file: 160 U.S. SCHOLARS IN APPEAL TO CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
In an unusual move, a group of 160 senior American scholars have appealed to the Chinese Government to stop its crackdown on liberal intellectuals.
The scholars, in a letter sent today to the Chinese Ambassador in Washington, Han Xu, said they were ''deeply concerned by the punitive measures adopted against some of China's leading intellectuals in the sciences, social sciences and humanities.''
The authors of the letter, experts on China from 40 American colleges and universities, said they feared the campaign ''will adversely effect China's intellectual vitality'' and might ultimately ''undermine China's effort toward modernization.''
The letter marks the first time American scholars have spoken out as a group about domestic politics in China. 
By contrast with American experts on the Soviet Union, who have often been critical of Moscow for human-rights abuses, China specialists have remained silent and sought to maintain good relations with Beijing.
'We Tried to Be Neutral'
''In the past we tried to be neutral, objective scholars not passing judgment, even during the Cultural Revolution,'' said Merle Goldman, a professor of Chinese history at Boston University who was one of the two organizers of the petition.
''But that was like the Holocaust,'' she said. 
''We can't remain silent again.''
In the Cultural Revolution, from 1966 to roughly 1976, millions of Chinese, especially writers, artists and scholars, were attacked, beaten, shipped off to exile in the countryside or killed.
Mrs. Goldman said the signers of the letter might risk angering the Chinese Government and lose their chance to do research in China, a highly coveted privilege after years in which China was closed to the outside world.
Among the prominent American scholars signing the letter was John K. Fairbank, professor emeritus of history at Harvard University, who is widely regarded as the father of modern Chinese studies in the United States. 
Others included Frederic Wakeman, professor of history at the University of California at Berkeley; Lucian Pye, professor of political science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and Wm. 
Theodore DeBary, professor of East Asian civilization at Columbia University.
The letter was also signed by Chinese-American scholars, including Tu Wei-ming, a professor of history at Harvard; Victor Nee, a sociologist at Cornell University, and Leo Lee, a professor of Chinese language and East Asian civilization at the University of Chicago. 
Professor Lee was the other organizer of the petition.
Â 
University of Michigan Statement
In a separate effort, 21 China specialists at the University of Michigan, which has one of the largest China studies centers in the country, signed a statement that was read in Congressional testimony earlier this month expressing ''concern'' about the campaign in China.
Another open letter to Mr. Deng, expressing shock at ''the severe criticism and punishment'' of intellectuals, has been signed by mostly ethnic Chinese authors and scholars in the United States and Hong Kong, including Chen Ruoxi, who is perhaps the most important Chinese writer outside China.
The statement from Michigan, read by Kenneth Lieberthal, a professor of political science, said events since the ouster in January of Hu Yaobang, the General Secretary of the Communist Party, were ''sadly reminiscent'' of the beginning of the anti-rightist campaign of 1957 and the Cultural Revolution in 1966.
Mr. Lieberthal testified before the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on Asian and Pacific Affairs.
In a telephone interview, Mr. Lieberthal said, ''People here felt it was not productive for American scholars to write directly to China telling them what policies to have.''
But at the same time, he said, the scholars at Michigan, who have been heavily involved in intellectual exchanges with China, felt ''it was not too early to voice our anxieties.''
Â 
Opinions Vary on Crackdown
Among those who signed the Michigan statement was Michel Oksenberg, a professor of political science who was the China specialist on the National Security Council under President Carter and helped work out the normalization of relations between Washington and Beijing in 1978.
Mr. Lieberthal and Mrs. Goldman differed in their interpretation of how serious the current crackdown is. 
The campaign, which began after a series of student demonstrations calling for greater democracy, has led to the ouster from the party of several promiment writers and scientists and widespread attacks in the Chinese press on ''bourgeois liberalism.''
Mr. Lieberthal acknowledged that ''serious damage'' had been done to the efforts by Deng Xiaoping, China's paramount leader, to arrange an orderly succession and build confidence among the country's intellectuals who are needed for its modernization drive. 
But he added, ''the events have not been as negative as one could have feared'' and fewer people have been purged than some experts expected.
On the other hand, Mrs. Goldman said she believed that ''the campaign seems to be intensifying, with the conservatives having the edge.''
Visiting Chinese have told her in the last few days that a famous writer, Liu Xinwu, has been removed as editor of the magazine People's Literature and that another writer, Wang Meng, may have been ousted as Culture Minister.

file: 2 American Tourists Are Still in Chinese Custody.txt
text:
ï»¿
Two Americans detained by the Chinese in Tibet during violent demonstrations a week ago remain in custody, a State Department spokesman said yesterday.
Officials of the Chinese Foreign Ministry in Chengdu told American officials that the two men - John Ackerly, 31 years old, of Cambridge, Mass., and Dr. Blake Kerr, 29, of East Hampton, L.I. 
- were still being held by the Chinese authorities, according to Nancy Beck, the department spokesman in Washington.
The Chinese did not disclose where the Americans were being held or whether they faced criminal charges.
News organizations had reported that the two Americans, who were described as tourists, were detained by the authorities in Lhasa, the Tibetan capital, during nationalist demonstrations last Sunday. 
But until yesterday, it was not known whether they remained in custody.
Â 
Mother 'Desperate to Know'
''We are very glad it has been confirmed that they are detained, that they are alive,'' said Margaret Kerr Richenburg, the mother of Dr. Kerr, who was traveling with his friend from college after graduating from medical school this year. 
''I am really desperate to know they are all right.''
Mr. Ackerly, a lawyer, and Dr. Kerr were in the middle of a three- to four-month tour of Asia and had been in Lhasa for five to six weeks before they were taken into custody, according to Dr. William C. Ackerly, Mr. Ackerly's father, who was interviewed at his home in Cambridge yesterday.
The two men had been friends since they were both undergraduates at Dartmouth College. 
Mr. Ackerly attended law school at American University in Washington, D.C., and Dr. Kerr attended medical school at the State Univesity of New York at Buffalo.
Dr. Ackerly, who last heard from his son by telephone two weeks ago, said: ''John never mentioned a word about politics to us; when he called, he said he was going to visit monasteries.''
''They had been having a wonderful time,'' the father said. 
''We thought they would be in Katmandu by now. 
They are experienced outdoorsmen.''
Climbed Mountains in Peru Dr. Ackerly, who described both men as tall and in good health, said that they had climbed mountains in Peru together and that they liked roughing it and meeting natives in foreign cultures.
The last postcard the family received, on Aug. 
23, seemed untroubled and did not mention political unrest, Dr. Ackerly said.
''This place is like Peru, no showers, no fresh food,'' the postcard from Tibet said. 
''The restaurant serves three things: beer, tea and yak dumplings.''
Telephone calls yesterday from the State Department to the families of the two men in Massachusetts and New York provided their parents with the first official information after 24 hours of anxious waiting. 
They were first told of their sons' plight on Friday in calls from news organizations, and they had been trying to learn more by telephoning China and State Department officials in Washington through the night.
According to Ms. Beck of the State Department, an American consular official from Chengdu will be sent to Lhasa to learn more about the situation.

file: 2 ARRESTED IN SILICON VALLEY THEFT CASE.txt
text:
ï»¿
In the latest of several arrests aimed at curbing the theft of sophisticated technology from companies in California's Silicon Valley, the Federal Bureau of Investigation said yesterday that it had arrested two men on charges of attempting to sell stolen electronics hardware to an agent posing as a representative of the Chinese Government.
In an affidavit filed in New York, the agency said the electronics components involved in the case had been stolen from a division of the General Electric Company in San Jose. 
The parts, worth about $200,000, included integrated circuits, diodes and other components used in the control systems of nuclear plants.
In the latest of several arrests aimed at curbing the theft of sophisticated technology from companies in California's Silicon Valley, the Federal Bureau of Investigation said yesterday that it had arrested two men on charges of attempting to sell stolen electronics hardware to an agent posing as a representative of the Chinese Government.
The affidavit also charged that one of the defendants, John Henry Jackson, had told the F.B.I undercover agent that he would be able to obtain and sell about $20 million worth of hardware used in military radar systems. 
Mr. Jackson, 44 years old, also faces criminal charges that he led a crime ring that stole and remarketed more than 100,000 semiconductors in recent years. 
He is awaiting trial on those charges.
Â 
Inquiry Began Last September
The F.B.I. said the other defendant in the case, Gary Wayne Dotson, 33, was a stockroom employee at General Electric's San Jose facility for three years until he resigned in December. 
The agency declined to provide information on Mr. Jackson's occupation.
An F.B.I. spokesman in San Francisco, Larry Holmquist, said the arrests of the two men, both San Jose residents, followed an undercover investigation that began last September. 
The undercover identity of the agent on the case - a representative of the Chinese Government - ''was pulled out of the air'' and was not selected because of any suspicion that China is involved in the illegal acquisition of proprietary technology, he said.
A spokesman for General Electric's San Jose operation, Bob Bell, said yesterday that the case involving Mr. Jackson and Mr. Dotson was the most serious breach of his company's security that he could remember and that the company's attempts to prevent theft of its products were being intensified.
Nonetheless, Mr. Bell added that the parts involved in the case did not reveal any highly advanced or proprietary technology. 
''You could buy that stuff at any Radio Shack store,'' he said.
Â 
Growing Concern About Losses
The arrests of the two men came a month after the F.B.I. charged 18 Japanese businessmen, many of them employees of Hitachi Ltd. and the Mitsubishi Electric Corporation, with conspiring to steal confidential computer information from the International Business Machines Corporation. 
In that case, the F.B.I. used undercover agents who had established a small electronics company in Silicon Valley as a front for their investigation.
The agency's undercover work has been increased in response to growing concern about the loss of trade and military secrets at electronics companies where employees are sometimes able to conceal tiny, but sophisticated semiconductors in their pockets or clothing as they leave.
In its complaint, the F.B.I. said that in meetings between the two defendants and the F.B.I.'s undercover agent, who is of Chinese descent, an agreement was reached in which the agent would pay $200,000 for the the nuclear plant components. 
Although no money changed hands, the F.B.I. said the parts were shipped by the two defendants to Newark and seized by Federal agents there.
The complaint also said that Mr. Jackson, in conversations with the undercover agent, had said he needed to sell the nuclear plant parts to raise money so he could buy the military radar components. 
The agency did not say where Mr. Jackson had intended to obtain the military hardware.

file: 2 CLING TO CHINA, EVEN AFTER 21 YEARS OF NO CHOICE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Against the scale of suffering that was commonplace here in the first 30 years of Communist rule, the two women were minor casualties, incidental figures in a huge tableau of repression.
But they were Americans, and the punishment they endured seems to have been senseless even by the obscure standards of the time. 
Seraphine and Marjorie Fuller, a devoutly Christian mother and daughter living quietly by themselves in Shanghai, answered a knock on the door one day in 1959 to find agents of the feared Public Security Bureau waiting to take them to a labor camp.
They remained there, somewhere outside Shanghai, for 21 years, sleeping on bedrolls on concrete floors, often desperately hungry, always fearful of marauders among the other foreigners incarcerated with them. 
In the last nine of those years an American President, Richard M. Nixon, visited Shanghai, as did hundreds of other prominent Americans. 
But for all the good it did the Fullers the visitors might as well have never come.
Interview with two women--81-year-old Seraphine Fuller and 62-year-old daughter Marjorie--who from 1959 to 1980 were inmates in Chinese labor camp for foreigners; women, who now live at home for elderly foreigners in Harbin, have declined offer of opportunity to renew their American citizenship, which they renounced after Seraphine's husband abandoned them in 1930; photo; map (M)
To the Chinese the two women were technically stateless, although to guards and fellow inmates at the camp they were never anything but the ''meiguo nuren,'' or American women. 
Three decades before the knock on the door, in bitterness at a husband and father who abandoned them for another woman, they renounced their American papers and vowed to remain together in China.
Â 
Human Tourist Attraction
Five years after they got out of the labor camp, with no more notice or explanation than was vouchsafed when they were seized, they are still the ''American women,'' offered like a tourist attraction to American reporters reaching Harbin. 
In this northeastern China city, 1,000 miles from Shanghai, they live out their lives in a second-floor room of a home for elderly foreigners, the only one in China, resolved to neither regret nor reverse their decision to forsake the United States.
''We're not regretting anything,'' said Seraphine Fuller, 81 years old, sitting at a table on the second-floor landing with her daughter, Marjorie, 62. 
''There is just nothing to regret.''
It was one of the few times that the older woman spoke during a 45-minute conversation that Miss Fuller said was one of the longest she or her mother had had with anyone in years.
The serene look on Mrs. Fuller's face and the way she folded her hands calmly across her lap conveyed the impression of a proud woman at peace with her fate, content to allow her daughter to do the talking. 
From time to time, especially when the talk turned to religion, she smiled or nodded.
To an outsider, their story sounded like a tale of innocent lives wasted. 
But at the table in a ramshackle suburb of Harbin, amid a vista of muddy roads and redbrick factories, there was scarcely a trace of bitterness or even chagrin, save for a moment when a visitor suggested that in renouncing the United States the two women had struck out at the man who abandoned them in the only way they could.
Â 
An Evangelical Conviction
''I suppose in a way we were,'' Miss Fuller said.
The conversation was laced with the younger woman's quick wit and evangelical conviction. 
Her starting point was that they had brought their fate upon themselves by remaining in Shanghai in 1949 when thousands of other foreigners were fleeing before the advancing Communists.
''We elected to stay, so we can't complain,'' she said. 
''We thought they were going to be democratic.''
She laughed, and added, ''You know what the Italians say: Every liberation begins with the hope of freedom and ends in tyranny.''
Seraphine Fuller was born in Harbin at a time when the city was one of the liveliest in the Far East. 
Her father was a Russian who had come to build the railroads that ran east to Vladivostok and south to Port Arthur, now Dalian; her mother was a Polish woman born in the Ukraine.
Â 
European Flavor Once Strong
Though the city was in China the Russian concession at its heart gave it a strongly European flavor, enhanced after 1917 when thousands of White Russians poured across the border to escape the pursuing Red Army.
''Oh my, Harbin. 
It was a beautiful city,'' she said in one of her rare conversational sallies. 
''They called it the Paris of the Orient.''
In the 1920's she was drawn to Shanghai, an even greater center of European settlement. 
There she met and married her husband, a freewheeling merchant who was the son of an American and the child-bride whom he had married in the Chinese community in San Francisco.
Seraphine Fuller's brief marriage ended in 1930, and her husband left for San Francisco. 
Mrs. Fuller and her daughter were left in Shanghai, American citizens who had never been to the United States.
Marjorie Fuller saw her father again in 1939, when he visited the two women in Shanghai and brought his daughter a gift from Japan, an antique ivory carving of a geisha. 
It was one of a pair, and Miss Fuller's last memory of her father is him telling her that one day they would be reunited in America, where they would place the two geishas side by side on the mantelpiece.
Â 
Prized Possession Remains
Nearly half a century later the geisha is Miss Fuller's prized possession, next to her Bible, in the room she shares with her mother. 
In 1962 her father wrote to the two women in labor camp, suggesting that they resume their old lives. 
His daughter said they never replied. 
He would be 89 if he is still alive, but the two women said they had no idea what had become of him.
''It's too late for anything like that now,'' Miss Fuller said, in a phrase that recurs often as she talks of the perspectives that govern their lives. 
''Much too late.''
Although the Chinese provide three meals a day in a dining room at the home, and take residents on trips to the movies and parks, the Fullers keep their distance.
They eat in their room, and have asked to be excused from birthday celebrations. 
They spend much of their time reading the Bible and literature sent to them by an evangelical organization in the United States.
''Everything is dust compared with the word of God,'' Miss Fuller said. 
''Beside that, nothing matters at all.''
Confrontation Over Bible The women said that in the labor camp faith sustained them - but, they said, it also nearly cost them their lives. 
The Cultural Revolution that swept across China in 1966 penetrated even the labor camp, and militants who had set a fire seized their Bible along with other ''bourgeois'' possessions. 
The women clung to the Bible, telling their tormentors that if they wanted it, they would have to throw the women on the fire, too. 
The Bible survived.
In 1980, mother and daughter were summoned by camp guards, told to pack, and driven to the railway station in Shanghai, where they boarded a train for Harbin.
Miss Fuller says the greatest relief was not in leaving the camp but their fellow prisoners.
''There were decent people,'' she said, ''but there were also horrible ones, some of them were murderers, plain and simple. 
If anybody complained the guards would only say, 'You're all foreigners, you sort it out among yourselves.'
''
Since coming to Harbin they have been visited by the United States consul in Shenyang, an industrial city 300 miles south of here, and offered an opportunity to renew their American citizenship. 
Miss Fuller said they had refused because there is nothing for them in the United States that they cannot find here.
''We crossed the Rubicon on that one many, many years ago,'' she said, ''and there's no point in changing things now.''

file: 2 LEADERS FOLLOWED PARALLEL CAREERS WITH CONTRASTING STYLES.txt
text:
ï»¿
Though they have markedly different political styles and personal backgrounds, Zhao Ziyang and the man he replaced yesterday, Hu Yaobang, both owe their rise through the Chinese hierarchy to the same factor: the sponsorship of the country's paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping.
Until Mr. Hu's dismissal, the two men largely had parallel careers, and were often variously regarded as Mr. Deng's successors. 
Their fortunes climbed with Mr. Deng, and they fell into disgrace with him during the Cultural Revolution, only to be appointed to the most senior posts in the party and Government after Mr. Deng rose again and consolidated his power in the early 1980's.
Over the last six years, the two worked closely together but maintained a fairly clear division of labor. 
As Prime Minister, Mr. Zhao presided over the economic changes that are the centerpiece of China's modernization program and traveled widely overseas, including a visit to the United States in 1984, while Mr. Hu concentrated on party policy and internal discipline.
To many in Beijing, both foreigners and Chinese, the two men seemed ideally suited by personality to the roles in which Mr. Deng had cast them. 
Zhao Ziyang (pronounced JOW dzeh-YANG), son of a landlord family, emerged as a polished, articulate and well-dressed statesman, while the diminutive and fiery Hu Yaobang (prounced WHO yow-BANG), born to a poor peasant family, came to be known for his bluntness, earthy wit and impulsiveness.
Â 
'Good Cop' and 'Tough Cop'
As some foreign diplomats saw it, Mr. Zhao often played the role of the ''good cop'' to Mr. Hu's ''tough cop,'' and reaped the benefits that went with that role. 
But in replacing Mr. Hu as General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party, Mr. Zhao now also assumes responsibility for supervising the party's 44 million members, a task expected to test all of his considerable finesse and managerial skills.
Early in his career, in the years immediately following the Chinese Revolution in 1949, Mr. Zhao, now 67, supervised purges of ''class enemies'' in the southern Chinese province of Guangdong, where he was later to serve as party secretary. 
But he is best known within China for the sweeping economic experiments he introduced after he was appointed party secretary and Governor of Sichuan, China's largest province and Mr. Deng's home ground, in 1975.
By dismantling the commune system in the countryside and introducing material incentives, Mr. Zhao freed the pent-up energies of Sichuan's 100 million people and was able to turn the province into the breadbasket of China. 
That success, which led to the liberalization of agricultural policies across China, was particularly appreciated by the country's 800 million peasants, who quickly coined a rhyming couplet, ''for grain (liang), look to Zhao Ziyang,'' in his praise.
''The defect of management in China is that state control is too tight,'' Mr. Zhao said not long after his elevation to Prime Minister in 1980, explaining the decision to extend the Sichuan reforms. 
''It does not provide for enthusiasm for the enterprises.''
Â 
An Earlier Denunciation
Though seen as an innovator in the field of economics, in politics Mr. Zhao has demonstrated the ability to adapt himself to shifts in the party line. 
When the leftist ''Gang of Four'' led by the wife of Mao Zedong purged Mr. Deng toward the end of the Cultural Revolution, Mr. Zhao joined in the denunciation of his patron.
Earlier, at the height of the Cultural Revolution, Mr. Zhao had himself been purged as one of the ''capitalist roaders'' associated with Mr. Deng. In a humiliating public ceremony, Mr. Zhao was paraded through the streets of Canton, capital of the province in which he served, with a dunce cap on his head.
The ''consummate bureaucrat,'' in the words of one Western diplomat, Mr. Zhao has served as a member of the standing committee of the Politburo of the Chinese Communist Party while Prime Minister and has a strong following among younger, modernization-minded party members. 
His major weakness, according to diplomatic and academic analysts, is his lack of military experience or personal ties to leaders of the People's Liberation Army, an institution said to contain large numbers of hard-liners opposed to Mr. Deng's modernization program.
Mr. Hu, 71, is also said to have suffered from a limited military background, though as a teen-ager he accompanied many of the senior party and army leaders on the ''Long March'' through the Chinese countryside. 
Born in Hunan, Chairman Mao's home province, Mr. Hu, who measures less than 5 feet tall, first came into the party as a ''Little Red Devil,'' the Communist youth group.
Â 
Party Boss in Sichuan
Following the Communist victory in 1949, Mr. Hu became the party boss in northern Sichuan, where his performance attracted the attention of Mr. Deng. In 1952 he was transferred to Peking, where he became the head of the Communist Youth League and built up a strong network of relationships with young hopefuls who subsequently emerged, with his help, as party leaders.
Like Mr. Zhao, Mr. Hu was also purged during the Cultural Revolution as a ''revisionist'' and ''counterrevolutionary'' because of his associations with Mr. Deng, with whom he shares a passion for bridge and has often played as partners. 
He is said to have been ''sent down to the countryside'' for menial labor for three years and to have spent an additional five years under house arrest.

file: 30 YEARS OF SPYING FOR CHINA IS CHARGED.txt
text:
ï»¿
A Federal law-enforcement official said today that a former analyst for the Central Intelligence Agency had admitted that he provided the Chinese Government with extensive intelligence information for 30 years.
The analyst, Larry Wu-Tai Chin, was indicted today by a Federal grand jury on a single count of conspiracy to commit espionage. 
According to the law-enforcement official, the account of Mr. Chin's activities was based largely on his his statements to the authorities. 
The account included the names of the Chinese Communist officials who recruited him and Mr. Chin's rank within the Chinese intelligence service, the official said, Mr. Chin, who the authorities said had been under investigation since December 1983, was arrested early Saturday. 
He has not yet entered a plea but his lawyer, Peter Meyers, said in court last Saturday that Mr. Chin would plead not guilty.
The eight-page indictment said that Mr. Chin had access to classified material ''at all levels, including secret and above,'' in his job as an analyst at the Foreign Broadcast Information Service, an arm of the C.I.A.
Mr. Chin was able to see ''virtually all levels of classified information dealing with China and other aspects of American Far Eastern intelligence,'' another Federal law-enforcement official said.
An Administration official said the security breach caused by Mr. Chin was a serious one and that he ''could have done a lot of damage.''
According to the indictment, the broadcast information service monitors foreign broadcasts and does translation work for other components of the intelligence agency. 
Its analysts would use classified intelligence reports to help assess the foreign broadcasts recorded by the American authorities. 
Additionally, other officials said Mr. Chin's language skills could have involved him in translating documents for a variety of sensitive C.I.A. operations in other segments of the agency.
Â 
A 'Deputy Bureau Chief'
These officials noted that at some points in Mr. Chin's career, he might have been called on by the espionage branch of the agency, which deals with covert agents in the field, as a translator.
The indictment disclosed new details about Mr. Chin's frequent travels to China. 
It said he was promoted to ''deputy bureau chief'' in the People's Republic of China intelligence service in a 1982 trip to Peking.
Prosecutors revealed for the first time that Mr. Chin continued working for the intelligence agency as a contract employee after his retirement in 1981. 
The indictment said that from 1981 to 1985, he worked with the United States Joint Publications Research Service, a division of the agency that does translation for broadcast information service.
The indictment did not specify the type of information Mr. Chin dealt with in his four years with that division. 
But in a criminal complaint filed over the weekend, the Government charged that Chinese intelligence paid Mr. Chin $50,000 in 1982, about a year after he had become a contract employee for the Central Intelligence Agency. 
The indictment charged that Mr. Chin was paid more than $140,000 for all of his activities.
Â 
Kept in Touch at Agency
According to the indictment, Mr. Chin kept in contact with his friends and associates at the agency after his retirement. 
At one point, he told Chinese intelligence about a C.I.A. employee he believed was ''susceptible to recruitment.''
The picture of Mr. Chin that emerged from those who know his family was of an immigrant who had succeeded in the United States and was proud of the accomplishments of his three children.
A family acquaintance described Mr. Chin today as a ''sweet, kind good humored'' family man who had a close relationship with his two sons and daughter. 
One of his sons attended Dartmouth College and is an a doctoral program at Stanford University.

file: A FAIR FOR CHINA BIBLOIPHILES.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's first international book fair opened today in Peking, offering something for bookworms of all tastes - if they could get in.
Browsers who managed to obtain passes could skim 50,000 titles ranging from the Encyclopedia Britannica in Chinese - 10 volumes at $4 apiece - to such children's books as ''Little Panda Loses His Way.''
No books are for sale, but officials said Chinese buyers could place orders for their organizations through the national book importer.
The officials did not say how passes were distributed. 
But for those who obtained one, the weeklong fair was a bibliophile's dream since foreign books are rarely available and extremely expensive in China.
Most of the books are in English, although some of the cramped publishers' stalls at the Peking Exhibition Hall featured titles in French, Russian and other languages.
''I'm actually a fan of English literature,'' said a man leafing through Louis L'Amour's western novel ''Ride the River,'' ''but this is great stuff, too.''
''This place is amazing,'' said a woman whose taste ran to spy novels as she peered down aisles laden with copies of ''Wild California,'' a nature book; ''The Fannie Farmer Cookbook,'' and Edgar Snow's ''Red Star Over China.''
Chinese officials said they planned to hold similar fairs every two years to promote global friendship and the exchange of information. 
They said this was the first such fair in China since the 1949 Communist revolution.
At a news conference last week, the officials said they would screen all the books - 70 percent of them on technical topics - before the fair opened to make sure none contained material insulting to other countries; they did not elaborate.
A total of 1,055 publishing houses from 35 countries were taking part in the fair, with most coming from the United States, the officials said.

file: A HERO, SOVIET-STYLE.txt
text:
ï»¿
BORODIN Stalin's Man in China. 
By Dan N. Jacobs. Illustrated. 
369 pp. 
Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press. 
$25.
WHEN Dan N. Jacobs began his several years of research into the career of the famous Comintern emissary to China, the name ''Borodin'' probably called to most people's minds the Russian composer of ''Prince Igor.''
Even the few who do recall the ''other'' Borodin's role in the Chinese Nationalist revolution and the eventual failure of Lenin's and Stalin's attempts (1920-27) to bring China into the Soviet orbit will be intrigued and informed by this first full-length study of Mikhail Markovich Gruzenberg, alias Michael Borodin (1884-1951).
Albert L Weeks reviews Dan N Jacobs's book "Borodin: Stalin's Man in China"
Mr. Jacobs follows Borodin's serpentine trail from Russia to America, where he lived for eleven years in exile (1907-18), on to a dozen other countries, including Mexico and Britain, where he functioned as Lenin's personal envoy, a Comintern agent, an informer, an organizer of Communist apparats abroad, a recruiter of talented revolutionaries (e.g., M.N. 
Roy, the well-known Indian firebrand and later Comintern official and co-worker of Ho Chi Minh), and even as a smuggler of jewels and funds to finance subversion in foreign countries.
Borodin's biography is at once a tale of high personal adventure and an account of Soviet adventurism of ''world-historical'' proportions. 
His is also the story of an erstwhile Bolshevik ''hero of our times'' whose top-level political involvements and achievements ended in failure, martyrdom and premature death. 
But his is a case of Petrushka-like reemergence as well. 
In the early 1960's, Borodin was posthumously rehabilitated, along with General Vasily Blyukher (who helped Chiang Kai-shek plan the 1926 ''Northern Expedition'' to unite China) and other victims of Stalinist repression. 
And with the reburnishing of the Comintern's image under Leonid Brezhnev in the 1970's, Borodin has become a veritable model Soviet Man. 
Mr. Jacobs's book thus could not be better timed.
To Borodin, as to Lenin, Trotsky, Zinoviev and the other leaders in Moscow, China represented an attractive ''Eastern route'' to world revolution. 
With proletarian revolution bogged down in the West during the 1920's, the huge populations and the raw materials of the East, upon which Western capitalist industry depended, became strong inducements for the Bolshevik leadership to redirect the ''fire of revolution'' to the capitalist ''rear'' of Asia and the Moslem Near East. 
''The outcome of the struggle,'' advised Lenin, ''will be determined by the fact that Russia, India, China, etc., constitute the overwhelming majority of the population of the globe.''

text:
ï»¿
Simon Keswick dislikes being photographed against the Hong Kong skyline. 
''It's too Clavellian,'' he explained, wincing as he referred to the best-selling novels by James Clavell that loosely chronicle Mr. Keswick's clan and company.
A notion that a photograph of a man and a city would suggest a lord surveying his dominions would be absurd in New York or London - but not in Hong Kong. 
Mr. Keswick's company, Jardine Matheson Holdings Ltd., has towered over the British territory for 145 years, dealing in opium and silk in the last century and everything from ice cream to insurance today.
A few years ago, the international conglomerate nearly collapsed - a result of disastrous investments in real estate, shipping and the oil industry. 
As earnings plunged and debt soared, it seemed that the ''Noble House'' that was founded in China in 1832 might expire with barely a whimper, perhaps with control passing to one of several native Hong Kong entrepreneurs. 
But the typhoon appears to have passed.
A Slimmer Operation
Jardines has had to sell valuable assets to survive, but the slimmer company reported a near-doubling of profit in 1985 and a further 173 percent increase in the first half of 1986. 
Long-term debt has been cut in half. 
''I think the patient is out of the operating theater,'' the 44-year-old Mr. Keswick, who resembles a stouter and younger version of Robert Redford, said in an interview in his office overlooking Hong Kong harbor. 
''Now we have to get him strong and running again.''
Along those lines, Mr. Keswick last week announced a reorganization of the company. 
The changes amount to the dismantling of one of the territory's proudest names: the Hongkong Land Company, the world's largest property concern. 
The changes, which create a complex web of corporations that own each other, with Mr. Keswick controlling all of them, fortify defenses against a takeover, while reducing the group's debt.
But many in Hong Kong remain skeptical about Jardines' prospects. 
They doubt that it will ever again be the titan it was in its swashbuckling days at the peak of British influence in the territory. 
A new breed of Hong Kong Chinese entrepreneurs, such as Sir Y. K. Pao and Li Ka-shing, has proved more astute in recent years than the old British dynasties. 
And many wonder how much of a role can be played by a fundamentally British company after Hong Kong becomes a part of China in 1997.
Beyond that, there are widespread doubts about the company's commitment to Hong Kong, as well as about the Keswick family's commitment to Jardines. 
Two years ago, the holding company moved its formal home to Bermuda, sending Hong Kong stock prices plunging. 
Then, as part of the reorganization last week, a new unit that will be a bulwark in the Jardines group was also moved to Bermuda.
Â 
A Generation Gap
The Keswick family (pronounced KE-zick) is believed to own about 10 percent of Jardines and has been immersed in the company for more than a century. 
While earlier generations - such as Sir John Keswick, Simon's uncle - spoke several Chinese dialects and relished life in the colony, Simon's generation never learned the local language and seems more comfortable with steak and kidney pie in Britain than with fungus or bird's nest soup in the territory.
Simon Keswick reportedly told friends in 1982, when he arrived in Hong Kong from Britain, that he planned to remain for just five years. 
Today the tai-pan (big boss) insists that he will remain in Hong Kong for some time, and that Jardines will not abandon Hong Kong.
Jardines' return to fiscal health -albeit after five desperate years -belies the reputation Mr. Keswick has acquired as the inheritor of his family's looks, but not its business acumen. 
While he consults often with his older brother, Henry, who oversees Jardines' interests in London, it was Simon who first emphasized insurance broking, which has done extremely well for Jardines recently.
Mr. Keswick's grand strategy, as he describes it, is to maintain Jardines' volume of business in Hong Kong and China, while reducing the region's contribution to its earnings to about 50 percent, from 75 percent. 
He plans to do that by increasing the amount of business done elsewhere in the world. 
As he envisions it, Jardines would control an international network of subsidiaries involved in insurance, securities, food, hotels and real estate.
Â 
A Disastrous Investment
Mr. Keswick is not a squeamish man. 
He has shown no qualms about dissecting the Hongkong Land Company, of which he is also chairman. 
In 1979 and 1980, Jardines made a disastrous investment in the Land Company, acquiring 40 percent of it and allowing it to acquire the same percentage of Jardines. 
That was near the peak of Hong Kong's land boom, and the subsequent collapse in the property market and soaring interest rates became the single biggest burden on Jardines.
Mr. Keswick picked up the carving knife in October, when the Land Company's residential real estate portfolio was sold to the Australian investor Alan Bond. 
Its Dairy Farm food subsidiary also is being spun off as an independent company. 
And last week Mr. Keswick said the Land Company's Mandarin-Oriental Hotels unit -which owns two hotels that are considered among the best in the world - the Oriental in Bangkok and the Mandarin in Hong Kong -also would be spun off.
The Land Company will be reduced to its property core, and as a further indignity Mr. Keswick will insist on the conversion of an issue of convertible preferred stock into Hongkong Land common shares. 
That will help reduce Jardines' stake in the Land Company to 26 percent, from 35 percent. 
Some analysts expect Jardines to continue to pare its real estate holdings in Hong Kong because of concerns about having China as the territory's landlord after 1997.
''In Shanghai, Jardines lost a heck of a lot of money that was in fixed assets, and they have a phobia about it not happening again,'' said A. William S. Phillips, managing director of Baring Securities in Hong Kong.
The Communists in Beijing may be more gentle when they assume control of Hong Kong than they were when they took over Shanghai in 1949, nationalizing banks and all other corporate interests. 
But Jardines may not be willing to take the risk.
Â 
Executive Turnover
David J. Davies resigned as managing director of Hongkong Land Company in July, apparently because he disagreed with the Keswick strategy of dismantling it - and he was not the only executive to go. 
Upon arriving, Mr. Keswick evicted the previous chairman, David K. Newbigging, and about 40 other executives.
The upheaval was all the more striking because Jardine Matheson had been noted for its relaxed management style, cultivated by generations of young graduates of Oxford and Cambridge universities. 
In the last few years, Mr. Keswick has dumped several lines of business as well as businessmen. 
The departure from ship-owning was the most important, and the most traumatic, for Jardines, a trading company that had grown up with shipping.
''It's a genuine recovery, in that they've managed to get rid of the rubbish,'' said Christopher Chong, an analyst at James Capel Ltd. in Hong Kong. 
''They're out of shipping and oil, but where do they go from here?''
When the restructuring is complete in a few months, Mr. Keswick said, Jardines will focus on six semi-autonomous areas: engineering and construction; insurance and securities; transport, including ship broking and management; marketing and distribution, including wine, cars and the Pizza Hut restaurants and 7-Eleven stores that it operates under license; hotels, including 10 luxury hotels in the Mandarin-Oriental group soon to be spun off from Hongkong Land, and the real estate interests of Hongkong Land itself.
For all the diversification, most of Jardines' business is in Asia, and the company is trying to become more competitive in the region. 
Jardines is planning to promote more Hong Kong Chinese executives to improve competitiveness. 
And it is requiring all new employees to study one of China's two main dialects: Mandarin and Cantonese.
''I'm sure there'll be lots of ups and downs,'' said Martin C. Barrow, who is in charge of the effort to make the company more competitive in Asia, ''but we're here to stay. 
Come back and see us in 1998.''

text:
ï»¿
TEN years ago Shatin was a quiet patch of farmland in Hong Kong's New Territories, with water buffalo pulling plows through geometric acres of rice paddies and fishermen's cottages along the Shing Mun River. 
It was an evocation of rural China, even though it was only 10 miles north of the teeming city of Kowloon, separated from Hong Kong's busiest district by the steep Lion Rock Hills.
Today it is the most energetic of Hong Kong's so-called new towns, a city of more than 300,000 people that is expected to grow to 500,000 within a decade. 
There are forests of 40-story high-rises with highways, viaducts and overpasses crisscrossing about them, a new 17-story hotel, shopping plazas and malls, dozens of restaurants, even a race track. 
What had been virtually vacant countryside has become an urban showcase amply demonstrating the British crown colony's singular energy and its ability to expand and grow swiftly.
Shatin is a place of parks, urban plazas, cinemas and branches of Japanese department stores, a weekend getaway for the people of Kowloon - 10 minutes away by train -and a growing tourist destination.
Perhaps more significant, however, is that Shatin provides what is possibly a view of the Hong Kong of the future, because it sits in the New Territories, the 350 square miles of land between Hong Kong proper and the border of China that are the subject of immediate concern in negotiations on ending the lease on the colony held by Britain. 
The lease expires in June 1997. 
The New Territories are on a 99-year lease that was signed in Peking in 1898. 
Hong Kong Island and Kowloon were leased in perpetuity, but in fact the lease terms have come to include the entire colony. 
Many Hong Kong residents believe that in the years leading to the end of the lease, and immediately thereafter, Hong Kong's future expansion lies in these New Territories.
But there is more to Shatin than cement and polished granite and shopping malls like the New Town Plaza, where the waters of a computerized fountain dip and soar to symphonic music and recall the dancing waters many of us remember from Radio City Music Hall's earlier days. 
It has developed as a city but has managed to preserve some of the atmosphere of old China.
Just beyond the Lion Rock Tunnel, which now cuts through the hills around Shatin, across a small valley from a mountain the people of Shatin call Amah Rock - they say it resembles a nursemaid carrying a child on her back - lies Tsang Tai Uk, a preserved walled village. 
Here 200 people live the rural life of China, much as the inhabitants did when the village was built 140 years ago. 
Tsang Tai Uk is a compound enclosed by long parallel rows of two-story masonry houses. 
Each building contains an elaborate ancestral hall of red- and gold-gilded woods that is used for worship as well as an entry into the enclave, which is dotted with small gardens and chicken coops. 
Tsang Tai Uk translates literally as Mr. Tsang's Big House and to this day virtually all the villagers are named Tsang.
The earliest settlements in the area date to the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644), when it was reported that a village called Tai Wai had been founded four centuries earlier. 
People in Shatin say that the rice from Tai Wai's fields was so fine that it was sent to the Imperial Court in Beijing.
Shatin houses the Che Kung Temple, named for a general of the Sung Dynasty (960-1279). 
The temple, which is close to Shatin's main railroad station, is of stucco-covered stone, dark and exceedingly quiet. 
There are several carved Buddhas, but the feature that distinguishes the temple is the forest of circular incense hoops hanging from its ceiling. 
Che Kung is a favorite place for weekend visits by the Chinese of Kowloon, who come to burn the incense hoops, to pray to their ancestors and to celebrate the coming of the Lunar New Year and other traditional holidays. 
Close by is the Four-Face Budda, a statue with four faces carved in wood in Thailand. 
The shrine is always bedecked with flowers set before it by prayerful Buddhists.
ALSO near the station - 431 steps up from it - is the Temple of Ten Thousand Buddhas, where, if you care to count them, 12,800 small Buddhas of carved wood and sculptured clay, some painted bright scarlet, are set into its walls. 
The hillside temple is marked by a bright red nine-story pagoda. 
By climbing 69 more steps the visitor finds the Temple of Man Fat, dedicated to the monk Yuet Kai, who founded it. 
His preserved body, covered with gold, sits with closed eyes inside.
Though it has developed far more quickly than others, Shatin is typical of the new settlements that have sprung up throughout the New Territories, towns that have grown simply because Kowloon and Hong Kong Island, the core of the colony, cannot hold an ever-expanding population that is well above five million. 
In such New Territories towns as Fo Tan, Tai Po and Fanling, apartment buildings, owned and operated by the Hong Kong Government, continue to be built, along with markets and shopping centers. 
Shatin also has a luxurious racecourse, owned and operated by the Royal Hong Kong Jockey Club, where the diversion is flat racing on a grass track.
Some tour operators, particularly those in Australia, are booking groups into Shatin's new Hotel Riverside Plaza, where there are swimming pools, a health center, several restaurants and a discotheque. 
Guests who ride the hotel's shuttle bus to Kowloon's Tsim Sha Tsui shopping area walk through malls and boutiques selling everything from silks to the latest electronic gadgetry. 
In one of Shatin's mall developments, Shatin Inter-City, visitors strolling among the shops that are lively imitations of those in Kowloon find several restaurants, one of which, named for the complex, serves such Cantonese dishes as guinea hen and deer.
THEY may also discover the Palm Beach Sauna and a huge swimming pool that form part of the huge recreational center built for the residents of Shatin Inter-City. 
Nearby is Shatin New Town Plaza, next to a budding park called Shatin Central Park.
The cynosure of New Town Plaza is its fountain. 
Each afternoon, just before 12:45, hundreds of people, many elderly and children among them, pull up folding chairs and encircle the fountain, which sits in a multistory atrium in the middle of a shopping mall. 
At 12:45 the music begins, occasionally Western symphonic, though more often classical Chinese, and the waters begin to dance. 
People run out of the many bakeries and dim sum parlors, out of the Yaohan department store, out of the boutiques, to watch the free half-hour water show.
New Town Plaza also houses many new restaurants, most of them Cantonese and catering to families, with dim sum, roast duck and all manner of stir-fried dishes. 
One, the North Park, becomes a nightclub after dark. 
A Malaysian restaurant offers beef and chicken satays in hot peanut sauces and hot curried rice noodles; a Korean barbecue has grilled beef and lamb and that spicy cabbage salad called kimchee.
The most recent manifestation of Shatin's explosive growth is the Hotel Riverside Plaza, not yet two years old. 
On its 17 floors are 830 rooms and suites, some facing the Shing Mun River, others the hills and temples of the town. 
The hotel is built around a four-story atrium that contains a 60-foot-long pool with a sunken bar.
Among several restaurants in the Riverside Plaza is the Botania, where the menu selections range from Cantonese fried rice to duck pate with green peppercorns, from oxtail soup to open-faced Scandinavian sandwiches of salmon and cheeses. 
The Regal Seafood Restaurant offers a variety of hot pots, there is a Japanese restaurant and coffee shops like the Boulevard, serving pizza and hamburgers as well as roast pork and Chinese vegetables.
It is a place from which to contemplate Shatin. 
One evening my wife and I took the train from Kowloon to Shatin, walked to the Riverside Plaza, had dinner in the Botania and a late drink near the pool deck. 
I recall looking out at the hills, many of them now covered with lights, and wondering about 1997.
Â 
GUIDE FOR AN EXCURSION TO AN EXPANDING NEW TOWN
Â 
Getting There
By car, Shatin is about a half-hour's drive from Kowloon. 
The distance is less than 10 miles but the trip takes so long because traffic through the Lion Rock Tunnel is generally heavy. 
It is more convenient and less arduous to take the train. 
There are several daily trains between Kowloon Station and Shatin. 
A one-way ticket is about 50 cents. 
Buses also go to Shatin, from Causeway Bay on Hong Kong Island. 
The No. 170 leaves from the front of the Daimaru department store, and the fare is 50 cents. 
From Kowloon the No. 70 runs from the Jordan Road Terminal; fare: 45 cents. 
There are no charges at the temples in and around Shatin, although an offering box is placed at entrances and near altars.
Â 
Bus Tour
For a look at Shatin that is combined with a visit to other parts of Hong Kong's developing New Territories, visitors can take a Hong Kong Tourist Association bus tour entitled ''The Land Between.''
It departs every weekday from the pier opposite City Hall on Hong Kong Island; in front of the Holiday Inn Golden Mile Hotel on Nathan Road, Kowloon, and the Holiday Inn Harbor View Hotel, East Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon. 
The six-hour trip, which includes lunch, costs $23 or $18 for children. 
The Hong Kong Tourist Association (5-244191) can supply further details. 
General information is also available from the association's office at 548 Fifth Avenue, New York, N.Y. 
10036; 212-869-5008.
Â 
Meals and Hotel
Meals in the restaurants scattered about the Shatin Inter-City complex and New Town Plaza generally run about $10 to $15 a person. 
Eating such exotica as bird's nest, shark fins or fine pigeon dishes could add $5 to $10 to the bill.
A meal in the Botania in the Hotel Riverside Plaza will be about $20 a person.
Room rates at the hotel range from $70 for a standard room to $200 for a deluxe suite. 
All rooms have color TV and minibars.Â Â Â Â F.

text:

For Trini Sham, the 15-year-old accused of shooting a police officer in a Manhattan park last week, the path to jail led from the streets of Hong Kong to the alleys of New York's Chinatown, where shadowy gangs absorb many young Asian men.
Interviews with the boy's estranged mother and law-enforcement officials outline a portrait of a youth who, left without parental control, chose a life that promised action and power but instead yielded violence.
The story of Trini, who is now being held without bail on charges of attempted murder of a police officer, also reflects what scholars and authorities describe as a fundamental change in the power structure of Chinatown's community of more than 300,000 people.
The authorities said that traditional youth gangs, which act as the muscle for community organizations known as tongs, are in decline while smaller, independent squads, such as the one to which Trini is said to belong, proliferate.
Shooting Is Called Spontaneous
Investigators agree that the 4:30 A.M. shooting in Columbus Park of Officer James Dora, who was listed in good condition yesterday at Bellevue Hospital Center, was a spontaneous act by a surprised youth, not a planned operation by a gang.
In fact police officials said the shooting directly contradicts the most important rule among those who control Chinatown's underworld: that gang violence be kept strictly within the community, preferably within the gangs themselves.
The gang to which Trini is said to belong - the Fu Qing, meaning ''youth from Fujian,'' a province on the southeast China coast - is described by the police and by prosecutors as an amateurish but nonetheless dangerous group of young men who have tried unsuccessfully to claim territory in Chinatown for illegal activities.
Despite that failure, investigators said, attempts by the Fu Qing and other small groups have led to gun battles in the last two years in which gang members and innocent visitors from outside the community have been wounded or killed.
Â 
'Serious Crisis'
''The tongs are losing control of gangs like the Fu Qing,'' according to Dr. Peter Kwong, an expert on New York's Chinatown and professor of politics at the State University at Old Westbury. 
''Right now there is a serious crisis with the youth gangs because the tail is wagging the head.''
In contrast to the new groups, members of Chinatown's established gangs, such as the Dong An - ''Eastern Peace'' - or Flying Dragons, exercise control in clearly demarcated zones where they protect gambling operations and pry protection fees from local businesses, law-enforcement officials say.
The last exchange of gunfire between the police and members of such gangs, according to investigators, occurred in 1983 when officers giving chase to Dong An members were shot at in Brooklyn.
''They've never gone and intention-ally targeted a police officer,'' one official said.
Remaining are the questions of what investigators believe a 15-year-old was doing in a park at 4:30 A.M. armed with two powerful pistols and why he shot.
The answers, according to investigators, lie in the apparently explosive mixture of the boy's background and the increasingly anarchic nature of the Chinatown underworld.
Â 
Grew Up in Hong Kong
Trini grew up in Hong Kong, where he was raised by his father, a musician, after his parents divorced 10 years ago, the boy's mother, Rita Gillard, said in an interview from the Chinese restaurant in Brooklyn where she works.
The boy - one of a growing population of legal Chinese aliens from all over Asia who arrived at a rate of about 1,400 a month last year - settled in Queens, where his father still lives. 
The police declined to name the youth's father, who Mrs. Gillard called ''very upset.''
Attempts to reach him by telephone were unsuccessful.
Speaking only Cantonese, the Southern Chinese dialect prevalent in Hong Kong, the boy was enrolled in a Queens school, where he picked up a little English but stayed for less than a year, according to Mrs. Gillard, who said she speaks to her son about once a week.
Although investigators said Trini had declined to cooperate with them, detectives and his mother said he probably became involved with the Fu Qing gang while still in school and living with his father, whose work frequently took him away from home.
Like other young men who move to New York from Hong Kong or San Francisco's Chinatown, he was most likely recruited at his school or in a Chinatown arcade or other locale frequented by young people, according to law-enforcement officials.
Â 
Living in 'Crash Pads'
Dr. Kwong said the gangs seek out those who appear to have the desire and aggressiveness demanded by gang life. 
''Once you're in the situation, you can't back down,'' he said. 
''If you want to get out they threaten you.''
He added that families had been forced to leave Chinatown in order to extricate children from the gangs.
Once involved, Trini moved out of his father's home and began to spend nights in what the police describe as various ''crash pads.''
''It's a common practice for gangs to set up apartments in various neighborhoods where the members sleep and keep their contraband,'' one law-enforcement official said.
Working on numerous tips from Chinatown residents, detectives of the Fifth Precinct said they had to check at least six addresses for Trini before arresting the youth and a companion, 18-year-old Lee Lang Chiu, on Friday at a house in South Ozone Park, Queens. 
Mr. Lee was said by the police to have been in a getaway car outside Columbus Park at the time of the shooting. 
He has been arraigned on a charge of possessing a deadly weapon.
This weekend, two Asian youths entering the house, at 104-17 128th Street, declined to speak with a reporter. 
Neighborhood residents said 8 to 10 youths had been staying at the house for about two weeks.
''They were all very young and they were all alone all the time - no mother, no father, no adults ever with them,'' said one neighbor, who declined to give his name.
Â 
Previous Trouble
Before his arrest, Trini had been in trouble with authorities. 
In 1985, according to officers of the 110th Precinct in Queens and his mother, Trini was taken to Family Court on charges of stealing a bicycle but was later released to the custody of his father. 
And just two days before last Tuesday's shooting, the police said, Trini was arrested and charged with smashing a car window with a sawed-off pool cue after a minor car accident in the 110th Precinct.
On Monday night, according to the police account, Trini and Mr. Lee had gone to Chinatown and entered the territory of the Flying Dragon gang on Pell Street, when they were confronted by gang members, beaten and perhaps briefly detained.
The two youths returned to the Queens house, armed themselves and then drove to Chinatown. 
Shots were exchanged with Flying Dragons members at the intersection of Pell and Mott Streets.
Hearing the shots, Officer Dora ran into the park. 
He identified himself as a police officer and ordered a slim Oriental male to drop his weapon.
It was then that Trini is said to have fired.

A formal judgment of Mao Zedong's achievements and mistakes has been reached, Deputy Prime Minister Huang Hua said today.
After months of delay and debate, Mr. Huang, who is also China's Foreign Minister, said that the Communist Party leadership had reached a consensus that Chairman Mao's triumphs outweighed his debacles, thus clearing the way for a long-delayed party meeting and a subsequent party congress that is expected to formally approve the demotion of the current party chairman, Hua Guofeng.
In a two-hour meeting with A.M. Rosenthal, executive editor of The New York Times, Mr. Huang stressed that reports of a power struggle within the party leadership were ''untrue.''
''We can say that the present central leadership of the party is the most unified, stable, most effective and the most popular since the 1960's,'' Mr. Huang said.
Chinese Communist Party leadership reaches formal judgment of Mao Zedong's achievements and mistakesJudgment of Mao Was Delayed
He said the officially proposed judgment of Mao, which was reportedly delayed for months by objections from party factions because it was either too harsh or too lenient, would be submitted as a resolution to be debated, and perhaps amended, by the party meeting before it was submitted to the party congress, as yet unscheduled, for approval.
Wan Li, another Deputy Prime Minister, said this week that the party meeting would take place in early June, to be concluded in time for the 60th anniversary in July of the founding of the Chinese Communist Party.
Mr. Huang criticized foreign reports that China was abandoning the Maoist line. 
''Some people say there is a de-M@aoification campaign in China,'' he said. 
''This is completely untrue. 
Mao Zedong thought will remain the guiding thought of our party and our state.''
Â 
Mao's Mistakes Are Cited
Mr. Huang then summarized what he said was the consensus achieved by a wide cross-section of the party leadership on the judgment of Mao. 
While praising him as a ''great Marxist and a great revolutionary who was the first to combine the universal principles of Marxism with the concrete conditions of the Chinese revolution,'' Mr. Huang said that Mao also made mistakes. 
The Deputy Prime Minister called the system of setting up people's communes in the countryside, the so-called Great Leap Forward in 1957 and 1958, among the mistakes.
''But it was not comrade Mao Zedong alone,'' Mr. Huang said. 
''The mood of anxiety to build up our country quickly was quite prevalent at that time. 
Even cadres at the middle level were overanxious to build up our country quickly. 
So we must all be responsible for the mistakes. 
It is not fair to put the blame on Chairman Mao alone.''
Mr. Huang said that in starting the so-called Cultural Revolution, Mao compounded his earlier mistakes with much more serious ones.
''In his later years, he was detached from the real situation in China and from the masses,'' Mr. Huang said. 
''He was no longer good at listening to different opinions. 
Therefore, he made mistakes which caused serious results for our country.''
Mr. Huang said, however, that Mao's role was made up of contributions that were primary and mistakes that were secondary. 
''This is our consensus,'' Mr. Huang said.
Â 
'Collective Wisdom'

He said that the ''four modernizations'' - in industry, agriculture, science and defense - were also put forward originally by Chairman Mao.

Mr. Huang said that Mao put forward the policy of ''letting 100 schools of thought contend and letting 100 flowers blossom'' in arts, literature, science and technology.

He said it would take two or three five-year plans to complete a basic restructuring of ''economic systems and changing of the product mix.''

IN December 1967, Peng Zhen was dragged into a Beijing gymnasium, his clothes torn, his face bloated after a year in prison.
Young Red Guards yelled ''despicable swine'' and cheered as Mr. Peng, a leader of the Communist revolution and former Mayor of Beijing, was pushed and kicked by his captors.
Twelve years later, China's new leader, Deng Xiaoping, brought Mr. Peng, by then 77 years old, back into the ruling Politburo. 
He became one of the most vociferous detractors of Mr. Deng's moves to open up the Chinese economy and is now a chief orchestrator of the return to orthodoxy.
Other party leaders had returned to their posts three years before Mr. Peng and that delay is still often cited as a source of friction between the two men.
Of much greater significance, however, are the deep philosophical differences between them. 
While Mr. Deng looked to Western capitalism for China's economic model, Mr. Peng adamantly defended tight state control over economic, social and political life.
Some Western and Asian diplomats here say that even before this winter's crackdown on dissent, Mr. Peng used his position as chairman of the National People's Congress, the country's legislative body, as a brake on some of the reforms. 
And as the changes swept China, particularly in the countryside, reining in the absolute authority of party bureaucrats and diminishing the role of ideology, his was one of the few voices that railed against replacing Marxist doctrine with Western notions.
Â 
After the abrupt crackdown in
January that followed a series of student demonstrations, Mr. Peng and other hard-line Chinese leaders are dominating the country's newspapers and television screens with harsh attacks on ''bourgeois liberalization,'' code words for democracy and free expression. 
Diplomats and other experts here believe that Mr. Peng is one of the leaders charting the country's new course.
Last week, Mr. Peng, wearing a traditional high-collared Mao jacket, presided over the opening session of the annual meeting of the People's Congress. 
In a speech to the delegates, Zhao Ziyang, the acting party General Secretary since Hu Yaobang's dismissal in January, told the delegates that the economic initiatives would continue, but that ''pernicious'' Western ideas would not be tolerated. 
Earlier this month, the standing committee of the congress declined to act on a measure that would have given factory managers some freedom from state control and placed other limits on the party's power over the economy.
Mr. Peng has pushed strong central planning since the 1950's. 
In 1960, as Chinese relations with the Soviet Union rapidly deteriorated, Mr. Peng engaged in a shouting match with Nikita S. Khrushchev, who argued that Mao had lost touch with the world. 
Mr. Peng defended both Stalin and Mao, asserting that Mr. Khrushchev was betraying Communist principles.
Mr. Peng's political difficulties began in 1966 when he and other party leaders tried to stifle the Cultural Revolution, Mao's movement to ''cleanse'' the party. 
Like many other leaders, including Deng Xiaoping, Mr. Peng was swept from power and imprisoned, his family disgraced. 
His 86-year-old mother was forced to stand on a dunghill while she was denounced.
With his return to prominence in 1979, Mr. Peng focused his energies on building the power of the National People's Congress and establishing himself as a party ideologist.

''Some people look to bourgeois democracy as if capitalist society were even brighter than our sun,'' he said.

''Some people say that reform means 'de-Marxist-Leninization' and 'de-Maoization' and that upholding Marxism-Leninism means opposition to reform,'' Mr. Peng said in a recent speech. 
''Such an argument is put forward from ignorance or misunderstanding or is aimed at provocation.''
Mr. Deng and Mr. Zhao have insisted that the campaign for political conformity will not affect economic reforms.

file: A MELLOWING TAIWAN SEES A DIFFERENT MAINLAND.txt
text:
ï»¿
WHEN the Manchus toppled China's Ming Dynasty in 1644, supporters of the Ming emperors fled to southern China and the island of Taiwan, vowing that they would soon recover the mainland. 
They never did, of course, although the invading Manchus were gradually assimilated into Chinese society and culture.
When the Communists toppled China's Nationalist Government in 1949, supporters of the Nationalist leaders fled to Taiwan, vowing that they would soon recover the mainland. 
They have not, although some of the vitriol and dogmatism of the Communists seems to have dissipated.
Most analysts give Taiwan only a slightly better chance than the Ming emperors of regaining China. 
As that realization sinks in, tough questions are surfacing that go to the heart of the Republic of China, as Taiwan calls itself: What is to be done vis-a-vis the mainland?
How long can the Government claim to be the legitimate ruler of all China?
How long can it continue to refuse all contact with the mainland?
The contention that the Government here is China's Government may be maintained for the foreseeable future, but cracks have appeared in the facade. 
Last week, the ruling Nationalist party formally approved the lifting of the ban on visits to the mainland for family reunions. 
The Government is allowing publication of some mainland books. 
It is becoming easier to import traditional medicines that originate in China. 
There is talk here of cultural, scientific and sports exchanges, and some officials would even like to see trade and investment links.
Family reunions aside, the ban on visiting the mainland will continue. 
But officials here sometimes seem to suggest that the ban is mostly for show, to withhold legitimacy from the Communists, and will not be rigorously enforced. 
''It's very difficult to verify,'' said John H. Chang, the Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs. 
''If they say they went to see relatives, what can we do?
So the tendency is to be more lenient.''
The increased leniency (people who have made visits to the mainland are no longer jailed) reflects a general mellowing. 
Martial law was lifted in July. 
New political parties have formed. 
The press is increasingly bold, anticipating the lifting of certain press restrictions on Jan. 
1. Government film censors have relaxed, allowing the showing of ''Daughter of the Nile,'' a recent film with an unflattering portrayal of Taipei.
In part, the new attitudes seem to reflect the same pressures for liberalization that have appeared in South Korea and Hong Kong. 
Extremely rapid economic growth - 7 percent a year per capita over the last 20 years, compared to 2 percent in the United States - has fostered a prosperous middle class that increasingly wants to participate in the political process. 
At the same time, the number of students in higher education has surged from 10,000 in 1953 to more than 430,000.
An older generation that accompanied Chiang Kai-shek to Taiwan in 1949 is handing over power to a new generation - too young to remember the mainland, less ideological, and armed not with bazookas but with American Ph.D. degrees. 
Shaw Yuming, the new 49-year-old chief Government spokesman (Ph.D., University of Chicago), has books in his office that at one time could have been read only under the bed covers, including works from China and ''The Soong Dynasty'' by Sterling Seagrave, a harsh portrayal of Chiang Kai-shek. 
It is necessary, Mr. Shaw explains, to know your enemy.
While the younger generation is generally urging greater tolerance, there are concerns that this could also increase the pressure for Taiwan to declare itself independent, separate from China, perhaps after President Chiang Ching-kuo, son of Chiang Kai-shek, leaves the scene. 
The one thing Beijing and Taipei agree on wholeheartedly is that Taiwan is an integral part of China. 
However, the increased tolerance poses the risk that if people are allowed to say what they think, some - perhaps 25 percent, some analysts estimate - will say that Taiwan should be independent.
Â 
38 Years on the Island
Moreover, the two Chinas are moving farther apart. 
For the vast majority of Taiwanese, the mainland is an ethereal place that they have never seen and never expect to see. 
The Nationalist Government lasted on the mainland from early in 1912 to the fall of 1949, a bit less than 38 years. 
On Oct. 
1 the Communists celebrated 38 years of the People's Republic of China, which means the Nationalists have been on Taiwan longer than they ruled on the mainland.
Jaw Shaokong, a legislator, says visits to the mainland and other contacts will make reunification more likely. 
''If we keep away from mainland China, we'll be moving toward independence,'' he argues. 
But while more people from Taiwan are now expected to make legal and illegal visits across the Taiwan Strait, a Western analyst here warns that they may find the economic and social gulf is too great to be bridged. 
Per capita income on Taiwan is more than 10 times higher than on the mainland. 
In a revealing comment, Hsu Lu, a journalist who made an illegal visit last month, said afterward: ''I will never go back to mainland China as a reporter. 
It's too boring.''

text:
