China's most prominent dissident intellectual, breaking an imposed silence, today assailed harsh political controls on university students and teachers.
The dissident, Fang Lizhi, also disparaged the Communist Party's recent calls for liberalized intellectual and literary expression as insincere.
In his first interview with a foreign journalist here since he was expelled from the Communist Party last year, Mr. Fang dismissed his promotion last week to ''second-rank professorship,'' from ''fourth rank,'' as ''propaganda.''
It was not clear whether there would be any repercussions for his interview.
Student Demonstrations
Professor Fang, who is one of China's most distinguished astrophysicists, was dismissed as vice president of the University of Science and Technology in Hefei last year after a nationwide tide of pro-democracy student demonstrations that began at his school. 
Communist Party leaders, including the country's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, accused Mr. Fang of instigating the protests by encouraging students to speak out on a wide array of political and intellectual concerns.
After being stripped of his official position and expelled from the party last year, he went to Beijing, where he pursued his research at the China Academy of Science. 
Party officials prevented him from contacts with virtually all foreigners, especially journalists, until he was permitted to travel to Rome last summer to attend a scientific conference. 
While in Rome he gave an interview to the West German news weekly Der Spiegel in which he suggested that Marxism had reached the end of its useful life in China.
No single name evokes such fervent response on China's campuses and among intellectuals as that of Fang Lizhi. 
He is widely seen as the most articulate and forthright critic of China's Marxist orthodoxy and the country's pre-eminent champion of free speech.
Â 
Appearances Must Be Approved
He is permitted to appear in public only with the permission of the highest members of the Communist Party. 
In November, an invitation to speak on cosmology at his old university in Hefei, in Anhui Province, had to be personally approved by Li Peng, one of the five members of the Standing Committee of the party's Politburo and now acting Prime Minister.
Professor Fang derided suggestions that conditions for intellectuals in China have been improving since a major party meeting in October at which many elderly orthodox Marxists retired from leadership posts.
''On the surface, there is more tolerance,'' Professor Fang said. 
''but this is not so in reality.''
Professor Fang was particularly critical of many American and European China specialists who have described recent trends in China as increasingly liberal. 
''They're deceived,'' he said simply. 
October Party Congress At the October meeting, a congress of party representatives that gathers every five years, many new, younger faces appeared in the Politburo and on the Central Committee. 
Many Western diplomats and academics have pointed to this as an indication that economic liberalization coupled with a softer ideological line had triumphed.
But Mr. Fang maintained that it is too early to assess whether real change has occurred. 
''The students don't like the new members,'' he said. 
''Almost all the new members come from areas that treated student demonstrators harshly - Li Ruihuan from Tianjin, Jiang Zemin from Shanghai.''
''Power is still held by Deng and the older generation. 
Zhao is No. 1 in principle. 
But when they talk about who will talk with Gorbachev, it is Deng. 
It is clear who is in charge.''
He was referring to proposals by Mikhail S. Gorbachev, the Soviet leader, to hold a summit meeting with Mr. Deng, although Zhao Ziyang is now the party leader.
Â 
Changes Were Celebrated
When older hard-liners were voted off the Central Committee last October, many Beijing intellectuals celebrated. 
But Professor Fang said that these elderly leaders still exercised tremendous power. 
''They may not have a position, but their secretaries and their aides now are in positions of power. 
These old guys just get on the phone and say, 'Do this.'
''
Professor Fang, who is in his early 50's, said that the greatest evidence of the continuing influence of hard-liners was the crackdown on students and teachers on college campuses.
When he was granted permission to visit the University of Science and Technology last November, his schedule was rigidly controlled. 
''They limited me to a two-day visit,'' Professor Fang said. 
''I still have an apartment there and I was kept inside. 
When I was there, some people said I should speak in the big lecture hall, but the party secretary said no.
Â 
Four Lectures at Old School
So Professor Fang said that he delivered four lectures in a smaller hall.
''There were 80 security men there,'' said Professor Fang, his boyish face erupting in laughter. 
''The authorities are afraid of my having contact with the students.''
''There also is a new policy on study abroad. 
The Government wants to reduce the number of students abroad. 
On the surface they say they want to do this because not many are coming back. 
In fact, they are afraid of the returning students. 
They are afraid of what they have learned, of what they will say.''
Even in the rather abstruse fields of quantum mechanics and cosmology, Professor Fang said, China's ideologues have continued to interfere.
Â 
Marxism and Astrophysics
''Marxism thinks it has solved all the problems of man,'' he explained. 
''Two years ago, I wrote an introduction to a translated essay on quantum mechanics by Hawking for the magazine 'science.'
Hu Qiaomu said it could not be published, that it wasn't Marxist.''
Mr. Fang referred to Stephen W. Hawking, a theoretical physicist at Cambridge University who has done pioneering work in cosmology. 
Hu Qiaomu is an orthodox ideologue who retired from the Politburo last October.
''Cosmology is still concerned with the problem of whether the universe is finite or infinite. 
That question is not solved for us. 
In Marxism, they already have solved this question. 
In a letter, Engels said that the universe must be infinite. 
So for Marxists, it is.''
Professor Fang disdained suggestions that his academic promotion last week reflected a liberalization in the party's approach to unorthodox intellectuals. 
''It's just propaganda,'' he said. 
''I get 20 yuan more every month,'' a sum equivalent to $5.40.
At the moment, he said, he is waiting for permission to spend next year at Cambridge doing research. 
He said that approval would probably have to be granted by Mr. Zhao himself.
Mr. Fang's wife, Li Shuxian, a physicist who teaches at Beijing University, has been denied permission to do research in Rome and has been restricted in her contacts with students.
''I wanted to meet with some students outside class but they wouldn't let me,'' she explained. 
''I put up a paper sign on the wall saying I would meet the students on the side of the road. 
There were 100 students who showed up. 
There were 10 security officers watching the whole time.''
Professor Li shook her head slightly as she talked. 
''I'm not afraid,'' she said. 
''We're not afraid.''

file: A REPORT FROM PEKING.txt
text:
ï»¿
CHINA, Alive in the Bitter Sea. 
By Fox Butterfield. 
Illustrated. 468 pp. 
New York: Times Books. 
$19.95.
IN 1979 Fox Butterfield became the first New York Times correspondent to be based in Peking in 30 years. 
For the next two years, while China cast off the fetters of more than a decade of cultural revolution and wrestled with the legacy of Mao, he was there giving Americans a firsthand view of China. 
Educated in East Asian studies at Harvard, apprenticed in Hong Kong and Taiwan and fluent in Chinese, he traveled to remote areas of the country, visited the people in their homes, climbed sacred mountains, spoke with top leaders by day and met with dissidents at night.
B Michael Frolic reviews book, "China: Alive in the Bitter Sea," by Fox Butterfield
What he had to report was not pleasant, and this book, based on his experiences in China, is not always pleasant. 
After 10 years of Pollyanna-ish accounts by others, Mr. Butterfield and a few fellow American journalists have sent back messages of disappointment and despair. 
China is poor; China is autocratic; China is complicated and beset by massive problems that defy simple solution. 
China does not make it easy for outsiders to penetrate the various layers of her reality. 
China is dazzling in her uniqueness, yet banal in her backwardness. 
China is nearly a superpower, but her per capita income is less than $200 a year. 
China is a nation of survivors whose faith in Communism has been irrevocably shaken: men and women with broken careers and lost families, cynical party members, innocent victims denied justice, disenchanted young people enduring two decades of turmoil, individuals sacrificed to a system that is out of control. 
One's heart goes out to Lihua, a young woman whom Mr. Butterfield befriends. 
She tells him, ''I won't be happy till I die. 
I've never lived a good day in my life. 
My mother was beaten to death, my father was left senseless and I still have to beg for everything. 
â¦ My scars will never heal.''
Mr. Butterfield's view of China is gloomy and reminiscent of standard accounts of life in the Soviet Union. 
He describes an economy in permanent crisis, where per capita grain production has not increased since the mid-1950's, where reforms make no palpable impact, where outmoded management responds poorly to the demands of modernization. 
Within such a system inequities abound and are perpetuated by an alliance of party, army and police that arbitrarily makes decisions and maintains control for the elite. 
Sudden and unorthodox movements are dangerous. 
Everybody is keeping an eye on somebody else. 
It's best to go with the flow and keep quiet - not exactly the stuff of which industrialization is made. 
(A Peking University professor tells Mr. Butterfield: ''If you are not overly ambitious and don't have any political troubles, life in China is pleasant, like living on a slow-moving conveyor belt.'') The system cannot cope with China's massive population, nor, apparently, is it capable of stimulating the rapid economic growth required for a modernization breakthrough.
YET amid the grimness there are rays of hope. 
If the Socialist system has degenerated, there is still the positive legacy of Chinese culture and the strength of those individuals who dare to step forth and tell their stories to foreigners. 
Well-meaning leaders are developing pragmatic policies in an attempt to salvage the Chinese revolution, if not to restore China's greatness. 
Also, significant gains have been made since 1949: a doubling of life expectancy, the attainment of literacy for hundreds of millions of people, a better distribution of resources, elimination of foreign domination. 
Despite his pessimism, Mr. Butterfield occasionally evinces the hope that somehow China can still right herself, not as was wantonly promised during the Cultural Revolution, but through a more cautious form of development. 
No matter how bitter the Chinese sea may be, it is still ''alive'' for Mr. Butterfield.
His book, which is imaginatively organized, conveys his concern for the individual Chinese he meets. 
He divides his book into five sections that cut to the heart of daily life in China: ''Connections,'' ''Pas-sages,'' ''Systems,'' ''Persua-sions'' and ''Messages.''
In ''Connections'' he introduces us to the ways in which Chinese relate to foreigners and to each other, from ''taking the back door'' (getting scarce goods through sheer ingenuity) to ''the giant flight of stairs'' (a principle that acknowledges that ''beneath this facade of the classless society â¦ some people are much more equal than others''). 
In ''Passages'' Mr. Butterfield discusses the various stages of life, from child-rearing practices through love, sex, marriage, abortion, divorce and old age. 
The underlying theme is that, with some exceptions, Chinese ''passages'' are rather like ours. 
Bing, one of Mr. Butterfield's Chinese friends, reads Gail Sheehy's ''Passages'' and then tells him: ''It was a revelation. 
I was really going through a crisis, and it showed me there are turning points in your life. 
I fit right in to what Sheehy called 'Catch 30.'
''
The section on ''Systems,'' Mr. Butterfield's strongest, is reminiscent of some of the best parts of Hedrick Smith's ''The Russians,'' a book that Mr. Butterfield clearly would like to emulate. 
Drawing upon his long experience reporting on Chinese economic development, supplemented by his personal observations and by Western scholarly accounts, Mr. Butterfield provides an excellent analysis of contemporary Chinese agriculture, industry and bureaucratic structure. 
We see how these systems work and also why they respond so poorly to change. 
We meet Chinese officials who say, ''We are having trouble defining what our system is. 
We are trying a number of experiments. 
Those that work we will call Socialism. 
Those that don't we will call Capitalism.''
The last two sections, ''Persuasions'' and ''Messages,'' describe the pervasiveness of the Chinese system of control and the meager ways in which Chinese individuals can resist the persuasions of those in power. 
Comparison with the Soviet Union is unavoidable, and Mr. Butterfield finds himself trying to separate Chinese and Soviet experience, even while referring to a Chinese gulag and to control techniques that, for the most part, resemble those of the Soviet Union. 
Yet he notes that no Chinese Solzhenitsyn or Sakharov has appeared, and that Chinese dissent may be of a somewhat different stripe. 
''I'm a patriot, not a dissident,'' says Tan, a Columbiatrained economist. 
''I can see many faults. 
But I'm not a dissident because the present system is the best we have; there is no viable alternative to Deng. 
It would be traitorous of me to jeopardize our modernization.''
DESTINED for a wide audience, this book will undoubtedly influence American perceptions of China. 
It is informative, disturbing, poignant and absorbing. 
It is based on a range of personal encounters with individual Chinese that are almost unprecedented for any American journalist in recent times. 
It is a testament to Mr. Butterfield's skill in reporting, his training in Chinese studies and his personal commitment to China. 
However, in looking to him for the final word about China, we should proceed with caution. 
As a foreigner and a journalist, his experiences were extremely limited. 
The bulk of his reporting was confined to a few Chinese cities. 
He was basically isolated from the lives of China's 800 million rural dwellers. 
From his arrival until the day he left, his movements were monitored. 
He was an important ''foreign friend,'' an outsider who was constantly followed. 
Those Chinese whom he managed to befriend often were the desperate outsiders, the alienated, ''Westernized'' elements. 
We should stop and ask whether Mr. Butterfield's disaffected Chinese friends do justice to the mainstream of Chinese who may be relatively satisfied with their system and with their present lot in life.
Encounters between Westerners and Chinese have been unusual and painful over the centuries. 
It seems the more the Chinese resisted Westernization , the more exotic and remote China became. 
How many Americans have tried to discover the ''truth'' about China, and how many different truths have they found?
Yesterday's revolutionary simplicity gives way to today's oppressive Chinese totalitarianism as described by Mr. Butterfield. What will tomorrow bring?
Since the cultural revolution China has been rendered less remote, more tangible and vulnerable, somewhat more comprehensible to foreigners. 
Is this the image Chinese leaders want Americans to see and the one Americans prefer to have of China?
One recalls Jerry Rubin's remarks to Mr. Butterfield after Mr. Rubin's visit to China in 1979: ''One day as I was riding on a bus, I said to myself, either everyone is telling the truth or everyone is pulling my leg. 
It came to me that everyone must be telling the truth.''
Given our past encounters with China, how could he have been so sure?
Perhaps there is no one great truth that Westerners can find in China, only that she is big and poor and old, and struggling to reclaim a unique cultural tradition by means of a terribly painful revolution that is still far from complete.

file: A SHIFT TO CHANGE IS SEEN IN CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
Advocates of change in China won a solid victory at its 13th Congress of the Communist Party, but the balance between them and more cautious leaders has been carefully preserved, according to a number of academic specialists on China.
The experts held a four-day meeting here to assess Beijing's efforts at change.
Of the five members of the new Standing Committee of the Politburo, the highest decision-making body, the experts noted, two are clearly reformers, including Zhao Ziyang, the new Party General Secretary. 
But two others, including Li Peng, who is believed likely to be named Prime Minister, favor a more moderate approach, and the fifth member, Qiao Shi, is thought to be a swing vote capable of siding with either group.
''It's clear the reformers will be the dominant group, but the more cautious people still have a significant position,'' said Roderick MacFarquhar, a professor of government at Harvard University. 
''This reproduces the old balance so there will continue to be arguments.''
Â 
Judging Economic Changes
The experts, meeting at a conference sponsored by Brown University's Institute for International Studies, raised a number of questions about the success of Beijing's economic changes.
They agreed that the economic changes, notably in agriculture, had been far more effective than those in any other Communist nation in producing high growth rates. 
Since the reforms began in 1979, in fact, China's gross national product has grown at eight percent a year, more than six times the recent average growth rate in Eastern Europe.
But the participants, from the United States, China, Japan and the Soviet Union, stressed that Beijing had not reaped any gain in industrial productivity, and they suggested that the big jump in farm output in the early 1980's may have been a one-time increase, which has now stalled.
Indeed, some experts argued, the Communists have not gone nearly as far in reforming industry as they have talked about, especially in freeing prices and making factory managers responsible for profits.
Â 
Recent Spurt of Inflation
''They may have missed their best opportunity to do these things,'' said Nicholas R. Lardy, a professor of economics at the University of Washigton.
In part, Dr. Lardy contended, this is true because of a recent spurt of inflation, which has made all Beijing's leaders more nervous about experimenting with freeing prices previously fixed by the state. 
But it is also because the ''urban population is against further reform,'' he said. 
Many urban residents feel only the peasants have benefited from the changes so far.
The specialists were impressed that Deng Xiaoping, China's paramount leader and the champion of the reformers, was able to force the retirement from the Politburo of virtually all the senior conservative officials who have opposed him, including Peng Zhen, 85, the chairman of China's legislature. 
Mr. Deng himself stepped down from his Politburo seat in exchange.
But they expressed surprise that Hu Yaobang, who had been forced out as General Secretary by pressure from conservatives last January after a series of student demonstrations, was retained on the Politburo. 
Mr. Hu is Mr. Deng's closest disciple and the most outspoken advocate of political as well as economic change.
Â 
'Potential for Conflict'
Merle Goldman, a professor of history at Boston University, said Mr. Hu's continued membership on the Politburo raised ''the potential for conflict between him and Zhao,'' the new General Secretary. 
She pointed out that two of the five members of the new Politburo Standing Committee, Mr. Qiao and Hu Qili, both had served under Mr. Hu in the China Youth League, and that many of the provincial party leaders as well as heads of China's prestigious reserach institutes were loyal to Mr. Hu.
''Hu still has a mass base and Zhao doesn't,'' Dr. Goldman said, alluding to Mr. Zhao's background as a technocrat rather than as a party or military bureaucrat. 
On the other side of the ledger, Mr. Zhao has emerged as a smooth operator, more concilatory to old-line conservatives than Mr. Hu was, and less interested in the sensitive subject of changing the political structure through greater freedom of speech and more open elections, Dr. Goldman said.
Mr. Zhao's future, and that of the economic reforms, may rest on two factors, the participants agreed: how long Mr. Deng lives and how well the changes actually work.
Dr. Lardy argued that too much attention is paid simply to the names of the members of the new Politburo. 
''The people called conservatives are not opposed to reform when they find out how well it works,'' he said, pointing to the many rural officials who have now happily given up much of their former power to go into business under the new rules approving private enterprise.
Dr. Lardy also pointed to evidence that the changes in industry have not done as well as many foreigners believe. 
The best measure, he argued, should be increased profitability of factories, since China is trying to make the transition from a centrally planned economy, where the Government provides raw materials and labor and automatically takes all output, to a more market-oriented appproach.

text:
ï»¿
GRIEVER
An American Monkey King in China. 
By Gerald Vizenor. 
238 pp. 
Normal: Illinois State University/ Fiction Collective/Sun & Moon Press. 
Cloth, $15.95. 
Paper, $8.95.
IMAGINATION is the real world,'' claims the mournful clown Griever de Hocus, ''all the rest is bad television.''
Griever, hero of Gerald Vizenor's second novel, is a Native American of mixed blood who abruptly appears as one of an ill-assorted group of American teachers at a Chinese university in Tianjin. 
Here his trickster heritage of tribal folklore and myth, not to mention his readiness to dream, helps him to cope with a socialist cadre and the closed society it monitors. 
For despite the repudiation of the Cultural Revolution, China remains suspicious of foreign devils. 
At the same time, it struggles with population control and welcomes modernization in the form of plastics, dermabrasion and Western venture capitalism.
Griever screams his rage at these responses into what he calls ''panic holes'' or turns it into playful wisdom in the manner of the monkey kings that populate China's myths of the poor and oppressed. 
Like the monkey kings, other animals - bears, bats, spiders, even mosquitoes - are also seen by Griever to help shape human conduct. 
And so, with a pet rooster for a companion, he follows their lead, playing basketball with hogs and liberating both chickens and political prisoners. 
Later, he disrupts the opening of an extravagant French restaurant and begins a brief affair with a local translator, a dalliance that leads to tragic consequences when it is discovered by her sinister father, a chain-smoking bureaucrat who conceals his contempt for Westerners behind a snakelike smile. 
Among the other figures Griever encounters are an enigmatic Russian painter who protects his hands with white mittens while serving a prison sentence hauling coal and an actor-sage who preserves Griever's history on a picture scroll that introduces his adventures with a cloudy but comic shrewdness that sets the tone for much of the novel.
Like his hero, Mr. Vizenor attempts to overcome the stale political realities of a Communist state through the renewal of language. 
For the characters as well as the reader, his world is laid out like brush strokes in an ink painting.
It is technology, however, rather than metaphor that finally determines the outcome of the novel. 
And after a climactic carnival, the story's magical disregard for time and space collapses under the weight of a high-tech escape from the mainland. 
Griever's often burlesque encounters, like his visionary impulses, reflect his desire to escape rather than confront China's dusty streets and oppressive social conditions. 
Thus his opposition to injustice eventually dissolves into a mere expression of personal vexation. 
The real arena for Griever's wild history is poetic dreamscape.
Though grounded in the author's experience as a teacher in China and in extensive historical references that are scrupulously identified in an epilogue, the novel gains its strength more from associations of color and from the play of words than from bare facts. 
Beyond our need for them, words, as Griever realizes, need us to hold down a sense of place. 
They also need to take off on their own. 
When they do, this modestly experimental, often luminous novel, which won the 1986 Illinois State University/Fiction Collective Award, evokes a world that does not mirror but parallels our own.

file: ACCOUNTS OF RUSSIAN_S CHINA VISIT SUGGEST EXPECTATIONS ARE LIMITED.txt
text:
ï»¿
Official accounts today of the visit to China by a senior Soviet official offered new indications of the limited expectations both Governments appear to have for the occasion.
The official, Ivan V. Arkhipov, a First Deputy Prime Minister, is the most senior Soviet official to come here in 15 years. 
His visit is being closely watched for signs of any thaw in the chilly political relations that have prevailed for nearly a quarter of a century between Moscow and Peking.
Official accounts of visit to China by Ivan V Arkhipov, Soviet First Deputy Prime Minister, offer new indications of limited expectations both Governments appear to have for occasion; Arkhipov is most senior Soviet official to come to country in 15 years (S)
But so far, after two days, both sides have taken care to emphasize the differences that have prevented an improvement in their relations. 
At the same time, they have stressed their readiness to expand trade, economic and scientific exchanges, and to continue their search for better overall ties.
For both sides, the most important fact about the the visit is probably that it is taking place at all, after a last- minute postponement in May when Moscow evidently wished to show its displeasure over Chinese troop clashes with Vietnam and over the warmth displayed when President Reagan came to Peking in April.
Â 
Won't Return for Funeral
The symbolic importance of the Arkhipov visit was underscored today when the Russian remained here rather than return to Moscow for the funeral of Defense Minister Dmitri F. Ustinov, as unofficial reports from the Soviet capital Friday had suggested he might.
The Chinese wariness toward the visit was suggested by the coverage given in today's editions of People's Daily, the Communist Party paper, which put accounts of Mr. Arkhipov's arrival here and the banquet given for him Friday night on the bottom of its back page. 
Important official visitors from friendly countries are generally accorded front-page display.
At the banquet, Mr. Arkhipov and his host, Deputy Prime Minister Yao Yilin, struck a cordial personal note in their speeches that reflected an acquaintance dating back to the Russian's years here heading the Soviet aid program in the 1950's.
The two officials also spoke of their nations' common interest in better ties, Mr. Yao saying China ''sincerely hoped'' for improved relations and Mr. Arkhipov responding that it was in the fundamental interests of both nations ''to put these relations into the orbit of friendship and good-neighborliness.''
But the account given by the official New China News Agency said both men had also referred to the ''differences'' that had impeded normalization. 
The agency said Mr. Arkhipov had ''mentioned'' those involving ''major international issues and relations with certain other countries.''
Since political consultations between the two capitals were resumed in 1982, five sessions here and in Moscow have failed to bridge differences over the Soviet military intervention in Afghanistan, Moscow's backing for the Vietnamese occupation of Cambodia and the high troop levels each side maintains on their common frontier.

file: ADVANTAGES SHIFT SUBTLY IN A DELICATE THREE-HANDED GAME.txt
text:
ï»¿
The United States, China and the Soviet Union last week seemed to be playing another round in an international strategy game, with each side trying to avoid being isolated by the others. 
The stakes were high - if any two joined forces, they might endanger the country left out. 
Playing the game vigorously in Peking, Defense Secretary Caspar W. Weinberger met with Chinese leaders and announced that Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang would come to Washington in January and that President Reagan would be going to Peking in April.
Mr. Reagan's advisers saw the planned trip as a chance to play up his role as a world leader, an obvious asset if he seeks re-election seven months later. 
(The China visit may also provide a convenient reason for rearranging his Asian itinerary, delaying a visit next month to the Philippines, where anti-regime turmoil threatens security and political hazards.)
Subtle shifts in triangular relationships between US, USSR and China in recent years reviewed, with China now perceived as leading in obtaining US concessions without much concrete commitment; Sec Caspar Weinberger and Zhang Aiping illustrated (S)
After Washington reclassified China as a ''friendly power'' and thus eligible for more high technology exports, and the United States agreed to import $800 million of Chinese textiles, Peking seemed ready to reciprocate, at least on the protocol level. 
Washington had urged Mr. Zhao to come so Mr. Reagan could return the visit.
In China, Mr. Weinberger talked up the Soviet threat and the value of closer strategic ties between Washington and Peking. 
He dangled a list of possible ''defensive'' arms China could buy, notably antiaircraft weapons and antitank guns. 
But the Chinese seemed uninterested in pursuing an open military alliance (which could also be difficult for Mr. Reagan, after his repeated pledges of support for Taiwan). 
As a reminder that they were not tying themselves to Washington, the Chinese announced talks on normalizing relations with the Russians would resume on Thursday. 
As to Soviet-American relations, they remained in a frozen state. 
Mr. Reagan last week took a different tack with a ''high road'' speech at the United Nations, stressing the need for arms control accords. 
But he also continued his verbal assault on Moscow for shooting down the South Korean airliner and he accused the Russians of violating previous accords. 
Yuri V. Andropov, the Soviet leader, obviously concerned about the propaganda effects of the plane incident and angered by Mr. Reagan's insults, condemned the Administration on all fronts.
As a result of the poor state of relations with the Russians, Washington's ability to reap benefits from the triangular game is no longer what it was in the early 1970's when the Nixon-Kissinger Administration finessed both Communist countries while avoiding the appearance of ganging up against either. 
This was easier when the Soviet Union and China were in a state of mutual military alert. 
The ability to play the Chinese against the Russians ended in 1980, after the Soviet intervention in Afghanistan. 
President Jimmy Carter cut back relations with Moscow and put off seeking Senate ratification of a strategic arms limitation treaty.
Mr. Carter also sought a strategic relationship with China against the Russians. 
But although Peking had once sought better relations, Washington found it unreceptive when the Carter Administration got around to talking of a virtual alliance. 
The Chinese seemed to decide to stand aloof, although they, even more than Americans, had reason to be concerned about Soviet military actions in Afghanistan and Southeast Asia.
Testing the Waters
China's doubts about cooperating with the United States were fortified when Mr. Reagan, a long-time supporter of Taiwan, became President. 
Prolonged debate ensued about Taiwan and issues such as textile limits, handling of defectors, and whether Pan American World Airways should be allowed to fly to Taipeh.
By last year, the Kremlin sensed it could break out of its isolation in the triangle and try to turn the tables on Washington. 
The Russians began to court the new Chinese leadership, while Peking, seeking to depict itself as a leader of the nonaligned bloc - where being seen as an American ally is a liability - seemed more than willing to test the waters with Moscow. 
In so doing, China put pressure on Washington to yield on Taiwan.
Peking, which has extracted economic and technological assistance in return for normalization with Washington, now is insisting on security concessions from Moscow. 
China wants the Soviet Union to reduce its heavy troop concentration along the Chinese border, pull its forces out of Afghanistan and end its backing for the Vietnamese occupation of Cambodia.
If the United States was the major beneficiary from the triangular relationships of the 1970's, the Chinese seem to have learned the lesson well and emerged as the leading player now. 
Foreign Minister Wu Xueqian, in New York for the United Nations General Assembly, made that clear in a speech to the National Committee on United States-Chinese Relations. 
''China,'' he said, ''always adheres to an independent foreign policy, never attaches itself to any big power or group of powers and never yields to pressure from any big power. 
China has always adhered to principles, neither playing the Soviet card to put pressure on the United States, nor playing the American card to put pressure on the Soviet Union.''
Despite Mr. Wu's protestations, however, American officials were watching to see if Mr. Andropov, having virtually frozen relations with Washington, would now meet Chinese demands at least halfway. 
He could do so by agreeing to reduce Soviet troops in Afghanistan or to a troop pullback from the Chinese border area. 
With Mr. Reagan due to visit China in seven months, there is time for Moscow to act to stay in the game.

file: AFRICAN SCENES_ _GHOSTLY_ RAIDS TO CHINESE AID.txt
text:
ï»¿
A dozen Angolan soldiers, AK-47 assault rifles at the ready, dogged every step taken last week by a group of reporters looking at a refugee camp in Angola's east central province of Moxico. 
The soldiers' presence belied an official myth.
According to Angola's Marxist regime, there is no organized internal opposition. 
Jonas Savimbi and his National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, known as Unita, are ''phantoms.''
Bernard Nossiter discusses present conditions in Angola and Sudan
The only real threats come from South African troops or ''reactionaries,'' an official from the Ministry of Culture explained at great and vehement length recently when this reporter stopped in Angola during a swing through Africa.
In fact Moxico and neighboring provinces are frequently raided by Savimbi guerrillas. 
The military escort joined the group in case the Savimbi ''phantoms'' decided to stage a demonstration for the correspondents. 
They did not, but the gap between the official line and prudent practice was evident.
The Sudan's conservative Moslem society has been strained by female refugees from Ethiopia. 
Fleeing the wars of secession there, the women continue to cling to their form-fitting dresses and their relaxed and easy manner with men. 
They contrast strikingly with the Sudanese women, swathed in concealing robes and rarely present in mixed company.
The Sudan's Commissioner for Refugees, Abdul Rahman el-Beshir, acknowledges as much with a bureaucratic gloss. 
''We welcome strangers in this country,'' he said, ''but there are cultural problems of incompatibility. 
Moslems resent the liberal ways the Ethiopian females are having.''
On city streets, the Ethiopian women are often subjected to obscene taunts and gestures. 
Respectable Sudanese families avoid cafes that the refugee women frequent. 
Some of the Ethiopians are forced or induced into concubinage or prostitution. 
Mr. Rahman speaks with sympathy of ''these wretched people, compelled to leave their country.''
At the airport in Addis Ababa, about 60 Chinese men and one woman sit patiently, most of them dressed in neat Western suits. 
This is no package tour but a purposeful exhibition of Peking's attempt to win friends and influence distant people.
One member of the group looks up from Le Monde to explain that they are doctors, agronomists, engineers, and road and dam builders. 
They are fanning out to Tanzania, Mozambique, Mauritania and the Sudan to show Africans how things are done in China. 
Peking cannot afford much foreign aid in cash but it is rich in technical assistance, an effective way of making its weight felt.
Commissar Marques Wassowowa occupies the palace in Luena from which the Portuguese once governed the Angolan province of Moxico. 
The palace is still splendid with its flagstone courtyard, tiled roof, sweeping paneled dining room facing a curved marble veranda, plush chairs, delicate tiled bath and hospitable jug of Scotch for guests.
But the splendor is fading. 
The carpets are torn, the woodwork cracked. 
The window panes are broken and the plaster molding is chipped. 
The commissar evidently has other priorities.
Whether he should is a question raised by some students of Africa. 
A leading expert, Jean-Claude Concollato, on leave from the Sorbonne to work in the Sudan for the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, contends that much of Africa's instability flows from the lack of strong central government. 
Too many states, he says, are marked by a plethora of regulations whose writ does not run much beyond the ministries.
Even a revolutionary Government like Angola's might find some use in tangible symbols of authority, in keeping up Luena's palace. 
At the very least it would serve as a reminder that scarce capital equipment requires careful maintenance.
The 125-mile road from Khartoum, the Sudan's capital, southward to Wad Medani, runs through a bleak parched landscape almost denuded of trees, peppered with dusty shrubs. 
Walled villages of mud brick bake in the strong sun. 
Scrawny herds of goats and cattle search for fodder. 
The occasional incongruous textile or cement factory breaks the empty horizon.
The Blue Nile runs invitingly alongside, but there is neither capital nor manpower to tap its life-giving waters and irrigate the semi-desert.
When the road bends east to Gedaref, the scene suddenly changes. 
Gum arabic trees, green and promising, fill the skyline. 
Patches of soft green cotton emerge. 
The ground is covered with brown stalks from the sorghum crop. 
Conical thatched-roof houses show that nature is more abundant here.
This region gets three times the rain, and for twice as long, as the country below Khartoum. 
Gedaref is a rich town whose farmers and merchants hire Ethiopian refugees as laborers and servants. 
Failure and success in the Sudan depends not on man but on nature, on the presence or absence of rain.

file: AFTER A 37-YEAR ABSENCE, U.S. VESSELS VISIT CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
As brass bands played, three United States Navy warships, each flying China's flag, tied up here today and became the first American vessels to visit China since the Communists took power.
A gray early-morning haze shrouded the harbor as guns from the arriving American ships fired a 21-gun salute in honor of the Chinese Navy. 
Then, nudged gently by large white tugboats, the guided-missile frigate Rentz loomed through the mist with sailors in blue pea jackets and white caps standing at attention along her entire length.
Three elderly Chinese ships, a destroyer, a frigate and a submarine, were moored nearby with dozens of colorful signal flags flapping from their rigging. 
Chinese sailors stood at attention on deck while a United States Navy band aboard the guided-missile cruiser Reeves struck up ''Happy Days Are Here Again.''
Joining the Reeves and the Rentz on the seven-day port call is the American destroyer Oldendorf.
The visit, announced by Defense Secretary Caspar W. Weinberger last month on a trip to China, is being portrayed by American military and diplomatic officials as a major step in the increasingly close military ties between the two countries.
The visit also comes as details of a $550 million sale of equipment to the Chinese Air Force, announced in April, are being made public.
The commander of the United States Pacific Fleet, Adm. James A. Lyons Jr., was aboard the Reeves and spoke of the importance of the visit to the strategic interests of both countries.
''We recognize this as a historic port visit, a further step in developing and enhancing the relationship between our two countries,'' Admiral Lyons told American and Chinese journalists. 
''A key element in furthering stabilityI in this region is fostering the U.S.-China relationship. 
We also share a common concern that no one country should dominate Asia or the world.''
Â 
Some Advice for Newcomers
Despite the assertions of American officials that the 1,000 sailors had been given no special instructions on how to behave while in China, many of the sailors could be seen clutching a 32-page pamphlet titled ''A Sailor's Liberty Guide to China,'' a document filled with admonitions on proper behavior.
''China does not have bar girls,'' read one warning. 
''Drink in moderation,'' cautioned another passage, while the fiery Chinese liquor mao-tai was introduced with a blunt, ''Watch out.''
The first glitch of the visit did not involve onshore comportment, but naval etiquette. 
Although the Chinese ships across the pier were flying signal flags from their rigging in what the Navy calls ''full dress,'' the American vessels were not similarly bedecked.
Several Navy officers said the Chinese had protested the failure of the American ships to go to ''full dress'' and refused to proceed with the welcoming ceremony until a precise and formal equality had been established.
Hastily, sailors aboard the three American ships began clambering up masts. 
Piles of bright signal flags were produced from lockers, and after nearly two hours they were in place on the American ships.
Adm. Ma Xinchun, the commander of China's northern fleet, which is based here, then strode to the gangplank of the Reeves to officially welcome Admiral Lyons to China.
The last American naval visit to these waters ended on May 24, 1949, as Communist armies pressed south and east. 
The U.S.S. 
Dixie, a repair ship built to service destroyers, took aboard the last Americans in Qingdao and steamed toward Hong Kong.
Qingdao owes its genesis as a major city to 19th-century German colonial designs. 
The Germans held Qingdao for 16 years before losing it in World War I, and the broad avenues carved by German planners are still lined with heavy stone and brick villas.
While it has been more than 37 years since American sailors trudged up Jungshan Road, the main commercial street here, the memory of the Americans has lingered.
''The Jungshan was the world of the Americans,'' said a 79-year-old man who gave his name only as Lao Liang, or ''old Liang.''
''That's where all the action was,'' he said. 
''They paid with American dollars and we took in American dollars.''
Â 
'A Great Event'
Even younger Chinese possess a sort of collective memory of the Americans, a recollection that is usually less than kind. 
''The Americans, they grabbed women and didn't follow traffic signs,'' said Tang Tingxing, a 39-year-old shipyard worker.
Still, as he stood at the gate to the navy yard waiting for a glimpse of the American sailors, Mr. Tang said he was excited about the visit. 
''I think this is a great event,'' he said.
Along Jungshan Road today, the Americans soon found the tall, green bottles of Tsingtao beer that have made this city famous.
At a park dedicated to the 20th-century writer Lu Xun, Patrick M. Stevens, 22, lowered his camera for a moment. 
''I think this is great,'' said the sailor from Amityville, L.I. 
''This is the first ship here in 37 years. 
This is history. 
We're little ambassadors.''

file: AIDE SAYS INTERNAL FORCES STILL THREATEN HANOI.txt
text:
ï»¿
A senior Vietnamese official interviewed in a Polish newspaper has depicted his country with unusual candor as one troubled by grave military, economic and political problems.
The official, Hoang Tung, a secretary of the Vietnamese Communist Party's Central Committee, told a correspondent of the Communist daily, Trybuna Ludu, in an interview published here on Monday that Vietnam was threatened directly by China, which he said is supported by the United States. 
The external threat, Mr. Tung said, is matched inside the country by supporters of the South Vietnamese regime that was defeated seven years ago.
Mr. Tung said ''classes'' connected with the former Saigon Government, though overthrown, had not yet been completely destroyed. 
He also said the existence of ''more than a million people formerly closely connected'' with the old regime ''complicates the social situation.''
WARSAW, May 25 - A senior Vietnamese official interviewed in a Polish newspaper has depicted his country with unusual candor as one troubled by grave military, economic and political problems.
''To a large extent we have liquidated the burgeoisie as a class, but former property owners continue to live among us and even now still have a sense of their own strength,'' the party official said.
Â 
Ethnic Chinese Attacked
He added that many of the former entrepreneurs were members of the ethnic Chinese minority and charged that they were linked to a global ''network'' that was conducting economic war against Vietnam. 
He referred to alleged smuggling of goods into Vietnam from Bangkok, Hong Kong and Singapore.
Foreign residents and visitors tend to believe that the goods sent into Vietnam from abroad and traded largely on the black market have provided the people of Vietnam's cities with the margin of survival while the official, Government-run sector is unable to meet basic needs.
Mr. Tung accused China and other enemies of Vietnam of conducting what he characterized as ''small war'' against his country. 
He described this as consisting of ''continuous tension'' created by Chinese military strength on Vietnam's northern border and the fomenting of partisan movements in Cambodia and Laos.
Vietnamese troops are stationed in both of those neighboring countries, whose weak regimes are considered dependent on Hanoi. 
Mr. Tung's assertion that partisan movements in Laos and Cambodia are part of a war against Vietnam appeared to be an admission of his country's predominance over the two countries.
Economically, the Vietnamese official said, ''small war'' consists of the creating of ''economic confusion and disorganization'' of the Vietnamese market by the overseas Chinese.
Â 
'Economic Blockade' Charged
Furthermore, Mr. Tung charged, an ''economic blockade'' is being carried out against Vietnam. 
Presumably, he meant the suspension of various Western and Japanese economic aid programs in retaliation for Vietnam's invasion of Cambodia in 1979 and its continuing occupation of that country.
The Vietnamese official said the three principal tasks facing the Hanoi Government were defense, feeding the population and laying the foundations of a socialist system. 
While southern Vietnam has been Communist for only seven years, the northern half of the country has been Communist since 1954 and governed by a socialist system that even Eastern European Communists consider of excessively doctrinaire rigor.
Referring to Vietnam's serious food shortages, Mr. Tung said that balancing defense requirements against food needs ''has influenced the standard of living.''
But he added, ''When even the United States has the dilemma of cannons versus butter, why shouldn't we have a dilemma, arms versus rice?''
Acknowledging ''serious difficulties in everyday life,'' Mr. Tung asserted that the Vietnamese were not meat eaters and accepted an annual consumption level of 22 pounds a person. 
The assertion, which is not supported by knowledge of Vietnamese eating habits, caused a Pole to remark that the only purpose of publishing the interview was to persuade Poles that some countries were even worse off than Poland.

file: AMERICAN IS ARRESTED IN CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
An American businessman has been formally arrested and charged with causing a hotel fire that killed 10 people in Harbin, his lawyer said today.
The businessman, Richard S. Ondrik, 34 years old, from Houston, had been detained for more than two months in connection with the fire.
Robert Goodwin, Washington lawyer, says he has been retained by American businessman Richard S Ondrik, who was formally arrested and charged with causing hotel fire that killed 10 people in Harbin, China (M)He was arrested Wednesday and transferred to a police detention center, according to the lawyer, Robert Goodwin.
''It is kind of like a dormitory, it is a lockup,'' Mr. Goodwin said in a telephone interview.
It remains unclear why the police waited two months to arrest Mr. Ondrik. He had been held under a law that permits the detention of suspects or witnesses during an investigation.
Mr. Ondrik, who represents a Hong Kong company called Energy Projects, Southeast Asia Ltd., was staying at the 15-story Swan Hotel when a fire destroyed the 11th floor on April 19. 
His business partner, Alan Eng, five North Koreans and four hotel workers died.
The police detained Mr. Ondrik and confined him to another hotel without formally arresting him.
Mr. Goodwin, a Washington lawyer retained by Mr. Ondrik, said he has been trying to find a Chinese lawyer to represent his client because foreigners are not permitted to practice law in China. 
The case has not been reported in the Chinese press.
Mr. Goodwin said he understood that Mr. Ondrik was charged with causing the fire through negligence and that the maximum penalty is seven years in prison. 
He declined to say how Mr. Ondrik planned to plead.
The businessman had said in earlier telephone interviews that he did not remember what happened.
American sources said Commerce Secretary Malcolm Baldrige raised the issue of Mr. Ondrik's detention during a visit here last month.

file: AMERICAN TRIAL PUTS CHINESE JUSTICE TO THE TEST.txt
text:
ï»¿
When Richard S. Ondrik flew from Peking to this city on April 18, he was as prepared as an American can be for the trade opportunities unfolding in China.
Fifteen hours later, choking on acrid smoke, the Indiana-born energy expert was trapped in a nightmare. 
A fire had broken out in Harbin's Swan Hotel. 
On the 11th floor, an American working with Mr. Ondrik on an oil equipment deal, Alan Eng, was dead. 
The bodies of nine other men who had chosen to jump rather than endure the intense smoke and flame lay on the ground. 
Seven others were seriously injured. 
Chinese investigators quickly zeroed in on Mr. Ondrik as the cause of the fire, accusing him of having fallen asleep with a lighted cigarette. 
After days and nights of interrogation without a lawyer, and a 10-week delay while the matter was bounced around the bureaucracy in Peking, Mr. Ondrik was formally arrested and taken to a detention center where a naked light bulb burned throughout the night. 
After a few days he was formally charged with the ''unintentional crime'' of setting fire to the hotel.
Article on trial of Indiana businessman Richard S Ondrik, who had been accused by Chinese authorities of 'unintentional crime' of causing fire in Harbin's Swan Hotel by falling asleep with lighted cigarette; trial ended in July and verdict is expected by August 15; photos (M)Verdict Expected by Aug. 
15
The ensuing trial ended in July after four days of hearings, and a verdict is expected by Aug. 
15. At the worst, Mr. Ondrik could end up with a seven-year jail term and a bill for compensation to the hotel of $87,600.
Even if the court is lenient, as the chief judge suggested in his closing remarks, the American could spend years paying off damages for which he is uninsured. 
Worse, he may never again be able to function effectively as a businessman in China, a career for which he studied Mandarin and otherwise prepared himself for 10 years.
In some ways he is caught in a web of circumstances that are peculiar to China. 
Long after the case is closed what happened will stand as a warning to Westerners.
Unlike United States courts, Chinese ones do not require a plea of guilty or not guilty, and Mr. Ondrik has staked out a position somewhere in between. 
His account to the investigators, repeated in court, was that he had no recollection of lying down on his bed with a cigarette, but that after the shock of the fire he could not be sure.
Â 
An American Attorney
In affidavits presented to the court by his attorney, Richard C. Goodwin Jr. of Washington, five former roommates attested that they had never seen the American smoking on a bed.
In the end Mr. Ondrik's case rests less on whether he was responsible for the fire than on the more basic question of whether he should be on trial at all. 
Although the article of the Chinese criminal code under which the charge was laid bears some similarity to the United States crimes of criminal negligence and involuntary manslaughter, Mr. Goodwin, for one, says that he knows of no case in which those charges have been laid in an American court against somebody accidentally setting a fire with a cigarette. 
Was the Hotel Safe?
Mr. Ondrik's dinner was sponsored by the Harbin Oil Refinery, to whom the American's Hong Kong-based company, Energy Projects Southeast Asia Ltd., was hoping to sell a compressor. 
At the end of a day that saw the American fly 750 miles and conduct hours of talks, he consumed, by his own testimony, eight to 10 glasses of maotai, four glasses of wine and several beers.
Everything seems to have conspired against the victims. 
Prosecution evidence showed that rooms in the 16-month-old hotel had been designed for smoke and fire detectors, and were wired for them, but the devices themselves remained in storage. 
Plastic wallpaper and hollow plywood doors speeded the fire and there were no emergency exit signs. 
The only fire extinguisher did not work, and there was no alarm. 
The floor attendant, on a 24-hour shift, was off taking a bath and a meal on the eighth floor. 
Some of the testimony implied that the fire exit was locked.
Worse yet, the fire department was not answering its telephone. 
Later, taxi drivers at the hotel said that when the the firetrucks finally arrived, 37 minutes late, they had been fetched by a hotel car.
Â 
North Koreans Died in Fire
After Mr. Ondik's arrest on June 26, Mr. Goodwin had argued at the Foreign Ministry and elsewhere that a trial would be harmful to trade and other ties with the United States. 
But the Chinese were confronted with a more compelling diplomatic consideration, the fact that five of those who died and four of the injured were members of a North Korean Government delegation. 
In the lawyer's view, that ultimately made a trial inevitable.
Barely a week separated Mr. Ondrik's indictment from the opening of the trial, and by the time Mr. Goodwin reached Harbin there were only four days left. 
As a foreigner he was barred from appearing in court or seeing his client in detention, and had to work instead through a Chinese attorney he had engaged in Peking.
The careful collection of physical evidence and statements supporting the state's case marked an improvement on the past, when criminal trials, when they were held at all, were arbitrary in the extreme. 
But once Mr. Ondrik reached court it seemed clear that one fundamental, the assumption of guilt, had changed hardly at all.
By the end of the trial Mr. Goodwin had concluded that challenging the state case in a criminal prosecution here is largely fruitless, ''because the Government cannot be seen to lose.''
Rather than deciding innocence or guilt, he said, the court's function appeared to be ''assessing degrees of responsibility,'' a task it addressed at length in the Ondrik case by reviewing the deficiencies in the hotel's fire equipment and the bungling that ensued once the blaze broke out. 
Two Chinese, the hotel supervisor and the absentee floor attendant, face trials of their own for ''dereliction of duty.''
For his part, Mr. Ondrik seems to have resigned himself to a conviction. 
''It is difficult for me to accept that I am a criminal,'' he told the judges in his final plea. 
''This is partly because the law in my country and in China toward accidents is different. 
However, I am a friend of China and a guest in your country, and if this court decides that vengeance and punishment are necessary according to your laws, then I will accept that.''

file: Among the Multitude of Ayes, Nays in the Chinese Congress.txt
text:
ï»¿
There, on page 3 of People's Daily, organ of the Communist Party, was a postcard-sized photograph of three men in China's Parliament sitting with their hands in their laps while around them hands fluttered aloft. 
It was an extraordinary display of official discord.
The occasion was a vote during the current session of the Parliament in a country where the appearance of public unanimity by Government is hallowed ground.
A good deal of sacred turf has been trampled this week as more than 2,900 delegates to the National People's Congress gather in annual session to hear reports on the Government's performance and to ratify new laws and constitutional amendments. 
But the lockstep behavior of past congresses has dissolved in instances of genuine debate, negative votes and - even more remarkably - substantial coverage of events by China's press.
China's news organization have been awash with reports on the congress, interviewing delegates, publishing accounts of debates in working sessions and explaining contentious issues, like the intransigent and politically volatile problem of inflation. 
Even foreign reporters were invited for the first time to sit in on delegate discussions.
As soon as the congress opened it was clear that this year was going to be different. 
Liu Yiu-chu, a Hong Kong lawyer and delegate from Guangdong Province, abstained on a vote for the members of various committees.
A gasp went through the auditorium. 
The chamber exploded in the flashes of photographers' strobe lights. 
And then she did it again. 
Delegates joined in.
''I do not know how the lists of candidates were formulated, nor do I know the criteria for choosing them,'' Miss Liu told reporters afterward. 
''As a deputy I think I should have such information and clearly know what the procedure is.''
Miss Liu's behavior proved contagious, and at one point 69 delegates voted against the composition of a congress working committee.
Huang Shunxing, who once served in Taiwan's legislature but who now works in China as a scientist and is a delegate to the congress, urged the defeat of 89-year-old Zhou Gucheng as chairman of a committee.
Â 
Some Blunt Language
''He is too old and should be given more time for a rest,'' Mr. Huang said, in the bluntest language heard in public so far. 
After a moment's hesitation, applause surged across the auditorium in the Great Hall of the People.
For the first time in the People's Republic, not a single committee of the congress was elected unanimously.
Not all the delegates were impressed by the collapse of orchestrated tradition, however.
''If we all cast dissenting votes or abstained from voting for our own personal reasons, wouldn't this be extremely disruptive?'' the influential Economic Daily, an economic newspaper, quoted an unnamed delegate as saying.
But another saw that China was looking at something new and more recognizably democratic. 
''Those delegates who abstained or who voted negatively have brought up a new problem in how to conduct elections properly in the future,'' the delegate said. 
''Much attention should be paid to this.''

file: ANDOVER_S OPENING TO CHINA STUDIES.txt
text:
ï»¿
TO a casual observer the three students sitting around a table in government class at Phillips Academy, a private secondary school in Andover, Mass., look like typical Asian-American teen-agers. 
Wearing jeans and jogging shoes, their books stowed in backpacks on the floor, they listen as Ronald Speirs, the teacher, discusses the checks-and- balances system of the United States Constitution.
But all three of the students are Chinese, who arrived only six weeks previously from the Harbin Institute of Technology in Manchuria. 
They are the fifth group of three students each from the People's Republic of China that have enrolled in the last five years in senior classes at Andover.
Three students from Harbin Institute of Technology study at Phillips Academy in Andover, Mass, in exchange program started in 1980; school is committed to developing intensive four-year Chinese studies program and is one of 36 public and private US high schools to receive Dodge Foundation funding for language and other courses (Education: Winter Survey) (S)
Like their predecessors, who are already enrolled in American colleges and universities, the three Chinese students - Jia Yantao, a man, and Ma Tianyi and Chu Xiaoming, all 19 years old - are spending this year at Andover polishing their spoken English. 
In Harbin foreigners are a curiosity, and they find everything, not only the language, confusing. 
At Andover, however, the three will make new friends and will gradually need each other less and less. 
Surrogate families in the community have already welcomed them into their homes during school holidays.
''It's a tradition at Andover to recruit students from China,'' said Joshua L. Miner, dean of admissions. 
''And it's consistent with the diversity we seek in the student body - we have students from 19 foreign countries this year. 
But having representatives from the world's most populous nation wasn't enough. 
We had to develop a full curriculum for non-Asian students that would include a four-year Chinese language program as well as the courses we already offered in East Asian history, religions and art.''
Established in 1980 through private contacts, the exchange quickly gained approval from the Ministry of Education in Peking. 
There are still problems, however; five years after the first Harbin students arrived on the Andover campus, and three years after instruction in Chinese was first offered, ''The Chinese studies program has not yet begun to grow,'' according to Hale Sturges, chairman of the foreign language department.
Last year at Andover only nine students signed up for beginning Chinese, and this year there are 14. 
The immediate goal is to add a more advanced level of instruction each year, so that taking Chinese will eventually satisfy a student's language requirement. 
Other long-term goals include increasing the number of students of Chinese to 50. 
Many of these advanced students could then continue their studies in Harbin, making the program a real exchange.
This year, for the first time, Harbin sent a visiting scholar, Ni Xiaomin, to perfect her English and to help with Chinese instruction. 
Each Harbin student tutors a few first-year Chinese students. 
Last summer, for the first time, five Andover students visited China for six weeks.
Expenses for the three Harbin students - room, board, tuition, travel and vacations - run about $50,000 a year. 
But Andover's commitment to developing a four-year Chinese studies program is estimated at an additional $100,000 a year. 
These costs are now covered by initial funding from the Geraldine R. Dodge Foundation's $1.3 million China Initiative program, Andover's Kemper Fund for foreign students, general scholarship funds and individual contributors. 
But in the future, according to Dean Miner, Andover must begin a large fund-raising effort to endow the program.
SCHOOLS like Andover face a number of obstacles in setting up strong Chinese programs. 
As of 1980, the year of the most recent study, there were only 1,980 high school students nationwide taking Chinese. 
Geography, inertia, parental bias toward the traditional Romance languages and obsolete teaching materials work against a curriculum balanced between Western and non-Western languages. 
This year, for example, 43 percent of all Andover students take French, 24 percent Spanish, 16 percent Latin, 8 percent Russian, and only 1 percent Chinese.
According to Mr. Sturges, Chinese pedagogy is far behind America's. 
The five available texts, with no graphics, he described as boring. 
''We make do,'' he says, but new texts, correctly paced, with audio-visual aids are needed for students of the 1980's.
Things are improving, however. 
This year Andover was one of 36 public and private high schools, 22 more than in 1983, to receive Dodge Foundation funding. 
Schools willing to make a long-term commitment to teach Chinese language can participate in annual forums such as one held at Ohio State University last summer, in which teachers of Chinese met to share their concerns and explore new ways to help students.
And at the college level, the 13,178 enrollment in Chinese language classes in 1983-84 represents a 16 percent increase over 1980. 
''It's important to get a head start on Chinese,'' said Richard Brod, director of foreign language programs at the Modern Language Association. 
''Unlike the Western languages, without the base of pre-collegiate Chinese, it's not easy to gain functional proficiency in Chinese at the college level.''
The three students at Andover are the youngest of the 10,000 mainland Chinese now studying in the United States, which is only about 3 percent of all foreign students in the country. 
Of the total number of Chinese here, China pays for 5,400. 
The balance are sponsored either by relatives and friends in the United States or through private scholarships. 
Except for a student exchange in the planning stage between the Sidwell Friends School in Washington, D.C., and Peking Middle School No. 2, there is nothing comparable to the Andover-Harbin program at the high school level in the United States; the Chinese students at Andover are the only ones from that country attending American secondary-level schools.
China's population is four times that of the United States but its 800 colleges and universities are barely a quarter of this country's. 
China sends less than 1 percent of its college students here, most at graduate and postgraduate levels in subjects like engineering, computer science or management, which Chinese universities cannot yet offer. 
Most are also trained as teachers.
Those who do come are a highly select group, and the three now at Andover are no exception. 
To gain entrance to Harbin Institute, one of 14 institutions in China that are considered to have special status, they received the highest scores on college-entrance examinations given to 50,000 qualified high school seniors. 
This year at Andover they are taking advanced physics and math, economics, and English and American history for foreign students. 
Eventually, after five or more years of study in America, they will return to the Harbin Institute to teach.
Terry Hoyt is a freelance writer based in New York City.

file: Arabs Lands Said to Be Turning to China for Arms.txt
text:
ï»¿
Arab diplomats say that some Arab countries are turning to China for weapons at a time when the Soviet Union appears reluctant to provide arms.
The Soviets have been building bridges with the Arab world for three and a half decades. 
But in the Arab diplomats' view, a crisis of confidence appears to be developing over what many Arabs see as a shift in Moscow's policy in favor of Israel and toward closer cooperation with the United States, Israel's main backer.
Criticism in the Arab press of Soviet moves on this issue has prompted an official retort from Moscow and set in motion a publicity campaign to reassure Arabs that there has been no basic change in Soviet attitudes.
Â 
Chinese Missiles Sought
The diplomats say Syria and Libya, Moscow's closest Arab allies, have been negotiating with Beijing to buy a sophisticated shorter-range missile known as the M-9, which is still under development.
Syria and Libya are armed with Soviet-built Frog-7, SS-21 and SS-1 surface-to-surface missiles, which have ranges of 37 miles, 62 miles and 150 miles, respectively. 
The Chinese M-9 is estimated to have a range of 375 miles.
On Wednesday, As Safir, a daily newspaper in West Beirut, carried reports that Moscow has refused to supply Syria with the SS-23 missile, which has a range of about 300 miles.
Arab-Chinese economic ties have also increased. 
Libya has announced that it was investing in a Chinese silk factory, while Kuwait and Tunisia have set up a joint venture with Beijing to produce fertilizers.
Â 
Assad to Visit Moscow
Diplomats said President Hafez al-Assad of Syria plans to visit Moscow soon for talks with Mikhail S. Gorbachev, the Soviet leader.
Mr. Assad's last trip to the Soviet Union was a year ago. 
A joint communique at the end of that visit said the two countries, joined in a treaty of friendship and cooperation, were to upgrade their military cooperation.
But sales of Soviet military equipment to Syria are reported to have fallen off over the last year, partly over Moscow's insistence on being paid in cash.
Another reason, diplomats say, is unease over recent Soviet-Israeli contacts and the perception of what has been described in Arab publications as ''Soviet complicity with the United States'' against the Palestinian cause and in favor of Israel.
Gennadi I. Gerasimov, spokesman for the Soviet Foreign Ministry, issued a statement Tuesday rejecting the charges. 
Tass, the Soviet press agency, quoted Mr. Gerasimov as emphasizing that Moscow and Washington were in fact discussing measures to stop an intensification of the arms race in the Middle East.
On Tuesday the Soviet Embassy in Beirut released to the press an Arabic translation of an article by the Soviet press service Novosti, explaining recent Soviet overtures toward Israel but emphasizing that they did not constitute a lessening of Moscow's support for the Arab and Palestinian causes.
The article denied that Moscow had concluded a deal with Israel to allow more Jews to leave the Soviet Union. 
A planned visit to Moscow by an Israeli consular delegation is only a ''technical matter,'' it said.
Novosti asserted that a meeting at the United Nations in New York this month between the Soviet Foreign Minister, Eduard A. Shevardnadze, and the Israeli Prime Minister, Yitzhak Shamir, was intended merely to exchange views and did not constitute a first step toward resuming diplomatic relations.

file: ARMS TO CHINA_ DUBIOUS MOVE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Warnings by American officials that the United States might sell weapons to China if the Soviet Union invades Poland raise questions whether such a threat has any serious validity. 
The dominant view among intelligence officials of the United
States and other Atlantic alliance countries is that it does not, and that the hardheaded professionals of the Soviet military and security forces are aware it does not. 
Some analysts with a wide knowledge of China's military situation deplore what one called a ''knee-jerk reaction'' on the part of American politicians whenever the Soviet Union invades a neighboring country, as in the case of Afghanistan, or appears to be on the verge of doing so, as in the case of Poland.
This reacton, they say, takes the shape of public assertions that Soviet action will be followed by American arms aid to China. 
They cite as examples statements by Secretary of Defense Caspar W. Weinberger and Senator Charles H. Percy, the Illinois Republican.
Military Analysis questions warning by U S to provide weapons to China if Soviet Union invades Poland
Most politicians, the analysts assert, do not understand the difficulties involved in an attempt to modernize China's obsolete or obsolescent forces.
Â 
Chinese Forces Lag Years Behind
The first, and possibly the most important, of these difficulties would be the absorption of modern arms by the Chinese forces. 
A Defense Department study completed under the Carter Administration estimated that the Chinese forces lag 15 years behind the United States in technological training.
''Even the maintenance of low-technology equipment would be problematical in the hands of China's relatively unsophisticated common soldiers,'' the report said.
A study by a subcommittee of the Congressional Joint Economic Committee concluded that even if China got a huge infusion of foreign defense technology and other arms aid, the impact on China's combat abilities would not become apparent until late in this decade.
Without such aid, the Chinese economy is unlikely to be able to provide the modern weapons required to put an army of 3,600,000, an air force of 490,000 and a navy of 360,000 on a basis of equality with the Soviet Union.
Lieut. Gen. Eugene F. Tighe Jr., director of the Defense Intelligence Agency, told the committee that the prospects for China's becoming a powerful military state by the end of this century are very slim - ''as a matter of fact almost nonexistent in terms of counter-United States or counter-Soviet Union.''
Analysts emphasize that to become even a marginal threat to the Russians, China would have to reverse present economic trends in addition to receiving foreign - meaning American - arms aid.
Â 
China Shifts Industry to Peace
As an Atlantic alliance source pointed out, while the Chinese public is warned continually about the imminence of Soviet attack, planners give priority to agriculture, light industry and some segments of heavy industry. 
The NATO report declared that ''a sizable proportion of Chinese military manufacturing capacity'' has been converted to civilian production. 
The Xingtan tank plant, which has started to produce sewing machines, electric fans, bulldozers and tower cranes, was cited as an example.
This shift in priorities is risky, analysts agree. 
The Soviet Union has 46 divisions - six armored and 40 motor rifle - deployed along the frontier with China. 
This force, supported by an air force of about 3,500 planes and a large number of surface-to-air and surfaceto-surface missiles, is regarded by analysts as far better equipped and more modern in its military doctrine than the lumbering Chinese forces south of the frontier.
Any American or other foreign aid would also have to take into account the primitive internal communications system and other aspects of the military infrastructure. 
China's ability to deter Soviet attacks along a frontier that, including Mongolia, extends 5,813 miles is regarded as severely limited.
''Let us suppose that the Russians do invade Poland and that the Administration decides to rearm China in retaliation,'' one analyst said. 
''Does anyone really understand the costs of doing this or the strain that it would put on the present American military-industrial complex?''
Â 
Aid Would Cost Up to $63 Billion
As evidence he cited a 1979 Pentagon study estimating that procurement of sufficient military goods and services from the United States to give China ''a confident capability'' to defend itself against Soviet attack by conventional forces would cost $41 billion to $63 billion.
Projected programs for the modernization of China's forces would include, among other items, 3,000 to 8,600 improved medium tanks. 
8,000 to 10,000 armored personnel carriers, 16,000 to 24,800 heavyduty trucks, 6,000 air-to-air missiles, 720 mobile surface-to-air missile launchers, 200 air-superiority fighters and 240 fighterbombers.
Under present industrial conditions, analysts said, the production of weapons in such volume is out of the question. 
They expect an expansion of the United States arms industry to meet the Reagan Administration's military expansion plans. 
But they do not expect that expansion to be large enough to accommodate both American needs and a modernization of China's weaponry.
If by a miracle of industrial mobilization the United States was able to provide even half of China's needs the question of absorption would remain.
Threatening statements by American leaders do not alter China's vulnerability, one NATO analyst said. 
No promises of military assistance, he added, can change the fact that the three Manchurian provinces - vulnerable to the nearby Soviet Union - are of the greatest strategic importance to China. 
They supply 35 percent of China's coal, 70 percent of its crude oil, 40 percent of its steel, 68 percent of its trucks and railroad rolling stock and most of its civilian and combat planes.
