file: BREZHNEV CHARGES U.S. IS THREATENING NUCLEAR CONFLICT.txt
text:
ï»¿
Leonid I. Brezhnev told a gathering of Soviet military leaders today that the United States was threatening ''to push the world into the flames of a nuclear war.''
He also said the Soviet Union would do ''everything in our power'' to normalize relations with China.
In a speech to some 500 generals and Defense Ministry officials summoned
Â 
Excerpts from speech, page A7.
to the Kremlin, the Soviet leader accused the United States of pursuing a foreign policy of ''adventurism, rudeness and undisguised egoism.''
MOSCOW, Oct. 
27 - Leonid I. Brezhnev told a gathering of Soviet military leaders today that the United States was threatening ''to push the world into the flames of a nuclear war.''
Perhaps by coincidence, Mr. Brezhnev spoke on the eve of the 20th anniversary of the day in 1962 when Nikita S. Khrushchev bowed to President John F. Kennedy's demands for the dismantling of Soviet missiles in Cuba. 
Mr. Khrushchev's retreat left Soviet generals vowing never again to be caught short of military strength in a confrontation with the United States.
Â 
Brezhnev Seeks to Assure Army
Most of Mr. Brezhnev's speech dealt with assurances that the Soviet leadership recognized the need for military strength and was prepared to commit the necessary resources.
He said that, while the Soviet Union continued to stand for detente, it recognized that ''not only words'' but military strength were needed to deal with what he called the American threat. 
Accordingly, he pledged support for a drive to increase the combatreadiness of the Soviet armed forces and for an upgrading of military technology.
His speech also marked an explicit Soviet use of the ''China card.''
For months Soviet leaders have been calling for an end to the deep-seated ideological and territorial disputes that have divided Moscow and Peking for two decades. 
After a break of three years, the two sides resumed talks in Peking earlier this month and agreed to continue them in the two capitals.
Â 
Connection With U.S. 
Policy
Previously, the Soviet Union had called for improved relations with China as a goal in itself. 
Today, Mr. Brezhnev made an explicit connection with the strained Soviet-American relationship. 
He said United States policy had made Soviet relations with other nations ''very important,'' and he mentioned specifically China.
In a passage that suggested that the Soviet Union was not discouraged by the first phase of the renewed talks, he noted that the Chinese leaders, too, had expressed interest in closer ties.
''Of no small importance are rela-tions with China,'' he said. 
''We sincerely want a normalization of relations with that country and are doing everything in our power toward this end. 
In Peking, they also say now that normalization is desirable.
''No radical changes in the foreign policy of the People's Republic of China are to be seen so far. 
But the new things which appear must not be ignored by us.''
Both Chinese and Soviet officials said after the Peking talks that they expected no early resolution of the differences between the two nations.
The unusual nature of the Kremlin gathering, and Mr. Brezhnev's assurances of backing for the armed forces, suggested that the party leadership was seeking to ease concern in the military that responses to the United States had not been tough enough.
This interpretation was strengthened by a new emphasis in Mr. Brezhnev's remarks. 
In previous speeches during the 21 months of the Reagan Administration, the main theme was generally the importance of detente and of restoring an equilibrium through arms negotiations, trade and other contacts.
This time there was only a brief passage about detente and no mention of the two sets of nuclear arms reduction talks under way in Geneva, on strategic, or long-range, weapons, and on medium-range weapons in Europe.
Instead, there was a strong hint in Mr. Brezhnev's remarks that a Soviet freeze on the deployment of medium-range missiles might be abandoned soon if American preparations for the deployment of equivalent missiles in Europe were to continue.
Western diplomats said that, while the change in tone owed something to the fact that Mr. Brezhnev was addressing a military audience, it also implied a stiffening of the Soviet posture.
''The masses of people on all continents,'' Mr. Brezhnev said, ''angrily protest against Washington's aggressive policy, which is threatening to push the world into the flames of a nuclear war. 
The adventurism, rudeness and undisguised egoism of this policy arouse growing indignation in many countries, including those allied with the U.S.A.''
The occasion had implications for Soviet domestic politics. 
Diplomats could not recall a previous occasion when a Soviet leader felt obliged to offer such public assurances to the military. 
Moreover, the speech contained a passage in which Mr. Brezhnev, who is 75 years old and in failing health, appeared to be trying to scotch rumors that he was no longer in command.
In the presence of five other members of the ruling Politburo - including the two men favored eventually to succeed him, Yuri V. Andropov and Konstantin U. Chernenko - Mr. Brezhnev noted that Defense Minister Dmitri F. Ustinov, ''constantly reports'' to him about military matters. 
His words slurred, he added:
''I also constantly handle matters of consolidating the army and navy in the performance of my official duty, so to say, and know about the state of affairs.''
Some of the solutions to economic problems, including increased investment in agriculture, appear to have created anxieties in the military about a budget squeeze. 
But Mr. Brezhnev, who has gained a reputation in 18 years as a Soviet leader for giving the armed forces almost everything they want, promised that they would be getting even more in the future.
''We are equipping the armed forces with the most advanced weapons and military hardware,'' he said. 
''The party's Central Committee is taking measures to meet all your needs.''
It was at this point that he indicated concern that the Soviet forces were falling behind in military technology. 
''Competition in military technology has sharply intensified, often acquiring a fundamentally new character,'' he said. 
''A lag in that competition is inadmissible. 
We expect our scientists, designers, engineers and technicians to do everything possible to resolve successfully all tasks connected with this.''

file: BREZHNEV STRESSES ISSUE OF CHINA TIES.txt
text:
ï»¿
Leonid I. Brezhnev today underscored the importance he ascribes to improving relations with China in a brief survey of foreign affairs that was marked by its temperate tone.
The Soviet leader spoke to local Communist leaders in the course of a visit to Baku, the capital of Azerbaijan in Soviet Central Asia. 
''As regards Asia, we would deem it very important to achieve a normalization, a gradual improvement of relations between the U.S.S.R. and the People's Republic of China on a basis that I would describe as that of common sense, mutual respect and mutual advantage,'' Mr. Brezhnev said.
He did not pursue the subject further, and Western analysts saw the statement in the context of continuing Soviet efforts to reduce the animosity that has separated the two Communist giants for the last two decades.
MOSCOW, Sept. 
26 - Leonid I. Brezhnev today underscored the importance he ascribes to improving relations with China in a brief survey of foreign affairs that was marked by its temperate tone.
Mr. Brezhnev made a strong appeal for improved relations with China last March in Tashkent, and since then the Russians have made several tentative overtures to Peking. 
During the Chinese Communist Party Congress this month, Soviet commentaries were notable for their constrained and factual approach in comparison with the more combative tone used in the past. 
Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher of Britain said during a visit to Peking last week that Soviet-Chinese talks were expected to start next month.
Â 
Unusual Moment of Levity
Mr. Brezhnev's nationally televised appearance before Azerbaijani party members had an unusual moment of levity and confusion when it turned out that the Soviet leader had started reading the wrong speech. 
A hurried consultation was visible among officials seated on the rostrum, and Andrei M. Aleksandrov, Mr. Brezhnev's aide, hurried to his side with a sheaf of papers just as the cameras turned away.
The 75-year-old leader displayed good humor and presence of mind when he said with a smile: ''It's not my fault, comrades. 
I have to start from the beginning.''
He did, and proceeded without evident trouble through the 40-minute address.
Since his return from his summer residence in the Crimea early this month, Mr. Brezhnev has pursued a vigorous schedule, including two state visits to Moscow by foreign leaders and his current trip to Baku, where his program has included a full range of official functions. 
He has appeared to be in relatively good health and fully recovered from whatever affliction kept him out of public view earlier this year.
Â 
Moderate Tone on U.S. and Israel
In his speech, Mr. Brezhnev touched relatively briefly on foreign affairs and avoided the acrimonious references to the United States and Israel that have characterized recent Soviet pronouncements. 
Instead, he affirmed Soviet constancy on international detente, which he said had struck ''deeper roots'' in Europe than elsewhere.
''But there exist possibilities for its strengthening everywhere and they must be used intensively,'' he added, continuing, ''I shall not speak here about our attempts to develop relations with the United States of America, to achieve just, mutually acceptable agreements on questions of the limitation and reduction of both strategic and medium-range nuclear weapons, for you know well about them.''
One reason for the shortage of references to the difficulties with Washington and of condemnations of Israel, diplomats suggested, may have been Mr. Brezhnev's reluctance to pre-empt the impending discussions between Foreign Minister Andrei A. Gromyko and Secretary of State George P. Shultz.
Â 
Mrs. Gandhi's Visit Hailed
Mr. Brezhnev declared his ''sincere satisfaction'' with the visit to the Soviet Union by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi of India. 
A joint declaration issued today on Mrs. Gandhi's return home repeated the effusive expressions of friendship made in earlier speeches and toasts.
It also reported a joint resolve to ''insure a 1.5- to 2-fold increase in the volume of trade'' between the two countries by 1986 and to maintain a high rate of growth in trade until 1990.
The Soviet Union has edged out the United States as India's largest trading partner, according to Indian diplomats here, and India ranks as Moscow's major trading partner among developing countries. 
In 1980 the trade amounted to 2.4 billion rubles, or about $3.3 billion at the official rate of exchange.
Much of the trade has been in the form of Soviet arms sales to India, but that area was not mentioned in the communique. 
The statement said the two countries agreed ''to examine possibilities for the further expansion of cooperation in such areas as ferrous and nonferrous metallurgy, coal and oil, machine-building and power.''

file: BREZHVEV PRESSES OVERTURES TO THE CHINESE LEADERS.txt
text:
ï»¿
Leonid I. Brezhnev issued a new appeal to Peking today to revive the search for ways to end the Chinese-Soviet feud. 
The Soviet leader's comments in Tashkent, about 250 miles from the Chinese border, were the latest and most direct in a series of overtures that diplomats said were designed to take advantage of the United States-Chinese rift over the proposed sale of American jet fighters to Taiwan.
The specific proposals made by Mr. Brezhnev broke little new ground. 
But the tone in which they were couched was more conciliatory than the invective of most Soviet references to China in the two decades since the two nations drifted apart over ideology, territory and other issues.
Leonid I. Brezhnev issued a new appeal to Peking today to revive the search for ways to end the Chinese-Soviet feud.
Western diplomats said Mr. Brezhnev's speech was Moscow's most positive signal to the Chinese in several years, and certainly since the downturn in Soviet-Chinese relations following the Soviet intervention in Afghanistan.
Â 
Claim to Taiwan Is Backed
Mr. Brezhnev said the Soviet Union recognized Peking's claim to Taiwan, and rejected the ''two Chinas'' concept over which Peking has increasingly fallen out with Washington.
The Soviet leader denied that the Russians posed a threat to China or that they claimed any Chinese territory. 
He said the Soviet Union was ready to resume talks on disputed border segments, adding a proposal to discuss ''possible measures to strengthen mutual trust in the area of the Soviet-Chinese frontier.''
There was no elaboration, but the offer seemed to imply a mutual reduction in military buildup.
''We remember well the time when the Soviet Union and People's China were united by bonds of friendship and comradely cooperation,'' Mr. Brezhnev continued. 
''We have never considered normal the state of hostility and estrangement between our countries.
''We are prepared to come to terms, without preconditions, on measures acceptable to both sides to improve Soviet-Chinese relations on the basis of mutual respect for each other's interests, noninterference in each other's affairs and mutual benefit, certainly not to the detriment of third countries.
''This refers to economic, scientific, cultural as well as political relations, to whatever extent each side is prepared to take concrete steps in any of these spheres.''
Â 
Brezhnev Disavows Meddling
Mr. Brezhnev took pains to assure the Chinese that criticism of their foreign policy did not imply meddling in their internal affairs.
''We have never denied and do not deny now the existence of a socialist system in China,'' he said, ''even though Peking's association with the policy of the imperialists around the world contradicts, of course, the interests of socialism.''
Mr. Brezhnev made no such distinction a year ago at a Soviet party congress in discussing Chinese relations. 
At that time, he said that China's social and economic development demonstrated ''what a distortion of the principles and essence of socialism in domestic and foreign policy can lead to.''
Today's speech by Mr. Brezhnev followed a call by Prime Minister Nikolai A. Tikhonov last month for the resumption of a dialogue with China ''on the basis of equality and in the spirit of mutual understanding.''
Â 
U.S.-Chinese Strains Noted
Before Mr. Tikhonov's remarks, an article in the Government newspaper Izvestia had pointed to the strains between Washington and Peking, saying that ''as long as Americans are scaring themselves stiff with the 'Soviet threat,' they will always be haunted by the nightmare of normalization in Soviet-Chinese relations.''
Part of the present efforts at rapprochement was a visit here last week of three Chinese economic experts. 
Their purpose, Chinese sources said, was to study Soviet management methods, and they were received by Aleksandr V. Bachurin, a deputy chairman of the State Planning Committee. 
The visit was the first of the sort since the Chinese-Soviet break in the early 1960's.
In subsequent years, Moscow made several approaches to restore ties, but all overtures foundered. 
Border negotiations that began after frontier clashes in 1969 have been dormant since 1978, and some preliminary discussions on normalization were abandoned after the Soviet intervention in Afghanistan.
The souring of American-Chinese ties, however, revived speculation that China might be ready to play its ''Russia card,'' and Mr. Brezhnev's remarks suggested that the Soviet Union was prepared to play along.
Â 
Soviet Objectives Appear Limited
Diplomats believe that Soviet ambitions are limited, and Mr. Brezhnev seemed to support this view when he underlined the possibility of modest agreements.
The Russians are unlikely to believe that they can quickly remove the accumulated resentments and restore the alliance they had with China in the 1950's. 
A 30-year friendship treaty lapsed last year. 
Tensions over Afghanistan, India, Vietnam and the 4,500-mile Soviet-Chinese border are unlikely to dissipate soon. 
And China's trade with the United States, totaling $5.5 billion last year, far exceeds Chinese-Soviet trade, which was $400 million in 1980.

file: BRITAIN AND CHINA GIVE NO SIGN OF PROGRESS IN TALKS ON HONG KONG.txt
text:
ï»¿
China and Britain completed their latest round of negotiations on the future of Hong Kong today without indicating whether there had been further progress toward framing a mutually acceptable plan for the colony.
A three-sentence communique issued after the end of the eighth round of talks called the meetings ''useful and constructive,'' a standard phrase that has been used to describe the last four rounds of talks.
The communique did not elaborate. 
The statement after the seventh round of negotiations in December said that ''both sides reviewed the course of the talks and the progress made so far,'' raising expectations that the gap between their positions was narrowing.
China and GB complete latest raound of talks on future of Hong Kong without indicating wheter they have made further progress; set new talks for Feb 22 (M)Next Talks in February
The statement today said the ninth round of talks would take place in Peking on Feb. 
22 and 23. 
Western diplomats in Peking agreed that the omission of a brighter characterization did not necessarily mean that the negotiations had run into new difficulty. 
The British and the Chinese have agreed not to disclose details while the negotiations are in progress.
Britain and China have been trying to reach agreement on the status of Hong Kong after 1997, when Britain's 99-year lease over most of the territory expires. 
China has insisted on regaining sovereignty and has refused to allow Britain an administrative role in the transition to Chinese rule.
There have recently been reports in the British and Hong Kong press that Britain has agreed to concede the issue of sovereignty and a transitional presence in return for China's assurance that Hong Kong could retain its existing social and economic system for 50 years after 1997.
Such reports have been neither confirmed nor denied, but they have coincided with a greater confidence on the issue expressed by China's Prime Minister, Zhao Ziyang, and the party General Secretary, Hu Yaobang.
Â 
Deadline is September
Such optimism may not signal a breakthrough in the near future. 
There has been some speculation that the Chinese could be exuding hopefulness as a device for pressing the British to accept Peking's terms and for blaming London if the talks do not produce tangible results by next September, the deadline that China has set for an agreement.
However, a Western diplomat who has followed the talks said he believed the latest round had started to focus on the technical details involved in a transfer of power, including the means of putting into effect a 12-point Chinese plan for Hong Kong, which could explain why today's communique made no mention of progress.
The Chinese proposal, details of which have been publicized by Chinese officials this month, would let Hong Kong keep its capitalistic system and way of life, including its stock, gold and foreign-currency exchanges and the convertible Hong Kong dollar.
The colony would be run by its residents as a newly created special administrative zone of China, with Peking handling only Hong Kong's military and foreign affairs.
The first round of talks got under way in Peking last july, after a preliminary phase of negotiations that began with Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher's visit to China in September 1982.
Â 
Differing Descriptions
The first round of talks was described as ''useful and constructive,'' and the second round, two weeks later in July, was called only ''useful.''
The third and fourth rounds, in August and September, were not characterized at all, indicating that they had run into difficulty, and were followed by Chinese charges that Britain had taken a colonial attitude.
The climate began to improve by the fifth round in October and the sixth round in November, and the first allusion to progress came at the seventh round in December. 
Each round of talks has lasted two days, but since last fall they have been supplemented by informal contacts in Peking between the British Ambassador, who heads the British delegation, and the Chinese Foreign Ministry official who heads the Peking delegation.
The latest negotiations had two new chief delegates - the newly arrived British Ambassador, Sir Richard Evans, and China's Assistant Foreign Minister, Zhou Nan. 
Despite the changes, they hewed to the old format in their communique.

file: BRITISH AND CHINESE AGREE TO TALK ON HONG KONG.txt
text:
ï»¿
China and Britain agreed today to negotiate the future of Hong Kong through diplomatic channels but did not reach any consensus on the fundamental question of who would have sovereignty over the colony.
Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher of Britain, after spending 2 hours 20 minutes with Deng Xiaoping, China's paramount leader, read a carefully phrased joint statement to reporters that said:
''Today, the two leaders of both countries held far-reaching talks in a friendly atmosphere on the future of Hong Kong. 
Both leaders made clear their respective positions on the subject. 
They agreed to enter talks through diplomatic channels following the visit, with the common aim of maintaining the stabilityI and prosperity of Hong Kong.''
PEKING, Sept. 
24 - China and Britain agreed today to negotiate the future of Hong Kong through diplomatic channels but did not reach any consensus on the fundamental question of who would have sovereignty over the colony.
At a news conference, Mrs. Thatcher repeatedly refused to go into any details of her discussions with the Chinese leaders, including the issue of who had the right to Hong Kong.
''I think the people of Hong Kong will recognize that to maintain confidence, you must also maintain confidentiality,'' Mrs. Thatcher said.
Â 
Chinese Add a Paragraph
But the New China News Agency, in releasing the joint statement as Mrs. Thatcher's news conference was about to start in the Great Hall of the People, added a further significant paragraph:
''The Chinese Government's position on the recovery of the sovereignty of the whole region in Hong Kong is unequivocal and known to all.''
A Hong Kong journalist whom the Chinese briefed privately said that the Chinese sought to include their position on sovereignty in the joint statement but that the British refused. 
Mrs. Thatcher was apparently not aware that the New China News Agency had added the paragraph.
Britain acknowledges that its lease on 90 percent of the colony's territory will expire in 1997 but has insisted that the rest, including the island of Hong Kong, was ceded to Britain in perpetuity.
China insists that the entire colony was seized illegally by the British through unequal treaties in the 19th century and must in principle be given back.
In responding to one of the 30 questions at her news conference, which concluded her talks in Peking, Mrs. Thatcher also confirmed rumors that new Chinese-Soviet talks would take place next month.
She replied that the Chinese view of the Soviet Union had not changed, then added, ''I do know that talks are being held, is it next month?
October, yes.''
Â 
Familiar Format for Talks
A Western diplomat here noted that the format adopted by Britain and China to continue discussing Hong Kong paralleled the one used by the United States and China in arriving at their communique last month on American arms sales to Taiwan. 
The negotiations on this issue were also carried on through the embassies in each other's capitals, with Vice President Bush calling on Mr. Deng last May.
The Chinese and British Embassies have been consulting on the Hong Kong question since spring in preparation for Mrs. Thatcher's visit. 
Today the British Prime Minister stressed that future talks would be more than just a continuation of existing contacts.
''The whole thing must now be speeded up and discussed much more intensely and in much greater detail than it has been before,'' Mrs. Thatcher said.
Although she seemed to allude to the delicate question of business confidence in Hong Kong, Mrs. Thatcher insisted that the joint statement, with its reference to stabilityI and prosperity, should sufficiently encourage Hong Kong's residents.
''Now and then, if you're entering into talks and you wish to be successful, you must in fact keep those talks confidential,'' Mrs. Thatcher said. 
''You must. 
That should inspire more confidence than blabbing all over the place.''
She observed that no one had expected a solution to emerge from the current meetings, which are the first on the issue at the head-ofgovernment level. 
''It would not have been possible today to get much further than we have,'' said Mrs. Thatcher, who called the issues complex.
The Prime Minister may have dug in her heels on the sovereignty issue to gain a good bargaining position. 
But she also said that ''my responsibility as Prime Minister of Her Majesty's Government is to the people of Hong Kong, and that is how I tackle it.''
Â 
Nervousness in Hong Kong
There has been financial nervousness in Hong Kong over the 1997 deadline because mortgages and other long-term planning are already being affected. 
There have been reports that some capital is shifting to Singapore and other commercial centers.
When a journalist asked Mrs. Thatcher today what she would advise British businessmen who were considering new investments in Hong Kong, she replied tartly: ''I'm not an adviser on investment to any company. 
I'd make a lot more money if I were.''
The British recognize that Hong Kong island could not survive as an independent entity without the rest of the colony and want to resolve the status before the deadline.
China also has an interest in an orderly transition because it earns 40 percent of its foreign currency from Hong Kong and does not want its commercial value to dissipate.
One proposal unofficially floated by the Chinese has been the gradual transition of Hong Kong into a ''special administrative zone'' under China's flag, a favored status similar to the one offered to Taiwan for peaceful reunification.
Mr. Deng has said that Hong Kong investors should set their minds at ease. 
Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang said Thursday that Hong Kong need not be concerned about the future. 
But both leaders have also made clear that China expects to reassert sovereignty.

file: BRITISH OFFICIAL CONFERS IN PEKING ON HONG KONG.txt
text:

The British Foreign Secretary met today with China's Foreign Minister to review the negotiations on the future of Hong Kong.
Britain's lease over most of the colony expires in 1997.
Sir Geoffrey Howe, the British Secretary, discussed the issue of Hong Kong in separate sessions this morning and this afternoon with his Chinese counterpart, Wu Xueqian.

The talks were to evaluate the progress already made and to study what needed to be done to reach an agreement on Hong Kong's future, the spokesman said.
Â 
September Deadline for Accord
China, which intends to reassert its sovereignty over Hong Kong, has said it will announce its own plans if an accord is not reached by September.
The spokesman gave no details of today's talks, which were conducted with the same air of confidentiality that has covered 12 rounds of direct negotiations on Hong Kong.
Sir Geoffrey is the most senior British official to visit China since Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher first raised the subject in her official visit here in September 1982.

Â 
Speculation of Breakthrough
The British Foreign Secretary's visit has raised speculation in Hong Kong that some breakthrough might be forthcoming. 
Sir Geoffrey tried to dampen this hope Sunday by calling his visit ''only one stage in the complex and difficult process'' of agreeing on the best way to preserve Hong Kong's stabilityI and prosperity.
After his arrival Sunday aboard a Royal Air Force plane, Sir Geoffrey was quoted by his spokesman, John Goulden, as saying: ''A good deal of progress has already been made by our negotiators. 
It is now timely to review the position at the ministerial level and to decide how best we can take the process forward from here.''

5 million inhabitants of Hong Kong.

For this reason, Sir Geoffrey is expected to withhold any subtantial comments on his talks here until after he arrives in Hong Kong on Wednesday.

Top Company Leaving Colony Hong Kong's stock market fell sharply late last month after one of the colony's leading companies, Jardine Matheson, announced that it would move its legal domicile to Bermuda because of uncertainty over the colony's future.

file: Business and the Law_Legal Ties With China.txt
text:
ï»¿
IN two weeks, Xi-Qing Gao, a 33-year-old associate at a large New York firm, is scheduled to be sworn before a judge to practice law in the United States. 
Last summer he became the first citizen of China to pass the New York Bar examination.
Mr. Gao, who was working on a railroad in southwest China 15 years ago during the Cultural Revolution, is the latest in a growing number of lawyers who are able to make their way through the thicket of complex American and Chinese commercial laws and rules.
For a long while after relations between China and the United States began to thaw during the Nixon Administration, companies in the West were hard-pressed to find lawyers who could understand the intricacies of Chinese law. 
Furthermore, China had relatively few ''legal workers,'' as they were then called. 
Not many American schools taught courses in Chinese law and even fewer firms had employees who knew anything about the subject.
It was not just a shortage of lawyers that made deals more difficult. 
''They didn't have words to express the same meanings as our words: words such as contract, offer, acceptance,'' said Jerome A. Cohen, one of the first Americans to become a scholar of Chinese law. 
''When you're drawing a contract and one side says arbitration and the other thinks it means mediation, it can create lots of problems.''
But all of that is beginning to change. 
Last year, China began to institute examinations for its 50,000 lawyers. 
Chinese officals have said they expect to increase the number of lawyers to more than 500,000 by the turn of the century. 
Some Chinese law schools, closed during the Cultural Revolution, are now larger than law schools in the United States.
''One young student from Beijing said to me not long ago that law used to be undesirable because after studying it, it used to be the case that graduates would have to go back to the farm,'' said Mr. Cohen. ''But now, the student said, a law degree was a 'hot ticket.'
''
In the United States and Canada, 10 law schools have exchange programs with schools in Beijing and Shanghai.
''The first time we had a Chinese student back in 1982 was an exceptional transaction,'' said Paul D. Carrington, dean of the Duke University School of Law. 
''It seemed like such a remote place then. 
Now it is becoming a common occurrence, with people coming and going all the time.''
By most accounts, such exchange programs are expected to grease the wheels of trade between the two countries.
''Every year we have a few Chinese citizens who spend some time with our firm before going back to their country,'' said Mr. Cohen, a partner at Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison, which has one of the largest practices representing clients with business interests in China. 
''Now when we sometimes negotiate with the Government we run into people who worked in the United States and know how we operate.''
Other firms that have a significant practice of clients with Chinese investments include Baker & McKenzie, Coudert Brothers, Graham & James and Haight, Gardner, Poor & Havens.
Mr. Cohen, regarded in the field as one of the earliest and brightest players - he taught Chinese law at Harvard Law School for 17 years, wrote a book on the subject and speaks Mandarin, a Chinese dialect - declined to name any of his firm's clients. 
But among the American companies with some of the 8,000 contracts worth $20 billion in investments that have been signed in the last eight years are Gillette, H. J. Heinz, American Motors and Foxboro.
Many more companies are expected to invest in China, according to Craig Allen, an international trade specialist at the Commerce Department, despite recent figures that American investment had fallen last year.
Still, China forbids foreigners to practice law or appear in its courts, although some observers have said that Japan's decision earlier this year to open up its legal system to foreigners has been looked upon in Beijing as a favorable development.
For Mr. Gao, who teaches Chinese law in the law schools of Fordham University and American University when he is not working on bonds at Mudge, Rose, Guthrie, Alexander & Ferdon, the move to train more Chinese lawyers means more than just being able to conduct international commerce.
''I consider myself to be lucky because I had many friends who are much brighter than I who either died on the railroads or have been moved to factories,'' he said. 
''It's as much an incentive as anyone needs to work harder and do more.''

file: C.I.A._S SECURITY WAS LAX, ACCCORDING TO CONVICTED SPY.txt
text:
ï»¿
Larry Wu-Tai Chin, the former C.I.A. analyst convicted last week of spying for China for 30 years, said today that it was ''easy'' to evade the Central Intellience Agency's security procedures and steal reams of classified documents.
In his first interview since his arrest last November, Mr. Chin said he was never searched when he left work at the Foreign Broadcast Information Service, an arm of the C.I.A. that translates and interprets material gathered from radio broadcasts and newspapers.
''It was easy to do,'' he recalled. 
''They do not search your body when you go out.''
Mr. Chin said he was giving the interview to two reporters because he was eager to tell his story. 
He said he originally talked to F.B.I. agents about his activities because ''consciously or unconsciously I wanted the world to know what I did was for the good of U.S.-Chinese relations.''
Mr. Chin was convicted last week by a Federal jury on charges of espionage, conspiracy and filing false tax returns. 
No date has been set for his sentencing. 
C.I.A.'s Security Questioned The case has raised several questions about the C.I.A.'s security procedures. 
A memorandum filed by the prosecution shows that Mr. Chin was given only one polygraph, or lie-detector, test in his 30 years as a contract employee and staff officer.
Mr. Chin was given the polygraph test in 1970, after he was hired as a full-time intelligence officer in the headquarters of the foreign broadcast service in northern Virginia. 
It was the standard polygraph given to all prospective C.I.A. employees.
In the next 11 years Mr. Chin never again underwent a polygraph exam, even though in 1974 his security clearance was upgraded from top secret to top secret, codeword, a higher classification, according to trial testimony.
In the same period Mr. Chin was audited seven times by the Internal Revenue Service, which questioned whether his salary as a Government employee could support the expenses he was showing from his rental property.
Â 
Defector Tipped Off Officials
But suspicions at the C.I.A. were not aroused until 1983 when, intelligence sources say, a high-level Chinese defector tipped off American officials.
Prosecutors contended that Mr. Chin was paid more than $150,000 by the Chinese. 
They said he maintained multiple foreign bank accounts, owned gold overseas and held title to about 30 rental properties.
Mr. Chin said he believed that a security agent from the C.I.A. covertly interviewed him once, in 1974 or 1975. 
He recalled that a person identifying himself as a Commerce Department official came to his house in Dale City, Va., and asked him about his sources of income and where he bought his furniture. 
He said he believed the person was really a C.I.A. agent.
''I said most of my furniture was bought from yard sales, which was true,'' said Mr. Chin. '' I lived very modestly.''
Â 
Turner Found Security Lax
Stansfield Turner, Director of Central Intelligence under President Carter, said in an interview last year that potentially lax security at the agency was a major concern in his tenure. 
Mr. Turner said he had instituted random searches of briefcases at the agency's headquarters offices in Langley, Va., but he said he was unsure whether these procedures were used at the Foreign Broadcast Information Service office.
''One of my first impressions when I went to work at the C.I.A. was that security was terrible,'' said Mr. Turner.
Mr. Chin testified at his trial that he hid documents in his coat.
A C.I.A. spokesman declined to say whether the Chin case and the conviction on espionage charges of Sharon Scranage, another C.I.A. employee, had prompted any specific changes. 
''We're always looking at security procedures, said Kathy Pherson, the spokesman. 
''It's not going to be one event that causes us to look at things.''
In a 30-minute interview at the Prince William-Manassas Regional Adult Detention Center, Mr. Chin quoted from Chinese military strategists and world history to justify his decision to steal classified documents and provide them to the Chinese.
Â 
Motivation Sets Him Apart
One of only two C.I.A employees convicted of espionage while employed by the agency, Mr. Chin's motivation and character set him apart from others charged in the recent spate of spy cases. 
His C.I.A. personnel files show that his supervisors were impressed with his ability as a linguist and interpreter of Chinese political developments.
Mr. Chin said he had no regrets about his decision to talk with F.B.I. agents last Nov. 
22. The agents confronted him with an account of his activities that intelligence sources say was gleaned from a high-level Chinese defector. 
Mr. Chin told the agents that night that he began spying for the Chinese in 1952, when he told a Chinese intelligence agent about his interviews of Chinese prisoners of war in Korea.
But today Mr. Chin said he did not begin stealing documents until 1970, when he joined the broadcast service and was given a clearance to top-secret material. 
That year, he said he came across a classified message from President Nixon to Congress that revealed the Administration's hopes for a reconciliation with China.
He said he was hoping to bolster the pragmatic faction in China, led at the time by Zhou Enlai. 
With the secret documents, Mr. Chin said he hoped to accelerate a warming of relations between the United States and China.
''When I think about what I have accomplished - the improvement of the livelihood of one billion Chinese people - my imprisonment for life is a very small price to pay,'' he said. 
''It was worth it. 
I have nothing to regret.''
Mr. Chin, a tall, thin man, read from a single handwritten sheet of paper on which 20 points for the interview were set out in Chinese characters. 
He called himself a ''patriotic American'' and acknowledged that he had no right to make on his own momentous decisions about American foreign policy.
Still, he said, ''The ends justify the means.''

file: CANADA, AWAITING ZHAO, RECALLS WARM FRIENDSHIP.txt
text:
ï»¿
On a quiet street in this tidy, conservative village of 8,000 is a yellow gingerbread parsonage that stands as a symbol of how differently Canada and the United States have dealt with China.
The house in this resort community 100 miles north of Toronto is the birthplace of Dr. Norman Bethune, a Communist who died while serving as a frontline surgeon with the guerrilla forces of Mao Zedong. 
For the last eight years it has been maintained by the Federal Government as a museum.
''There's never been any controversy at all about this place, no problems or protests'' said Helen Winters, one of the Ministry of Parks guides who gives tours of the former parsonage. 
Dr. Bethune, the son of a Presbyterian minister, spent the first three years of his life here in the 1890's.
''I suppose the exhibits emphasize Dr. Bethune's humanitarianism more than his political views,'' said Mrs. Winters, who was awaiting word on whether Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang would visit the parsonage during his weeklong state visit to Canada that begins on Monday.
Article on expected arrival in Canada of Chinese leader Zhao Ziyang focuses on Dr Norman Bethune, Canadian-born Communist who died while serving as frontline surgeon with guerrilla forces of Mao Zedong; for the last eight years Bethune's home located 100 miles north of Toronto has been maintained by Federal Government as a museum (M)18,000 Visitors a Year
As it turned out, it was announced that Prime Minister Zhao and his party would not visit the museum. 
''There simply wasn't enough time,'' said John Hadwin, the Canadian diplomat in charge of the visit.
Mrs. Winters said that of the 18,000 people who visited the museum in each of the last few years about 4 percent were Chinese travelers paying homage to the man whom Mao once glorified in an essay on selflessness that became mandatory reading during the Cultural Revolution.
Dr. Bethune is a greater hero in China than he is in Canada but here, too, schoolchildren learn of his heroism. 
All of this is in keeping with Canadian attitudes toward China that were shaped in part by Canadian missionaries to China, who unlike their United States counterparts generally favored Mao over Chiang Kai-shek.
Then, too, Canada's Prime Minister, Pierre Elliott Trudeau, wandered through China in the civil war years. 
He returned to China in 1960, 10 years before Canada recognized Peking and before he entered politics, and as a result of that visit wrote a book with his traveling companion, Jacques Hebert, entitled ''Two Innocents in Red China.''
Occasionally the book has been cited by right-wing critics as proof that the Prime Minister is or was infatuated with Marxism. 
Others might regard the work as the enthusiastic writings of two young men infused with the thrill of travel and discovery.
Â 
A Special Relationship
The special relationship between Peking and Ottawa, a tie that has been much less contentious than the links between Washington and Peking, will be reaffirmed this Tuesday when Mr. Zhao becomes the first Communist leader ever to address a Canadian Parliament. 
Though some members of the Conservative opposition are known to have bridled privately at the invitation, there has been virtually no public outcry or political controversy about the speech.
Mr. Zhao will also visit the Canadian side of Niagara Falls and travel to Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver.
''Unlike the United States we have always had a one-China policy,'' explained Mr. Hadwin, who heads the Chinese section within Canada's Department of External Affairs. 
''We have considerable trade with Taiwan but it is on a private basis and we have no official representation there; furthermore, we have no arms sales at all to Taiwan,'' he added in explaining the differences in the current Canadian and United States relationships to China.
Starting in 1981 Canada committed 90 million Canadian dollars in aid to China over a five-year period. 
The sum was not intended for capital projects but for management training and technical education programs - about 1,500 Chinese are studying in Canadian universities. 
But for the Chinese delegation arriving here, trade is clearly a greater concern than aid.
Â 
$1.5 Billion in Sales to China
Since 1979 Canada has extended lines of credit to Peking with financing terms averaging around 10 percent. 
The umbrella trade agreement between the two countries runs out next year and it is expected that the Chinese delegation will be seeking greater concessions. 
This year China will be buying more than $1.5 billion worth of Canadian goods, mostly raw materials, while Canada is to purchase only about $200 million of Chinese wares, all of them manufactured products.
Mr. Hadwin pointed with pride to Canada's recognition of the Peking Government in 1970, three years before the United States opened official contact with Peking. 
Many Canadians cherish this decision not only in terms of the relationship with China but as an example of maintaining an independent foreign policy distinct from that of the United States, Canada's closest and sometimes overwhelming ally. 
The United States did not formally recognize Peking until Jan. 
1, 1979. 
The Canadian economy has also benefited: Ottawa was selling surplus wheat to Peking in the 1960's.
Yet coinciding with Mr. Zhao's visit have come suggestions that the Canadian decision to recognize the Chinese Government was delayed for years because of pressures from Washington, notably from President Eisenhower. 
As early as the autumn of 1949, while war between Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists and Mao's Red Army continued, the Canadian diplomatic legation in Nanjing was urging recognition of the People's Republic of China.
The head of that mission was Chester A. Ronning, a former diplomat and teacher who now at the age of 89 has written an article for Peking's China Daily outlining the delays that took place since he first urged Ottawa to recognize the newly formed Government in Peking.
''As weeks went by, I despaired because it was obvious that the fund of friendship in China for the West was being dissipated,'' Mr. Ronning wrote, adding that finally on June 25, 1950, he was instructed to enter into negotiations on recognition.
Â 
Delayed by War in Korea
''It was too late,'' Mr. Ronning recalled. 
''On that day, war broke out in Korea.''
He added that he was ordered to close the embassy and return to Ottawa to head the Far Eastern Department in the Foreign Ministry. 
In 1953, he wrote, he again sought to reestablish ties but the idea met resistance from the Canadian Government of Prime Minister Louis S. St. Laurent. 
Some of Mr. St. Laurent's papers, released here recently by the archives, show his resistence to the idea of recognition despite the urgings of Foreign Ministry officials. 
In 1958, wrote Mr. Ronning, he was advised by Foreign Minister Lester B. Pearson that Canada had decided to recognize Peking and that he would be named as the first Canadian Ambassador to Peking.
''Shortly before the formal announcement was to be made,'' wrote Mr. Ronning, Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Pearson went to Washington to inform President Eisenhower of the decision.
''To their surprise, President Eisenhower, who was embittered by the Chinese intervention in the Korean War, protested,'' wrote the retired diplomat. 
''He said other nations would follow the Canadian example and this might result in the People's Republic being admitted to the United Nations. 
If China was seated, the President warned, the United States would withdraw from the United Nations.''
It was not until Oct. 
13, 1970, that Canada formally recognized China. 
In his article for the Peking newspaper, Mr. Ronning wrote that this event lent support for President Nixon's decision to visit Peking and the eventual United States recognition. 
He wrote that it came about ''21 years and 13 days after my initial recommendation.''

file: CAPITALISM LIFTS CHINA BANK.txt
text:
ï»¿
As recently as eight years ago, the Bank of China here was a stodgy outpost of the Beijing Government that barely mattered on the local banking scene.
Since China's opening to the West in the 1970's, however, the bank's growth has been extraordinary. 
Since 1979, deposits have increased 5.8 times, loans have gone up 8.5 times and revenue has increased twelvefold. 
The Bank of China group has taken to capitalist-style competition so swimmingly, in fact, that it has become the second-biggest bank in the colony.
The bank seems to think this is just the beginning. 
It is building a 70-story headquarters that will be Hong Kong's tallest building, with executive offices that offer a view down on the headquarters of the giant Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, the only bank in Hong Kong that is larger.
''It's extremely competitive, both in terms of service and in terms of interest rates,'' said David K. P. Li, chief executive of the Bank of East Asia, another Hong Kong bank that has been expanding. 
''It's very dynamic.''
For some Hong Kong businessmen, deeply apprehensive about what will happen after the colony reverts to Chinese control in 1997, having the Bank of China as a competitor may be strangely reassuring. 
It provides evidence of the Beijing Government's willingness to tolerate capitalistic practices and of its expanding financial stake in the well-being of Hong Kong. 
In the process, China has been gaining financial experience and raising funds for investment on the mainland.
This growing presence in Hong Kong has not been painless, however. 
The Bank of China group seems to be sacrificing profits to gain market share, and diplomats and other bankers have doubts about the quality of its loan portfolio. 
It is also taking some significant risks as it develops its expensive new headquarters in the face of an extremely uncertain property market, and as it makes very long mortgage loans that lead to a mismatch between short-term deposits and long-term loans. 
There are also signs that the Bank of China group will face increasing competition, in Hong Kong as well as China, from other Government-owned financial institutions.
The Bank of China remains secretive, and it refused to make its two top executives in Hong Kong available for interviews. 
One other senior executive did grant an interview, after three months of prodding, but his information was limited. 
He could not say, for example, when the chief executive in Hong Kong, Huang Diyan, assumed office; how old Mr. Huang is; where he lives, or whether he has a car at his disposal. 
Other information was gathered from interviews with competitors, financial analysts and diplomats and from analysis of the limited financial records the bank provides.
Â 
Group of 12 Banks
The Bank of China, which is based in Beijing, heads a group of 12 other Chinese banks and one finance company operating in Hong Kong and the nearby Portuguese enclave of Macao. 
These sister banks operate exclusively in Hong Kong, although eight of them are technically registered in Beijing. 
They remain under the control of the Bank of China, although they have separate boards of directors and distinct specialties.
This Bank of China group missed the profits made by Hong Kong banks in the late 1970's, when the economy was booming and land prices were soaring. 
So the sister banks tried to catch up after China's dramatic policy shift of 1979. 
They hurried into property lending without waiting to develop their skills in credit analysis. 
It was an inauspicious start. 
The property market collapsed in 1982, along with much of Hong Kong's economy, and there are indications that many members of the banking group lost substantial sums of money.
Court records show that several of the banks had lent heavily to the Carrian Group, a Hong Kong investment firm that failed in 1983. 
Apparently, the individual banks did not know that other members of the group had also lent to Carrian. 
To avoid such credit risks, the Bank of China formed a Hong Kong and Macao regional office, which oversees the sister banks and approves large loans. 
The sisters are also linked by computer, and they clear checks among themselves.
Huang Diyan, the chief executive of the regional office, assumed the leadership in late 1985, and shortly thereafter began to shuffle people into retirement. 
Mr. Huang, who previously headed the Bank of China's international division in Beijing, appears to be highly regarded in the Communist hierarchy. 
He is still in his mid-50's -young for a position of authority in China - and last year was named vice chairman of the overall Bank of China. 
Because Mr. Huang is often traveling, the daily management rests with Zhang Xueyao, a pipe-smoking, English-speaking former diplomat who previously headed the Bank of China operation in New York. 
Mr. Zhang, and to a lesser extent Mr. Huang, are playing a more active role in the banking cocktail circuit than their predecessors. 
Neither man, however, speaks Cantonese, the Chinese dialect spoken in Hong Kong.
This has been no obstacle to growth, however, particularly among working-class and middle-class families, who are attracted by a good branch network and excellent mortgage terms. 
Since 1983, the Bank of China has advertised widely.
Â 
Politics Brings New Business
The Bank of China group has also picked up a great deal of commercial business, but it is not clear how much of this is based on merit. 
Many of the group's business clients are the 3,000 companies from China that have opened offices in Hong Kong in the last half-dozen years. 
And many others appear to be corporations, mostly based in Hong Kong, that think it is good politics to maintain at least one account at the Bank of China.
The bank group's staff has doubled since 1979, to 11,000, but reportedly there have been tensions between the recent university graduates and the less-educated middle managers they work under. 
Although some young managers have been promoted very rapidly, many have quit out of frustration, banking rivals say.
''There is a gap between the abilities of the employees and the demands of the job,'' conceded Chen Wen-jing, a senior executive of the Bank of China's regional office. 
As a result, he said, the bank has set up training programs that have been attended by thousands of employees.
Nevertheless, there are strong indications that bad loans are substantial and that profitability is low. 
The problem in making such assessments, however, is that the group's financial reports are sketchy and (with the exception of the four sister banks registered in Hong Kong) are unaudited by outside accounting firms.
Even by their official earnings statements, the profits of many of the banks in the group have fallen in the last few years, after adjusting for a devalued Chinese currency. 
One fairly typical member of the group, for example, the Bank of Communications, reported a $25.3 million profit in 1983, but just $14.9 million in 1985, the most recent year for which figures are available.
The 1985 profit amounted to just a 6.9 percent return on capital, compared with 17.8 percent at the Bank of East Asia, an independent Hong Kong bank.
Some rival bankers complain privately that the cut-rate mortgages and long repayment periods offered by the Bank of China have aggravated an already very competitive banking environment.
''Foreign banks can't match them,'' complained the head of one foreign bank operating in Hong Kong. 
In the last few years, several local banks have failed, and several foreign banks - including the Bank of America and Barclays Bank of Britain - have cut back their presence. 
One reason for these moves may have been the declining profitability of retail banking because of the Bank of China's policies, bankers say.
''They are taking business away,'' said Teresa Ma, an analyst in Hong Kong for Jardine Fleming Securities, ''not from the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, but from the medium-sized Chinese banks.''
Although the Bank of China is often cast as a warrior in a titanic battle with the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, most bankers and analysts see it differently. 
In 1985, the last year for which figures were reported, the Hongkong and Shanghai bank gained market share, analysts said. 
And the two giants tend to pursue somewhat different markets: The Bank of China is after the smaller depositor and borrower, and the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation seeks larger customers, both individual and corporate.
''We are two big players in a very competitive banking scene, but there are a great many others,'' said Michael Broadbent, a spokesman for the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation. 
''We're pretty confident that we can retain our market share.''

text:
ï»¿
Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang and former President Jimmy Carter called tonight for a continued strengthening of Chinese-American relations in after-dinner toasts at the Great Hall of the People that were directed more toward the Reagan Administration than toward each other.
The Prime Minister used the welcoming banquet for Mr. Carter to publicly thank President Reagan for his expressions of readiness to continue to develop the relations that the Carter Administration formalized two and a half years ago. 
Specifically, he thanked Mr. Reagan for a personal letter of friendliness delivered by Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. in June.
Mr. Carter said that when he decided to establish full relations with China, he hoped that Chinese-American ties would be seen as ''of such obvious value that the processes would be irreversible and able to withstand the inevitable shocks of changing political times.''
Chinese Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang and former President Jimmy Carter call for continued strengthening of Chinese-American relationsPeking Wary on Arms Sales
Despite efforts at reassurance by the Reagan White House, the Peking leadership remains wary that Mr. Reagan may still decide to authorize the sale of advanced jet fighter planes to Taiwan - a move that Peking has said would be a severe blow to Chinese-American relations. 
Mr. Reagan has shelved the issue so far, but Peking fears that if it accepts offers for military aid from the United States, it might be eventually forced to accept American arms sales to Taiwan.
The former President arrived in Peking last night on a private 10-day visit. 
It was not Mr. Carter's first visit to China, however, as Prime Minister Zhao learned to his surprise at a reception before the banquet. 
When Mr. Zhao asked the standard warm-up question of whether this was a first visit, Mr. Carter replied, '' No.''
Mr. Carter said that as a young submarine officer, he visited Shanghai and Qingdao in 1949. 
In the latter city, he said, he could see the campfires of the surrounding ''Mao forces,'' which had Qingdao surrounded and were preparing for conquest.
Â 
'Outstanding Contributions'
This trip was Mr. Carter's first major sojourn abroad since he left the White House, and the Chinese treated him, as the President who formally recognized China, with great respect. 
Prime Minister Zhao, at the beginning of a meeting this morning that lasted 1 hour 45 minutes, said he had made an ''outstanding contribution'' to Chinese-American relations. 
''We will never forget it,'' he said.
According to Jody Powell, the former White House press secretary who accompanied Mr. Carter, Mr. Zhao revealed that he, like Mr. Carter, was a jogger and suggested that they run together in the future.
This afternoon, the former President, his wife, Rosalynn, and daughter, Amy, toured the Forbidden City. 
Mr. Carter was expected to meet Thursday with China's principal leader, Deng Xiaoping, who is the senior deputy chairman of the Communist Party.
Â 
Strong Ties Emphasized
Like other members of his Administration who have preceded him to China, Mr. Carter emphasized the theme that Chinese-American relations were too valuable and too strategic to trifle with over the unmentioned issue of Taiwan.
''There is no doubt that the cause of world peace has been advanced by this Sino-American friendship,'' Mr. Carter said in his toast tonight. 
He went on: ''It is important that bilateral cooperation in economic, scientific, cultural, and defense areas continues to grow.
''The strategic importance of the Sino-American relationship can only be understood in the context of these three global problems: expansionism, the pressure of natural resources, and the worldwide threat to peace.''
Premier Zhao noted that the relationship between China and the United States, both strategically and economically, ''enjoys the extensive support of U.S. political circles, a support that is bipartisan.''
Before he came to China, Mr. Carter talked by telephone to Secretary Haig and to the former United States Ambassador to China, Leonard F. Woodcock.

text:
