TO THE STORM The Odyssey of a Revolutionary Chinese Woman. 
By Yue Daiyun and Carolyn Wakeman. 
Illustrated. 405 pp. 
Berkeley: University of California Press. 
$17.95.
WITH their belief in the individual and progress, intellectuals in the 19th century never conceived of 20th-century totalitarian terror. 
Yue Daiyun, the narrator of ''To the Storm,'' had 19th-century views.
A third-generation intellectual who has triumphantly survived waves of political purges, she was born in 1931 in Guizhou province in southern China. 
She was an active member of the flourishing student Communist underground, one of 20 at Peking University admitted to the party in 1949. 
In 1952, when she graduated, there was much revolutionary optimism among her peers.
Miss Yue was elected valedictorian of her class, secured a faculty position and was about to make a brilliant marriage to Tang Yijie, a philosophy professor and the son of the president of the university. 
She had also received early acclaim as a poet -though in 1966, out of fear that her work would be seized and used as incriminating evidence, she burned it all, including the prescient poem ''To the Storm,'' from which the title of this unusual and intimate memoir of a revolution is taken. 
For instead of taking an assured place as part of China's intellectual elite, the couple spent most of the next 30 years in a state of terror of political reprisals.
Like so many bourgeois Communists, Miss Yue was more bourgeois than Communist. 
Her cultural referents included ''Gone With the Wind'' and ''Jean Cristophe''; her father translated Somerset Maugham into Chinese, and her brother liked to sing ''My Old Kentucky Home.''
Her notion of being a good Communist was to to shun a fancy wedding while voicing what she took to be Russian Marxism.
Her idealism too was 19th-century; she was filial and wifely, and she wanted her children to carry on the family's academic tradition. 
She failed to perceive the contradictions in her position: as a student member of the Party, she helped to purge individuals she considered rightist, yet she gloried in her in-laws' social status.
Mao Zedong, whose own origins had been bitterly humble, never trusted intellectuals like her. 
He recognized that they ''tend to be subjective and individualistic, impractical in their thinking and irresolute in action.''
More important, their education and skills in a country where more than 80 percent of the population is rural peasantry gave them oligarchic power to rule and to transfer their power to their children.
When the government moved to smash such intellectuals, one obvious place to attack was the universities. 
Miss Yue was a member of a prominent family and a campus personality as a result of her poetry and academic standing. 
I N 1958 her ordeal began. 
She was declared a rightist enemy of the people by the party and abruptly removed from her nursing infant son and sent to the countryside. 
In Zhaitang she tended pigs and took orders from peasants on a collective farm. 
She endured hard labor, near starvation, isolation and constant physical degradation.
Miss Yue was caught in a familiar trap: to preserve some sense of her own identity while living in demoralizing conditions, she needed to cling to her faith in the revolution she had helped create and believe in the correctness of the party. 
But when she returned to her family in Peking in 1960, infested with lice, her small children were suspicious of her, and her friends avoided contact.
Then, after a brief respite, the Cultural Revolution of the mid-1960's resumed and intensified the purge of intellectuals. 
Miss Yue, Mr. Tang and most of their friends were hunted down and abused; many members of the professional class were killed.
During this anarchic period, many academics were forced to work in what amounted to chain gangs; they had to confess their crimes by singing ditties to jeering children. 
The scholars had to wear dunce caps; their children were deprived of an education and sent to the countryside to become peasants. 
Mr. Tang was branded a member of the ''black gang'' - an academic warlord opposed to Mao - and suffered permanent physical injury.
The chaos finally evolved into rival Red Guard groups. 
The intense Red Guard warfare took a little heat off the academics. 
Ironically, during the next round of political developments, the new Clean the Class Ranks Movement had to sort through so many purged teachers it was difficult for them to know whom to elevate to positions of responsibility. 
Clearly, the soldiers and workers in charge of restructuring the universities had no idea who was who.
Reading between the lines of this detailed and unremorseful account, one senses that the desperate need for well-trained intellectuals that began to be recognized at this point was the reason Miss Yue and Mr. Tang survived and rose again. 
If you are a member of a small, highly trained elite and manage not to be killed, then you might always have a chance for political resurrection when a new group needs you. 
T HE last section of the book gives an interesting account of the machinations of those close to Mao. 
In 1970, as the terror of the previous years subsided, Miss Yue was appointed a ''five same-thing teacher'' - she ate, lived, labored, studied and reformed her thoughts with her students.
During this period Mr. Tang managed to regain some political standing. 
The Clean the Class Ranks Movement, begun in 1968 with the support of Mao's wife, Jiang Qing, needed intelligent leaders like him. 
Miss Yue is a loyal wife in her description of the ensuing events, so a reader can't tell from this distance whether Mr. Tang had a real alternative to becoming a leading member of Liang Xiao, the group of scholars that prepared criticism of Lin Biao. 
Miss Yue says he did not. 
After Mao's death, Mr. Tang was found guilty of leftism in a national trial, and the family was again disgraced.
But by 1977 the terror had waned. 
The couple were rehabilitated and their children allowed to continue their education. 
In a postscript, Miss Yue says her daughter, now married, works in computer science and lives in New York City and her son, a physicist, also lives in America. 
She and her husband have top university jobs in China, and she has been able to visit the United States.
It is an amazing sign of the changes in China that she feels free to publish her story. 
At the end, she reaffirms her faith in the revolution and says she has rejoined the Communist Party -one can't tell whether from continued idealism or expediency.
The book is the result of an unusual collaboration. 
Yue Daiyun and Carolyn Wakeman became friends while Miss Wakeman was teaching English in 1981 in Peking, and Miss Wakeman has shaped Miss Yue's extensive conversations and notes into a first-person memoir. 
It is a valuable report on a world from which we have had little news, by an intelligent woman survivor who was at the center of the turbulence.

file: Chasing the Heroin From Plush Hotel to Mean Streets.txt
text:
ï»¿
Group 41 of the Federal Drug Enforcement Administration has been assigned to break up the Chinese Drug rings that transport heroin along ''the China White Trail,'' from the mountains of Thailand to the secret criminal societies of Hong Kong to the quiet Chinese neighborhoods in Queens.
What follows is a firsthand description of undercover drug buys in New York City, of surveillances and arrests.
The account is a kind of diary of impressions and observations of the people and events in the life of Group 41 as it seeks to fulfill its mission in the summer of 1987. 
Plaza Hotel, Wednesday, Time: 5 P.M. Inside the drug world, nothing is quite what it appears. 
Faces are often mirrors. 
Answers are mostly lies. 
Cases have beginnings, but never really end.
So here at the center of an international drug enforcement operation - two rooms under chandeliers and molded ceilings -the drug agents of Group 41 react with a start in their suite at the Plaza Hotel each time the phone rings. 
They know anything can go wrong.
Three agents, ties askew, lean over a coffee table scattered with slices of cold pizza and cans of Diet Coke. 
Another agent, in T-shirt, jeans and sneakers, munches on a tuna sandwich from a delicatessen down the block.
Although renting the Plaza suite may be necessary for an undercover operation involving lavish drug traffickers, the agents are not willing to pay the price of room service. 
''Jeez, $12.50 for a bottle of nuts,'' said one of the agents, looking down the price list of snacks in the room's refrigerator. 
''Can you believe that. 
Who can pay $12.50 for nuts?''
Today's operation involves an undercover American drug agent who has posed as a courier and brought heroin with a street value of $46 million from Bangkok.
If all goes according to plan, representatives of the people who bought the drugs, major Chinese heroin dealers in New York, will pick up the shipment in the lobby of the Plaza.
The agents do not expect to make arrests at the hotel. 
Instead they will follow the drugs, hoping the trail will lead to the major buyers.
At that point the drug agents, in coordination with the Thai and Hong Kong police, will arrest the buyers and sellers on both sides of the Pacific.
''It's a tricky operation,'' said Richard, the 39-year-old special agent who heads the group. 
''But it could pay double dividends.''
For 19 months the 10 agents of Group 41 have performed such operations in an attempt to penetrate the hidden world of Chinese heroin traffickers, As a result of intelligence gathered by the group of white, black and Chinese-American agents, law-enforcement officials recently were able to sketch a striking new picture of the New York heroin industry, a multibillion-dollar business that is now dominated, they say, by Chinese drug traffickers.
In the lives of drug agents each arrest is really just a beginning that leads to new information, new cases and new arrests. 
Each face, each license plate, each address and each criminal relationship is a small piece in the puzzle of the China White Trail. 
The phone rings. 
An agent listens for a moment and hangs up. 
He smiles and says: ''It's show time.''
Plaza Lobby, An Hour Later No one in the milling crowds would notice the middle-aged man in a tan suit, sitting with a green cloth suitcase by his side. 
He is, in fact, an undercover agent playing the part of a corrupt diplomat who has smuggled the heroin on a flight from Bangkok.
Eight feet away, Richard is slouched by a doorway, appearing weary but relaxed. 
His gaze drifts slowly around the lobby but never falls directly on the undercover agent. 
A two-way radio is hidden in his folded newspaper.
Richard is regarded as one of the few experts on international Chinese drug traffickers by United States and European law enforcement officials. 
He is fluent in French, Thai and the Chinese dialects of Mandarin and Cantonese.
Suddenly, a round Chinese man pops through the grand revolving door at the hotel entrance. 
He beams a smile to the undercover courier. 
The courier rises and disappears through the door and down the hotel's front steps.
''We have movement,'' Richard whispers through his radio to a platoon of agents hidden on corners, on benches and in cars. 
Their best protection is the camouflage of New York street life.
Just beyond the hotel awning the Chinese man and the courier lift the suitcase into the trunk of a blue Buick with the New York license plate ZMC 223. 
The car, with two other Asian men in the front seat, pulls out into traffic.
Â 
'Who Is On the Blue Buick?'
In an instant, the undercover agent portraying the diplomat has slipped back into the hotel and Richard is alone on the street, watching the Buick fade away. 
His face freezes. 
Something is definitely not working.
''Who is on the blue Buick, New York plates, Zebra - Michael - Charlie 223?''
Richard says into the radio. 
There is no response. 
''Who is on the blue Buick?''
Richard repeats.
No response. 
Richard mutters a curse.
Somehow, even with seven cars on surveillance and more than a dozen agents in the area, everyone but Richard missed the deal. 
He has one minute, possibly two, to save the New York end of the operation by finding the Buick. 
Richard jumps into a Group 41 car parked nearby. 
#58th Street Chase ''Let's move,'' he says.
The agent behind the wheel, a former surveillance specialist with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, puts his foot on the gas and his car swings down 58th Street after the blue Buick, now the only link that connects the sellers in Hong Kong to the buyers in New York. 
Thanks to several traffic lights, the two agents spot the Buick at the entry ramp to the Queensboro Bridge.
The driver of the Buick, as he careers between lanes and cuts off other cars, may now have noticed a car 50 feet behind, mimicking his every move. 
The agent driving says he has no choice. 
His is the only car trailing the Buick.
Back at the hotel an agent had substituted imitation blocks of heroin for the real drug. 
74th Street In Queens, Time: 1 A.M. A day at the Plaza has turned into dark night in a parked car in Jackson Heights.
The night has brought a pounding summer rainstorm, followed by a cool breeze. 
In the darkness, the smell of fresh-cut lawns and wet sidewalk wafts through the car window as Richard and another agent listen to the sputtering voices of other agents on the radio.
They are parked in a driveway around the corner from the blue Buick. 
The car, with the suitcase still inside its trunk, has sat five hours, ever since the driver parked and entered a brick three-story house on 74th Street in Jackson Heights. 
Four other drug agency cars are parked nearby.
Six times a white Oldsmobile with a bashed fender has circled the block, stopping twice by the side of the Buick. 
The driver, a slender Chinese man with a beeper on his belt, has even stepped out and walked the street. 
Yet he has not opened the trunk.
Â 
Questions on Both Sides
The slender man knows something may be wrong, Richard explains. 
So now he must confront the classic quandary of a drug dealer: Is this really worth the risk?
Am I just being paranoid?
And Richard is facing the classic questions of a drug agent: If he picks it up, should I arrest him here ?
If I follow him, will he lead me to his compatriots?
Such ruminations are interrupted by a distant scream.
''He's gonna kill me!'' yells a voice with a Hispanic accent. 
''He's crazy!''
The two agents jump out of their car and see a small man running down the middle of the street, through the pools of light cast by street lamps.
''He's gonna kill me!'' the man says again, running past.
The agents stare at each other in confusion. 
A gypsy cab is abandoned in mid-road a block away. 
Another man, barrel-chested, with biceps like ham hocks, is running towards them. 
The agents block his path.
Â 
'Please, Let Me Kill Him'
''Please, don't stop me,'' says the pursuer, panting. 
''He tried to sell crack to my 14-year-old sister. 
That's how they sell it, these Colombians, from gypsy cabs. 
Please, let me kill him!''
Richard slaps a palm onto his forehead.
''Oh, just what we need,'' he says. 
''A homicide over crack.''
When there are no police officers around, Federal drug agents must intervene to stop a violent crime. 
Agents on the street sometimes have been drawn out of undercover roles to prevent bank robberies, assaults, even murders. 
But agents are reluctant to jeopardize major drug cases.
Suddenly, a red gypsy cab screeches to a halt at the intersection. 
Seconds later six more cabs from the same company come piling into the area to help their comrade.
A taxi drives onto the sidewalk, a driver jumps out of his cab with a knife in hand. 
An agent leaps on him, thrashing his body up against the car. 
The knife drops inside the car.
By the time the agent looks up again, a row of gypsy cab drivers is out in the street. 
Nine drug agents have come out of hiding and stare back like a line of well-disciplined troops. 
A crowd of onlookers gathers.
''Move on, now,'' Richard yells, flashing his badge. 
''We're taking care of this.''
A precinct patrol car appears and two uniformed officers issue warnings. 
The taxis, the enraged pursuer and the crowd disperse into the night. 
No one is arrested.
The confrontation came and went like the summer thunderclap: sudden, frightening and apparently meaningless. 
Yet it may have had a lasting impact. 
The driver of the white Oldsmobile does not reappear. 
74th Street, Time: 8:30 A.M. The agents of Group 41 stand in the sunlight beside the blue Buick. 
The suitcase is still inside the trunk. 
The agents's eyes are red and some stomachs are raw from too much bad coffee.
The agents hold in their frustration as they question a teen-age Chinese boy who lives in the house on 74th Street where the driver parked the Buick. 
The boy says the driver's name is ''Sammy.''
He entered the house and left through a rear door. 
The boy says he does not know where Sammy is or how to find him. 
The boy's father interrupts. 
''I am so worried about this kid,'' says the father, who was visibly shaken by the arrival of Federal drug agents at his door this morning. 
''I am trying to save money and give him a good home. 
I am going to buy a house in Jersey. 
But he gets involved with gangs.''
Â 
'We'll Try to Do Better'
''It is a very serious business,'' an agent warns.
'' I know, I know,'' says the father. 
''We'll try to do better with him.''
Drug agents in Manhattan have arrested a man they believe was a look-out at the Plaza Hotel. 
The police in Hong Kong are about to arrest four men, one of whom is believed to be associated with 14K, a powerful criminal secret society based in the Crown Colony.
And agents plan to check the home addresses of people who rented the cars seen in yesterday's surveillances. 
The agents will record the names and addresses. 
They will remember the faces.
The operation in New York has ended in disappointment. 
Yet a few new pieces have been fit into the puzzle. 
D.E.A. Office, Tuesday, Time: 10 A.M. ''Sometimes I wish I hadn't chosen this profession,'' Richard says. 
''It is so all consuming, it is impossible to get away. 
It is impossible to have another life.''
A soft-spoken man with a near-academic manner, Richard's eyes dart around an office adorned with the souveneirs of a 16-year career: a plaque from the police in Malaysia and Hong Kong, a bulletproof vest, a poster of the Galerie Roussard in Paris and a poster that says, ''A cleaner Chinatown is up to you.''
Officials say it is from Richard's work in the last year and a half that they learned the size and importance of the China White Trail in the New York region.
Raised in an Italian-American family in Pittsburgh, Richard had no interest in the Chinese until he joined the agency's New York office in 1971 and fell into a group that happened to be handling numerous Southeast Asian heroin cases. 
Soon Richard developed a passion for things Asian, a passion his parents in Pittsburgh would never really understand.
Â 
Advised French Police
In the years that followed he worked in Thailand, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Paris. 
While serving as a special adviser to the French police, he met and married a woman from Korea.
In January 1986, Richard was brought back to New York to form a new group of agents targeting solely Chinese traffickers. 
It was an imposing task, for practically no one in New York had informants inside Chinese drug organizations and no one in law enforcement knew the scope of their activities.
In the first months, the agents of Group 41 walked the streets of Chinatown and cultivated the friendship of agents overseas, hoping that eventually they would get a tip on a heroin shipment coming in.
On Sept. 
10, Group 41 got its first major break. 
They seized 33 pounds of heroin hidden inside Thai furniture and made one arrest. 
A string of other arrests and seizures followed. 
Some defendants agreed to cooperate, introducing the agents to their contacts, suppliers and other organizations.
Â 
'No Letup'
What emerged was a subculture of drug traffickers in New York, with links that extended throughout the overseas Chinese communities of Asia, Europe and South America. 
In some cases the trafficking groups were loose confederations of businessmen and smugglers who associated for a single deal. 
In other cases, they involved complex organizations of dozens of people in Asia, Europe, South America and the United States.
''There's really been no letup since,'' Richard said. 
Shortly after their arrival in New York, Richard's wife began to notice that he was never home. 
Almost everyday she would signal him on his beeper. 
He would call back and say he had no idea what time or even what day he would return.
One evening at their house, she showed him a newspaper advertisement for Jacoby & Meyers, the law firm, and pointed to the firm's telephone number. 
She said with a smile that someday his beeper will tell him to call that number back. 
It will be her new lawyer asking for a divorce.
Â 
Strained Family Relations
Now, whenever Richard's beeper goes off, another agent is likely to crack, ''Uh oh. 
Jacoby & Meyers.''
The joke has a sharp edge to it. 
Many drug agents experience one or more divorces in their careers. 
Few family members can tolerate the tortuous schedules year after year, the exhaustion, the irritation and worst of all, the agents's inability to explain what they are doing with their days and nights.
Despite the hours, the isolation and the anonymity, however, many agents seem almost obsessed with their profession.
Most admit that it is not a crusader's zeal that keeps them on the job - some agents believe they are helping to stop the spread of drugs, others do not. 
Rather, veteran agents say they are people who cannot part with the unspeakable thrill of a chase and the mystery of entering hidden worlds. 
More important, perhaps, they realize that only agents and their informers truly understand what life is like inside a case. 
Once they have left this quiet fraternity, they know, in some strange way, they will always be alone.
''A lot of the time it seems we are tilting at windmills,'' Richard said. 
''I don't know. 
But maybe, when you retire somebody will say 'He was a good manager. 
He made some good cases.'
That is all I ask for.''
Tuesday, Time: 11 A.M. Two agents are loading the last thick wads of $100 bills into the green suitcase that carried the courier's heroin a week ago. 
Every bill has been counted and every serial number has been recorded. 
The suitcase is filled with $850,000.
A Chinese-American agent of Group 41, playing the undercover role, will show the money to two heroin sellers as they sit inside a stretch limousine on the Upper West Side.
He is wearing a gold Rolex watch and a crisp khaki suit. 
His hair is slicked back to suggest he was a tough street youth in Chinatown not long ago. 
Another agent will play the part of his chauffeur, a muscular man clad in a cream-colored jacket, chomping a thick cigar.
This case, one of dozens of cases the group is working on these days, began recently when the undercover agent was introduced to a Chinese couple from Queens who said they could provide large shipments of China White on a regular basis. 
Richard says he believes the couple works for a group of smugglers active in the Bangkok-New York trade.
Â 
An $86,000 Deal
On June 30, the Chinese-American agent met the couple on the corner of Third Avenue and 63d Street. 
The couple and two other men gave the agent a brown paper bag containing a pound and a half of China White. 
Mr. Wong paid them $86,000 in cash.
Group 41 followed the four suspects to Chinatown where, they say, the money was handed off to a fifth person, a short, young Chinese man with a thick mustache. 
They followed the man with the thick mustache to a string of massage and gambling parlors.
The first deal was designed to gain the couple's trust and identify their associates. 
Today the group plans to make arrests. 
The West Side, Tuesday, Time: 5 P.M. Following the flash of the cash as the limousine sat parked on West 66th Street, Group 41 has trailed the couple through Manhattan for hours. 
Now the agents and their quarry have converged on this block across the street from Lincoln Center waiting for the heroin to arrive.
The undercover agent stands with the couple in front of a Coward shoe store. 
A white Camaro pulls up to the curb. 
The undercover agent gives a signal.
''Bingo,'' says another agent who has spent the day as the driver of a yellow taxi.
Â 
Guns at Lunchtime
Suddenly, diners lunching at outdoor tables of the Saloon restaurant see a cab driver jump from his car armed with a revolver. 
Two young, well-dressed women jump from a sports car, also carrying guns. 
Even some diners jump up from their tables, and they, too, are brandishing pistols.
In a moment, a semicircle of agents have surrounded the couple and placed them under arrest.
The couple will later be identfied as 28-year-old Dong Hsiang Chen and Yin Yuen Wong, 29, both of 4045 Ithaca Street in Jackson Heights, Queens, and charged with conspiracy and the sale of narcotics.
Other agents grab the driver of the white Camaro, Lee Hong of 3 Doyers Street in Chinatown. 
From inside his car, they say, they have recovered $7.5 million worth of heroin and a .38-caliber revolver.
''Who are you guys?'' yells a uniformed police officer with his hand on his pistol. 
He confronts what looks like a crowd of Manhattanites suddenly bristling with guns.
Often drug arrests take place before the officers of the local precinct can be warned. 
At such times, the agents can only hope the patrolman on the beat has cool nerves.
''D.E.A.,'' says Richard, flashing his identification.
''Oh,'' says the officer, putting his hand to his chest. 
''That's a relief.''
These arrests again are just a few more pieces falling into place. 
Since last September, Group 41 has seized 155 pounds of heroin and arrested 39 more people - an impressive record by the standards of law enforcement. 
And yet as long as Group 41 is among the few law- enforcement groups in the nation pursuing the mysteries of Chinese organized crime, officials acknowledge that most of the players and their activities will probably never be apprehended or known.
Today's work will continue into the night and into tomorrow morning. 
The prisoners must be read their rights and asked other names, faces and deals. 
The agents must search three houses with warrants. 
And they must pay a visit to a gambling parlor where someone last saw the man with the thick mustache.
And Richard must remember to call his wife. 
No, he will tell her, he cannot say when he will be home.

file: CHINA AGAIN CENSORS REAGAN TV TALK.txt
text:
ï»¿
For the second time in two days, China has deleted portions of remarks made by President Reagan on prime time Chinese television.
A significant part was deleted from an interview that Mr. Reagan gave Saturday with the Chinese television network. 
In it, he asserted that ''Americans are people of peace'' who did not threaten China or any other nation and had ''no troops massed on your border.''
This latter part alluded to the heavy concentration of Soviet troops and missiles on China's northern frontiers.
China, for second time in two days, has deleted portions of remarks made by Pres Reagan on prime time Chinese TV; significant part is deleted from interview in which Reagan said that Americans are people of peace who do not threaten China or any other nation and have 'no troops massed on your border;' latter part alludes to heavy concentration of Soviet troops and missiles on China's northern frontiers; photo (M)
On Friday, Chinese television omitted passages of a speech that Mr. Reagan gave to a select Chinese audience in the Great Hall of the People that were even more explicitly critical of the Soviet Union.
Â 
Allusion to Airliner's Downing
In that speech, Mr. Reagan also said that ''American troops are not massed on China's borders'' and occupied no lands. 
''Nor do we commit wanton acts such as shooting 269 innocent people out of the sky for the so-called cause of sacred airspace,'' Mr. Reagan said, alluding to the shooting down of a South Korean airliner by a Soviet jet fighter last September. 
Both cases of deletion reflected Chinese sensitivity over criticism that Mr. Reagan has leveled against the Soviet Union during his visit here. 
Peking has entered into talks with Moscow aimed at normalizing relations, though Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang told Mr. Reagan that there had been no substantive progress. 
It has also invited a Soviet First Deputy Prime Minister, Ivan V. Arkhipov, to visit China in mid-May.
While Chinese-Soviet relations are still cool, China evidently does not want to appear to be returning to the doctrine of strategic cooperation with the United States, which it shelved two and a half years ago in favor of greater identification with the third world.
On Saturday, the Presidential party brushed off the significance of the earlier deletion of Mr. Reagan's remarks.
Â 
President Is Queried
When the President stopped before television cameras during his sightseeing at the Great Wall Saturday afternoon, one television reporter asked him, ''What did you think about your speech being censored?''
Mr. Reagan said he was not upset. 
''You fellas do it all the time,'' he said.
''We don't cut out all the best parts,'' another television reporter said. 
''Yes, you do,'' Mr. Reagan replied,
The Chinese Foreign Ministry's information director, Qi Huaiyuan, when asked about the editing of the videotape of Mr. Reagan's speech Friday, indicated that his Government did not want to let the leader of one country publicly attack another country while in China.
''I have no more comment than that it is inappropriate for the Chinese media to publicize the comments by President Reagan on a third country,'' Mr. Qi told reporters at a news briefing. 
Larry Speakes, the White House spokesman, gave reporters a statement Saturday expressing ''regret'' that the statements in Mr. Reagan's Friday speech that ''would have given the Chinese people a better understanding of our country and its people'' had been cut out of the later rebroadcast.
Â 
U.S. Said to Have Been Told
But Mr. Qi said he had informed the White House office of the deletions before Friday's broadcast. 
''I said some paragraphs that concern a third country, and so forth, will be left out,' the official said. 
Mr. Speakes had said earlier that the speech would be transmitted in its entirety.
In the parts of the interview deleted Saturday, Mr. Reagan also said that ''economic growth and human progress make their greatest strides when people are secure and free to think, speak, worship, choose their own way and reach for the stars.'
In a subsequent passage that was omitted, he asked the Chinese rhetorically to ''resolve that communication, not confrontation, and commerce, not conflict, will always govern Chinese- American relations.'
However, Chinese authorities allowed Mr. Reagan's defense of continuing United States support for Taiwan. 
He said that ''we don't believe it would be right to cast aside longtime old friends in order to make new friends,'' but added that ''we will do anything we can to encourage the peaceful solution of this problem by the peoples of China'' on both sides of the Formosa Strait.
Â 
'Faith and Freedom' Stressed
In the passages that the Chinese removed Friday, Mr. Reagan went even further, asserting that Americans ''have drawn tremendous power from two great forces - faith and freedom.''
The President went on to speak of the importance of belief in God and American-style democracy.
A senior Chinese journalist played down the omission of these latter sections, contending that they might have been left intact if Mr. Reagan had not so conspicuously attacked the Soviet Union, even though he did not mention it by name.
However, some authorities here noted that Mr. Reagan's comments were in conflict with the Communist Government's four ''cardinal principles.''
These are adherence to the leadership of the Communist Party, the Socialist road, the people's democratic dictatorship and the official ideology of Marxism, Leninism and Mao Zedong thought.
Although China has in recent years tolerated a supervised resurgence of religious belief, the Government formally professes atheism and does not allow public proselytizing of belief in God.
Chinese officials, while defending the censorship, complained today that too much attention was being given it by Western reporters. 
Mr Qi asserted that his Government was not being ''petty'' or ''unfair'' by refusing to air all of Mr. Reagan's convictions.
Â 
U.S. Coverage of Zhao Cited
''I think we have given a lot of coverage to the visit and I think during Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang's visit to the United States, there wasn't so much coverage on Prime Minister Zhao's speech,'' the spokesman said in response to questions.
When an American reporter reminded him that Mr. Zhao's speech in the United States last January had been transmitted in full by the Cable News Network, Mr. Qi replied that China had only one television network while the United States had five.
By China's standards, heavy coverage has been given to Mr. Reagan's visit this week.

file: CHINA AND SOVIET PLEASED BY MOOD OF PEKING TALKS.txt
text:

As the most important Soviet visitor in 15 years left for home today, officials on both sides asserted that an important watershed had been passed in the long struggle to re-establish good relations between the two Communist powers. 
Attention among Soviet and Chinese officials here focused less on the economic and technical agreements reached during the nine-day visit of First Deputy Prime Minister Ivan V. Arkhipov than on the warm atmosphere that prevailed throughout his stay.
One Soviet official recalled the situation after President Nixon visited here in 1972, a trip that he said was important more for the fact that it occurred, and for its friendly atmosphere, than for any notable political breakthroughs.
Â 
'Atmosphere Has Been Changed'
''Now,'' the official said, ''our side has come, and although we haven't overcome the big problems, the atmosphere has been changed.''
Chinese Foreign Ministry officials who discussed the trip privately made a similar assessment. 
Peking stuck to its demands that disagreements over Afghanistan and Cambodia and tensions along the Chinese-Soviet border be tackled before normal political ties are resumed, but the officials said there was ''no doubt'' that Mr. Arkhipov's visit had changed matters considerably for the better.
(In Washington, a Reagan Administration official said that the talks represented ''a significant new development'' in relations between the two nations, but added that it was ''not unexpected.'')
For the moment, there is no talk in Peking of a reconciliation as far-reaching as that achieved between China and the United States, and realists on both sides say that factors such as geographical proximity, rivalry within the Communist world and differing domestic policies probably rule out anything like that between Peking and Moscow for many years.
Nonetheless, the new beginning that was referred to frequently by Mr. Ark hipov and the Chinese Politburo members who met him here has many aspects, by no means all of them limited to the basic issues of a five-year trade pact and Soviet technological assistance to outdated Chinese industry that dominated the talks. 
Just as much else in Peking has changed drastically over the last decade, so has the prevailing attitude toward the Russians.
For several years after the border clashes of 1969, antipathy toward the Soviet Union was encouraged. 
The Soviet aid program that had helped China onto its feet after 1949 was derided, with special visits provided for Westerners to Yellow River dam projects and other undertakings that the Russians were said to have botched. 
Children's books depicted Soviet border troops as menacing, and nearly everything the Soviet ''social imperialists'' did at home and abroad was held in contempt. 
Much of this receded with the other excesses of the Cultural Revolution, the leftist-inspired turmoil that gripped China for a decade beginning in 1966. 
But it is only in relatively recent times, since the resumption of six-monthly talks at the Foreign Ministry level in 1982, that a much more tolerant attitude toward the Russians has emerged. 
Though only limited momentum has gathered so far, the manifestations are striking.
Â 
Intererst in Russia Voiced
No longer can Westerners hope to gain points here by adopting a supercilious attitude toward the Soviet Union. 
Inquiries about life in Russia put to Americans who have lived there are sympathetically phrased. 
And not only among the high officials who met Mr. Arkhipov is there a new appreciation of the money and effort expended by the Kremlin on its aid program here during the 1950's.
To a far greater degree than has been the case for 20 years, ordinary Chinese can now learn something about Russians and their culture. 
On the anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution last month Chinese television showed its first contemporary Soviet film in two decades, and the one it picked, ''Moscow Doesn't Believe in Tears,'' a moving depiction of a young woman of rural background struggling to make her way in the capital, won widespread popular acclaim.
About 30 other exchanges have taken place this year. 
China has been host to an exhibition of 20th century Soviet painting, a Soviet writers' group has visited for lectures and discussions and a Russian tenor, Yuri Marusin, won a standing ovation for a concert in which he sang Russian folk songs and selections from Tchaikovsky and Verdi. 
A photo exhibition on Soviet life that was held at the National Gallery during the Nov. 
7 anniversary drew large crowds.
At the Waiwen Bookshop on Wang Fu Jing Street, Peking's principal source of foreign books, an effort has been made to upgrade the selection of Soviet publications. 
Several new Chinese- Russian dictionaries have been printed, there are coffee-table books about the beauties of the Soviet Union and Soviet children's albums offering a glossy view of Russian life are on sale.
However, as in the broader relations between the two countries, reservations remain. 
While the English-language selection at the bookstore includes P. G. Wodehouse, Anthony Burgess and Henry James, among others, the Russian fiction available is mostly 19th or early 20th century classics by Pushkin, Lermontov and Chekhov. 
The only recognized writers of the Soviet period are early ones like Vladimir Mayakovsky, and there is nothing by any Soviet leader, even Stalin.
The choice of Mr. Arkhipov to be the first senior Soviet official to come here since Prime Minister Aleksei N. Kosygin's brief airport stop in 1969 was well taken, since he had headed the Soviet aid program here and evidently made strong friendships with several of the men now in power. 
Insistent gratitude was shown by Politburo members like Chen Yun, who spoke of having got along ''swimmingly'' with the Soviet official in the 1950's.
Mr. Arkhipov responded with some ingratiating remarks of his own about ''the great changes'' now taking place in China under the regime of Deng Xiaoping, which have had a chilly reception from the official Soviet press.
The official New China News Agency even quoted Mr. Arkhipov as having said that the changes constituted ''a magnificent plan for the future.''

An unannounced work committee has begun mapping details of the campaign for discussion and endorsement shortly by a plenary session of the party's Central Committee, according to Chinese and foreign diplomatic sources.
The campaign, known as a ''rectification of party style,'' could result in the expulsion of a million or more party members who are found to be corrupt, incompetent or too radical for the leadership headed by Mr. Deng.

The correct new party line follows the political pragmatism set out by Mr. Deng in speeches and writings that were published here to great fanfare as his ''Selected Works'' last July. 
A 4,000- character commentary on the front page of People's Daily today pointedly called Mr. Deng's works ''an important ideological preparation for the overall rectification campaign'' that will get under way throughout China this autumn and winter.

Mr. Deng introduced practical measures to spur productivity in agriculture and industry and opened the door to commerce with the West while rejecting Western values and ''bourgeois'' freedoms. 
Many of his innovations have been at variance with the dogma of Mao Zedong.
Â 
Maoists Are a Major Target
A primary target of the new rectification drive will be Maoists who have been obstructing change. 
Many got their government and party sinecures during the Cultural Revolution. 
But the party leadership has also said it wants to clear out those guilty of corruption and other abuses of authority who have damaged the party's prestige among ordinary Chinese.
The campaign was originally announced by the party's General Secretary, Hu Yaobang, at the 12th party congress in September 1982. 
Mr. Hu admitted then that ''it is true that impurities in ideology, style and organization still exist within the party and no fundamental turn for the better has as yet been made in our party style.''
To correct the situation, Mr. Hu said, ''the Central Committee has decided on an overall rectification of party style and consolidation of party organizations, which will proceed by stages and by groups over a period of three years beginning from the latter half of 1983.''
Since then, pilot projects to swing the party rank and file into line have been instituted throughout the nation. 
People's Daily complained last June that ''some problems still remain unsolved.''
It said some party committees were afraid to confront ''the malpractices of some leading cadres.''
Â 
Resistance in the Army
The objections to a rectification drive are believed strongest in the army, but there are also reports of Maoist resistance to Mr. Deng's policies in provinces like Hunan and Guangxi in southern China.
Mr. Deng has already shuffled some key jobs in the provinces and military regions. 
Today's commentary in People's Daily hinted that the new drive would scrutinize the loyalties of party members in the middle echelons.
''All party members, those holding positions at and above county level in particular, must acquire a clear understanding of the stand, point of view and methods Comrade Deng Xiaoping used in dealing with all kinds of problems,'' it said.
The official press has insisted that the campaign will not turn into the kind of witchhunt that the Maoists mounted during the Cultural Revolution. 
''With regard to criticism launched by comrades, we must adopt a comradely approach, stress reasoning and seek truth from facts,'' said Lu Dingyi, a Central Committee member, in a speech People's Daily published in late August. 
''We must oppose the trumping up of charges and exaggeration.

Â 
'Handful Will Be Expelled'
Mr. Hu said at the party congress 13 months ago that following political study and self-criticism, all party members would have to register anew.

The leadership has avoided mentioning any percentage, possibly for fear of suggesting a quota of miscreants that zealous subordinates would try to fill.

This was two more than his poorest showing yesterday, but most Council members now regard his candidacy as all but hopeless.
UN Security Council fails to choose new Secretary General as China continues to veto Kurt Waldheim's candidacy for third five-year term
China's intentions remain the central question. 
It vetoed Mr. Waldheim twice in 1971 to demonstrate its insistence that the United Nations should be run by someone from Asia, Africa or Latin America. 
Later China relented, abstaining on the third round.
This time there have been six inconclusive rounds of voting thus far. 
Whoever is nominated by the Security Council must still be approved by the 156-nation General Assembly, where election is by a simple majority.
Council members believe that China is waiting for the Latin Americans to put forward a candidate in the expectation that the Soviet Union will then cast a veto and share with the United States the onus of thwarting third-world aspirations.
The Waldheim backers hope that China will then lift its veto, satisfied that it has done its best for a third world whose Council members have been unable to vote together as a solid bloc.
The Soviet Union would not like saying ''no'' to a third-world figure.

There is no assurance that the Soviet Union would veto every Latin American. 
Ten years ago, it blocked Carlos Ortiz de Rozas of Argentina. 
But since then, Argentina has shipped much needed wheat to the Soviet Union. 
Mr. Ortiz de Rozas is again a potential candidate.
The first Latin candidate to appear openly may be Javier Perez de Cuellar of Peru, until recently a United Nations Under Secretary General.

Those present at today's voting behind closed doors said 11 nations had voted for Mr. Waldheim on each round and four against, including the critical Chinese ballot.

file: CHINA CRACKS DOWN ON _DECADENT_ CAPITALIST VALUES.txt
text:

With a major Communist Party congress scheduled for autumn, the Chinese leadership has been swinging the country back toward its old orthodoxy, with new constraints on foreign contacts and study abroad and a revival of ideological attacks on Western values.
The sour mood developing over the last few months evokes the xenophobia that existed in China before Peking opened its doors to Western influences in the mid-1970's. 
Some diplomats are finding unofficial access to the Chinese people increasingly difficult. 
One European journalist with several tours in China calls the climate the tightest he has seen since before the death of Mao Zedong in 1976.
PEKING, July 30 - With a major Communist Party congress scheduled for autumn, the Chinese leadership has been swinging the country back toward its old orthodoxy, with new constraints on foreign contacts and study abroad and a revival of ideological attacks on Western values.
This all seems to be linked to the 12th Party Congress, at which Deng Xiaoping, China's foremost leader, is expected to try to purge the policy-making bodies of Maoists and supporters of Hua Guofeng, whom he ousted as party chairman last summer. 
Chinese sources expect the congress to begin sometime in September.
Â 
A Protective Maneuver?
Consequently, some Western diplomats speculate that Mr. Deng is using the crackdown to protect his agricultural and economic programs from criticism, since ideological hard-liners fear that his open-door policy of trade with the West is letting in bourgeois ideas that will corrupt the Chinese people.
''The influence of decadent capitalist ideology on certain people, the ideological poisoning it causes and the pollution it produces in the social mood are now much greater and more serious than in any previous period,'' the Weekly Digest said last month.
Such statements in the official press, which inveighs against what the ideological journal Red Flag called ''the corrosive influence of capitalist ideas,'' suggests that positions are already being staked out before the congress.
One Western European diplomat also views such ideological attacks as a ramification of an anticorruption campaign that was begun earlier this year and now appears to have bogged down.
Â 
Foreigners as Scapegoat
The campaign against economic crime never reached the higher echelons of the party and the Government, despite public expectations, and the diplomat said he believed foreigners were now being made a scapegoat because of internal resistance.
''The argument is that corruption isn't basically Chinese and wouldn't exist but for foreign influence,'' the diplomat said. 
''They don't admit that it takes two to make a bribe.''
The most visible sign of the times here has been what another Western diplomat called ''a fairly extensive clampdown'' on unauthorized contacts between Chinese and foreigners. 
Circulars have gone out warning Chinese not to mix socially with foreigners. 
Some Chinese who have Western friends have been summoned for police interrogation, according to the friends.
Foreigners teaching English at some institutes in Peking have been shifted out of communal dormitories into segregated quarters where their students need written permission to visit them.
Â 
Warnings to Schoolchildren
The warnings against foreigners have extended to schoolchildren. 
Ideological guidelines recently promulgated for primary schools by the Ministry of Education instruct third-graders to be wary of foreigners and not to follow them about or accept presents readily.
The case of Lisa Wichser, an American teacher detained and expelled early last month for allegedly stealing state secrets, has been introduced in political study sessions, according to a Chinese student, with an implication that all foreign teachers are possible spies.
Miss Wichser's ''state secrets'' were unpublished economic and agricultural statistics that she had collected for a doctoral thesis. 
Her friend, Yi Xigong, is now in jail here.
Since April 1, the children of high-level Government and party officials have been effectively barred from going abroad to study. 
The unpublished directive, which is understood to apply generally to the children of officials with the rank of deputy minister and above, has reportedly engendered resentment because Mr. Deng and other leaders sent their children abroad before it went into effect. 
Mr. Deng's son is studying at the University of Rochester.
Other Chinese graduates wishing to study abroad must now work for a year before applying, when they will presumably be more ideologically mature. 
In another indication of concern about Western influence, some returning students are being sent through ''reorientation'' courses lasting up to eight weeks, according to a Peking source.
Â 
No Effect on Delegations
The latest prohibitions on foreign travel do not seem to affect official delegations visiting the West. 
A United States Embassy spokesman said the number of Chinese going to the United States on official business rose 54 percent in the first six months of this year over the same period last year.
But delegations are evidently being told to stick together to avoid bourgeois contamination. 
The Workers Daily earlier this month severely criticized several members of a Chinese delegation who split off to enjoy the seamier sights of Hong Kong.
A renewed obsession about state secrets, which in China means whatever the Government chooses not to publish, was evident in an interview with Deng Yingchao, the widow of Prime Minister Zhou Enlai, which Peking newspapers published on July 1, the 61st anniversary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Miss Deng was quoted as saying that she and her husband never discussed classified information with each other and that Mr. Zhou never let relatives and friends into his private office. 
One Western diplomat inferred from this that some other officials probably do, to show off their status.
Â 
'The Sacred Duty'
''Keeping party and state secrets is the sacred duty of every Communist Party member, especially of middle-level and senior officials,'' Miss Deng was quoted as saying.
There has also been a campaign against so-called Western ''pornography,'' which includes rock music tapes as well as racier videotapes and books. 
According to news reports, some young people in Peking and Shanghai were punished for dancing at ''obscene'' private disco parties earlier this year. 
And Canton residents last month were ordered to pull down thousands of ''fishtail'' antennas, which let them watch Hong Kong television.
Such bans reflect a fear within the Chinese leadership that exposure to the West will undercut the appeal of the Communist Party, which already suffers from credibility problems with youth.
The Weekly Digest, a sister publication of The People's Daily, warned in an article last month that ''external reactionary forces'' were waging a campaign of ''peaceful evolution'' to blur the distinctions between capitalism and Marxism and that Chinese students abroad were a main target.
The article went on to label as ''sinister'' such Western ploys as academic and scientific exchanges, foreign radio broadcasts and publications aimed at ''shaking the faith of our younger generation in the party's leadership and the socialist system.''
It remains unclear how long the crackdown will prevail. 
''I don't think it will last beyond the party congress,'' a Western diplomat said. 
But another took the crackdown as proof that the headier days of post-Mao liberalization were over.
The crackdown seems bound to discourage news leaks at the congress, which should be preceded by a closed meeting of the Central Committee. 
Earlier this year, a Chinese editor, Li Guanyi, was sent to prison for five years for divulging details of last summer's session to a foreign journalist.

file: CHINA EXPELS TIMES REPORTER FOR ENTERING RESTRICTED AREA.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Peking bureau chief of The New York Times was expelled from China today after being detained for nearly six days on suspicion of espionage.
The correspondent, John F. Burns, was ousted from the country for ''activities incompatible with his status as a journalist.''
The official New China News Agency said he had been involved in ''deliberately breaking into Chinese areas closed to aliens, thereby violating the law governing aliens' entry into and exit from the People's Republic of China.''
In a statement issued in New York last night, Arthur Ochs Sulzberger, publisher of The Times, said, ''We are grateful for the prompt resolution of the problem facing John Burns, though we regret his expulsion from China after so many years of distinguished reporting for The New York Times.''
Accused of 'Act of Spying'
The Chinese authorities told A. M. Rosenthal, executive editor of The Times, that they considered Mr. Burns guilty of an ''act of spying and intelligence gathering which will not be tolerated by a sovereign state.''
Mr. Rosenthal, who arrived in Peking on Saturday with the newspaper's foreign editor, Warren Hoge, said of Mr. Burns: ''I believe in his innocence of any espionage and intelligence gathering.''
The Times editors were told by the Chinese authorities today that Mr. Burns and an American traveling companion had broken into ''a military restricted zone of our country'' and had taken ''numerous photographs of classified objects.''
Mr. Burns arrived in Hong Kong after being put aboard a flight of the Chinese state airline that left Peking at 9:30 A.M. (8:30 P.M. yesterday, New York time). 
His wife, Jane Scott-Long, and their two children, Jamie, 5, and Emily, 2, were allowed to remain in Peking for the time being.
Mr. Burns said by telephone from Hong Kong that he had been taken from his cell to another area of the prison where a brief deportation order was read to him in Chinese and English. 
He said the statement asserted that he had ''engaged in espionage'' and had ''endangered the security of the People's Republic of China.''
Mr. Burns said the trip out of which the charges grew had been ''a legitimate journalistic venture.''
Â 
First Accusations
Until today, Mr. Burns, who spent most of his incarceration incommunicado in a small cell, had not been accused of any offense. 
On Monday he was allowed to see his family, British and American Embassy officials and his editors.
Mr. Rosenthal voiced regret over Mr. Burns's expulsion, adding, ''We'll soon be asking the Foreign Ministry to accredit another New York Times correspondent to China.''
He said he had been assured by the authorities that the newspaper would be allowed to replace Mr. Burns.
The last Western journalist ordered out of China was Tiziano Terzani, an Italian reporter for the West German magazine Der Spiegel who was ordered to leave in 1984 for purportedly trying to smuggle artifacts out of the country, a charge that he denied.
Â 
Tour of Central China
The case against Mr. Burns arose from a motorcycle tour of central China that began late last month. 
He was accompanied by Edward McNally, a lawyer on leave from the United States Justice Department to teach constitutional law at Peking University, and Zhang Daxing, who had recently returned to China after studying in the United States.
During their trip, the three were stopped by the police near the border of Shaanxi and Sichuan provinces and told they were in a restricted area. 
They were held for two days but were allowed to return to Peking after writing long ''self-criticisms.''
Mr. Burns, who said he had thought the matter had been resolved, was taken into custody for a second time on Thursday at the Peking airport as he and his family prepared to leave China on vacation. 
He was questioned at the airport for 15 hours, his home was searched and he was taken to a detention center early Friday morning.
Photographs taken on the trip were confiscated, and Chinese officials told the Times editors this morning that the materials would not be returned.
Mr. McNally had left China to attend to business in Hong Kong before Mr. Burns was detained. 
Mr. Zhang was reported to have been questioned for a day and ordered to write a second self-criticism. 
His whereabouts were not known.
Mr. Burns, who is 41 years old, was born in Britain and travels on a British passport. 
He became The Times's Peking bureau chief in 1984.
He reported from China for The Globe and Mail of Toronto from 1971 to 1975, when he joined The Times. 
He has also served as The Times's bureau chief in Johannesburg and Moscow.
Mr. Rosenthal and Mr. Hoge were informed of the correspondent's expulsion by an official named Xu Hui, who identified himself as ''the responsible official'' of the State Security Bureau. 
Mr. Xu informed them that Mr. Burns had been put on a plane to Hong Kong.
Referring to ''the Burns-McNally case,'' Mr. Xu said his Government considered the matter ''a grave one.''
He said there had been ''no action taken yet'' regarding Mr. McNally.
Â 
Ministry Summons Envoys
The meeting between the Chinese official and the Times editors came after earlier summonses from the Chinese Foreign Ministry to the British Ambassador, Sir Richard Evans, and the United States Ambassador, Winston Lord, as well as Mr. Rosenthal and Mr. Hoge. Three vice ministers met separately with the envoys and the Times editors.
Mr. Lord was notified by one of the ministers, Zhu Qizhen, of Mr. Burns's impending ouster. 
Mr. Lord reported the development to Washington, where a spokesman for the State Department, Deborah Cavin, issued a one-sentence statement: ''We are grateful that the incident has been resolved.''
Another official, Qi Huai Yuan, told the Times editors that he understood they had been trying to see him for several days. 
He now wanted to tell them, he went on, that they had to understand that Mr. Burns had broken the law and that the matter had to be handled according to legal procedure.
Mr. Qi said he was convinced that the case would not damage ties between China and the United States nor the relationship of The Times with his country.
In reply, Mr. Rosenthal said: ''I've said it before: I know that Mr. Burns is a newspaperman and only a newspaperman. 
He also is a good friend of China, and so is The New York Times.''
Mr. Rosenthal had previously stated that Mr. Burns had gone on his 1,000-mile journey, from June 29 to July 7, to gather material for several articles, including one for The New York Times Magazine.

file: China Gives Managers Greater Control in Industry.txt
text:
ï»¿
A law intended to strip grass-roots Communist Party committees in state enterprises of much of their power and concentrate decision-making in the hands of technocratic managers was approved by China's legislature at its closing session today.
In the last year an intense debate, sometimes spilling into the public press, has raged over how much authority should be given to managers and how much power should be relinquished by the party. 
Although the text of the new law has not yet been made public, a paraphrased version released by the official New China News Agency suggested that party bureaucrats have not been completely frozen out.
The action was taken on the closing day of the National People's Congress, whose 2,970 delegates met here for 20 days in their annual session. 
The congress earlier confirmed Li Peng as Prime Minister and ratified the composition of a new Cabinet.
Late this afternoon, the 59-year-old Mr. Li answered questions from foreign and Chinese reporters for nearly two hours at his first news conference since he assumed his post. 
The Prime Minister has been portrayed by many diplomats and Western scholars as more cautious in his economic views than Zhao Ziyang, the party leader.But Mr. Li disparaged suggestions of disagreement between the two men.
''Now there is some comment in the foreign press that Zhao Ziyang is in favor of reform and opening to the outside world, while I'm in favor of stabilizing the economy,'' the Prime Minister said. 
''They somehow pit these two views against one another. 
As a matter of fact there is a misunderstanding involved. 
The two aspects form an integral whole and cannot be separated from each other.''
He also ridiculed suggestions that he was pro-Soviet because of his extensive education in the Soviet Union or that the new members of the Cabinet, many of whom also studied either in the Soviet Union or Eastern Europe in the 1950's, were sympathetic to Moscow.
''If you follow that kind of logic,'' Mr. Li said, ''you may think that China will have a pro-United States government in 20 or 30 years because it now has some 20,000 students in the United States.''
The 20-day congress confirmed a series of laws and constitutional amendments intended to formalize further China's decadelong effort to embrace a more Western-style economic structure, one less constrained by Soviet-style socialism. 
Among the actions taken included formal constitutional approval for private enterprise and the right to sell land-use rights. 
In what has the potential to be equally significant, Western diplomats said, is the law approved today on the authority of enterprise directors.
Until now, nearly all state industrial enterprises, which account for 70 percent of industrial output, were managed by committees of managers and party bureaucrats, with the party exercising the final say in all decisions.
Â 
Greater Control for Managers
Under the new law, factory directors are to assume principal control for the performance of their industry. 
Broadly, the law will allow enterprises to determine their own management structure, grant greater leeway to industries to negotiate contracts with foreign partners, permit factories to change their products in response to market demand and make it easier for workers to be hired and dismissed.
It also declares that a manager who causes an enterprise to suffer heavy losses ''shall be dealt with for criminal responsibilities,'' the news agency said.
It is unclear precisely what role the Communist Party will now have in newly organized industries. 
But the news agency said the party would ''guarantee and supervise the implementation of the guiding principles and policies of the party and the state.''
The congress also approved a plan today to establish the southern island of Hainan as an independent province with broad autonomy to encourage foreign investment and rapid economic development. 
Foreigners will be able to visit there without a visa and many Chinese laws governing the import and export of goods and services will not apply to the island.

We should not let the old issues from the past hold us back. 
The Chinese side has already made significant efforts for the removal of the obstacles existing between our two countries. 
It is hoped that the U.S. side will make corresponding efforts.''
Although Mr. Zhao did not specifically mention Taiwan, the reference seemed clear in his allusion to China's hope that ''both sides will strictly abide by the mutually agreed principles'' of the communiques they signed in 1972, 1979 and 1982, in which the United States recognized that there was only one China, governed by Peking, and agreed to gradually reduce the arms sales. 
The sales are expected to total $760 million this year, down from $780 million in 1984.
When speaking of China's own efforts to remove obstacles, Mr. Zhao apparently was referring to Peking's position that Taiwan can keep its political and economic systems, as well as its army, if it agrees to reunification with the mainland. 
The country's paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping, whom Mr. Bush will be meeting, has described the bid for unity with Taiwan as China's top priority, ahead even of Mr. Deng's ambitious program of economic change.
Â 
Bush's Reply
Mr. Zhao's use of the first public exchange of the trip to revive an issue that Washington has been playing down appeared to surprise Mr. Bush, who amended his own text in reply. 
Having catalogued the progress the two nations have made in trade, academic exchanges and other ties, the Vice President departed from his text to note that Mr. Zhao had referred to ''problems'' in the relationship. 
He added: ''We know that, and we should work to solve them.''
United States officials had characterized the Vice President's trip as an opportunity to underscore Washington's support for Mr. Deng's program of change. 
Mr. Zhao also cited progress the two nations have made in other areas, and spoke of Mr. Bush, who was chief of the United States diplomatic mission here a decade ago, as ''a friend well known to the Chinese people.''
But the jarring edge to his remarks on Taiwan underscored the somewhat cooler attitude Peking has adopted in the last year to ties with Washington.
One of the changes that has affected the relationship since Mr. Bush was last here - the thawing of relations between China and the Soviet Union -was not mentioned at the dinner. 
But there were salient reminders of it in the presence here of several Soviet delegations. 
One of them is a high-ranking parliamentary group that includes Georgi A. Arbatov, the Kremlin's top adviser on United States relations.
Â 
Signs Are the Same
Officials in Peking and Washington have maintained that ties between China and the United States are independent of the progress being made in Peking's contacts with Moscow.
But Mr. Bush's entourage of 110 officials and journalists could hardly avoid being struck by the sudden budding of the sort of contacts between Moscow and Peking that were the prelude in the 1970's to the flowering of Washington's own relationship here.
Mr. Bush finds himself in China at a time when two major Soviet cultural attractions are being offered here: a tour by the Moscow City Ballet and a series of poetry readings by Yevgeny Yevtushenko, 51 years old, the writer who was in the forefront of the Soviet avant-garde in the 1960's. 
There is even a visit by a group of blind Russians renewing contacts between their organization and its Chinese counterpart.
Mr. Bush is expected to hold talks over the next two days with several of China's top leaders, including Mr. Zhao and Mr. Deng. On Wednesday, Mr. Bush will fly to Chengdu, capital of Sichuan Province, to open the fourth United States Consulate in China. 
He will go on from there to the resort city of Guilin, the southern city of Canton and to the Special Economic Zone of Shenzhen, near Hong Kong.

text:

China's new era of orderly development and modernization will stress the role of competent managers and be guided by a team of leaders instead of a single all-powerful ruler like Mao Zedong, the new chairman of the Chinese Communist Party said today.
In his first speech since assuming China's most important office on Monday, the party chairman, Hu Yaobang, said the ''liquidation'' of leftist ideology that nearly destroyed China during the Cultural Revolution of 1966-76 ''is under way.''
The 66-year-old protege of Deng Xiaoping, the senior deputy chairman who is the country's principal leader, called for strict obedience and discipline within the party to help restore its ''greviously damaged'' prestige. 
The leftist radicals most responsible for the damage, including Jiang Qing, Mao's widow, he said, have been ''swept into the garbage bin of history.''
Hu Yaobang discusses plans for China's new era of orderly development and modernization
Mr. Hu spoke at a televised rally of 10,000 people gathered at the Great Hall of the People to celebrate the 60th anniversary of the party's founding in 1921.
Â 
Flanked on Dais by Deng and Zhao
Mr. Hu was flanked on the dais by Mr. Deng and Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang, who is also a newly named deputy chairman of the party. 
Hua Guofeng, who is now a junior deputy chairman, sat three seats away.
Mr. Hu described Mao as ''the greatest national hero in Chinese history,'' adding that ''his immense contributions are immortal.''
But he said Mao had made ''grave mistakes'' that the party, because of the personality cult around Mao, failed to prevent.
In a 35,000-word assessment of its 32 years in power, the party yesterday formally criticized Mao's errors. 
The critical assessment and Mr. Hu's assumption of the party chairmanship, replacing Mr. Hua, Mao's handpicked successor, were regarded here as the formal closing of the era of Maoist rule and an attempt to unify the party behind Mr. Deng's brand of pragmatism.
Whether these moves did so is not clear. 
There have been continuing reports from Chinese sources of deep continuing division within the party leadership.
Â 
Need for Obedience Stressed
Perhaps for that reason, Mr. Hu stressed the need for obedience in his speech. 
''Comrades at a lower level must respect and obey the leadership of comrades at a higher level,'' he said. 
It was something Mao would not have had to mention, but Mr. Hu raised his medium-pitched voice several times to the level of shrillness in making his point.
''They must not feign compliance while actually violating or resisting instructions from the high level,'' he said. 
Earlier this year, when Mr. Hu was serving as the party's secretary general, he was reported by knowledgeable Chinese to have been shocked that the documents for study and speeches he carefully composed and sent down to provincial and district leaders, had not been read. 
As a result, a propaganda campaign was launched on the need to study documents from party headquarters.
Mr. Hu stressed in his speech the need for collective decisionmaking at all levels, saying ''no one individual is allowed to have the final say.''
Criticism, he said, is welcome and ''retaliation is impermissible.''
Â 
Individual Initiative Welcomed
Individual initiative in party matters is welcome, he said, ''but no party member is allowdd to impair the party's interest and the common goal by turning the department or unit entrusted to him by the party into his own independent kingdom.''
Just because the Communist Party, with 39 million members, is in power, he said, ''some of our comrades feel conceited and succumb to bureaucratic practices.''
Mr. Hu was as adamant as other party officials have been in eschewing competition for the party.
He said the party's most serious task was to develop a new generation of younger leaders to replace old revolutionaries who should step out from day-to-day party matters and think about longrange problems.
Mr. Hu challenged reports of disunity within the party and said only ''a handful of people '' were sowing disunity. 
Then, shaking his fist as his voice cracked, he added:
''Now, reality has given them a clear answer: no force on earth can break the Chinese Communist Party's strong unity based on Marxist principles.''
