file: CHINA_S UNHAPPY CHOSEN_PROTESTS REVEAL AN UNSUSPECTED DISCONTENT AMONG ELITE YOUTH AND FEARS ABOUT F.txt
text:
ï»¿
The pro-democracy demonstrations by university students over the last several weeks have revealed a depth of discontent among the elite of China's youth that was unsuspected until now.
That university students, the chosen young, should demonstrate in such numbers in favor of political principles closely associated in the minds of Chinese with the non-Communist West, particularly the United States, has raised disturbing questions among many here about the direction of economic and political change in China.
The largest rallies were in Shanghai last weekend, where close to 50,000 people were estimated to have gathered on Sunday alone. 
But they also occurred in Beijing and about half a dozen other cities. 
Today there were reports that 3,000 students demonstrated in the port city of Tianjin to show their solidarity with the Shanghai protests.
Marches in Province Capitals
In the provincial capitals of Hefei and Wuhan, several thousand students marched under banners calling for greater democracy and freedom. 
They also protested university living conditions, which are primitive by Western standards.
Students in Hefei in particular derided the elections to the local legislative people's congress as a sham, saying they did not even know the candidates they were supposed to vote for as student representatives. 
As the protests continued, local leaders agreed to postpone the elections to give the students an opportunity to run their own candidates.
But it was the five days of demonstrations in Shanghai that were the most visible sign of widespread student discontent. 
Even in the beginning, the demonstrations were large, with more than 10,000 students marching. 
Quickly, the protests grew until more than 50,000 students were packed into People's Square in downtown Shanghai.
Students carried banners with the words ''Freedom'' and ''Democracy'' in passionate red brush strokes.
Many of the students interviewed during the Shanghai protests, while unable to describe in any sustained fashion what they meant by greater democracy, fervently argued that they had no control over their lives and that the Chinese people had no say in how their country was run.
Repeatedly over the last year, China's top leaders, including Deng Xiaoping, the senior leader, have said political ''reform'' would accompany China's economic restructuring, a process that has drawn much of its character from Western economic and financial models. 
But, uneasy about the implications of political reform - a widely used but only vaguely defined term that seems to embrace some form of decentralization in economic and adminstrative decision-making -the leadership has stressed that real political change will take two or three decades to achieve.
Â 
Economic Controls Loosened
The economic liberalization, a loosening of central controls over the economy so that individual enterprises are free to prosper or flounder on their own without state support, is intended to envigorate an economy that functioned in only the most rudimentary sense in the three decades until 1980. 
Now, companies go bankrupt, raise money through stock issues and dismiss workers for incompetence, practices inconceivable just a few years ago.
Even the party theoretical journal, Hongqi, has urged that the work of John Maynard Keynes be explored. 
''Whether one is a Marxist or a non-Marxist,'' the journal said, ''and whether one is a supporter of Keynsianism or its opponent, one needs to study the doctrine of Keynsianism.''
But with this shifting economic orientation, many intellectuals have insisted that responsibility in the workplace must be accompanied by rights in the political sphere. 
If people are allowed to take individual risks for economic gain, they should also be able to express their views individually, and collectively through some form of electoral system, on the country's political direction.
In 1979, when a hint of intellectual liberalization surfaced, there was a brief explosion of free political expression that became known as the Democracy Wall Movement, named for wall posters calling for democratic rights that were plastered on a wall in downtown Beijing. 
Although at first endorsing the movement, Mr. Deng quickly reversed himself and ruthlessly suppressed it, jailing its leaders for ''counterrevolutionary acts.''
That crackdown, while firmly consolidating Mr. Deng's power over the party ideological apparatus, succeeded in cowing China's intellectuals.
Â 
Easing Controls on Intellectuals
But Mr. Deng was aware that he could not successfully increase China's openness to the West while intimidating the country's intellectuals, the very people needed to propel the country out of its economic backwardness. 
So in the last five years he has gradually eased controls on intellectuals. 
Indeed, there is now virtually nothing that cannot be discussed in academic journals, according to many intellectuals.
''Nothing is taboo,'' said a young graduate student at Beijing University who is a regular contributor to the journal Reading Books.
But even as this intellectual liberalization proceeds in the highest reaches of university life, the absence of substantive liberalization in the daily lives of Chinese has become increasingly apparent to students on Chinese campuses. 
Students have no decision in who their representatives to student councils are, have no role in picking student candidates to local people's congresses, a sort of local legislature, and no freedom to chose where they will work after graduation.
A professor at Beijing University said the Government could not react harshly against the students.
''What can they do?'' he asked. 
''If they attack the students, no one will ever trust them again. 
They cannot be committed to intellectual freedom on the one hand and attack students calling for democracy on the other.''
At the same time, many students realize the fragility of their positions, that university administrators can ruin their lives through bad job assignments upon graduation. 
As the demonstrations petered out, many students explained the calm by citing such pragmatic considerations over their future.
Â 
A Warning in Editorials
For the Government, of course, those concerns and the threats it can make to enhance those concerns are its best hope for containing future protests.
Today, for instance, China's leading newspaper, People's Daily, and other major newspapers warned in front-page editorials that those who deviated from Communist Party policies would ''have to eat their own bitter fruit.''
People's Daily noted Mr. Deng's efforts this year to ''invigorate party and state organs, bring into play the initiative of grassroots units and the masses, overcome bureaucracy and increase efficiency.''

PEKING, Saturday, May 7 - China, embarrassed by the first successful hijacking of one of its civil airliners, today dispatched an official delegation for discussions with authorities in South Korea on the return of the hijackers as well as the plane, its crew and passengers.105 People on Plane
The British-made Trident jet was on a domestic flight from Shenyang in Manchuria to Shanghai Thursday when it was seized by the Chinese hijackers. 
They shot and wounded two of the crew before forcing the plane, with 105 people on board, to land at a military airfield in South Korea.
Mr. Shen sent a telegram on Friday to Chol Yong Kim, director of the South Korean Civil Aviation Bureau, expressing ''deep concern'' for the passengers and crew.
''In order to deal with this matter,'' the telegram said, ''I will go to Seoul personally as quickly as possible.

The text of the telegram was released by the New China News Agency.

Foreign Ministry Statement
The Chinese aviation agency said details of the discussions would have to come from South Korea. 
China's intentions, however, were spelled out in a statement issued Friday by the Foreign Ministry.
The statement said, ''The Chinese side requests the South Korean authorities immediately return the aircraft together with all the crew members and passengers and hand over the criminals that hijacked the airliner to the Chinese side in accordance with related articles of international civil aviation conventions.''
The New China News Agency identified the leader of the ''group of armed thugs'' as An Weijian, but gave no other details.

Strict Security Measures
China, which joined the international antihijacking convention in early 1979, has set up tough security measures at its airports, including body searches and luggage inspection. 
As a result, there was amazement among some Chinese that the hijackers managed to smuggle weapons on board.
Chinese officials have denied or refused to confirm stories of other unsuccessful hijackings here, some of which have been reported in the Hong Kong press.

The destination of all previous hijacking attempts has been Taiwan.
China's discreet trade with South Korea through Hong Kong has been sharply cut back, possibly under pressure from North Korea, after South Korean exports alone, mostly of industrial goods, approached $140 million in 1981.

file: CHINESE AIDE LEAVES WASHINGTON WITHOUT FORMAL ARMS SALES PACT.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese Defense Minister, Zhang Aiping, left here today without reaching formal agreement with Secretary of Defense Caspar W. Weinberger on United States military sales and assistance to China, according to Defense Department officials.
The chief Pentagon spokesman, Michael I. Burch, issued a statement saying discussions would continue on a technical level toward ''the possibility of agreements being reached in the future.''
Defense Department officials said Mr. Zhang and Mr. Weinberger had ''agreed in principle'' to the potential United States sale of antiaircraft missiles and antitank weapons to China. 
They also said China might buy military technology and possibly set up plants to produce weapons under license from American companies.
The officials cautioned, however, that no specific sales had been decided. 
The expression ''to agree in principle'' is often used in Asia to avoid specific or formal agreements but expressing a willingness to continue negotiations.
Â 
No Arms Sales Since '49
The United States has not sold weapons to China since the Communists took power in 1949. 
After that China and the United States were enemies in the Korean War, and formal diplomatic relations were established by President Carter only in 1979.
On Monday Mr. Burch said Mr. Weinberger and Mr. Zhang had ''reached agreement on a number of important matters'' but declined to say what they were. 
He suggested then that an announcement would be made before Mr. Zhang left Washington.
The Chinese asked for a news blackout over the negotiations because, officials said, they did not want to appear to be moving closer to to the United States. 
Mr. Burch said Monday that the Chinese had asked that the meetings be considered ''private'' and that Mr. Weinberger had agreed.
The officials said that a Chinese delegation of technicians and military officials had been in Washington since March and that several officials who came with Mr. Zhang had remained behind after he left. 
Mr. Zhang is continuing his visit with tours of United States military bases and visits to military contractors.
Officials said no specific agreements had been reached because the Chinese had not decided what arms they want and were exploring all possibilities. 
Mr. Zhang is expected to continue that search as he visits General Dynamics, Boeing and other arms contractors.
Â 
Interested in High Tech
In addition, officials said that the Chinese had been more interested in high technology but that the Americans had sought to steer them toward weapons more in keeping with the relatively rudimentary nature of the Chinese military forces.
The Chinese, who have limited amounts to spend, have long said they are more interested in buying technology than in arms themselves, but the Administration wants to sell weapons, the officials said. 
A compromise between those two positions has still not been achieved.
The initiative in forming a military relationship between the United States and China has largely come from the United States, both in the Carter and Reagan Administrations. 
Mr. Weinberger, in his public statements during a visit to China last fall, made clear that the Administration would welcome an anti-Soviet posture by China.
The Chinese, however, have made equally clear that they are not interested in allying themselves with the United States against the Soviet Union, with which they share a 5,000-mile border. 
Soviet military power along that border is much greater than China's.
The Nationalist Government in Taiwan has vigorously objected to possible United States arms sales to China. 
The Government in Peking, in turn, has strenuously objected to continued American arms sales to Taiwan. 
The Reagan Administration has slowed the sales to Taiwan but has refused to stop them.
Â 
'When They're Ready'
After Mr. Zhang left today for the remainder of his visit to the United States, one official said: ''We think they'll go back home and look over all their notes and then make a presentation to us. 
Maybe it will be just one system at a time, when they're ready.''
Officials said the Chinese evidently had a long list of weapons in which they appear interested but had not given the list to American officials. 
They also said that arms sales to China would be subject to Congressional approval and that a formal announcement might not made until it was time to notify Congress.
Among the weapons apparently high on the list of potential sales, the officials said, were Hawk antiaircraft missiles, which are supersonic, can reach to 60,000 feet and have a range of 25 miles.

For nearly a decade the United States and some of its principal NATO allies have sought to sell arms to China. 
Recently they have been joined by Japan.
Success in the form of large, long-term contracts has proved elusive; of 25 major negotiations since 1972, only nine have resulted in sales.

Intelligence agencies in the West say that the Chinese need modern arms and have needed them since the late 1960's, when the last weapons delivered by the Soviet Union moved toward obsolescence. 
But two American scholars, Dr. William T. Tow and Dr. Douglas T. Stuart, concluded in a recent study that although in this decade China can be expected to acquire NATO and Japanese weapons systems gradually to maintain ''a minimum defense posture,'' the shopping list will be limited by ''overall economic constraints and by the low priority accorded to defense by the current Peking leadership.''
In addition to a scarcity of foreign exchange, a serious obstacle to modernization is resistance in the Communist Party and the army to the acquisition of new equipment. 
Many senior officers and party officials, it is said, are convinced that if the Russians invade they will only be ''drowned in the human sea'' of a billion Chinese.

Inspection Teams Sent
Peking's practice has been to send inspection teams to the United States, Western Europe and Japan to study the weapons systems most appropriate to Chinese needs. 
A small quantity of weapons or of dualpurpose equipment such as Boeing 747 jet transport planes is then purchased so that the Chinese can develop their own models.
The study reported that in some instances Peking used a so-called reverse engineering method, buying, for example, 10 Boeing 707 jets, stripping them down and building its own versions, meeting particular needs and responding to production limitations.
Arms transfers from the West have been almost negligible when China's requirements and the scale of Soviet forces on its frontier are considered. 
In 1978 it bought 600 antitank missiles from West Germany, about two days' supply for a division in modern war. 
Two years later Marconi, a British company, sold it five sets of fieldartillery-control equipment.
Chinese military doctrine holds that a large helicopter force would be essential in meeting Soviet forces invading along a number of routes, but the number purchased would hardly suffice. 
So far the Chinese have bought 80 French helicopters, 8 American helicopters and an undisclosed number of West German craft.
Â 
Soviet Protest to Britain
The Soviet Union has been highly sensitive to the development of arms deals between members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and China. 
When Britain and China were conducting negotiations on the Harrier jet fighter, Leonid I. Brezhnev, the Soviet leader, wrote to Prime Minister James Callaghan and other NATO heads of government warning that sales of such weapons would harm relations with the Soviet Union.
West Germany has been the most wary of offending the Russians in this area, probably because of the thriving West German-Soviet trade. 
China's interest shifted from the Harrier to the Tornado supersonic fighter co-produced by Britain, West Germany and Italy, but the TowStuart study expressed doubt that Bonn would agree to a sale to Peking ''because of its determination to avoid the wrath of Moscow.''
An interesting aspect of China's reluctance or inability to ''buy big,'' in the view of Western analysts, is that its need for advanced weapons has increased since it reopened trade with the West.

file: CHINESE AS IT_S WRITTEN_ WILDLY DIFFERENT STROKES.txt
text:
ï»¿
Cao Xianzhuo is worried.
Despite his efforts, the efforts of bureaucrats who preceded him and perhaps because of the weight of 3,000 years of history, people in China refuse to write Chinese all the same way.
Street signs, billboards, newspapers, books and the signs over shop windows sometimes use forms of Chinese characters that are irregular, obscure or downright wrong.
Last month Peking Daily published two pages of Chinese characters, the ideograms that make up the written Chinese language, and declared that once and for all this was the way Chinese should be written. 
It was at least the sixth time in the last 25 years that such a list has been published. 
A Posse of Schoolchildren?
Earlier this year exasperation with the spread of irregular written characters seemed to reach a fever pitch, and schoolchildren were urged to patrol the streets looking for public signs with incorrectly written Chinese as part of a campaign dubbed ''Let the spring wind drive away wrong characters.''
Thousands of signs were repainted but now, six months later, a short stroll down any street in Peking will uncover dozens of miswritten characters.
''In our society, people use many different ways of writing,'' said Mr. Cao, the secretary general of the State Language Commission, an agency created to try to lend some unity to the written language. 
''It's not very good.''
Throughout its history, China has endured a lack of uniformity in its written language. 
Over the centuries Chinese characters have changed their appearance. 
In some cases, two or three ways of writing a single character emerged, each correct and each commonly recognized by China's tiny literate population.
Â 
Characters With Fewer Strokes
When Mao Zedong took power in 1949, the cultural officials within the Communist Party's bureaucracy set out to simplify radically the way Chinese was written. 
The goal of total adult literacy meant that characters, some with more than 30 individual strokes, needed to be redesigned with fewer strokes so they would be easier to remember and write.
Since then, batches of these ''simplified characters'' have been published as the new standard. 
But disagreements among cultural officials, grumbling by scholars and confusion among the people led to the recalling of some lists, which created further disarray in the written language.
Even People's Daily, the official newspaper of the Communist Party, entered the fray. 
In a long editorial, the paper wrote, ''At present, the indiscriminate use of the original complex form of Chinese characters, the indiscriminate creation of new simplified characters, and wrongly written characters are quite common.''
The paper wryly observed, ''The standardization of a written language usually reflects the extent of the civilization of a country, nation or region.''
Â 
Faux Pas on Sunny Street
In one block along Chaoyang, or Sunny, Street in Peking, more than a dozen shops and businesses advertise their presence with a melange of incorrect or miswritten characters. 
On the eave of a tire-repair shop, the proprietor wrote one character in the old style and then painted the next one incorrectly.
Down the block, a shop that sells false teeth proclaimed its wares with a simplified, but officially disapproved, version of a character. 
And even the city street sign used a supposedly irregular simplified version of the word for ''street.''
The spread of multiple written forms of the language has been accompanied by a misleading official description of how the standardizing has been carried out. 
It has also been accompanied by a popular stubborness that resists, however subtly, arbitrary decisions by an invisible bureaucracy.
In explaining the choice of several characters with a greatly reduced number of pen strokes compared with the original versions, Mr. Cao said that some of the new characters had been used by ''the ordinary people'' during the Song and Yuan Dynasties, or from the 10th to the 14th centuries.
Â 
The Real Story: Illiteracy
''This is one way the new characters are chosen,'' he said, in what is now a politically acceptable recourse to history. 
''The other way is often to ask for the opinion from society. 
Simple words were obtained from the people.''
But in reality, when most of the decisions were made to simplify the written language, very few Chinese could read at all, much less offer a view on the constitution of the written aspect of their tongue. 
The most recent national census taken in 1982 disclosed that 23.5 percent of China's citizens remained illiterate.
Despite the repeated efforts to simplify the written language, remedial literacy requires the memorization of 4,000 or more individual characters, a number that makes typing, computer entry and telegraphy nightmarish.
In 1958 the Government adopted a plan to use the Roman alphabet to spell phonetically the northern Chinese dialect known in the west as Mandarin. 
More than half of China's one billion people speak other dialects or languages as their first language, a fact that has impeded broader acceptance of an alphabetized Chinese. 
Because the characters are ideograms, they convey the same meaning among China's dialects, although the words themselves may be pronounced quite differently.
Â 
Pinyin Is Growing Slowly
Nonetheless, schoolchildren across the country can receive newspapers printed in a combination of Chinese characters and Pinyin, the name of the Romanization system devised by the Government.
Still, the Pinyin system is not used extensively. 
''We may use Pinyin in telegrams,'' said Mr. Cao. ''Some dictionaries are now organized this way. 
There is some thinking now to expand the use of Pinyin.''
But, he said, ''the development of Pinyin is very slow now.''
''At the moment,'' he said, ''scholars have different opinions. 
Some think Chinese should be alphabetized. 
Some scholars think it should not. 
Chinese characters are considered traditional things by old people.''
The major problem, he said, is not how to induce people to switch to an alphabet, but how to settle upon a single written form of the language.
''The most important thing is to make the form of Chinese characters stable and regular,'' he said. 
''I myself see many characters that are wrong. 
We have decided on regulations to correct characters.''
With the new list just published, Mr. Cao said, there will be no further changes in the Chinese written language.
Even with regulations, Mr. Cao said, complete standardization will remain elusive. 
''It's no problem if signs still are not correct,'' he said. 
''We can't force them to correct the characters. 
If the problem is solved in the big places, in books, in business, that is important.''

file: CHINESE CHIEF OF STATE AN ASTUTE OLD WARRIOR.txt
text:
ï»¿
Li Xiannian's knack for survival has served him well over many years. 
His appointment as China's new President, its first in 15 years, caps the career of a crusty old revolutionary who still commands the nation's respect.
In his time, Mr. Li has been a tough soldier and an astute negotiator. 
He has no known formal education, but his self-taught grasp of the complex Chinese economy made him its leading exponent. 
He has traveled widely in Communist and developing nations, while displaying a deep suspicion of both the United States and the Soviet Union.
PEKING, June 18 - Li Xiannian's knack for survival has served him well over many years.
Though he has been known as a political moderate, his inate conservatism made him a rallying point for hard-liners who distrust the economic policy changes instituted by Deng Xiaoping, China's paramount leader. 
''He is an embodiment of China, far more than Deng,'' said a Western diplomat here.
Li Xiannian is believed to have been born in 1905 to a poor family in Huangan County north of the Yangtze River in central Hubei Province. 
In 1927 he joined the Communist Party and the Red Army and quickly displayed an aptitude for command that brought rapid promotion. 
He helped organize the Communist base area in Hubei and later joined the celebrated Long March. 
By 1941 he was a seasoned combat veteran with 60,000 troops under his charge.
Â 
A Top Commander in Civil War
He was elected to the party's Central Committee in 1945. 
With the defeat of the Japanese, he rose to general commands in the renewed civil war against the Nationalists. 
After the Communist victory in 1949 Mr. Li was rewarded with top party and government posts in Hubei Province.
Mr. Li became interested in economic affairs while Mayor of the industrial city of Wuhan, which was recovering from the ravages of long warfare. 
After two years as Mayor, Mr. Li was brought to Peking in 1954 to confront the problems afflicting the national economy. 
He soon succeeded Deng Xiaoping as Finance Minister and also became a Deputy Prime Minister, a post he would hold for 26 years. 
He joined the party's ruling Politburo in 1956.
As Finance Minister in the 1950's, Mr. Li was assigned two Soviet advisers, with whom, he said later, he quarreled daily. 
The experience fueled his suspicion of the Soviet Union, but he also disliked the United States for its continuing support of the Nationalists on Taiwan.
Mao Zedong reportedly never quite trusted Mr. Li but kept him on because of his competence and Prime Minister Zhou Enlai's support. 
Mr. Li's responsibilities covered almost every facet of the economy, from industry and agriculture to trade and the budget.
Mr. Li was less astute in anticipating the political winds of change. 
When Mr. Deng was sent into disgrace for a second time, Mr. Li called in a speech in October 1976 for the nation to ''deepen the struggle to criticize Deng Xiaoping.''
Mr. Li, who at one point was expected to succeed Hua Guofeng as Prime Minister, had to step down as Deputy Prime Minister in September 1980 in a maneuver by Mr. Deng that gave the top Government post to Zhao Ziyang. 
Mr. Li has kept his seat in the Standing Committee of the Politburo.
Â 
Critical of Deng Policies
Though Mr. Li had disapproved of Mao's rash economic panaceas, his later identification with the faction of the bureaucracy that wanted to sustain heavy industrial growth set him at cross purposes with Mr. Deng, who pressed changes that emphasized light industry and the consumer.
Mr. Li has suffered in recent years from frail health, with rumored ailments ranging from cancer to kidney problems. 
But he is apparently strong enough to carry out the mostly ceremonial duties of the presidency.
The new President is married to Lin Jiamei, who has worked in the Ministry of Public Health as well as the State Council's Office of Finance and Trade.

file: CHINESE DAILIES CHANGE TACTICS AS IMMIGRANTS POUR INTO CITY.txt
text:
ï»¿
Some of New York's 10 Chinese-language daily newspapers - once genteel bulletin boards for marriage, business and community announcements -are sending their reporters out to hunt down stories on crime and justice.
Last fall, the second largest of the dailies, The Centre Daily News, began to get more aggressive and assigned a reporter to cover the Manhattan Criminal Court complex on Centre Street in lower Manhattan - like all courthouses a repository of compelling stories and sometimes gripping details.
Almost immediately, the city's largest Chinese daily, The World Journal, based in Flushing, Queens, followed suit.
Now at least four papers have reporters covering crime and the courts part time, all of them concentrating on crimes or lawsuits involving Chinese-Americans.
Some journalists and Chinese community leaders say that the new attention to the judicial process by the Chinese papers - in both civil and criminal cases - is a result of broader changes in the community.
Low Crime Rate
For example, they point to the diminished impact of the tongs, or associations, which in the past would mediate in many disputes among Chinatown residents. 
Community leaders say that the authority of the tong leaders, most of whom speak Cantonese, has deteriorated as immigrants with widely different dialects have entered the community.
''There are some very complicated problems,'' said Louis Liu, a longtime reporter who was also one of the first journalists to begin covering the courts, for The Sing Tao Daily. 
''The old immigrants are settled down, many have businesses. 
The new immigrants mostly have no money and must work hard, long hours, mostly for those older immigrants.''
''The Chinese used to hide among themselves,'' said Emile Bocian, a reporter for the United States-China Economic Journal. 
''Now they're more involved in the community, in the government.''
Almost all the papers are not shy about trumpeting their political views in the news columns - which range from The World Journal's strong pro-Taiwan position to The China Daily's pro-Peking stance.
Some of the papers have subdued graphics and a conservative tone. 
Others are more daring. 
The World Journal is a four-color broadsheet with a generous use of large pictures.
Â 
Greater Resources Available
Journalists at the papers say that although the courts are in Chinatown's backyard, they have never been covered regularly by the Chinese-language media.
Partly, they say, this is because the Chinese population in New York - and thus the number of civil and criminal actions involving immigrants -has never been large enough to warrant it, and partly because none of the papers had the financial resources for such coverage.
But the waves of new Chinese immigrants over the last decade have changed all that. 
For the papers, the new immigrants have brought greater circulation and advertising revenues than ever had been imagined a few years ago - thus allowing staff increases at many papers.
At the same time, as the Chinese immigrant population has doubled in the last five years to at least 250,000 - mostly in Manhattan and Queens - the number of civil and criminal court actions involving Chinese-Americans has risen sharply. 
The increase has swamped the old Chinatown associations, which once dealt with the kind of disputes now ending up in the courts.
''Chinese papers have become much more sophisticated,'' said Justin Yu, president of the Chinese Language Journalists Association of New York. 
''A few years ago, they were in a very primitive state - they were all community news, marriages, who was opening a business. 
Now they're just Chinese versions of American papers. 
Sensational stories - blood, sex, crime - they're the most popular.''
Â 
Change in the Newsroom
Despite changes in the community, however, the Fifth Precinct, which includes Chinatown, has one of the lowest crime rates in the city. 
Moreover, in the first six months 1985, the total number of felonies dropped 5.6 percent, to 2,020, from 2,139.
A spokesman for the department said the drop was partly a result of an increase in police manpower in the precinct that followed a rise in crime in the previous several years.
The emphasis on court coverage has created new pressures in the newsrooms. 
First, reporters must be fluently bilingual - not a requirement in covering Chinatown or the Chinese community in Queens.
Also, reporters must have some familiarity with the United States legal system. 
And for the papers, it is a major financial commitment to assign a reporter to cover the courts. 
The staffs at all of the papers are relatively small - The World Journal, for example, has 10 reporters in New York and the Centre Daily has eight.
Editors say that the pool of potential candidates -college educated, fluent in both English and Chinese and able to write well in Chinese - is relatively small, and that competition for good reporters is intense.
Â 
A Personal Rivalry
For example, three papers have hired a reporter to concentrate on the courts in the last six months, and all three of the reporters were educated in colleges in the United States.
At the city's two leading papers, there is a personal, though friendly, rivalry, between two former classmates at Michigan State who began covering the courts last December - Huang Yuan-Ling, a 27-year-old native of Taiwan who works for The World Journal, and Carol Huang, a 31-year-old Taiwan native, who is on the staff of The Centre Daily News.
The two reporters, who are not related, said that they have encountered difficulties, partly because of the sometimes arcane rules of the system, and partly because they are new to New York. 
But both also feel they serve an important function.
''I think that many Chinese papers created a false impression in the past,'' said Carol Huang. 
''We would report an arrest - then nothing. 
We didn't tell our readers anything about what happened after that, what the punishments were, or how the legal system worked.''
''We haven't built up a relationship with the court,'' said I-Der Jeng , assignment editor at The China Daily News, which hired a reporter to cover the courts about four months ago. 
''The time is very short.''
Â 
Administrative Problems
Court officials say that the number of cases involving Chinese-Americans remains small but can often lead to administrative problems, especially in regard to language.
A case pending next week in State Supreme Court, for example, involves two different Chinese dialects - one spoken by the family of a murder victim, the other by the accused murderer. 
And since there are no Chinese language interpreters on staff in New York City, according to the State Office of Court Administration, the two interpreters needed for the trial will have to hired on a freelance basis.
Circulation figures for the city's Chinese-language papers, many of which are only a few years old, are sometimes exaggerated, according to officials at the Chinatown Planning Council, which oversees economic development in the Chinese-American community. 
Moreover, none of the papers are members of the Audit Bureau of Circulation, which accredits circulation numbers.
However, the council estimates that the four largest papers are The World Journal, with a circulation of about 100,000 nationwide - about 50,000 of it on the East Coast; The Centre Daily News, with about 65,000 nationally; The China Daily News, with about 50,000, and The Sing Tao Daily, with about 25,000. 
Other papers are The Sino-Daily Express, The China Post Daily, The United Journal, The China Tribune, The Pei Mei News and The International Daily News.

A Chinese student educated in the United States has been identified by his wife as one of the demonstrators detained in China's crackdown on political dissent.

11 in Shanghai after taking part in the student demonstrations there for freer speech and democracy last December.
His wife, Che Shaoli, said the family's request to visit her husband in prison was denied and ''we do not even know where he is.''
She asked that Chinese authorities release him or ''try him according to legal procedure.''
Ms. Che, who is still in the United States, said in an interview Friday that ''this kind of treatment to a returned student is frightening to all students now studying in the West.''

The 31-year-old Mr. Yang was detained in his parents' home in Shanghai on Jan. 
11, Ms. Che said, relating the events as told by friends and relatives.

Ms. Che stressed that Mr. Yang's father and mother were both senior members of the Chinese Communist Party.
''The old generation believed in the party but the young generation doesn't believe in the way Communism is practiced in China,'' Ms. Che said. 
Neither she nor her husband were party members, she said, but they were not against the party and supported its reform.
Dr. Wang Bingzhang, a former Chinese student who founded the Chinese Alliance for Democracy here in 1982, said Mr. Yang was the first student returnee from the United States known to be arrested in the current crackdown.

The Chinese Alliance for Democracy has received reports of the arrest of 3 students and 11 young workers in the last 10 days in Shanghai, Canton and Tianjin, according to Dr. Wang. These arrests also seem related to the recent demonstrations.
Ms. Che said her husband had written her about taking part in the Shanghai student demonstrations. 
She said that Mr. Yang's position was difficult because he was not currently enrolled in a Chinese university but planning to return to get his Ph.D in the United States.

file: CHINESE DISSIDENT DERIDES A DOGMA.txt
text:
ï»¿
In his first public political remarks to students since his expulsion from the Communist Party, China's most prominent dissident spoke to a gathering of 300 students today about democracy and modernization.
The speaker, Fang Lizhi, derided the idea that China could develop economically in its own way, a central thesis of current Chinese Communist ideology.
''There's no such thing as physics with Chinese characteristics,'' Professor Fang said as the students crowded in around him. 
''The same goes for modernization. 
Modernization is modernization.''
''First we must recognize the concept of human rights above all,'' he continued. 
''And we must use democratic means. 
For human rights, all the people must have freedom of thought and freedom of speech.''
After an address to university students in Hefei 18 months ago, Professor Fang, an astrophysicist and vice president of the University of Science and Technology there, was expelled from the Communist Party and dismissed from his post. 
Party leaders accused Mr. Fang of instigating the protests by encouraging students to speak out on political and intellectual concerns.
Â 
Anniversary of Student Movement
The occasion today was the 90th anniversary of the founding of Beijing University, one of China's most prestigious institutions, and the 69th anniversary of a student movement that catapulted China into the modern era. 
On May 4, 1919, students from the university marched in Beijing to protest the ceding to Japan of Germany's rights to Shandong Province. 
They were beaten by the police, and subsequent demonstrations exploded into nationalist and reformist sentiment that gave birth first to an intellectual iconoclasm and later to the Communist Party.
Professor Fang was not included in the official anniversary festivities, in which Li Tieying, a Politburo member and the chairman of the State Education Commission, addressed 25,000 alumni, faculty and students.
As Mr. Li urged students ''to carry forward the good tradition of diligence, rigor, honesty and creativeness,'' hisses were heard from students listening on outdoor speakers.
Almost since its inception, Beijing University, which now has 25,000 students, has been at the heart of China's intellectual and political life. 
In December 1986, Beijing University students tramped through the snow to demand greater freedom of expression. 
Protests there and in other cities led to the dismissal of Hu Yaobang as Communist Party leader and six months of intellectual repression.
Â 
Students Offer Their Views
At about 3:30 this afternoon, Professor Fang arrived at a locust grove on his bicycle to the cheers of students who were seated in a circle. 
The students offered their views on China's political organization and future. 
Some urged collective action, others reflected on the country's complexities.
''There's a long tradition of intellectuals sacrificing themselves passively,'' a young man said, his hand jabbing the air. 
''I think we should change methods. 
We should be more inflammatory. 
One can sacrifice oneself passivley, or make a splash in the process.''
Another student rose. 
''A revolution in thought must come first,'' he said.
A third stood up. 
''Democracy in China must have Chinese characteristics,'' he said, adding, ''Do you really think that you would be able to import American democracy wholesale into China?
Much progress has been made over the past decade, but progress has to be made step by step.''
Later, when asked whether the students should take to the streets to press their views, as they did more than a year ago, Mr. Fang replied, ''Maybe they should keep quiet for a period.''

file: CHINESE DOCTORS VISIT U.S. UNDER YALE PROGRAM.txt
text:
ï»¿
THROUGHOUT his childhood in China, it was common to step over the bodies of the dead and dying in the streets, recalled Dr. John McLean Morris, a professor at Yale University.
''Unwanted female infants were disposed of by throwing them through a small hole in one of the dozens of stone huts erected for the purpose around the countryside,'' he said.
Dr. Morris's experiences in Anhui Province as the son of a Presbyterian missionary were the genesis of his medical career. 
Dr. Morris, 67 years old, is now the chief of gynecology at the Yale-New Haven Hospital.
His lifelong contacts in China, which he left as a teen-ager, were cut off when the Communists took over in 1949. 
But they were revived two years ago when China's Ministry of Public Health invited Dr. Morris and a medical committee from Yale to reestablish an exchange program at Hunan Medical College in Changsha, capital of Hunan Province.
Contingent of 8 Chinese doctors and professors of medicine begin a year as observers at Yale-New Haven Hospital in Connecticut
Hunan Medical College, an affiliated hospital, nursing school and Yali High School (named for Yale), were built in the 1920's by the Yale-China Association with funds contributed by the philanthropist Edward Stephen Harkness. 
The complex flourished as a teaching and treatment center until the revolution, and remains one of the leading facilities of its kind in China.
But in 1951 the American staff was asked to leave the country and the property was nationalized by the Chinese Government. 
Today it is administered and operated by the Chinese, with Yale doctors serving only as visiting professors and surgeons.
In New Haven, an old, red-frame building on Temple Street houses the staff of the 80-year-old Yale-China Association, plus Chinese art, memorabilia and literature. 
The house vibrates these days with the excitement of Yale students and faculty preparing to depart for China, or introducing their newly arrived Chinese counterparts to life in New Haven.
A few months ago a contingent of eight Chinese doctors and professors of medicine began a year as observers at Yale-New Haven Hospital. 
Two American doctors are currently in China through the program, and others will be going later this year. 
Other American doctors have already been there on the Yale program and are now back in the United States.
Expenses of $10,000 for each Chinese doctor are paid by the association, which also pays for the Yale representatives at Hunan College and Hubei Medical College in Wuhan. 
The association's endowment fund of $1.2 million will increase by $500,000 through a settlement in which the Chinese Government agreed to make restitution for the property that was nationalized.
To help underwrite the $750,000 cost of the medical exchange and also a language program in China, the association conducts two annual tours of China for small groups of Americans, priced around $4,000 and tied to joining the 1,000-member association. 
It receives no financial support from Yale University, but operates ''in confluence with university policies,'' said John Bryan Starr, executive director of the association.
''The basis for the successful reestablishment of Yale-China ties is the overwhelming interest of the Chinese Government in scientific technology,'' Mr. Starr said. 
Chinese medicine, in Dr. Morris's opinion, is ''about where the United States was 40 years ago.''
At a recent gathering in Dr. Morris's office, his Chinese colleagues discussed some of the differences between medicine here and at home.
For one thing, ''women have taken over the field of gynecology,'' said Dr. Zhang Shichun, head of surgery at Hunan Medical College. 
Dr. Cheng Suqian, chief of gynecology at Peking Medical College and wife of a surgeon, noted that in China ''examinations for cervical cancer are mandatory for married women every other year. 
Most women are visited in their homes to obtain the (Pap) smear.''
The use of acupuncture, which Dr. Pei Wusun said enables his patients ''to remain conscious and take nourishment during open-heart surgery,'' is also used in the delivery of babies. 
''Anesthetics limit contractions and reduce the levels of oxygen for the infant,'' Dr. Cheng said.
''There are some Chinese practices that we might learn from,'' Dr. Morris said. 
''Certain aspects of acupuncture and herbal medicine, and their reluctance to take extraordinary measures to preserve a life.''
''Of course, the economics are taken into account to a greater extent there, but I think we may be going too far with these heroic procedures,'' he said, using as an example the use of mechanical means to keep premature infants alive.
The fact that American doctors may perform surgery in China, but no foreign doctor may do so here without an American medical license, has been a contentious issue with the Chinese.
''Observation is useful, but it is not the same,'' said Dr. Lu Xinsheng, a Hunan surgeon. 
Nevertheless, Dr. Morris receives an increasing number of applications each month from Chinese doctors who wish to come here and learn, he said.
A second and equally important program run by the association is the sponsorship of ''Bachelors,'' Yale graduate students with at least two years of Chinese language instruction, who are sent to China for two years as English teachers at the colleges in Hunan, Hubei, Wuhan and Hong Kong. 
About 14 students are involved in the program this year.
Leaving for China July 1 as a Bachelor is Julian Chang, a Chinese-American who visited China for the first time recently and experienced ''the old roots feeling that China is my homeland,'' he said. 
''There were minor cultural differences â¦ no ice cubes on a hot day in Peking, but you get over that very quickly.''
As fluent in Russian as he is in Chinese, Mr. Chang majored in political science at Yale and contemplates a career in international relations.
''I'm interested to see how I deal with the bureaucracy of a Communist government. 
To me, China is like the United States of the 1860's - it has a huge potential.''
The numbers of students eager to become Bachelors are an indication that ''America's love-hate relationship with China is on an upswing of the pendulum,'' said Susan O'Sullivan of the China Council of the Asia Society, which is headquartered in Washington D.C. 
The Yale-China Association is a member of the Southern New England council of the society.
''Education is not the only basis for rekindled interest in China,'' Miss O'Sullivan pointed out. 
''North Carolina had strong ties with the Chinese tobacco industry at the turn of the century, and that council is becoming active again.''
Yale University has taken initial steps to institute a cooperative exchange program between the Yale School of Music and the Shanghai Conservatory, Mr. Starr said. 
Apart from the United States, where Stanford University in California and other institutions have been organizing exchange programs, the pursuit of person-to-person relations with China seems to interest only France among Western nations, he noted.
''A two-year stint teaching French in China is an alternative to military service for both men and women,'' he said of the French program. 
''There is a large colony of French nationals at Wuhan University,'' most of whom are involved in language programs, he said.
Jean Heller, a Bachelor going to China in July, looks forward to ''the excitement of seeing what is worthy of imitation on both sides.''
''Every relationship we form will be magnified and will send out waves of influence,'' she said.

text:
ï»¿
Social unrest is unavoidable as China continues to change its economic and political structure, Prime Minister Li Peng told a meeting of senior security personnel on Tuesday.
Today, the Chinese Public Security Minister, Wang Fang, said at the same forum that riots and ''anti-revolutionary activities'' were growing in frequency across the country and must be dealt with harshly.
Mr. Wang also said that foreign-instigated sabotoge had recently increased, although he refused to specify which countries were responsible.
These admissions of social upheaval, and of sabotage, are remarkable in a country where the leadership takes pains to present a portrait of a society at peace with itself despite occasional publicized incidents of protest or disturbance.
While Chinese leaders have acknowledged the fact of criminal activity -pictures of criminals on trial are regularly broadcast on the evening news -crime is routinely described as relatively minor and under control. 
The statements by Mr. Li and Mr. Wang seem to belie these contentions.
Â 
Unruly Students and Monks
Since late 1986, China has had several instances of acute social disturbance, including a wave of student demonstrations that was crushed by the police in January 1987 and a series of violent protests late that year and early in 1988 by Tibetan Buddhist monks calling for independence of the region from Beijing.
But the Chinese leadership remains aware of the possibility of spreading social upheaval as the country's ambitious program of economic restructuring spurs sudden and intense inflation, a recent phenomenon that has unsettled most urban residents who see their already small incomes being rapidly eroded.
Mr. Li's remarks were not reported in full; brief excerpts were published by the official New China News Agency on Tuesday night.
''Li said that deepening the reform will unavoidably cause some 'social upheavals' and sharpen various contradictions,'' according to the Government press agency's account. 
''Organs of public security should be fully prepared to deal with any kind of trouble-making, riots, sabotage and serious crimes, Li urged.''
Â 
Veiled Political Reference
The Prime Minister, who assumed his post in March, also called for more serious penalties for ''crimes harmful to the country's political stabilityI,'' the press agency said.
Although he was not specific, he apparently referred to the sporadic outbreaks of protest by college students as well as the continuing unrest in Tibet. 
Chinese authorities regularly denounce student protests, saying they threaten to upset political stabilityI. 
Several Chinese journalists said their papers have been instructed to play down news of strikes in Eastern Europe related to economic reform policies there and to ignore incidents of domestic unrest.
Late last month, 1,000 people from a village southwest of Beijing, who were protesting the dumping of polluted water through their community, were clubbed by hundreds of police officers who broke up the demonstration. 
Only after the incident was reported in foreign newspapers did the official press mention the protest, and even then it ignored the actions of the police.
Mr. Wang's remarks, the first of this kind in many years, acknowledged the spread of antistate agitation, sabotage and rioting. 
As with Mr. Li's comments, the Chinese press agency only paraphrased his speech.
''While riots - especially ones involving anti-revolutionary activities -are on the rise,'' Mr. Wang said, ''sabotage instigated from abroad has also recently been intensified.''
No reports of sabotage by foreign agents or of Chinese acting at the behest of foreign powers have appeared in the country's newspapers in recent years, so it was not clear to what exactly Mr. Wang was referring.
Â 
Potential for More Trouble
Last month, groups of students at Beijing University organized a series of demonstrations to protest against inadequate living conditions and price increases. 
The protests, quickly stifled by university authorities and the police, exposed the potential for wider unrest caused by urban inflation.
As the Chinese economy shifts toward a more market-oriented system, prices, especially in urban areas, have risen sharply in response to pent-up demand. 
The cost of food and basic consumer goods, the two largest expenditures for city families, are now climbing at an annual rate of nearly 20 percent, far exceeding salary increases.
While it appears that there have been no organized protests by workers in urban areas over the price increases, it is clear that the degree of strain is worrying Chinese leaders. 
Already, some income subsidies have been granted in an effort to alleviate the squeeze.
But the leadership has so far given no indication that it intends to retreat from its economic policies, even if they mean some short-term pain for urban dwellers, who make up about 20 percent of the national population.

file: Chinese Official Lists 6 Grievances Against U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
In the strongest language to date, China has described its relations with the United States as potentially unstable and attacked what it said was interference in its internal affairs.
''Over the past year or so a succession of unpleasant incidents has led to disputes which have introduced some instability in Sino-U.S. relations,'' said Huan Xiang, the director of the Center for International Studies, writing in the authoritative Beijing Review.
''The influence of destabilizing factors on the development of relations between China and the United States may haunt us for the next decade or more,'' Mr. Huan said. 
He outlined six problems in relations between the two nations, among them American sanctions for what the Reagan Administration has charged were Chinese arms sales to Iran; Congressional displeasure over China's record on human rights; Washington's continued arms sales to Taiwan and the Administration's continuing criticism of China's family planning programs. 
He also cited Congressional resolutions that criticized China's handling of demonstrations in Tibet and - in the one area where he conceded some unhappiness might be warranted - impatience with the pace of China's ''opening up to the outside world.''
'Political Blackmail' Charged
''The six problems,'' Mr. Huan said, ''amount to nothing short of interference in China's internal affairs and political blackmail. 
They are a blatant demonstration of hegemonism and represent a threat to stable Sino-U.S. relations.''
Insisting that China has not ''directly sold weapons to Iran,'' Mr. Huan lashed out at the Administration's decision to suspend consideration of further high-technology exports to China.
''This is purely political blackmail, and by no means conforms with the principle of equality in international relations,'' Mr. Huan said. 
''It is both damaging to the future of bilateral relations, as well as to the image of the United States.''
Mr. Huan also assailed the Congressional resolutions dealing with China's handling of pro-independence demonstrations in Tibet late last year, during which at least a dozen Tibetan Buddhist monks and civilians were killed.
Â 
Different Views of Human Rights
''Regarding American attacks on China under the guise of safeguarding human rights,'' Mr. Huan wrote, ''I must say that we define the term 'human rights' differently, according to our value concepts. 
Neither of us should force his views on the other.''
''The U.S. 
Congress is the legislative body of the United States, not of China, nor the world. 
Neither the Chinese nor the American people have authorized it to administer Chinese affairs,'' wrote Mr. Huan, a member of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, the country's legislature.
Chinese officials and the Government-controlled press have criticized American policy toward China repeatedly in recent months. 
But Mr. Huan's essay is by far the longest and most severe assessment of the state of relations between the two countries and it employed a harshness of language not seen in some time.
In the one instance in which Mr. Huan suggested that United States criticism of China might be warranted, he wrote: ''The United States has leveled criticisms at China's bureaucracy and inadequate legislation in its work of opening up to the outside world and especially on the issue of foreign investment. 
Some of the criticisms are reasonable and China has accepted them and is ready to make further efforts to improve its work.''

file: CHINESE OFFICIAL URGES MODERATION.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's acting Prime Minister, Li Peng, opened the annual session of parliament today with a call to continue the economic and political initiatives that have dramatically affected the lives of the nation's one billion people.
But his call was tempered by an insistence that China should not go too far too fast.
''The Government should put reform at the center of all our undertakings,'' Mr. Li said, but urged officials to ''take into account what the state, the enterprises and the masses can tolerate.''
Mr. Li delivered his remarks, a review of the nation's accomplishments and prospects, at the opening session of the National People's Congress, China's lawmaking body. 
Attended by 2,978 delegates, the congress is to solidify the constitutional and legal bases of the country's economic restructuring, approve the appointment of new ministers and ratify the reorganization of parts of the Government.
For the first time in the four decades of Communist rule, constitutional protection will be accorded to private enterprise and the right of people to buy and sell the right to use land in what amounts to the re-emergence of private property.
Â 
Hard-Liners Are Quiet
Gone from this year's congress is the ideological breast-beating that dominated proceedings 12 months ago, when party hard-liners sought to whip up opposition to ''bourgeois liberalization.''
Instead, pragmatism, economic growth and Government restructuring are the new orthodoxy.
The public is being barraged with newspaper and radio coverage of the day's developments at the congress.
Debate among the delegates, often vigorously pursued, is also being shown on television for the first time.
Mr. Li, a 59-year-old engineer who was trained in the Soviet Union, is expected to be confirmed as Prime Minister at the congress. 
He was named to the post in an acting capacity when Zhao Ziyang resigned to become head of the Communist Party last November.
Many diplomats here said they were watching Mr. Li to see how aggressively he would push the policies of economic restructuring and rapid growth propounded by Mr. Zhao.
Â 
Grain Policy Is Upheld
Standing behind a thick wooden lectern, Mr. Li spoke to the delegates for slightly more than two and a half hours, outlining plans for the coming five years.
He began by addessing China's policy of self-sufficiency in grain, a central economic concern of the more traditional wing of China's leadership. 
Many young Chinese economists disparage this policy, arguing that some farmland is more profitably used for cash crops.
''The steady growth of agricultural production, especially grain production, is the foundation for sustained economic development,'' Mr. Li said.
Mr. Li cajoled, exhorted and occasionally rebuked the lethargic bureaucracy that is to carry out his Government's policies, which were set forth last fall by the Communist Party.
He said China's enterprises, from state factories to local general stores, must abandon archaic management practices and encourage autonomy for directors and managers.
Mr. Li said housing must be commercialized so that it is bought, sold and rented like refrigerators or bicycles. 
Housing is now the most heavily subsidized element of the economy and something often doled out in a system of party and Government patronage.

file: Chinese Order a Japanese Reporter to Leave.txt
text:
ï»¿
China ordered a Japanese journalist to leave the country within 10 days today, after accusing him of stealing information related to national security.
The expulsion order marked the third time in 10 months that China had forced a foreign journalist to leave the country and came at a time of mounting tension between China and Japan.
The reporter, Shuitsu Henmi, a correspondent for Kyodo News Service of Japan, said he was informed by officials from the Ministry of State Security that he would have to leave China because he had collected information that was regarded as intelligence. 
Mr. Henmi said he was not told the nature of that information.
In the last week, Chinese officials have heightened their verbal attacks on Japan over a range of issues, including accusations of growing Japanese militarism, complaints about a continuing trade deficit with Japan and an adverse ruling by a Japanese court that gave a contested parcel of real estate to Taiwan.
Mr. Henmi's expulsion order comes after the deportation of a journalist for Agence France-Presse in February on charges of receiving restricted internal documents, and the arrest and expulsion of a correspondent for The New York Times last July for entering a restricted area.
Â 
No Response to Queries
Someone who answered the phone at the Ministry of Public Security told a caller to phone again Saturday, and the telephone at the information office of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs was not answered this evening.
Mr. Henmi, who spoke Chinese fluently and who is well-regarded among foreign journalists here, is known for his extensive contacts with Chinese officials. 
His reports in recent months have focused on the tensions within the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party since the dismissal of Hu Yaobang as Party leader in January. 
He has also written extensively about internal Party documents that criticized Mr. Hu and that outlined the campaign against Western ideas.
Â 
He Denies Impropriety
Mr. Henmi, who has been in China since June, tonight denied any impropriety in his news gathering. 
''I absolutely did not use any irregular means,'' he said, referring to his acquisition of documents from the Central Committee of the Communist Party. 
''Even some Chinese officials of the information department of the Foreign Ministry said they were not national intelligence because some parts of them were published.''

file: CHINESE PREMIER, IN MAJOR SPEECH, ADOPTS HARD LINE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang told the Chinese people today that his Government's economic initiatives would continue. 
But he denounced ''pernicious'' Western ideas and demanded a tight rein on intellectual and artistic expression.
In the opening address to the National People's Congress, the country's legislature, Mr. Zhao acknowledged serious economic problems, including low productivity, widespread inefficiency, trade and budget deficits and runaway spending on construction projects.
The speech offered the first broad insight into both the Government's economic plans and the political temperament since the ouster of Hu Yaobang as leader of the Communist Party in mid-January in a campaign against Western ideas and values.
The 2,719 delegates to the People's Congress, gathered in the Great Hall of the People for a 16-day session, applauded as Mr. Hu strode onto the stage in his first public appearance in three months. 
On Tuesday a spokesman for the National Peoples Congress said Mr. Hu had been re-elected to the 157-member presidium.
The spokesman, Zeng Tao, also said the assembly would not name a new Prime Minister despite the fact that Mr. Zhao holds both the senior Government and senior party posts. 
Mr. Zeng said there would be no major changes in China's leadership at least until September, when a Communist Party congress is scheduled.
Â 
Many Difficulties Remain
Prime Minister Zhao, in his nationally televised address, said, ''We must be keenly aware that we still face many difficulties in our advance and that our work is not free from mistakes and problems.''
In addressing those difficulties, Mr. Zhao said, the nation must dramatically increase agricultural and industrial output, stem the increase in consumer spending and maintain Marxist political orthodoxy.
He said Government spending will be cut by 10 percent from last year's expenditures and investment in projects like hotels and office buildings will be reduced.
Nonetheless, Mr. Zhao insisted that China's economic initiatives, intended to infuse the economy with Western management techniques and market mechanisms, would continue, although he acknowledged that some would be slowed.
Since January, a group of hard-line party leaders, represented most prominently by the chairman of the National People's Congress, Peng Zhen, have spoken repeatedly about the need for caution in pursuing the economic program and have urged a reassertion of some traditional socialist economic practices, such as a renewed emphasis on central planning.
Â 
A Sartorial Contrast
Mr. Zhao, in a light gray suit, blue shirt and dark tie, provided a sartorial contrast to Mr. Peng, seated on his right in a dark blue, high-collared Mao jacket.
The Prime Minister urged the fulfillment of what he called the ''two major tasks'' for the coming year: to ''increase production and practice economy'' and to ''combat bourgeois liberalization,'' the catch phrase for Western political and ethical ideas.
In outlining the economic program, Mr. Zhao stressed the need to increase agricultural output, particularly grain production. 
Hard-line leaders have expressed dissatisfaction with with the growing number of peasants who, instead of rice and wheat, are growing vegetables or other crops that can be sold on the free market at higher prices.
Mr. Zhao devoted a significant portion of his speech to ideological questions and repeatedly denounced the intrusion of Western ideas into China. 
''Immense efforts must be made to eliminate the pernicious influence of this erroneous ideological trend,'' he said.

file: CHINESE REPORT THEY BEAT BACK VIETNAM ATTACK.txt
text:
ï»¿
China announced Friday that its frontier guards repulsed a large-scale attack by Vietnam Thursday across their tense border after 10 hours of heavy combat.
A dispatch by the official New China News Agency from what it said was the front line in Yunnan Province, where another battle was reported a month ago, said that after the fighting, ''the invaders fled in utter confusion.''
It said Chinese troops, working in the rain, had fortified their positions in preparation for a new attack.
Â 
First Reported by Vietnam
The border hostilities were confirmed by the Vietnamese News Agency. 
It accused China of shelling Ha Tuyen Province, which abuts Yunnan, with artillery and rockets since early July, killing civilians and seriously damaging property.
Vietnam has accused China of creating border incidents to tie down Vietnamese troops and take pressure off guerrillas in Cambodia who are fighting Vietnamese occupation forces there. 
China supports the Cambodian guerrillas, while the Vietnamese, who invaded Cambodia at the end of 1978 and installed the regime of Heng Samrin, are allies of the Soviet Union.
Chinese newspapers and radio carried the first domestic reports of the fighting Friday morning. 
The armed forces newspaper, Liberation Army accused Vietnam of taking ''a new ferocious step on its wrong road against China.''
The initial dispatch of the New China News Agency Thursday night said a Vietnamese division with artillery support mounted an incursion into Malipo County in Yunnan at 5 A.M. Thursday local time. 
But it said the Vietnamese ran into stiff resistance from Chinese frontier guards, who stood their ground and inflicted heavy casualties.
Â 
Battle Reported Over
''Fierce fighting was still going on at sunset,'' the Chinese press agency said Thursday night. 
Its report Friday implied that the battle was over, at least for the time being.
A broadcast by the Voice of Vietnam, monitored in Bangkok today, repeated the Vietnam News Agency report that Chinese gunners had fired 5,000 artillery shells into two districts of Ha Tuyen Province this month. 
But it made no mention of the battle that China said took place Thursday.
The Vietnamese radio also said more than 200,000 artillery shells had been fired into Vietnam's six northernmost provinces from China in the last two months, wounding hundreds of civilians and destroying homes and property.
There was no way to confirm the accuracy of either version, since independent observers have not been allowed into the remote area. 
Similar recriminations have been traded off and on over the last three months. 
Foreign diplomats in Hanoi and Peking believe that reports on both sides tend to be exaggerated for greater propaganda effect.
The reports of border clashes have been circulated since early April, which is far longer than the duration reported in previous years. 
The tensions in the past coincided with Vietnam's spring offensive against Chinese-backed guerrillas in Cambodia and tapered off as the fighting there wound down.
Members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations reportedly told the United States and other ''partner'' nations at a meeting in Indonesia Thursday that the anti-Vietnamese coalition in Cambodia was ''working very well'' and causing serious military problems for Hanoi.
Â 
Frontier Guards Exhorted
Liberation Army Daily, which is read in the Chinese armed forces, contended today that hostilities with Vietnam were continuing. 
If the Vietnamese provoked border incidents, the newspaper said, ''we can do nothing but hit them back in self-defense and fight to the finish.''
It urged China's frontier guards, who operate as light infantrymen with artillery support, to defend every inch of Chinese territory and hit back hard at Vietnamese attackers. 
Liberation Army Daily is not permitted reading for foreigners, but the New China News Agency took the unusual step of circulating extracts of the article to give it greater authority.
Liberation Army Daily charged that Vietnam was committing fresh troops to its continuing border conflicts because it regarded China as the biggest obstacle to its aggressive ambitions of controlling Southeast Asia.
Â 
New Strains With Soviet
The latest reports of fighting come at a time when Moscow's support of Hanoi has caused new strains in Chinese-Soviet relations. 
On June 25, Liberation Army Daily accused the Soviet Union of inciting the Vietnamese to engage in ''armed provocations'' along the border. 
Otherwise, it said, ''the Vietnamese authorities could not have been so brazen in their outrages.''
Last week the weekly magazine Outlook called Vietnam's ''strategic alliance'' with the Soviet Union the root of tension and turbulence in Southeast Asia. 
Peking has charged that Moscow is using Vietnam as a forward base for its hegemonistic strategy in Asia and the Pacific.
Vietnam has leveled similar charges at China. 
On Thursday, Vietnam's Foreign Minister, Nguyen Co Thach, said China had launched an ''absolutely unprovoked attack'' at several points along their border. 
Mr. Thach, who was flying to Mongolia, another Soviet ally, for a visit, contended that Asia should guard against China's ''new expansionist designs.''
Â 
Terrain Is Rugged
The clashes along the Chinese-Vietnamese border are confined to a rugged terrain of densely vegetated mountains, limestone cliffs and narrow valleys and streams, which would normally restrict the scope of military operations. 
The reported fighting seems to be over the high ground that can dominate both sides of the border.
Friday's Chinese press accounts observed that Vietnam mounted a regimental-sized attack in the same area of Malipo County earlier on June 11. 
Chinese frontier guards said then that they repulsed six Vietnamese assaults that day, inflicting heavy casualties.
By contrast, the Vietnamese claimed to have retaken three Chinese positions dug a half mile inside Ha Tuyen province, capturing ''many'' Chinese prisoners and seizing 12 artillery pieces and 6 mortars.
The New China News Agency quoted Chinese military sources as saying the Vietnamese spent a month preparing for Thursday's attack, a period that would have given Chinese troops time to reinforce their positions.

file: CHINESE SAYS TAIWAN IS STILL MAIN ISSUE.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's Foreign Minister called on the United States yesterday to cease any ''official or semiofficial'' relations with Taiwan.
In his first public speech in this country, the Foreign Minister, Wu Xueqian, said the continuing contacts between Washington and Taipei were the basic obstacle to improved relations between the United States and China, and he demanded that the United States reduce its arms sales to Taiwan.
''As far as the bilateral relations between China and the United States are concerned,'' he said, ''the principal obstacle is the issue of Taiwan.''
China's Foreign Minister, Wu Xueqian, in New York for opening of UN, says continuing contacts between Washington and Taiwan are basic obstacle to improved relations between US and China; claims Taiwan is 'inalienable part of China's territory' (M)His First Visit to U.S.
It was the first visit to the United States by Mr. Wu, who was appointed Foreign Minister in November 1982. 
He is in New York for the opening of the United Nations General Assembly, which he will address on Tuesday. 
Mr. Wu's remarks came in an speech before the National Committee on United States-China Relations at the Waldorf- Astoria Hotel.
''If the United States truly desires to see a peaceful settlement of the Taiwan question,'' Mr. Wu said, ''it should refrain from doing anything detrimental to the peaceful reunification of China, refrain from having any offical or semiofficial relations with Taiwan and gradually reduce, both qualitatively and quantitatively, its arms sales to Taiwan, leading to a final termination.''
''Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory, and the people of Taiwan are our own flesh and blood,'' Mr. Wu said. 
''Therefore, the question of Taiwan is an important one involving China's sovereignty and the national feeling of the one billion people.''
Â 
Two-Edged Approach
Mr. Wu's comments reflected Peking's two-edged approach to the issue of Taiwan. 
On the one hand, China has tried, largely through public pronouncements, to persuade other nations to cut off their relations with Taiwan. 
On the other hand, Peking, whose posture has continued to evolve in the last 18 months, has most recently sought to reassure Taipei that Taiwan would be able to retain its social and economic systems after reunification.
After reunification, Mr. Wu said, ''while it is the People's Republic of China alone that will continue to represent China on the international arena, Taiwan as a special administrative region can maintain systems different from those of the mainland.''
Mr. Wu delivered only the opening and closing paragraphs of his speech. 
The body of the address was read to the 200 guests of the National Committee in English by a Chinese Government interpreter.
The Chinese Foreign Minister responded to American concerns that his country's relations with the Soviet Union might also affect relations with Washington.
''Such views do not tally with reality,'' he said. 
''China has always adhered to principles, neither playing the Soviet card to put pressure on the United States, nor playing the American card to put pressure on the Soviet Union. 
Mr. Wu said in response to a question after his address that while China regretted and was shocked at the shooting down of the Korean Air Lines jet by the Soviet Union, his country had abstained from the Security Council vote condemning the Soviet action because ''some circumstances leading to the downing are not quite clear.''

file: Chinese Student Is Convicted For Role in Shanghai Protests.txt
text:
ï»¿
An American-educated student was convicted in Shanghai today of conducting ''demagogical propaganda for counterrevolutionary ends,'' the Government-controlled New China News Agency announced.
The student, Yang Wei, a 32-year-old molecular biologist, is the first person to be tried for counterrevolutionary acts supposedly committed in the protests a year ago.
Foreign observers were banned from observing the trial.
In recent months, the case has become a source of friction between China and the United States because of a Senate resolution calling on the Chinese Government to release him. 
In addition, a group of Chinese students in the United States signed a petition to Zhao Ziyang, the Communist Party leader, urging that Mr. Yang not be prosecuted.
Â 
Arrested in January
Mr. Yang, who studied at the University of Arizona, was arrested Jan. 
11 and has been detained since. 
Senior officials from the United States Government have repeatedly sought to obtain an explanation for Mr. Yang's arrest from the Chinese but have been rebuffed, according to American diplomats here.
Mr. Yang's wife is a doctoral candidate at the Baylor College of Medicine in Houston and a physician, Officials at the Shanghai intermediate court and the city's foreign affairs bureau both confirmed earlier in the day that Mr. Yang had gone on trial, but they refused to say what the charges against him were, how long the trial would last or where it was being held. 
They also refused to say when they would provide information about Mr. Yang's fate. 
But late this evening, the New China News Agency announced Mr. Yang's conviction. 
[In New York, the head of a Chinese dissident group said Mr. Yang was sentenced to two years in prison, The Associated Press reported. 
The official, Wang Bingzhang, president of the New York-based Chinese Alliance for Democracy, said he had learned of the sentenced from Mr. Yang's relatives. 
Mr. Wang called the sentence light and credited pressure from the United States.] 'Changing the System in China'
The New China News Agency said that Mr. Yang joined the Chinese Alliance of Democracy while was in the United States. 
The agency contended the group's aim was ''fundamentally changing the autocratic system in China.''
Mr. Yang was said to have written articles for the magazine China Spring, a banned publication that often attacks the suppression of human and democratic rights in China.
''After he returned to Shanghai in May 1986, the court was told,'' according to the press agency report, ''Yang was active in collecting information about students' unrest at the end of 1986 and secretly sent materials back to the headquarters of the alliance.

file: CHINESE TAKE A LIKING TO THEIR GUEST.txt
text:
