For all the controversy over the earlier censorship of some of his televised remarks, President Reagan appears to have created a positive impression among many Chinese.

President Reagan, visiting China, appears to have created positive impression among many Chinese; interviews with Chinese people indicate his skill as great communicator has served him well in China; photo (M)Thousands Line the Streets
Monday, hundreds of thousands of curious Chinese lined the streets of Shanghai to watch his motorcade go by, and the turnout testified to the interest that has been generated by the first visit of an incumbent United States President since Chinese- American relations were established more than five years ago.
But interviews with more than two dozen Chinese in Peking and Shanghai suggest that many people have been interested not only in what he had to say but how he said it. 
Indeed, President Reagan has shown that his skill as a great communicator at home has served him as well here in China.None of those interviewed seemed aware that Mr. Reagan's implicit criticisms of the Soviet Union and his affirmations of God, capitalism and Western-style freedoms had been deleted from his remarks that were subsequently televised to an audience estimated at more than one million people on Friday and Saturday nights.

Looking for Practical Results
The students at Fudan University who listened to Mr. Reagan Monday seemed to be mainly interested in the practical ramifications of closer cooperation between China and the United States. 
Many educated Chinese hope that increased contacts will accelerate the infusion of United States technology that China wants for its modernization drive.
''We think Reagan's visit is good because it will help develop economic relations on both sides,'' said a science undergraduate who was one of 700 students, mostly from the Communist Youth League, who were selected to attend Mr. Reagan's university speech. 
''It will be beneficial and open more opportunities for Chinese students to go and study in the United States.''
A couple of other Fudan University students said Mr. Reagan's visit had produced some immediate dividends: the university authorities had allocated money to renovate the auditorium where the President spoke Monday and to spruce up the campus.

Limited Exposure to China
Just as Mr. Reagan's brief sojourn of six days has given him a limited exposure to China, not unlike that of any tourist, so the issues that Mr. Reagan discussed with the Chinese leadership have been filtered through the official press, giving Chinese a selective acquaintance with his views.

A Chinese journalist said Mr. Reagan's visit, for all its glamour, would have to be measured in retrospect by progress on the Taiwan question.
Most of the Chinese interviewed answered questions on such political issues as if they were being tested on their knowledge of People's Daily. 
''The Chinese people warmly welcome his visit to China,'' recited a telecommunications engineer. 
''It will play an important role in relations between our two peoples.''
Â 
Flattered by Use of Proverbs
Several Chinese said they were flattered by Mr. Reagan's frequent use of Chinese proverbs, which were supplied by United States specialists on China and subsequently put back into Chinese by the translators.
''It seems that he understands China very well,'' said a cheerful clerk sitting behind the counter of one bookstore. 
''He quotes our proverbs very well.''
Despite the substantial publicity given to Mr. Reagan's visit in the press, some people paid it little or no attention. 
A grizzled peasant visiting from the countryside acted startled to discover that President Reagan was indeed in China. 
And an army officer used the conversation to reminisce about the ''excellent performance'' that he had seen an American basketball team give in China.
Though Mr. Reagan clearly generated good will among the Chinese, several of those interviewed indicated that they were waiting to see what emerged from his visit.

text:

China today announced plans for its first high-level official visit to Laos since relations between the two Communist neighbors were frozen in 1979.
The Foreign Ministry spokesman, Ma Yuzhen, said Deputy Foreign Minister Liu Shuqing would visit Laos from Saturday to Thursday at the invitation of the Laotian Foreign Ministry.
Diplomats said it would be the first such visit since China and Laos froze relations at the charge d'affaires level after the 1979 Vietnamese invasion of Cambodia.
Laos is a close ally of the Soviet Union and Vietnam, which has about 50,000 troops in Laos.
In August, the Foreign Ministers of Laos, Vietnam and Vietnamese-occupied Cambodia issued a statement calling for talks with China. 
The overture came less than a month after the Soviet leader, Mikhail S. Gorbachev, urged closer ties between the Communist nations of Asia.
Beijing responded that it welcomed proposals for improved relations with Vientiane but said there was ''no point'' in talking with Vietnam until it withdrew its estimated 140,000 troops from Cambodia.

But he rejected recent Soviet and Vietnamese calls for closer ties between Beijing and Hanoi.

''But Vietnam must withdraw all its troops from Cambodia and stop its hostilities against China.''
Vietnam and China fought a monthlong border war in 1979 after Hanoi's forces ousted the Chinese-backed Khmer Rouge regime in Cambodia. 
The two nations have reported many border clashes since.

file: Chinese Visitor Admires Home Built for Disabled.txt
text:
ï»¿
An official guest from China came to the Parrinos' home here in this Westchester County village today, and as he pushed himself from room to room in a wheelchair, he commented on the wide, smooth hallways and the picture-window views of the outdoors.
Features such as those, he told his hosts through a translator, could help disabled people like himself to forget they were restricted at all.
The visitor was Deng Pufang, the eldest son of China's pre-eminent leader, Deng Xiaoping. 
His public role as director in chief of the China Fund for the Handicapped, which is intended to aid disabled people in his country, stems from personal misfortune.
Nearly 20 years ago, during China's Cultural Revolution, Deng Pufang was paralyzed from the waist down in his senior year at Beijing University.
Â 
Active and Visible Spokesman
The cause was not accidental, but coincided with the period of political disfavor for his father, who at the time had been stripped of his post as Secretary General of the Communist Party and made a factory hand.
Red Guards came to Deng Pufang's room on the upper floor of a dormitory, where they attacked him and then either pushed him or forced him to jump to the ground.
Mr. Deng will probably never walk again, but the changing political fortunes of his father have allowed him in recent years to become an active and visible spokesman for the disabled in China and abroad. 
The connection to his father has apparently also allowed him, through treatment abroad, a measure of health not available to thousands of others who were victims of physical attacks in the Cultural Revolution.
The road that led Deng Pufang to Briarcliff Manor, at the start of his first trip to the United States, began with a meeting last year in China with Sandra Swift Parrino, chairwoman of the National Council on the Handicapped, an independent Federal agency.
Â 
Understanding and Respect
Mrs. Swift's eldest son became a quadriplegic shortly after his first birthday because of an illness that has never been fully diagnosed. 
When she and her husband, Dick, built a house in Briarcliff Manor, they designed it, wherever possible, to be accessible by wheelchair.
Mr. Deng, who is 43 years old, took a particular interest in the Parrinos' home. 
He and a variety of Chinese officials, in advance of a series of meetings this month in New York City, Washington, Florida and California, visited the Parrinos' home, where they asked questions about policies toward the disabled in this country. 
Mr. Deng later took a brief tour of the home, perhaps looking for ideas for his own home in Beijing, although an official in his position would be unlikely to concede such a thing.
The discussion on programs here ranged from centers for independent living to automated lifts in public buses, which caused Mr. Deng to ask who paid for such amenities. 
''There must be a conflict between your Council for the Handicapped and your Department of the Treasury,'' he said.
Mr. Deng, whose vigorous hand motions and square, deep jaw seemed to reflect the same determination as his father, listened intently and nodded when the executive director of the National Council on the Handicapped, Lex Frieden, described the ''subtle, psychological and often inadvertent'' ways that handicapped people face discrimination in this country.
That problem was no different in China, Deng Pufang said. 
The toughest battles faced by the disabled are often not against their own disability, he said, but against the reactions of others.
For that reason, Mr. Deng said he was urging a policy of four steps to treatment of the disabled, which he said could apply not only in his country but anywhere.
''First must come understanding of the disabled, and then respect,'' he said. 
''Then concern, and then help. 
Otherwise, if it's only the last two, then it is not really help at all, but only pity.''

file: CHINESE VISITOR LEARNS OF LAWS AND U.S. WAYS.txt
text:

A most unsettling thing happened one night while Shen Shiao-ming was studying at her carrel at the law library of Southern Methodist University.
''Someone knocked on my door with a long terrible white face, and long white hair,'' she recalled, ''So white, so long, it scared me. 
I thought it must be a poor American person. 
I thought I didn't get in touch with the poor people here, and now they are coming here for me.''
Shen Shiao-ming becomes first person from People's Republic of China to receive law degree from US law school
Only after she fled in horror did she learn that the ogre was a Halloween prankster, celebrating a holiday that she did not know existed. 
But keeping up with American holidays was the least of the adjustments in the last year for Miss Shen, who this month became the first person from the People's Republic of China to receive a degree from an American law school.
Â 
Awarded Masters Degree
For Miss Shen, law school in America meant coping with a new language, a different legal tradition and a different academic world. 
But in her 10 months here, she completed 11 courses worth 24 hours of credit to earn her master's degree in comparative laws.
Miss Shen, a 33-year-old specialist in China's new law on joint business ventures with foreign countries, also published a study on that law in the university's law journal.
Among the joint ventures between China and foreign companies that have been authorized by China's Foreign Investment Commission are an airline, several hotels and a textile corporation.
Miss Shen now plans to work with the New York law firm of Sherman & Sterling before returning to China sometime next year.
Â 
Education in China
Miss Shen grew up in Hangzhou, a cultural and university center of about one million people. 
She received her first degree from the Peking Institute of Political Science and Law in 1964 and completed graduate work, specializing in civil law, at the Law Institute at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences in 1967.
Her law career was interrupted for almost 10 years by China's Cultural Revolution, which virtually closed down research at the Law Institute. 
From 1970 to 1972, she and her colleagues spent their time in the countryside working with farmers, but by 1975 she was able to resume her studies in law and foreign languages.
She is now associated with the Law Institute, which is instrumental in drafting China's legislation. 
Miss Shen was involved in various projects, including research in the areas of admiralty law, trademarks and investments, and in 1978 met a delegation from the American Bar Association traveling in China.
Among the group was Beverly May Carl, a law professor at Southern Methodist University, who suggested that Miss Shen study at the university here. 
Four corporate sponsors, Hunt Oil Company, Ensearch Company, Mobil Oil and LTV Corporation, paid her expenses, and Miss Shen spent the last year specializing in law that will facilitate trade between the United States and China.
Â 
Differences Are Noted
''It is very different here,'' Miss Shen said. 
''Ours is civil law; yours is case law. 
And the law courses are very different here. 
Law students here study very hard. 
Every day undergraduates here have a party as if it is always someone's birthday. 
I don't think law students have so much fun. 
Maybe Friday night, they have a drink or go to a party or something, but everyone mostly just studies.''
She is also aware that lawyers here seem to be viewed with a good deal more suspicion than those in China. 
''Here someone said: 'They don't like the lawyers, but they need them. 
Everywhere they need them.'
In China, there is not such a strong feeling toward lawyers.''
Miss Shen's year at the university here has been marked by a steady stream of businesses and law firms seeking to consult with her about Chinese trade. 
Most are interested in China's trade laws, particularly its joint venture law.

text:

The drive to professionalize China's armed forces took a step forward today with the announcement that 47,000 officers, about a tenth of the officer corps, will be retired before the end of 1986.
The announcement had political ramifications since the officers involved are mostly men who joined Mao Zedong's guerrilla forces before the Communists seized power in China in 1949. 
Although there has been an official retirement policy for 25 years, the practice had been to allow those who took part in the guerrilla struggle to remain in uniform until they died or voluntarily stepped aside.
Deng Xiaoping, the 80-year-old army veteran who holds pre-eminent political power, has made the remaking of the army one of his priorities. 
He wants to replace the poorly educated peasant boys who made the revolution by younger, better-trained men.
Chinese Government announces that 47,000 military officers, about 10% of officer corps, will be retired before end of 1986 in effort to professionalize country's military; political impact noted in light of fact that most officers joined Mao Zedong's guerrilla forces before Communists seized power in 1949 (M)Aim Is to Curb Army Influence
Mr. Deng has political as well as military objectives. 
By clearing the officer corps of revolutionary veterans, he hopes to curb the political influence wielded by the army in the past, often in favor of the so-called leftist policies Mr. Deng has discarded. 
He has also said that the army, which had a woeful experience in the 1979 war against Vietnam, must be modernized.
The New China News Agency said the officers being retired were men who joined up in the war against the Japanese occupation forces in the 1930's, or in the civil war against the Nationalists between 1945 and 1949. 
Most of them had achieved junior rank up to regimental level, the agency said, indicating that they were mostly the equivalent of majors, or less.
The retirees were said to be part of a larger group of 70,000 to 80,000 officers designated to retire in the next few years, the press agency said. 
Western military attaches said this suggested that a decision had been taken to retire officers as they reach the nominal retirement age of 60, except at higher command levels. 
An example is the commander of the armed forces, Yang Dezhi, a Deng appointee who is 75.
The move to purge the junior officer corps has been accompanied by pressure on veteran senior officers, thousands of whom have been retired since 1980. 
Late last year, Mr. Deng obtained the retirement of 40 officers on the command staff who held ranks equivalent to lieutenant general and higher.
The halting progress in carrying out the retirement policy appears to reflect resistance among those affected as well as constraints on Mr. Deng's own political power. 
At times he has sounded testy on the subject, as when he struck out in 1982 at officers whom he called ''undisciplined, arrogant, extravagant and lazy.''
When he was purged twice during the Cultural Revolution, between 1966 and 1973 and again in 1976-77, Mr. Deng was under army guard in provincial exile.
Â 
Better Pensions Offered
As compensation for retirement, there has been a drive to improve pensions and other benefits. 
The New China News Agency said today that 30,000 apartments had been built for retiring officers and that the Ministry of Civil Affairs, which cares for the retirees, had appointed a special staff to look after their needs. 
One point of strain has been an order that retiring officers vacate their army quarters.
Similar policies have been applied among the nine million party workers in civilian jobs. 
The Central Committee's Party Organization Department, in charge of personnel, said recently that 900,000 party workers over the age of 60 had retired, allowing 80,000 professionally competent middle-aged party workers to be appointed to responsible posts.
Mr. Deng has laid stress on promoting men in their 30's and 40's, saying that it is to them that China must look for leadership for the rest of the century. 
In the armed forces, General Yang has stipulated that division commanders should be about 45, with regimental commanders 40 or younger.

file: CHINESE-U.S. RELATIONS TAKE A MORE REALISTIC DIRECTION.txt
text:
ï»¿
If China's rhetoric can be believed, two of its fondest friends are the North Korean President, Kim Il Sung, and the ousted Cambodian guerrilla leader Pol Pot, whose notoriety has isolated them elsewhere. 
By contrast, the United States gets lumped with the Soviet Union as hegemonistic superpowers who pose the real threat to the peaceloving world.
But an old Chinese proverb counsels: ''Listen to what a person says and then watch what he does.''
This week Chinese Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang visits the United States as head of a Government that has distanced itself from Washington since diplomatic relations were established on Jan. 
1, 1979, but that nonetheless retains common interest on a range of issues.
In the last five years, perceptions on both sides have matured, sometimes painfully, into a more sober realism about the limitations as well as the potential of the relationship. 
Antagonisms persist over the future of Taiwan and lesser problems, even as interdependence increases on other fronts. 
Mr. Zhao, who is expected in Washington tomorrow and will see Mr. Reagan Wednesday, set a conciliatory tone for the visit last week when he spoke at a news conference of ''great progress'' in relations between the two countries.
For complex reasons, China welcomed strategic cooperation with the United States in 1979. 
The Vietnamese had invaded Cambodia, ousting Pol Pot's regime. 
Before retaliating with a punitive invasion of Vietnam, China wanted a link with the United States to discourage a comparable Soviet response on its northern border. 
The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan that year confirmed the value of such an alliance for Peking. 
The Chinese and American outlooks still coincide on the Cambodian and Afghanistan invasions, and converge on some other areas threatened by the Kremlin's ambitions. 
But the bilateral relationship suffered from an American failure to live up to China's grand expectations. 
Peking hoped that the severing of official ties between the United States and Taiwan would demoralize the nationalist regime there and force it to negotiate with the mainland. 
Instead, Taiwan has prospered, while enjoying new infusions of American military aid. 
Mr. Zhao said last week he would not press for an immediate end to arms shipments to Taiwan but indicated he would remind Washington of its pledge to phase the sales out. 
Peking also expected its friendship with the United States to produce a cornucopia of capital and technology for China's modernization. 
This was obstructed by high interest rates and tight controls on the export of computers and other sophisticated hardware. 
The lack of a quick technological fix from the United States was interpreted by China as a deliberate slight. 
Coziness with the United States also hurt China's standing with other developing countries, where American policies are not popular. 
This discovery produced a shift in late 1981 toward conspicuous nonalignment. 
China shelved strategic cooperation and revived its superpower label for the United States - a change owing in large part to the election of Ronald Reagan, whose campaign remarks in support of Taiwan upset the Chinese. 
Mr. Reagan's tough approach to Moscow also left China freer to moderate its hostility toward the Soviet Union and agree to talk about improving strained relations. 
The Chinese-American communique of August 1982 clarified the Reagan Administration's position on Taiwan but fell short of dissipating the ill will. 
By last winter, the Chinese seemed to see little prospect of getting along with Mr. Reagan. They were consequently surprised by his decision to relax substantially controls on technology exports, which involved reclassifying China from a potential adversary to friendly nonaligned country. 
This week, an accord on industrial cooperation by which both sides would facilitate private investment in China is due to be signed during Mr. Zhao's stay in Washington. 
A treaty defining investors' rights may be ready when Mr. Reagan visits Peking, probably in April.
Other aspects of the relationship have also expanded. 
Although bilateral trade declined in 1983 because the Chinese stopped buying grain to protest a temporary imposition of import quotas on its textiles, total trade is still expected to exceed $4.2 billion. 
That is four times the figure for 1978, before diplomatic ties were established. 
United States officials estimate that at least 120,000 Americans visited China in 1983, compared with fewer than 10,000 in 1978. 
Some 13,000 Chinese students and scholars are studying in the United States, up from virtually zero five years ago. 
Chinese delegations are visiting the United States at the rate of 200 a month, a tenfold rise over five years ago. 
China remains beholden to its self-image as a revolutionary nation. 
''The Chinese want to think of themselves as Communists,'' said an Eastern European diplomat. 
This may help explain why they claim to feel more comfortable with Kim Il Sung or Pol Pot than with President Reagan. 
But when Mr. Zhao comes to Washington this week, his baggage will be lighter with the absence of the old illusions about Chinese-American relations.

file: COMMERCIAL RENTS IN CHINATOWN SOAR AS HONG KONG EXODUS GROWS.txt
text:
ï»¿
A flood of immigrants from Hong Kong has pushed commercial rents in New York's Chinatown up to the levels of midtown, making the real estate in one untidy corner of Manhattan among the most expensive in the United States.
The demand for space is so strong, local real estate brokers say, that the operators of vegetable stalls near the bustling intersection of Catherine and Division Streets pay more rent per square foot than the owners of Tiffany & Company at Fifth Avenue and 57th Street. 
City officials describe the frenzy in the Chinatown real estate market as ''hysteria.''
''Everytime you turn around the prices have shot up again,'' said Michael Dirzulaitis, an assistant commissioner in the city's Division of Real Property, which has been involved in several development projects in Chinatown this year. 
''It's hard to believe that there is enough money around to keep it going, but there is.''
The pressures on Chinatown have been building for some time. 
But they have been given added urgency by the exodus of people and capital from Hong Kong in advance of the 1997 deadline for Britain to turn the colony over to China.
New York's Chinatown is not big enough to absorb much of Hong Kong's wealth. 
The largest real estate deal in the works in the neighborhood is about $18 million, tiny by Manhattan standards and modest even by those of other cities.
The money coming in from Hong Kong, however, is not the big fortunes, counted in millions of dollars, but nest eggs measured in the thousands - just enough money to stake a newcomer in business. 
In Chinatown, where newcomers are isolated from the outside world by language and culture and where severe zoning restrictions prevent the addition of space to accommodate a larger population, these sums are enough to run up the bids for every available nook.
Two decades ago, Chinatown was a neighborhood of 20,000 people, most of them men and most of them of Cantonese extraction, squeezed into about 35 square blocks at the foot of the Manhattan Bridge in the shadow of City Hall. 
The population is estimated now at 100,000 or more and is growing geometrically. 
If Chinatown were an independent municipality, it would rank as one of the fastest-growing communities in the United States.
With new arrivals squeezing in at a rate at nearly 2,000 a month, the district spread north through what was once a Jewish section on the Lower East Side and west across Little Italy, turning Yiddish into Mandarin and fettucine into won tons. 
The frontier of Chinatown has crossed into TriBeCa and SoHo, and new Chinatowns have blossomed in Queens and Brooklyn, bringing the total Chinese population in the city to about 300,000.
Â 
Hundreds of Entrepreneurs
Wherever they live, the immigrants are drawn back to downtown Chinatown to work and shop, creating an atmosphere of an old city market, with hundreds of entrepreneurs tending their own stalls or shops.
Bushels of live blue crabs, crates of bok choy and hordes of intense shoppers crowd the sidewalks of Canal Street, the central business district of Chinatown. 
Shopkeepers hawk wares from every available nook: batteries and audio tapes, scarves, T-shirts, jewelry and food of every description, from lobsters to doughnuts.
''We Chinese are very independent people,'' said Danny Li, owner of a chain of bakery shops and an investor in real estate and restaurants. 
''The first ambition for a Chinese person is to have his own business. 
It gives jobs to everyone in the family.''
On East Broadway, a new arrival sublets enough space under the awning of a fish store for a dozen open crates of vegetables. 
''He might pay the owner of the fish market $1,500 a month for a place to stand in front of the store window,'' said Kwok Ming Chan, a restaurant owner and real estate investor. 
(He describes the lease as if it were hypothetical. 
In the intimate, small-town atmosphere of Chinatown, where neighbors and partners often know each other's business, no one admits to knowing details.) Mr. Chan said that, to obtain the lease in the first place, a lease that might run for as little as two years or as long as five, he might pay $20,000 or more in ''key money,'' an illegal but universal - and universally acknowledged - fee assessed everytime a tenant moves in or renews his lease.
When the key money is amortized over the life of the lease, the operator of the vegetable stand might pay the equivalent of $275 a square foot a year for the privilege of selling his apples, snow peas and mushrooms. 
Some of the shops in the atrium of Trump Tower on Fifth Avenue, among the most expensive retail space in the city, pay little more than that.
Yet the competition is so fierce that retail prices at many of the stalls are considerably lower than those uptown. 
Apples that sell for 89 cents a pound on the upper West Side go for 33 cents on Henry Street. 
Snow peas cost a third of what they bring at greengroceries in other parts of the city.
''They can make a living only by working 14 hours every day,'' Mr. Chan said. 
''And everyone in the family must work, too.''
Despite the drab exterior of the neighborhood, Chinatown is not poor. 
''People have plenty of money,'' Mr. Li said. 
''If they do not have enough to open their own business, they work as waiters in the Chinese restaurants. 
You can put aside a lot when you work as a waiter. 
You have no time off to spend what you earn.''
The drabness comes in part from the compulsion to do business. 
''A few years ago, a group of us convinced the city to commit several million dollars to rebuilding the sidewalks and planting trees and shrubbery in the area,'' Tieh Chi Ho, an architect and developer, said. 
''But the merchants objected. 
They said the construction would drive away customers.''
When the Golden Pacific National Bank, one of the many banks in Chinatown, failed last year, Federal regulators who examined the books were surprised to find so many waiters with savings accounts of $20,000 or more, Mr. Chan said. 
He pointed to a vendor selling hot noodles from an aluminum pushcart on the corner of East Broadway and Pike Street. 
''He takes in $500 a day,'' Mr. Chan said. 
''One day soon he will have enough to lease a stall.''
Those who lack the capital for a pushcart settle for a cardboard box on which they spread a half-dozen mackerel or a dozen scarves.
Â 
Restaurants and Curio Shops
The customers who support this multitude of merchants come not only from Chinatown but also from the Chinese communities in Queens, the non-Chinese residents of the lower part of Manhattan and the tourists drawn to the hundreds of inexepensive restaurants and curio shops.
''With so many people passing by, the owner of a small stall can sell a lot of merchandise,'' Mr. Chan said. 
''You can watch him in the morning unload a truckload of goods to sell, maybe $2,000 worth, and by the end of the day it is all gone.''
But the day does not end until late at night, he added.
Mr. Chan and nine other stockholders hope to take advantage of the demand for space with a new shopping center they are building on East Broadway underneath the Manhattan Bridge on land leased from the city. 
It is one of the few sites available for new construction.
''Most of the real estate in Chinatown is owned by family associations with many members,'' said Irwin Liu, an American-born lawyer who with several partners founded a title insurance company on Pell Street in Chinatown. 
''It is very hard to get so many different people to agree on a plan for development.''

file: DENG IS GIVEN A SHARP TALK BY MOYNIHAN.txt
text:

A decade after he lectured America's foes from the podium at the United Nations, Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan brought some of the same style into a meeting this week with China's pre-eminent leader, Deng Xiaoping.

As the United States representative to the United Nations under President Ford from 1975 to 1976, Mr. Moynihan gained a reputation for taking the offensive against critics of the United States and its allies and for assailing those critics for what he characterized as hypocrisy.
At a meeting with Mr. Deng on Tuesday in the Great Hall of the People, he used less flowery language than he often used in the General Assembly.

Sen Daniel Patrick Moynihan, in China with Congressional group, complains to Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping about China's overwhelming record of voting against side taken by United States at United Nations; notes State Department tally of last year's General Assembly session shows China and United States on opposite sides 86 percent of time; official New China News Agency, in its report of meeting, says Deng acknowledged that 'certain problems' exist between two nations (M)

Â 
Tally of Assembly Votes
Mr. Moynihan entered the session with a State Department tally of last year's General Assembly session that showed China and the United States on opposite sides 86 percent of the time when a for-or-against vote was taken. 
He said at a news conference later that he had told Mr. Deng that this put China ''in the same column'' as the Soviet Union and the countries espousing nonalignment, with patterns of voting overwhelmingly against the United States.
Mr. Moynihan said he had chided Mr. Deng for what the Senator called China's ''two United States policy,'' a friendly attitude in direct relations between Peking and Washington, and a sharply different posture at the United Nations.

In the Shanghai communique in 1972, the United States accepted that Taiwan was part of China.
Mr. Deng, who celebrated his 81st birthday last week, appeared to be in a genial mood as he greeted the Americans.

Visitors Do Most of Talking

From the senators' accounts at the news conference, Mr. Moynihan's seemed to have been the most sharply worded of the American statements.

text:

Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, will not be a member of the new Central Committee of the Communist Party, delegates to the party congress said today.
Mr. Deng's expected departure from the Central Committee, which debates and approves policy, means that he will apparently also have to quit the Standing Committee, or inner circle, of the Central Committee's Politburo, the body that rules the country, But Mr. Deng is expected to remain a forceful presence behind the scenes, relinquishing little of his actual authority.
Diplomats and knowledgeable Chinese agree that Mr. Deng, who is 83 years old, will stay on as chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces, in keeping with Mao's dictum that ''political power grows out of the barrel of a gun.''
Â 
Chairmanship Eliminated in 1982
The Central Committee seat would be the first party post that Mr. Deng has given up since he eliminated his job as deputy party chairman at the last party congress in September 1982. 
The party chairmanship, which was created for Mao in 1945, was also abolished with its deputy slots.
Mr. Deng's refusal to accept the mantle of chairman then underscored the shift to a more collective leadership and left the General Secretary as the top official of the Communist Party, which has 46 million members. 
Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang is now the Acting General Secretary.
Mr. Deng was twice purged from the Central Committee, in 1966 and in 1976, when he ran afoul of leftists in the Cultural Revolution, but each time he returned to power. 
Since 1978, he has been the most powerful man in China, despite his unwillingness to assume formal leadership posts. 
He declined to succeed Hua Guofeng as Prime Minister when Mr. Hua was forced out in September 1980.
Word of Mr. Deng's decision to step down from the Central Committee emerged during a series of strictly controlled interviews today with four delegates to the party congress.
Pressed by foreign reporters, Lu Guangqiu, a prosperous 44-year-old chicken farmer from Hangzhou, blurted out his astonishment that Mr. Deng's name had not appeared on the list of potential candidates that was presented to delegates of the congress.
''I never thought I wouldn't find Deng's name on the list,'' Mr. Lu said to the foreign reporters who crowded around him.
Â 
Wants the Aged to Retire
Mr. Deng, who designed China's economic resurgence over the last decade, has called on all the party's elderly leaders to retire in favor of younger leaders.

The list of 172 names represents a sharp drop in the size of the Central Committee from its current 209 members.

Â 
'New Nucleus of Leadership'
There had been some speculation, particularly among Eastern European diplomats, that Mr. Deng would remain in the Politburo. 
Several Chinese familiar with the deliberations of the congress said today that it was clear now that Mr. Deng would leave the Central Committee.

With a visit to Peking planned next month by its party leader, East Germany is stepping up a reconciliation with China that appears to have the cautious blessing of the Soviet Union, according to scholars and Bonn officials.
Since 1982, when the Soviet Union made its first overtures to China, East Germany has been quietly mending the relations that were ruptured two decades earlier in the course of the ideological confrontation between Moscow and Peking.
The visit to China in the latter half of October by the East German leader, Erich Honecker, 74 years old, is expected to consolidate relations and possibly open the way for other Eastern European Communist chiefs to follow. 
Poland's leader, Gen. Wojciech Jaruzelski, and Hungary's leader, Janos Kadar, are the main candidates.
For Mr. Honecker, the steady opening to China is a strand in a larger strategy of gaining recognition for East Germany as a sovereign and autonomous country. 
The timing of the China trip felicitously offsets an apparent veto by Moscow on a long-planned milestone visit to West Germany.

Pressure on Moscow

Conspicuously, Mr. Sindermann recalled that German Communists and the Communist movement in China have hoary connections, including a friendship struck between Mr. Hu and Mr. Honecker in the 1950's when they were the leaders of their countries' respective Communist youth groups.

Lo Chengxun, whose 10-year sentence as an American spy was disclosed in Peking yesterday, was one of several Chinese or Hong Kong journalists and officials who have informal license from the Chinese Government to maintain contacts and exchanges with foreigners in Hong Kong.System No Longer as Important
The system of informal contacts and exchanges, still in existence but no longer as important in these days of China's more outgoing foreign policy, seems useful both to the foreigners, including many Americans, and to the Chinese Government. 
Even though the Chinese involved are known not to divulge information that has not already appeared in the official Chinese press, foreigners find the meetings helpful in interpreting policies of the Peking Government.
Most of the diplomats and journalists assume that their meetings with the editors and others are routinely reported to the authorities in Peking, who are interested in gathering information about individual specialists on China and on Western attitudes toward the country. 
The system of contacts is also widely regarded as part of China's ''united front'' work, a series of activities by which the Peking Government builds ties with foreigners and with Chinese outside China proper.
Mr. Lo, though he did not speak English, was a prominent and highly valued participant in this system. 
It was well-known in Hong Kong that Chinese-speaking diplomats and journalists frequently sought him out. 
A lively, affable man who spoke with the accents of his native Guangxi, Mr. Lo was regarded as a pragmatic thinker who generally favored a greater political openness in China.
Hong Kong newspapers reported last fall that Mr. Lo, who was known in Hong Kong by the name Lo Fu, had been arrested while traveling in Guangdong Province with his family. 
The newspapers said that during that trip in May 1982, Mr. Lo was suddenly called to Peking. 
After that, the papers said, his family heard nothing from or about him except for a brief handwritten note to his wife that arrived a few weeks later.
Similar incidents have been reported involving other Hong Kong residents, who are considered Chinese nationals by the Peking Government.
The Chinese police have detained members of human rights groups based in Hong Kong who were traveling in China to collect information about dissidents. 
One of them, Lau San-ching, disappeared in Canton after visiting the relatives of some human rights activists who had been arrested in that city.
Another case involves Hanson Huang, a 1976 graduate of Harvard Law School who went to China in 1979 to teach law at Peking University and work as an adviser for the China International Trust and Investment Corporation, a Government body that arranges business contracts with foreign companies.
According to reports gathered in Hong Kong and published in The Wall Street Journal and SPEARHead, a magazine published in New York that monitors human rights in Asia, Mr. Huang called his mother in Hong Kong early in 1982 to tell her that he was moving out of his hotel room. 
There has been no word of him since, and it is assumed he is under arrest.

file: EMBASSY SECRUITY_ PROBLEMS EXIST FOR U.S. AROUND THE WORLD.txt
text:
ï»¿
Some of the security problems that have arisen at the American Embassy in Moscow are present in a number of other American missions around the world, according to Administration officials, intelligence experts and current and former American ambassadors.
Missions in China, Eastern Europe and other areas with a large Soviet presence have been particularly vulnerable, American security officials said. 
But they said there were also problems in certain Middle Eastern and African countries.
Americans serving in friendly countries where internal security regulations are more relaxed are also susceptible to Soviet and other subversion, they said.
Security lapses elsewhere have not drawn the same attention as those in Moscow, the specialists acknowledged, although many of the problems have existed for decades and are considered as serious. 
Nor has the attention directed at the problem in Moscow been duplicated elsewhere.
Â 
'Problems Are Widespread'
''What the incident in Moscow should awaken us to is that the problems and vulnerabilities are widespread,'' said Adm. Bobby R. Inman, retired, a former Deputy Director of Central Intelligence, who headed a special State Department advisory panel that investigated embassy security in 1985.
''While the Soviets most skillfully exploit them, they are not the only ones trying,'' he added, ''and vulnerabilities are at least as large if not larger in other places where the guard is not so high.''
An Assistant Secretary of State for Diplomatic Security, Robert E. Lamb, acknowledged that hostile espionage is a global problem confronting United States diplomatic facilities.
''Moscow has a threat level unmatched in the world, but there are other places that are just as vulnerable,'' he said. 
''Espionage is a worldwide problem and not confined to just hostile countries.''
Â 
Break-Ins in Eastern Europe
In discussing security problems in Eastern Europe, the officials said that embassy buildings in Prague, Budapest, East Berlin and Sofia, Bulgaria, are next to buildings that is some cases are owned by the host government. 
American investigators have turned up evidence of break-ins in buildings in Eastern Europe and electronic bugging.
Outside the Eastern bloc, the least acknowledged but the most serious security problems are at American facilities in China, according to intelligence officials.
When Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigators visited the three Beijing embassy buildings last year, they discovered a maze of tunnels from the basements to other buildings. 
Doors to the tunnels were locked but did not have alarms. 
One tunnel led into the basement of the Czechoslovak Embassy, said one committee staff member who went on the trip.
The consulate in Canton, meanwhile, is considered impossible to protect, since it is situated on several floors of a high-rise hotel and even ''secure areas'' where only Americans are allowed are guarded by the Chinese police, not American marines.
Â 
Many Local Employees
American installations are also made vulnerable by the extensive use of local employees. 
While West Germany, France and Britain hire an average of one local employee for every three of its own officials, the average number of local employees at American posts far exceeds the number of Americans.
Last December there were 10,766 Americans and 15,327 local employees working full-time at American posts around the world. 
In some countries, the difference was dramatic. 
In Japan, for example, local employees numbered 407, compared with 269 Americans. 
In France there were 583 local employees and 291 Americans, and in Morocco 268 locals and 96 Americans.
Local employees outnumbered Americans even in some posts in Eastern Europe. 
In Czechoslovakia, for example, 46 locals worked for 27 Americans, while in Poland there were 119 locals and 52 Americans.
In Moscow, 210 Russians worked at the American Embassy, but all have been withdrawn.
Â 
Many Natives Used in China
Because of language and cultural barriers, American posts in China employed 336 locals and 155 Americans.
The United States can hire its own local employees in countries with large numbers of Soviet officials, such as Cuba, Nicaragua, Iraq and Syria, but it is assumed that some of them are intelligence agents and that all must report to their governments.
In November 1985, for example, the State Department issued a strong protest when Nicaragua subjected local employees of the American Embassy in Managua to several hours of intense interrogation. 
American diplomats in both Baghdad, Iraq, and Damascus, Syria, have reported problems with electronic surveillance.
Government investigators assert that the problem of socializing between American embassy staff members and local employees and residents is more widespread than is generally acknowledged by many officials.
Â 
'Sleep NATO'
''The basic rule, especially in the Eastern bloc, is 'Sleep NATO,' but that's not always followed,'' a former Foreign Service officer said.
American officials working at the United States Interests Section in Havana and the embassy in Managua have been sent home in recent years after they were caught dating local women. 
In Havana, investigators believe there was a serious intelligence loss because of an incident three years ago.
It is common practice for the Soviet intelligence services and their surrogates to use their nationals to seduce Americans in countries outside the Eastern bloc, where there is a tendency to be less suspicous and where socializing may not be forbidden.
Â 
Bill Would Ban Locals
In many emerging nations, where salaries are low, local employees have been particularly susceptible to offers to spy for Soviet-bloc governments and, to a lesser extent, ostensibly friendly countries.
This month, Representative Jim Courter, Republican of New Jersey, submitted a bill that would ban all local workers from American posts in Eastern Europe.
Although the State Department opposes the bill, it is working on a plan that would eliminate local employees from sensitive areas of American offices in Eastern Europe. 
It is also investigating regulations that would further prohibit socializing.
Reducing the number of local employees would require budgeting enormous resources to substitute Americans in many jobs. 
It would also shrink significantly the services offered to Americans abroad.
Â 
Locals Called Vital
Extensive renovation or replacement of more than 100 embassies to deter terrorism and espionage, as recommended by the Inman panel, would be even more expensive.
But despite the concern about the widespread use of locals, many diplomats argue that on the whole they benefit the Foreign Service.
They provide valuable services that in some cases could not be duplicated by American contract employees, according to State Department officials. 
And without local employees, they say, American embassies could turn into closed fortresses with little connection to the populace.
The officials say that native employees know how to resolve problems with local bureaucracies, know the language and dialects and often provide insight into culture and politics.
Â 
'Tremendous Benefits'
''There are tremendous benefits to being surrounded by foreign nationals, and if one is careful the benefits outweigh the liabilities,'' one Foreign Service officer said.
''There's a lot of sentiment in Congress for building new embassies when you're saving lives, but not for espionage,'' Mr. Lamb said, referring to the readiness of Congress to make embassies more secure against terrorism. 
''If this Government is going to make embassy security a priority, this Congress can help.''
Mr. Lamb is expected to raise this and other issues in testimony before the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on International Operations on Wednesday.

file: EX-PRISONER TO SEE CHINA, BY INVITATION.txt
text:
ï»¿
John T. Downey came home to Connecticut a decade ago after spending more than 20 years in a Chinese prison on charges of being an American spy.
This week, for the first time since his return, Mr. Downey will go back to China. 
He said his 18-day visit was a gesture of good will that had attracted the attention of the White House.
''If I had one strong conviction coming out of there it was that a solid relationship between the two countries was very important to our national interest,'' Mr. Downey said at his New Haven law office.
John T Downey, who returned to Connecticut 10 years ago after spending 20 years in jail in China on spy charges, will visit China for 18 days by invitation from Chinese Government; Downey says he hopes trip will be viewed as good-will gesture by Chinese; photos (S)
''It just seemed to me that maybe this was the time to go back,'' he said. 
''I'm hoping it will be seen as a good- will gesture by the Chinese.''
Â 
'Interest and Curiosity'
Mr. Downey, 53 years old, said he was ''looking forward to it with great interest and curiosity, but no trepidation.''
In 1952, at the height of the Korean War, Mr. Downey was 22 years old - fresh out of Yale University and working for the Central Intelligence Agency - when his plane was shot down over the mountains of Manchuria.
He was captured and sentenced to life imprisonment. 
He spent more than 20 years in prison before he was released in 1973 as relations between the United States and China began to improve.
Mr. Downey resumed his life almost as if the 20-year gap had never existed.
After his return, he went to Harvard Law School, got married and began practicing law with occasional forays into Connecticut Democratic politics.
Â 
A Race for the Senate
Last year he ran for the United States Senate but lost the Democratic nomination to Representative Toby Moffett, who in turn lost to Senator Lowell P. Weicker Jr., the Republican incumbent.
Speaking this month to the Western Connecticut Retired Officers Association in Westport, he said his experience in China was ''not one I would like to repeat.''
But he said it had convinced him that America society was ''the best hope for mankind.''
Mr. Downey said he began thinking about a return visit last winter when problems cropped up in United States- China relations over such things as arms sales to Taiwan and textile quotas.
''It just kind of set off alarm bells,'' he said.
He sounded out people who were familiar with China, such as Vice President Bush, a former chief of the United States Liaison Office in Peking.
They were enthusiastic about the idea of a visit but did not know how the Chinese would react, Mr. Downey said. 
They suggested that he get in touch with the Chinese on his own, which he did in March with a telephone call to the Chinese Embassy and a follow-up letter from his wife, Audrey, who was born in China but raised in Taiwan.
Mr. Downey, who will leave Wednesday with his wife and 3-year-old son, John, is going at the invitation of the Chinese People's Association for Friendship with Foreign Countries, which he described as an unofficial arm of the Chinese Foreign Office. 
The Chinese are not paying his way, he said.
Â 
A Chat With the President
Earlier this month, Mr. Downey discussed his trip at a meeting in Washington with Mr. Bush, who took him to the Oval Office for a brief chat with President Reagan.
Mr. Downey also had lunch with a staff member of the National Security Council for a background briefing. 
Despite the meetings, he said, his visit will be ''strictly private.''
Mr. Downey said he expected to find many changes since 1973. 
''The fact we are going is a sign of that,'' he said.

file: FEW IN HONG KONG SEEK DEMOCRACY.txt
text:
ï»¿
In Hong Kong's colonial system of government, a relative handful of Britons have complete control, even though 98 percent of the city-state's five-million-plus residents are Chinese.
Yet with the negotiations over Hong Kong's future just under way, begun two weeks ago when Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher of Britain met in Peking with Chinese leaders, the vast majority of the British crown colony's people want to retain the British administration without any real changes for the foreseeable future, according to public opinion polls.
Under the present setup, the Governor, Sir Edward Youde, in consultation with the executive and legislative councils, makes all policy decisions. 
Though there are some Chinese members of the two councils, they are all appointed by the British administrators, not elected by the populace.
HONG KONG, Oct. 
6 - In Hong Kong's colonial system of government, a relative handful of Britons have complete control, even though 98 percent of the city-state's five-million-plus residents are Chinese.
The system of government is, in many ways, as contradictory and anomalous as Hong Kong itself - a colony in an anticolonial era. 
For example, when Mrs. Thatcher was in Peking, Hong Kong was engaged in its largest exercise of democratic expression in its history, the election of representatives to so-called city district boards. 
These boards have been established as a vehicle for gathering views from the people on matters of public concern.
Â 
Reluctance to Vote
Despite a big get-out-the-vote effort by the Government, only 12 percent of the two million people eligible to vote bothered to exercise their privilege.
''The Government is pushing people to the polls,'' acknowledged Joseph Cheng, a professor of political science at Hong Kong's Chinese University and a leading critic of the Government. 
''It is the people who are reluctant to vote.''
There are several reasons for the apparent political apathy in Hong Kong. 
With more than 40 percent of the population immigrants and the colony's future uncertain, there is a sense of impermanence to Hong Kong that makes people less inclined to be politically active.
Moreover, even the Government's harshest critics describe British rule as a ''benevolent dictatorship.''
In the mid-1970's, for instance, the Government established statuatory holidays. 
In 1979 and 1981, rent control legislation was enacted. 
In both cases, social programs were enacted by government fiat that the labor unions were too weak to push for and the business community resisted, according to political experts.
Â 
Hands-Off Government
In addition, Hong Kong is renowned for its brand of hands-off government with low taxes, and public-sector spending and services, while expanding, is kept to a minimum.
Because of the Government's limited scope, some residents are not particularly anxious to have a voice in shaping its activities. 
''The Government does very little for us,'' said Shirley Woo, a 25-year-old office worker, who did not vote in the district board elections. 
''Why should we care about it?''
Rising wages and living standards afforded by Hong Kong's rapid economic growth and a policy of giving the Chinese elite appointed positions in Government have also blunted demands for a more democratic system.
However, the portion of Hong Kong's population that is seeking more direct participation in Government, though still a minority, is growing. 
About 60 percent of all residents are under 30 years old, and their levels of education and expectations are higher than their parents, many of whom were refugees.
Â 
Talks on Hong Kong's Future
One force that should heighten political awareness, analysts say, is the Peking-London negotiations over the future of Hong Kong after 1997, when the lease covering 90 percent of the colony's land runs out.
China has stated that it will reassert its sovereignty over all of Hong Kong by 1997. 
Britain says that the 19th-century treaties that created the colony are still valid, though they can be altered.
For years, it has been understood that the Peking leadership would not permit Hong Kong to become an independent, self-governing state, or ''a third China,'' Taiwan being the second. 
This has allowed Britain to run Hong Kong without opening the Government up to elected representatives from the local Chinese community.
Now, one likely compromise in the British-Chinese talks appears to be a long transition period, up to 40 years, during which the British presence is gradually phased out. 
Presumably, local Chinese would then be phased in. 
''It's very clear that there will be a transition period,'' Mr. Cheng said. 
''There can be no excuse for keeping local Chinese out anymore.''
Â 
System Characterized as Relic
As a first step, Mr. Cheng thinks that there should be elected representatives on the legislative council within five years. 
Many British Government officials here agree. 
In private conversations, they are among the first to characterize the present system as a relic of a bygone era. 
But first, they emphasize, an agreement must be worked out with China, preferably within a year to restore business confidence by removing uncertainties about Hong Kong's future.
So for the time being, the British administration must remain as the reassuring symbol of the ''stabilityI and prosperity'' in Hong Kong that Peking and London agree are key objectives of the current negotiations.
''This benevolent dictatorship isn't 100 percent what I'd like, maybe not even 80 percent,'' said Ronald Li, chairman of Hong Kong's Far East stock exchange. 
''But 60 percent is better than a lot of the alternatives.''

file: FIELD DAY FOR BRITISH PRESS_ PHILIP_S REMARKS ON CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
Britain's tabloids had a field day today insuring that remarks attributed to the Duke of Edinburgh about Chinese ''slitty eyes'' and how ''ghastly'' he had found Peking would become the longest-remembered happening of the royal tour of China by Queen Elizabeth II.
The most sophisticated headline was in The Daily Mail, which asked, ''Does Britain Need a Terracotta Duke?''
Under it was a photograph of a grim-faced Queen inspecting the terra cotta warriors guarding the imperial tomb of the Chin Dynasty emperor near Xian and a heading that said, ''They're tall, dignified, ceremonial and above everything else, they are silent.''
There was also a cartoon of the Queen's husband with a gag over his mouth.
Â 
A Barrage of Puns
Headline writers on other newspapers let loose with a barrage of outrageous puns to show why British diplomats on a tour that had earlier been heralded as ''historic'' were now choking with embarrassment.
''Philip Gets It All Wong,'' screamed the front page of The Sun, a mass-circulation tabloid, which was illustrated with a photo of the Prince retouched so as to give him darting Fu Manchu eyebrows and eyelids. 
''Prince Philip torpedoed the royal visit to China,'' the newspaper reported.
''Great Wally of China,'' cried The Daily Mirror, using a British colloquialism applied to bumblers and buffoons. 
Taking a more somber line, the newspaper Today's front page declared simply, ''Philip Drops a Clanger.''
Reporting from Peking, the BBC found some consolation in the fact that the Chinese press had ignored the remarks, which were made in Xian in conversation with a group of University of Edinburgh students.
Â 
Chancellor of University
The Prince, who is the university's chancellor, was reported to have asked one of the students how long he had been in China. 
When the young man replied that he had been there six weeks, the Queen's husband then wisecracked, ''If you stay here much longer, you will go back with slitty eyes.''
Asked by one of the students how he had found the Forbidden City, the Prince seemed momentarily confused about where that was. 
His wife's response - that she had found it fascinating and wished she could have spent more of her time in Peking visiting it -appeared to refresh his memory. 
''Oh yes,'' he was quoted as having said. 
''But Peking was ghastly.''
A journalist then repeated the Duke of Edinburgh's remarks to a British diplomat. 
''Thank you for spoiling my evening,'' the diplomat replied.
Michael Shea, the Queen's spokesman, was rushed in to explain that the Prince's remarks had been entirely jocular and that ''the Duke of Edinburgh is in no way disparaging of the Chinese people.''
Â 
A Pained Expression
Wearing what was described as a pained expression, the spokesman went on to try to explain the statements. 
He said: ''It's a well-known physiological fact that people in different parts of the world have eyes that are differently shaped. 
My eyes are round.''
Asked today, when the royal party stopped in Kunming, about the uproar over his remarks, the Prince commented offhandedly that he thought it had been ''a little tactless'' of the Edinburgh students to repeat them.
Queen Elizabeth II is the first British sovereign to visit China, but a distant ancestor, George III, sent an envoy to Peking in 1792, an occasion that became the first of many embarrassments and misunderstandings in relations between the two countries. 
The Chinese assumed the envoy had come to pay homage on behalf of George III to the reigning Ming emperor and to make Britain a tributary state.

file: FIRST CHINA-TAIWAN TALKS YIELD ACCORD.txt
text:
ï»¿
China and Taiwan today concluded their first face-to-face negotiations in 37 years, with Peking agreeing to allow the Nationalist Government to reclaim a cargo plane flown to the mainland by its pilot, who defected.
The agreement, after three days of talks here, will also involve the return of two crewmen who were flown to China on the plane by the defector.
During talks on Saturday and Sunday, representatives of the airlines of Taiwan and China disagreed on where the transfer of the plane should occur. 
China wanted Taiwan to pick up the plane, a Boeing 747, on the mainland, while Taiwan said China should fly it to Hong Kong.
Today China agreed that a crew from its national airline, the Civil Aviation Administration of China, would fly the plane and the two crewmen to Hong Kong. 
Another meeting was scheduled for Tuesday to work out the details.
Â 
First Talks Since 1949
The talks have been the first direct contact between Taiwan and China since the Nationalists fled the mainland for Taiwan after losing a civil war to the Communists in 1949.
The Nationalists, who say they are China's rightful Government, had until now shunned all contact and had rebuffed initiatives by China to set up commercial, postal and communication links with the eventual goal of reunification.
Both sides have said the talks did not have political significance, but were a business matter between two airlines, not Governments.
But political commentators said they believed Taiwan's decision to negotiate directly must have been approved by President Chiang Ching-kuo, whose Government has been criticized by some legislators for rejecting all contacts with China.
Western diplomats in Peking have said that China, which views Taiwan as a Chinese province and has hopes of gaining its agreement to a new relationship, scored a victory by getting Taiwan to negotiate, whatever the outcome of the talks.
Â 
A Desire to Appear Reasonable
China has sought to appear reasonable and it was in its interest to reach an agreement quickly to avoid the impression that the two crew members who want to return to Taiwan were being held hostage, according to the diplomats.
Zhang Ruipu, the head of the Chinese delegation, said today that China had accepted Taiwan's proposal as a gesture of sincerity.
''We always maintain that there is no problem that cannot be solved between fellow countrymen through friendly and sincere discussions,'' he said in a news conference.
Chung Tsan-jung, the head of the Taiwan delegation, said China's concession was ''not a victory but a right'' of Taiwan.
The China Airlines cargo plane, which had left Bangkok bound for Hong Kong, landed in the southern Chinese city of Canton on May 3. 
Aboard were the pilot, Wang Hsi-chueh, 56 years old; the co-pilot, Tung Kung-shin, 57, and a technician, Chiu Ming-chiu, 40.
Â 
Father Is in Sichuan
Mr. Wang said in a news conference in Peking that he had defected in order to be reunited with his 82-year-old father in the central province of Sichuan.
Officials of Taiwan have said that they believed Mr. Wang had been kidnapped and that they reserved the right to ask China later for the pilot's return. 
Mr. Chung said China had refused to let members of the Taiwan delegation telephone Mr. Wang to clarify the situation.
In Taipei, a spokesman for China Airlines, Larry Lin, said the carrier did not regard the outcome of the talks as a victory ''because the release of all three crewmen, including Wang Hsi-chueh, is our final goal.''
Wang Fu-yao, the pilot's son, said in a telephone interview that relatives still refused to believe his father had defected. 
''I hope he is allowed to visit Hong Kong to clarify the situation,'' he said.

file: For China, _Rejuvenated_ Leadership.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's parliament approved a new lineup today of Government leaders who are widely seen as committed to its ambitious program of economic restructuring.
As the National People's Congress approved the new leaders, men who in general are slightly younger and better educated than the previous leadership, it also voted to give constitutional protection to private enterprise and to the selling of land use rights, activity that is tantamount to selling land itself.
Last Saturday, the congress approved Li Peng, a 59-year-old Soviet-trained engineer, as Prime Minister. 
The congress, which meets annually, has been marked by a degree of open discussion not seen since the founding of the People's Republic in 1949, but its real power is essentially confined to ratifying decisions already made by the Communist Party's Politburo.
The official New China News Agency described the new group of state councilors, the equivalent of a cabinet, and ministers as ''a group of technocrats, who are younger in age, pragmatic and enthusiastic in the reform.''
''China is rejuvenating its leadership, making it professionally more competent as a measure to insure the continuity of its current policies for reform and the opening to the outside world,'' the press agency said.
Western diplomats here generally subscribed to that view, saying that the new group of officials reflects a continuing shift toward a more nuts-and-bolts and less politically motivated government.
Among the most prominent appointments made today was that of Qian Qichen, 60, as Foreign Minister. 
He succeeds Wu Xueqian, 66, who was named a Deputy Prime Minister and who is expected to retain overall control over China's foreign policy apparatus.
Mr. Qian, who has spent nearly all his career in the diplomatic ranks, has been heavily involved with the Soviet Union, where he was stationed for a total of 10 years, and with Eastern Europe. 
He has been a Deputy Foreign Minister since 1982.
Other significant appointments include the naming of Li Guixian as a state councilor and governor of the country's central bank, and Li Tieying as Minister of the State Education Commission..
Neither man brings visible experience to his new position. 
Li Guixian is a chemical engineer who has been a senior party bureaucrat, and Li Tieying, an electrical engineer who studied in Czechoslovakia, has worked in the electronics industry and as a senior party official in the provinces.
Qin Jiwei, 73, a veteran military man, was named Defense Minister. 
He replaces the ailing Zhang Aiping, 80. 
The party's Central Military Commission, headed by Deng Xiaoping, has most of the military power in China.
Altogether, three Deputy Prime Ministers, two fewer than there were previously, were appointed: Yao Yilin, Tian Jiyun and Wu Xueqian; 11 state councilors, down two from before; and 41 ministers, down from the previous 45. 
The slight shrinking in the number of senior posts is evidently part of an effort to streamline the cumbersome governmental apparatus.
Both constitutional amendments approved today are intended to give legal weight to the continuing remolding of the economy. 
By granting constitutional legitimacy to private enterprise, a radical step here,the leadership has given recognition to the need to protect the most rapidly growing segment of the economy.

file: FOR NEW CHINESE ENVOY, A PARTY ABOARD THE QE2.txt
text:
ï»¿
It was not an accident that Han Xu, China's Ambassador to the United States, chose a reception and a luncheon in his honor, a forum provided by the China Institute in America, for his first public appearance in New York before an American audience. 
He said with a broad smile yesterday: ''My predecessor made that choice and I make the same choice because you are a force for Sino-American mutual understanding and friendship.''
So, only one and a half months after he became China's Ambassador, he boarded the Queen Elizabeth 2 for a cocktail party followed by a luncheon of avocado and crabmeat and sliced tenderloin, with a 1982 Macon-Lugny. 
A speech by the Ambassador called the British cruise ship a symbol ''that will take us on a common journey.''
Han Xu, China's new Ambassador to United States, choses reception and luncheon in his honor, forum provided by China Institute in America, for his first public appearance in New York before American audience; photo (M)
''The wind is up,'' Ambassador Han said. 
''Let us sail to a splendid tomorrow.''
That was the sort of good fellowship that continued through the afternoon in the QE2's Princess Grill as a crowd of 50 people toasted the new ambassador and his wife, Ge Qiyun. 
A marimba band, getting tuned up for the ship's departure last evening for Bermuda, played softly.
The Ambassador called for an increase in American-Chinese trade, a relaxation of what he called a ''rising protectionist trend'' here, and a renewal of efforts to bring China and Taiwan together without interference from the United States. 
That done, the Ambassador seemed to enjoy dropping by the various knots of people to introduce himself and his wife.
Among those at the party were Wan-go H.C. 
Weng, president of the China Institute; Ji Lide, Consul General of China in New York, and his wife, Ma Shaoping; Gillian Martin Sorensen, the city's Commissioner for the United Nations and Consular Corps, C. Douglas Dillon and his wife, Susan; Von Sung Yang, one of the oldest members of the institute's board of trustees; Denise Sze, sister to I.M. 
Pei, the architect, and Dr. William Shaw.
Â 
Businessmen Present
The luncheon crowd was liberally sprinkled with American and Chinese businessmen, including Morley Cho, a Hong Kong shipping executive; Phillips Talbot, former president of the Asia Society, and Zhou Zhenxing, representative of the Bank of China here. 
Winston Lord and his wife, Bette Bao Lord, were there as well, and Mr. Lord was placed in a seat of honor at Ambassador Han's table. 
Mr. Lord has been mentioned as a leading candidate to be United States Ambassador to China.
Mrs. Han, sipping a Perrier water, spoke of growing up in Shanghai, of her three children - her 33-year-old daughter, who is a doctor, and her sons, one a philosophy teacher, the other an engineer - but she became animated when she spoke of her only grandchild, a girl.
''The Chinese have a saying,'' she said. 
''A little girl is like a pearl in one's palm. 
My granddaughter is the pearl in our family's palm.''
Mr. Weng, who was the ambassador's escort for the occasion, took pains to introduce him as ''no stranger to us.''
He pointed out that from 1973 to 1979 Ambassador Han had been stationed in Washington with China's liaison team, as negotiations for resumption of relations between the United States and China went on. 
In Peking he was head of the Foreign Ministry's American and Oceania Department and his expertise was in the field of United States foreign relations; he was later head of protocol. 
He came to the United States on May 3.
Mrs. Han also worked in the Foreign Ministry, she said, specializing in disarmament problems. 
When it was suggested that her specialty could be used at this time, she laughed loudly. 
''I am my country's hostess now,'' she said.
Miss Sorensen welcomed the Hans on behalf of Mayor Koch and used the occasion to announce that an exhibition of photographs entitled ''New York City: The City and Its People'' was about to open in Peking as part of the New York-Peking sister city exchange arrangement. 
Mr. Weng then took the floor and invited ''all of you to the Workers Cultural Palace in Peking to see New York.''

text:
