THINKING IN TIME The Uses of History for Decision-Makers. 
By Richard E. Neustadt and Ernest R. May. 329 pp. 
New York: The Free Press. 
$19.95.
Â 
IN 1948 George C. Marshall, then President
Truman's Secretary of State, was concerned that the Communists seemed to be winning the civil war in China. 
He therefore asked Gen. Albert Wedemeyer, who had been the American commander in China at the end of World War II, to go to the Far East and see what, if anything, could be done. 
Upon his return, Wedemeyer recommended that Washington dispatch a few thousand military advisers. 
Attached to Chinese Nationalist forces, those advisers might well halt the Communist advances and perhaps even allow the Nationalists to win.
General Marshall rejected the advice, concluding that the United States should not go beyond giving the Nationalists money and supplies. 
He later explained this decision to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee: ''It would be impossible to estimate the final costs. 
. . . It certainly would be a continuing operation for a long time to come. 
It would involve this Government in a continuing commitment from which it would practically be impossible to withdraw.''
Marshall's judgment is cited by the authors of ''Thinking in Time'' as a stunning example of how a statesman can - and should - look at ''an issue in the present with a sense both of past and of future.''
Marshall's first assignment as a young soldier had been in the Philippines after the Spanish-American War, when American public opinion turned against imperialism and in favor of the Filipinos who were resisting occupation. 
He had witnessed the public's disenchantment over American involvement in World War I, its dislike even for small military actions that lasted too long, such as sending the Marines into Nicaragua in the 1920's. 
He had even served in China before World War II. 
But it was not his firsthand experience in the Far East that made him reject sending military advisers to China - General Wedemeyer had served there too but came to the opposite conclusion. 
It was Marshall's habit of thinking in ''streams of time'' - identifying what is worth preserving from the past to carry into the future.
Richard E. Neustadt and Ernest R. May, distinguished professors, respectively, of public administration and history at Harvard University, believe that readers of this book can learn how to use history in the manner of a Marshall. 
They suggest a methodology that may or may not produce wise statesmen, but will at least provide the means to avoid the usual pitfall of American decision makers - excessive reliance on solving the problem at hand as quickly as possible, with little regard for the history that led up to it or the future consequences of actions taken. 
Students too often believe that international relations can best be understood by constructing abstract models of behavior, or relying on historical analogies that fail to question ''some presumption the decision-makers cherish.''
In their formative years they would do far better to read history and literature - how the Athenians' preparations for their ill-fated Sicilian expedition in the fifth century B.C. so weakened them that they ultimately lost their freedom, or Stendhal's antiheroic description of the battle of Waterloo.
Before making a final decision on events of grave consequence, the authors urge the following as standard practice: list the key elements of the immediate situation, namely, those Known, Unclear and Presumed. 
That simple procedure, they point out, ''puts attention on the situation itself instead of on the question 'what to do?'
(which thus is kept at bay a little while).''
Then identify any past situations that appear analogous -and quickly note the Likenesses, as well as the Differences that can block use of potentially misleading analogies. 
Before defining the desired objective, examine the history of the issue. 
First, ask: what's the story?
And note any significant changes in the story so far. 
Next, ask what the authors call ''the journalists' questions'' - where, who, how and why?
Finally, place the organizations and the people concerned with the situation at hand - what are their histories?
We are treated to cases of how the method was employed successfully (for example, the Cuban missile crisis, when President Kennedy and his executive committee used analogies sparingly and subjected them to careful scrutiny) and unsuccessfully (for example, President Johnson's Vietnam policy in 1965, when he ''relied on the supposition that [the North Vietnamese Government] would respond to pain as a person might''). 
The Carter Administration, not surprisingly, was apt to ignore history. 
(The President himself, an engineer by training, cared little for history; his instinct was to get things fixed and move on to the next problem.) A signal instance the authors provide of how things went wrong when they need not have was the ''discovery'' in 1979 of the Soviet brigade in Cuba.
The story of the Soviet brigade begins in late July, when the Democratic Senator Richard Stone of Florida wrote the President of rumors that the Russians had combat troops in Cuba. 
If true, the Senator said, Moscow was violating agreements with Washington made after the 1962 missile crisis. 
Mr. Carter's national security adviser, Zbigniew Brzezinski, asked for more data, and sure enough, there the troops were. 
With the second strategic arms limitation treaty with the Russians just signed but not ratified, the last thing Mr. Carter wanted was evidence that the Russians did not keep their word. 
Nonetheless, calm prevailed until Senator Frank Church, the chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, learned of the brigade from Secretary of State Cyrus Vance. 
Church was up for re-election in 1980 and was under fire for having supported the arms control treaty and for having gone to Cuba to meet Fidel Castro. 
He reacted to news of the Soviet brigade by saying the treaty should be scrapped and the brigade removed.
Secretary Vance then declared, ''I will not be satisfied with the status quo.''
Mr. Brzezinski, in turn, saw the brigade as further evidence of Soviet adventurism all over the world. 
As the mini-crisis continued through the fall, the President and his aides finally learned more about the history of the brigade. 
In fact, the brigade had been there since 1962, and did not violate past agreements made by Kennedy. 
Although Kennedy had asked the Russians to remove the troops, they had not promised to do so, and finally he dropped the subject. 
Because the Carter aides failed to discover the true history of the Soviet brigade soon enough, however, valuable time was wasted that should have been spent getting the arms treaty ratified, and when the Russians invaded Afghanistan in December any chances of ratification disappeared forever. 
''C OULD this farce have been avoided?'' the authors ask. 
Mr. Carter's staff say the intelligence agencies should have dug deeper earlier. 
But no one seems to have asked what motive the Russians could have possibly had to test Mr. Carter, particularly with an arms control agreement pending. 
Mr. Neustadt and Mr. May believe this episode ''underscores the uses of an issue's history and the consequences of habitually slighting it.''
They add: ''The brigade became an issue only because Carter and his aides did not know the brigade had been there all along, hence supposed it indicative of some new move by the Russians, hence reacted with their own form of the sovereign's complaint, He can't do that to me.''
Nor did the intelligence agencies have the historical data at hand, the authors tell us, ''because they were not accustomed to answering historical questions. 
Carter did not ask them. 
So his aides did not ask them either. 
Nor were they accustomed to pursuing them with persons out of government, but formerly with it, who might have known the answers, as some surely did.''
Indeed, Dean Rusk, who was Secretary of State in 1962 when the Soviet brigade was first discovered there, tells us he could have ''straightened them out . . . in five minutes - but no one called.''
There are other rich illustrations scattered throughout ''Thinking in Time,'' and they are fascinating (though the style often lapses into dreadful jargon -''credentialed,'' ''sophisticating'' - and so, along with history, I would recommend English composition). 
As for reading the great historians of the past - from Thucydides to Henry Adams - we should not look to analogies as a guide to present problems, a generally dangerous habit. 
Rather, the authors suggest, we should understand ''Thucydides' proposition that human nature remains constant - or better, perhaps, that dilemmas of human governance remain so.''
CHARMING JIMMY CARTER ''Someone from another country ordinarily has little American history in his head. 
. . . [The West German Chancellor Helmut] Schmidt seems to have taken no notice of events and details offering him possibly useful inferences about Carter. 
. . . With a little simple question-asking, Schmidt might have seen Carter's details against the special events of Southern, even Georgian, history. 
. . . Schmidt might then have assumed that he would be greeted with a sermon and that a great deal of courteous ritual would have to precede any getting down to business. 
One veteran of the Carter Administration, also long acquainted with Schmidt, feels sure in retrospect that, with only a little imaginative effort, Schmidt could have made Carter a dogged friend and ally. 
We are inclined to agree. 
With a good deal less brainpower than Schmidt but, partly for that reason, more experience in the exercise of personal charm, British Prime Minister James Callaghan managed to use Carter occasionally as the equivalent of an extra Labour Party whip.- From ''Thinking in Time.''

A week ago, a British professor decided to rush his blond daughter, a student, out of West Beirut after a secretary at the French Embassy was kidnapped.
The secretary's abduction, three days before, deepened the apprehension among Westerners still in Beirut because it showed that foreign women were no longer immune from kidnapping.
The apprehension did not ease after the French secretary, Danielle Perez, was freed. 
The wife of a French businessman, for instance, dyed her hair jet black so she would not look quite as foreign.
Â 
'Scouts' Survey Streets
For many months, Westerners, Eastern bloc nationals and even Arabs, Lebanese and non-Lebanese alike, have lived in constant fear of being kidnapped or killed. 
Now, after a new wave of abductions of foreigners in the last month, an even more oppressive atmosphere has settled on Beirut.
Article on deepening apprehension among Westerners still in Beirut, Lebanon, following recent abduction of secretary at French Embassy, sign that foreign women are no longer immune from kidnapping; secretary, Danielle Perez, has been freed but new wave of kidnappings of foreigners has led many to consider that bodyguards are no longer sufficient and 'scouts' are being hired; photo (M)
Bodyguards are no longer considered sufficient. 
''Scouts'' have been hired. 
They are posted outside homes or offices to signal their employers when it is safe for them to venture out on the street.
Foreigners now avoid keeping a pattern for their movements, since most of those kidnapped were seized by gunmen while on their way to their offices.
At first, foreigners lived under the illusion that only Americans and French nationals were targets of the kidnappers, most of whom, if not all, are believed to be Shiite Moslem fundamentalists backed by the Iranian Government.
Two British kidnapping victims, Geoffrey Nash and Brian Levick, said they were freed after their Moslem abductors realized that they were not Americans. 
Nevertheless, the British Embassy closed its premises in West Beirut and confined its business to an annex it established in East Beirut.
Life in the eastern sector is no longer safe either. 
A revolt on March 12 by Christian militiamen against President Amin Gemayel raised the danger of violence among Christians.
Last month, the United States Embassy evacuated 29 staff members from its East Beirut annex to Cyprus. 
Threats by Moslem fundamentalists and the unstable situation in Christian areas were cited as the reasons.
Â 
Many Embassies Move
Most Western embassies have moved either totally or partly to Baabda, a Christian suburb of the capital where the presidential palace and the residence of the American Ambassador, Reginald Bartholomew, are situated. 
Those that remained in West Beirut are heavily guarded or run by skeleton staffs.
The Japanese and the West Germans are the least threatened, because, one authority here said, Tokyo and Bonn are on good terms with the Islamic Government in Teheran. 
There was not one policeman at the West Beirut residence of a West German diplomat when he gave a reception two months ago.
Nevertheless, the street where the West German Embassy is situated is closed to traffic by huge concrete blocks. 
The Japanese Government has decided not to repair its embassy in West Beirut, which was badly damaged by a rocket during fighting last year. 
''There is no guarantee that the embassy would not be wrecked again in future if we undertake repairs,'' a diplomat explained.
The diplomat is one of five Japanese Embassy officials left. 
Of a group that once numbered 1,000, only 9 Japanese are left in Lebanon.
The diplomatic cocktail-party circle has dwindled to nil. 
There were more local friends than foreigners at a reception given by the Ambassador of the Netherlands for the wedding of a staff member last month.
Â 
Dutch Priest Is Slain
But panic has now spread to the few Dutch nationals here after the body of a Dutch Jesuit priest, the Rev. Nicolas Kluiters, was recovered from a pit in eastern Lebanon this week. 
The priest, who had lived in Lebanon for many years, was kidnapped on March 14. 
He appeared to have been strangled.
Soviet bloc diplomats try to convey the impression that for them, business is as usual. 
But the Soviet Embassy is heavily guarded. 
The bomb shelter at the basement of the Soviet Cultural Center, in a separate building, was made livable again after the building was twice attacked by rockets last year.
Shiite fundamentalists took responsibility, saying that they were acting in solidarity with the Mujahedeen, the rebels who are fighting Soviet troops in Afghanistan.
The Islamic Holy War organization has taken responsibility for most of the kidnappings in the last year. 
Islamic Holy War is believed to be only a convenient title used by Shiite fundamentalists who uphold the principles of the Islamic revolution of Iran's religious leader, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.
But at the same time, the two leaders of the Party of God - Shiite clerics and lay activists who strongly support the Khomeini regime - have deplored the abductions.
Â 
Photographed With Sheik
Last month, the Party of God's spokesman, Sheik Ibrahim al-Amin, agreed to have his picture taken with an American correspondent. 
He told the American that if he was ever kidnapped, he should show the photo to the gunmen and they would release him.
Nevertheless, the correspondent left town after learning that Terry A. Anderson, the chief Middle East correspondent of The Associated Press, was kidnapped on a West Beirut street in daylight only a day or two after he had interviewed Imam Mohammed Hussein Fadlallah, beleived to be the spiritual guide of the Party of God.
Islamic Holy War took responsibility for kidnapping Mr. Anderson and for holding four other Americans seized in West Beirut in the last year. 
The four are William Buckley, a political officer at the American Embassy; the Rev. Benjamin Weir, a Presbyterian minister; the Rev. Lawrence Martin Jenco, a Roman Catholic priest, and Peter Kilburn, a librarian at the American University of Beirut.
A former president of the university, Dr. Malcom H. Kerr, was slain outside his office on campus 15 months ago. 
In the summer of 1982, the university's acting president, David S. Dodge, was abducted on campus; he was released after a year in captivity.
His abductors were described as Teheran-linked Shiites who were retaliating for the reported kidnapping two weeks before of three officials of the Iranian Embassy at a Christian militia checkpoint north of Beirut.
Â 
Most Prominent American
Dr. Calvin H. Plimpton, Dr. Kerr's successor, is regarded in Beirut as a man of courage. 
He is the most prominent American living in the Moslem part of Beirut.
Several of the American professors have remained at the American University. 
They avoid being interviewed, but friends said they had resigned themselves to the danger of kidnapping. 
One, an Arabist, always carries with him a message in Arabic addressed to would-be kidnappers quoting verses from the Koran instructing the faithful to be kind to non-Moslems.
From 12,000 Americans living in Lebanon when the civil war broke out a decade ago, only 1,400 are here today. 
An American Embassy source said the majority of those remaining were Lebanese-Americans. 
Only about 250 American citizens are still in West Beirut, most of them associated with the university.
Some 2,500 foreign companies have move out of Beirut, which was once the Middle East's business and banking center.
All but a handful of foreign correspondents have left the city, which used to be the listening post from which events throughout the Middle East were reported. 
All Western embassies had maintained regional sections here, but have now relocated them.
Â 
Tenth of Former Total
The number of foreigners, including Arabs, in Lebanon once totaled 400,000, living among three million Lebanese in a country the size of Connecticut. 
Not more than a tenth that number of foreigners are in Beirut now. 
The Westerners are a mere few hundred.
Not even the Chinese have been spared. 
China's Embassy, in a Moslem suburb, was hit by a rocket-propelled grenade in February.
''Why us?'' an Arabic-speaking Chinese diplomat said, when he accompanied his Ambassador to the Foreign Ministry in East Beirut to lodge a complaint. 
There was no answer to the question.
Formerly, 300 Chinese lived in the 10- story building housing the embassy, complete with a swimming pool and Ping-Pong tables. 
Only 17 officials now reside there.
Arab foreigners have not done much better. 
Of 22 Arab ambassadors, only those from Algeria and Southern Yemen felt safe enough to stay.
Worst hit was the Saudi Embassy, which was ransacked and set ablaze by pro-Khomeini demonstrators last year, three months after the Saudi Consul General, Hussein Farrash, was abducted at gunpoint in West Beirut.
Â 
U.N. Recalls Its Staff
Gone are the days when Arabs from the Persian Gulf came here with their fortunes to invest in real estate and build skyscrapers.
The United Nations decided last week to recall what was left of its foreign staff in Beirut, after a British journalist working for the agency aiding Palestinian refugees was kidnapped. 
The Briton, Alec Collett, is still missing.
The foreigners who remain in Beirut are either tied to their work or have lived in Lebanon so long that they could not adjust if they returned to their countries of origin. 
''I cannot bear the cold weather in Austria anymore,'' said an Austrian restaurateur who has lived in Lebanon for 30 years.
''We're not any better than the Lebanese themselves,'' a West German woman said, noting that more than 3,000 Lebanese had been kidnapped since the civil war began.
A Western news agency official said, ''The foreigners who cannot take the heat and who cannot live under civil strife conditions must not stay.''

text:

IRON & SILK By Mark Salzman. 
211 pp. 
New York: Random House. 
$16.95.
IF there were a prize for most winning writer, Mark Salzman would cop it. 
After studying all things Chinese at Yale University, he took a job teaching English to doctors in the city of Changsha in Hunan Province. 
During his two-year tour of duty, in addition to his teaching, he managed to study calligraphy as well as more than one of the Chinese martial arts. 
He also played the cello, tuned a piano, killed a rat with his American College Dictionary and generally kept his eyes and ears open. 
If there has ever been a better American ambassador to China, I don't know of him. 
Well aware of the antipathetical philosophy of the society, irked by a crabbed bureaucracy whose instinct is to holler ''no'' after any request and depressed by the lack of physical charms with which Communism has cemented itself upon a charming people, Mr. Salzman retained and indeed enlarged his deep affection for China and its people. 
It should come as no surprise that their feeling was reciprocal toward this courteous, friendly young American.
''Iron & Silk'' is a collection of anecdotes, each intended to give a glimpse of a circumstance of life in China or a trait of the Chinese, and all written in a jerry-built teen-age prose that is oddly appealing for all its habit of bumping into itself. 
Ah, but for that I prefer to put the blame on Yale rather than the author. 
It would be swinish to carp about a book that kept a smile on my face from cover to cover. 
Besides, where is it graven in stone that one must write stately Latinate phrases in a hand still pudgy with baby fat?
None of the anecdotes in this book is anything less than compelling. 
For instance, Mr. Salzman once assigned his student-doctors to write a composition entitled ''My Happiest Moment.''
Mr. Zhu, after recounting in minutest detail his having dined on Peking duck in a famous restaurant in Beijing, confessed that he had never actually eaten duck in Beijing. 
He had never even been to Beijing. 
It was his wife who had done that, ''but she often tells me about it again and again, and I think, even though I was not there, it is my happiest moment.''
Struggling to satisfy the seemingly cruel demands of his Chinese weaponry teacher, Mr. Salzman had to practice mutual staring and scowling for minutes at a time and always in a state of anticipation of the unexpected blow. 
The art of wushu, we learn, draws its strength from the eyes. 
By staring at his student, a teacher passes it on. 
When Mr. Salzman clumsily lost control of his weapon and injured himself, the teacher remarked with admiration, ''Sweating and bleeding. 
Good.''
About calligraphy he learned that there are several tens of styles and that to make a single dot may involve five distinct motions of the wrist and shoulder.
Some of the ways of China ought to be adopted immediately by the West. 
One of these is the means by which the Chinese endure the endless, boring speeches to which they are subjected. 
Actual listening is optional. 
Nor do they pretend to pay attention, but openly doze or get up and walk around or chat among themselves, none of which offends the speaker in the least. 
Very sensible. 
Most touching and most hopeful is Mr. Salzman's rendering of the relationship between teacher and student. 
It is clearly one of profound respect and devotion, a blend of expectation and obligation. 
Any distance between East and West shrinks to inconsequence alongside instruction and learning on a one-to-one basis, as with his calligraphy and wushu teachers. 
What stirs is no less than the yearning for world peace. 
STILL, despite Mr. Salzman's sincerity and eagerness, East remains adamantly East, where ''The World According to Garp'' is ''very, very unsuitable'' reading and one cannot be treated for athlete's foot because it has been ''declared successfully driven out of China.''
Reaching out, Mr. Salzman asked the young man who taught him calligraphy what two things he thought about most. 
''Eating and sleeping'' was the reply, which was a far cry from Mr. Salzman's own confession that he more than anything wanted to be liked, especially by women, and that he wanted to master something, anything, well enough to earn recognition for it. 
The Chinese teacher was incredulous: ''But these goals can be achieved so easily!
All you have to do is be kind and work hard. 
But to eat and sleep well, that is a difficult wish, because you cannot control these things yourself.''
For all the moments of mutual pleasure in each other's companionship, the Chinese and the American were rarely able to cross over the cultural gap. 
Still, Mr. Salzman will have us believe it is enough to understand that the gap is there and that much hard work lies ahead for both countries.

text:
ï»¿
Over the last 10 years, China's intellectuals have visibly if slowly shaken off the effects of decades of re-education and imprisonment, public humiliation and private despair.
And yet, while some of those who endured labor camps and prisons have managed to leave China, to speak from the safety of adopted homelands, almost no one here has been willing to talk with candor about the past treatment of the intelligentsia, to reflect on the larger meaning of a society that so easily turned on its best and brightest in pursuit of one man's notion of class struggle and communism. 
And few have spoken publicly about the implications of this tortured history on writers, artists and academics today.
Seldom does an individual Chinese intellectual speak critically of his country. 
Fang Lizhi, the astrophysicist who was expelled from the Communist Party in January 1987 for his discordant views, is almost alone in challenging Government and party policies. 
A journalist, Liu Binyan, who was expelled from the party at the same time for similar views, held his tongue until he journeyed abroad this year.
Retribution for dissonant opinions remains a constant threat. 
Not long ago, Professor Fang was denied permission to visit the United States to attend a scientific conference because of what he said was ''displeasure by the leaders over my views.''
Â 
'We Must Be Careful'
A well-known young writer here in the capital talked quietly of this reluctance. 
''You know, people like us worry about this, but because our futures are controlled we must be careful,'' he said. 
''Of course it's very important to know what happened to the older generation because that could happen again. 
We need to know what older intellectuals went through. 
We don't want that for our generation.''
Prof. Wu Ningkun, who now teaches English literature at the Institute of Foreign Relations in Beijing, is one of that older generation. 
He agreed to recount his experiences, not because they are so much different from those of others, he said, but because they tell much about what China has been since Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic in 1949. 
He said his treatment, and that of others like him, suggests the limits of intellectual life in this society.
''I had heard a lot of good things about China,'' Professor Wu recalled of letters he received in 1950, when he was in the United States. 
''I had been very dissatisfied with the Kuomintang regime, like most of my contemporaries. 
So everything we heard about the Communists was good. 
China was turning over a new page.''
That year, a friend on the English faculty at Yanjing University urged him to leave the University of Chicago, where he was finishing a doctorate, and return to China to teach. 
After wrestling with the attraction of American academia and the tug of patriotism, Professor Wu finally gave way and arrived in Canton in 1951.
Â 
A Revolutionary University
''The most unforgettable experience in Canton was that we were taken to visit a revolutionary university,'' he continued. 
''It was a very dingy old place. 
We were taken into a room.
''We didn't see any revolutionaries, but there were pamphlets, handwritten pamphlets on display. 
They were all autobiographies - meaning confessions of the students, to say how they had committed this or that crime or sin against the people. 
The political commissar came and spoke to us and told us what this place was for, to help the intellectuals reform themselves, for ideological remolding. 
So we were given a foretaste of our own future.''
From Canton, he went to Beijing and joined the English department. 
Life changed rapidly for the young assistant professor during a series of political campaigns intended to purify the ideological consciousness of the country. 
''The academic atmosphere changed greatly after that,'' he said.
''Now, what was uppermost in your consciousness was whether to be for or against,'' he said. 
''You either have to go along or resist. 
That's how you got into deeper and deeper trouble.''
''In 1955 came this movement to uproot the hidden counterrevolutionaries, to smoke them out,'' he said. 
''So my house was searched for counterrevolutionary evidence. 
I was denounced. 
They made me sit in the center of the room, and I was surrounded by a whole group of my accusers, the entire department. 
I had read 'Darkness at Noon' and '1984,' and I said, 'My god, it's all happening, this is going to be the future.'
''
Â 
A New Day Dawns
The denunciations tapered off toward the end of 1955. 
When 1956 dawned, many intellectuals, including Professor Wu, felt more hopeful that the party would be more accommodating to a diversity of views. 
That year, a short-lived explosion of opinions, many extremely critical of the Communist Party, swept through the press, part of the so-called Hundred Flowers period. 
Professor Wu was transferred to the Institute of Foreign Relations.
''Everybody was elated, even the leftists, people who had been very active in denouncing me,'' Professor Wu said. 
''They said, 'Now China will be different.'
'' Then, in the summer of 1957, the official press published editorials attacking outspoken intellectuals. 
Mao called for a purge of ''rightists.''
''I didn't consider myself a rightist,'' Professor Wu said. 
''I didn't know I qualified. 
My understanding of politics was very naive and limited. 
Well, I was the number one rightist. 
I was officially labeled an ultra-rightist. 
That meant there would be practical consequences. 
Most of what I had said had to do with freedom of speech. 
As an intellectual that was my uppermost concern: people are not only born equal but they're born free to speak.''
Leading the national campaign against so-called rightists was Deng Xiaoping, now the country's senior leader. 
The new mood of repression swept campuses, publishing houses and film studios.
Â 
Sent to a Labor Camp
At the Institute of Foreign Relations, Professor Wu said, it was decided that he would be sent to a labor camp to be re-educated. 
He and other academics labeled as rightists were shipped to a swampy area near the border of Soviet Siberia, an area near Xingkai Lake in Heilongjiang Province.
''They didn't need any legality,'' he said. 
''It was to educate me, except that it's in prison. 
The worst part about it is that it's indefinite. 
We were even laughed at by the prisoners, by the penal criminals. 
They said, 'I serve five years, I go home. 
How do you know you'll ever get out of here?'
'' In 1960, as China was enduring its worst famine of the century, he was transferred with many other rightists to a walled prison farm outside Beijing.
Although many other writers, poets and academics were imprisoned with him, no one talked about literature or politics, he said. 
''Nobody dared, and nobody was interested because they were hungry all the time,'' he said. 
''They were dying of hunger.''
When Professor Wu began digging graves to bury cell-mates who had died of starvation, he decided to write to his wife, Li Yikai, to tell her to come for a last visit. 
His wife, who herself had been deprived of her academic job simply because she was married to a rightist, was shocked by the frail man who met her that day in 1961. 
She left the prison and went to the Institute of Foreign Relations, the only entity that could win freedom for her husband. 
Some weeks later, Professor Wu was handed a train ticket and taken to the station on a donkey cart.
Â 
Half a Million Rightists
There were in 1962, by official Government count, more than half a million people classified as rightists, people who had been persecuted since 1957, from imprisonment of the sort endured by Professor Wu to losing their jobs at universities and institutes -virtually the entire intelligentsia of the country. 
Once again, the repressive intellectual environment seemed to ease.
He returned to teaching at Anhui University. 
From 1962 to 1966, he and his family lived quietly until the morning of June 6, 1966, the day the Cultural Revolution came to Anhui University.
''We were sleeping and my wife nudged me,'' he said. 
''She said, 'Ningkun, you hear the shouting. 
They're shouting your name.'
So I began to hear closer and closer, 'Down with Wu Ningkun, down with ultrarightist Wu Ningkun, down with U.S. imperialist element Wu Ningkun.'
''
''They took me to one of these public places on campus,'' he said. 
''A student leader was making a long speech. 
He was haranguing against the crimes, sins and counterrevolutionary activities of all the teachers. 
And I was hit and kicked so hard, I was on my knees.''
The next year, Professor Wu was sent to a village to perform hard labor and, in the words of his tormentors, to be educated by the peasants. 
''We were shifted around, to different villages and criticized from village to village,'' he said. 
His wife and children were sent to another village in Anhui Province where they too were to be re-educated. 
After five years, they were reunited in his wife's village.
Â 
'I Had No Identity'
''I was nobody,'' Professor Wu said of arriving in his wife's village. 
''I had no identity. 
My children had changed their names. 
Wu Yiding became Li Nong, Li the Peasant, Wu Yimao became Li Zhong, Li the Faithful, that is faithful to Chairman Mao's thought. 
The name Wu was odious.''
He lived in this village in western Anhui Province until 1974, when he and his family were sent to the small town of Wuhu where he was to resume teaching. 
Again, in 1976, in the last gasps of the Cultural Revolution, Professor Wu was denounced. 
''People started shunning me again,'' he remembered. 
''I said oh-oh, here we go again.''
Finally in 1979, three years after the death of Mao and the arrest of his wife and her radical associates in the party leadership, Professor Wu was summoned back to Beijing to the Institute of International Relations to be politically ''rehabilitated.''
In the years that followed, he has been promoted to full professor, given a three-bedroom apartment and allowed to travel abroad. 
His children - once denounced as ''little ultra-rightists'' and ''little cow monsters'' - now live in the United States. 
But What of the Future?
For China's young writers and academics, it is the experiences of people like Professor Wu and the tens of thousands of others like him that may insure some greater measure of intellectual freedom. 
Indeed, a recent television series, ''River Elegy,'' issued the bluntest warning of this threat.
''Although 20th century Chinese intellectuals are now rid of the misfortune of being categorized as 'stinking ninth elements,' their social status has only been marginally raised,'' wrote the program's authors. 
''Economic and psychological pressures still affect them. 
There are constant reports of their early deaths.
''What is more horrifying is that a country where Confucius was most respected is now treating its teachers so badly. 
The old generation is dying and the younger generation is unwilling to follow in their footsteps. 
They are desperately in need of cleaner air and more freedom.''

text:
ï»¿
ONCE UPON A TIME THE BRIT-ish, masters of half the world, built a modest palace for the Governor of their easternmost possession, Hong Kong, which they had acquired as booty of the Anglo-Chinese Opium War of 1839-42.
It was a pleasant, white building, classically pillared, and from its hillside slope it dominated the magnificent harbor that lay below, where the traffic of Empire came and went.
A century and more later, Government House still stands, but there have arisen stupendously around it, all but blocking that prospect of the harbor, the overwhelming skyscrapers of commerce and finance, glittering with the investments of a dozen nations and towering grossly over the Union Jack flying from the mansion's flagstaff.
For, yes, although 98 percent of its people are Chinese, Hong Kong, which lies 6,000 miles from London, is still a British Crown Colony, and a Governor still occupies the mansion - Sir David Wilson, who came to office earlier this year, the 27th in a line of succession that began in 1841. 
He lives in the unmistakable style of the late Pax Britannica, with its wry ambiance of slightly amused but dignified restraint. 
He assumes, when the occasion demands, all the old trappings of Empire, the plumed hat and the striped trousers, and he is attended, of course, by elegant aides and considerate Chinese servants. 
He is driven about in a Rolls-Royce Phantom, he sails across the harbor in a gloriously elderly yacht, and he performs, as British colonial governors always have, all manner of ceremonial functions, presiding over legislatures, receiving visiting swells, representing Her Majesty at celebrations of the Queen's Birthday.
But he is also the all-powerful chief administrator of Hong Kong, and just as the posture of his mansion has been transformed by the turns of history, so Sir David Wilson now plays a role that would have seemed inconceivable to most of his predecessors. 
His prime function is to supervise preparations for Hong Kong's departure, in 1997, from the British Empire - its return to the motherland, China, and the absorption of its colonial-style capitalism into the body of Chinese Communism.
It is possible that Wilson may be the last British Governor of Hong Kong; almost certainly he will be the last to exert any real power. 
After him all will be mere formality. 
Hong Kong is, in effect, the end of the British Empire, its population, at 5.6 million, being some 35 times greater than the population of all the other remaining overseas possessions put together.
Sir David is a courteous and intellectual Scot, a 52-year-old Sinologist who was once editor of the authoritative China Quarterly, a distinguished mountaineer who has climbed in the Chinese Karakoram and a diplomat with 30 years' experience of Asian affairs; just the person, one would think, for the job and for the moment.
Ten years before its return to China, Hong Kong is in a ferment of change. 
It is earnestly, anxiously, often angrily bracing itself for the denouement. 
Its colonial character is fading fast, and Wilson's successors are already jostling for position - not only the agents of the People's Republic of China, but ambitious Hong Kong citizens of many persuasions. 
New political movements are springing into existence, the territory buzzes with rumor and speculation, rascals and philanthropists alike are taking up advantageous positions. 
For it is generally believed that what happens now, while the British are still in control, will decree what happens in Hong Kong far into the 21st century.
THE WORLD AT LARGE thought the Hong Kong question settled in 1984, when the British Government agreed to return the colony to Chinese sovereignty in 1997, and the Chinese Government promised that for 50 years thereafter Hong Kong's ''capitalist system and life style shall remain unchanged.''
The colony would become a Special Administrative Region - S.A.R. for short - part of the People's Republic of China, but specifically excused for half a century from China's socialist ideology. 
As the Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping himself put it, two systems would coexist within one country.
The concord was generally hailed as an acceptable conclusion to Britain's imperial career upon the China coast, enabling it to maintain satisfactory economic relations with the People's Republic. 
Deng assured the people of Hong Kong that they need have no worries about their future.
But, from the start, they did. 
They put no dependence on Deng's assurances -and who honestly could, after China's volatile changes of style and temper during the last few decades?
And they suspected that Hong Kong, none of whose inhabitants had played any part in the treaty negotiations, was being regarded chiefly as a source of foreign currency and technology for China, a base for international financiers and conglomerates - not as the home of more than five million people, many refugees from Communist China and few possessing any nationality other than that of British colonial subject.
In Chinese semantics, an American Sinologist once observed to me, ''words are like rubber,'' and the terms of the 1984 agreement are certainly elastic. 
The Chinese, for example, undertook to draw up a constitution for the S.A.R., to be known as the Basic Law, which they are preparing in consultation with notables within Hong Kong. 
It is expected to be made public next year, but nobody knows whether it will really work as a constitution in the Western sense, guaranteeing the rights of the people, or a constitution in the Communist sense, entrenching the powers of the state. 
The 1984 agreement promises that the legislature of the S.A.R. will be chosen ''by election'' - but what that signifies, and whether it will be any more popularly elected than the People's Congress in Beijing, is anyone's guess.
And what do the Chinese mean when they promise the ''accountability'' of the executive to the legislature - an obligation to obey, or simply an undertaking to report?
What do they mean by ''capitalism,'' or for that matter ''socialism''?
What indeed do they mean by ''life style,'' which sounds more like an adman's concept than a diplomatic definition, and are they referring to Hong Kong's life style as it is now, or as it will be in 1997?
It is Sir David Wilson's job to make the most of this equivocal concord, which he helped to negotiate. 
I asked him recently what he saw as his chief historical obligation toward the colony. 
He said it was to insure that Hong Kong was handed over to China in good working condition, but I suspect he may have been deliberately ambiguous in his response. 
He is careful with his words.
Certainly there are many people in Hong Kong, Chinese and British, who believe that his duty is more profound. 
They think he owes it to the conscience of the British and their lost Empire to leave Hong Kong with a government of its own, composed of Hong Kong people, elected by Hong Kong citizens, a government strong and experienced enough to stand up to the Chinese Communists when they formally arrive with their party secretaries and their propagandists on July 1, 1997. 
''Fair play'' was the ideology of the British Empire at its best; the fount of its authority, after all, was the mother of parliaments at Westminster. 
And fair play seems to demand that the last of the imperialists should leave the people of Hong Kong as much in control of their own destinies as is politically possible.
READERS OF HONG KONG newspapers cannot fail to have noticed a recent change in the nomenclature of Sir Y. K. Pao, one of the colony's richest and most powerful citizens, who for years has been known to everyone as Sir Y. K. - a truly imperial colloquialism. 
Lately, he has been identified in the press as Sir Yue-Kong Pao, and one wonders how long it will be before he forgets his imperial honorific altogether and tactfully returns to his original persona - citizen Pao Yue-Kong, from the Chinese province of Zhejiang.
Several such colonial grandees have already made their peace with Communism, and the powerful international financial community seems at the moment similarly sanguine. 
At the level of high finance, the reunion of Hong Kong with China seems to be going well enough. 
It is true that there has been a steady exodus of middle-rank, middle-aged business people, and many more plan to leave before 1997, but at the top there is no sign of panic.
There is hardly a Hong Kong businessman - Chinese, Japanese, European, Australian or American -who would not prefer this marvelously profitable city to remain just as it is. 
But faced with the certainty of change, many of them appear to think that whatever happens after 1997, they can at least reinforce their fortunes in the meantime. 
For the most part, they have little to lose anyway. 
The conglomerates can easily switch their cash and their operations elsewhere; the Chinese tycoons are so rich that they can move where they like when they like, and, indeed, many of them have already acquired homes and thriving bank accounts in Canada, Australia or the United States.
So big business still flourishes in the doomed colony, and the place clicks, flashes, fizzes, blinks, roars, rumbles and pullulates as vigorously as ever. 
Property values are stunningly high, the stock market is bullish, new office blocks are going up everywhere. 
One international consortium is building a new tunnel under the harbor, and another is hoping to build a new airport and a new seaport on an artificial island.
Hong Kong is the second-largest container port in the world, and one of the world's half-dozen key financial centers. 
The city's gleaming new Exchange Square swarms with young brokers and bankers from all over the world. 
When I asked one American why he and his colleagues seldom left the office before 8 in the evening, his reply adequately expressed the flavor of this marketplace: ''Because we're aggressive young men trying to make as much money as possible in the shortest possible time.''
To some entrepreneurs, reunion with China itself promises a bonanza, and already Hong Kong money is hard at work searching for new profits within the People's Republic. 
Some 2,000 factories in nearby Guangdong province are owned, or partly owned, by Hong Kong concerns, and thousands more operate for Hong Kong industrialists under subcontracts. 
Countless Hong Kong concerns have offices or branches in Beijing. 
Conversely, within Hong Kong there are now hundreds of concerns owned wholly or partly by the agencies of Communist China, including banks, insurance companies, airlines, hotels and newspapers.
The truth is that now, as always, to the big moneymakers the existence of Hong Kong is no more than a convenience, and if reconciliation with Communist China offers the best hope of future profit, so be it. 
Sir Y. K., whose family came to the territory as refugees from Communism, is now almost as honored in Beijing as he is in Hong Kong, and he has handsomely subsidized a new university in his birthplace of Ningbo, where he is already referred to as Mr. Pao.
CONSIDER, HOW-ever, the group of young people on the upper deck of the ferry to Lantau Island. 
They are extremely lively, extremely neat, extremely polite, extremely engaging young people. 
Laughing a lot, with their bright blue rucksacks, their sneakers and their Walkman radios, they might easily be, were it not for the chirpy Cantonese of their conversation, students at one of the more genial and go-ahead universities of the West.
They are Sir David Wilson's particular wards and charges, an educated young bourgeoisie brought into being entirely by the presence of Britain in Hong Kong. 
There is nobody like them in China proper, and they are the colony's chief cause for pride. 
Admirably fit (Hong Kong has one of the highest life-expectancy rates in the world), highly numerate and literate, they seem as clever, as promising and as thoroughly normal a young society as you can find anywhere on earth.
I use the word ''normal'' advisedly, because this is the first ordinary generation Hong Kong has been able to foster. 
The territory was born and bred to abnormality. 
Peculiar in its origins, unique in its functions, until 20 or so years ago it was, above all, a city of refugees, intent as refugees must be on establishing themselves and accumulating enough cash to give their children security.
It was the pressure of these communal anxieties, plus, of course, the Chinese genius for commerce and finance, that gave rise to the old canard about the people of Hong Kong being interested exclusively in the making of money. 
This was certainly true, as it still is, of most of its expatriates, generally transients making a quick and easy buck before returning home to Europe, America, Australia or Japan. 
It is, however, no more true of the new educated middle-class young Chinese on that ferryboat than it is of young people anywhere else.
Their interests and emotions are the same as those of young Americans or Europeans. 
They are just as idealistic, no more, no less; just as concerned with a proper balance of life, between the necessary making of money and enjoyable ways of spending it. 
They were nearly all born into this temple of capitalism, with its seductions of wealth and financial power, but they are by no means all blinkered in materialism. 
Indeed, a British employer of my acquaintance tells me that his junior executives and secretaries sometimes seem to him almost alarmingly altruistic, so preoccupied are they with good causes and high intentions.
A decade from now the British Empire will be delivering this generation, by then in its 30's and early 40's, into the unpredictable hands of the People's Republic of China. 
Its members do not generally have the option, as do foreigners and the very rich, of going somewhere else. 
Nurtured as they were beneath the British flag to British citizenship of a kind, they, nevertheless, have no legal right to go to live in Britain. 
When 1997 comes, they will be utterly dependent upon the good faith and the political constancy of China - which has shown itself, during their lifetimes, almost preposterously inconstant.
The historical duty of the British, says the Governor, is to hand over Hong Kong in good working condition, but essential to that condition will be the support of this formidable new bourgeoisie. 
In such countries as South Korea, Singapore and even Taiwan, these are the very people who have lately forced their Governments into political concessions; and in the years before 1997 they might still plunge Hong Kong into confusion, sending stock prices and land values plunging, driving the foreign financiers out, thus killing the golden goose before the Chinese even get hold of the nest.
So in the first generation of their existence, they seem to me to hold the fortunes of Hong Kong in their hands. 
It is because the British are still there, because they have kept the colony in orderly equilibrium through many hazards, that Hong Kong remains a world financial center, and a vital instrument of China's own economic policies. 
What a prize the People's Republic will be acquiring, if Hong Kong is transferred in its present state of prosperous efficiency!
All depends, though, upon the young bourgeoisie. 
Keeping them content, encouraging their sense of responsibility, is a sine qua non of Hong Kong's continued success; and keeping them content must surely entail giving them a proper share in the running of their own territory.
THERE'S THE crunch. 
Politics!
As never before in its history, Hong Kong today is in political tumult. 
This is all the more startling because British Hong Kong has never been anything like a democracy. 
It has honorably fostered freedom of speech, thought and opportunity, but its Government has always been of the standard Crown Colony pattern, in which an all-but-omnipotent Governor, subject only to London, has been supported by an administration firmly under his thumb. 
The Executive Council, the policy-making body, is entirely officially nominated, and only a minority of the Legislative Council, Legco, is elected. 
Nobody on Legco is chosen by direct vote in a public ballot box, and its electorate is drawn from an infinitesimal part of the population - about 71,000 out of 5.6 million - who are members of various local councils and professional or trade organizations. 
The Governor personally presides over both councils.
The notion of adversarial politics, with all its concomitants of party dissent and economic fluctuation, has been anathema to the financiers of Hong Kong, and to many of its ordinary people. 
Until now the only organized political activists have been the Communists, and when in 1967, under the impulse of the Cultural Revolution, they came into the streets of Hong Kong with riots, bombs and Little Red Books, the populace at large was unfeignedly grateful to a colonial autocracy that brusquely put them down.
But there have always been voices to criticize the archaic order of Hong Kong. 
For years, visiting parliamentarians have expressed their dismay at the spectacle of this territory, so rich, so capable, so modern, yet so stuck in the political forms of fin de siecle. 
And they have been backed within Hong Kong by a persistent handful of Chinese and some progressive-minded expatriates.
So fierce had these criticisms become by 1984 that in order to get the Sino-British agreement accepted by the British Parliament, Margaret Thatcher's Government had to promise a measure of constitutional reform for Hong Kong. 
Almost simultaneously, the British announced their intention of making the colony's legislature more properly representative.
Since 1984, the voting franchise for Legco has, in fact, been somewhat widened, and the Government is committed to a further review next year. 
Three years have passed, three years out of 13, and Hong Kong is now in a dangerous frenzy of debate about the reforms that haven't yet happened. 
Scores of political organizations, mistily identified by names like the Group of 71 or Meeting Point, are now posturing and arguing, petitioning and protesting. 
Everyone talks of it, everyone writes about it, everyone has a view, whether it be that of the fiery liberal lawyer Martin Lee (''The Government cannot stifle the wave of public opinion without facing the consequences'') or that of the former Chief Secretary, Sir David Akers-Jones (''What we must do is adjust gradually and maintain the balance between the various parts of the system'').
Some want immediate universal franchise and direct elections, on the ground that a community that has reached a certain level of maturity has the right to run its own affairs. 
Some demand exactly the opposite -the firm maintenance of the status quo, on the ground that tampering with it can lead only to trouble. 
Don't risk upsetting Beijing, says one school of thought; make sure, says another, that the people of Hong Kong have some genuine political experience before they are handed over to the Communists.
On the whole, I suspect that big business, whether Chinese or foreign, would prefer as little change as possible. 
Anyway, what's the use of introducing democracy now, runs a favorite Exchange Square argument, when the Chinese are sure to abolish it in 1997?
Pollsters, however, report that the majority of the population at large now wants representative government, and that probably includes most of those young, educated people who are likely to provide Hong Kong's civic leadership by 1997.
Views are, however, by no means stereotyped. 
Some conservatives believe repressing political instincts is likely to be more dangerous to stabilityI than satisfying them. 
Some liberals believe party politics would soon be subverted and manipulated by the Chinese Communists. 
Already, one hears horror stories about Beijing's interfering with the political processes - ''Do we gather you support the idea of political reform?
Oh?
Well, about that contract now. 
. . .''
As for the Government, it keeps its own counsel; although generally benevolent, it has always been a reticent regime. 
Last May, it published a Green Paper outlining possible alternative constitutional developments for 1988. 
Skeptics maintain that this is merely camouflage, and that under Chinese pressure the British are really reneging on assurances of reform, or at least tempering them to suit the forthcoming Basic Law. 
Who knows?
When I asked the Governor for his personal view about what should be done, he replied, with a gentle Foreign Office sort of smile, that this was the only question to which he was not prepared to give a direct reply.
IRONY HAS BEEN A pervasive characteristic of the British Empire in its last years, its silver years, during which it has watched its own dispersal with a blend of regret, relief, pride, cynicism and self-amusement. 
It is an attractive quality in many ways, puncturing pomposity and bitterness, and clothing one of history's truly grand processes - the dissolution of the greatest of all Empires - in a dressing of humor.
But time is running short for irony. 
Already one senses the shift of power in Hong Kong as the British prepare to go, the Chinese to take over. 
An ever-decreasing cadre of Britons is all that is left of the old imperial administration, and an American now heads Jardine Matheson, the most famous of Hong Kong's old British concerns. 
If you enjoy watching history speeding up, like a movie running too fast, Hong Kong is the place to be.
Everything the British do now is in reflex to the attitudes of China across the border, and in anticipation of 1997. 
Yet even now, they alone can decree what ideological legacy they will bequeath to the Special Administrative Region of Xianggang. 
They can play it safe, so as not to upset the money market or exacerbate Chinese suspicions. 
Or they can be bold, and make of Hong Kong, just in time, a democracy in their own image.
Whichever course the British take as they calculate the risks and assess the advantages, they have one gigantic imponderable to face: they do not really know what they are preparing for. 
Neither Sir David Wilson, nor Sir Y. K. Pao, nor the chairman of the Hongkong Bank, nor the shrewdest of American company lawyers, nor the most cunning of Australian property millionaires, can possibly know what China itself will be like in the year 1997, when Deng Xiaoping is gone and a new generation dominates party thinking in Beijing. 
It may well honor its commitments, or it may scrap them. 
It may be freer than it is now, or more despotic, more open to the West or more closed, loyal to the memory of the pragmatic Deng or pursuing once again the philosophies of the dogmatic Mao Zedong. 
Perhaps it will respect the status of democratically elected politicians in Hong Kong, or perhaps it will parade them in dunce hats outside Government House.
It is impossible for the 27th Governor to know, and when I asked one of the best-informed of all Western Sinologists how he thought the present Chinese leaders really saw the future of Hong Kong, he said they didn't know either. 
Nobody knows - an ironic text, with a vengeance, for the British Empire's epilogue.

BY L.R.SHANNON
Many American travelers to foreign countries optimistically arm themselves with English-to-Ruritarian phrase books to help them navigate through menus and ruins, to restrooms and post offices. 
Generally, such language guides are divided into categories - dining, drinking, touring, and so on - with what are considered useful words and phrases for each.
At first blush, these books seem a good idea, although only someone already fairly skilled in the language in question might be able to tell from reading one whether ''zhay fam'' is likely to indicate you are hungry or henpecked, or ''ic MOC-tuh I-nuh pen-SYOHN'' get you a German boardinghouse or retirement pay. 
And they all leave you in the quandary of wondering what to do if you rattle off ''How much time have you spent doing manual labor in the countryside?'' in perfect Mandarin and the rehabilitated revisionist actually answers.
Discussion of language guide books for travel in China
As travel to China has increased in recent years, the number of guidebooks and phrase books for visitors to that country has increased at a rate that would warm the hearts of a publishers' production brigade. 
The idea is that you find what you want to say in the English translations and then point to the adjoining Chinese characters. 
(Given the recent abominable record of most publishers' proofreading of English, one does wonder how trustworthy the Chinese is.) Some of the books also offer English phonetic renderings of the Chinese.
A trial of the phonetic version of ''I am happy to be visiting your commune'' on a Chinese-speaking friend produced the testy reply that it was rather late in the day to bring up Quemoy and Matsu and threaten to unleash Sen. William F. Knowland.
A recent day spent armchair-traveling in China in the company of three guidebooks, each containing a supplementary language section, plus a pocket Chinese phrase book, underlined some of the potential pitfalls. 
(Actually, I did it on a sofa, but when you travel in imagination you have to say you did it in an armchair. 
Sofatraveling is very cumbersome.) Most of the sentences are basic and undoubtedly apt, but among them are several questions one doubts ever got asked and propositions one doubts ever got proposed.
Following is a lightning imaginary trip to China, as illustrated by useful sentences and helpful hints drawn from ''The Morrow Travel Guide to the People's Republic of China,'' by Ruth Lor Malloy (Quill); ''The American's Tourist Manual for the People's Republic of China,'' compiled by John E. Felber (International Intertrade Index); ''China Companion,'' by Evelyne Garside (Farrar Straus Giroux), and ''China Traveler's Phrase Book,'' by Bennett Lee and Geremie Barme (Eurasia Press). 
They are all available in paperback.
At the Hotel
''Your room boy or girl will probably walk into your room unannounced but be nowhere to be found when you want something.''
(Garside)
''Where do I register?''
''What is my room number?''
''When will it be ready?''
''The hot water is cold.''
''Do you have a megaphone?''
On Tour
''A combination public address and radio speaker bring forth marches, classics and setting up exercises in the morning. 
One will find the Chinese trains in immaculate condition and quite modern.''
(Felber)
''Trains are fairly comfortable, although heating and ventilation are dispensed sparingly and radio broadcasts over-generously ...you may discover that the standard of cleanliness and service varies.''
(Garside)
''Usually no air-conditioning. 
Very hot in summer. 
The toilets are filthy.''
(Malloy) ''How much money do you make a month?''
''If she is nursing her baby, how many hours with pay does she get a day to feed it?''
''Please forgive me if I am asking too personal questions.''
''May I see your composting techniques?''
''Is there a barefoot doctor in this production brigade?''
''What a bore!''
Dining
''Many say (the food) is the finest in the world.''
(Felber) ''It is only in the large and relatively modern cities ...that you can hope to find a good restaurant.''
(Garside) ''To best enjoy a meal, never ask what a particular morsel is.''
(Malloy) ''Where is the dining room?''
''We would like four dishes and a soup.''
''What was the name of that dish?''
''My stomach is upset.''
''How long bed rest?''
Drinking
''One of the stronger wines is Mou T'ai Chiew or better known in its short form, 'mou t'ai' (chiew) meaning wine in Chinese. 
It has a very high proof, some say stronger than vodka. 
It is served in tiny shot glasses and it's not uncommon for ten or more to be served or at least offered at special occasions.''(Felber)
''Where is the bar?''
''But you have been so kind and I feel I will be indebted to you for the rest of my life.''
''How many work points would you make per day if you spent the day weeding?''
''Bottoms up.''
Most language guides suggest that you master a handful of sentences (however many sentences make up a handful) of wide utility - of the ''hello,'' ''pardon me,'' ''where is the bathroom?'' sort. 
Western travelers to China, in this writer's opinion, should thoroughly learn to say ''wo bu xihuan chi gourou'' and use it frequently, even compulsively, whenever in the slightest doubt.
How much trouble can you get in by constantly repeating that you do not like to eat dog meat?

text:
SPEAKING VOLUMES
Bookshops in New York tend to grow in clusters, the remnants of the old Fourth Avenue secondhand center still in the neighborhood of 12th Street and the larger general-trade emporiums on Fifth Avenue in the upper 40's and 50's. 
One of the most exotic bookstore regions anywhere is on lower Fifth Avenue, between 18th and 21st Streets, where four stores each carries large stocks for completely different clienteles.
The Soviet Union has a literary corner in the Four Continent Book Corporation at 149 Fifth, at 21st Street (533-0250). 
This large store stocks Soviet letters, Russian grammars, periodicals and other publications from nonpolitical to most political. 
The bulk of these are in Russian, with one larger section in Ukrainian and smaller sections in such other tongues as Armenian and Yiddish, which is placed on a hard-to-get-at bottom shelf but has perhaps a few dozen titles. 
Open 9:30 A.M. to 5:30 P.M. Mondays through Saturday.
Going Out Guide highlights upcoming cultural and entertainment events
At No. 125, north of 19th Street, is China Books and Periodicals (677-2650), less imposing quarters than those filled by books from the Soviet store a block north. 
The books are mostly in English, although one wall is devoted to works in Chinese. 
The publications here also deal with third-world politics as well as with grammars for learning Chinese and nonpartisan guides for visitors to China. 
Open 10 A.M. to 6 P.M., Mondays through Saturdays.
There is a distinctly continental change by the time one reaches the attractive and vast French and Spanish Book Corporation, 115 Fifth, just north of 18th Street (673-7400). 
One section is for French books of all sorts, another for Spanish, while a third is a marvelous repository of dictionaries for all languages, including the most obscure. 
As visitors enter, they can get into training for the stock here by choosing from the language-learning books clustered in a small enclave. 
Open from 9 to 6 Mondays through Fridays, from 10 to 6 Saturdays.
The doyen of bookish lower Fifth Avenue is Barnes & Noble, 105 Fifth, at 18th Street. 
The language in this large store of texttooks and instructional material is mostly academic, although general and avid browsers can pleasantly exhaust themselves in the equally large annex across Fifth Avenue, which is filled with paperbacks, publishers' overstocks and other books, ad infinitum. 
Open Mondays through Fridays, 9:45 to 6:45; Saturdays from 9:45 to 6, Sundays, 11 to 6.
ART
They take cultural matters seriously at District 1199, which has a gallery in the union headquarters, 310 West 43d Street (947-1944), in which exhibitions are regularly on display as part of the organization's ''Bread and Roses'' program of art, theater, dance and other forms of artistic expression offered to members and others.
The current show, ''Latino New York,'' the first exhibition of Latin-American artists by a union, displays the work of five painters born in this country or in Puerto Rico, but all working in New York.
They manifest a variety of approaches to a variety of subjects, from whimsy to social message by way of Exit Art to collages. 
The artists are Papo Colo, Marina Gutierrez, Vilma Maldonado Reyes, Lee Quinones and Juan Sanchez, all young people whose minds follow new and independent paths.
Open, free, Mondays through Fridays from 10 A.M. to 8 P.M. through March 4.
WRITING
Four talented writers will be discussing how they make the change from the teamwork of working on films to the lonely discipline of novel writing in a program at 8 P.M. sponsored by the American PEN Center (255-1977) at the American Place Theater, 111 West 46th Street.
''Double Identities - a Screenwriters Roundtable'' will involve Steve Tesich (''Division Street,'' ''Breaking Away''), John Sayles (''Union Dues,'' ''Return of the Secaucus Seven''), Judith Rascoe (''Yours and Mine: A Novella and Short Stories,'' ''Road Movie'') and John Guare (''House of Blue Leaves,'' ''Atlantic City''). 
They will speak with Nora Sayre, film critic and writer.
Admission: $8, first come, first served, doors open at 7:30. 
After the talk, a reception.

text:

The espionage case against a retired Central Intelligence Agency analyst began in 1983 with a tip from a Chinese defector, Government sources said today.
Prosecutors have said in court documents that the analyst, Larry Wu-Tai Chin, had admitted to Federal agents that he was a spy for the Chinese. 
According to a motion filed by prosecutors today, Mr. Chin was impressed at the agents' knowledge of his activities, so much so that he speculated aloud that his principal Chinese contact might have defected to the United States.
The motion did not disclose whether Mr. Chin's suspicions were accurate, but intelligence sources said today that the case arose from information provided by a Chinese official who fled to the West.
The prosecutors' motion, filed in Federal District Court in Alexandria, offers a rare glimpse into the techniques used by F.B.I. agents to elicit admissions from a spy suspect. 
It describes the dramatic moment on Nov. 
22 when two F.B.I. agents confronted Mr. Chin in his Virginia apartment with what the bureau says was evidence of 30 years of espionage activity.
Â 
Talk of Double Agent
The document filed today said that Mr. Chin first denied the charges, then offered to be a double agent for American intelligence and finally gave details of his career as a spy for the Chinese beginning in 1943.
Mr. Chin has pleaded not guilty. 
His attorneys have moved to suppress his statement to the agents on the ground that the F.B.I. violated his constitutional right to counsel and that he had been coerced.
The document filed by prosecutors today was a response to this motion.
It quotes Mr. Chin as questioning whether the agents had sufficient evidence, asking, ''How do I know you're not bluffing?''
In response, prosecutors said, Mark Johnson, an F.B.I. agent, described a September 1983 trip to China in which Mr. Chin was said to have met with Ou Qiming, described as his Chinese handler. 
Mr. Johnson said that Mr. Chin talked to Mr. Ou of the possibility of recruiting a fellow C.I.A. employee as a spy. 
He also mentioned his marital difficulties.
Â 
'Only Ou Knew'
Mr. Chin then told the agents, ''You have details that only Ou knew,'' according to the motion.
''Chin said the details about his wife were only known by Ou and asked where the agents obtained their information,'' the motion said. 
Mr. Chin, it said, ''speculated that Ou had defected.''
The Government sources, who asked not to be identified, would not comment on whether Mr. Ou was the defector they said was involved in the case.
Mr. Chin worked for nearly 30 years for the Foreign Broadcast Information Service, an arm of the C.I.A. that translates and interprets broadcasts and publications. 
Administration officials have said that because of his language skills Mr. Chin was also used by other sections of the C.I.A. and had access to virtually every classified intelligence document on the Far East for a period of years.
The F.B.I. said in an affidavit filed last month that from 1961 to 1967, Mr. Chin met with Mr. Ou and others while visiting Hong Kong. 
He was paid money and given an address in Canton where he could send correspondence, the F.B.I. said.
Â 
Contact in Canada
In 1976, the F.B.I. affidavit said, Mr. Ou gave Mr. Chin procedures to be used to reach Chinese agents in Canada. 
According to the F.B.I. statements, Mr. Chin would take documents home from work hidden in his clothes and briefcase and then deliver them to agents of the Chinese in Canada.
The motion said that when the agents appeared at Mr. Chin's apartment and identified themselves, Mr. Chin said, ''Why sure, come on in.''
They sat at the dining room table and said they were investigating ''the passage of classified information to the Chinese Intelligence Service.''
Mr. Chin denied any involvement in the case, the motion said.
Mr. Johnson of the F.B.I. read details of Mr. Chin's 1982 trip to Peking. 
''Chin appeared surprised with the detailed information,'' the motion said.
The agents then said they had been investigating the case a long time, the motion said. 
It continued: ''They had come to offer him a chance to explain what happened. 
They told him if he didn't want to talk to them that they would get up and leave and present the case to the Department of Justice.''
According to the motion, Mr. Chin said, ''Maybe I should seek legal counsel.''
Â 
Not Arrested at First
Mr. Johnson said Mr. Chin was not under arrest and was free to call an attorney, the motion said. 
The F.B.I. agent identified himself as an attorney.
After being confronted with the details that he thought only Mr. Ou could have known, Mr. Chin offered to confirm or deny what the agents knew, the motion said. 
They refused this offer. 
According to the motion, Mr. Chin said ''it would take a long time for him to tell everything'' and that he wanted to think it over and decide the following day whether to cooperate.
The agents then told him, ''This was his only chance to cooperate,'' the motion said.
After a pause, Mr. Chin offered to work as a double agent for the United States. 
The agents said they were not authorized to approve such an arrangement and they could only relay what he had to say to their supervisors.
''He said he would start with an outline and go back and fill it out,'' the motion said. 
''He then began with 1943.''

file: HONG KONG MARKETS SLUMP AFTER TALKS.txt
text:

The one clear reaction to the Chinese-British talks over Hong Kong's future has been in the colony's financial markets.
In the two trading sessions since discussions between Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and Chinese leaders ended last Friday, prices on the Hong Kong stock markets have fallen by more than 9 percent. 
In addition, the Hong Kong dollar dropped to its lowest level against the United States dollar since the local currency was allowed to float in late 1974.
''There has been nothing in the talks to give any comfort to Hong Kong investors and people,'' said Lawrence Chui, a director of Jardine Fleming & Company, an investment firm. 
''The reaction in the markets is what you would expect.''
HONG KONG, Sept. 
28 - The one clear reaction to the Chinese-British talks over Hong Kong's future has been in the colony's financial markets.
Yesterday, stock prices, as measured by the Hang Seng index, fell 83.74 points, the second-largest one-day decline this year. 
Today, the index retreated 23.96 points, closing at 988.66. 
The trading volume was extremely heavy both days, nearly twice the average daily volume last week.
Â 
Exchange Rate Declines
The United States dollar closed yesterday at $6.20 (Hong Kong), up from $6.11 on Saturday. 
After opening lower this morning, the local currency closed at about yesterday's level, largely because of Hong Kong dollar purchases by the Government, dealers say.
As a barometer of reaction to the British-Chinese talks, the weakness of the local currency is viewed as less significant than the stock market drop because the United States dollar is now unusually strong against all major currencies.
Stock market analysts cited three reasons for the big declines in share prices. 
First, the British-Chinese joint statement on Hong Kong, released last Friday, was less specific than many investors had hoped, giving only a general assurance that both sides wanted to maintain the ''stabilityI and prosperity'' of Hong Kong.
The differences of opinion between the two sides appear to be greater than many in Hong Kong had expected. 
Britain has made it clear that it considers the 19th-century treaties, which established its rule in Hong Kong, still valid. 
''Britain keeps her treaties,'' Mrs. Thatcher emphasized yesterday, though she added that theyzcould be ''modified.''
Â 
Chinese Seek Sovereignty
For its part, Peking has stressed that it must regain sovereignty over all of Hong Kong. 
Britain controls Hong Kong under a 99-year lease of 90 percent of the colony's land, which expires in 1997.
''The market was not expecting a sharp difference of views over the treaties,'' said Barry Yates, research director of Hoare Govett Far East Ltd.
The third factor in the big declines has been concerted selling by wealthy Chinese investors in Hong Kong, several market participants believe.
''It is not in the big guys' interest to see confidence or the stock market go higher at this time,'' one executive said. 
''This is a way of showing Peking and London that prosperity in Hong Kong is a very fragile thing.''
The stock markets are watched as a key indicator of business confidence in Hong Kong. 
Real estate issues represent about 40 percent of the market capitalization. 
Real estate prices, in turn, are viewed as an index of how much people want to live in Hong Kong and set up offices and factories here. 
Though still high, property values have, on average, declined 30 percent during the past year.
The Hong Kong stock markets are notoriously volatile. 
Analysts were reluctant to make specific predictions about the market outlook. 
Most agreed they would probably fall further in the near future, though they observed that the markets could stabilize and even turn up if the big Chinese investors decided to step in.
''They don't want to see things go down too much,'' one securities executive said. 
''After all, they do have the most to lose.''

file: Hong Kong Sees Rising Emigration as Peril.txt
text:
