In a reversal, the Hong Kong Government has begun to acknowledge that rising emigration among skilled and professional workers is hurting the thriving economy of this British colony, which is due to be returned to China in 1997.
As part of an effort to confront the problem, the Government this week announced the formation of a task force on emigration. 
The announcement marked an important policy shift for the Government, which has consistently denied that middle-class residents have been emigrating in unusually high numbers to escape the Chinese takeover. 
The official position was growing less tenable each week as new reports and surveys detailed new labor shortages linked to emigration.
The Government's position had long been that emigration patterns in this prosperous colony were normal.
But two weeks ago, Hong Kong's Governor, Sir David Wilson, acknowledged during a news conference that ''we have to face the fact that there is a problem because even though the figures have not gone up enormously, there are more people from the key middle management sector leaving.''
Cautioning that its figures are sketchy, the Government has estimated that 27,000 residents emigrated last year, almost double the number in 1986. 
The latest figure is also sharply higher than the 20,000 who emigrated annually before 1984, the year Britain agreed to return Hong Kong to China.
Experts said the official figures are conservative, and the Government said collecting reliable emigration numbers will be the first job of the task force, which will ultimately recommend measures to stem the flow.
Peter Tsao, the colony's secretary for administrative services and information, attributed the increased emigration to opportunities abroad as well as to a lack of confidence in the colony's future.
Last month, a private survey of major businesses found that emigration had increased, and that executives said they were losing college-educated, mid-level managers, many in their 30's. 
Two key sectors of the economy -trade and the finance - are among those hardest hit.
''This isn't a blip,'' said Paul Kirkbride, the author of the survey and a lecturer at City Polytechnic of Hong Kong. 
''The trend is up.''
The Government has maintained that many who leave the territory return here to work once they have the insurance of a second citizenship. 
But companies surveyed by Mr. Kirkbride estimated that only 2 in 10 emigrants return.
The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, the largest bank here, said it had lost 8 percent of its employees to emigration last year, compared with 3 percent in 1986. 
Two other major banks have announced cash bonuses for employees who recruit friends or neighbors to work as clerks and tellers, and one has offered a reward of more than $1,000 for any employee who brings in an assistant vice president.
While China has promised to grant the territory ''a high degree of autonomy,'' most people here are immigrants or relatives of immigrants who fled the political and economic policies of the mainland and have little faith in Beijing's promises.
Business executives and Western diplomats said privately that while they expected some professionals to emigrate as 1997 approached, they did not expect the rush to begin this early. 
As in the private sector, the Government also faces labor shortages caused by emigration. 
The colony's firefighting force, for example, has lost 10 percent of its senior fire officials, all ethnic Chinese who have emigrated in the past two years.
Both British and Chinese officials have sought to reassure the jittery, distrustful middle class that Beijing wants to preserve Hong Kong's successful free-enterprise system.
But some observers said confidence has been undercut by, among other recent political developments, the release of a draft of the basic law that will govern the territory after 1997. 
The draft was criticized by advocates of democracy here, who said it failed to safeguard the rights and autonomy of the territory.

text:
ï»¿
Hong Kong has never been permitted an elected government by Britain, and until recently its residents left the running of the colony to British paternalism while they earned money.
''Hong Kong people by and large have been apathetic toward politics,'' said Stephen Cheong, a textile factory director who serves as an appointed legislative councilor. 
''We have in the past devoted all our energy to making a living and building up Hong Kong economically to what it is today.''
On July 18, however, the British-run government here is expected to take a small but significant step toward granting the territory's 5.5 million residents a greater voice in their future.
A green paper, as the British call draft legislation, will be issued proposing some phased electoral changes to let Hong Kong's citizens choose more of their own officials in advance of 1997, when China intends to reclaim sovereignty over Hong Kong.
Â 
Officials Are Appointed
Hong Kong has no elected government beyond its local district boards. 
Instead, the British Governor appoints unofficial members of the Executive and Legislative Councils, more commonly known by the acronym Umelco. 
The appointees are heavily drawn from Hong Kong's influential business leaders. 
Eleven of them sit on the Executive Council, an advisory cabinet, and 29 on the Legislative Council. 
Five members are appointed to both bodies.
The absence of elected representatives has left Hong Kong's inhabitants with no appropriate mechanism to have a say in the negotiations on their future that Britain and China are conducting in private.
Since China declared that it would take Hong Kong back when Britain's lease over most of the territory expires on July 1, 1997, some younger educated people have come to view the creation of an indigenous political system as a way to insure that their freedoms and living standards continue.
The Peking leadership has promised that Hong Kong can keep its own socio- economic system and way of life after 1997. 
But the people of Hong Kong - 2.5 million of whom fled the Communist regime on the mainland - remain nervous about its assurances.
''We have a very wide communications gap,'' said Allen Lee, another legislative councilor. 
''Umelco has been trying to close that gap, and I can tell you, we haven't been successful.''
Â 
Rude Reception in Peking
The advisory councils' difficulty in trying to express Hong Kong's concerns became embarrassingly clear in June when Sir Sze-yuen Chung, a respected businessman, and two other councilors went to Peking to see Deng Xiaoping, China's leader.
Their explanation of Hong Kong's confidence problem was undercut by Mr. Deng's uncharacteristic rudeness. 
He accused his guests of being under the influence of colonialism and said they did not speak for the people of Hong Kong. 
For the next week, Hong Kong talked of little else, obscuring the fact that the councils had put across their message. 
''This argument that we are not elected so we cannot represent their views is a real red herring,'' Lydia Dunn, one of the three councilors, said in retrospect.
''As long as one is knowledgeable,'' she said, ''as long as one is in contact with the people, anybody is able to reflect the worries and anxieties of Hong Kong. 
We never claimed to have representative status.''
Â 
'Stooge for the British'
Indeed, the councils, which advise the British Governor and address public complaints, have greater independence than China's nominal Parliament, the National People's Congress. 
But as a longtime British resident observed, ''The Chinese Government sees any representative of Umelco as a stooge for the British colonial system.''
The electoral changes in the green paper will make little initial difference. 
It will reportedly propose that some or all council members be selected from the elected members of local district boards. 
The Legislative Council may eventually be presided over by an elected official.
But direct elections have evidently been ruled out, in part because the emergence of a Western political democracy could anger Peking. 
China has suggested that Hong Kong residents should run Hong Kong, as long as they are, in Mr. Deng's words, ''patriots.''
Â 
'A Bit of a Dilemma'
''I have a feeling that the Chinese are very uneasy about Hong Kong's move toward a more representative type of government,'' a council source said. 
''But I also detect that they are in a bit of a dilemma. 
If they obstruct this form of government, it would be politically hard for them to justify, given what they have previously said.''
There is also little enthusiasm in Hong Kong for a plunge into representative government. 
The only established political factions are either staunchly pro-Taiwan or pro-Peking. 
A fresh struggle between them could spark social unrest and drive away investment, removing China's grounds for not interfering in Hong Kong's stabilityII and prosperity.
''There is a fear among the wealthy that democratization will become a free-for-all, and sound and prudent fiscal policies will be undermined by political factionalism,'' a British businessman said.
For those who plan to move out, the prospect of democracy does not make much difference.
''I don't know of a single Chinese executive of tertiary education or successful businessman who has not worked out plans to leave,'' the British businessman said. 
''The only people who say they won't leave are those who have no chance.''
Â 
68% Thinking of Leaving
An unpublished survey found that 68 percent of the professional people polled in Hong Kong were considering leaving. 
Allen Lee, who serves on Umelco, said his business acquaintances were getting visas to other countries simply as insurance. 
He said he expected many of them to wait and see after 1997.
The interest in confronting China with a working democratic system when it reasserts sovereignty in 13 years is stronger among younger businessmen, lawyers, teachers and other professionals who do not have enough money to finance a new life abroad. 
''People who are 35, if they are going to the United States or Canada, will be 48, and it will be difficult to start another career,'' said P. H. Yu, a corporate planner who is deputy chairman of the Hong Kong Observers, a group that discusses issues affecting Hong Kong. 
''The majority are still very confused. 
They have not decided what they are going to do.''
The electoral changes envisioned are unlikely to be fully put into effect until 1992, a scant five years before China reclaims Hong Kong. 
Many people think the shape of Hong Kong's future will be decided by then.
China has rejected the notion of a ''three-legged stool'' in which Hong Kong joins Peking and London as a partner in the 1997 talks. 
The Peking leadership maintains that it alone can represent the interests of Hong Kong.
Still, many younger educated people like Yeung Sam, deputy chairman of Meeting Point, another prominent discussion group, say they see an indigenous democratic system as the best guarantee of Hong Kong's future.
''If Hong Kong people don't want to run their affairs, China will send its own people,'' Mr. Yeung said. 
''We want to fight for more chance to participate, and Britain should help us before it is too late.''

file: HONG KONG TO BAR NEW BOAT PEOPLE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Hong Kong announced today that newly arriving Vietnamese boat people who could not prove they fled religious or political persecution would be incarcerated as illegal aliens until they could be returned to Vietnam.
Until now, the thousands of arriving boat people have been put in camps in Hong Kong until they could be resettled in a third country.
Under the new criteria, the vast majority of boat people landing here will be isolated in detention centers and cut off from relief and resettlement agencies.
Geoffrey Barnes, the Hong Kong Secretary for Security, said the new policy was meant to send the Vietnamese the message: ''Do not come here.''
Sir David Wilson, the Governor of the British colony, called the new policy ''humane and just.''
He said the colony would use international criteria, as defined by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, to screen the boat people streaming into Hong Kong. 
#16,000 Already in Camps More than 7,700 refugees have arrived this year alone, compared with 650 for the same period last year, and the colony's overcrowded camps now hold more than 16,000 people, the highest number since 1980.
The new requirement for proving refugee status does not apply to refugees already in Hong Kong. 
Those who arrived since 1982 have been housed in camps surrounded by high wire fences and patrolled by guards. 
Under the new policy, the Government says, they will be given more freedom of movement.
As of midnight tonight, new arrivals who do not turn back will be detained in guarded camps on outlying islands.
Those who are eventually deemed refugees will be housed with the present refugee population. 
But those who cannot prove a ''well-founded fear of persecution'' will remain in detention. 
Officials estimate that barely 10 percent of the future arrivals will be deemed refugees.
Western countries have been taking increasingly fewer Vietnamese refugees for resettlement. 
At the same time Hong Kong's residents, 98 percent of whom are ethnic Chinese, have bitterly opposed the Government's previous policy of allowing Vietnamese to remain here while awaiting resettlement but forcing illegal immigrants from China to go back. 
The colony, with a population of 5.6 million, took a stand in the mid-1970's that it had absorbed as many mainland Chinese as it could.
Â 
Political Strain Is Cited
A senior Government official said today that it was ''political strain'' more than any economic one that had led to the new policy.
Most of the recent arrivals, Government officials said, are poor farmers and fishermen from the north and central parts of Vietnam fleeing poverty, food shortages and an economy in a state of near-collapse.
Those who are not accepted as refugess will eventually be forced to return to Vietnam, a process that Government officials said could probably not begin for at least two years.
A senior Government official said that Hanoi has made no significant movement in its refusal to discuss repatriation of the boat people, except on a case-by-case basis.
Government officials said that while Thailand and Malaysia had a surge in Vietnamese refugees since the beginning of the year, Hong Kong had the biggest jump.
Thailand now puts all arriving Vietnamese in camps without access to resettlement workers, and has reduced the number of new arrivals to virtually nothing, a Hong Kong official said. 
Malaysia has continued to accept all boat people as refugees, but has warned that its policy will be changed.
Â 
Ex-Leper Colony Will Be Used
The first camp for the Vietnamese arriving illegally will be on Hei Ling Chau, a small rock of an island that was once the site of a leper colony. 
Refugees housed in a camp there will be transferred to a new camp.
Relief agencies, which now provide educational and recreational services in the refugee camps, will not be allowed access to the detention camp.
Some relief officials questioned how immigration interviewers would be able to determine which boat people were fleeing persecution and which were ''economic migrants.''
Keith Holcombe, director of World Relief, an agency that aids refugees here, told of a case last summer involving four Vietnamese brothers.
''The United States uses the U.N. criteria for a refugee, and American screening officials found that two of the brothers were refugees and two were economic migrants,'' he said. 
''It's going to be sad and tricky.''
Mr. Barnes said he believed that most cases would be ''clear cut.''
A spokesman for the United States Consulate in Hong Kong said Washington had not commented on the policy.

file: Hong Kong, Wary of China, Sees Its Middle Class Fleeing.txt
text:
ï»¿
Four decades after their parents and grandparents swarmed from revolutionary upheaval in China to the safety of Hong Kong, a wave of young Chinese professionals is again fleeing Communism, packing their bags for Canada, the United States and Australia.
With less than 10 years to go before Hong Kong is returned to the Chinese motherland, more and more of the British territory's brightest lights are deciding that they do not trust China to allow Hong Kong to remain capitalist, decadent and efficient.
This year more than 10,000 will say farewell to the ''fragrant harbor,'' as this city is known in Chinese, and dolefully brace themselves for Canadian winters and other hardships still only dimly understood.
''People used to ask me vague questions about the future,'' said Wong Shikeung, a traditional fortuneteller whose premises attract middle-class Chinese. 
''Now they ask more focused questions: 'Should I stay in Hong Kong after 1997?' or 'Will foreign countries offer brighter career prospects?'
''
Â 
Date for End of British Rule
On July 1, 1997, it will be the marriage of the century: China, one of the most regulated societies in the world, enormous and sluggish; and Hong Kong, a monument to laissez-faire, a tiny, pulsating territory that already economically dominates a broad swath of southern China.
The amalgam will have far-reaching implications for all of China, and even now, 10 years before the nuptials, expectations of what it will bring are transforming Hong Kong.
But it is an arranged marriage, and one that gives the 5.6 million inhabitants of Hong Kong deep reservations. 
The apprehensions, which seem to be a particular preoccupation of the middle class, are compounded by the belief that Britain and China are conspiring to thwart the emergence of democracy, so that Hong Kong will not develop political institutions that could challenge Beijing. 
The colony is now governed by officials appointed by Britain.
Iris W. Y. Lam, 30 years old, a slender, curly-haired banker with an easygoing manner reminiscent of her stu-dent days at the University of Southern California, is one of those leaving. 
''My dad was in Shanghai in 1949, when the Communists took over,'' she said. 
''The Communists promised people freedom then, but they lost everything.''
Miss Lam, who leaves next month for Toronto, worries about finding a new job and regrets having to leave the world she knows in Hong Kong. 
But she has no doubts about the wisdom of her decision to emigrate. 
In time, she says, she will find new friends, or old friends will join her. 
So far this year, five good friends have left Hong Kong, and she says others are planning to leave as soon as they have earned a little more money. 
''Everybody is thinking about leaving,'' she said.
Â 
The Rush for Visas And a New Life
Miss Lam is just a face in the crowd of emigrants, another professional leaving behind a vacant office and an empty bank account at a time when the fall of the stock market underscores the uncertainty and volatility that will accompany the integration of the two economies.
No one knows just how big the exodus is, because Hong Kong does not keep emigration statistics. 
The Commission for Canada in Hong Kong, which gets more applications for immigration visas than any other Canadian diplomatic mission, issued 16,000 immigrant visas in the first nine months of 1987. 
That compares with 8,800 in all of 1986, although part of the increase this year is the result of a backlog of applications from last year. 
Australia granted 5,200 immigration visas in the 12 months that ended June 30, compared with 4,460 in the same period a year earlier.
The United States Consulate in Hong Kong issued 7,585 immigrant visas last year, and the numbers have been fairly steady since then because of strict limits. 
Meanwhile, about 15,000 people from Hong Kong are studying in the United States, apparently more students proportionally than from anywhere else.
Until the end of September, the United States limited to 600 the number of Hong Kong-born people who could receive immigration visas in any year, not counting spouses and minor children of American citizens. 
Many more visas were granted because many recipients were spouses or underage children of Americans, and because many were born in China but now live in Hong Kong. 
The limit was raised to 5,000 in the fiscal year that began Oct. 
1. The United States gives preference to family members of Americans and to those with special skills.
Some of those going abroad will return to Hong Kong in a few years, clutching their new foreign passports. 
But emigration advisers say that as 1997 nears, more and more of the emigrants, especially younger ones, say they will build their lives abroad.
Â 
Over the Decades, Rise and Fall of Tensions
The latest worries are part of a long history of tensions between Hong Kong and China. 
Lord Napier, the British officer who more than 150 years ago sought to wrest Hong Kong island from China, was mocked and given a Chinese name meaning ''laboriously vile.''
Britain obtained Hong Kong only by defeating China in the 1839-1842 war that forced the Chinese to accept the opium trade.
More recently, the Communists have sometimes seemed ready to take back Hong Kong by force. 
In 1962 a wave of 70,000 refugees suddenly poured across the border from China to Hong Kong in a 25-day period, straining the territory's resources and raising concern that China had finally begun an unorthodox invasion. 
Just five years later, China encouraged riots in the center of Hong Kong that for six months shook the territory to its core. 
While the Bank of China branch in Hong Kong used loudspeakers to call on the people of Hong Kong to overthrow the imperialists, the British drowned out the incitements with loudspeakers broadcasting the thunderous screech of Chinese opera.
Now China is again expanding its influence in Hong Kong, although in a more cooperative manner. 
Businesses based in China have acquired real estate and corporations in Hong Kong apparently worth well over $5 billion, while others are issuing stock on the Hong Kong market. 
The Bank of China is snatching business from other institutions by offering highly competitive terms, and it is building Hong Kong's tallest office tower for its new headquarters in the territory.
The head of the New China News Agency branch in Hong Kong, Xu Jiatun, is China's top official in Hong Kong and functions as the ''shadow governor,'' the counterpart of Britain's top official, Sir David Wilson. 
Ironically, neither Mr. Xu nor Sir David speak the Cantonese dialect of Chinese spoken by 98 percent of Hong Kong's population.
The main reasons for China's expansion of influence in Hong Kong seem to be to gain experience in capitalism generally and Hong Kong particularly, and to reassure residents that China does not plan radical changes in Hong Kong's way of life after 1997.
Although the brightest young professionals are unconvinced, many of Hong Kong's manufacturers are optimistic that China will allow Hong Kong to remain a place to make and keep money.
Â 
The Sun Is Setting On British Influence
As Chinese influence has expanded, British influence has declined. 
Last year, for the first time, Americans outnumbered Britons among the expatriate residents of the territory. 
The Hong Kong Chinese who hope to emigrate seek visas to America or Australia more than to Britain. 
And the old British companies that dominated commerce are being replaced or acquired by Hong Kong Chinese concerns. 
The tai-pans, or big bosses, had names like Jardine, Dent, Sassoon and Swire. 
Now the inheritors of the tradition of the greatest of the tai-pans - William Jardine, founder of the Jardine Matheson trading company, known to the Chinese as ''iron-headed old rat'' - have names that trip English tongues: Pao Yuekong, Li Kashing, Siu Yatfoo, Wu Yingseung.
The British tai-pans still flourish, of course. 
But as a final indignity to the old order, a New York lawyer, Brian M. Powers, was appointed this year to be the next tai-pan of the Jardine Matheson group. 
In a relatively formal society, the 38-year-old Mr. Powers is a maverick. 
He calls people by their first names unless they are over 70 years old and worth more than $1 billion.
Â 
The Border Blurs For Shopping and Play
Hong Kong is changing in another important way; it is becoming a part of China. 
For much of the postwar period, tight Chinese entry restrictions made it extremely difficult to cross the border and prevented information from flowing to the outside world. 
In the late 1960's China-watchers in Hong Kong assessed the violence of the Cultural Revolution partly by noting the number of bodies drifting down the Pearl River from China.
Hong Kong is becoming more integrated with cities like Shenzhen, on the China side of the border. 
Working-class families in Hong Kong take advantage of lower prices in China by crossing the border for doctor and dentist appointments and to shop for vegetables on the weekends. 
Middle-class families cross the border to tee off on Shenzhen's golf course. 
And students attend university in Guangdong Province, both because tuition is low and as a way to ingratiate themselves with their future rulers.
Among those who are neither middle class nor wealthy, there is some apprehension about the future, but it is tempered by the feeling that they have little to lose and that there is not much they can do about it. 
In addition, some with strong nationalist feelings believe that Hong Kong belongs to China and should be ruled by Chinese rather than foreigners.
A few people in Hong Kong seem to welcome the Chinese takeover; they are particularly represented in labor unions, newspapers and independent high schools that have long been associated with the Communists.
The jitters about 1997 are concentrated overwhelmingly in the middle class - which numbers somewhere less than a quarter of the population -particularly among young people who have been educated abroad. 
They may have more to lose and may feel they can do something about it - leave Hong Kong.
Not all the Chinese who go abroad will be welcomed. 
Reports abound that Chinese criminal gangs known as triads are expanding overseas from Hong Kong as 1997 approaches. 
The Hong Kong police force says it has no evidence that this is so, but a report this summer by California's Attorney General, John K. Van de Kamp, warned that Chinese triads are believed to control 20 percent to 30 percent of the heroin smuggled into the United States.
Â 
The Passport Merchants: Profits From Fear
''People leave Hong Kong because of fear,'' said Horatio C. S. Cheung, the director of a nonprofit organization that advises people on how to get a foreign passport. 
''They came to Hong Kong with nothing, worked hard and accumulated some wealth. 
They don't want to lose it.''
That fear has spawned more than a dozen businesses that, like Mr. Cheung's, help people emigrate. 
Tucked in the phone book between Ice Skating Rinks and Importers & Exporters is a category called Immigration & Naturalization Consultants, with 14 listings. 
They charge hundreds or even thousands of dollars to help someone obtain a foreign passport.
Even some foreign countries see the alarm in Hong Kong as a source of funds. 
The island nation of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean offers a passport in exchange for an investment of about $50,000. 
Industrialized countries are more expensive. 
Canada, which primarily admits people who are joining relatives or have special skills, offers immigration visas for some investments of $200,000 or more.
The fear of China's takeover strains the fabric of life in other ways. 
''The 1997 issue has an indirect influence on marriages, although not a major one,'' said Elsie Lam, a marriage counselor in Hong Kong. 
Families are being separated so that a member with a visa can be sent abroad to get a toehold in the hope of bringing the rest of the family later. 
In freewheeling Hong Kong, where there has been little compunction about extramarital liaisons, the separation of spouses reportedly has led to a boom in such affairs.
Chinese parents are even relaxing their standards about their children's marriage partners. 
Parents usually want their children to marry other Chinese, preferably those who trace their origins to the same region of China. 
But these days ''gweilos'' - ghostly people, as foreigners are called - are in demand on the marriage market. 
''Marrying another Chinese is important,'' said a woman in her 20's, ''but getting a foreign passport is even more important.''

file: HONG KONG_S BANKING GIANT.txt
text:
ï»¿
This British colony pursues commerce and wealth so single-mindedly that its magnificent natural setting has become a mere backdrop to its driving purpose. 
Tall buildings sprout everywhere, their walls often dense with advertising. 
Open stretches of sidewalk turn into crowded markets.
Within this hectic landscape, the sleek new headquarters being built by the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation is a striking reminder of its leading role in the colony.
In recent years ''the Bank,'' as it is known here, has grown into a force beyond the colony, too. 
The bank's modernistic headquarters - with 43 floors suspended from round steel masts, looking like a cross between a bridge and an offshore oil platform - is a fitting monument to the kind of dynamic institution it has become under Michael Sandberg, chairman since 1977.
Profile of Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corp, focusing on rapid expansion undertaken by Michael Sandberg, its chairman since 1977, and uncertain future as Hong Kong prepares to revert to Chinese control; William Purves, who is expected to succeed Sandberg, discusses his plans for consolidating bank's operations over next few years; photo of new headquarters; graph shows bank's assets and return on assets, 1970-83 (M)
Â 
In Past, an Era of Plenty
But with the colony nervously preparing for eventual transfer to Chinese rule, the innovative skyscraper will say more about the era of plenty gone by than the tougher years ahead. 
Mr. Sandberg, 57 years old, took over the bank in the midst of a boom that carried Hong Kong into immense prosperity. 
His aggressive management transformed Hongkong Bank from a regional leader into an international giant, the 23d largest in the world in 1983. 
Since 1977 its reported net earnings quadrupled to about $319 million last year. 
Like the new building's architecture, the bank Mr. Sandberg fashioned was bold and imaginative.
The days of soaring expansion have ended now. 
The bank's earnings rose less than 6 percent in 1983, with the colony's uncertain future making a return to high growth rates unlikely. 
Hongkong Bank is having to adjust to a new environment, all the way up to the top.
Â 
A New Kind of Executive
At a bank run by consensus, the consensus seems to be that the new headquarters' formal opening late next year will bring Mr. Sandberg's tenure, already waning, to a close.
William Purves, 52, the deputy chairman and Mr. Sandberg's likely successor, is cut from different cloth. 
He is a large, heavy-set Scotsman, with a stern gaze that can wither subordinates. 
Colleagues and competitors describe him as cautious and iron-willed.
Asked about his leadership ability, colleagues recalled Mr. Purves's military experience. 
As a 19-year-old officer in the Korean War, he won one of Britain's highest military honors for rallying a unit given up as lost after an attack. 
His reputation is for tackling problems head-on and in no- nonsense terms.
Where Mr. Sandberg accepted risks like an entrepreneur, maneuvering to increase the bank's size, Mr. Purves says his objective is consolidation.
Â 
Aspects of Bank's Efforts
''Now I don't happen to think that growth and acquisition are necessarily the route this bank should be going,'' Mr. Purves said recently during a long interview. 
''We should be concentrating on what we've got, trying to make it work better and trying to make more profit out of it. 
A restriction on balance sheet growth may be a good thing for the next few years.''
Whether Mr. Purves becomes chairman soon or not, he already has the influence to effect that strategy. 
He controls Hongkong Bank's commercial and merchant banking operations, powers his predecessor as deputy chairman did not have.
The institution he is shaping stands apart from other international banks. 
On the positive side, Hong Kong has proved an exceptionally profitable base. 
Hongkong Bank controls nearly half of all deposits in the colony, issues more than 80 percent of the currency and acts as central banker to the colonial government.
Â 
Economic Projects in Asia
Hong Kong has also been a springboard into the rest of Asia, economically the world's fastest-growing region. 
Hongkong Bank is strong in China, too, having financed most of the limited opportunities open to foreign banks there, about 150 projects in the last three years, according to Anthony Russell, the bank's China area manager.
''They have their greatest strength in the area where most financial institutions most want to be,'' said Lawrence Toal, senior vice president and head of the Chase Manhattan Bank's Hong Kong operations. 
''Their intelligence and contacts in this market make you feel you have to have a relationship with them to do business here.''
In addition, Hongkong Bank shunned lending to Eastern bloc and developing countries when other banks plunged into that market. 
Instead, it has been a net lender to other banks of the Euromarket.
Â 
Transition to Chinese Rule
However, Hongkong Bank's once- solid base is starting to look shaky. 
It must now contend with the changes that are going to sweep capitalist Hong Kong as it begins a transition to Chinese sovereignty. 
Britain has conceded to China that in 1997, when its lease on most of the territory expires, British rule will end.
Both sides promise that Hong Kong will become an autonomous, self-administered territory with its current system largely unchanged. 
Still, most residents worry whether China's Communist authorities can resist tampering with a society so contrary to their own. 
Several senior Hong Kong government advisers acknowledged recently that any Chinese-British agreement would be an experiment, and could wreck Hong Kong if it fails to find popular support.
These uncertainties have forced businesses to ask themselves difficult new questions. 
Up to now, they could work like British companies, Asian companies or hybrids, depending on what suited their needs.
Â 
'Still a British Colony'
''Although they've changed the name to a territory, this is still a British colony,'' Mr. Purves said. 
''Therefore, we're a British bank. 
Having said that, we're a Hong Kong-based bank, proud of our heritage here. 
We've achieved things being based in Asia that would never have been achieved in London.''
But the colony and the companies in it may not be able to sit on the fence much longer.
Jardine, Matheson & Company, a trading concern involved in Hong Kong's founding in 1842, decided to change its legal domicile to Bermuda to assure that it will remain under British jurisdiction.
All is not gloomy in Hong Kong, though. 
Stock prices are depressed, but brokers say some investors are nibbling at undervalued shares. 
''There are short-term gains to be made here,'' said Hugh Bolland, managing director of Schroders & Chartered Ltd., a merchant bank.
Â 
Investment by Americans
There is steady United States investment, too, according to Mr. Toal, who is also president of the local American Chamber of Commerce. 
He explained that some American companies are attracted by the prospect of investing in what will eventually be part of China.
Even before the 1997 issue claimed headlines, Hongkong Bank decided it was too heavily concentrated in Asia, so it sought to diversify. 
Expansion overseas became Mr. Sandberg's chief objective. 
He described his strategy as creating three equal legs for the bank - in Asia (including the Middle East), in Europe and in North America.
Just months after becoming chairman, Mr. Sandberg began Hongkong Bank's largest overseas move, a bid for 51 percent of New York's Marine Midland Bank. 
The $314 million deal succeeded, but only after a long battle with state banking authorities.
Â 
Outsider's Role in Britain
In 1981 Hongkong Bank bid for the Royal Bank of Scotland, topping an offer by the Standard Chartered Bank. 
This time Mr. Sandberg was greeted like a party crasher. 
Standard Chartered and Royal Bank had already reached an understanding that had approval from the Bank of England. 
The central bank frowned on the uninvited guest's behavior, and the British Government intervened.
Ultimately, both bids were rejected. 
The bitter lesson for Hongkong Bank was that in Britain it was treated like a foreigner.
More important, Mr. Sandberg's international ambitions had foundered. 
Hongkong Bank spoke of another acquisition attempt in Europe, but nothing happened. 
There have been small moves, such as the purchase of the trade financing house TKM International. 
But TKM's heavy Latin American exposure made the investment a poor one. 
Hongkong Bank still has just over 40 percent of its assets in Asia and the Middle East, an additional 40 percent in North America and about 15 percent in Europe.
Â 
Cautious About Expansion
Mr. Purves concedes that Hongkong Bank may have run out of growing room in Asia, but he talks cautiously of overseas moves.
''We don't have to dive out and buy something in Europe,'' he said. 
''If we see the right thing, I believe we would like to make that investment, but there are not too many things we see as the right thing.''
Mr. Purves said, though, that Hongkong Bank is considering buying an interest in a London stockbrokerage firm. 
Other banks have made such acquisitions recently.
Another shift under Mr. Purves is Hongkong Bank's control over subsidiaries. 
While Mr. Sandberg often delegated operating autonomy, some are now being reined in under Mr.Purves's authority.
An example of the change is how Hongkong Bank's merchant banking unit, Wardley Ltd., renamed Wardley Holdings Ltd. last year, operates.
Â 
Wardley's Brisk Growth
In a break with Hongkong Bank custom, Mr. Sandberg had installed an outsider as Wardley's chief officer instead of a bank-trained executive, and it enjoyed heady growth during the boom years.
However, it lent heavily to property developers. 
When the market collapsed in 1982, millions of dollars in real estate loans went sour. 
Particularly embarrassing were Wardley's large loans to the Carrian group, which has since become the largest bankruptcy in the colony's history.
Wardley's earnings plunged to about $9.6 million in 1983 from the peak of about $25.7 million in 1981, and Hongkong Bank had to inject $25.5 million into the unit last year.
When Mr. Purves became Wardley's chairman in 1982, several executives were eased out and its loan portfolio was shrunk, with some credits transferred to Hongkong Bank. 
Now Wardley arranges financing but does little lending.
''They should be handling investment management and trying less to be like a bank,'' Mr. Purves said.
Â 
Tight Control Over Units
Hongkong Bank has also tightened its control over other units. 
Antony Gibbs Holdings Ltd., a British merchant bank, is now Wardley London.
All branches of the wholly owned Mercantile Bank were either merged with the Hongkong Bank's branches or sold. 
Marine Midland's Paris branch was closed and the business taken over by Hongkong Bank. 
And Hongkong Bank sharply scaled down its retail business in Britain.
Strategy may also be changing at Marine Midland. 
Mr. Purves backed off from any suggestion that its autonomy was being trimmed, but he indicated that Marine Midland was likely to become less ambitious, following its parent's formula.
Marine Midland's bottom line, Mr. Purves said, ''has not been quite as good as we would have liked, and they still have some distance to go to be up with their peer group.''
Marine Midland is re-examing its strategy, and the findings will be reported to Hongkong Bank shortly, according to Mr. Purves. ''It may be too early to say what the findings are, but I think they're finding they are likely to concentrate on their own domestic backyard.''
Â 
Looking for Biggest Return
''Perhaps,'' Mr. Purves said, ''they are finding that their international banking has been less profitable and less attractive and that perhaps they should build on the existing strengths of their wide branch network.''
Hongkong Bank's empire-building seems over for the moment. 
Its emphasis, Mr. Purves said, will be on profits, not size.
What Mr. Purves suggested he wants to guard against is letting Hongkong Bank's pretensions get ahead of what it can manage, with the costs of growth rising too high.
As an example, the brief given Foster Associates, the architect for the bank's new headquarters, was to create ''the best building in the world.''
Hongkong Bank got a fabulous structure - at a fabulous price of $638 million that, Mr. Purves acknowledged, will reduce profits.
''Maybe at this uncertain time in the world financial community and with the added political uncertainties over Hong Kong's future,'' Mr. Purves said, ''it will be a period of wait and see.''

file: HONG KONG_S HOME AWAY FROM HOME.txt
text:
ï»¿
A Canadian banker recently told of a visit from a Hong Kong businessman who said he had come to Vancouver to buy property but could spare only a week.
The banker asked how much the visitor wanted to spend. 
The reply: ''About $50 million.''
Such tales no longer astonish the citizens of Canada's most westerly province, which has been busy forging commercial and cultural links with nations around the rim of the Pacific Ocean.
Article on growth of Hong Kong investment in British Columbia, whose forests and minerals as well as port facilities have attracted resource-scarce Asian countries; recent investments from Hong Kong have included $60 million shopping mall, big hotel and high-rise office towers; Asian investors were reported two years ago to own 12 to 15 percent of downtown Vancouver (M)
''What we've done is to prepare our citizens and trading partners for the age of the Pacific,'' said Vancouver's Mayor, Mike Harcourt. 
''We're into it for the long haul.''
British Columbia's ties with Asia date to the late 19th century and the first Chinese immigrants, who helped complete the Canadian Pacific Railway and worked the mines. 
British Columbia's distance from Eastern Canada has led it to seek out commercial links with Asian countries as well as with the Western United States. 
Such regionalism is characteristic of Canada's provinces, which often find more in common with American neighbors or other countries than with each other.
The appeal of British Columbia to Asians also reflects current political uncertainties, notably those created by the British agreement to turn Hong Kong over to China when the British lease expires in 1997. 
Even before the agreement was reached, Hong Kong businessmen were pumping money into real estate in Vancouver, which claims one of North America's largest ethnic Chinese populations. 
Mayor Harcourt estimates that 125,000 ethnic Chinese live in greater Vancouver, whose population totals 1.2 million.
Recent investments from Hong Kong in Vancouver have included a $60 million shopping mall with 140 shops in suburban Richmond, a big hotel and high-rise office towers. 
Two years ago, the Vancouver Sun reported that Asian investors owned 12 to 15 percent of downtown Vancouver. 
Andrea Eng, a broker who deals with clients from Hong Kong for the real estate firm of Macaulay Nicolls Maitland International, called such estimates exaggerated but confirmed that money was flowing in from Hong Kong people who want to hedge their bets.
Â 
Chinese Are Welcome
The suspicions that fueled white prejudice against Chinese immigrants in the 19th and early 20th centuries have faded. 
''The Chinese are very welcome here,'' said Brian Power, a Vancouver Sun reporter who has covered the Asian scene. 
''The feeling here is that we're really blessed with these people.''
Canada's immigration policy favors entrepreneurs who will set up a business that generates jobs rather than just buy property. 
Canada, with its high living standard and political stability, becomes an attractive second choice for many who cannot qualify under the United States's tougher immigration quotas.
Yet Asian investors in British Columbia have generally stuck to real estate because they balk at the province's high taxes and aggressive labor unions. 
The more adventurous investors leapfrog to Toronto, Canada's financial center. 
Of a group of 600 entrepreneurs from Hong Kong who got immigration visas last year, 336 went to Ontario and only 94 chose to stay in British Columbia. 
But some Hong Kong Chinese, at least, find that Vancouver reminds them more of home, with its lovely harbor, mountains and vestiges of British colonial culture.
In addition to the Hong Kong-Canada Business Association in Vancouver, there is the Mokuyokai Society, which promotes trade ties and cultural links with Japan, and the Canada-Korea Business Association. 
Another group is being formed to promote trade with the countries of Southeast Asia.
British Columbia has been hoping that trade with Asia would help pull it out of a recession that has left 15 percent of the work force unemployed. 
Seventy-nine percent of Canada's exports to China, 75 percent of its exports to Japan, 64 percent of its exports to South Korea and a third of its exports to Hong Kong flowed from or through British Columbia last year.
The province's forests and minerals as well as its port facilities have attracted resource-scarce Asian countries. 
When a delegation of business and labor leaders from British Columbia visited China last month, their Chinese hosts talked about buying into a sawmill or pulp mill in British Columbia. 
China already gets three-quarters of its wood imports from British Columbia.
The province's Premier, William Bennett, proposed in February that Vancouver develop into an international banking center. 
British Columbia may find it difficult to emulate Hong Kong's success as Asia's financial capital, but the idea attracted local interest.
''I look to the west as Canada's front door, as part of a national initiative,'' said Vancouver's Mayor Harcourt, who will shortly lead his own trade delegation to Asia. 
''We're not just representing British Columbia. 
We're representing Canada.''

text:
ï»¿
The fight started as a routine quarrel between a tenant and the landlord who wanted to evict her from her home in the teeming Jinhua neighborhood of western Canton.
When such petty harassment as exploding firecrackers on her threshhold did not budge the tenant, Hu Siye, the landlord and his two sons battered down her door one night. 
One son beat Miss Hu's son, She Huxiaqn, with a heavy pole.
Frantic neighbors summoned not the police but the local mediation committee, who arrived as Mr. She was flourishing a cleaver.
Article on neighborhood mediation committees in China which handle nearly seven million local disputes each year and which, according to Ministry of Justice, prevented 80,000 incidents of homicide, suicide and bodily injury as well as saving considerable time and expense in judicial litigation; says recourse to mediation is rooted in Chinese tradition; photo (M)
''We talked to these two families and stopped She from using the cleaver,'' said Li Lixin, the mediation committee director. 
In the bargaining that followed, the landlord agreed to pay for Mr. She's medical treatment and repair the broken door. 
The son who hit Mr. She submitted to police detention for 10 days.
''After education and our work, the families stopped fighting,'' Miss Li reported.
Â 
Rooted in Chinese Tradition
In the United States, such a fight would probably have ended in court, but not in China, where neighborhood mediation committees handled nearly seven million local disputes last year. 
According to the mediation department of the Ministry of Justice, neighborhood mediation prevented 80,000 incidents of homicide, suicide and bodily injury in 1983 as well as saving considerable time and expense in judicial litigation.
The recourse to mediation is rooted in Chinese tradition, but it was also popular in the 1950's before radicals scrapped the nation's legal system in the Cultural Revolution. 
Mediation was incorporated into the civil procedure code adopted in March 1982 to revive the rule of law.
The physical limitations of China's legal system, which has only 15,000 full- time and part-time lawyers, is just one reason for the popularity of mediation. 
Ordinary Chinese have an inherent suspicion of courts and prefer to settle disputes within the family or neighborhood rather than before strangers.
As a result, most cases never reach court. 
Last year Chinese lawyers handled 72,000 criminal cases and 37,000 civil cases, according to Minister of Justice Zou Yu. 
By contrast, neighborhood mediation comittees, which have grown to more than 927,000 nationwide, resolved 6,978,179 cases in 1983.
''The purpose of setting up mediation committees is so the people themselves, not officials, can resolve problems,'' said Liu Dadan, a Jinhua committee member. 
''We have the advantage of knowing the people well, so we can accomplish the work more easily.''
While mediation has attracted the attention of some Western legal experts as a way to alleviate overloaded courts, it seems to work in China because the Communist Party promotes it and because many Chinese are sensitive to the opinions of their neighbors.
In the Jinhua neighborhood, the mediation committee handled 98 cases last year and referred only three to the courts, said Miss Li, an affable woman who displayed an indefatigable interest in the lives of those around her.
The mediation committee, whose half-dozen members are mostly retired workers with little else to do, tries to head off problems before they develop by putting up posters in Jinhua, a neighborhood of narrow lanes and quaint row houses with red tile roofs.
Miss Li said the committee had reformed all but 17 of the neighborhood's 129 known juvenile delinquents and that the remaining miscreants ''have gotten better.''
Â 
A Little Arm-Twisting Helps
In theory, mediation can take place only with the consent of all parties, but the Jinhua committee has sometimes done a little arm-twisting.
In one case, Li Xiaoyun, a textile worker, broke off a romance with Xie Penghui, a laborer. 
The lovesick Mr. Xie kept coming to Miss Xie's house and, when her father refused to admit him, followed her when she went out.
''She became frightened of him,'' Li Lixin said. 
''She didn't dare to go to work and stayed at home.''
The committee tracked down Mr. Xie and, Miss Li said, ''we educated him not to do this because love and marriage are something both sides must agree to.''
The mediation committee is not timid about rushing into a marital fray. 
After Li Junan, a factory worker, began beating his wife, Lan Xiaoyun, during their quarrels, she packed up and went back to her mother. 
The mediation committee visited his home and, despite his hostility, ''we stayed there and talked to him for several hours,'' Miss Li said. 
''He was moved by our serious attitude and enthusiasm.''
Mr. Li agreed to treat his wife properly and she returned home.
The committee has been as determined to discourage divorce, which still carries a stigma in China. 
Li Wenting also beat up his wife, Li Yelan, on 15 occasions. 
She returned to her mother and then applied for a divorce.
''We talked to them by turns more than 10 times over eight months,'' said Zhu Hua, a committee member. 
''We educated her husband in the marriage law and made him correct his attitude.''
His wife kept demanding a divorce until last November, when the committee got her to withdraw the application.
Miss Li conceded there were cases where mediation had failed. 
An old woman named Li Chong said that her son and daughter-in-law mistreated her by feeding her poorly and tampering with her sewing machine. 
After four tries, the committee gave up and referred the case to a court because they feared for the woman's health. 
The court ordered the couple to pay Li Chong subsistence money each month as part of their duty to support her.
When violence is likely, the committee may turn the matter over to the Public Security Bureau, as the police are called. 
''If both sides are holding knives or cleavers and it affects the peace and security of our neighborhood, we'll get help from the Public Security Bureau,'' said Liu Didan.
But in most cases, it seems, the persuasion of the mediation committee wins out.''We are convinced that with effort we can get people to adopt the right opinion and they will get on better,'' Mr. Liu said.

'There Are Many Questions'

file: HU_S OUSTER_ DENG_S ROLE__Did He Drop Protege Or Was He Forced_.txt
text:
ï»¿
The abrupt ouster of Hu Yaobang, China's Communist Party chief, raises the question whether the move was engineered by Deng Xiaoping, the country's paramount leader, or was forced on Mr. Deng by increasingly powerful hard-liners in the party.
State Department officials sought today to play down the importance of the dismissal of Mr. Hu, long the protege of the 82-year-old Mr. Deng and apparently his choice as successor.
''Deng has now got to find a new successor, but there is evidence that he decided he wasn't ready to retire and didn't like feeling being pushed out by Hu,'' one official said.
But a number of academic specialists disagreed, contending that Mr. Hu's ouster could be a serious setback to Mr. Deng's plans to create a more orderly political system and modernize the country's economy.
''This has to be seen as a serious development and one that runs counter to much that Deng was attempting to change over the past eight years,'' said Michel Oksenberg, a professor of political science at the University of Michigan who was the China specialist on the National Security Council under President Carter.
Among the effects of Mr. Hu's ouster, Mr. Oksenberg said, could be the disruption of Mr. Deng's plans to insure an orderly succession and to reassure the country's intellectuals that the Communists will not slip back into the political struggles of the Cultural Revolution.
Mr. Oksenberg, like other academic experts, acknowledged that he had been caught by surprise by the dismissal of the 71-year-old Mr. Hu, a leading advocate of introducing more market forces in China's economy and loosening the Communist Party's tight political controls.
Â 
Protests by Students
Mr. Hu's ouster came after a wave of demonstrations by students demanding greater democracy and after resistance by hard-line Communist officials to Mr. Hu's efforts to offer more freedom. 
But exactly what caused Mr. Hu's downfall remained uncertain, Mr. Oksenberg and others said.
''I think the student demonstrations were only a pretext, the straw that broke the camel's back,'' said Merle Goldman, a professor of Chinese history at Boston University. 
''His fundamental problem was that he had alienated the conservatives, who put pressure on Deng.''
As an example of the political changes that Mr. Hu championed and that annoyed the hard-liners, Mrs. Goldman recalled that in 1984 he overturned a decision to have the Communist Party present a pre-selected slate of officers at a national writers conference.
Instead, after some writers appealed, Mr. Hu told the gathering to vote by secret ballot, and several outspoken liberals were elected, including Liu Binyan, China's most popular and widely read author.
Â 
'It's a Great Shame'
Mr. Liu, whom Mr. Deng attacked by name earlier this week for helping foster the liberal mood in which the student protests took place, was a close friend of Mr. Hu. He had told associates that only Mr. Hu protected him from earlier reprisals for his frequent writings about corruption among party officials.
Roderick MacFarquhar, a professor of government at Harvard University, said Mr. Hu's ouster raised the question whether a Communist nation such as China ''can liberate itself'' to pursue the kind of rapid economic growth that has transformed the other countries of Asia.
''The rights and wrongs of what happened to Hu are not as important as the institutional question,'' Mr. MacFarquhar said. 
''What Deng has done is undermine the succession process which he had so laboriously set in place. 
It's a great shame, because China is now no further along than it was under Mao. 
When Deng goes, struggle will break out again over the succession.''
Mr. Hu, who joined the Communist Red Army guerrillas as a 14-year-old and took part in the Long March, was like a son to Mr. Deng, Mrs. Goldman said. 
He served under Mr. Deng as a youthful army political commissar in the late 1930's and they were purged together in the Cultural Revolution.
But Mr. Hu also had a brusque, impetuous personality that often brought him into conflict both with hard-liners in the party and some intellectuals, who found him uneducated.
Â 
Resistance in the Army
A State Department official said today that there had been indications for a year that Mr. Hu was in trouble and might not end up as Mr. Deng's successor. 
Mr. Deng had been expected to give up his post as head of the party's Military Affairs Commission at a scheduled party congress next fall. 
But there were reports that senior army officers did not get along with Mr. Hu and would not accept him on the military commission, the official said.
''It's possible Deng decided Hu wasn't up to his shoes and then saw the reaction to the student demonstrations as a neat opportunity to get rid of Hu,'' he added.
The official recalled that Mao Zedong had turned on several of his supposed successors, including Liu Shaoqi, then the head of state, and Lin Biao, the military commander who was actually designated the successor in China's Constitution during the Cultural Revolution.
Mr. Oksenberg agreed that Mr. Deng may have been outraged by Mr. Hu's failure to curb the student protests, which spread to at least 11 cities. 
But he said it was difficult to discern whether Mr. Deng had acted under pressure from the hard-liners or just moved dramatically, as he has done inthe past, to assure his own authority.

file: In China, Signs of a Power Struggle.txt
text:
ï»¿
The orthodox Marxists who have dominated politics and culture in China for more than five months are coming under increasing attack from other Communist Party members who support the economic and social changes introduced by the country's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping.
Western diplomats here infer that a serious struggle for power is under way within the country's leadership four months before the party's 13th National Congress is scheduled to begin in October. 
The congress, normally held every five years, charts the country's direction and names its new leaders.
''Clearly there is a major struggle going on,'' a senior Western diplomat said. 
''Now it seems that the reformers led by Zhao are coming out on top.''
Zhao Ziyang is both Prime Minister and Acting General Secretary of the Communist Party.
Â 
Warnings on 'Leftism'
Since the former party chief, Hu Yaobang, was forced to resign in January, a coalition of ideological hard-liners has clamped down on freer expression in the press, the arts and in universities and has opposed those who advocate Western political ideas. 
The hard-liners also have sought to rein in components of the economic modernization pushed by Mr. Deng and Mr. Zhao.
Now, in newspaper editorials, public statements and private meetings, supporters of the policies of Mr. Deng and Mr. Zhao are warning of the dangers of leftism and ossified political views.
''The conservatives don't have any credible alternative,'' a Western European diplomat said. 
''They don't have any economic program.''
A Communist Party member who identifies closely with those who support change said: ''What do the conservatives want?
They want to go back to the 50's. 
Who wants that?
Nobody.''
Â 
A Sign of Change
One sign that the hard-liners may be on the defensive, according to diplomats here, was Mr. Zhao's choice of Wan Li, a Deputy Prime Minister, as Acting Prime Minister, and Hu Qili, a senior Politburo member, as temporary party head when Mr. Zhao visited Eastern Europe two weeks ago.
Both men are regarded as strong proponents of economic change. 
Prominent party conservatives were overlooked for the temporary appointments, according to these diplomats.
Still, some diplomats said, it is by no means certain that Mr. Zhao and his supporters have regained the political initiative necessary to dominate the upcoming congress. 
With Mr. Hu's political demise, a new party leader must be named and a new Politburo must be formed. 
The faction that controls the Politburo, diplomats here say, can set China's economic and ideological course through the end of the decade.
The diplomats pointed out that the inner workings of the Communist Party leadership remained tightly guarded. 
Their conclusions came from close readings of newspapers and scrutiny of public statements.
Â 
Accounts of Crime for Profit
Western diplomats are divided about whether Mr. Zhao and his supporters have beaten back the hard-liners. 
The articles championing the benefits of economic innovation have coincided with a crackdown on illegal publications and criticism of some private business practices.
In recent weeks, China's papers have been full of accounts of illegal dealings by private businessmen and brazen crimes for profit. 
In an economic climate that encourages making money, a diplomat said, unequal wealth and crime are easy targets for hard-liners who believe that innovations not only depart from true Communism but also induce social disorder.
In their counterattack, the so-called reformers have equated strident leftism with poverty. 
The phrase ''socialist poverty'' revives memories for many Chinese of the hysteria and social upheaval of the Cultural Revolution of 1966 to 1976, when Mao Zedong and his allies maintained that ''eating socialist grass'' was better than partaking of capitalist food.
''As poverty is not a characteristic of socialism, it is imperative to develop productive forces,'' Shanghai's party secretary, Rui Xingwen, said in a recent speech.
Â 
Support for 'Open Policy'
For such advocates, this means strengthening programs intended to loosen central controls and relying more on market forces to stimulate production.
Even the party's theoretical journal, Red Flag, which has become an outlet for hard-liners in the last six months, defended economic change recently. 
''Without reform and the open policy,'' the journal said in a major editorial, ''our socialism would have stagnated or ossified and socialist construction with Chinese characteristics would be nothing.''
For the first time in six months, a vague program for separating the Communist Party from the state's administrative apparatus is being discussed. 
This week, Mr. Deng told a Yugoslavian visitor that ''political reform is the order of the day and will be the major topic for discussion at the 13th National Congress.''

file: IN HONG KONG_ OF THE NEWEST, 10 OF THE BEST.txt
text:
ï»¿
Hong Kong is a city of ceaseless conspicuous wonders. 
It supports the world's biggest neon sign, the 328-foot-long Citizen watch sign atop Elizabeth House in Causeway Bay. 
It has the densest concentration of Rolls-Royces, 580, or one for just about every mile and a quarter of Hong Kong road, according to Asia Magazine. 
Its new stainless steel subway carries 1.2 million people a day over its 16-mile length. 
It has the world's longest escalator ride, a 700-foot moving stairway in its Ocean Park recreation center. 
Its Star Ferry boasts a 9-cent harbor ride. 
It is the largest exporter of clothing, watches and toys in the world.
As if all of that weren't sufficient, Hong Kong also has perhaps the best collection of restaurants anywhere. 
To be sure, there may be better individual restaurants in other cities, though even that opinion might occasion some argument in Hong Kong, but there is no place that boasts so many good restaurants.
Not only is the eating wonderful in Hong Kong, so are the varieties of its restaurants, their vitality and their restlessness. 
The restaurant scene is one of constant change. 
Last year I made two trips to Hong Kong, the last just before the end of the year, and in the eight months between those visits scores of new restaurants were opened, this in a city that boasts more than 20,000 restaurants as it is. 
Each time I go to Hong Kong I try as many new places as I can to determine if they are indeed new, exciting, yet true to their Chinese culinary heritage, and each time I find many that please.
Following are 10 of the best of Hong Kong's new restaurants, all of them opened in the last year. 
Unlike what I found on some earlier visits, these restaurants are not all in East Tsimhatsui, that burgeoning enclave of malls, hotels and restaurants in Kowloon. 
Some are in Kowloon proper, and some are on the developing waterfront on Hong Kong Island, across Victoria Harbor from Kowloon.
As with virtually all restaurants in Hong Kong, they are not expensive. 
Such delicacies as shark's fin soup and bird's nest soup can, of course, run up your bill, but for two to three courses of the foods mentioned below, dinner should not be more than $15 to $20 a person. 
The food is the thing; the more rare the more expensive. 
Nor is elegance a sole index of price. 
Such restaurants as Lai Ching Heen and Ziyang Szechuen are decorated in good taste and can be a bit more expensive, but food in far less glossy places can cost as much or more.
All of these restaurants are open from about 11 A.M. to 11 P.M., but those noted as serving dim sum will customarily open several hours earlier, usually about 8 A.M. As important as being new is the fact that these restaurants represent all of the four regional cuisines of China.
Perhaps the most outlandish is the North Sea Fishing Village (first and second basements, Auto Plaza, East Tsimshatsui; telephone 3-7236843), which has a full-size Chinese junk moored in its center. 
On the deck of the junk is a sushi bar at which fresh raw octopus, abalone, conch, lobster and many varieties of raw fish are prepared. 
Sushi, while not common in Hong Kong, is becoming more well known. 
The Chinese call it yueh sang, which translated literally means live fish. 
Tanks of live turtles, crabs and lobsters are piled on the deck of the junk as well.
The restaurant's specialty is the freshest of seafood, and on the junk sit many tanks of filtered water in which swim sea bass, garoupa and pomfret. 
You select your fish; it is netted and cooked as you wish. 
The best method, in my opinion, is to have it steamed with shredded ginger, mushrooms and scallions. 
The restaurant is also fine for dim sum, that traditional Cantonese brunch of different kinds of dumplings and scented tea.
For elegance and Cantonese cookery raised to the level of high art, Lai Ching Heen (Regent Hotel, Salisbury Road; 3-7211211) has few competitors. 
This restaurant on the basement level of the hotel, which sits on the border between East Tsimshatsui and Kowloon proper, is all gray velvet walls and antique Chinese blackwood furniture. 
The table setting consists of a square plate of green jade, a holder of carved green jade that contains a spoon of silver with a jade handle and ivory chopsticks banded in silver and a condiment dish, also of green jade.
Do not miss roast suckling pig in Lai Ching Heen, a dish served nouvelle style, glistening, cross hatched and crisp, or other Cantonese classics such as steamed crab with its roe or roasted pigeon with freshly ground spicy Sichuan peppercorns. 
And all the while enjoy the traffic of the harbor as it passes by your window.
Outstanding examples of the cooking of the people of Chiu Chow, many thousands of whom live, and cook, in Hong Kong, are found at City Chiu Chow Restaurant (East Ocean Center, 98 Granville Road, East Tsimshatsui; 3-7245383). 
The food of the Chiu Chow, who live on the southern coast of China, is one of sharp tastes. 
They use much garlic and white vinegar in their cooking and season the food with a sauce of tangerine juice and ground chili peppers. 
A specialty of the Chiu Chow is pomfret fish, smoked in tea leaves; this restaurant does it superbly. 
Another specialty is large crabs from the China Sea, boiled then served at room temperature so that they can be cracked and eaten in the style of a New Orleans crab boil. 
A custom here is to have Iron Goddess tea before and after the meal, initially to cleanse the palate, finally to cut the pungency of what has been eaten and to help you digest it. 
The tea, widely available, even in the United States, is also known as Ti Kuan Yin.
In Kowloon, one of best of the new is the Ziyang Szechuen Restaurant (45D Chatham Road South; 3-687177), the brainchild of Allan Koo, whose two previous Hong Kong restaurants were Italian and named Valentino and Leonardo. 
Why?
''Because I spent so much time in Italy. 
Italian food is family-style food. 
I like spaghetti,'' says Mr. Koo, all of whose reasons seem sensible.
Ziyang has gray suede and pink marble walls, caged parakeets that chirp incessantly, a guitarist nightly, chairs from Italy that cost Mr. Koo $200 each, and Sichuan food of an exceptionally high order. 
We had wonderful fried dumplings, thinly sliced loin of pork in a garlic, soy and vinegar sauce, bean threads dressed with hot peanut and sesame sauce, prawns in searingly hot chili and dry-fried shredded beef, a difficult dish to make because it often resembles used shoelaces. 
Not here.
The Shing Tao Restaurant (6-8 Jordan Road, Jordan House; 3-7243832) divides its menu equally between Sichuan and Peking cooking. 
It is just off Nathan Road, in the traditional back lot of Kowloon, away from much of the Tsimshatsui glitter, but its food is worth the trip.
When you sit down, a plate of peanuts that have been stewed in cinnamon, eight-star anise and Sichuan peppercorns is put before you to nibble on while you consider the menu. 
We had Yunnan ham with fresh honey in steamed buns, duck smoked in tea leaves and camphor and as a final course Mongolian-style grilled beef. 
A curved cast-iron grill that looks like one side of a waffle iron is placed over a small fire in the center of the table. 
Beef is placed on the grill and cooks in seconds. 
This is then dipped into a bubbling mixture of soy sauce, wine, sugar, white pepper and peanut oil and eaten with shredded leeks. 
A spectacular dish.
A fashionable, though tiny, establishment in Kowloon that is serving some of the best Shanghai food in Hong Kong is the Wu Kong Shanghai Restaurant (27 Nathan Road, Alpha House; 3-667244), a white marble place entered from Peking Road, just around the corner from its nominal address. 
The restaurant is the creation of Bill Kong and his chef, Wu Chow, who was born in Shanghai and has been cooking the food of his native city for 30 years.
The food is classical Shanghai in execution: so-called drunken pigeon, the bird marinated in Hsao-Shing wine before being lightly braised; tiny shrimp poached with egg white and sauteed quickly so that they look like a snow drift; eel, shredded so that it resembles pasta, then braised with bean sprouts and minced garlic in wine vinegar and soy sauce.
Across the harbor, on Hong Kong Island, many new restaurants have opened in recent months. 
Most of them are Cantonese, as are most restaurants in Hong Kong, but one of the best is the East Ocean Seafood Restaurant (25 Harbour Road, third floor, Harbour Center; 5-8938887), where, as its name suggests, the menu is heavily accented with fish and seafood. 
The restaurant's strength lies in elaborate, banquet-quality preparations, and even though you might not want to indulge in a 10-course binge, a selection from the banquet menu is advised.
We had, for example, whole prawns steamed with garlic and served in small bamboo steamers; double-boiled whole shark's fin cooked with wintermelon and Yunnan ham and octopus fried with snow peas and fresh ginger. 
Then as a respite from seafood we were served a whole chicken that had been marinated in Grand Marnier, fried, then presented with a bit of lemon juice and Sichuan peppercorns and sea salt, ground together. 
It was outstanding.
In Hong Kong Central, up the slope from Queen's Road, is the West Villa Restaurant (1-5 On Lan Street; 5-212196), which is one of Hong Kong's best fowl, bird and game restaurants. 
The dishes are classic (but often overlooked) Cantonese. 
For example, you can eat, as we did, partridge cooked in a closed porcelain jar with sugar cane, Yunnan ham and ginger, a striking preparation. 
We have had pigeon stuffed with shark's fin, then braised, and crab meat with beaten egg whites, a snow white mountain of softness bordered with bright green flowers of broccoli.
The chef, Peter Tang, cooks what he calls ''the food of the home'' and says he pays ''obedience to the old masters'' of Chinese cookery, those master chefs called Mon See Fu, and when he cooks such delicate things as eel, first double boiled, later steamed in hollowed bamboo, his respect for elegance is understood. 
There is a similarly named restaurant on the Hong Kong waterfront, the West Villa Admiralty Restaurant (18 Harcourt Road, ground floor, Admiralty Center; 5-298333), which is said to have several partners in common with the other West Villa. 
Whether it does or not, the restaurants are totally different, the West Villa Admiralty specializing in Shanghai cuisine.
It serves drunken shrimp, a rare delicacy consisting of live shrimp marinated in rice wine, then slowly cooked in the wine in their shells. 
The restaurant cooks shredded beef with fermented black beans and fresh shallots, makes quite a rich wintermelon soup filled with duck meat, shrimp, fresh lotus seeds and frog legs and steams Hong Kong's native fish, the garoupa, with scallions and fresh sliced ginger.
Finally, there is another of those new and elegant Cantonese restaurants, the Tao Yuan Restaurant (23 Harbour Road, third floor, Great Eagle Center; 5-738080) near the new Hong Kong Arts Center. 
It looks out over the harbor, and on its tables are pink cloths and table settings that are adequate copies of Ching Dynasty porcelain.
The Tao Yuan has wonderful dim sum in the morning, then in the afternoon it becomes a place to eat minced quail, mushrooms, cucumbers, water chestnuts and celery wrapped in cool lettuce leaves, crisp goose with sweet plum sauce, scallops stuffed with mashed taro root, then fried, and hot bouillon into which are dropped puffy fried vegetable fritters.
This is the sort of food being cooked in Hong Kong. 
It is inventive, yet true to its Chinese roots, and is extraordinarily well prepared by a growing band of young Hong Kong-born and Hong Kong-trained chefs. 
It is food worth making a trip more than halfway around the world to taste.

file: IN SHANGHAI JAIL, A GLIMPSE OF A _LOST GENERATION_.txt
text:
