He was seated at a table in the prison dispensary, dressed in a white dustcoat. 
From the anguish in his eyes and the awkward way he rose to his feet, it was plain he was no ordinary doctor.
What brought Zhao Guomin to the Shanghai Municipal Prison was not medicine but murder. 
On Dec. 
28, 1968, he and four other men beat to death the 38-year-old scientist who was head of the Shanghai Pharmacological Institute in a case that was swallowed up for a time in the general tumult of the Cultural Revolution.
Now 43 years old, Mr. Zhao has about 18 months of an eight-year prison term still to serve, and he counts himself a lucky man. 
''I could have been executed,'' he told a visitor. 
Tears welled in his eyes as he spoke of his victim's family and of the travails of his own wife and son as they await his return.
Article describes conditions at Shanghai Municipal Prison, China, where many young people arrested during country's Cultural Revolution remain incarcerated; some efforts have been made by Government of Deng Xiaoping to help prisoners prepare for better life (M)
Mr. Zhao's story is one of many in the forbidding edifice at 147 Changyang Street in central Shanghai that have their origin in the ''10 years of calamity,'' as the Cultural Revolution is officially known. 
When Mao Zedong set out in 1966 to turn Chinese society upside down, he unleashed forces that shattered hundreds of thousands of lives, and the legacy is still felt in every corner of the nation's life.
A tour of the Shanghai prison is a sobering affair. 
More than 60 percent of the 3,700 inmates are under 35, men and women who belong to what Chinese call the ''lost generation'' of youth whose education and family life were uprooted when the Cultural Revolution closed schools, set children against parents and licensed mayhem against anybody standing for the established order.
Â 
Cultural Revolution Is Blamed
''What we have here in many respects are the victims of the Cultural Revolution,'' said Wu Jichen, the prison's deputy governor, as he led a visitor through workshops and classrooms that cluster around granite cell blocks built by the British between 1903 and 1923. 
''They belong to a generation that was told by the Gang of Four that education was useless, so they grew up without culture, without any sense of right and wrong.''
''What we try to do is to engage in a process of remolding, to try and help the inmates distinguish what is right from what is wrong, what is beautiful from what is ugly, what is lawful from what is not.''
Similar accounts have been offered for many years in Chinese jails, but officials acknowledge now that much of what was said in the past was false or at least exaggerated. 
The picture that has emerged since the ascent of China's current leader, Deng Xiaoping, is one in which the country's vast network of jails and labor camps, indeed the entire legal system, was fatally prejudiced by arbitrariness and brutality.
Not all of this has changed. 
In two years, under a crackdown on crime begun by Mr. Deng, thousands of people have been executed, some within days of their offenses. 
The central authorities' insistence on a broader use of the death sentence has led to thousands of executions since the autumn of 1983, nine in Peking on one day in January alone. 
Troubling questions remain about the fairness of court procedures, including limited opportunities for defense.
Â 
Greater Effort Visible
Nonetheless, a visit to the Shanghai prison suggests that greater effort has been made under Mr. Deng to give substance to Mao's instruction that prisons be turned into factories, farms and schools where inmates can prepare for a better life. 
A visitor passing through workshops where prisoners make clothing, electrical components and ornaments has the impression of generally healthy men and women unafraid to talk about their yearning for life outside.
The prison sits off a busy street, shielded by a succession of three steel doors, by guards with automatic rifles and by a 20-foot granite wall topped by glass shards. 
According to Mr. Wu, the deputy governor, sentences range from 20 years to six months, with ''seven or eight'' inmates under suspended death sentences that can be commuted for good behavior after two years.
The case of Dr. Zhao suggests that there is still much that is arbitrary in the sentencing. 
As he told it, he was press-ganged into joining an ''investigation team'' that came to the pharmacological institute to press charges of spying against the party secretary. 
Because torture was to be involved, the team wanted a doctor present, but as things progressed Dr. Zhao became an accomplice in the beating.
Dr. Zhao said the death was covered up at the time, but the case was reopened at the widow's instigation after the overthrow of the so-called Gang of Four - Jiang Qing, who was Mao's wife, and her associates - in 1976. 
Two of the five assailants were tried, and Dr. Zhao received the stiffer sentence. 
After two years at hard labor and two more in another prison, he was assigned to the dispensary. 
On his release next year, he expects to be reassigned to medical work in Shanghai.
Â 
Song Shows New Attitude
Against this, other sentences seem relatively severe. 
Chen Jingcai, conductor of the prison orchestra, is serving a 15-year term for ''molesting women'' while interviewing them for posts with a Shanghai ensemble. 
Since there is a charge of rape under Chinese law, his offense evidently was less severe. 
Now he spends his days teaching prisoners the violin, flute and other instruments and rehearsing lusty renditions the ''Ode to Joy'' movement of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony and American songs such as ''Oh!
Susanna'' sung with Chinese words.
Even in the orchestra, prisoners are expected to work at remolding attitudes. 
Zhao Derong, a former glassmaker serving a four-year term for stealing bicycles, exercises his strong tenor in a prison ballad he composed, ''Don't Worry About Me, Mother.''
In the refrain, he sings of his wish to study hard, learn skills and ''make my contribution to the motherland.''
Work is the center of prison life. 
Inmates labor eight hours a day, six days a week for three yuan, or $1.07, plus monthly bonuses of up to 20 yuan. 
All are required to attend classes and to work toward at least a junior middle school certificate, the equivalent of 10th grade. 
Each block has a television set, a library and a Ping-Pong table. 
A half-hour family visit once a month is permitted, and about a fifth of the prisoners are allowed to go home for a couple of days each year.
At night, two inmates are locked into each of the cells, which measure about 8 feet by 5 and have steel doors and a sliding peephole that opens from the outside. 
Bedrolls stacked against the wall are laid on concrete floors. 
Regulations pinned to the wall forbid discussion of crimes and sentences between cellmates and command them to ''seriously repent'' their wrongdoing.
According to Mr. Wu, the deputy governor, the last time anybody escaped was in 1975, clinging to the underside of a delivery truck, and he was caught in hours. 
Although guards are unarmed, officials say none have been attacked in memory. 
''What we aim for is to achieve the kind of relationship doctors have with patients,'' said Mr. Wu. ''You can see for yourself, there is no hostility between wardens and prisoners.''

text:
ï»¿
Dragonair, a 22-month-old airline that owns one plane and leases another, has a burning ambition. 
It wants to become a major international carrier.
Standing in its way is Cathay Pacific Airways, which has everything Dragonair does not: passengers, profits and prospects.
Regarded as among the world's best airlines, along with other Asian carriers such as Singapore Airlines and Thai Airways International, Cathay Pacific has expanded rapidly in recent years and now uses Hong Kong as the hub of 494 flights each week, on 22 aircraft. 
Most of the flights are within Asia, but it also serves destinations ranging from Amsterdam to San Francisco. 
More than 4.3 million passengers flew Cathay last year.
Â 
Byzantine Struggle
The battle is more than just for business: It is a prime example of the Byzantine struggles in Hong Kong for China's patronage before Beijing resumes control of this territory in a decade's time.
''Cathay Pacific is the image of Hong Kong past, and we're the image of Hong Kong future,'' said Stephen H. Miller, the feisty general manager of Dragonair, formally known as Hong Kong Dragon Airlines Ltd.
Seven weeks ago, many analysts might have agreed with that assessment. 
Dragonair was viewed as having Beijing's backing, through the crucial web of relationships known in Chinese as ''guanxi,'' the key to getting what you want in China. 
Of the Chinese businessmen associated with the airline, the most prominent is Sir Yue-kong Pao, a shipping magnate who is one of Dragonair's largest backers and is serving as chairman. 
He has good links with Beijing and is often mentioned as a future candidate for governor of Hong Kong. 
Meanwhile, Cathay Pacific, with its crew of 100 percent non-Chinese pilots and flight engineers, was seen as being British-backed.
Then abruptly, at the end of January, China's investment bank, the China International Trust and Investment Corporation, purchased a 12.5 percent stake in Cathay Pacific for $245 million (United States).
Dragonair's managing director, Helmut Sohmen, likened the Cathay move to ''pushing panic buttons,'' but in the airline industry it was seen as a brilliant maneuver that robbed Dragonair of its status as the fighter in Beijing's corner.
Dragonair has hardly wilted under the pressure. 
On New Year's Eve, it announced that it had placed firm orders for two of the McDonnell Douglas Corporation's new long-haul planes, the MD-11 - even though Dragonair as yet has no long-distance routes.
Then, shortly after the China International investment in Cathay, Dragonair's shareholders announced they would double the paid-up capital, to $51 million.
Cathay formerly was 70 percent owned by Swire Pacific, a Hong Kong conglomerate that in turn is controlled by John Swire & Sons, a diversified London concern. 
The remaining 30 percent was owned by the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation. 
However, last year, the two owners decided to make a public offering and issue stock.
Traded on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, the issue was 52 times oversubscribed, a measure of Cathay's premier role in the territory - and of the profits that are anticipated. 
In 1985, the last full year for which figures are available, Cathay Pacific earned $100 million on revenues of $965 million.
For the present, Dragonair is losing money - reportedly $500,000 a month - although Mr. Miller, the managing director, said that when two more planes are in service later this year the airline could break even.

Iran's Foreign Minister forcefully denied today that his country had received any weapons from China, including antiship missiles, and he warned both the United States and the Soviet Union to stay out of the Persian Gulf.
He added that if Iraq would stop attacking ships in the gulf, Iran would do likewise.
Iran has manufactured its own missiles, the Foreign Minister, Ali Akbar Velayati, said while speaking to reporters at the Iranian Embassy. 
He added that China did not help build the missile production installation.
He made his remarks in response to reports that China has sold Iran surface-to-ship missiles of the type known in the West as Silkworm.

''We meet our armament requirements from any place we deem suitable,'' he said.
Â 
Arms Traced to North Korea
The Foreign Minister, who met today with the Chinese head of state, Li Xiannian, has just completed a visit to Pyongyang, North Korea. 
Several European and Asian diplomats said this week that Iran had obtained great quantities of Chinese arms via North Korea.
Mr. Li told Mr. Velayati that the United States and the Soviet Union ''have taken advantage of the situation, making the turbulent gulf situation even more complicated and tense,'' according to the New China News Agency.
Both the United States and the Soviet Union have agreed to fly their flags over Kuwaiti tankers to deter attackers and justify protection by their warships. 
China said earlier this week that it, too, was considering a request by Kuwait to register vessels under the Chinese flag.
Â 
A Warning to the Kuwaitis
Mr. Velayati said Kuwait's effort to protect its ships by using the flags of other nations would not succeed. 
What the Kuwaitis have done, he said, is to provide a kind of invitation to intervention.
He added that Kuwait had ''miscalculated the political situation.''
Instead of easing dangers in the Persian Gulf, he said, the reflagging has contributed to a hightening of tensions.
The Foreign Minister refused to specify what action his country might take if foreign warships tried to protect Kuwaiti ships or refused to respond to Iranian Navy challenges.

file: JARDINE MATHESON_S HEIR-ELECT_ Brian M. Powers_An Asian Trading Empire Picks an American _Tai-Pan_.txt
text:
ï»¿
Struan and Company (was) the greatest house in Asia, and so rich and powerful that the other China traders had named it in awe and jealousy The Noble House - noble because it was first in riches, first in largess, first in trade, first in clippers, but mostly because Dirk Struan was Tai-Pan, the Tai-Pan among all the tai-pans of Asia.
- ''Tai-Pan,'' by James Clavell
Â 
Â 
IT is not power so much as magic that swirls about the tai-pan of the Jardine Matheson group - a legacy of opium and intrigue that goes with being the ''big boss'' of Asia's famous trading company. 
Chronicled as Struan and Company in James Clavell's novels, Jardines is more than an international conglomerate; it is a legend.
At least nine streets in Hong Kong are named for tai-pans at Jardines, which has towered over the British territory for 145 years, dealing in opium and silk in the last century and everything from ice cream to investment banking today. 
The tai-pan of the Noble House - or the Princely Hong, as Jardines is also known - inherits the mantle of William Jardine, the first tai-pan, a shrewd Scotsman nicknamed by the Chinese ''iron-headed old rat.''
Most of the tai-pans - whose arrivals in earlier days sometimes were greeted by cannon salutes - come from branches of the same family tree, serving in the Hong Kong hot seat before retiring to London or the family estate in Scotland. 
So Hong Kong gasped at the announcement that a 37-year-old American investment banker, with just 14 months' experience at Jardines, is set to become its next tai-pan.
Brian M. Powers is a 6-foot 2 former football player, sandy-haired with a hint of gray, who looks a bit too affable to be tai-pan. 
But he can rake the landscape with his speech: Ideas and quips and analyses fly through the air like shotgun pellets. 
And for years - ever since his first job at a New York law firm - he has set himself apart from others with his long workdays, even in offices where absurd hours were the norm.
On his wedding day eight years ago, Mr. Powers was busy with a real-estate transaction and had to rush to the church at the last minute - only to discover that he had left the ring behind. 
The bridal party watched aghast as he searched his pockets before racing back home to get the wedding band.
Last fall, during negotiations on a Jardines sale of some of its American oil interests, he flew to San Francisco for the day to try to get a better price - a move that worked and that impressed the man who counts most at Jardines: Simon Keswick, the current tai-pan and a distant relative of William Jardine.
''People in Hong Kong think they work very hard,'' Mr. Keswick said in his office 48 floors above Hong Kong's bustling central district. 
''I think Brian has demonstrated that people in New York work even harder.''
And so the 45-year-old Mr. Keswick (pronounced KEH-zick) announced earlier this month that he would relinquish his position of managing director of the Jardine companies to Mr. Powers. Mr. Keswick will remain as chairman, but, he says, he will spend more time outside Hong Kong than in it. 
He calls Mr. Powers the ''heir-elect,'' and says he already regards Mr. Powers as tai-pan.
THAT may be a bit premature, so long as Mr. Keswick is still in town. 
But the expectation, within Jardines and without, is that moving vans will appear sometime over the next year or so at 35 Mount Kellett Road, the residence of the tai-pans, on the Peak on Hong Kong Island. 
Mr. Keswick, the whispers say, will retain the title of chairman from London, just as his uncle, Sir John Keswick, did two decades ago.
Mr. Powers will presumably inherit the keys to the Mount Kellett Road home, as well as to the tai-pan's second residence at Shek O, along the water. 
He apparently will also assume a seat on the board of the Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corporation and the coveted position as steward of the Royal Hong Kong Jockey Club.
But most of all, there is Jardines to command. 
As managing director, Mr. Powers will head up a network that sells cognac in Japan, operates the renowned Oriental Hotel in Bangkok; runs Pizza Huts in Hawaii and 7-Eleven stores in Malaysia; oversees ship management in the Pacific, construction in China and investment banking throughout Asia.
The empire - with 1986 revenues of $1.3 billion and after-tax profits of $61 million - employs 61,000 people in 22 countries and includes Jardine Matheson Holdings, Jardine Strategic Holdings and controlling interests in the Hongkong Land Company, Mandarin Oriental Hotel Group, and Dairy Farm International Holdings.
To this may be added some large American company. 
Mr. Powers says the group is looking for acquisitions in the United States and Britain, though he says this could be a single $2 billion deal or a string of $100 million purchases. 
Mr. Keswick says he would like a major American presence, and he adds that Mr. Powers might want to return to the United States in five years or so and run the American wing of Jardines.
But familiarity with the American market was not the reason for choosing Mr. Powers. Indeed, his nationality may even have worked against him a little, in the clubby world of British-run Hong Kong companies. 
His Yankee frankness has ruffled some feathers here, he acknowledged. 
''The business style is different,'' he said. 
''The Brits are much more civilized than Americans.''
And though Mr. Powers has joined the Jockey Club and he and his wife have dutifully entertained at their home on the Peak, their presence in Hong Kong's social circuit is subdued. 
''I like Hong Kong,'' he said, ''but I work very long hours and I'm very committed to my job.''
But if Mr. Powers has not always displayed proper enthusiasm for drinking port, no one doubts his mastery of law and finance. 
Those skills seem to have been key to his meteoric rise, after arriving at Jardines in April 1986 as ''chief strategist.''
The conglomerate was then in the process of slimming down - after some disastrous investments in real estate, shipping and oil.
Rivals for power within Jardines had their own credentials, but they could not compete with a financial alchemist at a time when the group was so absorbed by financial matters. 
Mr. Powers immediately set to work planning a restructuring of Jardines that included spinning off subsidiaries and creating a complex web of corporations that own each other. 
He also registered some more of the group's assets in Bermuda, in the belief that foreign-registered corporations might fare better when China takes over Hong Kong in 1997.
That grasp of finance and corporate strategy seems to have impressed many people in Hong Kong, in and out of Jardines. 
''Maybe U.S. financial people are more on the ball than British people,'' mused one British executive at Jardines. 
''Nobody here has the financial know-how to take all those companies apart and register them elsewhere and watch those share prices rocket.''
FOR Brian Powers, the road to becoming tai-pan began in Massapequa, L.I. 
The second-youngest of four children, and the son of a stockbroker, he devoted most of his energy in high school to football. 
He even turned down Yale initially to go to Holy Cross because of its more rigorous approach to athletics. 
He transferred to Yale after two years.
''When he played football, his favorite position was defensive end,'' his wife recalled. 
''I think that's because reading the other side is what he finds fun and intriguing about a situation.''
An economics major, Mr. Powers graduated with average grades and then went to the University of Virginia Law School, where he excelled. 
He graduated near the top of his class and, after a year as a teaching fellow at Stanford Law School, he became an associate in the New York law firm of Debevoise & Plimpton. 
He is remembered there as a hard worker and a quick study who was fortunate to specialize in mergers and acquisitions just as the wave of mergers was beginning in the United States.
After two years at Debevoise & Plimpton, Mr. Powers accepted a job as an attorney with the Ford Foundation. 
However, almost immediately he was put in charge of a large investment portfolio that included venture capital and real estate.
One of his first acts was to foreclose on two big real estate developments in the belief that the Foundation could run them better than the developers. 
Colleagues noticed that. 
Some thought him brash. 
Most - including his boss, Jon L. Hagler -were impressed. 
''I haven't seen a better negotiator,'' said Mr. Hagler, who now runs a Boston investment firm. 
''He had it all.''
Mr. Powers was at the Ford Foundation when James D. Wolfensohn, an Australian-born financier, gave him a call. 
Mr. Wolfensohn was planning to set up a New York investment bank, and had heard about Mr. Powers from a Debevoise & Plimpton partner. 
So after four years at the foundation, Mr. Powers joined Mr. Wolfensohn, becoming his right-hand man at James D. Wolfensohn Inc.
SOON after the firm opened, a man named Simon Keswick called. 
He was in the New York office of the Coudert Brothers law firm, and wanted to know if Mr. Powers could come by that evening to help structure a deal. 
With characteristic bluntness, Mr. Powers asked the tai-pan: ''This is a terrible question, but who are you?''
From that inauspicious beginning, a relationship grew between the two. 
Mr. Powers handled more and more Jardines business, including an extremely complex sale of sugar interests in Hawaii that included a leveraged buyout with commercial and government financing. 
''That was an extraordinary piece of work,'' recalled Mr. Wolfensohn.
Indeed, it was one of the accomplishments that led Mr. Keswick at the end of 1985 to ask Mr. Powers if he would like to come to work for Jardines. 
Mr. Powers's initial response was that he was happy at Wolfensohn and that his wife, Paula, had a job in New York and was not mobile.
Mr. Keswick persisted, and Mr. Powers finally arrived in April of last year, with a seat on the board and a mandate to direct financial strategy. 
Paula Powers, who was teaching at Columbia Law School, was willing to move to Hong Kong, and both parents thought it was the ideal time for their son, Jeremy, to live abroad. 
Mr. Powers has so far not studied Chinese, but six-year-old Jeremy is learning the local dialect and already knows important words like ''su tiu,'' which means french fries.
Mr. Keswick seems to have raised the possibility of succession with Mr. Powers when he was first hired, but both say that no commitment was made. 
There were a number of other candidates: David J. Davies, the head of the Hongkong Land Company until he resigned last year rather than see it dismantled; Martin G. Barrow, board member and head of a key subsidiary until he was promoted out of both positions earlier this year, and Nigel Rich, the current chief executive of Hongkong Land.
As the new tai-pan, Mr. Powers will face a number of challenges. 
Despite diversification, a large share of the company's assets remain in Hong Kong. 
The property market and business climate here are extremely sensitive, even though Beijing has promised that it will allow Hong Kong to maintain its capitalist way of life for at least 50 years after 1997.
Then there is the rise of a new breed of competitor in Asia: local entrepreneurs who in the last two decades have built their own conglomerates to challenge British interests. 
In Hong Kong, such Chinese entrepreneurs as Sir Y.K. 
Pao and Li Ka-shing have often outmaneuvered Jardines in the last decade.
These entrepreneurs are not only rivals but also potential threats, for Jardines could become an acquisition target. 
One reason they have gained on British interests is that they know the market better - and that could be all the more true when Jardines is run by a man who is a newcomer to the region.
Nor is it clear exactly how much control the Keswicks will continue to exert. 
The family is the company's largest shareholder, with about a 10 percent interest. 
Simon's older brother, Henry Keswick, is a former tai-pan now living in London who remains deeply involved in Jardines.
''I think the Keswicks will still pull the strings from London,'' said William Phillips, the managing director of Baring Securities Hong Kong Ltd. 
Others say Jardines will still be run out of Hong Kong, but that there will be constant consultations.
Mr. Powers may want to keep an active chairman. 
He says he approves of separating the top job, to spread the power. 
Otherwise, he says, there is a risk for the tai-pan that ''if things go reasonably well, you can easily believe you're God.''

file: JARDINE MOVING PLAN IS JOLT TO HONG KONG.txt
text:
ï»¿
After Jardine Matheson, the Hong Kong trading company, disclosed last Wednesday that it planned to move its legal residency to Bermuda, The Hong Kong Standard likened the shock to hearing that the Queen of England was emigrating to Australia.
Jardine Matheson & Company Ltd., after all, helped found the British Crown Colony in 1841, only nine years after the company itself was born in Canton, China. 
Jardine has long since outgrown its opium-running origins to become a major conglomerate with investments in Asia ranging from real estate to financial services to shipping. 
More than any other company, it epitomized Hong Kong's commitment to free-wheeling capitalism.
Article examines impact on Hong Kong of disclosure by Jardine Matheson & Co Ltd that it plans to move its legal residency to Bermuda; full details of relocation decision will not be known until company's annual report on May 14, but number of Hong Kong business people and other analysts have concluded that Hong Kong Government's characterization of legal relocation as only 'a commercial decision' is not far off; illustration (M)
The full details of the decision to move will not be known until the company's annual report is issued to the stockholders on May 14. 
The decision will then come up for approval at a general meeting in June.
But in the few days since the jolting announcement was made, a number of Hong Kong business people and other analysts have concluded that the Hong Kong Government's characterization of the legal relocation as only ''a commercial decision'' is not far off.
There are potential psychological ramifications, say the analysts, but they believe that it will not touch off a hemorrhage of business confidence in Hong Kong's future after 1997, when China intends to reclaim sovereignty.
''Nobody wants to pull out of Hong Kong,'' said one United States businessman. 
''There is too much money to be made. 
There are no sales in Bermuda.''
In making the unexpected announcement, Jardine's chairman, Simon Keswick, acknowledged that the plan to set up a parent holding company in Bermuda reflected the prevailing uncertainty over what will happen to businesses when Hong Kong reverts to Chinese sovereignty.
Mr. Keswick, who came from Britain to take over as chairman less than a year ago, said that as an international corporation allocating its investments, Jardine found it ''undoubtedly a disadvantage to have to deal with questions regarding the long-term future of Hong Kong.''
As a British-run business, Mr. Keswick said, ''we wish to remain as long as possible under that jurisdiction.''
As Mr. Keswick noted, Jardine is not physically pulling out of Hong Kong in changing its legal registration. 
The head office and fixed assets will remain in the colony and business activities here will continue.
But the Bermuda connection is meant to ensure that Jardine continues to operate under British laws after Britain's lease over most of the colony expires in 13 years. 
One business analyst described the plan as ''a legal maneuver on where the tax will be paid.''
In practical terms, this means canceling the company's shares issued in Kong Kong and replacing them with equal new shares issued in Bermuda. 
Jardine's Hong Kong stock is now valued at about $5 billion (Hong Kong), or $641 million (United States).
Mr. Keswick linked the decision in part to an 80 percent drop in his company's net earnings last year over those of 1982, caused by financial jitters over the colony's future.
Jardine's announcement has already affected the colony's equities market. 
Last Thursday, the Hong Kong stock market plunged more than 61 points in the worst one-day loss this year. 
On Friday, it slipped nearly 43 more points, to close at slightly over 1,014 points on the Hang Seng index. 
The Hong Kong dollar has been unaffected because it was pegged to the United States dollar following its fall to a record low of 9.5 Hong Kong dollars to the United States dollar last September.
A local architect who follows the stock market suggested that ''now is the time to buy. 
The stocks are cheap and they'll come up again.''
Â 
Political Reaction Sharper
Politically, reaction has been even more negative, since the decision came while Britain and China remain engaged in sensitive and secret negotiations on a Hong Kong agreement before the September deadline set by Peking.
Several members of the colony's Legislative Council called Jardine's plan bad news. 
One council member, Selina Chow, told reporters ''this is definitely a manifestation of the lack of confidence of some of the business community in Hong Kong's future.''
Stephen Cheong, another member, said that ''the damage to the delicate flower of confidence has been done.''
The Chinese Government, apparently caught off guard, has been conspicuously silent. 
But the leftist Hong Kong press, which tends to reflect Peking's thinking, has criticized Jardine's plans and questioned its motives. 
The daily newspaper Wen Wei Po contended that the ''unwise'' decision could not have been made without the collusion of the British.
Other analysts do not fault Jardine for refusing to wait until China and Britain announce their plans for the transition of authority in Hong Kong. 
The secrecy surrounding the talks, which resume in Peking on April 11, prompted Hong Kong's legislative council to vote last month to open its own debate on the colony's future. 
Peking has objected to such a public voice.
Â 
A 'Justifiable Question'
''What Jardine has done is to raise a very justifiable question,'' said a Western resident of Hong Kong. 
''Under which law are we going to operate once China takes over this place?
How can we stay here to play a game whose rules are not known to us?''
Chinese officials have promised that Hong Kong can operate with its own political, economic and legal system as a special administrative region after it reverts to Chinese sovereignty. 
The Foreign Minister, Wu Xueqian, was quoted in a recent magazine interview as saying that China would ''scrupulously implement'' the agreement that it reaches with Britain.
The major concern now is that other companies, seeing Hong Kong's most prominent firm register an apparent lack of confidence in the future, may decide to follow suit and look for their own bases outside Hong Kong, a move that could dampen further investment in the colony. 
Particular attention is focusing on Swire Pacific, another company that originated as Jardine's major rival nearly a century and a half ago.
Another question is whether Peking may be angry enough to retaliate in some way against Jardine's business ventures in China. 
Such vindictiveness could also hurt China's credibility with Hong Kong investors, the analysts say.

South Korea continued tonight to hold a Chinese torpedo boat that drifted into its waters with six dead crew members, killed in what some reports described as a mutiny after some crewmen tried to defect.
The South Korean Government made no direct response to a Chinese request for the return of the naval vessel and its crew ''as soon as possible.''
(China and South Korea were reportedly holding talks on the return of the boat and crew through officials they maintain in Hong Kong.)
Â 
2 Reportedly in Hospital
Two crew members, reportedly shot but not critically wounded, were in a hospital in the South Korean port of Kunsan, on the Yellow Sea. 
A total of 10 or 11 other crewmen were also believed to have been taken to Kunsan, but their whereabouts could not be determined. 
Their boat was apparently offshore.
South Korea continues to hold Chinese torpedo boat that drifted into its waters with six dead crew members, killed in what some reports described as mutiny after some crewmen tried to defect; two crew members, reportedly shot but not critically wounded, are in hospital in South Korea, and South Korean Government makes no direct response to Chinese request for return of vessel and its crew 'as soon as possible'; photo (M)
It was not clear whether any of the sailors sought political asylum in South Korea or preferred to be sent home.
South Korean officials seemed to deal cautiously with the episode, which threatened to undercut recent attempts by the two countries to pursue friendly contacts even though they have no diplomatic relations.
Â 
'A Simple Scuffle'
A statement issued tonight in Seoul by the Minister of Culture and Information, Lee Won Hong, did not mention a mutiny or any deaths.
''It was determined, based on facts so far obtained, that casualties aboard the Chinese torpedo boat were due to a simple scuffle among the crewmen and that no political reason was involved,'' Mr. Lee said.
Officials interviewed by telephone from Seoul declined to give details. 
But several foreign diplomats in South Korea described the incident as a mutiny that seemed to have begun on Friday when some Chinese crew members tried to defect to Taiwan.
Â 
Demand by Crewman
A Western diplomat said available information suggested that one crewman had held a rifle and demanded that the vessel - apparently part of a naval exercise in the Yellow Sea - be diverted to Taiwan. 
The Japanese press, citing unidentified sources, reported that at least two Chinese crew members sought political refuge.
No details were available about who shot whom or what happened after the gunfire ended.
But according to Mr. Lee and other officials, the torpedo boat's engines failed during the incident, and the vessel drifted into South Korean waters, where it fired flares to signal it was in distress.
By then the Chinese Government had become aware that one of its boats was missing and was heading toward South Korea. 
China alerted the Seoul Government through the South Korean Consulate in Hong Kong, diplomats said.
Â 
Sighting by Fishing Boat
On Friday night, a South Korean fishing boat sighted the torpedo boat and towed it to Hawangdung Island, 45 miles west of Kunsan. 
From there, survivors and the bodies of slain crewmen were taken to the mainland.
Through American diplomats, South Korea sent a ''stern protest'' to Peking over the entry of three other Chinese military ships into South Korean waters. 
The three ships apparently followed the torpedo boat, and one was said to be a missile destroyer.
A Government statement issued this afternoon in Seoul said the three ships had returned to international waters after warnings and a ''show of force'' by the South Korean Navy and Air Force. 
The nature of the ''show of force'' was not clear, but diplomats said no shots had been fired.
China later acknowledged that its vessels had entered South Korean waters. 
But it said they had done so ''inadvertently'' while searching for the stricken boat and had turned around once they realized the error. 
Peking did not respond directly to a South Korean demand for an apology.
Â 
Seoul Plays Down Episode
By tonight, Mr. Lee's statement dropped all references to the three intruding ships and his Government's earlier protest.
It appeared to reflect a decision to play down the episode after an evening of meetings by senior officials, including Prime Minister Lho Shin Young and Foreign Minister Lee Won Kyung. 
A decision on a matter of this importance almost certainly had the imprimatur of the South Korean leader, President Chun Doo Hwan.
The fact that South Korea had not said after more than 24 hours what it would do with the Chinese boat suggested to some diplomats that officials in Seoul were weighing political as well as diplomatic consequences.
The closest parallel to the situation was a hijacking in May 1983 in which six Chinese seeking asylum in Taiwan forced a Chinese airliner on a domestic flight to land in South Korea. 
In that incident, senior Chinese airline officials visited Seoul to negotiate the return of the airplane, a journey regarded by South Korea as a political coup.
Diplomats said Seoul may hope for similar gains this time.
Â 
Trade Is an Open Secret
Both China and South Korea have given signs of wishing to ease the deep bitterness that has divided them since they fought during the Korean War. 
Trade between them is more or less an open secret, with most goods passing through Hong Kong.
South Korea expects China to attend the Olympic Games in Seoul in 1988. 
It also regards Peking as a moderating influence on North Korea. 
A fundamental assumption in Seoul is that Chinese pressure has been a main reason for the mildly improved climate between two Koreas over the last 15 months.
In the 1983 hijacking, South Korean courts convicted the six Chinese but handed out mild sentences. 
Last Aug. 
13, adhering to a pattern set in previous defections, South Korea ignored China's objections and allowed the hijackers to go to Taiwan, where they were given homes and jobs.

file: LAW FIRMS CAPITALIZE ON CHINA TRADE BOOM.txt
text:
ï»¿
In keeping with the rapid expansion of United States trade with China in the last few years, five American law firms have now established what amount to permanent offices in Peking.
The new legal interest in China was underscored last month when Jerome Alan Cohen, who is widely regarded as the foremost American authority on Chinese law, resigned as professor of law and associate dean at the Harvard Law School to accept an offer as a senior partner at the New York firm of Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison.
Mr. Cohen, 51 years old, had been intensely courted by at least two other major Wall Street law firms, including Coudert Brothers, for whom he had worked as a consultant on American-Chinese trade over the last 10 years. 
He had also been one of the leading candidates for dean of the Harvard Law School last spring.
5 American law firms establish permanent offices in Peking (China)
Mr. Cohen took a two-year leave of absence from Harvard to help Coudert Brothers set up an office in Peking after the normalization of relations with China in 1979.
Â 
A Doubling of Trade
American trade with China last year amounted to $4.8 billion, more than double the 1979 figure. 
American trade with the countries of East Asia as a whole has also climbed rapidly in the past decade and reached $139 billion in 1980, more than the total of the United States' imports and exports with Western Europe, which amounted to $114 billion, according to the Department of Commerce.
''But American law firms were very slow to take note of this trend,'' Mr. Cohen said in an interview. 
Officially, China still does not permit Western legal firms to have offices in Peking. 
This is partly because of Chinese suspicion about what the foreign lawyers are doing and partly because of a shortage of housing and office space.
There is intense competition among foreign businessmen, bankers, lawyers and journalists for hotel rooms in Peking. 
Mr. Cohen will use a suite at the Peking Hotel that he got when he was working for Coudert Brothers in 1979.
Â 
Seminars Paid Off
Coudert Brothers was able to secure permanent rooms there because Mr. Cohen gave a series of legal seminars to officials of the Peking city government, which runs the Peking Hotel.
In this stay, Mr. Cohen will give a course for a Chinese Government ministry on United States contract, investment and trade law.
The other American law firms that have offices in Peking are Baker & McKenzie of Chicago, Graham & James of San Francisco and Heller, Ehrman, White & McAuliffe of San Francisco.
Stanley Lubman, a partner with Heller, Ehrman, said he now spends one-third to one-half his time in China. 
Mr. Lubman, who speaks Chinese, said that, from 1979 and 1980, a series of laws issued by the Chinese Government on taxation, foreign investment and joint ventures had made it easier to do business with China.
Â 
Legal System Is Different
But he cautioned that lawyers should not expect the Chinese legal system to be as complete and relatively free of ambiguities as United States codes.
In negotiating any deal with the Chinese, he said, it was his experience that ''it is a matter of shrinking the American contracts and stretching the Chinese ones.''
''The Chinese contract,'' he said, ''will emphasize what should be done, the American contract will also emphasize what happens if the project isn't done, and that's where the big differences come up between us.''
Both Mr. Cohen and Mr. Lubman began to study Chinese law in the early 1960's with grants from the Rockefeller Foundation. 
At the time, Mr. Cohen recalled, China and the United States were bitter enemies, and his wife and friends thought ''I was losing my mind.''
''It's a wonderful thing to study,'' his wife, Joan Leobold Cohen, counseled him, ''but this is a field that has absolutely no practical application. 
We'll have to live off our academic salary.''

file: MACAO PLANS FOR A FUTURE UNDER CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
Not quite two years after Britain and China fashioned a formula for the return of Hong Kong to China, Portugal and China have agreed to open negotiations on a similar deal for Macao, the oldest European enclave on the China coast.
The talks will begin at the end of June in Peking and are expected to conclude more quickly than those on Hong Kong, which took three years.
Compared with the frenetic British colony that lies 40 miles away across the mouth of the Pearl River, this has always been a quiet and unstressful place, and so it is proving as the China talks approach.
Unlike Hong Kong, which went through a stock market plunge and associated jitters on the road to agreement with Peking, Macao's 400,000 people, only about 12,000 of them Portuguese, are generally sanguine about the prospect of returning to Chinese sovereignty sometime in the next 10 to 15 years.
'Hope for the Best'
''I wouldn't say that people here like the idea, but they accept it and hope for the best,'' said the Rev. Domingos Lam, the vicar general of the colony's Roman Catholic Church.
Father Lam has more to worry about than most, given the repression experienced on the mainland by priests who insist on their loyalty to Rome. 
But even on this score he is optimistic, saying he doubts the Communist authorities of the future will require him to remove the oil paintings of popes and bishops that line the upper gallery in the 18th-century villa that serves as the church's main office here.
''If they ask for that, they may as well tell me to get out,'' the chain-smoking priest said, chuckling. 
''I will simply tell them, 'No!'
''
Besides the Catholic Church the mainland rulers have much else to contemplate as they prepare for their negotiations with Portugal's chief delegate to the United Nations, Ruy Barbosa Medina, who will head Lisbon's delegations in the talks.
Macao's largest source of revenue is its 24-hour casinos, which draw more than three million Hong Kong gamblers a year onto the ferries and high-speed jetfoils that cross the choppy waters between here and Hong Kong.
Although gambling and licentiousness have raised their heads in China, the authorities repeatedly crack down on what they call the threat to China's ''spiritual civilization.''
In Macao, unless there is a radical change in the colony's economic fortunes, they are not so much a threat to the way of life as the pillar of it.
Â 
Peking Seems Little Bothered
So far, Peking seems little bothered by the colony's ways. 
Tens of thousands of mainlanders make their way here each year, and it is easy to spot the short haircuts and baggy suits of the typical Communist officeholder among the pleasure-seekers at the Lisboa's ''crazy Paris show.''
Along with this, the authorities in Kwangtung Province, beyond the archway that straddles the border with China, have boosted the mainland's stake in the Macao economy, to the point where Communist-owned banks, construction companies and trading houses account for 10 to 20 percent of local business.
Partly to protect the economic upswing Macao is experiencing, Peking has sketched out the agreement it expects from the talks. 
The basic pattern will be the same as those for Hong Kong, which provide for the extension of the British colony's capitalist system and the laws that underpin it for 50 years after the handover in 1997. 
But a Peking political newsweekly, Outlook, recently spoke of the need to meet the ''specific conditions of Macao,'' implying that there may be some special provisions here.
Portuguese and Chinese opinion leaders hope that one difference will be the timing of the transition. 
With 1997 barely a decade away, they say, Macao is far less prepared for the autonomous existence envisioned in the Hong Kong formula.
''We will need more time,'' said Joaquim Marinho de Bastos, the Portuguese lawyer who is the colony's tourism director as well as the leader of its Social Democratic Party, which has majority support among the Portuguese officials, professionals and businessmen.
Â 
Few Chinese Officials
Mr. Marinho noted that the administration here remained almost entirely in Portuguese hands, unlike Hong Kong, where the bureaucracy is predominantly Chinese and has begun to yield some of its most important posts to local people.
China is unlikely to want Macao back before 1997. 
Hong Kong, which has 5.5 million people and is one of the world's most important economic centers, weighs far more heavily with Peking than the six square miles of Macao.
A recovery date for Macao that preceded Hong Kong's would risk the confidence that British and Chinese officials are trying to develop in the British colony. 
''If things went wrong here, it could have a devastating effect in Hong Kong,'' Mr. Marinho said.
An important role in the bargaining over Macao's future is being played by wealthy Chinese businessmen who have fostered close ties with Peking. 
The most important is Ma Man-kei, a multimillionaire in banking and real estate, who makes his priorities clear in the portraits that adorn his office above an antiques shop on the Praia Grande promenade. 
A large photograph of Deng Xiaoping, the Chinese leader, dwarfs a much smaller shot of the former Portuguese President, Antonio Ramalho Eanes.
Mr. Ma has already helped obtain revisions to investment rules on the mainland, and Portuguese officials, including some who have not always trusted him, say they believe he can perform a similar ''educating'' role for Macao.

file: MACAO WILL REPORT TO CHINA IN 1999 UNDER PORTUGAL PACT.txt
text:
ï»¿
China and Portugal reached agreement today on returning this small gambling haven, a Portuguese colony for 430 years, to China in 1999.
The agreement means that Portugal, which here became the first European power to establish a beachhead on the Asian mainland, will be the last colonial power to leave.
Macao, a dot on the South China coast 40 miles southwest of Hong Kong, is home to 420,000 people, 97 percent of whom are ethnically Chinese. 
The enclave is sprinkled with casinos and massage parlors and has a reputation as Hong Kong's playground. 
The economy depends on the 4.2 million tourists who visit each year, mostly from Hong Kong.
'The Holiday Is Finished'
''We have had a long summer holiday, but the holiday is finished,'' the Rev. Domingos Lam, the Roman Catholic Vicar General of Macao, said today. 
''Everything will change.''
The agreement, which followed nine months of negotiations, was announced in a brief statement by negotiators in Beijing. 
The terms of the accord were not disclosed, and apparently will not be, at least until it is initialed in Beijing on Thursday by chief negotiators for both Portugal and China. 
[A Portuguese diplomat in Beijing said the accord would be signed next month by Prime Ministers Mario Soares of Portugal and Zhao Ziyang of China.] But reports in Macao, Beijing and Lisbon agree on major aspects of the agreement. 
The accord is similar to the one by which Britain will return Hong Kong to China in July 1997.
According to these reports, Macao will return to Chinese control on Dec. 
20, 1999. 
Like Hong Kong, Macao will be guaranteed 50 years of noninterference in its way of life and capitalist system. 
A committee of Portuguese and Chinese negotiators will resolve other issues, such as the political institutions and legal system.
''I think the agreement can be considered a fairly good one,'' said Carlos Monjardino, the acting Governor. 
''But for now there is no significant reaction here.''
Indeed, most people interviewed here seemed relatively unconcerned about the agreement. 
In part, this reflected the lack of information about the accord. 
In part, many people said, it also reflected the view that there is not much that residents can do about it, whatever they think. 
'Small People Cannot Go'
''We have worries, but what can we do?'' asked Danny Cheung, whose small shop here sells traditional medicines and bird nests used to make soup. 
''We are not millionaires, or we could fly to another country. 
We are small people; we cannot go.''
Mr. Cheung and several others interviewed said they doubted that China would continue for long to tolerate the gambling casinos and strip shows that are the enclave's economic foundation. 
But a senior Government official here said that the gambling would definitely continue, and other analysts note that China would face substantial economic pressure if it closed the casinos -which supply 20 percent of economic output here and a large proportion of government revenue.
''The mind-set here is entirely different from China's,'' said the 36-year-old well-dressed owner of a small shop. 
''But I'm not worried. 
I have a green card to go to the United States. 
I figure I have 10 more years here.''
#1999 Is Considered Distant Many people here stressed that 1999 was still very distant, and that much could happen before then.
''I'm not anxious about 1999,'' said C. K. Lo, a pawnbroker. 
''My main worry is whether I can find a meal today.''
Macao's economic dependence on vice has caused problems for China before. 
Soon after the Portuguese revolution of 1974, some Portuguese officials traveled to Beijing to suggest that the colony be returned to China. 
They were rebuffed. 
Chinese officials said they wanted Macao back but not just yet. 
Apparently they were unsure how to reconcile Communism with blackjack, and afraid that if they interfered the jitters would spread to Hong Kong and disrupt that territory's economy.
Although Macao, which was permanently settled by the Portuguese in 1557, has the architecture and relaxed atmosphere of Portugal, and shop signs must be in Portuguese as well as Chinese, the Portuguese influence is minimal. 
Only 3 percent of the population speaks Portuguese, and almost no one knows streets by their official Portuguese names. 
Instead, they are known by their Chinese names.
A Portuguese official here said that his country had insisted in the negotiations on favorable trade arrangements as parthedding its colonies - such as Angola, of Macao. 
No formal trade concessions - such as increased purchases by China of Portuguese exports - were adopted, but an informal understanding was reached, the official said. 
Issue of Dual Nationality A more contentious issue was the rights of some 80,000 ethnic Chinese residents of Macao who hold Portuguese passports. 
China refused to regard them as dual nationals, and at one point last week Portugal reportedly threatened to suspend the talks because of disagreements on the subject.
But China is reported to have agreed that while it would regard dual passport holders as solely Chinese nationals, they could retain their passports and claim Portuguese nationality while traveling outside China.
The agreement also serves Portugal's interest in allowing it a more gracious departure than it experienced from its other colonies. 
Portugal was widely criticized in the mid-1970's for shedding its colonies - such as Angola, Mozambique and East Timor - without adequately preparing them for self-government. 
In the final years of its stewardship, Portugal is trying to increase its role in Macao, and is considering leaving a ''farewell gift'' such as an airport or other major project for Macao.

PEKING, Oct. 
11 (UPI) - A man tried to hijack a bus full of American tourists in north central China Sunday but was overpowered by the police before he could carry out his plan to defect to Taiwan, tour sources said today.Sources said the man boarded the bus clutching a package and handed a note written in Chinese to one of the American tourists.

file: MERRILL_S HONG KONG LINK.txt
text:
ï»¿
HONG KONG In Hong Kong, where making money is a national pastime, nothing is more applauded than a consummate deal, and no individual is more revered than the businessman who can make one. 
Most revered of all is Fung King Hey, an immigrant from China whose formal education stopped at about the eighth grade. 
Widely recognized as king of the deal makers, he has built a real estate, securities and banking empire larger than any other in Asia.
Mr. Fung and Merrill Lynch & Company are planning to sign a deal early next month which, although beneficial to both parties, has clear advantages for Mr. Fung's Sun Hung Kai Securities and Sun Hung Kai Bank. 
And it advances what some people believe is a rather eerie company motto: ''With our feet in Hong Kong, with our back against China, with our face towards the Asia-Pacific region, with our eyes open, we scan the world.''
Colleagues describe the financial wizard in terms that suggest science fiction rather than high finance. 
Physically, he could have been designed by a graphic artist: a pencil-thin body which seems to be powered by a dozen glasses of water a day, an angular head and spare features with hardly a wrinkle after 60 years.
Profile of Fung King Hey, Hong Kong entrepreneur, describes his new deal with Merrill Lynch & Company
Mr. Fung does not grant interviews, but his efforts to stay out of the limelight have been thwarted by his deals, which have brought much attention his way. 
Those deals are considered here to exemplify a business encounter of the most ingenious kind.
''He is an exceptional businessman,'' said Robert Fell, Hong Kong Commissioner for Securities. 
''He has a keen sense of timing and he is not afraid to take chances. 
He has made some mistakes, but he is very clever.''
The latest development, under which Merrill Lynch is acquiring 25 percent of Sun Hung Kai Securities and 15 percent of the Sun Hung Kai Bank, could make Mr. Fung the largest individual shareholder in Merrill Lynch & Company, parent of the United States' largest securities firm.
The arrangement, said William R. Arthur, chairman of Merrill Lynch International, ''will greatly strengthen our ability to serve individuals, corporations, institutions and governments throughout the Pacific region.''
But it is Mr. Fung who is being congratulated on this side of the world for pulling off a classy deal. 
He personally will make $60 million, and it gives him possibly the largest foothold of any Hong Kong businessman in the United States market. 
Through it, his companies are expected to gain considerable foreign expertise, security and clout.
The Merrill Lynch agreement, which has been valued at $81.5 million, calls for Merrill Lynch to buy 20 percent of the outstanding stock of Sun Hung Kai Securities directly from Mr. Fung. Sun Hung Kai Securities has assets of $478 million and reported 1981 aftertax profits of $32.6 million.
Merrill Lynch will also buy 17.3 million shares, or 10 percent, of the outstanding stock of Sun Hung Kai Bank directly from Mr. Fung. Formerly known as Sun Hung Kai Finance, the bank received its license only two months ago. 
The bank has assets of about $760 million and its aftertax profits were $12.5 million in 1981.
Mr. Fung will be paid in Merrill Lynch convertible debentures, which if exercised will give him 4 percent of Merrill Lynch. 
No decision has been made yet on whether or when Mr. Fung might convert his debentures.
In the same deal, Compagnie Financiere de Paris et des Pays-Bas, known as Paribas, will sell some of its holdings in Sun Hung Kai Bank to Merrill Lynch, cutting its holdings in the bank to 25 percent from 30. 
By reducing Paribas' holdings, the bank can now offer higher deposit rates than allowed by top-tier banks, which include banks with foreign bank holdings of more than 25 percent. 
But Paribas will lift its holdings in the securities firm to 10 percent from five and with Merrill Lynch, it plans a limited tender offer for another 10 percent of Sun Hung Kai Securities.
By bringing Merrill Lynch into the bank and the securities firm, Mr. Fung took care of his obligations to Paribas and his plans for expansion into the United States while realigning operations and eliminating the need for numerous foreign partnerships.
''Even before Banque de Paris et des Pays-Bas became a minority shareholder in 1978, Sun Hung Kai had already mapped out a strategy for cooperation in Europe, America and Asia,'' said Mr. Fung through the buffer of executives who isolate him from the press. 
''Objectives were set for the desirable distribution of share holdings. 
After that, it was a question of waiting for the right opportunity. 
When this presented itself, Sun Hung Kai was able to reach agreement with Merrill Lynch almost immediately.''
Sun Hung Kai is expected to end a five-year-old joint venture with ACLI International, a commodities brokerage house owned by Donaldson Lufkin Jenrette, a rival of Merrill Lynch's, and end a nine-monthold arrangement with Bear, Stearns & Company to market United States securities.
ALTHOUGH there are no figures to substantiate the claims, Bear S terns and Sun Hung Kai, which controls 25 percent of the trading in H ong Kong stocks, were said to be the largest brokers of United S tates securities in Hong Kong last year.
Bear Stearns will stay in Hong Kong, but the partnership will be dissolved because ''obviously there would be a conflict,'' said Michael Tarnapol, general partner of Bear Stearns. 
In Hong Kong it is felt that Bear Stearns was just an interim step for Mr. Fung, who wanted an American link to market United States securities.
Mr. Fung has not just been working on strengthening ties to the United States market. 
Mr. Fung, who had a money-exchange business in Canton before the Communist takeover and began his China trading ventures in 1978 with his Sun Hung Kai China Ltd., is considered the chief China link in Hong Kong. 
There are no other businessmen quite as well connected with China trade as Mr. Fung or with a company big enough to handle the trade on a large scale.
In Hong Kong, it is felt that although Merrill Lynch was able to get a foothold in Hong Kong, it wanted China trade connections and broader access to Southeast Asian markets. 
Sun Hung Kai China has liaison offices in Peking and Shanghai, and it enters joint undertakings with American and European multinationals mostly in equipment and technology projects.
Mr. Fung, who lives in Hong Kong's exclusive Victoria Peak area, is quiet and unassuming, say people who know him. 
He loves European antiques and has an exceptional memory, but he is most excited by a deal, his associates relate. 
The deal, not the money, interests him. 
He is, some say, embarrassed by his wealth and prefers to ride in a Cadillac than in the Rolls Royce that serves as his company car.
Yet he is not a traditional Chinese businessman. 
His son is in training on the company's board, but Mr. Fung recruits managers from all over the world to run the company while he plans for the future and does his deals. 
He does not get involved much in day-to-day operations, but delegates authority and likes innovation. 
He is considered a gentleman and not vindictive, but most executives here are careful not to offend him - in word or deed - because his business empire is so vast that they will have to deal with him sometime or other.
In style, Merrill Lynch and Sun Hung Kai seem well suited. 
In Hong Kong, Sun Hung Kai was the first to market stocks to the man in the street. 
Stock markets had been exclusive clubs. 
No one offered shares to taxi drivers and hawkers until Sun Hung Kai set up retail brokering operations.
A trial-and-error businessman, Mr. Fung came to Hong Kong after the Communist takeover to take advantage of trade opportunities. 
In one of his earliest efforts, he tried to ship tropical fish to Taiwan. 
But en route he became so seasick that he was unable to keep the oxygen bubbling through the containers holding the fish. 
When he arrived, the fish were dead. 
Undaunted, he loaded the ship with bananas for the return trip, but bad weather delayed it and the bananas rotted.
During the Korean war, he made money selling supplies to Macao. 
When refugees began pouring into Hong Kong from China in the 1950's, Mr. Fung with two partners began a property concern, which prospered until 1967 when riots inspired by the Cultural Revolution soured Hong Kong business. 
He fled to Canada.
After returning to Hong Kong, in 1969 he began building the Sun Hung Kai empire with the formation of Sun Hung Kai Securities and Sun Hung Kai Finance. 
His retail-brokering operations were helped by a credit plan that allowed small investors to finance stock purchases through Sun Hung Kai Finance. 
Most of these investors do not speak English so the firm does stock research in Chinese. 
Because Mr. Fung also does not speak English, he has developed an entire department that translates, interprets and analyzes documents, publications and research in Chinese.
Sun Hung Kai Securities was the first non-banking financial Asian institution to enter the Eurobond market, and with Marsh & McLennan, it began an insurance brokering and consulting business. 
Last year it established a joint venture with West Germany's A.E.G.-Telefunken to set up a link between China, Germany and Hong Kong. 
''Mr. Fung makes wonderful deals,'' said David K.P. 
Li, manager of the Bank of East Asia. 
''He's a natural.''

file: MILITARY AID FOR CHINA CONSIDERED AS HAIG PREPARES TO VISIT PEKING.txt
text:
ï»¿
In preparing for the visit of Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. to China next week, the Reagan Administration is moving toward decisions that will give more of a military cast to Chinese-American relations.
Specifically, according to American officials, there is strong pressure to remove China from the list of Communist countries subject to special export controls. 
This would allow for the transfer of military technology such as the engine and electrical equipment from the new F-16 fighter plane and for the sale of TOW antitank missiles.
Â 
Common Anti-Soviet Front Sought
A number of officials see this as a way of strengthening a common anti-Soviet front, but some also see the prospective offer as an effort to induce Peking to accept the sale of an advanced type of fighter plane to Taiwan.
Military aid for China considered as Haig prepares to visit Peking
It is the prospect of this sale to Taiwan, and the concern that ''Taiwan not be allowed to get in the way of the Chinese-American strategic consensus against Moscow,'' as one Chinese diplomat put it, that has activated Chinese lobbying.
Ambassador Chai Zemin held two dinners last week for Reagan aides and State Department officials. 
While circumspect in these talks, the Chinese said they were concerned that the pro-Taiwan lobby in the Republican Party would succeed in turning the clock back in the relationship between the United States and China and that selling the FX fighter to Taiwan would damage relations most of all.
The National Security Council met today in the White House to consider whether the Chinese were bluffing, what negative reactions might be expected from Moscow and Tokyo and what could be done for Taiwan to keep the Republican right wing happy. 
The council also intended to work out the objectives of the Haig mission.
Officials said earlier that no specific decisions on sales of military equipment would be made, but that there was a consensus to transfer more arms and technology to both China and Taiwan. 
The major decision on China is expected to come in proposed visits by Defense Secretary Caspar W. Weinberger to China or by Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang to the United States.
In interviews, American officials have discussed these elements:
- Government experts are still reacting to a remark by a visiting Chinese military delegation last year that China wants the same kind of security relationship with the United States that Egypt has. 
In the absence of a more specific Chinese explanation, the Americans have taken this to mean the desire for military credits and the F-16 plane. 
The Chinese have long held the public position that they do not want an explicit security relationship with any country.
- Pentagon officers, reversing their judgment, have concluded that Taiwan does not need the advanced FX fighter, which is still on the drawing boards. 
The officers have come around to the view that China does not pose a major threat to Taiwan and that China is more important to the United States than Taiwan. 
But the officers do not want to make this judgment public for fear of a fight with conservatives.
- Chinese diplomats are stressing their policy of seeking an ''evolutionary'' reunification, which they say would leave Taiwan ''autonomous'' with its own government, armed forces and economy and possibly give its ruling Nationalist Party a role in Peking.
Â 
Key Issue Is Export Controls
The major specific issue for the White House meeting today was to be the largely symbolic, but important question of the export control category in which China should be placed.
It could continue to be treated in the same category as the Soviet Union, meaning restrictions on exports of materials with potential military applications. 
It could be put a special category with Yugoslavia, in which exemptions can be made for items of a military use. 
Or it could be placed in the general category with Britain and India, with virtually no restrictions.
In any event, when it comes to exports of potential military items, the Commerce Department makes the decision case by case, regardless of the category.
There is virtually total agreement in the Government that China should not be treated the same way as the Soviet Union. 
A typical statement, from the State Department, was: ''It is nonsense to treat China like an unfriendly state like Russia and be prepared, in principle, to sell anything to a state like India which buys arms from and has a friendship treaty with Moscow.''
Â 
Only Nonlethal Equipment Allowed
A related decision is what to do about China's standing on the munitions control list, or list of actual weapons, which is administered by the State Department. 
As of now, China is restricted to nonlethal equipment such as trucks and radios.
If the United States were to go ahead and actually sell arms and transfer the technology to build weapons, the most likely candidate seems to be the antitank missile. 
The Chinese prefer buying the technology and producing the weapons more cheaply themselves.
As an economy measure, for example, they are understood to seek only the engine and the electrical equipment of the F-16 so that thay can install these components in a plane they would design themselves. 
But in the case of the antitank missiles, they have told the United States that they need them now and that it would take too long to produce their own.
In the meantime, the Chinese have made clear that they want the Haig visit to be a success, and that they regard him as the one in the Administration who best understands their situation. 
Administration officials say the Chinese have been the ones pushing for the visit, urging that it take place soon, and saying that unless policies are satisfactorily clarified soon, there could be retrogression in the relationship.

file: MORE CHANGE DUE IN CHINA_S ECONOMY.txt
text:
ï»¿
The acting Chinese party leader, Zhao Ziyang, said today China must intensify the restructuring of its economy along Western lines if it is to escape poverty.
Mr. Zhao, who is also Prime Minister, speaking at the opening session of the Communist Party's 13th congress, lashed out at ''major defects'' in the party leadership. 
He also declared that Government offices needed to be completely overhauled and called for the creation of a civil service system.
''We must be soberly aware that we still face a great many problems and difficulties, many more than we anticipated,'' Mr. Zhao told the 1,936-member congress. 
''There are not a few failings in our work of leadership.''
Mr. Zhao's speech marked the first party congress China has held in five years. 
Leaders who have gathered from around the country will spend the next week discussing and approving plans for the Government and the economy, which has already undergone the biggest changes in any Communist nation.
Before adjourning, the congress will also elect a new Central Committee, which in turn will name members of the new Politburo that will rule China.
It was the first time that the party, which was founded in secrecy in Shanghai in 1921, has opened its congress to foreign reporters. 
As copies of Mr. Zhao's address were handed out in six languages, spokesmen said China was permitting foreign reporters to attend as part of its efforts to become more open to the world.
The congress started this morning with Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, striding into the auditorium of the Great Hall of the People to applause from the delegates. 
He was followed onto the dais by the rest of the leadership, including the former party chief, Hu Yaobang, who was removed in disgrace in January after a tide of nationwide student protests. 
Mr. Deng, who looked tan and fit, was praised by Mr. Zhao for ''his courage in developing Marxist theory'' and ''his foresight and sagacity.''
For two and a half hours, Mr. Zhao read his 32,000-word report to the congress, sitting and pausing to sip tea from a white ceramic cup. 
As he spoke, some delegates appeared to nod off. 
Chen Yun, an 82-year-old member of the Politburo's standing committee, left the dais supported by two nurses in the middle of the speech.
While reaffirming the nation's adherence to socialism, Mr. Zhao said China would accelerate the introduction of many economic and financial methods integral to Western capitalist economies.
''Some of the things we have introduced in the process of reform such as expanded markets for means of production, funds, technology and labor service and the issuance of stocks and bonds are phenomena which are not peculiar to capitalism,'' he said. 
''Socialism can and should make use of them, trying in the meantime to minimize their negative effects in practice.''
The 68-year-old Prime Minister also called for a thorough reordering of China's pricing system, so that market forces would regulate supply and demand.
Whenever Mr. Zhao or his supporters discussed the need for pricing changes over the last year, party hard-liners blocked his proposals by labeling them capitalist. 
The opponents object to having market forces govern the decisions of industrial managers, a traditional role of state planners. 
Today, Mr. Zhao appeared to have imposed his position on the party.
''We should gradually establish a system under which the state sets the prices of a few vital commodities and labor services while leaving the rest to be regulated by the market,'' he said.
While the state should have a role in industrial policy, he said, other mechanisms besides free prices, like taxes, bank credit and other new financing arrangments, would also influence industrialization.
Â 
To Maintain Private Sector
He acknowledged that China's small private sector would continue to play a role in development.
A growing class of private entrepreneurs has emerged in both urban and rural areas. 
Orthodox Marxists in the leadership have voiced opposition to the growth of individual private enterprise because of its unabashed capitalist nature.
''Practice has proved that a certain degree of development of the private sector promotes production, stimulates the market, provides employment opportunities and helps in many ways to meet people's needs,'' Mr. Zhao told his fellow Communists. 
''It is thus a necessary and useful supplement to the public sector.''
Mr. Zhao spoke repeatedly and with unusual bluntness of problems of leadership, corruption in the party and a bureacratic style in Government.
''There are major defects in our system of leadership, in the organizational structure and style of work,'' he said. 
He cited as problems the overconcentration of power, excessive bureaucracy and lingering ''feudal influences.''
He described in broad terms how the Communist Party should remove itself from the administration of Government, industry and public life.
Resistance to economic restructuring has been most pronounced among the party organizations that oversee many industries and rural areas. 
By calling for the reduction of the party's influence in day-to-day management, Mr. Zhao appeared to be devising a way to overcome the resistance.
He proposed establishing a civil service system based on examinations, which he said would help make the Government less subject to the caprice of party officials and more professional. 
He said a state administrative college would be established. 
Government posts are now filled by party committees, which select officials from lists they maintain.
Mr. Zhao concluded his address by attacking widespread imperiousness and corruption in the party, which he said meant that ''members of a party in power tend to become divorced from the masses.''
But, he said, the restructuring of the economy and China's opening to the outside world should not change just because of ''those few cases of corruption.''

text:

When the propaganda loudspeakers atop the concrete bunkers of the Nationalist-held island of Quemoy blast away at the Chinese mainland barely a mile distant, the anti-Communist broadsides are mercifully interspersed with the songs of Teresa Teng.
Taipei's most effective psychological weapon against the Communist Government in Peking is not Taiwan's higher living standards or its less stringent society, but Miss Teng, its pop singing star, who is known on the mainland by her Chinese name of Deng Lijun.
The Nationalist authorities like to tuck in a recording of Miss Teng when they loft a balloon laden with propaganda and small gifts across the Strait of Formosa.

Â 
She Says She Is Puzzled
Miss Teng is a kind of Debbie Boone of Chinese pop music, not only on the mainland but also in Hong Kong and elsewhere in Southeast Asia. 
In an interview before one of her sold-out performances in Taipei, Miss Teng professed puzzlement that her music was objectionable to Peking.
''I don't know why,'' she said in graceful English learned when she studied in Los Angeles for a couple of years. 
''I think it is rather disappointing, rather sad. 
I don't understand it.
''They're basically love songs,'' she said. 
''In my music, I express a lot of my feeling, my emotion. 
Everything I have, I sing out. 
That's probably why they don't like it.''
Miss Teng said she had received fan mail addressed to ''The Famous Deng Lijun'' from the mainland, so she knew she was popular there. 
''They say they love my singing and they admire my songs,'' she said.

Girl-Next-Door Innocence
Yet Miss Teng projects a girl-next- door innocence.

The family was from suburban Peking, and she was raised on the folksongs sung by her mother.

She Has Toured Widely
