file: New Refugees Crowd Camps In Hong Kong.txt
text:
ï»¿
Growing numbers of Vietnamese have been arriving in Hong Kong by boat in the past few months, crowding into refugee camps with thousands of other Vietnamese, most of whom have only a slim chance of finding new homes outside the chain-link fences of the bleak compounds.
So far this year, more than 1,500 Vietnamese refugees, most of them poor farmers and fishermen from north Vietnam, have landed in Hong Kong, four times the number of arrivals during the same period last year, according to Govennment figures.
Waves of refugees have been arriving in Thailand and Malaysia as well, and the Thai authorities have pushed some boats back out to sea.
Hong Kong has so far resisted such an extreme measure, but a recent newspaper survey revealed that 65 percent of those polled here want any new refugee boats turned away. 
And the Governor of this British colony, Sir David Wilson, said last week that Hong Kong is reconsidering its policy of allowing all boat people to land.
'Compassion Fatigue'
The Governor said resettlement countries are experiencing ''compassion fatigue,'' and are simply not prepared to accept all the boat people Hong Kong is sheltering.
Relief officials said people have been fleeing Vietnam in greater numbers this year because the country's economy is near collapse, and crop failures threaten famine in some areas.
The new swell of immigrants has left Hong Kong with a total of 10,400 Vietnamese refugees - a Vietnamese refugee population second only to that of Thailand, according to Nigel J. French, the Hong Kong Government official in charge of refugee policy.
Refugees sail north to Hong Kong from the northern Vietnamese port of Haiphong, a 500-mile journey through the South China Sea that takes about 15 days with good luck and fair weather. 
Refugees from the north, Mr. French said, are poor people with few skills, no foreign languages and no ties to countries outside Vietnam.
''More and more we have the men, women and children nobody else wants,'' Mr. French said.
Â 
Barracks-Like Buildings
A teacher at a closed camp on Hei Ling Chau, a tiny rocky island that was once the site of a leper colony, said there are children there who had never seen a dog or walked on grass.
Hei Ling Chau is about an hour's boat ride from central Hong Kong, and a recent visitor was asked to send picture postcards of the city because most of the refugees had only caught a glimpse of it as they landed.
The camp's barracks-like cinder-block buildings house 2,900 people in spaces meant for 2,400. 
Two meals a day and a snack are served and there is one toilet for every 90 people.
''We try to take the children on field trips, to see what real life looks like,'' said Nilda Bernardo, a teacher with World Relief, which runs programs in Hei Ling Chau.
''Sometimes we take them into a flat there so they can see what a kitchen and a living room and a bedroom look like,'' she said.
Christopher Bale, the director of the Oxfam relief agency in Hong Kong, said the three closed camps, surrounded by high steel fences and supervised by prison guards, are ''just barely adequate for short-term stays, but there are almost 5,000 people who have been living in these places for three years, and 3,000 who have been in them for more than five years.''
Â 
'No One Has Asked to See Us'
Bao Ntuyen, a 12-year-old from Haiphong, said he had been living in Hei Ling Chau for four years and no resettlement official had ever interviewed him or his uncle, a farmer who has no ties to anyone outside Vietnam.
''No one has asked to see us,'' the boy said, ''so we are learning English. 
We want to go to a free country, somewhere where they play football.''
Hong Kong has had a continuous flow of refugees since 1975, but the numbers had begun to drop, from a high of about 8,500 arrivals in 1981 to only 1,200 in 1985. 
But by 1986 the flow of refugees began to increase once more.
Hong Kong now plans to build a fourth closed camp to handle the increasing numbers of Vietnamese. 
In addition to the closed camps, Hong Kong has one ''open'' camp, where about 3,000 refugees who arrived before mid-1982 may come and go freely and hold jobs in the community.
Â 
Ethnic Chinese Resentment
Many Hong Kong residents, 98 percent of whom are ethnic Chinese, resent the fact that the Vietnamese are allowed to stay when immigrants from mainland China, even those with close relatives here, are treated as illegal aliens. 
An average of 40 a day are shipped back.
Only the United States, Britain, Canada, Australia and Hong Kong itself have active resettlement programs here, and all require that refugees have some link to their countries. 
The United States, which last year accepted only 340 refugees from Hong Kong, also requires refugees to prove they have a ''well-founded fear of persecution.''
Malaysia Sees Sharp Rise
Â Â  BANGKOK, Thailand, April 28 (Special To The New York Times - The number of Vietnamese arriving on Malaysian shores has risen sharply since Thailand began turning back refugee boats in January.

The South Korean service carried the reports of Mr. Kim's presence at the airport as the main item on its noon broadcast, followed by the accounts of the loudspeaker announcements. 
That suggested that greater weight was being placed on the report that Mr. Kim, 74 years old, was still alive.
U.P.I. quoted the Austrian trade representative in North Korea, Wolfgang Entmayer, as saying of Mr. Kim: ''I saw him with my own eyes, and he seemed to be in good health and smiling. 
He was walking on his own, and there was nothing unusual about it.''
U.P.I. said the interview was conducted by telephone from Peking.

And the Defense Minister, Lee Ki Baek, told a National Assembly committee that ''serious signs of an emergency in North Korea'' suggested that Mr. Kim had died or that a power struggle was in progress.

Mr. Lee, who has been the most outspoken South Korean Government official in discussing the Kim matter, told members of the National Assembly that on Saturday morning the Government received intelligence reports from Japan saying Mr. Kim had been killed by soldiers a day or two earlier. 
These military men defected to China, which has thus far rejected North Korea's demand for their repatriation, he quoted the reports as saying.

'A Severe Power Struggle'
''Judging from information gathered from various sources, North Korea is suffering from a severe internal power struggle,'' Mr. Lee said.

Says It May Be a Ploy

North Korean diplomats in Peking and New Delhi strongly denied the death reports and accused South Korea of inventing them. 
''The South Korean side always spreads such fabrications,'' the North Korean Embassy in Peking said.
There were few signs on Seoul streets that anything unusual had occurred, let alone something that could have huge importance for South Korea as well as the North.
The national police were put on special alert, and busloads of officers filled some downtown streets. 
But the police presence is normally thick and has been especially so in recent weeks after large anti-Government demonstrations.
South Korea's armed forces were said to be kept to a normal state of readiness, as were the 40,000 United States soldiers stationed here.
Â 
North's Borders Tightly Sealed
Determining political developments in North Korea is extremely difficult because that country has tightly sealed its borders, revealing little of itself to outsiders, even Communist countries.
There have been periodic reports in recent months of unhappiness among North Korean military officers with the Kims' plans to transfer power from father to son, and several political analysts in Seoul said today that the displeasure might have spilled over. 
Close allies of Pyongyang, notably the Soviet Union and China, have also hinted at dissatisfaction with the transition plan.
Another possibility, the political analysts said, was that certain officers had disapproved of Kim Il Sung's recent tilting toward Moscow in the balance that his country traditionally has sought to achieve between the Soviet Union and China. 
The North Korean leader made a visit to Moscow late last month, an unusual trip in that he made the journey by plane. 
Mr. Kim is known to have a strong aversion to flying and in the past had traveled the nearly 4,000 miles from Pyongyang to Moscow by train.
The two Koreas share one of the world's most heavily fortified borders, and, unlike the two Germanys, they are implacable enemies. 
In the South, Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il are depicted as almost demonic personalities, and their pictures are rarely seen.
Several political analysts said the developments in the North could also affect South Korean politics. 
The Government of President Chun Doo Hwan has begun a crackdown on dissidents, and the possibility of unrest north of the DMZ may make the political opposition think twice before further challenging the Government's authority.
Â 
North Korea At A Glance
Â 
Government
Â Â In the four decades since he was installed by the Soviet forces that took over from occupying Japanese, Kim Il Sung has been the absolute ruler of North Korea, running the country almost like a personal fiefdom. 
The national ideology, while officially Communist, is primarily based on the glorification of Mr. Kim's thinking. 
In recent years Mr. Kim has elevated his son, Kim Jong Il, to a position of almost equal influence and has named the son to be his successor.
Â 
History
Â Â Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and retined control until the end of World War II. 
Korean customs and nationalism were brutally suppressed. 
The Cairo Declaration of 1943 called for a free and independent Korea after the war, but Stalin accepted a 1945 American plan for two military zones to be established after the Japanese surrender, divided along the 38th Parallel. 
Free elections were to be held.
After the Japanese surrender, political exiles came home. 
In the South, Syngman Rhee returned from the United States; in the North, the anti-Japanese resistance leader, Kim Il Sung, returned from the Soviet Union.
With Soviet backing, Mr. Kim was named head of the new Government of the North, which was proclaimed the Democratic People's Republic of Korea in September 1948. 
Mr. Rhee became the first leader in the South, which had been founded a month earlier. 
American forces were pulled out of the South in June 1949.
Â 
The Korean War
Â Â The Korean War began on June 25, 1950, when North Korean forces invaded the South. 
Seoul, the South Korean capital, was captured after four days. 
United States troops returned, at the request of Seoul, at the end of June. 
Responding to a United Nations call, 16 other nations sent military contingents to the defense of the South.
In October 1950, the North Korean capital was captured, and in November, the allies reached the Yalu River on the Chinese border. 
Peking had committed troops to the fighting in October, and they were able to push the South Korean and United Nations forces back to approximately the 38th parallel.
Fighting continued back and forth until an armistice was signed at Panmunjom in July 1953.
Â 
Military Strength
Â Â Counting all branches, North Korea has approximately 785,000 troops, according to the International Institute for Strategic Studies. 
By comparison, South Korea has 622,000 troops. 
United States forces in South Korea number approximately 40,000.
Â 
Geography and People
Â Â North Korea has a population of about 20 million, about half that of South Korea. 
Its area is 46,540 square miles, somewhat larger than the South and about the size of New York State.
Â 
Resources
Â Â Seventy percent of the mountainous Korean Peninsula is forested, and most of the best timber is in the North. 
Iron ore and coal deposits are concentrated in the North. 
Rice and corn are the major crops, and extensive efforts have been made to reclaim land for agriculture.

A NUCLEAR plant under construction in China just 30 miles from Hong Kong is generating enormous heat in this crowded British territory. 
The project, which is not scheduled for completion until 1992, has already aroused a political typhoon and caused tension between Hong Kong and its vast neighbor to the north.
No one in Hong Kong paid much attention to China's proposal to build the nuclear plant at Daya Bay when it was first discussed early in this decade. 
But in the last several months, after the accident in April at the Chernobyl plant in the Soviet Union, Hong Kong residents have been distressed at the prospect of such a facility on their doorstep.
Perhaps even more fundamentally, the situation raised new doubts about whether China can be trusted after it absorbs Hong Kong in 1997. 
If China does not heed the British colony's wishes now, some say, why should it pay attention to such concerns after the territory becomes a part of the motherland?
A Chinese official in Hong Kong grimaced at that logic. 
''A lot of resources already have been committed to the project,'' he said. 
''China says, 'Why should we give it up because of a lot of people who don't know about nuclear power?'
It's a very difficult situation for China.''
Of course, Hong Kong has been gripped by political events in the past. 
In the late 1960's the colony was shaken by riots sponsored by admirers of Mao Zedong, the late Chinese leader. 
But Daya Bay marked the first time that many Hong Kong residents had signed a petition or taken a controversial stand.
The Hong Kong Government, led by a British-appointed governor, is also in an awkward position. 
At first it refused to release a 1984 study it commissioned to examine the Daya Bay proposal. 
Later the Government backed down and released part of that report. 
This unusual concession to public opinion hurt the antinuclear campaign; the report strongly favored the plant.
''A lot of people think if they can't get the plumbing right in Peking, how can they get nuclear power right,'' said Peter B. Harris, chairman of the political science department at Hong Kong University. 
Like many others, he believes that concern over the Daya Bay plant has forced Hong Kong for almost the first time to take a substantial interest in politics. 
Normally apathetic Hong Kong residents have rallied against the project, and 20 percent of the territory's 5.5 million residents have signed a petition objecting to it.
''The middle class woke up,'' explained Albert W.Y. 
Chan, a social worker and politician. 
Mr. Chan says that Daya Bay has for the first time created a political system based on mass participation, not small interest groups.
Professor Harris agrees: ''There are signs that a political consciousness is beginning to emerge for the first time. 
In politics, you've taken the cork out of the bottle, and you won't be able to put it back again.''
Â 
British Engines
''Hong Kong people are quite reluctant to take a stance, especially on a political issue,'' explained the Rev. Fung Chi-Wood, a 30-year-old Anglican who is leading the campaign against the Daya Bay plant.
Despite the protests and opinion polls showing that most Hong Kong residents favor a halt or delay in the construction of the plant, neither Hong Kong's Government nor Britain's seems to have done anything to dissuade China. 
Indeed, some Hong Kong residents charge that Britain has accepted the risk to Hong Kong because a British company will supply turbines for the $28-billion plant.
Pushed into a defensive alliance, Britain, China and Hong Kong all assert that the plant will be safe, that it is sufficiently far from Hong Kong and that it will be the cheapest source of power. 
Southern China is desperately short of electricity, to the point that industrial growth must be curtailed, and Hong Kong is expected to face a shortage in the next decade. 
While 70 percent of Daya Bay's output will be sold to a Hong Kong utility, some will be left to ease the shortage in the area around Canton, China.
The Daya Bay protests may not be enough to stop the nuclear plant, but they are likely to reverberate through Hong Kong's emerging political system. 
Proponents of direct elections to choose territorial leaders say their movement has gained support as a result of the nuclear controversy.

PEKING, March 6 - The passengers aboard C.A.A.C. 
Flight 1506 from the southeastern city of Fuzhou arrived in Peking on schedule, but their luggage did not. 
The passengers waited for nearly an hour before an airline employee explained that heavy air cargo had been piled on top of the luggage.
When the luggage finally appeared, the employee murmured a rare apology to an American traveler. 
''I know that C.A.A.C. is bad,'' she said.
Her admission would not be challenged even in China. 
The official Chinese press has taken up the incessant complaints about the surliness, incompetence and sloth of the Civil Aviation Administration of China, as the state airline is officially called. 
Now it is promising to undo its reputation as arguably the world's worst major airline.
A new directive issued recently by the airline's officials announced it had embarked upon a shake-up under the slogan, ''A people's airline for the people.''
According to People's Daily, incompetent managers and employees who do not shape up will be dismissed.
Â 
Delays to Be Announced
From now on, the party newspaper said, there should be no more rude and uncivilized behavior, bad meals, rough baggage handling and soliciting of gifts. 
It said the airline planned such startling changes as announcing flight delays honestly and feeding stranded passengers.
The campaign has been remarkable so far for the skepticism that it has evoked. 
''We'll see,'' a Government official in Peking said. 
''Deeds are more eloquent than words.''
Other veteran travelers recalled earlier pledges. 
In August 1980, the airline promised to improve after newspapers exposed cases of mismanagement, surly service and disrespect for passengers, including an argument in which one employee spat in the face of an African Ambassador's wife.
A year ago, Shen Tu, the airline's director general, admitted at an international conference of travel agents in Peking that his airline had ''many aspects which are far from satisfactory, such as deficient management, low efficiency and poor services, which caused difficulties and unpleasantness to our passengers.''
Mr. Shen added, ''We have the confidence to overcome them.''
Â 
Airline Earned $100 Million
Any Western airline that arbitrarily canceled flights, refused to make connecting or return reservations and was generally slovenly would most likely go bankrupt. 
But the Chinese airline earned $100 million in profits last year, thanks to a monopoly on air travel inside the world's most populous country and such practices as charging foreigners two-and-a-half-times the fare for Chinese.
The airline also restricts competition on regional flights. 
It has only five direct flights a week between Peking and Hong Kong, and applicants for a seat have to wait up to two weeks. 
C.A.A.C., which manages every aspect of civil aviation in China, refuses to let other airlines share the lucrative route. 
British Airways was finally granted the right to carry Hong Kong passengers once a week on its London-to-Peking run.
Flights on the Chinese airline are seldom full because a few seats are saved in case an important party or Government official shows up at the last minute. 
Overbooking, however, was resolved on at least one flight by setting up canvas stools in the aisle.
Â 
Many Need an Explanation
The airline treats flying as a privilege, and ordinary Chinese need a letter of explanation from their work unit to get a ticket. 
Sales offices tend to ignore telephone reservation requests, but appearing in person is not much better. 
A Chinese traveler reported lining up at the airline's Canton's office only to have the ticket window slam down for lunch. 
It was 10:55 A.M.
The airline has made some improvements in the last few years. 
It has upgraded its fleet of 160 or so aircraft by buying some Boeing and Douglas jetliners, although aging Soviet-made Ilyushins, Tupelovs and Antonovs still fly the provincial routes. 
The airline's pilots, trained in the Chinese Air Force, are competent, though a Western airline official said ''they do come in a little fast.''
A European military attache compared his landing in Canton to ''a strafing run.''
The Chinese, like the Russians, do not disclose air crashes unless foreigners are involved. 
In the worst incident reported, an airliner slammed into a mountain near Guilin in April 1982, killing all 112 people aboard. 
According to Hong Kong reports, an air controller gave the wrong altitude to the plane's pilot.
Â 
Combs for Souvenirs
Safety briefings are nonexistent on the airline's flights, and flight attendants approach their responsibilities with sometimes engaging innocence. 
A first-class traveler on a flight to Urumqi recalled how the flight attendants lounged in the spare seats eating tangerines and never offered her one.
One duty of the flight attendants involves distributing key rings, plastic combs and other inexpensive souvenirs. 
Small nail clippers were doled out on one trip, and the bored passengers set to work.
The airline tolerates an almost unlimited amount of hand baggage stuffed into overhead compartments and piled along the aisles. 
On one Shanghai-to-Hong Kong flight, a shipment of live crabs broke loose, and they scuttled under the seats.
Occasional defects in maintenance are more serious. 
A Western airline representative found a Chinese ground crew washing out and reusing disposable filters. 
When a Chinese pilot discovered problems with an engine last December, he took off from Hong Kong with his passengers aboard and flew over to Canton, where the repairs could be done more cheaply, before arriving in Peking eight hours late.
An Ilyushin-18 caught fire on its approach to Canton in December 1982 because a passenger was smoking in the lavatory. 
Some airport fire trucks had not filled their water tanks, and 23 people died in the blaze.
Â 
Hijackers to Be Resisted
One policy unlikely to change became apparent after an internal flight was hijacked to South Korea last May. 
Mr. Shen, the director general, said at a subsequent news conference that crews had been ordered to resist hijackers ''if the safety of the passengers is assured.''
Until now, the airline's attitude has been that disgruntled passengers could take a train, or walk. 
After the hijacking last spring it banned air travel for everyone except ranking officials, military officers and foreigners until X-ray security devices could be installed at airports.
Its wholesale cancellation of flights left stunned travelers crowding aboard trains. 
The situation has since returned to normal, which People's Daily said at the Peking airport meant ''filth, chaos and rudeness.''

text:
ï»¿
INTELLECTUALS AND THE STATE IN MODERN CHINA A Narrative H istory. 
By Jerome B. Grieder. 395 pp. 
New Y ork: The Free Pres s. 
$22.50.
CHINA'S INTELLECTUALS Advise and Dissent. 
By Merle Goldman. 
276 pp. 
Cambridge, Mass: Harvard University Press. 
$22.
FOR ordinary mortals who have not acquired through study or practice the art of deciphering Chinese thought and politics, such matters can seem forbiddingly unfamiliar or quite simply impenetrable. 
The Confucian heritage sounds impossibly archaic and the Marxist-Leninist present is hardly inviting. 
In the past 30 years, debates about philosophy and politics have usually been conducted in code: Today's leaders and issues wear the disguise of figures and events from the past, from a literary and historical culture unknown to most people in the West. 
Those brief moments during which the Chinese have spoken en clair, such as the Hundred Flowers campaign of 1957 and the Democracy Movement of 1978-79, have riveted our attention but ended almost as suddenly as they began.
Roger Garside reviews Jerome B Grieder's "Intellectuals and the State in Modern China," and Merle Goldman's "China's Intellectuals"
So we still need interpreters - though many books by China specialists thicken the mystery instead of dispelling it. 
Not so Jerome Grieder's ''Intellectuals and the State in Modern China.''
Convinced that China's modern history is not an item of intellectual exotica but ''something that belongs to all o f us,'' Grieder set out to write about China's intellectuals from the middle of the 19th century until the Communist victory in 1949, in a manner that would be intelligible to the general reader.
The result is no facile work of popularization. 
It will make demands upon the stamina of any reader. 
At times the author overestimates the layman's capacity to absorb detail, and Grieder's style can be wordy, even portentous. 
But his broad learning and vitality of spirit make him an excellent narrator and companion for this eventful journey. 
This is intellectual history in the sense defined by Joseph Levenson: ''The history not of thought, but of men thinking.''
Grieder engages the reader emotionally as well as intellectually as he recounts the fate not only of ''men thinking'' but of ideas living, and dying, in modern China. 
It is worth noting in this regard that neither America nor Europe has in modern times been through an identity crisis of the intensity the Chinese have endured since the middle of the 19th century.
Grieder makes a major contribution to our understanding of the intellectual adjustment China has had to undergo in the face of overwhelming pressures from outside and massive economic imbalance within. 
He shows us that many of the most difficult and sensitive issues that confront China today faced Chinese intellectuals 50 or 100 years ago. 
Pragmatism in conflict with dogma, pluralism versus an ideological monopoly, how to absorb the best of foreign culture without destroying China's own sense of identity, how to devise political and legal institutions that will balance freedom and order, how to modernize the economy - all these are themes of the book as well as issues in Peking today.
''Intellectuals and the State in Modern China'' provides sketches of the lives of the protagonists, and with deft economy Grieder evokes the conditions of the China they have inhabited. 
But he concentrates on their sense of themselves, their values, philosophies and proposals for reform or revolution. 
He conveys the agonizing of those who wanted to save the imperial system but realized it could not be done by drawing on the resources of traditional philosophy. 
Men like the early Communist leader Chen Duxiu icons of inherited culture with verbal violence. 
We hear the quieter voice of the liberal pragmatist Hu Shi calling on China to adopt a different strategy, to choose pluralism instead of totalitarianism.
Since the death of Mao Zedong, China has been engaged in a sober reassessment of its socialist revolution, and it is enlightening to look back now with Grieder at what Hu Shi wrote. 
''Civilization is not created wholesale,'' he cautioned in 1919. 
''It is created bit by bit and drop by drop. 
Progress cannot be achieved all at one go, of an evening.''
After the traumas of the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, such words must sound more persuasive to Chinese ears now than they did in the 1920's. 
But in those days, as Grieder points out, in a nation with no tradition of tolerance for a party of loyal opposition, and at a time of growing anarchy, it was not surprising th at China's leaders should have been drawn to authoritarian political forces, Chiang Kai-shek at one pole and the Communist Party at the other. 
Events in the 1920's and 1930's were pressing, and people were too impatient for Hu Shi's ''drop by drop''philosophy.
Nevertheless, from Grieder's account, Hu Shi emerges as a thinker no less radical than his Communist contemporaries: China must ''accept without prejudice the scientific-industrial world culture and the spiritual civilization that underlies it,'' he said, and declared that ''the only way to have democracy is to have democracy.''
In one of those connections that make his book so stimulating, Grieder moves from Hu Shi in the 1920's to Wei Jingsheng, the most radical activist of the Democracy Movement of 1978-79, and places them both in the line of those who have struggled for a pluralist China.
But Grieder does not deal with the period after 1949 in any detail. 
Our understanding of the continuities between the old China and the new is thereby impoverished. 
So few of those who study the new China possess his combination of boldness, historical perspective and ability to relate Chinese thought to the world outside. 
Intellectual history of the post-l949 period has been largely in the hands of craftsmen, not artists.
Merle Goldman is a fine artisan. 
In the serried ranks of Sinologists, there is no more skillful code breaker than she. 
Her earlier book, ''Literary Dissent in Communist China,'' chronicled literary developments up to the Great Leap Forward at the end of the 1950's. 
In her new book, ' 'China's Intellectu als: Advise and Dissent,'' she has broadened her focus to inc lude not only literary writers but philosophers, historians, journal ists and scientists.
The most valuable part of this book is the chapter in which she interprets the veiled debates that took place in the early 1960's, in the aftermath of the disastrous Great Leap Forward. 
With scholarly precision Goldman indicates how intellectuals, enjoying the patronage of powerful Communist Party leaders opposed to Mao, expressed an amazing array of heterodox ideas, reopening questions that seemed to have been settled by the Communist victory in 1949.
She presents the playwright Wu Han calling for the breakup of collective farms, eminent historians speaking of the need to unite the country around common goals, and philosophers like Liu Jie arguing that the Confucian ideal of human kindness produced in China an evolutionary rather than a revolutionary process. 
No one to my knowledge has researched and written so comprehensively on this aspect of the period. 
But the rest of the book is disappointing. 
Its title leads one to expect an intellectual history; one finds instead a history of the bureaucratic politics of the intellectual culture.
Merle Goldman is so preoccupied with Lenin's question ''Who: Whom?'' that she presents intellectual ideas and values as functions of these bureaucratic politics, whereas we have abundant evidence that there is an autonomous life of the mind and spirit in China.
This has been plain to see each time the lid has been lifted on post-1949 China: during the Hundred Flowers campaign and the Cultural Revolution, and in the years since Zhou Enlai's death in 1976. 
A volcanic eruption of poetry has provided evidence that traditional patterns of expression are being married to contemporary thought and feeling. 
For an intellectual history to be published today without a proper examination of that evidence - let alone of the earlier evidence - is just not good enough.
That is not all. 
Goldman has not developed the vital connections between what has happened in this later period and the point at which Grieder stopped. 
The social context in which Chinese intellectuals operate is all but invisible. 
Finally, Goldman's acknowledgments and notes on sources confirm what the text itself makes clear: Discussions with Chinese played no significant part in her study.
Such detached and dispassionate writing is sometimes regarded as ''scientific.''
Certainly it is justifiable if one is writing about molecules or plants, neither of which have been known to die for their ideas. 
But when transposed to the realm of people, this approach becomes unscientific; it filters out too much of the essence of our untidy lives.
Oh, ye watchers of latter-day China, open your doors and bring into your studies other men's emotions, suffering and dreams!
Nations and their politics are not made by power play alone.

text:
ï»¿
When Secretary of Defense Caspar W. Weinberger arrives in China on Sunday for a five-day official visit, he will be introduced to an army that was at one time considered the world's best light infantry but has been overtaken by progress.
China's People's Liberation Army, with over 4.2 million men and women under arms, is largely obsolete, lacking sophisticated antitank and antiair craft missiles and electronic communications gear, among other modern necessities.
The army, which was born as a guerrilla band 56 years ago, remains mired in its traditional dual role of defending the country and ''serving the people,'' as the old Maoist slogan put it.
Â 
Soldiers Still Harvest Rice
Its soldiers still routinely fix roads, plant trees, raise pigs and harvest rice. 
Yu Qiuli, the army's political commissar, declared recently that the armed forces had contributed 100 million work days of public service over the last four years.
Yet an effort has now begun to transform the army into a more modern fighting machine. 
''The P.L.A. is no longer in the era of millet plus rifles,'' a commentary in the official newspaper People's Daily said last May. 
Mr. Weinberger, who is making his first visit to China, according to a Pentagon spokesman, is scheduled to review an armed forces honor guard on Sunday in Peking. 
On Tuesday he is to visit the elite Third Division of the Peking Garrison, and two days later he is to visit an aircraft factory in Xian and inspect a naval vessel in Shanghai.
The Chinese leaders are expected to ask Mr. Weinberger about the Reagan Administration's decision to liberalize its export to China of dual-use technology - primarily civilian computers and other hardware that can be adapted for military purposes.
Â 
U.S. Offer Remains Open
Washington's offer, made two years ago, to consider Chinese requests for United States weapons remains open, though some Western military observers here doubt that the Chinese will present Mr. Weinberger with a specific shopping list, for two reasons.
The Chinese leadership is thought to be concerned that its purchase of American arms might give the Reagan Administration a pretext to sell more weapons to the rival Nationalist regime on Taiwan. 
This issue remains a key sticking point in Chinese-American relations, since Peking interprets the joint communique of August 1982 as committing Washington to phase out its military deliveries to the Nationalists.
But China is also too poor to re-equip the world's largest army with foreign weapons. 
Mr. Yu was quoted by The Beijing Review in August as saying:
''We have never pinned our hopes for modernizing our military equipment on imports. 
China is a big country with a big army. 
We cannot afford to buy all the weapons we need. 
Even if we could afford it, it is hard to acquire really advanced weapons of important military value.'
Â 
Foreign Arms Used as Prototypes
The Chinese seem interested in acquiring small quantities of foreign arms that could become prototypes for eventual weapons of Chinese manufacture. 
Some Western diplomats expect the Defense Minister, Zhang Aiping, to raise this issue with Mr. Weinberger, if only in an inconclusive way, though they point out that it would be faster for China to buy the arms than the production technology.
But the indications are that China, which canceled a multimillion-dollar deal with British Aerospace earlier this year, wants to do things cheaply. 
The Chief of Staff, Yang Dezhi, assured army delegates to the National People's Congress in June that ''we will mainly rely on our own efforts to improve our weapons and equipment while introducing advanced techniques from other countries.''
Statements by Chinese military leaders, articles in the official press and analysis by Peking-based diplomats and military attaches indicate that the problem of modernization of the army extends beyond arms alone to basic tactics and leadership competence.
The army's arsenal consists of copies of Soviet weapons mostly predating 1960, when the Soviet Union stopped its military and economic assistance to China. 
Light weapons like the Chinese version of the Kalashnikov assault rifle are highly enough regarded to make China a major arms seller to developing countries.
Â 
Military Aircraft Outdated
But heavier equipment is badly out of date. 
The Chinese Air Force uses copies of Soviet combat aircraft that go back to the MIG-15 of Korean War days. 
Its more modern Shenyang jet fighters, painstakingly updated from the MIG-19 and MIG-21, were described by one United States analyst as ''the world's most advanced obsolete aircraft.''
China has obtained some MIG-23's from Egypt to copy and its version is now believed to be in production, but even this new plane is no match for supersonic fighters like the Soviet MIG-25 or the American F-16.
The Chinese T-59 tank is likewise copied from the old Soviet T-55. 
A newer Chinese model, the T-69, has a gun stabilizer for high-speed firing, infrared searchlights and a laser range-finder, but it remains inferior to the T-72 that spearheads Soviet armored units.
Lacking self-propelled artillery, China has tried to mount heavy 122-millimeter guns on some of its armored personnel carriers, straining their suspension systems. 
Its antitank weapons resemble first-generation Soviet models dating back at least two decades.
Â 
Troops Still Move on Foot
The Chinese Army still basically moves on foot. 
Of the 200 or more divisions it is estimated to have, only 11 are armored and three are airborne. 
The Chinese have mechanized three to five infantry divisions, though it is unclear whether all their battalions are included. 
By comparison, the 45 or so Soviet divisions positioned along China's northern borders are all motorized.
The Chinese Navy has at least one nuclear-powered submarine capable of firing ballistic missiles from underwater. 
Presaging a move away from the traditional role of coastal defense, two Chinese naval vessels made a nonstop 6,000-mile voyage into the South China Sea and Western Pacific earlier this year. 
But the navy remains old-fashioned.
A military attache from a North Atlantic Treaty Organization country who has watched Chinese ground military tactics said, ''It is just like World War I with trenches.''
The Chinese Army is now trying to transform its old strategy of static defense, which is vulnerable to armored and airborne assault, into what the Liberation Army's daily newspaper has called an ''active defense.''
As some Chinese officers describe it, this means combining fixed defensive positions with mobile forces for counterstrikes and guerrillas for harassment behind enemy lines. 
Wu Xiuquan, head of Peking's Institute of International Strategic Studies, told visiting American members of Congress in August that China was also prepared to use nuclear weapons against an invader.
Â 
'Combined Operation' Maneuvers
Last year, the Deputy Chief of Staff, Zhang Zhen, said that tank battles would be emphasized over set-piece infantry warfare and that officers would be trained to use more sophisticated weapons. 
The press has disclosed ''combined operation'' maneuvers that coordinate infantry, artillery and armor with supporting signal and engineer units.
There has also been talk of slimming down the swollen forces by 10 percent or more and relieving them of nonmilitary duties. 
More than 20 divisions, by one estimate, are being transferreed from the army to a newly formed paramilitary People's Armed Police whose duties range from guarding public buildings and embassies to manning frontier posts. 
It was reported last month that a 30,000-man army construction unit was being demobilized and reformed as a construction engineering corporation in Peking.
One of the toughest challenges is to rejuvenate the upper echelons of the army, which have been dominated by aging guerrilla veterans too conservative to accept change. 
A plan to restore military ranks, which were abolished in 1965, has yet to be put into effect, partly because there would be so many elderly generals.
Â 
Higher Education Required
Other steps have been taken to create a younger and more professional officer corps. 
Mr. Yang, the Chief of Staff, reported in June that officers would no longer be chosen from the enlisted ranks but must graduate instead from military academies. 
The Political Commissar, Mr. Yu, told The Beijing Review that ''we have made it a rule that officers above the platoon level must have received a college education.''
The military has ranked last in China's ''four modernizations'' campaign, behind industry, agriculture and science and technology. 
The army's military budget this year has been put at 17.87 billion yuan - less than $9 billion - which is about the same as those of the last two years, though some programs like nuclear weapons and missile development have been tucked away in the budgets of ostensibly civilian ministries.
China's leader, Deng Xiaoping, has reportedly persuaded the army leadership to accept this low priority, arguing that industrialization will create a base for the domestic production of sophisticated weapons.
Â 
Technical Renovations Cited
''We have devised and produced our own atomic and hydrogen bombs, long-range guided missiles and other sophisticated strategic weapons for self-defense,'' the Communist Party journal Red Flag said last year in encouraging the army to stretch out the equipment that it already has. 
A few days ago, Mr. Yang, the Chief of Staff, said at an army meeting on arms production that over 12,000 technical renovations had been made on Chinese wapons in recent years.
But Mr. Deng has also maintained his grip over the armed forces by retaining the chairmanship of the party and state military commissions, while giving up other Government and party posts. 
He has installed in key slots senior officers who, if not enthusiastic about his policies, are at least unwilling to oppose them. 
Five of the commanders of China's 11 military regions have been replaced in the last year.

Bo Yang is a mild-mannered, bespectacled scholar who scribbles Chinese characters on notebooks in his small study, and infuriates people throughout the Chinese-speaking world.
Taiwan once labeled Mr. Bo a Communist agent, and imprisoned him for nine years. 
On the Chinese mainland, the authorities this year banned his books and condemned him for insulting the Chinese people. 
And in Chinatowns in the United States, as well as Hong Kong and Southeast Asia, Mr. Bo's acid pen has earned him bitter criticism as well as adulation.
Mr. Bo is a Chinese Voltaire, a social critic who is prolific, biting, and read.

text:

A former foreign leader and frequent visitor here once asked Deng Xiaoping about the best strategy for regaining office. 
''Be patient,'' Mr. Deng said, laughing. 
It was advice born of experience. 
Few leaders have been as far down as Mr. Deng was between 1966 and 1973 and again between 1976 and 1977, when Mao Zedong and his cronies reduced the disputatious little man from Szechuan to the status of an ordinary worker. 
The Red Guards called him a ''Napoleon'' for his imperious ways, but the nickname proved more apt than they imagined.
Like the French Emperor returning from exile on Elba, Mr. Deng came back, in his case to a new hold on power beyond any he had known.
Last week, seven years after he gained control of the Communist Party, China's pre-eminent leader made his boldest move yet to outmaneuver those who oppose his ''open door'' reforms.
At a special conference, more than 130 high-ranking veterans of the party's days as a peasant guerrilla force were gently shunted aside in favor of middle-aged officials selected for their loyalty to Mr. Deng's vision of a modernized, competitive future.
The resignations were the culmination of a campaign that has already resulted in the forced retirement of more than a million civil servants and tens of thousands of military officers.
Almost all the retirees were in their 70's or 80's and had marched with Mao. 
Among the more prominent were Marshal Ye Jianying, 88 years old, one of the five men who sat with Mr. Deng on the Politburo's Standing Committee, China's inner circle; Deng Yingchao, 81, the widow of Zhou Enlai and the country's highest-ranking woman, and Wang Dongxing, 72, the former head of Mao's bodyguard. 
Surprisingly, two Cabinet members, Defense Minister Zhang Aiping, 75, and Culture Minister Zhu Muzhi, 69, were also removed.
In part, the retirements - 64 from the Central Committee, 10 from the Politburo - were designed to bring new vitality into the overaged hierarchy. 
But by pressing for the departure of dozens of leaders with ties to the party's inward-looking obscurantist past, Mr. Deng was also attempting to slay the Maoist dragon once and for all.
It seemed an appropriate time. 
After six weeks at a seaside retreat, Mr. Deng returned to the capital for his 81st birthday on Aug. 
24 with a walnut tan. 
But his age is beginning to show. 
He has developed a minor speech impediment and a miniaturized aid in his left ear has only slighly improved his hearing. 
He banters about going to see Hong Kong after China gets the colony back in 1997, but virtually everyone assumes that the post-Deng transition cannot be far away.
Because he trod carefully in securing his power after 1978, Mr. Deng is in a hurry now. 
At the Party Congress in 1982, the first under his control, he pulled nine of his allies onto the Politburo, but was left with a rump of holdovers from the Mao era who continued to snipe at his reforms. 
In 1983, the policies came under heavy pressure during a ''spiritual pollution'' campaign that was blatantly anti-Western, and it was several months before Mr. Deng mustered the political muscle to suppress it.
At that time, he and his allies devised an expedient for consolidating their position: the special conference now in session. 
Only two such meetings have been held since the party's founding in 1921, one in 1937 to approve the policy of a ''united front'' with Chiang Kai-Shek's nationalists against Japan, and another in 1955, when Mao needed the party stamp on his ouster of a major rival, Gao Gang, and Gao's associate, Rao Shushi. 
One of the keynote speakers on that occasion was Mr. Deng.
The 1982 party Constitution envisaged special conferences for the discussion of ''major problems that require timely solution.''
Although they have never been used for wholesale political housecleaning, the Dengists used their Central Committee majority to deem that the phrase covered the need to ''rejuvenate'' the committee, a task that would normally be handled by the next Party Congress in 1987.
That they were sensitive to mumblings about irregular proceedings was implied by a constitutional exposition that Hu Yaobang, the General Secretary, offered the conference's opening session.
This week, Mr. Deng will unveil the list of those he has recruited to the Politburo. 
At the top will be two men who have emerged under his stewardship as heirs-apparent - Hu Qili, 56, favored to succeed the unrelated Hu Yaobang as General Secretary, and Li Peng, 57, the insiders' choice to take over from Zhao Ziyang as Prime Minister.
Â 
Economic Growth
Both are university-educated, tough and economically literate, particularly the Soviet-educated Mr. Li, who impressed his hosts on a tour of the United States this summer.
Beyond their talents, the new elite inculcated by Mr. Deng will have the advantage of the vaulting popularity of his reforms. 
Statistics released at the conference showed that since they took hold in 1980 there has been an average annual growth rate of 10 percent, against a best rate of 2 or 3 percent under Mao.
There have also been huge leaps in basic living indices - a 600 percent increase in retail shops and services, a 120 percent rise in retail food sales, an 85 percent increase in the income of peasants and a gigantic leap, to 15 million, in the number engaged in private business.
But to describe the strengthening of Mr. Deng's hand on the Central Committee as ''a guarantee'' of the reform policies, as the People's Daily did in its editorial, is to discount party history.
The contest between the Maoist levelers and those such as Mr. Deng, who see Communism as a means of making China rich and strong, has deep and bitter roots, and there is the example of the immediate post-Mao period to show that majorities evaporate rapidly when sentiment shifts in the innermost councils of power. 
The Dengists are stronger, but the opposition is still there.

Mr. Liao's letter also reflected the concern among the aging Peking leadership that successive generations of Chinese would grow less emotionally interested in Taiwan's return to the mainland. 
''Time does not stay, and brief is the day,'' Mr. Liao wrote.
Pointedly noting the Taiwan President's advancing age and poor health, Mr. Liao told Mr. Chiang, who is 72 years old, that his reconciliation with Peking would be a patriotic act insuring his place in Chinese history.
''You would be doing a meritorious service to the country and your name would be inscribed in the temple of fame,'' Mr. Liao wrote, adding, ''hesitation, procrastination or leaving the problem to other days would only lead to difficulty and distress and you, my brother, would hardly be able to escape the blame.''
Â 
Periods of Cooperation
The letter, which must have been approved if not drafted by the Peking leadership, recalled two previous periods of cooperation between the Kuomintang and the Communist Party, first in the 1920's and later in the late 1930's and 1940's against the Japanese invaders. 
Both were followed by a return to hostilities.
Mr. Liao declared that Mr. Chiang could not hold out forever. 
''Taiwan is bound to return to the embrace of the motherland eventually,'' he wrote. 
''An early settlement would be in the znterests of all.''
The letter also reiterated that after reunification, the remains of Mr. Chiang's father, the late Chiang Kai-shek, should be returned from Taiwan for burial ''in the native soil - in Fenghua, Nanjing or Lushan - in fulfillment of your filial wishes.''
Such an invitation was extended last October by the Communist Party Chairman, Hu Yaobang, at a rally here celebrating the 70th anniversary of the 1911 revolution.

file: PEKING AIDE ADMITS ERRORS OF IDEOLOGY.txt
text:

A prominent cultural official has offered an apology for his own ideological shortcomings in a move interpreted here as a signal that stricter ideological conformity is again being demanded of China's writers and artists.
Zhou Yang, an adviser to the party's propaganda department and chairman of the state-controlled China Federation of Literary and Art Circles, offered a self-criticism for ''shortcomings and mistakes'' in a major address to a symposium commemorating the 100th anniversary of the death of Karl Marx.
His self-criticism, in the form of an interview with the New China News Agency, was featured today on the front page of Guangming Daily, a newspaper read by many educated Chinese, and also appeared in the party newspaper, People's Daily.
In his speech, which he gave last March, Mr. Zhou contended that alienation - the estrangement of an individual from society - could exist in Marxist as well as in capitalist countries. 
He also suggested that humanitarianism was a legacy shared by Marxists and Western thinkers.
Zhou Yang, prominent cultural official in China, offers apology for his own ideological shortcomings in move interpreted as signal that stricter ideological conformity is again being demanded of country's writers and artists (M)'Socialist Society Is Superior'
''Socialist society is undoubtedly superior to capitalist society, but this by no means says that there is no alienation in Socialist society,'' Mr. Zhou had said, and went on to cite some instances in China.
''A thoroughgoing materialist ought not to be afraid of admitting facts,'' Mr. Zhou had continued. 
''Only by admitting that there is alienation will he be able to overcome alienation.''
Such seemingly arcane philosophical points are watched carefully here because they define the parameters of creativity permitted in the Communist state. 
Mr. Zhou had seemed to imply that writers and artists should be allowed to portray contemporary China more realistically.
But his interview circulated by the New China News Agency quoted Mr. Zhou as saying, ''I did not pay proper attention to drawing a clear line ideologically between Marxist and bourgeois views on this question.''
Mr. Zhou said his report last March was ''open to distortion'' by some people with anti-Marxist views and had created ''some ideological and theoretical confusion'' about the nature of Marxist society.
Mr. Zhou's self-criticism, which was a common device used to correct divergent views under Chairman Mao, seems linked to a new drive against ''spiritual pollution,'' a code word for values, ideas and trends from the West.
Â 
What Is Significance of Move
The significance of the drive, and Mr. Zhou's self-criticism, is debated by Western diplomatic analysts here. 
Some believe that Mr. Deng decided to rein in literature and the arts to get wider support from hard-liners for his ''rectification'' or bloodless purge of the party, which was launched last month.
But some other diplomats think that the spiritual pollution campaign indicates that Mr. Deng has run into tougher opposition than was evident from party conservatives who opposed not only a shake-up of the party but also the changes that he has introduced over the last few years.
The new campaign reflects the assumption that life in capitalist societies is inherently pessimistic and degenerate and that therefore life in Communist societies should be portrayed as unfailingly optimistic.
Mr. Zhou, who is believed to be 75 years old, made his reputation both as a translator of Tolstoy and as a literary theoretician and propagandist. 
He was disgraced after the Cultural Revolution got under way in 1966 and then was rehabilitated 11 years later, becoming a deputy chief of the party's propaganda department.
At the 12th party congress in September 1982, he joined Mr. Deng and some other aging officials in retiring to the newly created advisory committee, but he remained with the propaganda department as an adviser.
Though he was active in the anti- rightist campaign of 1957 that persecuted writers who had veered from the party line, Mr. Zhou developed a more liberal reputation in recent years.

file: PEKING AND MOSCOW GET REACQUAINTED.txt
text:
ï»¿
PEKING IF it did not quite match the drama of Richard M. Nixon's visit in February 1972, there was nonetheless unusual interest in the arrival here last week of Soviet
deputy Prime Minister Ivan V. Arkhipov for the start of the most important encounter between China and the Soviet Union in 15 years.
Mr. Arkhipov's visit began on an upbeat note when his Chinese counterpart, Vice Premier Yao Yilin, first grasped the Russian's hand, then embraced him. 
Later, four Politburo members greeted the Russian in similar fashion, telling him of their pleasure in seeing him and of the gratitude China still feels for the Soviet assistance immediately after the Communist takeover in 1949. 
The warmth persisted as Mr. Arkhipov held four days of talks here, then flew south for a tour of the Shenzhen special economic zone, the showcase of China's distinctly un- Soviet attempt to modernize with the help of foreign investment, private enterprise and competition.
At the end of the week, as Mr. Arkhipov wound up his visit, assessments of it were mixed but the official upbeat note was maintained through the final banquet Friday. 
From the frequency with which Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang and other Chinese leaders referred to the 77-year- old economic specialist as ''an old friend'' and as a man who had ''worked swimmingly together'' with the Chinese during his years as chief of the Soviet aid program here in the 1950's, there was no doubting that the atmosphere was good. 
Nor was there any disposition to belittle the value of personal contact between high-ranking leaders for dispelling some of the bad blood that has bedevilled relations between Moscow and Peking.
All the same, there was plenty of evidence that it will take more than affection toward an old comrade to solve the knotty problems blocking the normalization of political relations that both sides have avowed as their goal. 
The talks ended with the announcement of four new economic and technical agreements, including a long-term trade pact, that were already in the works in May when the Arkhipov trip was scrubbed in a fit of Soviet pique over President Reagan's successful talks here in April and renewed border fighting between China and Vietnam. 
But the Chinese leaders were careful to restate the conditions for a broader political accommodation, which the Kremlin has already refused.
What emerged more strongly than before was China's decision to allow commercial and economic ties to move ahead on an independent track. 
In this, there is less sentiment than hard-headed calculation about the benefits China can reap by allowing natural flows to resume. 
In the decade up to the border clashes in 1969, the heavy trade built up in the 1950's was reduced to barely $30 million a year, and this crept back up to only $300 million by 1982. 
Once China's leader, Deng Xiaoping, decided to emphasize economic growth, inhibiting the potential that the two economies have for servicing each other became self-defeating. 
Thus, it was agreed that for 1985, trade would be increased by 22 percent, to $1.8 billion. 
The Russians also agreed to modernize several dozen factories built in the 1950's with their help. 
The commitment to a five-year trade pact signalled a willingness on both sides to put matters onto a surer footing than year-to-year arrangements have allowed. 
But even the most generous estimates by Chinese and Soviet officials place a ceiling of about $6 billion on the barter trade the two nations will be conducting by 1990, when the trade pact will expire. 
This is about as much trade as the United States and China will do in 1984. 
Peking's hunger for American technology suggests that the total will go much higher in future years. 
The trade figures reflect a wider truth. 
Although the fashion among Chinese officials these days is to play down the strategic relationship that developed with the United States after Mr. Nixon came, there is much that attests to the strength of the American tie. 
The Arkhipov visit has to be balanced in this year alone against the trips to Washington made by Prime Minister Zhao and Defense Minister Zhang Aiping, and the visits here by Mr. Reagan, Navy Secretary John Lehman and the American delegate to the United Nations, Jeane Kirkpatrick.
A Threatening Presence
On the other hand, there is still much in the relationship with the Russians that the Chinese consider threatening. 
The ''three obstacles'' to normalization that were emphasized again last week - Soviet support for Vietnamese actions in Cambodia, the Soviet presence in Afghanistan and Soviet troop deployment along Chinese frontiers - are examples of Moscow's muscle-flexing on Peking's doorstep. 
In 27 months of Foreign Ministry talks, the Soviet Union has shown no readiness to compromise on any of the three, a stand that leaves 50 Soviet divisions arrayed along the border and nuclear-armed aircraft at Mongolian bases barely half an hour away from Peking. 
And far from preparing to move out of Afghanistan, the Soviet Army marked the fifth anniversary of its entry into that country with a continuing offensive in the countryside against stubborn guerrilla resistance. 
(For President Reagan also, the Soviet occupation was ''a serious impediment'' to improved relations.)
The part of the Arkhipov visit that seemed particularly interesting was the Russian's visit to Shenzhen, the area bordering Hong Kong, where the Chinese have granted tax and tariff concessions to foreign investors eager for low-cost labor. 
Together with the unleashing of market forces and the decentralization of economic authority sponsored by Mr. Deng, the experiment embodied at Shenzhen makes for a stark contrast with the halting reforms the Kremlin has launched at home. 
Soviet propagandists have predicted confidently that the Chinese policies will fail, but the fact that Mr. Arkhipov went there - on his own initiative, the Chinese say - suggests that Moscow was at least curious and wanted to look things over all the same.

file: PEKING FINDS A NEW ENEMY_ _SPIRITUAL POLLUTION_.txt
text:
ï»¿
China has begun a major campaign against what it disparagingly calls ''spiritual pollution'' - the influx of unwelcome Western trends and liberal values that have been attributed to China's open-door policy toward the West.
The crackdown has come in the aftermath of last month's full session of the Communist Party's Central Committee, which announced a three- year program to clean up the party and rid it of radical and corrupt members.
Deng Xiaoping, China's foremost leader, raised the issue of spiritual pollution in a major speech to the closed session of the committee. 
The text of his speech has not been made public, but some Western diplomats speculated that it was part of Mr. Deng's strategy for undercutting opposition to the party's so-called rectification campaign.
China begins major campaign against what it disparagingly calls 'spiritual pollution,' influx of unwelcome Western trends and liberal values that have been attributed to open-door policy toward West; campaign is directed principally against literature and the arts; photos (M)
The party's propaganda chief, Deng Liqun, recently confirmed that the crackdown on spiritual pollution was ''closely linked'' with the party's rectification campaign. 
He went on to identify four categories of cultural contamination.
Â 
'Indulgence in Individualism'
These were, he said, the spread of ''obscene, barbarous or reactionary things,'' vulgar artistic performances, gainseeking and ''indulgence in individualism, anarchism, liberalism, etc.'' and writings or speeches that contradicted China's Communist system.
The campaign has been directed principally against literature and the arts, familiar scapegoats in previous ideological crusades. 
The broad scope became more apparent today when People's Daily published a self-criticism by Minister of Culture Zhu Muzhi, in which he apologized for his ministry's ''slow reaction and weak attitude'' in fighting the cultural contamination.
In the same newspaper, Ai Qing, a prominent poet who suffered under the Maoists, was also quoted as complaining that some Chinese literary magazines were ''polluting'' the minds of readers with material that ran counter to the official ideology. 
Several regional literary magazines have been suppressed for not being orthodox enough, according to reports in the Chinese press.
There was evidence earlier that a tougher line was being taken toward liberal trends. 
In September a play by Jean-Paul Sartre was closed down in Shanghai. 
Mr. Sartre's writings were criticized last year for having a negative impact on young Chinese.
Last month the China Youth newspaper denounced a light musical performance at a hotel in Canton, partly because the singers wore the traditional tight-fitting dress with a slit up the side, called a ''qipao,'' that revealed their thighs.
Â 
'Bourgeois Spiritual Pollution'
Peking Daily said last month that workers in the capital, over half of whom are 35 or younger, would undergo two weeks of ideological study because they lacked enough experience to recognize ''bourgeois spiritual pollution.''
Lin Jianqing, a senior party official, recently told a trade union congress here that ''we should help workers distinguish the beautiful from the ugly so that they favor the good and oppose what is ugly, vulgar and self-centered.''
The head of China's Academy of Social Sciences, Ma Hong, said last month that Chinese scientists, while studying the experiences and opinions of foreign scientists, must be on guard against the ''pollution by bourgeois ideology.''
The major assault recently on spiritual pollution has come in the current issue of the party's ideological journal Red Flag, which called it ''like air pollution, a public hazard.''
It also railed against vulgarity in literature and the arts, suggesting that these would be visible targets of the campaign.
Red Flag complained that ''frivolous and depraved drama and literature'' were increasing in China. 
It also said pornographic videotapes, photographs and hand-copied manuscripts were circulating ''with demoralizing and poisonous effect.''
Â 
Ideological Debate Within Party
The article, which was signed Shi Youxin, a pseudonym for a collective editorial effort, took a hard-line position when it said that ''many comrades'' were aware of the decadent trend but ''dare not resist for fear that they may be accused of being 'left.'
''
Red Flag also hinted that an ideological argument was under way in the party when it asserted that ''alienation'' was not possible in a Communist society. 
This contradicted a previous assertion by Zhou Yang, an adviser on literature and the arts to the party's propaganda department, that alienation was a universal phenomenon.
Last month Peng Zhen, a leading Politburo member and ally of Mr. Deng, told a forum that concern about liquidating spiritual pollution did not mean a change in the party's policy of encouraging diversity. 
Mr. Peng explained that such a policy of ''letting a hundred flowers bloom and a hundred schools of thought contend'' was intended to promote a Communist culture. 
''It is wrong to mistake it for a policy of liberalization,'' the official New China News Agency quoted him as saying.
Wang Zhen, a member of the Central Committee, indicated recently that some party officials had been careless about letting liberal tendencies develop. 
According to the New China News Agency, Mr. Wang said ''a few people on the ideological and theoretical front had spread in publications and classrooms many erroneous theories and viewpoints'' that ran counter to Marxist fundamentals.

file: PEKING FINDS THE AIRWAVES FILLED WITH UNKIND REMARKS.txt
text:
ï»¿
When President Reagan arrived in China late last month, a radio station broadcasting in Chinese likened Mr. Reagan's visit to ''the weasel going to pay his respects to the hen,'' an old Chinese proverb for treachery.
Its broadcast the next day, taking note of Mr. Reagan's smile, warned that ''a smiling tiger is the most treacherous.''
A broadcast on the third day lamented that the Chinese leaders failed to understand the danger of receiving an anti-Communist like Mr. Reagan. The radio likened Mr. Reagan to Hitler.
Article on clandestine broadcasts by August First Radio, Peking, China, made during visit of Pres Reagan to China; notes broadcasts, purporting to speak for disgruntled elements of Chinese armed forces, have been traced to Soviet Union and are part of effort to undermine policies of Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping (M)
All the broadcasts came from a station calling itself ''August First Radio,'' after the date the People's Liberation Army was founded in China, and purporting to speak for disgruntled elements of the Chinese armed forces.
In fact, its broadcasts have been traced to the Soviet Union and are part of an effort to undermine the policies of China's leader, Deng Xiaoping.
Â 
First Heard 5 Years Ago
A monitoring service of the British Broadcasting Corporation discovered in October 1982 that when the August First radio failed to appear one day, its frequency carried Moscow radio's domestic programming, ''Mayak.''
The station, first heard five years ago, is one of many clandestine radio stations around China's borders.
Another station calling itself ''The Voice of Democratic Kampuchea'' has reported the successes of Peking- backed guerrillas fighting the Vietnamese in Cambodia. 
The station is believed to be based in southern China.
Since last year, other clandestine radio stations pretending to represent China's armed forces have gone on the air with criticisms of Peking. 
They use such names as ''Radio Spark,'' ''Radio October Storm,'' ''The Voice of the P.L.A.'' and ''The Contingent of Proletarian Fighters.''
Some references to Nationalist ideology led to speculation that they come from Taiwan, but their signal has prompted theories that they are based in Vietnam.
A Western diplomat said the August First broadcasts were not aimed at ordinary Chinese so much as at soldiers along the northern border. 
He said the soldiers - young, poorly educated and sometimes homesick - were considered ripe targets for such propaganda.
The August First radio and its companion stations try to sound patriotic, staunchly Communist, anti-Western and sympathetic to army gripes. 
They charge that Peking insulted the armed forces by giving the military last priority in the four modernizations, after industry, agriculture and science.
Â 
Press Anti-Deng Campaign
The broadcasts also articulate the resentments of hard-liners who have had to yield to Mr. Deng's policies. 
They have accused him of creating a personality cult and letting degenerate Western values into China. 
The broadcasts have also attacked the party consolidation drive to weed out leftists and criminals from the rank-and-file. 
The sharpest diatribes have been directed against China's relations with the United States. 
The clandestine broadcasts have played up the size of continuing United States military sales to Taiwan and said the promise of United States technology was meant only to ''bribe and blackmail'' China.
The worst vilification in recent months was voiced by the August First radio against Secretary of Defense Caspar W. Weinberger, whose trip to Peking last September opened the way for the subsequent exchange of visits by Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang and President Reagan.
A month later, the August First radio said that Mr. Weinberger and his delegation had said ''these yellow-skinned dogs of China are all odius and impolite.''
The radio also accused the Americans of making obscene remarks about Chinese women.
Not surprisingly, the August First radio also stresses the need for closer relations with the Soviet Union.
The Chinese press has publicly ignored the clandestine broadcasts, which have not incited any visible disquiet. 
But the sensitivity exists. 
When a Western military attache paid a courtesy call on a senior Chinese Army officer, he inquired about the broadcasts. 
The officer, he said, smiled coldly and changed the subject.

file: PEKING FIRES ITS FIRST SUBMARINE-LAUNCHED MISSLE.txt
text:
ï»¿
China has successfully test-fired its first submarine-launched missile, the official New China News Agency reported tonight.
The agency said a ''submarine-based carrier rocket launching test'' was carried out in the East China Sea between Oct. 
7 and 16. 
Earlier, the Japanese daily Yomiuri Shimbun said test firings of intermediate-range ballistic missiles from a nuclear-powered submarine took place last Tuesday. 
The first official Chinese reports indicated that only one missile had been fired.
PEKING, Oct. 
16 (Reuters) - China has successfully test-fired its first submarine-launched missile, the official New China News Agency reported tonight.
The successful test makes China only the fifth country to have developed submarine-launched missiles. 
The others are the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain and France.
Â 
Launched ICBM's in 1980
China has already developed intercontinental ballistic missiles, or ICBM's. 
In May 1980, China fired what were initially described as carrier rockets in the central Pacific Ocean. 
They were later identified as ICBM's, and a handful of them are now believed to have been deployed. 
Last month, China announced it had successfully launched its 12th space satellite, and Western experts believe the Chinese are capable of placing multiple nuclear warheads aboard the ICBM's.
The New China News Agency said the Communist Party Central Committee, the Government and the party's Military Commission had sent a telegram of congratulations to all personnel involved.
The agency said after the launch button was pressed, ''a rumbling was heard, followed by a slight tremor, and the rocket broke through the sea surface with the force of a thunderbolt.''
Observers aboard nearby naval surface ships monitoring the launch burst into cheers, it said. 
The command post for the launch was on a hill near the sea, the agency said, with the entire operation directed by a commander and his deputy sitting at a control console.
Observers in helicopters watched the missile land in the target area, it added. 
The agency said the danger area had now been reopened to sea and air traffic. 
China had declared the area closed between Oct. 
7 and 26 for a missile test but had not said that it would be launched from a submarine.
Â 
100 Attack Submarines
This week's missile test would have taken place in waters controlled by China's east sea fleet, based at Ningbo, south of Shanghai, Western experts said.
This is the biggest of the navy's three fleets. 
The others are the northern fleet with headquarters in the former German concession port of Qingdao and the southern command sailing out of Zhanjiang.
Western experts say the Chinese Navy remains essentially a coastal defense force. 
It has a large number of patrol boats equipped with guided missiles and more than 100 attack submarines, according to latest Western estimates, but the experts see them as vulnerable to the superior technology of potential foes.

file: PEKING PAPER FOR OUTSIDERS FINDS A NICHE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Anyone who wants his National Hockey League scores along with news of the Xinjiang cotton harvest, the latest results of basketball tournaments in New York and light industry in Shanghai, tips on bridge-playing and bridge-building need look no further than a newspaper called China Daily.
As China's first English-language newspaper since the Nationalists shut down their presses and fled to Taiwan in 1949, China Daily has become a success six months after it started formal publication, with a circulation up from an initally cautious 20,000 copies to 50,000 today.
It was devised for foreigners, but two-thirds of its readership is Chinese -often ranking bureaucrats - who brush up on their English while enjoying a less restricted view of the world than is normally found in the Chinese press.
''Our newspaper is mainly geared to foreign readers,'' said Guan Zaihan, who serves on the China Daily editorial board. 
''That's why we serve so much foreign news. 
But we also want to tell our foreign friends about China.''
Profile of China Daily, Peking's first English-language newspaper since 1949
China Daily prints overseas news from foreign wire services, domestic news from the New China News Agency and merciful abridgements of the verbose ideological exhortations that fill the Chinese-language papers.
Â 
Lively Mix of Stories
The resulting mix is lively if sometimes curious. 
Last week, China Daily related at some length the tale of a married medical student in Shanghai who was expelled for adultery after he began spending his nights with an undergraduate notorious for her ''bourgeois ideology.''
The adjacent story was a report, translated from The People's Daily, on an animal husbandry farm, which had increased its profits twentyfold in the last five years by giving the peasants more responsibility.
China Daily is considered a ''sister publication'' of The People's Daily, and occupies the same compound in Peking, the gate of which is guarded by a soldier with a fixed bayonet.
Bicycles are parked in the building hallway. 
Upstairs, one of the English-language signs cautions: ''Do not fall into bad habits. 
The easy way is quite often the incorrect way.''
While China Daily has been subsidized by a loan from The People's Daily and is printed on its new English offset presses, the new newspaper has avoided the self-conscious propaganda image that China's other English-language publications project.
''We have a different readership, very different from The People's Daily,'' said Zheng Defang, a deputy editor who learned her profession at the New China News Agency. 
''If we tried to preach, you know what the reaction would be,'' she said.
Â 
'Under the Leadership of the Party'
Miss Zheng, a genial, matronly woman who wears her graying hair in a bun, added, ''This paper is run in China, and China is a country where the party leads, so any paper printed in China would be broadly speaking under the leadership of the party.''
Mr. Guan, who was a Professional Journalism Fellow at Stanford University several years ago, explained: ''We are not a party organ and we do try to be as objective as we can. 
In other words, we don't deviate from the party line but we do have our own editorial policy.''
The newspaper's resulting soft sell offers something for almost everyone. 
China-based diplomats and journalists increasingly rely on it to catch developments that they missed in the Chinese-language press.
Tourists get two pages of sports news as well as overseas news, even a daily crossword puzzle. 
Chinese hone their English on some articles that would not be found outside the Reference News, a classified daily summary restricted to reliable officials.
The managing editor, Feng Xiliang, has encouraged the young staff, which is mostly recruited from foreign language institutes, to write feature articles that will enlighten foreigners about all aspects of China. 
There have been recent interviews with Wu Tunan, a lithe 96-year-old master of taijiquan, the meditative shadow boxing, Yu Zhixue, a noted landscape artist, and Wang Shix@iang, who collects Ming Dynasty furniture. 
Other features have explained the arcane theatrics of classical Peking opera and, among other food recipes, have shared hints on how to catch and cook a turtle.
Â 
Limited Promotion Overseas
Though China Daily has yet to be promoted overseas, 8,000 copies are now printed for readers in Hong Kong. 
The Hong Kong edition costs 18 cents an issue, or three times the price of the Peking edition.
China Daily gets about 100 letters a week from readers, whose comments offer an insight into what concerns the Chinese. 
Chen Yunde, in Shanghai, expressed shock the other day that some young women were having their ears pierced, a practice that he equated with the binding of feet. 
Two other readers complained that the Chinese habit of spitting on the ground was giving foreigners a bad impression.
Miss Zheng and Mr. Guan said they could not give financial details about the newspaper because, Miss Zheng said, ''we don't handle the business part.''
But she did say that ''we get more money from our advertisements than from our circulation.''
The advertisements, which cost about $15.50 per column inch, are used by the Chinese to promote such products as carpets, pumps, pharmaceuticals and sandals and by foreign companies to sell watches, banking services and airline flights.
China Daily's biggest problem, Miss Zheng said, is its shortage of English-speakers in a staff that now numbers 40. 
The reporters start at a monthly salary of $33 for college graduates. 
Experienced editors like Miss Zheng earn about $90 a month.
''You know, at the present moment,'' Miss Zheng said, ''we don't have enough people. 
A lot of young people are eager to work for us, but they don't have the English.''

file: PEKING PARTY MEETING OPENS_ MAJOR CHANGES ARE EXPECTED.txt
text:
