file: SECRECY IN A DISMISSAL BY STANFORD FUELS ACADEMIC FREEDOM DISPUTE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Stanford University's expulsion of a graduate student, on the basis of a secret report by faculty members who investigated his anthropological work in China, has touched off a dispute about academic freedom.
The student, Steven W. Mosher, was dismissed from Stanford's doctoral program by an 11-0 vote of the anthropology department last February, with no reported dissent. 
But the secrecy surrounding the decision and conflicting accounts of the charges against the student have raised questions over whether Stanford had bowed to pressure from Peking to retaliate against Mr. Mosher.
Mr. Mosher, 34 years old, conducted research in a village near Canton in 1979 and 1980. 
He was one of the first American scholars allowed to work in China after normal relations between Peking and Washington were restored.
Stanford University's expulsion of a graduate student, on the basis of a secret report by faculty members who investigated his anthropological work in China, has touched off a dispute about academic freedom.Work Led to Chinese Ban
He gathered a highly unusual collection of local police and government documents that the Chinese consider secret, and he later published an article in a Taiwanese magazine that described a campaign to force many women to undergo abortions as part of China's birth control program.
The Chinese were angered by Mr. Mosher's activities, and soon after his departure, whether by coincidence or not, banned all further field research by American academics. 
In conversations with other American scholars, Chinese officials also began accusing Mr. Mosher of a long list of charges, including spying, smuggling and immoral conduct with a woman. 
Several of the scholars reported the charges to Stanford.
Stanford then set up a three-member investigating committee that reported that Mr. Mosher had engaged in ''illegal and seriously unethical conduct'' in China. 
But the anthropology department has refused to release the 47-page committee report on which the vote to expel Mr. Mosher was based, contending that it ''contains information that may be injurious to innocent parties.''
In a statement this spring responding to critical letters and editorials, Donald Kennedy, president of Stanford, termed the dispute over Mr. Mosher ''one of those unfortunate cases in which we find two important social values in collision.''
He said the university would like to be able to release the information to answer questions about ''possible infringements on academic freedom or about the operation of political influence.''
''But an equally strong set of values attaches to the need for privacy,'' he went on, saying that the information might be ''damaging'' to other people.
A spokesman for the university said Mr. Kennedy had not read the investigating committee's report.
Â 
Ex-Wife Said to Be a Source
Although members of the anthropology department have offered differing accounts of the charges against Mr. Mosher, several professors said the critical evidence had been supplied by his former wife, Maggie So, a Chinese born in Hong Kong.
In the spring of 1980, after a bitter quarrel over Mr. Mosher's demand for a divorce, Miss So went to the United States Consulate in Canton, where she accused him of bribing local officials to obtain documents, the anthropology professors said. 
She complained that Mr. Mosher's actions were endangering her relatives who still lived in the village, they said.
In early 1982, after the couple were divorced, the professors said, she repeated her accusations to the Stanford investigating committee, calling collect from France. 
One professor said Miss So had also charged Mr. Mosher with financing his operation by smuggling Chinese antiques to Hong Kong, though other professors said this was untrue. 
Miss So's current whereabouts are unknown.
Â 
'Abolutely False,' He Says
Mr. Mosher derides Miss So's information as ''absolutely false and unsubstantiated slander'' from a ''scorned woman who vowed to ruin me.''
In a telephone interview from Taiwan, where he now lives, Mr. Mosher said he had been dismissed because of Chinese anger over the abortion article and pressure from American China scholars eager to please Peking.
Stanford has denied both charges. 
Clifford R. Barnett, the chairman of the anthropology department, insisted that the department had been fair and had, for example, excluded China specialists, who might have appeared to be subject to pressure from the Chinese Government, from the investigating committee and the departmental vote.
Â 
Stanford Widely Criticized
The university, however, has been widely criticized for its handling of the case. 
Editorials in The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal questioned the need for secrecy and suggested that Mr. Mosher might have been expelled to mollify the Chinese. 
Arthur Wolf, a Stanford anthropology professor, said all department members had received critical letters from groups that oppose abortion.
Several professors at such universities as Harvard, Brown and Yale, who asked not to be named to avoid cooler relations with colleagues at Stanford, have raised questions about how much authority a university should exercise over students' actions off campus. 
They pointed out that Harvard University, along with some other Ivy League schools, had adopted a policy of limiting disciplinary action to offenses connected with a student's academic record or behavior on campus.
Irving Louis Horowitz, the editor of Society magazine and a professor of political science and sociology at Rutgers University, said there was a serious question whether Stanford could withhold a degree from a student without making public the charges against him.
Â 
Quality of Work Termed Issue
''The issue is not whether Mosher's a nice man but the quality of his work,'' said Mr. Horowitz. ''I've read his manuscript,'' he added, referring to Mr. Mosher's proposed dissertation, ''and I'd be glad to have him as a graduate student.''
''I think Stanford felt they had to deliver a head to the People's Republic,'' Mr. Horowitz charged. 
''If Mosher had done the same things in the Soviet Union, he'd be a hero.''
He noted that many American academics disliked the Soviet Union but had a favorable attitude toward China.
Thomas Grey, a professor at the Stanford law school and one of the three members of the investigating committee, disputed Mr. Horowitz's contention. 
''We were aware from the beginning that the Sinological community had a bias in this, so we kept them out,'' Mr. Grey said.
''I certainly didn't have any ax to grind,'' he added, ''and it took a lot of time away from my work at the law school.''
As an indication of Stanford's sensitivity, Norman K. Wessels, dean of the School of Humanities and Sciences, has appointed a panel of three scholars, including one from outside Stanford, to hear a threepage grievance Mr. Mosher has filed against the school. 
Mr. Wessels asked the panel to recommend how he should deal with the case and requested a report that could be published.
Â 
Student Says He May Sue for Libel
Mr. Mosher, who has the investigative committee's report on the charges against him, has not released it. 
He has said he might sue Stanford for libel and that releasing the report himself would undermine his case.
Mr. Barnett, stressing that he had tried to insure a fair investigation, said the department had rejected a number of unsubstantiated accusations made by Peking and by fellow China scholars, including the charge that Mr. Mosher was a spy and that he illegally imported a van into China and gave it to village officials.
Still, Mr. Barnett asserted that some of the Chinese charges, including one that Mr. Mosher traveled without authorization into Guizhou Province, which is closed to foreigners, indicated a pattern of questionable behavior.
One Stanford professor said Miss So's evidence had been corroborated at least in part by Richard Williams, who was the United States Consul General in Canton when Mr. Mosher was in China. 
Mr. Williams, now deputy consul general in Hong Kong, said by telephone that it ''wouldn't be appropriate'' for him to comment on the case.
To support his contention that Stanford bowed to pressure by China scholars, Mr. Mosher cited a letter from Kenneth Prewitt, president of the Social Sciences Research Council in New York, to Stanford after he talked with Chinese officials late in 1981.
The exchange program between China and the United States ''could be harmed if the American scholarly community took no action on what the Chinese regarded as improper behavior by Mosher,'' Mr. Prewitt warned.
Stanford itself has conducted an active exchange program with China.
Â 
Abortion Campaign Described
In a book, ''Broken Earth: The Rural Chinese,'' to be published in September, Mr. Mosher paints a portrait of apathy, corruption and poverty among China's peasants and village officials.
He also describes, as he did in the article published in Taiwan, a campaign in his village in the spring of 1980 to force abortions on pregnant women who were not permitted to have children under Peking's strict birth control rules. 
At a family planning meeting he attended, he wrote, a local official told the pregnant women, ''None of you have any choice in this matter.''
''The two of you who are eight or nine months pregnant will have a Caesarean,'' Mr. Mosher quotes the official as saying. 
''The rest of you will have a shot that will cause you to abort.''
In a nearby village, Mr. Mosher asserted, a woman seven months pregnant who had no sons had an ordered abortion and was found to have been carrying twin boys.
The woman's husband, Mr. Mosher wrote, went in a fury to the home of the official who had ordered the abortion. 
''Seizing the man's two sons, aged 8 and 10,'' he wrote, ''he heaved them into the courtyard well and then leaped in himself. 
All three drowned.''
The magazine article, published in May 1981, brought accusations from Peking that its content, and its publication in Taiwan, was an attack on China. 
And the head of Mr. Mosher's dissertation committee at Stanford, the anthropologist G. William Skinner, wrote Mr. Mosher that he was ''appalled at your irresponsibility and insensitivity'' in not concealing the identity of the women facing abortions. 
Concealing subjects' identity is a canon of anthropological ethics.
Â 
Chinese Had Been Complaining
Chinese officials had already been complaining to American scholars about Mr. Mosher, and Stanford decided to set up the investigating committee. 
When it began its work in October 1981, however, it lacked proof. 
The committee head, Prof. Jane F. Collier, wrote to Zhao Fusan, a deputy director of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, appealing for evidence. 
''Much of the information we have received on these charges,'' she said, ''has been indirect and secondhand, consisting of reports by American scholars of complaints made to them by Chinese officials.''
Mr. Zhao's response only reiterated the allegations that had been gossiped about, said Mr. Barnett, the anthropology department chairman.
But in December 1981, Miss So began making her accusations to Stanford, according to several professors familiar with the investigative report.
Mr. Mosher asserts that Miss So had little first-hand knowledge of the village, though she had cousins there, because she visited him infrequently. 
Instead, she was either finishing graduate school at the University of California at Berkeley or working out of Hong Kong for an import-export company.
Â 
'I Will Ruin You'
''Matters came to a head in March 1980,'' Mr. Mosher said. 
''She came to the village and I said I wanted a divorce.''
''She replied, 'You can't, I will ruin you,' '' Mr. Mosher said. 
About the confidential documents, Mr. Mosher insists he was given access to them legally after three Chinese officials from Peking visited the village shortly before his arrival in 1979 and ordered the local authorities to cooperate with him.
The documents included land registers, household registers and class status registers, giving a social and economic profile of each peasant going back to the 1940's. 
Mr. Mosher also obtained crime reports prepared by the local secret police. 
Scholars say no American had ever gained access to such material.
Mr. Mosher said he did give his Mazda van to the village and turn over to his wife's cousins a house he built. 
But his only other gifts, Mr. Mosher said, were dinner invitations to peasants who helped him.
Â 
Gifts Held Improper
Professor Barnett concedes that anthropologists routinely provide their research subjects with money or gifts in exchange for their information or time. 
But, without elaborating, he asserted that Mr. Mosher ''went way over the line'' with his gifts.
Before he was expelled, Mr. Mosher had planned to give all his documents to the Hoover Institution on War, Revolution and Peace at Stanford. 
An official of the politically conservative institution said he had already turned over some materials on education and a microfilm file of the local county newspaper, a valuable tool for scholars.
Unfortunately, the film he took was of such poor quality that it is unusable, the official added.

file: SENATOR JACKSON, IN PEKING, SAYS BETTER TIES ARE AHEAD.txt
text:

Senator Henry M. Jackson said today that Chinese-American relations were improving at a pace that could soon bring an exchange of visits between President Reagan and Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang.
Mr. Jackson, Democrat of Washington, commented after a meeting with Deng Xiaoping, China's paramount leader.

Sen Henry Jackson, in Peking, says improving Chinese-US relations could lead to exchange of visits between Pres Reagan and Prime Min Zhao Ziyang; meets with Deng Xiaoping, who gives Jackson bear hug; illustration; delivers Reagan letter (S)

Chinese ties with the United States, strained since Mr. Reagan was elected, have improved in the last three months and ''the opportunity is now present to expand our relations,'' Senator Jackson said at a news conference.

When questioned about the possibility of a visit by Prime Minister Zhao to the United States, Senator Jackson said, ''I think things are improving for that visit and some time after the first of the year, hopefully, the Premier's visit would be reciprocated by the President of the United States.''

'Movement Is Favorable'
The Senator said no decision has been made, but the ''movement is favorable'' for a Zhao visit in November or December. 
Mr. Jackson said a Reagan trip to Peking could probably come in early 1984 before United States election campaigns intensify.
Mr. Zhao accepted a Reagan invitation last year, but the trip was shelved as relations faltered over continuing United States arms sales to Taiwan and Chinese complaints that Washington was holding back purchases of United States technology.

file: SHULTZ ON CHINA_ ACCENTING THE POSITIVE_News Analysis.txt
text:
ï»¿
Despite some tough language in China's official commentary on Secretary of State George P. Shultz's four-day visit to Peking, there seems to be considerable agreement by American and Chinese officials on what Mr. Shultz did and did not accomplish there.
In interpreting the results of the Shultz mission, however, the two sides appear to be practicing what one of Mr. Shultz's aides today called ''half full, half empty diplomacy.''
The aide meant that Peking persists in seeing the same ''cup'' of relations as half empty that the Americans see as half full.
Mr. Shultz was informed of the New China News Agency commentary when he awoke this morning. 
He read the text along with senior advisers, Paul D. @Wolfowitz, the Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian Affairs, and Thomas Shoesmith, Mr. Wolfowitz's deputy. 
The commentary said Mr. Shultz's visit had helped Chinese-American relations ''to some extent'' but unless the Taiwan issue was resolved ''mutual trust between China and the United States is out of the question.''
SEOUL, South Korea, Feb. 
7 - Despite some tough language in China's official commentary on Secretary of State George P. Shultz's four-day visit to Peking, there seems to be considerable agreement by American and Chinese officials on what Mr. Shultz did and did not accomplish there.
The initial American reaction was one of relief that it had not closed the doors to improved relations, and was less negative than some early news accounts suggested. 
One aide, in talking to reporters, said, ''We don't see anything startling: in fact, there are some positive things in it.''
Â 
Shultz Limits Claims of Success
This assessment, of course, was in keeping with the traditional American approach to Chinese relations. 
Every secretary of state leaving China has described the results in a more positive way than have the Chinese. 
For instance, Cyrus R. Vance in 1977 said some progress had been achieved, only to have the Chinese call the visit a failure. 
Alexander M. Haig Jr. 
In 1981 was exuberant about moves in the strategic field, only to have the Chinese lash out at the Reagan Administration, and to suspend military contacts.
Mr. Shultz has limited his claims of ''success'' to having achieved a better understanding of each other's position, more mutual trust and a laying of groundwork for closer ties in the future. 
He did not claim any breakthroughs on Taiwan or anything else.
The reason Mr. Shultz's party was not unhappy about the press agency commentary was that much of it meshed with what the Americans were saying about the visit. 
These points were made by Mr. Shultz's aides:
- The two sides agreed that the visit improved relations ''to some extent'' by allowing a full airing of differences, even though problems remained.
- The press agency said the two countries were ''close in their analyses of the current international situation as well as in their views on the issues of Afghanistan, Cambodia and arms control.''
That was an even more positive statement than Mr. Shultz had made at his farewell press conference and was the first time publicly Peking said it agreed with Washington on arms control matters.
- The press agency commentary did not take issue with two potential developments made public by Mr. Shultz. The first was that the two sides had agreed to hold talks on ways of bringing about closer military relations. 
The second was that Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang had agreed to come to the United States and a date would be worked out. 
The White House said he had agreed to come this year, but Mr. Shultz was not that specific.
- Even though the Chinese raised the Taiwan issue repeatedly during the talks with Mr. Shultz, the press agency article quoted Mr. Shultz correctly as saying that he and President Reagan fully intended to live up to last August's communique calling for phased out arms sales to Taiwan.
The article went on to list what it said were violations of agreements on Taiwan, such as officials attending Taiwan receptions in Washington and the setting up of a new Taiwan office.
''Obviously, the point they are making is that Taiwan is a problem in relations,'' one American said. 
''We know that.''
What is unknown, of course, is whether the Chinese side will seek to focus so heavily on Taiwan and other problems such as the difficulty of getting licenses to buy certain advanced technology so as to prevent relations from developing further.
Mr. Shultz and his aides who sat through the long hours of talks insist the Chinese made it clear they wanted to advance the relations, even though differences persisted.
Â 
Felt Chinese Were Ill Informed
As a longtime mediator, Mr. Shultz believes that with patience and trust most problems can be solved, or at least ought to be. 
As he made clear on the plane flying here from Peking, he came away from the talks feeling that the Chinese side was not as well informed on American policy as it should have been and this, in his view, created distortions. 
One reason, some of his aides said, was that the former Chinese Ambassador, Chai Zemin, spoke no English, and was not able to become closely enough involved in Chinese-American relations in Washington.
The new Chinese Ambassador to Washington, Zhang Wenjin, is an old American hand, speaks fluent English, and was involved in the opening of relations in the early 1970's. 
Mr. Shultz's hope is that Mr. Zhang will become involved in such matters as licensing problems for exports, and can better appreciate the political realities in Washington that makes it impossible for any administration to renounce the Taiwan Relations Act, which obliges the United States to provide for Taiwan's defense.
It is assumed by the Americans that the Chinese harp on the differences to make clear they remain independent in their foreign policy - something crucial to their relations with the Soviet Union and the third world. 
And the Chinese may feel, American officials say, that by stressing the problems they can bring pressure on Washington to make compromises.

file: SHULTZ-GROMYKO MEETING POSSIBLE AT ARMS CONFERENCE IN JANUARY.txt
text:
ï»¿
Secretary of State George P. Shultz indicated today that he might meet with the Soviet Foreign Minister, Andrei A. Gromyko, at an East-West conference on disarmament in Stockholm Jan. 
17.
Several Western European nations, especially West Germany, have been urging that the 35-nation conference on developing safeguards against surprise attacks be begin with foreign ministers present. 
Mr. Shultz, at a breakfast meeting with reporters, indicated he would not oppose that effort, although he declined to say specifically that he would meet with his Soviet counterpart.
''It seems to be shaping up as a meeting to which foreign ministers will go,'' he said. 
''If that's the way it emerges, then the United States will be represented.''
State Sec George P Shultz indicates that he might meet with Soviet Min Andrei A Gromyko at East-West conference on disarmament in Stockholm Jan 17; several Western European nations are urging that 35-nation conference begin with foreign mins present; other points made by Shultz outlined (M)
Such a meeting would be the first high-level Soviet-American encounter since the chilly exchange between Mr. Shultz and Mr. Gromyko in Madrid on Sept. 
9 after the Soviet Union shot down a South Korean passenger airliner. 
The tension between Moscow and Washington has worsened with the deployment of American medium-range nuclear missiles in Western Europe and the Soviet suspension of the talks in Geneva on medium-range missiles.
Â 
Kohl Backs Deployment Schedule
In Bonn, Chancellor Helmut Kohl said he favored adhering to the deployment schedule for the American missiles as a way to to persuade the Soviet Union to return to the Geneva talks. 
(Page A13.)
In Geneva, Soviet and American negotiators met for 3 hours and 35 minutes in the current round of talks on limiting strategic, or long-range, weapons. 
They agreed to meet again next Tuesday. 
(Page A10.)
Â 
Joint Decision Expected
As for the Stockholm meeting, Mr. Shultz said he and other North Atlantic Treaty Organization foreign ministers would decide whether to attend when they met in Brussels next week. 
He said his attendance would not depend on whether Mr. Gromyko was coming. 
An aide said later that while there were no arrangements for Mr. Shultz to meet Mr. Gromyko in Stockholm, ''it would be logical'' for that to happen.
The United States is reported to have privately suggested to Moscow various possible topics for talks, such as technical exchanges or navigation agreements to prevent events like the Korean jet incident. 
But Administration officials are skeptical that much can be done while the state of health of Yuri V. Andropov, the Soviet leader, remains uncertain.
When asked about Mr. Andropov, Mr. Shultz replied: ''He's obviously ill. 
How ill he is and what is his illness, I don't know. 
I know that statements are issued in his name. 
There's all sorts of speculation. 
Obviously we follow these matters closely. 
But what we have to do is not try to base our policies on what we think may be happening there, but base our policies on what we think is right for us.''
In his wide-ranging one-hour session with reporters, Mr. Shultz made these other points:
- Recent conciliatory statements by the Nicaraguan Government were ''good to hear'' and ''vastly different'' from what the Sandinista junta was saying six to eight months ago. 
But Mr. Shultz said there is ''always a question of whether there is a reality behind the words.''
- Planning continues for the visit of Zhao Ziyang, the Chinese Prime Minister, to the United States in January, and for President Reagan's visit to Peking in April. 
Mr. Shultz said he assumed the visits would take place despite Chinese objections to two Congressional measures that referred to Taiwan as the Republic of China. 
The Administration has since reaffirmed its position that the Peking Government ''is the sole legitimate Government of China.''
- The Salvadoran Government risks erosion of its support unless it can take some action quickly to curb right-wing death squads and bring suspected killers to trial. 
Unless improvement from the current ''grave'' situation is made by January, Mr. Shultz said, it would be ''very difficult'' for him to report to Congress that progress on human rights was being made in El Salvador.
- Supplies of American-made cluster bombs to Israel will depend on working out a satisfactory agreement on their use, an indication that the Reagan Administration is looking for tighter restrictions to insure that such weapons are not used in areas with heavy civilian populations.
Â 
Conditions on Sale and Use
During this week's visit to Washington by Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir, the Reagan Administration indicated that it was ready to consider resuming supplies of such weapons. 
Those shipments were suspended 18 months ago as a sign of Administration unhappiness over Israel's invasion of Lebanon.
In response to a question about the cluster bombs, Mr. Shultz said: ''What we have said is that the suspension on sales of cluster munitions will be lifted if there is a satisfactory agreement on usage. 
We will have to see whether such an agreement can be made in the course of our meetings. 
I assume there's interest. 
If there's no interest, why, that's fine.''
Several times, he defended President Reagan's agreement with Mr. Shamir to set up a new American-Israeli political-military group as a necessary move to offset ''the buildup of Soviet arms and troop presence in Syria.''

file: SLAYING WAS ORDERED FROM TAIWAN, LAWYER SAYS.txt
text:
ï»¿
A lawyer for the family of a Chinese writer who was slain here asserted today that the identification of the killers as leaders of an underworld gang with good political connections in Taiwan showed the killing had been ''ordered and planned by powerful figures in Taiwan.''
The lawyer, Jerome M. Garchik, asserted that Chen Chi-li, leader of the gang, had links to a number of officials in Taiwan, including a son of President Chiang Ching-kuo.
Mr. Chen was named last week by the Federal Bureau of Investigation as mastermind of the slaying of Henry Liu, who was shot in his home in nearby Daly City on Oct. 
15 shortly after publishing a critical biography of President Chiang and his family.
Lieut. Thomas G. Reese of the Daly City police said the department was still uncertain about a motive. 
Taiwan has denied any involvement in the incident.
President Chiang's son, Chiang Hsiao-wu, is Deputy Secretary General of the National Security Council on Taiwan, a powerful umbrella security agency, and was formerly head of the China Broadcasting Corporation, where he had contact with a number of movie stars and singers. 
Mr. Garchik contended that some of the performers were members of the underworld organization, known as the Bamboo Gang.
Â 
Political Repercussions
The killing appears to have touched off political repercussions in Taiwan.
Since the Nationalist Government maintains tight political control over Taiwan with a highly effective police network, many Chinese assume the gang must have had good relations with the Government to survive, said a Chinese scholar at Stanford University. 
The Bamboo Gang has grown rapidly in recent years and has been heavily involved in extortion, gambling and prostitution.
The scholar, who asked that his name not be used because of fear of retaliation by Taiwan or the gang, said President Chiang appeared to be above suspicion in the killing.
On Nov. 
13 the Taiwan Garrison Command suddenly began a major crackdown on the gang, arresting more than 300 members, including Mr. Chen and Wu Tun, another suspect in the killing. 
Among those detained was a senior police official in the city of Kaohsiung and a former officer of the Garrison Command who now serves as head of the Prominent Merchants Club, a private club run by Mr. Chen, according to accounts in the Taiwan press.
Â 
'Looking for the Answers'
Paul Mao, a spokesman for the San Francisco office of Taiwan's unofficial mission in the United States, the Coordination Council for North American Affairs, said today that his Government had begun the crackdown on the Bamboo Gang and other underworld groups precisely to find out what was the extent of their power and political connections. 
''We are looking for the answers,'' Mr. Mao said.
Both Lieutenant Reese and an agent of the F.B.I. familiar with the case said they had been told by various Chinese about a friendship between Mr. Chen, the gang leader, and President Chiang's son. 
''I've heard about it, but I'm not at liberty to comment on it,'' Lieutenant Reese said.
Mr. Garchik, in a news conference, said several other unresolved questions suggested the involvement of the Taiwan authorities in the killing. 
For example, he noted that Mr. Chen himself had come to San Francisco, even though he is the head of a gang with perhaps 4,000 to 10,000 members. 
Mr. Garchik also said Mr. Liu had never written about the Taiwanese underworld and had no connection to it.
''There is no other explanation than a political assassination,'' Mr. Garchik said.
In addition, Mr. Garchik pointed out that Taiwan has recently banned two magazines that reported on Mr. Liu's writings and killing and noted that the head of the Government Information Office in Taiwan last week had threatened to sue anyone who said anything critical about Taiwan.
Mr. Garchik contended that the killing and recent identification of the suspected killers had serious international implications. 
''We feel this is a case of international terrorism, and if Taiwan doesn't extradite these criminals, they will be harboring terrorists,'' Mr. Garchik said at a news conference here.
Â 
State Department Is Silent
A State Department spokesman in Washington said the department would have no comment at present because the case is a criminal matter and is being handled by the F.B.I.
Mr. Chen and two of the others named by the F.B.I. as the killers fled to Taiwan after the shooting. 
A fourth man identified as the driver of the car used by the killers, David Yu, a business executive from San Gabriel, near Los Angeles, was arrested at his home but then released last week because of insufficient evidence, the police said.
On Monday the San Mateo County District Attorney's office near here issued an arrest warrant for Mr. Chen, which is being forwarded to the United States Attorney's office in San Francisco to obtain Federal warrants for illegal flight from justice, a first step in trying to extradite Mr. Chen. However, the United States does not have an extradition treaty with Taiwan, with which it broke diplomatic relations in 1979.
Â 
Statement Is Demanded
Mr. Garchik, who represents the Committee to Obtain Justice for Henry Liu, demanded that Taiwan make it clear whether it would cooperate in extraditing the suspects.
Lieutenant Reese of the Daly City police said the police were close to getting warrants for the other suspects. 
''We know how it went down,'' Lieutenant Reese said of the slaying, which took place in Mr. Liu's garage.
The incident comes as the Reagan Administration is taking a heightened interest both in international terrorism and in the new development of Asian crime gangs in the United States.

file: SOVIET AIDE HINTS AT A CUT IN TROOPS ON CHINESE BORDER.txt
text:
ï»¿
A key member of the Central Committee of the Soviet Communist Party has told a group of Japanese journalists that talks with China could result in a pullback of troops from the Soviet-Chinese border.
Participants in a conference of Japanese and Soviet journalists being held here confirmed today that the Soviet official, Viktor G. Afanasyev, who is the editor of Pravda, the party newspaper, made the remark on Tuesday during a meeting at Pravda's offices.
The suggestion was similar to one that a Chinese official was reported as having made to Western journalists in Peking during a background discussion last month after the resumption of Soviet-Chinese negotiations.
Â 
Efforts at an Accommodation
Kyodo, the Japanese news agency, quoted Mr. Afanasyev as having said: ''It is possible that the two sides might promise each other a reduction of military forces in border areas.''
A reporter for the agency later said the quotation was accurate. 
(Although the United States has deliberately not been voicing public concern about the improvement of Soviet-Chinese relations, Washington officials say privately that they find the trend worrisome. 
Page A7.)
MOSCOW, Nov. 
17 - A key member of the Central Committee of the Soviet Communist Party has told a group of Japanese journalists that talks with China could result in a pullback of troops from the Soviet-Chinese border.
The indication that the Soviet Union might consider troop reductions along the frontier in the context of a general improvement of the relationship was not in itself new. 
But it attracted attention in the context of the change in the Soviet leadership and the renewed Soviet overtures to the Chinese.
Â 
Unusual Warmth for Chinese
The new Soviet leader, Yuri V. Andropov, signaled his attitude when he greeted the Chinese Foreign Minister, Huang Hua, with what appeared to be unusual warmth at a reception that followed Leonid I. Brezhnev's funeral on Monday. 
The next day Mr. Huang met with Foreign Minister Andrei A. Gromyko for 90 minutes in what was the highestlevel discussion between the Soviet Union and China since their Prime Ministers met in 1969.
The Soviet press has also given unusual prominence to Chinese condolence messages, printing them with those from the Soviet-bloc nations.
On Tuesday, Pravda and Izvestia, the two principal Soviet newspapers, published excerpts from an interview that Mr. Huang gave to the New China News Agency. 
In it, he said:
''Peace and friendship between China and the Soviet Union fully correspond not only to the interests of both peoples and both countries, but also to the interests of peace in Asia and the whole world.''
Western diplomats assessed the remark about a possible troop pullback as another carefully considered signal. 
Mr. Afanasyev, as the principal conveyor of official news to the Soviet people, is close to the Kremlin leadership. 
When he met with an American editor two weeks ago, he spoke in general terms about the new contacts with China and did not mention the possibility of troop reductions.
In his talk with the Japanese, he said that he thought Soviet troops ''will eventually withdraw'' from Afghanistan and that he did not think the issue could be settled militarily. 
The remark was not inconsistent with Soviet policy, which has called for a political settlement, but its timing seemed significant.
Mr. Afanasyev was quoted as having said that a senior Soviet official, whom he did not identify, had been conducting discussions on Afghanistan with ''concerned'' parties, including Pakistan. 
This appeared to be a hint that the Kremlin had been making a hitherto undisclosed bid to find diplomatic maneuvering room over the issue. 
Western proposals for an international conference have been repeatedly rejected.
The editor's remarks appeared to be fashioned as a response to the demands that China has made a condition for a return to normal relations. 
The demands, restated in recent months, are for a reduction of troops on the border, a Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan and an end to Soviet backing for the Vietnamese-installed Cambodian Government.
Mr. Afanasyev's remarks, as reported by Kyodo, also included references to the new political situation here. 
According to Kyodo, the Pravda editor alluded to some kind of power struggle after the death of Mr. Brezhnev. He did not elaborate, but Kyodo quoted him as having said that Mr. Brezhnev's chief of staff, Konstantin U. Chernenko, ''had the possibility'' of succeeding Mr. Brezhnev.
However, the Pravda editor was quoted as having said that ''many responsible, sincere men'' had chosen Mr. Andropov instead. 
The editor said vacancies would be filled in the two key bodies in the Soviet power structure, the Politburo and the Secretariat of the Central Committee, which together make up the Soviet leadership group. 
These additions are expected to be announced next week. 
However, Kyodo said, Mr. Afanasyev did not expect major changes of top figures because Mr. Andropov is ''a man of prudence.''

file: SOVIET ANNOUNCES DECISION TO TRIM ITS AFGHAN FORCE.txt
text:
ï»¿
Mikhail S. Gorbachev said today that the Soviet Union would withdraw six regiments from Afghanistan by the end of the year, and asked that the move be matched by a reduction of Western aid to the guerrillas.
In a televised speech from the Pacific coast city of Vladivostok, he also gave a noncommittal response to President Reagan's recent letter on arms control, and called for closer relations with China.
Western diplomats said the troop withdrawal would cut Soviet forces in Afghanistan by 6 percent. 
The number of soviet troops in Afghanistan is estimated at 120,000, and the number of Afghan guerrillas as high as 30,000.
Â 
Call for Verification
Mr. Gorbachev said the six regiments would be withdrawn in such a way as to make possible verification by ''anyone interested,'' presumably meaning American spy satellites. 
[In Washington, the Reagan Administration indicated it did not attach great importance to the announcement. 
In another move, the State Department proposed to a visiting Soviet official that the foreign ministers meet in mid-September to begin planning for a summit meeting. 
Page A7.] In the Vladivostok speech, Mr. Gorbachev said Mr. Reagan's reply on arms control had been delivered over the weekend. 
The letter ''sets one thinking'' and is being studied with ''responsibility and attention,'' Mr. Gorbachev said.
He said the Soviet reaction would depend on whether the American positions ''meet the principle of equal security'' and ''make it possible to reach effective joint solutions in the field of ending the arms race and preventing its spread to outer space.''
In Washington last week, officials said Mr. Reagan was prepared to delay deployment of space-based missile defense systems for up to seven years on condition that the Soviet Union agree to deployment after that period. 
Western diplomats said the fact that Mr. Gorbachev did not criticize or reject the latest American offer was a positive sign. 
But they cautioned that the Soviet Union was likely to have reservations since the offer was contingent on the continued development of space-based defenses.
On Afghanistan, Mr. Gorbachev said that the withdrawal of the six regiments ''must be answered'' by a reciprocal curtailment of Western aid to the guerrillas fighting Soviet and Afghan Government forces.
It was the first announced withdrawal of Soviet troops since they entered Afghanistan in December 1979.
Western diplomats said the withdrawal of the six regiments - one armored regiment, two motorized rifle regiments and three antiaircraft artillery regiments - was a token gesture that would not significantly reduce Soviet influence in Afghanistan, but might improve the climate for efforts to reach a political settlement.
Â 
Contingent on Western Response
Mr. Gorbachev indicated that no additional withdrawals would occur without a cutback in Western support for the guerrillas. 
If aid continues, he said, ''the Soviet Union will stand up for its neighbor.''
In the 1985 fiscal year, the United States gave the Afghan guerrillas $280 million in aid, mostly in the form of small arms, ammunition, support equipment and clothing, according to American officials.
Mr. Gorbachev said, ''The Soviet Union is striving to speed up a political settlement, to give it another impetus.''
He said that the Soviet Union and Afghanistan had worked out a timetable for the withdrawal of all Soviet forces, and that this schedule might be speeded up if a political settlement were worked out. 
He said there had been progress in indirect United Nations-mediated talks between Afghanistan and Pakistan.
At a round of talks in June, the Afghans said their agreement with the Soviet Union provided for a phased withdrawal over a four-year period. 
Pakistan and the United States called such a drawn-out schedule unrealistic.
Â 
View on Summit Talks Affirmed
On a second meeting with President Reagan, Mr. Gorbachev insisted that the talks should promote progress in arms control and help reduce tension.
The Soviet leader said he could not agree with the view that the accords reached at the first summit meeting in Geneva could ''be reduced simply to the promise of having more meetings.''
''No,'' Mr. Gorbachev said. 
''The main thing on which we agreed last time with President Reagan, and what we signed, is a consent to strive for normalization of relations and for improvement of the international situation and to speed the course of talks on the reduction of armaments.''
On the issue of medium-range missiles, he insisted that any proposed elimination of Soviet missiles in Europe would mean just that - elimination - and not the transfer of such missiles to Asia.
Mr. Gorbachev spent considerable time on the issue of Soviet-Chinese relations. 
He said these had noticeably improved in recent years, and offered talks on additional measures aimed at transforming what he described as the world's longest land frontier into a ''line of peace and friendship.''
Troop Cuts Offered to China He proposed talks on reductions in Soviet and Chinese land forces and noted that the two nations had similar priorities in developing and modernizing their economies. 
He suggested that the two countries might discuss the best ways of achieving these aims.
''Why not support each other?''
Mr. Gorbachev said.
He disclosed that the Soviet Union and China were working out an accord to renew joint water management projects in the Amur River basin on their border. 
Such a program had been worked out in the 1950's, but was canceled when the two countries began to drift apart.
Mr. Gorbachev said the Soviet Union was also preparing a ''positive reply'' to a Chinese proposal to renew construction of a railroad linking the Xinjiang Uighur Autonomous Region of China and the Soviet republic of Kazakhstan. 
Such a project was also begun in the 1950's.
The Soviet leader added that Moscow had offered to train Chinese astronauts for a joint space mission. 
Relations in Pacific Basin Reviewing political and economic relations in the Pacific basin, Mr. Gorbachev said, ''We clearly realize that that the United States is a great Pacific power with legitimate economic and political interests in the region.''
But, since the mid-1970's, he went on, the United States has conducted a military build-up that is turning the Pacific Ocean ''into an arena of military-political confrontation.''
During the same period, according to the Pentagon, the Soviet Union has also strengthened its forces in the Pacific.
To reduce tension, Mr. Gorbachev proposed, as a long-term objective, a conference of Pacific nations that would work out an agreement for cooperation similar to the 1975 Helsinki accord in Europe.
Even before such an ambitious undertaking, he added, the Pacific nations might come together to consider confidence-building measures and the nonuse of force, similar to measures now being worked out by the European nations in Stockholm.
He said such an Asian-Pacific security conference might be convened in a Soviet Pacific city, possibly even Vladivostok, which as a naval base is among Soviet cities now closed to foreigners. 
He said the Soviet Union might consider ending this restriction.
''We would like it to be our widely opened window to the east,'' he said, drawing an apparent analogy to the construction in the 18th century of the city of St. Petersburg (the present Leningrad) as a ''window to the west.''
Among other diplomatic initiatives, Mr. Gorbachev called for an improvement of relations between the Communist countries of Indochina - Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos - and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, a regional grouping made up of Burnei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand.
Mr. Gorbachev also proposed Soviet-American negotiations aimed at a reduction of Pacific naval forces, particularly nuclear-armed ships, and limitations on the deployment of antisubmarine weapons.
He suggested that the United States consider removing some or all of its military forces from the Philippines.
''If the United States gave up its military presence, say, in the Philippines, we would not leave this step unanswered,'' he said.

file: SOVIET PREMIER HINTS AT OVERTURE TO IMPROVE RELATIONS WITH CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
Prime Minister Nikolai A. Tikhonov said in an interview published here on Sunday that the Soviet Union is ''not going to keep from concrete steps'' toward improved relations with China, but that the process ''must not be one-sided.''
Mr. Tikhonov did not elaborate on the steps he had in mind. 
But his remark, in prepared answers to questions submitted by the Japanese newspaper Asahi, appeared to be the most positive signal from Moscow in several years on the frosty relationship with Peking.
Diplomats said it was not clear whether Mr. Tikhonov was giving an advance signal of a breakthrough or was summoning up the possibility of a rapprochement as a lever in the Soviet bid for improved relations with the United States. 
Since Washington and Peking began normalizing relations in 1971, all three capitals have engaged in feints and maneuvers of this kind.
Soviet Union's Prime Minister Nikloai Tikhonov hints at overture to improve relations with China
The Soviet Prime Minister coupled his comments on China with a review of Soviet-American relations and the situation in Poland. 
He urged the United States to abandon the ''language of power and diktat'' and to accept a ''smoothing'' of relations, and he said that it was ''staggering how reckless'' the United States and its allies were being in using the Polish situation to sour international relations.
But it was his comments on China that seemed to strike a fresh note. 
The 75-year-old Prime Minister balanced his overture to Peking by saying that ''the Chinese leaders, as is known, persistently follow in international affairs a course of animosity toward the Soviet Union, its allies and its friends.''
But even this formulation was milder than most that Soviet leaders have used in the two decades since the two nations fell into a rancorous dispute over ideology, territory and other issues.
Â 
'All This Cannot Be Ignored'
Mr. Tikhonov also alluded to the role that the closer relations between the United States and China have played in the equation by saying that ''there exist also other forces in the world that are pressing in every way for a further worsening of Soviet-Chinese relations.''
But it was his reference to possible improvement in the relationship that caught the eye of diplomats. 
Embassies here and in Peking have been alert to the possibility of a thaw since Moscow approached Peking last fall with a proposal that they revive talks about a new relationship that were broken off after the Soviet intervention in Afghanistan in late 1979.
''We have proceeded and continue to proceed from the view that there are no problems in Soviet-Chinese relations that could not be decided on the basis of equality and in the spirit of mutual understanding,'' Mr. Tikhonov said. 
''We are not going to keep from concrete steps that would meet vital aspirations and interests of the Soviet and Chinese peoples.''
''But this process must not be one-sided,'' he said. 
Any move to improve relations is likely to confront obstacles. 
Among them are the border dispute that led to armed clashes in 1969 and the Soviet role as the principal backer of Vietnam, which is in a state of tension with China over the Vietnamese occupation of Cambodia and other matters. 
In recent years the Kremlin has made a number of approaches to Peking seeking better ties, but the initiatives foundered each time.
Â 
'Scaring Themselves Stiff'
An indication of the Kremlin's perspective came in an article two weeks ago in the Government newspaper Izvestia, in which a commentator, Aleksandr Bovin, pointed to recent strains between Washington and Peking and predicted that the relationship would ultimately founder on differences in ideology and global interests. 
In the meantime, he said, ''as long as Americans are scaring themselves stiff with the 'Soviet threat,' they will always be haunted by the nightmare of normalization in Soviet-Chinese relations.''
Mr. Tikhonov's remarks on relations with the United States broke no fresh ground but were notable for continued stress on the need for the ''constructive dialogue'' that the Prime Minister advocated in a speech three weeks ago. 
Since then, Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. and Foreign Minister Andrei A. Gromyko met in Geneva for talks that produced no breakthroughs on arms control, Poland and other issues.
Mr. Tikhonov said ''a smoothing of Soviet-American relations'' would lessen international tensions and the risk of war, but added, ''Regrettably, there are so far no signs that things are moving in a favorable direction.''
Mr. Tikhonov also said that the American military buildup was futile. 
''Washington will not gain anything either by striving to introduce in diplomacy the language of power and diktat,'' he said.

The Soviet Union said today that President Reagan's remarks yesterday at a news conference confirmed his ''militaristic ideology.''
It said an American offer to sell weapons to China was ''provocative.''
Detailed reports by the official press agency Tass on the President's remarks and on the visit to China by Secretary of State Alexander M. Haig Jr. made it evident that Soviet leaders had found nothing to their liking in either.
Soviet Union says President Reagan's remarks at new conference confirmed his "militaristic ideology"
Describing Mr. Reagan's comments on arms controls, the plight of Communism, relations with China, military aid to Pakistan and American support for Israel, Tass said the President ''immediately made it clear that his Administration intended to pursue its objectives not by lessening tensions and building up mutually beneficial international cooperation and mutual understanding but by escalating nuclear terror and building up military strength as an instrument in blackmailing other countries.''
Â 
'Provocative Decision'
Tass asserted that the decision to lift restrictions against selling weapons to China was a ''provocative decision of the White House to supply Chinese hegemonists with offensive weapons which they could use against neighboring countries and peoples.''
But a separate dispatch on Mr. Haig's three-day visit to Peking gave only a tentative assessment of the development and no indication of its potential ramifications for Soviet foreign policy.
Tass accused Mr. Haig and the Chinese of joining in a conspiracy of aggression, imperialism and domination of other countries. 
The agency said that the United States would create opportunities for the Chinese to buy up-to-date American technology and equipment, ''including modern weapons.''
Tass noted that an agreement had been reached to expand military cooperation, and that a Chinese military mission would visit Washington to discuss it.
''Judging by the initial reports of the foreign mass media,'' Tass continued, ''this agreement has given grounds for legitimate concern not only to the Asian countries neighboring on China, against which Chinese expansionism is directed, but also to other parts of the world.''
The agency accused the Americans and Chinese of finding a ''commonality'' of aggressive aspirations around the world. 
Referring to Afghanistan and Cambodia, Tass said that the two sides ''confirmed their support for the Afghan counterrevolutionary rabble, the Pol Pot cutthroats and other Khmer reactionaries.''
The friendship proclaimed between Mr. Haig and his Peking hosts, Tass said, ''shows that the U.S. has found in Peking a welcome partner in carrying out its military strategic objectives and that Peking has stooped to teaming up directly with imperialism.''
The sharpest comments were predictably reserved for Mr. Reagan's critical comments about the Soviet Union and its governing system. 
''He besmirched in every way the socialist system and grossly slandered Soviet foreign and domestic policies,'' Tass said. 
On arms controls, Tass said that Mr. Reagan had ''mentioned only in passing'' a need to limit nuclear arsenals.

Nuclear Weapons in Europe

file: SOVIET SEEKS STATUS IN GATT.txt
text:
ï»¿
Faced with falling foreign trade volume and declining oil prices, the Soviet Union has recently made public its interest in becoming an observer at the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
At an unusually candid news conference here recently, Mikhail Pankine, who heads the Soviet Foreign Ministry's Department for International Economic Organizations, said Moscow viewed it as ''essential'' that it be granted such status, and be allowed to observe a new round of world trade talks expected late this year or early next year.
But diplomats here, headquarters of the 90-member GATT, which works to expand and liberalize world trade, say there is little chance that the Soviet Union would gain such observer status anytime soon. 
They said industrialized nations such as the United States and the European Economic Community would block the consensus decision needed for Soviet membership or observer status, for political as well as economic reasons.
'System Isn't Compatible'
''The fundamental thing is that the GATT is an organization for free trading countries and one which is geared on the free, open market system,'' one Western diplomat said. 
''The U.S.S.R., on the other hand, is so enormous that there's some fear that it could skew the whole system. 
Their system isn't compatible with the GATT anyway, and their form of state subsidies wouldn't lend itself to GATT discipline.''
A nominal precedent exists for letting a state-trading nation such as the Soviet Union join the GATT, since Soviet-bloc allies Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia and Rumania have long been members, and China already has observer status. 
But there the comparisons end, the diplomats say, because the four Warsaw Pact nation's economies are too small to make a difference, and China has already begun major economic reforms more adaptable to the GATT structure.
''First of all, China is actually seeking to return to membership in the organization, since it was in fact a founding member,'' the diplomat said. 
''Their economy, though one of state trading, is in a state of change and flux so I think that if negotiations with them do begin, it will be partly because people forsee a change in the Chinese system, and believe that membership in the GATT would encourage that, whereas we don't believe letting the Russians in would change anything.''
Â 
Way to Expand Foreign Trade
For the Soviet Union, joining the GATT would conceivably be one way of expanding its foreign trade, still regarded as minor in comparison to the United States, Western Europe and Japan. 
And such expansion could also shore up exports that declined dramatically last year.
According to the new report of the United Nation's Economic Commission for Europe, Moscow's exports to the Comecon countries stagnated last year, while exports to market economies plummeted by a staggering l4 percent. 
The report blamed winter disruptions of production and transport of Soviet raw material and fuel exports in early 1985, and the decline in world oil prices toward the end of the year.
The continued drop in oil prices could cost the Soviet Union between $4 billion and $5 billion in hard currency this year, or about 25 percent of its export earnings, the report noted. 
That is seen as a major factor that could spur the Soviet Union to move more aggressively into the world trading system by trying to join GATT.
Â 
Push to Soviet Union
''You can see the effects in the decline of oil revenues and how this could clearly be giving a push to those inside the Soviet Union who have been arguing for the advantages of getting into the trading system on a bigger scale,'' the diplomat said.
But besides the economic considerations cited by diplomats here, several envoys spoke of political considerations as well. 
The primary concern among Western nations, they said, is that Soviet entry into the GATT - one of the few United Nation specialized agencies they have refrained from joining - could politicize an agency that has so far largely avoided overly political debates.
''Clearly, the relationships with the Soviet Union are different, and many countries would be reluctant to have them join,'' another Western diplomat said. 
''There is the question of whether they would act in a political manner, rather than an economic manner, like they do in the General Assembly.''
Â 
'Different Size of Fish'
He continued, ''The East European nations which are already members don't tend to do that. 
They haven't been digested well by the GATT, but they're so small that we can handle it. 
The Soviet Union is a different size of fish altogether.''
The Soviet Union has yet to apply formally for observer status, which would be a stepping stone to membership, but it has been sounding the waters at the organization for three years. 
Nevertheless, some Western diplomats suggest that though the Soviet Union might see membership as ''essential,'' there is little likelihood of it being granted.
''Given the size of their economy, they couldn't avoid becoming a major player,'' one diplomat commented. 
''If we let them in, I don't think the GATT could continue to function as it has. 
We believe in fact that the GATT would cease to function as we know it.''

text:

The faculty council at St. John's University in Queens voted yesterday to reproach the president, the Rev. Joseph T. Cahill, for removing the Asian studies program from the Liberal Arts College and the Graduate School and making it a separate entity more directly under his control.
''The liberal arts faculty council hereby expresses its concern and displeasure at the removal and the manner of removal of the Asian studies program from St. John's College and the Graduate School,'' faculty representatives declared in their statement.
By its vote, the faculty registered its disapproval, but it has no power to change the president's action. 
Father Cahill could not be reached for comment yesterday, according to Charlotte Tomic of the school's public-information office.
The faculty council at St. John's University in Queens voted yesterday to reproach the president, the Rev. Joseph T. Cahill, for removing the Asian studies program from the Liberal Arts College and the Graduate School and making it a separate entity more directly under his control.
Asked before the vote why he had taken the action, Father Cahill said through a spokesman that it was ''an administrative decision made to insure the viability of the center's academic programs.''
But faculty members throughout the university asserted that the president should have sought their approval before acting. 
The vote stems from a longstanding dispute between the administration and the faculty over how to treat the study of China. 
The Asian studies program has become the arena for the conflict.
The administration continues to maintain ties formed in earlier years with Taiwan. 
Some faculty members feel this jeopardizes the academic integrity of the program.
While programs at other universities have been increasingly open to scholarly links with China, the mainland government, St. John's has not.
Directors of the program have served in the Taiwan government, there have been publishing ties with Taiwan and money from Taiwan has supported the program and helped build its headquarters.
The differences between Father Cahill and the faculty came to light last Memorial Day weekend in connection with a conference on Chinese literature in which scholars from China participated.
Â 
Asian Scholars Are Summoned
Three weeks later, the Asian studies faculty was summoned to meet with Father Cahill in his private dining room in Alumni Hall. 
''He called my conference 'diabolical,' '' said Jeffrey C. Kinkley, the professor who organized the conference and invited scholars from both China and Taiwan. 
Dr. Kinkley's observation was corroborated.
''Father Cahill has no recollection of making a statement like that,'' Martin Healy said on behalf of the president, who refused to speak to a reporter, but agreed to respond to questions submitted to Mr. Healy, the university's public-relations spokesman.
Last fall, Father Cahill appointed Yih-Young Chen as a vice president of the university and director of Asian studies. 
Dr. Chen until then was director of a bureau in Taiwan's Ministry of Education. 
He has a doctorate in computer science from Tulane University.
Dr. Peter Nosco, who was associate dean for Asian studies until his removal after he had approved plans for the literature conference, Dr. Kinkley, who has a doctorate from Harvard in East Asian languages, and several other young scholars were hired in recent years, signifying an apparent intention to upgrade the program.
The Asian studies program was established at St. John's in 1959, and its first director was Paul K.T. 
Sih, who headed it until his death in 1978.
Dr. Sih had served Taiwan in its embassy in Rome, according to his autobiography. 
He took great pride in the building that was erected in 1973 to house the Asian studies program.
It is a pagoda-like structure with a yellow tile roof, contrasting with the nondescript, boxy buildings that make up most of the rest of the campus in Jamaica, Queens, overlooking the Grand Central Parkway.
Asked where the money had come from to erect the building, Mr. Healy said he would not release the names of donors, but Dr. Chen said the structure was ''a gift from the Republic of China,'' Taiwan.
In the mid-1970's, the program was prodded to give up its authority to grant doctorates, after a review by the State Education Department.
One of the outside reviewers, Charles O. Huck, a professor at the University of Michigan, said recently that ''the whole operation seemed pro-Taiwan,'' and that objective scholarship in that atmosphere would have been ''impossible.''
The program continues to offer bachelor's and master's degrees. 
Although the university press stopped operating in the 1970's, St. John's published a biography of Chiang Kai-shek under its imprint in 1981.

file: STAMPS_FROM THE FAR EAST.txt
text:
ï»¿
While diplomats negotiate and nations go to war over international boundaries, stamp collectors remain unaffected by the winds of change. 
Nowhere is that better found than in the treatment of China. 
In stamp catalogues there are two Chinas.
The Scott Standard Postage Stamp Catalogue begins its China listings with the 1878 issues of the Imperial Maritime Customs Post. 
The large and small dragon issues have been the subject of intensive study and award-winning exhibits. 
The Imperial Chinese Post issues of 1898 were overprinted in 1912 to serve as the first issues at the time of the Chinese revolution.
The Communist revolution led by Mao Tse-tung changed the political geography of China in 1949. 
But in the catalogue, the China listings are the ''Republic of China (Taiwan)'' including the provincial issues and a separate section for ''China (People's Republic).''
Pre-Communist China listings end with Scott number 1006. 
The first Taiwan stamp is assigned N1007, while the first People's Republic stamp is assigned N1, the treatment normally accorded the issue of a new nation.
This arrangement reflects philatelic reality. 
While the issues of China have taken on increasing popularity, most serious collectors emphasize the early issues and continue their collections with the stamps of Taiwan and China.
The China Stamp Society is the major specialist group in this country devoted to the stamps and postal history of China. 
The society's quarterly journal is entitled ''China'', emphasizing the unified collecting approach. 
Information on the society can be obtained from Mr. Frederick deRidder, Secretary, The China Stamp Society, 100 Font Boulevard, San Francisco, Calif. 
94132.
Much of the challenge and the frustration encountered by collectors of Chinese stamps and covers stems from complexity of Chinese characters. 
The identification of Chinese stamps and cancellations is the subject of a new study by Michael Rogers of Winter Park, Fla. 
''The English-Chinese Philatelic Dictionary & Identification Key'' is a 59-page, 8 1/2 by 11-inch publication that unravels much of the mystery in understanding these characters.
The guide includes a dictionary that translates 300 philatelic terms, dates and colors, a section that translates Chinese characters and another that identifies and locates the towns and provinces.
Guides to the two Chinese systems of year numbering - essential in dating covers - and conversions of Chinese names using the three major translation systems plus an index for character identification and a locator map complete this comprehensive work. 
It is available for $11 from Michael Rogers, Inc., 340 Park Avenue North, Winter Park, Fla. 
32789.
Also available is a copy of the catalogue for their latest specialized Asia and worldwide airpost postal auction and their all-China Price List. 
Each is offered for $1 or will be sent free of charge with the Dictionary & Identifier.
The China area offers new issue collectors the dual advantages of some of the loveliest issues found anywhere and the existence of two postal entities to maintain a steady flow of new material. 
Despite their political differences, the historical, cultural and social similarities of China and Nationalist China are evident in their new issues.
China does lean more towards industrial and political themes, while Nationalist China emphasizes the great traditions of Chinese culture. 
But there are common themes, such as the 1984 Summer Olympics and the veneration of Sun Yat-sen.
The latest releases from Nationalist China are highlighted by four colorful stamps issued Feb. 
20 that depict Chinese flower arrangements. 
A yearbook picturing all issues of 1985 also was released on that date. 
March 20 saw the release of a souvenir sheet and four singles celebrating the 90th anniversary of the postal service.
On March 26 a single commemorative honoring the revolutionary martyr Chen Tien-hua was issued.

These stamps are available from local dealers and mail order new issue specialists.

Hospitals Issue
A United States commemorative stamp honoring this nation's public hospitals was issued Friday by the United States Postal Service. 
Peter E. Voss, vice-chairman of the Postal Service Board of Governors, was the principal speaker at the first day of issue ceremony conducted at New York's Bellevue Hospital Center which is celebrating its 250th anniversary this year.
The history of public hospitals dates back to the almshouses in 16th century England. 
The closing of religious institutions in the 1530's by Henry VIII made care of the sick a public responsibility. 
Acts of Parliament subsequently placed on local communities the responsibility for physically and mentally ill, aged and homeless.
The almshouses and workhouses brought together the poor, the sick and the petty criminals. 
The able-bodied were forced to earn their keep, while those who could not work were housed in cheap, often-unhealthy quarters.
By the 1700s, voluntary hospitals supported by charity and run by prominent citizens began to flourish in England. 
These institutions attracted distinguished physicians through the social contacts of board members. 
They also offered medical teaching facilities.
The American colonies adopted this dual system of hospitals. 
The earliest public almshouse to evolve into a hospital was opened in Philadelphia around 1731. 
It eventually became Philadelphia General Hospital. 
In New York City, the House of Correction, Workhouse and Poorhouse opened in 1736. 
That facility was the forerunner of today's Bellevue Hospital Center, a complex that is one of the largest hospitals in the country. 
With the closing of Philadelphia General in 1977, Bellevue became America's oldest active public hospital.
The Public Hospitals stamp follows a growing pattern caused by the need to limit the number of commemoratives issued each year while still recoginzing deserving institutions and organizations. 
The Postal Service's announcement and selection of a first day site singled out Bellevue on the occasion of an important anniversary, but the stamp is a generic salute to public hospitals.
In contrast, a 1964 commemorative singled out the Mayo brothers, who founded the Mayo Clinic in Minnesota. 
These are the only two United States stamps issued to honor health institutions in this country.
The sterile modern design by Uldis Purins of Newton, Mass. is an abstract presentation of a hospital with the familiar blue and white ''H'' road sign that leads motorists to hospitals. 
The artist demonstrates an ability to produce attractive traditional work in the 1985 Public Education issue.
Collectors desiring first day covers are encouraged to purchase the Public Hospital stamps and affix them to envelopes before sending for first day cancels. 
The stamps are on sale at local post offices. 
Deadline for placing orders is May 11. 
A return address should be placed in the lower right of each envelope submitted, with a peelable label suggested for this purpose. 
Such envelopes should be sent to Customer-Affixed Envelopes, Public Hospitals Stamp, Postmaster, New York, N.Y. 
10001-9991.
The address for covers without stamps affixed is Public Hospitals Stamp, Postmaster, New York, N.Y. 
10001-9992. Covers without stamps affixed should be accompanied by personal check or money order for 22 cents per stamp, to a maximum of 50 covers. 
Postage stamps are not acceptable as payment.
Â 
Spellman Museum
The Cardinal Spellman Philatelic Museum will conduct its annual Philatelic Literature Fair and stamp bourse next Saturday and Sunday. 
The museum is one of the few of its kind in the United States. 
It is located at 235 Wellesley Street, Weston, Mass.
The museum was founded in 1963 through a generous gift to Cardinal Spellman from the estate of Mrs. Mabel Gilman Corey. 
Cardinal Spellman was an avid philatelist who donated his collection to the Sisters of St. Joseph in Boston. 
The Sisters administer Regis College in Weston and it was on a grant of land from Regis that the museum was built. 
The collection of the National Philatelic Museum, formerly located in Philadelphia, also is housed in the Spellman Museum.
The museum's facilities and services includes meeting space for local clubs and national conventions, adult courses in philately, research and circulating libraries and a publications program. 
Information is available on membership privileges and the tax-deductibility of donations to the museum.

Opinions III
The Philatelic Foundation recently released ''Opinions III'', the latest volume in its highly-regarded series. 
The book is available for $29.50 from dealers who carry philatelic literature or from The Philatelic Foundation, 270 Madison Avenue, New York, N.Y. 
10016. The Opinions series was initiated in 1983. 
Each of the books issued to date contains articles by America's leading philatelic experts. 
They provide insights into the examination and evaluation of stamps and covers and information on how collectors can avoid costly purchases of misdescribed material and fakes.
Opinions III comprises 226 pages and 36 articles on some of the more challenging or revealing pieces to have been submitted to The Philatelic Foundation in its 40-year history. 
United States, British Commonwealth and general foreign material is covered. 
Because the same expertizing techniques and tools can be applied in a variety of situations, the Opinions books are useful to most collectors interested in the examination of stamps and covers and in the condition factors that affect their value. 
A liberal use of photographs, including high-magnification views, adds to the usefulness of the book.

Literature
Further information on the 1851-57 issue, and on stamps generally, can be found in the Scott Specialized Catalogue. 
It is available from stamp dealers and in many libraries.

10036.

On March 7 the Marshall Islands released two high-value definitives as the fourth section in its current maps and navigation series. 
A $2 issue depicts two atolls in the Radak Chain. 
A $5 stamp shows a map of Bikini atoll.
In addition to the atolls on the $2 issue, a depiction of Mercator's terrestrial globe is depicted. 
Mercator is credited with solving the problem of displaying the earth as a flat surface, using a cylindrical projection that is cut open. 
The navigational aid on the $5 is one-half of a stick chart, the first half having been shown on a previously-issued 20-cent issue.
Each stamp in the series illustrates a map of one or more atolls that make up this trust territory administered by the United States on behalf of the United Nations.

In conjunction with the First Day of Issue, the World Federation of United Nations Associations (Wfuna) will offer an exquisite First Day Cover that features a reproduction of Chinese artist Chen Yifei's ''Bridge of Peace'' oil painting.

Chen Yifei will be at the Wfuna counter in the lower concourse of the United Nations General Assembly Building on May 10 to greet collectors and autograph First Day Covers.

Two new additions to the United States Transportation Series were issued last month in Oil Center, N. M. A 10.1-cent stamp depicts an 1890's oil wagon and a 12.5-cent stamp features an 1880's pushcart.

Please note that covers must bear at least 22c postasge to cover the first class rate. 
All stamps affixed by the collector must have been issued no later than April 18. 
For Postal Service affixing, one oil wagon and one pushcart stamp will be applied to each cover at a charge of 23 cents per envelope submitted.
All orders must be postmarked no later than May 18. 
Cash or postage stamps are not acceptable. 
Personal checks are accepted up to a limit of 50 covers. 
The address for customer-affixed envelopes is Customer-Affixed Envelopes, Oil Wagon (or Pushcart) Stamp, Postmaster, Oil Center, NM 88266-9992. 
$10.75 Stamp On Monday in San Francisco, the United States Postal Service will issue a $10.75 stamp intended primarily for use on items weighing up to two pounds and sent via Express Mail Service. 
Available in singles or in booklets containing one pane of three stamps, the $10.75 stamp is similar in design to its predecessor $9.35 edition.

94188-9991.

94188-9992. Personal checks or money orders will be accepted at $10.75 per stamp to a limit of 50 covers.

text:
