Molly Yard, who was elected Saturday to guide the National Organization for Women through politically critical times, described herself today as a born feminist and the spiritual descendant of Eleanor Roosevelt.
At a news conference this morning, Ms. Yard recounted the circumstances of her birth in China, as the third daughter of Methodist missionaries there, and said her upbringing there helped mold her feminist views.
''My father's male Chinese friends said that was a fate worse than death, to have daughters and no sons,'' she recalled. 
''They gave him a gift of commiseration, a brass wash basin, and I grew up in a society that devalued girls and women.''
Â 
Efforts on NOW's Agenda
Ms. Yard, who is in her 70's but steadfastly refuses to divulge her precise age, is taking over as NOW's president as the 150,000-member organization enters its third decade. 
On its agenda are determined efforts to block the confirmation of Judge Robert H. Bork for a seat on the Supreme Court, to insure the continuation of legalized abortion and to promote Representative Patricia Schroeder of Colorado for the Democatic nomination for President.
But Ms. Yard's election also comes at a time when some are questioning whether NOW represents a broad spectrum of American women, many of whom are concerned with subtler and more personal issues, like the family and career goals.
But her sweeping victory, along with those of her running mates for vice president and secretary, was interpreted here as approval by the NOW membership of the approach to public issues taken by the departing president, Eleanor C. Smeal, who favored visible confrontational tactics.
Ms. Yard vowed repeatedly during the three-day convention in the Wyndham Franklin Plaza Hotel here that the organization would continue to be heard in the most public ways possible, including street demonstrations.
''Our first action will be to continue what has already been begun: to stop the Bork confirmation,'' Ms. Yard said. 
She also vowed that the group would picket the Vatican mission in Washington for five days starting on Aug. 
26 to protest the Vatican's position on abortion and birth control. 
''In October,'' she added, ''we will participate in a major way in a march for lesbian and gay rights.''
But, clearly in response to criticism of the group's past confrontational efforts, she emphasized that NOW would be active on other fronts, too: filing lawsuits, promoting legislation favorable to women, working for the election of women at all levels of office and leading the bandwagon for the Mrs. Schroeder candidacy. 
$350,000 for Schroeder On Saturday, NOW members pledged more than $350,000 to Mrs. Schroeder's campaign, enough to qualify for Federal matching funds. 
That, Ms. Yard said, demonstrates the organization's clout and ''said volumes about where our heads and hearts are.''
In addition to continuing Ms. Smeal's policies, Ms. Yard will apparently also follow her predecessor's style. 
As Ms. Smeal does, she speaks in ringing, emotional tones. 
In her final campaign speech she vowed to rally more than a million marchers on behalf of an equal rights amendment to the Constitution and in opposition to military spending and toxic waste. 
She declared: ''The only war we seek is the war to end poverty, ignorance and disease.''
Ms. Yard is reticent about divulging details about her life. 
A close associate said that although she had known Ms. Yard for 30 years, she knew little about her personal life.
Ms. Yard was born Mary Alexander Yard but prefers to be called Molly. 
She reminds many of the old-school liberal activist of the Roosevelt era, and indeed, she described Eleanor Roosevelt as ''my second mother.''
She said that in the 1930's she was a member of the American Student Union, a radical organization that was critical of Roosevelt's New Deal policies. 
She said Eleanor Roosevelt called her once to discuss her criticisms. 
''Out of that we became close friends,'' she said.
Â 
A Protest at Swarthmore
After having been educated in China, both by a tutor at home and later in the school system, Ms. Yard attended Swarthmore College, graduating in 1933.
It was there that she got her first taste of public protest. 
After a Jewish student was denied admission to the sorority to which Ms. Yard belonged, she was so angered that she worked to abolish the sorority and fraternity structure on the campus.
After graduation, and with the nation still in the throes of the Depression, she became a social worker in Pennsylvania. 
But she soon became disillusioned with the system and turned to political activism.
Through the years she has been active in trade union and civil rights causes, and she was involved in efforts that led to the equal apportionment for men and women of delegate positions at the Democratic National Convention.''I worked for years in the Democratic Party,'' she said, ''but as a woman I always felt left out of the process. 
I never dreamed of going to the convention as a delegate, for example.''
Ms. Yard was also active in Philadelphia politics, serving in the early 1950's in the Democratic administrations of Mayor Joseph Clark.
Mrs. Yard moved from Philadelphia to Pittsburgh in 1953 and in 1956 she helped coordinate Mr. Clark's campaign for the United States Senate.
She herself sought public office in 1964, winning the Democrat nomination for a seat on the state legislature but losing in the general election.
In the mid-1970's she turned her efforts to NOW causes and became a key figure in the organization's campaign for ratification of the proposed equal rights amendment. 
Securing a constitutional amendment remains the centerpiece of her program.
Before being elected president, she served as NOW's political director. 
She is also vice president of the Americans for Democratic Action.
Â 
Met Mao in China
Since her childhood, Ms. Yard has returned to China twice, the first time in 1938 when she met Mao Zedong and other leaders. 
In June of this year, she visited Beijing and presented leaders with a journal from her years in China.
Ms. Yard, a resident of Ligonier, Pa., has been married for 48 years to Sylvester Garrett, a labor arbitrator. 
They have two sons, James, a 43-year-old assistant United States attorney in Pittsburgh, and John, 39, a doctoral candidate in forestry at the State University of New York at Syracuse, and a daughter, Joan Garrett-Goodyear, 45, a professor of English at Smith College. 
They also have four grandchildren.
Few people at the convention were neutral about her candidacy. 
Some said they were concerned that, as a longtime friend of Ms. Smeal and her close ally in the organization's frequently bitter internal politics, Ms. Yard would continue to run an autocratic administration and would be a surrogate for Ms. Smeal. Some also contended that her stirring rhetoric masked a lack of pragmatic strategy.
But the vote to elect her, 940 to 629, and the comments made in meeting rooms and hallways indicated that those criticisms represented a minority view.
Alma Steed Fox, a national board member from Pittsburgh, and a longtime colleague in rights battles with Ms. Yard, said: ''One reason I support her is that to a certain extent she will be a continuation of Ellie. 
But she has a mind of her own, too. 
And she certainly will not be a quiet leader.''

text:

During World War I, thousands of illiterate Chinese laborers were brought to France to help dig trenches. 
They were desperately homesick, working 14 hours a day and unable even to write to their families. 
A young Chinese-born Yale University student arrived eager to help.
''I made a discovery there,'' Dr. Y. C. James Yen recalled the other day. 
''I discovered these human beings, in effect, buried for 3,000 years, despised and rejected.''
He became first their scribe and then their instructor.
International Institute of Rural Reconstruction founder Dr Y C James Yen to be awarded People to People Eisenhower Medallion for his work with poor worldwide; his portrait (M)
Dr. Yen, who is approaching his 90th birthday, looks back on his ''discovery'' as the starting point of a career teaching and training millions of illiterate peasant farmers in the developing countries of Asia, Africa and Latin America.
In recognition of the success of the international movement he still helps lead, Dr. Yen is to be awarded the People to People Eisenhower Medallion on Oct. 
26, his birthday.
Â 
Dinner to Be Given at U.N.
The date also marks the 23d anniversary of the founding of his International Institute of Rural Reconstruction, the network through which his program works. 
And there will be a dinner at the United Nations on the same day given in his honor by David Rockefeller. 
Several generations of Rockefeller family members have supported Dr. Yen's work.
''The institute is what I call a 'power- releasing' organization,'' said Dr. Yen, sitting in his office on Broadway in Manhattan, which serves as the American headquarters of the institute. 
''We do not offer relief to the poor, but release,'' he said, underscoring the institute's self-help approach.
The institute's main training center is in Cavite Province in the Philippines. 
There are affiliated organizations elsewhere in the Philippines, Thailand, Ghana, Guatemala, Colombia and India. 
But much of the work is carried out in villages in impoverished rural areas where the institute's staff tests the agricultural, public health, family planning and educational techniques developed in the Philippines.
Â 
Self-Help Concept Preserved
Methods have changed over the years. 
Computers are now used to check research in crop improvement, for example. 
But the basic concept of self help has been preserved and has been a continuing thread through Dr. Yen's work since his wartime encounter with the Chinese laborers in France.
When World War I broke out, Dr. Yen volunteered to go to Europe with the Young Men's Christian Association. 
At first, the homesick Chinese workers begged him to write their letters and he obliged.
But then he stopped, insisting that the workers had to learn to read and write. 
He began with ''40 daring souls willing to spend an hour each night struggling to learn.''
Because they lacked textbooks, he started a newsletter, he said, adding, ''I was in my 20's, a good age for a revolutionary, and I didn't know the difficulties I faced and I was not timid.''
The experience in France led him to return to China, committed to helping the poor through a mass education movement. 
He moved from Peking to a district of villages in Hopeh Province, persuading fellow scholars to join and bring their families.
Â 
Simplified Vocabulary Used
He developed teaching methods using a simplified written vocabulary of 1,000 Chinese characters. 
He also broadened the instruction to include improved farming methods and public health. 
Health workers were trained to teach disease prevention and immunize the villagers, a practice that gained acceptance throughout China.
In 1928, Dr. Yen returned to the United States, in part seeking support for the growing movement. 
He was introduced to John D. Rockefeller Jr., who offered a personal gift of $100,000 if other donors would contribute. 
In all, $500,000 was raised.
In 1936, the work in Hopeh Province was shifted to the west when the Japanese invaded China. 
After the war, Dr. Yen returned to the United States seeking assistance for rural reconstruction. 
As a result, Washington authorized a $27.5 million program under a Chinese-American Joint Commission on Rural Reconstruction.
The commission's work in China was aborted 16 months later, however, when civil war erupted, but was continued on Taiwan. 
Later, Dr. Yen's work was moved to the Philippines. 
Besides the six autonomously operated affiliates, the institute has trained 600 specialists from 37 countries since its establishment in 1963.

Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang of China addressed a joint session of Canada's Parliament today and praised Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau for his efforts to quell a nuclear arms race that ''is becoming white hot.''
Mr. Zhao, the first Communist official ever to address a joint session of the Canadian House of Commons and Senate, was warmly received by politicians of all parties.
In his speech, the Chinese Prime Minister assessed his country's relations with Canada, the United States, the Soviet Union and Britain. 
The speech, for the most part, repeated views expressed in Mr. Zhao's visit to the United States, but it also included references to the Canadian leader's peace initiative in which Mr. Trudeau has had consultations with more than 30 world leaders in the last two months.
China's Prime Min Zhao Ziyang addresses joint session of Canada's Parliament and praises Canada's Prime Min Pierre Elliott Trudeau for his efforts to quell nuclear arms race (S)Zhao's Visit to Last a Week
''We appreciate the efforts made by Prime Minister Trudeau to safeguard world peace, relax international tension and promote nuclear disarmament,'' said Mr. Zhao, who started his weeklong visit to Canada, the first by a high Chinese official, with the address in the House of Commons.
As opposition politicians listened to the translation from Chinese, Mr. Zhao continued, ''We support his appeal for participation from all political leaders of the world in the cause of safeguarding peace.''
''There are hot spots in the world,'' he said, ''and the nuclear arms race is becoming white hot.''
A key element of Mr. Trudeau's proposals has been to open up the issue of disarmament to political debate and political pressures, removing it from exclusive jurisdiction of bureaucrats,
Â 
whom he has disdained as ''nuclear accountants.''
Â 
'Nations Go Into Action'
Mr. Zhao alluded at one point to Mr. Trudeau's attempt to stimulate action by nations other than the superpowers in the face of United States-Soviet standoff on disarmament and military balance.
He expressed his hope that all ''peace-loving nations go into action to urge the two major nuclear powers, who represent 90 percent of the world's nuclear weapons, to stop the nuclear arms race, resume disarmament talks and agree on measure to drastically reduce nuclear arms to create conditions for joint disarmament by all nuclear countries.''
There was no mention, however, of a conference of the five avowed nuclear nations, which was the hardest item in Mr. Trudeau's proposal. 
The Chinese leadership brushed aside the proposal when Mr. Trudeau raised it on his visit to Peking in November.
After praising what he termed the historic and special relations between Canada and China, Mr. Zhao assessed his visit to the United States, characterizing his talks with President Reagan as ''friendly, candid and serious.''
Â 
'Fairly Big Progress' He said relations with the United States ''have made fairly big progress'' since the establishent of diplomatic relations, with the question of Taiwan reminaing the outstanding obstacle.
By contrast, he said, Peking's relations with Moscow have only ''somewhat improved'' after three rounds of talks.
In these meetings, he said, the Soviet Union has ''evaded'' discussion of what he described as the three major obstacles - Moscow's support for the Vietnemese in Cambodia, its military involvement in Afghanistan and its deployment of troops on the Chinese border in Mongolia.

text:

A San Francisco newspaper characterized him as ''more an amiable panda than a Chinese tiger.''
Michael K. Deaver, a White House official, called him ''very charming and most pleasant to be with.''
With a warm personality and a message of friendship and cooperation, Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang of China seemed to evoke a positive response wherever he has appeared.
But beyond the atmospherics, he presented another side, the competent and tough Communist leader holding firm to positions on Taiwan and other touchy subjects.
Article on visit to US by Chinese Prime Min Zhao Ziyang, who, despite positive response he has presented during visit, is holding firm to positions to Taiwan and other touchy subjects; notes Zhao has indicated he is flexible enough not to make Taiwan obstacle to cooperation with US and at same time stressed importance of issue (M)
''He has the ability to be charming,'' said Mr. Deaver, ''without giving up any of his positions. 
Sort of like Reagan.''
A former United States Government official who met Mr. Zhao said he had been impressed with this blend of sophistication and realism.
''He is intelligent and well prepared and he knows quite clearly why he came here,'' the former official said. 
''He was not conciliatory on matters that he felt he needed to be clear and strong on. 
But he also indicated areas where he thought United States and Chinese interests coincide.''
Mr. Zhao seemed successful in accomplishing two aims: maintaining the momentum that has marked American-Chinese relations, and showing that he has the ability to handle foreign policy as well as economic affairs at home.
Before his visit, experts said that the way he handled the Taiwan issue - whether he let it become a sticking point - would be the key to the success of his trip.
In Washington, San Francisco and New York, Mr. Zhao put forth a clear message. 
He indicated that he was flexible enough not to make Taiwan an obstacle to cooperation with the United States. 
At the same time, he stressed the importance of the issue as ''the principal obstacle to the growth of Chinese-United States relations.''
In a 40-minute meeting yesterday with Zbigniew Brzezinski, President Jimmy Carter's national security adviser, Mr. Zhao voiced concern that people in the United States might not understand the attitudes of the Chinese Communist leaders on the issue.
''They are concerned that we don't appreciate the depth of their feelings on the subject, and they are probably right,'' Mr. Brezinski said later. 
''But I told him that if he makes the issue the main bone of contention, it could have consequences neither we nor they wish.''
In speeches across the country to Chinese-American groups and businessmen, Mr. Zhao sought to educate the public on China's stance and to marshal support.
In San Francisco, he promised that Taiwan could maintain its own military, trade policy and judicial system.
''China's reunification and rejuvenation is the common aspiration of the whole Chinese nation, including those living in Taiwan and abroad,'' Mr. Zhao said. 
''We will respect history and reality and will take into consideration the wishes of the Taiwan people. 
It is not a case of the mainland swallowing up Taiwan.''
At a news conference the next day, he refused to rule out the use of force against Taiwan, in words similar to those that his aides said he had used with President Reagan.
''We cannot undertake the commitment only to use peaceful means because it is an internal affair to be resolved by the Chinese themselves,'' Mr. Zhao said, adding that Peking wanted the United States to stay out of the problem and ''not place any obstacles'' in the way of reunification.
He indicated that Taiwan would not be a roadblock. 
When asked whether Peking would drop talks with Washington if the Taiwan Relations Act were not repealed, he said that, if the law could not be repealed, he hoped the United States would act in accord with joint communiques on Taiwan.
In exchange for diplomatic relations with Peking as of Jan. 
1, 1979, Washington ended its diplomatic and treaty ties with the Nationalists in Taiwan, but reserved the right to supply Taiwan with defensive arms.

First a small flashing robot stepped on the Chinese Prime Minister's toes. 
Then a 7-foot Colombian boa constrictor stuck out its forked tongue at him.

Mr. Zhao was on the road in America, seeing unofficial pursuits and ordinary citizens after leaving the high- level talks and cocktail parties of Washington behind him.
Chinese Prime Min Zhao Ziyang continues nine-day tour of US with visit to students and scholars at University of California's Lawrence Hall of Science, Berkeley, Calif; White House chief of staff Michael K Deaver, who is traveling with Zhao on his California visit, comments (M)

The visit showed off the style that has endeared Mr. Zhao to many Chinese - a down-to-earth practicality, an unassuming but self-confident air and an easy manner.
Â 
'Charming and Most Pleasant'
''He's very charming and most pleasant to be around,'' said Michael K. Deaver, the deputy White House chief of staff, who is traveling with the Prime Minister on his California visit. 
''And he has a wonderful sense of humor.''
Mr. Zhao's visit to Berkeley started with a welcome from students waving the Chinese flag and a greeting from a 2-foot-high robot named RE5X that was a ringer for R2D2 of ''Star Wars'' fame. 
Wearing a T-shirt emblazoned with a panda, the robot wheeled up to the Prime Minister and failed to stop, as planned, nudging the Prime Minsiter's toe.

Enjoy your visit.''
Â 
Visits Elementary Students
After a break for Chinese green tea, the Prime Minister visited some grade- school students who were performing experiments in the biology and physics labs.

Â 
exhibit of dead insects by Donald Dahlsten, a professor of entomology.

Agriculture a Main Interest

The Prime Minister's style on this trip contrasts somewhat to that of Deng Xiaoping, the paramount Chinese leader, who toured the United States in 1979.

By contrast, Mr. Zhao is friendly and warm but somewhat stiff.

His style is perhaps best illustrated by the way he has handled the Taiwan issue.

Mr. Zhao pressed his case for reunification strongly and clearly with President Reagan and in meetings with business leaders and Chinese Americans. 
At a cocktail party with Chinese- American leaders, he promised that Taiwan could maintain its own military, trade policy and judicial system.

'He's Done His Homework'
But he did not let himself be backed into a corner.

Mr. Zhao said he had not yet considered what to tell his family about his American visit when he returns home.

Zhao Ziyang held his Tiffany's crystal seal of New York aloft, showing the assembled crowd his latest American gift.
''Turn it around,'' Mayor Koch told Mr. Zhao. ''You're holding it backwards.''
And so began an encounter yesterday between the Mayor of New York and the Prime Minister of China. 
For the first time during his nine-day tour of America, Mr. Zhao shed his deliberate, and somewhat stiff, demeanor and seemed to relax and enjoy himself at a Gracie Mansion lunch in his honor.
Chinese Prime Min Zhao Ziyang visits New York City during his 9-day tour of US; appears to enjoy banter with Mayor Koch during luncheon in Zhao's honor at Gracie Mansion; photos (M)
Catches the Mayor's Style
He caught the Mayor's bantering style and deftly lobbed it back, with a wit and animation that charmed the 80 assembled guests, mostly New York City and State officials.
The Mayor quickly set the tone when he said that, in a private meeting, the two men had exchanged views. 
''But because of protocol,'' he said, ''I can't tell you how we disposed of Hong Kong, Vietnam and other problems.''
Then Mr. Koch strayed from his prepared remarks to tell the Prime Minister about the recent visit to New York of the Mayor of Peking, Chen Xitong. 
''You should promote him,'' he said, adding an aside to the audience that he hoped that Mayor Chen would ''do the same for me.''
Then it was Mr. Zhao's turn. 
He raised his arm above his head and said archly, through an interpreter, ''As far as my personal wishes are concerned, I would like to see Mayor Koch promoted to an ever higher and higher position.''
As the Mayor and his guests roared with laughter, Mr. Zhao continued with a neat jab at the Taiwan issue he has been talking about all week in more serious tones.
''But I don't think I can make this a commitment in front of the reporters because if I did that, the State Department will complain that the Premier of China is interfering in U.S. internal affairs.''
That is exactly the phrase he has been using to explain why the United States should not interfere in the Taiwan issue.
And so they went, back and forth. 
Asked why he was serving the Prime Minister marinated scallops and chicken Florentine instead of the ''authentic American beef stew'' he had promised, Mr. Koch shrugged, ''I looked in the wrong pot.''
Before lunch, the Prime Minister was given a grand - and swift - Gotham tour. 
As hundreds of police officers blocked off city streets, his 30-car motorcade left the Plaza Hotel.
Most New Yorkers didn't give the procession a second look, except those who loudly cursed the traffic snarl it caused.
One tourist staying in the hotel, however, turned to another in wonder.

''Do you think it's a soap opera star?''
''I hope it's Burt Reynolds,'' her friend replied.
Â 
Visits the Met
Accompanied by a coterie that included the United States Ambassador to Peking, Arthur W. Hummel Jr., and the Chinese Ambassador to Washington, Zhang Wenjin, Mr. Zhao started with an early trip to the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

He was given two presents by museum officials: a book on the Met's Chinese treasures and a film showing the construction of the Ming garden, which opened in 1981.
At the World Trade Center, Mr. Zhao received yet another gift, this time a silver medallian showing the activities of the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey.
''I hope you will recommend businessmen here participate in China's modernization,'' Mr. Zhao told Alan Sagner, chairman of the Port Authority.
Â 
Sees Statue of Liberty
It was a theme he has repeated often in his meetings with Americans, both in Washington and in San Francisco, where he spent two days before coming to New York.

Some suggested that the resignation would be felt most keenly in Europe, where Mr. Haig had special ties dating from his days as commander of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization's military forces, and in China.
At the same time, specialists throughout the political spectrum praised Mr. Haig's successor, George P. Shultz, but raised questions about his business connections in the Middle East.

file: _WHITE RAJAHS_ LINGER IN A MALAYSIAN TOWN.txt
text:
ï»¿
This is the town the White Rajahs built, and it revels in the distinction of having been the heart of one of the most eccentric ventures in the history of European colonialism.
From the polished brass cannon at the small fort on the hill to the stuffed animals in the museum near the Anglican Cathedral, there are reminders of the family that once ruled this territory on the northwest coast of Borneo with a mixture of pluck, paternalism and absolute authority.
Though Sarawak has been part of Malaysia for a quarter of a century, the people of Kuching are proud of their special geography and history. 
''It is hard to express to the rest of the world how we feel about Sarawak,'' Caroline Goh-Cheong, a publisher, said. 
''We have a special place.''
From 1841 to 1946, three men -James, Charles and Vyner Brooke -more or less owned Sarawak, a gift to James from a Brunei sultan grateful for help in quelling a local rebellion.
Â 
A Colonial Oddity
The Brookes were British, but England wanted nothing to do with this troublesome territory, populated by headhunters and perenially short of income. 
So the Brookes were free to rule as potentates, with the help of Malay aristocrats and tribal warriors.
Until 1946, when the territory was turned over to the Crown, there was no British colonial service here, only a few hardy freelance Europeans.
Resentful of Western intrusion, Chinese gold miners and traders from the interior attacked Kuching in 1857, burning the newly created symbols of authority and killing members of the first Rajah's entourage.
His nephew Charles (later the second Rajah) replied by unleashing his upcountry Iban tribesmen on the Chinese. 
The Ibans, headhunters, quickly sent the Chinese back to the hills.
Â 
Architectural Treasures
When James Brooke saw Kuching for the first time in 1839, the small village was the nearest permanent settlement to the muddy Sarawak River delta, where as early as the 11th century a ramshackle bartering center had been established. 
To the delta in their wooden boats came people from the interior and coastal settlements to trade their turtle eggs, feathers, camphor and hornbill ivory for manufactured goods from China and India - ceramics, textiles and metal objects.
Kuching grew rapidly under the Brookes. 
A classic, cloistered courthouse was built in 1874. 
A fort followed in 1879. 
In 1891 a museum opened. 
There were other homes and public buildings of distinction, among them several noteworthy Chinese temples.
Kuching has kept much of its character intact. 
Small wooden sampans are still ''taxis'' to the 300,000 residents, ferrying them along and across the river from dozens of landings. 
The fare is about 5 cents.
Â 
The 20th Century Encroaches
Lucas Chin, curator of the Sarawak Museum - housing one of Southeast Asia's most remarkable ethnic collections - told a visitor how committed Kuching was to saving and embellishing its architectural heritage.
''This whole part of Kuching has been preserved as a cultural center,'' he said, gesturing to take in the hill where his museum stands and the old downtown area, its open, grassy square leading to the waterfront markets.
But high-rise buildings are in evidence, primarily on the less-populated western bank of the river, and Kuching has begun to experience some of the problems common to urban life elsewhere.
Squatter settlements are mushrooming on the city's edges, the product of what the state's Chief Minister, Abdul Taib Mahmud, calls the ''one-way drift'' from Sarawak's interior with its mammoth rivers and uncharted jungles.
''We have been very secluded here,'' said Miss Goh-Cheong, the publisher. 
''We have not really been in touch with the world. 
TV came here only six years ago.''

file: 1,000 Chinese Journalists Call For Greater Freedom of Press.txt
text:
ï»¿
In the strongest appeal so far for freedom of the press in China, more than 1,000 journalists from official news organizations signed a petition that was presented to the Government today calling for talks with China's leaders.
The goal of the talks would be to discuss independence of the press, broader coverage of major events like the recent student demonstrations, and the dismissal of the editor in chief of a Shanghai newspaper.
''The reason we are calling for such a dialogue is that our press coverage has attracted criticism at home and abroad,'' said Li Datong, an editor at the China Youth News. 
''We think that the press in Beijing has failed to be comprehensive and fair in its coverage. 
And we think this is the direct result of our current press system.''
The petition, which was presented to the All-China Journalists Association by about 100 journalists, criticized press censorship in coverage of the recent student demonstrations and demanded a change in the Communist Party's role in press coverage.
Â 
'Some Reports Were Distorted'
''Some reports of the demonstrations were extremely distorted and they have severely damaged the reputation of China's press both here and abroad,'' the petition said.
Because domestic news organizations have been restricted in their coverage of the demonstrations, many Chinese people have learned of the recent events from foreign reports, such as those on the Voice of America and the British Broadcasting Corporation.
During the big student protest last Thursday, about 300 reporters from leading publications demonstrated at the headquarters of the official New China News Agency. 
Several newspapers also printed articles, albeit brief ones, on the event the next day.
''We saw more than you did, but you wrote and published more than we did,'' Yuan Xiaolu, a journalist at China Youth News who signed the petition, told a foreign reporter.
Several reporters said they did not know whether their newspapers were going to publish articles about the petition today. 
But a reporter at the Science and Technology Daily, which was forced to delay distribution of an issue recently because it included articles about the demonstrations, said the newspaper planned to cover the event.
The single action that seems to have aroused the greatest dissatisfaction among journalists is the dismissal two weeks ago of Qin Benli, who was the editor in chief of China's boldest newspaper, the Shanghai-based World Economic Herald. 
Mr. Qin, 70, seems to have become a symbol of the need for more press freedom.
Journalists for the newspaper said the authorities have again intercepted the Herald and delayed its publication. 
They said officials refused to allow the current issue of the weekly newspaper to be printed because of a front-page letter declaring Mr. Qin's dismissal improper. 
The letter was removed and the newspaper was printed 36 hours late, they said.
Zhang Weiguo, a reporter in the Herald's Beijing bureau said the staff members also intend to sue the Shanghai Communist Party leader for his decision to dismiss Mr. Qin and reorganize the newspaper.

file: 150,000 March in Defiance of Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
More than 150,000 demonstrators openly defied official warnings and a concentration of troops today to march for 14 hours through the capital, repeatedly and effortlessly puncturing lines of policemen and soldiers sent to stop them, in one of the biggest displays of dissatisfaction in 40 years of Communist rule.
The student-organized demonstration in support of democracy and against corruption was a stunning humiliation for the Government, which responded this evening by agreeing conditionally to the students' demand for discussions with officials.
Most worrying for the authorities was the fact that crowds of cheering workers lined the entire route and hailed the core of student marchers almost as a liberating army. 
Workers vigorously applauded the students, waved encouragement from office windows, and frequently sent them food and drinks to show support.
Soldiers Are Surrounded
On at least three occasions thousands of workers surrounded hundreds of soldiers and and prevented them from approaching student marchers.
Workers sometimes pushed aside police blockades even before the students drew near, and the marchers in the four-mile-long parade were easily outnumbered by supporters who walked and bicycled along with them for at least part of the way.
Beijing residents said the security forces, including army troops called in from surrounding areas, had made their greatest show of force in recent memory, but it was dwarfed by the sea of demonstrators.
Including the onlookers who waved and cheered as the parade went by, perhaps half a million people took part one way or another, often climbing trees and lampposts when there was no ground to stand on.
The only comparable protest came in the first week of April 1976 when angry crowds gathered in Tiananmen Square to mourn the death of Prime Minister Zhou Enlai and oppose the ''Gang of Four'' then in power. 
Several Chinese who took part in both demonstrations said the one today involved more people and more general defiance of the authorities, who had warned of a crackdown on demonstrators.
Â 
New Themes Are Raised
For the first time, the pro-democracy movement, which in the past has been overwhelmingly limited to students and intellectuals, seemed to draw fervent support from others. 
The students encouraged this not only by pressing their previous demands, like freedom of the press and more money for education, but also by raising populist themes like official corruption and inflation.
The perception of Government impotence was most vivid when the crowds burst through the last police barricade to get to Tiananmen Square in the center of the capital. 
Nearly 1,000 soldiers in 20 trucks did not flee quickly enough and mobs swarmed around them, clambering onto the hoods and sides of the vehicles and appearing ready at first to lynch the troops. 
But when it became obvious that the soldiers were terrified and thinking only of retreat, the mobs cleared a way for them to escape.
Shouts of ''Brothers, go home and till your fields'' could be heard from the crowd as the trucks raced off.
Aside from some shoving, there was no violence. 
Indeed, students once rescued soldiers sent to block their march. 
Several truckloads of troops were surrounded by angry mobs, who allowed them to leave only when persuaded to do so by students waving their university identification badges.
Â 
An Appeal to the Workers
''We're deeply moved by the students' audacity,'' said a young Government ministry official who came out of his office to applaud as the students passed. 
''They say what is in our hearts.''
The procession was full of signs and banners, ranging from ''Vive la liberte,'' erected by French-language students, to a large black banner aimed at workers: ''You work but you get nothing; your life is bitter.''
The students were far better organized than they have been in the past, and some with megaphones were assigned to rally worker support. 
When the march passed a large factory, whose gate was promptly locked, a student made a small speech:
''Dear workers, we are all citizens, and we all have the right of free movement. 
If anyone stops you from getting out and joining us, that's against the Constitution.''
Of the 150,000 or more marchers, about half were organized students carrying banners and the rest were workers or students taking part on their own. 
One worker who marched was Zhou Jingping, a library clerk, who said he was an enthusiastic supporter of the students.
''Inflation has given us a lot of difficulties because prices rise but salaries don't,'' Mr. Zhou said. 
''Students voice that desire of ours to suppress the inflation. 
And then there's corruption. 
Bribery is evident everywhere, and people are sick of it. 
Education is another reason - the Government hasn't paid enough attention to education.''
To many workers, the students seemed to represent not a focused, alternative agenda, but simply a cry of discontent that struck a deep chord.
''They represent people's thinking, the sense that we the people are in control,'' said one of the marchers, Lin Yulin, a 52-year-old worker wearing a Mao Zedong button as a sign of his discontent. 
''The leaders cover everything up. 
People don't know anything, and we are no longer the masters. 
That's why there is this uprising.''
The outpouring of support for the students was humiliating for the entire leadership, but for no one so much as the senior leader, Deng Xiaoping. 
In the last 10 days of protests, the students have often expressed contempt for Mr. Deng, and he more than anyone appears to have been behind the hard line that the Government has taken in the last few days. 
Harsh Words From Deng?
Chinese with close Communist Party connections say the Politburo raised the matter of student unrest this week and asked Mr. Deng for his views. 
He is said to have answered particularly harshly, saying that if necessary some blood could be spilled and that repression would not seriously harm China's image in the world.
The students said tonight that they would continue their boycott of classes and some predicted that there would be more demonstrations on May 1 and May 4. 
It was not clear how the students would regard the Government's offer of discussions, which was a major concession but which appeared to be linked to the students' willingness to avoid street demonstrations.
The Government appeared dumbfounded by the size of the day's demonstration, and the television news did not mention it tonight. 
The official New China News Agency mentioned it briefly and suggested its effect only indirectly when reporting that it had caused ''huge traffic tie-ups'' affecting 300,000 people.

A1 & 6)

file: 2 CHINA DISSIDENTS DETAINED IN MAY.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese authorities have recently detained at least two democracy advocates, including one who spent a decade in prison for political beliefs, Chinese familiar with the cases say.
Students at Beijing University said a fellow student, Peng Rong, was detained on Friday, one day after President Bush recommended the renewal of most-favored-nation trading status for China.
Two weeks ago, Liu Qing, a leader of the Democracy Wall movement in 1978-79, was picked up and accused of not having a valid permit to live in Beijing, associates said.
One of the most prominent dissidents in China, Mr. Liu was freed from prison at the end of 1989 after having served 10 years for advocating democracy and human rights and also for publicizing prison conditions.

Exact Charges Unclear
Although the poster echoed the official position, it is illegal to put up posters or petitions without approval. 
A year ago, posters at Beijing University helped set off student demonstrations.
University authorities deny that Mr. Peng was detained because of the poster, students said.

Three other students who also signed the May 11 petition have not been arrested so far.

Mr. Peng took part in the students' demonstrations a year ago, but he was not detained in the months after the army's June 4 suppression of the demonstrations and he was not on the list of 21 students sought after the violence.

file: 2 in Race Disagree On Defense And Trade.txt
text:
ï»¿
With a troublesome economy and social issues as focal points of their rancorous race for the United States Senate, Senator Alfonse M. D'Amato and Attorney General Robert Abrams have virtually ignored any discussion of foreign policy issues.
Even on those rare occasions a foreign policy issue has been raised, like military budgets and the future of Russia, their answers have been framed in domestic concerns, like the impact on jobs and trade possibilities.
But a broader examination of their positions on world affairs reveals a striking difference between them despite their relative agreement on narrow issues like favoring improved relations with Israel after the periods of strain through the last four years.
In essence, Mr. D'Amato, a Republican seeking his third Senate term, and Mr. Abrams, a Democrat in his first bid for national office, embrace fundamentally different visions of the future, in that Mr. Abrams sees a world less threatening to the United States than Mr. D'Amato does.
Â 
Quick-Strike Force
The disparity emerges through the role they see the United States playing in the near future and the degree to which they would reduce the current national defense budget of $290 billion over the next five years.
While both envision the kind of mobile, quick-strike military force used in the Persian Gulf war in 1991, with a strong presence in Europe and other strategic places, Mr. D'Amato's force would be larger. 
He favors reductions of $85 billion in the defense budget over the next five years, and a decrease of 400,000 troops, to 1.5 million. 
Mr. Abrams would cut spending by more than three times as much, $280 billion over the same period, and require only 1.1 million troops.
Both see the need for reducing the 300,000 troops stationed in Europe -- Mr. Abrams to 75,000 to 100,000; Mr. D'Amato, to about 100,000.
In a recent interview, Mr. D'Amato assailed the continuing presence of Saddam Hussein in Iraq and the ethnic wars in Yugoslavia, citing them as reasons for slower defense reductions. 
He said the demise of the Soviet Union and Communist governments in Eastern Europe was no guarantee military threats had evaporated. 
He called North Korea "still a military threat" and said he worries about countries like Iran and China buying weapons on the open market.
Â 
Similar Concerns
Mr. Abrams cited similar concerns in a separate interview but not to the degree expressed by Mr. D'Amato, who he said "hasn't yet realized the cold war is over."
Mr. Abrams argued that the cuts and troop levels he advocates, drawn from a recent study by the Brookings Institution, would be sufficient to safeguard the interests of the United States.
While he would keep the United States military advantage over other countries, he played down the need for the United States to act as "the world's policeman," saying he preferred what he described as the "collective action" of the gulf war.
In an election year in which voters are far more focused on domestic concerns, Mr. D'Amato's approach of seeking smaller cuts in military spending is tied to jobs. 
He says slashing the military further would not only undermine national security but also devastate New York's economy by eliminating hundreds of thousands of jobs from defense contractors like Grumman on Long Island and General Electric in Schenectady.
But Mr. Abrams argued that the longer-term economic stability of New York requires conversion of military production to consumer businesses and reallocating dollars saved from military spending into programs to rebuild the nation's infrastructure. 
Mr. D'Amato favors the same kind of programs but a more gradual conversion rate.
Â 
'Responsible Reductions'
"With the end of the cold war, we cannot bury our head in the sand and miss this opportunity," Mr. Abrams said. 
"We can remain the strongest military power in the world, but at the same time get the benefit of the end of the cold war with responsible reductions in the military budget."
On trade issues, Mr. D'Amato favors approval of the North American Free Trade Agreement with Canada and Mexico, which means he supports the measure as written.
Like Gov. Bill Clinton in the Presidential race, Mr. Abrams supports the agreement in principle but would prefer amendments or parallel legislation to require Mexico to enforce its environmental standards and insure worker safety and the United States to provide retraining programs for Americans losing their jobs when their employers move to Mexico.
Both candidates contend that trade relations with China, specifically most-favored-nation status, should be tied to improved human-rights policies in China, especially in the wake of the Chinese Government's crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square in 1989.
But Mr. Abrams takes a harder line against the Chinese Government than Mr. D'Amato, saying "the furthering of democratic principles and human rights should be at the cornerstone of foreign policy" with China.
The Senator called China a "very, very difficult situation."
In July 1991, he voted against granting most-favored-nation status to China because of Tiananmen Square. 
Less than two years later, when the issue came before Congress a second time, he voted with the minority to grant most-favored trade status as a way to encourage the Chinese leadership to adopt more democratic principles.
But a month later, after the President vetoed Congressional rejection of favored-nation trade status, the Senator joined 59 other senators in an override vote that fell 7 votes short.
Mr. Abrams contended that Mr. D'Amato's change in position represented either an inconsistency in position or political opportunism, in that it never appeared that the Senate would gather enough votes to deny China the preferred status.
The Senator disagreed, saying his initial support in 1991 was based on the President's satisfying concerns of Congress through an executive order that, among other things, protected Chinese students living in the United States by not forcing them to leave. 
His override vote, he said, was cast in the spirit of supporting human rights.
Both candidates chided the Bush Administration for reacting too slowly to help Russia toward democracy and a market economy. 
Both would encourage investment to further open Russia to American products.

file: 2 U.S. Officials Went to Beijing Secretly in July.txt
text:

The White House said today that the national security adviser, Brent Scowcroft, made a secret trip to China in July, shortly after President Bush suspended high-level meetings with the Chinese Government over the June crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators. 
Deputy Secretary of State Lawrence S. Eagleburger also went on the trip.
Word of the July visit came as the White House was still fielding criticism about a more recent visit to Beijing by Mr. Scowcroft and Mr. Eagleburger. The two men went to China 10 days ago to mend relations after hundreds of students died in June at the hands of the Chinese military in Tiananmen Square. 
That crackdown stirred deep anger and calls for sanctions among the American public and in Congress.
The second trip was announced by the White House only after Mr. Scowcroft and Mr. Eagleburger arrived in Beijing. 
July's trip had been kept secret, and it was made public by the White House today after it was reported by Cable News Network.
The pictures of Mr. Scowcroft during the visit this month, toasting Chinese leaders by candlelight ''as friends to resume our important dialogue,'' set off a wave of criticism in the United States. 
Many critics responded strongly again today to the news of the July visit, saying Mr. Bush has misled the American people.
Senator George J. Mitchell, Democrat of Maine, the majority leader, said he was ''astonished'' to learn that Mr. Bush had sent the two officials to China on ''another midnight mission, barely a month after the brutal killing of pro-democracy student demonstrators.''
''At that time, the President was saying there could not be business as usual with a Government that took such actions,'' he said. 
''Yet this is increasingly what seems to be happening.''
He said the trips ''make a mockery of our profession of concern for human rights and the stated ideals of our democratic system of government.''

text:

China faces a difficult battle in Congress this summer to retain its preferential access to the United States market, but you would hardly know it from the unconciliatory remarks being made by Chinese officials.

Retaliation Is Likely
China will also use high tariffs to drive American companies out of its markets if the United States does not renew the current trade privileges, Mr. Zhu added. 
Billions of dollars in contracts and thousands of jobs in industries from aircraft manufacturing to agricultural chemical production would be at risk, he said.
Mr. Zhu's remarks were only a little more strident than other policy statements by Chinese officials. 
For China has pursued a pugnacious four-pronged lobbying strategy here that has dismayed its friends and gladdened its foes.
Mr. Zhu's comments were not what members of Congress had hoped to hear. 
The massacre at Tiananmen Square in 1989, along with reports in the last month by a human rights group and a Congessman that political prisoners are being forced to produce goods for export, have so stained the reputation of China's leadership that diplomats' assurances carry little credibility.

A motion of disapproval, which seems likely to be introduced, would have to pass both houses of Congress within 90 days, and it probably would provoke a Presidential veto.
When President Bush renewed China's trade status last year, the House voted to disapprove the renewal. 
The Senate considered similar action but did not take a vote before the 90-day time limit expired, so the renewal stood.

Another possibility is that Congress will pair its disapproval of the status for China with approval of a renewal for the Soviet Union, said one lobbyist who favors a renewal for China.

file: A New Novel by Amy Tan, Who_s Still Trying to Adapt to Success.txt
text:
ï»¿
Success, Amy Tan has learned, is never what you expect it to be.
"In some ways it's like being a kid in a candy store," the 39-year-old best-selling author says, pouring coffee in her suite at the Carlyle Hotel. 
"But there's also the loss of privacy. 
I'll be getting up from a nap on an airplane, and someone will come over to me and say, 'You're Amy Tan.'
And I'll realize that I look like everybody else does when they've just awakened on a plane, and I want to say, 'No, I'm not.'
"
Three years ago, Ms. Tan was a freelance technical writer living in San Francisco and working on her first novel. 
That book turned out to be "The Joy Luck Club," a tale of Chinese-American women and their immigrant mothers. 
It jumped onto the best-seller lists in the spring of 1989, and a few weeks later its paperback rights were sold for $1.2 million.
Ms. Tan's second novel, "The Kitchen God's Wife," is being published this month by G. P. Putnam's amid much promotional fanfare. 
Early reviews have been glowing and it would be surprising if the novel, in which an elderly immigrant woman tells her daughter the story of her harsh and oppressive life in China before the revolution, did not wind up on the best-seller list.
With money sometimes comes celebrity, a status that Ms. Tan says has affected her life on the ground as well as in the air. 
For one thing, she has had to move. 
"I was determined at one point to keep everything the same," she says. 
"Which is a very idealistic, romantic notion. 
We lived in a very nice house, but we were on the first floor, and every day there were people walking by and pointing at it. 
My mailman would tell everybody what mail I had received. 
I felt very exposed."
So she and her husband, Lou DeMattei, a tax lawyer, packed up and headed a couple of blocks away, to the third floor of a condominium. 
As she speaks, Ms. Tan carefully rearranges a shimmering orange-gold cape that is wrapped around her shoulders. 
Her legs are crossed, and much of the time so are her arms, as if she is shielding herself from public prying. 
She is trying very hard to be outgoing and cheerful, but her nervousness shows. 
She seems, surprisingly, a little shy. 
It is not that she is still a novice at interviews; it's that she really doesn't like them.
"I have a different personality in public than I have in private," she says. 
"I put on the public personality. 
I ironed these clothes for you this morning. 
Otherwise what I would be wearing would be really grungy."
Â 
Different in Private
She is a lot sillier in private, she says, "and a lot bitchier."
She is more comfortable, she says, "when I'm walking around back home with my husband, or when I'm having a conversation with him, and he's sort of drifting off trying to read the paper, and I say: 'Well, this is good; I'm as boring as I always was.'
"
"The Kitchen God's Wife" didn't come easy, she says. 
While she was writing it, she was very much aware of another aspect of success: the fear that the second book will not be as good, or as well received, as the first.
"I see all the faults," she says. 
"I know what's been put in and what's been taken out. 
I know where the mistakes are, and I'm always afraid someone's going to catch them and say, 'You put the wrong emphasis on this,' or 'You used the wrong angle on that.'
"
She also didn't want to be typecast. 
"I didn't want to be pegged as the mother-daughter expert," she says. 
So at first she tried writing something very different from "The Joy Luck Club."
But that something wasn't working, and there were a number of false starts. 
"It was an attempt at rebellion," she says. 
"And I realized that rebellion was not a good reason to write what I was writing."
Then, suddenly, her mother provided the inspiration. 
"My mother kept complaining about how she had to tell everybody she was not the model for the mother in 'The Joy Luck Club,' " Ms. Tan says. 
"She told me that next time I should write her true story. 
And then one day she said something that I thought was remarkable.
"I knew she had lived in China during World War II, that she had been married to someone else before my father, and I asked her what the war had been like. 
I expected to hear all these exciting tales, and instead she told me, 'I wasn't affected.'
"But then she mentioned that maybe two or three times a week, when the bombs fell, she would have to run to the east gate or the west gate. 
'We were always running,' she told me. 
'We were always scared that the bombs would fall on top of our heads.'
So I said to her: 'Wait a minute. 
You told me you weren't affected by the war.'
And she replied: 'I wasn't. 
I wasn't killed.'
"
For Ms. Tan, the statement was a remarkable revelation about the difference between her own perspective on life and her mother's. 
"I decided I wanted to try to capture the shock of that difference," she says.
She changed many details, but the novel keeps close to the basic outlines of her mother's life in China before, during and after the war: "Everything from her horrible marriage, to her children dying, to being in jail, to escaping right before the revolution in 1949."
Â 
An Effort at Understanding
Her goal, she says, was to try to understand her mother. 
"She is such a strong person," Ms. Tan says. 
"And I could never understand why she lived with such a horrible man for 12 years of her life. 
She once told me that she might even kill him if she ever saw him again. 
If she hated him that much, why didn't she leave him?"
But Ms. Tan came to learn more and more about the subservient role of women in that Chinese society. 
"My mother was repressed so much by her family, by the society she lived in," Ms. Tan says. 
"And then I started thinking about all the different myths we grow up with, all the assumptions and the expectations. 
There are these things that form and control our lives that we never question."
The novel's title, Ms. Tan says, is a reference to a Chinese tale about a man who wronged his wife and was then elevated to the status of a deity -- "a perfect metaphor," she says, for those unquestioned governing myths.
Ms. Tan wrote the novel in 1989, while the student demonstrations were taking place in Tiananmen Square in Beijing. 
"People would always say that the students were so brave," she says. 
"I wanted to understand what it is like to live a life of repression and to understand the fear that one has, and what you have to do to rise above that fear."
Ms. Tan says she has already done research for her next novel, and expects to begin writing it as soon as she has finished promoting "The Kitchen God's Wife."
And with the writing, she knows, will again come the pressure.
"If I get an award, I look at it and I thank somebody and I give it to my mother," Ms. Tan says. 
"And if my mother wants to throw it away, she can throw it away. 
I don't keep that stuff around. 
I don't keep my books on my coffee table. 
I don't want to see any reminder of them. 
There's an unreality about it. 
My life with the last book ended when I made the final corrections."
She takes a sip of coffee and looks up expectantly. 
Is the interview over?
Yes, she is told, it is. 
She laughs, the carefree laugh of a schoolchild at dismissal.
"Great," she says.

text:

WHEN British India shuddered on the faultline of religion and split apart at independence in 1947, a new nation for Muslims, which they called Pakistan, was born.
But Pakistan, washed in the sun-seared south by the Arabian Sea, and fringed at the north by the soaring, snowy peaks of the Hindu Kush and the Karakorams, was new in name only. 
This narrow land, enclosed on three sides by India, China, Afghanistan and Iran, was where much of the subcontinent's culture originated.
India may have taken the name, but Pakistan got a lot of the history -- prehistoric, Hellenistic, Persian, Buddhist and Mogul. 
Alexander the Great rode into its valleys. 
So did the Emperors Darius and Cyrus the Great. 
Archeological sites at Mohenjo-Daro in Sind and at Taxila in the North-West Frontier Province reveal sophisticated cultures thousands of years old. 
Museums at the sites preserve their artifacts and tell the stories of the ruins.
Pakistan also has good samples of the Indian subcontinent's dramatically varied geography. 
There is an undeveloped seacoast, quiet mountain valleys with cool, clear streams, deserts - camels loom over cars at traffic lights in Karachi - and fertile agricultural plains that bloom and die and bloom again in rhythm with the rains.
The Indus, the river that gave life to the subcontinent's earliest civilizations, flows nearly the full length of Pakistan, from mountains to sea.
One of the world's great overland journeys can be made from the north of Pakistan to China along the recently completed Karakoram Highway, a contemporary addition to the ancient Silk Route, which opened West Asia to the Orient.
What Pakistan doesn't have is tourists, at least not many of them, not yet. 
The country, emerging from more than a decade of military domination, returned to democracy recently and exuberantly, and now hopes to welcome more visitors, while considering how to develop its tourist attractions, and what kind of tourists it wants.
Pakistan remains at heart a pious, though not fundamentalist, Islamic nation. 
Women are dressed modestly in trousers and tunics - the comfortable shalwar-kamiz suit that Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto is helping to raise to new fashion heights. 
No alcoholic drinks are served or consumed in public places, though non-Muslim foreigners may buy local beer, whisky, gin and rum from room service menus in international hotels. 
Bringing alcohol into the country is illegal and gambling is forbidden by both law and religion.
Most Pakistanis, however, are friendly and tolerant people. 
Outsiders who understand and generally respect their customs - avoiding shorts or other skimpy clothes in public places and removing shoes in mosques - feel little or no hostility or sense of opprobrium. 
Service, if sometimes unpracticed or erratic, is never disingenuous or slick. 
Accommodation is adequate to excellent in most towns and all cities, where good cars can be hired for free-lance trips.
Urdu is the national language, but all the regions have their own languages and English is sometimes used as a link. 
English will be spoken in all tourist areas and in most hotels. 
The best time to travel is in the spring, when snows melt in the north and temperatures are pleasant. 
Summer is hot almost everywhere except high in the hills. 
Temperatures in Pakistan's cities, especially in the south, can rise above 100 degrees, and the desert sun is punishing. 
After October, snows close the mountain passes, including those along the Silk Route, which reopens for the season on May 1.
Pakistan used to be accessible overland from Kabul to the west and Delhi to the east along the old Grand Trunk Road until war in Afghanistan and separatist unrest in India's Punjab state closed those routes to most travelers.
The country is now most easily reached by air, and perhaps in the future will be served by cruise ship. 
Pakistan can be sampled as a side trip to an Indian vacation, or as a stopover on the way to Southeast Asia or China. 
Pakistan International Airlines, which is both a domestic and international carrier, is one of South Asia's most pleasant travel surprises, with efficient service and clean, well-cared-for aircraft. 
Flying inside Pakistan is cheap and safe, and most tourist destinations can be reached by plane from larger cities.
There are two international gateways to Pakistan by air: Karachi in the south and Lahore (or on some days Islamabad) farther north. 
Karachi, Pakistan's largest city and a busy seaport, is the best base for exploring the lower end of the Indus River valley and the archeological ruins of Mohenjo-Daro.
Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first Prime Minister, called the Indus civilization the precursor of all later cultural periods in India. 
At Mohenjo-Daro, connected to Karachi by air, a metropolis with educational institutions, civic buildings and a drainage system flourished before 2500 B.C.
Like another apparently large and highly developed city at Harappa, in Pakistan's Punjab state to the northeast, Mohenjo-Daro appears to have vanished into history, leaving no clues to its language and thus locking away its secrets. 
The site was not unearthed until 1922, and restoration work since then has been sporadic. 
But some of the city's street plan is visible, and a collection of pottery, weapons, toys and household objects can be seen in the museum at the site.
From Karachi, tourists can also go west to the country's largest and most remote province, Baluchistan. 
The Baluchi capital, Quetta, like Peshawar to the north, is a frontier town populated by fierce-looking, often armed, men true to the past. 
It is not a city of either charm or historical interest, since much of it was destroyed in an earthquake in 1935 that killed 23,000 people. 
But it serves as a base for hiking and for drives into mountain passes and valleys. 
Its bazaars are full of colorful Baluchi handicrafts, including embroidered clothes and jackets and pillows decorated with tiny mirrors.
The city of Karachi is not regarded as a tourist attraction, but it is not without its points of interest. 
In the seaside suburb of Clifton, where the Bhuttos and other wealthy and influential Pakistanis - as well as a few oil sheiks from the Persian Gulf - have homes (or minor palaces), there are camels to ride along the beach. 
Families come out to stroll on Fridays, the Pakistani day of rest, when children don their finest clothes. 
Curbside, makeshift shooting galleries are popular here, a reminder of Pakistan's long fascination with guns.
A visit to Karachi should include a stop at the tomb of Pakistan's founder, Mohammed Ali Jinnah, known as Quaid-e-Azam, or Father of the Nation. 
The white marble, domed mausoleum stands on a hill, visible from some parts of the city. 
It is set in a large public park where families come to relax or picnic. 
Jinnah, whose Karachi home has also been made into a small museum, is Pakistan's most revered leader, and a hero on whom politically fractious Pakistanis agree.
The National Museum of Pakistan is in a garden off Dr. Zia-uddin Ahmed Road in Karachi, the country's first capital. 
Open every day but Friday from 10 to 4, the museum offers a panoramic look at Pakistan's history and regional cultures. 
Like several other exceptionally good museums found in Pakistan - two others are at Lahore and Peshawar - the National Museum is housed in a building erected during British colonial times. 
A Muslim Gallery in the museum is devoted to the rich Islamic cultures that converged in Pakistan.
It is the northern part of Pakistan, rather than Karachi or the southwest, that is most popular with tourists, who can travel easily and comfortably along the Lahore-Rawalpindi-Peshawar route, making as many side trips as time and interest permits.
Lahore is a classic Mogul city with added elements of Victorian brick and stone. 
Its character is intellectual and political. 
Rawalpindi, four or five hours away by road or rail or less than 45 minutes by air, is the military center of Pakistan, and a thriving commercial city. 
Peshawar, near the entrance to the Khyber Pass, is vintage frontier, embellished now by millions of Afghan exiles who walk the streets selling carpets, or lay out tables of chunky Turkoman jewelry and fine woolens hand-knit by refugee women.
These three cities have three of Pakistan's four oldest hotels: Faletti's in Lahore, Flashman's in Pindi and Dean's in Peshawar. 
The fourth in the chain, now owned by the Government, which toys now and then with the idea of tearing them down, is the Cecil in the hill town of Murree, east of Islamabad.
Rawalpindi or Islamabad, Pakistan's new capital city only a few miles away, is the takeoff point for trips by road or air to the remote regions of Gilgit, Balistan and the Pakistani part of Kashmir. 
From here, the trip along the Silk Route to China can also begin. 
The Chinese Embassy in Islamabad issues the necessary travel documents in three to seven days, for a nominal fee of about $3.50.
For people who prefer to travel in a group, Pakistan Tours, with offices at Flashman's Hotel in Rawalpindi and at the Chinar Inn in Gilgit, offers 8-day and 15-day trips into and back from China across the 16,500-foot Khunjerab Pass. 
The tour costs about $70 a day, including all transportation, meals and accommodation, from Rawalpindi to China and back. 
Trips begin in mid-May with one a month minimum.
The tour operator has vans equipped with oxygen for high altitudes, tourism officials say. 
Privately hired cars may go only as far as the Chinese border. 
Further information is available from Pakistan Tours, 23-24 Flashman's Hotel, The Mall, Rawalpindi; telephone 65449 or 64811.
A trip through the Khunjerab, however, is not necessary to get a sense of the majesty of Pakistan's northern mountainous frontier. 
In good weather, travelers can fly to the towns of Skardu or Gilgit, or drive into the northern valleys, known for their good hiking and climbing terrain, fishing streams, clear air and solitude. 
By jeep, the trip to Gilgit can take between 12 and 20 hours; most car-rental companies recommend breaking the journey into two or more day trips. 
There are small inns and rest houses of varying quality along the way. 
Flying to Gilgit, however, is subsidized, and costs only about $12 from Pindi. 
This means the daily flights are often full. 
Buses also make the trip from Pindi for under $15.
The towns in Pakistan's northern territories are in high mountain valleys, Gilgit-Hunza at 4,770 feet and Skardu, to the east, at 7,500 feet. 
Skardu has the more dramatic scenery. 
Backed by some of the highest mountains in the world, the Skardu Valley has lakes, sand dunes and an old mountain fort. 
There are more than half a dozen approved hotels and lodges in Skardu.
From a base at Rawalpindi, a day trip can be made to the archeological sites of Taxila, most of them an hour or less away by car.
Taxila, at the heart of the Gandhara civilizations of the North-West Frontier, is a collection of several excavated sites that together document an extraordinary confluence of religions and cultures. 
There are Hellenistic influences - Buddha figures in Greekstyle robes, for example - as well as Bactrian, Scythian and Persian.
India's first Emperor, Chandragupta Maurya, was crowned at Taxila; here his grandson Ashoka later ruled as viceroy. 
During Ashoka's time, in the third century B.C., Taxila became a center of Buddhist learning and pilgrimage. 
Some of the finest of early Buddhist art has been found here, including the startling, skeletal Fasting Siddharta, often called the Gandhara Buddha, now on display in the Lahore Museum.
A visit to the Taxila sites takes a visitor into the hearts of poor, dusty Pakistani villages, a poignant contrast to the glories of the past, when the land was kinder to the people who lived here. 
One word of caution: villagers have become adept at reproducing Gandhara artifacts, which they offer to tourists as originals ''dug up over the hill.''
Government guides at the archeological sites say that no metal or pottery items are found these days, but that occasionally a coin will be genuinely old.
However, the reproductions of tiny bronze pots or jewelry are often so pleasant to look at that visitors buy them, once the price has been bargained down from antique to trinket level.
West and northwest of Rawalpindi lie more beautiful mountain valleys: Swat and, beyond that, Chitral. 
The capital of the Swat region, named for its river, is Saidu Sharif, the seat of the Kings of Swat, who ruled until 1969. 
Good small hotels begin here and dot the villages - Miandam, Bahrain and Kalam - to the north. 
Over these towns tower the mountains of the Hindu Kush. 
Across the border to the west is Afghanistan.
It is forever-unruly Afghanistan that has dominated the life of Pakistan's most fascinating city: Peshawar. 
Now the capital of the North-West Frontier Province - and the headquarters of seven Afghan resistance armies trying to overthrow the Soviet-backed Government in Kabul - Peshawar is a town full of energy and intrigue.
The bazaars hereabouts are legendary, so a traveler might be wise to look around ahead of time in other cities to get a working knowledge of fair prices, but then save the shopping for Peshawar. 
Here there are warrens of markets with copper and brass, woolens and leatherware. 
Afghan carpets - some with latter-day symbols like automatic weapons or Soviet tanks woven into them - and colorful Afghan dresses with trousers to match are sold in shops run by exiles.
There are beads and powder horns, camel bags and icons stolen from Russian soldiers who died across the border in a war that must have baffled them. 
Soviet officer's hats and decorations are also available, along with a smuggler's cornucopia of imported foods and luxury goods seen nowhere else in South Asia. 
Trekkers can stock up here on comforting home-town goods like real chocolate bars and mustard.
In the past, travelers who came to Peshawar from the east almost invariably took a day trip through the Khyber Pass and back. 
Lately, however, that trip has been off limits because of fighting around the Afghanistan-Pakistan border town of Torkham on the other side of the pass. 
Hotels in Peshawar keep in touch with local authorities, and can tell visitors whether the route, with its wild mountain scenery and fortified villages behind mud walls, is open or not.
Meanwhile, it is possible to drive west of Peshawar far enough to pause at the large Afghan refugee colonies to see first-hand the overwhelming human tragedy Pakistan has on its border.
When traveling in isolated valleys or through mountainous terrain, tourists should avoid being on lonely roads after sundown, when armed bandits sometimes stop and loot vehicles, particularly in regions near the Afghan border. 
Roads are also dangerous at night because of the mix of animals, unlighted farm wagons and speeding cars, trucks or buses, usually elaborately decorated. 
For both reasons, it is a good idea to settle down early in the day, and plan an evening around the hotel, whether in town or countryside.
Peshawar is not a dangerous city because of the Afghan war. 
But it is a city with spies, gunrunners and narcotics agents where weapons are abundant, demanding circumspection on the visitor's part. 
It is also the home of some of the most conservative Muslims in Pakistan or Afghanistan. 
Western women, who almost universally don Pakistani attire here, sometimes say they feel uncomfortable in Peshawar. 
But hundreds of them are working happily with more than three million refugees from Afghanistan, and have come to understand, as have their Western male counterparts, the ways of this barren frontier.
Â 
FOR REAL AND ARMCHAIR TRAVELERS
Because Pakistan has not been a major tourist destination, not many travel books have been written on the country. 
But those that are available are excellent, partly because they assume a certain unfamiliarity on the reader's part.
Â 
General
Pakistan: A Travel Survival Kit, by Jose Roleo Santiago (Lonely Planet Publications, Post Office Box 2001, Berkeley, Calif. 
94702; $7.95; about $12.50 in international hotel bookshops in Pakistan). 
Like its companion guides to other little-known countries, this Travel Survival Kit begins with ancient history and moves through almost every topic of interest - food, vocabulary, accommodations and so on - to descriptions of places and attractions detailed enough to help a traveler plan a tour.
A Traveler's Guide to Pakistan, by Hilary Adamson and Isobel Shaw (The Asian Study Group, Post Office Box 1552, Islamabad; about $6.95 in bookshops in Pakistan). 
A private project, thoroughly researched by two Westerners who lived in Pakistan for several years, this guide with its many hand-drawn maps covers nearly every corner of the country.
To the Frontier, by Geoffrey Moorhouse (Sceptre Books, Hodder & Stoughton; about $5.55 in Pakistan.) Here's a book to read for its initial insights into Pakistani daily life. 
Mr. Moorhouse, a skilled travel writer with a gifted eye for detail, describes his own first, solo encounter with Pakistan. 
No shopping or accommodation details here, except when part of the narrative. 
But there is enough atmosphere to make Pakistan memorable, even for those who may never visit it.
Â

Trekking in the Himalayas and Karakoram, by Hugh Swift (Hodder & Stoughton; no price given). 
Trekkers and climbers consider this work a classic, though the area it covers is large - Chitral to Bhutan. 
The book contains scholarly information on local wildlife, history and customs.
Trekkers Guide to Hunza, by Haqiqat Ali (published privately for sale in Pakistani bookshops at about $6.95). 
One of the first local efforts to fill the gap in details about some of the more remote valleys of northern Pakistan, this book was written by an experienced climber and guide born in Hunza. 
It includes realistic advice on the dangers of this isolated, high-altitude terrain.Â Â Â Â -Â Â B. 
C.

ACCOMMODATIONS FROM DESERT TO MOUNTAIN
In general, Pakistani hotels that tourists might choose have private baths and very often, in the north, fireplaces. 
Credit cards -especially American Express and Visa - are accepted in all big hotels. 
Traveler's checks are also used widely. 
Cash will be necessary in small lodges outside cities.
