text:
ï»¿
President Bush said today that he was willing to seek Security Council authority to create a United Nations security force in northern Iraq that would pave the way for the withdrawal of American and allied military forces from the Kurdish region.
The announcement came a day after the Secretary General of the United Nations, Javier Perez de Cuellar, indicated that his envoy in Baghdad was making progress in negotiating conditional Iraqi support for such a security force. 
The State Department spokesman, Richard A. Boucher, also said today, "There may be some preliminary agreement on some type of guard arrangements to be associated with the U.N. humanitarian effort."
A compromise on the security force issue that is acceptable to Washington and Baghdad could spare Mr. Bush a stalemate in northern Iraq, a development that could turn the humanitarian effort into a political liability at home.
Also, a compromise security force that won Iraq's approval would defuse a potentially bruising dispute between Mr. Bush and the Security Council, where the Soviet Union and China have expressed strong reservations against a United Nations military role in Iraq that is not approved by the Iraqi Government.
In a sign that Mr. Bush may be courting Security Council votes, the President also stated publicly today that he favored renewing China's most-favored-nation trade status, linking his decision to China's cooperation at the United Nations during the Persian Gulf conflict.
Last fall, when Mr. Bush needed critical Chinese and Soviet votes to authorize the use of force against Iraqi troops in Kuwait, the President broke his own ban on high-level visits by Chinese officials imposed after the Tiananmen Square crackdown.
The United Nations police force, if it is approved, would provide protection for the relief operation under way in the Kurdish security zone that stretches from Zakho on the Turkish border to the outskirts of Dohuk, a major Iraqi provincial capital. 
More than 8,000 American, British and French forces occupy the zone and thousands more are stationed in Turkey and the Eastern Mediterranean as a "quick reaction" force.
Responding to a question about the United Nations police force proposal, Mr. Bush told reporters on the South Lawn of the White House, "We're contemplating going to the United Nations on that to get further authority."
Â 
Compromise Possible
Mr. Bush added that, in his opinion, the authority to create such a police force has already been granted "under existing resolutions" of the United Nations that require Iraq to cooperate with humanitarian relief efforts.
But his public remarks indicated that Mr. Perez de Cuellar's negotiations with Baghdad may have produced a formula that the United States and its allies will be able to accept.
On Tuesday, Mr. Perez de Cuellar said that his special envoy, Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan, was negotiating approval from Iraqi officials to add an armed United Nations security force of 400 to 500 men to the United Nations relief workers already in northern Iraq.
A permanent reconciliation between the Kurds and the Iraqi Government is the subject of separate negotiations now headed by the Kurdish guerilla leader Massoud Barzani. 
Mr. Bush also said today that these talks "could offer some hope."
But Mr. Bush emphasized that until relations between the Kurds and the Iraqi Government are normalized, the United States will adhere to its security commitment. 
"I don't think we can entrust the fate of the Kurds to the word of Saddam Hussein."
At the State Department, Mr. Boucher said "we don't have the details" of the security force proposal that is emerging from the talks in Baghdad. 
"But we understand that discussion will continue this week between the U.N. and Iraqi authorities."

file: Aided by U.S. Waiver, China Launches First Foreign Satellite.txt
text:
ï»¿
China launched a foreign telecommunications satellite tonight, setting off a national celebration to mark its entry into the international launching business.
As television viewers watched, a Chinese Long March 3 rocket carrying the American-made satellite blasted off from a launching pad in the central province of Sichuan. 
It is the first time that China has launched a foreign satellite.
The launching took place around 9:30 P.M. after being delayed for more than an hour and a half because of bad weather, officials said.
The launching of the satellite, Asiasat, built by the Hughes Aircraft Company and owned by a consortium based in Hong Kong, was made possible when President Bush temporarily waived a ban on weapons exports to China to allow the export of the satellite in February. 
The ban was imposed in June in response to China's military crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Beijing.
Â 
U.S. to Export 2 Others
Although President Bush said he was exercising the waiver for the sake of ''national interest,'' the move was viewed by many diplomats and politicians as a conciliatory gesture to Beijing. 
President Bush also cleared the way for the export of two other satellites manufactured by Hughes Aircraft that are to be launched on Chinese rockets over the next two years.
Asiasat has the capacity to relay television, telephone and facsimile signals to about 2.5 billion people in more than 30 Asian countries. 
Many live in remote areas with little access to telecommunications services.
A Chinese company, the China International Trust and Investment Corporation, is a partner in the consortium, but apparently has no control over the satellite's operations, which will be monitored from Hong Kong. 
Other partners are Cable and Wireless P.L.C. of Britain, and Hutchison Telecommunications Ltd. of Hong Kong.
It was the second time that the 2,732-pound satellite, formerly called Westar-6, was launched into space. 
On its first journey, it failed to reach orbit and was recovered by a United States space shuttle in 1984. 
Officials hope it will settle into orbit this time about 22,500 miles above the Earth.
China has successfully sent 26 of its own satellites into space, with one failure in 1974.

file: American on Their Own Terms_The Complete Other Side of the World_.txt
text:
ï»¿
TYPICAL AMERICAN
By Gish Jen.
296 pp. 
Boston:
Seymour Lawrence/Houghton Mifflin Company. 
$19.95.
Migration and mutation form a persistent, characterizing theme of our unsettling time. 
In her first novel, "Typical American," which explores the transformation of Chinese immigrants in the United States, Gish Jen has engaged this theme with distinction. 
More than that, she has given us "natives" (that is, the less recently settled) back to ourselves with a jolt of sharpened self-recognition.
"It's an American story," so the tale begins. 
"Before he was a thinker, or a doer, or an engineer, much less an imagineer like his self-made-millionaire friend Grover Ding, Ralph Chang was just a small boy in China, struggling to grow up his father's son."
The novel charts the progress of "Ralph" (an Americanization of Lai Fu -- "Come Fortune"), who leaves China in 1947, amid the "wreckage, and inflation, and moral collapse" that follow the war with Japan. 
Ralph's aim is to pursue engineering studies in New York.
He has six subsidiary goals, carefully listed. 
Two are resolutions to cultivate virtue and bring honor to his family. 
The succeeding four, culminating in a resolve to have nothing to do with girls, are abandoned without recall as Ralph comes to realize that he is alone, that he has journeyed "to the complete other side of the world."
It is during his first year abroad that Manchuria falls to Communist control -- the opening in a series of moves that will utterly transform China, sundering Ralph's link with his parents and ancestral traditions and leaving him unmoored, adrift in a new world.
Then, one day, Ralph is found slumped on a park bench, in the depths of despair. 
The finder is none other than Theresa, his long-lost older sister, who had emigrated before him. 
" 'Was miracle.'
This was Ralph's version of the story. 
'Miracle!'
" There's yet another miracle in store: Theresa happens to be rooming with a beautiful young Chinese woman named Helen, who is destined to become Ralph's wife. 
Together Ralph, Helen and Theresa set up housekeeping and, as they progress from permanent residents to citizens, each -- in his or her own way -- begins to undergo a sea change.
It is greed that most powerfully transforms Helen and Ralph. 
From their former playfully defensive recital of "typical American" characteristics ("typical American no-manners," "typical American no-morals," "typical American use-brute-force," "typical American wasteful") comes a new chant. 
Helen's is a litany of enraptured consumerism; Ralph's, of high-venture capitalism. 
Hers: "Double garage with separate entrance. 
Finished basement. 
Sliding glass doors. 
. . . breakfast nook with built-in benches. 
. . . wall unit. 
. . . extras galore."
His: "Got to spend money to make money. 
. . . What you can conceive, you can achieve. 
. . . The whole trick is. 
. . . Sky's the limit. 
. . . Can do, can do, can do!"
And, in time, as his own restaurant -- Ralph's Chicken Palace -- takes tangible shape, Ralph's dream of America as "every wish come true" seems to be realized.
I won't reveal what comes next, although no mere plot recital could possibly spoil the rest. 
No paraphrase could capture the intelligence of Gish Jen's prose, its epigrammatic sweep and swiftness. 
There's no pause, no underlining, no winking aside to the reader to signal how clever this is, how humorous that is. 
The author just keeps coming at you, line after stunning line. 
Even her incidental description seems new-minted -- purely functional, bone clean yet lustrous -- whether it's focused on the wilting of an elaborately curled hairdo in a discouraging social situation, or on children facing their first move, kissing the walls of their old apartment goodbye, or on death threatening one of the family members as "a man to sit at supper and never eat -- a man with his eye on everyone."
Here is Theresa, succumbing to the seduction of a pair of highly colored, voluptuously curved new shoes:
"These shoes had snagged her -- so vital, there in the store window, that they did not look like shoes so much as some highly adapted life form, mimicking shoes the way lizards mimicked desert rocks. 
Whereas the shoes she'd had on were plainly the real thing: worn out, dried up, cracking. 
Like their owner -- her reflection in the window was spindly and stiff, separated just this way, by a pane of glass, from some more vibrant world. 
At the center of her image, the red shoes had seemed to pulse, like her own true heart."
My only quarrel with this book is a backhanded tribute to its virtues, to the interest created in character and situation. 
There were times when I wanted to know more -- deeper and more -- moments when Helen and Ralph's capitulation to all-American greed seemed too easy, too headlong, verging on the simplicity of fable. 
This simplicity is clearly not wrong in itself, but it struck me as fundamentally at odds with the complexity, the multifaceted richness, of the novel as a whole.
Were there no contending forces?
No dim remembrance of Confucian harmonies or Buddhist detachment before Ralph's obsession gained full sway?
Wouldn't even passing reflection on the austerities of life under a Communist regime in China have raised a little point-counterpoint, exerted a chastening influence?
There were numerous references to church (Ralph, unconverted, attending with Theresa), rosaries, prayers, parochial school for the Chang children, yet not a word of admonition, not a whisper, concerning thralldom to material things. 
Was the church completely captive to culture, then?
It would seem so. 
Two perfunctory lines -- slogans, really -- from a homily ("Risk faith. 
Doubt doubt.") would suggest that the priest speaking was well attuned to typical American one-sound-bite attention spans. 
I wanted to know more.
It may be that this reader's lingerings and wonderings stem, in large part, from just plain reluctance to close the book on the Changs. 
For I came to care about all of them -- Theresa at first meeting, Ralph belatedly. 
And as the Changs seemed so hopelessly to drift apart, each one off in pursuit of some bright fragment of the American dream, I waited eagerly for them to return -- quan jia tuan yuan, the whole family together -- quite as if they had become my own family.
Â 
Â 
'I DREW ON WHAT I KNEW'
Gish Jen was once asked if the publishers of her first novel, "Typical American," had pressured her to change her name to something sounding less Chinese. 
"My real name is Lillian," she said, laughing, in a telephone interview from her home in Cambridge, Mass. 
She playfully adopted Gish -- as in the actress -- in high school. 
"It was part of becoming a writer," she said, "not becoming the person I was supposed to be."
That person was the dutiful daughter of Chinese immigrants, who expected her to get a practical job. 
Ms. Jen did attend business school briefly, and even took a typing test after marriage and house renovation had led her to put fiction aside. 
But before she became a secretary, Ms. Jen, an alumna of Harvard and the Iowa Writers' Workshop, successfully applied for a fellowship at Radcliffe's Bunting Institute. 
Her submission -- a story about the immigrant Changs -- grew into "Typical American."
"I drew on what I knew," she explained. 
"But even though I can see the elbows and knees and noses of people from my past, the relationship is like that between a dream and life. 
It's similar, but highly transformed."
Ms. Jen, who is 35 years old, once lived in Yonkers, where her family was called names and pelted with stones. 
But the experience, she said, did not define her childhood, and she refuses to emphasize it. 
In fact, the comedy of "Typical American" came most naturally. 
"I felt like a stereo with no bass," she said. 
"I had to learn to hit the low notes."
Although "Typical American" does include sadness, Ms. Jen still feels it is upbeat. 
"Not everyone has to be like Ralph," she said of her hero. 
"You can use the freedom of America differently."
When asked if she was working on a new book, Ms. Jen, who is now pregnant, replied simply: "I'm hatching."
-- LAUREL GRAEBER

file: American Women In Final In Soccer.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a plain stadium where a loudspeaker boomed out rousing Chinese folksongs, the United States women's soccer team defeated the German team tonight, 5-2, and won the right to take America into its first world championship soccer match.
Having reached the final of the first women's soccer championship, the United States team now has a chance to bring home a new trophy, and create a new image for American soccer.
"If we win this championship, I think the win will give us an international identity," said Anson Dorrance, coach of the United States women's team.
Dorrance, whose women's team garnered 49 goals to 0 for its five opponents during the qualifying matches for this tournament, said that while soccer is a very popular sport in the United States, "it's a sport with an inferiority complex. 
It's a sport most Americans feel is better played abroad."
But, he added, "The statement we're making is that we can play soccer in the United States."
Â 
Good Publicity for World Cup
Moreover, American soccer officials believe a championship women's team would focus attention and interest on the sport as the United States approaches 1994, the year it will be host to the World Cup soccer championship for men.
The championship match, which will be played Saturday in this sprawling, prosperous city in southern China, will pit the United States team against its archrival, Norway.
Norway has defeated the American team the last two times they were matched. 
In its semifinal game today, Norway beat Sweden by 4-1.
The United States women's team, which has played aggressive, entertaining, high-scoring soccer throughout the competition here, has "captured the attention of even the old stodgies here," said one soccer official, referring to some of the officials of FIFA, the organization governing world soccer, who are attending the event.
Â 
Making Up for Deficits
April Heinrichs of Littleton, Colo., the captain of the United States women's team, said that while the Americans might lack "the sophistication and the subtlety of the European players who grew up watching soccer on TV, we make up for that lack with speed, guts and determination."
Heinrichs, who is now head women's soccer coach at the University of Maryland, said that winning the world championship would be a watershed event for women's soccer in America.
"Females play soccer more than any other sport in America and I think this championship could draw attention to the sport, increase enrollment, sponsorship and audience interest," she said. 
"I think in four to eight years, soccer could dominate women's sports in America."
America's growing interest in soccer comes at a time when women's soccer is beginning to come into its own around the world, with 65 of the 165 countries involved in FIFA now sponsoring women's teams, officials said.
Â 
Sport Maturing in U.S.
The interest in soccer that began with boys and girls in America's suburbs and small towns in the mid-1970's is now maturing, bearing fruit in the form of the very players on the United States women's team here.
Carin Jennings, from Palos Verdes, Calif., said she had been playing soccer since she was 8 years old. 
Jennings scored three of the goals tonight against Germany, the defending European champion. 
Heinrichs scored the other two.
If they have impressed the other soccer teams and officials here, the 18 American players, aged 19 to 26, have also impressed the local Chinese.
Polite and smiling, the Chinese have asked the players for autographs, photographed them on the street and brought their families to the glitzy hotel where the American team is staying, ambling through the marble lobby hoping to catch a glimpse of some of the young women.
Corporations, government buildings and even a local meat market are decked out in huge red-and-white banners welcoming the international players in English and Chinese with the greeting, "Hail the 1st FIFA World Championship for Women's Football."

file: Army Tests Defenses Against Biological Weapons.txt
text:
ï»¿
The United States Army laboratories responsible for defending American troops against biological weapons are testing potential treatments in China and Argentina, the laboratories' commander has disclosed.
Col. David L. Huxsoll, commander of the Army's Medical Research Institute of Infectious Diseases at Fort Detrick, Md., said in an interview that his organization has also tested disease therapies in Liberia and South Korea and has supplied emergency pharmaceuticals to Egypt and other countries.
Critics charge that Army biological warfare experts ought not play any role in public health programs. 
In January, at the annual meeting of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, Colonel Huxsoll was confronted by civilian scientists concerned that an international race for new biological weapons may begin.
American biologists at the meeting, including Dr. Keith R. Yamamoto of the University of California at San Francisco, argued that field trials like those under way in China and Argentina should be managed by the National Institutes of Health rather than the Defense Department.
Â 
Question of Military Oversight
Research funds would be used more efficiently by the civilian agency, Dr. Yamamoto said. and trials would not arouse suspicions that military research was masquerading as public health.
But Colonel Huxsoll said in a subsequent interview that the Army remains responsible for protecting American troops against both natural diseases and biological warfare agents. 
He said it would be wrong for the armed forces to yield this responsibility to any outside agency.
If an enemy were ever to use biological weapons against American forces, the Army believes, such weapons would probably be based on organisms or viruses already known to scientists. 
Among the possibilities are variants of diseases that ravage many underdeveloped countries but are rare in industrial nations.
To develop defenses against such diseases, scientists must test vaccines and drugs in areas where the diseases are endemic.
''It would be absurd for us to create disease-causing organisms just to test therapies we develop,'' Colonel Huxsoll said. 
''We therefore conduct tests in cooperation with the host governments of countries where diseases are already claiming victims. 
It is in the interest of both the United States armed forces and the peoples of other countries to find defenses against lethal or incapacitating diseases that occur naturally but which might also be encountered in warfare.''
Â 
China Cooperates With Army
One nation cooperating with the Army is China, which charged in the 1950's that the United States had used germ-warfare weapons against North Korean and Chinese troops. 
The United States has denied the charge.
The current testing program in China is managed jointly by Hubei Province Medical University and the United States Defense Department. 
The trials have been carried out on more than 200 hospitalized volunteers suffering from a group of diseases known as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome. 
A victim is rapidly felled by vomiting and fever, sometimes followed by kidney failure that leads to death.
Some patients were treated with an antiviral drug called ribavirin, while others served as a control group. 
Colonel Huxsoll, who holds a doctorate in microbiology, said the test so far suggests that ribavirin sharply reduces the death rate from the disease. 
Ribavirin is made by ICN Pharmaceuticals of Costa Mesa, Calif.
''We have found,'' he said, ''that if a patient is treated with the drug within four days of developing symptoms, his or her chance of dying is only one fifth what it would be with no treatment. 
Treated survivors also recover much faster.''
In the Korean War, many soldiers, including Americans, were infected with the hemorrhagic fever and some died. 
The disease still is found in Korea, but the majority of its victims, 100,000 cases a year, are in rural areas of China. 
It is spread largely by rats.
Â 
Testing Program in China
The Army's testing program in China, which began two years ago, was in response to a Chinese initiative, Colonel Huxsoll said.
''We had been doing some work with that virus and the drug ribavirin in animals,'' he said, ''and the Chinese recognized the importance of the work and approached us.''
A different type of test began in Argentina last fall, in which about 6,500 volunteers, most of them farmers, are participating. 
The United States Army and the Argentine Government are inoculating part of this group with a vaccine developed at Fort Detrick against Junin virus, a disease also called Argentine hemorrhagic fever. 
Although many symptoms are similar to those of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, the Argentine disease is caused by a different virus.
The Argentine disease and a Bolivian hemorrhagic fever are caused by closely related viruses. 
They are spread by rat urine, particularly in the harvest season, which in the Southern Hemisphere peaks in May. 
Depending on the virulence of the strain and other factors, the death rate of victims can reach 30 percent, Colonel Huxsoll said.
The current treatment for Argentine and Bolivian hemorrhagic fever is a serum administered to a patient after the disease has been diagnosed, and this treatment is quite effective. 
The vaccine would render people immune before they become infected.
The trial will continue for several years, Colonel Huxoll said, and will be extended to many more volunteers to improve the statistical basis of the test. 
But by the end of the harvest period four months from now, Army experts expect to observe a clear difference between vaccinated and unvaccinated volunteers. 
The vaccine has already passed initial safety tests on animals and a small number of humans in the United States.
Limited trials of ribavirin were carried out in Liberia in the early 1980's as a therapy against Lassa fever, a dangerous virus also spread by rats. 
The tests were promising, Colonel Huxsoll said, and larger-scale trials are planned.
Â 
Critics Suspicious of Research
Still, critics remain suspicious of the Army research. 
At the meeting last month of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, Dr. Erhard Geissler, an official of East Germany's Central Institute for Molecular Biology, said that in 1943 and 1944 the Nazis developed biological weapons while calling their program ''defensive research.''
That is why, Dr. Geissler said, his Government is suspicious of all defensive biological warfare research, including that of the United States.
At the conference, Colonel Huxsoll denied that his organization's defensive research has any offensive application. 
He said that all the work conducted at the Fort Detrik laboratories is unclassified and is solely intended to protect people against disease.
The United States, for its part, is one of 111 nations, including the Soviet Union, that have ratified the Bacteriological and Toxin Weapon Convention of 1972. 
The treaty prohibits the development, production and stockpiling of biological weapons. 
But it does not prohibit research and development of defensive measures against biological agents.
Colonel Huxsoll noted that vaccines developed at Fort Detrick have been used not only to immunize patients abroad, but have protected Americans at home.

file: Arriving in Tokyo, Baker Starts 3-Nation Asia Tour.txt
text:
ï»¿
Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d arrived in Tokyo today at the start of a politically risky Asian tour likely to determine whether relations between China and the United States remain strained or can begin to recover in the aftermath of Beijing's violent crackdown on democracy advocates in 1989.
After stops in Japan and South Korea, Mr. Baker is to travel on Friday to Beijing in the highest-level visit by a Bush Administration official since the Tiananmen Square killings of June 1989. 
Although Mr. Baker's trip is going ahead as planned, President Bush last week responded to domestic political concerns by canceling a planned Asian tour beginning late this month.
Administration officials say that secret contacts between Washington and Beijing have assured Mr. Baker that he will not leave China empty-handed or embarrassed. 
But it is far from certain that members of Congress will be satisfied with what he extracts from the Chinese in the key areas of arms control, human rights and trade.
Â 
Solarz 'Uneasy'
"I am uneasy with this trip," said Representative Stephen J. Solarz, the Brooklyn Democrat who heads the House Foreign Affairs subcommittee on Asia, and a leader of efforts to punish China for the crackdown. 
"If Baker comes back and demonstrates that the trip was justified in the areas of our concern, fine. 
If he comes back as empty-handed as some others in the Administration before him, the trip will be rightly judged as not only a failure, but a mistake."
Mr. Solarz argued that if Mr. Baker "gives the present Chinese leadership gratuitous legitimacy" without getting anything substantial in return, the debate over the Administration's China policy will likely be rekindled. 
An unimpressive result might also give new impetus to efforts to strip China of "most-favored-nation" trading benefits, which the Administration renewed in June.
Â 
Movement Is Seen
An Administration expert involved in planning the trip said, "The Chinese have been doing some things -- not in the human rights area -- in a direction which we see as more positive than negative and we would like to encourage them to continue that movement.
"Look, everyone has mixed feelings about this trip," the official added. 
"I supported it because you cannot talk credibly about Asia, about Japan becoming a regional power, about the future security architecture in Asia and leave China unattended. 
It is too important. 
You avoid China at your peril."
Chinese leaders, the official said, "will want the maximum to give themselves face out of this visit. 
They will limit their cooperation in the absence of such meetings in order to get that. 
You go into it aware of that, and it is just a question of how you deal with it."
Bush Administration officials cite several areas where they contend the Chinese are moving in the right direction. 
The first is their agreement in principle to sign the treaty against the spread of nuclear weapons. 
Others include Beijing's limited cooperation on Middle East arms control -- which primarily involves not yet delivering missiles contracted for by Syria -- and its commitment in principle to join the Missile Technology Control Regime. 
Finally, on Sept. 
23, the Chinese agreed to begin talks on assuring Washington that it will not export to the United States goods produced by prison labor.
Â 
Cooperation With Iran
And then there are the areas where Washington will try to prevent further deterioration, like China's increasing nuclear cooperation of with Iran.
What Mr. Baker will apparently try to win from the Chinese is some sort of ironclad commitments not to sell nuclear technology to countries like Iran, Syria or Pakistan, nor any ballistic missiles. 
Even if the Chinese sign the treaty controlling missile technology, the question is how closely they will abide by it. 
The treaty against the spread of nuclear weapons is before the Chinese legislature and the Chinese authorities are saying it must be passed there first, although the regime could push it through any time.
"The Chinese are very good at appearing to make concessions and then not doing it," said a Congressional staff expert on China. 
"That is why the assurances have to be ironclad."
Because so many other issues have captured the headlines in recent years, American trade problems with China have been largely lost from view, but they are extremely serious. 
To control inflation in recent years the Chinese have clamped down tightly on imports, devalued their currency and erected import-license trade barriers to support their state-owned enterprises -- including those that depend on prison labor. 
This has led to diminished American exports to China and a trade defict in 1990 of about $10.5 billion.
Â 
Talks on Market Access
The United States is already engaged in negotiations with the Chinese over market access. 
Another yardstick for the success or failure of Mr. Baker's trip will be the extent to which it can speed up these negotiations.
The area where Congress will be most closely watching Mr. Baker's trip, however, will be in the field of human rights. 
Legislation that would strip China of its preferential trading status is now on hold in Congressional committees; whether the legislation is revived will depend in part on how many political prisoners the Chinese release amonng those arrested since the 1989 crackdown.
Amnesty International estimates that there are roughly 800 such political prisoners, and Congressional experts hope that half will be freed, including some prominent dissidents.
Before Mr. Baker visits Beijing, he will be making his inaugural stopover in Seoul, the South Korean capital.
The most pressing issue now on the Korean-American agenda, say American officials, is what can be done about quickening pace of North Korea's nuclear arms program. 
Some experts believe North Korea is only 6 to 12 months away from producing a bomb.

file: As Hong Kong Elite Are Leaving, Japanese Investors Are Moving In.txt
text:
ï»¿
At a time when thousands of Hong Kong's elite are vying for Canadian passports and its oldest companies are registering in the Bahamas, something unexpected is happening. 
The Japanese, usually among the world's most cautious investors, are moving into town.
As the countdown continues to 1997, when Britain will return Hong Kong to China, money is rapidly flowing out of the colony. 
Economic growth this year, the Government said last week, has slowed to just above zero.
But this does not seem to bother the Japanese, who - though they acknowledge a glimmer of self-doubt - see a giant buying opportunity, a chance to build a bigger base camp for doing business in China a decade from now.
Filling a Vacuum
Though exact statistics are not available, by most estimates Japan invested about $2 billion here last year, a record. 
That brings its total investment to roughly $8 billion, more than that of the United States for the first time.
The result is that Japan now has, at least for the time being, power and prestige in Hong Kong on a scale not seen in 45 years. 
As native businesses and even a few remnants of British colonial power decamp, sped by memories of the Chinese Government's crackdown on the democracy movement in Tiananmen Square last June, Japan is filling the vacuum, a vacuum of both money and power.
Hong Kong's richest and most influential executives are still the Hong Kong Chinese. 
But today Japanese investors are courted and dined, primarily because their presence is seen as another insurance policy against China's intervention in the city's freewheeling and largely unregulated ways.
The British, by contrast, are viewed as lame ducks, powerless to enforce the guarantees they received from China when they agreed to cede control of the colony.
''Japan is China's biggest provider of foreign aid,'' one prominent Hong Kong executive said the other day. 
''We have to hope that China will see that it is not in its interest to anger the Japanese here.''
The Japanese, in turn, tend to view Western nations, particularly the United States, as hopelessly romantic about China, overly enthralled about the country in the 1980's and too quick to flee when the crackdown came.
Traditionally, Japanese and American businesses have regarded Hong Kong as not only a convenient regional trading center but also a steppingstone to China. 
From Hong Kong, they could commission manufacturing work on the mainland and test Beijing's hospitality to investment. 
When things turned sour on the mainland, they could retreat to Hong Kong. 
Now, with each passing month, the colony seems increasingly like an abundantly rich corner of an otherwise poor nation.
So, Japan's approach has been to build up steadily, assuming that liberals and hardliners will come and go but that all will discover the lure of Japanese capital. 
There are more than 50 Japanese banks here now, with effective veto power over big projects like the $16 billion airport the Hong Kong government is trying to build, and more than 30 Japanese securities firms.
''I think Japan has big confidence that after 1997, Beijing will understand that Hong Kong is special,'' said Hiroshi Zaizen, the chairman of the Mitsubishi Corporation's subsidiary here and one of the city's most influential Japanese executives.
Â 
Big Money to Be Made
While China is the main reason that Japanese companies come to Hong Kong, there is still big money to be made in the colony itself.
Most Japanese department stores have opened in the tourist centers here to serve Japanese tourists -usually selling them products at lower prices than they could find at the same department stores in Tokyo. 
But Japan's Yaohan Department Store Company has opened a giant store in a boom town in the New Territories - part of the colony that is near the mainland border - hoping to tap the market for the half-million Hong Kong workers who live in giant new apartment buildings in the area.
The Japanese confidence in Hong Kong's future is hardly ironclad. 
Japanese companies have for the most part avoided big real estate purchases, preferring more liquid investments. 
If disaster should strike, much of the money can be pulled out -much the same strategy Japan has pursued on the mainland. 
''On June 29, 1997, we can always press a button, I guess,'' Mr. Zaizen said.
Meanwhile, evidence mounts that Hong Kong's natives are already pressing that button. 
A recent study by the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation showed that the transfer of capital abroad last year increased 10-fold, though no one knows what that figure means because Hong Kong does not measure capital inflows. 
Putting the best face on things, the Government said the figure was a measure of the health of the economy because it showed Hong Kong companies were investing abroad. 
The more common explanation is that people are leaving the country and taking their bank accounts with them.
Â 
Japan's 'Sky High' Investor
But then there are exceptions like Kazuo Wada, the owner of Yaohan. 
Mr. Wada surprised both Tokyo and Hong Kong when he decided last year to move his corporate empire here.
Earlier this month, in another symbol of the shifting power structurehere, Mr. Wada became the new owner of ''Sky High'' - a palace of turrets, a half acre of floor space and views of the South China Sea from all windows - perched atop ''the Peak,'' the striking hill that dominates Hong Kong Island. 
The sprawling villa had been built, at exorbitant cost, by Hongkong and Shanghai Banking, one of this city's oldest and richest institutions, as the official residence of its chairman.
But these are more conservative days for Hong Kong institutions, and so the bank company, after three unsuccessful tries, persuaded a reluctant Mr. Wada to buy the house for $11 million. 
His company said the purchase was mostly intended to cement good relations; Mr. Wada himself plans to live in modest accommodations.
''Perhaps it would make a nice guest house,'' said Yuji Sakuma, the managing director of Yaohan's Hong Kong operations.
Â 
The Social Whirl
The wedding of Mr. Wada's daughter a few months ago was viewed as an enormous social event in Hong Kong, and it was one example of how mightily Japan has risen in the social pecking order in Hong Kong.
Another was the creation of the Dynasty Club, an exclusive club intended to rival Hong Kong's legendary Jockey Club, a bastion of the British establishment. 
The wealthy Hong Kong Chinese who started the club asked three people to act as initial ''patrons'' to draw Hong Kong's rich and powerful. 
The three were the head of the New China News Agency - China's unofficial diplomatic representative - and the senior American and Japanese diplomats here.
The American official declined, but few here missed the symbolism of the fact that the British were not asked.
Â 
Some Deep Resentments
But if many people in Hong Kong are reassured by Japanese investment, not everyone is pleased. 
Resentments of World War II run deep, and the city still holds a ceremony each August to mark its liberation from the Japanese forces at the end of World War II, though attendance grows sparser every year.
''The businessmen need Japan, so it is convenient for most of the city to forget,'' said Jack Edwards, who heads a group of former prisoners of war who have mounted a campaign here to recall Japanese war crimes. 
Older Chinese often refer to the Japanese in derogatory terms, he said, ''and my generation doesn't like their arrival at all.''
He added, ''I guess it was inevitable.''
Today the Peninsula Hotel, once Japan's military headquarters here, swarms with Japanese tourists. 
Executives in the growing Japanese population here, estimated at 16,000, often leave their families in Hong Kong and spend the week across the Chinese border in Guangdong province, where companies like Sanyo have large factories.
Â 
Japanese View of the Risk
The risk of investing in Hong Kong is viewed by Japan as no worse than the risk of investing in China itself. 
And Japanese businesses say they are eager to do more, as soon as World Bank lending resumes and the Japanese Government releases $500 million in economic development assistance that has been withheld since Tiananmen Square.
The World Bank has put forward two loans to China for its board to approve on Tuesday. 
The United States has said it can support one of the loans - $300 million for tree planting to combat deforestation - because its meets basic human needs. 
But the United States is opposed to the other loan, $150 million to upgrade roads and inland waterways in Jiangsu province.
''We are still nervous,'' said Fumio Hashimoto, who heads the Bank of Tokyo office here. 
''No one would say that we have 100 percent confidence in the future of Hong Kong. 
But in the medium to long term, we know it is important.''
Â 
Plans for New Airport
Still, Japan is carefully picking and choosing in its investments. 
And it is in those choices that Japan's presence is likely to be felt most strikingly in coming years.
Plans for the new airport illustrate the tensions in the relationship. 
No one questions the need for a far larger airport. 
Hong Kong's enormous volume of air traffic is currently funneled through a single, short runway. 
The runway approach comes perilously close to one of Kowloon's densely packed neighborhoods - so close that passengers about to land can see families preparing dinner in nearby apartments.
So last year the Hong Kong government planned a giant airport to be built on an outer island and connected to Hong Kong by a long bridge. 
Roughly half the $16 billion cost is expected to be picked up by private investors. 
Japanese engineering and cement companies are eager for a piece of the action; so are companies like the Bechtel Group in the United States, which has been chosen to coordinate the project.
Â 
Need for China's Blessing
The problem is that the Hong Kong government barely consulted China before laying out details of the plan. 
The Chinese are suspicious that Hong Kong will use the airport to empty the colony's coffers before 1997. 
They have signaled general approval of the project, but not enthusiastically.
As a result, the Japanese banks -already burned by lending to hotels on the mainland that today have few guests and little way to pay back debt - say they will be very cautious. 
Recently, a senior Hong Kong government official went to Tokyo - the first such visit - to drum up support. 
He got smiles but few commitments. 
''We need the Chinese blessing,'' said Mr. Hashimoto of the Bank of Tokyo. 
''We still have no detailed studies, and the time is short.''

file: As Things Ease in China, an Envoy Departs.txt
text:
ï»¿
Two months ago a man named Zhang boarded a train with nearly $2,000 in life savings, disembarked more than 400 miles later at the nearest United States Consulate and plunked his money down as a contribution to helping American soldiers wounded in the Persian Gulf.
That would never have happened two years ago, when the embassy in Beijing was surrounded by armed Chinese soldiers and ordinary citizens did not dare linger by the compound, much less attend a banquet at the Ambassador's residence.The difference in atmosphere reflects how some things have changed in the two years that Ambassador James R. Lilley has been in Beijing. 
In recent weeks, Mr. Lilley, who retires as Ambassador on Friday, has been able to draw large crowds of Chinese to his farewell parties.
Mr. Lilley, a blunt-speaking China hand who has given brief news conferences in Chinese and who was an officer for 27 years at the Central Intelligence Agency, was instrumental in navigating Chinese-American relations out of a stormy period. 
He arrived weeks before the military crackdown on the democracy movement in 1989."He's tough and won't let the Chinese pull the wool over his eyes," an American diplomat said. 
"He knows how to negotiate with the Chinese. 
Relations would have been much worse without him."
But while the guns in front of the embassy have disappeared, relations are still tense. 
As the deadline approaches for determining whether to extend most-favored-nation trade status, negotiations between American and Chinese officials over human rights, weapons sales and trade have accentuated the strains in the relationship.
The embassy even refused to disclose Mr. Zhang's full name -- it is also returning the money to him -- for fear of getting him into trouble with the authorities, and today, the Foreign Ministry spokesman, Wu Jianmin, warned that China would not bow to foreigners.
"The Chinese side will never accept the attachments of various kinds of conditions to the extension of most-favored-nation treatment of China," Mr. Wu said at a news conference today. 
"Attempts to force the Chinese Government to change its policies by exerting pressure on it will lead nowhere."
Nonetheless, the China of the last two years was a China with which Mr. Lilley is intimately familiar, although he has faced an uphill battle since he arrived. 
Only days after he got to Beijing, he rode his bicycle on the streets to get first-hand knowledge of what was going on at the pro-democracy demonstrations on Tiananmen Square.After the crackdown, Mr. Lilley found himself a host to two of China's most prominent dissidents, Fang Lizhi and Li Shuxian, who had sought asylum at the embassy. 
Because of the secrecy surrounding the asylum, Mr. Lilley sometimes delivered meals personally to Mr. Fang and Ms. Li. The next year was consumed with negotiating the release of the two dissidents.
Mr. Lilley was born 63 years ago in the eastern Chinese city of Qingdao, and returned again to China to open the Central Intelligence Agency's station in Beijing in 1973. 
He also was here when George Bush came to open the diplomatic mission a year later. 
The two men, both of whom graduated from Yale University, became close associates, and their wives are also friends.
Mr. Lilley's close ties with the President have led many people to suggest that he is a candidate for Director of Central Intelligence. 
Other possible jobs are deputy national security adviser or Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian Affairs.
While Mr. Lilley's last tenure here lasted only two years, which has fanned rumors that he is being called home to take the Central Intelligence Agency job, his associates say that his post all along was to last only two years. 
Mr. Lilley declined to respond to questions about his next career move, and he declined to be interviewed for this article.
But he has hinted that he will not assume a high profile on China policy after he leaves on Friday. 
His successor in Beijing has not been named, but for a long time, it has been expected to be J. Stapleton Roy, who is executive secretary of the State Department.

file: Asian Games_Chinese Athletes Stun Their Foes.txt
text:
ï»¿
For a country that has lately grown accustomed to the agony of defeat, the Asian Games under way here have been a rare joy. 
China has rebounded from its disappointing performance in the 1988 Olympics in Seoul, South Korea, to overwhelm nearly all comers and stack up an enormous number of gold medals.
When the Asiad ended today, save for a closing ceremony Sunday, China had won 183 of the 308 gold medals at stake. 
South Korea was a distant second, with 54, and Japan third, with 38.
China has stunned its competitors by winning even in events in which it has little experience. 
China took up boxing only three years ago - the sport was previously banned here - yet it managed to get six boxers into the finals and won one boxing gold.
China's performance is remarkable in that at the last Asian Games, held in Seoul in 1986, it barely edged out South Korea by a single gold medal to win first place in the tally. 
The Korean athletes were bolstered by a heavy haul in boxing medals, and that left an impression on China. 
It was a major reason why Beijing reversed its ban and began cultivating its own boxers.
Â 
More Than Sportsmanship
Beijing regards the Asian Games as being about far more than sportsmanship - as the last Sports Minister discovered when he was dismissed after the poor showing at the 1988 Olympics - and the hard-line leadership is exultant with the outcome since the games began Sept. 
22.
After a string of unremitting bad news for the Government - demonstrations, martial law, international ostracism, economic slump, as well as the disappointment in the Olympics - the leadership finally has something to crow about. 
The official newspapers are even suggesting that the victories underscore the virtue of socialism.
''What is our secret?'' asked the People's Daily, the Communist Party newspaper, in a front-page headline one day last week.
It answered the question: training has been merciless, and athletes have also been coached rigorously in ''ideological education.''
Â 
'A One-Man Show'
China has been preparing frantically for the Asian Games, which offered it an opportunity to win back international respect and domestic support after the 1989 crackdown against the democracy movement. 
The respect from competitors has been forthcoming, tinged with a certain amount of envy and incredulity at the Chinese success.
''It's incredible the way they're walking away with the whole show,'' grumbled a South Korean, one of an enormous contingent here to see the games. 
Yonhap, the South Korean news agency, reportedly declared: ''Interest has subsided as China has swept the gold medals and turned the Asiad into a one-man show.''
So far no single athlete has overwhelmed the public imagination with a string of gold medals, but several athletes have turned in outstanding performances and won national fame. 
On Thursday, a 14-year-old boy edged out the world champion to win a gold medal in platform diving with a stunning set of dives, which included a dive that earned one perfect mark of 10 and six scores of 9.5.
The boy, Sun Shuwei, had won a competition in Canada earlier this year, but Thursday's victory was his first in a major international competition. 
A backward 3 1/2-somersault dive helped clinch his victory over the current world champion, Xiong Ni, a 16-year-old who finished second to Greg Louganis at the 1988 Olympics.
Â 
No Single Star
Another star is 97-pound Xing Fen, the 17-year-old daughter of a farmer from southern China, who surpassed her own world record by lifting barbells of 209 pounds, more than twice her body weight.
Gao Min, a 20-year-old diver from Sichuan Province, won three gold medals despite insisting that her best performances will not come until the next Olympics, in Barcelona in 1992.
Another standout was Zhou Lingmei, a 22-year-old woman who won a gold medal and beat a six-year-old world record by clocking 1:13:899 in the one kilometer cycling time trial. 
The overall winner in the medals race was Shen Jianqiang, a 25-year-old swimmer who won five gold medals during the Asiad, but he is unlikely to do so well at Barcelona when faced with other powerful sprinters.
So far the games have gone smoothly, but they were marred by the crash of a hijacked plane Tuesday in the southern Chinese city of Canton. 
At least 127 people were killed, after the crew apparently refused to follow the hijacker's instructions to fly to Taiwan or Hong Kong. 
Instead, an attempt was made to land in Canton, and the hijacker is believed to have fought over the controls or perhaps set off a bomb when he realized he hd been tricked.
A foreign diplomat suggested that Chinese officials were aparently so concerned at foiling the hijacking and preserving the integrity of the games that they put the passengers at risk by trying to trick the hijacker.

file: Aspiring Party Leaders At Forefront of Revolt.txt
text:
ï»¿
Many of the early leaders of the student demonstrations in Beijing were sons or daughters of ranking Communist Party officials studying at People's University, a school intended to produce future senior Communists, an American scholar who has been doing research there says.
The scholar, Lee Feighon, a professor of Chinese history at Colby College in Maine, said the key role of these young Communists suggested that the pro-democracy protests in China ''were originally not a movement against the party but a movement to reform the party.''
''These were students who thought of themselves as the future leaders of the country and were upset by all the corruption and rigid bureaucratism they saw in their own party,'' Mr. Feighon said. 
''Their goal was to restore the prestige of being a party member, not to destroy the party.''
Mr. Feighon said that many foreigners as well as some Chinese had misunderstood the origins of the demonstrations, attributing them to students at nearby Beijing University, China's most prestigious school, where the students have fewer ties to the Communist Party and more interest in the West.
Â 
Leaders of Protest Movement
Students from Beijing University did play an important role later in the movement as it grew, Mr. Feighon acknowledged. 
But he said that, based on his own observations, it was students from the lesser-known People's University who had taken the lead at critical times.
Mr. Feighon, who spent a month living in a dormitory on People's University campus during his fourth stay there in recent years, said the organizers were all students from the Party History Department, the only department at any Chinese university devoted to studying the history of the Chinese Communist Party.
''These kids have all been carefully screeened before they are admitted to the Party History Department,'' Mr. Feighon said in a telephone interview. 
''Everybody knows they are well-connected and are being groomed to be the future Communist leaders of China.''
Among the students at People's University, for example, is a grandson of Mao Zedong. 
He was initially admitted to the Party History Department, Mr. Feighon said, but an order from the Central Committee later prohibitted him from joining it, so he was made a student in the general history department. 
But the younger Mao ''hangs around with the Party History Department crowd,'' Mr. Feighon related.
Unlike most of China's best college students, Mr. Feighon said, the students in the Party History Department are not studying with hopes of going abroad. 
''They are traditionalists in the Chinese sense, seriously interested in Chinese history and the Party.''
Â 
Party's Loss of Prestige
Nevertheless, he said, they recognize that since the Cultural Revolution in the late 1960's the party has suffered a huge loss of legitimacy and they are not as eager for a career in the Party as earlier generations of Chinese were. 
A poll he took of 34 undergraduates in the Party History Department found that 30 of them had wanted to be assigned to other fields. 
In China, the Government decides which students will be admitted to which department and which university.
Still, it was a group of graduate and undergraduate students from People's University Party History Department who took the action that sparked the student demonstrations. 
Late in the evening of April 15, after the announcement of the death of Hu Yaobang, the ousted party General Secretary and a leading advocate of liberalization, they went to Tiananmen Square to lay wreaths in his honor. 
What made their action even bolder, Mr. Feighon said, was that they put the name of their school and department on the wreaths.
Two days later, students in the Party History Department began a boycott of classes, demanding a reappraisal of Mr. Hu's career. 
He was removed in early 1987 after being charged with being too lenient toward an early series of student protests. 
Students in the department then formed a militia enforcing the strike throughout People's University, and the idea later spread to other schools in the city.
On April 17, Mr. Feighon said, it was again students from the Party History Department who formulated plans for a large march into Tiananmen Square on the day of Mr. Hu's funeral, the first large student march into central Beijing.
Â 
Defiance of Crackdown
And most important, on April 27, after Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, had called for a crackdown on any futher student activities, it was students from People's University who led a procession into central Beijing, pushing past police lines for the first time. 
''The night before, you could hear loudspeakers all across campus warning students not to go out, but the next morning the kids from the Party History Department came out in formation, like a Roman legion, with their arms linked,'' Mr. Feighon said.
''They were out front all day, putting their bodies on the line,'' Mr. Feighon recalled. 
''When they came back that night, for the first time workers and other people treated them like heroes, joining in to give them food and support. 
Those students who hadn't marched felt pretty left out.''
Each time before the students set out, they called their parents or grandparents, many of whom hold high office. 
''If the troops fire on the students, I just want you to know they'll be firing on me,'' Mr. Feighon reported the students saying telling their relatives.
At first some of the students had treated the demonstrations like a panty raid, he said, with some simply throwing small bottles out their windows as a prank. 
Mr. Deng's given name rhymes with the word for small bottle.
But most of those in the Party History Department were serious, taking their inspiration from the Cultural Revolution, Mr. Feighon said. 
''They weren't looking to re-enact it, but to learn lessons from it. 
It taught them that students do have the power to topple a corrupt bureaucracy and that one old man should not have too much power,'' he said.

file: AUG. 30 - SEPT. 5_ New Abuses Charged_More Democracy Activists Detained in China.txt
text:

The police in Beijing last week detained three more pro-democracy activists, including Shen Tong, a leader of the Tiananmen movement in 1989 and a graduate student at Boston University who had returned to China to set up a chapter of a pro-democracy organization that he heads.
Also detained were two associates, Qi Dafeng and Qian Liyun. 
They were taken from the family home of Mr. Shen about 4 A.M. Tuesday. Li Yixian, Mr. Shen's mother, said the police passed her a note written by her son that said he was being questioned at a hotel but giving no location.

file: Baker Denounces Executions of Chinese Protesters.txt
text:
ï»¿
Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d joined a chorus of Western leaders today in denouncing China's execution of three men for their role in political demonstrations in Shanghai. 
But he said the Bush Administration was not planning any additional actions against Beijing ''at this time.''
''We deeply regret the fact that these executions have gone forward, notwithstanding appeals from the United States, appeals from the Federal Republic of Germany, and perhaps other countries, for clemency,'' Mr. Baker told reporters at a briefing at the White House. 
The briefing followed a meeting between President Bush and Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher of West Germany.
The United States, Mr. Baker added, ''is not contemplating any additional action at this time.''
''I ought to also say that there is an important relationship here which we should seek to preserve if we possibly can,'' Mr. Baker said.
Â 
Thatcher 'Utterly Appalled'
Reacting to the events in China today, Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher of Britain said, according to Reuters, that she was ''utterly appalled'' by the executions, and said she and Prime Minister Bob Hawke of Australia were discussing possible sanctions against China.
The Associated Press reported that Foreign Minister Roland Dumas of France told the National Assembly in Paris: ''What is happening in China is atrocious. 
The totalitarian machine, in all its horror, is rolling. 
It turns what should be judicial decisions into veritable murders.''
The A.P. quoted a Dutch Foreign Ministry spokesman as saying the executions were expected to be discussed at next week's European Community summit meeting in Madrid.
As with many other decisions on China, the actions Tuesday to suspend high-level exchanges between American and Chinese officials and to postpone consideration of new loans to China by international financial institutions were made by the President and the Secretary of State, along with a tight circle of aides. 
It took not only many White House staff members by surprise but many in the State Department as well.
Â 
Events in China
While the move obviously had a heavy domestic political component, aimed to demonstrate that the Administration was not being indifferent to the suppression of pro-democracy demonstrators, it also seems to fit with the overall analytical framework with which Mr. Baker and Mr. Bush are understood to be operating.
A senior Administration official said President Bush and Mr. Baker are acting on the assumption that events in China will go through several stages in the coming years.
The official described the first stage, encompassing the present situation, this way: ''The Chinese leadership is entirely focused on their short-term survival. 
They determined that their basic system of authority was being challenged by the pro-democracy movement and they were ready to pay any price - both foreign and domestic - to preserve that system.''
The official said of this stage: ''There is nothing that the United States can do or say that will really influence the behavior of the Chinese leadership. 
They are motivated by basic impulses of survival.''
The moves the Administration took Tuesday were done with the full awareness that they would have no immediate restraining effect, officials said. 
Rather, they were aimed at the next stage in developments in China, when the authorities in Beijing consolidate their rule and try to restore the economic modernization program they were on before and then confront the full domestic and international price of their repression.
That includes the postponement of loans, the halt in military sales from the West, the decrease in Western investment in China, the falloff in tourism, international diplomatic isolation and, maybe most important, the passive resistance of their own people.
That passive resistance, as Administration officials see it, could take a variety of forms, from sabotaging of production in state-owned factories, to work stoppages, to decreases in productivity, to sporadic demonstrations.

file: BAKER FAILS TO WIN ANY COMMITMENTS IN TALKS IN BEIJING.txt
text:
ï»¿
Two days of talks between Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d and China's top leaders have yielded none of the gestures on human rights, arms control and trade sought by Washington as requirements for improved relations with Beijing, a senior American official said today.
Mr. Baker, making the first public high-level visit to China by an American official since Beijing's violent crackdown on democracy advocates in 1989, has one more scheduled meeting with the Chinese Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen, on Sunday. 
The American official said Mr. Baker hoped that at this session the Chinese would be more forthcoming than they had been up to now.
Â 
A Last-Ditch Appeal
This evening's briefing by the State Department official seemed at times like a desperate, last-ditch appeal to the Chinese to respond before Mr. Baker departs with the kind of specific concessions he had anticipated in making the visit, which has already bestowed some much-sought legitimacy on the Chinese leadership. 
If Mr. Baker goes home empty-handed, the Bush Administration is likely to face growing domestic criticism of its China policy and greatly increased pressure in Congress for sanctions against Beijing.
"We cannot want an improved U.S.-China relationship more than the Chinese," the official said after today's six hours of meetings. 
"There are obviously certain things that need to transpire for that to move forward. 
For whatever reasons, if there is anything they have to say to the Secretary, it will be said tomorrow. 
They know when we are leaving, they know that we have that meeting tomorrow, and I think I will leave it right there."
The official said Mr. Baker came here expecting at least some firm commitments from China on human rights, missile proliferation and trade.
He was understood to be seeking the release of some of the 800 political prisoners rounded up by Beijing after the Tiananmen Square killings in 1989, a halt to the transfer of Chinese missiles and nuclear technology to Middle Eastern nations and an end to restrictive trade practices, which have created an American trade deficit with China of about $13 billion.
Up to now, the official said, Mr. Baker has received neither positive nor negative commitments from China in any of these areas.
Mr. Baker met today with China's Prime Minister, Li Peng; the Communist Party leader, Jiang Zemin; the Minister of Justice, Cai Cheng, and President Yang Shangkun.
The American official said that in the meetings Mr. Baker repeatedly emphasized to the Chinese that they had been asking him to come to Beijing for two years and that now he was here they would be making a big mistake to send him home with nothing to show for his politically risky trip.
The Chinese presented a somewhat different view of today's talks. 
The common theme running through their comments to the Secretary, judging from the briefing given by the Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman, was that the Chinese greatly value their ties with Washington and want them improved, but not on Washington's terms alone.
Each of the Chinese leaders emphasized to Mr. Baker that they would not respond to any pressure from Washington, that the United States had to learn to continue dealing face-to-face with China, despite differences in the relationship, and that Washington should appreciate more the strategic value of Chinese-American ties. 
If it did, some of the differences in the relationship could be more easily muted or overlooked.
For instance, President Yang was quoted by the official New China News Agency as having told Mr. Baker: "Some problems can be solved through discussions, while others need several rounds of discussion. 
Those which cannot be solved for the time being can be shelved. 
We call this 'seeking common ground while reserving difference.'
"
Â 
A Warning on Pressure
So long as both the United States and China can adopt such an approach, Mr. Yang continued, it will be easy to solve the problems between them. 
But he added that "the practice of exerting pressure can only lead to tension in the bilateral relations, and is of no use in solving problems, " the official press agency reported, that
The Chinese President went out of his way during his opening comments to Mr. Baker -- while American reporters were in the room -- to praise President Bush and talk about what good friends they were.
With Mr. Baker at his side, President Yang recalled that he first went to the United States at the invitation of Mr. Bush when he was Vice President.
"After our meeting, we had a long and pleasant talk," he said. 
"We didn't use diplomatic language. 
We talked about a lot of things about China. 
Actually, Mr. Bush asked me a lot of questions concerning China. 
Though we had a long talk, time was passing very quickly. 
Actually, we had this long talk on a boat, and when we finished the boat tour it was already very late. 
So Mr. Secretary, when you return to Washington, please convey my greetings to my friend Mr. Bush."
When the Foreign Ministry spokesman, Wu Jianmin, was asked whether Minister of Justice Cai responded to Mr. Baker's appeal for the release of imprisoned democracy advocates he responded brusquely, "Actions that the Chinese judicial organs will take are entirely something that the China side shall decide."
His remark seemed to suggest that if China did release some prisoners in response to Mr. Baker's appeal it would not be during this visit.
Another issue high on Mr. Baker's agenda is arms proliferation. 
China is believed to have provided help to the nuclear programs of Iran and Algeria, among other nations, raising concerns that it is helping third world countries develop nuclear weapons. 
Beijing is also believed to have pursued sales of medium-range missiles to Syria and Iran despite pledges not to sell such weapons in the Middle East.
What seemed to have distressed the American delegation was not only that Mr. Baker received no concrete commitments from the Chinese leaders, but also that the same was true for the experts he brought along. 
These went over the human rights, arms control and trade issues in detail with their Chinese counterparts.
When the senior American official was asked to characterize the talks that the Assistant Secretary of State for Human Rights, Richard Schifter, and the Under Secretary of State for International Security Affairs, Reginald Bartholomew, held with their Chinese counterparts, she said curtly, "The only characterizations I would give is that they were meetings between experts."
The Chinese press omitted all references to Mr. Schifter's presence in the American delegation.
During Mr. Baker's talks with Prime Minister Li, the Chinese leader told the Secretary that while there were some problems between the United States and China, they could not be solved if the two sides did not sit down and talk "face to face," the Chinese press agency reported.
Mr. Li was quoted as adding: "China may share the same view with you on some questions and have different viewpoints on others, but this is very natural. 
The Chinese nation, with a history of more than 5,000 years, has a strong sense of national dignity. 
For more than 100 years we the Chinese people suffered very much from foreign aggression and humiliation, so we cherish so much our independence and sovereignty. 
We hope to see gradual restoration and improvement of the bilateral relations through contacts."
Jiang Zemin, General Secretary of the Communist Party, used his meeting with Mr. Baker to emphasize that "it is very abnormal and not in keeping with the interests of our two big countries that you don't have high-level contacts with us," the Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
Â 
Nixon's Approach Recalled
Mr. Jiang explained to Mr. Baker that "the world is a colorful one which has various kinds of social systems, cultural heritages and ideologies, so it is dangerous to model such a colorful world on one form."
The Communist Party leader recalled fondly for Mr. Baker the approach to relations taken by former President Richard Nixon and former Secretary of State Henry A. Kissinger with Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai, the late Chinese leaders. 
He seemed to be trying to encourage Mr. Baker to harken back to those days, when the United States and China supposedly did not seem to worry so much about questions of human rights, but focused on the global game of nations in which Washington viewed China as a critical counterweight to the Soviet Union.
Mr. Nixon and Mr. Mao, he said, "came to realize that the common interests count most for both sides."
Mr. Jiang concluded by telling Mr. Baker: "I remember two lines of an ancient Chinese poem. 
It says that if you want to have a longer vision you should move to a higher level. 
We should look further by moving to a higher point, and have our eyes on the future and in this way we should surely be able to restore Sino-American relations."
In all of his meetings today, Mr. Baker was never photographed shaking hands with any Chinese officials. 
Before each meeting, reporters and photographers were kept out of the room until after Mr. Baker and his Chinese hosts had greeted one another, and were ushered in only when the Chinese and American delegations were seated stiffly around the conference table.
Chinese officials told American reporters that Mr. Baker's delegation had requested such arrangements, although American officials denied this.
