file: Baker Warns China Against Selling New Missiles.txt
text:
ï»¿
Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d warned China today that there would be "profound consequences" for Chinese-American relations if Beijing sold newly developed ballistic missiles to Syria and Pakistan.
China's arms exports have become a matter of controversy as Congress considers President Bush's proposal to renew Beijing's preferential trade status. 
Mr. Baker said the United States had no "evidence or any indication" that China had actually shipped surface-to-surface missiles to Syria, despite a recent press report suggesting that a deal was near completion.
He said the Bush Administration had also cautioned Beijing against sending sophisticated new missiles to Pakistan, asserting that this "would constitute grave threats to the region and could have bilateral consequences."
Mr. Baker did not elaborate further.
A group of Republican and Democratic senators is seeking concessions from the Administration in exchange for legislative support for President Bush's decision to renew trade privileges for China for another year.
Â 
Bitter Rift With Lawmakers
The White House and Congress are bitterly divided over how to handle relations with China. 
Many Republican and Democratic lawmakers are concerned that Mr. Bush has reacted too mildly to Beijing's crackdown on the democracy movement two years ago.
Mr. Bush prevailed last year in extending trade privileges to China, but he faces stronger opposition this year in both the House and the Senate. 
The renewal of China's trade status has become one of the most contentious foreign policy and trade issues facing Congress this summer.
At a meeting this morning with Mr. Baker and Brent Scowcroft, the national security adviser, Senator Bob Dole, Republican of Kansas, presented a proposed letter to Mr. Bush that was drafted by Senator Max S. Baucus of Montana and co-signed by three other Democratic senators.
The letter calls for five concessions from the Administration, a participant in the negotiations between the White House and Congress said. 
The biggest concession would be for the United States to end its opposition to Taiwan's immediate entry into the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
Such a move would infuriate China, Deputy Secretary of State Lawrence S. Eagleburger told a House panel today.
The letter also suggests that the Administration take legal steps to fight China's import barriers, insure that Chinese products made with prison labor are kept out of the United States market, block loans to China by multilateral agencies until the country's human rights record improves, and enter negotiations to curb the spread of ballistic missiles in the third world.
"My understanding is they are willing to make virtually all the concessions I've asked for in my letter," Senator Baucus, the chairman of the Senate's International Trade Subcommittee, said in an interview today.
Â 
Risking China's Anger
Several Administration officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said that no final deal had been struck. 
They said White House officials were divided on whether to risk China's anger by supporting Taiwan's application to GATT.
Senator Baucus said he had not decided whether he would support the renewal of China's so-called "most-favored-nation" status if the Administration refused to grant the concessions.
A Congressional resolution canceling the renewal of China's trade privileges is considered likely. 
To sustain a Presidential veto of such a resolution, Mr. Bush would need the votes of nearly a dozen Democratic senators led by Senator Baucus who strongly support free trade but are troubled by China's human rights record.
The participant in congressional negotiations with the Administration said that Senator Dole was asking other Republican senators to co-sign Senator Baucus's letter, which is to be released on Thursday.
Senator Baucus said that 8 to 12 Democratic senators and 25 to 30 Republican senators were likely to support the renewal of China's preferential trade status if the Administration granted the concessions.
Such a tally would not prevent the Senate from approving a resolution rejecting renewal of China's trade status, he said, but it would insure that a Presidential veto could not be overridden.

file: BAKER WILL VISIT CHINA THIS MONTH.txt
text:
ï»¿
After several months of secret negotiations, Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d announced tonight that he would visit China this month, a trip that is bound to revive the debate over the Bush Administration's stance toward the hard-line Beijing Government.
Mr. Baker will be the highest-level Bush Administration official to visit Beijing since the violent crackdown on democracy demonstrators at Tiananmen Square in June 1989. 
His announcement of the trip, in a news conference at the close of Middle East peace talks in Madrid, came only a few days after reports that China may be helping Iran develop a nuclear bomb.
Clearly aware that his trip will re-ignite the debate between the Admministration and Democrats in Congress over how tough the United States should be in dealing with Beijing, Mr. Baker immediately took the offensive.
"China has almost one fourth of all the people in the world," he said, echoing Mr. Bush's argument that China, no matter how repressive its domestic policies, is simply too big to ignore. 
"It has nuclear weapons, it has great influence in the region and it has immense economic potential."
Â 
Invokes Human Rights
Seeking to justify the timing of the trip, Mr. Baker said his mission was the only way of persuading Beijing to make changes in its arms control and human rights policies.
"We cannot make headway unless we discuss them," he said. 
"Ignoring them will not make the problems go away."
Mr. Baker's trip will also take him to Korea and Japan.
The Administration's policy toward China is widely believed to be governed by President Bush himself, who was the top-ranking American diplomat in Beijing in the mid-1970's.
It was Mr. Bush who dispatched thenational security adviser, Brent Scowcroft, on two secret trips to China in 1989, a decision that stirred wrath in Congress when the visits were disclosed late that year. 
Mr. Scowcroft made the first trip only a month after the killings of the -democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square.
In addition to China's poor human rights record, American critics have assailed its reported sales of ballistic missiles to the Middle East and growing trade surplus with the United States. 
Tensions in the trade relationship have increased with reports that China uses prison labor to make cheap exports.
Negotiations about the possibility of a Baker visit are believed to have been under way for months, with the United States seeking specific assurances from Beijing that some kind of formal agreement could be reached during the visit. 
Most expectations focus on arms control accords.
Â 
Signing Arms Pacts
During a visit in August by the Japanese Prime Minister, Toshiki Kaifu, China said it would sign the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty. 
During Mr. Baker's visit, it is possible that China will also declare its willingness to sign the Missile Technology Control Regime, an accord that curtails the transfer of medium-range missiles, or other agreements limiting the sale of conventional weapons.
Chinese leaders have pressed hard for a visit by Mr. Baker, who even journeyed to the tiny neighboring country of Mongolia in July without stopping in Beijing. 
China feels that Mr. Baker's visit would be an important propaganda victory, demonstrating China's continued importance in the new world order and Washington's willingness to work with its hard-line leadership to resolve the strains in their relationship.
While other foreign leaders are now regularly visiting Beijing -- albeit complaining each time about human rights violations -- Chinese officials have expressed frustration that ties with Washington are not improving. 
They argue that their relationship with Japan has been normalized and relations with Europe have "basically recovered" since the Tiananmen Square crackdown, and that only the United States has held back on repairing ties.
Aside from arms control, issues on Mr. Baker's agenda will presumably include trade and human rights. 
The Chinese now profess a willingness to discuss human rights in general, though they reject specific criticism as interference in their internal affairs. 
Mr. Baker may ask for assurances that certain dissidents or their family members will be allowed to travel to the United States.

text:

In Tokyo, where Medina Dixon has been a popular professional basketball player for the past seven years, she must practice three hours a day, an endless but typically Japanese routine she could do without. 
Still, as the imported American star, she gets off easy.
"Everyone else has to practice six hours, three in the morning and three in the afternoon," she said.
That she is also an assistant coach for her team, Nippon Electric, makes no difference. 
Dixon sleeps in, and worries about practice after lunch.
On the United States women's Olympic team, there are no prima donnas, no special treatment, no exemptions from pressing and defending the basket as you would your wallet. 
With Dixon leading another all-out defensive assault with 5 of her team's 30 steals, and adding a team-high 19 points, Coach Theresa Grentz again demonstrated the truly unmatchable advantage she is holding here. 
As the United States women pursue a third straight gold medal, Grentz possesses the ability to look down her bench, like Chuck Daly, and know everyone there is as good as everyone on the court.
"That's how we selected this team, with that in mind," said Grentz after the United States wore down China and its 6-foot-8-inch, 273-pound center, Haixia Zheng, 93-67, to improve its record to 2-0.
The Chinese players could pass and shoot, and Haixia, a 25-year-old great wall from Zhengzhou who had her picture taken with Magic Johnson last week, could certainly take up space. 
As the 6-3, 165-pound Dixon said, "If I set a back pick on her, you wouldn't see me."
"She's not one to run up and down the floor," said Dixon.
Zheng, who scored 8 points and had 9 rebounds, spent most of her time looking at the backs of the United States players fast-breaking upcourt.

China might have been able to do some serious damage had its best player, Dongmei Zheng, who hit five 3-pointers in China's victory over Spain on Thursday, not inexplicably fouled out late in the first half.
Grentz has instructed her players to go as hard as they can on the press and the break, and expect that fresh troops will not be far behind. 
The result has been an outbreak of turnovers by the opposition, with the United States being credited for a total of 70 steals in its two games.
"I'm enjoying playing the defense, something that's unusual for me," Dixon said, admitting the star system practiced in Japan occasionally creates a jealousy problem.
That is one of the reasons why the upcoming season will be her last as a player in Japan. 
The Japanese players, she said, complained that the American stars make too much money, so the Americans will be banned for two years, and when they return, they will have a salary cap.
Out of respect for her fame and tenure, Dixon has been offered the head coaching job for the season after next, but she has not decided to accept it.
"I'd have to cut practice to three hours a day," she said. 
"I don't know how that would go over."

file: BARCELONA_ DIVING_China and U.S. Divers Make Different Splashes.txt
text:
ï»¿
The men's 10-meter platform diving competition teetered today between moments of sublime perfection and frightening failure.
A disastrous plunge that will make the year's highlight films showed the possibility of what happens to a dive out of control from three stories up.
"It was definitely agony and it was definitely defeat," quipped an aching but intact Matt Scoggin of Austin, Tex.
In the standing, his dive was at the other end of the point spectrum from the spectacular closing attempt by the soon-to-be champion, 16-year-old Sun Shuwei of China. 
On Sun's final dive, trying to keep his first-place lead over Scott Donie of Fort Lauderdale, Fla., the Chinese diver refused to play it safe. 
He produced one of the highest scores in Olympic history -- four of the seven judges awarded him perfection, a 10.
Sun wound up with 677.310 points, scoring seven perfect 10's on his 10 dives, and finished comfortably ahead of Donie's 633.630. 
China ended up with three golds in the four men's and women's diving events. 
Donie's silver medal, meanwhile, gave the United States its third diving medal over all. 
Xiong Ni of China took the bronze.
"I've been diving great all my life, but no one's noticed," said Donie. 
It was an ironic statement, coming on a day when everyone noticed his teammate, who didn't dive great but who survived.
Scoggin's memorable Olympic moment came on Dive 7, a back 3 1/2 somersault tuck. 
Dives are scored in part by their degree of difficulty, and for Scoggin, this was his most demanding of the day with a difficulty of 3.3.
He stood ramrod straight, back to the water, outlined against the blue-gray Barcelona sky and the city's skyline, high above the outdoor pool atop Montjuic. 
Then Scoggin, at 28 the oldest diver in the competition, took off. 
If you looked up at him, you would have thought he was soaring over the city. 
The dive called for him to grab his knees and tuck them under his chest. 
He leaped backward off the board, somersaulted once, and reached for his knees with both hands. 
His right hand latched onto the right knee. 
But the left hand missed.
"It slipped," Scoggin said afterward. 
He started to spin like a broken helicopter, going sideways. 
The water was coming fast and he was out of control.
"I tried to find the water," he said.
Â 
Shadows Cause Problem
But there was another problem. 
The pool is laid out east to west, and the shadows of the late afternoon played havoc with some divers' perceptions. 
It was so dark on the water they couldn't tell which was the bottom of the pool and which was the water.
He hit the water on his back. 
The water splashed, the only tidal wave of the day.
"That was the worst hit I ever had," Scoggin said.
The crowd moaned, seemingly feeling his pain. 
Despite the sickeningly loud splatter, he didn't swallow any water and pulled himself out of the pool quickly.
"I started to run," he explained, "hoping to run off the pain."
He was taken to an emergency medical room, but released within a minute.
"It hurt for 20 or 30 seconds," he said. 
"I don't think I ever felt pain like that. 
Ever."
His coach, Mike Brown, a former Dartmouth diver, described Scoggin as "being in shock."
"It was like running into that wall over there," Brown said.
Scoggin was, essentially, out of the competition now. 
He had started the dive in sixth place, not far removed from medal contention. 
Instead, it was recorded as a "failed dive" -- the only one of the competition, and worth zero points.
Still, he returned.
"It never crossed my mind not to compete," he said. 
"I came here, I gave it a shot. 
All athletes know it can happen, that's why winning is so great -- you know you overcame danger."
His next dive was a forward 3 1/2 somersault pike. 
He mounted the platform to growing applause, took off, and completed the dive without a hitch, producing a decent score of mostly sevens.
How did he feel about going up again?
Did he want to get right there and do it?
"I could definitely wait," he said.
Despite his failed attempt, Scoggin beat out two divers and finished 10th.
"I'm happy that I don't have to do that again," said Scoggin, who is going to sell real estate and retire. 
"I don't have to do that dive again. 
Or any other dive."
Brown predicted that Scoggin's fall will make a lasting Olympic impression. 
"I think Matt will make the new 'Agony of Defeat' poster," he said.

file: BARCELONA_Chinese Beam With Pride.txt
text:
ï»¿
If bicyclists are swerving even more than usual these days, if factory workers are nodding over the assembly lines, if Government officials are excusing themselves from evening banquets, the problems have less to do with the sultry weather than with collective pride at the leaps and plunges of a few pint-sized teen-agers 7,200 miles away.
Many Chinese, who can barely tell a shot-put from a discus, have been transfixed by the Olympics -- and that makes them insomniacs. 
Because of the seven-hour time difference from Barcelona, Spain, the live television coverage lasts well into the night, but many are alternately delighted and impatient to watch the triumphs of their Olympic athletes.
"It's about time we picked up some gold," said a shopkeeper in his 20's. 
"With 1.1 billion people, we should be winning all the golds. 
Hey, did you see Li Xiaosahuang?
Stunning. Absolutely beautiful."
Li Xiaosahuang, whose name translates as "Little Twin," earned a gold medal for the floor exercise in men's gymnastics. 
His twin brother, Li Dasahuang, or "Big Twin," also competed but did not win a medal.
Â 
15 Gold Medals
China has done much better than anybody expected in the Olympics, excelling in diving, swimming and gymnastics. 
It won only five gold medals in the 1988 Olympics in Seoul, but already it has earned 15 in the 1992 Games, including three of the four golds in diving.
In a nation that has been deeply divided politically in the last few years, the Olympics have provided a rare occasion when everyone from Communist Party bosses to student dissidents can join together and cheer China's performers. 
The nation's newest heartthrobs include Lu Li, the bright-eyed 15-year-old who earned a perfect 10 as she won the gold medal for uneven bars in gymnastic competition, and Fu Mingxia, the 13-year-old sensation who dominated in women's platform diving.
For three years, the Government has tried to find a way to unite the nation. 
It tried to win support with the Asian Games, which were held here in the fall of 1990, but those games annoyed many people who were forced to contribute money and labor for the preparations.
But the daily news from Barcelona of the rising medal count, which stood at 48 after today's events, has functioned as a nationalistic adhesive to rally the nation.
Whatever they think of their Government, many Chinese bristled at the way American journalists were reported to have treated the swimmer Qian Hong after she won the gold medal in the women's 100-meter butterfly. 
When Qian, 21 years old, was asked what her mother did, she replied "environmental sanitation."
As reported in the Chinese press, the American reporter pressed Qian with another question: "Does that mean she collects garbage?"
The room filled with raucous laughter and Qian ended up crying.
"Those American reporters really have no manners," the report said, a statement that was echoed in many conversations with Chinese about the Olympics.
Â 
Stir Over Steroid Issue
Allegations that Chinese athletes may be using steroids -- a charge that is not backed by any clear evidence and that the Government denies -- also have caused an uproar.
Chinese appear to be divided on the issue, with some convinced that their athletes have learned from Eastern European coaches how to take steroids. 
Some say that the athletes probably take Chinese herbal medicines to improve their performance.
One instance of the use of Chinese medicine was confirmed today in Barcelona when Wu Dan, a Chinese women's volleyball player, was banned after she tested positive for strychnine. 
The official New China News Agency said she had absorbed the strychnine in a Chinese medicine after she was feeling ill.
Wu's case, the first positive result after 1,080 tests, was a clear embarrassment for the Government. 
The news agency indicated that Wu took the medicine of her own volition, apparently without realizing that it contained a forbidden substance.
Official television and radio news programs did not report the test results this evening, and so Chinese were not aware of the violation. 
In any case, the positive test for strychnine does not shed light on whether Chinese athletes take steroids -- a suggestion that offends many people in Beijing.
"Are you kidding?" said a Chinese clothing salesman. 
"If it were discovered that Chinese athletes were really taking steroids, think of all the heads that would roll at the National Sports Commission. 
The Government definitely wouldn't let them take the stuff."
Â 
Wide TV Coverage
The Government has given the Games extensive publicity. 
For the last week, national television has broadcast about 19 hours a day of Olympic coverage.
By the end of the Olympics, China will have aired about 250 hours of Olympic programs. 
Replays of events in which Chinese athletes have won gold medals occur throughout the day, along with commentary and interviews of the athletes.
Companies, radio stations and newspapers have sponsored Olympic guessing games, with prizes that range from cars to televisions and refrigerators, and free trips to Hong Kong or Singapore.
To encourage athletes, the National Sports Commission will give about $14,000 to each winner of a gold medal, The China Youth Daily reported last week. 
The article added that companies, factories and other sponsors have also made contributions so that each gold medal winner could bring in about $37,000, or 95 times the annual salary of an average factory worker.
One company, Jianlibao, which makes a sports drink, said it would give a gold can, worth about $6,500, to each gold medalist. 
It had already prepared 30 cans of gold, partly in expectation that the Chinese women's volleyball team would win a gold medal. 
But the team lost to Brazil.
"The volleyball players were too proud and thought they would get the gold without having to try," said a private businessman, who said he stayed up regularly throughout the night to watch the live coverage.
The Government is hoping that its performance will enhance its chances to win the right to be host to the Summer Olympic Games in the year 2000. 
A Chinese sports official expressed the thought cautiously: "We hope the achievements of our athletes in Barcelona will leave a very deep impression on the decision-makers."

Incident During Bush Visit

text:

China announced today the release of 97 people who had been involved in last year's pro-democracy movement, including two student leaders, in a move that diplomats described as an attempt to ease domestic tensions and win favor in Western countries.
The announcement came two days after the anniversary of the crackdown on the democracy movement, and some diplomats said it reflected a mild reduction in tensions now that the Government does not have to worry about protests on the anniversaries of last year's key protest dates.
China said that 76 prisoners were released in Beijing, while 21 were released in Shanghai.
The action brought the total officially reported to have been released in the last six months to 881, but it is unclear how many remain behind bars.

Releases Last Month
In mid-May, when it released 211 prisoners, China said only 431 were still ''under investigation.''
After today's announcement, that would leave 334 people in detention, according to the Government figures.
Most Western diplomats say, however, that there are probably more than a few hundred being held, and some estimates run into the thousands. 
Partly because of the uncertainty about how many dissidents are still being held, diplomats interviewed were cautious about judging the significance of the releases.

The release is one of the latest examples of mixed signals by the Chinese leadership.

file: Beijing Invites Chinese Abroad to Return Home.txt
text:

The Government today invited Chinese living abroad to return "to serve the construction of the motherland," but it also hinted that it might bar Chinese students from returning if they oppose Communism.
The issue has arisen because the authorities are refusing to allow Gong Xiaoxia, a Chinese student at Harvard University, to return to China for a visit. 
Ms. Gong, who has been critical of the Government, is waiting in Hong Kong, hoping that the Chinese Government will relent and allow her back.

Fate of the Outspoken
In fact, thousands of Chinese have been allowed to return to China without difficulty after trips abroad, and there seems little chance that a loyalty test will be imposed.

To be sure, many Chinese students would be delighted to stay in the United States.

Only 50,000 have returned.

file: Beijing Journal_A Weekly Bath, and a Good Brain-Scrubbing Too.txt
text:
ï»¿
It is less verdant and spacious than Beijing University, and far more isolated and gloomy than Tiananmen Square: a guarded compound in the southwest part of the capital that may be the next home for many leaders of China's democracy movement.
Surrounded by 13-foot walls topped by an electric fence, Beijing No. 1 Prison is a gray and dilapidated compound built in 1908, in the dying days of the Ching Dynasty. 
Its cells have been home to thieves and rapists and political idealists, and it leaves its mark on all of them.
There are eight hours of political education a week, intended to make inmates acknowledge their guilt and inspire them to support the Communist Party and the Government.
''The political education is effective,'' said Wang Hehao, a 25-year-old man serving an 18-year sentence for killing a man in a fight. 
''Before we did not understand anything about the law, but now we know about the need to respect the law and society.''
Â 
Where Minds Are 'Cleansed'
Beijing No. 1 Prison is for felons who have been convicted and sentenced to terms of more than 10 years, and so far it has not received any prisoners from the democracy movement. 
But in the coming months, as those people are brought to trial, some will end up behind the jail's walls, left to struggle for self-respect and the faith of their ideals in a system that aims not only to isolate criminals but above all to cleanse their contaminated minds.
Wei Jingsheng, an electrician serving a 15-year sentence for leading the 1978-79 democracy movement, was kept in solitary confinement early in the decade before being transferred to a prison camp in the desolation of Qinghai Province, in western China. 
The official press says he has a bad attitude and refuses to repent.
Xu Wenli, another leader of the Democracy Wall movement of a decade ago, remains in a cell here. 
Prison officials do not much like to talk about him, although when asked about his ideological progress they say it is ''about average.''
Â 
Bleak and Austere
No one knows how many people have been detained or arrested throughout China in connection with this year's democracy movement. 
Most estimates by diplomats range from 10,000 to 20,000. 
Some people are released after several days of interrogation, but arrests continue.
A visit to the No. 1 Prison offered a window into the life that many dissidents can anticipate for the next decade or two. 
It presented glimpses of an existence that is bleak and austere, but perhaps not so harsh as might be imagined.
In part, this may be because No. 1 Prison is a model institution, in contrast with places like the Gongdelin Prison, in the north of Beijing, where the guards are said to torture inmates by manacling them so tightly that they are unable to use their hands for days afterward.
And there is Qincheng No. 1 Prison, in the northern suburbs, where some intellectuals are believed to be confined behind an arched entrance known as the Atheists' Gate to Hell.
Still less accessible are the labor camps in remote areas of the far west and far north. 
Two Chinese officials with access to high-level information say a senior leader has proposed that new labor camps be built in the areas along the border to accommodate large numbers of those deemed counterrevolutionaries.
Â 
Bunk Beds and Guitars
Xu Jizhuang, the lean, affable warden of Prison No. 1, led the tour of the prison, showing how a dozen inmates are packed into six bunk beds in a room the size of a large American bedroom - crowded, but not strikingly so by Chinese standards. 
Many prisoners have guitars, which they play in their free hour each evening or on their day off each week. 
A few have books: some political or inspirational, but also a few novels.
About 2,000 prisoners live here, including 100 women and 30 people serving sentences for counterrevolutionary offenses. 
Inmates work eight hours a day, six days a week, in two prison factories, making socks and plastic objects like sandals and lunch boxes. 
They are paid about $1 a month, and the state turns a $300,000 annual profit on the operation.
Mr. Xu said 5 percent of former inmates were arrested for new crimes in the three years after their release. 
He attributed the rate to political education, along with technical and academic training programs.
The prisoners are allowed some access to television news and newspapers, and they were aware of the democracy movement when it was happening. 
But if there was any thrill at seeing the anti-Government demonstrations, it is dead now.
Â 
'Stable Environment'
''During the unrest, we were very indignant,'' said Liu Xuewen, a 23-year-old man serving a 12-year sentence for robbery. 
''What we want most is a stable environment.''
Of course, Mr. Liu was speaking not only to a foreign reporter but also to a half-dozen prison officials eyeing him with apprehension. 
While the reporter selected Mr. Liu at random for the interview, it was hardly a realistic probing of his attitudes.
Mr. Liu and the other inmates interviewed in these circumstances expressed considerable enthusiasm for prison conditions, sometimes with such apparent sincerity that it seemed they might be reluctant to leave. 
But three former inmates interviewed independently confirmed that while the No. 1 Prison is hardly idyllic, it is bearable.
The worst aspect is the winters, they said, because the prison is not centrally heated and the small stoves never raise the temperature enough to be very comfortable. 
In addition, they noted that some political prisoners have been kept in isolation -even guards are not allowed to talk with them - and that this takes an enormous toll on the prisoner's well-being and sanity.
Â 
One Bath Each Week
Ordinary prisoners, who appeared relatively healthy and well fed, are usually allowed to receive mail and to write two letters a month. 
They bathe weekly and receive one family visit a month. 
Particularly well-behaved prisoners are even allowed outside to visit their families on the Chinese New Year, and 15 percent have their sentences reduced for good conduct. 
Some have their sentences lengthened for fighting or other misconduct.
Inmates and officials say that torture and fighting are rare in the No. 1 Prison, and that brutality or rape among inmates is much less common here than in the United States.
But the official press has indicated that torture and wrongful imprisonment do occur on a large scale in some parts of the country. 
China Legal News reported that in the first half of 1986, 949 people were known to have been detained illegally, and 140 of them were killed or injured by ''cruel and vile methods.''
