ï»¿
Behind the armed guards at the grand main gate of the compound, beyond the cafeteria in a pleasant park-like setting, is a building that is identified as No. 5, but which might better be labeled as a battleground for the future of China.
It is the editorial office of People's Daily, the most important of the 1,459 newspapers published in China. 
In a nation where power struggles are constant and camouflaged, People's Daily functions for people here and abroad as a window - heavily frosted - into the minds of the Chinese leadership.
During the democracy movement in the spring of 1989, the walls of building No. 5 were plastered with posters in which many of the newspaper's 1,900 staff members endorsed the movement, and expressed embarrassment at the pablum they felt they were writing.
Now it seems that the battle for People's Daily has ended in a remarkable stalemate: The hard-liners have gained clear control of the newspaper, but many people no longer read it.
Â 
Mood at Paper Seen as Bleak
''It's so boring that I don't look at it anymore and neither do my friends,'' an economist in Beijing said. 
''We would rather read other papers, which at least contain some social news and crime news.''
The new publisher of People's Daily, Gao Di, a 63-year-old former provincial party secretary who lives in the same compound on Wanshou Road as Prime Minister Li Peng, declined to be interviewed. 
But other editors who spoke in officially arranged interviews asserted that stabilityI had returned to the newspaper.
''Last year the newspaper had some incorrect guidance, and we had to rectify our errors,'' said Zhang Yongwen, a senior editor. 
''Some people made mistakes. 
But with some political study they were able to improve their understanding and raise their consciousness. 
Some had unrealistic ideas. 
But once they had a proper understanding, they could return to work as normal.''
Other People's Daily reporters -interviewed privately in defiance of a ban on unauthorized contacts with foreign journalists - said the mood in the newspaper was bleak.
Â 
Promoting Hard-Liners' View
''Most people are quite depressed,'' said a reporter for the paper. 
''And there's little sense of hope that conditions will improve.''
But the reporter said that as the investigations and political study wind down, life is returning to a routine and that the new editor in chief, Shao Huaze, an army man, had proved to be more reasonable than some people had expected.
Under the newly arrived editorial team, including not only Mr. Gao and Mr. Shao but also a fresh deputy editor and deputy publisher, People's Daily has taken the lead in promoting the hard-liners' view that only Communism can save China. 
A typical front page carries articles about the activities of top leaders, along with a call for unity, a few items about improved economic performance, and perhaps an inspirational account about a model worker.
If gloom and frustration are the primary emotions in the People's Daily compound these days, it is not for the first time.
''There's only one thing that's accurate in People's Daily each day -the date,'' a former top editor once said to a group of friends, according to a Chinese who was there. 
And a poll in 1988 of 1,800 Chinese journalists found that only 1.1 percent thought that the public believed the press.
Â 
Role of 'Positive Propaganda'
One of the ways in which People's Daily has tried to build credibility is by soliciting letters to the editor. 
Each day the newspaper receives about 1,000 letters, and those are carefully scrutinized by a staff of 54 people for possible publication.
''Those letters we publish are those reflecting what people most care about and what people most want to read,'' said Li Youchun, the first vice director of the Masses Letters Department of People's Daily. 
Some of the published letters criticize traffic jams, pollution, rude clerks and other problems. 
But no attacks are permitted against Government policies.
''Criticism is an aspect of our jobs,'' said Wang Yongan, a deputy director of the Masses Letters Department. 
''But it's just a part. 
The main function is still positive propaganda.''
One problem for People's Daily is that the propaganda zigs and zags along with China's policies, and the newspaper's editors tend to be get in trouble at each twist. 
According to a book about People's Daily published last year, Chairman Mao Zedong warned the editor in chief in 1957 that in taking the job he should accept the risks of dismissal, expulsion from the party, divorce, imprisonment and even execution. 
So far no one has been executed, But Mr. Gao is the fourth publisher in the last seven years.
Because People's Daily is published by the Central Committee, the paper's editor and publisher have ministerial rank - along with perhaps 1,000 other current and former office holders in China - and the publisher in the past has been entitled to sit in on expanded meetings of the Politburo.
With a claimed circulation of 3.5 million, based overwhelmingly on subscriptions from offices rather than individuals, People's Daily is probably the most widely circulated newspaper in the country. 
The closest competitor is Reference News, a digest of positive news reports about China from abroad, which claims a circulation of 3.3 million. 
Because it has such a large circulation, People's Daily is able to charge foreign advertisers $40,000 for a full-page advertisement - insuring the newspaper a measure of prosperity.
''The People's Daily used to be very prestigious, and young journalists wanted to work there,'' said a reporter who turned down the chance to join People's Daily and now works for a rival newspaper. 
''Now smart young people would rather look elsewhere for jobs, because the People's Daily is absolutely inflexible. 
Rigor mortis is setting in.''

file: Beijing Journal_China_s Campus Life_ A Torrent of Self-Criticism.txt
text:
ï»¿
A university professor sighed as he described the long self-criticism that he had written painstakingly in a small notebook and then read aloud to a critical audience of colleagues and Communist Party officials at a political meeting.
''I was humiliated, but I had to do it,'' said the professor, whose self-criticism detailed his involvement in the democracy movement this past spring.
Now, he says, he feels a deep loneliness, an emptiness that grows when he recalls the violent crackdown in June. 
To fight his depression and to cleanse away his anger, he is pouring his energy into teaching, nearly tripling his number of hours in the classroom, to 26 a week.
Throughout China, university students and teachers have returned to school, with the last of them - those from Beijing University, the most active in the protests - officially beginning classes this week. 
Teachers and students say they are profoundly changed by the events of the spring, but in the gloomier atmosphere, they are struggling to smooth over their pain so that they can get on with their lives.
Â 
A String of New Worries
Students are nervous about a new guideline that would require them to work for as much as seven years in China before they are allowed to study abroad. 
Their lives have also changed enormously this academic year, with new ideology sessions, new mandatory labor in the ''grass roots'' after graduation, and at some institutions a new requirement of military training.
At Beijing Normal University, a 21-year-old student, who lasted for seven days without food during a hunger strike this spring, said she was surprised how lightly the authorities had reprimanded her. 
All she had to do was write a 3,000- to 5,000-word essay on her ''reflections,'' a task that many of Beijing's university students were obliged to undertake.
''They must have categorized me as a follower,'' said the student, who was even selected to lead some of the recent political study sessions.
In her essay, she was extremely careful, writing that a ''collective consciousness'' moved her to take part in the hunger strike, and that once she began the hunger strike she felt she had a duty to her classmates to stay with it until the end.
Â 
Copying the Right Words
''I didn't know the posh language of the Government, so I copied it from the newspapers,'' she said. 
''I studied the papers and speeches for a week and then wrote it all down in one day.''
''Only socialism can save China,'' she said, and then laughed at the words she had copied in her essay.
She says she will never forget the spring, but now she rarely talks with her friends about the experience and she no longer asks about how the crackdown has affected others.
''We don't ask about other students,'' she said. 
''What good is asking?''
She says she believes that the authorities have been gentle to them simply because so many took part and the Government cannot throw them all in jail. 
This gives her hope.
''The future is bright,'' she said, quoting Mao. 
''But the path is crooked.''
Â 
Off to Military School
Students and teachers at Beijing University, historically a symbol of political protest, have been chastised more severely. 
The class of 748 freshman, down from about 2,000 last year, has been sent to a military academy in the nearby city of Shijiazhuang for one year of military training and political indoctrination. 
Some other schools this fall have offered a couple of weeks of military training; others have none at all.
Moreover, four of Beijing University's departments considered too liberal-minded for the Communist orthodoxy - history, philosophy, administration and international politics - have been closed to new students.
The school's returning students, like those elsewhere, are studying the speeches of China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, along with propaganda documents and videotapes on the ''quelling of the counterrevolutionary rebellion,'' as the democracy movement is called by the Government.
Rumors at the school about the numbers detained range from tens to more than 100, and some say a teacher was sentenced to 12 years in prison. 
For those who escaped jail, however, there is still intimidation, confession-writing and endless hours of questioning. 
And the school may add a note to their file, hurting their careers.
''They don't need to arrest you,'' a university teacher said. 
''They have so many other ways of influencing you: your work assignment, your salary, where you live. 
They don't need to put you in jail to control you.''
Â 
Keeping the Record Clean
Some students have turned to focusing on their careers once again, and so they are doing their best to avoid black marks on their records. 
But even good political records do not mean good jobs these days.
One of the greatest worries among young people now is a new policy that recent college graduates work for a year or two at the ''grass roots'' level before taking up good jobs in the cities. 
The most worrying aspect of the new policy is that the housing registration is transferred as well, so that many fear they will not be allowed to live in Beijing again if they make a political mistake.
The new policy is supposed to apply to all those who graduated from college beginning in 1985, but the emphasis has been on those who graduated this year.
Â 
Reluctance to Speak Out
At Beijing University, several groups refused to talk to a foreign journalist, whose reports could bring trouble to them. 
Others talked, but hesitantly, in low voices.
One angry student took the offensive in the conversation.
''I don't believe there really is free speech in the United States,'' he said. 
When asked if he would join demonstrations again, he paused for a long time.
''Definitely,'' he eventually responded. 
''But we can be patient. 
That's one virtue we Chinese have: endurance.''
His friend disagreed. 
''Endurance also has its shortcomings,'' he said. 
''We have endured, yes. 
But that's why China has never gotten very far.''

file: Beijing Journal_Chinese Cartoonist Is the Master of the Fine Line.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a country where bold is bad, artists sometimes think more about diplomacy -- about tiptoeing on a thread of silk -- than they do about drawing. 
Ding Cong is such a diplomat: he is a consummate political cartoonist who never raises the topic of politics.
At a time when people are thrown in jail for openly criticizing the Government, Mr. Ding's black and white drawings stand out because they dare to satirize the leadership and the tensions in Chinese society. 
But these days, Mr. Ding has mastered tact and subtlety, a far cry from his younger days when he would paint scrolls streaming with flashy evil-doers, distorted and contorted, to portray his views of the Chinese Nationalists.
Like poetry, his drawings now often convey layers of meanings, but the most sensitive meaning is usually masked behind an image of everyday experience. 
For that reason, by American standards, Mr. Ding's cartoons are tame. 
They never explicitly portray any of China's current leaders. 
Instead, they sometimes draw on allusions, plucking out characters from way back in China's history to illustrate a point relevant to current events.
"He's a very slippery cartoonist," said a Chinese writer who is a fan of Mr. Ding's works. 
"How can the leaders catch him?
If they point to a cartoon and say, 'This is critical of the Government,' all he needs to ask is, 'Where is it critical?'
And he'd be right, because you can't pin his cartoons down."
Â 
A Difficult Social Climate
Mr. Ding's drawings often capture the alienation of intellectuals in society, or the chasm between the leadership and the people, or the system's corruption. 
Sometimes, the political zap is so veiled that a political explanation seems far-fetched, but Mr. Ding's background is rooted in politics and many of his cartoons have a bitter edge. 
To Mr. Ding, cartooning is wedded to politics.
"In China, all cartoons are political," Mr. Ding said with a loud, nervous laugh. 
"To be a cartoonist, if you want to satirize something, it's political."
And then with another laugh he added, "But because our social climate is not so good, there are not too many political cartoons these days."
In many ways, his demeanor and personality mirror his style of cartooning. 
Physically, the 74-year-old Mr. Ding is a plump, bubbly man whose features are bold and accentuated, like many of his cartoon characters. 
His manner of conversation -- winding and dodging around a point -- resembles his style of cartooning.
Part of the reason he is careful is simply that he wants to keep drawing. 
His cartoons have always contained critiques of society, often with severe consequences. 
After the Chinese-Japanese war broke out in 1937, Mr. Ding's cartoons so offended the Japanese that in 1938 he had to flee to Hong Kong. 
In 1945, Mr. Ding worked for an underground unit of the American armed forces based in the southern city of Kunming. 
He and his colleagues would sneak out at night, rip down posters put up by the Japanese troops, change them subtly so they poked fun at the Japanese, and then stick them up again.
Â 
10 Books of Cartoons
During the next couple of years, some of his most biting satire was aimed at the Chinese Nationalist regime of Chiang Kai-shek, and in 1947 he fled to Hong Kong once again to escape persecution. 
He returned to China to support the Communist revolution, but then in 1957 he was labeled a "rightist" and sent to the countryside to do manual labor. 
For the next 22 years, Mr. Ding did not draw a line.
Since 1979, when he was rehabilitated and allowed to draw again, Mr. Ding has published 10 books of cartoons. 
He has not been active in the democracy movement, but in early 1989, before the crackdown, he signed a petition calling for greater freedoms. 
He was not punished for this.
Even though Mr. Ding is probably the best-known cartoonist in China his drawings are rarely published in the official national newspapers. 
These days, Mr. Ding knows how far he can stretch a point before he must stop. 
But this is the hard part of his work, he says.
"It may take me only a few hours to draw, but days and days to think about what to draw," Mr. Ding said. 
"As soon as you look at a cartoon, one meaning jumps out at you immediately. 
But if you draw so that the real satire can be seen right away, ah, then you're finished."
Many ordinary people simply do not catch the underlying point of his cartoons. 
In a cartoon that appears completely nonpolitical, an obese woman is holding a picture of a young woman with a flowered dress. 
The woman is wearing an exact replica of the dress that her tailor just completed, but after looking at the slim shapeliness of the woman in the dress, she complains to him, "You didn't do it exactly according to the picture."
Â 
A Political Meaning
Mr. Ding, who published the sketch more than four years ago, says the cartoon has a political meaning as well. 
The obese woman can be thought of as the Government, slovenly and out of shape. 
No matter how many people it orders around to help dress it up, it cannot hide its bulges and mistakes.
A much more recent drawing portrays a string puppet in the image of a fierce general, Cao Cao, in the third century A.D. The cartoon derives its satire through interplay with an accompanying poem, "An Ode to a Puppet," which Mr. Ding did not write:
With pieces of string, it dances gracefully,
Yet, few people see through the small trick.
Black-haired, white-faced, it looks the image of Cao Cao
Without a soul behind the curtain, it's a good-for-nothing.
The crucial question is this: Does the puppet represent Prime Minister Li Peng, manipulated by China's octogenarian leaders?
Some intellectuals look at the cartoon and immediately say that it must be Prime Minister Li. 
Others take a look and are sure it does not refer to Mr. Li. Mr. Ding denies he had any intention of referring to the current leadership.
"I just drew a picture according to the poem," he said. 
"Where is it critical?"

file: Beijing Journal_English Spoken Here (by Would-Be Expatriates).txt
text:
ï»¿
A class of 40 nervous students looked blankly at the teacher who had just asked a sample question on an English test, about the purchase of shoes from a catalogue. 
''Class, what is a catalogue?'' the teacher asked.
Several students squirmed in their seats, for none of those in the cold, damp classroom had ever heard of buying from a catalogue. 
Shoes were bought in shops, not catalogues. 
They shrugged, and hoped that the issue would not come up in a test of English as a foreign language.
They had signed up for this series of English classes to prepare for the test, which is required of foreign students by American universities. 
Many young intellectuals, thrown into a depression after the military suppression of the democracy movement in June, regard study abroad as the best escape hatch out of China.
The more the Chinese authorities attack the United States, the more many intellectuals perceive the political climate to be worsening, and the more fanatically they study English to try to get to the United States.
''We are all trying to get out,'' said a young Chinese man planning to study abroad. 
''There is little hope for us here.''
Â 
Pointless to Remain, They Say
It is not so much that they are afraid of being arrested; rather, they say they believe there is no point in remaining, for they will be given no opportunity to use their talents in China.
Paradoxically, the biggest obstacle for many is not permission from the Chinese authorities, at least for the moment, but American immigration law. 
The United States Embassy here is reluctant to give visas to those who cannot show a good reason why they must return, such as a spouse who is remaining behind, and so a large number of single men and women who have been accepted at universities abroad find that they are denied visas.
''I don't think I'll be able to go abroad because it's nearly impossible to get a U.S. visa,'' said a young Chinese woman who was taking a class to prepare for the English test.
Because of their passion for getting away, many Chinese with only an inkling of English are brushing up on their Americanisms. 
In Shanghai, novice English-speakers boldly walk up to foreigners and offer to be their guides, just for the sake of speaking English to a foreigner.
Â 
Some Use Connections
Those hoping to take the English test are not just from the universities. 
Technicians, physicists, philosophers and computer programmers are among the thousands flocking to English classes and standing in line to register for the test, which is given four times a year.
The next test date is in January, and some people lined up for two days to insure a spot on the registration list at one of about a dozen locations in the city.
Yet the authorities have already started to make it difficult for Chinese people to prepare for and take the test. 
Late in October, the authorities closed down the English Corner, an officially designated area in Purple Bamboo Park in Beijing where people could go to practice English. 
About 100 Chinese gathered in the English Corner last Sunday in defiance of the Government ban.
It has also been hard for Chinese who work in units that are being scrutinized because of the pro-democracy demonstrations this spring. 
Most Chinese must obtain permission and a letter of introduction from their work unit to register for the test, and some Chinese without connections say they have been denied that permission.
''This Government controls nearly every aspect of our lives, down to the very food we eat,'' said a young woman who, like many Chinese, lives in a dormitory and eats at a cafeteria run by her work unit. 
She also planned to take the English test, but was denied permission.
Â 
Rumors of a Rules Change
One Chinese worker infuriated officials when they found out he had used a letter of introduction written months before for an earlier test date to register for the January test.
The rush to study English has been fanned by rumors that the Government will change the regulations for studying abroad sometime next year.
Among the fears is that the Government will not allow Chinese people over 35 years old to go abroad for study, although they may make an overseas trip as part of a business delegation or other work. 
Others fear that the Government will not let students who have just graduated from college go overseas to study until they have worked in China for four to seven years.
Â 
A Fear of Rejection
Some Chinese are confident they will obtain passports, a process that sometimes can take as long as six months, but are concerned they will be rejected by foreign embassies.
But a United States Embassy official said the visa approval rate for study, now about 50 percent or higher, has remained essentially the same as it was before June. 
Moreover, the official said there had not been a noticeable drop in the number of passports issued, although many of the people applying for visas now had applied before June for their passports.
But figures for visas issued from April to September at the United States Embassy suggest that fewer lecturers and researchers have applied to go to the United States since June. 
The largest drop in applications was in the category of business travel.
''This category had grown 20 to 30 percent a year,'' the official said. 
''It's usually a barometer of the state of economic relations.''

file: Beijing Journal_For Jailed Scholar, a Wife_s Daring Voice on Rights.txt
text:
ï»¿
Hou Xiaotian's face brightens with an innocent grin as she weaves her bicycle through the traffic. 
But her girlish demeanor belies a life these days composed more of tears than smiles, more of prison than family, and of memories of a husband whom she is not scheduled to be reunited with again until the year 2002.
Ms. Hou, 28 years old, has become virtually the only person in Beijing now who dares to speak out for human rights to the foreign press. 
She assumed the role after her husband, Wang Juntao, was sentenced in February to 13 years in prison for his role in the Tiananmen Square democracy movement.
"Why am I doing this?" she asked. 
"If I can speak freely, if this can take place in China, then it shows that China is making progress. 
I am nudging the Government. 
This is an opportunity and I must not abandon it."
Since April, her husband has been confined alone in a small jail cell where he eats, sleeps, and uses a toilet, Ms. Hou said. 
A scholar of economics, with a passion for democracy, he can barely read because of the dim light. 
His family said he suffers from hepatitis B, a potentially fatal ailment of the liver.
Â 
Husband on Hunger Strike
Last week, Mr. Wang began a hunger strike as a protest against his treatment and in response to the authorities' decision not to allow Ms. Hou to visit him this month. 
Normally she is allowed one monthly visit for 30 minutes, but this month the session was cancelled -- apparently because the authorities were annoyed at Ms. Hou's contacts with foreign journalists.
For more than a year, Ms. Hou's battle has focused on improving prison conditions for her husband, and she has repeatedly approached various officials in different Government departments to solicit help. 
She brought cakes and gifts to the prison doorsteps on his birthday, their wedding anniversary and the new year, but both she and her gifts were turned away.
The setbacks, she said, have taken a toll on her emotional and physical health. 
Earlier this summer, she became weary and severely depressed, crying every day, and she spent more than a month in the hospital.
"They are really villains, trying to exploit the love a woman has for her husband to attain to their means," Ms. Hou said in an appeal printed earlier this year by a human rights organization. 
The authorities wanted to know what she had told foreign reporters, threatening to reject the presents she had brought for her husband, she said.
Â 
Served 5 Months in Prison
"I knew the life inside prisons because I had been inside one, and so I was very concerned about my husband," the appeal continued. 
"How dare they blackmail me using this relationship and my feelings. 
They are really not human beings at all."
Ms. Hou was jailed for five months until April 1990 in a jail cell separated from the outside world by eight layers of doors or gates. 
The authorities charged that she helped her husband attempt to escape the law in the months after the June 1989 crackdown. 
She insists, however, that she did not help him. 
But now she suggests that she wished she had.
"I was full of despair and thought I would never come out," Ms. Hou said of her time in prison. 
"I know what my husband must be going through. 
He must be losing his respect. 
I have wronged him. 
In jail I thought that if I got out, I would help my husband."
Mr. Wang is just as concerned about his wife. 
When he first decided in July to begin a hunger strike, he told his parents in confidence, but not Ms. Hou, for fear she could not bear the news. 
After his trial in February, he sent a letter to his lawyers and closed with a request that they look after his wife for him.
Â 
Allowed to Provide Medicine
"Please help me comfort Xiaotian," he urged in the letter, which was later published by newspapers in Hong Kong. 
"Let her calm down, not to get into any more trouble, not to break any law, especially not to become impolite to those who are handling my case. 
I still need her to help me in many things on the outside, so she must take care of herself."
For a long time, the authorities denied that Mr. Wang was ill, but finally in June, they admitted to his family that he had hepatitis and allowed them to bring him some medicine.
But the family has not been allowed to give him medicine regularly, and earlier this month the Government denied to a visiting United States Congressional delegation that Mr. Wang was sick. 
Mr. Wang apparently contracted hepatitis while he was being treated by injection for a toothache during his detention in Qincheng prison, family members said. 
In April, he was moved to Beijing No. 2 prison, as was another dissident, Chen Ziming, who was also sentenced to 13 years. 
The two men were detained in 1989, two years before their trial, and this period will count toward their jail terms.
"I speak about the most basic right of man, what God gave man -- even though I don't believe in God -- and I tell them that you must give back what man is born with," Ms. Hou said. 
"This is what I fight for."
Â 
'I Can Be Taken In Anytime'
She talks little about the shortcomings of socialism or of the need for freedom of the press and political reform, and says she believes that this may be one reason why the authorities have been relatively tolerant of her outspokenness. 
She is still concerned, however, that she could be detained or arrested at any moment, and one stark reminder of the risk came when Zhang Weiguo, a prominent journalist who spoke openly against the political system, was detained for three weeks this summer in Shanghai.
"I've been waiting for them to come get me," she said. 
"When Zhang Weiguo was detained, it made me realize what a thin tightrope I am walking on. 
I can be taken in anytime."
Eased out of her job in an employment center, she has no means of livelihood and no place to live. 
Instead, Ms. Hou, who has a graduate degree in psychology, moves from place to place, relying on handouts from friends who dare to help her as she continues to fight for her husband so that she can go on with her life.
"What I really want is a family, to be a housewife -- a virtuous wife and a good mother," Ms. Hou said. 
"I want a child, but now I can't have one."

file: Beijing Journal_Marxism Died and Left a Big Hole in Their Lives.txt
text:
ï»¿
A secular age of faith appears to have collapsed in China, turning into a time of despair and doubt in which many people have no heroes and nothing to believe in.
When Chinese bare their souls to foreigners these days, they sometimes speak of a ''spiritual crisis'' that they blame for increases in petty crime, as well as for a disintegration of social values and cohesiveness.
This sense of emptiness and purposelessness has been on the rise in recent years, but many Chinese, interviewed in different parts of the country, say it has become particularly acute since the suppression of the democracy protests last June 3-4.
''We used to believe that Chairman Mao or Deng Xiaoping could solve our problems,'' said a disgruntled Communist Party official in Beijing. 
''But now we've lost hope. 
Now there's nothing for us to believe in.''
'We Feel an Emptiness'
In the central Chinese city of Chengdu, a young university teacher searched for a way to explain her malaise. 
''There's nothing left,'' she said. 
''We feel an emptiness.''
A university student in Beijing said some of his friends were turning to Christianity and Buddhism, as a new source of moral values.
''Without doubt there's a spiritual crisis in China,'' he said. 
''I don't have any friends who believe in Marxism now. 
Even my parents don't believe in Marx or Deng anymore. 
There's a vacuum.''
''This also existed in the 1980's,'' the student added. 
''But then we could live by our dreams. 
My friends and I dreamed of studying abroad, of working for joint venture companies, of going south to make more money. 
Since June 4, those dreams have died, and now we have nothing to live by.''
Not everyone is so melancholy, and many people continue to be absorbed by the challenges of daily life rather than by existential crises. 
For all the concern about the effects of nihilism on society, the impact so far has been confined mostly to petty vandalism, thievery, a relatively minor drug problem and an aggressive discourtesy.
Â 
Life Seems Grayer
China's family structure is intact, crime is low by Western standards, and people continue to marry, find jobs and go about their daily lives pretty much as ever. 
But the texture of life seems grayer, and gloomier, particularly in the cities.
In the countryside, where about three-fourths of Chinese live, peasants are usually more absorbed by fluctuations in weather than in politics, and in any case regarded Mao and Mr. Deng as rather remote deities. 
Moreover, while many peasants and workers have lost their faith in political leaders, they can still sound quite reverent when speaking of new consumer goods or ways to earn the money to buy them.
''These days we don't believe in political leaders,'' a worker in his mid-20's said. 
''But we still believe in something. 
The new god is money.''
Chinese say that just 25 years ago, almost all of their compatriots believed in Mao, and just a few years ago, there was overwhelming support for Mr. Deng. These days, it is difficult to find a young person who believes passionately in anything or anybody, and despair is more common than faith.
Â 
Disparaging a Legacy
The loss of faith has been complicated because it has not only discredited China's political leaders but also the value of the Chinese cultural legacy itself. 
Whatever their political beliefs, Chinese used to share a common pride in a 4,000-year-old heritage, but now more and more intellectuals worry that China's poverty and authoritarianism are rooted in the culture itself. 
They disparage their historical legacy and stress the need to turn to the West for help in modernizing China.
A university teacher in his 30's, who like many others is trying to find a way to the United States, described what to him is one of the most painful aspects of the present society: the obligation to take part in meetings where everyone is forced to profess beliefs they do not feel.
''In the West, if you lost faith in Christianity, you could still believe in yourself, or in existentialism, or in whatever you wanted to,'' the teacher said. 
''But here you are forced to say you believe in what you don't: in the party, and in the 'glorious crackdown.'
''
China was also swept by a great wave of disillusionment in the late 1970's, after the Cultural Revolution. 
But many Chinese, as well as foreign specialists, say the situation is worse now - partly because people see no way out of the nation's difficulties and because there is no obvious candidate to lead them to safety, as Mr. Deng seemed to do after his return to power in 1978.
Â 
Campaigns to Build Spirit
''I sense greater despair this year than in my 11 previous years of visiting China,'' said David L. Shambaugh, a China scholar from the University of London. 
''In the reform period, people at least had a sense of the future, for there was progress and social mobility. 
Now, most of those who benefited from the reforms are losing hope.''
The Chinese leadership seems to be aware of the malaise, for there have been a series of campaigns recently to build national spirit by emulating the legendary soldier Lei Feng, who died in 1962, and other Communist heroes. 
Those campaigns seem to be greeted with indifference by most of the population, and by resentment among intellectuals.
''It's very serious when people don't believe in anything,'' said a business executive in his 30's. 
''Even my friends who are foreign-trained intellectuals do nothing but play the game mah-jongg all day. 
It's disastrous for the long run, and the central leaders know it.''

file: Beijing Journal_No Praise, Please! He Wants to Be the Premier.txt
text:
ï»¿
Of all the names being bandied about these days as potential prime ministers, one evokes a special tingle -- depending on your vantage point -- of either hope or horror.
Zhu Rongji, a former rightist who has spent more years in disgrace than in power, is the fastest-rising star in China's political firmament. 
But Mr. Zhu, a fluent English-speaker and aggressive advocate of economic change, faces a horrendous image problem within the party leadership: admirers abroad have affectionately dubbed him "China's Gorbachev."
This helps Mr. Zhu about as much as it would benefit President Bush for China's hard-liners to hail him as "America's Mao Zedong."
"You're not going to write a story saying how great Zhu Rongji is, are you?" a Chinese official who likes Mr. Zhu asked reproachfully. 
"Because whenever there's an article like that, he gets whacked politically."
Â 
Specter of Gorbachev
Vice President Wang Zhen, an acid-mouthed octogenarian who peppers his conversations with village expletives, is said to have warned colleagues last year that "there is a Gorbachev sleeping beside us."
Mr. Wang did not mention any names, but that's the kind of comment that would have Politburo members craning their necks to look at Mr. Zhu.
Still, the 63-year-old Mr. Zhu (whose name is pronounced joo rong jee) has managed to survive both the attacks and the compliments. 
In his spacious, air-conditioned second-floor office, just inside the north gate of China's park-like leadership compound of Zhongnanhai, Mr. Zhu has amassed prestige and authority along with the calligraphy that he hangs on the wall.
Named a Deputy Prime Minister last year, Mr. Zhu is one of several contenders hoping to replace Prime Minister Li Peng when his five-year term expires early next year. 
It is unclear, however, if the position will be vacant; Mr. Li is a skilled tactician who is fighting for a second term.
"Zhu Rongji is doing really well right now," said a family member of a top official. 
"But in China, the better things look for you, the worse your prospects really are. 
It's the bird in front of the flock that gets shot."
Some officials say the present fragile consensus at Beidaihe, the beach resort where China's elderly leaders are playing bridge and deciding the nation's future, is to allow Mr. Li to retain the post of Prime Minister. 
But they say that even according to this plan, Mr. Zhu would become first deputy prime minister in charge of the economy, so that he would be breathing down Mr. Li's neck.
"Even if Zhu Rongji isn't made Prime Minister, it may not matter so much," said a party member who has discussed policy with Mr. Zhu. "Because in any case, he'll be in charge of economic policy."
When summoned to Beijing last year from his previous post as Shanghai's Mayor, Mr. Zhu was given the task of unsnarling endless debt chains among state-owned companies. 
Partly because he was more successful than most people expected, he was named head of a new department called the Economic and Trade Office. 
It is emerging as a super-ministry with overall responsibility for managing the economy.
Â 
Nominal and Real Power
Officials say that a deal has been struck for Mr. Zhu to vault onto the Politburo's standing committee, the nation's top policy-making body. 
It is exceeded in authority only by the so-called sitting committee of octogenarians who are nominally retired but continue to hold ultimate power.
The key to Mr. Zhu's success is that Deng Xiaoping, the nation's 87-year-old senior leader, is acting as his campaign manager. 
Mr. Deng has gone out of his way to praise Mr. Zhu's understanding of economics.
Mr. Zhu is disliked not only by some hard-liners, however, but also by many midlevel and senior officials. 
They find him a terror to work for. 
Extremely demanding, Mr. Zhu scolds people publicly in a society where it is considered more polite to stab them in the back.
"Some comrades are kind of muddled, and even when you point out some problems they figure they're in the right," Mr. Zhu said in a recent confidential speech, defending his style. 
"Even their self-criticisms are superficial. 
So then you've got to criticize those laggards by name.
"I also encourage everyone to criticize me," Mr. Zhu added in the speech, parts of which appeared in a restricted-circulation publication for party officials. 
"A couple of times, the criticisms were pretty nasty, and they weren't entirely fair. 
But I listened. 
Whether or not the complaints are correct, it's good for them to let off steam."
Mr. Zhu still speaks Chinese with a trace of a Hunan Province accent, reflecting his childhood there, but he studied electrical engineering at Qinghua University in Beijing and has spent most of his life in the capital. 
He took up Mao's invitation in 1956 to offer the party constructive criticisms, and a year later he fell victim, along with others who spoke out, to the "anti-rightist campaign."
By a fluke he escaped with extremely lenient punishment: he was allowed to hold on to a job in the central Government, but in disgrace. 
In 1978, when Mr. Deng came to power, Mr. Zhu was rehabilitated and climbed onto the fast track.
Â 
An Embarrassing Encounter
While many Chinese believe that Mr. Zhu is different from other leaders, the last thing he wants is for this to be pointed out. 
When he once found himself seated beside an American correspondent at a dinner, he studied the reporter's name card and then asked accusingly, "Weren't you the one who wrote that article?"
The journalist asked if he meant an article that had appeared 10 months earlier, reporting that Chinese like Mr. Zhu much more than other leaders. 
"Yes, that article," Mr. Zhu said coolly, and he switched to English and quoted the headline word for word.
When the reporter acknowledged writing the article, Mr. Zhu paused for a moment in horror, and then pivoted. 
For the rest of the dinner he engaged in conversation exclusively with the person on his other side.

file: Beijing Journal_On the Stifled Campuses, Faint Echoes of Dissent.txt
text:
ï»¿
At one of Beijing's elite universities not long ago, students were subjected to another of a series of propaganda films intended to insure the reindoctrination of China's future leaders along the correct Communist road.
These same students had led ''the counterrevolutionary rebellion'' crushed so brutally in June, and they have since been subjected to steady, numbing sessions of political education.
The film that evening, ''Wei Wei Kunlun,'' which translates roughly as ''Towering Mountain,'' depicted China before the Communist takeover in 1949. 
A scene of a demonstration being violently broken up brought cheers because unlike the case in June no tanks were used.
Party officials asked the students why they had applauded. 
''Because it was such a good film,'' they said.
Â 
Common on the Campuses
Stories of quiet mockery of this sort are common on the campuses. 
The familiar slogan ''Only socialism can save China'' has been slightly altered to become, ''Only without socialism can China be saved.''
Freshmen at Beijing University have been sent off to Hebei Province for military and political training for a year; older students say that when the freshmen return they will practice ''peaceful evolution'' on them -the party catch phrase for the supposed capitalist strategy to undermine Chinese Communism through the introduction of alien cultural influences. 
One upperclassman, a party member, said, ''We will pass on to them their proper education in the four evils'' - excessive eating, drinking, gambling and promiscuity - and he seemed to be quite serious about the task.
The rapid changes in Eastern Europe, and especially the overthrow and execution of Nicolae Ceausescu, the Rumanian leader who was a longtime ally of the Chinese leadership, have brought a few daring gatherings and posters. 
Like the mockery, they are indicative of a lasting disgust and a resoluteness of spirit largely untouched by the ideological corset being tightened everywhere in intellectual and academic life.
But while the investigations are winding down and students and teachers await the party's judgments on punishment, there is wariness and mistrust everywhere and a general depression about the future that argues against any rapid re-emergence of the sort of demonstrations that electrified the world last spring.
Â 
A Sense of Caution
The unexpected death of a prominent figure like Deng Xiaoping or Zhao Ziyang, the party leader who lost his job after showing some sympathy with the June demonstrations, could create a pretext for students to gather and march, but few believe the leadership would react a second time with so much confusion and delay.
Students and teachers interviewed over the last three weeks described caution and lack of purpose. 
Among many students there is a self-imposed cap on political discussion and an aimless escapism. 
There are increasing experiments in casual sex and alcohol abuse. 
''We're watching trashy movies and reading trashy novels,'' one student said. 
''Sidney Sheldon is very popular now, and so is 'I'll Take Manhattan.'
''
Students speak of a sense of isolation from the larger society. 
''The campus is a very small world,'' one said. 
''It's like living in a cage, and you feel watched all the time.''
People are ''depressed and discouraged,'' she said. 
''Life seems meaningless now, and they are cynical. 
They feel bored. 
Life is boring if you're in school or out, boring if you have a boyfriend or not, boring if you work or not.''
Students still speak of politics to their closest friends, ''but that gets boring, too,'' the student said. 
''We don't disagree about anything. 
We all want change. 
But politics once again seems like empty talk.''
Â 
Something to Hide
The analogy of Rumania frightens the Government right now, another student said. 
''All the killing frightens us, too. 
We don't think the Chinese Army will crack so quickly as in Rumania, and many more could die.''
Most students, one said, had made less than fully forthcoming self-criticisms and protected their friends, and there is a feeling that many teachers and deans are also protecting students from the authorities. 
''But there are a lot of people who participated and have something to hide,'' he said. 
''So people don't trust one another. 
It is one of the biggest successes of the Government.''
Some students said many wanted either to go abroad or to make a lot of money and live an easy life. 
Everyone seems to be learning English and trying to pass the language examinations required to study abroad. 
But freshman are now judged too young to study abroad, and graduating students are told they must stay in China and work off their debt to society. 
''It's a way of keeping people here,'' a teacher said.
Teachers describe relatively open political discussion in the faculty rooms, but they are under strict orders not to discuss politics in class or with students. 
''The party tells us, 'If you have your own views, O.K., but don't pollute them,' '' a teacher said.
Another described a faculty meeting with the party secretary, who complained that while some students had informed on others, no teachers had done so, behavior that set a bad example. 
The party secretary was particularly outraged because he had received anonymous letters purporting to inform on him. 
''We felt he had no sense of shame,'' the teacher said. 
''Only the die-hard leftists or the careerists pursue this witch hunt.''
Â 
Caution Is Still Needed
One must nonetheless be careful, another teacher said. 
She was teaching a night class in English to adults who were behaving passively while she was trying to explain the prefix ''octo.''
''So I finally said: 'Why don't you talk?
You're as stubborn as octogenarians!'
''The class laughed, but the next day she was called in by the party secretary and asked why she had made fun of the party leadership, which is largely composed of elderly officials. 
''I said that it was in the textbook,'' she said, ''and that was that, but it worried me. 
Someone obviously made a report.''
Another teacher said that while he understood his students' anger and shared it, he tried to caution them that the situation could get worse, as it did in the 1950's and '60's.
''The students are impatient, of course, and want rapid change, and they have their own ideas. 
But I don't want them to get into trouble or waste their lives. 
We've all been inspired by a few demonstrations and by Rumania, but I tell them: 'Right now, your lives are more important. 
Don't throw them away.'
''

file: Beijing Journal_Tiny Counterrevolutionaries Facing Reform From 200,000 Fly Swatters.txt
text:
ï»¿
A few months ago, the authorities started noticing something very strange, scratched their heads and called in specialists who also scratched their heads but couldn't come up with an explanation to the mystery: why, all of a sudden, does China have so many flies?
No one seems to know the answer, but with the same Communist zeal that the Government hunts down "counterrevolutionaries," it has launched a grand campaign to wipe out flies.
"To build a 'City of No Flies' is a requirement of a highly civilized modern city," a senior official, Tie Ying, was quoted as saying recently in the official Beijing Daily. 
"It is a requirement of reform and openness and a means to push the economy to a higher stage."
China's leaders are calling on the masses to make greater contributions in the front against the flies, and the expression "City of No Flies" has become a rallying cry. 
Front-page news articles describe the latest battlegrounds of the fly war, the different tactics used and the successes in diluting the density of flies per room.
Â 
A Bid for the Olympics
A major reason for the campaign, which began in March, is to boost Beijing's chances of being host to the Olympics in 2000. 
The International Olympic Committee will decide on the location of the games next year, and the Chinese Government believes that if it stamps out flies -- in part by cleaning out hidden repositories of squalor and feculence -- it will be more likely to be chosen.
"Our goal is to create a city of no flies," said Gao Yukun, a senior health official in Beijing's Eastern District. 
"But we won't just kill flies. 
We want to create clean cities."
As part of the campaign, Beijing, which has a population of about 10 million people, purchased 130 tons of pesticides and held training courses to teach people the most advanced methods for eradicating flies.
Officials hold high-level meetings to discuss strategy and exchange status reports. 
Everyone is urged to study models of cleanliness, like the Foreign Ministry, which won praise from Beijing's Mayor, Chen Xitong.
Â 
Even in the Wonton Soup
Early in the summer, when the authorities sent their work teams into the dirty bowels of China's cities, they were alarmed to discover that flies were buzzing all over: in the gutter, in the toilet, in the dusty rooms, in the wonton soup.
"By June, we found that there were significantly more flies than before," said Zhang Xizeng, a senior health official in the Beijing Government. 
"It was this way all over the country. 
We don't know why."
The campaign bored deeper and the city held special "attack weeks," or cleaning festivals. 
Citizens posted banners bearing the slogan, "Mobilize the Masses to Build a City of No Flies," and distributed two million pamphlets to publicize the campaign.
Scores of children and elderly citizens joined special swat teams. 
They swatted flies, sprayed and sprinkled poison and cleaned out the garbage cans and bathing areas.
During one of the "attack weeks," the city distributed about 15 tons of pesticides, along with 200,000 fly swatters. 
In mid-July, after the first blitz, the density of flies had dropped 20 to 30 percent from the previous month. 
During another "attack week" in August, 1,000 teams of elderly people and young children hunted down flies, using 17,600 pounds of poison.
As in any major political campaign, citizens throughout the nation feel obliged to declare their support. 
Privately run restaurants post the slogans on the walls, hotels hang red banners and senior officials, like the Mayor, go on inspection tours.
A group of Beijing sixth-graders wrote a letter to Mayor Chen to propose that they use their summer vacations productively by swatting flies and cleaning up alleys filled with garbage.
To an outsider, Beijing does not seem to be particularly plagued by flies any more than, say, New Delhi or New York. 
But China is still trying to hold its cities to a tough standard for its showcases to the world: out of every 100 rooms, only one room is allowed to have two flies. 
In some parts of Beijing, the density was as high as 33 flies per room in June.
Â 
The Dry- Dish Test
Aside from taking aim at flies and rats, the campaign also promotes other ways of improving hygiene. 
Restaurants must pass a three-step dish-cleaning test that includes using water hot enough that it evaporates on the plates after rinsing. 
One joint-venture hotel, the Tianlun Dynasty Hotel, was fined about $735, partly for failing the dry-dish test.
Officials say that statistics on flies and rodents are difficult to collect. 
A few decades ago when the Government wanted to clean up the city by promoting campaigns against rats, it had citizens cut the tails off the rats they killed and mail them to the unit that collected the statistics. 
But then the Government discovered that children were picking up diseases from handling the dead rats.
Now, one of the rat tests consists of sprinkling piles of powder in several parts of a room, waiting 24 hours, then checking how many footprints there are. 
If two out of three piles have prints, then the room fails the permissible standard.
The campaign is producing some clear results. 
According to official statistics, the city of Beijing alone has cleaned up 26,000 dirty areas that bred flies and disposed of 270,000 tons of garbage that had been left on the streets or in vacant lots. 
Workers installed screens for 300 public toilets and cleaned 47,000 dustbins.
Â 
Dissent Even on This Issue
The Government knows it is up against extraordinary odds. 
When the weather is hot and damp and there is plenty of garbage for fly food, female flies can lay batches of 100 to 150 eggs every 18 days, according to Yang Jianmei, an entomologist at Beijing University.
Most citizens agree with the aims of the campaign and are fond of pointing out that even the United States and European countries still have flies. 
But for some people, the Government propaganda is nettlesome.
"A cleaner city is something that no one would normally oppose," said a young Chinese researcher. 
"But the Government turns everything into a political campaign. 
I don't like flies, but the way the Government forces you to kill flies, I'm almost tempted not to side with the Government."

file: Beijing Memo_As the Crackdown Continues, China Starts to Seem Just Like Old Times.txt
text:
ï»¿
Swept up in liberalization and a mood of relaxation until a few weeks ago, China suddenly seems more familiar to people who lived here or visited 10 or 20 years ago than to those who may have arrived recently.
It is not that China has returned to the days when the population was awakened at 6 A.M. by propaganda loudspeakers or when it was an offense, punished by a ''struggle'' meeting, to wrap garbage in a newspaper bearing a photograph of Mao.
But the repression sweeping China has brought back many once-common practices and controls - from the numbing repetition of a few authorized statements to a modest cult of personality.
The televised reports of trails of ''thugs'' who were said to have attacked troops during the crackdown two weeks ago illustrate the point.
Â 
'Open' Trials Now Closed
For a time, China made efforts to open up its criminal procedures. 
Trials were attended by foreign journalists and other observers. 
A system that for decades had been shrouded in secrecy emerged into the open.
But this week, when journalists asked the authorities if they could attend one of the ''open'' trials of people involved in the recent protest movement, they were told that it would be ''inconvenient at present.''
The near absolute management of information and the practice of conducting ostensibly public affairs behind closed doors are the sorts of practices that seemed to be falling into abeyance in the recent past.
To observe them again provides a shock of recognition to the Chinese and foreigners alike whose memories stretch back to the 1960's and 1970's, when China was not only far more secretive but also more closed in on itself than it has been in recent years.
''This is a place I recognize,'' an Italian journalist, absent from China for several years, said on his return after the crackdown two weeks ago. 
The journalist had read accounts of a country far different from the one he knew when he lived here in the early 1980's. 
It is, he said, far less different now.
''After these few relaxed years, these changes will have a deep psychological impact,'' one analyst said. 
''People will think that China is moving backward, no longer forward.''
Â 
Some Gains Still Stand
In fact, the backward move does not represent a wholesale reversion to the Maoist era when the very right to a private sphere of life went unrecognized. 
It is not yet forbidden in China to do things like listen to foreign radio broadcasts, play Beethoven, try to become wealthy or get married without the permission of the local party secretary.
The situation of the last two weeks is perhaps well represented by the anchorwoman on the evening news broadcast. 
She is chicly coiffed and dressed in a pink silk blouse, a style that would have been condemned as ''bourgeois'' in the worst of days past. 
But she presides over news broadcasts reminiscent of the saturation propaganda campaigns not known in this country for years.
In today's broadcast, for example, a coal worker from China's northeast was shown expressing his anger at those who conducted the ''counterrevolutionary disturbance'' in Beijing. 
The disturbance, he said, was aimed at ''overthrowing the Communist Party and the socialist system and at beating, smashing, looting, burning and killing.''
Two minutes later, the television anchorwoman read a statement by a local party leader. 
Word for word, right up to the ''beating, smashing, looting, burning and killing,'' the statement was the same.
Â 
End to Freewheeling Talks
The incident reminded some who first came to China in the early to mid-1970's that, in those days, practically all Chinese felt constrained in public to utter only a few correct phrases and little else - a stark contrast with the freewheeling discussions of recent years.
China specialists attribute some of the restorations of past practices to the current prominence of the group of aging revolutionary veterans who, in the face of the recent challenge to their authority, fell automatically back on older, familiar ways of doing things.
The ceaseless repetition of the same small number of phrases is, in this sense, a sign of the revival of another once-common technique that had fallen into abeyance in recent years, the use of a mass propaganda campaign to establish the leadership's authority.
The overall changes could be described as ones of mood and degree. 
Propaganda and sloganeering, Government secrecy and political intimidation, have never entirely ceased in China. 
But those with long memories here say the intensity of the present repression has not been reached since the moderate party faction, led by Deng Xiaoping, returned to power in the late 1970's.
Â 
Speech as Gospel
Analysts here, for example, say they cannot remember a time since the death of Mao and the arrest of his closest followers in the Gang of Four when the speech of a leader became the basis for a mass campaign.
But some remarks made by Mr. Deng to the Military Affairs Commission more than a week ago have not only got much publicity - even though Mr. Deng's actual words have not been released - but have become the objects of a national study campaign being promoted every day in the state-controlled news media.
The emerging pattern of political life also bears striking resemblances to a pattern that had virtually disappeared for more than a decade, that of a new unpredictability at the top.
One of the clear goals of Mr. Deng's leadership was to establish a kind of schedule of government, to run things according to clear rules. 
And so, since about 1983, key meetings of the party or of the National People's Congress, China's parliament, have been announced in advance and held on schedule.
Â 
Behind-the-Scenes Maneuvers
Now, for the first time in several years, the leadership seems likely to return to its older method, which was to hold meetings in secret and to announce them only later.
This week a scheduled meeting of the National People's Congress was postponed indefinitely. 
The assumption is that the leaders wanted to hold a meeting of the Central Committee before the congress. 
But while rumors have circulated for a week about a Central Committee meeting, there is no indication yet when or if it will be held.
The point is that after several years of apparent stabilityII, the leadership has returned to a pattern when behind-the-scenes maneuvers were so intense and difficult that it was impossible to keep schedules. 
Analysts say that the business of the party and the Government are likely to become, as they were in previous decades, enshrouded not only in secrecy but in uncertainty.
In this sense, one of the most conspicuous aspects of an earlier era to reappear is the spectacle of an aging leadership clinging to its power.
Â 
Comparing Deng With Mao
Some Chinese are quietly comparing the current period of Mr. Deng, who is 84 years old, to the last years of Mao, which were marked by an ever more intense personal tyranny.
The saturation campaign to advertise Mr. Deng's speech is the sort of thing that used to surround Mao's pronouncements. 
In a subtle but perhaps telling shift, Mr. Deng is being referred to as Chairman Deng - he is chairman of the Military Affairs Commission but not of the Communist Party.
To be sure, the modest cult of personality growing up around Mr. Deng falls far short of the mass adoration of Mao, during which his statue and picture were ubiquitous and his every word was given Delphic authority.
And yet, one of Mr. Deng's stated goals when he returned to power more than a decade ago was for the old leaders to step aside in favor of younger ones. 
Like Mao, however, Mr. Deng has destroyed the younger figures that he himself anointed.
Â 
'Love the Party'
In allowing a cult to grow up around himself now, Mr. Deng seems, in the view of analysts, to be returning to an effort to re-establish the authority and prestige of the party as the sole source of wisdom and legitimacy.
One result is the constant repetition of slogans that had almost disappeared. 
''Without the Communist Party, there would be no new China'' is one incessantly repeated lately. 
Another is ''Love the party, love the socialist motherland.''
In the last few years, particularly in speeches at party congresses, such slogans have been occasionally spoken, particularly by the veterans of Mr. Deng's generation, but they have not become parts of intense campaigns to build up the party's authority.
Since the mid-1980's, the party was something certainly to be obeyed; but the people have not for many years been called on to ''love'' it.

file: Beijing Orders 2 More Americans to Leave China.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a sign of continuing diplomatic tensions, two Americans have been ordered to leave China, presumably because of their activities during the recent pro-democracy demonstrations, an American official here said today.
The two Americans, Mark Radicia, 25 years old, a teacher at Nankai University in Tianjin, and Helen Qubain, 21, a student at the same univesity, were given until the end of the month to leave, the official said.
The two are believed to have maintained close ties with pro-democracy demonstrators in Tianjin, a large industrial port in northeast China.
An official at Nankai University said in a brief telephone interview that the university was ordered by the Tianjin public security bureau to tell the two Americans to leave China. 
He gave no reasons for the order.
Peace Corps Program on Hold
An American official said Mr. Radicia, who is from Omaha, and Ms. Qubain, from Buena Vista, Va., were now in Beijing. 
They are expected to leave the country within the next day or two, the official said.
The expulsions bring to five the number of Americans ordered expelled from China since the violent crackdown on the protest movement more than three weeks ago. 
Three journalists have also been expelled.
The order to the two Americans to leave followed notification by China that it was putting off a Peace Corps program that had been due to start this fall with the arrival of 20 American teachers in Sichuan Province. 
A United States official said today that the Chinese had given no reason for postponing the program, which would have been the first of its kind in any Communist country. 
The program was agreed to in April.
The official said the Chinese move, which was announced by the China Education Association for International Exchange, a Government organization, did not mean that the program would not eventually go ahead.
''We're not reading anything retaliatory into it,'' the official said. 
''It's not by any means canceled.''
The indefinite postponement of the Peace Corps program, however, seemed almost certainly to be linked to Chinese irritation with the United States, both for imposing sanctions against China after the crushing of the protest movement and for providing shelter in the American Embassy here for China's best-known dissident, the astrophysicist Fang Lizhi.
Â 
Visa Requests Are Up
But in one sign that China is allowing some aspects of relations with the United States to continue, American officials reported today on a rapid rise in the number of visa seekers already holding newly required exit permits. 
The Government said after the crackdown that all Chinese would have to have exit permits issued by the Public Security Bureau before they would even be allowed to enter foreign embassies to apply for visas.
An American official said that on Monday 100 people came to the embassy seeking visas, compared with just a handful in previous days. 
The English-language China Daily reported today that 8,520 of the newly required permits have already been granted.
A Chinese here said that the permit can generally be obtained when an applicant furnishes the Public Security Bureau with a letter from his workplace testifying that he had no part in the recent demonstrations. 
#24 Killed in Train Blast The Chinese also announced today that 24 people died when dynamite exploded on a passenger train traveling near Shanghai late Monday night.
While the explosion seemed to be an act of sabotage, it was unclear whether it was related to the protest movement or to the sweeping repression that has followed it.
The explosion recalled an incident three weeks ago when a train in Shanghai ran into demonstrators who were blocking tracks to protest the crackdown in Beijing. 
Six people were killed in the incident, and some protesters, apparently angered by the failure of the train to stop, set fire to the train. 
China later announced that three ''ruffians'' were executed for setting the fire and for burning police motorcycles.
While that incident made it seem possible that the sabotage Monday night was an act of retaliation, diplomats here pointed out that acts of vandalism on trains, including the setting of explosions, were known to take place in the months before the outburst of protest. 
Moreover, even if the sabotage Monday night was an act of retaliation, it seems unlikely that such acts of terrorism will become widespread here.
''China is just not a very likely place for that sort of thing,'' a diplomat said, referring to the tight control and pervasive surveillance here.
A television report on the incident showed a gaping hole in the side of a green passenger train, which was making the trip from Hangzhou, a major tourist city about 100 miles southwest of Shanghai. 
It said 11 people were seriously wounded in the blast.
Â 
Draft of New Law Approved
As details of the blast were announced, China's State Council today approved the draft of a new law on rallies and demonstrations. 
The draft is in preparation for a meeting of the standing committee of the National People's Congress, China's parliament, which is due to meet on Thursday.
There were no details of the law, but it is widely expected to impose formal restrictions on the rights of Chinese to hold demonstrations.
The laws being drafted by the State Council, which is a kind of Government cabinet, have been under discussion for months. 
When the discussions began, many analysts were expecting the laws to expand citizens' rights. 
Since the protests, however, the mood has changed dramatically.

file: Beijing Ousts Governor Tied to Zhao.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a sign that Beijing is trying to crack down on freewheeling economic policies in the provinces, China today announced the dismissal of the Governor of the nation's most experimental economic region.
The official, Liang Xiang, the Governor of Hainan Province in southern China, is a close associate of the ousted Communist Party leader, Zhao Ziyang. 
Mr. Liang is the highest-ranking official to be purged in connection with the Government's recent campaign against corruption.
The former Mayor of Shenzhen, the bustling city adjacent to Hong Kong, Mr. Liang, 71 years old, is a symbol in China of economic restructuring. 
Like many local officials, he put his faith in capitalist-style incentives and foreign investment rather than Marxist orthodoxy.
Accused of Corruption
The Chinese authorities accused Mr. Liang of ''serious mistakes by abusing power for personal interests'' and said he allowed his wife and son to profit from illegal business dealings. 
Mr. Liang is also said to have close ties to Mr. Zhao's second son, who has repeatedly been criticized for corrupt commercial practices.
The announcement said that Mr. Liang was replaced by Liu Jianfeng, a deputy party secretary of Hainan and former deputy minister of the electronics industry. 
In a dispatch by the official New China News Agency, the 53-year-old Mr. Liu said that Hainan's policies of restructuring and opening to the outside world would not be changed and indeed would be ''stepped up.''
Some analysts say they believe the dismissal of Mr. Liang is part of a broader attempt by hard-liners to clamp down on local officials who were closely associated with Mr. Zhao's style of economic change.
''It ties in with the overall politics of China and the overall attitude toward south China,'' a foreign official in Canton said of the dismissal. 
In a telephone interview tonight, he said the new leadership ''is going to try, as every political movement does, to reinforce itself and cut down opponents.''
He said a test of how far the purge would go may be the treatment of the party leader of Hainan, Xu Shijie, who has also been a vigorous proponent of foreign investment and economic restructuring.

Mr. Liang developed a national reputation as Mayor of Shenzhen, which expanded rapidly in recent years and is one of the most capitalist Chinese cities, partly because of foreign investment.

Symbol of Economic Goals

The announcement on national television this evening did not cite specific crimes of corruption committed by Mr. Liang, but it said he violated regulations when he allowed a local company to import cars.

file: Beijing Rejects Deadline for Talks And Students March in Defiance.txt
text:
ï»¿
Waving banners commemorating a similar demonstration 70 years earlier, thousands of university students marched through the capital this morning to press their demands for greater democracy.
The march followed the Government's rejection Wednesday of the students' conditions for formal talks to resolve their differences. 
Today, demonstrators shouted slogans criticizing the Government's recent meeting with student leaders as a sham, and demanded that students themselves pick their representatives to meet with the authorities.
By the middle of the day, thousands of students had swept past police lines and into Tiananmen Square, the center of the capital, and policemen who had ringed it were unable to hold back the columns of marchers from at least eight universities and thousands of onlookers who also rushed to the square. 
Other student groups, including several from out-of-town schools, had yet to arrive at the square.
Aside from some pushing, there was no serious confrontation with the police. 
The authorities seemed to want to avoid any violence, perhaps partly because it was the 70th anniversary of the nationalist demonstrations in Beijing that sparked the May Fourth movement, which had a major influence in China's political, economic and cultural modernization, and foreshadowed the rise of the Communist Party.
Â 
Confrontation Expected
The demonstration could be highly embarrassing for the Government because, among other things, it might disturb the opening session of the Asian Development Bank annual meeting, for which China is host in the Great Hall of the People. 
Tiananmen Square is adjacent to the Great Hall.
The Government said Wednesday that it would cordon off the square, setting the stage for a confrontation between demonstrators and the police.
It was unclear what measures the security forces would use against the demonstrators, but the Government spokesman, Yuan Mu, suggested that the police would use the same methods they have in the past -principally long lines of unarmed men to block protesters from going farther.
The General Secretary of the Communist Party, Zhao Ziyang, appealed to a gathering of Chinese youths and officials Wednesday afternoon for political stabilityI and unity.
Â 
Student Demands Refused
''Haven't we had enough social turmoil?'' the official New China News Agency quoted him as saying.
Students had demanded that the Government agree by noon Wednesday on their conditions for direct talks with China's leaders, but the Government refused. 
The authorities insisted that any dialogue be carried out through the official student unions, which the protesters reject.
In an unusually harsh attack against the nation's best-known dissident, Mr. Yuan also suggested that Fang Lizhi, the astrophysicist, had played a role in the current unrest. 
When pressed, however, Mr. Yuan refused to give details on Mr. Fang's involvement.
Mr. Yuan accused a ''handful of people of manipulating the student unrest from behind the scenes,'' and he seemed to be saying that Mr. Fang was one of them. 
Mr. Yuan also asserted that the New York-based Chinese Alliance for Democracy, which publishes a magazine in support of greater democracy in China, was behind the student unrest. 
Fang Denies Any Role Mr. Yuan also criticized recently reported remarks by Mr. Fang that suggested foreign countries might exert pressure on China to improve its human-rights situation by withholding investments.
''His remarks and future facts will show what a role he is playing in the current unrest,'' Mr. Yuan said.
In a telephone interview Wednesday night, Mr. Fang denied any role in the student unrest. 
''They should show some evidence that I am behind the scenes,'' he said.
At an outdoor news conference of their own, students declared their intention to march today, after a vote by 47 student delegates representing universities throughout the capital. 
The vote was not unanimous, but the delegates said 40 universities would take part. 
Student representatives who had traveled from Shanghai, Hefei, Sichuan and Tianjin also said they supported the demonstration.
Â 
Informal Talks Faulted
Surrounded by a thick circle of students and journalists, Wuer Kaixi, the president of the independent student union, denied that the association was influenced by Mr. Fang or the Chinese Alliance for Democracy.
He also criticized the recent informal talks that had taken place between the Government and the students.
''I think that Mr. Yuan Mu and some of those he represents lack the sincerity with which to carry out a dialogue with us,'' said Mr. Wuer, who is from Xinjiang Province.
In a sign that dissatisfaction is spreading among intellectuals, a group of reporters for official publications met Wednesday to plan a peaceful demonstration of their own. 
They said that more than 100 reporters would gather in front of the New China News Agency today to protest the dismissal of a Shanghai newspaper editor, Qin Benli, who had insisted upon reporting controversial events.

file: Beijing Seals Off Square_ Protest Fizzles.txt
text:

Faced with the threat of renewed protests in Tiananmen Square, the authorities sealed the area to the general public today while arranging for thousands of schoolchildren to sing and dance in the square.
Overseas dissidents had called on Chinese to mount a peaceful protest today by quietly gathering in large numbers on Tiananmen Square and walking around it. 
Word spread through Beijing in recent days about the planned protest, and students said posters were put up at two or more universities calling for people to take part.
Apparently in response, the authorities sealed off the square around dawn and kept ordinary people behind a line of policemen. 
But while the crowds of onlookers seemed a bit greater than normal, it was clearly not the large turnout that dissidents had hoped for.
In the evening, when the police reopened Tiananmen to the public, about 1,000 people strolled onto the square, but most appeared to be tourists from other parts of China rather than dissidents making a political point.
Â 
Protest Planned for Thursday
The failure of Beijing residents to turn out in large numbers for the quiet protest suggested that it would be difficult for the democracy underground to mount other protests this spring, in the delicate period that includes the first anniversaries of the democracy movement. 
The quiet protests on the square were supposed to take place not only today but also on Thursday - the traditional day when Chinese honor the dead - but it is not clear if the authorities plan to close Tiananmen Square on that day as well.
Chinese leaders appear to have been concerned about the risks of unrest. 
Not only were most Chinese work units ordered to advise employees to stay away from the square, but some university students were given special bus trips today to the Great Wall and other distant sites, and foreign tourists were also told to stay away from the area.
A wreath and a floral arrangement, presented at the Monument to the People's Heroes on Saturday by two elementary schools, were removed overnight.
