file: BEIJING SENTENCES, THEN RELEASES FOE.txt
text:
ï»¿
In what appears to be the last political trial related to the Tiananmen Square democracy movement, China sentenced an influential economist today to three years in prison for counterrevolutionary crimes and then released him for time served.
Wu Jiaxiang, a 37-year-old theorist who was detained on July 17, 1989, was allowed to return home this afternoon after his sentence was read out to a courtroom, a family member said. 
Mr. Wu was jailed for five weeks more than his official jail term, and one of the reasons appears to be that officials wanted to end the three-year series of Tiananmen political trials by allowing the last person tried to walk away from his sentencing a free man.
"This is the last trial," said John T. Kamm, an American businessman and human-rights campaigner who met this week with justice and police officials. 
"They wanted to close it with a release."
Officials told Mr. Kamm that all Chinese who were detained in connection with the Tiananmen Square democracy movement have now been tried and that a handful of other Chinese prisoners also have been released recently. 
But they evaded questions about what would happen if Chinese dissidents still wanted by the Government returned to China.
Â 
'Brain Trust' Member
Mr. Wu was a senior researcher at the Communist Party Central Committee General Office and was held in Qincheng Prison, where he was allowed to read but not write.
He was charged with counterrevolutionary incitement and propaganda. 
Mr. Wu did not actively take part in the protests, although he is believed to have been accused of writing a set of counterrevolutionary" slogans that were used in Tiananmen Square demonstrations.
A native of a remote village in Anhui Province, Mr. Wu grew up in the countryside. 
After the Cultural Revolution, he attended Beijing University and his career soared.
In the late 1980's, Mr. Wu became a member of the "brain trust" of young intellectuals surrounding the Communist Party leader, Zhao Ziyang. 
Mr. Wu wrote several important policy speeches and a book on the theory of Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader. 
He was close to Gen. Wang Ruilin, Mr. Deng's chief of staff.
Â 
Reports of Breakdowns
But those contacts did not help him after his arrest.
"He's one of them," said a Chinese journalist. 
"And they think he betrayed them."
There have been reports that Mr. Wu also suffered from mental breakdowns, and the family member reached today suggested that Mr. Wu would need some rest to recuperate mentally from his ordeal.
"On the outside, he looked okay," said the family member, adding that he did not have a chance to speak much with Mr. Wu.
Â 
Steel Worker Reported Freed
A poet and prominent essayist, Mr. Wu was one of the original proponents of "new authoritarianism."
That theory held that Chinese required enlightened despotism, rather than Western-style democracy, to promote the growth of a healthy economic system and prepare for broader freedoms later on.
Mr. Wu was a close associate of Bao Tong, the former political secretary of the Politburo, who was sentenced last month to seven years in prison.
The Government also told Mr. Kamm that it had released Zhu Jianbin, a 37-year-old dissident who had been imprisoned for 11 years because of his involvement in the Democracy Spring movement that began in 1978. 
Mr. Zhu, a steel worker who edited a pro-democracy journal, The Bell Tolls, was detained in 1981 and virtually nothing has been heard of him since then.
Officials told Mr. Kamm that Mr. Zhu was tried and sentenced in April 1981 to six years in prison for counterrevolutionary incitement. 
They said he broke prison regulations when he assaulted someone in a brawl and then had his sentenced increased by "several years."
Â 
Prisoner's Wife Released
The authorities would not say when Mr. Zhu was released. 
They told Mr. Kamm that Mr. Zhu has returned to his home in Wuhan and now has a job.
Another dissident, Hou Xiaotian, said today that she had been released after four days of questioning about her plans to protest on behalf of her imprisoned husband. 
Ms. Hou said she was released late Sunday night but had been kept in a guest house rather than a prison and had been well treated.
Her husband, Wang Juntao, is serving a 13-year sentence for his role in the Tiananmen democracy movement. 
He began a hunger strike on Aug. 
11 to protest actions by authorities to block two suits he is filing against the court and a prison.
Ms. Hou said the authorities told her that her husband had lost about 22 pounds since he began his hunger strike, but that he was eating again on an irregular basis.

file: Beijing Stops Key Dissident From Meeting With Bush.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a harsh rebuke to the growing enthusiasm here for more democracy, China on Sunday prevented the country's best-known dissident, Fang Lizhi, from attending a banquet to which he had been invited by President Bush.
Earlier in the day, China's top leaders told President Bush in the bluntest terms that the United States should not raise human rights issues in China. 
Their comments and the police action against Mr. Fang were not only an embarrassment for Mr. Bush, but a clear sign of the Communist Party's alarm at the growing calls for democracy.
The Chinese comments and action against Mr. Fang were surprising, partly because Mr. Bush had not raised human rights issues in his discussions Sunday, as he had been expected to.
The Communist Party General Secretary, Zhao Ziyang, himself raised the topic Sunday afternoon, sharply warning Mr. Bush that demands for democracy are a serious obstacle to economic change in China. 
The subject came up toward the end of their conversation, and Mr. Bush did not respond.
But on leaving China early this morning, President Bush told the ranking Chinese official present, Deputy Prime Minister Wu Xueqian, that he regretted that Mr. Fang had not been allowed to attend the dinner. 
A spokesman for the American Embassy in Beijing also said that Mr. Bush had asked Ambassador Winston Lord to follow up on the matter with the Chinese Foreign Ministry. 
The spokesman said that Mr. Lord would request a meeting to discuss the issue.
Â 
Harshest Comments Yet
In their discussions Sunday, Mr. Zhao told Mr. Bush that ''the fact that some elements in American society support people who are dissatisfied with the Chinese Government will not contribute to China's political stabilityI and reform, nor will it help China's friendship with the United States.
Mr. Zhao's statements, and milder statements in a similar vein by the senior leader Deng Xiaoping and Prime Minister Li Peng in their meetings with Mr. Bush, were by far the harshest official comments so far on the increasing demands here for democracy and for the release of political prisoners.
Together with the action against Mr. Fang, the comments reflected Chinese alarm not only at the speed with which the democracy movement has gained ground but also the support it has received in America from Congress, news organizations and citizens.
Mr. Fang, a 53-year-old astrophysicist who was expelled from the Communist Party two years ago because of his criticisms of Marxism and calls for democracy, was first stopped by the police several blocks from the Great Wall Sheraton Hotel, where Mr. Bush was hosting a Texas-style banquet for about 500 people. 
Mr. Fang was with his wife, Li Shuxian, a Communist Party member who is a bitter critic of the Government, and Perry Link, a prominent American scholar of Chinese language and literature, as well as Mr. Link's wife.
Mr. Link's driver was accused by the police of a traffic violation, and so they decided to walk the short distance to the hotel. 
Mr. Fang said the police there refused to allow them to enter the hotel, and told them they were not on the guest list. 
When they tried to take a taxi to the American Embassy, the taxi was immediately pulled over for a traffic violation as well.
Â 
Buses Told Not to Pick Them Up
The police also ordered buses not to pick them up, so the four of them walked for an hour and a half to the American Ambassador's residence, followed the entire way by teams of police on foot and in cars. 
Two Canadian diplomats found them in front of the residence and helped them contact American officials and reporters.
''This is a fresh example of the human rights violations in China,'' Mr. Fang said in an interview Sunday night.
Most of the guests at President Bush's banquet were Chinese officials, but at least two other dissidents were allowed to attend. 
Su Shaozhi, a Marxist theorist and open critic of the Government, said he had encountered no difficulties, nor had a dissident and playwright, Wu Zuguang.
Mr. Bush and the guests were unaware that Mr. Fang had been turned away. 
The White House spokesman, Marlin Fitzwater, had earlier said that Mr. Bush probably would not meet with Mr. Fang at the banquet.
In addition to Mr. Zhao's comments, Mr. Deng and Prime Minister Li made remarks in a similar vein during their meetings with Mr. Bush. Mr. Deng told the President that China's economic modernization required a stable environment, and that without such stabilityI the achievements of the last few years would be lost.
Â 
'Cast a Shadow Over Relations'
Mr. Li also seemed to warn Mr. Bush against raising human rights questions. 
The spokesman said that Mr. Li had cautioned that a small number of Americans are trying to influence China's foreign policy and internal affairs. 
''If this comes from Government officials,'' Mr. Li added, ''this will cast a shadow over the good relations between the U.S. and China.''
The fact that the Chinese side released such remarks to reporters suggested that the comments were intended as a warning both to Chinese democracy advocates and to Americans who support them.
Mr. Zhao said that there were two extreme points of view in China: those who wish to retreat from change and those who ''call for the introduction of a multiparty political system and the parliamentary system of Western countries.''
Referring to the proponents of democracy, Mr. Zhao said:
''In practical terms, they do not promote reform; they provide a pretext for retreat from reform, and therefore stir up social disorder. 
They will block the way of reform. 
They will make the reform suffer setbacks or fail. 
This is very serious.''
Such comments were particularly unusual coming from Mr. Zhao, who in the past had been regarded as a patron of intellectuals and a supporter of a more tolerant political climate. 
But in the last six weeks, at the same time that the dissident movement has bloomed, some of Mr. Zhao's supporters have called for a ''new authoritarianism,'' which they say is necessary to provide a stable framework for economic development.

file: Beijing University Students Mark the 1989 Crackdown.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a bold protest against China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, students at Beijing University early this morning smashed nearly 100 glass bottles to mark the second anniversary of the military crackdown here on the democracy movement.
Shortly after midnight, students began clapping, cheering and throwing bottles outside three graduate dormitories where policemen were patrolling, a witness said. 
In Chinese, "xiao ping," meaning "little bottle," is a homonym for Mr. Deng's given name, and protesters often express their feelings about Mr. Deng by shattering bottles.
The protest came despite the large-scale presence of policemen and other security officers, and despite threats issued to students in recent days that they faced severe punishment if they tried to commemorate the anniversary of the 1989 crackdown. 
The authorities already had reportedly tried to gather up all the glass bottles in the area so that students could not break them.
Â 
Center of Student Demonstrations
Beijing University, the most famous in the country, was a center of the student demonstrations that ended with the Tiananmen Square crackdown on June 3-4, 1989. 
The university also has particular significance because many of the children of senior officials, including Mr. Deng's oldest son, have gone there.
China's best-known student leader, Wang Dan, who is serving a four-year prison sentence, was a history student at Beijing University.
On Monday night, at least 200 students had gathered outside the campus library. 
Some wore white, the color of mourning in China, and they started to sing songs, but were silenced by dozens of plainclothes policemen.
The bottle smashing appeared to be loosely organized, and no group took responsibility. 
It was difficult to tell how many students were involved, but the witness said at least several dozen took part. 
The protest lasted about two hours, but the police did not raid the dormitory and no arrests were reported.
Â 
A Protest Last Week
After a small protest last week, in which a banner was unfurled and leaflets distributed, the police waited for more than a day before raiding the dormitory. 
And a year ago, when Beijing University students also smashed bottles and sang protest songs, the security forces waited for several days before arresting an organizer, who is still in prison.
An organization called the Young China United Association took responsibility for last week's protest.
Although security has been dramatically increased around Tiananmen Square, around the university district and particularly near Beijing University, there appeared to be no clashes between students and the police.
In the last few days, teachers and staff members at Beijing University were reportedly summoned to meetings where they were told about several displays of student protest that had taken place recently.

file: BEIJING UNMOVED BY STUDENT_S PLEA.txt
text:
ï»¿
After banging his head against bureaucracies throughout this city, a Chinese graduate student prepared today to return to Texas, after failing to win any sympathy from the authorities in his mission to bring his jailed friend closer toward freedom.
Ge Xun, a student of experimental physics at Texas A & M University, waved an air ticket he obtained today for a Wednesday flight back to the United States. 
When Mr. Ge first arrived eight days ago on a quest for clemency for his friend, a democracy advocate, the authorities seemed so irritated that they did not provide documents he needed to be allowed to leave China.
But his ticket did not bring him any closer to influencing the case of his 32-year-old friend, Wang Juntao, one of the most prominent dissidents who has been detained for more than a year because of his role in the Tiananmen Square democracy movement. 
Last month, Mr. Wang was formally charged with counterrevolutionary crimes and sedition.
Â 
One-Way Ticket to Beijing
Mr. Ge read the news in the United States, and out of frustration and anxiety, he bought a one-way ticket to Beijing and traveled 9,000 miles to see what he could do to help his friend. 
The trip carried some risk, because Mr. Ge is a Chinese national who -- although he has lived in the United States for four years -- could be denied permission to leave China if he offended the authorities here.
As it turned out, Mr. Ge could not accomplish much. 
But Mr. Ge's tortuous trip points to the difficulties in gleaning any information at all about the trials and fate of dissidents jailed in connection with the Tiananmen demonstrations in June 1989. 
For eight days, Mr. Ge scoured the trial notices outside the courthouse and he pounded on the doors of the courts, the prosecutors offices and the public security bureau, hoping to find out where Mr. Wang's case stood.
He didn't find out a trial date, he didn't find out if the case would even be brought to trial, and he didn't find out if the trial, if held, would be open.
Â 
'A Tool of Punishment'
"The law has become a tool of punishment, a tool of revenge," Mr. Ge said in an interview.
The only thing Mr. Ge found was that Mr. Wang's case had not yet been brought to court. 
In one of his last nights, Mr. Ge met with his friend's wife, Hou Xiaotian, but she told him she didn't know anything.
Instead, she told him of her feelings of depression and of her uncertainty about trials that are expected soon. 
Ms. Hou said she had exchanged letters with her husband, but had not been allowed to see him.
"They are depressed," Mr. Ge described the wife and her friends. 
"They hurt in their hearts, but there is still a kind of hope that their family members can be treated fairly."
During his stay in Beijing, Mr. Ge refused to call on any of own his friends for fear of getting them in trouble. 
His family gave him a rather ambivalent welcome, for while they were delighted to see him -- it was the first time he had returned to China -- they were horrified at the attention he was attracting by talking to foreign reporters and at the risks he was taking. 
He saw his mother only three times, including the time she kicked him out of the house after reporters tried to interview them. 
Mr. Ge stayed in a hotel.
Â 
'For a Single Cause'
Mr. Ge also did not inquire in detail about other dissidents, who have also been formally charged recently and are expected to go on trial soon.
"I came back for one person, for a single case," said Mr. Ge, who met Wang Juntao when they worked together at a research center in the early 1980's. 
"I hope my visit helps change the way they look at Wang."
Mr. Ge had wanted to stay longer in Beijing, trying to help his friend, but his family here is pressing him to return to the United States and his wife in Texas is ill, so Mr. Ge says he is ready to return. 
He admits the trip was "very poorly planned," but he says he is glad he came, and he points out that his education in the United States gave him the strength to pursue his journey.
"There were two things I learned at A & M," he said. 
"Honesty and courage."

file: Beijing Welcomes _Old Friend_ Nixon, Hoping for Thaw With U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
Former President Richard M. Nixon arrived today for a visit of about six days in which he will meet with top Chinese leaders, and although it is billed as an unofficial fact-finding trip, both the United States and China seem to hope that it will help smooth relations.
Mr. Nixon is regarded here as an ''old friend'' of China because his trip in 1972 led to the normalization of Chinese-American relations. 
He is by far the most prominent American to visit since Beijing's violent suppression of the democracy movement in June, and officials here say they hope that the trip will reduce the antagonisms that have roiled relations since then.
Mr. Nixon's staff said the former President had discussed his plans with President Bush. 
It said that after Mr. Nixon returns to the United States, he will give the White House a written assessment of the Chinese leaders, their policies and prospects for Chinese-American relations.
Sanctions imposed shortly after the crackdown prevent most high-level contacts between American officials and their Chinese counterparts, and for political reasons few American office-holders would be willing to be photographed shaking hands with those who planned the repression.
During the summer, some Americans said they hoped that Mr. Nixon's visit would lead to some breakthrough, such as an arrangement for the emigration of the dissident couple Fang Lizhi and Li Shuxian. 
Mr. Fang and Miss Li have taken refuge in the American Embassy here, and are certain to be arrested if they step outside.
Now, however, diplomats and Chinese officials doubt that Mr. Nixon will be able to resolve that problem. 
They say that the value of the visit lies in opening a new channel of communication between the two Governments, and in the possibility that Chinese officials will listen to his counsel.
Mr. Nixon is expected to meet with Deng Xiaoping, the senior leader; Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party leader; Prime Minister Li Peng, and other top officials.
''Sino-U.S. relations are at a crossroads,'' Foreign Minister Qian Qichen said tonight at a banquet for Mr. Nixon, according to the official New China News Agency. 
''We sincerely hope that the U.S. 
Government will weigh the pros and cons and take a forward-looking approach so that Sino-U.S. relations may return to the track of normal development at an early date.''
The agency said that during the banquet, Mr. Nixon described himself as a ''friend of China.''
It said he had expressed confidence in the growth of American-Chinese relations.
Mr. Nixon's former Secretary of State, Henry A. Kissinger, is expected to visit China beginning Nov. 
7, shortly after Mr. Nixon has left.

file: BEIJING_S LEADERS REPORTED TO MEET.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's top officials were believed to be meeting in secret today to resolve the nation's political crisis, but while there were many rumors in the capital there was no confirmation of an outcome.
All week there have been reports that the Politburo was meeting in an enlarged session, but the meeting today appeared to be a long-delayed plenum of the Central Committee. 
There was no official confirmation, but Chinese in a position to know described it as the fourth plenum of the 175-member Central Committee; the third plenum met last fall.
An Asian diplomat said that he had been told by Chinese that a large meeting was under way, but that he was unsure whether it was the Central Committee meeting, a party work conference that might precede the plenum or simply another enlarged session of the Politburo.
Â 
Search for 7 Intellectuals
The meeting appeared to have been called amid secrecy unusual since the end of the Maoist era even for the normally secretive Communist Party. 
One official said today that provincial governors and party leaders had been told that they could bring just one aide with them to Beijing, to prevent word from spreading too much.
As reports of the party meeting circulated, an all-points bulletin was obtained here today for seven prominent intellectuals who are accused of agitation during the recent democracy movement. 
Among the seven are one of China's best-known social scientists and one of its best-known businessmen.
While these seven appear to have escaped arrest so far, and at least one is reported to have escaped to Hong Kong, the television news reported extensively tonight on the arrest of a well-known literary scholar who was accused of being a ''black hand'' behind the democracy movement.
Â 
Changes at People's Daily
The all-points bulletin carried a Government seal, as well as photos of the seven intellectuals, and was almost certainly genuine. 
It was issued to top officials at security agencies and is to be posted at all airports, train stations, police stations and elsewhere, to help find and arrest the fugitives.
In another sign of the sweeping changes taking place in the corridors of power throughout the nation, People's Daily said today that its director and its editor had been changed ''for health reasons.''
The newspaper is published by the Communist Party and is by far the most important daily in the country, so the change in its leadership is a sign of the political transformation now taking place.
The new director is Gao Di, a Central Committee member who is believed to have links with Prime Minister Li Peng. 
The new editor is Shao Huaze, a military man who has ties to the family of President Yang Shangkun and is currently director of propaganda in the army's General Political Department.
''It brings one back to the Cultural Revolution, when army men were sent to run nearly everything,'' an American Government analyst said. 
''They belong to the same gang, which is now in control.''
The Asian diplomat said of the reported party meeting: ''Something is going on right now. 
None of the national or even local leaders were on television tonight, and that also is evidence that some kind of meeting is going on.''
One Chinese said the new Communist Party leader was Jiang Zemin, the Shanghai party leader. 
Mr. Jiang, a 63-year-old engineer who speaks English, Russian and Rumanian, has been mentioned as a possibility for the post of General Secretary, but the leading candidate has been Qiao Shi, a Politburo member in charge of internal security.
A Western diplomat said some associates of Mr. Qiao had indicated that he might not want the position, and if this is true it might make room for another person, like Mr. Jiang.
The new party leader would take the post of Zhao Ziyang, who has not been seen in more than five weeks and is believed to have been purged in a power struggle that began because he took a conciliatory attitude toward student demonstrators.
Â 
Prominent Political Scientist
Among the seven intellectuals cited in the all-points bulletin obtained today is Yan Jiaqi, one of China's most prominent political scientists and a scholar with many friends in the United States. 
Mr. Yan, who is 47, was one of China's most outspoken scholars and with his wife, Gao Gao, had written a study of the Cultural Revolution. 
Mr. Yan and Miss Gao are now reported to have escaped to Hong Kong, although this could not be confirmed.
Another is Wan Runnan, the 42-year-old head of the Stone Corporation, an extremely successful high-technology company in Beijing. 
Mr. Wan, a scientist who started the company with several colleagues, may be in trouble because a research foundation financed by his company was involved in an attempt to overturn martial law by calling an emergency session of the National People's Congress Standing Committee. 
The head of that research foundation, Cao Siyuan, has disappeared, and Mr. Cao's absence from the list suggests that he has already been arrested.
Chen Yizi, the head of the Government's Institute for Restructuring the Economy, is also on the list.

text:
ï»¿
LEGACIES
A Chinese Mosaic.
By Bette Bao Lord.
245 pp. 
New York: Alfred A. Knopf. $19.95.
Above all other virtues, the Chinese treasure ren. 
Translated literally, ren simply means ''to endure.''
But as Bette Bao Lord explains in this stunning collection of oral histories, the Chinese ideogram is far more telling than the English definition: the character for ren is written by placing ''the cutting edge of a sword above a heart.''
Ren, the ability to survive the calculated cruelties and everyday betrayals of Chinese life as well as calamities such as last June's Tiananmen massacre, runs through these intimate accounts. 
Based on interviews and tape recordings Bette Lord made with Chinese men and women while her husband, Winston, served as the United States Ambassador in Beijing from 1985 to April 1989, ''Legacies'' is franker, more penetrating and infinitely sadder than most journalistic accounts of the brave and tragic uprising at Tiananmen Square.
Because the Shanghai-born Mrs. Lord is connected to China by threads of family, education and experience, she enjoyed unusual access to all levels of Chinese society. 
The salon she created at the American Embassy in those fleeting years when China's doors were wide open to the West drew scores of Chinese artists, writers, historians and other intellectuals. 
Many stayed after the disco dancing ended, befriended their hostess and spilled out their harrowing stories. 
Since returning to the United States last summer, just days before the crackdown, she has woven their stories together with her own reminiscences and somewhat more upbeat tales of her own vast clan. 
''Legacies,'' the work of an expert storyteller (Mrs. Lord is the author of three previous books, including a novel), is an assemblage of indelible portraits that get at the essence of what it means to be Chinese in our times, of what the Chinese Communist Party has bequeathed its people.
''How many riddles are there in one life?'' one of Mrs. Lord's troubled confidantes wrote in a poem. 
Plenty, judging from these stories.
Consider the young actress, alienated since the age of 7 from a father who was branded a ''rightist''; his political crimes dashed her hopes of attending a special school for the gifted and of joining the party. 
''I would not speak to him,'' she admits to Mrs. Lord. ''He would bring me candy and fruit. 
I refused to touch it. 
. . . So ashamed was I of my father that I wished he would leave and never come back.''
Eventually, he did just that. 
And it was only when she was sent to collect his ashes from the prison where he spent the Cultural Revolution that she realized that, instead of being a traitor, he was something of a hero. 
Although the official explanation was that he had committed suicide, a prison warden told her that her ''father's ears were torn off'' because he refused to inform on others.
The Cultural Revolution figures in many of these portraits, but Mrs. Lord makes it clear that Communist repression - and lunacy - preceded that traumatic decade. 
One former fiery revolutionary confides to Mrs. Lord that he first got into trouble as a volunteer during the land reform movement of 1950. 
In the small village he was administering, he couldn't find enough landlords to satisfy the 5 percent quota designated by the party for vilification. 
''I could not believe that the Party truly meant for me to name an arbitrary number of landlords,'' he recalls. 
His integrity earned him a long sentence in a prison camp where he was forced to play female roles in Chinese opera productions - and, as additional punishment, to grow his hair to shoulder length and wear ladies' costumes all day.
Not everyone in this book is a tragic figure. 
Bette Bao Lord, on an early visit to China, was astonished that her Uncle Jieu Jieu, an engineer who survived years of hard labor, somehow managed a cheerful, even carefree manner. 
''What makes you so different from the others?'' she asks him. 
''An unwashable brain,'' he boasts. 
Not only had he never accepted any of the shifting ideologies peddled by the party over the years but he had come to realize that he and other critics were ''truly indispensable'' to the regime. 
''Without people like me,'' he points out, ''the Party has no objects of struggle or excuses'' for its failures.
The writing in ''Legacies,'' devoid of sentimental pity, saves the book from becoming a catalogue of miseries, just as some internal mechanism spares many Chinese from deep depressions or other mental illnesses. 
Through the interviews and her own commentary, the author captures the texture of Chinese life: the endless gossip (Prime Minister Li Peng's unflattering nickname, she reveals, is ''Comrade No Talent''); the Chinese wariness of making new friends (''old ones were safe'' while ''new ones were risky''); the tendency for every dinner conversation to become ''a seminar on the state of the nation.''
Appalled though she is at the horror stories, Mrs. Lord confesses that she misses China every time she leaves. 
''Life there was difficult,'' she writes, ''but because this was true, everything seemed to matter more.''
Mrs. Lord's final days in Beijing coincided with the student occupation of Tiananmen Square, but she does not attempt to chronicle those events systematically. 
There is one engaging tale, however, of a prosaic marriage saved from collapse when the bored husband discovers, to his delight, that his dull homebody of a wife has been cooking for the students in the square. 
Mrs. Lord is a storyteller, not a political analyst. 
And yet the powerful voices she orchestrates here explain eloquently why ordinary Chinese, pushed throughout their lives to endure the unendurable, might stand up to a tank.

text:

At Public School 102 in Elmhurst, Queens, there are a lot of new students and nowhere to put them. 
A special projects class is held on the auditorium stage, while an English-as-a-second-language class is held behind it. 
The stage dressing room has been transformed into the school's resource room. 
Two students sit in front of a computer in a stairwell for a math lesson, as their teacher stands two steps above them.
"We use every bit of space," said Dale Dancis, the resource room teacher. 
"We'd use the ceiling if we could."
P.S. 102 is one of several schools in Elmhurst, Corona and Ridgewood spilling over with new students as immigrants from China to Colombia flock to Queens. 
On Wednesday, the Board of Education announced that its annual enrollment had leaped by nearly 18,000 students. 
Every school district in Queens was affected. 
District 24, which includes P.S. 
102, saw the greatest jump in the city: More than 1,200 unanticipated students enrolled during September.
Â 
'A Steady Increase'
These numbers were no surprise to schoolteachers and administrators in District 24, which has 27,000 students in kindergarten through eighth grade. 
"We have had a steady increase in immigrant population for several years now," said Carlos LeDee, the supervisor of bilingual and English-as-a-second-language programs for the district. 
The biggest increase, he said, is in Spanish-speaking students: from 9,335 in 1986-86 school year to 12,005 now. 
Chinese and Korean-speaking students are increasing as well, he said, along with children from Eastern Europe, Pakistan and Africa.
Mr. LeDee said that the district has made accommodations for the new foreign students, looking hard to fill vacancies for bilingual education and English-as-a-second-language teachers. 
"Of course we have Spanish bilingual teachers," he said. 
"But we've also had to find Korean bilingual teachers and Chinese bilingual teachers."
The diversity the immigrants bring to the schools is a source of pride to principals in the district. 
But they are worried that if the wave of immigration continues, their resources will be stretched to the breaking point, especially as the school system faces the prospect of huge budget cuts. 
They worry about teacher layoffs next year, about rising class sizes and about finding ever more bilingual and English-as-a-second-language teachers. 
Most of all, they worry about the lack of space and what it will do to their students.
Harvey Sherer, the principal of P.S. 
102, said he calculated that his 900 students have two-and-a-half square feet of space each -- just enough to bump elbows when they stand behind their desks to pledge allegiance to the flag. 
"Could you sit in a room like this all day?" he said, pointing to a third-grade classroom with 39 desks.
The teacher of the class, Elizabeth Jennings, said that she continually rearranges the desks to find the most room.
"No matter what," she said, "I have them bumping into each other."
To give the children breathing room, she said, she puts class materials in a corner near her desk so children can walk up and "stretch their legs."
"They also sign a sheet to go to the bathroom," she said, adding with a sigh, "It's a popular sheet."
P.S. 102 has 900 students in a space used four years ago by 650. 
In the school's minischool, where kindergarten and first grade are taught, English-as-a-second-language classes are held in vestibules. 
Mr. Sherer has asked the district to rent space in a parochial school on the same bus route. 
"If there are budget cuts, I don't think we'll get it," he said.
Many of P.S. 
102's new students were picked up from neighboring Public School 89, which dropped its fifth grade classes and began teaching only kindergarten through fourth grade four years ago so it could fit 1,400 students in its 48 classrooms. 
P.S. 102 picked up 150 of P.S. 
89's students, easing the pinch for P.S. 
89 just a bit.
District 24 broke ground last week on a new elementary school, and has begun installing modular classrooms at some buildings. 
P.S. 89 is expecting a new wing, but not until 1993.
"We have new students registering all year long," said Cleonice LoSecco, principal of P.S. 
89. "Just this morning, the office was full of parents waiting to register."
P.S. 89, a turn-of-the-century four-story structure built to hold 900 students, has turned every available inch into classroom space. 
Assistant principals' offices are classrooms. 
Teachers' lounges are classrooms. 
The gym holds three classes: a second- , third- and fourth-grade class, where three teachers hold group and individual lessons.
The classrooms look like United Nations postcards; there are 35 languages spoken and the students -- mostly Asian, Latin American, East Indian and African -- share their native foods at an international festival each May.
There is a lot of sharing at P.S. 
89. There are five doubled kindergarten classes, with 42 or more students in each, three doubled first-grade classes and one doubled second-grade class.
Virginia Quinones teaches 42 bilingual Spanish kindergarteners with another teacher and two paraprofessionals.
"The hardest part is just moving around the room," she said. 
"On nice days, we take them outside and give them lessons out there. 
Today we made pinwheels and walked around the building, giving them a lesson on wind."

A month ago, for a variety of reasons, China briefly became the capital of the international bridge scene. 
Two weeks of activity began with the Far East Championships in Canton.
The home country won the titles in three divisions, Open, Women and Junior, but the members of the Chinese Open Team suffered a disappointment: although they were overall winners, they did not win the right to compete in the Bermuda Bowl in Yokohama, Japan, in October. 
Australia and New Zealand regularly compete in the Far East contests, but because they are from another zone, their results do not count in qualifying for world championships.
Hong Kong, which did badly against the South Pacific countries and finished fourth, won the top spot when the Far East countries were ranked and will go to Yokohama. 
Nevertheless, China will be represented by its women's team in Japan and by its junior team in Ann Arbor, Mich., for the World Junior Championships in August.
After the Far East Championships, many of the competitors moved to Beijing where they took part in the Epson Worldwide Bridge Contest on June 7. 
They were among the 1,400 players in the Great Hall of the People.
As in previous years, the bridge enthusiasts in the Chinese leadership took part: Wan Li, chairman of the National People's Congress; Wu Wenying, Minister of Textiles; Ding Guanjen, a member of the Politburo; Qian Jiwei, Minister of Defense, and Liu Zhongyi, Minister of Agriculture. 
As he has for several years, Deng Xiaoping, the country's leader, played in a private Epson game.
In a separate event June 8 and 9, an American squad was among those invited to play in the International Friendship Teams. 
The winners were the Shanghai "Poker" team, named for the playing-card manufacturer that sponsored them rather than for a different card game.
Earlier, during the Far East event in Canton, Wan Li not only presented the trophies to the Far East champions, but received one himself from Ernesto D'Orsi of Brazil, the president of the World Bridge Federation. 
The award was for finishing second in a field of 87,000 in the 1990 Epson Contest, a remarkable feat for an octogenarian.
After receiving his award, Wan called for a table to be set up and settled down to a social game. 
On the diagramed deal, as South, he was using the Precision System, which has been popular with Chinese players ever since it was invented a quarter-century ago by Charles C. Wei, a Chinese-American shipbuilder in New York City. 
Kathie Wei, his widow, was sitting in the North seat as the chairman's partner.
In a pair game, it is likely that many North-South partnerships would arrive in four hearts. 
That would be in serious jeopardy after a spade lead, although it can be made, double-dummy, by winning with the ace, cashing two top hearts and leading the diamond queen: a diamond trick is established in the South hand to take care of the potential spade loser.
But North-South avoided this trap. 
After the strong one-club opening, a one-diamond response would have been negative. 
South therefore bid two diamonds, showing length in the suit and positive values. 
After both players had rebid their long suits, a series of cue-bids led to the good contract of six diamonds.
The success of the slam depends primarily on the trump suit. 
Viewing this suit in the abstract, there are five possible approaches aimed at avoiding the loss of two trump tricks: Cash the ace and continue; lead the queen for a finesse and if it loses, cash the ace; lead the queen for a finesse, and if it loses finesse again; lead to the queen, and if it loses to the king, cash the ace; lead to the queen, and if it loses, finesse for the jack.
The obvious play, which most players would adopt, is to cash the ace. 
That succeeeds 65 percent of the time, but it is the worst plan. 
Leading to the queen, with a decision to be made later about the jack, is about 6 percent better than cashing the ace. 
But 5 percent better still, because it deals with four trumps in the East hand, is to lead the queen from the dummy, again with a jack problem if West has the king.
In practice, however, the five options dwindled to two. 
An opening club lead went to dummy's ace, and South threw one of his remaining clubs on the heart ace. 
He then ruffed a low heart, ruffed a club and reached the moment of truth.
Leading to the diamond ace would still have been wrong, but by a smaller margin. 
Since South cannot deal with K-J-5-4 in the East hand, his advantage in running the queen is only 6 percent, not 11 percent. 
Nobody could calculate that at the table, but South made that play, which was right in both theory and practice.
This may have been the product of good intuition, but it is quite possible that South detected a slight hesitation on his right when the queen was led from the dummy and the four appeared. 
In any event the slam was now safe, for the heart king was available in dummy to take care of the potential spade loser.
Wan had bid and played well to make his slam. 
As an Epson silver medalist, he is the only top government figure around the world to own 10 World Bridge Federation master points, a large step on the road to becoming a world master.

But whether teams from India, Pakistan and other countries holding strong anti-apartheid positions will actually sit down to play South Africa is far from clear. 
The world body, following precedent, is sure to divide the teams into several groups and keep incompatible countries apart.
In Yokohama, with 16 teams competing in both the Bermuda Bowl for open teams and the Venice Cup for women's teams, a complete round robin could have been organized, since neither South Africa nor Israel was involved. 
That method would have been preferred by many, but the teams were divided into two groups, playing a double round robin. 
That introduced an element of luck, since one section can prove to be stronger than the other.
About a decade ago the problem of Taiwan was settled, for bridge purposes, when that island agreed to give up calling itself the Republic of China in tournaments. 
Instead of Taiwan, it is now listed in international bridge events as Chinese Taipei, the equivalent, perhaps, of describing the United States as American Washington.
China and Chinese Taipei met head-to-head in the quarterfinal of the Venice Cup, their first clash in a world event. 
China trailed early but pulled ahead in the closing stages to win by 52 imps. 
The margin would have been bigger if a Chinese player had guessed correctly on the diagramed deal.
North and South for China were Gu Ling and Zhang Yalan, who have long been the cornerstone of the Chinese women's team. 
They climbed rather optimistically to six clubs, in which the declarer has problems in both clubs and hearts. 
South may reason that if the heart queen does not fall eventually, she may be able to maneuver a heart ruff in the dummy after discarding a heart on the second round of diamonds.
If you ignore the presence of the eight, the club combination in the North-South hands represents a theoretical problem. 
There are four reasonable ways to play: cash the ace and lead to the queen; cash the ace and duck the next time if East plays low; lead to the queen and if it loses, finesse the 10; lead to the queen and if it loses, play the ace at the next opportunity. 
These all offer about a 50 percent chance of making three tricks and losing one.
In practice South led to the ace, continued with the three, and was at the crossroads when East played the nine. 
South was now guessing about the trump suit. 
She needed to find West with exactly one of the two missing honors, and the king and jack were equally likely. 
She guessed to play low and lost 11 imps as a result, instead of gaining that number. 
In the replay the opposing North-South rested in game.
In the context of the hand, the play of the queen was indicated. 
If it won, South would then have been able to maneuver to discard a heart if necessary from the dummy and establish that suit with a ruff. 
But that would not have been possible if the ducking play had succeeded. 
It is better, in general, to leave the opponents with a winning trump than a losing trump.
China later recovered from this blow, won the match and eventually took the bronze medal for placing third in the Venice Cup.

U Sein Win came to Washington last week to remind the Bush Administration that his popularly elected Government in Myanmar, formerly Burma, remains powerless because of a military dictatorship that is building an alarming weapons arsenal with the help of China.

"There is only one superpower left in the world," Mr. Sein Win said in an interview on Saturday.

That China is heavily arming the law and order council, known by its acronym Slorc, has caused concern in other Asian nations, particularly India, said David I. Steinberg, a Georgetown University Asian specialist who has written several books on Myanmar. 
Mr. Steinberg said Beijing has sold $1.2 billion in arms, aircraft and patrol boats to Myanmar since 1988.

He said that the country of 40 million people was being run by "uneducated criminals."

text:

Handing President Bush a major defeat, the House of Representatives today overwhelmingly reaffirmed legislation protecting Chinese students in the United States from deportation. 
The Senate is expected to vote on Thursday, and the outcome is too close to predict.
The Administration's setback in the House came in the form of a 390-to-25 vote to override the President's veto of a bill allowing Chinese students to remain in the United States, with 145 House Republicans joining 245 Democrats. 
Only 25 Republicans and no Democrats sided with the President.
When he vetoed the bill Nov. 
30, the President argued that he could protect the Chinese students with the same effectiveness as the legislation through administrative measures that would be less offensive to the Beijing authorities.
Extensive Lobbying Effort
The vote marked a direct, but not unexpected, repudiation by the House of Mr. Bush's handling of relations with China, despite what has probably been the most extensive lobbying effort by the White House on any foreign policy issue since Mr. Bush was elected.
At a news conference this morning, Mr. Bush acknowledged that he was ''a little late'' in trying to block a two-thirds majority of House members from lining up against him and that he was focusing his energies on trying to prevent a similar majority in the Senate. 
If a two-thirds majority there also votes to reject the veto, the bill will become law.
In today's floor debate, Congressmen repeatedly criticized the President's decision to send two top aides on two secret missions to Beijing, despite his public claim to have banned all high-level exchanges, and his willingness to ease many sanctions on Beijing in the absence of any significant improvement in human rights. 
They said these steps caused them to lose confidence in Mr. Bush's judgment on China and convinced them that a different approach must be mandated by legislation.
''Make no mistake about it, this vote is a referendum on human rights that will be heard around the world,'' said William S. Broomfield of Michigan, who is the ranking Republican member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. 
''I appreciate the difficulties President Bush finds himself in. 
America cannot always choose the foreign leaders it has to deal with. 
Yes, we should deal with the Chinese Government. 
However, let's do it on our terms. 
America should be remembered for providing a launching pad for Chinese leadership of the future and not for providing crutches for its tyrants of the past.''
The President had breakfast this morning with a group of Republican Senators in an effort to convince them that he has fully protected all 40,000 Chinese students who want to remain through administrative measures he implemented through the Immigration and Naturalization Service. 
Therefore, he argued, the legislation was both unnecessary and provocative.
Opening his news conference this morning, the President warned that Congress ''will have only itself to blame'' if it overrides his veto, because, he added, the authorities in Beijing have threatened to stop all Chinese students from coming to the United States if the bill is passed.
Â 
Called a Question of Pride
The President did not explain, though, why the Chinese would retaliate for the legislation and not for what the President ordered, if his executive orders were identical to the legislation. 
The only explanation, say many Congressmen, is that the Chinese know that a law cannot be easily changed, while an executive order can be reversed or amended by the stroke of the President's pen.
An Administration official said it was a question of pride. 
The Chinese, he said, can live with a ''quiet'' administrative order but not an open, and embarrassing, repudiation by Congress.
Mr. Bush said today that immediately after the crackdown on democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square last June, ''I moved to protect the Chinese students in this country.''
''Not one was sent back,'' he said. 
''They were safe then, and they are safe now, and they will be safe in the future. 
If I signed the bill, the students would still be safe, but China would retaliate and cut off future student exchanges. 
I want to keep contact. 
I do not want isolation.''
Since the Bush Administration imposed sanctions on China in the wake of the killings in Tiananmen Square last June, Beijing has allowed more than 7,000 Chinese students to come to the United States. 
There are currently about 40,000 Chinese students in this country, 32,000 of them holding visas that would require them to return to China before applying to change their American visa status.
Â 
Congress Not Impressed
Most members of Congress simply were not impressed by Mr. Bush's argument. 
They countered that if the Beijing leaders want to punish themselves and their country by stopping all Chinese students from benefiting from an education in the United States, they can go right ahead.
Speaking in the House debate before the vote, Stephen J. Solarz, the New York Democrat who heads the House Asia subcommittee, argued: ''If the President can send some of the highest foreign policy officials in his Administration to Beijing at the same time as he is telling the American people that he has suspended all high-level contacts then he simply cannot be relied upon not to rescind the executive order at some time in the future.''
Judging from the vigor with which Democratic House members denounced the President's approach in the floor debate, they relished not only repudiating his China policies, but also delivering him a political blow at the very start of the Congressional new year. 
Their rather assertive start to the second session of the 101st Congress seemed to signal that despite the President's soaring approval ratings, Democrats would not shrink from challenging his policies on a broad front.
Â 
Defense of Administration
Republican House members who voted with the President cited this, and other arguments, in trying to defend the Administration in the floor debate. 
Lamar S. Smith, Republican of Texas, said: ''I think the real question here is if the students are protected, what is the rush to override the veto of the President?
It sounds rather suspiciously that the bash President Bush brigades are on the prowl.''
Robert H. Michel of Illinois, the House Minority Leader, said: ''President Bush knows China as well, if not better, than any member of this House. 
He knows their people. 
He knows their special traits and he must be given the room to make the foreign policy moves he feels are in the long range best interest of our country.'
According to The New York Times/CBS News Poll, the American public is about evenly divided on the question of the proper approach to dealing with China. 
Asked on the weekend of Jan. 
13-15 whether it was more important to criticize the way China suppresses human rights, as the Congress seems to favor, or to avoid criticism in order to maintain good relations with China, 42 percent favored outspoken criticism, while 46 percent said their priority was maintaining good relations. 
The survey questioned 1,557 Americans by telephone and had a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3 percentage points.
Trying to sway Senate Republicans this morning, Mr. Bush said the Chinese authorities have permitted Peace Corps volunteers to work in China, have accredited a correspondent from the Voice Of America and muted hostile propaganda against Americans.

text:

President Bush has ordered a wide-ranging investigation into Chinese import barriers that could lead to punitive duties on imports from China, Administration officials said today.
Scheduled for announcement on Thursday, the President's decision reflected a broad consensus among Federal agencies that China is discriminating against American products and shows no willingness to change its policies, they said.
But the decision reflects not only international trade strategy but also domestic political maneuvering.
The Administration waged a fierce political battle this summer to win the renewal of China's most-favored-nation trade status. 
Part of the price it paid for the support of seven Democratic senators from farm states was a commitment to start an investigation if China did not change its policies soon.
The investigation ordered today would look at four ways in which Administration officials believe that China unfairly restricts imports. 
They are import quotas and outright bans on some products; complex import licensing requirements; highly specific technical standards that only match domestically produced goods; and a refusal to publish rules so that American businessmen can avoid legal pitfalls.
Administration officials contend that these import barriers are a major reason why China will accumulate an estimated $12 billion trade surplus with the United States this year, exporting more than $3 worth of goods to the United States for every dollar worth of imports. 
Chinese exports to the United States have soared while American exports to China fell slightly last year.
The Chinese Ambassador, Zhu Qizhen, said at a news conference this summer that weak Chinese imports of American goods reflected a slowdown in the Chinese economy, and not discrimination against American exports.
China is one of the largest foreign markets for American grain and agricultural pesticides, and senators from states producing these products were under pressure from constituents to vote against legislation this summer that either would have canceled the preferential trade status immediately or made any renewal next year subject to a wide range of conditions, such as an improved human rights record.
China threatened to retaliate against American exports if either measure passed, and Administration officials said President Bush would veto any legislation that did not call for an unconditional renewal.
The Senate voted 55 to 45 to impose conditions, failing to reach the two-thirds majority required to override a veto. 
The House passed similar legislation by slightly more than a two-thirds margin. 
Neither house has moved to iron out differences between the bills.
A resolution to cancel the trade status entirely passed the House by a narrow margin and was never put to a vote in the Senate.
In a letter on July 19 to Senator Max Baucus, Democrat of Montana, one of the seven farm state Senators who supported the Administration on this issue, President Bush wrote that if talks with Chinese officials in mid-August "fail to produce Chinese commitments to take substantial measures to improve market access," the Administration would take action.

30, but Administration officials concluded that it represented no change.

file: By the Sea, China_s Leaders Chart the Nation_s Path.txt
text:
ï»¿
A Chinese worker circled a small pavilion tucked among the sleepy hills here, and when the guard wasn't looking, he stole a peek at the red-tile roof of a mansion that for the next month may be the most important building in China.
Under the roof of the mansion, which is surrounded by trees, Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, is taking counsel on whom to promote and dismiss, and on how to redefine the Communist road.
Each summer, when the political heat follows the mercury upward, China's leaders retire to this seaside resort to debate the nation's future alongside the sand and salty water of the Bohai Gulf. 
Although their movements are never announced, Chinese say that Mr. Deng arrived in mid-July and that most of his associates have joined him to occupy the adjacent mansions on the hillside.
"That's where it's all happening," a foreign diplomat said, referring to Beidaihe (pronounced bay-dye-huh).
Â 
The Place for Negotiating
In a nation where the most important decisions are made not by a parliament or even a politburo but by consensus among a handful of old men, Beidaihe is usually the forum where the bargaining takes place and an agreement is thrashed out.
This year the Beidaihe meeting will be even more important than normal. 
Even the winds off the sea have an unusual whistle to them.
The party elders will have to determine the new roster of leaders and set the agenda for the 14th Communist Party Congress, which meets this fall to select a new Central Committee. 
A party congress takes place only once in about every five years to set the nation's direction and pace.
Many Chinese intellectuals expect the congress to legitimize a bold program for liberalization. 
Even Chen Yun, the elderly hard-liner who is Mr. Deng's most powerful rival, recently endorsed special economic zones and other new methods for economic reform.
Â 
Many Changes Are Expected
"We expect a lot of changes at the 14th Party Congress," a university lecturer said. 
"Next year will be much more open than this year."
Another urgency probably nags at Mr. Deng these days: his mortality. 
Three of his close revolutionary colleagues have died this year, so Mr. Deng, who is 87 years old, must be anxious to complete the task of deciding on succession.
"Deng is in a tough spot," a Chinese journalist said. 
"It all requires a delicate balance, to accommodate all the different groups and factions. 
And all this is being sorted out at Beidaihe."
Those holding formal positions often commute to Beijing for meetings, but most of the octogenarians remain in Beidaihe in the July and August heat. 
Since they have arrived, Beidaihe has gushed with gossip about who has come and who has not come, who will step aside and who will step ahead.
The fate of Prime Minister Li Peng may well be determined in Beidaihe this summer. 
Mr. Li's five-year term expires early next year, and there are whispers that Mr. Deng would like to move him aside into a less powerful post, like the largely ceremonial position of the presidency. 
Mr. Chen and other hard-liners are unlikely to agree to that without a tussle.
Mr. Chen, who apparently rarely comes to Beidaihe, may retire at the party congress from his job as chairman of the Central Advisory Commission, which Mr. Deng has been trying to dissolve for years.
Mr. Deng is believed to have arrived in mid-July, followed a few days later by Yang Shangkun, China's President, and then Prime Minister Li.
Bo Yibo, another elderly leader, and Wan Li, Mr. Deng's bridge partner and chairman of China's legislature, are also believed to be here.
Â 
Tight Security for Deng
"Deng came on a special train with three cars," said a local driver who has been inside Mr. Deng's compound. 
"He rode in the middle car, and army men were in the front and the rear ones. 
When he arrived, none of us were allowed to be at the station. 
They shooed away the buses and the taxis."
Tight restrictions are imposed when leaders come to town, and Mercedes-Benzes snake through the tree-lined streets in the hills. 
The police have set up checkpoints around town, and at night they sometimes refuse to allow cars to pass.
One minibus was stopped three times in the middle of the night and told to take a detour to its destination, said a Chinese business executive who was in the bus. 
The policemen beamed a searchlight at the bus, searched the luggage of the passengers and asked if anyone had knives.
Mr. Deng stays in Lianfengshan Park in Mao Zedong's old house, part of a compound of villas where several elderly leaders stay. 
The Deng villa was apparently renovated a few years ago, said a Chinese who visited the compound.
Â 
Summer Brings Life
Two town workers said separately that Mr. Deng's children spend most of their time on a large red-and-pink brick estate built into the cliffs of the Jinshan peninsula, where the streets wind through patches of pruned poplars and red roses.
Beidaihe sleeps in the winter and then booms all summer. 
Yellow-sand beaches are crowded these days with screaming children, old cadres and young couples who come in droves under the guidance, and expense accounts, of their Government ministries.
Almost all Government departments operate resorts here for employees. 
Along the beach are the State Council Resort, the Beijing Old Cadres Sanitarium, the Public Security Resort and the People's Daily Resort. 
Beidaihe, a town of 50,000, also has local bureaus of the New China News Agency and The Guangming Daily.
Some of the buildings are high-ceilinged colonial houses built by foreigners early in this century, while others are modern round-windowed compounds partly hidden behind high hedges. 
Brown-eyed Susans peer out of flower gardens and darkened windows appear through tufts of trees.
Nobody knows what happens inside.

file: Campus Life_ M.I.T._Officials Seeking Grant to Establish Course in Chinese.txt
text:
ï»¿
Five days a week during the academic year, Andrea Li boards the No. 1 bus at the steps of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's main building for a 15-minute ride to Harvard University, where she is studying Chinese.
Like 16 of her M.I.T. classmates, Miss Li, a senior from Stony Brook, L.I., who is majoring in brain and cognitive sciences, must take Chinese at Harvard because M.I.T., where students of Asian heritage account for 19.3 percent of the student body, does not offer the language. 
Four other M.I.T. students studied Chinese at Wellesley College last fall, making the 45-minute commute four times weekly.
But that situation may change, perhaps as soon as this fall.
Last month, M.I.T. applied to the Chiang Ching-kuo Foundation in Taiwan for a three-year, $300,000 grant to establish a Chinese language program at M.I.T., said David L. Lundberg, director of development for the School of Humanities and Social Sciences.
Â 
Satisfying Language Needs
The newly established, private foundation has an endowment of $100 million. 
Its function, Mr. Lundberg said, is to give grants ''exclusively to Americans to promote Chinese culture and things related to Chinese culture in America.''
Should M.I.T. be awarded the grant, the language classes would satisfy the needs of many, from students who want to talk to relatives in their native tongue, to others with a general interest in Asian cultures, to others who may find knowledge of Chinese useful in business. 
Mr. Lundberg expects a reply within two months.
For Miss Li, whose parents were born in Hong Kong and speak Cantonese at home, she wanted to study Chinese to learn about the culture.
''Since I am Chinese, I feel the need to be familiar with the language,'' she said. 
''There are a lot of people in my position, brought up understanding Chinese, but not fluent.''
Â 
Survey of Student Interest
Yet most like her do not have time to commute, said the vice president of the Chinese Students Club, Min-yuan Tung, a senior in the department of electrical engineering and computer science, from St. Clairesville, Ohio.
The club, representing a group that makes up the larger part of M.I.T.'s 800 Asian undergraduates, distributed surveys to several hundred students during the first week of December, asking about their interests in studying Chinese. 
One club member, Rebecca Kao, a senior from Framingham, Mass., who is majoring in electrical engineering and computer science, said the survey results indicated that a large number of students would be interested in studying Chinese if classes were taught at M.I.T.
''Our long-range goal,'' Mr. Lundberg said, ''is to establish an area studies program for Asia.''
''We've got lots of bits and pieces,'' he said. 
''But a big gap is that we don't teach the Chinese language.''
M.I.T. offered courses in Chinese from 1976 to 1980 jointly with Wellesley, but the program was discontinued after a disagreement. 
Several M.I.T. groups, including the Chinese Students Club and the Asian Working Group, have since sought the reinstatement of the Chinese classes.
The Asian Working Group is made up of faculty members like Richard J. Samuels, who directs the M.I.T. 
Japan science and technology program, and Tunney Lee, head of M.I.T.'s urban studies and planning department, who are interested in promoting awareness of Asian cultures and values.
Last fall, the Chinese Students Club members met with various administration officials, including Ann F. Friedlaender, the dean of the School of Humanities and Social Sciences. 
As acting head of the foreign languages and literature section, Mrs. Friedlaender would be responsible for the establishment of the Chinese classes.
''Institutionally, if you were to ask anyone if Chinese should be taught at M.I.T., the answer would overwhelmingly be, 'yes.'
'' she said. 
''But M.I.T. is in a budget deficit. 
In that situation there is a reluctance to start new programs.''
If M.I.T. receives financing from the Chiang Ching-kuo Foundation, it may take up to a year for the institute to find and hire faculty members to teach the courses, Mrs. Friedlaender said. 
In that case, M.I.T. may accept help from Wellesley College's Chinese department, which would provide instructors until M.I.T. hires permanent ones.
Miss Li, whose parents speak Cantonese, said she wanted to study Chinese to learn about the culture. 
(The New York Times/Rick Friedman)

file: Capital Flees an Edgy Hong Kong.txt
text:
ï»¿
The signs of fear are everywhere in Hong Kong, economists, bankers and brokers say, from the Chinese women crowding into little shops to buy small bars of gold, to the thousands of residents patiently lining up in the hot June sun for immigration forms from the Canadian, Australian or American consulates.
''In one day, our bank received $25 million in new business, most of it attributable to the China situation,'' said one foreign banker. 
Another Western banker estimated total new business at $5 million.
From the bustling Chinese street stalls of Mong Kok to the glittering skyscrapers of the central business district, the British colony of Hong Kong has become anxious and edgy because its future is so closely tied to the repressive Chinese regime just across the border.
In the last few weeks, as the tumultuous events in China have moved from a student rebellion to a military crackdown, overseas investment and property brokers have reported a surge in requests from residents who want to get their money off the island.
Â 
Sharp Stock Market Decline
One measure of the disquiet is the decline in the Hong Kong Stock Market since May 18, the last stable trading day before the Chinese turmoil. 
The Hang Seng Index at that market has fallen by 922.47 points, or 28 percent, to 2,355.10, in that period. 
Brokers say that most small investors here have been dumping stocks, and that foreigners have also been selling.
One broker said, ''Unless they like gambling in a casino, locals won't put money back in the market in the near future.''
Foreign banks also report increased business from Hong Kong Chinese who want to open offshore accounts.
''There are no statistics on this subject, just vague estimates and gut feelings about what is happening,'' said one American banker. 
''And my feeling is money is moving. 
But we're talking about personal accounts of wealthy Chinese,'' not pullouts by major businesses. 
Investment capital, he said, ''isn't that mobile, and it takes more time to detect movement there.''
Â 
'Money Is Moving'
Just how much capital is fleeing Hong Kong is anyone's guess. 
The Government, celebrated for its laissez-faire approach to business, places virtually no controls on the movement of money into and out of Hong Kong, and banks here respect secrecy laws that rival those of Switzerland.
Robert Broadfoot, a consultant, said, ''Much of the direct investment capital here now will stay because it is tied up in big projects, but I think new capital investments will slow down. 
Business money will be looking for overseas opportunities, hotels in Canada or the United States, that kind of thing.''
He added, ''I think foreign institutional investors will be liquidating their stock holdings here with each slight rise in the stock market.''
Hong Kong reverts to Chinese control in 1997, and as China continues its violent repression, residents here are losing faith that officials in Beijing will abide by their pledges to leave the colony's economic and political freedoms intact. 
Moreover, half of the 5.7 million residents here are Chinese immigrants who fled the violence and persecution of the Communists in the 1950's and 1960's, many losing homes and profitable businesses.
Stephen Yu, vice president and branch manager of the National Bank of Canada, said the recent repression in China had made some of his depositors so edgy that ''they insisted we redomicile their deposits, even though these were Canadian dollar accounts in our bank.''
He added, ''We are a branch of the main bank, not even a subsidiary, but they wanted that money moved offshore because they were so worried the Chinese Army might march in and seize it here.''
Â 
Outflow Started in '84
Since 1984, when Britain agreed to return Hong Kong, businesses here have been moving large blocks of their capital overseas, but offsetting that move have been investments in Hong Kong by ompanies, which are anticipating trade and business opportunities in China.
''While substantial capital has been leaving Hong Kong, that outflow has been balanced by an inflow of foreign money from Japan, Europe, the United States, and I am not certain now that that balance will continue,'' said Miron Mushkat, director of economic research at Baring Securities. 
''In light of the events in China, I think the outflow is intensifying, and I think there is a chance the inflow will diminish.''
''There is a lot of panicky conversion going on now among wealthy Chinese, and while some of that will taper off when there is stabilityI, even negative stabilityI in China, it won't stop,'' he added.
Mr. Broadfoot, who is managing director of Political and Economic Risk Consultancy Ltd., said he thought the Chinese were ''liquefying all their assets now - stocks, houses, cars.''
He added: ''They are putting their deposits in offshore accounts, making significant movements into gold. 
They are poised for flight, but I don't think it has really started yet.''
Alex Fung, manager of the investment department of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, said that in the last few weeks, the Hong Kong Chinese had been moving ''a substantial amount'' of money, transferring it out of the colony through offshore accounts, bond purchases or other short-term foreign investments.
Â 
'Confirmed the Worst Fears'
''The events in China have confirmed the very worst fears of many Hong Kong people, and if they were even thinking of leaving or sending their money out, their decision is now definite,'' said Mark Michelson, vice president of Business International Asia/Pacific, a consulting firm.
Another Hong Kong banker said a number of local Chinese were so fretful that ''they have been breaking into fixed-deposit accounts and accepting the penalties.''
He added, ''They want to move their money right now, because they are very uncertain about the future.''
Last year, the Government estimated conservatively that 45,000 people emigrated from Hong Kong, taking their assets with them. 
Most went to Canada, Australia or the United States. 
And experts expect those numbers to be even more dramatic now.
Richard Grams, a manager of overseas investment and migration, said: ''Calls about emigrating have increased fourfold. 
Yesterday alone, we received 273 phone calls or visits from people interested in emigrating.''
He added: ''The people who leave Hong Kong take with them substantial amounts of money, plus their own business expertise and skills.''
And residents who once thought they had time to make more money in Hong Kong before they left, ''now want out as soon as possible, and they want their money out too,'' Mr. Grams said.

file: Cheney Presses Israeli on China Missile-Aid Issue.txt
text:
