Four members of a human rights delegation who came from the United States to investigate conditions of political prisoners in China were detained overnight before apparently being expelled from the country today.
The American and Canadian Embassies said they were told late this afternoon that the four had left the country. 
The four, all ethnic Chinese, are Yang Chen Borchert, a 53-year-old American who was leading the group; Liu Qiyang, a 53-year-old American scholar; Ning Chyn, a 34-year-old Canadian national living in the United States, and Hsu Ru-hsueh, a 46-year-old Taiwanese who had worked for China Spring, a magazine that China considers counterrevolutionary.

file: China Detains Two Dissidents During Baker Visit.txt
text:
ï»¿
With Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d visiting here in part to press for the release of hundreds of Chinese dissidents, two more of them were detained over the weekend as the Beijing authorities apparently sought to prevent them from meeting with Mr. Baker's aides.
Before Mr. Baker arrived in Beijing on Friday for a three-day visit, American officials had tentatively arranged meetings between his deputies and several dissidents in Beijing.
But tonight one dissident, Hou Xiaotian, the wife of a prominent democracy advocate now serving a 13-year prison sentence, said she was awakened at 1 A.M. Saturday, taken briefly to a police station and then driven to a Beijing suburb. 
There she was kept in a comfortable guest house, where she was allowed to watch television but was not permitted to leave or to make telephone calls.
Ms. Hou said her guards were reasonably cordial and indicated that she had been detained because of Mr. Baker's visit. 
The authorities drove her home tonight, a couple of hours after Mr. Baker left Beijing.
"I had hoped that through his efforts, Wang Juntao and Chen Ziming and other political prisoners would be released, but I know this requires a long time," Ms. Hou said when asked to discuss what she would have told Mr. Baker. "But before then, I think there are practical needs that should be met, problems such as improving their health care."
Mr. Wang, who is Ms. Hou's husband, and Mr. Chen were sentenced to 13 years for their reputed roles in the Tiananmen democracy movement that was crushed in June 1989.
Dai Qing, a journalist who had been denied an exit permit to take up a fellowship at Harvard University this fall, also reportedly was detained this weekend because of tentative plans to visit with American officials. 
Her telephone number produced a busy signal all night, and it is not clear if she has been released yet.
Mr. Baker was asked at a news conference before his departure about the detention of Ms. Dai. He said, "If it's true, it would be distressing news."
Â 
Churchgoers Barred
It was not clear how the Chinese authorities knew of the tentative meetings, which apparently were not arranged on the telephone. 
But Chinese officials knew that there had been suggestions that Mr. Baker or his assistants might meet with dissidents.
Earlier this morning, when Mr. Baker attended a service at a local church, seven or eight regular Chinese churchgoers were denied entrance because the authorities suspected that they were troublemakers, one of them said.
"For some reason, they didn't let me into church today," the churchgoer said. 
"I even went to the service when President Bush was here. 
It's my right to go to church, and when they didn't let me in, I felt very shaken and disturbed."
One of Mr. Baker's aims in his talks with Chinese officials was to achieve the release of some Chinese dissidents. 
China so far has not released any, but it did give information on about 800 dissidents whose names were on a list presented by American officials to Beijing.

file: CHINA ENDS PURGE OF PARTY_S RANKS.txt
text:
ï»¿
A year after the Communist Party announced a purge of members who were involved in the democracy movement, party members say, with relief and a bit of surprise, that the purge has fizzled.
Hard-liners who ordered the purge succeeded in making life miserable for many of their opponents, and in forcing a significant share of the nation's 48 million Communist Party members to go through a complex process of ''re-registration'' that was intended to weed out those who ''deviated from the correct political stand.''
But after months of meetings, self-criticisms and essay writing, virtually everyone has managed to stay in the party.
The ineffectiveness of the purge suggests the extent of the deadlock that has brought the Chinese political system to a virtual halt, officials say. 
The hard-liners have been pre-eminent for more than a year, but they have been unable to consolidate their gains by eliminating large numbers of their antagonists.
A Stalemate in the Party
''Neither side can overcome the other,'' said an official with first-hand experience in China's power struggles. 
''There's a sort of agreement reached now: you don't do anything, and I won't do anything either.''
The leadership called for the purge on June 25 last year, and the entire party membership in Beijing was obliged to re-register to retain party membership. 
Outside the capital the process was far looser and generally involved only party officials, party members say.
The re-registration is now completed or nearing completion in most work units, and party members say that the vast majority - perhaps 99 percent or more - have been approved to remain in the party, even in certain sensitive departments under the Central Committee that are hotbeds of quiet opposition to the hard-liners.
Officials say privately that only a few prominent liberals have been prevented from re-registering so far. 
Among them are Zhu Houze, a former director of the Central Committee's propaganda department; Du Runsheng, the head of an influential research center, and Li Rui, Li Chang and Yu Guangyuan, all members, along with Mr. Du, of the party's powerful Central Advisory Commission.
Â 
Five Left in Limbo
Although these five people have not been allowed to re-register, they have not been expelled from the Communist Party either. 
Nor has there been a definitive judgment on their cases; instead they have been labeled ''registration postponed,'' officials familiar with their cases said. 
The result has been to leave them in limbo.
Despite reports to the contrary, another prominent liberal - Yan Mingfu, nominal head of the Central Committee's United Front Department, who has been removed from decision-making - has tentatively been allowed to re-register, an official said. 
And the most prominent person to fall from power last year, Zhao Ziyang, the General Secretary, remains in the party although investigations into his conduct are continuing.
Even those in the ''registration postponed'' category may receive a favorable decision soon. 
Chen Yun, the 85-year-old mastermind of central planning, has recently argued against expelling people from the party for political reasons, Chinese officials said. 
Mr. Chen is said to have cited the case of Wang Ming, a rival of Mao Zedong. 
Mr. Wang lost a power struggle with Mao in the 1930's but not only kept his party membership but also retained a seat on the central committee.
Holding onto party membership can be important for senior officials who still hope to make a comeback. 
Deng Xiaoping, the senior Chinese leader, was dismissed from all his posts in 1976, but his return to power a couple of years later was facilitated by the failure of his enemies to strip him of his party membership.
Â 
'The Purge Isn't Working'
''The conservatives would like to kick out a lot more people,'' a young worker said. 
''But they are too high up, and they don't control the re-registration at the grass roots. 
That's why the purge isn't working.''
Others say the purge fizzled because the hard-liners lost their nerve and were afraid of creating enemies of large numbers of people by expelling them.
''What could they do?'' a university teacher asked. 
''Expel all intellectuals?
That would just make them more unpopular than ever.''
Of course, with 48 million members, the expulsion of even a tiny fraction adds up to a large number of individuals. 
In 1989, 33,400 party members were expelled - a modest increase over the figure in previous years, but still less than one-tenth of 1 percent of the national membership.
Those who have not been allowed to re-register seem to fall into several categories. 
Some are party members whose involvement in the democracy movement was so flagrant that it could not be overlooked, as in the case of people who were imprisoned. 
Others tried to resign from the party, but found themselves expelled instead. 
Some people have also been purged for reasons that have little to do with politics: they took bribes, engaged in sexual misconduct or were otherwise judged unfit.

file: China Ends Silence on Deal U.S. Rescinded.txt
text:
ï»¿
When President Bush voided the sale of a Seattle aerospace supplier to a Chinese Government agency, the company's executives and employees saw themselves caught in political crosswinds stemming from the killings of demonstrators in Tiananmen Square in June.
For two weeks, the Chinese Government did not comment on Mr. Bush's action, but today the silence ended. 
The official New China news agency asserted that the deal by the China National Aero-Technology Import and Export Corporation, or Catic, to buy Mamco Manufacturing Inc. was entirely legal and did not pose any threat to the United States, the Reuters news agency reported.
The Chinese said the United States would be responsible for any financial losses that resulted from President Bush's order. 
The statement did not specify what recourse Beijing might seek.
In Compliance With Laws
An official of Catic was quoted by Reuters as saying the acquisition ''is solely a commercial activity in the area of civilian aircraft manufacture, the whole procedure of which was in full compliance with the Federal and local laws and regulations of the United States.''
The official added, ''This acquisition does not involve any high-technology leakage, nor does it impair or threaten the national security of the United States,'' Reuters reported.
Roger Bolton, a spokesman for the Treasury Department, said: ''We are going to withhold comment until we hear directly from the Chinese Government. 
We haven't heard from them yet.''
On Feb. 
2, Mr. Bush had ordered Catic, a Chinese agency that exports military and civilian planes, to divest itself of Mamco, saying Catic's continued control of the airplane parts maker might threaten the national security of the United States. 
A panel comprising officials of eight agencies and headed by Stephen Canner, the director of the Office of International Investment in the Treasury Department, had recommended that the purchase be rescinded. 
Catic had acquired Mamco on Nov. 
30.
Mr. Canner has declined to comment on the reasons for the panel's recommendation.
Â 
Boeing Is Main Customer
Mamco supplies small mechanical parts, built to customer specifications, for commercial aircraft. 
Its largest customer is the Boeing Company, and it reported sales of $19 million in 1989.
''I find it hard to believe we pose a threat to national security,'' Kenneth A. Keller, president and chief executive of Mamco, said in a recent interview. 
''We're no different than literally hundreds of other machine and job shops around the country.''
Mr. Keller said officials of the Chinese agency had attempted to persuade United States officials to rescind the ruling, which requires that Catic divest itself of Mamco by May 1, unless an extension of up to three months is granted.
Mr. Keller said Catic was ''exploring all other avenues'' to prevent the divestiture. 
But if those attempts are not successful, he said ''we'd probably talk to Catic about a re-acquisition of the company.''
''It is just too early to speculate what will happen,'' he added.
Mamco makes no parts for export. 
In addition to Boeing, its customers include McDonnell Douglas, Bell Helicopter and Cleveland Pneumatic. 
Mamco does not employ full-time designers or engineers and does not own the rights to the designs of its products. 
None of its products are on Government lists of militarily significant high-technology parts. 
205 Employees A 50-year-old company that had been privately held before its sale to Catic, Mamco operates in an industrial area of Seattle. 
Its 205 employees work two shifts on weekdays and one on Saturday and Sunday.
Catic is responsible for much of China's imports and exports, and some American officials have contended that it has close ties to China's military. 
The Seattle Times, quoting unidentified Congressional sources, has reported that Catic provided two General Electric jet-turbine engines to the military, which dissassembled them for study, breaking agreements that the engines would be for civilian use only and would be left intact.
The order involving Mamco is believed to be the first in which a President has ordered a foreign corporation to sell an American company it had already purchased. 
President Bush acted under a 1988 trade bill that authorized the President to block sales of companies to foreign interests if the sales are seen as threats to national security.
Mr. Keller, who is 45 years old, a certified public accountant from Oregon, purchased Mamco in 1988 with two partners, James Young and Barry Allen. 
The three men had met and worked together for six years at Security Properties Inc., a Seattle real estate company, where Mr. Keller was chief financial officer. 
They left that company with the intention of buying a number of businesses in the Pacific Northwest at a rate of one a year. 
Mamco was their first acquisition.
Â 
Joint Venture Sought
Mr. Keller said that as the partners searched for other companies to acquire, they decided to bring in joint-venture partners. 
In early 1989, an accounting firm introduced them to officials of the Chinese agency.
''Catic was not interested in our proposals, but a few months later offered to buy Mamco instead,'' Mr. Keller said.
After the deal was concluded in November, the company's managers stayed on to insure that it remained under American management. 
Catic did bring two executives to the operation, including Shan-Jun Xiong, Catic's chairman of United States operations. 
He is not involved in day-to-day operations of Mamco, Mr. Keller said, but oversees Catic's other interests in the United States, including its dealings with Boeing and McDonnell Douglas.

file: China Enlivens Hong Kong_s First Direct Vote.txt
text:
ï»¿
For the first time in the 150-year history of Hong Kong, people here will be able to vote directly for some of their legislative representatives in an election scheduled for Sept. 
15. And in the final days before that vote, the most compelling, most emotional campaign issue in this British colony is China.
While the 54 candidates competing for the 18 directly elected seats in the legislature have been discussing pollution, traffic and crime, their positions are often interchangeable and their debates dull -- until the subject of China is introduced. 
Then, voices are raised, tempers flare and charges and countercharges fly.
One candidate told voters that he had publicly opposed China's crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in 1989, but that his opponent was "scared to death when dealing with China."
Another candidate accused his opponent of trying to pretend now that he had taken part in demonstrations against China in 1989.
With Hong Kong scheduled to revert to Chinese control in 1997, many here would like to see a strong, independent local government set up before then.
"The main political issue here is the growing influence of China," said Anthony Cheung, a political commentator and a senior lecturer in the City Polytechnic's Dept of Public and Social Administration. 
"Voters want to know how candidates have reacted to that."
While only 18 seats are up for direct vote in the legislature of 60, which has largely been a rubber-stamp body, voters and politicians are taking this election seriously, hoping that if it is a success, they can press Britain for further reforms.
In Hong Kong, where officials are often criticized for bowing to pressure from China, polls show that two of the most popular candidates are Szeto Wah and Martin Lee, both outspoken critics of China who have been publicly branded as "subversive" by Beijing.
Newspaper polls indicate that Mr. Lee's party, United Democrats of Hong Kong, may take more than half of the directly elected seats. 
The party's 14 liberal candidates have been critical of China's abuse of human rights and its interference in Hong Kong affairs.
Several other parties are fielding a few candidates, but most contestants are running as independents.
While pro-Beijing groups are supporting several candidates, and half a dozen other candidates are known for their mainland sympathies, Mr. Cheung said, "Today, in Hong Kong, to be branded pro-Beijing is a liability."
Indeed, one candidate endorsed by a pro-Beijing trade group has complained that his posters have been defaced with slogans like "running dog of the Chinese Communists."
The apparent popularity of the United Democrats and their allies has made both China and the British Government anxious, political experts say.
Recently, China's semi-official China News Service advised Hong Kong voters that "apart from considering the political platform of each candidate, they should also take into consideration the attitude of each candidate towards Hong Kong's relationship with the mainland."
"Without a good relationship with the mainland, there will be a great impact on Hong Kong's prosperity and stabilityI," the agency said.
The 18 popularly elected legislators will take their seats in the Legislative Council alongside 21 Government-appointed lawmakers, and 21 indirectly elected representatives from constituency groups defined by the Government, including doctors, lawyers and teachers.
Francis Ho, of the Government's Constitutional Affairs office, said that of the four million potential voters, about half were registered to vote.
And no one maintains that Hong Kong's six million residents are in the grip of election fever.
The local television and radio stations do not cover the campaigns on their regular nightly news programs, for fear of violating tough equal time laws laid down by the Government. 
And the Government does not permit political advertisements to be carried on radio or television.
Campaigning is largely a matter of handing out leaflets and knocking on doors.

file: China Exile Starts Life in Britain.txt
text:
ï»¿
Fang Lizhi, China's most prominent dissident, said today that he and his wife were looking forward to ''a chance to rest and recuperate and to have some medical tests'' as they started a new life in Britain.
Mr. Fang and his wife, Li Shuxian, arrived Monday night at the United States Air Force Base at Upper Heyford, near Oxford, after the Chinese authorities allowed them to leave their refuge in the United States Embassy in Beijing and go into exile.
Cambridge University said Mr. Fang, a distinguished astrophysicist, had accepted a post as a senior visiting fellow at the university's Institute of Astronomy, where he would study the early universe.
Research Is Backed
In a statement issued through the Royal Society, the academy of sciences that has agreed to support his research for at least a year, Mr. Fang said:
''The past year has been difficult for us but we have received strong support from the international scientific community and friends everywhere. 
My wife and I would also like to express our heartfelt appreciation to President Bush, Ambassador Lilley and the staff of the U.S. 
Embassy in Peking. 
We look forward in the next few days to a period of quiet, a chance to rest and recuperate and to have some medical tests.''
Mr. Fang and his wife took refuge in the United States Embassy on June 5 last year after the Communist authorities - who issued a warrant for the couple's arrest for committing crimes tantamount to treason -used troops and tanks to crush student-led pro-democracy demonstrations. 
The officials have said that the couple had asked to go abroad for medical treatment.
Â 
'A Family Reunion'
Mr. Fang said that his son, Fang De, who is still in China, would soon be able to study abroad and that he and his wife were ''naturally looking forward to a family reunion.''
''As citizens of China,'' Mr. Fang said in the statement, ''we hope to do whatever we can in the future to help China's continuing progress and development.''
The Royal Society had planned to have Mr. Fang speak at a news conference today, but the briefing was canceled after he met with British diplomatic officials. 
When the couple were allowed to leave China, the Chinese Ministry of Public Security said they had agreed not to engage in activities against China.
Britain's Foreign Office said today that the Government had not imposed any condition of political silence on the couple, who are here on a six-month renewable visa.

file: China Faults Report on 2 Rebels.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a toughly worded statement, China today rejected as ''speculations pure and simple'' recent reports that the dissidents Fang Lizhi and Li Shuxian would be allowed to leave China soon.
While the statement did not rule out the possibility of the couple's release, the wording suggested that there has been no decision yet on allowing the two to leave. 
The statement hinted that as a minimum step the Chinese Government would like them to apologize before they go.
Mr. Fang, an astrophysicist who is China's best-known dissident, sought refuge with his wife in the United States Embassy soon after the violent crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Beijing in early June. 
His presence in the embassy has been a major source of tension between the United States and China.
A Western diplomat said today that he had been informed by Chinese officials that the stumbling block in arranging a compromise was that the Chinese authorities were demanding that Mr. Fang write a self-criticism, but that Mr. Fang refused to do so.
Â 
Widespread Rumors
In the last few weeks, there have been widespread rumors that Mr. Fang and Miss Li would be allowed to leave before the end of January. 
It has been rumored that the Chinese Government wanted to appear conciliatory to reduce the chance that the United States Congress might adopt further sanctions against China, and that the Chinese leadership wished to reward the Bush Administration for its decision to send Brent Scowcroft, the national security adviser, to Beijing on two secret missions.
The latest report, which led to the Chinese statement, appeared in Pai Shing Semi-Monthly, a China-watching magazine published in Hong Kong. 
The magazine said that Beijing and Washington had reached an understanding that Mr. Fang and Miss Li would be allowed to travel to Australia or Italy.
The magazine said that Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, had approved the plan.
White House officials have dismissed the report, saying there are no new developments in the case.
The Chinese statement, which was issued by the Foreign Ministry and carried by the official New China News Agency, seemed intended to dampen such speculation.

file: China Gains in Mideast Crisis But Loses Cold War Benefits.txt
text:
ï»¿
Less than a year and a half after China's leaders sent tanks and machine guns to crush the Tiananmen democracy movement, Western sanctions are being dismantled and China is regaining status in the international community.
Japan is resuming subsidized loans to China. 
The European Community last month lifted economic sanctions against China. 
A group of American Congressmen is expected in Beijing this month for the first time since the crackdown. 
Countries like Saudi Arabia and Singapore have in the last few months established diplomatic relations with Beijing.
"China has withstood the international anti-socialist environment and safeguarded the socialist system," crowed the official New China News Agency.
While most of the world has suffered from the gulf crisis, China has been a beneficiary. 
Scholars, diplomats and Chinese themselves say China benefited in two ways: Saddam Hussein's behavior gave the West a new enemy and China won gratitude for its cooperation in imposing sanctions against Iraq.
Â 
'Best of All Worlds'
"The gulf crisis accelerated a process that was already under way, of them waiting us out," said a Western diplomat in Beijing. 
"It's the best of all worlds for them, because they'be been able to reintegrate themselves with the West without sacrificing any third world credentials to do it."
Yet there are signs that over all China is a loser in the geopolitical reordering that has accompanied the end of the cold war. 
China has lost the leverage it had in playing the Soviet Union and the United States against each other, and its leaders may also be at a disadvantage in an environment in which nuclear weapons matter less than economic strength.
"People don't pay much attention to China any more," a European ambassador said the other day. 
Most experts agree that China matters less than it used to -- a proposition that drives some Government officials here to alternate between despair and fury. 
Visiting Americans these days are sometimes greeted with almost obsessive explanations of why China is still of fundamental importance to American interests.
Â 
Never Much of a Threat
The West's sanctions were never threatening to China in any fundamental sense. 
The sanctions included delays in new World Bank loans, a freeze on most military cooperation, and a halt to most high-level exchanges. 
Ordinary imports from China were never curbed, and in fact they have risen sharply: China's trade surplus with the United States could exceed $10 billion this year, up from $3.5 billion in 1988, before the crackdown.
Military cooperation remains on ice, but World Bank loans are gradually being resumed, and high-level exchanges are increasing. 
Zhu Rongji, Shanghai's mayor, visited the United States this summer; Wan Li, the head of China's legislature, will tour Great Britain this month; and Wu Xueqian, a politburo member, is leaving in a few days for Tokyo.
"The pace is very slow, but I can see that the direction is toward improvement in relations" with the West, said Yuan Ming, an international relations expert at Beijing University.
In any case, sanctions affected China's relations with only a relatively small number of countries. 
Most of China's neighbors were uncritical of its behavior and continued to do business with China as before.
In some respects, China now has broader international support than ever: Saudi Arabia and Singapore have newly established diplomatic relations with China, while Indonesia has resumed ties. 
South Korea will open an office in Beijing very soon, and would like to establish diplomatic relations.
"We were never so upset about the crackdown," said a diplomat from an Asian country that has its own human rights problems. 
"It's their business."
Â 
Communist Legitimacy Eroded
This is not to say that the crackdown on the democracy movement was painless, for the killings of peaceful protesters deeply eroded the Communist Party's legitimacy at home and among Chinese overseas as well as in the West. 
But some Chinese officials say the hard-liners probably regard the foreign sanctions as an acceptable price to pay, given that their alternative may have been loss of power. 
The price may be acceptable even if, as many believe, the Government's relations with the West will never again be as warm as before.
"Things will return to business as usual, but that emotional enthusiasm for China won't come back any time soon," a Western diplomat said.
One reason is that while the Bush Administration is gratified by China's cooperation in the Security Council, China's critics are less impressed. 
Their quarrel with Beijing was not about diplomacy, but about human rights, and they see no fundamental easing of the domestic repression.
While the Bush Administration is expected to favor further dismantling of sanctions, Congress may have other ideas. 
John T. Kamm, president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, expects Congress to make a new attempt next year to end China's Most Favored Nation status. 
He also is bracing for an effort to establish a code of conduct for American corporations dealing with China.
"We may well find ourselves in a position where Japan and the European Community are lifting sanctions, and we're adding sanctions," Mr. Kamm said.
Â 
Mutual Resentment and Suspicion
China wants a resumption of cooperation with the West, but it is wary that too much interaction might again lead to unrest. 
The resentments and suspicions are mutual and may slow the reconciliation on both sides.
A classified Communist Party document, obtained from a well-connected Chinese in Beijing, conveys these apprehensions. 
The document, an analysis of international affairs published at the end of last year by the Central Committee Propoganda Department, warns that "the struggle between the two systems" will be prolonged and intense.
"Since the appearance of the first socialist state in 1917, this kind of struggle has never ceased," the analysis reads. 
"It only varies in its form, intensity and the tactics employed. 
Now the struggle has entered a new stage, and the struggle will be sharper, more complex and more intense than before. 
We must be highly vigilant."
While most nations are celebrating the end of the cold war, China has been saying, even before the invasion of Kuwait, that the new environment is not so wonderful after all.
Â 
Emerging Regional Powers
One difficulty for China is that a multipolar world is likely to see the emergence of new regional powers including Japan, South Korea, Vietnam, India and Indonesia. 
China has had wars or bitter disputes with each of these countries in recent decades.
"They've always hailed, in theory, the emergence of a more multipolar world," said Harry Harding, a China scholar at the Brookings Institution in Washington. 
"But now that it's finally happening, the problem for China is that its relations with many of these emerging poles are rather strained."
Chinese leaders are most anxious about the rise of Japan, which they remember fighting in the 1930's and 1940's, and they often regard Americans as naive in playing down Japan as a military and strategic threat. 
Some Chinese are even warning that the Soviet Union and Japan could form a threatening alliance in the Pacific, creating a reason for cooperation between the United States and China.
China has clearly lost leverage in that it can no longer play the United States and the Soviet Union against each other. 
But Mr. Harding says that in a larger sense China has fewer cards to play in a world in which money increasingly seems to matter more than guns.

file: China Gives Light Sentences To Advocates of Democracy.txt
text:
ï»¿
China said today that it had handed down relatively short sentences for 11 protesters tried recently in connection with the Tiananmen Square demonstrations of 1989 and subsequent democracy protests.
These are believed to be among the last cases of people who have been held without trial for more than two years after the military crackdown on June 4, 1989. 
The sentences, reported in Ta Kung Pao, a Hong Kong newspaper controlled by Beijing, ranged from immediate release to five years in prison. 
Sketchy details on some of the convictions were provided earlier this week in Beijing by people familiar with some of the defendants' families.
By the standards of the hard-line Government, which earlier sentenced two prominent democracy advocates to 13 years each, the sentences reported today were mostly on the mild side.
The disclosures come as Beijing officials are calling for faster economic change and seem to be a sign that China is finally willing to resolve many of the cases in which dissidents have been held without trial. 
Such cases have figured prominently in its discussions on human rights with Western nations.
Â 
Public Barred From Trials
While the relative leniency, by hard-line standards, is probably a response to Western pressure on China, there is not necessarily a specific link to the vote by the United States Senate this week to add conditions on an extension of low tariffs for Chinese exports.
The trials were held at various times, effectively closed to the public and the press, and the timing seems mostly to reflect the aim of resolving the Tiananmen cases by the time the national legislature convenes for its annual session, around March 20.
Wu Xuecan, a former editor at the official People's Daily who was arrested for distributing a leaflet during the demonstrations, was sentenced to four years. 
Zhai Weimin, whose name appeared in 1989 on a list of 21 most-wanted university students and who later tried to organize an anti-Government underground movement, was given three and a half years.
Sentences begin from the day of detention, so those who were taken into custody at the time of the 1989 crackdown have already served more than two and a half years. 
The sentences were also released in a State Council letter to John T. Kamm, a Hong Kong-based American businessman active in promoting human rights.
One dissident, Bai Chunxiang, about whom little is known, was released without punishment. 
Peng Rong, a Beijing University student who was arrested for organizing a survey about demonstrations, was sentenced to two years and is expected to be released in May. 
Li Minqi, a student arrested for his role in a commemoration on the first anniversary of the military crackdown, was also given two years and will presumably be released in June.
The Hong Kong report suggested that China had now closed all of the cases raised by the State Department in its human rights report this year. 
In fact, a number of cases remain unresolved. 
China has not given information on about a dozen other dissidents whose names appeared on a list presented to Beijing in November by Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d.
Moreover, Bao Tong, a top aide to the former Communist Party leader Zhao Ziyang, was officially arrested in January and is expected to be tried soon. 
Wu Jiaxiang, a party official as well as a writer and researcher, was also arrested recently and is awaiting trial.
Little is known about the six other people sentenced, but presumably they were workers who had taken part in the demonstrations: Li Baoqin and Wang Guoqing, five years each; Dong Huaiming, four years; Wang Zhong xian and Wei Ren, three years each, and Wang Lidong, two years.

file: China Imposes Tighter Curbs on Foreign Reporters.txt
text:
ï»¿
China imposed new restrictions on foreign journalists today and banned articles that in the view of the authorities ''distort facts'' or violate ''the public interest.''
The rules, signed by Prime Minister Li Peng on Friday, took effect today on their publication in People's Daily.
''Foreign correspondents and news agencies must observe journalistic ethics, and must not distort facts, fabricate rumors or use improper means in their reporting,'' read the most sweeping of the new rules. 
''Foreign correspondents and news agencies must not engage in activities that are incompatible with their status, or those that endanger state security, national unification, or the public interest of Chinese society.''
In serious cases, journalists who are found to have violated the regulations could be expelled from China.
The rules specified that they were to be interpreted by the Chinese authorities, so the practical effect was not immediately clear.
It would be possible for the Chinese to expel reporters under the new rules on the vague ground that the reporters' articles harmed the public interest.
It is also not clear whether it is permissible to interview people on the street, or students on a university campus, or customers in a shop.
Such interviews were all explicitly banned during the period of martial law in Beijing, from May 20 to Jan. 
10.
The new rules state only that all interviews with any ''work unit,'' including any university, factory or Government institution, must be officially arranged.
A strict interpretation would ban interviews on university campuses, and street interviews might be banned on the ground that they are an ''improper means'' of reporting.
The relationship between foreign news organizations and the Chinese Government has often been strained, particularly since the military crackdown on dissent in June.
The authorities have accused foreign correspondents of distorting what it describes as a successful and restrained operation to crush a counterrevolutionary rebellion.
China has always regulated foreign journalists, and most of the 22 new rules were simply restatements of previous written or unwritten rules. 
The new regulations apparently were intended in part to take the place of the martial-law restrictions.
Those rules, which were not scrupulously obeyed, purported to ban virtually all unauthorized reporting, including unscheduled interviews in any factories, schools or neighborhoods.
The new regulations stipulate that reporters must obtain permission before leaving Beijing on any reporting trip, and that when on such a trip they cannot do any reporting outside the topics for which they have received authorization.
The rule is more explicit than one already in existence. 
The result is that authorization must be obtained even for trips to cities accessible to tourists, like Shanghai or Canton.
In the past, that rule and others were often ignored by the authorities and the journalists, and it is unclear whether passage of the new regulations means that they will now be more rigorously enforced.
As before, foreign news agencies cannot freely hire Chinese nationals, but must use only staff provided by the Government.
The new rules go a step further by stipulating that agencies must obtain Government permission even when hiring foreign nationals.
Â 
U.S. EXPRESSES 'GREAT CONCERN'
WASHINGTON, Jan. 
20 (Special to The New York Times) - An Administration official said today that the new restrictions on foreign journalists were cause for ''great concern.''
He said the United States would ask China to clarify what it meant.
Under the rules, he said, ''It is not clear if you can go out and freely talk to people on the street for a news story.''
The rules, he said, apparently do not authorize the Chinese Government to censor articles before publication, but they seem intended to encourage ''a little self-censorship by journalists.''

file: CHINA IS PLANNING 2 YEARS OF LABOR FOR ITS GRADUATES.txt
text:
ï»¿
In an effort to rekindle Communist values, the authorities disclosed today that most college graduates will have to work for a year or two in villages or factories before being permitted to enter graduate school.
The new policy, reported by the official China Daily, appears to be part of what well-placed Communist Party officials describe as a wider program to compel college graduates generally to put in at least a year at manual labor on farms or in factories before taking up their comfortable white-collar jobs.
The Chinese officials said that in the aftermath of the student unrest this spring, the leadership felt that one way of combating ''bourgeois liberalization,'' as Western democratic influences are now labeled, was to send students to rural areas to teach them to endure hardship, work hard and appreciate the daily difficulties faced by China's mostly rural population.
Â 
Cultural Revolution Recalled
The steps are reminiscent of the practice in the Cultural Revolution of the 1960's and 70's, when youths and others were sent to the countryside by the millions for re-education.
''Instead of going to graduate school this September, students, especially those in the social sciences, will have to work for a year or two,'' The China Daily reported today, citing a circular issued by the State Education Commission.
While some top leaders apparently would like all college graduates to get experience toiling in the countryside, it is not clear how rigorously the policy will be put in place. 
Resistance among young people is certain to be immense, and employers may also be less than enthusiastic about losing new recruits for a year.
Â 
Administration Headaches
If it comes about, the policy would not only deepen the alienation among university students, but could create vast administrative headaches for universities and for the villages that are supposed to be the hosts of the graduates.
China already has a surplus of labor in the countryside, and villages are unlikely to welcome intellectuals who speak with urban accents and are unenthusiastic about wading barefoot in the rice paddies all day.
Although there has been no announcement of the new policy requiring those who graduated since 1985 to work at manual labor, word already is spreading among young people, who are scrambling to avoid it. 
Most are convinced that the policy is retribution for the student-led democracy movement this spring, which the authorities violently suppressed, or at the least a reflection of the new-found enthusiasm for revolutionary values that the leadership is trying to foster in the society.
''This is part of the brainwashing now going on,'' said a young businessman who graduated from university a half-dozen years ago. 
''They want to send you to a horrible place so that when you get back to the city you'll appreciate it and won't cause them any problems.''
Â 
Information in Report
The businessman, who has access to information about high-level party decisions, said the policy on sending students to the countryside before giving them white-collar jobs was contained in the party's Central Committee report No. 5 now circulating among senior officials.
Today's article about requiring work experience before young people can enter graduate school did not indicate how the policy would be administered, nor how rigorously it was expected to be pursued. 
While the article seemed to say that the change would take effect immediately, that would require a degree of swiftness and cooperation among authorities that would be highly unusual in the Chinese bureaucracy.
The article suggested that it would apply in particular to graduate schools in social sciences, presumably because students of politics and history and related subjects were at the center of the democracy movement.
Under the new program, young people will have their household registration transferred to the rural area where they will work. 
In theory, there should be no problem in transferring it back to the city a year later, but many people are suspicious that they will be forever exiled in the countryside. 
Those people who tried to return to the city without also having their registration transferred would find it difficult to get jobs, housing, ration coupons and perhaps even to get married.
While most young people are appalled by the new policy, a university teacher who was sympathetic to the democracy movement said that most students had been coddled and would benefit from a year learning the value of responsibility and hard work.
Â 
'Take Out the Garbage'
''Most students don't even know how to take out the garbage for themselves,'' the teacher complained. 
She added that in any case the policy was unlikely to be pursued widely, and said that at her institution no steps had been taken toward putting the policy into effect.
A senior party official said the policy initially had been agreed upon in 1984 but was never implemented, and would apply to students who had graduated from college in 1985 and subsequent years. 
Throughout the country, about 1.8 million people have graduated from institutions of higher learning since 1985 and apparently would in theory be subject to the new policy.
''Many of them are very arrogant,'' the party official said of college students. 
''This will be very good for them, by teaching them how most Chinese people live.''
The official said he was sending the newly hired college graduates in his department who have no experience in manual labor to work either in the fields or in a factory. 
In some cases, his department will pay them a subsidy to make sure they do not suffer hardship, he said.
The official said this can't be compared to the Maoist method of sending people to the countryside. 
He said that except in extreme cases of people who performed very badly, graduates would be allowed to transfer their household registrations back to Beijing and begin assigned white-collar work after a year.

file: China Is Said to Execute 500 to Reduce Crime.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese Government does not report how many people have been sentenced to death and the real figure is believed to be much higher, the organization said.
It said the number of executions this year was the highest since 1983, when an anti-crime campaign resulted in 5,000 to 10,000 executions.
Those executed this year included people convicted of ''counterrevolutionary'' religious activities and violence during pro-democracy protests last year, the report said.
''The dramatic increase in death sentences is particularly disturbing because China's trial system falls far below international standards,'' Amnesty said. 
It said trials were often a formality with the verdict decided in advance and with little chance for appeal or pardon.
Almost all those sentenced to death this year were tried under emergency regulations that gave them virtually no opportunity to prepare a defense, Amnesty said. 
Some were executed within two weeks of their arrests.
Amnesty said courts had been ordered to crack down on crimes like drug trafficking, embezzlement, gang robbery and theft. 
But despite more death sentences, crime has not declined in the last decade.
Amnesty said a Chinese legal journal noted last October that several people tried under the emergency regulations believed that a death sentence was inevitable and did not try to appeal.
Â 
Beijing Frees Student Leader
BEIJING, Sept. 
12 (Reuters) -China has freed a student leader held for 13 months at a maximum security prison on charges of organizing pro-democracy protests last year, university students and instructors said today.
Yang Tao, prominent in the uprising crushed by tanks and troops in June last year, was quietly released from China's main jail for political prisoners, Qincheng, said the students and instructors at Beijing University.

file: China Issues _61 Deng Speech Stressing Shift From Ideology.txt
text:
ï»¿
China today published a 30-year-old speech by the nation's patriarch, Deng Xiaoping, in what appeared to be a call for greater attention to the economy and less concern for ideological campaigns.
The People's Daily, the official newspaper of the Communist Party Central Committee, said it had Mr. Deng's permission in publishing the speech at the top of the front page in today's issue. 
Its publication appeared to be an effort by the 88-year-old Mr. Deng to refocus the nation on economic development and restructuring after nearly two years of hard-line political and economic policies.
"If campaigns continue year-round, they will turn into superficial and exaggerated fanfare, and we will exhaust ourselves," Mr. Deng said. 
"In fact, they will breach the will of the masses, and alienate us from them."
The People's Daily gave no clear reason for publishing the speech, which was originally given to the All-China Women's Federation in December 1961. 
But China has a tradition of dredging up long-forgotten speeches to signal shifts in the political winds.
Â 
Full of Mixed Signals
China has been full of mixed signals since the army crackdown on dissent nearly two years ago, and it is not clear whether the reprise of the speech today indicates any major change of direction. 
Even if Mr. Deng intends to push for a more rapid move toward the market, he has given no indication he favors toleration of dissent. 
And in any case he is ailing, and must negotiate with other retired octogenarians with whom he shares power.
The focus of the speech is the need for improvement in the daily work of the party and Government, and less emphasis on grand projects and slogans. 
As in all such speeches, it is ambiguous and in places scarcely relevant to national policy -- it calls on the Women's Federation, for example, to improve relations between mothers-in-law and daughters-in-law -- but the theme is to shift the balance toward pragmatism and away from ideology.
"As for proposing this or that slogan, or this or that guideline, only when we have done enough daily, grass-roots work can we hope that they will materialize," Mr. Deng said. 
"Otherwise, our words will sink like stones into the sea, leaving not even a trace."

file: China Legal Scholar Faces Death Penalty In Democracy Trial.txt
text:
ï»¿
A legal scholar went on trial today for "conspiracy to overthrow the Government," the most serious criminal charge known to be leveled so far in the latest round of trials of Tiananmen democracy advocates. 
Conviction could bring the death penalty.
The scholar, Chen Xiaoping, a 29-year-old law lecturer with a reputation for intellectual brilliance, is one of at least four democracy advocates known to be charged so far with "conspiring to overthrow the Government."
Mr. Chen, who helped organize a citizens' group to support demonstrating students at Tiananmen Square, was a teacher at the University of Politics and Law until his arrest sometime shortly after the military crackdown on June 4, 1989. 
A graduate of Beijing University, Mr. Chen had a background in constitutional law and had taken part in previous student demonstrations.
If convicted, he would face a minimum jail sentence of 10 years, and if his case is deemed particularly serious, he could receive the death penalty. 
The trial was closed to foreigners, and it was not clear whether it ended today but no sentence was announced. 
In the past, sentences have been announced sometime after the end of the trial.
Â 
Cooperation Brings Release
Many foreign diplomats and Chinese lawyers say they rule out the death sentence, or even life imprisonment, for any of the students or scholars who took part peacefully in the Tiananmen democracy movement.
But most defendants brought to trial are convicted, although some have then been released because of their cooperative attitude. 
In China, legal punishment is often governed by the principle, "leniency to those who confess, harshness to those who resist."
The court has recently held political trials for nearly 30 Tiananmen democracy advocates, sentencing students to under four years and intellectuals and workers to longer terms.

file: CHINA MAKES A BID TO HOLD OLYMPICS.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's leaders have a special dream for a patch of empty ground in northern Beijing: the hope that in September 2000, in a 100,000-seat stadium to be built on that spot, they will preside over the opening ceremonies of the Summer Olympic Games.
After months of preparations, the Chinese leadership formally announced its bid today to become the host of the 27th Olympiad. 
Prime Minister Li Peng said in a letter sent today to the International Olympic Committee that China would try "to make the 2000 Olympic Games a grand celebration in sports marking the advent of a new millennium with a better prospect of peace and friendship."
Politics, not sports, underlie the Government's enthusiasm. 
The Games would be an important opportunity to win back international respect after the 1989 crackdown on democracy protesters, and a chance to unite the Chinese people behind a patriotic cause.
The Olympics would also give the Government a chance to redirect the spotlight of foreign attention from human rights issues to its achievements in building prosperity and a smoothly functioning capital with clean streets, excellent hotels and clear telephones.
Â 
Decision Due in 1993
The decision on the site of the 2000 Olympics is to be made by the International Olympic Committee in September 1993, and already there are a half-dozen contenders in addition to Beijing: Berlin, Braslia, Istanbul, Manchester, Milan and Sydney.
"Each site has its advantages, so for all of us the starting line is the same," said Wu Zhongyuan, a member of the executive board of the Beijing 2000 Olympic Games Bid Committee. 
"The competition is very tough."
Mr. Wu spoke in an interview in the bid committee's bustling office in donated space in a second-grade Beijing hotel.
As Beijing's advantages, Mr. Wu cited the city's existing sports installations, including 33 sports grounds and 46 practice grounds, which he asserted provide a better base than any other contender. 
In addition, he appealed for sympathy for an ancient nation that is home to 22 percent of the world's population but has never been host to the Olympics.

file: China Offers Cautious Economic Plan.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's Communist Party Central Committee concluded a major six-day meeting today, after approving a moderate, cautious new blueprint for the 1990's and warning that the next decade could determine the rise or fall of the nation's Communist system.
At the long-awaited meeting, the Central Committee formally approved the five-year plan that is supposed to govern the economy from 1991 to 1995 as well as a broader 10-year "program" for the 1990's. 
No specific measures or targets were disclosed today, but the party leaders issued a communique acknowleging that the Central Committee had held the meeting and mentioning some elements of the economic plans.
The communique cautioned against rapid economic growth and emphasized the need to raise efficiency and improve the nation's industrial structure.
Chinese officials and economists had said earlier that the conclusions of the meeting would reflect the compromises struck between the various leadership factions -- in particular, between provincial and central leaders and between hard-liners and liberals. 
The communique showed little sign of the conflicts between those groups, but its remarkable vagueness suggested that no single faction had dominated the blueprints.
Â 
Over 500 Leaders Attend
National television showed the party General Secretary, Jiang Zemin, dressed in a dark Mao-style jacket, giving a speech, as the party's Politburo members sat somberly beside him on the rostrum. 
The meeting included 171 Central Committee members, plus 107 alternate members and about 300 other Chinese leaders, according to the official New China News Agency.
"Success or failure in our efforts in the 1990's to consolidate and develop the achievements made in the 1980's and to greatly promote economic growth and social progress will have a direct bearing on the rise or fall of China's socialist system and the future and destiny of the Chinese nation," the communique said, as issued by the press agency.
In a later passage, it apparently alluded to the collapse of Communist systems in Eastern Europe, saying, "In the face of a complicated and ever-changing international stituation, it is crucial that we manage our domestic affairs well."
The leaders called for self-reliance, but also endorsed the policy of economic openness. 
They only briefly mentioned specific areas of economic restructuring, like prices, taxes, labor and enterprise. 
It also suggested that Chinese leaders did not want to repeat the economic mishaps, including inflation and economic overheating, that accompanied high growth during the last five years; they contributed to the pro-democracy demonstrations in May and June of 1989.
Â 
Zhao's Fate Not Mentioned
The document did not mention the fate of the former Communist Party General Secretary, Zhao Ziyang, who was ousted during the Tiananmen Square crackdown more than 18 months ago. 
Mr. Zhao has been said to be under investigaton, and the party, at least publicly, has still not made any formal determination of his role during the democracy movement.
No changes in the leadership were announced, and the party did not appear to expand the 14-member Politburo, on which three seats have been vacant since the crackdown.
The document gave no target economic growth rate, but the official press has said the economy should grow at about 6 percent annually in the next few years. 
This is dramatically slower than the previous decade's average annual growth, which was about 10 percent.
Â 
Splits With Local Authorities
According to Chinese economists and officials, the meeting had been delayed until now because of serious disagreements between the central Government and the provincial governors over the degree of regional autonomy and taxes that the provinces must hand over to Beijing. 
Because of severe fiscal deficits, central leaders had been seeking higher taxes from the provinces and greater influence over local markets, but the governors reportedly rejected earlier versions that they felt would have been too onerous.
One characterstic of the last decade had been the devolution of authority from Beijing to the localities, in an effort to raise economic incentives and spur the economy. 
In contrast, the new five-year blueprint includes an attempt by central leaders to take back some of that power. 
Officials have said the plan will give the central Government greater power but not quite as much as it had sought.
China's leaders also hope to spur ailing state enterprises -- one third of them are losing money -- and preserve the household responsibility system that allows individual farming.

file: CHINA OFFERS PEEK AT FAMED PRISONER.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Government said today that Wei Jingsheng, China's most famous political prisoner, is living in a private cell at a prison farm and that he refuses to admit that he has done anything wrong.
The disclosures today marked the first time that the Government has provided extensive details of the imprisonment of Mr. Wei, a 42-year-old essayist who has just begun the 14th year of a 15-year sentence.
Several senior officials of the Justice Ministry handed the information over to John T. Kamm, an American business consultant visiting Beijing on a Government invitation. 
Mr. Kamm, who lives in Hong Kong and has done business with China for 20 years, has been active in recent years in lobbying China to improve its human rights record.
Â 
Essays on a Wall
Mr. Kamm said the Justice Ministry officials complained bitterly about Western news articles suggesting that years of imprisonment had caused Mr. Wei to lose his teeth, his hair and his sanity. 
They denied the reports, saying Mr. Wei was in good health and constantly debated with the guards.
An electrician at the Beijing zoo, Mr. Wei emerged as the most famous essayist of the 1978-79 Beijing Spring movement, which created a "Democracy Wall" and covered it with posters demanding a political tolerance.
After the Government called for the "Four Modernizations" -- agriculture, industry, defense and science -- Mr. Wei wrote a passionate essay saying that China desperately needed a "Fifth Modernization" -- democracy.
Ever since his arrest and trial in 1979, there have been reports that Mr. Wei was physically and mentally ill; it was even reported once that he had died. 
But it was difficult to gauge the accuracy of these reports.
Mr. Kamm said the Justice Ministry officials had told him today that Mr. Wei occupies a single cell at a "reform through labor" farm near the central China city of Tangshan. 
They described him as a voracious reader, who keeps books in his cell and reads several newspapers each day.
Â 
TV and Debates
The officials said it was wrong to characterize Mr. Wei's situation as solitary confinement, because his cell opens onto another room in which there are several guards and a television set. 
They said Mr. Wei spends much of the day, when he is not reading, watching television and debating with the guards.
Mr. Wei is excused from the labor program but he tends some vegetables he is growing for himself, they said. 
The officials said that Mr. Wei occupied a private cell at his own request, and that he liked to go to read late at night and get up late.
While Mr. Wei basically abides by prison rules, he is "unclear" about his guilt, the officials said. 
When pressed by Mr. Kamm, they added that Mr. Wei neither acknowledges his guilt nor believes he has done anything wrong.
Mr. Wei's younger sister and a younger brother visit him every few months, the officials said. 
They added that Mr. Wei's father, a retired official who lives in Beijing but refuses to talk to reporters, does not visit his son and apparently does not get along with him.
While Mr. Kamm said he had no way of corroborating the Government account, he said the description sounded plausible. 
He said the treatment described was not so different from the conditions afforded to other sensitive prisoners, including Luo Haixing, a Hong Kong businessman who was released last year.
"In two years of working on these cases, they've never lied to me," Mr. Kamm said of the officials. 
"They don't tell me the whole truth, but they don't lie to me."
Mr. Kamm said the officials also told him that Wang Dan, a student leader who is serving a four-year term for his role in the 1989 Tiananmen demonstrations, was also proving difficult to "re-educate."
The officials said that Mr. Wang was being held at the Beijing No. 2 Prison, where he reads extensively, and that the guards have found it difficult to reform his ideology.

file: China Orders Expulsion of Hong Kong Journalist.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Government said today it had ordered the expulsion from China of a Hong Kong journalist who has been detained for a week on charges that she offered bribes for secret documents.
The journalist, Leung Wai-min, a 32-year-old reporter for The Hong Kong Express newspaper, was detained in the early hours of Oct. 
25 and kept incommunicado. 
She was not allowed visits from her husband or editor or from British Embassy officials.
China said that Ms. Leung would be forced to leave "within a limited period of time," but there was no indication she had been released. 
Her editors and her husband were unable to locate her and did not know her whereabouts.
By deciding to deport Ms. Leung, instead of putting her on trial, the Chinese authorities were apparently trying to calm anxieties in Hong Kong over the issue. 
Ms. Leung's detention underscored the prickly relations between the Chinese Government and the foreign press, and reminded Hong Kong journalists that they will be working under Communist rules after the territory reverts to China in 1997.
The official New China News Agency said Ms. Leung had bribed a Government employee into obtaining a "most confidential" document, a copy of which she then forwarded onto her Hong Kong headquarters.
On Oct. 
5, Ms. Leung's newspaper published the entire text of the keynote speech by the Communist Party leader, Jiang Zemin. 
The speech was delivered at an important Communist Party Congress that was held in mid-October.
The New China News Agency said Ms. Leung had destroyed her copy of the speech by burning parts of it in her hotel room bathroom, before discarding the remains in several trash cans on the streets. 
The dispatch added that Ms. Leung had obtained many secrets from the Government employee in exchange for a "large sum of money."
Patrick W. T. Wong, deputy editor at The Express newspaper, did not deny that Ms. Leung had obtained an advance copy of Mr. Jiang's speech. 
Asked if she had paid for a document, Mr. Wong said he had not seen her and so could not comment, but he added that his newspaper did not approve of paying money for information.
Â 
An Apparent Confession
National television this evening showed Ms. Leung, calm and steady, affixing her fingerprint to what appeared to be a signed 15-page confession. 
She was filmed answering several questions and then the camera displayed a bundle of money, suggesting that it had been found as evidence.
Until Ms. Leung is released, it will be impossible to confirm this account. 
Chinese Government versions of events have not always been noted for their accuracy.
The authorities say they treated her with leniency because she confessed to her crimes and was acting under the direction of her editor. 
The report said her editor had given an apology and promised that such a case would not happen again. 
The New China News Agency did not say what would happen to the two Chinese who obtained the document and provided it to her.
In May, Chinese State Security authorities searched the office of the Beijing-based reporter for The Washington Post, Lena H. Sun. They confiscated documents and issued a stern warning that she was involved in activities "incompatible with her status," but there have been no further repercussions.

file: China Orders Students Going Abroad to Pay Fees.txt
text:
ï»¿
China has issued new rules that would toughen restrictions on young people planning to study abroad, including a requirement that they first work for five years in China or pay large sums of money to the Government as deposit, officials say.
The new guidelines, issued by the State Education Commission last week and effective beginning Saturday, are apparently a result of months of deliberation on how to revise the program for overseas study, and to insure that greater numbers of students return.
The pronouncements were disclosed by several different Chinese officials and foreign diplomats, and they were confirmed by a spokesman at the State Education Commission.
Chinese officials have admitted privately that they are highly concerned that so few of their students have returned from studying overseas. 
Yet, the number of students preparing to apply to schools in the West has risen significantly since the military crackdown in early June, and word of the new rules, particularly the staggering amounts of money required for deposit, has worried many of them.
Despite assurances from Chinese leaders, many students say they fear that this new rule may represent a retreat from China's 12-year-old policy of promoting study in the West.
Two weeks ago, China's Education Minister, Li Tieying, told a group of returning students that ''the policy of sending people abroad to study will not, and has no reason to, change,'' according to the official People's Daily, which paraphrased Mr. Li's remarks.
The guidelines would require college graduates, who want to waive the work requirement and go abroad immediately, to pay the equivalent of about $530 for each year of college they attend. 
A student with a master's degree would have to pay the equivalent of $850 for each of the years in a master's program, and a doctoral student would need to pay about $1,275 a year. 
#2 Categories of Students It is not clear if graduate students would also have to pay for each of their years spent in college. 
The students would presumably get their money back if, and when, they returned to China. 
In contrast to these sums, a typical worker earns a salary of about $32 a month, and would need to save his entire salary for more than five years to pay for his child's college fee.
The Education Commission spokesman who confirmed the rules refused to elaborate on whether they applied to self-sponsored students or Government-sponsored students. 
Most students who study in the United States, for example, receive tuition assistance from the American university, but can be regarded by Chinese authorities as Government-sponsored students for visa purposes if the Government picks up at least a part of the educational bill.
Currently, however, self-sponsored students are not as strictly monitored as are sponsored ones, presumably because the Government has greater control over students it agrees to send overseas. 
According to the Chinese definition, the number of sponsored students tends to be higher than self-sponsored students, but in the last few months there are indications that the proportions have switched.
According to the United States Consulate in Beijing, there has been a marked decline in visa applications from Government-sponsored students, while those from self-sponsored students have risen. 
It is unclear if these new stipulations represent fundamental changes in an overall policy or merely stricter versions of a policy or regulation previously in place.
In China, the effectiveness of policies often depends on how thoroughly they are carried out. 
It is not clear if other ministries besides the State Education Commission are subject to similar rules, and even universities that fall under the jurisdiction of the Education Commission may not wish to carry out all parts of the regulation.
One Western diplomat suggested that, since the rule applies only to college graduates, students who had not yet received their bachelor's degrees may apply to study abroad and thereby circumvent the retroactive school fee and the five-year work requirement. 
''It's a possible loophole,'' he said.
