file: China Waits Anxiously for Ruling On Its Trade Status With the U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
A highly charged issue is looming in relations between the United States and China, and it has Chinese officials and intellectuals concerned over their future, their standard of living and their contacts with the West.
The issue is most-favored-nation trading status, and the concern is over whether the United States will renew favorable treatment on tariffs to China. 
By June 3, President Bush will make a recommendation to Congress for a vote, and Chinese officials and business executives are worried that Mr. Bush might not recommend renewal or that Congress would block it.
As a clear gesture of conciliation toward the United States, China announced Thursday that it had released 211 political prisoners, and had earlier lifted martial law in Lhasa, the capital of Tibet, but diplomats reacted cautiously. 
They said it was not clear whether one or two actions would be enough to ease American indignation at political repression in China.
Benefits of Trade Status
China, which exported about $12 billion worth of goods to the United States last year, has benefited enormously in the last decade from most-favored-nation status, which gives Chinese exports the same relatively low tariffs of 10 percent to 25 percent that the United States imposes on goods from most other countries. 
If the status were revoked, China would have to pay up to 90 percent duty on some items, mostly apparel, toys and electronics.
''If most favored nation is not renewed in June, and if Congress approves, then it could hurt both countries,'' Wei Mingyi, president of China International Trust and Investment Corporation, said in a recent interview. 
''Trade between the two countries could be set back by 20 to 30 years.''
The issue comes a year and a half after China began an austerity plan that has left the economy virtually stagnant, with zero industrial growth in the first quarter this year compared to the same period last year. 
Inflation is down and growth rose slightly in April, but some Chinese and Western economists say it will be a tough task to stimulate the economy significantly again without bringing back inflation, which reached double digits in 1989.
Â 
Threat to China's Exports
From China's point of view, the threat to its exports could not come at a worse time. 
Revocation of most-favored-nation status could cut China's exports to the United States by about 50 percent in the first year, and more in the following years. 
This would mean a decline in China's exports of about $6 billion in the first year alone, amounting to about 11 percent of its total exports last year of $52.5 billion.
Trade between China and the United States has soared in recent years, and last year it rose by 43 percent over 1988 to $17.8 billion. 
But trade frictions between the two countries could rise regardless of whether most-favored-nation status is revoked, because of China's mounting trade surplus with the United States. 
In the first two months of this year, its trade surplus with the United States was $1.3 billion, or 79.2 percent higher than the surplus for the same period last year, according to statistics from the United States Department of Commerce.
At that rate, American economists estimate, China's trade surplus with the United States could reach $11 billion this year, possibly making it the country with the second highest trade surplus with the United States, after Japan.
A small minority of Chinese intellectuals interviewed say they are so disillusioned with the Government that they support revocation of most-favored-nation status, but the great majority appear to favor continuation of the trade benefits.
Â 
'Torn Over the Issue'
''We feel torn over the issue,'' a Chinese researcher said. 
''On the one hand, we want the United States to punish the Chinese Government for what it did. 
But on the other hand, we know that such a punishment would affect our own personal lives, and frankly, we don't like the thought of having to endure the suffering.''
Most intellectuals say the Chinese Government would retaliate, probably at first by raising tariffs or restricting American imports, such as wheat and technology and equipment. 
But their anxieties go far beyond the impact on trade between the two countries. 
They say the Chinese Government would close its doors at least slightly to the world, restricting travel to America, cutting cultural exchanges and access to a wide range of Western things from books to fashions to ideas.
It is uncertain how the revocation of most-favored-nation status would affect Chinese politics. 
On the one hand, it would hurt the economy and perhaps increase the pressure within the leadership for the removal of Prime Minister Li Peng, who is in charge of the economy.
On the other hand, many Chinese say that the most likely outcome is that the hard-liners would seize the occasion to begin a campaign for self-reliance instead of openness, and encourage a new wave of anti-Americanism.
''It will deal a blow to the reformers,'' said a Chinese businessman. 
''It will foster an anti-Western attitude.''

file: China Whispers of Plots and Man Called Yang.txt
text:

When people here lower their voices and speak frankly about politics, their suspicions and hostilities frequently focus on a sprightly 82-year-old man whose most important hour may not yet have arrived.

Diplomats Suspicious, Too
There is particular suspicion and uncertainty because major personnel shifts are said to be under negotiation in the army leadership. 
Mr. Deng is considering leaving his last official post, Chairman of the Military Commission, and Mr. Yang is one of the contenders to succeed him, although Defense Minister Qin Jiwei is believed to regard himself as a better choice.
Many foreign diplomats are just as suspicious of Mr. Yang as are the Chinese, and some go so far as to say that the President is part of a new ''gang of four'' conspiring to consolidate power just as the original gang sought power as Mao was dying 13 years ago.

Relationship Is Disputed
The most common accusation against Mr. Yang is that he is building up a dynasty in the armed forces.

The President is often regarded as a hard-liner, but many Chinese with access to high-level information say that is not quite right. 
One Chinese who knows Mr. Yang says he has the best sense of humor among the elderly leaders, and that he has generally backed the wing of the leadership supporting further change rather than the group favoring more central planning.
''Right now he's a reformer, backing Deng on everything,'' said another official. 
''Of course, after Deng goes, who knows what he'll do.

text:

In a significant shift in its strategy to modernize the country, China said today that it would restrict the number of graduate students it sends to the United States and other nations, and would begin producing far more members of its technological elite in Chinese universities.

The Government has contended that its students have been over-influenced by the West.
In an interview published in the English-language China Daily, the Vice Minister of Education, He Dongchang, said that a ''screen'' must be placed over China's windows to the world to prevent ''flies and worms'' from infesting the country. 
''Opening to the outside world does not necessarily mean seeking knowledge from only a few Western countries,'' Mr. He said. 
#26,000 Enrolled in U.S. 
Schools According to statistics compiled last year, about 26,000 Chinese nationals were enrolled in American universities in 1988.
The move comes at a time when China, which has depended heavily on foreign technology and education in recent years, is trying to loosen its dependence on the West. 
That drive accelerated after the crackdown on the democracy movement in early June.
For example, meeting today with scientists developing China's space program, Prime Minister Li Peng said that after the June demonstrations ''we have come to the sober conclusion that China's space industry, either for national defense or civil purposes, must be developed through self-reliance and hard struggle.''
He urged them to use as much domestic technology as possible.

Fewer Doctoral Studies Abroad
In the new policy described today, Mr. He did not specify how many students China would allow to go abroad. 
But the Vice Minister, who is considered a close ally of Mr. Li's, said that ''China will concentrate on producing its own doctors in the future instead of sending students overseas for doctorates.''

Lack of Jobs Is a Problem
Mr. He himself conceded in the interview that China often does not find ''appropriate occupations'' for its returnees, and said that would improve, along with pay and quality of housing.
Presumably, the Government is also concerned by the thousands of Chinese students abroad who have organized a movement in exile, with extensive contacts back in their homeland. 
Mr. He suggested that ''patient and painstaking ideological work'' should also be conducted by Chinese students living overseas.

Users of Exit Visas

Mr. Bao was an ardent proponent of political change and headed the Central Committee's Political Reform Research Center. 
He had great influence over domestic and international policy.
The court would not tell family members today whether they could attend the trial, the Chinese said. 
Family members are normally allowed to attend trials in China, but they can be barred in cases that involve state secrets or other sensitive issues.
Mr. Bao's lawyer was also apparently notified of the trial, but it is not clear whether the court authorities will give him access to Government files he believes are necessary to prepare a defense. 
The lawyer is Zhang Sizhi, who has represented other political prisoners and is expected to put up a spirited defense for his client.
Normally, defense lawyers do not contest their clients' guilt but merely ask the court for mercy. 
When Mr. Zhang represented other dissidents last year, and vigorously defended them in court, he was reprimanded afterward by the judicial authorities.
In March, the Politburo expelled Mr. Bao from the party and stripped him of his Central Committee seat. 
A guilty verdict is virtually certain, and the Politburo has presumably decided on the penalty the court will impose.
Mr. Zhao's case has been handled strictly as an internal party matter, through an investigation that is believed to have been completed. 
It is unclear what the party will ultimately do with Mr. Zhao.

file: China Wins a Bigger Say in Hong Kong.txt
text:
ï»¿
Britain and China announced a breakthrough today in their bitter 18-month dispute over the future of Hong Kong, agreeing that the colony can build an expensive new airport, but on the condition that China will gain even more influence over Hong Kong's affairs.
It was an ambiguous resolution at best to the highly emotional airport battle, which was seen by each side as a test of the other's good faith and by some as a sign of China's impatience for control over the prosperous capitalist enclave.
Britain received the assurances it sought that China will honor any debts the $16.2 billion airport incurs, even after Hong Kong returns to Chinese sovereignty on July 1, 1997. 
That guarantee was considered essential to attracting private capital, on which the project depends.
In return, Britain acceded to China's demand that it be formally consulted on all major decisions about the airport. 
China also received extensive financial influence over Hong Kong, with Britain promising that when the colony is turned over it will have at least $3.2 billion in cash reserves.
Â 
British Leader Plans Visit
Hong Kong has never disclosed the size of its reserves, but they are believed to amount to tens of billions of dollars. 
China hinted during the dispute over the airport that it believed Britain was trying to empty the colony's coffers before China took control. 
China will now be able to influence both the financing of the airport project and the colony's overall finances.
The British Government also announced that Prime Minister John Major would travel to the Chinese capital soon to sign a memorandum of understanding containing the agreement.
That, too, could prove a bonus to the Chinese; the leaders of the industrialized nations agreed to halt all high-level visits after China's violent suppression of demonstrations in Tiananmen Square in June 1989. 
Mr. Major's visit would be the first by a major Western leader since then.
"We have an agreement that enables us to go ahead with this project with the confidence and certainty we've been looking for," said Hong Kong's Governor, Sir David Wilson.
He added, "I don't think this is a bad deal for Hong Kong."
Â 
The Key Phrase
The Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce praised the accord, and Martin Lee, a lawyer who has pushed for open elections in Hong Kong, said he welcomed the agreement's assurances. 
But Mr. Lee added that the threat to the colony's autonomy was worrying. 
"This would be most unacceptable," he commented.
The key phrase in the agreement is, "Any decision will give full weight to the Chinese Government's views."
The problem of what Britain will do if China continues to object to some aspect of the airport project after it is consulted remains unresolved.
"We think it's reasonable and makes sense to consult China on these issues," said Peter B. Davies, a spokesman at the British Embassy here. 
He added that "there are no secret annexes" that stipulate how disputes would be handled.
Britain had pushed for construction of the airport as a vote of confidence in the future of Hong Kong and to help insure its prosperity after it is returned to China.
Â 
Private Capital to Pay
The current airport, which juts into busy Hong Kong harbor from a crowded residential and commercial district near the heart of the city, will be replaced by a complex on the adjacent island of Lan Tao.
It will require huge amounts of excavation and landfill and construction of a suspension bridge nearly a mile long. 
Private capital is expected to pay for much of the project. 
Morgan Stanley & Company, the American securities firm, is the adviser on raising the billions of dollars that will be required.
China insisted it had a right to influence the airport plan, even though it has no formal say in the colony's affairs until 1997. 
At one heated moment a top Chinese Government official said that only the Chinese Government had the right to speak for Hong Kong's people.
Such remarks and Beijing's relentless criticisms were perceived by many in Hong Kong as meddling, a worrying sign that China would interfere in the colony's capitalist system in spite of a promise it will remain unchanged for 50 years after the 1997 handover. 
The bickering undermined already fragile confidence in Hong Kong.
Â 
A Form of Veto
Particularly worrisome for the British and many in Hong Kong was a sense that China was exercising a form of veto over a major Hong Kong issue. 
The project needed China's promise to honor the airport's debts to attract private capital. 
China had conspicuously withheld that promise; today it was offered.
As part of this financial understanding, the Bank of China was promised a large role in raising the loans needed for the airport. 
In addition, a Bank of China official will sit on the governing airport authority.
The Chinese Government said it would support "necessary and reasonable borrowing by the Hong Kong Government," even if it is to be repaid after 1997. 
What would count as reasonable was left unclear.
But China will hold a veto over any steps that would leave the airport with more than $640 million in debt after 1997. 
A joint committee will be formed, half of whose members will be Chinese, to review all major contracts and franchises that will run beyond 1997.

file: China Worried by Clinton_s Linking of Trade to Human Rights.txt
text:
ï»¿
If the Presidential campaign isn't going so well these days for President Bush, the Chinese leaders seem to think it's going even worse for them.
Most horrifying of all to the Chinese leaders, there is the prospect that next month United States voters will elect Gov. Bill Clinton, who has called for linking China's trade privileges to its human rights record. 
Mr. Clinton sent shivers down octogenarian spines here this summer when he called for "an America that will never coddle tyrants, from Baghdad to Beijing."
But even Mr. Bush, long regarded by the Chinese as an "old friend," has proved distinctly unfriendly on the campaign trail. 
Many specialists on China say relations are already severely strained and may get worse.
Â 
'Tense, Delicate Relationship'
"I think that we're going to see a very tense, delicate relationship and that we're going to see the relationship continue to go downhill irrespective of who wins the White House," said John T. Kamm, a Hong Kong-based business consultant and specialist on Chinese-American relations. 
"Of course, they'll probably go downhill a little faster if Clinton wins."
Chinese officials have long shown a preference for Republicans, and they often speak glowingly of former President Richard M. Nixon and Henry A. Kissinger for opening up relations, while giving much less credit to the Carter Administration for formally recognizing China.
Beijing seemed to regard the Democrats in the 1970's and 1980's as too weak-kneed in opposing Moscow.
Â 
U.S. Patience Wearing Thin
But there are a number of signs that the Bush Administration's patience with Beijing has worn thin, and that it is no longer willing to pay a political price for cultivating ties to China.
For example, the Administration is threatening that unless Beijing agrees by the end of this week to take major steps to open up its markets, the United States will retaliate against up to $3.9 billion in Chinese exports.
Just as bad, from Beijing's point of view, Mr. Bush announced last month that Washington would permit the sale of up to 150 F-16 fighter planes to Taiwan, which China regards as a renegade province. 
The sale of the fighter planes is regarded by many experts, American and Chinese, as a violation of a 1982 accord in which the United States pledged that it would not increase arms sales to Taiwan.
Â 
Taiwan Is Still Ticklish
"By brazenly selling F-16's to Taiwan over China's opposition, the United States has again revealed its hegemonist policy of using arms sales to interfere in other countries' internal policies," the official People's Daily said this week.
Beijing reacted to the F-16 sale by dropping out of arms talks with Western countries and by rejecting a longstanding proposal for a joint Chinese-American commission on human rights, and China has hinted it may retaliate further.
For now, the dominant issue is the deadline Saturday on reaching agreement on talks to open up the Chinese market to foreign competition. 
But experts say there is still time to avert a trade war, and note that past trade accords with Beijing have typically been reached at the very last minute.
"Given the importance of the issues at stake and given the progress that has been achieved so far, which is not insignificant, I think that there's a better than even chance that we'll be able to overcome the last hurdles," said a Western diplomat in Beijing.
For all their resentment at the Administration's recent toughness, the Chinese leaders do appreciate that Mr. Bush has vetoed Congressional efforts to put conditions on the most-favored-nation trade privileges that China enjoys.
Mr. Clinton, on the other hand, has advocated linking trade and human rights.
Ending most-favored-nation status would be a major blow to the Chinese economy, which counts on the United States as a crucial market for shoes, clothing, toys and other exports.
Last year 26 percent of Chinese exports went to the United States, and the figure may be even higher this year: in the first six months of this year, Chinese exports to the United States were running nearly 32 percent above the corresponding period in 1991.
Mr. Clinton has apparently given relatively little thought to China, and it is possible that he would work with Congress to put pressure on China without revoking most-favored-nation status.
But Chinese officials have been alarmed by his speeches and dismayed by the Democratic Convention, where the largest foreign delegation reportedly was Taiwan's, and even Tibet had nearly as many representatives as China. 
Two exiled dissidents, Li Lu and Chai Ling, were invited to the podium and hailed as heroes.
Among those advising Mr. Clinton on China are Richard Holbrooke, a former senior State Department official who is now an investment banker, and Michael Mandelbaum, an academic expert on international relations.
Mr. Mandelbaum visited Beijing earlier this year and held discussions that the Chinese say they found somewhat reassuring, in that both sides still seemed to care a good deal about the relationship, and Mr. Holbrooke came in July for a day-and-a-half visit on behalf of his banking clients.
Â 
Emphasis on Long Term
Mr. Holbrooke said he did not come as an emissary of Mr. Clinton, but he told the two Chinese leaders with whom he met that Mr. Clinton was very serious about human rights issues.
Mr. Holbrooke also told them that a victory by Mr. Clinton would be good for China because Mr. Clinton was more likely to invigorate the United States economy, providing a basis for healthy trade and sound relations in general.
Aside from listening to his advisers, Mr. Clinton is also believed to have consulted other experts on relations with China, including Stephen J. Solarz, a Congressman from New York, and Winston Lord, a former United States Ambassador to Beijing.
Whoever wins the election, there are other conflicts on the horizon, including the possibility that the United States will set up a new radio service -- perhaps called Radio Free China -- to broadcast across the bamboo curtain. 
China disapproves of the Voice of America, which it calls "voice of rumors," and it would be outraged if a more aggressive broadcast service were established.
Even now, some Chinese officials hope that the problems will ease.
"We want good relations with the rest of the world, above all with the United States, and even if Clinton wins I don't think that there will necessarily be a big change," a senior Chinese researcher said. 
"Of course if Bush wins, that's better, but that wouldn't mean that relations will be smooth either.
"Before Reagan was elected President, he was also very hostile to the Chinese mainland. 
But after he won the election he was very pragmatic and he had to face reality. 
Maybe after this election, it won't be quite the same as it was in the campaign."

file: China, in Shift, Accepts U.S. Shipping Concerns.txt
text:
ï»¿
China agreed today to allow two American companies to compete directly with Chinese rivals in shipping the nation's cargo, resolving a longstanding dispute over market access.
The Chinese concession, which comes at a time of mounting trade frictions between Washington and Beijing, is expected to facilitate trade with China and perhaps reduce transportation costs. 
It also is the first time that foreign companies will operate wholly owned subsidiaries in China's transportation business and directly compete with Chinese rivals.
China's decision averted a possible upward spiral of retaliatory measures that ultimately might have affected as much as half of the total two-way trade, estimated to be about $24 billion last year. 
The decision coincided with unrelated trade talks in Washington, in which a deal was struck this evening on protection of intellectual property.
"The company is very pleased," said Gary D. Gilbert, a Hong Kong-based vice president of Sea-Land Service Inc., a CSX Corporation subsidiary and one of the two American carriers granted approval to conduct business in China without Chinese agents. 
The other is American President Lines Ltd.
Â 
'We're Free Traders'
"We're free traders," Mr. Gilbert said. 
"We're in the business of moving commerce between countries, and the more free trade there is the better we like it."
Limited access to the Chinese market has been a major complaint of American companies and trade negotiators. 
The maritime dispute was reportedly raised by Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d during his visit to Beijing in November. 
It apparently was not directly linked to other trade issues.
"In so far as the individual negotiations, it is unrelated, but when looking at things like the attitude in Congress, it becomes one more log in a big fire," said a foreign businessman involved in trade between China and the United States. 
"It's all part of what we feel are barriers to market access."
China had effective control over the flow of goods into and out of the country, requiring American carriers to work solely through two Chinese booking agents, who in some aspects of the business were their direct competitors. 
In contrast, Chinese carriers were free to operate relatively openly in the United States.
Â 
Inquiry Was Begun
In July, the United States Federal Maritime Commission began an investigation into the treatment of American shipping companies in China. 
If the commission had determined that China indeed was unfairly restricting access, it could have imposed a charge of $1 million on each Chinese vessel that called at an American port. 
The Chinese side could also have retaliated with corresponding measures.
Presumably to avoid such stiff penalties as well as an ensuing trade war, China agreed to loosen its restrictions and allow two American shipping companies to establish subsidiaries and operate branch offices in China.
Half of all trade between the countries is carried by Chinese or American ships and would have been affected by the dispute, while the remainder is hauled on ships of third countries.
Sea-Land hauls about 13 percent of the trade between the United States and China; American President holds about 10 percent of the market.

file: China-Hong Kong Dispute Rattles Colony_s Stock Index.txt
text:

Hong Kong stocks collapsed today after Premier Li Peng of China blamed the British colonial Government for the market panic.
The market's leading indicator, the Hang Seng stock index, dived 205.13 points, or 3.8 percent, in the first 15 minutes of trading. 
At the close of the morning session, the index was down 400.6 points, or 7.4 percent, to 5,011.05.
Â 
Four Days of Panic Selling
The plunge was the fourth in as many days. 
In the first three days, the index lost about 10 percent of its value.
Panic selling has gripped the market since Beijing threatened to revoke contracts with the colonial Government that it had not approved after Hong Kong returns to China in 1997.
On Wednesday, Premier Li joined China's barrage of attacks on plans by the colony's Governor, Chris Patten, to make the 1995 legislative elections a bit more democratic.
Speaking on a visit to Hanoi, Premier Li blamed Governor Patten's administration squarely for the sell-off. 
"The responsibility lies entirely in the British Government's part and not the Chinese part." he said.
The Premier said Britain was disregarding past agreements with China on Hong Kong's status through the transition period to Chinese rule.
The turmoil comes despite soaring company profits and an economy expanding an annual rate of 5 percent. 
Some dealers insisted that stocks had been oversold and were ripe for a rebound, but Barry Yates of Asia Equity said the index could fall below 5,000 points, a full 23 percent below the all-time high of 6,470 it reached last month.
The slump was likely to last as long as the fate of Governor Patten's proposals on extending democracy in Hong Kong remained undecided, Mr. Yates said.
Mr. Patten's plans lie at the heart of the dispute with Beijing. 
Pro-China newspapers in Hong Kong on Wednesday called the proposals invalid and warned the Governor not to underestimate the mainland.
Â 
Overseas Investors Nervous
Dealers said overseas institutions, whose investment in Hong Kong stocks earlier this year helped push the market to its record levels, were beginning to take fright along with local investors.
Lehman Brothers said a compromise between Britain and China would bring a strong rebound in share prices.
"Conversely, if the Governor remains steadfast in his attempt to introduce a greater number of directly elected officials prior to 1995, we believe that the market could move considerably lower," the firm said.

file: CHINA-JAPAN LINK ON MISSILES SEEN.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Toshiba Machine Company, which was penalized by the United States for selling equipment that helped the Soviet Union silence its submarines in the 1980's, also sold a machine that may now be helping China build better missiles, a Japanese magazine reports.
Toshiba Machine concedes that in 1985 it sold an electron beam machine, a sophisticated piece of equipment used in making integrated circuits, to a company in Hong Kong. 
Both the company and the machine mysteriously vanished.
Toshiba Machine says it still does not know where the machine is. 
But the October issue of Bungei Shunju, a respected magazine here, reports that the machine is in use in China, at the Shanghai Metallurgical Research Institute. 
The article, by Koei Kaga, suggests that the machine possibly is being used to make chips for missile guidance.
Selling such equipment to China would have been a violation of export control rules in 1985, but a sale to Hong Kong would have been allowed.
Â 
Toshiba Says It Heeded Laws
Tetsuo Kadoya, a spokesman for Toshiba, said the company complied with all laws that were in effect in 1985 in selling the electron-beam machine. 
It received an export permit from the Japanese Government and a customs certificate from the Hong Kong Government that specified that the equipment would not be re-exported.
Between 1982 and 1984, however, Toshiba Machine had sold milling machines to the Soviet Union that allowed it to make quieter propellers for its submarines. 
After those sales came to light in 1987, Washington prohibited Toshiba Machine from exporting any products to the United States for three years. 
And it barred Toshiba Corporation, the electronics company that owns half of Toshiba Machine, from bidding for United States Government contracts for a year.
After the sales of the milling machines were disclosed, Toshiba and its subsidiaries tightened their export-control practices so that even if there was some laxity in 1985, there is none now, Mr. Kadoya said. 
He also said the electron beam machine in question had been removed from the export-restriction list in 1990.
The possible diversion of the Toshiba electron beam equipment, which is used in the process of imprinting microscopic circuit patterns on a silicon wafer, was first reported by another Japanese magazine, Foresight, in 1990. 
The Associated Press, following up on that Foresight article, said it had seen a copy of a receipt for the machine from the Shanghai research institute.
Â 
Sale Was Scrutinized in '90
Two years ago, the incident was examined by Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry, which had given permission for the equipment to be exported to Hong Kong. 
The Pentagon is also believed to have reviewed the sale.
Not much appears to have come of their investigations, and it is unclear whether the new article, which quotes a researcher at the Shanghai institute confirming that the machine is in use there, will prompt a new look. 
The article is starting to circulate in Congress, where there is concern about China's sales of missiles to other nations.
Senator Jeff Bingaman, a New Mexico Democrat who is chairman of the Armed Services Subcommittee on the Defense Industry and Technology, cited the article in a speech on the Senate floor on Monday. 
He called the sale "one additional reason we need to have a total review of our trade relations with China."
He said the Bungei Shunju article "pointed out that in 1985 a Japanese firm knowingly violated" export controls by shipping semiconductor manufacturing equipment that was "used to improve the guidance system in China nuclear missiles and perhaps to develop MIRV warheads as well."
Still, some people close to the Defense Department say the issue is considered old and not very important. 
Experts say that it takes many different pieces of equipment, not just an electron beam machine, to make computer chips, and that many different technologies besides chips go into making missiles.
While Toshiba Machine insists it was fooled by the Chinese operation, details in the article, confirmed by Mr. Kadoya, seem to suggest that the company should have at least suspected that the equipment was being diverted.
Â 
Buyer Had No 'Clean Room'
The Hong Kong buyer, Scientific Instrument Ltd., did not have a special factory, known as a clean room, which is needed to manufacture semiconductors. 
But Mr. Kadoya said the company had shown blueprints to Toshiba Machine indicating it was planning to build a factory.
Toshiba Machine's own engineers would usually install such a sophisticated piece of equipment in the customer's factory. 
In this case, the customer asked only that the machine be shipped. 
And Toshiba never got a call to service the machine, another unusual circumstance.
Takashi Suzuki, director of the export division at Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry, said that it investigated the matter after the first article appeared in 1990 and that it did not find any violation of export controls then.
"If new evidence is found I will re-investigate and give another hearing to Toshiba," he said. 
Asked if the new article provided new evidence, he replied, "I can't say."

file: China_s Army Is Cared For in a Lean Budget.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Government acknowledged today that it faced grave budgetary difficulties, but at the same time proposed a budget for 1990 that includes a sharp increase in military spending.
The National People's Congress, now meeting in Beijing for a 15-day session that will give pro forma approval to the budget and other proposals from the leadership, also agreed today to accept the resignation of Deng Xiaoping from his last formal post, as chairman of the Government's Central Military Commission. 
Mr. Deng announced in November that he would retire from the post, and today's move was a formality.
The Congress did not name a new chairman, but it is widely expected to be Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party leader and Mr. Deng's choice to succeed him as China's paramount leader. 
In November Mr. Jiang succeeded Mr. Deng as chairman of the Communist Party's Central Military Commission, which in practical terms is the same as its Government counterpart.
The military spending increase, by $6.2 billion, or 15.2 percent, had been expected as a signal of the leadership's appreciation of the role of the People's Liberation Army in crushing democracy protests last year. 
The army was the major beneficiary in a budget report that was otherwise bleak.
''The condition for the state budget this year is grim,'' Finance Minister Wang Bingqian told the congress in an address. 
He presented a draft budget that included a nominal deficit of $1.89 billion, down slightly from last year.
But those figures were calculated under the Chinese practice of counting borrowed funds as revenue. 
Using Western accounting practices, the budget gap this year reaches $9 billion, up 14.5 percent.
Most Western and Chinese economists agree that China's economic difficulties are related less to the military crackdown last June than to the 18-month-old austerity program. 
The economic slowdown has made it more difficult for the central Government to raise funds, and has meant increased subsidies to money-losing state enterprises.
The budget proposal also included a 9.9 percent increase in education spending and a 7.9 percent increase in funds for agriculture. 
It is not clear how such numbers are derived or how reliable they are, and some university faculties have been told that education spending would drop this year.
Most Western diplomats regard the figure for military spending as a significant understatement of the total, partly because the budget allocation apparently does not incorporate sums the army earns from weapons sales and from civilian products produced by army-owned factories.
China's leaders have given strong hints - particularly after seeing the Romanian Army help topple a Communist Government in December - that they want to insure the loyalty of the army. 
In addition, the leadership has been trying to give the army a greater role in maintaining domestic security.
According to the Finance Minister's report, the two largest allocations, each amounting to about $14 billion or about 20 percent of the budget, are for capital construction and subsidies to money-losing enterprises.
China has tried to cut spending for inefficient enterprises by introducing a bankruptcy law, but the Government has been reluctant to allow money-losing companies to go bankrupt.

file: China_s Babies_ Better _Elegant_ Than _Red_.txt
text:
ï»¿
While there are no free elections in China to use in judging the popular mood, one gauge of the people's sentiment is the names bestowed upon children.
By that standard, the hard-liners who run China are in trouble. 
Names with political meanings, redolent of the Communist past, are decidedly out of fashion. 
Almost no self-respecting parents now name their children Red, which used to be the most common name of all. 
Today's babies often get names that have an association with prosperity or the West, like Xiu, a name now common that means Elegant.
"These days people don't want political names like Red that are reminiscent of the Cultural Revolution," said Zhang Shuyan, a senior researcher in China's State Committee for Reforming the Chinese Written Language. 
"Now many names are unusual. 
Parents search the dictionary for a character that has a good meaning and is uncommon."
These days, parents strive for names that sound more cultured or cosmopolitan. 
Some children born in September, for example, were named Yayun, meaning Asian Games, after the mini-Olympics of which China was host at the time -- an international event that symbolized sophistication.
For baby girls, the character na, often used in transcribing Western names into Chinese, is common. 
It has little meaning, but because of its use in transcriptions it has the allure of associations with the West.
Almost all Chinese names have a meaning and are plucked from daily life.
For example, tens of thousands of people are named Li Jianguo (Build-the-Country Li), Zhang Hong (Red Zhang) and Wang Jun (Army Wang).
Those names proliferated during more orthodox moments of Communist history, and it used to be that a name offered an instant clue to when the person was born.
Anyone named Build the Country was probably born in 1949 or 1950, around the birth of the People's Republic. 
Yuanchao, meaning Assist Korea, is a common name of people born during the Korean War. 
Many who were born in the late 1950's, when Mao Zedong began an effort to catch up with Western industry, are named Chaoying, or Surpass England. 
And someone named Weidong, meaning Protect Mao Zedong, probably was born in the Cultural Revolution.
China's official newspapers reported approvingly that one soldier named his child Pingbao -- Suppress Rioting -- in honor of the crackdown against the democracy movement last year. 
In past years, that kind of name would have been ubiquitous, but in an indication of changing attitudes the newspaper report caused only mirth and ridicule.
A vast study of names by Ms. Zhang found that the single most common character used for names in the Cultural Revolution was Red. 
But since then, she says, the most common character in names has been hua, meaning magnificent and prosperous, and also signifying China.
Feng Yingshu, a sculptor, said, "It used to be that the time period provided a context, a frame in which to come up with a name for a child."
His own name reflects a drought at the time when he was born in 1948. 
The last character, shu, means a timely rain and includes the symbol for water.
Fortunetellers and astrology are still sometimes used in Hong Kong and Taiwan to derive names, but this is not common on the Chinese mainland today. 
Superstition is still evident in villages, however, where the desperate desire to give birth to a son leads to names for daughters like Zhaodi, Yindi and Ladi. 
All can be translated as 'Bring a Younger Brother.
As the Cultural Revolution generation enters adulthood, some people are changing their revolutionary names for more mundane ones -- as did many of the Soviet children who received similar names, particularly in the 1920's and 1930's, when Traktor, Elektrifikatsiya or Vladlen, for Vladimir Lenin, were not uncommon. 
A Chinese who deals regularly with Taiwan or Hong Kong business executives, for example, might feel a bit embarrassed if he was named Dongfeng, meaning East Wind, or Dajun, meaning Great Army.
While names are becoming more bourgeois, the names are still different from those that preceded the 1949 revolution. 
At that time, villagers often used ordinary characters from daily life. 
A child might, for example, be called Yuliang, meaning Surplus Grain, in the hope that he would always have enough to eat. 
Very feminine names, based on varieties of flower or jade, were common for girls before the revolution but have not made much of a comeback.
Mao Zedong's name meant Anoint the East. 
Deng Xiaoping's name is a common one and means Little Peace. 
Mr. Deng's partner and rival, Chen Yun, has a name that simply means Cloud.
One of the biggest changes in selecting names is that more and more people are getting names with only two syllables, consisting of one character for the surname and one for the given name. 
Chinese say that two-syllable names make it easier to hail somebody. 
But officials are concerned that a proliferation of two-character names will worsen the problem of large numbers of people having the same names.
Of the 1.1 billion people in China, about 100 million bear the surnames Wang, Chen, Li and Zhang. 
There were lots of mix-ups even when most people had three-character names, and with the popularity now of two-character names officials expect a good deal more duplication and confusion.

file: China_s Communists Prepare Party Congress.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Communist Party is preparing for a rare congress that will convene next week to shuffle the national leadership and establish a party line that is supposed to last for the next five years.
The party congress, the first to be held since 1987, is expected to confirm the rise of more pragmatic, change-minded officials within the leadership and to launch a new slogan: the building of a "socialist market economy."
No one knows just what a "socialist market economy" is, and that may be part of the attraction: the term is vague enough to be acceptable to all groups, while still sounding bold and reform-minded.
The authorities have given few details about the party congress, the 14th since the Chinese Communist Party was formed more than seven decades ago, except that it will begin on Monday. 
Still, they have hailed its importance, with Prime Minister Li Peng describing it last week as "a major event in our country's political life."
"We are sure that it will give a fresh impetus to reform, opening up and our economic development, and become an important milestone in the history of the Chinese Communist Party and China's socialist modernization," Mr. Li said.
The party congress will approve a work report that is supposed to set the tone for the next five years, and it will also choose a new Central Committee. 
The Central Committee, in turn, will choose a new Politburo.
In fact, all the crucial decisions have been made in advance by the handful of octogenarians who hold ultimate power in China, and the congress is less a forum for decisions than a platform for self-promotion -- a Chinese version of a national political convention in the United States. 
Among the key differences are that party congress speeches can last for hours, many of the proceedings are secret, and there is no election afterward to put it all in perspective.
The 14th party congress is expected to be important in that it will presumably anoint the team of leaders who will preside over the transition after the death of Deng Xiaoping, the ailing paramount leader. 
But the same was said of the 13th party congress in 1987.
Â 
Deng Not Expected to Appear
Mr. Deng appeared at the 1987 congress but there is no sign that he will turn up this time. 
He is 88 years old and rarely appears in public now.
Since the beginning of this year, Mr. Deng has been pressing behind the scenes for more rapid economic growth and restructuring, to the point of borrowing some elements from capitalism. 
The congress may be his last hurrah, and it is expected to endorse his preferred combination of free markets and one-party rule.
"There seems no question that the congress is intended to be a strong reaffirmation of the Deng Xiaoping line of reform and openness," said a Western diplomat in Beijing. 
"We expect that the new Central Committee and the new Politburo in particular will basically reflect that, in the sense that there will be a strengthening of the reform and moderate forces."
While the personnel decisions have presumably already been made, the rumors about who will be promoted vary considerably. 
By almost all accounts, the Politburo will be expanded from its present membership of 14, and most of the likely candidates are relatively young and enthusiastic about markets -- for goods if not ideas.
The most powerful rulers of China, all octogenarians like Mr. Deng, are nominally retired and will not be shuffled. 
Among the younger leaders who hold formal positions, the two most important -- Prime Minister Li and General Secretary Jiang Zemin -- are generally expected to hold onto their posts, at least for now.
Â 
Small Role for Delegates
The 1,991 delegates to the party congress, which will last about a week, will be entrusted with a minor role in addition to approving decisions already made. 
They will elect a Central Committee from a list of names that is a bit longer than the number of positions, so that a small percentage of candidates will lose the election.

file: China_s Intense Love of Education Cools Off.txt
text:
ï»¿
The director of a research institute here made a novel proposal the other day: he suggested that full professors receive the same salary as waitresses at the nearby Shangri-La Hotel.
There is little chance that the Government will approve the proposal, which would involve huge pay increases for the professors. 
But his idea underscores the humble circumstances of teachers in China, contributing to what is widely perceived today as a crisis in education.
At the annual session of the National People's Congress that adjourned on Tuesday, one of the topics that generated the most complaint was education. 
The outpouring of criticism appears to have galvanized top officials to acknowledge the problem and take action.
Prime Minister Li Peng said at a news conference Monday that he would convene a special committee to examine the nation's education problems. 
He also said he agreed with Deng Xiaoping's remarks on education.
''Our biggest mistake in the last 10 years has been that education has not been developed sufficiently,'' Mr. Deng, the senior Chinese leader, told Uganda's leader, Yoweri Museveni, who was visiting in the opening days of the legislative session.
In another sign of official recognition of the problem, Li Tieying, the Minister of Education, told reporters late last month, ''Our education is backward, our people's attainments fall short, and the low level of education has become a major constraint on our country's modernization and reform.''
While the Government is cutting spending on most programs, it has pledged to raise education expenditures by 15.4 percent to the equivalent of $10 billion. 
But some delegates said that sum is not enough. 
In some areas, children trudge hours each way through fields to classrooms in dilapidated shacks, or they learn from teachers with barely a high school degree, or are forced to share ragged books. 
In Beijing, some children bring their own chairs to school. 
Even in top universities, students often live six to a room that snugly fits one desk and three bunk beds.
Some rural children attend school in converted Buddhist temples or abandoned buildings, where conditions are often unsafe. 
Ninety percent of primary schools and 60 percent of junior high schools lack proper buildings and books, according to official figures.
Across the country, 220 million people are illiterate in a country with a population of 1.1 billion, and the average adult has only five years of schooling. 
While virtually all children enroll in primary school, one-third do not continue on to junior high school. 
High school enrollment has plunged by 27 percent over the last decade.
With China's rapid economic development, the symbols of achievement are no longer a college diploma or the rank of a scholar, but a new color television or a videotape player. 
While students still covet a scholarship to an American university - a possible route to permanent residency in the United States - the value of a local education is diminishing.
Â 
Professors Average $39.50
''If I had to make the decision again, I wouldn't become a graduate student,'' said a doctoral candidate in computer science at Beijing University. 
The student, who began his program six years ago, said that now not only the students but even the professors are going elsewhere.
A professor in China averages $39.50 a month, a bit less than the average for employees in Chinese business enterprises, and much less than taxi drivers or waitresses at international hotels.
When a college student advertised for a wife recently in a local newspaper, a young woman responded with a sarcastic scolding.
''Of what use is studying?'' she wrote. 
''Scribblers are not even as good as beggars. 
You can't eat culture, and you can't put ideals in the bank.''
The delegates to the National People's Congress admitted that the small increase in state funds will do little to improve the situation. 
The Education Ministry has suggested a school tax and higher tuition fees.

file: China_s Newspapers, After Crackdown by Beijing, Revert to a Single Voice.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's newspapers today show little trace of the independence and pluralism that they displayed last month before the Government cracked down on pro-democracy demonstrators.
Now the newspapers have reverted to a single voice, with little reliable domestic news, and if the reporters and editors are not satisfied, the only hint of it is the absence of bylines and an occasional indirect jab at the Government in articles on foreign news.
In the week after the military crackdown in China on June 4, a prominently placed headline in People's Daily read, ''The North Korean Labor News Criticizes Roh Tae Woo's Fascist Regime, Which Indiscriminately Kills Innocent Students and Citizens.''
Â 
Finding a Hidden Message
The reporter criticized Roh Tae Woo of South Korea, saying, ''The state of affairs makes clear that if Roh Tae Woo's military fascist regime is not overthrown, then the South Korean people will have no way to break away from bloodshed and death.''
But it was not farfetched to imagine that many Chinese would find a hidden message: that China's own military Government, which killed innocent students and civilians, needs to be overthrown, too.
Chinese newspapers have habitually been rife with such subtleties as reporters and editors try to work around the curbs ordered by the Government.
Â 
News More Constrained
The course of press freedom in a sense illustrates the trajectory of the entire democracy movement. 
There were tremendous initial gains, resulting in a relatively independent press, but then there was a crackdown that left news organizations even more constrained than before the protests.
Before the crackdown, criticisms were a bit more obvious and political analysts did not have to examine the international news so carefully.
About two months ago, readers found the front pages blanketed with national articles written by a newspaper's own correspondents, with perhaps a Government news item or two written by the official organ, the New China News Agency. 
But now, as part of a chorus of Government indoctrination, newspapers have yielded the front page to the official propaganda committee so that page 1 of each newspaper looks practically identical.
In bolder moments in the student movement, multiple perspectives were printed on the front pages, and some editors were openly sympathetic to the hunger-striking students. 
Just as the students had pushed their demands further than anyone expected, so, too, it seemed that news organiations had achieved much more independence and ''toumingdu,'' or ''openness,'' than anyone anticipated.
Â 
Propaganda Committee
But the swiftness with which the Government seems to have wrested control again over news organizations raises the concern that perhaps the newspapers will be indefinitely muzzled and that ordinary people will again have almost no source of information other than the official line.
For now, at least, newspapers are tightly controlled by a special propaganda committee that was formed after martial law was declared. 
In the absence of such committees, top editors and chief advisers, many of whom are elderly, were usually prestigious enough to defend a paper's decision to publish a particularly bold article.
''The passing of that generation might have several effects, and one is that people with very distinguished histories within the party are going,'' said Lynn T. White, a professor of Chinese politics at Princeton University.
''The independence or the social prestige of that kind of person can be very important in determining whether committees like this can make everything uniform,'' said Professor White, who is now doing research in Hong Kong.
Â 
'Concerned About Events'
''I'm concerned about the recent events because they might result in a structural change to some extent in the Chinese press by making the heads of newspapers less prestigious at least in normal times and so less able to have published what they feel is O.K.''
In the large protests at Tiananmen Square, where hunger-striking students had camped out before military soldiers forced them out on June 4, many journalists demonstrated to support the students and to demand greater press freedom.
Reporters at many large newspapers, including People's Daily, marched under their own banners. 
Moreover, thousands signed a petition to the Government protesting the dismissal of the editor in chief of China's boldest newspaper, World Economic Herald, based in Shanghai.
Journalists have been forced to abandon their demonstrations, and now they seem to be concentrating on retaining their jobs. 
While no reporters are known to have been arrested, there are fears that many will be.
Â 
'Subtle Passive Resistance'
If journalists are more careful now, that does not mean that they are satisfied, and there are signs they are resisting.
One possible indication of resistance is simply the near absence of staff-written articles in most newspapers. 
While it could mean that editors are ordered to publish mostly articles by the New China News Agency, that is not what the newspapers were originally intended to do. 
If it were, there would be no point in having so many newspapers, or in the newspapers having so many reporters of their own.
''There is obviously some kind of subtle passive resistance,'' said Byron S. J. Weng, a China scholar at Chinese University in Hong Kong. 
''I'd be surprised if there were none.''
In one sign of the continuing uncertainty at People's Daily, the Communist Party newspaper, a spokesman turned down a request to interview the editor in chief, Qian Liren.
Â 
Contacts Are Impossible
''Mr. Qian is in the hospital,'' the spokesman said. 
''And everyone else is too busy to receive you now.''
In China, when a senior official is unreachable because he is in the hospital, it usually means he is in political trouble, at least for the moment.
Before, it was relatively easy for foreign journalists to get to know counterparts on People's Daily and other newspapers; now it is impossible.
Recently, People's Daily has been publishing a string of articles that seem to be intended as subtle rebukes of the leadership.
The newspaper wrote about about President Raul Alfonsin of Argentina, ''President Alfonsin announced today that in order to prevent the nation from falling into a deeper crisis and to prevent the people from further suffering, he would leave his post early.''
Â 
Comparison With Argentina
The reporter for the newspaper continued: ''Now, the Alfonsin Government has already completely lost administrative ability. 
The majority of people in the ruling party propose that he should retire early from his political post to prevent the entire party from further loss of reputation.''
The suggestion seemed to be that China's Prime Minister, Li Peng, should resign.
When Prime Minister Nikolai I. Ryzhkov announced changes recently in the Soviet bureaucracy, a bold headline in People's Daily read, ''Three special characteristics of the new Government: Number of ministries and commissions reduced; Experts increase to some extent; The average age is 55.''
The subtle hint appeared to be that the Chinese Government bureaucracy could use similar trimming, more expertise and younger people.
Â 
Signs of Resistance
The article itself was written by the official New China News Agency, the Government organ through which most of the print propaganda has been disseminated. 
But the editors of People's Daily placed the article in the main position and wrote the headline.
There are also signs of resistance at other newspapers.
An article a few days ago in the China Youth News reflected on the death of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, saying, ''After the Iranian leader died on June 3, he left behind him a nation of feudal subjects in a state of utter stupefaction.''
In referring to the Iranian leader, the article seemed to be really describing Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader: ''Whenever a contradiction of political power suddenly became apparent, all that was required was a few words by him and calm would be restored.''
In another reference, the article said, ''The new Iranian leader was also decided by the word of Khomeini.''

file: China_s Peasantry Takes Measure of Its Prosperity.txt
text:
ï»¿
Ignoring a light drizzle, the women emerged from their houses carrying small plates of potatoes, goose livers and pickled cucumbers, and placed them on tables clustered outside a shiny white three-story house.
The focus of attention was a tiny boy bundled up like a bushy red ball and cradled in the arms of his new mother. 
He had just turned one month old, a magic age in the hardscrabble Chinese countryside, traditionally signifying that a baby is likely to survive, and nearly a hundred peasants had come with gifts of little red packets bulging with money.
"He's the first son," said Mai Shunjing, the scrawny grandfather, as he let out a smile filled with broken teeth and big aspirations. 
"This is an important day for our family."
Half a dozen years ago, there would have been a similar celebration, but without the food, the money or the wine. 
Life has overwhelmingly improved over the last six years, even the last six months, for the 440 people in Pan Shi, a village in a land of rich, rolling rice paddies in southern China's Guangdong Province.
Â 
Well Off and Typical
Pan Shi (pronounced pahn sher) is a bit wealthier than the average Chinese village, but customs and conditions here are still fairly indicative of how China's 900 million peasants -- three-quarters of the nation's population and nearly 17 percent of the world's -- go through life.
The great issues that absorb residents of Beijing, and through them catch the attention of the West, are of subdued interest here. 
The peasants seem little interested in challenging the Government on freedom of expression, for instance, preferring to put their energies into defying Government limits on having children.
They do not seem intrigued by macroeconomic questions, like whether China's economy now trails only that of the United States and Japan, but rather by such mundane matters as whether they will be able to afford running water instead of having to fetch water from a well.
Yet even here, the peasants feel vulnerable to what happens 1,000 miles away in the capital. 
The Communist Party's policies may change tomorrow. 
Or some official may arbitrarily decide to ruin one family or another.
"Our life is so much better now than before, but in China, you never can tell what the Government will do," said a young entrepreneur who runs a factory in another village. 
"I don't know how long this economic policy will last. 
So whenever I get the chance, I'm going abroad. 
Life is stable in America."
Â 
Knowing When to Clam Up
While they may not know much about politics, the peasants here in Pan Shi know enough to clam up when the topic comes up. 
As the festivities for his grandson continued over a 10-dish banquet by the porch, Mr. Mai turned sheepish when asked what he thought about the growing gaps between the rich and the poor.
He managed a faint smile before mumbling something about there being no gaps at all. 
Immediately, however, his son came to his rescue, and Mr. Mai slipped away.
"We don't talk politics in this house," said Jinsheng, his 29-year-old elder son. 
"My father has suffered too much in his life, from the Cultural Revolution, from this and that movement.
"He is old and afraid. 
I don't want anything to happen to him again because of politics. 
I have to protect my father. 
If it weren't for him, I wouldn't be here today."
Â 
Politics Is Passive
For most villagers, politics is not an interactive process but a passive one. 
A new political movement means that they must change the slogans on the village walls, or -- worse yet -- attend silly meetings instead of working the fields.
To be sure, the Government now holds elections for village chief, but only one person runs. 
That is partly because villagers cannot quite imagine a political race, and partly because it is no longer a very attractive position.
"Most people don't want to do that kind of work," said Chen Qiumei, a 33-year-old woman with two children, both boys. 
"The Government wants you to do a lot of work that offends other people."
A few others echoed her view. 
In a place where much of life is lived outside, there are few secrets. 
The village leaders often have take sides with one villager over another.
Â 
Spying for Family Planning
The worst part is reporting on mothers who get pregnant for a second, third or fourth time. 
The village chief risks being regarded as a traitor for turning in his friends.
Mai Ruiqian, a 46-year-old sturdy fellow with a rounding stomach, became the new Mayor this year. 
He is a member of the Mai clan that dominates the village: nearly all men are named Mai, and only their wives, who came from other villages, have other surnames. 
It is common in China for a village to be made up of a single clan, and many villages are known only by the surname of the people who live there: the Mai Village, the Wu Village, and so on.
One sign that the job is not as enviable as it was in the past is that the last chief declined to run for a second term. 
Still, Mayor Mai says he has found a way around the difficulty of picking on his neighbors: He leaves the troublesome tasks to his superiors in the township government a few miles away.
"The township sends its family planning people here," Mr. Mai said, expressing relief that he does not have to worry much about it. 
"They have the family planning rosters."
Â 
A Phone but No One to Call
Mr. Mai enjoys a few perks, like lunching in the township with officials nearly every day. 
But there are problems: arranging for water for crops and for more electricity to meet the growing demands of modernization. 
In a small triumph, the village also got a public phone recently; the only problem is that since few peasants have a phone, there is no one to call.
The phone, however, is a sign that the peasants are pretty well off in Pan Shi. 
Indeed, in addition to the public phone, two families have their own phones -- not including the Mayor.
Being moderately well off, in Pan Shi's case, means that peasants here earn an average of about $175 per person per year, instead of the national average for peasants of about $125. 
The figure may be a bit misleading because the peasants grow most of their food themselves and have few expenses.
Another reason they are doing well is that people throughout this region called Taishan have many relatives in Hong Kong, the United States and Canada. 
Taishanese is still a common dialect in Chinatowns in the United States, although in the last few decades it has been partly eclipsed by Cantonese and, more recently, Mandarin.
The gates to Pan Shi itself are a reminder of the overseas connection, having been built with money sent home from migrants abroad and carrying a tablet with the names of dozens of contributors.
Â 
Plastic for the Crops
Still, it was only when someone here introduced a new farming technique -- protecting the vegetable crops with plastic covers -- that life for everyone seemed to get better. 
The plastic serves to keep moisture in the soil and protect the vegetables from freezing, and the practice has since become widespread throughout China.
Mai Caidong, 26, is among the new entrepreneurs who are branching in new directions. 
Not content simply to spend her days wading in the rice paddies or bending over the cabbages, she is taking advantage of opportunities to go into business.
Up at 3:30 A.M., she and her husband roar off on their motorcycle to the Taishan city center every day to sell fruit and vegetables, a business that brings them about $2,600 a year. 
Last year, they saved $1,700 of that in the bank, although Ms. Mai recently diversified her assets by investing some of that in a gold necklace from Hong Kong and other jewelry.
"They let us go into private enterprise, and most people don't feel bad if they stay behind in the village," said Ms. Mai, sitting in her clean, spacious living room. 
"Of course, my husband wants to go to Guangzhou and set up a rice shop."

file: China_s Prime Minister Arrives in India.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a visit that portends major realignments in Asia, China's Prime Minister, Li Peng, arrived here today. 
It was the first trip by a Chinese head of Government in more than three decades.
India, long allied with the Soviet Union, has been thrown off balance by the calamitous disintegration of its former ally and has struggled to find a handhold in a changing world order. 
Now, presented with overtures from China -- like India an enormous, largely rural, developing country -- India sees the potential in establishing a new structure of international relations involving a newset of alliances.
Not since Zhou Enlai met with India's first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, 31 years ago, has a Chinese leader set foot on Indian soil. 
Since Mr. Zhou's visit in 1960, relations between the two Asian giants, which together embrace some 40 percent of the world's population, have wavered between outright belligerence and merely chilly. 
In that time, India, for decades an ally in all but name with the Soviet Union, and China have fought a vigorous border war, have jousted verbally over international disputes in Cambodia and Afghanistan and have differed over India's granting refuge to the exiled Tibetan leader, the Dalai Lama.
A major concern for India in discussions with Mr. Li is China's traditionally close and supportive relationship with Pakistan, with which India has fought two wars and which India insists is the major sponsor of separatist militancy in Kashmir. 
Indian officials, according to a Foreign Ministry official, are hoping to extract some assurance from Mr. Li that China will not provide Pakistan with surface-to-surface missiles as part of its weapons sales to Islamabad.
Â 
Concessions Unclear
It was unclear this evening, from either officials at the Chinese Embassy or from Chinese journalists, what concessions China was willing to offer India in its dealings with Pakistan.
Mr. Li's visit was greeted with outrage and protests by Tibetans who have taken refuge in India from China's occupation of their homeland. 
Just hours before the Chinese leader's arrival, the police detained hundreds of Tibetans protesting his visit and engaged in bloody clashes with thousands of others attempting to march on the Chinese Embassy.
But now, China and India find themselves adrift and isolated amid the rapid changes in the Soviet Union and Europe. 
China, still ostracized internationally because of its human-rights record, and India, stranded by a self-imposed economic isolationism, are struggling to find new partnerships in an emerging global order neither appear to like very much.
"It is historic," said a Western diplomat watching the visit from the sidelines. 
"It is important. 
The Indians are feeling a bit lonely in the world. 
This visit holds a whole lot more for India than for China. 
The only thing the Chinese have to gain is to pick up an ally in terms of issues like human rights and to find a friend to resist U.S. hegemony."
Â 
International Scrutiny
India has reacted sharply in recent months to Washington's efforts to raise a whole range of bilateral and regional issues -- from nuclear proliferation to intellectual property rights -- which it regards as evidence of American efforts to erode Indian sovereignty. 
Similarly, China has been vocal in its resentment of Washington's pronouncements on the issues of human rights, Beijing's weapons and nuclear technology sales and on trade issues. 
To that degree, some senior Western diplomats here said, the leaders of both nations feel beseiged.
China and India face international scrutiny over their behavior in Tibet and Kashmir respectively, both territories where there is widespread sentiment for independence. 
Diplomats here said that the Chinese and Indian leaders would likely seek support from each other that neither issue be the subject of debate in international formus, particularly the United Nations.
Yet, there remain serious differences between the two countries. 
The most visible source of tension between the two countries is China's continued occupation of Indian territory it took in the 1962 border war.

file: China_s Students Seek To Avoid Ban on Travel.txt
text:
ï»¿
Sometimes Wang Jie dreams of achieving her goal and making it to America, but there is just a hint of apprehension about what will happen if she is admitted to an American prep school and later to an American college.
"I think of myself surrounded by all these people with blond hair, and my parents too far away to help," Miss Wang said with a laugh, adding that her parents share her trepidation.
"My mother is a typical Chinese woman," Miss Wang added. 
"Whenever she sees some hope of me getting a scholarship abroad, she smiles. 
And then she cries."
Miss Wang, a 17-year-old student at one of China's best high schools, the Shanghai Foreign Language School, is part of a growing number of Chinese high school students who are trying to earn their undergraduate degrees in the United States.
The surge in younger applicants reflects improving standards of English among Chinese high school students. 
But most of the applicants say the prime reason is a requirement instituted a year ago that prevents Chinese from going abroad for at least five years after they graduate from a university.
While the Government has used the five-year requirement to make it more difficult for Chinese to go abroad for graduate study, it has not prevented high school students from applying to undergraduate programs abroad. 
Because the rule applies only to those who have graduated from a Chinese college, some college students are dropping out and applying to American colleges as transfer students.
Miss Wang plans to go first to a prep school, essentially repeating the last year or so of high school, but most high school graduates are trying to go directly to American colleges.
Â 
More Undergraduate Applicants
China already has more students in the United States than in any other country, and they are almost all graduate students. 
Only now are significant numbers of high school students applying for undergraduate programs.
Political discontent does not seem to be a factor in the yearning to go abroad; rather, some students cite a general pessimism about the future and resentment at the stifling orthodoxy and lack of academic freedom that they say now prevails at Chinese universities.
In the 1986-87 school year, 1,500 Chinese took the Toefl (Test of English as a Foreign Language) exam to apply to American undergraduate programs. 
By the 1989-90 school year, the number had soared to about 9,750. 
It is unclear how many of these are high school students and how many are college students trying to transfer to American institutions.
Only a tiny number of the high school students obtain the scholarships and the visas they need to go abroad to study. 
But their determination is sometimes staggering.
"The five-year rule makes them all the more desperate to go, to avoid the rule," said M. Elizabeth Barr, a Shanghai resident who conducts interviews for Wellesley College.
Many young people, and their parents, seem to believe that unless they escape to earn their undergraduate degrees, they will be destined to spend the next decade, and perhaps the rest of their lives, in uninspiring curriculums and careers at home.
"My niece is trying to go abroad to earn her B.A.," said a newspaper editor in Beijing. 
"It's her last chance, because otherwise she'll have to do a year of military training at the beginning of university, then four years of college, then a year after graduation working at the grass roots, and finally five years of work before she can get her passport. 
What's the point?
Why wait?"
Chinese students have grown more and more resourceful in their efforts to evade the five-year rule.
One first-year student at a Chinese university, now undergoing a compulsory year of military training, smuggled her application materials from the military camp through friends who acted as couriers. 
A student at Fudan University in Shanghai refused to go through the graduation ceremony so the requirement would not take effect.
Another student, an 18-year-old applicant to an Ivy League university, said sourly, "I refuse to take the Chinese college entrance examination, because there's nothing I can learn at a Chinese university."
If the determination of some of the students to leave is striking, so is their brilliance. 
Shen Jie, for example, is a top student at the Shanghai Foreign Language School who is applying to Princeton University and other schools.
Because China does not offer the Scholastic Aptitude Test, he took the Graduate Record Examination. 
Competing mostly against students who are already completing their American undergraduate programs, Mr. Shen earned the highest score possible in the mathematics section.
But Mr. Shen and most other Chinese applicants need more than an admission slip. 
Admission to an American university is often useless to a Chinese student without a full scholarship, and some students also need financial help even to buy the airline ticket to the United States.

file: China_s Tranquillity Is Seen as Only Skin Deep.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Government assures foreigners that life in China has loosened up, but lately many Chinese are shaking their heads, whispering: ''Nei jin, wai song'' - ''tranquillity outside, repression within.''
The expression has also been used internally by the Government to describe its policy of managing China's image, Chinese officials say.
The result of this attitude, Chinese intellectuals say, is that there is a divergence between the texture of life on the surface and the inside reality. 
Moreover, as the Government tightens its control on certain groups, contours of repression emerge to separate the largely unaffected ordinary Chinese from those under special scrutiny.
''When they lifted martial law, they announced to the world that everything was smooth and peaceful,'' a Chinese worker said, referring to the lifting of martial law in Beijing in January.
''But the troops are still here hiding indoors,'' he said. 
''To the outside world, they say life is normal. 
In Beijing, they drill the troops even harder.''
What goes on in the army is often a mystery to many Chinese. 
But particularly after noticing the army's role in the collapse of Nicolae Ceausescu's Communist Government in Romania, China quietly tightened control over its army, and there is talk about changes among regional commanders.
China's leadership has also explicitly distinguished between doctrine for domestic consumption and face-saving propaganda for the outside world. 
In closed meetings, the party has criticized the Soviet President, Mikhail S. Gorbachev, implying that he is not a true socialist, but officials have told Chinese not to publicize the criticism.
''They explained to us why Romania collapsed, and why China was different from Romania and the rest of Eastern Europe,'' a teacher said. 
''They also told us not to discuss this with outsiders, especially foreign reporters.''
Chinese intellectuals say the Communist apparatus, with its strata of rank, bureaucracy and secrecy, has many ways to tighten control over clusters of people without influencing the rest of society. 
For instance, party members are now facing greater pressures because they must re-register in a new screening procedure intended to weed out problem members.
Tension is growing at the higher echelons, partly because of power jockeying over major decisions before the National People's Congress, which convenes on March 20. 
China's security agencies have issued orders to restrict the flow of information about China's internal matters to the outside world.
The state has also managed the press and broadcasting more tightly.
