file: Chinese Aide, Visiting U.S., Sees Room for Compromise.txt
text:
ï»¿
A top Chinese official met today with Vice President Dan Quayle and Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d and said there would be no bloodshed in Beijing if the demonstrators continued to exercise restraint, an Administration official said.
The Chinese official, Wan Li, the chairman of the National People's Congress, the legislature, told Mr. Quayle that the students' ''reasonable demands'' could eventually be met and that army troops had been deployed around Beijing to maintain order, not to suppress the students.
The Administration official said Mr. Wan seemed to position himself carefully between Prime Minister Li Peng and the demonstrators. 
Mr. Wan was reported to have said China must have internal stabilityI if it is to continue liberalizing its economic system, and must end the student unrest before it can take further steps toward democracy.
Â 
Broadcasts Are Jammed
At the same time, the Voice of America said today that the Chinese authorities had begun jamming its broadcasts to China for the first time since 1978, shortly before the United States and China established diplomatic relations.
Administration officials said Mr. Quayle had emphasized several themes: the need to avoid violence and the United States' interest in promoting human rights and democracy around the world.
Mr. Baker, repeating the Administration's cautious stance toward the demonstrations, said he had told Mr. Wan, ''The United States appreciated the restraint which at least so far the Government of the People's Republic has shown.''
Speaking to reporters, Mr. Baker said, ''The United States supports freedom of speech'' and reported he had urged Mr. Wan ''that there be no resort to violence or bloodshed on the part of both sides of this problem.''
Mr. Wan, who is 73 years old, is a longtime ally of Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, and is considered a key figure in the current political crisis in Beijing. 
As head of the Congress, he could play a critical role in reported efforts by supporters of the protesters to get the Congress to revoke martial law and remove Prime Minister Li Peng.
Â 
No Public Comment
Reflecting the seriousness of the situation in Beijing, the normally genial and outgoing Mr. Wan declined to make any public comments today after his meetings with Mr. Quayle and Mr. Baker. After his talk with the Vice President in the Old Executive Office Building next to the White House, Mr. Wan maintained a stony stare as Mr. Quayle read a prepared statement, and Mr. Wan's interpreter refused to translate several questions from reporters about the demonstrations.
Mr. Wan is believed to be caught in a difficult position by the power struggle in China. 
For he is both a close friend of Mr. Deng - sometimes serving as Mr. Deng's bridge partner - and is a leading exponent of China's changes in recent years.
In the late 1970's it was Mr. Wan, then the Governor of Anhui Province in central China, who first began to decollectivize agriculture by allowing peasants to farm their own land in an effort to increase productivity. 
His action, then a breathtaking break with Communist orthodoxy, was later copied nationwide and forms the basis of Mr. Deng's political changes.
Mr. Wan has also been an outspoken supporter of more political openness, having made a major speech in 1986 advocating a greater role for China's intellectuals. 
These actions have placed him on the liberal side of the Chinese political spectrum.
Â 
Bush Meeting Scheduled
Mr. Wan, who arrived in Washington after a trip to Canada, is scheduled to meet with President Bush on Tuesday, Defense Secretary Dick Cheney on Wednesday and receive a honorary degree from Johns Hopkins University on Thursday. 
On Saturday he is to visit Disney World in Florida.
A scheduled tennis match between Mr. Wan and President Bush was canceled because ''it would be inappropriate at this time,'' Roman Popadiuk, a White House spokesman, said. 
Mr. Wan is an avid tennis player and had played with Mr. Bush when the President was the American envoy in China in 1974 and 1975.
In his 55-minute meeting with Mr. Quayle, Mr. Wan said that before he left China 10 days ago, the Chinese rulers agreed that no violence would be used against the student demonstrators. 
But Mr. Wan said that he was not fully aware of all the decisions that might have been made since then.
A statement issued by the Vice President's office said that Mr. Quayle expressed a hope that the Chinese authorities ''could resolve the situation without resorting to violence.''
Richard W. Carlson, director of the V.O.A., said that there was ''jamming on three of the five V.O.A. 
Mandarin Chinese frequencies.''
The jamming was apparently designed to cut off the flow of information to Chinese students and others demonstrating for greater democracy.
Many demonstrators had been relying on V.O.A. broadcasts to keep informed during the five weeks of pro-democracy protests.

file: Chinese Apparently Halt Rights Talks With U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a rebuff to President Bush and a warning to President-elect Bill Clinton, China appears to have suspended its discussions with the United States on human rights issues, including American inquiries about specific political prisoners.
The action by the Beijing authorities halts a process that began in December 1990, when the Bush Administration hailed the talks as a sign of progress on human rights following the violent suppression of the democracy movement in June 1989.
The dialogue on rights was never especially productive, but it gave American diplomats and visiting officials a basis for raising inquiries about specific political prisoners. 
These on-again, off-again discussions, about broad human rights topics and individual cases, sometimes drew minimal Chinese responses and occasionally led to real improvements in people's lives.
For all the frustrations, the discussions meant that China at least acknowledged that human rights were a valid topic of discussion. 
Now, even that much seems to be in jeopardy.
Mr. Clinton sharply criticized China for human rights abuses during the Presidential campaign. 
Since the election, he has eased up a little on that criticism, but indicated that he would continue to take a tougher line on the issue than the Bush Administration.
Â 
Throwing Down the Gauntlet
In effect, then, the Beijing authorities were laying down a challenge to Mr. Clinton as he and his advisers fashion a China policy.
Their action also comes as disagreements are expected in coming months on trade and other issues.
The Chinese approach in the wake of the American election is still being developed, however, and may permit discussions about human rights with legislators and others who are not part of the Administration.
In a significant step, China is welcoming a delegation of five Senators next month, a visit in which rights concerns are certain to be raised.
The latest Chinese decision seems to be a response to Mr. Bush's announcement in September that the United States would permit the sale of F-16 fighter jets to Beijing's adversary, the Chinese Nationalists on Taiwan. 
The Government here was outraged by the sale, which appeared to violate American pledges, and some diplomats expect further retaliatory action.
"The United States Government decision to sell F-16 fighters to Taiwan has seriously hurt Sino-U.S. relations," the Foreign Ministry said in an oblique statement today, 24 hours after it was asked for details about the suspension of the human rights discussions. 
"The Chinese Government has expressed its solemn and just stance on this."
The United States is not without leverage. 
Beijing, for instance, is worried that if it reacts too strongly, it will lose its low-tariff access to the American market, known as most-favored-nation status. 
Mr. Clinton has said that he favors linking China's trade with its human rights situation, but much will depend on how this principle is drafted into legislation on extending this trading status.
A Western diplomat explained: "You're talking about the U.S. taking 30 percent of their exports, and their exports to the U.S. are growing 40 percent this year. 
And they're counting on this to continue to grow. 
It's something that their entire reform package is based on."
Mr. Clinton's changing tone in recent weeks leaves his intentions unclear. 
During the campaign, he said that President Bush had failed to win concessions from China on rights and trade issues, but last week he said that "in the last several months" China had begun to moderate its policies.
"We have a big stake in not isolating China, in seeing that China continues to develop a market economy," Mr. Clinton said. 
"But we also have to insist, I believe, on progress in human rights and human decency."
The Foreign Ministry did not directly respond to the questions about whether the rights discussions had been terminated. 
By avoiding a direct response, the ministry seemed to be offering tacit confirmation without painting itself into a corner.
In a sign of the sensitivity of the issue, the United States Embassy in Beijing took two days to provide this terse response: "We believe an active dialogue on the issue offers the best chance of furthering both countries' interests. 
We continue to press China on human rights at every opportunity."
The embassy declined to comment further, but at a meeting earlier this month, American diplomats are believed to have tried to give the Chinese Foreign Ministry an unofficial though written inquiry on political prisoners.
The Chinese refused to accept it, so the Americans left it on a chair as they packed up and prepared to leave the room. 
The Chinese picked it up and said that there would be no response. 
The Americans were apparently heartened that they at least picked it up.
China's growing trade imbalance with the United States, in which its exports far exceed its imports, is another prickly issue. 
The surplus, now second only to Japan's, amounted to $13.4 billion in the first nine months of this year, more than in all of 1991.
The Beijing leadership has also been slow to carry out an agreement with Washington on curbing the export of goods made with prison labor.
If that were not enough to worry about, the Chinese Government's fierce opposition to democratic changes in Hong Kong may cause further tensions with the United States.
There have been significant improvements in other areas. 
China seems to have curtailed its arms sales, and it has allowed many, if not all dissidents to leave the country. 
It has released some prominent Catholics from prison and sharply toned down its Communist propaganda.
Last month, Beijing caved in on American demands that it open its markets to more American goods, and it is taking other steps to allow parts of its economy to be run on market lines. 
And, in a bouquet to Mr. Clinton, the Chinese announced shortly after the election that they would buy two million tons of American wheat, the first such purchase this year.
The suspension of human rights discussions was apparently decided at the highest level. 
The leadership informed various Chinese ministries that they should not discuss rights issues with American officials.
A test of how the Chinese will apply the suspension is expected during the Senators' visit. 
According to current plans, the delegation is to be led by Senator David L. Boren and to include Senators Bob Kerrey, Carl Levin, Claiborne Pell and John W. Warner.
In an important suggestion that it wants to be conciliatory, China plans to let the Senators visit Tibet. 
It ordinarily controls access to Tibet very tightly, effectively barring Western journalists from visiting the region.

file: CHINESE CHIEF SETS HARD POLICY LINE.txt
text:
ï»¿
In its most sweeping declaration of policy since leadership changes in June, the Communist Party acknowledged some mistakes today but called for vigilance against what it described as efforts by the West to subvert the Chinese Government and institute capitalism.
''Hostile forces, international as well as internal, are still engaged in activities of sabotage and subversion against us,'' Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party leader, warned in an 80-minute address shown on national television. 
The speech, part of the commemorations of the 40th anniversary of Communist rule on Sunday, had been circulated among the leadership and reflected not only Mr. Jiang's views but also those of all other top officials.
Giving a methodical if vague survey of China's economic, political and ideological policies, the speech was generally harsher than expected. 
While it reaffirmed the need for economic changes, some of the phrasing was more reminiscent of the 1960's and '70's than of the last decade of the open-door policy.
Maoist Phrase Resurrected
Mr. Jiang said China was engaged in ''a serious class struggle,'' a term that has occasionally been used in recent months but that has generally been out of favor since the Maoist era ended 13 years ago. 
In the past, use of the phrase often accompanied repression. 
Mr. Jiang said Beijing would ''isolate and attack the handful of hostile elements'' behind the democracy movement this spring that ended with a crackdown in Beijing on June 4.
''The disturbances stirred up by hostile forces, both internal and external, were aimed at overthrowing the Chinese Communist Party's leadership and subverting the socialist system, at turning China into a bourgeois republic and reducing it once again to a dependency of the Western capitalist powers,'' Mr. Jiang said. 
A 63-year-old technocrat who was appointed Communist Party General Secretary in June, Mr. Jiang has been designated by Deng Xiaoping, the nations' senior leader, to be the next paramount leader of China. 
The speech was perhaps his most significant opportunity yet to gain credibility and authority by speaking on behalf of the entire leadership.
China's new leadership has given mixed signals since it took power after the violent suppression of the democracy movement. 
The speech does not resolve the uncertainties, but it suggests an outline of China's directions: vigorous repression of any sign of dissent, economic retrenchment, increased central planning, but apparently modest extension of some economic restructuring programs.
Â 
A Split Is Acknowledged
In the most explicit statement so far of the divisions within China, Mr. Jiang warned that ''two completely different views exist on the issue of reform and opening.''
One view, he said, was the correct one, which would result in modernization and perfection of socialism. 
The other aims for ''total Westernization'' and ''constitutes transformation into capitalism and brings China into the orbit of the capitalist system of the West.''
By declaring that those who favor more aggressive change are effectively agents of Western capitalism, the party was escalating the accusations against them and serving notice that favoring ''bourgeois liberalization'' is an extremely serious offense.
With members of the Politburo and other top leaders seated behind him to underscore unity, Mr. Jiang acknowledged that the Party had made mistakes that had cost support.
''After we became the party in power, some phenomena of bureaucratism, petty tyranny, abuse of power for personal gains, corruption and degeneration, which result in alienation from the masses of the people, have gradually emerged,'' he said. 
The problems became worse in recent years, he added, and he called for extensive new ideological education to restore the Communist spirit and faith in the party.
Â 
Small Role for Private Sector
The struggles against foreign and domestic rivals ''will continue for a long time,'' Mr. Jiang said.
In economic matters, Mr. Jiang called for more central planning and suggested that China for the next three years at least would have to pursue its policy of economic retrenchment. 
During this period, he said, China should increase centralization and the proportion of revenue controlled by the central Government.
Apparently in response to concerns about attacks by the Government on the private sector, Mr. Jiang vigorously stressed the need for private enterprise. 
But he emphasized that it would always occupy a small role in the economy and suggested higher taxation of entrepreneurs as a way of avoiding rising disparities in incomes.
Mr. Jiang denied that the economic retrenchment amounted to a slowdown in the policy of economic change, and he said that China would maintain and further develop policies related to special economic zones and open areas along the coast. 
Apparently in a reference to China's fledgling stock markets, he said that China would continue to experiment with various ''pilot reforms.''

file: Chinese Dissident Criticizes U.S. on Human Rights.txt
text:
ï»¿
Fang Lizhi, China's leading dissident, said in an interview broadcast tonight that the United States had a ''double standard'' for human rights that was tougher on the Soviet Union than on China.
In the interview, with NBC News, Mr. Fang, who went into exile in Britain last month with his wife, Li Shuxian, also criticized the Bush Administration's decision to send a special mission of senior Administration officials to China last year after the authorities crushed the democracy movement.
Speaking in both English and Chinese, he also talked of the need he saw to push China into the international community and of the type of life he and his wife lived in the United States Embassy in Beijing, where they took refuge for more than a year.
The London bureau of NBC News said the interview had been conducted by Tom Brokaw and had been taped on Thursday at a hotel in central London.
Fang Sees a Double Standard
On the issue of human rights, Mr. Fang was asked whether he believed that United States officials had a double standard and were ''softer'' on China than on other countries.
Speaking in English, Mr. Fang said: ''Yeah, I think without doubt there is still some double standard there. 
Of course, they are better than before.''
President Bush, in London for a summit conference of NATO leaders, was asked at a news conference today about Mr. Fang's view that the United States had a double standard for human rights.
''I'd say that he's wrong,'' Mr. Bush said. 
''He's got a little time warp here, because we spoke out at the NATO meeting, indeed, I think we took the lead at the last, at a meeting in Europe, I guess it was the G-7 meeting, not NATO, where we took the lead in expressing our joint indignation in terms of the abuses of human rights at Tiananmen Square.
''We've kept certain sanctions on China. 
I am heartened that Fang Lizhi is free and free now to say what's on his mind. 
I would say that if he feels that way, he's simply not expressing the facts as they are. 
I don't agree with that. 
I know that some of my critics in the United States Congress say that, and I think they're just as wrong as they can be.''
Â 
Kept From Dinner With Bush
Mr. Fang said that he had not communicated personally with President Bush but that he hoped to meet him because the President still owed Mr. Fang and his wife dinner. 
He was referring to an incident in February 1989, when the Chinese Government prevented the couple from attending a banquet to which Mr. Bush had invited them at a hotel in Beijing.
Asked at his news conference whether he would invite Mr. Fang to the White House for dinner the President said: ''Well, he's here in this country. 
I thought he wanted to stay out of the public eye. 
I thought he himself said so, so you've got a little different information than that.''
Mr. Fang and Miss Li were in the United States Embassy in Beijing from June 5, 1989, until they were allowed to leave China last month. 
They took refuge in the embassy after the Communist leaders sent troops and tanks into Tiananmen Square to crush student-led pro-democracy demonstrations and after pro-Government demonstrators burned Mr. Fang in effigy.
The Chinese authorities issued a warrant for the couple's arrest and accused them of offenses tantamount to treason. 
Mr. Fang played no public role in the student campaign for political change, but China's leaders saw him as a major inspiration behind the protests and demanded that the United States hand the couple over to the authorities.
Â 
Medical Condition Cited
Chinese officials have been quoted as saying the couple asked to go abroad for medical treatment, vowed not to engage in activities directed against China and were allowed to leave after showing signs of repentance.
On June 26, the day after he arrived in Britain, Mr. Fang said he and Miss Li were looking forward ''in the next few days to a period of quiet, a chance to rest and recuperate and to have some medical tests.''
Mr. Fang, a distinguished astrophysicist, has accepted a post as a senior visiting fellow at Cambridge University's Institute of Astronomy, where he will study the early universe.
Mr. Fang said he did not ''think it was a good idea'' for President Bush to send the national security adviser, Brent Scowcroft and Deputy Secretary of State Lawrence S. Eagleburger to China last year. 
But he said China should not be isolated but should be pushed into the international community.
Mr. Fang said that he and Miss Li had sometimes felt alone at the United States Embassy but later received many letters and other ''information.''
He said he could communicate freely with foreigners during his stay.
Mr. Fang said he had lived the life of an ''American scientist'' in the beginning of his stay at the embassy but that he and his wife had become ''more and more Chinese,'' always eating Chinese food, which was prepared in a microwave oven. 
''And we used that modern machine to cook Chinese food,'' Mr. Fang said, ''so we give a new name called 'high-tech Chinese restaurant.'
''

file: Chinese Dissident to Study in U.S. (and to Speak Out).txt
text:
ï»¿
Fang Lizhi, China's most prominent dissident, said today that he planned to study in the United States for at least six months beginning in January. 
He also said that while he was there he would meet with exiled Chinese dissidents and speak out against his country's Government.
In an interview, Mr. Fang, an astrophysicist, said he might make the United States his permanent place of exile. 
He was allowed to leave China last month with his wife, Li Shuxian, more than a year after taking refuge in the United States Embassy in Beijing during the violent crackdown on dissent.
Mr. Fang's intentions seem likely to cause concern among the hard-liners in Beijing and could prove an irritant in relations between Beijing and Washington, but they do not appear directly to break any known elements of the agreement between the countries that allowed him and Miss Li to go free.
Face-Saving Measure
Although they were initially released to Britain, apparently as a face-saving response to Chinese concerns that Mr. Fang not go to the United States, there is no known agreement that prevents them from moving later on.
And while Beijing might regard Mr. Fang's speaking out against the Government as a breach of his pledge not to conduct ''anti-China'' activities while in exile, Mr. Fang was careful not to rule out criticism of the Chinese Government, as opposed to criticism of the nation itself.
In the wide-ranging interview, Mr. Fang, whose full name is pronounced fahng lee-jur (rhyming with burr), gave details of negotiations involving the United States Embassy in Beijing and the Chinese authorities that led to exile for him and his wife, who is also a physicist and a prominent dissident.
He said the authorities had asked him to agree not to participate in activities against the Government and to admit that he was a criminal. 
He said he had refused on both counts but agreed to other terms, including a demand that he say he was going abroad for medical treatment. 
Mr. Fang, who spoke in English throughout the interview, called that professed reason ''diplomat's language'' and said nothing was wrong with his health.
Â 
Urges Sanctions Against Beijing
Appearing relaxed and cheerful at his office at Cambridge University's Institute of Astronomy, Mr. Fang also touched on the state of the democracy movement in China, the need he saw for continued economic sanctions against the country and the role the Bush Administration could play in bringing about change.
Mr. Fang, who is here doing research into the structure of the universe, said that the Chinese authorities had allowed one of his sons, who had remained behind when the couple left, to travel to Britain a week ago and that the family, including a second son, had now been reunited.
Mr. Fang, 54 years old, said he had accepted an invitation from the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, N.J. 
- an independent institute that grants fellowships for research in various fields - and would conduct research there for at least six months.
Mr. Fang was asked whether he would meet Chinese dissident leaders while in the United States, where he would have a broader platform for his views. 
He said, ''I think so.''
Asked whether he would speak out, he replied, ''Yes, I think so.''
But he said that whether he would be willing to serve as the leader of exiled dissidents would ''depend on the situation.''
Mr. Fang said he might make his home in exile in the United States because it ''is very large and very easy to spend a longer time'' there than in Britain. 
He said he would visit various parts of the United States and had already received invitations from universities and institutes in California, Chicago, Colorado and New York.
Â 
Chose to Go to Britain
He said the Chinese authorities, for reasons that were unclear to him, had not wanted the United States to be his first stop after leaving Beijing. 
He said he had told the authorities he was willing to go to any developed country, and ultimately chose Britain, where he conducted research in 1979.
Mr. Fang and Miss Li flew to exile in Britain on June 25 after having been in the United States Embassy in Beijing since June 5, 1989. 
They took refuge in the embassy the day after the Communist leaders sent troops into Tianamen Square and after pro-Government demonstrators burned Mr. Fang in effigy.
Mr. Fang said he believed that the Government had allowed him to leave largely because it was feeling the pressure of economic sanctions. 
But the authorities also wanted to improve their image, he said, because ''intellectuals don't believe them and students don't like them.''
He said Western governments should relax sanctions against China only when it freed imprisoned dissidents and returned human rights to its citizens. 
He called on President Bush, whom he said he hoped to meet in the United States, to demand that pro-democracy demonstrators be released, adding that only about two student leaders had been freed.
He said Mr. Bush could not have acted to prevent the killings near Tiananmen Square because by that time, ''the Chinese Government had already become illogical.''
But he said a stronger response from the Bush Administration in the aftermath could have lessened the number of people who were detained or killed. 
He said at least 1,000 people were still in jail and gave 700 as the ''lower limit'' of the number of people who died when the Government sent troops and tanks into the square to crush the student-led demonstrations.
Â 
Long-Term Optimism

THREE times a week, 19 Chinese dissidents meet in Albert Einstein's former lecture hall to discuss how to bring democracy to their homeland.
Many of them fled to the West after the bloody crackdown in Tiananmen Square two years ago. 
Now they work from a safe haven inside the ivy-covered walls of Jones Hall at Princeton University, where Einstein, a refugee from another regime, Nazi Germany, once taught.
"We carry so much blood," said Su Wei, a 38-year-old writer and literary critic.
"I don't want to be a political leader," he said. 
"But there was so much blood we spent at the square, so big a price for the democracy hated in China.

'They Need Our Voice'

Some are working on plays, poems or books they hope will find their way into the hands, minds and hearts of the Chinese people.

Memorizing, Not Analyzing
Surrounded by Chinese calligraphy about human rights in the office of the Princeton Chinese Initiative, the scholars described their campaign over a constant stream of cigarettes and warm Coke, both reminders of home.
Bai Meng, 28, the poet who drafted the "Declaration of the Hunger Strikers" for the student protesters, said that before democracy could work in China the people's minds needed to be reshaped.
He said that in China, students were taught to memorize, and not analyze, the Government's version of history. 
They are exposed only to acceptable theories like Communism, he said.

Zhang Langlang, 48, is a painter, writer, philosopher and humorist.

It is not known what evidence existed against the three men, who appeared to be in their 20's or perhaps early 30's, or even exactly what role each was accused of having played in the incident.

Called Mentally Retarded

On U.S. 
Relations

'According to Law'
''The tiny minority of criminals will be punished according to law, and the Government will be lenient in dealing with most of the people who took part in parades and demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes, even those with extremist opinions,'' he said.

The statement cited ''bureaucratism,'' passivity and corruption as some of the practices that had helped to estrange party officials from the ordinary people, many of whom have privately expressed disenchantment with the party since the military crackdown on the Chinese pro-democracy movement last June.
''This means they are indeed keen on improving relations with the people, and getting support from the people,'' a foreign diplomat here said.

Laying the Groundwork
Diplomats and Chinese say the Central Committee meeting is preparing the groundwork for the coming session of the National People's Congress, China's Legislature, which is expected to announce an easing of austerity policies as well as changes of senior and mid-level Government personnel.

file: Chinese Seem to Be Risking More Open Protests.txt
text:
ï»¿
The campaign by Deng Xiaoping and other Chinese leaders for faster economic change seems to be having an unintended effect: Dissidents and ordinary citizens are becoming a bit bolder in challenging the authorities.
Partly because the hard-liners appear to be losing ground as the airwaves fill with calls for reform, many Chinese say they find the atmosphere looser and less ominous. 
Some say that the fear that has gripped the country for the last three years, since the Tiananmen Square crackdown of June 1989, is gradually easing.
Consequently, some dissidents are no longer hiding their activities. 
They now openly meet with foreign reporters, write for foreign publications and denounce human rights abuses in their country.
Â 
Overseas Publication
Zhang Weiguo, a Shanghai journalist whose newspaper, The World Economic Herald, was closed during the Tiananmen democracy movement, is one of several democracy advocates who seem less afraid of the leadership than it is of him.
"I'm writing more articles now than when I was at The Herald," Mr. Zhang said in a recent interview in Shanghai. 
Since his articles cannot be published in China, he writes about China for leading newspapers in Taiwan and Hong Kong, and he has given telephone interviews to the BBC's Chinese-language service.
The security apparatus is clearly alarmed about such growing boldness, but it seems at a loss how to react. 
So the authorities settle for harassing Mr. Zhang, summoning him periodically for interrogation, as well as threatening him and refusing to allow him to leave Shanghai. 
But Mr. Zhang, who spent more than 20 months in prison after the 1989 crackdown, continues to speak.
Perhaps the only effective way to silence someone so fearless would be to re-arrest him and sentence him to a long prison term. 
But this might provoke a furor abroad, reinforce the image of China as a brutal and repressive place and increase the chance of American trade sanctions.
Â 
Order vs. Freedom
The treatment of Mr. Zhang is relatively lenient compared with the repression of a few years ago -- in 1989, for example, a marine biology student named Chen Lantao was sentenced to 18 years simply for speaking against the Government.
As fear diminishes, China may be becoming a more open country -- but perhaps also a less stable one. 
For the three years after the army's crackdown, in which hundreds were killed, thousands hurt and many more imprisoned, the peace was preserved through a balance of terror: The people were afraid of the Government and the Government was afraid of the people.
Some of that fear lingers on both sides, but less than before. 
Some in the Government acknowledge their apprehension that people could eventually take to the streets and overthrow the Communists, but there is a clear division within the leadership about the nature of the threat.
Hard-liners say the risk comes primarily from the dissidents and from contact with the West, and so they favor harsh repression. 
But others -- including Mr. Deng, the 88-year-old senior leader -- suggest that dissidents will get nowhere as long as the economy is booming, and so the leaders fear trade sanctions perhaps more than outspoken critics.
Still, there are several indications that the greater boldness has affected not only dissidents but also ordinary Chinese, although in ways that are not overtly political.
When application forms to buy stock ran out in the southern city of Shenzhen last month, some 50,000 would-be investors accused the Government of corruption and rampaged on the streets.
"That rioting would never have occurred in the immediate aftermath of the Tiananmen crackdown," said a Chinese journalist in Beijing. 
"But this year, with all the new talk about reform, people are feeling more hopeful and braver than before."
The journalist added, however, that most people are still afraid of openly criticizing the Government. 
For now, a repeat of large-scale pro-democracy demonstrations is impossible, he said.
"Lots of people are willing to be followers," he said. 
"But no one wants to be the first to say anything. 
There's a saying: the first bird in the flock is the one that gets shot. 
So there are plenty of birds that want to fly, but not in front."
The greater public boldness reached Beijing late last month, when China's normally docile soccer fans stormed out of Workers Stadium in Beijing after a loss to South Korea and marched angrily down the middle of the street. 
They shouted curses at the Chinese team, the head coach and the police.
It was the third outburst in a week from soccer fans, and the authorities were quick to arrest a few people and denounce the behavior.
The official Beijing Daily wrote, "These riotous acts, totally alien to China's long-noted politeness and courtesy, smeared the image of Beijing as well as our country."
Chinese soccer hooligans may seem like paragons of obedience compared to the more violent British soccer rioters, but in one sense the disruptions here are much more significant than in Britain.
The glue that keeps most Western governments together is public support for the system; in China, according to many foreign diplomats and Chinese, the adhesive is fear. 
So if Chinese soccer fans dare to march on the streets because of dissatisfaction with a sports competition, there is at least some chance that they may dare to protest the form of government.
Â 
Pitfalls in Leniency
Recent history also suggests that a diminishing fear of the authorities might eventually lead to political protest.
Throughout the last four decades, the times when Chinese have protested against the Government have not generally been the periods of greatest discontent. 
Rather, they have occurred when people perceived -- usually incorrectly -- that the atmosphere was sufficiently lenient that they could get away with it.
To be sure, the authorities do their best to let people know that they will not get away with it. 
Some democracy campaigners, though not the most prominent ones, reportedly were quietly arrested over the last few months, and political prisoners in northeastern China recently smuggled out a letter complaining of continued beatings in their jail cells.
The latest police move occurred today, when the authorities detained Shen Tong, a democracy advocate who had returned from exile in the United States, as he prepared to hold a news conference. 
If Mr. Shen's return was a sign of the dissidents' new boldness, his detention was a signal that the authorities are willing to fight back.
So far, however, the Government has not reacted to another recent development that may cause security officials to furrow their brows. 
Three prominent independent-minded Chinese openly joined the board of a New York-based organization, Human Rights in China, that is often critical of the Beijing authorities. 
While the Government has not punished the three, it is not clear that it will allow them to leave China to attend a board meeting in the fall.
This relative restraint is having an unintended effect: It is skewing the incentive structure for dissidents. 
A few years ago, any Chinese knew that denouncing the Government would mean immediate dismissal, arrest and incarceration. 
But now, some critics suffer only harassment, and they achieve international renown and invitations to be visiting scholars at foreign universities.
Likewise, relatives of political prisoners used to believe that they were best off keeping quiet so as not to offend the authorities. 
But in several recent cases, family members have concluded that they are better off causing a fuss or at least speaking to the foreign press. 
In part they believe that attention in the West may result in shorter sentences for their loved ones, and in part they seem to feel more daring and assertive than they used to.
"With all the talk about reform, the Government has been telling us to be bolder in our actions," said a worker in his 20's, flashing a mischievous grin. 
"And so that's what's happening. 
We're bolder."

file: Chinese Set Off Their Biggest Nuclear Explosion.txt
text:
ï»¿
China today set off the largest underground nuclear test it has ever conducted, the State Department said. 
The explosion was thought to have a yield of about one megaton, equivalent to a million tons of TNT.
The blast, which took place about 1 A.M. Eastern daylight time, had 70 times the explosive power of the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima, and exceeded the 150-kiloton limit observed by Washington and Moscow under a 1990 treaty, scientists said.
The Bush Administration said it regretted the action by Beijing and urged restraint.
Â 
Limit on Underground Tests
There were sharp condemnations of China in Congress. 
Legislators from both major parties have been critical of what they see as an unacceptably conciliatory policy toward China by President Bush.
[The Chinese Foreign Ministry issued a statement confirming that Beijing had held a nuclear test. 
The statement said China was in favor of "complete prohibition on nuclear tests within the framework of effective nuclear disarmament."]
The Chinese test was only one-fifth as powerful as the largest underground test by the United States, a five-megaton blast in Alaska on Nov. 
6, 1971, the most powerful underground nuclear explosion on record. 
A megaton is 1,000 kilotons.
The largest underground test by the Soviet Union was a 2.8 to 4 megaton blast on Oct. 
27, 1973, a year before Moscow and Washington signed a treaty limiting the size of those explosions to 150 kilotons. 
The pact was ratified in 1990.
The Chinese test comes on the heels of persistent reports that Beijing is selling missile technology to Middle Eastern nations, and at a time when Beijing is rejecting all criticism of its human-rights record.
Arms-control experts also seized the chance to criticize the Bush Administration for its opposition to a comprehensive international test-ban treaty.
China's last and largest previous underground test, an explosion of between 50 and 200 kilotons, was on Aug. 
16, 1990.
The United States set off two underground nuclear explosions this year in Nevada, on March 26 and April 30. 
Both were reported to be less than 150 kilotons.
Large underground tests, even on the scale of today's blast in China, are considerably smaller than the atmospheric explosions of the 1950's and 1960's. 
On Feb. 
28, 1954, the United States tested a 15 megaton bomb at Bikini Atoll in the Pacific. 
The largest atmospheric test on record was conducted by the Soviet Union, a 58-megaton explosion on Oct. 
30, 1961.
Atmospheric tests were prohibited by the 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty, signed by more than 100 countries.
Today's Chinese underground explosion was situated in Xinjiang Province in northwestern China by Scandinavian seismologists, according to reports from Stockholm. 
In Hong Kong, scientists at first thought they were registering an earthquake.
"This suggests that the Chinese must be trying to develop large yield, offensive nuclear warheads for long-range missiles," said Gary Milhollin, director of the Wisconsin Project on Nuclear Arms Control. 
"This is a city-buster."
But he emphasized that China was still no threat to the United States in the development of intercontinental ballistic missiles.
Richard A. Boucher, the State Department spokesman, said, "We regret that the Chinese have conducted this test and that they are not demonstrating the same restraint as shown by Russia, ourselves, or the other nuclear weapons states."
Â 
Cold-War Mentality
China is not a party to the Threshold Test Ban Treaty between the former Soviet Union and the United States, which came into effect in December 1990. 
Under that pact, underground tests are limited to 150 kilotons.
"It is rather ironic that the United States would criticize other countries for testing," said Dunbar Lockwood, senior analyst at the Arms Control Association, a private research organization. 
"The United States under the Reagan and Bush Administrations has been one of the major impediments to progress toward a comprehensive test ban."
Mr. Milhollin described the Chinese test as illustrative of a cold-war mentality in Beijing. 
He added: "This is the price we're paying for not having a worldwide comprehensive nuclear test ban treaty. 
It means China can improve its ability to destroy U.S cities at long range by testing."
Leonard S. Spector, a nuclear-weapons expert at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace who has recently been in China, said in an interview that Beijing's test could take the pressure off the Bush Administration to agree to a comprehensive test ban. 
Pressure has been growing internationally and in Congress for that action.
Â 
Moratorium on Tests
In October 1991, the former Soviet President, Mikhail S. Gorbachev, announced a one-year moratorium on the testing of nuclear weapons. 
Boris N. Yelstin, the Russian President, has suggested in public remarks that he is preparing to resume testing this fall if there is no reciprocal movement from the United States.
The French have also stopped testing to encourage international action on a comprehensive ban.
"Thoughtful advocates of testing restraint think that a comprehensive test ban might draw in India," Mr. Spector said.
Senator Alan Cranston, Democrat of California and chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations subcommittee on East Asia, reacted to reports of today's test by calling China a "renegade nation."
"This test will strongly reinforce Congressional efforts, which I once again will help lead, to deny China most-favored-nation trade staus unless China complies with international non-proliferation standards," Senator Cranston said in a statement.

file: Chinese Trials End_ Fate of Hundreds Unclear.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a wave of trials ending Tuesday, Chinese courts sentenced 18 of the nation's best-known dissidents to prison for terms ranging up to 13 years. 
But while those trials have ended, almost nothing is known about the hundreds of others who are in prison for taking part in the Tiananmen democracy movement.
The Chinese have never given an accounting of those arrested in the crackdown beginning in June 1989, but most estimates are that more than 1,000 people are still in prison, detention centers or re-education camps for their involvement in the Tiananmen Square protests.
"Just the cases that will serve their purposes are announced, and the rest are never reported," said Robin Munro, a Hong Kong-based researcher for Asia Watch, a human rights organization. 
"We certainly believe these trials are the tip of the iceberg."
Among the others are such people as Han Dongfang, a 28-year-old railway employee who led a Beijing workers group in support of the students; Wu Jiaxiang, a Communist Party researcher who sympathized with the students and was arrested in July 1989, and Chen Ting, a worker arrested forhelping to organize protests in the central Chinese city of Hefei.
Asia Watch has compiled a list of 960 names of people believed imprisoned, and many others have been quietly sentenced without their cases coming to public attention. 
Family members often say they dare not seek help from foreigners.
"In our hearts, we feel terrible for not speaking out," said a relative of a young man who is serving an eight-year prison sentence. 
The family decided not to report the prisoner's name to foreign human rights workers for fear that the family members themselves would get in trouble."Some day, things will change," the relative said, "but for now we must keep silent."
The stiffest sentence in the latest trials was 13 years. 
But in occasional trials in the provinces, local leaders of protests were given even harsher punishments. 
In Shandong Province, for example, a 22-year-old worker named Zhang Jie was officially reported to have been sentenced to 18 years in prison for making a speech denouncing the army crackdown in Beijing.
Workers are typically given much longer sentences than intellectuals, and often face a more physically punishing prison regime. 
Although intellectuals may risk serving their terms in solitary confinement, workers are more likely to risk beatings, freezing nights in unheated cells, and near-starvation rations.In addition to those formally tried, a large number of protesters were sent to re-education camps. 
The police are allowed to send people to such camps for up to three years without going through the courts. 
The United States State Department report on human rights, issued this month, says that just two re-education camps near Beijing housed more than 800 youths detained extrajudicially for involvement in the Tiananmen protests.
So far, there has been no public reaction within China to the trials, and most Chinese express relatively little outrage or even interest. 
Some attribute the muted reaction to a yearning by people to withdraw from political affairs, which they say are burdened with painful memories and a feeling of hopelessness.
"People noticed the sentences, but itwasn't a big thing," said one Chinese who is moderately critical of the Government. 
"People are much more interested in the gulf war."
Family members of political prisoners have been warned not to talk to foreign journalists, and this places them in an agonizing position: do they disclose what they regard as outrageous injustices, if the consequence will only be further punishment inflicted on them and their loved ones?
"They are really villains, trying to exploit the love a woman has for her husband," Hou Xiaotian, wife of one of the dissidents who was sentenced to 13 years, wrote in an open letter last month. 
In the letter she described how prison guards refused to accept items she had brought for her husband unless she disclosed her contacts with correspondents.

file: Chinese Upheaval Shakes Italy_s Communists.txt
text:
ï»¿
The explosive events in China have sent shivers through Italy's faltering Communist Party, the largest in the West, and have emboldened Socialists who hope to emerge soon as the country's dominant left-wing group.
Communists here are bracing for what may prove to be unusually important elections for the European Parliament on June 18.
It clearly troubles party elders that because of China's turmoil Italians will vote with fresh memories of a Communist government that ordered its soldiers to shoot citizens demanding democracy. 
As a result, they have gone to considerable lengths to denounce Chinese leaders and to organize demonstrations of solidarity with the student-led democratic movement.
Perhaps more significantly for the future of Communism in Western Europe, the party secretary, Achille Occhetto, has gone further than ever to align himself with European social democratic movements in his continuing campaign to stop a decade-long slide at the polls. 
His efforts have even rekindled a public debate that arises periodically over whether it is time for the party to change its name. 
''We are not part of an international Communist movement,'' Mr. Occhetto said in a newspaper interview this week.
''In the East, communism is a term that has no relation any longerto its historic origins, and constitutes a political framework that is completely wrong,'' he said, adding, ''There is absolutely nothing left of communism as a unitary and organic system.''
Today, he called on the Government to freeze economic relations with China.
If Mr. Occhetto's damage-control strategy fails, the Socialist leader, former Prime Minister Bettino Craxi, is standing by to pick up the pieces.
Â 
Craxi Weary of Junior Role
Throughout the 1980's, the Socialists have been junior partners to the more numerous Christian Democrats in a series of coalition Governments, but Mr. Craxi is growing weary of the role. 
His ambition is to command an Italian left restructured under a single umbrella, but first his Socialists must overtake the Communists, who though weakening, have been second only to the Christian Democrats throughout the postwar era.
Thus, for him, the European parliamentary elections are far more critical than simply who will wind up going to Strasbourg. 
To drum up interest in the campaign, Mr. Craxi went so far as to help bring down the Government, through relentless badgering that finally impelled Prime Minister Ciriaco De Mita to resign three weeks ago.
While Mr. De Mita remains in office as caretaker over the shell of a Government, senior politicians have held endless consultations to figure out who should lead next. 
Their talks drag on and on, but a solution seems likely to elude them until after the so-called European elections.
Mr. Craxi was heartened last week by the results of local elections in 165 municipalities. 
For the first time, Socialist candidates won a bigger share of the vote than the Communists, 19.1 percent to 16.9 percent. 
In 1987 parliamentary elections, by comparison, the Socialists drew only 14 percent to the Communists' 22.6 percent.
The balloting in a relatively small number of localities was hardly conclusive. 
Mr. Occhetto dismissed it out of hand, saying his party lost primarily in Mafia-dominated towns in the South.
Nevertheless, political commentators say that if the results are duplicated on June 18, they may have a broad impact on the balance of party power, and could even trigger early national elections. 
At the least, it is said, they are likely to determine the shape of the next government.

"Our Town," Thornton Wilder's classic drama about life in turn-of-the-century New Hampshire, may seem the quintessential American play, but to ALAN ALDA, star of a production that opened in London last night, "It is universal."

file: Citicorp_s Hong Kong Deal Called Vote of Confidence.txt
text:
ï»¿
Citicorp, the largest banking company in the United States, yesterday gave Hong Kong one of the strongest votes of confidence it has received since the upheaval in China in June shook its markets.
Citicorp said it would arrange $5.2 billion (Hong Kong), or $667 million (United States), in loans to build two office towers in the territory's central district and may take an equity stake in the project. 
Citicorp plans to buy office space in the complex, and one tower may bear its name.
''We wouldn't have made the announcement at this time if we did not want to display in a dramatic way a vote of confidence and the fact that we intend to stay,'' said Steven Baker, Citicorp''s chief corporate officer in Hong Kong and division executive for East Asia.
Analysts noted that this also is a time to find property bargains in Hong Kong.
Â 
'A Very Good Price'
''Now is not a bad time to pick up assets,'' said Cheah Cheng Hye, head of research at Morgan Grenfell (Hong Kong) Securities. 
''If you don't think Hong Kong is going to fall apart after 1997, you're going to get in at a very good price.''
The invitation to participate in the project came from the Great Eagle Company, a major Hong Kong property developer that recently bought the last prime building site in the downtown business district.
The price Great Eagle paid at a Government auction, $2.7 billion, was well below expectations and about half the valuation placed on the site when Hong Kong's market was at its peak.
The territory's real estate market has been hard hit since the Chinese Government, which is scheduled to assume control of Hong Kong in 1997, suppressed pro-democracy demonstrations in June.
Â 
Completed in 1993
This is not the first time fears over Hong Kong's return to Chinese sovereignty have contributed to slumps in the local property market. 
Prices were notably weak in the early 1980's.
The high-rise project on Garden Road is to be completed in 1993. 
The site is next to the towering new Bank of China building, a highly visible reminder of Beijing's presence in the territory.
Citicorp's involvement in the development could be three-pronged: arranging a $1.9 billion bridge loan and a $3.3 billion term loan; possibly taking a 5 percent equity stake, which could be about $250 million dollars at the estimated development cost, and purchasing up to 400,000 square feet of office space.
At market rates for the district, that space would cost about $22 million, but Lo Ka Shui, managing director of Great Eagle, said office space in the development would be sold or leased to Citicorp below the going price.
Â 
Three Major Locations
Citicorp is one of the busiest foreign banks in the territory, with about 2,200 employees. 
But Hong Kong represents a small percentage of its worldwide business.
The bank now has three major Hong Kong locations: the stylish Exchange Square complex next to Victoria Harbor, Citicorp Center in Causeway Bay and Hopewell Center in Wanchai.
Mr. Baker said the planned move to Garden Road fits a ''two-building strategy'' that would group the bank's operations while expanding its existing Hong Kong office space of about 300,000 square feet.
Under the plan, the bank would have operations in one building in the central business district to house corporate and private banking businesses and a second, less-expensive site out of the central district to house its retail banking and credit-card operations. 
One alternative is to keep its Hopewell Center offices for that purpose.
In addition to the equity stake offered to Citicorp, Great Eagle said it had offered a 10 percent equity interest in the new project to the Singapore-based Robert Kuok Group, 5 percent to Wing Tai Exporters Ltd., 10 percent to Manhattan Garments Ltd., 7 percent to Sung Foo Kee Ltd. and 5 percent to a Japanese conglomerate.
Great Eagle will maintain about a 60 percent interest in the project, Mr. Lo said.

file: Clamor in Europe_Czech Students Belatedly Assail China Crackdown.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a belated expression of sympathy, several thousand Czechoslovak students marched here today to protest the violent suppression of China's pro-democracy movement in June.
When troops attacked and killed demonstrators in Beijing, students here said they were horrified but powerless to respond. 
Their own repressive Government supported the Chinese authorities, thwarting any chance of a student show of solidarity.
But after their own Government sent troops in to violently disperse a peaceful student demonstration here on Nov. 
17, prompting a backlash of protest that has caused the collapse of the Communist regime, Czechoslovak students decided to hold the demonstration they were prevented from holding months ago.
''It's important to stand up and say that what happened in Tiananmen Square and what happened here on the 17th should never be repeated,'' said Vera Krincvajova, a 20-year-old journalism student, who said she learned of the Chinese student uprising and the crackdown by monitoring foreign news reports on the radio.
Â 
'Dialogue - Yes!
Tanks - No!'
The students gathered in the freezing cold under threatening gray skies in a square opposite the philosophy department of Charles University, a center of the student movement.
They carried banners saying, ''Freedom for Prague and Beijing,'' ''Democracy Is Not a Crime'' and ''Dialogue -Yes!
Tanks - No!''
They wore headbands, as the Chinese students had, bearing the same messages.
The example of China has haunted the students of Czechoslovakia ever since they declared a strike two weeks ago and began working with leading dissidents to organize daily mass demonstrations and a two-hour general strike last week to force change on the Government.
This was the first large-scale demonstration in Prague in more than a week, because mass rallies were temporarily called off after the opposition group Civic Forum began negotiating with Prime Minister Ladislav Adamec over the formation of a new Government. 
For 10 days those protests had brought hundreds of thousands of people to Wenceslas Square.
Â 
'Guilty That I Was Silent'
Disappointed by the Government restructuring announced today, Civic Forum has called for a mass protest rally on Monday, a move the students say they endorse.
Students here have also said it is difficult for them to ignore that what happened in China might happen here.
''The possibility is in the back of everyone's mind,'' said Vladimir Kropacek, an 18-year-old math and physics student. 
''In the spring, I did not have the courage to express my sympathy, and in truth, I feel a little guilty that I was silent.''
The students had originally planned to march from the square to the Chinese Embassy, but Chinese diplomats protested to officials here.
After discussions with the authorities and among themselves, the students decided to avoid a confrontation by marching from the square through the winding, cobbled streets of an old section of Prague called Mala Strana, or the small quarter, and to a compound of dormitories for foreign students of Charles University.
''The most important thing to us was to show students' unity,'' said Simon Panek, a 22-year-old biology student and one of the leaders of the Student Strike Committee, who addressed the students after their hour-long march. 
''The world has been standing up for us, and now that we have the chance -it is late, we know, but it is our first chance - we are standing up for our fellow students.''

file: CLAMOR IN THE EAST_ China_Disgust With the West Is Reported, But Beijing Ignores the Wall_s End.txt
text:
ï»¿
Newspaper readers in China learned of the remarkable resignations of East German leaders this week, but they also picked up another bit of news: two East Germans who had fled more than a month ago to the West found the new society too disorderly and so returned home.
Chinese official newspapers have regularly, if sparingly, reported the developments within the East German leadership this week. 
But the brief reports included no explanations of the pressures that led to the unusual collective resignations. 
Lately, there has been little coverage of the mass demonstrations for democracy or the exodus to the West.
Such matters are presumably regarded as too delicate, too reminiscent of the democracy movement in China in the spring. 
Instead of giving in to some of the demonstrators' demands, as the East German leadership has done, the Chinese authorities called in troops and crushed the movement.
Today, there was no mention in the press or the national television about East Germany's opening of its borders to the West, although the trip to Poland by Chancellor Helmut Kohl of West Germany was reported.
Â 
'Period Full of Contradictions'
The recent articles - about one every two days, carried on the international news pages - have confined themselves to reporting excerpts from speeches by the new East German leader, Egon Krenz, about the necessity of reforming the party so that it can better exercise its leadership role.
''Democratic Germany is currently in a tense period full of contradictions,'' People's Daily today quoted Mr. Krenz as saying. 
''To make it through the difficult period, it is necessary to first carry out reform in the party itself.''
''The state economy is still the foundation of the socialist economy,'' Mr. Krenz was quoted as saying. 
''It is imperative to combine the superiority of the socialist planned economy with the regulation of the market.''
Chinese news outlets have tended to convey the impression that the ferment is coming from the top down, from a Communist leadership seeking to improve itself, rather than from a beleaguered party seeking to respond to enormous popular pressures. 
Still, many Chinese intellectuals listen to ''Voice of America'' or BBC radio programs, and often regard the changes in the Eastern bloc as a sign of the pressures that China could also face.
Â 
German Exodus Is Played Down
The newspapers have played down the exodus to the West, and have emphasized that some refugees found that capitalism was not as delightful as they had believed.
''When they first arrived, they were well treated,'' said a report in People's Daily early this week. 
''Yet they soon were given the cold shoulder and were treated unfairly.''
''Their general feeling is that society in West Germany is full of chaos, and there is no guarantee of life and property,'' the article said. 
''According to reports, quite a number of people have returned home.''

file: CLAMOR IN THE EAST_ The White House_Exchange With Gorbachev Leaves Bush Hopeful.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Mikhail S. Gorbachev has sent President Bush a message supporting the changes taking place in East Germany and expressing hope that the situation will remain ''calm and peaceful,'' the White House spokesman said today.
Marlin Fitzwater, Mr. Bush's press secretary, disclosed the message, which was received on Friday while the President was here to dedicate a memorial to soldiers killed in the Vietnam War.
The cable from Mr. Gorbachev was described by Mr. Fitzwater as ''an informal message.''
Although its text was not released, the spokesman said the Soviet leader spoke of ''the importance of the changes'' in East Germany and ''expressed the hope that the situation will remain calm and peaceful.''
Mr. Gorbachev also told Mr. Bush that he supported the actions of the new East German leadership to open its their country's borders.
Â 
U.S. Response Is Promised
Mr. Fitzwater said later that ''the President will respond, and he will repeat many of the things he said, as well as offering encouragement for the continuation of political and economic reforms.''
Mr. Bush, addressing thousands today at an emotional Veterans Day ceremony in which he dedicated a new Vietnam War memorial, said that the perforation of the Berlin wall shows ''a great truth shining brighter with each passing day.''
''The quest for freedom,'' he went on, ''is stronger than steel, more permanent than concrete.''
Recalling that his Administration had not foreseen the suppression of blossoming dissent in China, President Bush said in an interview published today that he has acted with ''prudence'' toward the developments in Eastern Europe because of concern that bolder action could ''contribute toward an unforeseen disorder'' in the Soviet bloc.
Â 
Inside View
In the interview, conducted on Friday with Texas reporters, Mr. Bush said he was prepared to discuss ''a wide array of economic questions'' with Mr. Gorbachev. But, in his first detailed response to the rapidly unfolding events of recent days in East Germany and other nations of the Warsaw Pact, Mr. Bush reflected the deep uncertainty within his Administration about how much the United States can become involved.
He seemed frustrated both at criticism that he has been reluctant to take the kind of leading role in Europe that the United States has pursued for four decades and at the limitations on American action created by the current upheavals.
Mr. Bush said his advisers believe that Mr. Gorbachev is irrevocably committed to his reforms. 
''They can't go back to Square One,'' the President said. 
But he and his aides are still uncertain, and debating among themselves, how the Kremlin will respond to the growing rift amomg its neighboring countries. 
What About Prague?
With Friday's change of leadership in Bulgaria, Mr. Bush went on, the Administration is eager to assess the possibilities for change in a remaining hard-line Communist country, Czechoslovakia. 
Mr. Bush said that Prague is now among ''the most egregious offenders of human rights, those that resist change the most clearly.''
Asked if he was concerned that the rapidity of events could lead to instability in Europe, he said, ''I think that's why I keep using the word like prudent.''
Still, he said, ''I am convinced, given not just the events of yesterday, but the cumulative set of events that have taken place, that this change is real.''
The President and his advisers have repeatedly insisted that China and Eastern Europe cannot be compared in political terms. 
But Mr. Bush would not disregard the Chinese crackdown on dissent that culminated in hundreds of deaths in Beijing in June, and he used that event to explain his seeming anguish over policy toward Eastern Europe.
Â 
'Keep Our Eyes Open'
''I think many of us felt that what happened in China set back the relationship there,'' he said. 
''I hadn't seen anybody predict that was going to happen.''
''And so we keep our eyes open, and we keep acting prudently so as not to exacerbate tensions but to encourage that democracy is whole and free. 
If we continue to do that, we can hopefully not contribute to an unforeseen disorder.''
Mr. Bush said he would like to return to Berlin ''to see it with the wall down, not just with holes in it.''
But he said he did not plan to stop there after his meeting with Mr. Gorbachev on ships off the coast of Malta on Dec. 
2 and 3 ''unless there were something that developed between now and then that would make the presence of the U.S. 
President catalytic for peace or for evolution of democracy.''
Â 
Possible Economic Help
Turning to questions about economic aid, the area in which the Administration has been especially reluctant to engage the Soviet Union, Mr. Bush said: ''I think the time is right, should the Soviets want to discuss how to improve their economy, that we do that. 
I'm perfectly prepared to talk to Mr. Gorbachev on a wide array of economic questions, and will be ready to do that.''
He added that he had had two ''interesting seminars'' with his advisers on economic issues to prepare for the meetings with the Soviet President.
Despite some conflicting statements in recent weeks about the Soviet-American relationship, Mr. Bush said he and his advisers agree on the substance of policy toward the East bloc. 
Still, they ''sit and argue back and forth - How quick will this happen?
Or, What will be next?
Or, what do you think is going to happen to Mr. A. or Mr. B.''
''Will Gorbachev remain committed to perestroika and indeed to glasnost?''
Mr. Bush said. 
''Absolutely.''

file: CNN Basks in Reaction to Its Beijing Coverage.txt
text:
ï»¿
These have been glory days for the Cable News Network. 
Its coverage of the upheaval in Tiananmen Square in Beijing has won praise from press analysts and attracted thousands more viewers, especially in the six days last week that CNN was able to transmit from its own satellite facilities in Beijing.
The network, its admirers say, was simply doing what it does best: showing a historic event unfolding - live. 
And being a round-the-clock all-news operation, it devoted many more hours to the story - 30 of them live that week - than could any of the three major networks.
''I think the Cable News Network really came of age,'' said Fred Friendly, a professor emeritus at the Columbia Graduate School of Journalism and a former CBS executive. 
''It performed a great national and even international service.''
Â 
Kudos for CBS
CBS, the only one of the three major networks to send an anchor, Dan Rather, and to set up its own satellite facility in Beijing, also performed ''an enormous service,'' he said. 
In an age when air time is enormously expensive and networks are cutting back, ''CBS did more than anyone else among the commercial stations,'' he said. 
''But they didn't have what CNN has, which is unlimited air time.''
CNN, a network of the Turner Broadcasting System, made its debut in June 1980, and has been turning a profit in recent years. 
It has grown rapidly, and now has 21 news bureaus, of which a dozen are outside the United States. 
It is seen in 83 countries besides the United States.
Its ''Prime News'' programs at 8 P.M. are normally watched by about 500,000 American households, roughly one-tenth the size of audiences for each of the three major networks' prime evening newscasts.
Â 
An Order on a Legal Pad
But 860,000 American homes watched CNN live last Friday night between 8 and 10:15 P.M., when a tense and curious exchange took place. 
Chinese officials told CNN to stop transmitting and CNN staff members asked for that in writing. 
A Chinese official complied on camera, writing the order on a legal pad. 
CNN members conferred with their network's headquarters in Atlanta, and the transmission ended.
That same night, 12.2 million viewers were watching CBS (and some called in to complain) as the network broke into the season's final episode of ''Dallas'' with a 21-minute special report that showed Chinese officials telling CBS to end its operations in Beijing.
During the past week, 400,000 American households tuned in daily to CNN on average - an increase of some 150,000 from usual.
Â 
'Logistical Nightmare'
The broadcasts from China were ''a logistical nightmare,'' said Eason Jordan, CNN's acting international editor, although events such as the 1988 Democratic National Convention required a larger staff.
CNN had 40 people in China last week, including the CNN anchor Bernard Shaw; Mike Chinoy, the Beijing bureau chief, and three other correspondents.
''They were working without sleep, as long as 20, 24 even 40 hours,'' Mr. Jordan said. 
''Even when they were told to get some sleep, they were too excited.''
In the view of Ed Joyce, a former president of CBS News, ''Bernard Shaw, and particularly Mike Chinoy, showed that nobody in commercial networks is doing anything better than they are doing. 
Chinoy, I thought, really seemed to have a grasp on the subtleties'' of the situation.
Â 
ABC and NBC 'Were Not Factors'
''What I found fascinating,'' Mr. Joyce said, ''was that the competition was between CBS News and CNN. 
ABC and NBC were just not factors'' - which he called a ''watershed'' development.
ABC and NBC were hardly in accord with this assessment.
''We're not at all ashamed - we covered it well,'' said Dick Wald, the senior vice president of ABC News. 
Noting that the original reason for the coverage was the Chinese-Soviet summit meeting, he said, ''The second story that captured the attention of the world wasn't part of anybody's planning.''
Comparing CNN to a wire story and the networks to newspapers, Mr. Wald said, ''The wire service is constant and constantly updating, but the newspaper creates a shape for things and a context.''
Joseph Angotti, a senior vice president of NBC News, said, ''I think its unfortunate that people have a perception that if your anchor is not there, you're not covering a story adequately.''
Â 
On the Camera's Presence
''The nature of CNN allows it to do things we simply can't do,'' Mr. Angotti added. 
Describing the coverage by CNN - and by all three networks - as ''terrific,'' he added that ''We think our pictures have been the best.''
Not everyone agrees on the impact of CNN's presence. 
Reuven Frank, a former president of NBC News, said the main point was that these days, ''the presence of the camera changes the nature of the event.''
Students, he said, were very much aware of the coverage, and timed their protest to the summit talks, just as antiwar demonstrators chose the Democratic National Convention to capture the cameras' eyes in Chicago in 1968.
And will CNN's achievement affect the way the commercial networks cover news?
''What I'm afraid of,'' said Mr. Frank, ''is that it may allow the networks to cop out. 
They could say, 'well, if you want it, it's there on CNN.''

file: COMPANY NEWS_China Will Launch U.S.-Built Satellite.txt
text:
ï»¿
A Hong Kong company signed a $30 million contract today to fire an American-built satellite into space on a Chinese rocket - the first time China will launch a foreign-built satellite.
''This marks China's first step in the international satellite business,'' said Terry Seddon, chief executive of the Asia Satellite Telecommunications Company, or Asiasat, which signed the deal with the state-owned China Great Wall Industrial Corporation.
Asiasat 1 is to be launched in April 1990, and China will be sending two other American-made satellites into space in July 1991 and February 1992 for an Australian satellite company, Aussat, Chinese officials said.
In addition, negotiations are under way for the Chinese to launch a second satellite from Asiasat and a weather satellite from Sweden. 
Asiasat 1 and the two Aussat satellites were made by the Hughes Aircraft Company.
The launchings on an unmanned rocket will provide China with much-needed foreign exchange and, if successful, help cement its position in the world of international aerospace.
Since 1984, China has successfully launched four of its own communications satellites. 
It started launching satellites in 1970 and has had 23 successful firings and one failure.
In December the United States agreed to allow China to launch American-built communications satellites after Beijing promised it would neither steal American satellite technology nor undercut private American companies.
China said it would limit itself to launching nine foreign communications satellites in the next six years.
According to some estimates, China's state-subsidized rocket industry charges 30 to 50 percent less per launching than its American or European competitors.
The Chinese launching will be Asiasat 1's second trip in space. 
In 1984, under the name Westar 6, it was sent up on the American space shuttle, but a rocket motor malfunctioned and the satellite was not delivered into orbit.
It was retrieved in a spectacular salvage operation in 1985 and sold to Asiasat, the company owned by a consortium consisting of Cable and Wireless of Britain, the state-owned China International Trust and Investment and Hutchison Whampoa, one of Hong Kong's biggest companies.

file: CONFRONTATION IN THE GULF_Iraq Voted Out of Asian Games.txt
text:
