file: Exiting Cabinet Member Leading China Trip.txt
text:
ï»¿
As many as three dozen political appointees who will leave office next month will first visit Beijing when Commerce Secretary Barbara H. Franklin flies there next week on a $13,000-an-hour Air Force jet, Government and industry officials said.
Bush Administration officials have frequently run into trouble for their use of Government aircraft. 
John H. Sununu, President Bush's first White House chief of staff, drew considerable public criticism when his extensive use of Government aircraft was revealed, although his travel appeared to be more personal than Ms. Franklin's trip.
The purpose of the trip is to review Chinese compliance with two bilateral trade agreements this year, to promote American exports and to hold broad talks on the two nations' economic relations, Ms. Franklin said at a news conference on Wednesday.
Â 
Administration Is Mum
When asked today for a list of who was going on the trip, Commerce Department officials refused, saying that releasing the names would threaten security. 
They also refused to say how many political appointees would be going but would not deny the estimate of three dozen. 
The trip comes at a time when budget cuts have resulted in severe travel restrictions for American trade officials.
Don Anderson, head of the U.S.-China Business Council and among those making the trip, said he knew of about 30 others who would be going. 
The American delegation will include several corporate executives and will travel on an Air Force C-137, a luxurious version of the Boeing 707 with office space and wide seats, he said.
Ms. Franklin's entourage is unusually large for the task, particularly since a half-dozen American civil servants originally negotiated the two agreements and the political appointees will have no more than a month after their return to use any insights they may develop in China. 
President-elect Bill Clinton is likely to replace them with Democrats when he takes office.
Â 
The Plane Clinton Refused
The C-137 is the same sort of plane the Bush Administration offered President-elect Bill Clinton for his first trip to Washington after the election. 
He turned it down as too expensive and chartered a cheaper plane.
According to the Pentagon, Mr. Clinton's C-137 would have cost $13,000 an hour for the four-hour trip. 
Air Force officials said that for Federal agencies outside the Defense Department, the White House and Congress, they charge $11,835 per hour of flying time.
A commercial round-trip flight to Beijing takes 37 hours in the air, suggesting a cost of up to $438,000 for the C-137, not including time the aircraft will spend on the ground during Ms. Franklin's six-day trip to Beijing, Shenzhen and Hong Kong.
Officials from the Commerce Department, State Department, the National Security Council and the Office of the United States Trade Representative will accompany Ms. Franklin. Some of them flew to Beijing as early as last week rather than joining the Secretary on the C-137.
Ms. Franklin's trip is partly intended to mollify the Chinese after a trip by Carla A. Hills, the United States Trade Representative, to Taiwan last month. 
Mrs. Hills took five aides and a commercial flight.
Â 
Negotiators Flew Commercial
Both trade agreements were negotiated with much smaller teams of civil servants who traveled on commercial flights, said Joseph Massey, the assistant United States trade representative for China and Japan who negotiated the first agreement, which provides for stricter protection of American copyrights, patents and trademarks. 
Before he left office last June to become a professor at Dartmouth University, Mr. Massey also negotiated most of the second pact, which was finished in October and calls for the elimination of Chinese restrictions on imports.
Each trip to China for those negotiations typically involved three or four officials from Mrs. Hills's office, one or two State Department officials and one or two Commerce Department officials, Mr. Massey said.
Mrs. Hills, a member of the Cabinet like Ms. Franklin, takes a half dozen aides on her trips and always flies on commercial aircraft, which tend to be much cheaper.
Â 
Travel Budget Crippled
Mrs. Hills faces deep cuts to her travel budget. 
Although her agency negotiated the two agreements that Ms. Franklin wants to discuss in Beijing, Congress cut her agency's $20 million budget by 10 percent this year, amid complaints by legislators from textile-producing states that she was too willing to abandon American restrictions on clothing imports.
The result has been a crippling reduction in the travel budget that has resulted in the United States' sending even smaller delegations to trade talks that could determine the future of multibillion-dollar American industries.

file: Fear of Chaos Grows as China_s Leaders Age.txt
text:
ï»¿
A young Government official paused over his dinner the other day when he was asked what the death of China's senior leaders might mean. 
''Chaos,'' he replied glumly. 
''Maybe civil war. 
It'll be back to the 1920's and 30's.''
Such pessimism is hardly universal, but many Chinese express growing concern that catastrophic social convulsions are possible over the next decade, particularly after the death of Deng Xiaoping and other elders. 
Indeed, this is perhaps the only issue on which many hard-line leaders and democratic dissidents can agree: A large number seem to think that widespread turmoil is a risk, though not necessarily the most likely outcome.
So these days, when Chinese ruminate about the future, they often say their prime fear is less a return to Maoism than a drift into turmoil.
Mr. Deng himself last month warned of the risks of instability in China. 
In comments published in Wen Wei Po, a Beijing-backed newspaper in Hong Kong, Mr. Deng cautioned that if the Communist Party lost its grip on China the result would be chaos that could lead 100 million Chinese to flee to Indonesia, 10 million to Thailand, and 500,000 to Hong Kong.
''Should a civil war break out in China, it would not cease,'' Wen Wei Po paraphrased Mr. Deng as saying.
Such warnings are clearly intended to drive home the message that China must stick with socialism. 
But these days many who see orthodox socialism as part of the problem also say that chaos is a possibility.
''China could just fall apart, with a return to warlords and fiefs and civil war,'' said a university student who like many others is reacting by trying to go abroad to study.
That concern about chaos is not new, but many students say they feel it more intensely than before. 
Last summer they were absorbed with apprehension that the so-called ''Gang of Elders'' would pull China back to the Maoist era. 
Now they are more relaxed about that possibility, for they say that in any case there is enough passive resistance to hobble the policies of the hard-liners.
Â 
Disintegration and Warlords
''The fundamental question in China is order, stabilityI, the state,'' said a Western diplomat with long experience in China. 
''The real fear among intellectuals now is not a challenge from the conservatives.''
Instead, he said, they fear that less capable leaders will take over after Mr. Deng dies and preside over the disintegration of China.
In this regard, many Chinese seem more pessimistic than Western diplomats and scholars. 
Many Westerners say they believe that civil war and upheavals on that scale are unlikely.
''All Chinese are concerned to a greater or lesser degree with centrifugal forces,'' said a Western diplomat, but he added that China probably would not revert to the turmoil of the 1920's and 1930's, when the country was torn among the ruling Kuomintang, regional warlords, the Communist rebels and Japanese invaders. 
''In the period of the warlords, you didn't have modern planes, fax machines, and the levers of control that we have now.''
Concern about chaos has a particular resonance in China because of the horrors of the last 150 years: The Taiping Rebellion in the mid-19th century left at least 20 million dead, and in the first half of this century famine and fighting killed millions more. 
Some Chinese say the recent experience of the Soviet Union, when Stalinism has declined while national minorities have pushed for autonomy or independence, has made the risk of disintegration more obvious. 
Many Chinese believe that a power vacuum at the center could lead to secessionist moves by Tibet and Xinjiang Province in the west, as well as growing assertiveness in other provinces.
Chinese and foreign specialists say the rapid spread of the democracy movement last year underscored the potential for such upheavals. 
Moreover, they say that the army's crackdown may have made unrest more likely in the long run, by robbing the Communist Party and socialism of legitimacy that otherwise might have helped hold the country together.

file: Few in Hong Kong Ask to Be British.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a surprising twist, a British offer of citizenship for a limited number of Hong Kong residents nervous about the Chinese takeover of the colony in 1997 has attracted only a fraction of the number of applicants expected.
The deadline for applications was midnight tonight for the program, which had been widely criticized as an offer of too little too late. 
But at midevening, government officials said they expected to receive about 60,000 applications for the 43,500 passports offered, a figure that falls far short of the 300,000 applications they originally anticipated.
On Wednesday the opposition Labor Party's home affairs spokesman in London, Alistair Darling, called for an investigation into why the plan had evoked so little response.
He said the limited number of applicants "flies in the face of everything I was told during three days in Hong Kong," he said. 
"I was told there would be a deluge."
With the Communist takeover of this lively capitalist colony growing closer, hundreds of thousands of residents have been lining up in front of foreign consulates in the last few years to apply for immigration papers. 
And with people actually emigrating from Hong Kong at a rate of more than 1,200 a week, officials here expected to be swamped with applications for the British passports.
Â 
Approved by Parliament
The package offered full British citizenship to 50,000 heads of households working in key businesses or professions. 
The 50,000 passports were to be distributed in two offerings, 87 percent, or 43,500, now, the remainder after 1993.
The British Parliament approved the package last year after months of intensive, often emotional lobbying by Hong Kong leaders who argued that after ruling Hong Kong for 150 years Britain ought to provide the colony's residents a place of refuge should life under the Chinese prove harsh. 
When Britain responded with an offer for only 50,000 families, many here felt betrayed and angered, especially the educated, professional families that the plan sought to attract.
Government officials, politicians and others here have offered a host of reasons for the lack of interest, but essentially, they say, most of the 5.8 million people here did not apply because they believed they would not qualify under the complex and limited plan. 
Experts said many here who would qualify did not apply because they simply would rather not live in Britain.
"It was a classic case of Hong Kong civil servants misreading the Hong Kong people," said Robert Broadfoot, managing director of the Political and Economic Risk Consultancy here. 
"They were people with good hearts, saying we have to help people here who face a future under the Communists. 
But the thing is, Hong Kong people have never longed to live in Britain. 
They don't like its economy or its weather, and if they want to escape the Communists, there are plenty of places they would rather go than Britain."
Â 
Not the Preferred Land
Paul C. K. Kwong, a demographer who has studied emigration trends in the colony, said he was not surprised that the British package was so coolly received because "for the past few years, survey after survey has shown that Britain ranks fairly low on the list of preferred destinations for Hong Kong emigrants, in some cases even after Singapore."
Mr. Kwong, a lecturer in the sociology department of the Chinese University here, said, "Anyone who could fill out the 32-page application for the British plan, and make his way through all its thick, pseudo-legal language, would be educated enough to go to the United States or Canada or Australia, which are the preferred destinations of Hong Kong people."
He said Hong Kong residents, 98 percent of whom are ethnic Chinese, prefer those countries because "they are perceived as having vital economies."
"These are places people think of as open, fair, full of opportunity, and Britain is just not seen that way," he said.
Â 
Million Forms Printed
Government officials, who printed one million application forms for the British plan, have still pronounced it a success, declaring that the comparatively low number of applicants shows that Hong Kong's people have regained their confidence.
"That was the goal of the nationality scheme, to restore Hong Kong's confidence by getting key people to remain here with the offer of a safety net," said Donald Tsang, Secretary for Administration and the man directing the plan.
Mr. Tsang said demands for British passports were highest after the violent suppression of pro-democracy demonstrators in China in June 1989.
"I think the level of confidence in Hong Kong has changed since then," he said. 
"Things have settled down."
Â 
'Always Too Small'
One Government official here said that offering British citizenship to residents of a British colony was unpopular "because people here did not want to apply for something they already thought they had."
But Mr. Kwong said a study on which he worked estimated that the number of "core" key workers Hong Kong would need to retain its vibrant economy through 1997 was 356,000 to 544,000.
"The British offer of 50,000 passports to keep key people in place here never even came close," he said. 
"It was always too small for its stated goals."

Saying it is ''shocked,'' China today condemned the American military strike in Panama as a violation of international law and demanded the immediate withdrawal of American forces.

'Shock and Strong Condemnation'
The statement concluded: ''The independence and sovereignty of Panama should be respected, and the United States should immediately stop the military invasion of Panama so as to prevent a deterioration of the situation.''
At the United Nations in New York, the New China News Agency reported, the Chinese Ambassador, Li Luye, told the Security Council last night of his ''utmost shock and strong condemnation'' of the American military attempt to topple the Panamanian leader Gen. Manuel Antonio Noriega.

Japan Backs President
TOKYO, Dec. 
21 (Special to The New York Times) - In a guarded statement of support for President Bush's actions in Panama, Japan today said it ''regretted'' that circumstances had brought the American intervention but that it understood the reasons why the United States felt it had to act.

file: FILM VIEW_What_s Adultery_ A Little Sex, A Lot of Politics.txt
text:

What Jane Austen did for marriage in the 19th century, film makers are doing for adultery today. 
In the past few weeks alone, eight films from seven countries have offered a view of infidelity around the world. 
It is an unmistakable sign of a turbulent social era.
''Ju Dou,'' set in China in the 1920's, and ''Tilai,'' set in a contemporary African village, are radically different films that share this single plot: an arranged marriage between a young woman and an older man leads her to an adulterous affair that results in murder. 
''The Sting of Death,'' from Japan, and ''A Woman's Revenge,'' from France, both depict a woman who discovers her husband's adultery and goes mad.
These films, shown at the 28th New York Film Festival (with ''Ju Dou'' and ''Tilai'' to open commercially later this season) echo the adulterous motifs in two current American films. 
''Henry and June,'' which glorifies the menage a trois among Anais Nin, Henry Miller and his wife, June, elevates marital infidelity to an artistic ambition. 
And ''Texasville'' is a slice of pure, commercial Americana whose adulterous tangles make ''Peyton Place'' seem like Mother Goose.
This overload of international adultery also includes films in which infidelity is significant but not central, such as the Australian director Paul Cox's ''Golden Braid'' and the Taviani brothers' ''Night Sun,'' from Italy, both of which were also shown at the recently completed festival.
In all these films, adultery is more than a matter of love or passion; in fact, with the exceptions of ''Henry and June'' and ''Golden Braid,'' there is surprisingly little eroticism in these films. 
But even passionate films such as ''Dangerous Liaisons'' and ''Sex, Lies and Videotape'' function like Austen's novels. 
They use an individual's tale of marriage and adultery to expose social hypocrisy, to analyze and criticize one of the most crucial standards by which any culture lives.
Most often, infidelity becomes a symbolic act of rebellion against the traditional social order. 
In those rarefied subcultures where adultery is acceptable, fidelity becomes the rebellious idea. 
And from the elegant, understated manner of ''Tilai'' to the soap opera commercialism of ''Texasville,'' the common motif is handled in a way characteristic of each country's cinematic style, offering a revealing cross-cultural view.
In films such as ''Ju Dou'' and ''Tilai,'' adultery is explicitly presented as heroic resistance to outmoded traditions. 
These films tell stories of passion and violence, but they are more concerned with social comment than with remaking ''The Postman Always Rings Twice.''
The first fact we learn about Ju Dou, the heroine who gives the film its title, is that she was a very expensive bride to buy. 
Every subsequent action she takes defies the tradition that binds her to an abusive husband. 
The affair and the illegitimate son she has with Tian Qing, her husband's middle-aged adopted son, are both symbolic and personal.
The old husband, so vile that he tries to murder the child, embodies the evil traditions (and by extension the Government control) that have held China back. 
And when the husband dies, a bearded family elder invokes the ancient teachings and banishes Tian Qing from the house because he is not a true son. 
Challenging such rigid social patterns is both heroic and tragic, eventually leading to the murder of Tian Qing by his own son. 
In this context, the persistent love between Ju Dou and Tian Qing is as much a failed social rebellion as it is a private passion.
In fact, when the lovers begin to writhe on the floor of the family's dye factory, the film cuts to a bolt of red cloth in a vat; it is the equivalent of old Hollywood movies that discreetly shift to the fireplace to suggest sex. 
But the director, Zhang Yimou, is not only working in a slow, symbolic Chinese tradition. 
He is circumspect in the way of film makers who must dance around censorship. 
The film was made after the Government repression that began with Tiananmen Square; though it is based on a novel that moves from the 30's to the 70's, the film is situated safely in the pre-Commmunist past.
Idrissa Ouedraogo of Burkina Faso is much more direct in his criticism of the old order in ''Tilai,'' a film whose crisp photography, spare dialogue and gently flowing narrative are typical of African cinema. 
But here, too, adultery is a form of social heroism. 
Nogma is in love with Saga, but is married off to his father. 
When the villagers discover the lovers' adulterous affair, Saga is condemned to death, with his own brother chosen as the sanctioned murderer.
As in ''Ju Dou,'' the film maker sympathizes with the rebellious lovers, whose passionate resistance to tradition carries symbolic weight. 
Nogma's adolescent sister and Saga's brother are also strong figures who question the arranged marriage and the punishment for adultery. 
But as in ''Ju Dou,'' this rebellion fails, leading to a death that functions as virulent criticism of tradition for its own sake.
''The Sting of Death'' is even more explicit in its use of adultery as a social metaphor, though much of that may be lost on an audience unfamiliar with the novel on which it is based or comments by the director, Kohei Oguri. 
The film ''uses the medium of the relationship of a husband and wife to graphically depict the character of the Japanese people in the postwar era,'' he has said.
The film does not make it clear that the time is the 1950's or that the wife was a naive bride who married a soldier about to be sent into battle - not an arranged marriage, though one colored by the exigencies of war and nationalism. 
When she discovers his infidelity after 10 years of marriage and two children, the screen oveflows with his guilt, her obsessive recriminations and mutual threats of suicide. 
If ''Ju Dou'' is ''The Postman Always Rings Twice'' in China, ''The Sting of Death'' threatens to become a low-volume, Japanese version of ''Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?''
But the personal story is connected to the political past by a flashback of soldiers on the island where the couple met. 
Such allusions tie the effectively tense domestic battles to the struggling self-image of the Japanese. 
And on the subway, the husband sees a poster advertising a department store. 
''Happy Family. 
Delightful Shopping,'' it reads, measuring the distance between this family and the social ideal that may not exist at all.
Mr. Oguri's elegant, formal compositions are in the Japanese line that extends back to Yasujiro Ozu; during a typical conversation between the couple, the husband is hidden in shadows that cover half the screen. 
Yet its most disturbing quality is not specifically Japanese at all. 
Both ''The Sting of Death'' and ''A Woman's Revenge'' - an agonizingly hermetic and banal French film directed by Jacques Doillon - contain the insidious idea that women go crazy when men desert them.
The mad wife in ''A Woman's Revenge'' is Isabelle Huppert, who looks up her dead husband's former lover and drives the woman to suicide. 
So much for the image of blase French infidelities. 
In fact, though the story is very freely transferred to contemporary Paris from Dostoyevsky's ''Eternal Husband,'' it challenges the idea that such liaisons are to be forgiven and dismissed. 
Where ''Ju Dou'' and ''Tilai'' see adultery as heroic defiance of the social order, in ''A Woman's Revenge'' and ''Night Sun'' adultery is the social order, so the films come down on the side of fidelity.
''Night Sun'' is another Russian transplant, this time moving Tolstoy's story ''Father Sergius'' to Italy. 
The 18th-century hero, played by Julian Sands dubbed into Italian by Giancarlo Giannini, is a soldier who wages a self-mortifying struggle to escape the sinful world. 
But it is a corrupt marriage contract that sends him fleeing from society in the first place.
The king plans to elevate Sergius's social status by arranging his marriage to a royal woman (Nastassja Kinski), with whom he falls in love. 
But when she confesses that she has been the king's mistress, the hero is so shocked at his personal betrayal and society's hypocrisy that he runs off and becomes a monk. 
The aristocratic, 18th-century world that he rejects is entirely familiar from ''Dangerous Liaisons.''
It is a world in which only a true innocent or a peasant (Sergius is both) could doubt that marriage is a social convenience and that infidelity without guilt is the way of the world.
By the early 20th century, of course, such sophisticated adulteries had been replaced by bourgeois fidelity - at least on the surface of polite society. 
''Henry and June,'' set in Paris in 1931, heralds Modernism and the shattering of bourgeois mores. 
Total sexual freedom and fidelity to one's own passionate experience is the central idea of the film, which reflects the precious, hothouse sensibilities of Anais Nin, on whose diaries the story is based. 
(To my literary taste that is no compliment, but it seems to be what the director, Philip Kaufman, desired.) Rejecting middle-class mores and accepting unrestricted sex go together in this story, where marital fidelity is an emotional prison for the artist-heroes. 
Underneath its self-consciously steamy surface, ''Henry and June'' is as much about society as it is about sex and art.
A potboiler like ''Texasville,'' however, has nothing so lucid to say about adultery and society, even though all of Jeff Bridges's married lovers seem to be sleeping with his son. 
In ''The Last Picture Show,'' the affair between the high-school athlete and the coach's forlorn wife was life-saving; it was also the emotional heart of the film's nostalgic portrait of a fading small-town way of life. 
But the sequel, where Mr. Bridges's character is a millionaire going bankrupt while the whole town goes bust emotionally, has the feeling of fiction rather than life, despite its detailed trappings of life in the 1980's. 
That everyone is sleeping with someone else's mate simply seems part of the soap opera plot of ''Texasville.''
So sometimes adultery is simply adultery, without much social weight. 
And sometimes it is truly mad and personal. 
In ''Golden Braid,'' a man is having an affair with a married Salvation Army worker, but develops an obsessive romantic attachment to an antique hank of golden hair. 
This may be the ultimate twisted infidelity, but none of these films suggests any easy morality or social standards. 
Instead, they question the muddled rituals of love and marriage. 
As Saga's brother says in ''Tilai'': ''It's all so complicated. 
We've all been so stupid.''

text:
ï»¿
On the banks of the West Lake, an enchanted region of islands and temples shrouded by mist and magic in this city 100 miles southwest of Shanghai, a love story has been unfolding before the cameras. 
It is a Chinese love story, in which the leading actress is both chased and - after a fleeting temptation - chaste. 
But it is also a Western love story, both unlikely and true, of a young American devoted to Chinese martial arts.
Mark Salzman may not get the girl, but he gets the martial arts. 
And, just as important, he gets the part of himself in the movie about his experiences filmed here and likely to open simultaneously on American and Chinese screens next fall.
After graduating from Yale University in 1982 with a degree - summa cum laude and Phi Beta Kappa - in Chinese language and literature, Mr. Salzman moved to China for two years. 
There he taught English, studied martial arts and encountered the absurdities and charms of the Middle Kingdom. 
His light, pointillist account of his experiences, ''Iron and Silk,'' was published in February 1987 and won excellent reviews.
Mr. Salzman, a muscular 28-year-old who jokes almost as easily in Chinese as in English, received several feelers from companies interested in buying movie rights to his book. 
But when he said that he wanted to write the screenplay himself, and even to star in the film as himself, they laughed.
He will laugh last, for his dream took shape during the fall and early winter under the camera lights along the West Lake. 
The filming of ''Iron and Silk'' ended Dec. 
21, and it will be edited in the United States by its director and producer, Shirley Sun, a Chinese-American film maker who was a consultant to Bernardo Bertolucci for ''The Last Emperor.''
Ms. Sun in 1984 produced and co-wrote ''A Great Wall,'' a low-budget comedy that attracted favorable reviews for its tale of a Chinese-American scientist who brings his family with him to visit his relatives in China.
Yet ''A Great Wall'' was largely a movie by Chinese for Chinese, or at least Chinese-Americans. 
Much of the dialogue was in Chinese, and it was too forbidding, too full of inside jokes, to capture a mass audience in the United States. 
''The Last Emperor,'' on the other extreme, used a distinctively foreign lens. 
It was about China more than it was about the Chinese. 
Its epic sweep of history and visual panoramas of old China were stunning but did not evoke the life of ''old hundred names,'' as the Chinese refer to their ordinary citizens.
That is the gap for which ''Iron and Silk'' is aimed: a work filmed with understanding, even sympathy, but conceived for Main Street.
''It's time that people who know about China made movies about China,'' said Ms. Sun, who was born in Shanghai but grew up in the United States, and later earned a Ph.D. in art history from Stanford University. 
''For so long the movies were so stereotyped,'' she said. 
''We hope that this and other movies we make will be more authentic about Chinese life.''
''Iron and Silk'' hardly follows a blockbuster formula. 
Ms. Sun declined to discuss the movie's budget, but it seems tiny by Hollywood standards. 
And two important ingredients of many important American movies, sex and violence, have been sublimated and Sinicized so that they are scarcely recognizable. 
Mr. Salzman and his opposite, the mainland Chinese star Vivian Wu, might share a bed if this were a typical American movie. 
Instead, in Chinese form, they share some yearning for each other's companionship but then decide it really isn't feasible after all. 
The other key ingredient, violence, is provided by the martial arts scenes. 
Mr. Salzman began to study kung fu when he was 13 years old, but it was during his two years in China that he practiced under two martial arts masters and learned to use the long sword - a rare skill even among Chinese.
Partly because it is not easy to find a well-known actor who can send a sword whistling among the cameras, the cast is perhaps the most remarkable element of ''Iron and Silk.''
Mr. Salzman had dabbled in acting but had no movie credits. 
Vivian Wu, on the other hand, is a gorgeous 22-year-old who has been appearing in movies in China since she was 16 and then was cast as the emperor's second wife in ''The Last Emperor.''
Now Miss Wu, who speaks fluent English and is studying at Hawaii Pacific College, says she would like to do more English language movies.
Then there is Pan Qingfu, ''The Iron Fist'' himself, a legendary martial arts expert who earned his nickname - and the acorn-size calluses on his knuckles - by his hobby of punching an iron plate a thousand or more times a day. 
Mr. Pan, whose fierce gaze can seem as lethal as his fists, was Mr. Salzman's kung fu teacher in China, and he also plays himself. 
Mr. Pan had appeared in Chinese kung fu movies, but he speaks only a few useful phrases of English taught him by Mr. Salzman, such as ''Don't worry, it's just a shoulder dislocation.''
Moreover, he was accustomed only to the exaggerated style and costumes of Chinese martial arts movies. 
When he showed up in Hangzhou for the filming, Mr. Pan brought with him several warrior costumes that have not been seen on the street in China for many centuries at least.
Except for Jeanette Lin Tsui, a well-known Hong Kong actress, the cast is rounded out by local English-speaking Chinese. 
Some were already English teachers or interpreters, and some were simply selected from Hangzhou's ''English corner,'' an intersection where people go every evening to practice their English on one another. 
Many of these play the roles of Mr. Salzman's English-language students, and for the movie they had to learn to sing ''Jingle Bells,'' with which they serenade him at a farewell dinner.
If Mr. Salzman and the other neophytes are daunted by the prospect of appearing for the first time in a motion picture, they give no sign of it.
''Making this movie is a whole lot easier than buying coffee in Changsha,'' Mr. Salzman said with a laugh, referring to the city where he lived for two years. 
Miss Wu, by comparison a veteran actress, appraised him highly, saying, ''This is Mark's first movie, but he's very good, very professional. 
He will make a very good movie actor if he wants to be one.''
The filming, in cooperation with a Chinese production company, demonstrated some of the cultural differences that are the very topic of the movie. 
Most Chinese movies, for example, do not record sound at the same time they film. 
Voices are dubbed in later in a sound room. 
Likewise, Chinese productions tend to be less meticulous about lighting and other technical matters, so that only about three times as much film is shot as is used in the eventual movie. 
On the other hand, a production like ''Iron and Silk'' typically shoots about 10 times as much film as eventually finds its way into the finished movie. 
That sometimes seemed like a waste to the Chinese on the set, who saw scenes shot over and over even if there was little wrong with the earlier attempts.
''We have a lot of differences in shooting,'' explained Jia Qi, a liaison officer from Beijing who helped the ''Iron and Silk'' crew deal with local authorities and get what they needed. 
''We say Americans are big, and their films are also big,'' he remarked. 
For example, Ms. Jia said that a Chinese film production usually requires three cars to transport equipment, while ''Iron and Silk'' required three large trucks, which had to be driven 800 miles over dubious roads from Beijing.
Another cultural difference was that the Chinese on the set did not quite understand what the film is about. 
They were used to Chinese movies with strong story lines, and ''Iron and Silk'' is in large part just a pastiche of Mr. Salzman's experiences as teacher of English and student of martial arts. 
To be sure, the movie does take artistic license in expanding into a central theme what in the book was a minor incident: an encounter between Mr. Salzman and a young woman, beautiful and intelligent, who is attracted to him but constrained by her situation and by a sense of propriety.
Aside from that liberty, the movie largely follows the book - as might be expected when the same person writes the book as writes the screenplay. 
That was the result of one of the many coincidences in the story of how the movie came to be made.
It all began in March 1987, about a month after the book was published. 
Ms. Sun had read the book - indeed, after starting it one afternoon, she had stayed up most of the night to finish it - but she had other projects underway and did not think of making a movie about it. 
Meanwhile, Mr. Salzman was a fan of ''A Great Wall,'' but he did not know Ms. Sun personally, and he was then considering offers from other companies for movie rights. 
At that point, they met at an Asian film festival at Yale, and they quickly decided to collaborate. 
For Mr. Salzman, one of the strongest attractions was that Ms. Sun would allow him to co-write the screenplay with her, as well as to star as himself.
''I thought he'd be great the moment I met him,'' Ms. Sun recalled. 
''I couldn't possibly get any other actor who knows China and martial arts the way he does, and who has his talents.''
Mr. Salzman acknowledges that writing the screenplay was much more difficult than he had expected.
''Every draft I did, I would think it was perfect,'' he said. 
''Then I would send it to Shirley, and after a couple of weeks I would get a call and she would say, 'I have a few ideas.'
And then I would totally redo it.''
Ms. Sun, who had worked often in China and had good contacts, had no difficulty getting approval from Chinese authorities for the project, but she was not certain where in China to film. 
In fact, the events took place in Changsha, the capital of Hunan province in central China, but neither Mr. Salzman nor anyone else was enthusiastic about filming in that drab city.
In May 1988, Ms. Sun planned a five-day trip to scout locations for filming, starting with Hangzhou and then hurtling to several other cities she was considering. 
But when she reached Hangzhou, she could not get a flight out of the city. 
The planes were all booked up. 
And so she spent all five days on the banks of the West Lake, soaking up the city, and the decision was made by default. 
''Iron and Silk'' would be filmed in Hangzhou.
There seemed little chance of finding Mr. Pan to play himself, when all of a sudden he arrived in Hangzhou by coincidence to participate in a martial arts tournament. 
He quickly abandoned other projects to participate in the movie.
''I really wanted to do this,'' Mr. Pan explained. 
''I'm very happy that Americans are interested in martial arts, and I think we should contribute to the world.''
Mr. Salzman acknowledged some apprehension about how Mr. Pan would react to some passages in the book and screenplay that seemed to poke fun at his considerable ego. 
But in fact Mr. Pan was happy to repeat the lines, which he regarded as entirely accurate, such as one where he said he never makes mistakes. 
Indeed, Mr. Pan said that one reason he took the part was to confirm the book's authenticity.
''When some foreigners read the book, they don't believe what it says about me - that my eyes are like an eagle's, and that I am very tough,'' he explained. 
''So this movie will show them that I really am like that.''

text:
ï»¿
A few months after public protests here over the violent repression of democracy in Tiananmen Square, it's business as usual in Hong Kong. 
After years in New York, a young Chinese remarked that his native city ''had become a gigantic shopping mall.''
The so-called Hong Kong dream, a vision of the good life parallel to the American Dream, however, shouldn't be reduced to pure mercantilism. 
For the film scholar Esther Yau, Hong Kong's precarious existence represents a utopia, the right not to choose between the Communist Party and the Kuomintang. 
Nowhere is this utopia better expressed than in the film industry - where audiences may enjoy a taste of paradise lost long ago in Hollywood. 
In Hong Kong, film making is an unpretentious industry, designed for profit, popular entertainment and export to Japan, Taiwan and Korea.
Paradise, however, is in danger of being lost. 
The Hong Kong film industry is a brilliant form of escapism, for there is something to escape from. 
In 1997, the 99-year British concession will expire, and Hong Kong will come under the jurisdiction of the Beijing Government. 
The June 4 crackdown has increased the residents' anxieties - and the film industry has been especially affected by the events. 
Producers, directors and stars, torn between rage, fear and the desire to keep working, might see their world disappear altogether. 
Hong Kong's film industry has its mega-stars (Sylvia Chang, Anita Mui, Cora Miao, Chow Yun-fatt, Tony Leung) and its kung fu idols Jackie Chang and Samo Hung; its major studios (Golden Harvest, Cinema City, D and B); its Spielbergian producers (Tsui Hark); its maverick auteurs (Allen Fong); and a handful of talented women directors (such as Ann Hui - of ''Boat People'' fame - and Mabel Cheung).
The most popular genres are action thrillers and a hilarious mixture of slapstick, martial arts and ghost story. 
Even when parodic, Hong Kong films still stand for the magic of cinema, its power to tell a story and to create a better and more exciting world. 
Gangster films are especially bloody, yet mythical. 
The protagonists are elegant, charming, brave, loyal friends, honorable adversaries, expert marksmen, extraordinary acrobats and, above all, paragons of manliness. 
Because they stick to genres and formulas, Hong Kong products might be described as exploitation films - yet they leave room for experimentation. 
Jackie Chang's humor, generosity and comical stunts have revitalized the action film, as in ''Project A, Police Story.''
Tsui Hark brilliantly combines traditional martial arts and high-tech special effects, as in ''Zhu, Warrior of Sacred Mountain.''
Since the 1970's, Hong Kong has become the Hollywood of Asia and one of the world's most prolific film centers. 
But a shadow looms over its creative energy - that of 1997, when Hong Kong is to be reunited with the People's Republic of China. 
And since June 4, 1989, the day of the Tiananmen violence, history seems to have quickened its pace.
''Chinese often use the past to talk about the present,'' says Po Chim Leong. 
Born in England to an emigre Cantonese family, he moved to Hong Kong in the 60's. 
Channel 4 in London produced his film ''Ping Pong,'' exploring the identity crisis of a young ''B.B.C.''
(British-Born Chinese). 
In Asia, he is famous for his 1986 film, ''Hong Kong 1941.''
The British colonials leave, the Japanese Army arrives, plunging the city into lawlessness and violence. 
Three young people struggle to survive. 
One of them (played by Chow Yun-fatt) gallantly dies to let his best friend escape with the girl they both love.
Beyond the romance, beyond the memory of the atrocities committed by the Japanese, ''Hong Kong 1941'' is pregnant with allusions to the present. 
''When the Japanese officer distributes rice, he says, 'Have faith in me.'
Those were the very words used by Deng Xiaoping to the Hong Kong businessmen who were preparing to do business on the mainland,'' explains Mr. Po.
In her 1984 film ''Love in a Fallen City,'' Ann Hui, a top New Wave director, also set a love story amid the havoc wrought by the Japanese Army. 
Tsui Hark's hits ''Shanghai Blues'' (1984) and ''Peking Opera Blues'' (1986), as well as Jackie Chan's box-office draw ''Project A, Part II'' (1987), used a similar strategy: though displaced in time and space, Hong Kong's anxiety concerning its future at the end of the British Mandate was clearly recognizable. 
Parallels are often drawn between Hong Kong in the 1990's and Shanghai in the 1940's, as exemplified by a recent action film, Teddy Robin's ''Shanghai Shanghai.''
Hong Kong is afraid of meeting the fate of Shanghai, a thriving urban metropolis (and film production center) that went into decline after 1949, following the Communist takeover on the mainland.
''The nightmare,'' says Tsui Hark, ''is that the Chinese Government itself does not know if it is capable of running Hong Kong . . .''
Born in Vietnam to a family from the south of China, he moved to Hong Kong in 1966 as a teen-ager, studied film in the United States, directed a series of successful films and now runs his own production company, Film Workshop.
''Hong Kong is the last place I would leave,'' he adds, aware that this is also the only place he could continue making and producing movies. 
''But I would hate living under an outdated Government. 
The question is not whether to stay or to leave, but whether or not we will be able to change that Government, and how.''
After producing a series of top-grossing gangster films directed by John Woo and starring Chow Yun-fatt, ''A Better Tomorrow Part I'' and ''II,'' and ''The Killer,'' Mr. Tsui went back to directing with ''A Better Tomorrow Part III'' (also known as ''Love and Death in Saigon'').
''Vietnam in 1974, at the end of the American presence,'' he said, ''offered an interesting background. 
The protagonists are the products of their times. 
The main character is less heroic, he's no Rambo, he doesn't stand a chance against a whole army. 
And the bad guys are more elements of the general corruption than typical gangsters.''
Here again, the spectacle of individuals fighting for their dignity and happiness in a country torn apart by opposing armies and rival factions, functions as a metaphor for the colony's worst fears.
Mr. Tsui started filming in Vietnam during the student movement, then went back to Hong Kong to complete production. 
''Then came June 4,'' he says. 
''The actors couldn't concentrate. 
They were crying, constantly turning the radio on to listen to the news. 
They would come to the set with black banners on their chests. 
I had to cancel many production days to allow them to participate in demonstrations.''
As a result, ''Love and Death in Saigon'' is Mr. Tsui's most somber film. 
Allusions to political repression, to the senseless violence of armed men, to student demonstrations, keep creeping in, belying the ''Better Tomorrow'' of the original title.
Can there really be a ''better tomorrow'' in Hong Kong?
It is no longer fun to watch ''Chinese killing Chinese,'' as many people say, and while the hero still gets the heroine (Anita Mui), she dies in his arms.
Since the ''open door policy,'' in which the Chinese Government sought to normalize commercial and cultural relations with both Hong Kong and Taiwan, Hong Kong film makers have been able to shoot on the Chinese mainland, making use of its extraordinary landscapes. 
Between 40 and 50 movies (mostly action films) were being shot annually in co-production with China. 
Since June 4, this number has decreased radically, but the trend seems only temporary. 
For both the Chinese Government and the Hong Kong producers, ''business is business,'' and real locations are more attractive than papier-mache sets.
Last April, Mabel Cheung was shooting ''Eight Taels of Gold'' in a rural area near Canton. 
A shy, overweight New York cab driver (Samo Hung, the kung fu star, creatively cast against type), comes back to the village he fled during the Cultural Revolution. 
There he falls in love with his beautiful cousin, already engaged to another man. 
A return to life on the mainland is impossible for Hung, who is left shouting his despair in an empty landscape.
''We were really excited about the democracy movement,'' says Miss Cheung. 
''We would go to Beijing to give food and supplies to the students. 
On June 4, during a night shoot, we picked up the news on a Hong Kong radio. 
We couldn't believe it!
So we went to Canton and called Beijing to confirm what we heard. 
And we wondered: What's the point of making movies?
We should be lawyers, doctors, farmers, or go to Beijing to help the students.''
The production was halted - a highly emotional moment described by Sylvia Chang, who stars in the film as Samo Hung's cousin: ''When I came back to Hong Kong, people were utterly destroyed. 
They were asking: 'How can something like that happen?
We are Chinese, and we are killing Chinese. 
What's the meaning of life if we cannot do anything to help our own people?'
''
When production finally resumed, mainland Chinese bureaucrats tried to censor the script. 
''We threatened to publicize their attempt at censoring us,'' said Miss Cheung. 
''They must have thought that they don't yet have control over a Hong Kong production - and they let us shoot the way we wanted.''
The immediate impact of June 4 on the film industry seems to be an increased commercialism. 
''Everyone wants to make as much money as possible,'' says Po Chim Leong. 
''They're afraid to think of anything else. 
It's like there's no tomorrow. 
Film makers seem to have lost confidence. 
They keep turning out old formula films.''
For the first time in years, the box office is down. 
Yet people still invest in building and refurbishing movie theaters - knowing that the younger audience will keep going to the movies until the Communists take over in 1997 - and probably after. 
And there is no shortage of interesting projects. 
Po Chim Leong wants to shoot a contemporary version of ''Hong Kong 1941.''
Mabel Cheung plans to direct a two-part film about what she describes as ''the Hong Kong countdown,'' one from a female, the other from a male point of view. 
Allen Fong hopes to make ''as many movies as possible before 1997, to document the last years of Hong Kong,'' then emigrate and give up film making.
Hong Kong's censorship law makes it difficult to produce and exhibit what the text calls ''political'' movies. 
Films ''which may seriously endanger the relationship between Hong Kong and its neighboring countries'' are banned. 
Last December, a Taiwanese video documentary titled ''They're Writing History'' could not be shown at the Hong Kong Art Center because it included interviews with Chinese dissidents and student leaders. 
Paradoxically, television, radio and newspapers are not submitted to censorship and vent, often violently, negative feelings toward China.
Last spring, ''the television networks were competing to report the student movement with as much detail as possible,'' recalls Shu Kei, a film maker and public relations representative. 
''From April 15 till Tiananmen Square, the students almost became our friends, our family.''''
When a Japanese television station approached Shu Kei last year to produce a documentary, he first intended to make a film on the legendary Taiwanese composer-singer Hou Dejian, who, in 1983,defected to China. 
Tiananmen Square thwarted the project. 
(Mr. Hou, on a hunger strike at the end of the student movement, disappeared during the violence and resurfaced in Beijing only two months later.) Instead, Mr. Shu made ''Sunless Days,'' a ''personal documentary'' about Hong Kong's reactions to the crackdown. 
Interviewing families and friends, he took his camera throughout the Chinese diaspora, from London to Australia and Toronto and back to Hong Kong - trying to find answers to the harrowing question: What does it mean to be Chinese in the post-Tiananmen world?
The film is composed of vignettes depicting various reactions to the events: from the radicalization of a couple of fun-loving artists to the self-analysis of writers in exile; from a mainland film maker's decision to go back, ''because there is work to do at home,'' to the middle-class strategy for a comfortable emigration; from demonstrations of Hong Kong students to images of his mother going about her daily chores.
''No one can conceptualize Hong Kong in the hands of mainland China,'' adds Shu Kei. 
''This is why people are so nervous.''
Initially he thought that his documentary would be banned in Hong Kong. 
But the theatrical version of the film won a prize given by the Roman Catholic press at the 1990 Berlin Film Festival. 
So, invited by the Hong Kong Film Festival, ''Sunless Days'' was finally passed by the censorship committee at the last minute and shown on April 15, the anniversary of the death of the ousted Communist leader Hu Yaobang, which had set in motion the democracy movement.

file: FILM_Grappling With Modern China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Three quarters of a century ago, the novel "Family" by Ba Jin, a devastating portrait of feudal culture in 20th-century China, disturbed and inspired a generation of young Chinese to seek and promote change. 
The novel set a tone for much of the influential art of China for the rest of the century.
Except for long periods of artistic control under the Communists, when a mandatory, socialist-realist optimism prevailed, Chinese artists, writers and film makers have seen their country mired in a deeply oppressive, superstitious conservatism that was, in turn, at the heart of its decline. 
Dwelling on China's tragedies, they have tried to puzzle out a basic question: why has their extraordinary and brilliant civilization fallen into such intractable difficulty?
Four new films dealing with aspects of China show that the artistic quest of Ba Jin continues even today -- or, more accurately, has been renewed since the 1989 student uprising in Beijing. 
The films are very different from one another. 
None, moreover, contains any explicit political message, any direct attempt to impart the lessons of history.
They are "Ju Dou," a portrait of a rural family; "Iron and Silk," a lighthearted account of the experiences of an American teaching English and studying martial arts in the city of Hangzhou; "Song of the Exile," a Hong Kong-made film about a mother and daughter coming to grips with a complicated past, and, finally, "Shadow of China," an adventure movie about a former Red Guard who escapes to Hong Kong and becomes a titan of finance -- until his own troubling history catches up with him.
Still, different as they are -- and they were directed, respectively, by a Chinese, Chinese-American, Hong Kong and Japanese film maker -- each touches on that most persistent and haunting theme of Chinese art: the tragedies of 20th-century China and how those tragedies have affected individual lives.
Certainly the most controversial of the new films is "Ju Dou," which opens in New York today. 
The movie, which tells the story of a cloth dyer, his young wife and his adopted son in an unnamed village in China in the 1920's, was nominated by China's national film board to be the official entry in the Academy Awards this year, before Chinese authorities demanded, in vain, that the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences withdraw the film. 
News reports from China indicated that "Ju Dou" fell victim to a conservative turn in the arts following the suppression of the Tiananmen Square student uprising.
"Ju Dou" is the latest work of Zhang Yimou, whose previous film, "Red Sorghum," won the Golden Bear award at the Berlin Film Festival in 1988. 
Mr. Zhang has consistently explored the boundaries of the permissible in China's tightly controlled film industry; like many artists in China, he is trying to express troubling concepts in a way that will pass the censors' scrutiny.
To gain official approval, Mr. Zhang, for example, is said to have set his story in the early 1920's, when the Communist Party was founded in China. 
His reasoning, apparently, was that by explicitly describing what the Communists like to call the "old society," he could not be accused of indirect criticism of present-day authority. 
The conclusion could be that he was showing why it was necessary for a Communist Party to exist in the first place.
Despite Mr. Zhang's efforts, China's film authorities are demanding that the work be recut. 
Their reasons are unclear. 
Perhaps it is because, by Chinese standards, the film is too erotic: the young wife of the tyrannical and much older dyer falls in love with his shy adopted son, eventually bearing his child.
Perhaps the objections arise from the fact that the film offers no escape from the stiflingly feudal traditions of China, no hope for a radiant future. 
In any case, of all of the recent offerings about China, "Ju Dou" is closest to the spirit of Ba Jin and other writers earlier in the century.
At first glance, "Iron and Silk," directed by Shirley Sun, an American born in China, seems far removed from the themes and depictions of "Ju Dou."
Ms. Sun's film, based on a book by Mark Salzman (who plays himself in the movie), is not aimed at the darker side of Chinese tradition. 
In the film, Mr. Salzman goes to China to teach English and realize his ambition of studying with a martial-arts master. 
He has various encounters with his students, especially with Pan Qingfu, a real-life martial arts master who, like Mr. Salzman, plays himself in the movie.
The encounters often puzzle and vex the young American, reminding him that a culture as self-contained, ancient and different as China's presents a tricky shoal for the foreigner to navigate -- even if challenging and often enjoyable.
Despite the film's sweet and gentle tone, authoritarian politics and China's continuing struggle to adapt to the challenge of the modern world are never far away. 
Mr. Salzman runs into trouble with the stern official in charge of the school's foreign affairs -- the very incarnation of China's humorless, inflexible, cautious bureaucrat. 
The bureaucrat sniffs out an innocent love affair that the American seeks with a medical student, played by Vivian Wu.
In this sense, youthful romantic yearnings -- which played a minor role in Ba Jin's "Family" and a major one in the Tiananmen uprising of two years ago -- are characteristically thwarted by the conservatism, the oppressive and life-denying social practices that, in a far more tragic way, spoil the lives of the characters of Mr. Zhang's "Ju Dou."
The dramatic center of "Iron and Silk" shows Mr. Salzman welcomed by ordinary people but isolated by Chinese officialdom. 
Mr. Salzman finds at one point that the door to his martial-arts master's studio is slammed shut. 
The reason: the campaign against "spiritual pollution" and "bourgeois liberalization," code words for the bad habits that supposedly come from Western influences.
Ms. Sun says that, even with the film showing in the United States, the authorities are demanding alterations. 
They have asked that she drop at least one segment of dialogue -- when the medical student tells Mr. Salzman they cannot continue seeing each other. 
"Things are not as free as they seem," she says. 
The Chinese insistence that the line be dropped seems to be an unintentional affirmation that the line is true.
Conflicts arising out of life in China's past are depicted in two other films. 
One, "Song of the Exile," by the Hong Kong director Ann Hui, begins when Hueyin, a student, returns home to Hong Kong for her sister's wedding. 
In so doing, she resumes a troubled relationship with her mother. 
Slowly, the many layers of that relationship, each corresponding to a layer of history, unfold.
Hueyin was a wartime child. 
Her father was a Communist soldier in Manchuria; her mother, Aiko, a Japanese citizen trapped there by the war's sudden end. 
When Hueyin and her mother visit Aiko's family in Japan, the daughter comes to understand her mother's moodiness and lack of affection, both stemming from her sense of estrangement as a Japanese living among the Chinese.
That historical intrusion is complicated by the burst of Maoist radicalism in China known as the Cultural Revolution, which affects Hueyin when she returns to the Communist mainland to visit her grandparents. 
In the beginning of the film, Hueyin believes she can escape the politics of China by going to England. 
Once she returns to Hong Kong, however, she discovers she is too deeply entangled to try to escape again; this time she chooses to remain.
There are similar notes in "Shadow of China," a thriller directed by Mitsuo Yanagimachi and starring John Lone as a member of the Chinese Red Guard who makes his fortune in Hong Kong. 
The opening sequences show the pain and sorrow of China amid the excesses of the Cultural Revolution, but the film, whose dialogue is mostly in English, is taken over by sexual infidelities, cutthroat big-business competition and drug traffickers who belong to the Triads, Hong Kong's main criminal underworld.
But even amid cinematic adventure, the Chinese past reaches out. 
The former Red Guard is, like Hueyin of "Song of the Exile," the child of a wartime marriage between a Chinese woman and a Japanese spy, and that fact, once exposed, leads both to his ruin and to a lonely walk back across the border from Hong Kong to China. 
The Red Guard, even in escaping China itself and creating a new, glittering life, is unable to escape the consequences of war and politics.
John K. Fairbank, the Harvard historian of modern China, used to say that there were three Chinas -- the mercantile country of the coastal port cities, the country of an immense conservative governing bureaucracy and the vast rural country of hundreds of thousands of villagers, nearly untouched by time.
These four films touch on all three Chinas. 
"Ju Dou" is the hinterland; "Iron and Silk" shines a light on bureaucratic China. 
"Song of the Exile" and "Shadow of China" take place on the commercial littoral, the part of China that is part diaspora and part Chinese. 
That spectrum of evocations should be useful to Western audiences who have seen few films about or by Chinese.
In "Iron and Silk," on arriving in Hangzhou, Mr. Salzman notes that here he is in a country of more than one billion people and "I don't know a single one of them."
These movies enable Americans to know at least some of them.

text:
ï»¿
I MYSELF AM A WOMAN
Selected Writings of Ding Ling.
Edited by Tani E. Barlow with Gary J. Bjorge.
361 pp. 
Boston:
Beacon Press. 
$24.95.
A model of the modern emancipated woman in prerevolutionary Shanghai, and an author of scandalous romantic fiction, the Chinese writer Ding Ling joined the Communists in Yanan in the 1930's and edited the literary columns of Liberation Daily, the party newspaper. 
At a critical juncture in party affairs, she allied herself with Mao Zedong's famous dictum that all art must hasten the revolution. 
Despite her efforts at political rectitude, she was hounded, exiled, and periodically imprisoned from the late 1950's onward.
''I Myself Am a Woman,'' augmented by a long interpretive essay by Tani E. Barlow, an assistant professor of history at the University of Missouri, is the most comprehensive selection of Ding Ling's work yet published in America. 
We now can ponder at close range the literary progression of a tempestuous rebel caught up in a revolution she believed to be necessary and good, who willingly sacrificed her ironic detachment and subtlest perceptions to the Maoist principle of ''serving the people.''
It is easy to see why the audacious stories from the 1920's established Ding Ling's literary reputation.
In ''A Woman and a Man'' (1928) the newly married, bored and provocative Wendy (she has dropped her Chinese name) arranges an assignation with Ouwai Ou, a pretentious, dissipated poet who has given himself a Japanese nom de plume. 
Ouwai Ou, alas, finds easier sexual satisfaction with Aijin, a back-alley prostitute who is grateful for his money. 
Her chastity, if not her feelings of sexual desirability, intact, Wendy returns to her husband armed with the small crumb of insight that Ouwai Ou is ''afraid of me!
Afraid of me!''
This delightful piece of fiction, which skewers the superficial bourgeois-intellectual circle that Ding Ling had come to detest, mixes a fine sense of place and a minute dissection of her characters' inner feelings with her inimitable signature from that era: a frisky, satirical poke at the double standard. 
The author of ''A Woman and a Man'' could be a spiritual sister to Jean Rhys.
In the winter of 1930, the father of Ding Ling's child and 23 other Communist activists and writers were executed by Chiang Kai-shek. 
Her response was swift and irrevocable: she joined the revolutionary struggle.
''Net of Law'' (1932) shows the effects of her Marxist transformation. 
The condition of woman is still close to her heart as she attempts to enter the world of China's proletariat. 
Alcoholism, wife beating, even murder, are rife in the slums of Hankou, a factory town, but the enemy is plainly the viperish capitalist system. 
An opaque veil hangs over the inner life of her characters; she prefers to show that the masses are in motion.
''When I Was in Xia Village'' (1941) demonstrates the transmogrification of Ding Ling, now a high Party functionary, into Maxim Gorky. 
Zhenzhen, a poor peasant raped by the Japanese, has contracted a venereal disease. 
When she returns to her backward village, she is ostracized by the elders. 
But there is hope for Zhenzhen: the Communist Party arranges for her to go to Yanan for treatment.
Innocuous on the face of it, this story was apparently a factor in Ding Ling's subsequent trouble. 
Ms. Barlow says that it ''upset literary policy enforcers because it reverted back to Ding Ling's earlier preoccupation with sex and justice. 
It also placed a woman seeking social redress at the center of the plot.''
I would offer a slightly different emphasis. 
More likely, Ding Ling's specific ideological heresy lay in placing an individual's social redress at the plot's center; in just such hairsplitting distinctions a generation of Chinese writers was destroyed.
In any event, the details of Ding Ling's fall from grace are still murky. 
Her class background, stormy personal life and high visibility were sufficient grounds for suspicion. 
A victim of the 1957 antirightist campaign, she was exiled to Manchuria, where she managed to continue writing under the patronage of some old friends in high places. 
She and thousands of other intellectuals fell into the hands of the Red Guards in 1966. 
Ding Ling underwent the ritual humiliations of the Great Cultural Revolution - the dunce cap, the public confession - and spent most of the next decade in solitary confinement. 
She was rehabilitated in 1978 under the aegis of Deng Xiaoping.
''Du Wanxiang,'' the final story in this collection, dated 1978 but written more than 10 years earlier, is a stolid parable about the hardships of a poor, industrious peasant with minimal skills (actually they are the feminine skills of cooking and cleaning) who triumphs in her desire to serve the people in a development outpost. 
The last lines read, after the fashion of the day, ''Du Wanxiang is our frontline soldier. 
We must learn from her. 
We must go forward with her.''
Officially restored to a position of eminence, Ding Ling was granted a trip to the United States in 1981, where she visited the University of Iowa's writing program and met with Arthur Miller. 
A new generation of Chinese writers, impatient for change and disappointed by her continued defense of literary censorship, took to calling her Old Shameful. 
She died a natural death in 1985.
Ms. Barlow's valuable though overly academic introductory essay proposes that Ding Ling's early feminist ideas were imported from the West, and thus were inevitably doomed in the larger context and priorities of the 1949 revolution. 
But most liberation theories - Marxist, feminist, anarchist, democratic - were imported from elsewhere to feudal, Mandarin China. 
The forcible suppression of the student rebellion this past June reminds us that feminism was not the only idea that lost out.

BECAUSE the Chinese words for fish and for prosperity or abundance are pronounced the same - yu - fish is one of the symbolic foods for the Chinese New Year celebrations that begin Saturday.
For this year's holiday banquets, an increasing number of chefs - especially in New York and California - will be scooping their fish live from tanks in the kitchens and sometimes in the dining rooms of restaurants. 
Cooks preparing fish at home can also buy fish live from markets in the Chinatowns of San Francisco, Los Angeles and New York -in Flushing, Queens, and the Sunset Park section of Brooklyn as well as Manhattan.
The trend reflects the growing influence of Hong Kong cuisine, the newest of Chinese cuisines to be imported to the United States. 
Restaurateurs in Hong Kong, anticipating the return of the British colony to China in 1997, have started establishing businesses in the United States, and more and more chefs are relocating.
In Hong Kong, restaurants with fish tanks are routine and shoppers in the city's Central Market often take their fish or shrimp home in plastic bags filled with water.
''As more chefs come here from Hong Kong, you'll see more restaurants with live fish,'' said Ken Hom, the author whose latest book, ''Fragrant Harbor Taste'' (Simon and Shuster, 1989, $24.95) is about the cooking of Hong Kong. 
He described the Hong Kong style as essentially a more elegant version of Cantonese cooking. 
The restaurants tend to be fancier and considerably larger than other Chinese restaurants.
''There is great emphasis on seafood because of Hong Kong's location,'' he added. 
''And whereas it may be easy to keep fish alive in a pond in a rural area in Canton, in a big city like Hong Kong it's expensive. 
That adds to its allure.''
Though his restaurants do not have tanks of live fish, Michael Tong has added a chef from Hong Kong to the staff of one of his establishments, Shun Lee Palace in midtown Manhattan. 
''Hong Kong cooking is the first really new Chinese style that has caught on in awhile,'' Mr. Tong said.
Several Hong Kong-style dishes, like gray sole on a bed of crispy, edible bones, are on his special New Year's menu at Shun Lee Palace, 155 East 55th Street.
Other restaurants in Manhattan that maintain tanks of live fish - usually freshwater varieties - include the Golden Unicorn, 18 East Broadway at Catherine Street, and Oriental Town Seafood Restaurant, 14 Elizabeth Street at Bayard Street.
The new Triple Eight restaurant, at 88 East Broadway at Forsyth Street, maintains tanks of both fresh- and saltwater fish. 
The fish are usually simply steamed with ginger and scallions so the freshness of the flavor can dominate.
Among the dishes at Oriental Town Seafood is steamed black carp with black beans. 
The Golden Unicorn serves live shrimp cooked at tableside in a broth.
Live shrimp is a delicacy that only a few restaurants carry. 
''They are very expensive - up to $20 a pound wholesale - and are so delicate that they can't be kept overnight,'' said Chuck Lou, one of the owners of Hy Fund, a fish market at 75 Mulberry Street in Manhattan, where at least six kinds of fish are available live on a given day.
The fish are freshwater varieties, like carp, buffalo fish, crappie and a type of large-mouth bass. 
Mr. Lou said the market does not carry live saltwater fish because maintaining the chemical balance in a tank is extremely difficult.
Some of the fish come from the Great Lakes and, increasingly, from fish farms around the country. 
Tank trucks filled with swimming white crappies, catfish, carp, blue gills and freshwater bass now make the 28-hour trip to New York from fish farms in Arkansas on a regular basis. 
At the New York Fish Exchange, a wholesaler at the Fulton Fish Market, several other varieties are available from time to time.
Prices in retail markets like Hy Fund in Chinatown range from $1.40 a pound for live carp to $8 a pound for large-mouth bass. 
The markets will dress the fish to order.
In the San Francisco area, live fish are kept in tanks at several Hong Kong-style restaurants, including Wu Kong, at 101 Spear Street near Mission Hill, Hong Kong Flower Lounge in Millbrae, North Sea Village in Sausalito and Suntung Lok in Burlingame. 
Markets in San Francisco that carry live fish include Wah Fat Fish and Sang Sang.
Bruce Cost, author of ''Asian Ingredients'' (William Morrow, 1988) and owner of Monsoon, a restaurant near the San Francisco City Hall that opened in November, is planning to install an aquarium for live fish. 
''For the time being I'm keeping live catfish in a couple of sinks in the kitchen, but I expect to install fish tanks between the kitchen and the bar where the customers can see them.''
The San Francisco restaurants and markets are supplied by fishermen who keep their catch in tanks on boats and by fish farms in Southern California and elsewhere. 
The fish, among them catfish, rock cod and striped bass are bought, cleaned and cooked the same day.
When Chinese cooks buy live fish in a market they usually steam it. 
One example suitable for a Chinese New Year's menu, is steamed buffalo fish with ginger and scallions, a recipe that Norman Weinstein teaches at his cooking school in Brooklyn, Hot Wok. 
Another is Mr. Hom's steamed fish with ham and vegetables.
Both these dishes are particularly appropriate for celebrating the Chinese New Year because they call for whole fish, a symbol of prosperity.

After years of being spurned on the international weapons marketplace, there are signs that these days Taiwan is finding Western countries willing to sell it modern military equipment to defend itself against mainland China.
Taiwan's relative success in buying modern weaponry shows the extent to which it may be reintegrating into the international community even though scarcely any important countries recognize it as the legitimate Government of China. 
The weapons purchases are also likely to inflame relations between Taipei and Beijing and cause tensions between the Chinese Government and Western Governments willling to sell such equipment.
Weapons specialists say that since the Persian Gulf war and the warming of relations between the Soviet Union and Western countries, military contractors -- and perhaps Governments -- are under greater pressure to find new markets, like Taiwan. 
While they may not yet be selling jet fighters, companies are talking to Taiwan about a wider range of weaponry and electronic warfare equipment.
"The business for us is shrinking in the U.S., so we have to start looking overseas for business," said a representative of an American armaments company, who was displaying advanced military communications systems at an exhibition recently in Taipei. 
"That's why we're here."
Armaments companies have always been willing to sell to Taiwan, but in the past, Western governments have frequently denied export licenses. 
Not all weapons specialists agree, but many say that the United States and several European countries may now be reconsidering the benefits of selling certain modern equipment to Taiwan against the risks of Chinese retaliation.
They add that with the collapse of Communism in the Soviet Union, the strategic importance of China may be diminishing, so that countries may be willing to stand up to pressure from the Chinese Government.
"Before, Taiwan could never pay billions of dollars for weapons and the French would never talk to us before," said Hei Youlong, a business executive and weapons expert in Taipei. 
"Now, Taiwan has money and when it talks, people start listening."
For example, in a deal many weapons specialists say is nearly completed, France plans to sell to Taiwan six Lafayette-class frigates, worth $2 billion, according to local news reports, with an option to buy 10 more.
Nearly two years ago, the deal fell through when China protested to France and successfully blocked the sale. 
Not only is the sale expected to go through this time, but China issued only a mild criticism of the deal.
In contrast, in the early 1980's, when Taiwan purchased two submarines from the Netherlands, China downgraded its relationship with the Netherlands to consular status. 
The relationship has since returned to normal.
More recently, the United States has approved the sale of four E-2 Hawkeye early warning aircraft, manufactured by the Grumman Corporation.
Taiwan, however, apparently wants a more modern version that the United States so far has not agreed to sell.
Currently, Taiwan's ability to detect approaching aircraft flying at low altitudes is relatively weak, as is its air capability in general, weapons analysts say. 
In the last two years, 19 to 20 jet fighters have crashed, including a prototype for a locally built fighter plane that Taiwan is trying to develop through a co-production arrangement with an American company.
The United States has consistently refused to sell F-16 jet fighters to Taiwan because they could be used to attack mainland China. 
It has sold the aircraft to other Asian nations, including Pakistan, Thailand and Singapore.
Taiwan and the United States cut off formal ties in 1979, when the United States and mainland China established diplomatic relations. 
At the time, the United States agreed to provide Taiwan with defensive arms but in 1982, it issued a joint communique with the Chinese that essentially limited American arms sales to Taiwan in quality and quantity to the level of those supplied previously. 
The United States was then supplying about $800 million in arms to Taiwan.
