ï»¿
The term ''pregnancy leave'' is taking on a new meaning here, as shown by a successful Hong Kong Chinese banker who is negotiating an unusual sweetener before he takes a new job. 
He wants his employer to pay to send his pregnant wife to Canada to give birth, insuring that their child will be born a Canadian citizen.
In the latest triumph of Hong Kong ingenuity, and the latest sign of Hong Kong's desperation, hundreds and possibly thousands of pregnant women are traveling to Western countries to give their babies what is regarded here as one of the most important things in the world: a foreign passport.
''In Hong Kong, when people ask you where you are going to have your baby, they don't mean which hospital,'' said Frank Ching, a writer and local newspaper columnist. 
''They mean which country.''
It used to be thought that the moment of truth for Hong Kong would come in 1997, when the British colony will revert to China, but now many people feel that the crisis is already here.
Â 
Mounting Frenzy Expected
Pessimists are drawing parallels with the surrender to Communism of Shanghai in 1949 and Saigon in 1975. 
They expect a mounting frenzy to leave, a surge in corruption as people try to buy a new future, and a social breakdown as the civil service abandons its loyalty to the lame-duck British administration.
''Hong Kong will all be destroyed before 1997,'' said George Hicks, an Australian businessman and writer who seats himself firmly in the pessimist camp. 
''The upheaval and disintegration will come way before 1997, as everybody tries to beat their neighbor out. 
This is like a game of musical chairs in which everybody knows when the music is going to stop.''
Of course, there are also optimists who believe that Hong Kong's economy is well positioned to continue to prosper, and that ballooning bank accounts will help salve anxieties about the future. 
Hong Kong has faced bouts of pessimism in the past, and few places in the world have displayed such a remarkable resiliency in overcoming wars, strikes, riots and trade embargoes.
In 150 years, Hong Kong has transformed itself from a pirates' lair to the world's largest container port, from an impoverished colony abounding in opium and skeletal rickshaw boys to an international financial center where impeccably dressed young men and women race along the streets, their Rolex watches peeking from under their sleeves as they chatter into portable telephones. 
Hong Kong today is richer and healthier than much of Europe, and it has more Rolls-Royces per capita than anywhere else in the world.
Â 
Despair Over Basic Law
Yet Hong Kong's fate seemed to be sealed in early April, when China's legislature approved the Basic Law that will govern the territory after 1997. 
The passage by China's National People's Congress was a formality, but it had the ring of finality for many Hong Kong residents who had hoped for a more democratic document.
Ever since the rise of China's hard-liners and the killings in Beijing last June, the mood in Hong Kong has been bleak and angry. 
Survey Research Hong Kong, a polling business that has measured confidence in the future since 1985, says its latest survey recorded a new low in public confidence. 
''People in Hong Kong are very discouraged at this time,'' said Louis Tong, director of the company. 
#1,000 Leaving Each Week Residents are emigrating at the rate of more than 1,000 a week, more than twice the rate in 1986. 
The obsession with emigration has spawned a new magazine, The Emigrant, as well as books and counseling services to help Hong Kong Chinese obtain foreign passports.
In one of the most unusual cases, a few people even paid about $5,000 each as a down payment on a passport from Corterra, which a brochure and advertisement identified as a South Pacific nation. 
They discovered too late that there is no such country.
Hong Kong does not officially report figures for capital flows, but John G. Greenwood, chief economist of G. T. Management (Asia) Ltd., an investment company, has derived estimates that suggest that Hong Kong began to shift capital abroad in 1984, the year that Britain agreed to return Hong Kong to China. 
By his method of calculation, the capital outflow soared in 1989 to nearly $5 billion, or almost $1,000 per inhabitant.
The apprehensions have been compounded by Hong Kong's unaccustomed encounter with economic difficulties. 
Economic growth tumbled to just 2.5 percent last year, about one-third of the usual level, and hotel occupancy rates dropped to 74 percent, compared with 92 percent in 1988. 
Over the last decade, Hong Kong's economy became integrated with southern China's, and so China's woes spill across the border into the British territory.
Â 
U.S. and China Imports Fall
The cause of the economic downturn is fairly straightforward: slowdowns in Hong Kong's biggest export markets: China and the United States. 
Thus the optimists, like George Baeder, director of the Pacific Rim Consulting Group in Hong Kong, argue that those are cyclical slowdowns and that when economic growth returns, the problems of Hong Kong will seem much more manageable.
''Think what happens when the U.S. economy picks up, when China rebounds from its cyclical downturn,'' he said. 
Then, he continued, if the leaders in Beijing ease out some prominent hard-liners and turn toward more pragmatic officials, Hong Kong will again be on the move.
Another source of optimism in some quarters is the belief that hard-line rule in Beijing is unsustainable. 
Albert W. Y. Chan, a local politician in the New Territories part of Hong Kong, is guardedly optimistic for the long term.
''With the democratization of Communist societies around the world, I don't think that the Chinese Communist Party can keep control indefinitely,'' he said. 
''Sooner or later, probably before 1997, there'll be major changes that will benefit Hong Kong.''
Â 
The Pessimism Deepens
The conventional wisdom in the business sector used to be that China would pursue its own self-interest in insuring Hong Kong's continued prosperity -because Hong Kong is China's biggest outside investor and trade partner, and because successful reunification might encourage Taiwan to return to the mainland as well. 
Arguments about China's self-interest are heard much less often today, for today's China seems to measure its self-interest more in control than in prosperity.
The multinational companies that have regional offices in Hong Kong are weighing the arguments, and more than half of them are considering moving elsewhere, one recent survey shows. 
Singapore is the most likely beneficiary, particularly for companies that focus on Southeast Asia, but many companies say they intend to remain in Hong Kong.
One source of concern for the private and public sectors has been the growing assertiveness of labor groups, and the threats of strikes by firefighters, taxi drivers, nurses and other groups.
''Everybody's scrambling for more money,'' said a longtime civil servant. 
''Nobody wants to wait. 
I don't see how the society can operate that way.''
The official, a Briton who regards Hong Kong as his home, added glumly: ''And I don't think that the real panic has set in yet. 
That's still ahead of us.''

file: From the Stone Age to Tiananmen Square.txt
text:
ï»¿
CHINA
A New History.
By John King Fairbank.
Illustrated. 519 pp. 
Cambridge, Mass.:
The Belknap Press/
Harvard University Press.
$27.95.
SLIGHTLY before the midpoint of John King Fairbank's latest and last book -- the eminent Harvard historian of China died last year at the age of 84 -- appears the only overtly autobiographical passage in the volume. 
It was in the early 1930's, Fairbank writes in "China: A New History," that he and his wife settled into Beijing life, and three things at once impressed the young newlywed graduate students as unusual. 
First, there was the extraordinary extent of their privilege as foreign residents; they were treated as members of the ruling-class elite from the first moment in China and were left unbothered by the ubiquitous police. 
Second, because of the incredible surplus of Chinese manpower the easiest form of transportation around the ancient city was by rickshaw: you lay back against the seats of the two-wheeled vehicle while the "intelligent human horse between the shafts" trotted and sweated his way to your destination. 
Third, in both city and country, all women of early middle age and over had bound feet, which left them "stumping about awkwardly on their heels as though the front sections of their feet had been amputated."
Why had this last practice in particular, Fairbank muses, been so little studied or discussed by either Chinese or Western scholars?
For close to a millennium, hundreds of millions of Chinese women had had the toes of their feet systematically bent under their arches, and the arches themselves strapped, tilted and broken, and then the women had performed the same protracted and agonizing ritual deformation on their own daughters. 
Why had no one tried to assess the "social and psychic repercussions" of this nightmare practice, reputedly performed for the sensual delectation of men, even though the physiological, esthetic or erotic effects of foot-binding were far from clear?
Perhaps, Fairbank concludes, Chinese scholars had dodged the topic because it would have forced them to confront the whole problem of women's subjugation; and perhaps the Westerners had dodged the topic as well because they were eager to avoid giving offense to Chinese sensitivities. 
Few scholars "are muckrakers by temperament," notes Fairbank, and since foot-binding was unique to China it was not a convenient topic for comparative sociological study. 
Furthermore, he observes, there is an "occupational quirk of sinologists, a secondary patriotism or sinophilia that may lead otherwise hard-headed scholars to want to say no evil of the object of their researches."
This last sentence is starred to a footnote on the same page, almost the only time in this entire history that Fairbank uses such a device, and the purpose of the starred note is clearly to deepen the autobiographical reflection further, and to carry it forward in time into another kind of dangerous psychic terrain. 
"For an outstanding example of sentimental sinophilia," Fairbank adds, "see my statement in Foreign Affairs, October 1972, that in a certain context the Maoist revolution was 'the best thing' that had happened to the Chinese people in many centuries."
In these brief passages we have a distillation of the historical stance that Fairbank adopted in the last years of his long and formidably productive scholarly life -- a stance that sought to present itself as both frank and skeptical, tackling the difficult questions and suggesting directions for new research, while making the author himself disarmingly vulnerable by his admission of past mistakes. 
Fairbank, this century's foremost promoter of Chinese studies, chose to bow out with a show of modesty.
I say show of modesty not with any intention to belittle this extraordinary man, but rather to underscore the incredible ambitiousness of his final work. 
"China: A New History" sets out to cover, in 432 pages of text, the entire span of China's history from the paleolithic cultures of 400,000 B.C. to the Tiananmen massacre of 1989, and it does so with a brisk and sprightly air but also with an awesomely thorough overview of the current scholarly work of scores of historians. 
The book is indeed a kind of reprise not only of Fairbank's life as a reader and teacher, but also of his long years as editor or co-editor of the many volumes of the monumental "Cambridge History of China," Volume 15 of which, on the People's Republic and Taiwan between 1966 and 1982, was published last year. 
Perhaps most surprisingly, for those who have followed Fairbank's extraordinary range of studies in the fields of Chinese-United States foreign policy, institutional history and missionary history, "China: A New History" is dedicated in large part to social history, to the infrastructures and daily life of the Chinese, and to the elusive world of "civil society" that obviously existed and flourished at many levels under the watchful eyes of the purportedly omnipresent autocratic state.
Despite Fairbank's attention to social movements in this volume, his intellectual energy seems still to be most concentrated on the problems of state power and dissonance that led -- among other things -- to those three aspects of exploitive hierarchy that he highlighted in the book's autobiographical musings. 
In one passage, arresting to the historian at once for its concision and for the vastness of the ideas tackled, Fairbank reflects on how a kind of unifying theory does seem to emerge from his lifetime's reading and research on China's long history, a theory that makes sense because it incorporates the rhythms of China's periods of fragmentation and conquest by others along with its own enduring institutional forms. 
In Fairbank's words:
"The hypothesis may be stated as follows: (1) that early China created a politicized state organized for purposes of central control both by bureaucratic methods of philosophic persuasion and by the imperial autocrat's use of violence; (2) that non-Chinese invaders from Inner Asia became integral participants in the Chinese polity by their military prowess and administrative skill; and (3) that the resulting Sino-nomadic imperial power continued to maintain the primacy of central political control over the subordinated processes of economic growth and cultural diversification."
Elsewhere in the volume, Fairbank produces a rather different formulation that he felt contrasted China succinctly with the main lines of Western development. 
Where the main line of Western national "style" had been "industrial-military-entrepreneurial," that in China had been "agrarian-nomadic-bureaucratic."
In many ways, as Fairbank's chapters on modern China show, both Chiang Kai-shek and Mao Zedong were caught in this cycle of values. 
Fairbank is distinctly unsympathetic to both these central leaders of 20th-century China, consistently with his earlier views in the case of Chiang, and perhaps seeking to bury the ghost of those 1972 "sentimental" deviations in the case of Mao.
Though the economic, educational and industrial reforms of Chiang's Kuomintang years are discussed fairly and thoroughly, Chiang himself emerges as a "vigorous Dr. Jekyll" who "metamorphosed" into a "sordid Mr. Hyde," and lost the civil war of 1946-49 through "stupidity" and "incompetence."
Similarly, though Communist attempts at national and rural reconstruction get their due, Fairbank writes that Mao's basic "organizational principle" was that of any traditional Chinese "bandit" who used "force and guile . . . to curry favor with the local people," before he emerged at last as an "updated emperor" whose final acts were to lead his people "up a mountain and into a volcano."
The only man to get an equally bad press is the leader of the massive mid-19th-century Taiping Rebellion, Hong Xiuquan, whose "bizarre and irrational" theocracy prompts Fairbank to search for parallels that range from Napoleon to Hitler. 
The invoking of such parallels is a device that Fairbank enjoys, and like his invocation of echoes from China's past it can be effective and arresting. 
Occasionally it illuminates the instant with a zany humor similar to that which did indeed bubble just beneath Fairbank's own often formidable public persona. 
One of my favorites is Fairbank's aside that the closest equivalent he can think of to Mao's massively publicized swim across the Yangtze River in 1966 would be "the news that Queen Elizabeth II had swum the Channel."
SUCH asides may not be good history, but they are good-humored and make a point. 
On other occasions, the aside can trivialize the moment. 
Thus to summarize the archeological finds of Stone Age Chinese skeletons with smashed-in skulls as showing that "Peking Man was a small-time cannibal or at least a head-hunter who savored brains" strikes me as a little tacky; to equate Han dynasty neo-Confucian imperial rituals with White House "foto-ops and sound-bites" is erratic; and to call the terrible famine that followed the Great Leap Forward "first-class" is truly odd.
Such ruminations aside, this book is an admirable achievement. 
And even if one cannot accept the idea that this history is entirely new, Fairbank has filled the analytic narrative with intelligent ideas and original contributions: on the long-term effect of the absence of early maritime trade in China, on frontier appeasement policies, on the inherent problems of translation of foreign texts into Chinese characters, on Confucian attitudes to the military, on the development of popular religion, on sweated labor, on the failures of democratic experimentation and the other quests of China's new elite of "Sino-liberals," on the politics of repression and the role of sycophancy. 
Fairbank dominated the field of China studies in the West for 50 years. 
In this volume, we see that even on the edge of death his hand had not lost its cunning.

file: Frustrated Chinese Look to U.S. as a Haven.txt
text:

''There are two kinds of people in China these days,'' said a worker in his 20's, continuing with a cheerful exaggeration. 
''First, there are those who simply want to go to the United States. 
And second, there are those who are already well along in their preparations to depart.''
Not everyone is afflicted by the ''emigration fever,'' as it is called here, but it is clear that the urge to leave has markedly increased since the army's crackdown on the democracy movement last year. 
That urge to relocate is motivated not only by political repression but by a far-deeper sense of frustration and discontent, as well as by rising economic expectations that China cannot meet.
''This place isn't stable, for all the official talk about stabilityI,'' said a woman in her 40's, who agonized over lists of English words to prepare for moving to the United States. 
''And everyone finds it stifling, with few opportunities to use your skills. 
What's more, Americans all have cars!''
Alarmed by the flood of students going abroad - compared with the trickle of people returning - the Chinese Government early this year imposed restrictions that on their face prevented college graduates from going abroad to study until they have worked for five years.
But ingenious young scholars are putting their minds to work evading the regulations. 
The most common method is to invent an aunt or uncle in Hong Kong or the United States, and take advantage of a clause allowing those with relatives abroad to pay fees instead of working for five years.
''We've had no significant change in the types of people who come in applying for student visas,'' an American diplomat here said. 
''We're still seeing lots of recent college graduates who come in. 
The number of applicants and the number of issuances are both up.''
In August, for example, the United States Embassy in Beijing received 1,550 applications for student visas, compared with 1,371 applications in August 1989 and 949 applications in August 1988. 
The portion receiving visas has also risen, to 60 percent from 43 percent two years ago.
There is no doubt that the new regulations have had an effect - many recent graduates say that they have postponed their plans to go abroad - so one explanation for the increase in the number of applicants is that it would have soared without the restrictions.
''Five members of my senior class are applying to American universities,'' a high school student in Beijing said. 
''I could do very well here, and join the Communist Party, and find a suitable husband, and get a good job. 
But there are lots of limits on what we can do here, and I think I'll be better off with training in America.''
A young business executive said that a few years ago, a Japanese executive offered to pay for her to study in Japan. 
She refused, and these days she thinks she made a terrible mistake.
''Now I can see that if you have talent here, you're suppressed and harassed,'' she said. 
She complained about her cramped dormitory room, which she shares with three roommates, and about her company's plans to send her to work in a factory to gain an appreciation for manual labor.
''I'm optimistic about my own future,'' she said, ''because I plan to go abroad, but I'm pessimistic about China. 
Anyone with talent is trying to leave. 
Absolutely everyone I know is looking for an exit.''

file: Furor Erupts Over Hong Kong Plan.txt
text:
ï»¿
Plans for a new airport here have led to a furor over who now speaks for this British colony's 5.7 million people -- Britain or China, which is scheduled to take control in 1997.
Hong Kong's British Governor is to visit Beijing on Monday and is expected to tell the Chinese authorities that the project will proceed, despite their angry objections.
Analysts and diplomats here say that while Beijing may have some justified concerns about the financing of the ambitious airport project, it also has decided to use the issue to assert control over Hong Kong, even before 1997.
In a war of words that has grown more and more bitter in the past two weeks, Chinese officials have insisted that Beijing has a right to a say in all important policies and projects that will affect Hong Kong after 1997. 
On Tuesday, in a statement that a prominent government analyst at the Chinese University here called "astonishing," the Deputy Premier of China asserted that "during the transition period, only the Central People's Government can, and is entitled to, speak on behalf of the people of Hong Kong."
Â 
Airport at Top of Talk List
Deputy Premier Wu Xueqian's remarks were quoted in official Chinese press reports. 
The Governor, Sir David Wilson, scheduled his trip before the latest exchanges began, but the airport is now expected to top the list of subjects to be discussed.
Today, Sir David was circumspect about the trip, saying only that Hong Kong wanted "a sensible relationship, a good relationship with China," adding, "That's the objective of my visit."
Sir David is expected to meet with Chinese Premier Li Peng and with Lu Ping, the new head of the Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office.
An experienced political analyst at Hong Kong University said that the dispute over the airport has grown into such an important political issue that "it is very doubtful that the question can be resolved at the Hong Kong level, during the Governor's visit."
"This is an issue that must be negotiated by Britain, by top-level officials," the analyst said. 
At most, he added, "The governor may be able to soften them up and help prepare for the visit of Lord Caithness," the British minister with special responsibility for Hong Kong. 
He is to meet with Chinese officials later this month.
Â 
China Seeks Project Suspension
Newspapers here have reported the airport dispute in front page stories with bold headlines, and in editorials they have called China's statements "hostile" and "bullying."
One political columnist said that if Britain acceded to Beijing's demands for veto power over projects here, the Hong Kong administration would go from being a "lame duck" to a "puppet" government.
Western diplomats said when a Hong Kong government team went to Beijing a week ago for talks on the technical and financial details of the $10 billion airport package, they were told to suspend the project until China's objections were answered.
As the three days of talks bogged down in Beijing, China's Ambassador in London was summoned to the British Foreign Office on two separate occasions to explain China's opposition. 
The talks ended on Jan. 
12 with Luo Jiahuan, who heads the Chinese airport team, telling reporters that the current Hong Kong government was only "a colonial government," and did not represent the Hong Kong people, who should be consulted more on the airport and given more information about it.
Another member of the Chinese airport team, an official with the Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office, Chen Zuoer, warned of "serious consequences" should the project proceed without China's full approval.
Â 
Total Cost Put at $16 Billion
Plans for a new international airport and an expanded shipping port, which the government now estimates will cost $16.3 billion, were announced in October 1989. 
Since then, China has bombarded the Hong Kong government with objections, but recently its criticism has grown more pointedly political. 
The project is still largely in the planning stages, though important contracts are scheduled to be announced soon, with work to begin before the end of this year and the first runway to be completed by 1997.

file: Games Offering China a Chance To Polish Image.txt
text:
ï»¿
With parachutists, panda balloons, 11,000 pigeons and 20,000 young Chinese dancers and martial arts experts, China opened the 11th Asian Games today as a mini-Olympics intended to win back international respect and domestic support lost during the military crackdown last year.
Flanked by other top leaders, President Yang Shangkun tonight opened the extravaganza before an international crowd of about 65,000 spectators in the Workers Stadium in the center of the capital. 
Determined that nothing should go wrong, the authorities arranged an enormous show of force and sent workers home this afternoon with the stern advice that they should stay off the streets and watch the ceremony on television.
Â 
Prelude to Olympic Bid
For China this has been far more than an athletic competition. 
It is the biggest international conference ever held in China, and more important it is an opportunity to rejoin the international community after the criticisms and isolation that followed the crackdown in June 1989. 
No effort has been spared to impress foreigners, from the new drug-testing center to the fake brick walls that have been erected around town to conceal the grim apartments that previously lined the roads.
If the Asian Games go smoothly, China intends to make a bid to be host to the Olympics in 2000. 
Officials from the International Olympic Committee arrived to see the Games, and they were treated as heads of state in the hope that they would back China's application to be host to the Olympics.
''This is my wish,'' the 83-year-old President Yang told Juan Antonio Samaranch, the president of the International Olympic Committee, in a meeting today. 
''If it is fulfilled, I shall be very happy, and China will build more stadiums and gymnasiums.''
The Beijing Asiad, which has been in the planning for eight years, is also intended to serve a domestic purpose: to unite the Chinese people behind a patriotic theme closely associated with the Communist Party. 
The torches used to light the Asiad flame were carried in an extensive relay race through every province in China, and some 180 million people were organized to line the route and applaud.
''China used to be called the 'sick man of East Asia,' '' the People's Daily declared today in a front-page editorial. 
''Over the past 40 years and more, ever since the establishment of the People's Republic of China, many Chinese athletes have made awesome achievements and now China has become host of the 11th Asiad. 
From a certain angle, this change reflects the great achievement of the Chinese people in socialist construction.''
Â 
Fear of 'Hostile Elements'
The Government's worst fear has been that ''hostile elements'' will take advantage of the international spotlight and create disorder, just as student demonstrators took advantage of the visit by President Mikhail S. Gorbachev of the Soviet Union in May 1989. 
But these days nearly everyone in Beijing seems cowed, and few people expect any significant unrest.
''We're not going to do anything at all during the Asian Games,'' said a member of an underground organization that grew out of the 1989 crackdown. 
''It's much too tense.''
After the crackdown, there were at first some calls for a boycott of the Asiad, but those soon fizzled and for a time it seemed that Beijing would be host to the first Asian Games ever in which every eligible country participated. 
Then the Gulf Crisis intervened, and on Thursday the Olympic Council of Asia voted overwhelmingly to exclude Iraq because of its invasion of Kuwait. 
It is not clear whether Jordan is sending athletes. 
54 Delegates From Kuwait Kuwait's 54 delegates were given a rousing welcome as they entered the stadium during a procession of delegations. 
While many Kuwaiti athletes were stuck in their home country and have not been able to participate, some had been training in Europe and were able to come to the Asiad.
Other enmities seemed mostly to have been forgotten today. 
South Koreans, thousands of whom have turned up for the Games even though Seoul has no diplomatic relations with Beijing, waved their flags and roared approval not only for their own delegation but also for that of North Korea. 
A Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister, the most senior official from Hanoi to make an official visit to Beijing since the two countries fought a border war in 1979, sat with top Chinese officials in the President's rostrum. 
And athletes from Taiwan and China, who grew up hearing tales of each other as dreaded ''Communist bandits'' or ''stinking capitalists,'' are mingling affably in the Asian Games Village.
While the level of competition in some sports may not be up to the highest international standards, Asian athletes are among the best in the world in diving, archery, shooting, judo, badminton, volleyball and table tennis, among other sports.
The 29 Asiad events will include, in addition to most of the typical Olympic sports, such Asian specialties as kabbadi, which has the advantage in poor countries that it requires no special equipment. 
The game is a bit like tag, except that attackers must continuously repeat the word ''kabbadi'' and are eliminated if they run out of breath.
Â 
Objective Is 100 Gold Medals
China, which takes sports very seriously, is hoping for about 100 gold medals, of the 308 possible. 
This will be a chance for China to redeem itself after a disappointing performance at the Seoul Olympics in 1988, when it won only five gold medals.
In the last Asian Games, which were held in Seoul in 1986, China won 94 of the 270 gold medals then at stake. 
South Koreawon 93 and Japan 58.
China's delegation of 838 athletes and officials is the biggest in the Games, followed by South Korea's with 757 delegates. 
Japan is third with 722, while Palestine - which many Asian countries recognize as a nation, and which is represented by Palestinian athletes living in various countries - has just two delegates.
Security was tighter than it has been in Beijing since the night of June 3 of last year, when protests erupted at Beijing University to mark the one-year anniversary of the killings of pro-democracy protesters.
Â 
Police Monitor Rail Stations
Tens of thousands of people without Beijing residence permits have been shipped out of the capital to their hometowns, and the police are monitoring the railway station and main roads to keep unauthorized people from coming to Beijing. 
University students have been subjected to bed checks to make sure they are not on the streets fomenting political mischief.
A large area around the stadium was sealed off in midafternoon, and everyone entering the stadium was searched with metal detectors. 
A helicopter hovered over the stadium during the ceremony, and thousands of police were in the nearby streets, but there was no hint of trouble.
It is difficult to gauge the attitude of Beijing residents to the games. 
In general, some intellectuals are contemptuous of the Asiad and complain that it is a terrible waste of money, while some children and workers are quite enthusiastic about the sports competition.
Â 
Cost Put at $530 Million
But the most common attitude seems to be one of only mild interest, mitigated somewhat by indignation at the forced contributions that were solicited to raise money for the games. 
China spent about $530 million preparing for the Asiad.
China's capital, normally a relatively drab city of endless apartment blocks whose color is measured in hues of gray, has taken on a new look for the games. 
Statues of Pan-Pan, an exuberant panda who has been chosen mascot of the Asiad, decorate the city just as portraits of Chairman Mao Zedong used to be the universal fixtures.
The most startling renovation has been the fake brick walls that have appeared along some major roads, to hide the dilapidated homes that used to line the way. 
Workmen even painted bricks on the outside of the new walls so that they appeared relatively elegant. 
But for Beijing residents, who sometimes have to wait a decade or more to be assigned an apartment, it has been galling to see such efforts dedicated to camouflage instead of to resolving the housing shortage.
Â 
New Buildings Draw Complaints
''Why don't they put those building materials into building us houses, instead of into hiding the problem?'' complained a worker in his 20's.
Officials have also made sure that shops are filled with merchandise to impress visitors. 
Nearly $900 million worth of merchandise - including eels from Fujian province, seedless grapes from Xinjiang Province and Phoenix brand bicycles from Shanghai - have been flown to the capital to lure visitors and startle longtime residents.
One problem, however, is that ticket sales to Asiad events have not been publicized much, even though they are an important source of revenue for the games. 
A Chinese American businessman complained tonight that he had been trying for days to purchase tickets to athletic events, and still had no idea where to buy them, or if they could be purchased at all.

file: Giving the Official Spin_ 6 Scenes on Chinese TV.txt
text:
ï»¿
Every evening in the last week, the official television news, viewed by millions of Chinese, seems to have reverted to the kind of indoctrination techniques familiar in the Mao era.
In the past there was never such a broad visual diplay, but today the methods have been adapted to television. 
Every night there are scenes of horror stories that inspire pity for the soldiers of the People's Liberation Army and hatred for ''the small number of conspirators'' who began ''a counterrevolutionary rebellion.''
In the first days after the military crackdown against pro-democracy demonstrators on June 4, in which soldiers killed hundreds or perhaps thousands of civilians in central Beijing, the television showed Government footage of civilians throwing rocks and stones at tanks and soldiers.
The Government has now moved beyond that, using other scenes to nurture a sense of outrage against the ''thugs'' and ''hooligans'' who are accused of inflicting damage to the city.
Tonight's national television news program was fairly typical. 
Here is some of what the viewers saw.
Â 
Scene 1
The camera pans to a large, sparsely furnished hall where several hundred high officials have come to listen to a reading of a speech first delivered by Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader. 
The speech is introduced by Prime Minister Li Peng, who appears wearing a Western-style suit for the first time in recent days.
''Comrade Deng Xiaoping's important speech made a profound analysis of the cause and nature of the counterrevolutionary rebellion and the correctness of the measures we adopted,'' Prime Minister Li tells the gathering.
Mr. Li's voice fades out and the announcer explains that Mr. Li had urged everyone at the meeting to study Mr. Deng's words carefully and to ''unify the people's thinking on the basis of Deng Xiaoping's speech.''
The camera passes through the rows of officials sitting in folding chairs as the announcer lists the names of some of the more important officials. 
Some officials are taking notes, some are reading and at least one participant is looking sleepy.
Â 
Scene 2
The camera opens on a street corner, called Xidan, where a great deal of the violence took place in the early-morning hours of June 4. 
Xidan was also where a soldier was killed and his body disemboweled and burned by civilians. 
For the last few nights, the television news has shown scenes of the charred body of the soldier propped against a truck, or lying flat on its back.
A few days ago, the television news showed citizens placing small wreaths along the bridge at the intersection, in memory of the soldier. 
Now, the camera shows how the railings are brimming with large, colorful wreaths as parades of citizens continue to lay more flowers in the soldier's honor.
The announcer relates the Government version of the events of that June 4 morning, when the soldier, Liu Guogeng, was killed, supposedly while trying to rescue a man from a boisterous crowd.
The soldier was on his way to seek help from colleagues, the announcer says, but when he was about 200 yards away from the Communist Party headquarters, on the Avenue of Eternal Peace, or Changan Avenue, he was beaten to death by ''thugs'' who then doused his body in petroleum, disemboweled it and then burned it.
The picture then switches to Jilin Province, where Mr. Liu's mother, father and younger brother live.
''I ask his younger brother to learn from the older brother,'' says his mother, who is sobbing with sorrow and anger. 
''Go annihilate the thugs.''
His father, lying sick in a hospital bed with an undisclosed ailment, says: ''We must resolutely deal with these thugs. 
They deserve no leniency.''
His younger brother says: ''I feel honored. 
I will learn from my brother.''
Â 
Scene 3
An announcer reports that as of Tuesday, the Beijing Public Security Bureau has received 1,227 letters giving details about ''counterrevolutionary thugs.''
Â 
Scene 4
The camera turns to a meeting of 31 leaders of China's ethnic minorities, including a Tibetan Buddhist, who are all voicing their support for the Government's efforts to ''put down the recent rebellion.''
The announcer reads a few remarks by one of the leaders. 
''The scheme of those who wanted to create contradictions and stir up riots among the ethnic groups have failed thanks to the joint efforts of the minority people,'' the announcer quotes the leader as saying.
Â 
Scene 5
Two students who were named on Tuesday among the list of 21 ''wanted'' student leaders are seen being led into a police station for interrogation.
One of them is Zhou Fengsuo, a 22-year-old physics student at Qinghua University in Beijing, who was arrested in the central city of Xian, where his family lives. 
He was reportedly turned in by his older sister and brother-in-law.
The scene turns to a livingroom couch in Xian, where Mr. Zhou's sister, Zhou Yanrong, is sitting with a baby in her lap and her husband next to her.
Miss Zhou and her husband, Yang Yibo, who works at the Institute of Communications Engineering in Xian, says she saw the Tuesday television news that showed the woman's younger brother as a fugitive.
The couple say they discussed what to do next and came to what the television announcer thought was the correct conclusion.
''They contacted the security office of the institute, and the officers there cooperated with five policeman to go to the town of Three Bridges to arrest Zhou Fengsuo,'' the announcer says.
''Zhou Fengsuo confessed that he was a member of the standing committee of the Beijing autonomous student union and that on June 9, he took the train to Xian,'' the announcer adds.
Â 
Scene 6
The camera focuses on an old, heavy-set woman, standing in the Chongwenmen district on a bridge covered with wreaths to commemorate a soldier. 
The soldier was reportedly beaten up by ''thugs'' on the evening of June 3.
The old woman says she witnessed the ''thugs'' kill the soldier by throwing him off the bridge.
''I stand in front of the people of this city as a witness,'' the woman says, speaking into a television microphone. 
''The People's Liberation Army soldiers did not shoot people.''
''I went up to the People's Liberation Army soldiers with some other old women and we pleaded with them not to shoot the people,'' the woman says. 
''They told us: 'We are the people's army. 
We will not shoot the people.'
''
''But then the thugs spread a rumor, telling the people that the soldiers had killed the son of an old woman,'' she says. 
The woman explains how the ''thugs'' then beat up the soldier and threw him off the bridge.
''When I saw the dead soldier, I felt terrible,'' she says. 
''He was still alive when he was thrown off the bridge. 
I feel I should bear some responsibility for the death of the soldier because I took the lead with two other women to go after the soldier, and this gave the thugs the opportunity to follow us.''

file: GORBACHEV ENDS CHINA AMITY TALKS.txt
text:
ï»¿
Mikhail S. Gorbachev left China today after a four-day summit meeting that ended 30 years of estrangement between the Soviet Union and China, taking with him promises of expanded party and government contacts and a general reduction of military tensions in Asia.
The reconciliation of the two Communist giants was interrupted and finally eclipsed by huge pro-democracy demonstrations in Beijing and other Chinese cities, dampening Mr. Gorbachev's hope of putting his policies on display to a wide Asian audience.
But the Soviet leader pronounced the summit conference an event of ''epoch-making significance.''
As Mr. Gorbachev concluded his visit with a side trip to Shanghai, the official Soviet and Chinese news agencies issued a joint communique promising new ties between the Communist parties of their two nations, which split in the late 1950's over ideology.
The agreements, which had been described earlier in general terms, included the reduction of military forces along the Soviet-Chinese border ''to a minimum level commensurate with the normal, good-neighborly relations between the two countries.''
Â 
Demilitarization Hoped For
Mr. Gorbachev said at a news conference Wednesday that he hoped this would eventually lead to full demilitarization of the border.
The Chinese and Soviet leaders also upgraded negotiations on several outstanding boundary disputes, now under the charge of deputy foreign ministers, to the level of foreign ministers.
The most extensive section dealt with the future of Cambodia, on which the two nations failed to overcome their remaining differences.
The Chinese repeated their call for the creation of a four-party transition government, including the Vietnamese-backed regime of Hun Sen and the three rebel factions headed by Prince Norodom Sihanouk. 
Prince Sihanouk would lead the government pending elections under this plan.
Moscow, which supports Vietnam in its 10-year-old war against the guerrillas, insisted that transition and elections were an internal Cambodian matter.
The two sides agreed that when Vietnam finishes withdrawing its troops in September, outside parties should gradually end military aid to any of the warring factions.
The communique declared that ''neither side would seek hegemony of any form'' in Asia or elsewhere.
Â 
Steers Clear of Protests
In Shanghai, Mr. Gorbachev steered clear of the student protests that have spilled into this city. 
He met with Mayor Zhu Rongji and the Communist Party leader, Jiang Zemin, laid a wreath to the Russian poet Pushkin, and toured the Minhang Special Economic Zone, one of the areas China has created to attract foreign investment.
The Soviet Union is contemplating establishing similar zones.
Compared with his three days in Beijing, where his schedule was cut and juggled to avoid the legions of protesters occupying the city center, the Shanghai visit was peaceful.
The only mishap occurred at the administrative building of the free trade zone, when an elevator carrying Mr. Gorbachev, his wife, Raisa, Foreign Minister Eduard A. Shevardnadze and Aleksandr N. Yakovlev, another Politburo member, balked and refused to move. 
First Mr. Shevardnadze got out, then Mr. Yakovlev, and still the elevator would not function. 
Finally, The Soviet leader was forced to descend the stairs from the sixth floor.
When a reporter asked if the group was too heavy, Mr. Gorbachev said, ''No, it's your Western technology.''
Shortly afterward, Mr. Gorbachev toured a Chinese-Japanese joint venture - an elevator factory.
The Soviet leader apparently saw nothing of the demonstrations that filled the port and city center here.

file: Governmental Candor Now Shortwave Staple.txt
text:
ï»¿
From Radio Afghanistan to the Voice of Zaire, more official government radio stations than ever before are broadcasting abroad on shortwave, and many have started downplaying strident propaganda and overt ideology in favor of more candor in their official newscasts.
The trend reflects the recent movement toward greater political and cultural openness in the Soviet Union and China, which has encouraged other countries to follow suit. 
It is also a response to the proliferation of other forms of communication in the developing world, which has fostered greater competition for listeners, government and private analysts say.
''The winds of openness are blowing in more ways than one,'' said Lawrence E. Magne, the editor of Passport to World Band Radio, an annual publication for shortwave users published by International Broadcasting Services, a private company in Penns Park, Pa. 
''There's been a decline in hard propaganda and a rise in more objective news.''
But with about 100 countries broadcasting abroad, the shortwave spectrum is becoming so congested that countries are building more powerful transmitters and taking other steps to insure that their official voices are heard abroad.
Â 
The New Candor
People who monitor international shortwave radio say the new candor has been evident in several countries, especially in the Soviet Union and China.
''Both are now surprisingly frank when it comes to dealing with domestic problems,'' said Kim Elliott, the director for audience research of Voice of America, which is operated by the United States Government. 
''They're doing a much better job of talking about themselves.''
During the recent earthquake in Armenia, for example, Moscow radio provided extensive news coverage. 
Shortwave monitors say the coverage included not only detailed reports of the estimated damage but also criticism of the Government's response.
In general, criticism of official institutions in the Soviet Union, the result of Mikhail S. Gorbachev's attempt to implement a sweeping reform program, is most apparent in the two official stations charged with external broadcasts, Moscow radio and Radio Peace and Progress. 
The economy, with its lack of consumer goods and lethargic industrial sector, has also been a subject of recent critical newscasts.
Â 
Coverage of Nanjing Riots
Beijing radio, which once began broadcasts with quotations from Mao Zedong, has similarly moved away from heavily ideological broadcasts. 
Its recent coverage of the riots in Nanjing, where Chinese students demonstrated against students from Africa, suprised Western analysts of shortwave programming.
''They hinted that there was racism in China,'' said G. Alex Batman, who monitors broadcasts for International Broadcasting Services. 
''That would not have happened in the past.''
And Vilnius radio, the official voice of Lithuania, a Baltic republic in the Soviet Union, has recently broadcast calls for more political autonomy.
Apart from the new openness, competition from other foreign stations, cassette players, videocassette recorders and improved domestic radio and television has forced countries to adjust their programming abroad to ''provide an attractive alternative to domestic media and cater to the international interests of the listener,'' Mr. Elliott said.
In many cases, he said, listeners wanted objective news about a country and would listen to stations they thought were providing it. 
This, he added, explained in part the vast international audience of the British Broadcasting Corporation. 
''One reason it's so powerful is because it's credible,'' Mr. Magne said. 
''Propaganda doesn't sell anymore. 
People won't listen.''
Â 
Medium for Propaganda
But ever since the late 1910's, when Bolsheviks used radio to try to foment revolution among vastly dispersed peoples, addressing broadcasts to, as its announcers intoned, ''all, all, all,'' propaganda has been and remains a key reason for broadcasting. 
Because of shortwave radio's range, countries have used it to project their messages across geographic and often ideological and religious divides.
Some countries have not been affected by the trend toward more candid and self-critical programming. 
Extremely strident propaganda can still be heard on Albania radio and Pyongyang radio, the official station of North Korea. 
And analysts in the West stressed that Moscow radio has not abandoned propaganda in its broadcasts; its message has simply become more subtle, they say.
Despite the Soviet Union's decision to end jamming of the United States Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty, radio warfare is not dead. 
The Soviet Union, for example, is still jamming foreign broadcasts aimed at Afghanistan in the Pashto and Dari languages, said Jonathan Marks, a Dutch shortwave expert at Netherlands radio.
Â 
A Crowded Spectrum
The medium's primary constraint, however, is the increasingly crowded shortwave spectrum. 
The number of national broadcasters has risen over the last 20 years to about 100; the number of hours broadcast has risen to about 30,000 hours annually, almost double the number in 1960. 
This has left too many countries competing for too few frequencies.
''It's a very crowded spectrum,'' said Mr. Marks. ''In order to be effective, countries are looking at ways to get their signal closer to their foreign audiences.''
Several countries, notably the United States and Britain, have embarked on ambitious programs to expand their broadcasting ability, building more powerful transmitters and establishing far-flung radio networks. 
But budgetary constraints will almost certainly delay the American expansion program.
Â 
Exchange Agreements
In addition, several countries have recently signed agreements to exchange radio facilities, essentially using one another as relay stations for broadcasting. 
A country transmits a program by satellite to another country's station, which then rebroadcasts the program by shortwave. 
This allows a country to broadcast from a position closer to its target.
''It's much cheaper than building a relay system overseas and then managing it,'' said Mr. Marks, who has counted more than 30 of these agreements, the majority of which developed in recent years.

file: Gulf Crisis Stirs Concern on Asian Games_ Fate.txt
text:
ï»¿
The crisis in the Persian Gulf is truly a terrible thing, a Chinese writer complained the other day.
''With this new situation, Kuwait may not be able to attend the Asian Games,'' he added. 
''And maybe some other Arab countries won't come either. 
It really is terrible.''
These days conversations here are frequently turning to the situation in the Persian Gulf, but usually people focus on the effect of the conflict on the Asian Games, which begin in Beijing on Sept. 
22.
It is not that people discount the horrors of a possible war, or lack sympathy for Western hostages in the region, but in most conversations those topics seems secondary to the impact on the sports competition.
Â 
Appeals to the Nation
China has been preparing lavishly and frantically for the games, which are held every four years as a regional version of the Olympics. 
After the Army crackdown last year, the Government has tried to win back loyalty and pull the nation together again with nationalistic appeals to make the games succeed. 
The Chinese leadership also hopes that if the games succeed, they will win back respect internationally - as well as tourists for China - and lead the way for China to be the host of the Olympics in 2000. 
Until the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait, China's diplomacy had seemed to be working, for all 38 countries in the region had said they would take part.
The dreams of a perfectly smooth event collapsed with the invasion of Kuwait. 
Among those killed was Sheik Fahd al-Ahmed al-Sabah, a Kuwaiti who was also the president of the Olympic Council of Asia, the group that coordinates the Games. 
The invasion thereby not only left the organization leaderless in the final month before the games, but also cast doubt on whether athletes from Kuwait would participate because of the annexation of Kuwait by Iraq.
Â 
Deadline for Lists
''Everybody's wondering about these questions, but our Government hasn't explained what's going to happen,'' a middle-age woman said. 
''We have no idea who's going to participate.''
One reason the authorities have not explained is that they apparently do not know. 
While all 38 countries said at first that they would in fact participate, the deadline for submitting name lists of competing athletes is tonight at midnight. 
It is not clear how many countries have submitted these name lists, and officials of the Asian Games have declined to be interviewed on the subject.
In recent days, the authorities have publicly expressed optimism that the Asian Games will succeed despite all the conflicts. 
Zhang Baifa, a Vice Mayor of Beijing, told a news conference on Saturday: ''We are confident that the Asian Games will surely be a meeting of unity, friendship and progress.''
Â 
Fans From Saudi Arabia
Despite the invasion, Kuwait might be able to send a team, as most of its athletes are said to be training in Europe. 
But other gulf countries may be too absorbed by the possibility of war to send teams, and even if they all do arrive in Beijing some teams may object to competing against political rivals. 
Saudi Arabian sports officials had advised China that if their soccer team reached the finals, they would send 3,000 fans to Beijing to root for their squad. 
Partly as a result, the Chinese authorities arranged the early opening of an unfinished expressway between Beijing and the nearby port city of Tianjin. 
The idea was that some fans could stay at hotels in Tianjin and commute to Beijing.
These days, however, some Chinese wonder whether there will be any Saudi Arabian entry at all.

file: Hong Kong After 1997_ Blueprint for Rule Expected in March.txt
text:
ï»¿
As alarm mounts over China's tough attitude toward Hong Kong and hopes rise that Britain will introduce greater democracy here, there is a growing sense that Hong Kong's future will be largely determined in the next few months.
The final version of the Basic Law, the blueprint for rule here after 1997, is expected to be determined by March, and the end game of sorts begins on Wednesday, when Hong Kong's Governor, David Wilson, visits Beijing for the first time since the crackdown on pro-democracy protesters there June 4.
''Everything's at stake,'' said David J. Clark, a senior lecturer in political science at the University of Hong Kong. 
''From now until March is the last opportunity to influence the content of the Basic Law.''
Opinion polls suggest that confidence in the future is waning, and more and more skilled professionals are applying for a ''lifeline'' to leave before 1997, when the territory reverts to Chinese rule. 
Each time the Beijing authorities criticize Hong Kong - as they have frequently recently - the mood becomes more bleak, many residents say.
Â 
Meeting With British Minister
As soon as Governor Wilson returns from Beijing, he is scheduled to meet with Foreign Secretary Douglas Hurd of Britain in Hong Kong. 
The two apparently will discuss the results of the talks in Beijing and possible measures to boost confidence in Hong Kong.
At issue is the extent to which the people of Hong Kong will be able to elect their legislators. 
The debate is not just over the elections in 1997, when the territory reverts to Chinese rule, but also over those in 1991, which some Hong Kong leaders believe are pivotal for determining the pace at which greater democracy is brought to Hong Kong.
For nearly two years now, British and Chinese leaders have tried to devise a plan that would provide for a smooth transition in 1997. 
Thus, Hong Kong would move slowly toward the system that China intends to put into effect after 1997. 
Beijing believes that only 30 percent of legislators should be directly elected, so that would imply that Britain should not allow election of a higher proportion before 1997.
Advocates of faster democratization want a greater proportion of directly elected seats in 1991, even if the percentage exceeds what is stipulated for 1997. 
This way, they argue, when China assumes control over Hong Kong, it will have to unravel a relatively advanced democratic system in order to implement the more conservative one spelled out in the Basic Law, and this could be embarrassing for the authorities in Beijing.
Â 
Fears of a Legislator
If the pace of democratization is to quicken, it must be encouraged by the British, at the risk of reprisals from China.
''In the present climate, the chances are nil - that is, the Chinese will not give in,'' said Martin C. M. Lee, an outspoken legislator who was recently barred by the Chinese from the Basic Law drafting committee. 
''The question is, 'What will Britain do?'
And I fear that Britain will kowtow.''
One test of how far London will go against Chinese wishes will be the fate of a British Government proposal to give 50,000 Hong Kong families, or about 225,000 residents in all, the right to live in Britain. 
The plan was recently condemned by the Chinese as a ''gross violation'' of British commitment to the Chinese-British agreement signed more than five years ago.
When the British and the Chinese agreed more than five years ago that Hong Kong would be returned to the mainland and that a joint committee would help draft a Basic Law, there was a strong sense of opportunity: the Hong Kong people would become a part of their motherland and have a say in forming the laws that would govern it after the territory was returned to China.
Â 
Basic Law Assailed
But there is now widespread skepticism among Hong Kong's 5.7 million residents that China will abide by the Basic Law, according to local polls. 
For many of the territory's legislators and leading intellectuals, who have worked over the last three years to help shape or influence the Basic Law, there is little pride in the final document as they envision it. 
Many people believe the Basic Law was largely dictated by Chinese leaders on the mainland.
''To me, the Basic Law is a total failure, a tragedy, an irony in itself,'' said Albert W. Y. Chan, a regional councillor for the territory's Tsuen Wan district. 
''The declaration of the Basic Law should have been a joy to most Hong Kong people, that they could have a system determined by themselves. 
But that is not the case. 
Their system will be dictated by the Chinese Government.''
Instead, these people look to the future with a mixture of resignation and defiance. 
On New Year's Eve, a cold, damp, dark night a few thousand Hong Kong residents huddled together outside to light candles for the victims of the Rumanian uprising and to demand the removal of the ''Ceausescus in China.''

file: Hong Kong And China Get Closer.txt
text:
ï»¿
Eight years before the marriage of the century, when capitalist Hong Kong and Communist China will be united in a ceremony here, they seem already to be melting into each other's arms.
The ''bamboo curtain'' that once isolated Hong Kong from its vast neighbor has been trampled down by the millions of Hong Kong Chinese who cross the border each year to shop, to see a doctor, find a wife, take a vacation, or to die. 
Several hundred thousand mainland Chinese also visit Hong Kong each year, either as tourists or on business, and residents of Guangdong Province in southern China watch Hong Kong television programs and occasionally even read Hong Kong newspapers.
Many Hong Kong residents remain deeply suspicious about whether China's intentions toward the territory are entirely honorable, and tens of thousands of the most talented young people are fleeing each year rather than live in Hong Kong after it returns to Chinese rule in 1997. 
But the millions of residents who remain seem to feel that if there is nothing to be done about it, they might as well enjoy the benefits.
That has already resulted in a reintegration of Hong Kong with the motherland, nearly 150 years after they were split apart by the persuasive efforts of British gunboats. 
Economically and culturally, China and Hong Kong are becoming one again.
Â 
'Enlargement of Hong Kong'
''We see no boundaries,'' said Gordon Y. S. Wu, chairman of Hopewell Holdings, a Hong Kong company that has invested deeply in China. 
''It's basically an enlargement of Hong Kong.''
It is not so much that the territory is returning to Chinese control; in some respects, China is coming under Hong Kong's control. 
The territory is already the largest source of China's foreign investment and its largest trading partner. 
More than two million people in Guangdong Province work directly or indirectly for Hong Kong companies.
Hong Kong songs and movies are popular throughout China, and adventure books by Hong Kong authors such as Jin Yong are popular among young Chinese. 
More and more Chinese companies are putting up signs bearing the old-style Chinese characters that were banished from the mainland decades ago but are still used in Hong Kong and Taiwan.
Perhaps most important, Hong Kong is increasingly seen as a model - economically, socially and even politically - for China.
Â 
Imitating the Capitalist Side
''They are trying to imitate the capitalist side of Hong Kong,'' at least in Shenzhen, the free-wheeling city across the border from Hong Kong, said David K. P. Li, chief executive of the Bank of East Asia.
Su Shaozhi, one of China's most prominent social scientists, told a Hong Kong interviewer recently that ''Hong Kong has a lot of strong points from which we must learn.''
In particular, he stressed that China should try to copy Hong Kong's development of the rule of law.
Already Shenzhen has announced that it will try to adopt Hong Kong's commercial and trade law. 
The city has even hired a Hong Kong institution, Sun Hung Kai Securities, to advise it on setting up a stock market.
But for many people here, what matters most is that the reintegration of Hong Kong and China has changed their daily lives. 
Poor families in Hong Kong take the train across the border each weekend to do their shopping. 
They also visit doctors and dentists across the border, where prices are much cheaper, and some send their children to university in China.
Â 
Brothels and Burial Plots
Burial plots are extremely expensive in Hong Kong, so families buy plots in Shenzhen. 
Some Hong Kong men regularly visit Guangdong's brothels; others find Chinese wives and install them in apartments in Shenzhen where they will be available for weekend visits during the 5-to-10-year wait for approval to immigrate into Hong Kong.
''Some Shenzhen women have a Hong Kong husband two days a week, and a local boyfriend five days a week,'' said Zhang Qingni, a Shenzhen lawyer sent by the Government to study Hong Kong's legal system. 
Miss Zhang recently represented a Hong Kong man seeking to divorce his Shenzhen wife.
Each year 27,500 mainland Chinese move legally to Hong Kong, and many more move illegally. 
In addition, more than 355,000 mainland Chinese visited Hong Kong as tourists last year, almost double the number in 1985. 
About two-thirds came on group tours, but many also came as business executives.
Just as Hong Kong is the largest investor in the mainland, so the mainland is the largest investor in Hong Kong, with $10 billion invested in the more than 2,000 mainland companies operating in Hong Kong. 
Many of them were set up by towns or counties in Guangdong as a way to shelter hard currency, and as an excuse for officials to visit Hong Kong regularly.
Â 
Resentment and Partnership
Some of them are also used to funnel investments back into China. 
That way, they get special incentives aimed at foreign investors that they would not receive as purely local investments.
Mainland residents often resent what they say is the trickery of Hong Kong people, while Hong Kong residents often say that mainlanders do not know how to work hard. 
Yet for all the resentment, the partnership is growing rapidly. 
It is also changing Hong Kong's role from a manufacturing base to a service center and hub for Guangdong Province.
Roderick W. Macneil, a lawyer who runs a China consulting company in Hong Kong, said, ''I really view Hong Kong now as the capital of Guangdong Province.''
