text:
ï»¿
After two bleak years in which it has lurched from one crisis to the next, exhaling confidence the way a punctured tire loses air, Hong Kong finally seems to be feeling good about itself again.
A new agreement was reached at the beginning of this month between Britain and China about a new airport to be built here -- and more broadly about how the territory will be governed until the hand-over to China in 1997 -- and it has elicited an enormous sigh of relief.
Spirits also rose today after the United States Senate vote Tuesday on trade benefits to China. 
Because Hong Kong depends a great deal on China for its economic livelihood, the vote, which makes likely the prospect of unconditional extension of the benefits, touched off even greater business optimism.
Â 
Stock Market at a High
For two straight days now, the Hang Seng stock market index has hit a new high, closing today at 4,028.77, up nearly 19 points from Tuesday's record. 
Housing prices are also estimated to have risen at least 10 percent since the airport agreement was announced on July 4. 
And for the first time since the Army crackdown in Beijing two years ago, there seems to be a measure of hope in the air here.
Hong Kong's confidence has been shaken not only by the political repression and ideological orthodoxy on the home turf of its future landlord, but also by the arrests of Hong Kong visitors on the mainland and a rising number of mainlanders sneaking into the territory and committing robberies. 
Emigrants continue to flee the territory at a pace of over 1,100 a week.
Now, with major uncertainties removed, politicians, business executives and bureaucrats here are turning to the nuts and bolts of the airport and port project, which is expected to dominate the economy until 1997 and cost more than $16 billion.
Â 
Caution and Foreboding
As with all bouts of optimism in Hong Kong in the last decade, however, this one is mixed with caution and a foreboding that China's verbal assaults may once again cloud the skies.
The agreement provides that China will support the construction of the airport in Hong Kong and will honor Hong Kong's debts after 1997. 
In exchange, Britain agrees to consult Beijing on all matters relating to the airport that will have an impact after 1997. 
Academics and politicians say the document is a crucial annex to the original joint declaration in 1984, which provides the basis for the handover of power. 
Some say it could set a precedent for power-sharing on all matters straddling 1997.
"China got what it wanted -- it got a formal acknowledgment of their role prior to 1997," said a diplomat in Hong Kong. 
The Chinese, he added, are believed to have suggested registering the memorandum as a treaty with the United Nations, as was the case with the 1984 Joint Declaration, but the British said no.
Â 
Risk of Imported Labor
As companies enter the contract bidding in the next few months for certain parts of the airport project, the Government is suggesting that the construction activity will add more than a full percentage point to Hong Kong's economic growth estimates in the near future. 
Costs for the airport and rail and bridge links will be $12.7 billion and billions more for the port development.
Although the political uncertainty may be removed for the moment, some economists and analysts say the endeavor will still stumble. 
For instance, a construction boom could be inflationary, unless the Government allows the import of labor. 
Another major risk that investors and bankers must consider is that all the connecting parts, such as the rail link, the suspension bridge and the airport, must be completed before any one can be used.
For the moment, the general public is busy with Hong Kong's favorite pastime: making money. 
Last week, the first Government land sale since the memorandum brought a price that was more than double the one reached for a similar plot in the same area last November. 
And there are some indications that the small investor also wants to keep investing in Hong Kong.

file: Hong Kong Calls China Talks Useful but Sees No Progress.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Governor of Hong Kong said today that his three days of talks with Chinese officials had been useful, but neither side reported major progress in easing tensions between Hong Kong and Beijing.
There was no sign of new conciliation on the Chinese side to accompany the lifting of martial law, which took effect on Thursday. 
On Thursday and again today, Chinese officials made comments that were widely perceived as reproachful of the British position.
The Governor, Sir David Wilson, who was on his first visit to Beijing since the army crackdown in June, said he told Prime Minister Li Peng and other officials about the opinions in Hong Kong about proposed democratic changes.
The June crackdown has increased alarm in the British territory that Beijing will suppress dissent and ignore local opinions after Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule in 1997.
Â 
Draft Law Faulted
China is now completing work on a ''basic law'' that will govern the territory after 1997, and many Hong Kong residents assert that the recent drafts of the law do not provide for enough democracy and will erode confidence in the territory's future. 
Sir David said he hoped that his comments on Hong Kong views would be taken into consideration by those drafting the basic law.
''I've been explaining the views that people in Hong Kong have both on short-term political developments and the hopes that people have for long-term development, for steady and continued development of the political structure,'' the Governor said at an airport news conference before returning home.
He said he also asked for Chinese assistance in reducing the flow of Vietnamese refugees, many of whom travel by boat along the Chinese coastline before landing in Hong Kong. 
He also said that the Chinese had repeated their criticisms of a recent British proposal to provide passports to 50,000 Hong Kong Chinese and their families before 1997, and that he had explained the reasons for the proposal.
''I can't say that in these discussions we have solved every problem,'' Sir David said. 
''But I do think that as a result of these meetings, it has been possible to increase understanding on both sides and get back to resuming the sort of practical dialogue which we need if we're to deal with practical issues in Hong Kong at the moment.''
Â 
Beijing Assertions of Subversion
The official New China News Agency tonight quoted Prime Minister Li as saying he was glad to see that ''on some issues, the two sides are drawing closer.''
The agency did not eleborate, but it said that Mr. Li also called on China and Britain to take steps to prevent damage to relations between Hong Kong and Beijing.
But earlier, there seemed to be some tension in the air. 
When Sir David referred in the presence of reporters to difficulties in the political climate, Mr. Li reportedly responded, ''Maybe that's your feeling, but I feel fine.''
On Thursday, Li Hou, deputy director of China's Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office, said to Sir David, in front of reporters, that some Hong Kong residents were trying to harm the relationship with China. 
He seemed to suggest that the Hong Kong Government should do more to stop such conduct.
At his news cnference today, Sir David addressed the Chinese concern that Hong Kong is being used as a base from which to subvert Communist rule in the mainland.
''We in Hong Kong have no wish, we have no intention, that Hong Kong should be used as a base for subversion against China,'' the Governor said. 
''In particular, we don't want people from outside Hong Kong to come to Hong Kong to use it as a battlefield against China. 
At the same time, we treasure our own liberties and freedoms in Hong Kong.''

file: Hong Kong Gets Wider Voting Rights in _97.txt
text:
ï»¿
The people of Hong Kong won a small battle today when China agreed to allow them a slightly greater degree of freedom to elect their own leaders as the territory passes to Chinese rule in 1997.
But the small concession by Beijing was unlikely to ease the tensions and alarm in Hong Kong over its future, and there have been calls for demonstrations to protest the overall restrictions and lack of democracy in the document that is now being prepared here in Beijing.
The final draft of the document, called the Basic Law, will be voted on Friday by the 51-member Drafting Committee. 
It then is to be sent to the National People's Congress, China's legislature, for approval.
A main issue in the draft of the Basic Law, which will govern Hong Kong after 1997, has been the composition of the territory's future legislature. 
China wanted to limit the number of directly-elected legislative seats to 18, or 30 percent of the legislature, while various Hong Kong leaders called for up to 30.
Today, the Chinese side agreed to allow 20 directly elected seats. 
China also decided to increase the limit on the number of foreign passport holders who would be allowed to serve in the legislature to 20 percent, from 15.

file: Hong Kong Journal_A Plea to the Motherland_ Listen to Your Heart.txt
text:
ï»¿
Dame Lydia Dunn, a senior member of the colonial government here, is a seasoned politician as celebrated for her perfect British reserve as for her establishment views.
And so the colony was stunned recently when Dame Lydia broke into tears as she testified before a British parliamentary committee investigating the problems confronting Hong Kong as Britain prepares to return it to China in 1997.
Dame Lydia lost her composure when she began to speak on the emotional issue of nationality and the fact that while Hong Kong's residents are British subjects, and have been for almost 150 years, they have no special right to live or work in Britain. 
As one legal expert put it: ''A native of Hong Kong has no more chance of being accepted for permanent entry into Britain than, say, a Japanese. 
Colonial ties count for nothing.'
Each time China routs demonstrators in Tibet or harasses a human rights militant in Beijing, Hong Kong residents flinch, reminded of the future fragility of their own freedoms. 
Tens of thousands of people here have already begun to cast about for some kind of escape hatch should Hong Kong life collapse under the Communists.
Â 
'Colossal Bitterness' Found
David Howell, a Conservative Member of Parliament and the chairman of the visiting foreign affairs select committee, said he was surprised by the ''colossal bitterness'' he had encountered over the issue. 
As the committee left for Beijing to continue its inquiry, Mr. Howell told reporters that while Britain would never grant all of the 3.2 million people born here the right to settle in Britain, proposals to relax some restrictions on immigration should be weighed.
For years critics have charged that the restrictive nationality laws are racist, and there is a feeling here that Britain might be more apt to make immigration concessions if Hong Kong natives were not almost exclusively ethnic Chinese.
Angry Hong Kong officials, politicians and professionals argue that for the first time in its history, Britain is relinquishing a colony to another sovereign power, a Communist power at that, and because Hong Kong's fate is unique, its people deserve unique immigration concessions. 
They say that if the British Government is not prepared to grant full right of abode in Britain to all Hong Kong natives, which most concede is a political impossibility, officials should at least make more liberal use of their discretionary powers and permit more civil servants and those with strong family, educational or cultural ties to enter Britain.
Instead, Britain has maintained a hard, unbending attitude, even refusing recently to grant automatic right of abode to a handful of Hong Kong war widows whose husbands died defending the colony against the Japanese in World War II.
Â 
Concessions Are Urged
The hearings last month, and the loud, bitter calls for help from Hong Kong, appear to have created some momentum for change. 
In the last few days, several important British publications, including The Economist and The Sunday Times, have declared that Hong Kong-born residents deserve special nationality concessions.
Britain took away all residency rights for colonials through four nationality acts passed between 1962 and 1981. 
Most Hong Kong people, who had no need or desire to live in Britain, originally viewed the mounting restrictions as churlish insults, but now they are seen as vitally affecting their future.
Britain's refusal to bend its restrictive policies is now seen as one more indication that it is abandoning the 5.7 million people in the colony, 98 percent of whom are ethnic Chinese.
Even the colony's top officials, usually unswerving in their defense of the British Government, which appoints and employs them, have been uncharacteristically critical of the laws. 
Dame Lydia, a member of the executive council that advises the Governor, called them ''morally indefensible,'' while the Chief Secretary, Sir David Ford, vowed the Hong Kong government would continue to press London for changes.
Sir David, in his testimony, pointedly reminded the visiting parliamentary committee that residents of the nearby Portuguese enclave of Macau, which reverts to China in 1999, will have right of abode in Portugal, which means that under European Community rules they may also reside in Britain - unlike this colony's own British subjects.
Â 
Grades of Citizenship
William S. Clarke, a lecturer in law at Hong Kong University specializing in nationality issues, said Britain is the only democracy that has grades of citizenship with vastly different rights. 
A full British citizen, he said, has the right to live in Britain, while those born in a British colony are merely British dependent territories citizens, who have the right of abode in their own colony but not in Britain. 
When China takes over Hong Kong, residents here will be downgraded to British overseas citizens ''who have no right of abode anywhere in the world,'' he said. 
''Their passport is really just a travel document.''
Moreover, China has already declared that all ethnic Chinese here will be considered Chinese nationals in 1997.
To gain entry into Britain, he explained, a Hong Kong resident would have to apply for permission like any foreigner and would be given right of abode, eventually, only if he were independently wealthy or had special skills or a British spouse. 
Mr. Clarke said there are probably no more than 100,000 Hong Kong residents with that right.
Hong Kong people have begun seeking foreign passports as an insurance policy against a Communist calamity in 1997. 
Last year, conservative government estimates placed the number of emigrants at 45,000, with most going to Canada, Australia and the United States.
Â 
How a Passport Would Help
''I sometimes wonder what the British people feel when they read about Hong Kong British subjects scurrying around the world to find somewhere else to take them in,'' Dame Lydia told the bipartisan committee from the House of Commons. 
Then, her voice choked, she added, ''It would do so much to help families commit themselves to a future here if they could be guaranteed a hope of last resort in Britain.''
The British and the Chinese are now conferring on the basic law that will govern Hong Kong after 1997. 
But as one political analyst here said, ''The British confer, but it is the Chinese who decide.''
In the end, ''granting full passports is the one real, practical measure Britain could take to help protect Hong Kong's people,'' he said. 
''The Chinese might not like it, but they could not stop it.',

file: Hong Kong Journal_Colony_s Cold Shoulder for Democracy_s Goddess.txt
text:
ï»¿
When an obscure documentary, ''Mainland China 1989,'' was screened in an art theater here last week, Hong Kong censors cut 17 minutes from the 78-minute film, deleting interviews with a mainland dissident and several pro-democracy student leaders. 
Officials said that without the cuts, the film could ''seriously damage our relations with other countries.''
Hong Kong, which is to be handed back to China in 1997, is now quick to censor itself, and equally quick to criticize any word or deed that could upset or offend China.
While democracy is sweeping Eastern Europe, in this colony the democratic impulse that gripped Hong Kong in the hopeful, heady months of May and June is fading. 
British and colonial government officials, politicians and community leaders have grown more and more fearful of China since it crushed the democracy movement in Beijing last June and adopted a sterner, more intrusive attitude toward Hong Kong.
Time of Anxiety
On the surface, Hong Kong still has the flash and flair of a wildly successful Western city, sleek, rich and self-assured. 
But as residents hear repeated Chinese warnings that it will not permit the colony to become a base for ''subversives,'' and as they watch Beijing attack liberal leaders here by name and draw up new provisions to limit political dissent after 1997, the underlying mood has become anxious.
''For years Hong Kong was afraid to speak out, but for a few weeks last summer all taboos were forgotten and they stood up to support democracy and protest the bloodshed in Beijing,'' said Joseph Cheng, a political analyst who has edited books on Hong Kong and China. 
''Now, the self-restraint, the self-censorship is creeping back and it is a sad thing to watch.''
The Governor of the colony, Sir David Wilson, set the new political tone here in October when he advised Hong Kong residents to use their rights and freedoms ''with self-restraint.''
Â 
No Symbols, Please
Recently, in an effort to reassure Beijing, British colonial officials have denied several Chinese dissidents with valid visas the right to enter Hong Kong, bundling them off on return flights to the United States. 
Pro-democracy groups have been denied the right to put up a permanent Goddess of Democracy, symbol of the Beijing democratic movement, in Hong Kong.
When Chinese families who for years have celebrated Taiwan's National Day on Oct. 
10 put out their Taiwanese flags this year, the police removed them, saying they obstructed traffic. 
When students from the April 5 Action Group, who held a permit to protest, gathered outside the celebration to mark China's National Day in September, they were pushed back by the police, there was a scuffle and several were arrested.
This fall, furious that Hong Kong had allowed a mainland athlete to declare himself a dissident and go to the United States, China suddenly stopped taking back its own citizens caught sneaking into Hong Kong. 
The crowded colony has reason to fear being overrun by a wave of mainlanders. 
After intense negotiations, the Chinese asserted that Hong Kong had made suitable concessions and once again accepted the return of the illegal migrants.
Â 
Damning Evidence
Hong Kong officials adamantly denied making concessions. 
But in a secret letter written the day the dispute was settled, and later obtained by a local newspaper, the colony's political affairs adviser wrote the director of the New China News Agency, whose Hong Kong bureau serves as China's de facto embassy, that ''the Hong Kong government has no intention of allowing Hong Kong to be used as a base for subversive activities against the People's Republic of China.''
''N.C.N.A. will have noticed the arrest of members of the April 5th Action Group,'' the letter continued. 
''They will also have noted that the 10 October celebrations passed off in a low-key way, and that the Hong Kong government has recently rejected a proposal for a permanent site for a replica of the statue of democracy.''
''The Hong Kong Government,'' the letter concluded, ''will continue to have a prudent regard for the special circumstances of Hong Kong and the interests and concerns of the Chinese Government.''
While government officials insisted that the letter showed toughness in the face of China's demands that they ban all dissident activities, others said the tone and substance of the letter were deeply disturbing.
In fact, this week a court found the April 5th demonstrators not guilty of all charges. 
But even the most ardent reformers concede that most of the colony's new political will has dissipated.
The Chinese themselves seem satisfied that Hong Kong's new political will is dissipating. 
Last week, a senior Chinese official told reporters that the time was ripe to discuss details of the colony's future political system, saying: ''Hong Kong people were not so calm over a considerable period of time after June 4th. 
They were too emotional. 
Hong Kong people are getting more calm now.''
Among the Hong Kong Government's recent moves to appease Chinese officials was the rejection of a proposal for a permanent site for a replica of the Statue of Democracy, which now stands in Victoria Park.

file: Hong Kong Journal_For Gentry_s Old Home, an Outstanding New Face.txt
text:
ï»¿
One day before long, when Dame Lydia Dunn joins the House of Lords, a legislative institution that has symbolized British male gentry for centuries, she will stand out not only because she is a woman but also because she is Chinese.
''It's rather intimidating,'' Dame Lydia said in an interview in her spacious wood-paneled office, accented with two reproductions of large antique Chinese screens. 
''Whenever I think about being introduced into that august body, I often think, 'I wonder what they think to have someone like me in their midst?'
''
A 50-year-old executive director at Swire Pacific Ltd., a British-run Hong Kong conglomerate, and the leading member in Hong Kong's Executive Council, Dame Lydia was honored on the Queen's birthday list in June with a life peerage. 
Only two other Hong Kong residents, both men, currently hold the honor here, and the flurry over it is a reminder of how this territory blends Chinese and British styles and traditions.
Hong Kong is run by a Briton who serves as Governor and periodically dons formal uniforms that seem to have emerged straight from history books of imperial Britain. 
And while more than 97 percent of Hong Kong's population is Chinese, the judges and lawyers here still wear white-powdered wigs in the courtroom, and prominent executives and public servants are knighted and called Sir. 
The result is some Chinese names, like Sir Yuekong Pao and Sir Runrun Shaw, that raise a few eyebrows among the British aristocracy.
Â 
In the British Tradition
If there is any symbol of that mix of styles in Hong Kong, it is Dame Lydia. 
Her cautious, conservative diplomacy during the territory's transition to Chinese rule, while it has won her prominence here and in London, reflects the delicacy with which Britain has approached China.
Dame Lydia is one of the few Chinese women to have risen so quickly in Hong Kong's British-styled society, winning appointments in the Parliament for more than a decade and senior positions in several business organizations. 
Her immaculate attire, sometimes a bold yellow dress or a V-necked red frock, has been a mark of her elegance, as is her knack for tact and diplomacy in the debating halls and corporate boardrooms.
While her roots are as Chinese as those of China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping - both have the same family name, but use different Romanizations - Dame Lydia is very much a product of British tradition: she is married to a British man, she travels often to Britain, she works at a British company and has a second home in London.
Now, with her seat in the House of Lords - an honor often given to reward the Prime Minister's political allies - the Hong Kong people may gain a voice in the British Parliament.
But if this greater access to the British Government gives Hong Kong a bit more influence in Britain, it comes just as the territory is moving inexorably toward becoming a part of China. 
On July 1, 1997, Hong Kong will become a part of China, by agreement between London and Beijing.
''I don't think she'll have a political future in Hong Kong,'' said Frank Ching, a local columnist currently writing a book about Hong Kong. 
''Lydia Dunn has a reputation for sitting on the fence.''
Â 
'I Am Not a Politician'
Dame Lydia would not rule out the possibility of seeking the post of chief executive, the top job in Hong Kong after 1997. 
But Mr. Ching and others say that her seat in the House of Lords may preclude her from gaining the requisite blessing from the Chinese, who may view her as an emissary of Britain.
For all Dame Lydia's prominence in Hong Kong, her views on some key matters remain a secret, because she rarely expresses them. 
She has never held an elected office, and says she will not run next year for one of the new 18 directly elected seats in the Hong Kong Parliament.
''I am not a politician,'' Dame Lydia said.
If her career has stressed cooperation with the colonial rulers, it is far from the only path taken by Hong Kong's British-educated Chinese professionals. 
Dame Lydia is probably one of two most prominent Chinese in the territory, and the other is a perfect contrast: Martin C. M. Lee, a leading lawyer and Queen's Counsel who dresses in sober suits and speaks in a posh accent but regularly infuriates the British Government by demanding more democracy for the territory.
Currently, none of Hong Kong's members of Parliament are directly elected, and although freedom of speech and of the press is generally allowed, no one asserts that the territory is a democracy.
Â 
Expelled From Committee
Mr. Lee was expelled by the Chinese authorities from the drafting committee of the Basic Law, the constitution for the territory after it becomes part of China. 
The British have not welcomed him much more warmly, and he seems unlikely to become a lord any time soon.
''Mr. Average would like somebody like me to speak up on occasion,'' Mr. Lee said in an interview.
Even Dame Lydia has indirectly expressed criticism of his outspokenness, saying that political leaders have responsibility ''to take the consequences of their words.''
But Mr. Lee says he believes such criticism is motivated by a fear of China's reaction, and he brushes it aside.
''They are beginning to think like a slave already,'' Mr. Lee said. 
''I don't want to antagonize my master and I don't want another guy to antagonize him either for fear that they will get less bread from the master.''
But Dame Lydia's refusal to take a stand on an issue has sometimes frustrated even a few British officials. 
In April, when the British Foreign Affairs Committee visited Hong Kong to hold a hearing on the pace of democracy in Hong Kong, Dame Lydia summarized the two diverging views -one faster, one slower - among the delegates.
''I can personally see the case for both,'' she said, diplomatically. 
When a British official then pressed her to state her personal view, she replied, ''That is difficult to comment, and I would say that I have an open mind on the pace.''

file: Hong Kong Journal_Frantic for Deliverance From China_s Clutches.txt
text:
ï»¿
When several local legislators recently suggested using Hong Kong's hefty budget surplus to buy an uninhabited island somewhere and resettle the colony's 5.7 million people there, other lawmakers agreed the idea was worth pursuing.
And when a millionaire businessman called a news conference to suggest that the United Nations take over Hong Kong, creating a neutral, independent state he envisioned as ''the Switzerland of Asia,'' his proposal drew the immediate support of the chief executive of the Hong Kong stock exchange and several community leaders.
Since the violent suppression of the democracy movement in China last June, the people in this British colony, plucky, resourceful and inventive, have been applying all their skills to the problem of how to escape or circumvent the Chinese Communists, who regain control of Hong Kong in 1997 under an accord reached with London in 1984.
Â 
Tens of Thousands Leave
In recent years, tens of thousands of professionals and wealthy entrepreneurs have left the colony to avoid the Communist takeover, but now some leading citizens are trying to devise plans that would protect millions of people here from the excesses of a mainland regime.
Hong Kong, known for its practical approach to life, is awash with schemes so wildly imaginative they must be regarded as either absolutely inspired or utterly desperate.
Some citizens, for example, want Hong Kong to declare its independence and seek international protection from the Chinese, and a British research institute has come up with detailed plans for moving all of Hong Kong to Europe, recommending a site on the coast of Scotland.
A group of industrialists is working on a plan that calls for ''re-creating'' Hong Kong in a remote spot near Darwin, Australia, that has been designated as a special economic zone. 
Another citizens' group proposes inviting three million residents to contribute to an investment fund that would be turned over to any country that lets the investors settle there.
Explaining the idea of moving Hong Kong to Darwin, Albert Cheng King-hon said: ''We're not talking about buying an island. 
That's useless because it means seeking independence. 
Our idea is to rent a site that would be a new British territory.''
He estimated the cost of the Australian Hong Kong at $100 billion.
''Most of these ideas are non-starters, but they are significant because they show the depth of the psychological despair here,'' said Richard Margolis, a former Government political affairs official.
Â 
'Insurance Policy' Is Wanted
Stanley Ho, the businessman who wants Britain and China to lease Hong Kong to the United Nations, said, ''I know the possibility is extremely remote, but as a citizen of Hong Kong, I thought I ought to try to do something to help.''
'' Thousands of people are leaving Hong Kong and taking their money with them. 
We must find ways to restore confidence in our future.''
Mr. Ho, whose vast business interests include the biggest gambling casino in the nearby Portuguese enclave of Macao, believes the protection afforded by a United Nations presence would encourage residents to remain past 1997.
In fact, most of the proposals for mass migration or resettlement stress the idea that with a home of last resort available in the event of a Communist calamity, many people would remain in Hong Kong and life in the colony could continue.
''Most people here love Hong Kong but they want an insurance policy against any problems after 1997,'' a senior politician said. 
''They want to know they can get out if things fall apart here.''
Many of the proposals for taking over distant islands sprang up after a major campaign here to persuade Britain to give the right of abode in Britain to the 3.2 million natives of the colony, a plea London has steadfastly refused.
Â 
Plans Are Called Unhealthy
Robert Broadfoot, a political and economic consultant on Asia, said he believes that, in the end, all the great ideas and grand plans being explored now are ''unhealthy because they deflect interest and energy away from the very real issues that need to be addressed here, such as a more rapid movement towards democracy, a greater autonomy for the Hong Kong Government as it approaches 1997.''
Beijing continues to promise that it will permit the colony ''a high degree of autonomy'' and preserve its economic and social systems for 50 years. 
But as Mr. Ho said, ''people don't seem reassured by Beijing's promises.''
Conservative estimates by the government put the number of Hong Kong emigrants at 45,000 last year. 
Foreign consulates here have been inundated with requests for resettlement, and the drive to leave the colony is so strong that there was a riot when Singapore declared that it had places for 25,000 Hong Kong immigrants and opened a booth to pass out applications.
Â 
Expert Help for a Fee
Sensing the special business opportunities, immigration consultants have been flocking to Hong Kong, where for a fee they will guide residents through the procedures of emigration to places like Canada and Australia. 
This week, the splashy new Hong Kong convention and exhibition center announced that it would no longer permit its space to be used for immigration exhibitions. 
Helene Li, the center's marketing director, said the center was built primarily ''to foster Hong Kong's image internationally,'' and ''anything that promotes the mass exodus of people'' from the colony is not in keeping with that goal.
Mr. Margolis, the former Government official who helped negotiate the terms of Britain's hand-over of Hong Kong, said the colony had weathered other crises of confidence just as frightening. 
But one longtime political observer insisted that the crisis of confidence today is even darker because ''there is little the colony can do to help itself.''
''The only real thing that will overcome this fear, this crisis, is a total change in leadership in Beijing.''

file: Hong Kong Money Shifts.txt
text:
ï»¿
Hong Kong residents are moving more of their wealth out of the British colony, bankers said this week.
This year alone, Chinese customers are likely to transfer about $770 million to Australia and four times that much to Canada, estimated Will Buttrose, a consultant to the private banking operation in Australia of National Westminster Bank P.L.C.
''The amounts are going to escalate in the next two years,'' he said, adding that ''people are very concerned about 1997,'' when Hong Kong is to come under Chinese control.
He said wealthy individuals in Hong Kong and Taiwan were transferring about $100 million a month to Canada, which many Hong Kong immigrants now call home.
''The bulk of the money is going to North America,'' he said. 
''Switzerland is a player, but more is going to North America.''
Participants at a conference on private banking in Geneva on Tuesday said Hong Kong investors are eager to place their money in overseas tax havens and trust funds before China takes control.

file: HONG KONG OPINION AGAINST REFUGEES.txt
text:
ï»¿
As foreign governments and international relief agencies condemn Hong Kong's forced repatriation of Vietnamese boat people, Hong Kong residents are expressing their approval of the radical measure, and even at times suggesting that harsher measures are needed.
''I don't think sending them back is inhumane,'' Chan Wai Shing, a Hong Kong electrician, said today. 
''Keeping them in Hong Kong is a waste of taxpayers' money.''
Â 
Threatening and Cajoling
For months now, legislators, community leaders and citizens' groups have been threatening and cajoling the British and Hong Kong Governments, demanding that they rid the colony of the 44,000 Vietnamese boat people who have crowded into the territory in the last year and a half, joining 13,000 already here and awaiting resettlement. 
Now that forced repatriation is under way, few here are debating the morality of the operation or even its possible political repercussions.
When the colony's Legislative Council met on Wednesday - one day after the forced repatriations began - council members discussed fire ordinances in boarding houses, kidney donor cards and trips abroad for district board members. 
In the middle of the session, the Chief Secretary made a brief statement defending repatriation.
Â 
Concerned About Cost
One member, concerned about the cost of returning the boat people, tried to ask a question about the repatriation, but he was ruled out of order, and nothing more was said on the subject. 
But politicians here are already preparing to fight new battles over the boat people, complaining that Hong Kong ought not to have to pay for the forced return of the Vietnamese, and arguing that other measures will be needed to curb the flow of Vietnamese.
''Mandatory return will not solve the root problem,'' said Kingsley Sit, a legislator who advocates scrapping the colony's policy of first asylum so that any new boat people arriving in Hong Kong's harbor would be pushed back to sea. 
And opinion polls show that Mr. Sit's position is popular with Hong Kong's residents. 
A recent poll by political leaders in the Central and Western districts - downtown Hong Kong and a heavily Chinese neighborhood adjacent to it - showed that 90 percent favored forcible repatriation of the Vietnamese and almost half wanted any new boats of Vietnamese shoved away. 
Other polls have shown even wider margins of support for that extreme measure.
A possible explanation for those views may lie in the makeup of Hong Kong's population of 5.7 million, which is 98 percent ethnic Chinese whose sympathies lie more with the thousands of mainland citizens who try to sneak across the border into Hong Kong each year. 
About 50 mainland Chinese a day are rounded up here to be shipped back across the border, handcuffed and under guard. 
Even though more than half the Chinese here were refugees themselves, fleeing the repression and poverty of China, they do not identify with the the Vietnamese who are fleeing similar problems in Vietnam. 
Instead, they have signed petitions and staged demonstrations against the boat people, and formed neighborhood vigilante groups to patrol in areas where Vietnamese are housed in squalid camps behind high-barbed wire fences.
Â 
'Britain Takes Responsibility'
While the British Government has ultimate responsibility for the harsh repatriation policy, British officials privately say that while they have no desire to send home the Vietnamese, Hong Kong's citizens have been growing mutinously angry over the situation and the Government had no other choice.
''Britain takes responsibility, as it should, for this act, but with a wink and a nudge and a nod at the Hong Kong Chinese,'' said one Chinese political analyst here. 
''They say they fear we would become ungovernable if the Vietnamese problem were allowed to persist. 
I don't know if that is true, but I do know that China has made it very clear they want this problem cleared up before they take over.''
When confronting forced repatriation, the Chinese here tend to pick their way through a thicket of paradoxes, ignoring thorny, contradictory issues. 
The colony's liberal conscience, the lawyer and legislator Martin Lee, is one of the very few here who have pointed out similarities between the desperate Vietnamese who sail here in their tiny open boats and the prosperous Chinese who were once refugees themselves here.
The hard line taken against the Vietnamese comes at a time when Hong Kong, which will be handed back to China in 1997, is asking British officials for assurances that its citizens will have a haven if the Chinese regime proves harsh and repressive. 
Rita Fan, a staunch supporter of forced repatriation and an outspoken critic of Britain's failure to grant Hong Kong citizens right of abode, has said: ''Some people try to connect the two issues, but there really is no connection between the Vietnamese coming here and Hong Kong people, who are British subjects, wanting the right to go and live in Britain. 
I see no connection.''
Mrs. Fan says Hong Kong must simply face the criticism that comes with forced repatriation and offer ''a thorough explanation of the difficult situation it faced.''
But Mr. Lee has warned that the operation was not only morally wrong, but could well endanger the Hong Kong people's quest for safety after 1997.

In a move certain to increase tension between China and Britain over the future of Hong Kong, the colonial Government announced today that it would spend $1.2 billion to prepare the site for a new airport here despite Beijing's refusal to approve the financing of the project.

A $22 Billion Project

China and Britain signed a so-called memorandum of understanding on the project last year, but China has yet to approve ways to pay for it.
Since some of the airport work would be completed after the Chinese takeover, in 1997, China's final approval is regarded as crucial. 
But talks on the airport have been stymied as Britain and China locked horns over the political development of the colony in the years leading up to the takeover.
Britain's Governor here, Christopher Patten, recently proposed political changes that would increase the democratic base of the Hong Kong legislature before 1997.

Maintaining the Debate
"If the Government had done nothing, it would have been tantamount to admitting any decision in Hong Kong already rests with Beijing," he said. 
"Now, they have at least maintained the debate, by asserting that they are the Government here after all."
A bid for the site preparation work, made by an international consortium and approved last July, was to expire at the end of this month.

file: Hong Kong Symbol Looks Away.txt
text:
ï»¿
From the days of opium and cannons to those of Valium and satellites, there has been one pre-eminent address in Hong Kong: 1 Queens Road, headquarters of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation. 
It is the nexus of power and money, and these days an emblem of the difficulties of big Hong Kong businesses and of international banking as well.
Confidence here was shaken recently when the Hongkong Bank, as it is universally known, announced that it was forming a new holding company with British registration. 
While the bank's headquarters and management will remain in the territory, the bank effectively decided to do what many of Hong Kong's 5.8 million inhabitants are doing: obtain a foreign passport as possible protection against the vagaries of Chinese rule, which is to begin in 1997 when Britain relinquishes control.
Â 
Passing through a Minefield
But many question whether the passport will be enough. 
The bank is known as a gweilo -- "ghost" or "foreign devil" -- institution in a territory whose control will soon pass from the gweilos to the highly nationalistic Chinese authorities. 
This raises two questions: first, will the Chinese leadership allow a gweilo bank to continue to dominate the local market, and second, in an increasingly Chinese environment, will the top executives of the bank, who are all British, continue to have the connections and information that have helped them run local operations so profitably over the decades?
To reduce the risks that will arrive along with Chinese rule, the bank has set out in the last decade to become a truly international institution, with a leg in each time zone. 
But its recent experience and that of many other banks suggests that the road to becoming fully international passes through a minefield.
The bank's assets have soared tenfold in the last decade to $143 billion, making it the 26th-largest bank in the world.
But much of the expansion was expensive and unprofitable. 
For instance, the bank acquired Marine Midland Bank of New York and 14.9 percent of Midland Bank P.L.C., a major British institution, only to see both investments go sour because of problems in the two banks' loan portfolios.
Because of the problems overseas, almost all analysts expect the Hongkong Bank to report a decline in earnings in 1990 for the first time since 1967. 
And this year will also be tough, though perhaps better than 1990, said William Purves, the chairman and chief executive of the bank.
"I'm sure shareholders would be happier if we'd stayed a regional bank," Mr. Purves acknowledged in an interview. 
But the silver-haired Scot, whose prestige in Hong Kong is reflected in his Chinese nickname, Pu Weishi, meaning "great man," added that in the long run the strategy of international diversification was sound and would continue.
Â 
Cosmopolitan From the Start
Mr. Purves's continuing enthusiasm for creating a more international banking company is natural: the institution has been cosmopolitan since it was founded in 1865. 
It claims to have been the first foreign bank in the United States, in 1875, and by the end of the 19th century it had a network of offices throughout Asia. 
But until about a dozen years ago, the bank remained highly focused on Asia.
That is when the management and board resolved to create a fully international institution. 
The conventional wisdom in banking circles for much of the 1980's was that international deregulation, technological strides and the integration of global capital markets would lead to the emergence of a small group of super banks that would straddle the globe. 
Seeking a place in the top tier, the Hongkong Bank acquired not only Marine Midland and a stake in Midland Bank, but also James Capel & Company, a London-based international securities firm. 
It also established a major presence in Canada and Australia.
Paradoxically, these diversification efforts led to a greater dependence on the Hong Kong base for profits. 
Because of the losses abroad at Marine Midland, James Capel and the Australian subsidiary, the share of profits derived from Hong Kong has risen and now probably exceeds 60 percent of global earnings even though assets in Hong Kong amount to less than one-third of the bank's total.
It is this lucrative Hong Kong base that could give the bank a significant advantage in scooping up other institutions while prices are depressed. 
The Hongkong Bank has its problems, but past indigestion has not curbed its appetite for further acquisitions if the right opportunity arises. 
While the bank announced this month that it would not raise its stake in Midland Bank, at least for now, Mr. Purves said it would very much like a larger presence in Europe.
Â 
Building as a Metaphor
Analysts note that the bank remains highly liquid and able to afford a big European bank. 
Traditionally a conservative institution, Hongkong Bank has few problem loans in its own portfolio and sits on a cushion of hidden reserves, which it is not required to disclose. 
Most analysts estimate that these reserves amount to $1.2 billion or more.
In its home market, the problem is not profits, which keep rolling in, but long-term uncertainties.
"If you look out your window, you see the Bank of China Building," said David Kowitz, an analyst at Jardine Flemming Securities Ltd. 
"That's pretty much a metaphor for what is happening."
The new headquarters for the Beijing-based Bank of China soars 1,209 feet, enabling it to look down on the 600-foot Hongkong Bank headquarters.
Many people here believe that the Chinese authorities will make some efforts in the years after 1997 to assert their mastery of local banking and reduce the influence of the Hongkong Bank.
"It's inconceivable to me that China will allow the Hongkong Bank to maintain its dominance of the Hong Kong banking environment," said John M. Mulcahy, the research director of Peregrine Brokerage Lt., a securities firm based in Hong Kong. 
"I don't think they'll nationalize it, but I think they'll try to establish a substantial presence of their own."
But China's strategy of using the Bank of China to gain market share seemed to collapse after the Army crackdown in June 1989. 
Thousands of Hong Kong depositors withdrew their funds from the Bank of China in protest, and these days the Bank of China and its sister banks are much less aggressive than they used to be.
Â 
A Question of Privileges
So China may now be looking for another strategy, which could involve acquiring an existing bank in Hong Kong. 
One possibility would be the Hang Seng Bank, a major Chinese-managed institution that is 61 percent owned by the Hongkong Bank. 
Another possibility would be the Hongkong Bank itself.
The Hongkong Bank is now incorporated under special bylaws that prevent any stockholder from accumulating more than 1 percent of its shares. 
The bank would like to keep this provision, but it is still unclear whether the Hong Kong exchange will grant the new British holding company the same privilege. 
A stake of 20 or 30 percent might be enough to control the bank, since there are no large shareholders, and some analysts believe that over the next 10 or 15 years China might seek to acquire such a position.
Also uncertain is whether Hongkong Bank's executives will be able to hold onto the privileges that have flowed from their institution's mystique. 
The taipan, or "big boss," of the Hongkong Bank has always been a member of the Executive Council, the territory's top policy-making body, and a steward of the Jockey Club, its foremost recreational institution. 
Such perquisites -- and many more -- insure that bank executives are always among the first to know of policies or trends that might affect finance. 
The extras also help executives nurture contacts and friendships that are a great lubricant in the business world of Hong Kong.
Hongkong Bank's franchise in Hong Kong is enormously profitable, as is its Canadian subsidiary, which is the seventh-largest bank in that country. 
Moreover, Hongkong Bank is well placed to benefit from continued high growth rates in Asia, and perhaps in China as well. 
But the strengths in the Hong Kong market could be undermined by the bank's image among young Chinese as a stuffy and discriminatory institution.
Â 
No Top Chinese Executives
While 98 percent of Hong Kong's population is ethnically Chinese, Mr. Purves and most other executives have not learned Chinese, and there is not a single Chinese face among the top tier of executives.
"This is still a gweilo institution, and they don't give a lot of opportunities to Chinese," said a mid-career Chinese employee of the bank. 
The perception of discrimination is magnified because these days there are plenty of Chinese in banking circles with college and graduate school degrees, while Mr. Purves himself has only a high school diploma.
"In the Hongkong Bank, it's very difficult for Chinese people to get to the top," said a Chinese employee of another big bank in Hong Kong. 
"That's the general view."
Cheah Cheng Hye, an analyst at Morgan Grenfell Asia Securities Ltd., said that incipient Hong Kong nationalism may become more of a problem for the bank, but that the executives could head off the problem by installing Hong Kong Chinese as general managers of the Hong Kong unit, and by taking other measures to give the bank a greater local identity.
As for Mr. Purves, he acknowledges the problems but puts the accent on Hongkong Bank's underlying strengths and historic resiliency.
"We've survived 155 years of buffeting," he said, "so why should we stop now?"
Â

file: Hong Kong Tastes Democracy, and China Chokes.txt
text:
ï»¿
Britain and China are engaged in an increasingly bitter dispute over the degree of democracy in this territory, and the resulting political typhoon has Hong Kong awash with fundamental new uncertainties about its economic and political future.
In recent months, the new British Governor has stunned almost everyone by calling for more democracy, reversing the approach of the last half dozen years, in which the British authorities went out of their way to squelch the colony's democratic impulses. 
China has responded with outrage, starting a new cold war against the Governor, Christopher Patten, whom it has promoted to the top of its list of foreign enemies.
The Governments in London and Beijing appear to be on a collision course over policy toward Hong Kong, which is now a British colony but which will revert to China on July 1, 1997. 
The dispute already has developed into a virtual cold war in which virtually everything is at stake: the territory's political system, the relationship between Britain and China, the transition of Hong Kong to Chinese rule, and perhaps even the long-term governability and prosperity of the territory.
Â 
China Would Undo Changes
In the latest from the north, China's National People's Congress Standing Committee this weekend asserted that if Mr. Patten went ahead with his proposals, Beijing would be obliged to undo the changes in 1997. 
That would create havoc in Hong Kong and make a mockery of the smooth transition that both sides say they want.
"If the British side wants to give China a 'stab in the back' during the remaining hours before sunset, the Chinese side will be forced to respond with a 'fatal weapon,' " Ta Kung Pao, a Beijing-controlled newspaper in Hong Kong, declared recently.
Wen Wei Po, another Beijing mouthpiece, said of Mr. Patten: "Deep in his soul are all the deep-rooted bad habits of an extremely arrogant colonist who benefits himself at the expense of others."
This barrage of insults is by far the fiercest that China has made against any foreign statesman in recent years. 
Normally, Beijing does not attack foreign leaders by name, and the level of vitriol is a reflection of the abruptness with which Britain has reversed its policy toward Hong Kong this year.
Â 
'A Distinct Change'
"I can see a distinct change of direction on the part of the British Government," said Martin C. M. Lee, a legislator who for many years tried without success to prod the British Government to introduce more democracy. 
"They don't want to be led by the nose any more."
Mr. Lee's administrative assistant, Thomas Boasberg, said of the British Government's new enthusiasm for democracy: "Every morning we have to pinch ourselves to be sure we're not dreaming."
One reason that China dislikes democracy in Hong Kong is that candidates like Mr. Lee -- who would probably be in prison if he lived a few dozen miles to the north -- won last year's limited Hong Kong elections with overwhelming majorities, while pro-Beijing candidates suffered humiliating defeats. 
China sees no reason why Britain, which ran Hong Kong as a benign dictatorship for more than 100 years, should suddenly introduce political changes in its last few years of power.
Despite the fury from Beijing, an overwhelming proportion of ordinary Hong Kong citizens seem to be standing by the Governor. 
One poll last month found that 73 percent of those surveyed supported Mr. Patten's proposals for a more representative government, with 11 percent opposed and the remainder uncertain.
Most of those surveyed doubt that China will ever endorse the changes, but say they still feel more hopeful for Hong Kong's future because of the proposals. 
A poll last week found that 57 percent of those questioned believed that Hong Kong should proceed with the steps toward more democracy despite Beijing's opposition, while 29 percent disagreed.
Still, the invective from China has clearly unnerved some people in Hong Kong, particularly those in business. 
Curiously, some of the territory's leading capitalists have joined the Chinese Communists in urging Mr. Patten to back down.
"To run the risk of developing a political system that will likely be dismantled in four-and-a-half years time is just not acceptable to us," Vincent H. S. Lo, the chairman of the Business and Professionals Federation, said on Monday. 
The Federation, which represents some of Hong Kong's most distinguished business leaders, called on Mr. Patten to withdraw some proposals.
To be sure, some taipans -- as the territory's tycoons are known -- support Mr. Patten's proposals, while others are desperately trying to preserve their neutrality. 
But the business community seems to be the sector of Hong Kong society that is most skeptical about the prospects for nurturing democracy in China's backyard.
Â 
'Red Rag to a Bull'
"It's like waving a red rag to a bull," said Sir Gordon Macwhinnie, a retired accountant and former chairman of the Royal Hong Kong Jockey Club. 
"China is just not going to accept any speeding-up toward democracy."
Sir Gordon added that the demands for democracy would simply lead China to withhold approval of a major new port-and-airport project, which he said mattered more than democracy in ensuring Hong Kong's long-term stabilityI and prosperity. 
He added: "We're hammering away at more democracy and while we do it, they're stalling on these other issues that we think are more important."
Michael Hanson, the Governor's spokesman, said that the debate over democracy was healthy, but he also noted that the concerns expressed by business leaders do not seem to be widely held by the public as a whole.
"I would be concerned if the business community found itself at odds with the rest of the community," Mr. Hanson said. 
"That would not be helpful."
Â 
Market Near Record
To everyone's surprise, the sniping between China and Britain has not punctured the Hong Kong stock market. 
Instead, the market has risen in recent weeks and is near its record.
The equanimity with which Mr. Patten accepts the attacks from China is particularly surprising because in the past British officials went to extraordinary lengths to avoid what they called "confrontation."
The British officials in Hong Kong not only did everything they could to undermine the local democracy movement -- even gerrymandering election districts and rigging public opinion polls -- but also censored films that criticized China, banned visits to the territory by Chinese dissidents and on at least one occasion handed back over to China a dissident who had arrived safely in Hong Kong and had applied for asylum.
Prime Minister John Major apparently felt increasingly that the conciliatory approach was both embarrassing and ineffective, and earlier this year he dismissed the previous Governor, Lord Wilson, a China expert. 
In his place he appointed Mr. Patten, a close friend and a former chairman of the Conservative Party.
"People feel that Britain has been kowtowing too long, and that it's time to give it to the Chinese," a long-time Hong Kong official said, with considerable relish. 
"Everybody's kind of enjoying it for a change."

text:
ï»¿
Almost everyone wishes he would confess to some counterrevolutionary crime or another, if only to get his sentence reduced, but Liu Shanqing sits in his unheated prison cell in China and obstinately refuses to admit that it was wrong to believe in democracy.
''I tried to get Liu Shanqing to confess, but it's no good,'' his father, a tiny, timid, sparrow-like man in his 70's, said in an interview. 
''He won't confess, because he didn't do anything wrong.''
Mr. Liu is regarded by some people here as Hong Kong's hostage in China. 
He has spent eight years in prison, the last three in solitary confinement. 
But even the Chinese authorities have never indicated that he did anything more than visit the wife of an imprisoned dissident and offer her a small amount of money to help pay the bills.
Thus Mr. Liu's 10-year prison sentence is widely viewed as a warning to Hong Kong people not to interfere in China. 
China's Government treated Mr. Liu, an ethnic Chinese who lived in Hong Kong and worked as a computer sales engineer, as a local citizen and imprisoned him, and so any Hong Kong resident would think twice about crossing the border to help dissidents. 
''They are deliberately warning people in Hong Kong not to interfere,'' said Martin C. M. Lee, a lawyer and democracy worker in Hong Kong. 
''They want to make an example of him to warn the people in Hong Kong.''
Mr. Liu's saga began on Christmas 1981, when he crossed the border from Hong Kong into Guangdong Province in southern China. 
He planned to spend two or three days visiting the families of two political prisoners. 
The two men, He Qiu and Wang Xizhe, were leaders of the democracy movement in Guangdong and are believed to be still serving prison sentences of 10 years and 14 years respectively. 
After meeting Mr. Wang's wife and giving her the equivalent of $51, Mr. Liu was arrested and sentenced to 10 years in prison for counterrevolutionary crimes. 
For the last three years, he has been kept in solitary confinement in a prison in a remote part of Guangdong more than 130 miles from the provincial capital, Canton.
Because they are frail and short of money, Mr. Liu's parents make the trip to see their son only twice a year. 
It is a day's journey each way, and they can see him for only 30 minutes, with a guard present to make sure they speak only about family matters.
Mr. Liu's father, who was nervous during the interview and asked that his name not be used for fear of offending China, said that he had visited his son just a week ago and had found him in fine health and good spirits. 
Now 37 years old, Mr. Liu is scheduled to be released at the end of next year, but it is not clear whether he will then be allowed to return to Hong Kong or whether he will be sent to some remote part of China to work. 
One of the most frightening aspects of Mr. Liu's case, from Hong Kong's point of view, is that the Chinese authorities are treating him as a local person rather than as a foreigner.
The reason for this is that China regards Hong Kong as its own territory, and thus considers all ethnic Chinese residents of Hong Kong to be Chinese nationals. 
Mr. Liu's plight was never pressed energetically by the Hong Kong or British governments.
Similar cases have occurred periodically in other parts of China. 
Among the most recent was the arrest, announced on Dec. 
25, of three Hong Kong Chinese and two Chinese from the Portuguese enclave, Macao, who were accused of helping the ''Underground Railroad'' that carries leaders of the democracy movement out of the country. 
The fate of the five is unknown.
For Mr. Liu, and the others being held, one of the surest ways to get a reduced sentence is to plead guilty and to implicate others. 
But his friends say he is unlikely to bow to the authorities, and they worry that his ''bad attitude'' will lead the authorities to ban him from returning to Hong Kong.
''He's a very tough guy, mentally,'' said a longtime friend, Stephen Y. C. Leung, a high school teacher. 
''You couldn't change his mind, unless you could really prove him wrong. 
And he's not afraid of anything. 
Once he sees justice, he'll pursue it.''

file: How Taiwan Wins Friends and Miffs Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
Armed with a new flexibility and immense reservoirs of foreign exchange, Taiwan is struggling for a seat at the international table, and in the process new tensions are surfacing between the rival Governments in Taipei and Beijing.
The Government here is aggressively cultivating developing countries, with considerable success. 
So far this year, four more countries have recognized the Republic of China, as Taiwan calls itself, bringing the total to 26.
''I'm hopeful more will come forward,'' Foreign Minister Lien Chan said in an interview, adding that contacts are under way with other nations.
China has been particularly upset because the recent diplomatic successes by Taiwan run counter to the previous trend. 
Until about two years ago, Taiwan was growing increasingly isolated. 
One by one, countries switched their diplomatic ties from Taipei to Beijing, and two of the more important nations still recognizing Taiwan - Saudi Arabia and South Korea - seemed to be preparing to switch to Beijing as well.
Then this pattern was abruptly reversed, partly because Taiwan no longer required other nations to cut their ties to Beijing before establishing ties with Taipei. 
Dual recognition was tolerated.
Even more important than diplomatic flexibility was money: Taiwan's per capita income is about $7,500, more than 20 times the level on the Chinese mainland. 
More important, Taiwan has foreign exchange reserves of more than $75 billion, highest in the world after Japan. 
Taiwan made it clear that it would offer aid to its ''friends.''
Beijing has reacted with indignation to Taipei's courtship of developing nations. 
The annoyance in Beijing is doubly strong because third world countries used to be its allies, and because it is apprehensive about a bidding war with Taipei for diplomatic support.
''Taiwan has been using its silver-bullet diplomacy to buy people's minds and hearts,'' People's Daily complained in October.
President Yang Shangkun, Prime Minister Li Peng and other top mainland officials have strongly criticized Taiwan's diplomatic policy, and the official New China News Agency suggested that dual recognition was aimed at establishing Taiwan as an entity independent from China.
So far the four countries that have recognized Taiwan this year are the Bahamas, Grenada, Liberia and Belize. 
Except for the Bahamas, which had not had diplomatic relations with either capital, each country previously had recognized Beijing. 
The Chinese responded by suspending relations with each of these countries, a step just short of severing relations.
Taiwan is offering the prospect of technical and economic aid, particularly a new Overseas Economic Cooperation Fund, endowed with a $1.2 billion this year. 
There has been some domestic criticism of the diplomatic offensive, on the ground that it is silly to buy friendships with tiny states, but many others back the policy.
''Now that we have money and now that we have declared to the world that we want to share our international responsibilities, when deciding who to give it to naturally we give it to countries with which we want to promote relations,'' said Tsai Chengwen, chairman of the political science department of National Taiwan University.
About a dozen countries have opened representative offices here in the last 18 months, and many others have sent trade delegations or relaxed visa restrictions for Taiwan passport-holders.
The upheavals in Communist countries are also regarded as presenting new opportunities, particularly since those nations are desperate for capital. 
Trade delegations are exploring opportunities with Vietnam, and the Government here this week eased restrictions on travel to Eastern Europe.
In the interview, Mr. Lien appeared to be wary of saying anything that would antagonize Beijing. 
Taiwanese officials used to seize every opportunity to denounce the Communists.
''To realize our national aspiration of unification,'' Mr. Lien explained, ''we must above all be rational and realistic. 
Verbal acrimony and hostile jargon are only for propaganda value. 
They serve no purpose.''

file: IDEAS & TRENDS_A Debate About The Inevitability, And the Fragility, Of Democracy.txt
text:
ï»¿
IN the 19th century, it could be said that there were two alternative predictions about mankind's future. 
Marx proclaimed the inevitability of world socialism while Toqueville asserted that democracy, which he saw with some trepidation as rule by the consent of the governed, would surely replace rule by the few.
Marx has proved to be wrong. 
But was Toqueville right?
Do glasnost and perestroika, the student marches in China, and the fall of dictators from the Philippines to Paraguay signal the realization of his prediction?
Milovan Djilas, the Yugoslav author of the dissident classic, ''The New Class,'' summed up an optimistic view on the issue at a conference earlier this month in Washington. 
''The only real, irrefutable progress of man is his freedom,'' the former Yugoslav vice president and political prisoner said. 
''Or, more precisely, expansion of his freedom is both the way and the condition of human existence.''
Mr. Djilas and people from two dozen countries spoke at a meeting sponsored by the National Endowment for Democracy, a group financed by Congress that gives money to democratic movements around the world. 
A few days earlier, some two dozen dissidents from China gathered in Bolinas, Calif., to talk about their country's present and future. 
The dominant assumption at both meetings was that totalitarianism has failed and is on the wane. 
Zbigniew Brzezinski, who moderated Mr. Djilas's panel, has written a new book called ''The Great Failure,'' a reference to the bankruptcy of Marxism. 
Meanwhile, in Latin America, in Eastern and Central Europe, in the Soviet Union, in China and in several African countries the trend is toward more freedom, less control.
Â 
Notes of Pessimism
But amid the optimism were notes of pessimism, recitations of remaining obstacles, including the obvious fact that many rulers do not want democracy. 
They want power. 
''We seem to be in a mood of self-congratulation and optimism,'' said Jean-Francois Revel, the French author of ''How Democracies Perish.''
But Mr. Revel, who is not among the optimists, went on to ask, ''Are we right?''
Many analysts believe that a kind of global village phenomenon is helpful to democratic movements. 
Monica Jimenez de Barros, who led a voter registration drive in last year's plebiscite on military rule in Chile, told the Washington conference how her son in Santiago had posters in his room celebrating the Solidarity trade union in Poland. 
The overthrow of Ferdinand E. Marcos, Mrs. Jimenez said, was also an example to Chile.
The move toward democracy also seems reinforced by what might be the most earth-shattering development of the late 20th century - the crisis of ideology in the Soviet Union and China. 
''The Soviet Union has entered the era of its decline and dissolution,'' said Janos Kis, a Hungarian writer, reflecting a common view in Eastern Europe that Poland, Hungary and even Czechoslovakia are moving toward democracy.
Wu Guoguang, a former reporter for the People's Daily, the official Chinese Communist newspaper, proclaimed that the student marches in his country, taking place despite a ban on such protests, show that ''a new force for change has arisen.''
Many of the Chinese dissidents meeting in California saw the recent demonstrations as reflecting not only a widespread loss of faith in socialist orthodoxy, but also a failure of confidence among the leaders who, in the past, quickly repressed all pro-democracy movements.
The most recent developments are different from previous surges of democratic feeling, the Chinese dissidents said, because now the dictatorships have lost the justification they once could claim - that only they could guarantee order and economic progress. 
The Chinese argued that the political leadership's intention to reform the economy without expanding political freedom cannot work.
Â 
Obstacles to Freedom
The words emerging to describe all this is ''the democratic revolution,'' a phrase that Vilem Precan, a Czechoslovak history professor who now lives in West Germany, defined as ''a system based on spiritual, political and economic pluralism and mutual tolerance.''
Its goal, he continued, apparently referring to what he sees as the flawed intentions behind the Soviet policy of glasnost, is not ''to modernize the Communist system and make it more efficient while retaining its essence.''
''The aim,'' he said, ''is to do away with it once and for all.''
And yet, as Mr. Precan acknowledged, ''democratic revolution'' may be overstating what is happening in the world. 
The rise of Islamic fundamentalism is one instance of a revived dictatorship, one that uses religion to justify itself. 
Terrorism is another force working against democracy. 
The weight of poverty and overpopulation are used time and again as justifications for authoritarian rule.
Leszek Kolakowski, the Polish writer and philosopher, pointed out that the dissolution of dictatorships can lead to chaos rather than to democracy. 
If democratic reform does not work in countries like China and the Soviet Union, the situation could be ripe for new demagogues and dictators. 
Hitler and Mussolini took power in floundering democracies in times of political and economic crisis, bringing an end to what might be seen as an earlier ''democratic revolution'' in this century after World War I. Jean-Francois Revel said last week that, in fact, the 20th century has on the whole been a disaster for democracy. 
If the democratic revolution has been renewed, it has so far only managed to bring some parts of Eastern Europe and Asia, Africa and South America to roughly the point they had reached when the last great anti-democratic cataclysm struck.
That may be progress, but as Mr. Revel pointed out, the century has already shown how fragile the progress can be.
