ï»¿
For hundreds of years Malaysia, the southernmost tip of mainland Asia, was an important crossroads for the great civilizations of China and India. 
A quirk of geography - the country's strategic position just north of the Equator, between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea - made it a historic meeting place for traders and travelers from West and East.
This mix of cultures is reflected in the country's eclectic architecture, especially in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia's most developed city and its capital. 
Kuala Lumpur is filled with Moorish buildings out of North Africa, colonial and Tudor structures from the English countryside, Chinese temples, Buddhist pagodas and Muslim mosques.
One of the particularly strong influences is the indigenous Malay house - cool, infinitely expandable or contractable, movable and well adapted to the exigencies of heat, rain, floods and large families. 
Another is the south Chinese shop house - here elongated in plan with louvered windows and verandas borrowed from Malay architecture, often with ornamented facades. 
Also influential are the Southern Indian and Mogul styles, with their exuberant domes and minarets, introduced by the British in the late 1890's.
During the last 30 years the skyline has shot skyward with an amazing variety of supermodern architecture. 
Even here, however, the international influence is mitigated by the solutions to the tropical climate. 
Many of the later buildings are also now striving for a more Malaysian identity - bringing back large overhanging roofs, verandas and columns.
Of the many memorable places to see in Kuala Lumpur, often called K.L., several are especially noteworthy.
National Art Gallery The city's last major colonial hotel was designed by a Dutch architect in 1932, and conveys some sense of its former grandeur with a curved driveway, mock-Roman columns and detailed cornices. 
The whitewashed Art Deco building on the Jalan Sultan Hishamuddin now houses the National Art Gallery and its 1,700 works of art, in 38 small oddly shaped former hotel bedrooms and bathrooms. 
The hotel-cum-museum was built around two open spaces that serve as sculpture courts. 
Historically a meeting place for planters and politicians, the hotel is now meant to serve as the showcase for Malaysian artists. 
There were plans to replace the building with a 22-story high-rise when the Government designated it a historic building, and in 1984 leased it to the National Art Gallery. 
It was opened as a museum on a permanent basis in January 1985. 
The works of art are arranged in chronological order, and room numbers have been replaced by picture labels. 
The inner courtyard has exposed, cheerfully painted slender pipes, a modestly tropical version of Paris's Centre Pompidou. 
The museum is directly across the street from the K.L. train station, and next to the fine and frequently overlooked Railway Headquarters building.
Admission is free, and the museum is open daily from 10 A.M. to 6 P.M., except on Fridays when it is closed from noon to 3 P.M. Kuala Lumpur Railway Station. 
Constructed in 1911, this is one of the most famous landmarks in Malaysia. 
Built in the northern Indian Mogul style with a variety of arched colonnades and domed and canopied turrets, this palatial station houses a hotel above the entry, and it has large glass and cast-iron roofs over the platforms. 
The Moorish exterior conceals large glass and iron train sheds, similar to those built in England at the end of the 19th century. 
The splendidly exuberant building was built by the firm of J. A. Russell. 
One of the brothers, P. C. Russell, was the architect, probably working under the direction of A. B. Hubbock, the official architect of Selangor State, of which Kuala Lumpur is the capital. 
Legend has it that the design was taken from a 1911 Moscow Trade Fair pavilion and that the roof is designed with snow gutters and the ability to withstand about six feet of snow, a condition that has never been seen in Malaysia.
In 1986 the entire building was gutted, renovated and enlarged in order to modernize the interior. 
Unfortunately, some of the original rhythm of the design has been lost, as the architects were not entirely successful in reproducing the shapes of the arches. 
Sultan Abdul Samad Building Infokraf (the Handicraft Information Center) is in the 1897 Sultan Abdul Samad Building, also known as the Clock Tower, on Jalan Raja. 
Kuala Lumpur's oldest landmark, it is of distinct and graceful Moorish design, and one of the most popular and photographed buildings in the city. 
Formerly the Selangor State Secretariat, it now houses the Federal and High Courts at one end, and at the other end, the country's official craft center, the function of which is to elevate the status and qulaity of local goods. 
The building, designed by C. E. Spooner, the state engineer, is topped by a large dome covered in copper sheet, with a 135-foot-high clock tower. 
Previously, the building had numerous pinnacles along the parapet. 
These were removed during World War II, and subsequently lost. 
In 1984, the building was restored by Haji Hajeeder, to accommodate the courts and the crafts showrooms. 
Kuala Lumpur National Museum. 
This building, completed in 1963 on Jalan Travers, is based on old Malay, Minangkabau architecture. 
(The word Minangkabau means buffalo horns, and the roofs in that style have two hornlike peaks.) On either side of the entrance hall are two immense Italian glass mosaic murals, 175 feet long and 115 feet high. 
Outside the museum a World War II airplane on permanent exhibition strikes a jarring contrast. 
The two-tiered pagodalike roofed building houses several collections of historical artifacts of Malaysia and a number of displays that relate to the country's history. 
There is an example of a Malaysian wedding feast, traditional costumes (of unusual interest was the beaded net work, worn under a wedding gown to protect the gown's fragile brocaded satin), Royal headdresses, demonstrations of customs, Malaysian etiquette, and more.
Admission is free, and the museum is open daily from 9 A.M. to 6 P.M., except on Friday when it is closed from noon to 2:45 P.M. Karyaneka Handicraft Village. 
This is a cluster of 13 small gaily painted wooden traditional Malay buildings, one from each state, around one main structure on Jalan Raja Chulan. 
The main building in this complex was built in 1982, along the lines of a traditional Malay house. 
In 1984, the additional houses were added. 
Inside each of the smaller buildings is displayed the indigenous crafts of every state. 
Demonstrations of techniques for various crafts are held daily from 9 A.M. to 5:30 P.M., except Sundays. 
The two most interesting houses to visit are the Sabah and Sarawak regional buildings.
The largest building has a comprehensive inventory of all that is housed in the individual cottages including handsomely shaped black, brown and terra cotta clay pots that I would guess are too fragile to mail. 
There are embroidered velvet purses, gold and silver threaded fabric and some elaborate weavings and carvings. 
Recently a Malay garden was added, including all the Malay indigenous plants and herbs.
Open Sunday to Friday from 9 A.M. to 6 P.M., and Saturday 9 A.M. to 6.30 P.M. Jame Mosque. 
This building, on Jalan Kuntun Perak, is in the style of a North Indian Mosque. 
The mosque is situated at the confluence of the Klang and Gambak Rivers, the birthplace of Kuala Lumpur (which means muddy waters). 
Built in 1909 on the site of the first Malay cemetery, the Jame Mosque is the oldest mosque in the city. 
Designed by the British architect A. B. Hubbock, who also designed the city's railway station, it has a walled courtyard and three domes flanked by two minarets. 
Fully renovated in 1984 the arched, white stucco building with gray granite floors is filled with strong white columns with gray capitals and bases. 
Non-Muslim visitors can walk around the grounds and the periphery of the building but generally are not admitted inside.
Multiracial, multicultural, multireligious - whatever their differences, Malaysians are all Asians, with a common heritage. 
The layering of cultures throughout Malaysia (in a country of 17 million, approximately 53 percent are Malay, 33 percent are Chinese, 10 percent are Indian and 4 percent are expatriates, with a smattering of Americans) is reflected in its ceramics, in the country's architecture, and the activities that go on in its colorful markets. 
In spite of the enormous problems of nation-building, they have managed to establish a political culture of compromise, and fashioned one of Southeast Asia's most dynamic cities.
This year, which has been proclaimed Tourism Year in Malaysia, the buildings of Kuala Lumpur are being displayed to special advantage: every element of the cityscape, from palm tree to street lamp, has been fitted with tiny sparkling lights.

file: Leaders in Beijing Bar Their Kin From Using Family Ties for Profit.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Communist Party Politburo announced today that the children of senior officials would be banned from engaging in business and that China's leaders would no longer have access to private supplies of food that are not available to the public.
The announcement was clearly intended to relieve popular outrage over the way children of top officials have used their connections to run trading companies and reap huge profits. 
Many people have also been indignant at the life of privilege and extravagance that top officials lead, and the announcements were apparently intended to show that top officials will live more simple and frugal lives.
Such objections to official privilege were often voiced this spring during the democracy movement, which was crushed by the Chinese Army, and there have been many attempts before to curb privilege and abuse of family connections among officials. 
The announcements today were more specific, but it was not clear whether they would be more effective than those in the past.
Deng's Speech on Corruption
The most striking of the announcements, which followed a two-day Politburo meeting that ended today, banned children and spouses of top officials of the party and the Government from commercial activities, and called on those holding business positions to give up their posts by Sept. 
1.
The Politburo also ordered the abolition of the Kanghua Development Corporation, which was closely linked to Deng Pufang, the eldest son of Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader. 
The company grew extremely quickly and was widely resented because of suspected corruption.
Deng Pufang and the organization of the disabled that he heads announced late last year that they had cut their ties to Kanghua Development.
In an unpublished speech last month Deng Xiaoping called on the party to wipe out corruption, said a Chinese who read the speech.
Mr. Deng's youngest son, who is working for a international investment company in Beijing, will apparently not be affected, as the new rules cover only the children of members of the Politburo, the Communist Party Secretariat and the Executive Committee of the State Council, which is China's cabinet. 
Mr. Deng has retired from the Politburo.
Â 
Economy and Family Ties
The Politburo's statement called for an audit of the China International Trust and Investment Corporation, also known as Citic, one of China's best-known companies. 
The audit is then to be published, but there is no indication that Citic will be otherwise affected.
Family ties are particularly useful in Chinese businesses because the economy depends only partly on market decisions. 
A company's success depends greatly on its ability to get scarce resources that are rationed not by price, as they would be in the West, but by officials who give them out to friends or relatives or those who offer bribes.
If a company can get permission to buy steel or coal at the low Government price, for example, then it is certain to make a fortune if it can resell the material at the higher free-market price. 
Partly for that reason, and partly because family members of senior leaders can cut through the bureaucracy, children of top officials have been extremely successful doing business in China.
The Politburo also decided that all top leaders will use Chinese-made vehicles instead of the Mercedes-Benzes that everyone from Mr. Deng down has enjoyed and that have been widely resented among ordinary people who complain about the drain on foreign exchange. 
In fact, the Government had said this year that no new cars would be imported for officials, so it is not clear whether this regulation represents much of a change. 
Food Rations for Leaders?
The Politburo also said leading officials should not entertain domestic guests with public funds, and should not accept gifts from subordinates. 
From now on, officials are to travel abroad only when it is relevant to their jobs, and they are not allowed to accept invitations from foreign business executives or from Chinese-financed companies that are based abroad.
It is not clear how the Politburo will interpret its ruling that officials should no longer have special supplies of food available to them, and that they will be assigned the same rations and made to pay the same prices for food as everyone else.
Until now, top leaders have been given everything they need - from cooks to maids to cars to food - and it would be quite a change if they were obliged to pay for the fancy meals that are served in the Zhongnanhai compound, where they live and work.

text:
ï»¿
The Commerce Department withdrew an export license for a $500 million sale of nuclear power plant parts to China after the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and Senator John Glenn protested, officials said today.
Senator Glenn complained in a letter to Commerce Secretary Robert A. Mosbacher that the shipment would undercut a 1985 Congressional resolution forbidding such sales unless the President certified that China is not helping other nations build nuclear weapons.
All of the equipment - non-reactor items like compressors, pipes, turbine generators and other electrical gear - was from a canceled power plant at Satsop, Wash. 
The plant belonged to the Washington Public Power Supply System, a consortium of publicly owned utilities.
The licensing actions occurred in May, before the suppression of student demonstrators in China.

file: LIFE STYLE_Every Day, 5,000 Chinese Meals.txt
text:
ï»¿
Anyone unfamiliar with Saugus might consider a little place like this an unlikely spot to construct a giant copy of Beijing's Imperial Palace where 1,500 people can eat Chinese food, some of it kosher.
But the opening of Weylu's, one of the largest Asian restaurants in the country, amid the liquor stores and muffler shops on Route 1 comes as no surprise to people who know the Boston area. 
The section, about nine miles north of downtown Boston, is known locally as a kind of highway version of Restaurant Row on West 46th Street in Manhattan.
The customers wait in line for hours to be served, or make reservations weeks in advance. 
Unlike Manhattan restaurants, the ones here serve thousands of meals a day and have parking lots larger than some city blocks. 
And Weylu's, which opened April 10, is the largest of them all.
''From Day 1, we have had waiting lines from noon until closing,'' said Rick Chang, the owner of the restaurant and several others by the same name in the Boston region.
Weylu's has been serving 5,000 meals a day - the average check is around $14 a person - and turning away some customers. 
The parking lot is full from 11:30 A.M. until closing (1:30 A.M. every night but Sunday, when it is 11:30 P.M.).
Mr. Chang predicted that Weylu's would become the highest-grossing Chinese restaurant in the country (it's not a faint hope: the nation's top-grossing restaurant of any style, Hilltop Steak House, is only a mile away and has 100 fewer seats). 
Before Weylu's opened, Hilltop was considered the most riveting of Route 1's offerings; it has a 68-foot neon cactus and a kitchen that cooks 20,000 pounds of red meat a week.
Food is only part of the attraction of the Saugus restaurants, which resemble small amusement parks. 
In addition to Hilltop, there is the Ship Restaurant, which is shaped like a schooner and serves seafood, and the Prince Restaurant, with a leaning tower marked ''pizza.''
Weylu's stands up to the architectural competition. 
A circular driveway leads up a hill to an imposing drive-through pagoda. 
Customers ride an escalator to the main dining room, where arched footbridges span a waterfall and a Chinese rock garden. 
The menu includes Mandarin, Sichuan and Hong Kong-style dishes.
The first floor has a room for catered kosher functions with its own kitchen and supply room, where Chinese dishes are prepared under the supervision of an Orthodox rabbi. 
The regular menu does not now include kosher meals.
''About 40 to 45 percent of my clients are Jewish,'' Mr. Chang said. 
''When they have a function that is kosher, they have a limited choice. 
I wanted to offer them more of a choice.''
The room is already booked for months in advance, and Mr. Chang said he would consider adding kosher food to the regular menu if the demand remains high.
There seems to be little competition among the restaurants: the owners agree that there are more than enough customers to go around. 
Other Route 1 restaurants put up signs in April wishing Weylu's good luck.
''We feel any business that comes to the area is good for all of us, not a detriment,'' Mr. Chang explained. 
''People like to try different cuisines and different restaurants.''
The Peking Acrobats performed at Weylu's last month to celebrate the restaurant's opening (The New York Times/Rick Friedman)

file: Macao Journal_Tiny Piece of Empire, Cringing in Giant Shadow.txt
text:
ï»¿
Once this was an international haven for spies and smugglers and political refugees, as colorful and corrupt as wartime Casablanca. 
But today most of Macao's waterfront sin and swagger have disappeared, leaving a small backwater port whose faith in the future and ambitious plans to become a commercial center have been rocked by the turmoil in China.
Macao, a tiny piece of mainland China appropriated by Portugal 400 years ago, does not return to Chinese control until 1999. 
But citizens of the oldest remaining European settlement in Asia already live in the shadow of Beijing and are careful not to try its patience.
''The people here have freedom -the freedom to fly around in a cage,'' said Nip Kwok Shi, a student leader at the University of East Asia here.
Always circumspect in its dealings with China, today Macao is just plain fearful.
''The people of Macao have lost their confidence,'' conceded Murteira Nabo, Under Secretary for Education, Health and Social Welfare, and the acting Governor of the territory.
Macao, with its narrow streets, city square and stucco houses, has the look and feel of a small Mediterranean town. 
But from their park benches under the banyan trees of the Avenida da Republica residents can look out over the Pearl River and see the rooftops of a Chinese village and watch battered fishing junks chugging back to China at twilight.
Â 
Retaliation by Beijing Feared
Just 50 minutes away by hydrofoil, in the British colony of Hong Kong, the ruthless military crackdown on students in Beijing galvanized residents politically, and many there are demanding speedier democratic initiatives in the colony and new rights of resettlement in Britain itself as a 1997 return to China draws near.
By contrast, Macao's 500,000 residents, 90 percent of whom are ethnic Chinese, appear to have grown quieter and more cowed. 
Having expressed their passionate support of the student movement in Beijing in rallies drawing up to 100,000 people, many now fear retaliation.
Some who once crossed into China almost daily just to buy cheap bananas and melons or sell appliances and blue jeans will not enter China for any reason. 
''After the demonstrations, there were rumors that if you crossed the border you would be kidnapped and punished,'' Mr. Nabo said. 
''That has not happened, but some people think it is so.''
Still, newspapers here and in Hong Kong have reported that Macao was part of an underground network helping students and dissidents escape from Beijing to Hong Kong and the West. 
''We do know there is a network,'' a Western consular official in Hong Kong said, ''and it makes sense that Macao would play a part.''
Many Macao residents still stroll through the handsome colonial arch that marks the border, most using only coupons they are issued as visas in packages of 100. 
The Chinese guards lounge on wooden chairs, barely glancing at the coupons or the people passing into China, including a young man in jeans and flip-flop sandals pushing a new refrigerator on a dolly and two men in business suits carrying briefcases.
Normally about 18 million trips a year are made into and out of the town of Zhuhai, one of China's special free trade zones. 
Macao officials say border traffic is almost back to normal, but scores of residents insisted recently that it was down by a third or more.
Most of Macao's political diffidence stems from the fact that, outside of the gambling casinos, much of its tiny economy - from wholesale foods to high-rise construction - is dominated by Chinese investment companies. 
And pro-Beijing officials control many of its labor unions and civic and neighborhood associations. 
Porfirio Gomes, a Portuguese lawyer who has lived in Macao for 10 years, said: ''Mention politics here and the locals will ignore you or change the subject. 
Here people cannot afford to be as open as in Hong Kong.''
The Chinese have promised that after 1999 Macao will continue to operate, as Hong Kong, with ''a high degree of autonomy,'' even tacitly approving the casinos. 
But as in Hong Kong, many here prefer to take no chances. 
''Many plan to leave Macao in three or four years,'' Mr. Gomes said. 
''They don't want to meddle in politics because that might mean trouble.''
Â 
Some Have Passports
While Portugal was described by one Macao businessman as ''a ghost government that does nothing real,'' it has given the 100,000 residents born here before 1981 the protection of citizenship, and they will be able to resettle in Portugal if they wish. 
There are also about 10,000 native Portuguese like Mr. Gomes living here.
When Macao begins this year to draw up its basic law - the constitution that will govern the territory under China - those with Portuguese passports, who make up the educated and professional class of the territory, have no incentive to get involved. 
Still, officials point out that the security of a passport means Macao today is a more stable place than Hong Kong, which is experiencing a brain drain as talented residents seek foreign abodes.
In the hard bright sun, much of Macao looks old and seedy. 
But several boxy new high-rises and a huge new horse racing complex are under construction. 
Plans are under way to make little Macao a regional commercial center. 
Three big projects - an airport, a deep-water container port and a bridge to China - are being considered.
''If China's political situation normalizes soon, we will have no problems,'' Mr. Nabo said. 
''But these projects are vulnerable because they need international financing and investors may be nervous about coming into this area now.''

file: Making Trouble in Shanghai.txt
text:
ï»¿
A CHINESE ODYSSEY
The Life and Times of a Chinese Dissident.
By Anne F. Thurston.
440 pp. 
New York:
Charles Scribner's Sons. 
$24.95.
THE Chinese dissident Ni Yuxian first had the chance to answer his Communist Party persecutors when the great investigative reporter Liu Binyan made him a hero of an essay, "A Second Kind of Loyalty."
Now, with Anne F. Thurston's biography, "A Chinese Odyssey," he has yet another opportunity. 
But sometimes those who try to clear their names get themselves into even more hot water by presenting their cases in public. 
Mr. Ni comes across in this book as a thoroughly unpalatable character -- abrasive, unfaithful, opportunistic and arrogant, a man who even as a dissident disappoints us.
What distinguishes Ni Yuxian from most well-known Chinese dissidents is that he is not a member of China's intellectual elite. 
Born in 1945 into a working-class family in a town near Shanghai, he got himself admitted to the army (one of China's sole routes of upward mobility) when he was 16. 
Eventually, the "dissident soldier" managed to attend the Shanghai Maritime Academy.
But he was in constant trouble from early youth. 
As Ms. Thurston explains, he organized fellow soldiers, workers and students against the authorities, wrote angry letters to Mao Zedong and put up written posters defying ultraleftist policies. 
During the Cultural Revolution, he was arrested and detained for printing a pamphlet of sayings from Lenin (even Lenin could be considered counterrevolutionary at the height of the fervor). 
In 1977, he was thrown into a detention center in Shanghai for putting up a poster attacking the Gang of Four. 
He spent two years in fear that he would be executed, until the authorities released him in early 1979.
Mr. Ni, Ms. Thurston tells us, was then reinstated at the Maritime Academy, where he was given work in the propaganda department. 
But he felt discriminated against when party leaders refused to facilitate his efforts to obtain a passport. 
He traveled to Beijing and headed to The People's Daily to join the lines of petitioners seeking to interest Liu Binyan in their cases. 
Finally, a letter caught the journalist's attention. 
In 1984, Mr. Liu went to Shanghai to meet Mr. Ni and investigate further.
At the Maritime Academy, Ms. Thurston says, officials tried to persuade Mr. Liu that Mr. Ni was no antileftist hero during the Cultural Revolution: on the contrary, they said, he was an extremist who attacked teachers and cadres; he had stolen a bicycle; he was an egregious philanderer and had once been accused of rape. 
But Mr. Liu persisted despite his reservations. 
"A Second Kind of Loyalty" appeared in 1985. 
The ensuing furor was one cause of Mr. Liu's expulsion from the Communist Party for a second time.
Fearful of being arrested again, Mr. Ni slipped into an elevator in the United States Consulate in Canton, eventually finding a sympathetic official who helped him obtain a visa. 
He arrived in the United States in 1986, where he became entangled with China Spring, a politically controversial emigre Chinese faction rumored to be funded by Taiwan. 
According to Ms. Thurston, he is now accused by former supporters of having misused funds from his own one-man organization, the Committee for the Promotion of Democracy in China.
GIVEN the questions that have been raised about Ni Yuxian's character and motivations, the reader cannot but wish to know more about Ms. Thurston's doubts concerning Mr. Ni's self-presentation or her own commitment to explore his life. 
For she suggests in her preface that he is "a narcissist" who "often failed in his basic obligations to those closest to him, disappointing, sometimes bitterly so, his wife and his family, his teachers, his loves, and his friends."
With this unimaginatively titled volume, Ms. Thurston, the author of "Enemies of the People," a book about victims of the Cultural Revolution, appears to have wanted to write both an academic biography of Mr. Ni and an impassioned history of the contemporary Chinese democracy movement. 
The fit is an awkward one, in part because Mr. Ni is a peripheral political figure who acted largely alone. 
In Shanghai, he had little connection with events in Beijing, and he was in the United States during the 1989 democracy movement. 
As biography, Ms. Thurston's account is oddly impersonal and distanced, though she spent hundreds of hours talking to Mr. Ni, and though she describes the relationships she developed during the years she spent interviewing his family as deep ones. 
We get only hints of the pain of Mr. Ni's wife or the bitterness of his mistress, even when the two meet in a minibus. 
Mr. Ni himself does not capture us, either as a man of courage or as one of interesting flaws.
Still, the book has gripping moments. 
When Mr. Ni is dismissed from the army in 1964 for his "mistaken, capitalist, and revisionist thought," he stumbles on an opportunity to wipe his slate clean when a lazy official allows him to carry his own file to his new workplace. 
Terrified, he eases it open: "Every transgression he had ever committed was recorded there, many of which had long since faded into the dark recesses of the mind."
By the time Mr. Ni is done burning the damaging evidence, the file is nearly empty.
Ms. Thurston's powerful description of Mr. Ni's experience in a Shanghai detention center in 1977 rivals that of Nien Cheng, who recounted her solitary confinement in the same city in "Life and Death in Shanghai."
Mr. Ni is placed in a 6-by-4-foot cell containing 19 men. 
Threats of execution, torture, disease and false accusations are constant. 
So filthy are conditions that soon "the prisoner's skin is marked by sores, his bottom covered with pimples, and the pimples are filled with blood and with pus, and when the pimples burst open the pus and the blood stick to his bottom like glue, so that when he has to remove his cotton trousers to use the matong the sores pull painfully open and frequently become infected, and every trip to the matong becomes a matter of dread."
Mr. Ni wakes one night to find himself covered with sticky liquid -- the blood of the man next to him, who has slit his wrists.
Ms. Thurston tells us that she was drawn to this story because she wished to write about "those rare cases where individuals manage to stay good" amid totalitarianism. 
But Ni Yuxian seems to have presented far more problematic a hero than either she, or Liu Binyan, had hoped.

file: Mao_s Cable Explains Drive Into Korea.txt
text:
ï»¿
The publication of a secret cable from Mao to Stalin in 1950 has provided the first documentary evidence of the Chinese leader's intentions in making the risky decision to enter the Korean War and engage American forces in combat.
Answering questions that have haunted scholars for decades, the telegram and other documents that have recently been smuggled to the West lend support to the theory that Mao acted out of fear that an American victory in Korea would threaten China. 
The documents have also convinced historians that Stalin agreed to, and then abruptly canceled, a Chinese request for Soviet air cover during the attack.
"If we allow the United States to occupy all of Korea," Mao wrote in the Oct. 
2, 1950, cable, "Korean revolutionary power will suffer a fundamental defeat and the Americans will run more rampant and have negative effects for the entire Far East."
Â 
Threat of U.S. 
Bombing
The cable explicitly recognized that the United States might bomb Chinese cities in retaliation for its entry into the war, but asserted that the destruction of the American forces in Korea was a goal worth the risks.
Two weeks after that summary of Chinese strategic thinking was sent to Stalin, Chinese soldiers invaded North Korea, where they surprised the American troops who were spearheading the United Nations military effort to protect the South Korean Government of Syngman Rhee.
The cable is among hundreds of documents that were published in Beijing in 1987 and 1990 as a collection of Mao's 1949-1951 papers. 
Although they were intended only for the eyes of senior Chinese officials and historians, several copies have been smuggled out of China and obtained by scholars in the United States.
Â 
Stalin's Air Cover
The documents also offer a glimpse at diplomacy between the Communist giants. 
Scholars now assert that after Stalin reneged on air cover and army supplies for the Chinese invasion, originally set for Oct. 
15, Mao froze preparations and reassessed China's position, but decided with his Politburo by Oct. 
13 to go ahead with the advance anyway. 
It began on Oct. 
19.
The invasion, by 260,000 Chinese troops, horrified American commanders in Korea and forced them into the greatest retreat in United States military history. 
The deadlock that followed, after three years of bitter and inconclusive fighting, left the Korean Peninsula divided, as it has remained ever since.
At the time the telegram was sent, Gen. Douglas MacArthur, the commander of United Nations forces in Korea, openly doubted China's willingness to enter Korea with an army that was fatigued from years of its own civil war. 
The Americans also ignored warning signals sent by Beijing as United Nations troops advanced north of the 38th parallel, which had separated the territories under Soviet and American control since the Japanese withdrew from the country in 1945.
Because the Chinese troops moved undetected at first, and then orchestrated successive feints, the size of their military presence was not fully grasped by MacArthur until late November, when the Chinese began unleashing huge nighttime assaults -- sometimes called "human wave" attacks -- on the Americans.
Â 
'Inside Information'
At the time, some policymakers in Washington believed that the Chinese troops had been sent on orders from the Soviet Union, and that Moscow controlled a monolithic Communist bloc. 
Although historians have since learned of the complex antagonism between Mao and Stalin, no documentary evidence has before been seen about what led Mao and his colleagues to their fateful decision.
"Now we really have inside information about decision-making," said Allen S. Whiting, a professor of political science at the University of Arizona who wrote "China Crosses the Yalu," a 1960 book about China's entry into the war. 
"These papers have been very illuminating."
Mr. Whiting, whose theory that Chinese leaders entered the war out of a feeling of defensive necessity has been borne out in the documents, said he was surprised by the extent to which Mao worried about anti-Government forces within China at the time of the war.
Mao at first hesitated to enter the war, Mr. Whiting said, partly because of what he perceived as a threat of lingering opposition to the Communist Government set up only a year earlier, in October 1949. 
But by late September 1950, Mr. Whiting said, Mao became convinced that a significant American presence in Korea might lead to an American-backed offensive by the Communists' enemy, the Nationalists, who had been expelled from the mainland but still posed a threat from Taiwan.
Â 
Altered Chinese Papers
Scholars who have studied the documents warned that they should be viewed with the knowledge that in the past, Chinese papers have often been altered to paint political leaders in a favorable or unfavorable light. 
Although the complexity and internal consistency of those documents point to their authenticity, there are other limitations.
"The problem is that they are fragmentary," said Michael Hunt, professor of political science at the University of North Carolina, who is also writing about the documents. 
"This is a cable in a series of exchanges between Mao and Stalin. 
We don't know what's been said so far."
In the Oct. 
2 telegram, Mao refers to much-needed assistance from Moscow. 
Stalin apparently agreed in the following days to provide air cover, but then reversed himself on Oct. 
10.
Prime Minister Zhou Enlai went on a secret trip to Moscow to try to persuade Stalin to support the Chinese attack, but was unsuccessful. 
In a cable to Zhou on Oct. 
13, Mao wrote that China's Politburo had backed the decision to go to war anyway.
Moving with stealth once they crossed the Yalu River border into Korea on Oct. 
19, Chinese troops were not discovered by American intelligence until they clashed briefly with United Nations soldiers on Oct.

file: Market Place_Funds Cautious On Hong Kong.txt
text:

SIR PIERS JACOBS, Hong Kong's financial secretary, is out ''beating the drum'' for the bustling market at China's door.
In New York, London and Paris last week, the No. 3 man in the Government worked to counter the the negative impact of June's massacre in Bejing's Tiananmen Square.
But the victory by the hard-liners in Bejing has raised some serious doubts among foreign investors who had been bullish on Hong Kong. 
And this attitude will affect the way the market is viewed until China's intentions are much clearer.
Several international funds are scaling back their exposure in Hong Kong. 
They are now looking at the market, said Gavin Dobson of Murray Johnstone International Ltd., as a trading market in which to see an opportunity and get in and get out quickly. 
The long-term view, for him, has become less attractive.
The stocks these funds are looking at are also different. 
The funds are moving away from companies with large property holdings, which had been popular. 
If there is a problem with China, property values will drop the fastest. 
Even with the recovery since June, prices are 10 percent to 15 percent below where they were, economists say.
''We see quite a lot of potential if developments in China are reasonable,'' said David J. Warren, executive vice president of Rowe, Price, Fleming International in London. 
''But we think there is a danger that hard-line forces allied with the army will consolidate their power, put a wall around China and say the capital road is not for us.''
Mr. Dobson of Murray Johnstone adds: ''With so much money to be made in politically safe countries, I don't see any reason to be overweighted in Hong Kong.''
The Hong Kong market tumbled in wake of the repression of the democracy movement and it stopped short only of its record fall in October 1987. 
But more important, the turmoil brought to the fore new concerns about what will happen to this free-market haven on July 1, 1997, when China takes over. 
The promise to continue the capitalist system for 50 years does not look so good now.
Sir Piers is optimistic, but he has to be - that is the party line. 
''I think we're going through the most difficult time now,'' he said. 
''In 1995, the situation could look good, far more optimistic than 1989 and 1990.''
Sir Piers argues that there are two factors favoring Hong Kong. 
The first is that China needs Honk Kong. 
''China is not going to turn its back on the world,'' he said. 
He and others estimate that there are now about 1.5 million to 3 million Chinese working across the border from Hong Kong in Guangdong Province that are directly or indirectly employed by businesses in Hong Kong. 
A major portion of foreign loans and foreign investment since 1979 has also come from the colony.
The other factor is the resilience of the Chinese in Hong Kong. 
It is assumed that they can bounce back from almost anything, as they did from the crash of 1987, the impact of the Chinese Cultural Revolution in the 1960's and as, Sir Piers says, they are bouncing back now from June 4.
He acknowledges the problems of the worker shortage and the resulting inflation. 
And he says the future does not promise economic growth so strong as in the past.
But, he notes, the stock market, according to the Hang Seng index, has recovered 732.60 points since June 4 and at 2,809.96 on Friday is poised to break through 3,000 by year-end. 
That the market did not close on Monday, June 5, shows the new Securities and Futures Commission is working well. 
And trade between Guangdong and Hong Kong continued during the crisis, he also said.
Sir Piers lists the deals that have been completed since June and the 11 new banking licenses. 
And he says an announcement on a new airport will come this week. 
He will not say what the decision is, but he does not deny that there have already been many stories saying the Government will go ahead. 
But he cannot dismiss the real problem -the problem of confidence that is so much more real now than it was nine months ago. 
''What you need to hold it together is the confidence,'' he said.
The so-called brain drain - the emigration of talented Chinese - is continuing. 
And it is not clear if the new British policy of guaranteeing ''essential'' people the right to move to England will help.
Andrew F. Economos, manager of the Scudder New Asia Fund, is not worried. 
''Before Tiananmen Square, people were overly optimistic about the People's Republic of China,'' he said. 
''Now they are overly bearish.''
But Mr. Dobson of Murray Johnstone and Mr. Warren of Rowe, Price, Fleming are not convinced. 
They have been cutting back their exposure in the stock market since Tiananmen Square and are now below the normal average in Asia.
Mr. Warren says many stock sales to foreigners now are by local Chinese, which he does not take as a good sign. 
And Mr. Dobson worries that even the best intentions, like the orderly transition to Chinese sovereignty, can go awry. 
''What seems to be totally impossible and can't happen,'' he said, ''can happen through sheer pigheadedness.''

file: MARKET WATCH_Hong Kong, Star of 1992, Begins to Dim.txt
text:

The world's major economic powers showed they could act together, for one day at least. 
And the world's stock markets showed they too could move in the same direction. 
They went down.
The carnage around the world last week was somewhat obscured in this country by the fact that Wall Street did relatively well. 
The Dow Jones industrial average fell 45.93 points, or 1.4 percent, to 3,285.71. 
Intervention by the world's central banks to support the dollar seemed to ease concerns over American stocks, but did not help shares in the rest of the world, where fears of slow economies combined with a host of local factors, not to mention the possibility of bombs over Baghdad, to produce selloffs.
Even Hong Kong went down, with the Hang Seng index losing 5.8 percent, its worst week since the fall of 1990. 
But it still is up 34 percent in 1992, and remains this year's craze among foreign investors, who now own about half the shares available for trading.
The news in Hong Kong that has justified that kind of performance has been the pending takeover, in 1997, of Hong Kong by China. 
To hear Hong Kong bulls tell it, what really is going to happen is the reverse, as Hong Kong's economic system takes over China, producing a wave of prosperity and a boom in consumer spending. 
"The potential growth of just changing China from an inefficient economy to an efficient one is staggering," says Victoria Goodwin, a Hong Kong watcher for James Capel Inc., the British firm.
Just three years ago, the prospect of a takeover of Hong Kong by the regime that brought the world Tiananmen Square was viewed as a reason to panic. 
But now investors are confident that, however repressive the politics, the movement to economic reform is irreversible. 
And Hong Kong is seen as the way to play China.
So what can go wrong?
A significant part of China's growth comes from its rising trade with this country. 
The American trade deficit with China, at $5.7 billion for the first five months of 1992, is now larger than with any other country except Japan. 
And while the Japanese figure is up 15 percent this year, China's has soared 60 percent.
President Bush has been China's best friend in Washington, staving off Congressional efforts to mess with most-favored-nation trade status, and the House vote to tie trade to human rights issues will not change the situation. 
But what about Bill Clinton?
"It's an issue where Clinton could be protectionist and wear a white hat at the same time," said David Shulman, the chief equity strategist for Salomon Brothers. 
"This could be a very big negative for the Hong Kong market," he said, adding that it also could hurt American companies that buy Chinese exports, ranging from Tyco and Toys "R" Us to Liz Claiborne and the Limited.
Occidentals have a way of applying straight-line forecasting to China, assuming that whatever trend is in place will continue forever. 
It won't, of course. 
Hong Kong stocks may have seen their highs for this year.

text:

China's Foreign Minister signaled to Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d today that Beijing would not block the United Nations Security Council from authorizing force against Iraq if diplomacy proved futile, a senior Administration official said.
The Chinese official, Qian Qichen, told Mr. Baker that his country rejected any "partial solutions" to the Persian Gulf crisis and insisted instead on a total Iraqi pullout from Kuwait, the Administration official said.
Mr. Baker and Mr. Qian met for 90 minutes while they were passing through Cairo. 
Earlier in the day, Mr. Baker met with President Hosni Mubarak of Egypt. 
Mr. Mubarak indicated his country's support for a United Nations authorization of force against Iraq if sanctions could not induce the Iraqis to pull out of Kuwait, which they invaded on Aug. 
2.
Â 
Trying to Galvanize Support
At each stop of his eight-city visit to the Middle East and Europe, Mr. Baker has been trying to galvanize support for a United Nations resolution authorizing force to enhance the credibility of the American military threat against Baghdad.
American officials say such United Nations approval would emphasize to President Saddam Hussein of Iraq that the international coalition arrayed against him would not crumble if there was a resort to force.
The Administration has still not decided when to press for such an authorization or exactly how. 
It apparently wants a blanket authorization that could be invoked when the United States and its allies chose.
Administration officials say they do not want to seek such authorization too soon and then simply wait around and do nothing, because that would undermine their credibility. 
But they do not want to wait indefinitely, because that might keep President Hussein from taking their threat seriously.
Since Sunday, Mr. Baker has won Bahraini, Saudi, Egyptian and Chinese support for some type of resolution. 
His strategy appears to be to try to line up support from Arab nations and China before he visits the Soviet leadership in Moscow beginning on Thursday.
Â 
Moscow's Critical Role
If Moscow can be brought around to endorse the idea, the Administration officials say, then any French hesitations would probably be overcome.
"If the Soviets come on board, I don't think the French would stand in the way," one official said. 
"The French can't be more Soviet than the Soviets."
At the opening of the Baker-Qian meeting, the Chinese Foreign Minister was asked whether his Government was willing to consider a United Nations resolution authorizing force, and he said: "The U.N. resolutions are intended to increase the pressure on Iraq for a peaceful solution. 
All of the armed forces have two roles to play. 
One is to fight a war, the other is to seek peace."
After the meeting, though, a senior Administration official said the Chinese official made it clear that Beijing would not block any such United Nations effort, which it could do by exercising its veto power as a permanent member of the Security Council. 
It would either abstain or vote in favor.
Considering the reluctance the Chinese have shown in the last few weeks about piling on more sanctions against Iraq, this apparently came as a pleasant surprise to American officials.
Mr. Qian renewed an invitation to Mr. Baker to visit Beijing, but the Secretary was noncommital, officials said.
Â 
Meeting Alone With Mubarak
As for the Baker-Mubarak meeting, the two men met alone, without even an interpreter, and both declined to speak to reporters about the substance of their discussions.
Margaret D. Tutwiler, the State Department spokeswoman, was asked whether Mr. Baker had won Egyptian approval for the basing of 20 American B-52 bombers on Egyptian territory, as some recent British newspaper reports suggested he would try to do. 
She responded, "No comment."
American officials said the two men agreed that there should be no partial solution to the crisis and that force should not be ruled out. 
They also discussed logistical support for Egyptian forces in Saudi Arabia, officials said, but disclosed no details.
Assistant Secretary of State John H. Kelly will go to Damascus on Wednesday to brief the Syrian leadership on American thinking about the gulf crisis. 
He will also go to Brussels to brief NATO representatives. 
Asked if anyone would go to Israel, American officials traveling with Mr. Baker said there were no such plans.

In the most substantial step to improve relations with China since the crackdown on democracy demonstrators around Tiananmen Square, President Bush met here today with the Chinese Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen, and declared that Beijing and Washington had "made common ground in terms of standing up against aggression" by Iraq.

Exchanges Barred in '89

file: MIDEAST TENSIONS_Chinese and Soviet Ministers Meet Hastily on Gulf.txt
text:

The Chinese and Soviet Foreign Ministers met today in western China for a hastily called conference on the Persian Gulf crisis, and afterward declared in a joint statement that the world should work for a peaceful solution if at all possible.
While the statement emphasized the Soviet and Chinese view that every effort should be made to avoid war, it did not rule out military intervention. 
Indeed, it could be read as a final warning to Iraq that Moscow and Beijing might endorse the use of force if Baghdad did not change.
The statement suggested that the United Nations Security Council would pass additional measures and said the Soviet Union and China would continue to work to insure the strict implementation of resolutions already passed, which call for an Iraqi withdrawal.
China and the Soviet Union have been the most reluctant of the permanent members of the Security Council to endorse a resolution authorizing the use of military force to drive Iraqi troops from Kuwait. 
While the statement was ambiguous, the two countries appeared to be positioning themselves so that they could, if necessary, declare that there was no longer hope for a peaceful solution and that they had no alternative but to back the use of force.
Â 
More Than 3 Hours of Talks
The meetings between China's Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen, and his Soviet counterpart, Eduard A. Shevardnadze, were held in the northwestern Chinese city of Urumqi and lasted more than three hours. 
Plans for the meeting were disclosed only on Thursday, suggesting that it was called on very short notice.
"Both sides stand for a political solution to the gulf crisis on the basis of relevant U.N. Security Council resolutons and support the positive efforts of Arab countries to resolve the conflicts," the joint statement said, according to a version released by the official New China News Agency.
"They strongly appeal to Iraq and demand that it withdraw its army from Kuwait unconditionally and immediately," the statement continued. 
"They hold that so far as there is still hope for a peaceful solution, the international community should continue to work to that end and try its best to avoid a war."
The statement was only a little bit different from a formula China has used in the last three weeks. 
But that formula is in itself a step away from China's initial reaction, which emphasized its opposition to force and seemed to offer no exceptions.
Â 
Political Credit for Support
A Western diplomat said he expected China to vote in favor of the Security Council resolution authorizing military moves against Iraqi troops. 
Mr. Qian is reported to have said that China would not veto such a resolution, and the diplomat said China believed that it would gain additional political credit in Western capitals if it voted for the resolution instead of abstaining.
"The two foreign ministers agreed that the two sides will continue to hold consultations with each other when the United Nations Security Council adopts additional measures, so as to insure that the relevant resolutions adopted previously by the Security Council will be implemented in real earnest," the statement declared. 
"The two sides are willing to work for a solution to the gulf crisis together with the other member states of the Security Council."
Mr. Qian and Mr. Shevardnadze had 90 minutes of private talks, accompanied by only one translator and assistant for each side. 
That meeting was followed by another 90 minutes of consultations in the presence of a larger group of Foreign Ministry officials. 
Mr. Shevardnadze returned to the Soviet Union late this afternoon.
The two foreign ministers also discussed bilateral relations, but the communique gave no details. 
Chinese-Soviet relations have improved dramatically in recent years, but a projected purchase of Soviet military equipment by Beijing has stalled in negotiations in recent months.
The statement said that Mr. Qian and Mr. Shevardnadze favored "further deepening of the good-neighborly and mutually beneficial relations in all the fields between the two countries."

Regained Some Legitimacy
Mr. Qian, however, said he saw no difference between contacts and exchanges, and said that his visit would be a "fairly important" event in American-Chinese relations.

text:

The United States is ready to seek a United Nations resolution this month authorizing offensive military action against Iraq, provided that final consultations with other members of the Security Council go as anticipated, a senior American official said today.
Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d arrived in Brussels tonight to begin an intensive round of country-by-country conferences, involving at least 9 of the Security Council's 15 members. 
He is seeking the backing of a half-dozen small countries, and confirmation that the Soviet Union and China will also cooperate.
The meetings will conclude on Nov. 
24, with a meeting in Bogota with Foreign Minister Luis Jaramillo Correa of Colombia, and the resolution could be introduced at the United Nations two days later.
"We do not know yet whether we will be able or not to go forward, because we don't know for certain that a country might not say no," said the senior American official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. 
"We haven't yet heard from China and the Soviet Union finally."
Â 
Congress Weighs Special Session
But other Americans involved in the talks said Washington had strong indications that most of the pivotal countries were ready to go along, despite statements made today in New York by a top Gorbachev aide, Yevgeny M. Primakov, who called for a political initiative to persuade President Saddam Hussein of Iraq to give up Kuwait peacefully.
United Nations action would greatly help an operation led by the United States to drive President Saddam Hussein's forces out of Iraq. 
All of Washington's major European allies except Britain and all of its major Arab allies have made Security Council approval a precondition to taking part in such an operation, according to a ranking European Community official.
Leading figures in Congress from both parties have said they would back a special session, in the event of a favorable vote in the Security Council, to debate President Bush's policy in the gulf. 
But it might prove difficult for critics of the policy to vote against it with a United Nations resolution already on the record. 
Congressional leaders decided Wednesday not to call for a special session now but reserved the right to do so later.
The Bush Administration considers it crucial that any resolution be brought to a vote before Nov. 
30, when the United States yields the chairmanship of the Security Council to Yemen. 
That small Arab nation has seldom been an American ally in the Persian Gulf crisis and could tangle a new resolution in parliamentary complexities, the senior official said.
Â 
'Don't Act Like Cowboys'
Top Administration policy makers have said in the last week that despite Mr. Bush's deployment of about 150,000 fresh troops to Saudi Arabia and the surrounding region, no decision has been made yet to start an offensive. 
No attack is likely, they have said, before January or February at the earliest.
A United Nations resolution, like the troop deployment, would be part of the effort to persuade Mr. Hussein that his only options are retreat or destruction. 
But it, like the troop deployment, runs the risk of frightening the American people, too, and convincing many of them that a war is imminent.
The senior American official said that, following Congressional and other advice, the Administration was making an effort "to not move precipitously, don't act like cowboys, proceed through the United Nations to the extent that you can."
Under Security Council rules, approval of a resolution authorizing the use of military force requires at least nine affirmative votes, and all of the five permanent members -- the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France and China -- must either vote yes or abstain.
Â 
Soviet and Chinese Votes
The Soviet Union and China have given preliminary indications, the senior official said, that they will not block a resolution along the lines the United States seeks, although there has been no sign that Soviet forces would play an active role in an offensive. 
Mr. Baker will try to clarify the Soviet position at a meeting in Paris on Sunday with Eduard A. Shevardnadze, the Soviet Foreign Minister.
Another American official said a definitive statement from China is expected within the next few days. 
Mr. Baker, who met Foreign Minister Qian Qichen in Cairo last week, is said to be confident that the Chinese will not veto the resolution but is not sure they will vote for it rather than abstain.
A Soviet decision to vote yes would probably have a major influence on the Chinese vote.
Britain and France have already signed up, as has Canada. 
Mr. Baker made a hasty trip to Bermuda on Tuesday to win the agreement of Joe Clark, the Canadian Minister of External Affairs.
Â 
No Overture to Cuba
If the Soviets and the Chinese eventually go along, that would give the United States the votes of all the permanent members and that of Canada, for a total of six. 
On Sunday, Mr. Baker will seek the backing of Finland, which is considered a likely supporter, and of Romania, whose support is thought to be a bit less certain.
That same day, he will also meet Douglas Hurd, the British Foreign Secretary, and Roland Dumas, the French Foreign Minister.
The United States hopes to get commitments of another two to four votes, giving it a total of 9 to 12, at the meeting in Colombia and at Mr. Baker's session in Geneva on Saturday with the Foreign Ministers of three African countries -- the Ivory Coast, Ethiopia and Zaire. 
State Department officials said a substantial margin was important to impress on Mr. Hussein his isolation from almost all of the world's other countries.
The other three members of the Security Council this year -- Cuba, Yemen and Malaysia -- are considered the least likely to support the United States, and Mr. Baker does not plan personally to solicit their backing. 
But the Administration has written off only Cuba, which has voted for only the mildest of the 10 resolutions on the crisis adopted by the Security Council.
Mr. Baker, who will spend Friday in Brussels, will be joined in Paris on Sunday by President Bush. 
Both will be there for the 34-nation summit meeting of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe, marking the end of the cold war, which runs from Monday to Wednesday.
After the summit conference, Mr. Bush will head to Saudi Arabia to spend Thanksgiving with American troops there and offshore, and then to Cairo.
Â 
BUSH PLAN FOR IRAQI ARMS
WASHINGTON, Nov. 
15 (Special to The New York Times) -- President Bush said tonight that an Iraqi withdrawal from Kuwait should be followed by international guarantees that would eliminate Iraqi chemical weapons and halt that country's nuclear weapons program.
In an interview on Cable News Network, Mr. Bush stopped short of making the elimination of chemical and nuclear weapons in Iraq a military goal of the United States. 
He said any effort to control those weapons after the current crisis is over would have to be carried out under United Nations auspices.
Mr. Bush went somewhat further than he had been willing to go in saying that in addition to forcing an Iraqi withdrawal from Kuwait, the United States was eager to eliminate Mr. Hussein's arsenal.
"Having demonstrated this recklessness," he said, "I don't think the rest of the world would say this is good enough, just what they call the status quo ante, going back to the way things were before the invasion."
Mr. Bush said that even if Iraq withdrew peacefully from Kuwait, "I think you'd see an understandable cry in the reinvigorated United Nations, under the peacekeeping function" to have controls on Iraqi weaponry.

file: MOSCOW IS SELLING WEAPONS TO CHINA, U.S. OFFICIALS SAY.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a move that is undercutting efforts to stem the spread of arms, Russia is selling missile-guidance technology, rocket engines and other advanced weapons systems to China, its onetime adversary, American officials say.
The exports to Beijing worry Bush Administration officials, who fear that a main reason the Chinese are acquiring the technology is to develop new weapons to sell to the third world.
"Re-export is a big problem," a Pentagon official said. 
"You don't know what the Chinese will do with the stuff once they get the high-tech capabilities."
Russia's arms sales have become a growing worry for Washington even as its military threat has shrunk. 
Moscow's reduction in military spending, combined with a desperate need for hard currency, has led arms factories and military-related institutes to look abroad for orders to survive. 
At the same time, conversion of military industries to civilian production has proved difficult.
Â 
Enriching Uranium
In addition to weapons, a senior Bush Administration official said, Moscow is selling technology to the Chinese that can be used to enrich uranium. 
Washington is concerned that Beijing will use the technology to improve the design of its nuclear power plants, making them attractive to third-world buyers and further undermining efforts to stop the spread of nuclear arms.
Despite a cooperative relationship with non-Communist Russia, the United States has so far been unable to stop the Russian sales. 
Russian officials seem to have decided that the proceeds from arms and technology sales are worth the risk of irritating American policy makers.
The Administration, for its part, seems to have concluded that supporting reform in Russia is more important than drawing a firm line against weapons sales and threatening a reduction in financial assistance.
Â 
U.S. Formally Complains
Moscow is proceeding with the sale of diesel submarines to Iran, and a Russian company, Glavkosmos, is selling a rocket booster to India in violation of an agreement restricting technology for ballistic missiles. 
A senior American official said the Administration had complained to Russia and China about the sale, apparently with no effect.
Undermining its leverage, the protests by Washington have come as Western nations, including the United States, have shown little restraint themselves in selling arms. 
The Administration, although it has exhorted governments of other industrial nations to control the spread of destabilizing weapons, appears to have placed emphasis on competing with its allies for arms deals as it faces a faltering economy and a difficult election campaign.
Two such deals -- the sales of combat jets to Saudi Arabia and Taiwan totaling $14.8 billion, announced in September -- exceed the value of American arms sales to all nations of the third world last year. 
Administration officials say that the Russians would be selling weapons to Iran and China regardless of American sales. 
But Russian officials have cited such deals to justify their exports.
The pattern of Moscow's arms sales has changed considerably since the cold war, when it provided billions of dollars in arms to nations like Cuba, Iraq and Libya, often at concessionary terms, in an effort to extend or maintain its military influence.
What the Russians are after is cash, not influence. 
That, plus the defeat of Iraq in the Persian Gulf war, which effectively removed Baghdad as a potential client, has limited the number of prospective customers. 
Two of the major customers are Iran and China.
Â 
Risky Business
"In absolute figures Russian exports have gone down," an Administration official said, "but the reality is that the customers that still want to buy from them are questionable."
And Richard F. Grimmett, an expert on conventional arms sales at the Congressional Research Service, observed: "The Russian focus is on those countries that are willing to pay cash. 
There is a tremendous focus on Iran. 
China has picked up, too. 
The Chinese cannot get high-technology weapon systems from other suppliers. 
What you have there is a marriage of convenience."
Russia has sold diesel submarines and SU-24 and MIG-29 aircraft to Iran, and is providing spare parts for some of the Iraqi aircraft that were flown to Iran during the gulf war -- planes that the Iranians have said they will not return. 
And along with Czechoslovakia, Russia has sold T-72 tanks to Syria.
Â 
Better Guidance Systems
American officials say Moscow has sold missile-guidance technology, rocket engines and rocket technology to China. 
China's air-to-air missiles are not well equipped to seek out enemy planes, and Russian technology is expected to enable Beijing to improve them. 
China's surface-to-surface missiles are also considered to have inferior guidance systems and could benefit considerably from Russian exports, American officials said.
Moscow has sold S-300 surface-to-air missiles to China, the officials say. 
The S-300 is a Patriot-like system designed to shoot down planes and missiles.
In addition, Russia has sold 24 SU-27 fighters to China. 
American officials believe that Beijing is buying the planes in hope of acquiring production technology so that future aircraft can be assembled at home. 
Adding to the American concern, there are indications of discussions between Russians and Chinese officials about the joint production in China of tactical missiles and other weapons systems, an Administration official said.
Russia is also selling tanks and tank technology to Beijing.
A further worry, a senior Administration official said, is the sale of advanced Russian dual-use technology, which can be employed to enrich uranium for nuclear power plants. 
The United States is worried that this technology transfer will help China modernize its nuclear power plants and make them more marketable in the third world.
Both Russia and China have recently announced the sale of nuclear power plants to Iran, a transaction that disturbs Washington. 
The Administration believes that even ostensibly peaceful nuclear programs will enhance Teheran's expertise and help it develop nuclear weapons.
Â 
Yeltsin Lays It Out
The Russians have not been secretive about arms sales. 
In February, President Boris N. Yeltsin said weapons exports would be a cushion for the Russian arms industry as the country tried to make the transition to a civilian economy.
More recently, a Russian Foreign Ministry spokesman justified the sale of three diesel submarines to Iran in blunter terms, saying it was a way of raising cash during a difficult period.
"Russia cannot in principle, taking into account the economic situation in this country, give up the receipts of freely convertible currency through the sales of armaments abroad," the spokesman said.
Whatever the rationale, Moscow has been stepping up sales efforts. 
In August, it held a major air show and used the occasion to promote arms, displaying surface-to-air missiles and self-propelled artillery. 
Signs in Russian and English said customers could buy military aircraft out of existing inventories or purchase specially configured planes off production lines. 
Chinese and North Koreans were among the foreign officials examining the weapons systems.
Norman Friedman, an American military expert, remarked, "They have got one product that is worth buying and they are selling it."

text:
