The most immediate tangible result promised here today from Mikhail S. Gorbachev's Beijing visit was Peking duck and a dozen other dishes. 
The arrival of 29 Chinese chefs is being expedited because of the summit meeting, according to officials working on the refurbishing of Moscow's dowdy, long-Russified Chinese restaurant.
Aside from that tidbit, Muscovites were stolidly unoptimistic in interviews about any short-run hopes for additional consumer goods from Mr. Gorbachev's mission. 
But they were genuinely relieved about the pledges of greater tranquility on the border after 30 years of hostile relations.
''We're tired of quarreling with the Chinese and I pray to God relations get better,'' said Olga M. Strepikheyeva, a 79-year-old retiree whose main point was that it is a long way from the Beijing talks to the empty shop shelves here.
Â 
The Fruits of Heroism
''Gorbachev is taken as a hero in China, but here his heroism has brought us nothing in the stores,'' she said. 
Then spotting a group of Chinese tourists passing her on Gertsena Street, the tiny woman smiled cherubically under her spring babushka and gestured to them with mock gaiety, ''Yes, let them see our fabulous life under Mr. Gorbachev.''
Muscovites were outspoken and well informed about the trip, but only within the limits of the official Soviet news reports on the Beijing events. 
These were notably deficient in explaining the mammoth size and libertarian politics of the Chinese demonstrations that disrupted Mr. Gorbachev's itinerary.
''The line people like to say about Gorbachev is that he is the stormy petrel of perestroika,'' said Yuri Bospalko, stressing the troubled seas that bring change. 
Word From the U.S. 
Mr. Bospalko was one of the few Muscovites to have an accurate idea of the street scenes in Beijing because he is deputy chief editor of the American news desk at Tass, the Soviet press agency, and privy to foreign dispatches not circulated here.
''I know about the one million demonstrators because we get Cable News Network on the dish upstairs and our correspondents fax us summaries of the American press,'' he said in the street outside the Tass office, asserting that fuller reports on the demonstrations would be made available in the Soviet press tomorrow. 
''I think Gorbachev is handling things in Beijing about as well as he handles things here in the Central Committee,'' he said admiringly.
Aleksandr G. Davidov, a construction engineer, said it was important to understand that the summit meeting was about ''more serious global problems'' and ''certainly not'' about the Soviet consumer's relentless troubles with scarce goods and the current panic buying of such commodities as matches and salt.
''To tell you the truth I have only a very vague idea about the demonstrations by the Chinese,'' he said when asked, reflecting the fact that Soviet television has been showing fleeting and colorfully serene pictures of the street crowds.
Â 
'I Am a Capitalist'
It was not until Mr. Gorbachev's televised news conference Wednesday night that viewers could tell from the emphasis of Western correspondents' questions that the Soviet leader was in a delicate position, being identified with the demonstrators' demands for political change.
''I know all about the demonstrations and I praise the students' reason,'' said Arkady P. Zorkin, who said he was a devotee of Western radio news broadcasts here. 
''They should get rid of their bureaucracy just like here.''
A retired veteran, Mr. Zorkin smiled and proclaimed, ''I am a capitalist,'' as he showed a dozen telescopes he has set up so visitors to the Lenin Hills promenade can rent peeks at the Moscow skyline below, an enterprise that was forbidden not too long ago. 
Such entrepreneur's savvy is what Mr. Gorbachev's summit meeting is all about, he said, predicting impressive economic growth from the visit, ''especially in the Far East.''
Farther up the hill wends Friendship Street, no longer an ill-fitting name for the address of the Chinese Embassy compound.
''There were awful incidents, tense relations,'' Valery I. Lukyanenko recalled of the cross-border fistfights and fatal shootings 20 years ago between the two nations' soldiers. 
''But now all around the world things are becoming more normal,'' he said in the sunshine.
''It's a revolutionary visit, a step beyond all the old problems and troubles,'' said Sergei A. Zhdanov, another passer-by outside the embassy.
Â 
A Time for Fantasies
Downtown at the Peking Restaurant, which saw its last Chinese chef over 30 years ago before the Chinese-Soviet troubles, Galina F. Gorinova, was preparing for a visit to Beijing on Saturday with five other Russians to make final arrangments for the 29 Chinese chefs and assorted restaurant managers who will be moving to Moscow. 
''The summit has expedited everything,'' she said. 
''And these chefs will be participating in the joint venture with a personal stake in the enterprise.''
Out on the street, Yuri Bychkov and Arkady Kostrolitin allowed themselves post-summit fantasies.
''Carpets, towels, sprinting shoes, hats,'' said Mr. Kostrolitin, summarizing what China means to him. 
''Remember those good raincoats in the old days?''
Both were curious about the demonstrations in Beijing. 
''Political freedom?''
Mr. Bychkov said when told what they were about. 
''We're also demanding political freedom,'' he said, smiling. 
''Some of the great Taiwan sound equipment would also be all right.''

file: Nanchang Journal_China Embraces U.S. Experts but There_s a Limit.txt
text:
ï»¿
Karen A. Krusich earns less than the other M.B.A.'s in her class back home, just $200 a month, but in her current job she does get plenty of respect. 
The first time she walked into a classroom here, the students applauded.
"Around here, they're not bitter and know-it-all," she said. 
They tend to be adoring -- and persistent.
"Every time I'm on my bike, people say, 'Hello, can I talk to you in English?'
" Ms. Krusich said with a grimace. 
"Sometimes I love it. 
Sometimes I want to scream."
Thousands of Americans like Ms. Krusich are getting respect, if not a lot of money, teaching English for a year or two at colleges throughout China. 
They leave an indelible mark.
In some cities, people sometimes cannot identify the Mayor but gossip knowledgeably about the foreign teachers. 
And English-speaking officials or academics often reminisce about American professors who taught them how to pronounce the "th" sounds, which are not found in Chinese, or introduced them to ideas of democracy.
Â 
An Experience to Relish
About 30,000 "foreign experts," including 9,000 or so Americans, work in China. 
Most are teachers, but their ranks also include doctors, crop specialists and even editors who polish English-language translations of Chinese propaganda.
Here in Nanchang, a provincial capital in east-central China, about 30 foreigners teach English in colleges.
"At first the little children here cried when they saw me, and ran away," said Ms. Krusich, a 42-year-old businesswoman from Chicago. 
"But then I started giving them candy, so now they're very friendly."
Now the children call Ms. Krusich "Auntie," and like most Americans she says she relishes the experience in China. 
Still, there seem to be two frequent minefields for foreign experts: romance and politics.
Many of the American teachers are single and in their early 20's, hormones coursing through their arteries in the same way that the veins of Chinese officials pulsate with prudishness and paternalism. 
While foreigners sometimes date and even marry local Chinese without difficulty, officials in some areas try to swat Cupid away.
Such officials tend to feel that when around foreigners, Chinese should never let down their guard, much less their clothes, and they fear infiltration of relative Western casualness about sex as much as Western seriousness about democracy. 
Such officials sometimes act as match-breakers and punish the Chinese involved.
Two years ago, a Chinese woman in Beijing was imprisoned on accusations of prostitution because of her steady relationship with a British boyfriend.
Today's foreign teachers are the latest in a long line of Western adventurers -- at least since the Jesuits of the 16th century -- who have come to China to teach Western ideas, technologies or languages. 
Early in this century, many Christian missionaries taught in schools throughout China, and then too some Chinese were suspicious of "foreign devils," as well as apprehensive about any intimacy.
Another delicate subject is politics. 
During the 1989 Tiananmen democracy movement, many foreign experts took to the streets with their students, but now most teachers and students alike seem to try to avoid direct criticisms of the Government, except in private conversations.
Still, teachers often introduce Western ideas in more subtle ways. 
Yingling Chin, a Chinese-American from Illinois who teaches in Nanchang, said that when he had a choice of two American films to show the class he asked the students to take a vote. 
Initially confused by the idea, the students have now caught on.
"It's an exercise in democracy," Mr. Chin said with a grin.
Salaries for teachers range from $120 to $200 a month. 
Most say they came because they wanted to experience life in an exotic foreign country, or because they wanted to learn more about China in particular.
They normally get rent-free apartments, with a telephone and often a maid. 
The accommodations are palatial by Chinese standards, but Westerners are often put off by the power failures, water shortages, and doormen who make Chinese visitors register their names.
"They tend to complain when they're there and rave when they come back," said Robert M. Pease, the executive director of the Princeton-in-Asia program, which has placed 25 college graduates in China in each of the last two years. 
"I don't think anybody regrets doing it."
Â 
The Numbers Are Up Again
Mr. Pease said the number of Americans in the China program peaked at 43 in 1988-89, right before the army fired on pro-democracy protesters in Beijing. 
The killings caused a sharp drop in applications, but now the numbers are up again.
Some foreign experts come through university programs like the one Mr. Pease administers. 
Others get in touch with Chinese embassies to volunteer their services, or write to the Foreign Affairs Office in the city or province where they want to work.
Chinese officials go out of their way to make their visitors feel at home. 
Some years ago, a group of American experts in the city of Chengdu were planning a grand Thanksgiving dinner and searched the region for a turkey, with no success. 
To universal delight, the Chinese hosts presented them on Thanksgiving Day with two turkeys, which were consumed with great merriment.
"Finally, someone asked them where they got the turkeys," recalled Jane Kenyon, a New Yorker who was then teaching English in Chengdu and who attended the dinner. 
"They said, 'The zoo.'
"

file: NATIONALISTS WIN TAIWAN ELECTIONS.txt
text:
ï»¿
The governing Nationalist Party won a major victory today in Taiwan's first full election in more than four decades, as voters appeared to rebuff opposition calls for a declaration of independence from China.
Communist leaders in Beijing, who had been intensely concerned about the election and had warned that they would attack if Taiwan declared its independence, are expected to be as relieved as their adversaries in the Nationalist Party, or Kuomintang.
The election, a milestone in the political restructuring of Taiwan, means that the Kuomintang will have the votes it needs to control a Parliament that will convene in March to revise the constitution and perhaps ordain a new system of government.
The Nationalists won 71 percent of the vote, on the high side of expectations. 
The main opposition group, the Democratic Progressive Party, which advocates independence, received 24 percent of the vote, well below its goal and also below its performance in national elections in 1989.
Â 
Two-Party System Seen
The rest of the votes were cast for smaller parties, but these groups did so poorly that Taiwan seems likely to continue as a two-party rather than a multi-party political system.
"We're very pleased that we've been endorsed by the electorate, in that they want stabilityI and development," Jason C. Hu, the chief Government spokesman, said tonight. 
"I hope that we can put aside the issue of reunification and independence and build up the country. 
The voters have seen no need to push an extremist position that may put us in danger."
Both the Nationalists here and the Communists in Beijing insist that Taiwan is an inseparable part of China, although each claims sovereignty over the other part. 
Taiwan formally calls itself the Republic of China, but the Democratic Progressive Party campaigned for a constitutional conference to formally decree the birth of a new "Republic of Taiwan" that would be fully independent of China and would apply for membership in the United Nations as a new country.
Â 
Looking to Next Election
The Democratic Progressives, at least initially, did not appear subdued by the election results.
"We think that Taiwan independence will still be an issue and that we can do better in the next election," said Yang May-sing, a spokeswoman for the party. 
"This is the first time that the issue has come up, and people are sensitive to it. 
But we think we can do better next year."
Analyzing the party's poor showing, Miss Yang cited an institutional tilt in Taiwan toward the Kuomintang, including a tendency by the three Government-controlled television networks to support Kuomintang positions. 
She also asserted that there had been vote buying by Kuomintang candidates.
Vote buying is a long tradition here, even though officials formally condemn it and there are rewards for turning in anyone who tries to buy a vote. 
Typically, a campaign worker offers $10 to $30 in expectation of a vote of thanks. 
In rural areas, farmers are sometimes made to swear on a statue of Buddha that they will vote for the candidate who provides the money.
Â 
All Parties Buy Votes
Local journalists and neutral officials say that while candidates of all parties buy votes, the Kuomintang perhaps does more of it because it has more money.
Parris H. Chang, a political science professor from Pennsylvania State University who is visiting here, said the opposition would have to do some soul searching about its strong backing for independence.
Of the 325 National Assembly candidates who were elected today, 254 were from the Kuomintang and 66 from the Democratic Progressive Party. 
Five were independent or non-aligned. 
Including 78 members who were elected in 1986 and who also will participate in the constitutional conference, the Kuomintang will have 79 percent of the seats. 
That will give it the three-quarters control it needs to approve a revised constitution.
Â 
Fewer Mainlanders
In a sign of the generational transition under way in Taiwan, less than 22 percent of the new legislators are originally from the Chinese mainland. 
In contrast, politics for most of the last 40 years -- ever since 1949, when Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek fled with the Kuomintang to Taiwan after his defeat by the Communists -- have been dominated by mainlanders.
The Kuomintang has threatened in recent months to disband the Democratic Progressive Party for supporting independence, which is nominally illegal. 
However, a government spoksesman gave no hint today whether the ruling party's election victory would make such a crackdown more or less likely.
Miss Yang, the opposition spokeswoman, said that the Democratic Progressives were not very worried about this possibility and that they could quickly reorganize even if they were disbanded.

file: New Strategy Suggested in Battle on China Trade Status.txt
text:
ï»¿
Anticipating that President Bush's decision to renew trade benefits for China this year will ultimately survive any challenge, opponents in Congress have started lining up behind legislation that would impose human rights conditions before similar benefits are granted next year.
The strategy was disclosed at a hearing today of the House Ways and Means Committee's Trade Subcommittee, where members of the international business community warned that should China lose most-favored-nation trading status, China would retaliate by not buying $6 billion of foodstuffs and other products it now purchases from the United States.
The warning had resonance. 
Representative Beryl J. Anthony, Democrat of Arkansas, said he did not want to see ''innocent producers of farm commodities punished'' by retaliation. 
Many farmers in his district grow soybeans.
Others Will Pick Up Business
Representative Frank J. Guarini, Democrat of New Jersey, said that since no other countries were contemplating any kind of trade action against China, ''our allies will simply pick up the business that we lose.''
Noting that the United States gives the preferred status to Iran, Iraq and South Africa, he added that ''to single out China is hypocrisy.''
Representative Robert T. Matsui, a California Democrat, said that a majority of the Chinese in his district ''tell me that by continuing trade there would be a more positive atmosphere.''
The trade status, which China has enjoyed throughout the last decade, provides the lowest available tariffs. 
Many members of Congress want to deny renewal this year because of Beijing's crackdown on dissent.
Resolutions of disapproval of the President's action have been introduced and will probably clear both chambers. 
But legislative analysts say that opponents did not have the two-thirds support in either chamber needed to override an almost certain Presidential veto.
A leader of the opposition, Representative Nancy Pelosi, a California Democrat, acknowledged as much when she predicted that one of the compromise bills ''I believe will have a good deal of support in the Congress.''
She was alluding to legislation proposed by Representative Donald J. Pease, Democrat of Ohio, which postpones the China trade battle until next year.
Under the Pease measure, before such trade status is extended, Beijing will have to show ''significant'' improvement in human rights, end martial law in China and Tibet and suspend support for the Khmer Rouge of Cambodia.
''I view this as a middle course between stopping trade altogether and making harmless and meaningless statements,'' Mr. Pease said at the hearing. 
He said that among his co-sponsors are 6 fellow members, of 36 on the Ways and Means Committee.
Â 
Extension Suggested
On a parallel track is a bill of Representative Peter J. Kostmayer, Democrat of Pennsylvania, that would grant a six-month extension, again on condition that China improve human rights.
But members of the business community today took exception to this approach. 
''Conditionality creates insurmountable problems in practice,'' said Roger W. Sullivan, president of the United States-China Business Council, representing American multinationals in China.
''The fundamental problem is that the Chinese leadership, by its intransigence over the past year, has made clear that it is unlikely to make fundamental changes in internal policy to accommodate U.S. concerns.''
Last year two-way trade between the United States and China amounted to $18 billion. 
American investment in China, in place and planned, exceeds $4 billion.
If Congress decides to withdraw the trade status, said Howard Lewis 3d, vice president of international affairs at the National Association of Manufacturers, business decision-makers in this country ''will conclude that China is just too risky.''
He added. 
''They may also conclude that other countries in transition are also too risky, from Poland to the Soviet Union to certain Latin American countries.''

file: New Tension Over Trade With China.txt
text:
ï»¿
As China's trade surplus with the United States rises sharply, diplomats and business executives say relations between the two countries could worsen because of China's import restrictions, software piracy and other issues.
"The tremendous growth in the trade deficit, and the proliferation of Chinese measures to restrict access to the market for imports, taken together, constitute a meaningful, significant trade problem," Joseph A. Massey, assistant United States trade representative, said at a news conference Friday night after two days of talks with Chinese officials on intellectual-property issues.
Â 
A Soaring Trade Surplus
China's trials of pro-democracy demonstrators seem to be largely completed, and so the human rights issue is expected to subside after two years in which it was the focal point of contention between the two countries. 
But since the Tiananmen crackdown in 1989, China has enjoyed a soaring trade surplus with the United States.
Kenneth G. Lieberthal, a China scholar at the University of Michigan who is visiting Beijing, said, "There is good reason to be concerned about the potential deterioration in Sino-American relations in the coming months."
While Beijing and Washington have differences on a range of issues, as well as in their ideologies and vision of the emerging international order, most people believe that trade disputes will be crucial in determining relations in coming months.
The United States trade deficit with China reached $10.4 billion in 1990, up from $6.2 billion in 1989. 
The only larger United States deficits are with Japan and Taiwan. 
By some estimates, the deficit with China will soar to more than $15 billion this year.
American imports from China include clothing, toys and shoes, with the value of the footwear more than double the level in 1989, according to figures for the first nine months of 1990. 
But while American imports were increasing sharply, American sales to China dropped sharply, from $5.8 billion in 1989 to $4.8 billion in 1990.
This trade imbalance, coupled with continuing indignation in the United States at the Chinese human rights situation, is expected to lead to another effort on Capitol Hill this year to withdraw China's "most favored nation" trade status. 
The effort failed last year, after the Bush Administration moved to quash it, but some experts say that Congress will try harder this year and that the Administration may devote less energy to the issue.
"Most favored nation" status is the key issue likely to emerge in coming months, executives say, and in the end most think it will be preserved after a fight. 
But they do not rule out the possibility that it will be revoked. 
That could cause a sharp drop in Chinese exports to the United States, retaliation by China and a significant chill between Washington and Beijing.
Â 
Property Rights at Issue
Another trade issue under negotiation concerns intellectual-property rights, which were the focus of Mr. Massey's talks with the Chinese. 
China has always ignored copyrights, to the point that pirated copies of President Bush's autobiography are available from a number of Chinese publishers.
American software manufacturers are particularly concerned and estimate that pirated software in China may cost them $400 million a year in lost sales. 
Mr. Massey said the piracy problem in China was one of the most serious in the world.
To address the criticism, China has adopted its first copyright law, to take effect in June. 
But its effectiveness will depend on carrying out regulations that have still not been published or completed.
If the United States is dissatisfied with Chinese progress on the issue, the Office of the Trade Representative could initiate an action under section 301 of the Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act of 1988. 
After an investigation, that could lead to imposition of retaliatory tariffs against Chinese exports to the United States.
Â 
'Dumping' Charged
There are also disputes about Chinese garment exports, and allegations that China breached its quotas limiting such exports to the United States. 
China is also accused of "dumping" certain products, at unfairly low prices, in the United States market.
John Frisbie, director of China operations for the United States-China Business Council, said that in the last few months China had begun to increase its imports and that this may help ease trade frictions.
Underlying the disagreements, Washington and Beijing seem to have fundamentally different perspectives on where the fault lies. 
In the United States, China is often viewed as recalcitrant, deceptive and repressive, as well as determined to adopt a mercantilist policy of bolstering exports and curtailing imports.
In China, officials complain that the United States is trying to subvert the Chinese Government and has ignored positive steps Beijing has taken, like the release of many dissidents from prison and the adoption of a copyright law.

file: Nixon Tells of China at White House Dinner.txt
text:
ï»¿
The White House was not exactly trumpeting it to the world, but Richard M. Nixon was back in the Presidential residence Sunday night, giving his former protege in the world of Chinese-American relations a firsthand report on his trip to China.
Mr. Nixon, who appointed Mr. Bush as the first American representative to Beijing since the Communist revolution in China, gave the President a confidential memorandum on his visit, on his view of Chinese-American relations after the crackdown on dissent and on the prospects for their improvement, Administration officials and associates of the former President said. 
Nixon aides and White House officials declined to make the report public.
But Marlin Fitzwater, the White House spokesman, and other officials suggested that the Bush Administration was not uncomfortable with Mr. Nixon's harsh comments to Chinese officials about the crackdown on dissent in May and June.
Mr. Nixon, who warned the Chinese against sinking into a ''backwater of oppression and stagnation,'' was much sharper in tone than Mr. Bush, Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d and other senior American officials had been in public.
Mr. Nixon spoke at length about his visit during the two-hour dinner in the White House residential quarters and then took questions from Mr. Bush, his wife, Barbara, Vice President Dan Quayle, Brent Scowcroft, the national security adviser, William H. Webster, the Director of Central Intelligence, and other top officials.
Â 
Crackdown 'Excessive'
The dinner was not announced in advance and was reported at the White House briefing today only in response to a question about Mr. Nixon's visit. 
During his visit to China, Mr. Nixon told his hosts that ''many in the United States, including many friends of China, believe the crackdown was excessive and unjustified.''
''The events of April through June damaged the respect and confidence which most Americans previously had for the leaders of China,'' he said during a banquet given by President Yang Shangkun in Beijing last Wednesday.
In response to the Chinese crackdown, the Bush Administration suspended sales of weapons and military visits and promised a sympathetic response to Chinese students who wanted to extend their stay in the United States. 
Critics in Congress and elsewhere called the response weak and, over the Administration's objections, both houses of Congress voted by large margins to impose stiffer sanctions. 
The Bush Administration and Mr. Nixon himself have been careful to note that Mr. Nixon was making a personal visit to China last week and was not representing the United States Government or Mr. Bush.
Â 
'Special Credibility'
But Mr. Bush has made a practice of taking relatively moderate stands on a variety of issues while letting surrogates deliver harsher messages. 
And Administration officials said they were aware that Mr. Nixon's comments carry a special weight, since his visit to China in 1972 paved the way for resumption of American diplomatic relations with that country.
''A tough message takes on special credibility when it comes from an old and very respected friend,'' one official said. 
''You may have noticed that we haven't said much about China since June, but I haven't heard any negative feelings about what Nixon said. 
Generally, my sense is that it was positively received.''
Asked about Mr. Bush's view on what Mr. Nixon told the Chinese, Mr. Fitzwater said: ''You know that the former President had some very direct things to say to the Chinese leadership about American reaction to what happened there. 
But we wouldn't want to embellish on those statements.''
Asked whether Mr. Bush agreed with Mr. Nixon's statements during his trip that China and the United States should put aside their differences and resume normal relations, Mr. Fitzwater replied, ''The President found those views quite interesting and productive but our general policy has not changed.''
Correction
In my previous column, I had President Nixon sending George Bush to China as envoy in 1974; it was President Ford.
An article yesterday about Richard M. Nixon's visit to the White House, where he discussed his recent trip to China, misidentified the President who sent George Bush to Beijing as chief American diplomat. 
It was Gerald R. Ford.
Correction-Date:Â November 9, 1989, Thursday, Late Edition - Final November 8, 1989, Wednesday, Late Edition - Final

file: Now Beijing Blames a Single Villain for All Its Ills.txt
text:
ï»¿
As China fills out its official version of the crushed democracy movement, a single villain has emerged who is held responsible for the student turmoil and virtually all of the country's economic woes: Zhao Ziyang, the ousted chief of the Communist Party.
Last week, virtually every newspaper here was jammed with front-page attacks on Mr. Zhao, who has not been seen since late May, when he had a tearful encounter with the students in Tiananmen Square. 
By week's end, China's leadership had openly joined in the fray, rarely missing an opportunity to heap more blame on the purged party leader.
Not surprisingly, then, the chief topic of conversation in Beijing these days -second only to the constant speculation over whether Deng Xiaoping, the country's foremost leader, is alive and active - is Mr. Zhao's fate.
Many believe that the torrent of articles and speeches is simply setting the stage to put Mr. Zhao on trial, in what would be the first formal charges against a top party leader since the Gang of Four - Mao's widow, Jiang Qing, and three radical colleagues -were tried in 1980 for their roles in the Cultural Revolution.
But many others say they believe the Government will stop short of formal charges because Mr. Deng, too, is closely tied to economic changes that Mr. Zhao undertook, changes that are now being scaled back.
''To put Zhao on trial is to put on trial the whole past decade of economic reforms,'' a Western diplomat said the other day. 
''That may be a little more than they bargained for.''
Indeed, the attacks are coming just as China is greatly scaling back a number of changes that occurred under Mr. Zhao. Many private businesses he helped allow to flourish are being disbanded or consolidated by the Government, or being labeled tax cheats.
The latest attack came on Friday as Qiao Shi, a member of the Communist Party leadership, said at a ceremony to mark the beginning of the autumn term of schools and colleges that ''international hostile forces have never given up their attempt to subvert the socialist system.''
Â 
Bourgeois Connivance
''For a period, Zhao Ziyang's connivance with and weak attitude toward bourgeois liberalization resulted in a surge of ideological attacks against socialism and the leadership of the Communist Party.''
The attacks have not gone so far as to roll back all that Mr. Zhao stood for, especially the encouragement of joint ventures and technology transfer from foreign companies.
Instead, they have consistently held him accountable for diluting the power of the party by turning more economic decisions over to local governments and private enterprises, and for suggesting that Western economies provided a good model for China to emulate in some respects.
In fact, in his public speeches, Mr. Zhao rarely sounded themes too far out of line with those of other leaders, especially as the economy expanded at a rapid pace. 
But examining his speeches in retrospect, the official Chinese press has concluded that the party leadership had a counterrevolutionary in its midst.
''Zhao Ziyang often told some people that capitalism was actually better and our socialist system had problems,'' Workers' Daily said the other day. 
Many articles have reconstructed Mr. Zhao's role in the days leading up to the student occupation of Tiananmen Square, accusing him of violating the party's constitution by advocating reduced economic interference, and of deliberately ''escalating the turmoil.''
The People's Daily said Thursday that Mr. Zhao ''betrayed us all'' when he addressed student demonstrators sympathetically on May 4, a month before the crackdown, and said his speech played the role of ''supporting the enemy, confusing the masses, suppressing the cadres and splitting the Central Committee.''
In an article on Friday, by indirection, Mr. Zhao was blamed for virtually everything that is wrong today with the Chinese economy: rampant speculation, the shortages of raw materials, tax evasion.

file: Official Says Beijing Won_t Copy Moscow_s Political Restructuring.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a rebuff to calls for a more democratic political system in China, Prime Minister Li Peng said today that China would not copy the Soviet Union's political restructuring and that China would not take ''hasty'' or ''excessive'' steps toward democracy.
''Democracy is a good thing,'' Mr. Li said, ''but it must arise from the conditions within a country. 
As far as China is concerned, we want to build a democracy, and we think that if we do this work well it will contribute to economic development and social stabilityI.''
He added: ''On the other hand, if the democratic process is carried out in haste, or excessively, then it will certainly affect our stabilityI and unity. 
If stabilityI is undermined, that will impair our work of reform and national construction.''
Mr. Li's statement follows a growing movement for more democracy and for an amnesty for China's political prisoners. 
Initially, some Government officials seemed sympathetic to calls for greater democracy, but in the last two months officials have seemed surprised and alarmed at the boldness and aggressiveness of the movement.
In a sign of official apprehension about the democracy movement, the Government-controlled press has mostly ignored the recent legislative elections in the Soviet Union in which challengers defeated many high-ranking Communist Party candidates.
Â 
Many Support Gorbachev's Views
Despite the lack of official interest in the situation in the Soviet Union, many Chinese intellectuals have emerged as strong supporters of Mikhail S. Gorbachev, the Soviet leader, and his efforts at political liberalization.
For their part, Chinese leaders have seemed distressed by the unflattering comparisons with the Soviet Union.
Asked about the recent developments in the Soviet Union, Mr. Li said, ''China's conditions are different from those in the Soviet Union, and we cannot mechanically copy the measures or policies adopted by the Soviet Union.''
Several times in the two-hour news conference, Mr. Li pressed the same theme: that China favors democracy, but in prudent doses, and that too much too soon could affect social stabilityI and economic development.
The news conference was arranged by the National People's Congress, the national legislature whose annual session ends on Tuesday.
Asked about economic policies, Mr. Li said China's economic liberalization would continue, even during the present retrenchment and austerity. 
He specifically cited the policy of rapid development of China's coastal areas, which is a favorite project of the Communist Party General Secretary, Zhao Ziyang. 
Mr. Zhao is generally regarded as more enthusiastic about rapid change than is Mr. Li.
China will draw on Hong Kong's experience in economic development, but will not adopt capitalism, Mr. Li said. 
''Hong Kong will keep its current capitalist system, and the Chinese mainland will cling to its socialist system,'' he added.
Asked about human rights and the call for amnesty of political prisoners, Mr. Li said China would continue to improve its human rights situation but stressed that social stabilityI was the nation's greatest need.

file: Pakistan Taking Steps to Modernize Its Air Force By BARBARA CROSSETTE.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Pakistani Air Force, concerned about the possibility of Afghan or Soviet air attacks to the west and wary of the military power of India to the east, is modernizing its inventory of fighter and trainer aircraft, according to diplomats and news reports here.
Two major projects are in the final stages of discussion here, diplomats say. 
The Government of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto is about to decide whether to go ahead with a purchase of 60 additional F-16 fighter planes from the United States and 75 upgraded F-7 fighters from China. 
In addition, Pakistan is planning to produce its own training plane with Chinese cooperation.
Pakistan already has 49 F-16's delivered or on order. 
The new F-16's would cost about $1.4 billion in all, at a time when Ms. Bhutto, who is also Minister of Defense, is under pressure to increase spending on social programs.
Diplomats expect that the moderization of the air force will provoke criticism from India even though the two nations have pledged themselves to establish better relations. 
In New Delhi, a spokesman for the Indian Government, declining Friday to comment on the newest Pakistani proposals, nevertheless called attention to earlier Indian statements deploring military and nuclear development in Pakistan.
A spokesman for the Pakistani Inter-Services Public Relations Directorate said he could not comment on aircraft purchases still under consideration, but did not deny Pakistani press reports of an air force overhaul.
The United States Congress has not been officially notified of the F-16 sale, pending final decisions by the Bush and Bhutto Administrations. 
But the notification to Congress, required by law, is expected within a month or two. 
Islamabad first raised the subject with the United States last fall. 
The purchase was also discussed during a visit here in January by three Democratic Congressmen - Stephen J. Solarz of Brooklyn, Ted Weiss of Manhattan and the Bronx and Chester G. Atkins of Massachusetts.
The Congressional delegation was left with the impression that Pakistan had yet to determine where to find the cash for the purchase, since there is no money left in the foreign military sales credit program for Islamabad under its current aid package.
The majority of fighter planes in the Pakistani Air Force are the 150 Chinese-built F-6's, which are based on Soviet technology of the 1950's. 
Pakistani military experts as well as diplomats in the region say these leave the air force well behind India's. 
Even with the additional F-16's, these experts say, Pakistan will still trail India by a ratio of 1 to 4 in aircraft numbers. 
In addition, India is building its own advanced fighter planes.
Under the regime of Gen. Mohammad Zia ul-Haq, Pakistan had also considered building its own fighter planes in cooperation with China.
Diplomats say the plan was abandoned last year because it became clear it would not be economically viable. 
But the Pakistani military had already budgeted $200 million a year in hard currency for the project. 
This can now be drawn on for the purchase of new planes, diplomats and Pakistani arms experts said.
Pakistan last month signed a final contract on an earlier order of 11 F-16's, which General Dynamics, the maker of the plane, has promised to begin delivering in 1992, diplomats said.
The Pakistani Air Force is already flying 38 of the planes.
The ease of incorporating new models of the same aircraft is one of the factors that makes the F-16 more attractive than the rival Mirage 2000, which France is offering to Pakistan, diplomats say.
Pakistan is beginning to test its own missiles and build guidance systems and other equipment locally.
A prototype of a new Pakistani-built jet training plane to replace 20-year-old Cessna T-37's and Saab MF1-17's may be ready in mid-1990, The Muslim newspaper reported today.
The Muslim, which has close ties to the Government, said the plane would be built in cooperation with China. 
Each plane will cost about $2.1 million.

file: Palaces of the Yi Kings.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE ghosts of the Yi dynasty, whose kings ruled Korea from 1392 to 1910, still haunt the palaces of Seoul,those oases of serenity amid the incessant motion and noise of this vibrant city. 
But the tranquil halls and exquisite gardens, a refuge from the Hyundai cars and the purple and white buses that rumble like elephants through the streets, mask a past rife with court intrigue, betrayal and war.
The Yi (pronounced ee) kings who built the palaces in Seoul reigned over the most intellectual period in Korean history. 
In the capital then known as Hanyang, movable metal type was invented early in the 15th century. 
Shortly after, King Sejong fostered the spread of phonetic writing that made the Korean language easier to grasp than the Chinese ideographs in which it had been written.These innovations led to an outpouring of books on Confucian philosophy, history, art, medicine, music, agriculture, mathematics, astronomy and military science.
Palaces in Korea, like those in China and Japan, are not single buildings as in Europe but vast complexes with towering gates, imposing halls where the rulers received their ministers and generals in audience, lavish living quarters and lovely gardens sprinkled with pagodas. 
The palaces of Hanyang were modeled on those of China, with their tiled roofs and sweeping eaves, but were given a Korean touch with their exteriors left in subdued ocher reds or natural wood and their interiors decorated with intricate, bright ornamentation.
In the Kyongbok Palace, there were once 500 buildings within the walls. 
Today, the Ch'angdok Palace with its adjacent Piwon, or Secret Garden, that was reserved for the king and his women, covers 180 acres. 
Add the Ch'anggyong Palace, a detached palace next to Ch'angdok, and the Chongmyo Shrine, where tablets commemorating the Yi ancestors are kept, and the entire complex rivals the Forbidden City in Beijing and the Imperial Palaces in Kyoto, Japan.
The palaces of Seoul are the only ones remaining in Korea, this city having been the capital for so long. 
Another center of culture, however, is the city of Kyongju, in southeastern Korea, where the Silla dynasty flourished from 661 until 935. 
Kyongju today is the site of Buddhist temples and the tombs of kings that are being carefully excavated to yield the secrets and treasures of Silla. 
Between Silla and Yi, the Koryo period was filled with strife, the Mongol invasion and war.
The Seoul palaces, burned in war and partly rebuilt several times, are, not surprisingly, a source of national pride. 
On almost any given day, throngs of schoolchildren ranging from kindergarten through high school can be found there.
Everywhere in the palaces are signs in Korean intended to nurture the deep-seated animosity toward the Japanese who invaded the peninsula in the late 16th century (and were driven out after six years) and who occupied Korea from 1905 until 1945. 
Signs in English remind visitors of the Korean enmity. 
Perhaps the nearest analogy in the West is the Irish enmity for the English. 
Koreans now emulate the Japanese in economic development but in their hearts, as in Irish hearts, are dark broodings about their former colonial masters across a narrow sea.
Three of Seoul's four extant palaces are in the northern sector of the city, on the opposite side from the site of the Olympic Games a year ago, with their backs to the jagged, rocky mountains that once were a barrier against invaders from the north. 
As with most palaces in East Asia, they face south to ward off the evil spirits thought to come from the northeast and, in the bitter Korean winter, to capture the rays of the southern sun. 
The fourth palace, Toksu, is in the center of Seoul and is a pleasant place to stroll but lacks the size and grandeur of the others.
The northern palaces, which are landmarks known to everyone in Seoul, are within walking distance of one another and it is perhaps best to start with Kyongbok, the oldest. 
The palaces are open to the public from 9 A.M. to 6 P.M. from spring to fall and close an hour earlier in winter. 
The visitor might want to plan his trek around the times that Ch'angdok is open. 
Unlike the other palaces, in which one may wander at leisure, Ch'angdok can be seen only on a guided tour. 
English- speaking guides generally lead tours at 11:30 A.M., 1:30 and 3:30 P.M.
The Kyongbok Palace was built in 1392, a century before Columbus sailed to America, and was burned by the Japanese warlord Hideyoshi in 1592. 
It then lay in ruins until 1865 when it was rebuilt. 
Most of the palace buildings were torn down by the Japanese when they annexed Korea in 1910 and what remained was blocked from view by the Japanese capitol erected on the southern edge of the grounds in 1926. 
Kyongbok was again damaged during the Korean War (1950 to 1953) when American and South Korean forces fought twice with Chinese and North Korean troops over the city.
IN the 1960's, as South Korea got back on its feet, the Government began to restore Kyongbok. 
The main gate, called Kwangwha-mun, was reconstructed in front of the capitol in 1969 so that it would dominate a broad avenue through the center of the city - and hide the capitol built by the Japanese. 
Government offices were moved in 1983 to convert the capitol building to a museum, which was opened in 1986. 
Though the gate was reconstructed, much of the palace is original and the restoration retains the site's ancient atmosphere.
Within the palace grounds, the main audience hall, called Kunjong-jon, may best be seen from the edge of the flagstone courtyard to its front. 
With the jagged mountains as a backdrop, the view is stunning.
Perhaps the loveliest spot is the pavilion called Kyonghoe-ru, or the Pavilion of Joyous Meeting, an open structure whose tiled roof and eaves rest atop 48 pillars. 
Sitting beside a calm reflecting pool, the pavilion was the scene of receptions for foreign envoys or sometimes dissolute court parties during the Yi dynasty.
The pavilion is also the scene of official receptions in modern times. 
One summer evening in the 1970's a retired South Korean general stood in a corner of the pavilion when, in one of those rare moments of amity between South and North, a North Korean delegation was being entertained. 
The general, who had fought as an infantry commander in the Korean War, said: ''I tell you, I never thought I'd see this, when we welcomed North Koreans here.''
He sighed: ''Well, I guess it's better than bullets.''
In the back of the palace grounds is the National Folklore Museum. 
It provides an excellent introduction into Korean life in the 19th century with vivid displays of Buddhist, shaman and Confucian rituals and of houses, living and farming tools, pottery and artwork.
The National Museum of Korea, housing 90,000 items in the northeast quadrant of the palace grounds, was closed recently for remodeling but the new museum in the former capitol building, has a splendid collection of 7,500 pieces from ancient and medieval Korea.
Two exhibits stand out. 
In one large room are Buddhist statues, including several of Maitreya, the god or goddess of mercy and healing. 
Art historians have not decided whether Maitreya is male or female but the gentle, graceful lines bring peace and serenity to the viewer's soul.
In another room is a trove selected from 22,000 Chinese ceramics of the 14th century found off the southwest coast of Korea in 1975. 
After a fisherman snagged seven pieces in his net, the Korean Government sent divers to find a sunken ship. 
From that came vases, dishes, statuary, bowls, incense burners and pitchers, some in delicate shades of green celadon, others in white porcelain or black glaze, still more with silver or bronze glazes or bluish tints.
About four short city blocks to the east of Kyongbok is Ch'angdok, built in 1405 as a detached palace. 
After both were burned by Japanese invaders in 1592, Ch'angdok was rebuilt in 1611 to become the main palace. 
It is the best restored of the palaces but, unhappily, cannot be seen at leisure as the authorities apparently fear vandalism. 
Guides help visitors find the way through the maze of halls, living quarters and private courtyards but they intrude on the sensibilities by dispensing information through a bullhorn.
In the courtyard outside the main audience hall, called Injong-jon, are tablets to the right and left of the raised walkway marking the ranks of ministers and generals as they awaited a summons from the king. 
Visitors cannot enter the hall but the ornate interior can been seen from the front door. 
Centered along the back wall is a raised throne behind which stands a screen on which are painted five mountain peaks to symbolize, in Confucian lore, the five happinesses, the five elements or the five points of the compass, the fifth being the center where stands the king. 
Overhead is an intricately inlaid ceiling, three stories high, of gold and red.
Perhaps the nicest part of Ch'angdok is the stroll through the quiet courtyards and, if one wanders a bit from the tour group, sensing the secluded life of the palace. 
That is especially true in the adjacent Piwon, or Secret Garden. 
Lush with pines and maples and cherry blossoms, flowers that bloom in different seasons, filled with flowing streams and lotus ponds and small pavilions where the kings and their women idled a pleasant afternoon, the Secret Garden is perhaps the ultimate escape. 
But the gardens can also be instructive as, in one corner, the home of a well-to-do commoner has been erected to give some idea of life outside the walls.
NEXT to Ch'angdok and Piwon is the Ch'anggyong Palace, also once a detached palace. 
The main audience hall, Myongjong, escaped destruction during the Japanese invasion of 1592 and survives today as the oldest of those Yi dynasty chambers. 
Like the others, it is very ornate. 
The rest of the palace grounds are much like those of others but, with a large pond, seem more relaxed than those of Kyongbok or Ch'angdok, a place for picnicking on Sunday afternoon or for taking the kids on an outing. 
It differs from the other palaces in that the audience hall and main gate face east instead of south in what may have been a touch of cultural independence from China.
Finally, just southeast of Ch'angdok is the Chongmyo shrine in which are preserved in stone tablets the memory of the kings and queens of the Yi dynasty. 
The shrine was originally part of Ch'angdok but Japanese occupiers built a road through the grounds in 1932. 
There is not much to see in the shrine, except the simple stone tributes to rulers that are housed in two halls. 
On the first Sunday of May every year, the Yi Dynasty Association honors rulers of the 500-year reign by reenacting a highly stylized ceremony of wine drinking, music and chants and elaborate liturgies for the dead.
But the mood of Chongmyo is worth experiencing. 
On the rare day when Chongmyo has few visitors, an eerie lull settles on the secluded grounds. 
A rustle of leaves in the wind sounds remarkably like the skirt of royal gown brushing along the stone courtyard and the slam of a distant car door sounds like a muffled cough. 
As one turns to look, a slight movement from another corner of the grounds catches the eye and there is an uncanny feeling of being watched by an ancient spirit.
Correction
A picture caption on Sept. 
17 about Seoul misidentified a building on the grounds of the 14th-century Kyongbok Palace. 
It was the Korean National Folklore Museum, which was built in 1972, not the palace itself.
Because of a production error, an article on Sept.

Political leaders receive awards frequently, but a double ceremony tentatively scheduled to take place in New York City on May 30 will be distinctly different. 
Two awards will be given to one of the leaders of the People's Republic of China for services to bridge.
Wan Li will be named ''Bridge Personality of the Year'' by the International Bridge Press Association and he will also receive an award from the American Contract Bridge League.
Mr. Wan has been involved as Deputy Prime Minister in his country's nuclear energy problems. 
He is now the chairman of the standing committee of the National People's Congress, and will be in Washington later this month as the guest of Vice-President Dan Quayle.
Mr. Wan and other members of the Chinese hierarchy including Deng Xiaoping, are enthusiasts who have encouraged the rapid growth of the game in their country. 
Team events sometimes draw 700 entries, and by the end of the century, China will probably have more players than any other country. 
Bridge is one of the few interests shared by the leadership and the student generation.
The diagramed deal played five years ago, earned Wan Li a different award from the I.B.P.A. 
He opened the South hand with one club, strong and artificial in accordance with the Precision system. 
The double showed major suits and North's one diamond was a ''positive-negative'' showing about six points. 
At the end of a contested auction South introduced an aggressive redouble, suggesting a willingness to raise the stakes.
The redouble might have induced East-West to retreat to five spades, failing by one trick barring a misguess in the trump suit. 
But they stood their ground and West made the imaginative lead of the spade eight. 
He was hoping to reach his partner for a heart lead, but South ruffed and studied his prospects. 
It was obvious that the hearts were on his left and he was in considerable danger of losing three tricks in that suit.
Most players would charge ahead, supposing that they could strip out the side-suits and eventually duck a heart to West. 
But South correctly saw that this would not quite work. 
By the time he had drawn trumps and ruffed two diamonds there would be no trumps left in the dummy and the endplay would fail.
The fact that West held major-suit length greatly increased the chance of finding East with both missing diamond honors. 
South therefore crossed to dummy and led the diamond nine. 
It would not have helped East to cover and he played low smoothly. 
South did likewise, holding his breath, and felt better when the nine held.
Now the declarer led a second diamond. 
A spade ruff would have been better, but would have led to the same result and this time East played the jack. 
South took the king and could see his way to an endplay. 
A trump lead to dummy and a spade ruff left this ending:
Â 
[Diagram]
The spade queen was discarded on the diamond ace and the diamond ten was ruffed. 
A heart was led to the eight, and West was forced to make a losing lead. 
Notice that the endplay would have been equally successful if East had held a singleton honor, for South would, of course, have played low. 
Wan Li made his redoubled contract and demonstrated shrewdness and ability.
Correction
The headline of the bridge column last Sunday misidentified Wan Li. 
He is Chairman of the National People's Congress in China, not Deputy Prime Minister.

file: PEARL HARBOR REMEMBERED_History_s Refraction Illuminates 2 Views Of a Date of Infamy.txt
text:
ï»¿
On Japan's airwaves this week, the battleship Arizona has sunk a dozen times, the aging Zero pilots have been interviewed so many times that dedicated viewers know their exploits by heart, and a stream of commentators have talked -- and talked, and talked -- about how the United States and Japan must seize this weekend to reaffirm the most critical alliance linking East and West.
But in subtle and telling ways, the images and explanations being offered here and in the United States to explain how two great powers came to battle each other are strikingly different.
For many Japanese, this has been a long week of trying, once again, to find comfort in a carefully sculpted interpretation of history that overarches the country's memories of the war. 
In dramas and documentaries, the Japanese have watched this week as their fathers and mothers made a futile effort to steer the country away from war, as a small group of military leaders drove a peaceful people to ruin, and as their country rose from its defeat to be as technologically powerful as the nation to whom it eventually surrendered.
Perhaps the clearest cleavage of interpretations came in the studios of NHK, the giant semiofficial broadcaster, which struggled for months with producers from ABC over a documentary that was aired this week in both countries. 
Although American and Japanese viewers saw nearly identical film, they heard very different scripts, and they were differences that went beyond the imprecision of translations.
Â 
2 Views of Rape of Nanking
In an 18-second clip about Japan's 1937 capture of Nanking, the then capital of China, ABC reported that "Japan's claim it was liberating China was ludicrous to Americans, particularly when hundreds of thousands of Chinese men, women and babies were murdered in what was called the Rape of Nanking. 
The U.S. sent China $50 million in war relief."
But in Japan, where the Rape of Nanking is not mentioned in textbooks and the country's right wing contends that the incident was a fabrication, viewers heard nothing about war atrocities.
Though NHK's version of the documentary showed vivid footage of Chinese being shot in a ditch, the voice-over said simply, "In a totalitarian attempt to grab land and wealth, the Japanese military had led the country into an eight-year war in Manchuria and China," an invasion that caused tension with the United States.
At a luncheon with foreign correspondents on Friday, Mikio Kawaguchi, the chairman of NHK, said there had been no effort to rewrite history for a Japanese audience, simply an attempt to explain things differently to American and Japanese viewers, who "have a different way of looking at history and life."
"Even though both sides were sincere in their efforts, the methods they wanted to employ to portray what they saw as truth were different," Mr. Kawaguchi said of his company's joint venture with the American network. 
"There were perception gaps. 
The two sides had such disagreements that they feared they might be headed into a second Pearl Harbor."
Â 
A Weeklong History Lesson
Without question, Japan learned a lot of history this week. 
Many young people said that until the flurry of programs, they had not been certain why Pearl Harbor prompted such strong emotions in America. 
At the same time, the tone of much of the coverage paralleled the tone of the little that is taught about the war in schools: Japan was more a victim than an aggressor.
Several broadcasts explored the internment of Japanese-Americans in the United States. 
Several reported arguments that President Roosevelt had known about the attack in advance and done nothing to stop it. 
Others found a simple answer for Japan's ultimate defeat: The country was simply outproduced by the United States. 
A lengthy program today, "The Secret Story of the War Over Steel," showed how the giant American steelmakers that provided the hardware for Japan's defeat later fell to Japanese competition.
Japanese television warmed to another popular theme here: that the Japanese military, rather than the Japanese people or even political leaders, was solely responsible for plunging the nation into war.
On Friday night, for example, viewers tuned into a vivid drama called "Defeat in Showa 16," a title suggesting that Japan lost the war as soon as it began in 1941. 
The Japanese calendar begins anew with the ascension of each new emperor, and 1941 was the 16th year of the Showa era, Emperor Hirohito's reign.
Â 
Shouting at the War Institute
Based on fact, the drama was the story of a railway executive, a bureaucrat and other Japanese who were drafted into the Government's "Total War Research Institute."
The institute was charged with determining what would happen if the country gave everything -- from its steel works to its samurai spirit -- to the cause of "liberating" the country from encirclement by Dutch, British and American colonialists.
In the show, the young men of the institute concluded that the Government's war plans were madness. 
There were frequent shouting matches with the military brass, but the young men's voices were drowned out. 
Many historians and older Japanese say that the spirit of such dramas is accurate.
"Everyone knew that relations were at a critical position, even though there was no indication war would be coming so soon," said Junnosuke Ofusa, who joined The New York Times bureau in Tokyo in 1930 and helped guide the newspaper's coverage of Japan for the next five decades. 
Mr. Ofusa, who retired several years ago, said that "no one said outwardly that it was a bad idea, because the military police were everywhere. 
But the Japanese people knew there was little chance of winning the war."
At the same time, some Japanese bridle at placing all of the blame on the military, because the argument is often used to absolve the rest of the country.
"Of course the military had much of the power," Seiki Nishihiro, a former Deputy Defense Minister, said the other day, discussing the coverage of the anniversary. 
"But the mass media and everyone else followed, so not only the military was responsible."
Bubbling just beneath the surface of the coverage was the question of whether, and how, Japan should apologize for the Pearl Harbor attack.
Government spokesmen, who have spent much of the last year fretting about the anniversary celebrations, were openly distraught. 
While they were issuing statements of "regret" or "remorse" or "self-reflection" -- a great deal of time was spent trying to figure out which word best described Japan's position -- Parliament was going in the other direction, scuttling any parliamentary apology altogether.
"Why should we fling mud at the history of Japan?"
Masayuki Fujio, a senior politician, asked the other day, in a remark that was quoted in the Japanese news media throughout the weekend.
But the week was so painful that this country, which planned no formal events to commemorate Pearl Harbor, seems eager to have the anniversary behind it. 
"In a sense it is a kind of Pearl Harbor week anyway," said a weary-looking Taizo Watanabe, the Foreign Ministry's chief spokesman. 
"So many questions asked, so many answers and apologies from us."
With one more apology on early Sunday morning here, after President Bush's address at Pearl Harbor, the Japanese hope it will be all over, so they can go back to topics that are easier to discuss.
"Ask me about anything else," a senior Government official said the other day. 
"Ask me why the trade deficit is getting bigger again. 
Ask me about why we are so slow to open the rice market. 
Just don't ask me about Pearl Harbor."

file: Perils of America as Seen in a Chinese Novel.txt
text:
ï»¿
Wang Qiming, a violinist from Beijing, grew up thinking of America as a paradise. 
Then he arrived in New York and had his luggage stolen at the airport. 
That was only the beginning of his troubles: he lost a small fortune gambling and his daughter became a drug addict before she was kidnapped and murdered.
Mr. Wang is a fictional character, but his creator, Cao Guilin, is a Chinese emigrant who lives in Queens and says the character is based on his own experiences.
In any case, his book, "A Beijing Man in New York," is the talk of the Chinese capital these days. 
It has been serialized in Beijing Wanbao, the most-read newspaper in the capital. 
A radio play based on the book is now being broadcast daily at lunchtime across the country, affording the public a tour through the seamy side of New York.
Many ordinary Chinese are reading with fascination about the experiences of a fellow Chinese who makes it to America and who initially strikes it rich by opening a small garment factory. 
Figuring out how to get to the United States is almost an obsession for many young Chinese, and Mr. Guilin's novel seems to offer a glimpse of what life might be like if they succeeded. 
At the same time, the Government is delighted to publicize how cruel life can be under capitalism.
Chinese newspapers have no shortage of reports about murders, rapes, robberies and homelessness in America. 
But many Chinese say they discount the reports as exaggerated or distorted. 
The novel, however, has captured the public imagination, and many readers seem genuinely surprised at its portrayal of the hardships faced by immigrants there.
"I picked it up accidentally and since then I've read every episode," said a college-educated restaurateur in Beijing. 
"Life in America is not a heaven, and this shows the ups and downs of an immigrant's life."
When the novel was first printed in a magazine, all 120,000 copies sold out immediately. 
Then it was published in book form in September, and that sold out. 
Now another magazine has published it, and it is being serialized in the China Press, a Chinese-language newspaper in New York.
"From a literary point of view, the craftsmanship is not very good, but the emotion is real," said Wang Hongxian, the magazine editor who first printed the story. 
"A number of students overseas write about their experiences. 
Some focus on the difficulties, some focus on the good things. 
This is not like those. 
It's more real, more objective."
In the novel, after Mr. Wang loses his luggage, he gets a job as a dishwasher while his wife knits for a garment factory. 
They are able to buy an old car and move into a decent apartment in their first year. 
Then Mr. Wang and his wife borrow money to start a knitwear factory. 
They become rich and buy a few buildings and a better car.
But life for the Wangs starts to turn sour when their daughter, corrupted by New York City schools, leaves home, turns to drugs and is kidnapped. 
Meanwhile, the factory goes bankrupt and Mr. Wang loses $40,000 when he gambles away the last of his money in the hopes of making enough to pay his debts. 
In the end, the kidnappers demand a ransom, which Mr. Wang cannot afford, so they kill his daughter.
"New York, ah, it really is a heaven in hell, a hell in heaven," moans the fictional Mr. Wang.
Mr. Cao, who was a violinist in Beijing before he left a decade ago for the United States, said he wrote the book because he wanted to dispel the fantasies that many young Chinese have about America. 
He admits he spiced it up to make it "more readable."
"You can achieve the American dream, but you can't just step off the plane and get it," Mr. Cao, who is himself a successful knitwear manufacturer, said in a phone interview. 
"You must go through a hard, bitter struggle that might make your heart bleed, but this cultural shock, you must go through all this before you can achieve the American dream."
Mr. Cao said he is surprised at the stir his novel has created in Beijing. 
Royalties, Mr. Cao said with a laugh, are no more than enough to cover a plane ride to Beijing. 
But he said he plans to publish another book soon.

file: PRESIDENT DEFENDS AIDES_ CHINA VISIT.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Bush today strongly defended his decision to send two senior aides to Beijing last weekend, rejecting criticism that he has forgiven Chinese leaders for the killing of democracy demonstrators there in June.
Mr. Bush's comments came as lawmakers and independent experts on China stepped up their condemnations of the surprise high-level visit as proof of the Bush Administration's willingness to sacrifice democracy and human rights in return for the normalization of relations with China.
The Senate majority leader, George J. Mitchell, condemned the American overture as ''embarrassing kowtowing to the Chinese Government.''
He added, ''These actions make a mockery of our profession of concern for human rights and our inconsistent with our stated ideals.''
The Democratic Senator from Maine also said that he will lead efforts to override Mr. Bush's Nov. 
30 veto of legislation to permit any Chinese student fearful of reprisal at home to remain in the United States beyond his visa's expiration.
Â 
Assurances on Missiles
It was the first high-level American visit to Beijing since President Bush banned such contacts after the military crackdown.
In defending his decision to send his national security adviser, Brent Scowcroft, and Deputy Secretary of State Lawrence S. Eagleburger to the Chinese capital, Mr. Bush said that Mr. Scowcroft won assurances from the Chinese that they would not sell missiles in the Middle East, and praised an announcement in the Chinese press to that effect as ''a very sound development.''
What Mr. Bush did not say was that there was no urgency on this issue since the missile, the M-9, is still under development, or that he had received the same assurances during a trip to China last February.
Mr. Bush, a former United States envoy to China who had previously said that Beijing must make the first move to improve relations, acknowledged to a group of editors that China has not apologized for the crackdown. 
But, he said, ''I don't want to see that China remains totally isolated.''
Mr. Bush said that relations with Beijing remain strained, but added, ''I don't want to make it any worse.''
The President also noted that the United States deals with a number of countries which violate human rights, suggesting that China should not be the exception. 
''We have contact with countries that have egregious records on human rights, so I am going to keep looking for ways to find common ground,'' he said.
Â 
Need to Brief Beijing Is Cited
Mr. Bush argued that the visit did not constitute a normalization of relations with China and criticized those who said so as people who ''simply do not know what they are talking about.''
He said that he planned no further sanctions against Beijing for its campaign of repression, which did not end with the crackdown on student demonstators last June but continues with executions and arrests of workers and students who participated in the democracy demonstrations.
Mr. Bush sought to justify the visit as a way to brief Chinese leaders on the results of the Malta summit talks. 
But the high-level nature of the briefing struck China experts as rather unusual. 
China was briefed on a higher level than some of the closest allies of the United States, including Australia and South Korea.
The President's remarks came amid criticism that the visit illustrates a continuing double standard in the Administration's approach to human rights.
''We don't expect the Chinese to be democratic and we don't hold them to the same standards that we hold the Soviets or the East Europeans,'' said Merle Goldman, professor of Chinese history at Boston University.
Representative Stephen J. Solarz, Democrat of Brooklyn and chairman of the House Foreign Affairs subcommittee on East Asia and the Pacific, said: ''We have to ask ourselves what our reaction would be if Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev were to unleash ther Red Army on demonstrators in Red Square. 
In such circumstances the President would hardly send his national security adviser to Moscow.''
Â 
Rejects Charges on Killing
Although Administration officials had discussed ways to brief the Chinese for some time, Mr. Bush made his final decision only last Thursday, cutting short a visit to Washington last week by James Lilley, the United States Ambassador to Beijing, senior Adminsitration officials said. 
The delegation was dispatched in secrecy to Beijing on Friday.
In other remarks, Mr. Bush denied charges that agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation had mistreated a potential witness to the killing in El Sal vador of six Jesuit priests. 
He said that he had investigated claims by Salvadoran Archbishop Arturo Rivera y Damas that American officials had tried to brainwash the witness, Lucia Barrera de Cerna, a Salvadoran housekeeper, to discourage the investigation of the crime.
''I have confidence that our attorney general would not permit the kind of inquisition process that was alluded to,'' Mr. Bush said. 
Mr. Bush also said he hoped to attend a February drug summit meeting with South American leaders in Cartagena, Colombia, despite security agency fears he could be a target of the drug cartels.

file: Prominent Dissident Is Freed by Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese authorities have released Wang Ruowang, a prominent writer and dissident, after 16 months of detention, but he remains subject to some restrictions, his wife says.
Mr. Wang's wife, Feng Suying, said in a telephone interview from her home in Shanghai that Mr. Wang could not come to the phone because he needed rest, and that in any case he was probably not permitted to speak to foreign journalists. 
But she confirmed that Mr. Wang had suddenly been released from a detention center on Monday, without any explanation from the authorities.
A prolific essayist and widely respected social critic, Mr. Wang is 72 years old and yet has retained the admiration of much younger intellectuals throughout the country. 
His influence and reputation seemed to gain when he was criticized and expelled from the Communist Party at the beginning of 1987, along with Fang Lizhi, the astrophysicist, and Liu Binyan, the journalist.
China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, personally ordered Mr. Wang's expulsion from the party. 
In a speech on Dec. 
30, 1986, which was later leaked to foreign reporters, Mr. Deng declared: "Wang Ruowang is indeed wayward. 
I said he should be expelled long ago. 
Why has this not been done?"
Â 
Accused by Beijing
Mr. Wang supported the 1989 democracy movement, but there is no evidence he was a leader of it. 
Nevertheless, the leadership in Beijing accused him of helping to inspire and spread the protests in Shanghai, where he was living, and accused him of being "a representative of bourgeois liberalization."
"Beijing Turmoil," a Government-sponsored book published this year, accuses Mr. Wang of taking part in street demonstrations, giving interviews to foreign reporters and wearing a sign reading: "Save the country, save the people, save the students."
After the crackdown on June 4, 1989, Mr. Wang was kept under house arrest at first, and in September 1989 he was formally detained in a prison that was nominally called a detention center. 
Ms. Feng said he had not been beaten or otherwise mistreated while under detention.
"They were rather humanitarian toward him," she said. 
"He's fattened up a bit, but he's not fit and he doesn't have any strength. 
When he writes, his hand shakes. 
His eyesight has deteriorated, and it's difficult for himto climb the stairs. 
If he exercises, he'll get better."
Â 
To Report Twice a Month
Ms. Feng said Mr. Wang would spent his time at home "studying" and would have to report twice a month to the authorities on his "ideological state."
He must receive approval to leave Shanghai, and it probably would be impossible for him to travel abroad, she said.
It is not clear why the authorities suddenly released Mr. Wang, without making any announcement. 
Ms. Feng said the authorities had given no reason for the release, but she suggested that her husband might have acknowledged making some errors -- which could give the Government an excuse to release him. 
The Shanghai Foreign Affairs Office and the Shanghai Public Security Department both declined to comment.
Ms. Feng said that there was no news on whether other dissidents would also be released soon. 
Shanghai's Mayor, Zhu Rongji, has said that only two other dissidents remain in prison in that city: Zhang Weiguo, a journalist, and another whom he did not identify. 
In addition, there may be hundreds of others who were sentenced to prison in Shanghai for taking part in violent protests after the crackdown, and whom the Government does not regard as political prisoners.
Throughout the country, hundreds or thousands of Chinese remain in prison or in detention centers for their involvement in protests and riots at the time of the crackdown. 
In addition, some political prisoners are still serving sentences from the Democracy Wall movement a decade ago.
