file: Pursued by His Dead Stepmother.txt
text:
ï»¿
TO ALL APPEARANCES A LADY
By Marilyn Bowering.
336 pp. 
New York: Viking. 
$18.95.
Those who think of Canada as a staid and proper place will have their misconceptions swept away by Marilyn Bowering's historical novel of the bad old days in Vancouver, British Columbia. 
Back then, vigilantes and smugglers, restless sea captains and idealistic reformers, Chinese gangsters and opium traders made the city as colorful and violent a community of misfits as could be found anywhere.
Ms. Bowering tells two linking tales: one of a modern half-Chinese bachelor seeking to discover his parents' true identities, the other of his mother's and father's adventures during the late-19th-century period of colonial expansion in the Far East and British Columbia. 
In 1957, Robert Lam sets off on a sea voyage with a briefcase full of just-discovered family documents. 
He is leaving behind, he thinks, his 100-year-old stepmother, who has just died and left him free to travel. 
But Lam Fan, the irascible old lady, appears on board as a ghost. 
She is determined to lead him - by guile if necessary - to understand the hard life his family once lived as immigrants to Western Canada, and to be proud of both his Chinese and British ancestors.
India Thackery, Robert's English mother, and Lam Fan, her Chinese adoptive sister, came to Vancouver from Hong Kong at the turn of the century, following a stormy voyage on a clipper ship via Kowloon and Saigon. 
Robert's father emigrated from China, driven by memories of mass famine and cannibalism. 
His mother's husband, Robert Haack, washed up in Canada from California.
All these people were in various ways sustained and undone by the opium trade that flourished quasi-legally in pioneer North America. 
Miss Thackery, a kind, idealistic Victorian lady, was quietly employed as a bookkeeper in an opium factory; Lam Fan was a lifelong addict of the factory's wares; and the hapless Robert Haack was a would-be opium smuggler who made enemies both among the Chinese who controlled the business and the white vigilantes who sought to exclude the prosperous immigrants.
Haack is the novel's most fully developed character, a drifter capable of both courage and cowardice, decency and hypocrisy, sentimentality and cold-bloodedness. 
His chance meeting with Robert Louis Stevenson and his love for the tender India Thackery inspire him to try bettering himself, but the impulsive ways he tries to gain respectability often land him in jail or worse. 
India Thackery, too, is appealing, as ingenuous and thoughtful as her young Chinese half sister is sly and impulsive. 
When the thieves who rob the opium factory maroon India on an island of quarantined Chinese lepers, she reacts to her predicament with great resourcefulness and charity.
Is this story beginning to sound melodramatic?
Well, it is, but that's all right. 
The 19th-century part of the novel is a tale of the times, featuring improbable plot twists and a cast of broadly drawn characters reminiscent of the fiction of Charles Dickens or Mark Twain. 
As fanciful as the story is, it provides a vivid picture of life in frontier Vancouver, which, like London slums or Mississippi River towns, could be as brutal as it was hospitable to newcomers.
Ms. Browering, an accomplished Canadian poet, has researched her material thoroughly and reports it with an eye to evocative details. 
When India and Robert go in search of a child prostitute India is intent on rescuing, they visit the makeshift lodging of some out-of-work settlers - ''a group of men sitting on an ice-covered floor around a small pile of leaves, which one man was attempting to blow alight. 
Another man was being shaved by a companion, and another lay on straw, smoking a pipe. 
They nodded politely to [a visitor] but had eyes for the food in his hands. 
In a corner, a man wrapped in rags and newspapers tried to hide the rat he'd been skinning with his fingers.''
The modern scenes, which take up about a quarter of the novel, are less successful. 
For one thing, they are overresearched; we learn a lot more about navigating the waterways of British Columbia than necessary. 
Also, neither Robert Lam nor Lam Fan develop well as characters in these sections. 
Robert has but one note to sing, that of a confused truth-seeker. 
Lam Fan is not a very interesting ghost; her one note is shrill and pedantic. 
Both characters seem willed into place as plot devices to give the book a complicated structure that it doesn't need.
Rather than holding the novel together, they constantly interrupt its flow. 
Juxtaposing stories from different centuries with their contrasting world views doesn't work. 
The technique almost forces the reader to skip over the present-day adventures of Robert and his ghostly stepmother in order to find out what will happen next in the much more compelling tale they are unfolding about their ancestors.
Marilyn Bowering does have a fascinating story to tell. 
If only she had told it more simply!
Still, ''To All Appearances a Lady,'' though not a completely satisfying novel, is ambitious and often enjoyable.
Â 
'DIRTY, DIRTY ROBERT!'
I sat on the broken steps and looked out into the darkened world I had known since childhood: the ghosting apple trees, the tilted greenhouses, and surmounting all the dark face of Christmas Hill. 
In this International Geophysical Year, in which nations had joined harmoniously together to observe the marvels of the earth, atmosphere, and space, in which boys in their twenties handled millions of dollars' worth of rocketry, I, Robert Louis Lam, three years from retirement, had quarrelled with a one-hundred-year-old woman over my future.
I sighed and thought about the Rose and what it would be like to set sail in her and never come back. 
And as I did, an icy hand gripped my shoulder and a voice shrill with anger cried out, ''Dirty Robert Lam!
Dirty, dirty Robert!''
I turned at that to see Fan standing there in her nightgown, holding a knot of papers in her shaking hand. 
. . .
I stood up and put my arms around her. 
Her head touched my chest, her arms felt like small dry sticks. 
She tried to say more, but her mouth was dry, and I could smell on her breath the sour fume of opium.
From ''To All Appearances a Lady.''

file: Reporter_s Notebook_ Turmoil in China_Seeing Shadows Where Once There Were Leaders, Facts and Inform.txt
text:
ï»¿
Writing about China's leadership these days must be a bit like covering the afterlife: Even if one is convinced it exists, confirming the details can be tough.
Indeed, covering China's leaders may well overlap with writing about the nether world, for there is some dispute about which world Deng Xiaoping now resides in. 
Mr. Deng, the country's senior leader, is variously said to be dead, dying or in even closer control of China than he has been in years.
In the last few weeks reporting about China has turned upside down, just as interest is exploding in what is going on in China. 
It used to be that there were leaders, and facts, and sources; now there are only shadows.
Take the simple question of who is in control in China. 
It should be easy to figure out who a country's leaders are; now, it is a puzzle. 
Aside from Prime Minister Li Peng, who appeared on television today and before that on May 25, no top leader has been seen in nearly three weeks.
The Communist Party General Secretary, Zhao Ziyang, almost certainly has been stripped of his power, and Prime Minister Li at least has the influence to get on television and to get some of his hard-line policies adopted. 
But does that really mean that his position is secure, or just that he has control over the television station?
Is Mr. Deng, assuming he is still alive, simply using Mr. Li as an instrument or does the Prime Minister have an independent power base?
Is President Yang Shangkun staging a coup against the Government, or is he working with other officials to reassert hardliner control?
Most Western diplomats and Chinese officials can make educated guesses to answer these questions, and journalists inevitably have to address the questions. 
But always there is uncertainty, because sources in China are increasingly fallible. 
Some journalists and diplomats have better sources than others, but probably none is regularly briefed by a Politburo member.
Instead, sources tend to come from a range of people: children of high officials, those who work for high officials and diplomats. 
The party is very careful about letting documents out of its possession, so most information comes not from leaked documents but simply from what people remember from meetings or from documents they have read previously. 
Confirming information is extremely difficult or impossible.
Â 
Witnessing Clashes
Covering the reports of skirmishes between military units has been particularly difficult, because probably no reporter has personally witnessed any of the reported clashes. 
Instead, reporters have relied on accounts from Chinese witnesses and from foreign diplomats, but almost inevitably there is uncertainty in the stories.
What was known was that army forces took up defensive positions with tanks, in a manner not normally associated with defense against civilians. 
In addition, artillery shells could be heard in the distance and occasional bursts of machine gun firing. 
Sometimes soldiers reported that they had been engaged in minor clashes with other troops, although they were usually vague on details.
Convoys of troops could be seen rushing around main roads, but it was often impossible to identify them. 
License plates of trucks are a clue -V11 plates mean that a military truck is from the northeastern city of Shenyang, for example - but it was then difficult or impossible to distinguish a group of Shenyang soldiers from the 39th Army from the Shenyang soldiers in the 40th Army.
Keeping track of soldiers was doubly difficult because they tended to shoot in all directions from their convoys, and they had a particular distaste for binoculars. 
Following along behind a convoy, in a car or on a bicycle, was impossible. 
Thus it became crucial to have a network of friends around the city who could report the latest troop movements.
Writing about the reports of skirmishes reflects a judgment that the accounts appear correct, and that they signify underlying tensions in the military that could be very significant. 
Many Chinese and foreigners have indeed feared that a civil war is a possibility, and that is consistent with the evidence. 
On the other hand, it is plausible that the skirmishes are many fewer than have been reported, and were not so serious as initially believed. 
Perhaps they were mostly bluffing, and attempts to scare and deter other armies instead of to attack them directly.
Â 
Friendships at Risk
Confirming information has been particularly difficult lately because sources are drying up in a time of political retrenchment. 
Many journalists an diplomats had friends and sources in the Zhao camp, and they have suddenly found themselves without information, or else too afraid of arrest to want to see any foreigners.
And even when Chinese friends are willing to maintain friendships with foreigners, there are agonizing questions about whether it is right to put them to risk. 
Thus the tendency has been to call on them much less, or not at all, for fear of inadvertently sending them to prison.
There are similar worries about quoting people by name. 
Most Western journalists like to use the names of ordinary people they quote: it adds a ring of authenticity, even when it is unpronouncable. 
It used to be that most Chinese never wanted to give more than their surname, even when they made the most inoccuous remark. 
Then, in the last few months, more and more seemed to find the courage to allow their full names to be printed in criticizing Beijing.
A few took an intermediate approach: they agreed to use their surname and initials, because that would make it more difficult to determine their Chinese characters and find them.
Now, since the expectations of a crackdown in the last few weeks, the mood has changed and nobody is willing to have their names used.
''Are you kidding?'' one young worker responded when he was asked if a reporter could use his name. 
''It's easy for you to get on a flight out of here. 
I'll be in jail for years.''
Â 
Getting Around Town
Even getting around the capital to find out what is happening has been difficult, for reasons of safety and transportation. 
Earlier this week, citizens erected barricades at many intersections, so that driving cars around Beijing became a nightmare. 
The result was that bicycles again became fashionable, and foreign correspondents rushed around town on bicylces.
However, bullets have become a major reason to stay away from some areas. 
On the first day of the shooting, many reporters were near the front lines, and two - one Japanese, one French - were shot and wounded. 
Since then, and especially after all the reporters visited the hospitals and wrote second-day stories about those who had been less lucky than themselves, many journalists have been more prudent.
Photographers have been particularly hard-pressed, because the soldiers have made it clear that they do not want their pictures taken. 
Some of the Chinese who were killed were shot because they were trying to take photos of the carnage.
Journalists have had to deal with the added problem that they are not really supposed to engage in journalism these days. 
Special martial law regulations ban coverage of what either the democracy movement or the troops are doing, and so there is no way to explain away one's presence as simply that of a journalist.
As a result, foreign correspondents have suddenly proven scarce in the capital, but a large group of foreigners has suddenly appeared who roam around the capital and pass themselves off as tourists. 
Their claims are belied by their notebooks and questions that few tourists would pose: ''So are the soldiers there from the 38th Army, and are they ready to fight with the 27th Army?''
Most ordinary residents seem fiercely supportive of foreign journalists, as well as curious about how foreign newspapers are covering the events in China. 
Workers or housewives sometimes guide journalists away from trouble, and everyone delights in the opportunity not to speak Chinese but to practice execrable English.
They push a journalist toward the most gruesome scenes, to drum into him what they regard as the Government's brutality. 
If there is a bloodstain from the attack earlier this week on civilians, the local residents will virtually drag a reporter to inspect it.
''Tell the world about it,'' a young worker said today as he pointed toward a trickle of blood on the ground from an old man who was shot by mistake near Tiananmen Square. 
''Make sure the world knows what is happening here.''

text:
ï»¿
China is a big country to survey in six days, even if you are an emperor, travel on a personal Boeing 747 with an army of fretting chamberlains and speed to the Great Wall with thousands of Chinese paramilitary police lining both sides of the road for 50 miles.
But the challenge is even greater for Emperor Akihito of Japan, because every stop on his itinerary must serve an unstated agenda: to set aside China's fear that Asia's other great superpower still harbors the sense of cultural superiority, one that led it a generation ago to try to conquer the Middle Kingdom.
So on the first visit a Japanese emperor has ever paid to China, Akihito's handlers have taken care that every moment resound with deep cultural significance, preferably one that will remind China of the arduous days centuries ago when Japanese envoys came here to learn at the feet of China's masters.
So today, while his hosts pondered the roles that the likes of Toyota and Sony might play as Chinese-style Communism begins to look more like Japanese-style capitalism, the Emperor had something else in mind: the Tang Dynasty.
Spending the day inside the giant walls of Xian, the eastern end of the Silk Road, the 58-year-old Emperor sought out some of his roots. 
He visited the Shaanxi Provincial Museum to see the stone tablets where scholars and Chinese emperors had first etched the pictographic symbol for the word pronounced in Japanese as "heisei," or achieving peace. 
Three years ago, hours after the death of Akihito's father, Hirohito, "Heisei" was chosen as the name for the new imperial era.
The Emperor spent a considerable time at the tablets (there are more than a thousand, bearing everything from Confucian classics to a cure for stomachache), asking detailed questions about the calligraphy.
"It is all very interesting," a Chinese official traveling with the Emperor said as he stood outside the building. 
"So tell me, do you think this visit will increase Japanese investment in China?"
The museum is not the only place where the Emperor has driven home the connections between two countries that, on the surface at least, seem among the most dissimilar in Asia. 
An accomplished student of certain types of fish, the Emperor visited the Chinese Academy of Science and talked about how his eighth-century ancestor, Emperor Shomu, used medicines from China. 
He has quoted from famous Chinese poets whose work he studied as a child.
So enamored was the Emperor of finding proof of the centuries of exchanges between the two countries that he skipped the one attraction virtually everyone else comes to Xian to see: The giant terra-cotta army, uncovered in the mid-1970's, whose thousands of soldiers and horses guard the burial mound of a Chinese emperor.
"It is something popular among the Americans and Europeans, I think," Hideo Kagami, the Emperor's spokesman on the tour, said Sunday. 
"I believe His Majesty has a stronger interest in stone tablets."
Â 
He Who Would Have Been
For most of the Emperor's trip, his schedulers have taken care to glide past sites that millions of Chinese remember with bitterness, places like the Marco Polo Bridge, where Japan staged an incident that prompted its full-scale invasion of China in 1937. 
But there was one moment, out of sight of most of his hosts, when there was a brief reunion with a figure from Japan's colonial control of parts of China.
It came on Sunday, just before the Emperor and his wife, Empress Michiko, left Beijing. 
At a reception by the Japanese Ambassador to China, Akihito was approached by a slight, elderly man in a tailored Mao suit. 
He was Pu Jie, the younger brother of Pu Yi, the "last emperor" of China and the central figure in the epic film by that name.
Pu Yi became a willing ally of the Japanese, who installed him as emperor of their puppet state, Manchukuo, in 1935. 
Pu Jie was trained to be the next emperor, sent to Japanese schools and married to a member of the Japanese aristocracy. 
But he never got to the throne: Japan was defeated and the Chinese sent Pu Jie for "re-education."
Today he is a member of the National People's Congress and a frequent visitor to Tokyo to promote bilateral relations.
Pu Jie left no doubt that he has a warm spot in his heart for Japan's royals. 
Asked what he told Akihito, Pu Jie did not hesitate: "I said today is one of the happiest days for the Chinese people."
Â 
The Non-Best Seller
Perhaps so, but many Chinese seemed a little confused about whose motorcade was blasting past bicyclists and farmers in their fields. 
And the Japanese seem to have a way to go before they change their image among the Chinese people, most of whom know Japan only as a one-time invader.
Biographies of the Emperor, on sale at major bookstores around Beijing, were not exactly leaping off the counters. 
The stores seem to have sold a few more than 2,000 copies, or one for every 500,000 Chinese.
Â 
No Sex Please, We're Royal
Pity the Japanese reporters who cover the Emperor every day!
First, by strictly enforced tradition, Japanese emperors never say much. 
Second, unlike the British royals, the people who surround the Chrysanthemum Throne do not seem given to sex scandals and failed marriages.
The biggest story at the palace these days is whether the Crown Prince, the heir to the throne, will succeed in his seemingly endless search for a bride. 
But the Japanese press cannot write about it: They agreed earlier this year to stop writing about the search because the speculation was driving away many potential candidates.
It is hardly surprising that Japanese reporters analyze every word for a glimpse at the Emperor's life. 
So a round of wondering began when, in the Forbidden City, the Emperor was taken to the bedroom of his former Chinese counterparts. 
Akihito, getting right to the heart of the matter, asked whether Chinese emperors and empresses had separate bedrooms. 
(It seems they did.)
This was quickly flashed back to Tokyo, raising the obvious question about the sleeping arrangements in the Imperial Palace. 
The Emperor did not say, and the Japanese reporters, polite to their core, did not ask.
Â 
Lost, Maybe, in Translation
The other utterance still under debate is how exactly what the Emperor said when he placed the blame on Japan for attacking China.
According to the English translation provided by the Japanese Foreign Ministry, he said: "In the long history of relationships between our two countries, there was an unfortunate period in which my country inflicted great suffering on the people of China. 
I deeply deplore this."
But in Japanese the comments seem far less judgmental. 
Though the words he used could be stretched to mean "deplore," a more literal translation would be, "About this, I feel deep sadness."
Japanese is a vague language, and it gets vaguer when the war comes up, but there was considerable suspicion that the Tokyo Government might have deliberately used phrases that could be spun differently in different countries.
Japanese officials deny this: "We did the best translation we could," a senior Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
Â 
My Wall's Bigger Than Yours
The Emperor was whisked past some of the most obvious evidence of Japanese influence in China (a new Matsushita electronics plant in Beijing, the Red Lips Karaoke Bar) to see the Great Wall. 
His guide was Chen Xitong, the Mayor of Beijing, and as they walked a considerable distance the Emperor remarked again and again on how large and impenetrable the wall seemed.
Mr. Chen shrugged it off.
"In time of emergency it was useless," he said, recalling invaders who sidestepped it. 
Then, reciting a lesson that the Emperor of a mere 120 million Japanese hardly needed, he added, "The real great wall is the people."

text:
ï»¿
When you tire of mashed potatoes and roast chicken, which should be any second now, a trip to Hong Kong may be just what your blanded-out taste buds require.
Fortunately, since Hong Kong restaurants have come to New York City, you won't have far to go. 
Triple Eight Palace, tucked away on the second floor of an all-Chinese shopping mall, is just under the Manhattan Bridge between Market and Forsythe Streets in Chinatown. 
And parking is right around the corner.
A vast Hong Kong food palace, slightly frayed around the edges, it has all the splendor of a Las Vegas casino: the glitter of gold embroidery on Chinese red fabric, twinkling neon lights, the sparkle of crystal chandeliers.
Triple Eight caters to the Chinese community: there were never more than two other Westerners there on any of our three visits. 
Toddlers arrive in strollers, infants in carriages along with their pre-adolescent siblings, parents and grandparents. 
Whatever the reason, we were the beneficiaries of the last remaining bastion of that wonderful old custom:that children should be seen and not heard.
If you would also like to take in a Chinese wedding celebration, Sunday evening is recommended. 
Along with our dinner one night, we were happy observers at the festivities of a beautiful young bride in a glittering red dress and a handsome, even younger-looking bridegroom. 
Their musical selections were ecumenical: Chinese words to Western music; country-and-western music in English, and Chinese music with Chinese words.
Perhaps because so few Westerners come here, not all of the staff is fluent in English. 
But all seem eager to warn you about the pricey dishes.
Patron: "Do you have bird's nest soup?"
Waiter: "Yes. 
Very expensive."
Patron: "Do you have abalone?"
Waiter: "Yes. 
Very expensive."
Patron: "Do you have shark's fin?"
Waiter: "Yes. 
Very expensive."
Moving right along, we ordered bird's nest soup and more dishes than five people needed.
Captain: "Order too much. 
Very expensive."
The bird's nest soup with chicken at $24 for four servings was wonderfully gelatinous. 
An acquired taste for most Westerners, it is a taste I have acquired.
In addition to the expensive dishes, Hong Kong restaurants are noted for their fish tanks. 
The patron picks the fish from the tank; the chef cooks it in one of many styles. 
To select mine, I was beckoned to a room off the kitchen where the captain netted a fish and suggested that it be prepared in the simplest manner -- steamed with soy, scallions and cilantro. 
It was impeccably fresh, of course, but slightly overcooked.
Though the menu is bilingual, the style of meals is not: there are no appetizers. 
For those, you must go for dim sum at lunch. 
You can have soup, or you can do as the Chinese do: order the entrees. 
Keep in mind that in a traditional Chinese restaurant there is an additional charge for steamed rice.
Many dishes on the menu will sound familiar to aficionados of true Cantonese cooking, the most popular regional food in Hong Kong. 
Whether you like the flavors of some of the more exotic dishes, like braised oysters with black mushrooms and fried dough, there are many well-cooked dishes. 
There were only two real clinkers: a light, freshly fried lemon chicken had a cloyingly sweet sauce, and a braised duck dish tasted reheated.
One of the most delicious choices was another duck, this one dipped in taro flour and deep-fried. 
The taro provides a very light but very crisp batter. 
There was a spectacular-looking gray sole in which the skin and bones had been deep-fried long enough to make the bones not only edible, but also irresistible. 
The flesh had been steamed and handsomely arranged on top with an assortment of vegetables that included the pleasingly bitter broccoli di rape. 
On one occasion, we thought we were ordering crabs with a spicy-sweet black-bean sauce. 
Better yet, we got clams.
The pork, a sophisticated version of the gloppy sweet-and-sour pork of our youth, is described by Grace Chan, one of the owners of the restaurant, as "a new creation begun in Hong Kong."
Ms. Chan and her husband, Ming, also own the H.S.F. restaurants in Chinatown and on the East Side of Manhattan.
Like American chefs who are exploring the regional cooking of their own country, those in Hong Kong have begun to borrow from other regions of China. 
Orange beef from Sichuan, for example, is skillfully interpreted at Triple Eight -- filet mignon is marinated in a savory mixture of garlic, dried orange peel, hot peppers, Sichuan hot sauce and vinegar and then pan-fried to form a crust over the tender cut.
The Chinese desserts are best skipped.
Lunch time at Triple Eight takes on all the characteristics of a Hong Kong dim sum parlor. 
Carts filled with steamers full of exotic "heart's delights," the poetic translation of dim sum, parade up and down the aisles, pushed by women singing in Chinese about their wares.
Point to what you want. 
The odds favor your chances of choosing something appealing from the dim sum cart as long as you stay away from anything that looks greasy. 
We tried 30 offerings and came away with many to recommend: shrimp bonnets, spareribs in black-bean sauce, seafood-stuffed bell peppers, steamed pork buns, meatballs, deep-fried taro pancakes, fried shrimp balls, turnip cakes, Shanghai egg rolls, and chicken feet for those who are fans. 
You might also like the sesame-seed buns filled with sweet bean paste.
Choose from five varieties of tea, including jasmine, at lunch.
Go early when everything is hot and fresh instead of hot and reheated.
And don't ask for fortune cookies. 
There are none.
Â 
Triple Eight Palace
*
88 East Broadway, near Market Street, in Manhattan, (212) 941-8886.
Atmosphere: A vast, slightly tattered Hong Kong food palace.
Service: Friendly, but some staff members are not fluent in English.
Recommended dishes: Bird's nest soup with chicken, fish from the tank with ginger, crispy duck with taro, fillet of gray sole with crispy fins, pork chop with Peking sauce, Triple Eight orange beef, hard clams with black-bean sauce. 
Dim sum: shrimp bonnets, spareribs in black-bean sauce, bell peppers stuffed with seafood, steamed pork buns, meatballs, deep-fried taro pancakes, fried shrimp balls, turnip cakes, Shanghai egg rolls, chicken feet, sesame-seed buns with sweet bean paste.
Wine: Very short list, and not always available. 
Tsing Tao beer is the better choice.
Price range: Dim sum lunch: $1.70 to $3.75, per dish; dinner: $6.95 to $35 per dish, with most dishes between $10 and $12.
Credit cards: American Express, Diner's Club, Mastercard and Visa accepted for for $25 or more.
Hours: Dim sum: 8 A.M. to 5 P.M. daily. 
Regular menu: noon to midnight seven days.
Reservations: Preferred.
Wheelchair accessibility: One flight up. 
Elevator on request; restrooms on the same level.

file: Rights Panel Scolds Cuba, Not China.txt
text:
ï»¿
The United Nations commission charged with encouraging respect for human rights worldwide refused to criticize China tonight for suppressing the student democracy movement last June.
But the Human Right Commission implicitly criticized Cuba by expressing concern about reported human rights violations there and by voting to examine its record again next year. 
The move, which came after a strenuous American diplomatic campaign, makes this the fourth consecutive year that the Government of President Fidel Castro will have been on the commission's agenda.
Seen as Test of Commission
The votes on Cuba and China had been seen as the most significant test this year of the 43-nation commission's ability to debate human rights records impartially. 
But the message for American diplomats seemed in the end to be ambiguous, with the United States getting its way against Cuba but unable to do so against China.
The United States delegation hailed the Cuba vote as a great victory. 
Armando Valladares, the Cuban-born writer and poet who is the head of the United States team here, called the outcome ''a great day for Cuba and a great victory for the human rights fight around the world.''
But he also said the defeat of a motion that avoided any direct criticism of China but merely provided for the commission to maintain pressure on Beijing by debating its record again next year showed ''a double standard'' in the debate. 
''It is inconceivable to me that the resolution could not make it through,'' he said, adding that ''I fought hard for that resolution. 
I criticized China in every speech.''
An American lawyer here said that the charges against China appeared far more serious than those against Cuba, which was accused of carrying out reprisals against citizens who gave evidence of human rights abuses to the commission two years ago.
''The violations of which Cuba is accused are little fish compared with Tiananmen Square,'' said the lawyer, Reed Brody of the International Commission of Jurists, a private human rights watchdog organization. 
''If the U.S. had made the same effort over China, it might have been different.''
The resolution on China, sponsored by the United States and most of its Western allies, welcomed the end of martial law, urged the Government ''to continue to take measures along the same lines'' and asked Secretary General Javier Perez de Cuellar to give its next session ''additional information including that provided by the Government of China.''
But a resolution introduced by Pakistan, Somalia and Cuba to take no action on this resolution was adopted with 17 in favor, 15 against and 11 abstentions.
Other countries siding with China on this vote included the Soviet Union, Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka, Yugoslavia, Nigeria, Iraq, Cyprus, Ghana and Ethiopia. 
Hungary and Bulgaria, the commission's two Eastern European members, voted with the West against the no-action motion.
Â 
Resolution's Language Is Mild
The resolution on Cuba, cosponsored by Poland and Czechoslovakia as well as the United States, was also mild, merely asking the Secretary General to give the next commission meeting a report on his ''ongoing contacts with the Government of Cuba.''
The resolution to maintain the Castro regime's human rights record on the commission's agenda was carried by 19 to 12 with 12 abstentions.
Once again, the Soviet Union voted for Cuba, as did China, Cyprus, Ethiopia, Ghana, India, Iraq, Yugoslavia and Mexico.

text:

The 14th annual Hong Kong International Dragon Boat Races began today and amid pageantry recalling the 2,000-year-old origin of this sport, and the United States team from Philadelphia qualified quietly and easily for the semifinals Sunday.
The wooden boats used are 38 feet long, weigh close to 4,000 pounds and use a crew of up to 20 rowers plus a coxswain to steer and a drummer, seated in the bow, to beat out the racing cadence. 
A dragon's head is mounted on the bow of each boat, and a dragon's tail is attached to the stern. 
The rowers sit two abreast in the boat, paddling in precise synchronization at a cadence of up to 100 strokes a minute.
Dragon boat racing was confined to Asian countries until 1976, when the first Hong Kong International Regatta was organized. 
This year, more than 3,000 rowers from 24 countries are competing. 
The United States first entered a men's team in 1982, placing second, a result it has yet to duplicate. 
This year's crew, from Philadelphia, is made up primarily of collegiate oarsmen and has altered its racing style in an attempt to find a winning combination.
Â 
Learning From the Chinese
''We're trying to emulate the style of Shun De,'' said Bob McNamara, the United States coach. 
The Shun De team from China has won this regatta the last four years, racing a short stroke at a cadence of 90 or more strokes to the minute.
''We've boated a lighter crew this year,'' McNamara said, ''averaging 160 pounds per man, which lets us use the Chinese style, eliminating the back lift heavier teams use.''
The United States team crossed the finish line two boat lengths in front of the Sai Kung team from Hong Kong. 
All the crews that failed to win today have repechage heats - a second chance to advance to the semifinals - Sunday morning. 
The semifinals and championship will follow.
Â 
Chants and Rice
Buddhist monks, clad in raspberry and black vestments, chanted the blessing ceremony officially opening the two-day regatta, which is raced along the Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront of Victoria Harbor.
The races commemorate the death of Qu Yuan, a Chinese poet and patriot who threw himself into the sea in protest against the corruption of the government of his time. 
The local fishermen were said to be so moved by Qu Yuan's sacrifice that they raced in their fishing boats to try to recover his body, beating the water with oars to ward off fish from eating it.
At the end of the opening ceremony today, rice was scattered over the competitors, invoking Qu Yuan's protective spirit for a safe regatta.

Near Broadway, which once marked a boundary between North Beach and Chinatown, it is possible to buy pasta or dim sum, focaccia bread or fortune cookies. 
Strolling past first-floor apartments on the way to the boccie court near Washington Square, the tiny park at the community's center, passers-by can hear the clicking of mah-jongg tiles through open windows.
And in the early mornings in front of Saints Peter and Paul Catholic Church overlooking Washington Square, Chinese immigrants silently exercise in unison to the ancient discipline of tai chi.
But a closer inspection discloses jagged scars left by rapid demographic change.
White residents at a bus stop in North Beach complain that the recent rerouting of a bus line to ease congestion in Chinatown was done for the convenience of ''those people'' at the expense of ''us.''
Others make jokes about the way Chinese drive cars. 
And half a block from Washington Square, the wall of a health center serving Chinese-speaking clients was spray-painted on the Chinese New Year: ''Kill You All Soon.''
''There's a lot of tension, a lot of animosity,'' said Henry Der, the executive director of Chinese for Affirmative Action, a civil rights and research group. 
''No matter how liberal we may be here, people still derive great comfort from having people like themselves living in their neighborhoods.''
It has been more than 100 years since anti-Chinese hysteria erupted here and unemployed whites led attacks against Chinese laborers, brutalizing them and vandalizing their stores and laundries. 
Since then tensions have seldom been evident until the last decade, when successive waves of immigrants from Asia burst the boundaries of what had long been a rigidly circumscribed Chinatown.
By the time of the 1990 census, the population of San Francisco is expected to be one-third Asian, half of them of Chinese descent. 
The growth is partly a result of Hong Kong's capitalists moving and investing their wealth on the West Coast in anticipation of the reversion of Hong Kong to control by China's mainland Government at the end of the century.
As this population has expanded, Chinese have bought up commercial and residential property in North Beach, jumping the psychological border at Broadway and sometimes, as landlords, bringing with them high rents that forced out established businesses.
Cultural differences are also causing friction. 
Some longtime North Beach residents complain about laundry hanging from balconies and the bins of bok choy on the sidewalks. 
They shake their fists at each home newly painted in the colors that signify good luck to the Chinese, pink with blue or green trim. 
The Chinese, meanwhile, wonder how their neighbors, many of them descendents of Genoa fishermen, could have come to prefer their homes in white or pale gray.
''The Italians perceive they are being driven out by the Chinese,'' said Dr. Grace Pung Guthrie, director of a study of North Beach financed by the Ford Foundation. 
''But the Chinese have an interest in preserving the unique quality of the neighborhood too.''
Thus it is especially irksome to the new residents that the old-timers are reluctant to acknowledge their contributions to the neighborhood, like the award-winning rehabilitation by a Chinese nonprofit group of a dilapidated hotel into 65 units of low-cost housing.
There are tensions within the Chinese community as well; one of Dr. Guthrie's findings is that established Chinese-Americans report feeling hostile toward the newly arrived Chinese. 
''They hate the rudeness of these newcomers, the shoving on the bus, spitting in the street,'' Dr. Guthrie said.
There are signs in North Beach of attempts to work together. 
The neighborhood association recently elected its first Chinese-American president.
But answers are not always simple. 
For example, nearly all of the dozens of Chinese businesses in the area were left out of a recent Chamber of Commerce guide to North Beach shops and services. 
Marsha Garland, founder of the North Beach Chamber, said she tried to make sure the Chinese were included by hiring a young man of Chinese descent who could speak Cantonese to approach the owners about paying to be listed in the guide as other businesses had done.
''They thought he was part of an extortion racket and they were afraid to talk to him,'' Ms. Garland said.
In the meantime, Chinese immigrants are bearing the burden of the racist stereotyping that occurs behind their backs and angry verbal attacks directed at them on the streets.
''They are bowing, smiling, saying, 'Sorry, so sorry,' to deflect aggression from Caucasians,'' Dr. Guthrie said.
Mr. Der agrees. 
''They don't confront, but they don't forget,'' he said. 
''It widens the gap.''

text:
ï»¿
DURING the maelstrom of this year's election campaigns, Junjiu Tan arrived in New Haven to begin his study of American politics. 
In an attempt to understand the election process, he said, he started by collecting literature from Connecticut's three gubernatorial campaigns. 
Then he visited campaign headquarters, interviewed street canvassers and took dozens of photographs.
Sitting in his office in Yale University's political science department, Mr. Tan, a Fulbright scholar on leave from his teaching position at Wuhan University in China, said he found that American voters appeared to be serious and well informed. 
"But," he added, "am I correct when I say that Americans have much to do to make their politicians more responsible?"
A few blocks away, at the Yale School of Music, another Fulbright scholar, Stefan Linev of Bulgaria, was participating in a far different investigation. 
With the help of Prof. Eleazar de Carvalho, Mr. Linev, who is a conductor at the Varna State Opera, analyzed the musical score to Beethoven's Second Symphony.
Â 
Scholars From 15 Nations
When Mr. Linev questioned the composer's use of tempo in one measure, the professor, whose students have included Zubin Mehta and Seiji Ozawa, raised his right eyebrow and paused. 
"As re-creators," he said leaning toward Mr. Linev, "we must be very careful."
Earlier, at a nearby coffee shop, Mr. Linev had discussed the political climate in Bulgaria, the beauty of its countryside and the contrast between New Haven and Varna, a city on the Black Sea. 
"It is quite something for me to be here," he said.
Mr. Tan and Mr. Linev are among the 28 foreign scholars lecturing or conducting research this year at universities in Connecticut under the Fulbright grant program. 
Selected on the basis of academic or professional merit, they represent 15 countries and are involved in academic areas ranging from political science and music to medicine and urban design.
In addition, more than 70 foreign students are now attending classes in the state under Fulbright grants, said Dr. Norman Kogan, the president of the Connecticut Fulbright Alumni Association and emeritus professor of political science at the University of Connecticut.
Initiated in the mid-1940's by Senator J. William Fulbright of Arkansas, the international exchange program awards 4,500 grants annually to American and foreign students, teachers and scholars. 
What makes the Fulbright program different from other educational exchange programs, said Dr. Kogan, is its role as a catalyst for change in the age of the global community. 
He said students and scholars are chosen for their ability to share ideas and experiences with people of different cultures.
"After they have spent time here, we hope that students and scholars will return to their home with a less superficial and a more balanced view of America," said Dr. Kogan, the recipient of three Fulbright grants to study in Italy. 
"In turn, we hope that students and residents in Connecticut, once exposed to Fulbrighters, will develop a more enlightened view of other cultures."
In a crowded auditorium at the University of Hartford recently, Perveen Shakir of Pakistan, dressed in a silk sari with embroidered flowers, gave an impassioned lecture on the history of her country, leading to the recent political demise of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto. 
Ms. Shakir, a poet and linguist, is visiting through May under the aegis of the Hartford Consortium for Higher Education. 
She will teach and lecture on the literature and history of her country at several colleges and universities in the area.
The author of three books of poetry and recipient of numerous writing awards, Ms. Shakir said in an interview that poets in Pakistan often have the status of film stars. 
In her country, she said, "even the least educated person has an ear for poetry."
She also said that she hopes to instill in her students a deeper understanding and appreciation of Pakistani culture. 
"Their picture of us is somewhat out of focus," she said. 
"They consider us very exotic. 
Some have even asked me if we have cars."
Amir Sagi's research may have nothing to do with intercultural relations, but by living in Connecticut, he is exposed daily to the details of American life. 
A biologist and oceanographer from Jerusalem, Dr. Sagi is researching hormonal activities in crustaceans with Dr. Hans Laufer, a biology professor at UConn in Storrs. 
Before coming to Connecticut a few years ago, Dr. Sagi worked as a researcher at the Life Sciences Institute at Hebrew University in Jerusalem.
He said he often discusses Middle East politics with colleagues and American friends, some of whom have formed their impressions of the region through television news reports.
"That gives you a brief glimpse of nothing," said Dr. Sagi, who was raised in an agricultural community outside of Jerusalem that was settled after World War II by Jewish refugees from Yugoslavia and Egypt. 
"The conflict between Arabs and Jews involves a long and very complicated political history."
Dr. Sagi, whose wife, Kei, a psychologist, and their two children are also living in Connecticut, said he had adjusted slowly to the pace and temperament of the state's residents. 
Recalling the day last year when he took his son to his first day at school, Dr. Sagi said he had assumed he would meet other parents. 
"Instead, they rushed in, dropped their kids off, then rushed off to their jobs," he said. 
"New Englanders are very slow at making new relationships, and that took some getting used to."
In his book "The Price of Empire" (Pantheon, 1989), Senator Fulbright recounted his hope that the scholarship program might erode "culturally rooted mistrust that sets nations against one another."
He called the scholars' experience "the acquisition of empathy -- the ability to see the world as others see it, and to allow for the possibility that others may see something that we have failed to see, or may see it more accurately."
This need to understand cultural values and actions applies particularly to Asha Basnyat of Katmandu, Nepal. 
Mrs. Basnyat, who is living with her husband and three children in West Haven, is working on an internship at the Mental Health Resource Center at St. Raphael Hospital in New Haven as part of a master's program in community psychology at the University of New Haven. 
With a caseload of six clients, Mrs. Basnyat said she focuses mainly on marriage and family counseling, adding that although problems arising from relationships are universal, solutions vary from culture to culture.
Â 
Shocked at Crime Rate
"When a woman is having difficulties in a relationship in Nepal, she is advised to compromise and to be more accommodating, since it is rare for a woman to divorce," said Mrs. Basnyat, who is training to be a psychotherapist. 
"But here, the emphasis is more on getting women to be assertive and to become independent. 
Therefore, I always must remind myself to deal with the individual and not let my cultural instincts interfere."
For many scholars, the level of crime in Connecticut cities came as a shock. 
For the first few weeks after he arrived, Mr. Linev, the conductor, said he often took late-night walks from the Yale campus to his apartment, about a mile away.
"Then I bought a television set and started watching the New Haven news," he said. 
"After that, I stopped my midnight walks."
Mr. Tan said that even the most commonplace activities for Americans can pique a visitor's curiosity. 
From his office window, which overlooks Sachem Street and the Yale skating rink, he often admires the abundance of trees, grass and shrubbery below, he said. 
"It is not something you see a lot in Chinese cities."
Walking down Orange Street one Saturday, Mr. Tan spotted a sign for a tag sale and decided to investigate. 
There, he said, "I found people selling everything from bicycles to used pencils."
Such a practice would be unheard of in China, he said, mainly because families are far less mobile than in the United States. 
He added, "the Chinese would be ashamed to sell used items from their homes."
Nevertheless, Mr. Tan said he felt that tag sales are a good example of Americans' pragmatism, a quality he appreciates.
Â 
Expanded Repertoire
Depending upon the type of research involved, Dr. Kogan said, Fulbright scholars often share their findings through lectures, articles or books. 
His own research on Italian political parties resulted in the two-volume "Political History of Post-War Italy," (Praeger, 1988), he said, which has been used by American Foreign Service officers in Italy.
Mr. Linev said his work at Yale and the private lessons with Professor Carvalho will help him expand his repertoire, which already includes operas by Mozart, Verdi and Puccini.
And Mr. Tan said that when he finishes his research on public participation in the American political process, he will incorporate his findings into his courses at Wuhan University. 
But before he leaves, he said, he would not mind immersing himself in one other all-American enterprise.
"Perhaps by May," he said, grinning, "I will be experienced enough to run my own tag sale."

file: Schools in China Try a Sideline_ Making Money.txt
text:
ï»¿
Peng Wenyi, a high-school principal, worries about absenteeism, lesson plans and his pupils' test scores. 
But these days, he also frets about the school's plans to expand its three clothing shops into a large department store.
Seven hundred miles to the north, the Sanyuanli Xiaoli Elementary School has a small sign at the main entrance. 
But it has an even larger sign next to that one, identifying its sideline venture: "Air-Conditioner and Refrigerator Repair Shop."
Throughout China, schools like those are diversifying into business. 
From elementary schools to universities, they are opening shops and factories to raise funds and join in the national entrepreneurial boom.
Making money has become a national obsession, and government bureaus, police stations and intelligence services are parlaying their expertise and staff into profits. 
But the fascination with money raises special questions when it is schools that are engaging in business, particularly when the success or failure of the business is what determines the facilities and opportunities that the students enjoy.
Â 
Profits and School Resources
Those questions are particularly striking -- and unexpected -- in a Communist-run country that prided itself on providing educational prospects to all pupils.
"This issue was debated for a long time, with people asking: Wouldn't this influence the school?" said Mr. Peng, a lanky, enthusiastic principal, who continues to teach physics to students. 
"But now, everyone is running businesses. 
And our school is in great demand. 
Lots of students want to come here, but we can't take them because we have no space."
Last year, nearly 680,000 school-run businesses across the nation, from textile factories and television manufacturers to book shops and fish farms, brought in a total income of about $850 million, and this year the figure is expected to soar much higher. 
In some areas, like the western district of Beijing, school-run businesses produce half the output of all industry.
One reason why Mr. Peng's school, the Fuxing Middle school, is so popular is that its enterprises make large profits that result in better academic conditions. 
At Fuxing, the 1,300 pupils may borrow books from a computerized library, learn BASIC computer language at one of 60 terminals, or watch television in one of the 40 classrooms.
Â 
Efforts to Make Money
In the last four years, the school has had a complete makeover.
It renovated its cafeteria, its basketball and volleyball courts, its jogging track and its Ping Pong recreation room and raised the bonuses for its teachers. 
Even after all that expansion, it is still hunting for new commercial investments to absorb its excess profits.
But the capitalist road to a good education has not been smooth. 
In local legislatures, Chinese officials disapproved of schools putting so much time and effort into making money instead of teaching their subjects. 
Schools had no expertise in negotiating their way through business deals and obtaining raw-material supplies, and many people said that the education of an entire generation could be impaired if too much time was spent on commerce.
And if the businesses lost money, would school funds go to pay commercial debts?
Â 
No Rent, Low Taxes
In a Beijing suburb, for instance, a school-run store selling cosmetics, soft drinks and toys, lost so much money that instead of getting their monthly bonus in cash, teachers were given a monthly credit at the store. 
Everyone complained, and the manager was changed earlier this year.
Sanyuanli Xiaoli elementary school, in the eastern part of Beijing, sorely needs money. 
State education funds next year will mean a mere $54 per student at the school, so it hopes its appliance repair shop will make money.
But the shop appears to be a dumping ground for unpopular teachers. 
The manager is a retired teacher of agriculture who seems to spend more time napping than selling. 
Another salesman, who appeared drunk when a reporter dropped by recently, is a former gym teacher who was asked to switch to the business side.
Even so, the shop brings in about $30,000 a year, partly because it pays no rent, since the school owns the property, and partly because it hardly pays any taxes. 
The school's recently launched mail-order book company also brings in nearly tax-free profits.
Â 
Finding Foreign Capital
"It's hard for these enterprises not to make money," said a teacher in a Beijing school. 
"If they don't make money one year, they just shift to something else."
With a national economy growing at nearly 10 percent a year, and increasingly prosperous consumers searching for all kinds of new goods and services, most businesses do indeed seem to be making money. 
That is especially true if, like most school-run ventures, they pay no rent and are run by local managers instead of by huge conglomerates.
This year, the Government offered even more tax relief to schools to encourage them to make money. 
In some regions, local and business taxes are also waived. 
Such tax breaks also give schools an advantage in finding foreign joint-venture partners, a practice the Government has supported by giving swift approvals.
In Beijing there are 67 school-run joint ventures, more than double the number for the year before, according to the State Education Commission.
Â 
Intellectuals and Merchants
"Of course there will be some schools that do better than others," said Wang Xiaoqing, a senior official at the Education Commission. 
"But this also follows the trend of the entire nation."
Mr. Wang and other teachers say the schools will not be hurt by commerce because the enterprises are small and flexible and can respond quickly to the market.
Moreover, the businesses are not staffed by students or regular teachers, and they are supposed to abide by guidelines to maintain their license. 
Instead, some teaching staff are detached from their regular academic responsibilities to run or supervise the businesses.
In China, intellectuals still turn up their noses at merchants, so that teachers say they do not fear a wholesale abandonment of educational standards.
"It took a while for me to get adjusted because, well, traditionally Confucius simply does not think highly of commerce," said Yang Jiajian, a 46-year-old history teacher who is now running Fuxing Middle School's successful clothing store. 
"Most teachers don't want to go into business. 
It's not easy to do and you have to have the gall to chase after money."
"Me?" he continued. 
"I still prefer to be called Teacher Yang."

It is hard to believe that CHINA MOUNTAIN ZHANG (Tom Doherty/Tor, $19) by Maureen F. McHugh is a first novel. 
The author, who has spent several years teaching in China, has imagined a 22d century unlike any other I have read about. 
It is full of believable details and surprises. 
What makes it so fresh is that it feels so ordinary. 
There is no trick to inventing an exotic future; what is difficult is to make the exotic sound familiar -- so that the people of the future inhabit a world that, however different from the reader's, appears every bit as real.
Ms. McHugh's 22d century is dominated by China; the United States, after undergoing a socialist revolution, has apparently settled down with only minor grumbling to play its assigned role as a secondary power. 
The main character, who lends his name to the book, is an "ABC" -- American-born Chinese -- which places him far above all non-Asians on the social ladder but far below the Chinese-born, who get all the good jobs even though everyone is theoretically equal. 
Zhang is smart, nonpolitical, good company and a good friend. 
He also has two secrets that he wisely keeps from the authorities: his mother is Hispanic (not good for his social standing) and he is gay (even worse).
Let me quickly add that "China Mountain Zhang" is not a book about racism or homosexuality. 
These facts of life are simply built into the world that Ms. McHugh unfolds for us, along with the triumph of a highly pragmatic socialism and the manned kites that race, for money and fame, in the dark night sky above a much altered New York City. 
The plot takes Zhang, who is 26 years old when the book begins, from New York to the Arctic Circle to China and back to New York. 
Each setting is beautifully realized, and the futuristic touches, while sparing, are entirely convincing. 
Besides the kite races, I especially liked the computer-assisted design technique called "daoist engineering" and the fact that no one in Zhang's New York ever worries about getting mugged on the subway. 
There is also a beautifully realized subplot about settlers on Mars, a woman alone and a man with a small daughter, who unexpectedly find that they are good for each other.
However, the focus never strays far from Zhang, even when other narrators take over; everything that happens touches his life in oblique but consequential ways. 
Ms. McHugh has chosen her protagonist well: Zhang is just enough of an insider to get beneath the skin of his society and just enough of an outsider to question what he finds there. 
A first novel this good gives every reader a chance to share in the pleasure of discovery; to my mind, Ms. McHugh's achievement recalls the best works of Samuel R. Delany and Kim Stanley Robinson, without being in the least derivative.
Indefatigable is the word for Orson Scott Card. 
His latest novel, THE MEMORY OF EARTH (Tom Doherty/Tor, $21.95), bears the subtitle "Homecoming, Volume One."
His publishers inform us that this is the first of a five-book series, which Mr. Card is beginning even before he finishes two other multivolume series (including his ambitious "Ender" saga). 
Some science fiction series are simply accretions of novels tied together by common characters or settings. 
But Mr. Card's "Ender" books form one long philosophical rumination on the question of whether taking life can ever be morally justified. 
"The Memory of Earth" poses the same question in the context of a planetary civilization, 40 million years in the future, that has been preserved in a kind of stasis by a nearly omniscient global computer.
Having kept the peace for millions of years by preventing its wards from developing destructive technology, the artificial intelligence known as the Oversoul realizes that it is breaking down, losing control over its own functions and over the human beings on the planet Harmony; to save the people and the planet, it decides to return to Earth to seek help from the artificial intelligence that created it. 
To assist it in this enterprise the Oversoul recruits members of a large extended family; it communicates with its chosen servants by stimulating visions of one kind or another in their brains. 
Some sacrifices are necessary; before the world-saving can even begin, a 14-year old boy named Nafai, through whose eyes we follow the story, is asked to kill a man in cold blood.
Mr. Card handles the biblical parallels with circumspection; the city-state of Basilica, where Nafai and his family live, is divided between matriarchal and patriarchal spheres, and the odd technological survivals that the Oversoul permits are constant reminders that while history may repeat itself, no one is a slave to the past. 
As always, Mr. Card writes with energy and conviction about agonizing moral problems, but I had the sense that this book would have profited from one more run through the word processor: some scenes go on long after their point is made; others feel sketchy and schematic, as if the author himself were eager to get to Earth and unlock the mysteries hidden there. 
Which, of course, is what sequels are for.
LORD KELVIN'S MACHINE (Arkham House, $19.95) by James P. Blaylock is an example of a new subgenre with the unfortunate label "steampunk."
Cyberpunk, as everyone surely knows by now, is fast-paced, technologically oriented fiction in which computers play a dominant role. 
Steampunk is cyberpunk set in the age of steam. 
The definitive steampunk work is "The Difference Engine" by William Gibson and Bruce Sterling, which takes place in an alternative 1855 when steam-driven cybernetic "engines" have brought the computer age to England a century early.
The machine of Mr. Blaylock's imaginings is far less interesting. 
Although it is capable of reversing the earth's magnetic field and traveling through time, neither it nor the large cast of characters who try to turn it to their purposes make much of an impact on their world, which is a sodden pastiche of Victorian England. 
"Lord Kelvin's Machine" (a sequel to Mr. Blaylock's "Homunculus") is full of intrepid derring-do and nefarious goings-on that pit the forces of good (led by the inventor- explorer Langdon St. Ives) against the forces of evil (led by the hunchbacked Dr. Ignacio Narbondo). 
But instead of building toward a climax, each confrontation has the effect of canceling out the previous one, so that the book seems to erase itself as it goes along, leaving behind a vaguely unpleasant aftertaste. 
The uses of the past are many, but journeying back in time in order to create villains whose evil is palpable in their physical deformities and funny-sounding foreign names seems regressive in more ways than one.

A team of Canadian, Chinese and French geologists has concluded that during the past 50 million years, the collision of India with Asia pushed Indochina more than 300 miles to the southeast and rotated it clockwise. 
This, they suspect, swung Vietnam more than 400 miles away from China, forming the South China Sea.
They have also identified the fault in the earth's crust along which this motion took place. 
It is a belt of severely altered rocks more than 600 miles long, from Tibet to the Gulf of Tonkin. 
The Red River, which flows from China across Vietnam into the gulf, follows this zone. 
This motion, the authors believe, also explains why mountain ranges along this river lie in the same northwest-southeast direction. 
This contrasts with the orientation of the Himalayas, which is more to the east and west.
According to this hypothesis, the northward pressure of India has severely squeezed Indochina, forcing it to slip southeast relative to the land farther north. 
The proposal is advanced in the Feb. 
1 issue of the journal Nature by a team that has been studying the geology of China and Southeast Asia for several years. 
They are associated with the Institute for the Physics of the Globe in Paris, the University of Quebec and the Institute of Geology in Beijing.

text:

Only when the sun goes down do they dare to congregate, and even then they speak in hushed voices as they discuss their plans to develop an underground movement for greater democracy.
Now there are no loudspeakers, printing presses or financial contributions, as there were in the flowering days of May. 
Only seven men remain of the hundreds of people who once were active in a workers' union that pressed for greater democracy.
They meet secretly, in considerable danger, and scribble their appeals for change on crackly, cheap pieces of paper and wait until twilight before they furtively paste up the messages on lampposts and signboards. 
They almost never say the name of their organization, the Workers' Autonomous Union, in public.
'Furious and Frustrated'
''You don't understand what it's like to live here in China,'' the union member said to a visitor. 
''Why do we keep pushing for democracy, even when we risk arrests?
We are furious and frustrated. 
The Communist Party and the Government is so corrupt, and yet it controls us all so completely. 
The officials skim off the country's money and there's hardly anything left for the workers.''
The group decided, after much discussion, to contact a foreign reporter to tell the world that their struggle for democracy was continuing, and to solicit assistance from foreigners, especially people on Taiwan.
So far the union's activities have been scarcely noticeable in Beijing, but if it is able to attract more participants and form a small underground organization, it could become a more significant embarrassment and nuisance for the Government. 
The union spokesman disclaimed any involvement in periodic attacks by snipers against the martial law soldiers who patrol the streets in Beijing. 
However, diplomats do not rule out the possibility of the formation of a sometimes-violent underground resistance to the authorities, and the union could become the core of such an organization.
Â 
Speaking Among Friends
''Do foreigners know what happened?'' the spokesman asked. 
Then, he abruptly proceeded to describe how he saw a young woman and two men killed just south of Tiananmen Square in the early hours of June 4, when the Chinese Army suppressed the democracy movement in Beijing.
''We are still continuing our fight for democracy,'' said the spokesman. 
''There is no democracy in China. 
We have so little choice in our lives here. 
The Government and the Party decide where we work, where we live, how many children we can have and when.''
They discuss democracy among their close friends, but not a word with fellow workers. 
The spokesman refused to divulge even the regularity of their gatherings, let alone the location.
Each of them has been writing essays on democracy and posting them in alleyways, residential lanes and occasionally on major streets throughout the city. 
At their meetings, they debate how to spread their message. 
At times they despair that their voice will not be heard.
Â 
Less Repression Than Feared
While martial law and the current political atmosphere have severely hampered their activities, they believe the repression may not be as severe as they had anticipated two months ago.
''I went to Tiananmen Square many times,'' the union member said. 
''I gave many speeches and I must have been filmed many times, but they haven't arrested me, have they?''
Some workers, he noted, had only been detained for interrogation, particularly about leaders of the union, and then released.
The group believes there have been about 40 arrests and detentions of members belonging to their unofficial, loosely formed union that had begun to expand its network throughout the city during May. 
The number, however, may be wrong because they have not been able to contact many colleagues. 
Some may have been arrested secretly, and some of those who they think were arrested may actually be in hiding.
Â 
Few Recent Court Sentences
Many workers and intellectuals who had been outspoken during the may protests have been frightened about being jailed or dismissed from their jobs if their role in the demonstrations were discovered. 
The Government has announced the execution of 12 people so far in connection with the turmoil, and nearly all of them have been workers.
Few additional court sentences have been announced since then, but the television images of people being sentenced to death still chill many workers.
''Many people are afraid to come out, but we know they support us,'' the worker said.

text:

Responding to China's human rights record, soaring trade surplus and continued arms exports to the Middle East, the Senate voted today to impose conditions on the renewal of China's favorable trade status with the United States in June.
The vote sends the legislation to President Bush after nearly three years of political maneuvering. 
The Administration has repeatedly threatened to veto the legislation, and the 59-to-39 vote today fell 8 votes short of the two-thirds majority that would be needed to override a veto if all senators voted. 
But the margin was wider than in last summer's vote on the same issue, when the Democrats also prevailed, 55 to 44.
The bill, a compromise between separate measures approved by the House and Senate last year, is the first penalizing China's growing exports to emerge from Congress since Beijing'scrackdown on dissent in 1989.
It would condition the renewal of China's most-favored-nation trade status on the Chinese Government's accounting for and releasing from prison all citizens accused of expressing their political beliefs nonviolently. 
It would also require as a condition of renewal that the President certify to Congress that China has made substantial progress in observing human rights, opening its markets to American goods and curbing exports of missile and nuclear technology.
The Senate's Democratic leadership insisted on the vote today to force the President and Republicans into the politically awkward position of publicly supporting the Chinese Government in an election year.
Several senators who changed their votes cited concerns about Chinese arms exports. 
Among them was Senator Jim Exon, a Nebraska Democrat who voted against the legislation last summer because he feared that China might retaliate against American corn exports. 
He said he voted in favor today because a recent Central Intelligence Agency report made him worry that China sought to replace the former Soviet Union as a superpower and the United States' leading adversary.
Arms exports are "the way you get to be a superpower," he said in an interview after the vote. 
"You surround yourself with a lot of your supporters, you give them a lot of nuclear armaments and then you become Mr. Big."
Senator George J. Mitchell of Maine, the majority leader and chief sponsor of today's bill, also cited China's occupation of Tibet and its $12.69 billion trade surplus with the United States last year, the second largest surplus after Japan's. 
Ten conservative Republican senators voted for the bill.
Â 
Five Democrats Vote No
Only five Democrats, all from farm states, crossed party lines to support the Administration. 
Their leader, Senator Max Baucus, the Montana Democrat who heads the Subcommittee on International Trade, said he supported the use of existing trade laws against specific Chinese exports.
Supporting the bill "is the politically easier course to take," he said. 
"It's easier to beat up on the Chinese and, for some Democrats, to beat up on the President in an election year."
The Administration lost today's vote despite weeks of strenuous lobbying to persuade Republican senators to vote with it. 
That effort concluded today with Republican senators meeting over lunch with Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d and Brent Scowcroft, the national security adviser.

text:

The Senate voted today to impose conditions on trade relations with China, but sponsors of the legislation failed to muster the two-thirds majority needed to overcome a likely Presidential veto. 
As a result, the day's action was a victory for the Bush Administration.
The 55-to-44 vote for trade restrictions was a setback for the Senate Democratic leadership. 
The legislation was sponsored by Senator George J. Mitchell, Democrat of Maine, the Senate majority leader.
The bill would attach conditions to any renewal of China's most-favored-nation trade status, as of next July, but would allow the President's recent renewal of the low tariffs to continue until then. 
The conditions would include an end to certain Chinese arms sales, the release of some political prisoners, and a halt in exports of products produced by prison labor to the United States.
Â 
Some Cross Party Lines
The Administration prevailed by retaining the support of 37 Republicans and persuading 7 Democrats from farm states to cross party lines. 
Only 6 Republicans voted against the Administration, led by Senator Jesse Helms, Republican of North Carolina, whose state has been particularly affected by a surge in textile imports from China.
Mr. Helms criticized China's human rights record and asserted that China continued to export products to the United States that were made with prison labor, a violation of American law. 
"For more than 40 years, these leaders have maintained themselves in power by the same means," he said.
Senator Bob Dole of Kansas, the Senate minority leader, said the 55-to-44 vote insured that a Bush veto would not be overridden. 
"This legislation is not going to become law," he said.
Â 
What the Status Does
The term "most favored nation" is a trade term that actually applies to almost all United States trading partners, including Iraq and Libya. 
Countries awarded this status ship goods to the United States at the lowest tariffs available for each category of import.
The House of Representatives voted two weeks ago to pass a similar bill. 
The House vote was 313 to 112, more than the two-thirds majority needed to override a Presidential veto. 
The bills must now be reconciled in a conference attended by members of both houses of Congress. 
The legislation will then go to President Bush, whose advisers say they will recommend a veto of any bill not providing for unconditional renewal of China's trade status.
As recently as two weeks ago, the Administration was still unsure whether it could muster the 34 votes needed to give it a strong chance of sustaining a veto. 
China's opponents and advocates alike focused their lobbying efforts on the Senate as the key battleground.
The Administration stressed party loyalty in a last-minute lobbying blitz and made limited concessions to fence-sitting Democrats and Republicans.
The Administration said it would back Taiwan's application to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, a move calculated to win support from anti-Communist lawmakers and free-trade advocates. 
The Administration said it would take legal action against Chinese import barriers if negotiations did not yield results in several months.
A combination of heavy lobbying and a package of limited concessions sent to Congress on Friday helped the Administration win a dozen or more votes in the last week. 
Business interests, led by grain and aircraft exporters and textile importers, joined the Administration in its successful lobbying effort over the last several weeks.
China was the largest importer of wheat from the United States last year. 
Grain exporters estimated that if China halted those imports in retaliation for action by the Congress, wheat prices could fall by 10 percent.
A group of mostly farm-state senators led by Senator Max S. Baucus, Democrat of Montana, chairman of the Senate subcommittee on international trade, sent a letter to President Bush on June 19 asking for concessions in exchange for their support. 
The President made some of the concessions but did not outline new initiatives on human rights or China's arms exports.
Senator Kent Conrad, Democrat of North Dakota, one of six Democrats to sign Mr. Baucus's letter, criticized the President's response today. 
"I found the President's response to be very weak," he said.
But Mr. Conrad said in the debate that he would still vote against the bill because modifying China's trade status was not an appropriate way to respond to address his concerns about China's record on human rights.
Mr. Baucus said the question facing Congress was how much China could be pushed to change its practices without persuading its leaders that the changes were impossible or involved an unacceptable loss of face. 
The conditions in Mr. Mitchell's bill are so extensive that Chinese leaders would rather cut themselves off from the United States than comply, Mr. Baucus said.
Backing Mr. Mitchell was an eclectic alliance of anti-Communists, human rights advocates and protectionists. 
Senator Donald W. Riegle, Democrat of Michigan, was one of several senators who focused on the growth in China's trade surplus with the United States, which reached $10.3 billion last year.
But Senator Lloyd M. Bentsen, Democrat of Texas, the chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, posed the same question as Mr. Baucus and reached a different answer. 
Recent changes in the Soviet Union, particularly a huge increase in emigration, show that conditions can foster change in Communist countries, he said.
Senator Dale Bumpers, Democrat of Arkansas, assailed the decision of the Chinese leadership to use force against demonstrators in and near Tiananmen Square in June 1989. 
Instead of arresting demonstrators, he said, "They chose to start mowing them down with guns and machine guns."
Before the final vote, the Senate added four amendments to Senator Mitchell's bill that made Chinese compliance more difficult. 
These amendments made it harder for Mr. Mitchell to gather votes.
An amendment introduced late in the evening by Senator Bentsen modified a provision in Senator Mitchell's bill that would have canceled the trade status immediately if China exported certain arms at any time in the coming year. 
The cancellation would instead take effect on July 3, 1992.
The amendment was a last-minute bid to soften the language of Senator Mitchell's bill and win support for it.
