file: Students Find U.S. Embassy a Barrier.txt
text:
ï»¿
In his news conference on Wednesday, President Bush pleaded with Congress not to ease the visa rules for Chinese students now in the United States. 
One of his arguments was that the action might lead China to cut back on future programs of study abroad, which he characterized as an important force for change in China.
Many students here share his concern. 
But their more immediate problem is that they cannot persuade the United States Embassy to grant them a visa.
'Making Life Difficult'
"Your consular section is making life difficult for some of these students," said Wu Ningkun, an American-educated professor of English at the Institute of International Relations in Beijing.
As an example, Professor Wu cited a distant relative, an engineer in his early 30's who had been accepted by an American university to study advanced engineering. 
An overseas relative agreed to provide financial support, and the young man resigned his job in order to get Government permission to leave.
He then applied for a United States visa and, since he was willing to leave his wife and child behind, thought he could show that he would return. 
But last month, his application was rejected, probably because the consular officer doubted that the relative would really provide all the money necessary.
Others also share their frustrations: a young man who was not allowed to go to the United States to visit his wife, who was studying there; a successful artist who was not allowed to take up a visiting position at an American university; a journalist with dissident connections who was denied a visa to attend the business school to which she had been accepted. 
Dreams are dashed each day at the United States Embassy, and because applicants have sometimes had to give up their jobs, they now find themselves with neither visas nor any means of support.
Â 
Proportion of Rejections Rises
While many Chinese focus on the number who are rejected, the Embassy and the American consulates elsewhere in China grant visas to more than 12,000 people each year to go to America to study. 
Since the military crackdown in June, the number of applications has risen by more than 60 percent. 
Some 7,000 Chinese students have gone to the United States to study since June.
In the early 1980's, it was difficult for Chinese to get passports and exit permits, and so most of those who did were granted American visas. 
But in the last few years, the Chinese made it much easier for people to go abroad, and so the American Embassy began to scrutinize applications and reject a larger proportion of applicants.
"The Chinese Government is very clever," said a young writer who is hoping to begin a graduate program in the United States in the fall. 
"They give almost everyone a passport now and let the Americans do the tight screening for them so they don't get the blame."
About half of those seeking visas to study in the United States are now rejected, because they cannot meet at least one of the three principal criteria for visas: that they be well qualified for the program they have chosen, that they have the necessary financial resources and that they intend to return upon graduation.
"Everybody gets the visa who convinces us they're qualified under U.S. law," said Karen Clark Stanton, consul at the Embassy here. 
Backlog on Immigration Visas
Some diplomats say that if the United States did open its gates, hundreds of thousands probably would seek to go. 
As it is, more than 82,000 Chinese have applied for immigrant visas at the American consulate in Canton, which handles those visas. 
At the current rate, someone applying now for an immigrant visa would have to wait for up to 21 years simply to have the case decided.
Some American diplomats admit privately that they are deeply uneasy with their role in destroying the dreams of those who want to go abroad. 
But they say that somebody has to be gatekeeper and that in any case they are only following American law. 
The burden of proof is on the visa applicant to show an intention to return to China, and these days many students find it difficult to sound sincere or enthusiastic when talking about coming back. 
Indeed, some Chinese, at the same time that they complain about the strictness of the Embassy, explain in the next breath that their dreams of starting a new life in America are now dashed.
"We are seeing privately sponsored people who feel that the Embassy rather than the Public Security Bureau is the greatest obstacle to getting to America," said Lee Travers, a program officer at the Beijing office of the Ford Foundation, which has not had difficulty getting visas for the scholars it sponsors. 
"However, it's also true that in those rejections I know about, consular officers have probably accurately predicted who does not want to return to China."

file: SUMMIT AT THE U.N._Bush Asks Security Council To Put Sanctions on Libya.txt
text:
ï»¿
In meetings with members of the United Nations Security Council, President Bush sought today to shore up support for a new resolution imposing sanctions on Libya for its refusal to extradite two suspects in the 1988 bombing of Pan Am 103 for trial in the United States, Administration officials said.
In his meetings at the United Nations, Mr. Bush spent 20 minutes with Prime Minister Li Peng of China, the first meeting between the leaders in nearly three years.
With the Administration facing another fight with Congress over the extension of China's trading privileges, Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d said Mr. Bush had told Mr. Li that the Chinese record on human rights was "insufficient" and needed "significant improvement."
Â 
Response 'Not Acceptable'
But Mr. Baker indicated that Mr. Li had merely dismissed Mr. Bush's concerns by saying that China did not accept the idea that its record on human rights can be judged by other countries' standards, a position that is increasingly likely to result in Congress's placing conditions on favorable tariff treatment for Beijing.
Mr. Baker said Mr. Li's response was "not acceptable under our standards."
Mr. Li's address to the Security Council earlier, which made the same point on human rights, offered little comfort to American officials.
Earlier today, Mr. Baker said Mr. Bush and President Francois Mitterrand of France, who met this morning at the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel, had discussed the wording of the proposed new resolution against Libya, which American officials said was being drafted and could be presented in early February.
The United States wants the resolution to go beyond merely condemning Libya for not complying with a resolution passed unanimously by the Security Council on Jan. 
21 demanding that the two suspects in the 1988 bombing over Lockerbie, Scotland, be surrendered.
"Terrorists and their state sponsors must know there will be serious consequences if they violate international law," Mr. Bush said in an address to a summit meeting of the 15 Security Council nations, seeking to link the Western standoff with Libya to the Council's concerted action against Iraq after it invaded Kuwait.
The Bush Administration wants some sort of sanctions imposed against Libya, at a minimum an embargo on airline flights to and from Libya and on sales of aircraft parts, officials said. 
"There's not much support at the Security Council for more than that," one official said today.
Â 
Policy Produces Little
Although Mr. Bush pressed Mr. Li to improve China's human rights record, American officials said Mr. Bush had already concluded that the current leadership in China is unlikely to do that.
They conceded that his policy of "engagement" with Beijing since the nationwide crackdown on dissent in China in 1989 has produced little in the way of results.
Still, the officials said, Mr. Bush is likely to veto any measure by Congress that would attach conditions to the extension of China's most-favored-nation tariff treatment. 
Such legislation could be passed as early as next week.
In this political climate, officials said, Mr. Bush hoped primarily to get through the meeting, which the Chinese requested, with as little embarrassment as possible.
"It was our judgment that we had to do this meeting and we're trying to do it with as little attention as possible," a senior official said.
Â 
Preparing for Yeltsin Meeting
While Mr. Bush met with his fellow leaders in New York, the Administration was preparing for the meeting at Camp David on Saturday with President Boris N. Yeltsin of Russia.
Officials traveling with Mr. Bush said the two were expected to announce a date for a formal summit meeting sometime between April and July. 
One said an earlier date seemed the likeliest possibility.
But American officials said arms control was not at the top of either leader's list of issues for their first meeting since the disintegration of the Soviet Union and the emergence of Russia as the successor to the old Soviet state.
Mr. Bush is eager, however, to get more details from Mr. Yeltsin on his recent arms control proposal.
The Russian leader's plan was a response to Mr. Bush's suggestion that both sides eliminate land-based multiple-warhead missiles -- the heart of Russia's deterrent force -- in exchange for a one-third cut in the number of nuclear bombs the United States keeps aboard submarines.
Mr. Yeltsin replied by calling for even deeper cuts than Mr. Bush suggested, and by proposing that the United States abandon its "Star Wars" antimissile program in favor of a global network to protect against missile attack.
The Bush Administration's initial response to that proposal was cool.
Because the two proposals remain inchoate and because the United States is still unclear about Mr. Yeltsin's arms control philosophies and the depth of his knowledge and engagement on the issue, the two leaders are expected to confine their pronouncements on nuclear disarmament to a vague commitment to "continue the process."
"Bush expects most of the discussion tomorrow will be on economic reform," a senior official said in New York.

file: Taipei Journal_Castaway From China Lands in Trouble in Taiwan.txt
text:
ï»¿
Seven years ago, Hou Dejian, a Taiwan-born folk singer, defected from here to mainland China on a quest for the meaning of life. 
In June, the Chinese authorities put him on a Taiwan-bound fishing boat, and now, like a refugee, he feels uneasy in both lands.
It was a strange homecoming: Mr. Hou went from detention in China to arrest in Taiwan, from being one of the most daring and outspoken dissidents in China to facing charges of illegal entry to Taiwan by fishing boat.
Chinese policeman flew Mr. Hou to Fujian Province in southern China, took him out to sea and then, when they came upon a fishing boat, ordered the Taiwanese fisherman to take him to Taiwan. 
Mr. Hou sat crouched for about 50 hours at the bottom of the boat, lost 10 pounds from his already lean frame, and had to be fed intravenously for three days after he arrived in Taipei.
After fame in China for his role in the democracy movement last year, Mr. Hou is facing a measure of notoriety back home. 
Rather than hear about his heroic deeds in China, the people here want to know why he left Taiwan in the first place. 
To many of them, Mr. Hou chose to live in the wrong China, and returned only because China no longer wanted him.
Â 
'They Don't Understand Me'
''When I returned, they said I had betrayed Taiwan,'' the 33-year-old Mr. Hou said in an interview. 
''They don't understand me.''
Mr. Hou, who is living at home while awaiting the Government's decision on his illegal entry, has admitted publicly that he now seeks an Australian passport and does not plan to stay long in Taiwan. 
He says that his calling is still to fight for human rights in China and that he feels uncomfortable waging his battle from Taiwan, whose ties with the mainland are slowly warming.
His latest music, whose Chinese lyrics often have political overtones, is not well known in Taiwan, but he says he plans to record tapes in both Chinese and English. 
While his music was relatively popular in China, his reputation grew from his involvement in the democracy movement, when he negotiated with the soldiers to allow students to leave Tiananmen Square in the early hours of June 4, 1989.
After the crackdown, he fled to the Australian Embassy, only to come out more than two months later and support the Government version of the events of that night. 
Mr. Hou was criticized by students for fleeing to the embassy rather than face jail - criticism that is being repeated now by Taiwan people.
Â 
How He Was Deported
But Mr. Hou became one of the few dissidents to continue speaking out against the Chinese Government, calling the leaders ''mad dogs'' and comparing the senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, to Nicolae Ceaucescu of Romania. 
He was taken into custody at the end of May, just before a news conference at which he planned to announce a petition to release political prisoners.
Mr. Hou says that on June 8 public security officials gave him two choices: he could go to prison in China or return to Taiwan. 
They added that they could expel him, but preferred that he write a letter asking to return to Taiwan, which he did. 
This way, they said, Mr. Hou could return to China at some later date.
Mr. Hou was kept inside a room of a suburban guest house during the 17 days of his detention, and was asked to write a self-criticism on 30 to 40 topics. 
This is a method Chinese authorities often use to alter the mind-set of prisoners. 
For the first 10 days, he said, the public security officials treated him rather amicably, telling him he had not committed any crime, but then they started threatening him, hinting that he could be sentenced to more than 15 years in jail.
After reading his long essays, they told him, ''You can never be reformed.''
They allowed him to collect $1,200 from his home and a few other belongings, then confiscated his telephone and more than 100 name cards of foreign friends.
Â 
'Peaceful Evolution' Is Goal
In Taipei, the anger against Mr. Hou is complicated by the fact that he left a wife and a baby in Taipei when he defected to China. 
In China, he took another wife, Cheng Lin, a famous singer; she left him to live in Paris with a well-known student leader, Wuer Kaixi, who escaped to France after the crackdown last year.
Not everyone criticizes him. 
''He is more advanced in his thinking than most people are,'' said a China-born woman who travels to Taiwan frequently on a foreign passport.
Mr. Hou still has his ideals. 
''My goal is peaceful evolution,'' he said, referring to a slow process of subversion of Communism, a policy the Chinese have accused the United States of using. 
''Even though the Chinese leaders hate that term, what they are doing, with their reform and open-door policy, is precisely peaceful evolution.''
And he hopes he can convince the Taiwan people that this is why he did not want to leave China at this moment. 
''I really wanted to continue being a noisemaker in China, which few other people can do these days there.''

file: TAIPEI JOURNAL_Taiwan Goes Fishing for Its Notion of Lost Souls.txt
text:
ï»¿
For nearly 40 years, defecting in a fighter plane was almost the only way for a citizen of China to visit Taiwan. 
These days Taiwan is cooling its invitation to pilots and instead is admitting private individuals from the mainland for the first time.
In December five mainland Chinese who are doctoral students in the United States became among the first officially sanctioned visitors, and their reactions have attracted great interest on both sides of the Taiwan Strait.
''Seeing is believing,'' one of the students, Qian Yingyi, wrote in a report published in a Shanghai newspaper. 
''Although our trip lasted only nine days and could give us only a superficial understanding, what we saw and heard was truly impressive.''
Here in Taiwan, people are patting themselves on the back after the students' favorable reaction - even smiling, with just a hint of condescension, at the mainlanders' observation that Taiwan residents drive like maniacs and that traffic signs ''are suggestions only.''
On the mainland, the first-hand observations are leading to embarrassing contrasts between the economic stagnation of China's socialist economy and the extraordinary vigor of Taiwan's capitalist economy.
Â 
'We're Open-Minded'
That is the effect that the visits are intended to have. 
James C. Y. Soong, the Deputy Secretary General of the Kuomintang, or Nationalist Party, said in an interview that visits by influential mainland figures are likely to do more to subvert Communism than the old strategy of hiring secret agents on the mainland.
''First we'll allow student groups,'' Mr. Soong said. 
''Then social leaders. 
We'll think about letting their reporters come here. 
We're open-minded.''
The mainlanders visiting Taiwan are enormously outnumbered by the Taiwan residents visiting the mainland. 
Since the fall of 1987, when Taiwan began to allow its citizens to visit the mainland, more than 400,000 have made the trip. 
Officially, Taiwan residents are allowed to go to the mainland only to visit relatives, but many also go to sightsee or even to do business.
Forty years after the Kuomintang was defeated on the mainland by the Communists and forced to flee to the island of Taiwan, it continues to assert that it is the legitimate government of all China. 
Officials remain deeply concerned that if the gates are opened too far, visitors from the mainland will turn out to be secret agents or will simply go into hiding and get good jobs. 
But almost everyone agrees that some mainlanders should be allowed to come.
Â 
Fate of 800 Taiwanese
Ma Yingjeou, a Cabinet member with special responsibilities for mainland relations, said the highest priority was to permit the return of native Taiwanese who were sent to the mainland to fight in the Chinese civil war but then became stranded after the Communist victory. 
Some 800 are still alive, and their names are now being checked to allow them to move back to Taiwan.
A few mainlanders have also been allowed to come to Taiwan to visit ill relatives, but the focus has been on mainland scholars and students. 
Selecting the right ones has been deemed so important that the former Secretary General of the Kuomintang traveled around the United States interviewing Chinese students interested in visiting Taiwan.
The Government still bans Communist Party members from visiting, but it is thinking of making exceptions. 
For example, Taiwan would like to welcome Fang Lizhi, an astrophysicist who is China's most outspoken proponent of democracy.
Mr. Fang, who was expelled in 1987 from the Communist Party, says he would like to go if China's Government allowed him to, but under present rules he would not be allowed to bring his wife, Li Shuxian. 
She is a Communist Party member, though a fierce critic of the party and of Marxism in general. 
Table Tennis, Anyone?
Taiwan is also thinking of inviting sports and cultural figures for exchanges. 
Table tennis, which played a role in the development of ties between China and the United States, may again be called upon to ease the tensions. 
China's Physical Culture and Sports Commission says Taipei has informally invited its team to play in exhibition matches, although no formal invitation has been announced so far.
Some mainlanders have not been waiting for permission. 
Instead, they have been paying fishermen the equivalent of about $2,000 to be dropped off on the Taiwan shore so they can try to find high-paying jobs.
Most of the illegal immigrants apparently work as manual laborers or, if they are women, occasionally as prostitutes. 
Because of rapid increases in Taiwan's living standard, employers have found it difficult to recruit local people in these occupations, and the illegal immigrants from the Philippines or Thailand who often fill these jobs are much more expensive than mainland immigrants.
No one knows how many mainlanders are now working illegally on Taiwan, but most estimates are in the hundreds. 
One mainlander who was discovered, Shi Longta, told reporters that he was one of 26 men who chartered a boat to Taiwan to earn extra money.
Mr. Shi, who worked in a plastics factory for less than a week before he was arrested, said it would be unfair to return him to the mainland. 
He said he was afraid to face both the Chinese Government and the friends and relatives who had paid for his trip.

file: Taipei Official Visits China Unofficially.txt
text:
ï»¿
Forty years after Communist forces sent China's Nationalist Government fleeing to Taiwan, Taiwan's Finance Minister today became the first Taiwan Government official to return.
While the Finance Minister, Shirley Kuo, has emphasized that she is here only to attend the annual meeting of the Asian Development Bank and that she will avoid political contacts with mainland officials, her presence behind what are technically enemy lines is the clearest sign so far of the easing of tensions across the Taiwan Strait.
The two onetime enemy Governments still do not recognize each other, but they stopped shelling each other a decade ago, and in the last 18 months contacts have multiplied frenetically.
Taiwan officials no longer refer to the ''Communist bandits,'' and hundreds and probably thousands of mainland peasants have sneaked into Taiwan to work illegally in its factories and brothels. 
Trade between Taiwan and the mainland via Hong Kong soared 80 percent last year to $2.8 billion, and on the mainland, ''Taiwan compatriots'' have invested more than $100 million and can now be seen wherever there is a sight to be seen or money to be made.
The New Look in Portraiture
Miss Kuo will sense the relaxed atmosphere when she visits Tiananmen Square in the center of the city. 
A gigantic portrait of Sun Yat-sen, who is honored by both sides, has been put up in the center of the square for the May Day celebration, but the traditional portraits of Stalin, Lenin, Marx and Engels were left off this year.
''This does not mean any change of political attitude toward Marxism,'' the official New China News Agency said today. 
It said that officials had decided that only national heroes would be honored, and noted that a portrait of Mao Zedong always hangs in a place of honor facing Tiananmen Square.
In a news conference late this afternoon, Miss Kuo announced that the Taiwan delegation would attend the opening ceremony of the development bank meeting. 
Miss Kuo had been expected to stay away, partly to avoid contact with President Yang Shangkun of China, who will apparently attend the opening session.
The opening session may be particularly interesting this year because it has long been scheduled to take place May 4 in the Great Hall of the People, facing Tiananmen Square. 
That date is also the 70th anniversary of famous Chinese nationalist demonstrations that began in Tiananmen Square, and this year students from throughout the capital are talking about a major rally for democracy in the square to mark the anniversary.
Beijing's last big march tied up traffic throughout the city, but if delegates did succeed in getting to the Great Hall of the People on May 4, it would presumably be an embarrassment for the Government to have its foreign guests witness another mass rally.
Â 
Other Signs of Easing Tension
Miss Kuo's arrival here today is the boldest move in a string of recent changes in Taiwan's policy toward the mainland. 
Last month, Taiwan announced that it would allow its reporters to visit the mainland on business, whereas previously reporters could get permission to visit the mainland only on the pretext of visiting relatives here.
More than 40 Taiwan journalists are here to cover Miss Kuo's visit. 
Even Nationalist-owned news organizations have sent reporters.
Last month Taiwan also allowed its first sports team, a squad of young gymnasts, to compete in a mainland competition and announced that direct telecommunications links would be open soon. 
At the moment such links are banned by Taiwan, although it is possible for people on the mainland to telephone or telex people on Taiwan.
Taiwan's Justice Minister, Hsiao Tien-tzang, even suggested that Taipei might give up its goal of recovering the mainland, if Beijing acknowledged that the Nationalists were an equally legitimate government of China, with sovereignty over Taiwan. 
Communist officials rejected that proposal.
South Korea's Finance Minister, Lee Kyu Sung, is also scheduled to attend the development bank conference, making him the first South Korean Cabinet minister to visit China.

file: Taiwan Ends Emergency Decree, Opening Way to Closer China Ties.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Lee Teng-hui declared an end to 43 years of emergency rule today, paving the way for greater democracy on the island and closer relations with China.
Mr. Lee took a symbolic step toward reconciliation with Beijing by ending the "Period of Communist Rebellion," a decree issued by the Nationalist Government a year before it lost the Chinese civil war and fled to Taiwan in 1949.
Emergency constitutional provisions under the decree blocked Taiwan's progress toward democracy by freezing in place hundreds of parliamentary deputies elected in mainland China in 1947.
"This will set in place the foundation for the future development of our country," Mr. Lee said at a news conference at the presidential office.
Â 
'Authorities' in Beijing
He said Taipei would now regard the Chinese Communists as "authorities," rather than merely as a "rebel organization," and reiterated his pledge not to use force to reunify China.
"From now on, we must accept the reality that the Communists control the mainland," Mr. Lee said.
He stopped short of declaring an end to the formal state of war that has existed between the two sides since 1949, or abandoning the Nationalists' claim to be the sole legitimate government of China.
Further improvement in ties would depend on Beijing's renouncing the use of force against Taiwan and allowing the island to join international organizations and establish links with foreign governments, President Lee said.
"If the Communists create military tension between us, or continue to fight us in the diplomatic arena, we will continue to view them as a hostile entity," he said.
Mr. Lee vowed to work toward the reunification of China, which both sides say they want, by encouraging cultural exchanges and unofficial contacts. 
A delegation from Taiwan is currently visiting Beijing to open up a channel for dialogue.
Links with China have grown rapidly since the late 1980's, when Taipei eased a ban on travel to the mainland by the island's 20 million people.
Tens of thousands of Taiwan residents have visited China and economic ties have blossomed, though Taipei insists trade and investment occur indirectly through third countries.
The aging deputies of Taiwan's National Assembly approved Mr. Lee's initial package of democratic changes last week, voting to rescind the emergency constitutional provisions and to authorize elections to the three chambers of Parliament.
All deputies representing constituencies on the mainland must retire by the end of this year, and most members of the new Parliament will for the first time represent areas in Taiwan. 
A minority of "mainland" seats will be retained to back Taipei's claim to sovereignty in China.
Passage of the changes set off brawls in Parliament and a 15-hour demonstration by about 10,000 supporters of the main opposition Democratic Progressive Party, which says the Nationalists are not sincere about full democratic change.
The new National Assembly, to be elected at the end of this year, will debate further changes like direct election of the President. 
The opposition has said the Nationalists aim to include undemocratic safeguards for their power.
Taiwan has been moving toward democracy since 1987, when it lifted martial law. 
After Mr. Lee took power in January 1988, the Nationalists allowed new political parties and considerable press freedom.
Most people say they believe the governing party's iron grip on political patronage, and its success in managing Taiwan's dynamic economic growth over the last four decades, mean the opposition will not pose a serious challenge for years.

file: Taiwan Envoys Seeking Access on Mainland.txt
text:
ï»¿
Taiwan legislators are slipping into mainland China these days, touting their political influence in hopes of meeting with the highest-ranking Chinese leaders possible, and carrying back messages they believe will play a role in the quiet diplomacy that is taking place across the Taiwan Strait.
The visits are only one way that the barriers between Taiwan and the Chinese mainland are breaking down -- not so dramatically as the destruction of the Berlin wall, but with scarcely less significance for this region.The four-decade ban by Taiwan on official contacts with mainland Chinese authorities is eroding, under the pressure of the legislators' visits and as well as joint meetings on repatriation of illegal immigrants from the mainland. 
Last month, Red Cross officials from Taiwan and China met secretly on Quemoy, an island administered by Taiwan off the coast of southern China, to negotiate repatriation of Chinese refugees who had fled to Taiwan. 
The news came out after the talks ended.
"Now there's a race to see who can meet the highest-level officials," said David J. W. Wang, a law professor atChinese Culture University. 
Mr. Wang accompanied a legislator to the mainland in August.
Taiwan opened its gates in 1987 and allowed its citizens to travel to the mainland, and since then, the contacts have expanded to included direct telephone calls, faxes and even some trade to the mainland.
In a step that could conceivably lead someday to two-way negotiations, the Government this month formed a Mainland Affairs Council to monitor cultural and commercial exchanges across the Strait. 
The council may also set up a subsidiary organization that could play a role in negotiating affairsbetween mainland China and Taiwan, and perhaps establish a branch in China.
Such a branch could help protect the interests of Taiwan citizens on the mainland. 
When 30 Taiwan travelers were killed on Oct. 
2 on a plane crash in Canton, travel agencies and private lawyers helped negotiate for information and compensation on behalf of Taiwan citizens. 
The Taiwan Government did not get involved.
Still, the plane crash and an increasing number of personal experiences have checked the "mainland fever."
Take the case of a young woman from Jiayi, a Taiwanese city, who visited the mainland this month with her father, and took a four-day bus ride to her ancestral hometown in a remote part of Anhui province.
"I didn't dare eat the food and my father had to explain to them that he and I are very light eaters," she said, relieved to be on her way back to Taiwan. 
"I couldn't take it in the village for more than two days."
Public opinion toward China was also jolted a few weeks ago, when Chinese officials blocked Taiwan's application to act as host for the 1998 Asian Games. 
The action was seen almost as a betrayal, because hundreds of Taiwan athletes and officials had enthusiastically traveled to Beijing to take part in the 1990 Asian Games.
Thousands of business executives are still flocking to China to build factories with cheap labor, but there is also a growing awareness that many of those ventures are not as successful as people had hoped. 
One report indicated that 40 percent of Taiwan operations on the mainland are losing money.The Taiwan Government is also playing a role in lowering the "mainland fever," for fear that Taiwan will become vulnerable, even hostage, to the mainland.
"That's why we want to reduce the temperature," said Ma Ying-jeou, who heads a commission on relations with mainland China.
In July, Saudi Arabia cut off ties with Taiwan to establish diplomatic links with China, and Taiwan's ally, South Korea, is setting up a commercial office in China. 
Beijing has also stalled Taiwan's application to join the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
"The Chinese authorities use isolation tactics to suffocate whatever room we have internationally," Mr. Ma said. 
"They want to cut off our international ties, hoping we would embrace the motherland."

file: Taiwan Opposition Pushes for Independence.txt
text:
ï»¿
Picking up on the fragmenting of the Soviet empire, Taiwan's opposition party is voicing the official heresy that Taiwan should not worry about reuniting with the Chinese mainland, but should forge an independent future.
"If the three Baltic republics can become independent, why can't Taiwan?" a legislator from the opposition Democratic Progressive Party, Hong Chichang, asked. 
"Taiwan is economically more powerful than they are, it has more people, and it has a military. 
If Taiwan is stronger than they are and China is weaker than the Soviet Union, then why can't Taiwan submit a vote to the people to declare independence?"
Since they fled here from the mainland 42 years ago, the Nationalist leaders have perpetuated the dream that they still are the legitimate rulers of all China, including Taiwan. 
But with China's turning a blind eye to the worldwide trend against socialism, even the leaders here acknowledge that reunification with the mainland under a capitalist system would probably have to wait some time.
The debate over independence is intensifying, as campaigning for elections in December starts. 
Nearly two-thirds of the seats in the National Assembly, which has been dominated by aging officials elected on the mainland for 40 years, will be contested in the elections, and the politicians, some too weak to attend sessions, are being forced to retire.
"In the upcoming election campaign, no one would advocate unification, and if someone did, people would think he was crazy," a prominent Taiwan magazine publisher, Antonio Chiang, said. 
"Independence is an issue, but reunification is not."
Pro-independence groups demonstrated last week to call for Taiwan's separate entry into the United Nations, and the success of the Baltic republics' struggle has given them increased inspiration, if not a more sympathetic public ear. 
But polls indicate that 12 percent of the population support independence, with no sign that that number is rising.
No one expects Taiwan to be permitted to join the United Nations any time soon, because China, which has a permanent seat on the Security Council, would veto an application.
Government officials here deny that the independence of the Baltic republics bears any similarity to Taiwan's situation. predicament. 
"The Soviet Union forcefully annexed the three countries, and now that wrong is being redressed," Foreign Minister Fredrick F. Chien said in an interview. 
"We believe in reunification. 
We do not think that independence would serve the interests of the 20 million people here."
Mr. Chien said that the situations of the other Soviet republics, many of which have declared independence but have not been recognized by foreign countries, are more comparable to Taiwan's circumstances. 
Taiwan, Mr. Chien argues, never was an independent country, and so the rest of the world would be unlikely to recognize it if it simply declared independence.

file: TAIWAN TO RELAX LIMITS ON SPEECH.txt
text:
ï»¿
The authorities are expected to take major steps this year to ease the remaining curbs on political debate in Taiwan.
Pressed hard by the opposition, the Government is easing its ban on seditious speech and will free some political prisoners. 
It is also expected to end its blacklist of Taiwan exiles, effectively fueling political debate.
Adding to the political confusion, a power struggle appears to be under way within the leadership, the Constitution is now being revised by a special conference, and the first free and full legislative elections in more than four decades will be held at year's end.
"This year is a threshold," said Alice H. E. Kao, a newspaper editor and member of the conference that is revising the Constitution.
Â 
Government Turnaround
Just a couple of months ago the Government seemed poised to move in the other direction. 
The authorities apparently came very close to dissolving the Democratic Progressive Party, the main opposition group, for advocating that Taiwan declare itself an independent country separate from China. 
In fact, while Taiwan is effectively run as an independent nation, it claims to be the Republic of China, with sovereignty over mainland China as well as the island of Taiwan.
Now the authorities are relaxing the old ban on seditious speech. 
While the ban has been widely ignored in recent years, and the opposition regularly excoriates the leadership and proclaims the heresy that Taiwan should abandon its claims to mainland China, the change in the law is still seen as a crucial step.
The sedition law, Article 100 of the criminal code, had provided for sentences as severe as life in prison and was sometimes used to stifle critics.
"My impression is that only those acts that involve violence will be prosecuted," said the Government spokesman, Jason C. Hu. "Expressions will not be prosecuted."
Â 
Dissidents to Be Freed
Once the law is changed, later this year, the Government is expected to free a handful of dissidents who are in prison for peaceful expression of their views. 
The most famous of these is Huang Hwa, a longtime champion of Taiwan independence who is serving a 10-year prison sentence.
These steps toward democracy and tolerance have caused concern within the Communist Chinese leadership, which fears that Taiwan is gradually moving toward formal independence from China. 
A senior Chinese official said the leaders were closely following the moves being taken by Taiwan this year.
Ending the blacklist, which for decades has kept hundreds of Taiwan's leading political figures and scholars from returning, will also be a major step toward opening up the political system. 
Ever since the late 1940's, large numbers of people from Taiwan have gone to the United States to study or work and have found themselves barred from returning because of their criticisms of the Taiwan Government policy at home.
The authorities are also moving to ease controls on radio and television, though not as quickly as the opposition would like. 
Mr. Hu said that it would take about a year to approve new commercial radio stations, which have been banned in part for fear that they would criticize the Government.
Â 
Allowing Cable TV
The Government is also allowing cable television systems, though with considerable restrictions. 
It is not clear that this relaxation will make much difference, because Taiwan already has a huge network of cable systems that are illegal but tolerated.
Another major arena for change is the governing Nationalist Party's 14th Congress, which will be held this year or next and is expected to revise the party structure to make greater use of elections by party members.
Hsu Hsin-liang, the leader of the Democratic Progressive Party, said he was optimistic that the opposition might even win a majority in the legislative elections late this year and form a government. 
This is a view that few others share, but Mr. Hsu indicated that the opposition would tone down its advocacy of Taiwan independence and turn to issues that have broader appeal among voters: taxes, pollution and delays in carrying out direct presidential elections.
"In last year's election for the National Assembly, our party platform was about Taiwan independence and that scared the middle class," Mr. Hsu said. 
"We talked about independence a lot last year, and this year we won't."

file: Taiwan_s New President Signals Major Softening in Relations With China.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Lee Teng-hui said today that he would soon revoke his Government's 40-year-old declaration of a ''Communist rebellion'' on the Chinese mainland, and would immediately restore the civil rights of nearly 30 dissidents, including 2 of the Government's most prominent opponents.
With the announcement, on the day of Mr. Lee's inauguration as the country's first Taiwanese-born President, the Government signaled its intent to end the formal state of war that has existed with the Communist Government since Chiang Kai-shek led the Nationalist retreat to Taiwan.
But the move will also chiefly have a domestic effect, because it will end the Government's reliance on emergency powers that took precedence over Taiwan's Constitution, a much-awaited milestone in the country's transition from authoritarian rule to a multiparty system.
By restoring civil rights for dissidents, Mr. Lee is permitting leaders of the country's fledgling opposition, the Democratic Progressive Party, to run for office.
Dissidents Gather in Protest
Mr. Lee's inauguration came as students and intellectuals pressed their protests for democratic reforms and in opposition to the appointment of Gen. Hau Pei-tsu, Taiwan's hard-line, conservative Defense Secretary as Prime Minister. 
Though General Hau has said he would resign his military posts and has begun wearing business suits instead of his uniform, 5,000 students and shoppers gathered today at the Chiang Kai-shek Memorial to protest against his appointment.
Mr. Lee has served as President since the death two years ago of his predecessor, Chiang Ching-kuo, the son of Chiang Kai-shek. 
In that time, he has presided over rapid changes in Taiwan's relationship with the mainland, including a startling number of Taiwanese business ventures in the People's Republic and a flood of more than a million Taiwanese visitors there.
But so far, those contacts have been indirect - mostly funneled through Hong Kong - because of the Taiwanese Government's insistence on maintaining its policy of ''three no's'' toward China: no direct contact, no negotiation and no compromise on the question of which is the legitimate government of China.
President Lee today appeared to back away from that policy, which has already been eroded by the widening network of business and family contacts across the Straits of Taiwan. 
He said that Taiwan wanted to establish direct ''channels of communication'' with the mainland, calling to ''completely open up academic, cultural, economic, trade, scientific and technological exchange.''
Â 
An Offer Likely to Be Refused
But President Lee presented conditions that Beijing has already said it would reject, including an opening of the Chinese Government's economy, a move toward democratic changes, and negotiations between the two governments on an equal basis. 
Beijing has said it would only negotiate party-to-party, treating Taiwan as a provincial government.
Even though few expect that Mr. Lee's overture will draw the two governments together for talks anytime soon, many saw it as a signal to Beijing of a softening of Taiwan's official line. 
It was a message, a Government official said, ''intended for the next generation of leadership'' in Beijing.
''What the President announced today is a big change,'' said Wu Wen-Cheng, a professor at Soochow University here, ''because it means that for the first time the Government is not insisting on the three no's policy. 
We are moving to a more flexible and pragmatic age.''
Three years ago, Taiwan ended martial law, touching off the beginning of a liberalization move that has in many ways closely paralleled South Korea's. 
But the Government still had broad powers under the ''temporary provisions'' in effect since Chiang Kai-shek led the retreat to Taiwan four decades ago.
Seeming to address the protesters who have been calling for quicker democratic change, Mr. Lee said today that ''if we proceed gradually, one step at a time, our system of party politics will naturally become sounder over time, our foundation of democracy will naturally become firmer, and the time when the country is well-governed and enjoys lasting stabilityI will naturally be in sight.''
Â 
Uncertain Political Climate
Despite the announcements today, President Lee still finds himself in a precarious political position. 
There are disagreements over what form of government Taiwan should adopt, including whether it should have a strong president.
Mr. Lee is being pressed by entrepreneurs who seek greater direct access to mainland China and reformers, including the students, who are seeking to acknowledge the reality of two separate Chinas, something neither government formally acknowledges.
On the other side, Mr. Lee needs the support of the far more conservative mainland-born politicians who dominate the political scene here. 
The legislature and electoral college are dominated by men in their 80's and 90's who represent regions of the mainland that have not been in the Taiwan Government's control for decades. 
Therefore,the Taiwanese themselves are vastly underrepresented in their own government. 
While the ruling Nationalist Party has asked the elderly mainlanders to step aside in the next two years, the party has stopped short of requiring them to do so.
Included among the 10 dissidents whose release was announced today are Shih Ming-teh, who has served 25 years in jail on two separate charges of sedition, most recently for his role in a 1979 anti-Government protest.
Â 
A Pardon Reportedly Refused
Mr. Shih, who has been hospitalized for four years since a hunger strike harmed his health, was reported by Chinese-language papers here to have refused the pardon, saying he wanted President Lee to apologize for the treatment of political prisoners in Taiwan.
Others involved in the 1979 protest, which turned into a riot in Kaohsiung had their rights restored today. 
They can now run for office and resume their work.
Also among those pardoned is Hsu Hsin-liang, perhaps Taiwan's best-known dissident, who spent most of the 1980's in exile in the United States. 
For years Taiwan blocked his return, sometimes sparking clashes between the police and Taiwanese waiting for his arrival at the airport. 
Mr. Hsu was arrested last year after he was caught trying to enter the country, and in December, he was sentenced to 10 years in prison.
Many dissidents accused of trying to undermine the Nationalist Government have been released in the last two years. 
With the latest group Taiwan appears to have relatively few political prisoners left. 
Many received pardons today, including top officials of the opposition Democratic Progress Party who are likely to run for election.

file: TALKING TO HIMSELF, BUT VERY LOUD.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE SECRET SPEECHES OF CHAIRMAN MAO
From the Hundred Flowers to the Great Leap Forward.
Edited by Roderick MacFarquhar,
Timothy Cheek and Eugene Wu.
561 pp. 
Cambridge, Mass.:
The Council on East Asian Studies/
Harvard University Press. 
Paper, $15.
Two Chinese texts for the day: ''It's good to have a bit of disturbance. 
Students making a disturbance is not equivalent to rebellion. 
. . . I say let them agitate to their hearts' content. 
. . . Make the process of the disturbance serve as an educational process, serve as a political course.''
And: ''The People's Liberation Army is for dealing with imperialism, not for dealing with the people. 
The People's Liberation Army is the son of the people. 
How could the son [of the people] ever oppose the father of the people?''
These observations, so poignant in light of the demonstrations in Tiananmen Square in May and June and the subsequent Beijing slaughter, were made by Chairman Mao Zedong 32 years ago, in February and March 1957. 
Mao was trying to get support for what became known as the Hundred Flowers Movement, a broad-based airing of views on the problems facing China, which he believed would dissipate the tensions that had arisen since the suppressions of the Hungarian and Polish risings in 1956. 
The reassurances Mao offered to intellectuals, party workers and students, in many informal speeches and off-the-record discussions, had the effect desired. 
By the spring of 1957 the movement was in full swing, and a deafening chorus of complaints was surfacing in every available forum.
Unfortunately for Mao, the complaints were directed not only at shortcomings in the political, economic and intellectual life of China, but at the Communist Party as an entity, and at Mao himself as an authoritarian and incompetent leader. 
Bitter and chagrined, Mao backed off from his support of the Hundred Flowers and joined forces with more conservative cadres who had never wanted the campaign in the first place. 
By the summer of 1957 the party was conducting a full-fledged ''Anti-Rightist Campaign'' against those who had been most outspoken. 
At least half a million Chinese were punished for having answered the chairman's call.
Mao gave hundreds of informal speeches, containing phrases and thoughts similar to those quoted above, but very few of them made their way into the five volumes of his official collected works. 
For the Mao canon was too important to be left to Mao, and batteries of senior comrades and editors were at hand to tidy up his work, remove indiscretions and try to reach a point of view consistent with whatever the party line of the time happened to be. 
However, for over 30 years Mao was the most revered and most feared person in China, and his words were stored in countless ways by those who heard them - in secret party archives, internal memos, private notebooks, tape-recorded transcripts. 
When the young Red Guards were encouraged by Mao in 1966 and 1967 to lash out at the senior officials in the party, the bureaucracy and the educational establishment, they customarily ransacked the homes and offices of their victims. 
In the course of these raids, much confidential material came to light. 
Some of it was used as evidence against the senior personnel concerned. 
If the words were Mao's, they were transcribed by Red Guards and circulated in various published or informal ways, as evidence - if more was needed - of Mao's creative originality as a thinker. 
Occasionally bits of these collections reached scholars in the west and were translated there; two important examples were the pieces published by Jerome Chen in 1970 as ''Mao Papers'' and by Stuart Schram in ''Mao Tse-tung Unrehearsed'' (1974).
Now, in ''The Secret Speeches of Chairman Mao,'' Roderick MacFarquhar, a professor of government at Harvard University, together with Timothy Cheek of Colorado College and Eugene Wu, the librarian of Harvard's East Asian collection, have edited a remarkably comprehensive collection of these informal Maoist texts. 
Wisely, I think, they have chosen to focus on just two key events in China's recent history, rather than using a scattershot approach that would give a little taste of many topics.
Their focus on The Hundred Flowers Movement of 1957 and the Great Leap Forward of 1958 is particularly apt, because each presents such a different side of Mao's character and his approach to politics. 
The Hundred Flowers texts show Mao almost as a petitioner among his own people, ''a wandering lobbyist,'' as he described himself in a talk to army cadres in Nanjing. 
He is genial, relaxed, sharp in comment but open to give and take. 
The Great Leap Forward texts, by contrast, show a much darker side of his character - angry, impatient, visionary, uninterested in arguments that might have brought him back to earth.
Obviously, these texts, by such a major political actor, collected in such informal ways, raise complex problems of authenticity. 
Mr. Cheek, in an opening essay called ''Textually Speaking,'' confronts this problem directly, reflects on the pros and cons of the authenticity of different texts, collates various speeches from different editions with their variant forms and with official published versions where possible, and concludes the speeches published here are genuinely the words of Mao. 
Mr. Cheek knows the field extremely well and has had the help of an international array of Chinese analysts, along with the bibliographic skills of Mr. Wu (who directs an essay of his own to similar problems), so I accept this judgment, especially since Mr. Cheek is not dogmatic about the works in question and tells us when he has doubts.
As Mr. Cheek nicely phrases it, in Mao's earlier official collected works, Mao himself accepted the need for a ''consensual approach to his own deification,'' whereas in the official collections published by the Communist Party since Mao's death in 1976, one gets a kind of ''academic theology'' in which '' 'scientific,' linguistic and historical analyses seek to contribute to a living faith.''
In contrast, the Red Guard editions that never ceased praising Mao, ''genius'' editions as Mr. Cheek calls them, provide both ''a gold mine of political and psychological data for Mao studies'' and ''a cesspool of run-on sentences, obscure grammar, and simple nonsense for the translator.''
Three other essays by eminent China scholars help to give us a valuable set of contexts in which to read Mao's informal texts. 
Mr. MacFarquhar's opening essay, as one would expect from the leading expert on both the Hundred Flowers Movement and the origins and implementation of the Great Leap Forward, gives an excellent overview of Mao's state of mind as he argued with his senior party colleagues over the need for change and criticism at the center. 
Benjamin I. Schwartz gives a moving analysis of Mao's ''deep anxieties, soaring exaltations, injured pride, deep resentments, and unexamined complacencies.''
Mr. Schwartz concludes that the ideas behind the Great Leap were more central to Mao's being than those of the Hundred Flowers, and presented an apocalyptically utopian view of the fusion of his mind with those of China's masses (as opposed to the bourgeois intellectuals) that represented Mao's ''final spiritual resting place.''
Merle Goldman, looking at the Mao of the late 1950's from the vantage point of her deep familiarity with the manifestations of political and literary dissent in China, explains how the Hundred Flowers slogans sprang from Communist Party intellectual history - specifically, from an earlier 1951 Maoist analysis of the Beijing Opera tradition and from the roots of a historiographical academic debate that Mao refused to pass judgment on. 
She also shows how Mao was enraged with his propaganda chiefs and newspaper editors, and concludes, forcefully, that Mao comes across in these talks as ''contradictory, repetitious, and obsessed.''
What, then, are the central contributions made by this new collection to our knowledge of China?
Perhaps the greatest is that they show us how much frank discussion was in the air during this strange period of Chinese history, and how difficult it sometimes was for Mao to get what he wanted despite his immense prestige. 
The final impression is that Mao felt so far above the fray, even while so grubbily absorbed in it, that he ceased to have any clear sense of the country's terrible suffering. 
People really had become ciphers to him, mere details on the way to some ultimate colossal goal. 
''In the past during the revolution numerous people died without asking anything in return. 
Why can't it be like that now?''
Mao asked his senior colleagues in August 1958 as he discussed the Great Leap. 
Maybe they should think of letting the peasants have two days' rest a month, he ruminated a little later, but then at once modified the thought: ''during the busy season, rest a little less,'' he said, and eat and sleep at the work site too, to save precious time. 
''This point should be written in the documents but not be talked about too much,'' he told his colleagues. 
Sometimes Mao's thoughts strayed to stranger zones: to great wide roads in every commune with no trees on their verges so that every road would be an airport; or to a world of Chinese so healthy that physicians would have no patients, and could go till the fields and do research.
Almost everything Mao was saying in 1957 was something students and workers wanted to discuss with their own Government in 1989. 
Perhaps most ironically, it was presumably Hu Yaobang, then directing the Communist Youth League, who tried to give Mao accurate information on student unrest. 
Hu Yaobang's own death in April 1989 was the initial spark that culminated in the June tragedy, even though the deeper causes had been smoldering a long time. 
As Mr. MacFarquhar says, this 1989 Tiananmen crisis ''would almost certainly have the same numbing effect on China's intellectual elite as the Anti-Rightist Campaign, and could deter rural and urban entrepreneurs and foreign investors.''
As we can now see, thanks to these texts, the paradoxes at the center of this Government were paradoxes that lay also at the heart of Mao's being. 
Or, as Mr. Schwartz puts it so beautifully in his essay: ''In the end, on the level of his final abstract vision, Chairman Mao may be not so much 'alone with the masses' as alone with himself.''
Â 
THE CHAIRMAN, UNEDITED
One added richness in this strange and absorbing book is that if we so choose we can take any one of Mao's off-the-cuff draft speeches and then see how it compares with the final party version (if there is one). 
To do this in the case of one of Mao's most famous speeches, ''On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People,'' is a fascinating exercise. 
The history of this speech is more than usually devious, since Mao initially delivered it on Feb. 
27, 1957, to a large group of nonparty intellectuals and bureaucrats, whom he was trying to persuade to join in the Hundred Flowers Campaign. 
It was not published at the time, to Mao's anger. 
But after he himself swung against the protesters, he apparently acquiesced in the publication of a totally revised version in The People's Daily of Peking on June 19, 1957. 
This latter version was doctored to make it appear that Mao wanted the Hundred Flowers Campaign to serve as a vehicle of class struggle, and that he anticipated trouble from the start.
The ''speaking notes'' for the original speech that have now surfaced bear almost no relation at all to the mood or content of the dogmatic and tedious June 19 version. 
The newly discovered version occupies 58 pages of ''The Secret Speeches of Chairman Mao,'' and there is a surprise on nearly every page. 
Some examples must serve for the whole: Mao's frank discussion of the troubles in Poland and Hungary, his sense that the people wanted two news agencies in competition with each other, his analysis of the way China's national bourgeoisie is not an enemy, his frank announcement that 770,000 Chinese were killed in the mass campaigns of 1950 to 1954, his portrayal of the constructive role of student protests in modern Chinese history, his analysis of problems in China's cooperatives and his estimate that in some areas 15 percent of the households were ''lacking grain,'' his mention that many Chinese now feel ''disgust with Marxism.''
Among other important things Mao discussed in February that never made it to the June text were the urgent need for birth control in China, the fact that 40 percent of school-age children had no schools to go to, and the fact that during 1956 China had been troubled by a mass of protests and strikes: 7,000 students protesting in 28 different cities, according to Communist Youth League figures, and 50 strikes conducted by urban workers, some involving over 1,000 workers, according to statistics Mao admitted were still incomplete.
Â 
JONATHAN D. SPENCE

file: Talks in Taiwan Urge a Popular Presidential Vote.txt
text:
ï»¿
After five days of strenuous national debate, a national conference on this island's future concluded today with a call for popular presidential elections.
The endorsement of popular elections by the 150 delegates seemed to give a considerable lift to proposals that would restructure Taiwan's political system along much more democratic lines in coming years. 
President Lee Teng-hui had chosen all the delegates and given them a mandate to grapple with the intensely emotional question of Taiwan's future.
It was the first time that the Government and its opponents had openly discussed on a public stage some critical questions about Taiwan's future. 
They included: Should the nation revise its Constitution or draw up a completely new one?
Should the Government adopt a presidential or parliamentary system?
How should the 20 million people on Taiwan build economic links with 1.1 billion Chinese on the mainland?
''This is a fantastic thing,'' said Kang Ning-hsiang, a prominent member of the Democratic Progressive Party, the opposition group. 
''To bring all these people together to talk about our future is the greatest political event.''
With bells ringing every so often to signal the end of a speaker's floor time, delegates stood up one by one on podiums to state their views on various issues. 
The conference delegates included a student, a Mongolian, a Tibetan, a handful of previously jailed dissidents, and Chinese scholars from the United States.
The conference has no legal authority, and so it is not clear how their conclusions will be carried out.
''Everyone feels a little funny,'' said Jaw Shau-kong, a legislator from the governing Nationalist Party and a delegate to the conference. 
''This is outside the legal system.''
The agreement on popular presidential elections was the most important decision at the conference. 
Currently, the President is elected through the National Assembly, an electoral college that is made up mostly of elderly men, who purport to represent constituencies on mainland China.
Â 
Charter Revision Proposed
While they agreed on presidential elections, delegates were divided on whether citizens should elect the President through an electoral college or bypass that step and hold direct elections.
The delegates also debated ways to restructure the island's legislature, which has passed only one minor law in its current session, which ends in a few weeks. 
President Lee and other Nationalist leaders have indicated that Taiwan needs a constitutional overhaul, but that that may not be easy to achieve.
In one move that will make Parliament more democratic, Taiwan's highest court ruled recently that those aging legislators - unelected in decades - must resign by the end of next year. 
Opposition members want an earlier deadline.
President Lee said in March that he would revoke within about a year the Government's 40-year-old declaration of ''Communist rebellion'' on mainland China. 
Changing that condition, which vests the President with special powers, would require altering Taiwan's Constitution, and there was no consensus on how to revise it.
The opposition party is demanding that the Government scrap the Constitution and write a new one. 
And while the party's voice has been more influential than its 30,000 membership would suggest, it is not clear that it has much support on this issue.
Still, delegates agreed that constitutional changes are inevitable and some hoped the conference would deepen the sense of urgency.
''We can keep the momentum of reform, and not just of the Constitution,'' said Ma Ying-jeou, a Nationalist Party delegate and Cabinet-level official. 
''The party structure has to be democratized to cope with new constitutional democracy.''
Probably the most delicate and emotional issue of the conference focused on Taiwan's policy toward mainland China. 
During the last couple of years, relations between China and Taiwan have warmed dramatically.

text:

HONG KONG
By Jan Morris.
Illustrated. 359 pp. 
New York: Random House. 
$19.95.
Fewer than nine years remain before Hong Kong will cease to exist as a British colony and become part of the People's Republic of China.
Never before have several million people been handed over to Communism. 
Jan Morris's unarticulated question in ''Hong Kong'' is: will Hong Kong continue to flourish as a bastion of capitalism, one of the world's leading financial centers, or will it slowly degenerate, turning into just another seedy and tacky Chinese city?
The story of Hong Kong, as Ms. Morris tells it, is full of drama, beginning with its birth as a colony a century and a half ago as the result of an encounter between the two dominant powers of the day, the Manchu dynasty, then in an advanced state of decline, and the expansionist British empire, which had yet to reach its zenith.
The colony was wrested from China in stages: first Hong Kong island was ceded in the aftermath of the Opium War in 1842; next, the Kowloon peninsula was seized in 1860; and finally, in 1898, the New Territories (the hinterland of the penisula and the rocks and islands immediately around Hong Kong) were added, enlarging tenfold the colony's area.
However, the last treaty contained the seeds of the colony's destruction, for instead of taking the land outright, Britain obtained a 99-year ''lease'' for which it did not pay any rent. 
No doubt, at the time, 99 years appeared to be close to eternity.
In the early 1980's, as the deadline loomed closer, the British asked for an extension and were sternly rebuffed. 
In 1984, Britain agreed to return the colony to China on July 1, 1997, along with its five and a half million people.
Ms. Morris, a historian, travel writer and author of the ''Pax Britannica'' trilogy, is fascinated by the story of Hong Kong, the last major colony not only of Britain but of any of the former colonial powers of Europe. 
She approaches the subject of Hong Kong ''as a student of British imperialism.''
She sets herself the task of portraying ''the last of the great British colonies as it is in its last years.''
She does a superb job.
Ms. Morris confesses that as recently as 1982 her sentiments toward Hong Kong were characterized by ''unmitigated dislike.''
Now, however, she finds a sense of poignancy as the territory faces a future that can be described, at best, as uncertain.
Ms. Morris alternates chapters of themes or analysis with chapters of historical description. 
She lovingly describes the historical setting, painting in broad strokes the colony's rise from a settlement of a few thousand fishermen to the present.
In the early years, she recounts, ''the Chinese Secretary was a Pomeranian clergyman, the Treasurer a former ship's mate, while in 1849 the Registrar-General dropped everything and joined the Gold Rush to California.''
Today, she says, tiny Hong Kong is the world's largest exporter of textiles, toys and watches. 
It has more Rolls-Royces per capita than any country in the world, makes more films per year than Hollywood and the pay of the Governor of Hong Kong is more than double that of the British Prime Minister.
One of the book's best historical chapters is on the Japanese occupation from 1941 to 1945. 
The Japanese tried to eradicate all vestiges of the British presence, to the extent of changing the name of the Peninsula Hotel to the Toa, of Jimmy's Kitchen to the Sai Mun Cafe and of Queen's Road to Nakameiji-dori.
Many in the Chinese community were compromised, Ms. Morris says. 
Some of the best-known Chinese citizens joined Japanese puppet bodies, such as the Rehabilitation Advisory Committee, the Chinese Representative Council and the Chinese Cooperative Council. 
''Some Chinese'' she writes, ''at least in the beginning, supported the Japanese simply as fellow Asians.''
But she concludes that, in general, ''they were not traitorous.''
For more than a century Hong Kong was essentially a transient community, offering haven for refugees from China who either returned home when things quieted down or who used the colony as a springboard from which to seek greener pastures abroad.
Only in 1981 did the census show a majority of the people actually born in Hong Kong. 
''Only recently,'' says Ms. Morris, ''has the emergence of a new, educated Chinese middle class, born and bred in the colony, made one feel that Hong Kong is approaching some kind of social equilibrium, becoming a real, balanced city - and with 1997 closing fast, perhaps it is too late.''
Only history will tell whether it is too late. 
So far, the signs are not good. 
Earlier this month, a China-appointed committee responsible for drafting the Basic Law that will govern Hong Kong after 1997 rejected demands for greater democracy and imposed additional hurdles to make universal suffrage unlikely even in the next generation.

text:

By SUSAN MERNITd wonders of Oriental cuisine, bao bing, a simple fruit dessert, has long stood out as one of the most ubiquitous in Asia. 
Yet it is almost unknown in the West.
A sweetened froth of seasonal fresh fruit and finely shaved ice topped with flavored sugar syrup and condensed milk, bao bing, or bing, has always been immensely popular throughout Asia. 
Now it is beginning to gain popularity in the United States as more Asians settle in this country.
Made with regional fruits like mangoes, litchis and rambutans, bao bing is ''Asia's answer to the ice-cream soda,'' said Gim Yee, owner of the Bamboo Garden, a restaurant in New York's Chinatown. 
In Taiwan, Malaysia, China and Vietnam, bao bing stalls do a brisk business; in Hong Kong, bakeries sell bao bing along with custard eclairs and pork bao.
Bao bing (pronounced bow-BING) can be traced back more than 1,000 years. 
According to Reay Tanahil, the author of ''Food in History'' (Stein & Day, 1973), bao bing, which means ''shaved ice,'' was eaten in China as early as the seventh century A.D. In 1972, when President Richard M. Nixon made his first visit to Beijing, bao bing was served during state dinners with Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai.
Not surprisingly, the dessert has evolved over the years. 
Nina Simmonds, the author of ''Classical Chinese Cooking'' (Houghton, Mifflin, 1982), said modern bao bing reflected westernization in Asian cuisine.
''The bao bing Asians eat today uses condensed milk and sweeter syrups, and is often served in tall paper containers,'' she said. 
''Classical bing skips the condensed milk, uses sugarcane juice and is served in a shallow bowl.''
Today, restaurants in Asian communities across the United States offer bao bing on their menus. 
Alfred Shu, owner of Memories of China, a Chicago restaurant, said bao bing is as popular with Asians in the United States as it is in Taiwan or Hong Kong.
Ten years ago, only one restaurant in New York's Chinatown sold bing. 
Today, more than 40 do. 
In Elmhurst and Flushing, Queens, and the Bay Ridge section of Brooklyn, restaurants catering to Asians make and sell bing, as do those in other large cities with Asian communities.
At the Bamboo Garden, at 22A Bowery between Pell and Bayard Streets in Manhattan, Mr. Yee and his staff sell 40 to 100 orders of bao bing a day. 
Mr. Yee, who was reared in New York, said he began to serve it only after customers began to request it. 
''A lot of the new immigrants, especially people from Hong Kong, really like bings,'' he said.
But Asian and Western tastes can differ. 
Red bean and custard are two of the most popular flavors in Taiwan, said Tony King, director of the China Council of the Asia Society in New York, while in New York, watermelon and litchi are favorites. 
Henry Hugh, a chef for a Manhattan investment house from Flushing, Queens, said many of his Asian-born friends prefer Malaysian-style bing, made with corn, green taro gelatin, starch beans and strawberry syrup.
Fortunately, there are many varieties of bao bing that please Western palates. 
Mango, litchi, mixed fruit and watermelon bing all have their Western devotees. 
''I have litchi bing at least once every two weeks,'' said Spencer Jarrett, an audio-visual producer based in New York. 
''I go to Maria's or Yuen Yuen Tea Parlor and get one to take out.''
There are signs that bao bing is gaining favor with an increasing number of Westerners. 
The Stony Wok, a Chinese restaurant in Flushing, Queens, has been serving bao bing to its customers every spring and summer for five years. 
The manager, Pai Kang, said: ''At first, customers ordered the ices out of curiosity, but then, they taste them and get hooked. 
Now, many people order them every time they come in.''

Cooking time: 5 minutes (for the sugar syrup)

1/2 cup sugar
1 tablespoon shredded orange peel (optional)

3 to 4 cups finely shaved or chopped ice, approximately.
1 3-ounce can condensed milk
1.Combine the water, sugar and shredded orange peel, if desired, in a heavy saucepan and bring to a boil. 
Reduce heat to medium-low and cook, uncovered, about 5 minutes, until you have a light sugar syrup. 
Remove from heat and let sugar syrup cool.
2.Open and drain the litchis. 
Reserve juice. 
For each serving, place 1/2 cup of the fruit in the bottom of a tall sundae glass or shallow bowl, and top each with about 1 cup of ice.
3.Top litchis and ice with 1/2 cup of sugar syrup, 1 tablespoon of reserved juice and 3 tablespoons of condensed milk. 
Serve.
Yield: 3 or 4 servings.
NOTE: This basic recipe will work with many types of fruit, including watermelons, mangoes and peaches.

Almond and Fruit Bing

1 cup cold water
Y cup sugar
3 cups milk, room temperature

Fresh or canned fruits, 16 ounces or 2 cups, peeled and chopped and juice reserved (see note in previous recipe)

For each serving, place about 1 cup of ice in shallow dish or deep container, then top with 1/2 cup of fruit and 1/2 cup of almond pudding.

Yield: 3 or 4 servings.

IN Chinatown in Manhattan, many coffee shops, restaurants and bakeries sell bao bing.
Yuen Yuen Tea Parlor, 61 Bayard Street near Elizabeth Street, offers one of the widest selections in the city for $1 to $1.25. 
Yuen Yuen's light, refreshing flavors include litchi, pineapple, watermelon and Yuen Yuen, the house special, made of fruit cup, litchis and red beans. 
The telephone number is 212-406-2100. 
The two Chinatown branches of St. Honore, a Hong Kong bakery chain, feature bao bing made with a delicate slushy ice. 
Watermelon, litchi and lotus-seed bing ($1.50) are among the most popular. 
The chain has shops at 28 Bowery near Canal Street (212-962-1012) and 6 East Broadway near Catherine Street (941-0735). 
At Wun Loy, 66 Bayard Street near Mott Street, an unusual fruit-custard bao bing ($1.50), made of sweetened egg custard and mixed fruit, resembles a version popular in Taiwan. 
The telephone number is 212-219-3822.

In Flushing, Queens, the Stony Wok at 137-40 Northern Boulevard (718-445-8535) also serves bao bing.
