text:
ï»¿
The British Foreign Secretary, Sir Geoffrey Howe, will visit Hong Kong in early July to assess problems in the British colony after the crackdown in Beijing, the Foreign Office said today.
The announcement came as officials explored ways of allowing Hong Kong citizens who hold British passports to settle here, although Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher has ruled out an ''open door'' policy.
Events in China have prompted widespread fears among the 5.7 million people of Hong Kong, which Britain is to hand over to Chinese rule in 1997. 
On Wednesday, the riot police fired tear gas to break up a crowd attacking Chinese banks and shops, and much of the colony was closed down by a strike.
Last year 46,000 people, mainly professionals, emigrated from Hong Kong to Canada, Australia and the United States. 
Analysts forecast that the trend would increase as 1997 approached.
The Hong Kong Governor, Sir David Wilson, held talks on Thursday with Mrs. Thatcher and the Foreign Secretary on the crisis in the colony.
After his meeting with Mrs. Thatcher, the Governor told reporters that she offered him ''more than tea and sympathy'' but turned down his appeal to give the colony's 3.25 million British passport holders the right of residence in Britain. 
Mrs. Thatcher earlier told Parliament that the Government was prepared ''to see if we can get increasing flexibility to allow an increasing number of people in here.''

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_China Seeks Arrest of Its Top Dissident.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Government issued a warrant today for the arrest of Fang Lizhi, China's best-known dissident, as official press organizations stepped up criticism of the United States.
The Beijing authorities also continued to arrest those involved in the democracy movement, as fear heightened in the capital that a a purge of students and dissidents was growing.
The warrant for Mr. Fang and his wife, Li Shuxian, was a sign of deteriorating relations with the United States because the American Embassy gave the two dissidents refuge last week. 
So long as Mr. Fang and Miss Li remain in the Embassy, the Chinese Government cannot enter to arrest them, but the warrant will make it more difficult to resolve the dispute by negotiation.
Â 
U.S. Discreetly Silent
The United States Embassy has refused all comment on Mr. Fang's case, apparently in fear of worsening tension with the Chinese Government, and the embassy again declined to comment tonight on the warrant for their arrest.
But in a television interview on the CBS News program ''Face the Nation'' before the warrant was made public, Ambassador James R. Lilley described the dispute over the dissidents as ''an irritant'' in Chinese-American relations, and said that he had discussed it with Chinese officials in recent days.
In Washington, a spokesman for the State Department said that there would be no immediate response on the Fang case and that the United States generally does not comment on such matters.
Â 
Pictures Hint at Brutality
There was no word from the Chinese authorities on how many people were arrested today in the capital, beyond the 400 who were reported on Saturday to have been seized in the last few days.
But television showed 20 newly arrested young men from Beijing, some of them bruised or cut as if they had been beaten, and many Chinese express fear that the number is in the thousands. 
A diplomat with connections in the security agencies said that the total would soon reach 1,000, if it had not already.
A week after the army cracked down on the democracy movement in Beijing, thousands of other Chinese intellectuals are in hiding in the capital or are fleeing to the provinces to avoid arrest. 
While it is not clear how those arrested will be punished, the purge is the biggest in more than a decade.
''I'm staying with friends each night because it's not safe to stay at home,'' said a young intellectual who fears arrest because he sometimes criticizes the Government even though he has not been active in the democracy movement. 
''And I'm going to leave Beijing for a while, just to be safe.''
Television news has shown a parade of the ''thugs'' and assailed them for supporting the ''counterrevolutionary rebellion,'' as the democracy move-ment is now being officially described. 
The television clips show that arrests are taking place in large cities all over the nation, although apparently nowhere in such large numbers as in Beijing.
Normal activity in the capital is slowly resuming, with more people than ever on the streets, bicycling to and from work, and there sems to be less danger now of being shot on the street.
But the arrests suggest that the atmosphere of fear and the strains with the United States are intensifying. 
The nation's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, and others in power seem determined to uproot the remnants of the democratic movement and to punish the United States for criticizing the violent suppression of the movement early this week.
The ''wanted circular'' for Mr. Fang and Miss Li charges them with ''committing crimes of counterrevolutionary propaganda and instigation.''
It says these crimes were committed both before and during the recent turmoil.
Mr. Fang is an internationally known astrophysicist, an ebullient 53-year-old who proclaims that Marxism is outdated and that China should move toward more democracy. 
''Teacher Fang,'' as young people call him, is enormously popular among university students, and he is relatively well-known abroad.
He was expelled from the Communist Party and transferred to Beijing from the central city of Hefei in early 1987 after the authorities accused him of inciting student pro-democracy demonstrations in December 1986. 
Miss Li, an associate professor of physics at Beijing University, remains a Communist Party member but has been outspoken in criticizing the party leadership.
Â 
Diplomatic Incident
Mr. Fang was at the center of an international incident in February, when the visiting President Bush invited him to a banquet that the Americans were giving for Chinese officials and citizens. 
More than 100 Chinese police officers intervened to keep Mr. Fang from attending, and the United States and China exchanged protests the next day.
Apparently fearful of being accused of misconduct, Mr. Fang and Miss Li did not participate in the demonstrations of the pro-democracy movement of the last two months. 
They avoided Tiananmen Square when it was being occupied by students.
The charge of counterrevolution made against Mr. Fang and Miss Li is an extremely serious one, equivalent virtually to treason. 
Two of China's best-known political prisoners, Wei Jingsheng and Xu Wenli, are serving 15-year prison sentences for counterrevolutionary activities, among other offenses.
Prison conditions for both are believed to be grim: Mr. Wei is widely believed to be suffering emotional problems because of solitary confinement broken only by annual visits by a younger sister. 
Until earlier this year, Mr. Xu was also in solitary confinement in a cell measuring 10 feet by 2 feet. 
Earlier this year, he was allowed his first visit from his wife and child in more than three years.
Â 
A Party Leader in Peril
The highest-ranking official thought to be under arrest is Bao Tong, an associate of the Communist Party General Secretary, Zhao Ziyang, who is believed to have been stripped of power. 
Mr. Bao is himself a member of the party Central Committee. 
While there has been no announcement, knowledgable Chinese and diplomats said he has almost certainly been arrested.
There is no clear word on the whereabouts of Mr. Zhao. Various rumors have the party moderate either under house arrest, in a hospital or dead. 
An Asian diplomat said that senior Chinese officials had told him that Mr. Zhao was being forced to write confessions of misconduct.
Chinese news reports today, particularly those on television, were full of criticism of the United States, as announcers read aloud from letters and telegrams that they said had been sent by viewers. 
One telegram questioned the United States Government:
''Can you tolerate people who trample on the U.S. 
Constitution and seek to overthrow the Government by force?
Can you tolerate those who burn the White House and the President's cars?
Can you tolerate those who attack and burn shops and banks?
Can you tolerate those who cruelly injure innocent U.S. soldiers?
''Look - so much Chinese property is damaged. 
Listen - so many Chinese mothers are extremely worried about their country. 
But you in the U.S. government wilfully criticize the Chinese Government, which banned the riots. 
You supply protection to the chief criminals who incited riots. 
Is this the freedom and democracy you advertise?''
Â 
Voice of America Scored
Several telegrams and letters also attacked American news coverage of recent events in China. 
The attacks were particularly strong against the Voice of America, which has a large following in China for its Chinese-language radio news programs. 
The Voice of America reports, while jammed, have usually been audible and the primary source of unofficial news for most Chinese.
''It is shameful of Voice of America to spread rumors,'' declared one telegram from Henan province. 
''We Chinese should be careful not to believe the U.S. 
Voice of Rumor.''
Another telegram, from Sichuan province, reported: ''During the riots, we studied propaganda by Voice of America and our own news reports, and compared them, and we thought that our reports are more reliable.''
Â 
Student and Labor Leaders
Most of those arrested who were shown on television were young men whom the Government said had fought against the troops entering Beijing last weekend. 
However, some were leaders of independent student and labor organizations that had promoted the democracy movement.
In the Western city of Lanzhou, for example, 32 people were arrested for joining citizen support groups that cooperated with student demonstrators. 
And in Shanghai, Yao Yongzhan, the head of the unofficial university student union, was arrested at the airport as he tried to board a flight to Hong Kong. 
Nine leaders of an unofficial labor union had earlier been arrested for ''meeting secretly, spreading rumors, sending leaflets, starting strikes and calling on people to 'overthrow the Government.'
''
The official media reported that in the southwestern city of Guiyang, the police arrested a total of 59 ''bad elements who stopped vehicles, placed road barricades to stop traffic, and disturbed social order.''
The most prominent of those seized so far seems to be Ren Wanding, a dissident and essayist who has written articles for The New York Times and other publications. 
A decade ago, Mr. Ren was one of the first people to raise the issue of human rights in China, and he later spent four years in prison for his activites in the 1978-79 Democracy Wall movement.
Â 
Obstacles to News Gathering
Several other prominent Chinese intellectuals were not in their homes today, but it was not clear if they had been arrested, if they had gone into hiding, or if they were simply away for personal or business reasons.
It has been difficult for foreign journalists to gauge the scope of the arrests, partly because it seems especially dangerous now for Chinese to have contacts with foreigners. 
This means that many foreign journalists are avoiding their Chinese friends and contacts, and are worried even about telephoning people to find out if they have been arrested.
As a result, journalists are relying more on official reports and on diplomats.
The Asian diplomat said that the authorities had decided to criticize and perhaps replace the top executives of major news organizations, including the People's Daily and the New China News Agency, but it was not known if any had been arrested.

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_Did Heavens Finally Fall on Deng_ Some See His Defeat in China Events.txt
text:
ï»¿
Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, used to reassure nervous foreign leaders that they need not worry about China after his passing because he had installed his own successors, several veteran analysts here recalled today.
''There is nothing to fear even if heaven should fall down,'' Mr. Deng liked to say. 
For Hu Yaobang, then the Communist Party General Secretary, and Zhao Ziyang, the Prime Minister and later party chief, would be there to prop it up.
But in the last two years, the analysts note, Mr. Deng, who is 84 years old, has overseen the waning first of Mr. Hu and now Mr. Zhao, leaving him without a political heir. 
Instead, it is his onetime hard-line rivals who now have succeeded in positioning successors, with Li Peng as the Prime Minister and Qiao Shi, a member of the Standing Committee of the Politburo, as a possible General Secretary of the party.
This is one of the reasons, the analysts here believe, that Mr. Deng's violent crushing of the pro-democracy movement was not so much a victory as a defeat for him.
Â 
A Difference in Interpretation
In their interpretation, the specialists in Hong Kong differ with some diplomats in Beijing and Washington, a difference that has surfaced frequently in critical moments in China in recent years. 
The Hong Kong-based analysts, who have pursued their craft for 20, 30 or even 40 years, tend to be more skeptical than the diplomats, less optimistic about China's condition and more prone to see continuing factional intrigue.
The major cause for the divergence is simply that the Hong Kong experts, most of them Chinese, tend to base their conclusions on a close study of Communist newspapers and radio broadcasts, the traditional tools of China watchers.
By contrast, the diplomats in Beijing, at least until the declaration of martial law, have enjoyed increasing access to Chinese officials and report back their conversations with them. 
One trouble with this approach, a Western diplomat acknowledged today, is that the Chinese officials who talk with foreigners tend to be liberals, while the conservatives shun them.
As a result, several diplomats said, they had been somewhat misled and underestimated the growing strength of the hard-liners over the last few years, power that broke into public view with the decision to use the People's Liberation Army to suppress the demonstrations in Beijing.
Â 
The First Sign
But the analysts here believe that the rise of the conservatives can be traced to as early as 1982 or 1983, soon after Mr. Deng maneuvered his way to the top and began his program in 1979 to return land to the peasants and allow private enterprise.
The first sign, said the Rev. Laszlo Ladany, a Roman Catholic priest who for many years published an authoritative newsletter in Hong Kong about developments in China, was when Peng Zhen became chairman of the National People's Congress, the nominal legislature.
Mr. Peng, one of the conservative elders, managed to appoint to the People's Congress several like-minded officials who had been removed by Mr. Deng from their Communist Party posts, Father Ladany said. 
More important, Mr. Peng virtually turned the People's Congress into ''his own headquarters,'' insisting that it be given greater power and the right to pass on new policies, Father Ladany said.
''It was an extraordinary defiance by Peng,'' said Father Ladany, who was a missionary in China before the Communists' triumph in 1949.
Another analyst, who long worked for the British Government here, said a further important clue to the resurgence of the hard-liners came three years ago when Chen Yun, a prominent octogenarian, revealed in a published speech that he had earlier engineered the appointment of Mr. Li as Minister of Electric Power.
In the speech, published in the third volume of Mr. Chen's collected works, he reported that initially Mr. Li, then the Deputy Minister of Electric Power, was not on the list of candidates for the Cabinet post.
Â 
A Protege Is Purged
But after intercession by Mr. Chen, Mr. Li was given the job. 
Mr. Li was soon to be promoted to be Prime Minister, where he announced the imposition of martial law. 
Mr. Chen's disclosure of his action, which would normally be regarded as a state secret in China, strongly suggests he wanted it known that he was behind the advancing career of Mr. Li, the analysts said.
Further signs of the conservative gains multiplied. 
In 1987, Mr. Deng had to jettison his protege and close friend, Mr. Hu, allowing him to be purged as party General Secretary after an earlier round of student demonstrations. 
(Mr. Hu's death two months ago touched off the pro-democracy demonstrations that were crushed by the military crackdown this month.) Last September, although Mr. Deng told visitors that China would soon begin the critical step of freeing prices, to move to a more market-oriented economy, the hard-liners won a victory and ordered economic initiatives frozen.
But the Chinese analyst who worked for the British Government, after insisting that the conservatives were making gains, was ordered to take early retirement last November in what some colleagues feel was an effort to silence his viewpoint.
In his view, and that of a Chinese analyst who worked for the United States Consulate General here, the rise of Mr. Qiao was still another sign of the hard-liners' gains at the expense of Mr. Deng.
Â 
Many Important Posts
Over the last two years, the 65-year-old Mr. Qiao, a career intelligence operative, was suddenly given a series of powerful portfolios. 
These included being head of the so-called Leading Group for Political and Legal Affairs in the Central Committee, which supervises the police and courts. 
It was a job formerly held by Mr. Peng and which Mr. Peng may have arranged for him.
Similarly, Mr. Qiao took over from Mr. Chen the post as head of the Central Discipline Inspection Commission, which investigates corruption in the party. 
In fact, Mr. Qiao was given so many important jobs that the Hong Kong analysts believed he was on the verge of replacing Mr. Zhao as party General Secretary even before the demonstrations.
The analysts here say they believe that Mr. Li and Mr. Qiao are now contending behind the scenes for the top party post. 
But whichever man emerges as the new General Secretary, he will be a follower of the conservative elders, not Mr. Deng, the analysts say.
A Western diplomat here said another problem in gauging the rise of the hard-liners was that most of them, like Mr. Peng and Mr. Chen, seemed to retire. 
''We may have been misled by their resignations,'' he said.

file: Turmoil in China_Far From Beijing_s Spotlight, A City Bears Scars of Clashes.txt
text:
ï»¿
Filling nearly a full square block of this city in the Chinese hinterlands is the burned-out rubble of collapsed roofs and melted shutters, of shattered glass and the mangled remains of bicycles and carts. 
All of it is testimony to the fact that the violence that gripped Beijing a week and a half ago was echoed in at least one major provincial city.
Foreigners and the few Chinese willing to talk to reporters these days say events in Chengdu, the capital of Sichuan Province, closely resembled those in Beijing. 
The city saw about three weeks of intermittent, large-scale protest demonstrations at the city's main intersection. 
Students occupied the broad pedestal holding a giant statue of Mao, a spot that is a kind of symbolic city center.
Then on June 4 and 5, there was a series of angry, violent clashes between demonstrators and armed platoons of police in which several dozen people were killed, by the more conservative estimates. 
American consular officials here say that on June 5 alone at least 100 seriously wounded people were carried out of the broad intersection in front of the statue where the battle took place.
Chengdu, the only provincial city in China where violent clashes similar to those in Beijing are known to have taken place, reflects a dramatic aspect of the turmoil that was most visible to foreigners in the capital.
Â 
Wreckage of Recent Turmoil
These days the city wears a double aspect. 
On one hand, the pattern of everyday life has reasserted itself so fully that in most parts of the city there is little to suggest that an upheaval took place here just over a week ago.
The many small restaurants and tea houses are crowded with customers; the free markets are loaded with produce. 
Sichuan Province was the place where Zhao Ziyang, now all but deposed as China's Communist Party leader, first instituted the eco-nomic liberalization later carried out in the rest of the country, and small-scale free enterprise is much in evidence here.
But the wreckage in the center of town, a stone's throw from the Mao statue, is conspicuous evidence of the intensity of recent turmoil. 
The fire destroyed a large complex of small shops known as People's Market. 
It destroyed a medical clinic, a restaurant, a police station, a bicycle repair shop, and most of the city's largest theater.
While a scene of greater violence than most provincial cities, Chengdu demonstrates that the events of the last few weeks represented a revolt against China's Communist Government that went far beyond Beijing.
Â 
Rumors of Violence and Looting
Chengdu was not the only city in Sichuan, China's most populous province with more than 100 million people, to be swept up in the movement for greater democracy in this country. 
Foreign students in the city of Mianyang, about 100 miles north of Chengdu, report that for nearly a month there were demonstrations there, though there have been no reports of violence.
Moreover, the pro-democracy protests in Chengdu drew thousands of supporters from all over the province. 
People here noted delegations of students occupying the pedestal of the Mao statute from as far west as Aba, near the Tibetan border, as well as from such cities as Leshan and Chongqing in the south.
Since the crackdown in Beijing 10 days ago, reports have circulated elsewhere in China to the effect that Chengdu, whose population, including the surrounding areas, is about four million, was the scene of terrible violence and looting. 
One widespread report had it that the city's largest hotel, the Jinjiang, which houses the United States Consulate here, had been partially burned down.
In fact, a two-day visit to the city revealed no damage to the hotel, which consulate officials said was briefly invaded by looters who apparently had little or nothing to do with the student-led protest movement outside.
Â 
Police Patrols and Arrests
But the reports and rumors reaching other parts of China nonetheless do not seem to have done justice to the size of the confrontation that took place in this city or to the number of casualties.
Posters seen around the city call on the citizenry to turn in those who took part in what is now being called ''the counterrevolutionary disturbance'' and provides four telephone numbers for people to call to make denunciations.
At night, platoons of armed police officers can be seen drilling in the square behind the Mao statue nearby the hulks of a dozen or so trucks and buses that were set ablaze in the violent confrontation there. 
They patrol in trucks or jeeps at night, their rifle barrels extending out the windows. 
On Tuesday night, a reporter observed two details of about 150 men each running in formation through the city streets.
There have been highly credible reports of arrests here, particularly at the city's several research institutes and universities. 
On Tuesday night, two uniformed policemen were seen arriving at Sichuan University, where they were reported to be looking for a person whose name was included on a blacklist drawn up by the local public security bureau.
Â 
Clashes at Midnight Rally
Some people, informed by friends inside the Government that their names are on the blacklist, are reported to be expecting arrest. 
Some are said to be already in hiding.
Like most Chinese provincial cities, Chengdu seems to have taken its cue from Beijing as the protest movement unfolded. 
Foreigners living here say the first big demonstrations took place on May 16, set off by news that students in Beijing occupying Tiananmen Square had gone on hunger strikes to demand democracy.
Wanting to avoid the attention of school authorities, students at Sichuan University set out at midnight that night and marched the several miles to the center of Chengdu, picking up marchers from other institutions on the route, including the Institute of Science and Technology and the West China Medical School.
The midnight demonstrators, estimated at several thousand, broke through a line of police officers blocking the way to the Mao statue and occupied the area. 
When the police forcefully evacuated the area the next morning and wounded some students, none of them seriously, the move seemed to set off larger demonstrations the following days. 
Foreigners estimate the size of some of the crowds that filled the broad avenues in front of the Mao statue at more than 100,000.
Â 
Tear Gas and Truncheons
The demonstrations were so frequent that they spawned a new elocution. 
A standard greeting in Chinese is ''Have you eaten yet?''
In Chengdu during the several weeks of protest, it sometimes became ''Have you demonstrated yet?''
One visitor to the city said that citizens donated some $15,000 to help the students. 
There were demonstrations by journalists, the police, and, as in Beijing, even the army marching under banners identifying them. 
A group of mostly unemployed people who formed barriers to protect the students occupying the area of the Mao statue were dubbed ''Society University.''
Visitors to Chengdu at the time of the crackdown of June 4 and 5 - the days that it took place in Beijing - say that detachments of armed police officers appeared on the square for the first time on those days. 
The armed police are a paramilitary group under separate command from the regular public security bureau whose forces do not carry weapons.
The armed police units cleared the area around the Mao statue on the morning of June 4, but, they and the demonstrators clashed sharply several times that day and the day after, with many casualties, people who compiled first-hand reports say. 
Some witnesses to the scene on June 5 said they did not believe that the police fired their weapons, but there was large-scale use of tear gas and beatings of demonstrators with truncheons. 
Some demonstrators, nonetheless, asserted that hospitals reported at least four people dying of gunshot wounds in the two-day battle.
Â 
Debris Cleared From Streets
''Things went crazy,'' said one visitor to Chengdu. 
''Sidewalks got ripped up. 
Construction sites were raided for steel pipes and pieces of wood. 
There were stones everywhere. 
The police beat people savagely. 
The crowd broke all the windows in the city government building when they attacked it. 
There were hundreds of injuries of all sorts. 
Buses and truckes were set on fire all over the place, especially near the Mao statue.''
The fire that destroyed a section of the downtown area started on the night of June 4. 
Some people sympathetic to the protest movement said that merchandise was seen being carried out of the area before it broke out, which has led to widespread suspicions that the blaze was started by the police as a means of harming the credibility of the demonstrators.
In the days after the violent clashes, the city government quickly cleaned up the streets so that not a shred remained of the hundreds of posters that had been put up all over Chengdu. 
The universities canceled classes for the rest of the term and many students returned to their homes.
But more than a week after the police cleared the streets of protesters, thick crowds of people were still seen walking slowly by the great heaps of scorched debris that was once the People's Market staring inside at the few concrete walls and pillars that remained standing, or looking up at the People's Theater across the street, where the immense neon characters identifying it were melted.

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_For Beijing, A Shortfall In Soy Sauce.txt
text:
ï»¿
Slowly, Beijing residents are peering out of their windows into the winding alleyways where they live to talk about the events of the last few days. 
But the more they look, the more they see that life is not normal, and it is not clear when it will return that way.
A high school teacher went to work this week because she knew her students were supposed to take a practice exam for entrance to college. 
As soon as they began the test, the sounds of gunfire and falling artillery shells rang throughout the classroom.
The teacher decided to send the students home and to distribute three days worth of material, including sample tests, to the students. 
''Students, please go home and take the tests by yourselves,'' she said.
Â 
Inaptly Named Thoroughfare
In the district of Xidan, near where much of the bloodshed took place, about 25 burned-out cars still stretch across the Avenue of Eternal Peace, or Changan Avenue, as a reminder of the unrest that overcame the capital a few days ago. 
But people have begun to emerge onto the streets, partly to buy food and partly to seek answers from their neighbors to the confusion that has reigned.
''We want to work but we can't,'' a middle-age office worker said. 
''We are petrified to go out, and besides, there is no transportation.''
Throughout Beijing, there are no buses, no subways, no newspapers, no stores, no work. 
There are watermelons, tomatoes and chopped meat, but there are long lines and the prices are rising as quickly as supplies are disappearing.
Â 
No Free Rides
Taxis are so hard to get that one driver demanded $1,000 from a Japanese-American passenger for a half-hour trip to the airport that normally costs $10. 
And rickshaw rides that usually cost less than $1 are now going for $8.
The broad streets are mostly deserted because without buses or trolley cars, there is no way to get around. 
People ride their bicycles, but even so, there are so many blockades that detours are inevitable. 
One large intersection was blocked by eight buses interwoven in a spiral, and others are blocked by burning cars.
Many people still do not venture farther than the alleyways where they live, and even so there are rumors that the troops are willing to chase citizens into these lanes to shoot them.
Although most of the main stores are closed, some smaller shops are open, and the smaller vendors are selling vegetables and chopped meat. 
For these, there are long lines. 
''The cucumbers and cabbage are two to three times the price they were last week,'' said a young woman waiting to buy vegetables. 
''And you can't even get salt, vinegar or soy sauce.''
Â 
The News Isn't Newsy
Life inside the home may be just as strange, especially if it revolves around television programs. 
Lately, there has not been much news on the main station. 
Almost the whole day is taken up with educational programs, like engineering mathematics.
In an almost eerie example of Government-orchestrated time lapse, the television news at noon today broadcast feature programs that were weeks old.
''International Children's day is approaching,'' the voice-over said. 
The holiday was on June 1. 
Another piece of footage was about an artist using an electric iron to create an artistic work. 
That, too, had been shown before.
Then after the news program ended officially at 12:30, the screen reverted to the middle of a mathematics lesson. 
Five minutes later, footage taken with Government cameras flashed across the screen, as an announcer explained that scoundrels and hoodlums were attacking tanks and armored personnel carriers.
The screen then cut back to several hours of educational programming.

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_From the Security Apparatus, An Obscure Leader Emerges.txt
text:
ï»¿
Qiao Shi, the Communist Party leader whose major role was reaffirmed by the Beijing radio early today, has had a long career in the shadowy Chinese security apparatus and is believed to be close to old-guard conservatives.
Before the crisis in Beijing, Mr. Qiao was officially listed as the third-ranking member of the standing committee of the party Politburo, following only Zhao Ziyang, the General Secretary, and Li Peng, the more orthodox Prime Minister. 
With Mr. Zhao reported to have been stripped of his post for taking too conciliatory a line toward student demonstrators and Mr. Li widely despised, Mr. Qiao could be in line for the top party or Government jobs.
Some analysts say that may have been what elderly party hard-liners had long planned as they maneuvered over the last few years to place the 65-year-old Mr. Qiao in a highly unusual combination of powerful positions.
While Mr. Qiao is little known to foreigners and had an obscure early career, his current roster of titles suggests he may have been groomed for power.
Â 
Top Internal Security Officer
Qiao Shi (the name is pronounced chow shur) is the Communist Party's top internal security officer, as head of what is known as the Leading Group for Political and Legal Affairs under the Central Committee. 
This agency oversees the work of the Ministry of Public Security and all the police and courts in China.
It was apparently because of this job that the Supreme People's Court sent him the message broadcast by Radio Beijing. 
This post was formerly held by Peng Zhen, one of the leading conservatives.
To some analysts, the message to Mr. Qiao also suggested the possibility that China's current leaders may be moving toward a new stage of the crackdown involving trials of some of the student demonstrators or even party leaders accused of joining with them.
Mr. Qiao, a native of Zhejiang Province near Shanghai, is also head of the Personnel Leading Group of the Central Committee, which oversees the party organization department and is responsible for making all promotions and demotions in the party.
Moreover, Mr. Qiao is secretary of the Central Discipline Inspection Commission, which investigates corruption within the party and any violations of party rules. 
He succeeded Chen Yun, another elderly conservative, in this post and may have been placed there by Mr. Chen, analysts think.
Â 
Underground Agent in the '40's
In addition, Mr. Qiao is president of the Central Party School, where he oversees the party's theoretical journal, Seeking Truth.
Chinese familiar with Mr. Qiao's early life say he was an intelligence agent in the Communist underground in Shanghai during the civil war against the Nationalists in the 1940's. 
His official biography says he attended college in Shanghai. 
Few senior Chinese officials have college or even high-school degrees.
In the 1960's Mr. Qiao worked in the International Liaison Department of the Central Committee, which has responsibilty among other things for foreign intelligence and subversion. 
He disappeared in the Cultural Revolution, but later was promoted to deputy director and then director of the International Liaison Department.
Little is known about Mr. Qiao's family or personal life.

file: Turmoil in China_Gorbachev Mutes His Voice in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
With the tumult in China continuing, the separate theaters of the new Soviet candor - adventurous at home, strategically crimped abroad - have never been clearer.
As President Mikhail S. Gorbachev returned today to the international stage, arriving for a summit meeting in Bonn, he left behind the jarring, exhilarating novelty of domestic outspokenness in the name of democracy in the new national congress. 
But this only underscored his own painstakingly uncritical view of China's violent repression of its pro-democracy demonstrators.
President Gorbachev was the most talkative man on the Soviet television, day in and day out, no topics barred, for two weeks of give and take on domestic issues. 
But he shunned the same garrulousness over China, as if glasnost were not for export.
Won't Risk New Opening
''He will stick to this policy, without a doubt,'' said an experienced Asian ambassador here.
''He's worked too long and too hard to rebuild the China tie to risk it now with a critical remark,'' said the diplomat, who estimated that Mr. Gorbachev personally weighed each word in the resolution adopted last week by the Soviet congress that defended China and condemned outside critics for stirring ''passions'' over Beijing's internal affairs.
In private, some Foreign Ministry officials concede their discomfort about the repression in China, but mainly in ways as pragmatic as Mr. Gorbachev's policy. 
One ranking official said that by attracting the world's news organizations to Beijing for his mid-May summit meeting there, Mr. Gorbachev may have unintentionally increased the stakes of civil demonstration and made the problem more difficult for the Beijing regime in the early stages.
Â 
Cautious and Terse
Unlike some Western leaders who condemned the violence, Mr. Gorbachev has been cautious and terse, declining even to match the restrained criticism of President Bush, which was accompanied by American military sanctions.
''Let Bush speak for himself,'' Mr. Gorbachev declared. 
He has remained resolute in his policy of noninterference, whatever the outrage of other nations, as he works toward links with China that could help to resuscitate the despairing Soviet economy.
In the view of a Western expert on Chinese-Soviet relations, Gorbachev's approach seems like basic, time-tested Machiavelli. 
But it is uncharacteristic Gorbachev after all the plain-spoken and world-stunning initiatives he has made in the name of disarmament and democracy.
''He's got to know he copped out on Beijing after all his months of talking about progress on human rights,'' the expert said. 
''And it's shameful, even if his reasons can be seen.''
Â 
A Call for 'Dialogue'
The most Mr. Gorbachev has allowed was a mention of concern about the violence and a hope that ''dialogue'' would settle it. 
But he never acknowledged the bloodshed inflicted on civil demonstrators by Chinese troops, and neither have Government-controlled news organizations here.
Instead, Soviet newspapers and television have presented what seems, in these giddily forthright days, like an exercise in the nostalgia of Communist censorship: a 1950's-steeped sympathetic parroting of official Chinese press reports about a responsible government dealing properly with ''reactionary forces'' who were supported by the ''incitement to hatred'' of foreign voices.
Lacking the shocking television coverage of the Beijing bloodshed, the Soviet public has spared Mr. Gorbachev moral pressure at home, making it far easier for him to stand strictly by the noninterference policy that has been one of the tenets of his laborious rapprochement with the Chinese after 20 years of bad relations.
Â 
Sakharov Plea Ignored
He stood fast particularly in the face of withering complaint in the final moments of the new congress's inaugural session from Andrei D. Sakharov, the Nobel Peace Prize laureate, who refused to be silenced and demanded in the name of humanity that the congress denounce the killings by the Beijing regime. 
''Enough, enough,'' Mr. Gorbachev said firmly, preferring the congress's resolution of support for Beijing.
''Remember that the Soviets did the most of the work to get back into China, and it was hard work,'' a Western diplomat said, speculating on Mr. Gorbachev's intensity in not seeing the new ties broken by one violent episode. 
''Still, you can question his strategy in the long run if moderates finally do gain control in China.''
Another diplomat stressed ''the glass house'' caution of Mr. Gorbachev. His full domestic realm, whatever the excitement over free-wheeling declarations in the congress, includes persistent, explosive mixes of civil demonstrations, grass-roots violence and martial-law standoffs in outlying republics and among ethnic groups.
Â 
Bush 'No Less Strategic'
''President Bush has been no less strategic in his approach,'' a pro-Gorbachev diplomat commented, saying that the White House criticism could have been more sweeping, considering public outrage in the United States, and that the White House also stopped short of altering commercial and ambassadorial ties to China.
''No doubt the violence took Gorbachev by surprise when he came back from Beijing,'' the diplomat said. 
''But he has to stick with his policy. 
He wants relations with China to be his model of normalization, of noninterference with other nations.''
The diplomat said the defensible denominator in both glasnost and Soviet policy in China was Mr. Gorbachev's overriding need to do anything it takes to rouse the Soviet economy.

file: Turmoil in China_Hong Kong Cancels Mourning Rallies.txt
text:
ï»¿
Plans for a series of rallies to mourn the victims of the Chinese crackdown were canceled here today after a violent confrontation between the police and a group described as provocateurs from the mainland.
But pro-democracy organizers, who canceled the rallies, continued their call for a token strike today, and many Hong Kong people shut their offices and shops or halted work to observe a moment of silence for the slain Beijing protesters. 
Schools were closed and many factories were idle.
Throughout the colony, people marked the deaths in Beijing with small personal tributes: flowers placed on Hong Kong's stone war memorial, a bit of black cloth draped along a window or tied to a car.
Violence Before Dawn
In its account of a predawn riot in the Chinese neighborhood of Mongkok, one of the most densely populated areas in the world, the Hong Kong Government said it was inspired by provocateurs from the mainland, assuring residents they were on the alert.
Several hundred police officers were called to Mongkok at 1:30 A.M. after a peaceful demonstration degenerated into a riot, with ''unruly hooligans'' hurling bottles and cans and battering storefronts with bamboo poles, the authorities said.
It was the first crowd violence since rallies and marches in support of China's pro-democracy movement began in Hong Kong several weeks ago. 
'These culprits were not those demonstrating in support of the Beijing students,'' a police official said. 
''They were criminal and nnruly elements who tried to exploit the situation.'
He added he had ''no information regarding their political motives, but I can't rule out any possibility.''
Â 
Organization of Crowd
Martin Lee, a legislator and a leader of the pro-democracy movement, said he believed the disruptive crowd ''was definitely organized,'' adding, ''In the beginning there may have been people having some fun, but toward the end we have witnesses who said they saw people brought in, carloads of people.'
He said there was a ''distinct possibility'' that the trouble was provoked by those wishing to discredit the demonstrations.
But the Secretary for Security, Jeffrey Barnes, said rumors that mainland agents had infiltrated the movement here, as they did in the 1960's in the Cultural Revolution, were unfounded. 
He said the Hong Kong Government was monitoring the situation closely. 
Another security official later said the riot was ''in no way political.''
A police spokesman said 'unruly hooligans in the crowd first tried to smash their way into a bank owned by China, and then turned to other shops and buildings on Nathan Road, later setting fire to a van. 
The police, wielding nightsticks, charged into the crowd, then set off tear gas to disperse the mob. 
Officials said the size of the crowd grew from 500 to about 7,000. 
The police said 15 people were arrested and 5 police officers were wounded.
Â 
Carnations for the Dead
Regina Lau, who was on strike from her job in a small trading company, said she was disappointed and very bitter that some people were not responsible and disrupted the demonstrations.
She had a small bunch of white carnations as a makeshift memorial for the students and citizens who died in the violence in Beijing. 
On the paper around the flowers she had written, ''We will miss you forever.''
The British colony, 98 percent ethnic Chinese, will revert to China in 1997, and the people here have been obsessed with the democratic movement in China, holding vigils, marches and demonstrations at first to express their hope and support for the cause and now, to show their anger and sorrow.
Despite the wilting heat, thousands of people stood in a line that stretched for more than a mile, waiting to sign the condolence book for China's dead that demonstrators have placed near the New China News Agency, the mainland's unofficial consulate here and the focus of many protests. 
Like Miss Lau, many brought flowers, and most wore black arm bands or head bands.
Â 
Many Shops Are Closed
In the business district, banks and the stock exchange remained opened but most of the fashionable boutiques like Gucci, Christian Dior and Baccarat were closed, as were beauty shops, computer and camera stores, tailor shops and dry cleaners.
Organizers had stressed that they did not want to disrupt commerce in the colony, but were simply calling for workday gestures to honor the dead.
Taxis, minibuses and limousines bore bits of black mourning cloth on their aerials, and many cars and trucks carried hand-lettered signs supporting the democratic cause in China and deploring the violence used to suppress it. 
Several thousand trucks and cars formed a caravan and paraded pass the New China News Agency.
The sleek new Bank of China tower, the tallest building in Asia and the pride of official Beijing, had two long slender black banners draped from its mirrored windows. 
The banners read: ''We are saddened for the thousands who were killed fighting for democracy,'' and ''We hate the wolves who betrayed the people.'

Two-thirds of Americans approve of the way President Bush is dealing with recent events in China, and majorities concur with several of the Administration's recent policies toward China, according to the latest Gallup Poll.

Seventy percent in the new survey approved of the way Mr. Bush is handling his job as President, up from 56 percent who approved in Gallup's previous poll, taken May 4 to 7.
The latest telephone survey, based on interviews with 1,235 adults nationwide, was conducted from June 8 to 11 and had a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 4 percentage points.
In reacting to the situation in China, 67 percent of the public approved of the way President Bush is dealing with events there. 
Majorities of the public also supported several of the Administration's recent policies toward the Chinese Government.
For example, 75 percent favored suspending the sale of American arms to China, a step already taken by the Administration. 
Seventy-one percent favored permitting Chinese students now in the United States to remain here after their visas expire.
But 72 percent opposed breaking off diplomatic relations with China, and 49 percent opposed recalling the American Ambassador from China.

file: Turmoil in China_Shanghai Issues an Appeal for Calm, and a Warning to Go With It.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Mayor of this city appealed in a televised address for an end to the ''chaos'' that he said has prevailed here for several days, warning that anyone causing disturbances or interfering with efforts to restore Shanghai's transportation system would be ''dealt with by the police in accordance with law.''
Mayor Zhu Rongji's speech on late-night television was one of several indications today that the authorities here are preparing to toughen their response to a student-led protest movement in Shanghai.
Earlier today, local newspapers carried an editorial warning that those causing disturbances would be severely punished. 
Nonetheless, in several small rallies and marches around the city, students called today for a mass demonstration Friday to protest the bloody repression of the democracy movement that took place in Beijing last weekend.
The warnings and the continuing efforts of an apparently dwindling number of students to maintain the protest were the latest development in a war of nerves between the Government and protesters that has been constant and intense in China's largest city since the crackdown in Beijing on Saturday and Sunday.
Since then, students and their supporters have succeeded in virtually blocking public transportation by commandeering buses and using them to barricade streets. 
Absenteeism at factories has been high and there has been a mood of near insurrection among many here outraged by the central Government's handling of protests in Beijing.
With foreign companies and some consulates evacuating their personnel, flights out of Shanghai have all been full. 
Foreign students at the universities, fearing violence there, have been leaving their dormitories and living in hotels in the city while they make their plans to leave. 
An emergency charter flight organized by the Australian Consulate took 400 people to Hong Kong this afternoon.
Â 
A Partial Return to Normalcy
Still, while anti-Government feelings clearly run high among local people, there have been many signs that, even without tough government measures, many elements of life in Shanghai began returning to normal today.
For the first time in almost a week, bus service on several main streets was restored. 
Visits to factories indicated that absenteeism, estimated at times to be as much as 50 percent of the work force, has diminished. 
There were indications that rail service, all but completely disrupted for two days, would resume soon.
All along, commercial life has been little affected by the protest movement. 
Stores have remained open; the shopping streets have continued to be crowded; students have allowed food to pass through barricades and there have been no reported shortages.
There were reports that many students, including many of the most politically active, have left their campuses in recent days and returned home, apparently in the belief that they have lost the struggle for now and would do better to work behind the scenes for a renewed pro-democracy movement in the future.
The Government's strategy seems to have been to avoid direct confrontations with local protesters, a policy that, by removing the police from the streets, often gave the impression in the last few days that large parts of Shanghai were entirely in the hands of the students and their supporters.
Â 
Rally at Party Headquarters
Even today, for example, students held a rally in front of Communist Party headquarters here during which they read a statement demanding that the United Nations expel China because of what they called its human rights abuses. 
There were about a dozen unarmed soldiers guarding the entrance to the building, but, even though the demonstration filled up the broad avenue that runs along the harbor here, there was no effort to stop it.
Similarly, students have circulated freely around the city, giving speeches, putting up posters, marching down city streets and commandeering buses. 
The police have made virtually no effort to interfere with them.
But the government has, particularly in the last couple of days, used that absolute control of the news media to mount a propaganda campaign, both in the newspapers and on television, appealing to the desire for order and accusing a ''very small number'' of people of trying to foment disorder.
Television stations, for example, have repeatedly shown footage of a train set afire two nights ago by Shanghai residents. 
Students and many others say the train driver, ordered by the police here to ignore a human blockade, plowed into a group of people, killing six of them. 
The television news has portrayed the train burning as an act of sabotage by ''bad elements,'' and its repeated reference to the incident seems aimed at persuading people of the costs of continued protests.
Â 
'Do You Want Chaos?'
Mr. Zhu's unscheduled appearance on television at about 11 P.M. tonight seemed aimed at encouraging the move toward the restoration of normal life here by combining warnings against the students with an appeal to trust the local government and the Communist Party to solve Shanghai's problems.
''Do you want chaos in Shanghai?''
Mr. Zhu, wearing a Western-style jacket and tie, said. 
Then, addressing what he called ''a very small number'' of ''unlawful elements,'' he said, ''the broad masses of Shanghai citizens can no longer tolerate your illegal activities.''
He said the city had organized major efforts to clear blockades across streets and to resume normal transportation. 
He said any efforts to interfere with the restoration of normal service would be ''punished by law.''
He blamed the disorder on unspecified ''foreign rumors,'' by which he presumably meant reports by foreign news organizations, particularly the Voice of America and the BBC, both of which are widely listened to in China, on the crackdown in Beijing.
While the foreign news reports have generally put the numbers of dead in the Beijing crackdown in the thousands, the Chinese news media have lately been reiterating a statement by Yuan Mu, the spokesman for the State Council, that about 300 people died in the army's action, most of them soldiers.

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_Shanghai Reports Dissidents_ Arrest.txt
text:
ï»¿
The state-controlled local radio and television stations reported today that nine labor dissidents and an undisclosed number of other people had been arrested for their roles in the protests that have swept this city in recent weeks.
The arrests, which followed official warnings two days ago that ''bad elements'' would be ''punished in accordance with the law,'' indicated that the roundup of protesters under way in Beijing was spreading to other cities.
Shanghai, China's most populous city and most important economic center, has been the scene of an active student-led protest movement since the army's savage crackdown in Beijing nearly a week ago. 
Earlier this week, it brought the public transportation system to a halt, and on Friday it brought tens of thousands of anti-Government demonstrators into the streets.
But today, in a move that seemed to signal at least a temporary move away from open protests, students from at least one university, the East China Teachers College, were reported to have voted to disband the autonomous student union formed early in the pro-democracy movement to coordinate student activities. 
Students elsewhere said they expected the unions at other universities to follow the East China Teachers College example.
Â 
'Don't Have the Strength'
''We simply don't have the strength to do more now,'' said a student union member from Fudan University, adding that many students ''feel that further activism now would get us nowhere. 
They think it would be better to reflect on our experience and to renew the movement sometime in the future.''
Still, several dozen students from Fudan University staged a sit-in today in front of the Shanghai police headquarters, protesting the arrest of nine members of the Autonomous Workers Union.
The Shanghai radio reported this morning that the nine were taken in by the police on Friday. 
There was no information on their identities or the charges against them, but their arrests were seen here as a sign that the crackdown against the democracy movement was intensifying.
While many workers have taken part in the last few days of protest, the Autonomous Workers Union does not seem to have played a major role in the pro-democracy movement. 
There are no officially recognized trade unions in China.
Â 
Others Reported Arrested
The state press also said today that several other people, described as ''hooligans,'' have been arrested in the last couple of days. 
The evening television news today showed footage of some of them being led to vans by the police and of others being interrogated, apparently at police headquarters.
The Shanghai radio, meanwhile, has been broadcasting almost continuous accounts of the ''counterrevolutionary'' and ''reactionary'' activities of students and others that ''brought great harm'' to the city. 
The radio has asked those who have engaged in ''illegal demonstrations'' and who have ''disrupted transportation'' to register with the police. 
So far, however, there have been no reports that any student leaders have been arrested.
It was unclear whether the crackdown in Shanghai would extend to intellectual circles.
Officials in Shanghai, in contrast with their counterparts in Beijing, have generally taken a moderate approach to the protest movement.
The authorities apparently have not wanted to arouse the anger of a population already seemingly bitter and shocked by the military operation in the capital six days ago.
At the small sit-in in front police headquarters today, for instance, there was no attempt by the police to remove demonstrators by force. 
After several hours, the students sent a small delegation inside police headquarters, presumably to discuss their grievances, while the rest of them returned to their campus.
Still, there have been signs of a toughening attitude on the part of the authorities here toward protesters. 
Brigades of workers militia, hastily organized by the authorities to aid the police, were visible at various points around Shanghai today. 
Their presence at major intersections and near the universities was evidently designed to forestall any resumption of efforts to disrupt the transportation system or to set up new street barricades.
Today for the first time local television showed footage of Friday's mass demonstration, characterizing it as illegal and charging that student demands against the Government were ''unreasonable.''
The students' demands were that flags be flown at half-staff in mourning for the students slain in Beijing, that the local governments agree to a ''dialogue'' with students and that videotapes of the army's operation in Beijing be made public.
At the demonstration on Friday, student speakers warned that if their demands were not met within 48 hours, they would step up their protests. 
Today, however, it seemed unlikely that the students retained the strength needed to follow up on the ultimatum.

file: Turmoil in China_Student Recounts 5 Days of Questioning by Police.txt
text:
ï»¿
A Chinese graduate student who disappeared last week on a visit home has returned to the United States and reported that Chinese police interrogated her for five days about American organizations aiding the pro-democracy demonstrators in Beijing.
Cheng Yu, a 31-year-old education student at the University of Chicago, said she was also struck by the sympathetic attitude among some of the half dozen Chinese police who questioned her. 
She said one policewoman had mocked a Government television broadcast that said Chinese citizens were enthusiastically welcoming the soldiers who cleared Tiananmen Square.
Ms. Cheng, her 1-year-old son, Payton, and a friend, Tong Boning, a graduate student at the University of California at Los Angeles, disappeared last week while on a two-week visit to China to help pro-democracy demonstrators. 
They were supposed to depart China on June 5 and were escorted to the airport departure area by relatives and friends, but they did not arrive on schedule in the United States and their worried relatives notified the State Department that they were missing.
In a telephone interview from their home in Chicago, Ms. Cheng and her husband, Li Sanyuan, gave a vivid account of her five days in captivity.
Ms. Cheng could not relate the story entirely on her own because she had to leave the telephone to console her baby, who, she said, has been upset by the ordeal. 
Mr. Tong could not be reached in Los Angeles yesterday to relate his account.
Â 
Under Constant Surveillance
Ms. Cheng, who is four months pregnant, her son, and Mr. Tong were arrested in the departure area of Beijing International Airport by police officers who had evidently kept track of them during the two-week visit, she said. 
They were taken to a guest house in a Beijing suburb that, Mr. Li said, is popular with Chinese officials who use the nearby golf course.
At the guest house, the two students' bodies and belongings were searched and they were interrogated for five days in separate rooms by a half dozen police women and men. 
Ms. Cheng said two policewomen accompanied her each time she went to the bathroom and remained in her room as she slept. 
Generally, Ms. Cheng indicated she was treated well but she said she broke down once because the authorities were refusing to notify her husband or her mother, a Beijing resident, of her whereabouts.
''I imagined how he must feel, and my mother, who is 70 years old, and I cried,'' she said.
Ms. Cheng said she had refused food for a day to press her demand that the police obey the law requiring notification of relatives.
Much of the interrogation, she and her husband said, centered on her knowledge of American organizations in China that may be sending money and providing other support for pro-democracy students within China. 
Ms. Cheng had brought into China more than $3,000 in donations she collected from Chinese students studying in Chicago and elsewhere. 
She distributed the money to people in Beijing who were helping the students camped in Tiananmen Square buy food and maintain sanitary conditions.
Â 
Questioned About Donations
''They wanted to know how the donations are collected,'' she said. 
''They think there must be an organization of some people who are in charge.''
Ms. Cheng said she told the police that she had collected the funds ''spontaneously'' and did not represent any organization.
''They wanted to find that I am the connection between some political organization in the United States and the student movement in China,'' she said. 
Her husband added, ''They wanted to know whether there was a conspiracy or any sort of organization behind her.''
Ms. Cheng has written articles for China Spring, a Chinese magazine published in the United States, and her interrogators asked her about the magazine's operations.
The police focused on a diary Ms. Cheng kept during her 15 days in China. 
In the diary, she described encounters in Tiananmen Square with the leaders of the protests there and with ordinary students. 
Ms. Cheng said she kept the diary because she wanted to let Chinese students in America know of the bravery of the protesters in Tiananmen Square. 
When she and Mr. Tong left for the airport, he warned her that it would be dangerous to try to bring the diary through passport control, but she rejected his urgings.
''She didn't take enough precaution,'' her husband said. 
''She thought she might get it through customs. 
After all it was a notebook. 
It was not a document.''
Â 
'The End of a Nightmare'
Ms. Cheng said that at one point policewomen guarding her watched a news program on the crackdown in Beijing and laughed when a reporter declared that Chinese citizens were welcoming the troops.
''One of them said, 'Why don't you show it to us?'
'' Ms. Cheng said. 
''There were no pictures on the screen and she said it very sarcastically.''
At another point, when pictures failed to back up the message, a policewoman scoffed, ''The TV has turned into a radio station.''
''I think they were sympathetic,'' she said. 
''They feel real concern for the baby. 
They told me: 'Don't be pessimistic. 
Things cannot be that bad.'
''
Ms. Cheng said she noticed that one policewoman was reading a book by an American author whose title she remembered as ''Tolerance.''
Ms. Cheng and her baby were released Friday night, and she promptly called her husband and alerted him that she would be returning on the next plane to San Francisco. 
She arrived in Chicago on Saturday night.
''It's the end of a nightmare,'' Mr. Li said yesterday, ''because no one knew where my wife was and what could happen to her next.''
Ms. Cheng said she had no regrets about her mission to China. 
''I have a personal mission,'' she said. 
''I want to be with my people at this historic time. 
It was worthwhile even if I had been there longer than five days.''

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_Students in Shanghai Wage War of Buses With Officials.txt
text:
ï»¿
First there are several disabled buses blocking the road to traffic and then, at the entrance to Fudan University, whose students put up the barricade, there are the signs of rebellion.
A Chinese flag is marked with a black band and under it the words ''China is Dead.''
Another sign hangs from a building declaring, ''National Disaster.''
Covering glass cases where school notices are usually posted are photocopied pages of Hong Kong and American newspapers showing pictures, not available in the Chinese press, of the violent crackdown over the weekend in Beijing.
Like most of the 40 or so institutions of higher learning in this city, Fudan, the most prestigious, is engaged in a strangely indirect battle with the local authorities, one that reflects the tension and unease in this city, China's largest, since the army's move on protesters in Beijing.
Â 
To Topple the Government
''Our goal is no longer, as it was before, merely to promote democracy,'' said one student, who gave only his surname, Wang. 
''Now, it is to encourage strikes, to disturb traffic and to help bring about the fall of the Government.''
Mr. Wang was standing next to a mobile speaker's unit, complete with microphone and loudspeakers, which students said is one of several being taken around this sprawling urban area so that the students' point of view can be spread, particularly about the brutality of the army's move in Beijing.
But a more intense battle has been taking place over the city's buses. 
They have been commandeered by students and supporters among the city's working class who let the air out of their tires so they can be used to disrupt the city's traffic and prevent people from showing up at work.
The crippling of the city's buses, which has all but eliminated public transportation in this city of about 12 million people, took place in broad daylight in the two days since the Beijing crackdown.
Â 
Counterattack at Night
The Government's counterattack takes place in the small hours of the morning when, presumably, most of Shanghai's aroused citizenry is asleep. 
Tonight, in fact, the state-controlled local television news showed a nocturnal police operation to tow the disabled buses off the streets and into repair yards.
A spokesman for the city transportation department, interviewed on the air, said 236 disabled buses had been recovered in this way, though he said they had not yet been put back into service because of a need for repairs and a lack of spare parts. 
Another view is that the city does not dare to restore bus service for fear that the buses will be commandeered and used as barricades again.
The students say the use of buses to make barricades is justified by the need to fight against a brutal Government. 
The action has the support of a large majority of people, they say, and the police have not interfered with their operations in what the students say is an effort to avoid arousing the people's anger. 
By contrast, the official propaganda machine attributes the sabotage of the buses to ''a very small number of bad elements'' who are seeking to use the current instability in China to stir up even more trouble.
Â 
No Public Transportation
Whatever the case, even as many of the barricades set up since Sunday have disappeared and the buses recovered by the city administration, there is still no public transportation in Shanghai.
The intensity of distrust here, and of the indirect conflict, could be seen when a train plowed into some people blocking the tracks a mile or so from the central station on Tuesday night, killing six and injuring six.
People who gathered about the scene of the accident said they believed that the train crew had been told by higher authorities to ignore the human blockade. 
They were so angry that they not only set the train's nine passenger cars ablaze last night, but also burned six police sidecar motorcycles parked on a road parallel to the tracks.
During a visit to the site this afternoon, a reporter discovered a large crowd of people, mostly workers in nearby factories, supporting the theory that the train accident was, like the Beijing army action, another instance of the reckless disregard by the authorities for the lives of ordinary people.
Â 
Tracks Blockaded
''All of the tracks have been blockaded for several days,'' said a man in the irate crowd examining the charred wreckage of the train and the heap of burned motorcycles. 
''So they knew there were people on the tracks, and yet they ordered the train not to stop.''
The official news accounts of the incident acknowledged that six people were killed in the accident but did not specify the cause. 
The account, carried on the local television news, along with pictures of the train engulfed in flames, went on to blame the arson on the ''very small number of bad elements'' who have been sabotaging the buses.
The Government's effort to quell the brooding crisis in Shanghai is, on the one hand, to try quietly, in the dead of night to repair the damage being done to the city's transportation system while, on the other, to portray its opponents as tiny, isolated bands doing harm to the people's welfare.
Â 
Mood of Defiance
The strategy also seems based on the hope that the student movement will die away, and indeed perhaps a half of the students have left the universities to go home, depleting their forces. 
Nonetheless, the mood at the partially depopulated Fudan today was defiant and even optimistic.
''The Government has lost its right to rule,'' said a student who, like virtually all of his colleagues, preferred not to give his name. 
''We are confident because we have so much support among the Chinese people. 
If we remain united in our effort, maybe we can succeed in forcing the Government to step down.''
Another student took a visitor on a tour of the campus slogans, drawing particular attention to one that made an allusion to a past martyr in the fight against tyranny.
According to legend, the student explained, a hero named Jing Ke tried to assassinate the cruel and ruthless first Emperor of China in the third century B.C. Before he set out on his doomed task, Jing Ke wrote a short poem reproduced at Fudan in black characters on red paper. 
It said:
Â 
The wind blows.
The river is cold.
The hero sets forth.
He may never return.

file: TURMOIL IN CHINA_U.S. Suggests Way Out Of Dispute on Dissidents.txt
text:

In an effort to resolve the dispute over two Chinese dissidents who have taken refuge in the United States Embassy in Beijing, Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d has suggested that the couple be allowed to go to a third country for asylum, Admnistration officials said today.
The idea of suggesting to the Chinese that they permit the dissidents, Fang Lizhi and his wife, Li Shuxian, to go to an unspecified third country originated with the United States Ambassador to Beijing, James R. Lilley, the officials said.
Mr. Baker accepted the proposal, which was one of several put forward by Mr. Lilley, and formally broached it with the Chinese Ambassador to Washington, Han Xu, during their discussions over the last three days. 
Mr. Lilley did the same with his contacts at the Foreign Ministry in Beijing.
Administration officials said that the Chinese have not responded to the American suggestion, but that an answer could be forthcoming at any moment. 
Repeated requests to the Chinese Embassy in Washington for a comment on the matter went unanswered.
'Left Ball in Chinese Court'
''We left the ball in the Chinese court,'' an Administration official said. 
''We have basically told the Chinese: You write the scenario and we will sign off on it. 
We want to find a quick solution. 
Our only bottom line is that we are not going to turn the Fangs over for arrest.''
Administration officials said the logic of the third-country proposal was that it would satisfy Washington's requirements that the dissident couple not be turned over for arrest, and spare Beijing the embarrassment of the couple's coming immediately to the United States for a media extravaganza.
Administration officials said they had no illusions that it would be easy to persuade the Chinese to accept such a compromise, particularly because the Beijing authorities put out an arrest warrant for Mr. Fang and Miss Li on Sunday and accused them of ''crimes of counterrevolutionary propaganda and instigation.''
The Chinese couple, both physicists, sought refuge in the American Embassy on June 4, after the military crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square.
Â 
Protection, Not Asylum
The embassy granted them temporary sanctuary on the ground that their lives were in danger. 
The couple made it clear at the time that they came to the embassy for physical protection and not in an effort to seek political asylum, which cannot be granted by the United States on foreign soil.
They insisted that they were Chinese patriots who wanted to remain in their home country, if at all possible. 
Given the position of the Chinese authorities, however, that is apparently no longer an option, unless they want to go to jail.
Administration analysts say they believe that the Chinese leadership remains divided on a variety of issues, including how to handle the Fang affair. 
It is known that Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, and President Yang Shangkun have a personal, visceral dislike for Mr. Fang, whose persistant and public demands for greater freedom in China have made him a folk hero among Chinese university students and an inspiration for the pro-democracy movement as a whole.
In addition, Administration officials believe that some circles in the Chinese leadership would like to use the Fang affair as a tool to worsen already tense relations with the West in general and the United States in particular.
Depicting Mr. Fang and Miss Li and their supporters as part of a broader ''conspiracy'' by foreigners to interfere in Chinese affairs might also be a useful way for Chinese authorities to undermine the legitimacy of the pro-democracy movement, the officials said.
Â 
The Economic Incentive
At the same time, the Administration is convinced that other elements of the Chinese leadership, possibly even Mr. Deng, have a powerful economic incentive not to damage ties with the United States and its Western allies any further and, as a result, might be ready to swallow their antipathy to the couple to get the matter behind them.
The State Department, though, showed no signs today of mincing its words or restraining its response to developments in China.
In a move that could itself inject further acrimony into Chinese-American relations, the State Department signaled today that it intended to expand and speed up processing of both immigrant and non-immigrant visas to accommodate those Chinese seeking to leave their country in the wake of the current wave of repression. 
Long lines of visa applicants are reported at the American Embassy in Beijing and American consulates elsewhere in China.
The State Department spokeswoman, Margaret D. Tutwiler, said: ''We will be monitoring the requirements to assure that staffing levels are adequate to provide the full range of consular services, including visa issuances. 
We will do whatever it takes to process visas in China.''
After the June 4 shootings in Beijing, President Bush ordered a halt to all military sales to China and extended the visas of Chinese nationals now in the United States until June 1990.
An inter-agency task force charged with preparing an additional list of possible sanctions the Administration might impose on China, should the situation there deteriorate further, has completed its work and presented its ideas to Mr. Baker. Officials said the options consist primarily of a variety of economic sanctions and limits on technology transfers.
Ms. Tutwiler cautioned, however, that this list of options was not presented to Mr. Baker ''in the form of recommendations.''
She added, ''They are merely a laundry list of possible options should the need arise.''
She declined to specify what actions by the Chinese authorities would prompt imposition of these additional punitive measures.
In light of the manhunt the Chinese police have begun for 21 fugitive leaders of the pro-democracy movement, and the mass arrests that have already taken place, Ms. Tutwiler once criticized the Beijing Government.
''Chinese media have reported the arrest of hundreds of persons,'' she said. 
''These arrests are very disturbing. 
Detention or arrest of people for exercising basic human rights of freedom of expression and free association is contrary to internationally recognized standards. 
We continue to believe that the solution to the problems in China lies not in repression and arrest, but in dialogue.''

file: U. S. EASING CURBS AS CHINA DECLARES MARTIAL LAW OVER.txt
text:
