China lifted martial law in Beijing today, and within hours the United States announced that it was easing its blanket opposition to World Bank loans to China.
Prime Minister Li Peng, who announced the lifting of martial law in a nationally televised speech, warned against unspecified foreign and domestic ''hostile forces'' that he said were working to subvert Communism in China. 
But he said that by and large, China had returned to normal.
Despite the official end of martial law, the Chinese authorities retain the ability and apparently a desire to suppress any signs of political unrest, experts on China said. 
[An article and excerpts from Mr. Li's speech are on page A10.] Administration's China Policy Vice President Dan Quayle said the lifting of martial law vindicated Mr. Bush's efforts to re-establish normal diplomatic ties with China. 
But experts on China challenged the Administration's assertion that Mr. Bush's policy had helped persuade China to lift martial law.
The Chinese action did not quell Congressional anger over the crackdown, in which hundreds of Chinese civilians were killed. 
Nor did it seem likely to mute Congressional criticism of President Bush's policy, which many lawmakers consider excessively sympathetic to the Chinese leadership.
The White House and the State Department praised China's decision to lift martial law as ''a positive step.''
Neither publicly acknowledged that strict laws banning dissent remained in force in China.
The State Department spokeswoman, Margaret D. Tutwiler, said that in ''a partial change of policy'' the United States would examine loans on a case-by-case basis.
Â 
Support for 'Human-Needs Loans'
Proposals for seven loans totaling $780 million have been held at the World Bank since the beginning of the crackdown in June.
Mr. Bush does not want economic sanctions to ''hurt the Chinese people,'' Miss Tutwiler said. 
''Our view is that basic human-needs loans - for instance, earthquake relief - should be permitted periodically to go forward,'' she said.
Miss Tutwiler said the United States' revised position had been under consideration for months and was ''not connected'' to the end of martial law. 
The timing, she said, ''is sheerly, honestly coincidence.''
Representative Nancy Pelosi, Democrat of California, said the lifting of martial law was ''an empty gesture.''
''Beijing can lift martial law because it does not need martial law to crush dissent,'' she said, noting that China had adopted a series of measures outlawing anti-Government demonstrations and authorizing security forces to stop protests.
Mrs. Pelosi is the author of a bill that would prohibit the United States from sending Chinese students back to China. 
Mr. Bush vetoed it on Nov. 
30. Congress is likely to override the veto soon after it reconvenes on Jan. 
23. Congress is also likely to approve a package of economic and military sanctions banning arms sales to China and suspending Federal insurance for private investments in the country.
Â 
Quayle Sees Policy 'Dividends'
Martial law was imposed in parts of Beijing on May 20, after more than a million people filled the streets of the capital to support demands for greater democracy.
Sweeping restrictions were imposed, including total bans on rumor-mongering, boycotts of classes, petitions, meetings and anything else that was deemed threatening to what Beijing called ''the normal order.''
After the June 3-4 military crackdown on the democracy movement, the Government banned all dissident organizations and gave the police the right to shoot demonstrators. 
Thousands of arrests and scores of executions followed.
It is not clear if China made a commitment to lift martial law when Mr. Bush's national security adviser, Brent Scowcroft, visited Beijing last month.
Mr. Quayle said today that the lifting of martial law illustrated the ''dividends from the President's policy toward China.''
A White House spokesman, Roman Popadiuk, said the Administration would like to think that the trips to China by Mr. Scowcroft, in July and December, ''played a part'' in China's decision to lift martial law.
Â 
Repression Said to Continue
But outside experts expressed doubt. 
A professor of Chinese history at Boston University, Merle Goldman, said ''the Chinese have been suffering economically'' and need financial assistance from the World Bank.
''The lifting of martial law is essentially a cosmetic or symbolic gesture to show that things are back to normal and to impress the outside world,'' she said in a telephone interview.
If China released student leaders, intellectuals and workers imprisoned in the crackdown on the demonstrators in Tiananmen Square, that would provide tangible evidence of political liberalization in China, Mrs. Goldman said.
Senator Claiborne Pell, chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee, said the lifting of martial law was ''a small step in the right direction.''
But Mr. Pell, a Rhode Island Democrat, said, ''It does not change the fundamental circumstance of repression in China or the many serious issues that remain - human rights and freedom for arrested students and workers, human rights and an end to martial law in Tibet, and a halt to Chinese arms for Pol Pot and the murderous Khmer Rouge in Cambodia.''
Mr. Popadiuk said: ''We are pleased with the lifting of martial law and see it as a positive step.''
He said that the lifting of martial law was ''another in a series of positive steps'' by China. 
In the last few weeks, he said, the Chinese Government has readmitted a reporter from the Voice of America, has discussed renewal of a student-exchange program suspended since June and has curtailed criticism of the United States in Chinese newspapers and broadcasts.
Mr. Popadiuk also said the Chinese had ''announced that they would not be selling medium-range missiles to the Middle East.''
But an Arabic-language newspaper published in London said this week that Syria had ''officially received assurances from the Chinese Government of its commitment to military cooperation between the two countries.''
The report said that China had rejected American pressure to stop selling weapons to Syria.
Â 
Pledge to Halt Missiles Sales
Chinese officials concluded that they needed to maintain the military capabilities of Syria and Israel's other Arab neighbors because ''Israel is being armed with the most technologically advanced weapons,'' the report said.
Asked about that report, Miss Tutwiler affirmed that China had announced that it ''would not be selling medium-range missiles to the Middle East.''
She said she did not know if the Administration was monitoring China's adherence to its pledge.
It was not immediately clear what types of World Bank loans would be acceptable to the United States. 
Miss Tutwiler said that though Washington might support some ''basic human needs loans'' to China, it would continue to discourage ''project loans.''
A spokesman for the Asia division of the bank, Pastor B. Sison, said the distinction was not obvious, because loans for specific projects could also serve basic human needs.

file: U.N. Panel Puts China on List Of Human Rights Defendants.txt
text:
ï»¿
A United Nations panel today placed China on a list of countries accused of seriously violating their citizens' human rights.
The panel, a subcommission of the United Nations Human Rights Commission, voted 15 to 9, by secret ballot, to have the full commission examine charges that China brutally suppressed the student pro-democracy movement in violation of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. 
It also appealed for clemency for those arrested in connection with the student demonstrations that were put down in June.
The 26-member subcommission is preparing a list of countries that it considers guilty of human rights offenses. 
The full commission will consider the charges at its annual meeting next March. 
Both bodies can do no more than exert moral pressure on accused governments to mend their ways by investigating the charges against them and publishing their findings.
Other countries accused of human rights abuses by the subcommission today included Iran, Indonesia, Guatemala, El Salvador, South Africa and Israel.
Â 
A First for a Big Power
But experts said the condemnation of China was particularly significant. 
It was the first time that a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council has been censured for its human rights performance in a United Nations forum. 
It was also the first time that a United Nations body assigned to enforce respect for human rights has passed judgment on the Chinese Government's suppression of the democracy movement this year.
On Wednesday, Amnesty International, the human rights watchdog, said it had evidence that China had decided to execute many leaders of the pro-democracy movement in secret and had announced only a few of the death sentences that were passed.
The document approved by the subcommission, which is composed of nominally independent experts appointed by their governments, said the panel was ''concerned about the events which took place recently in China and their consequences in the field of human rights.''
It asked the United Nations Secretary General to transmit information provided by China and ''other reliable sources'' to the full commission and appealed for clemency toward those ''deprived of their liberty.''
China's expert on the subcommission, Tian Jin, angrily rejected the resolution, saying his Government was acting within its sovereign rights in ''suppressing a rebellion.''
He accused Western countries of trying to ''blacken China's name.''
He also warned that if the resolution was passed, Western countries would then ''attack'' other developing countries. 
''The consequences will not be limited to China and this merits attention everywhere,'' he said.
Â 
Third World Seeks More Seats
Developing countries are seeking to increase the size of the Human Rights Commission to 53 from 43 members, awarding all the additional seats to the third world.
The developing countries argue that they are underrepresented on the commission. 
But Western governments contend that the effort is intended to make it harder for the commission to censure third-world governments for human rights abuses.
The Human Rights Subcommission decided to hold secret ballots on all resolutions relating to abuses today at the suggestion of the French expert, Louis Joinet, who said this would allow members to vote according to conscience, free from outside pressure. 
Only the representatives of Cuba, India, the Soviet Union, Rumania, Somalia and China voted against a secret ballot. 
Two members were absent.

file: U.N. Passes Voluntary Register to Curb Arms Sales.txt
text:
ï»¿
At a time when the international arms trade may be starting to grow again after a sharp decline, the United Nations General Assembly voted overwhelmingly today to establish the first register of international arms sales.
The aim of the register, which won strong support in the wake of the Persian Gulf war, is to curb the international traffic in arms by publicizing transactions and identifying potential trouble spots by showing where arm stocks are increasing.
Although the resolution calls on all nations to provide the world organization with an annual list of all imports and exports of arms, it does not require them to do so. 
Nonetheless, diplomats say most countries are likely to comply with the register because of the overwhelming support it has received and particularly because of its support from Britain, the United States, France and the Soviet Union, which together account for about 70 percent of the international arms trade.
The register will initially apply only to sales of heavy arms, like tanks, armored fighting vehicles, artillery pieces, combat aircraft and attack helicopters, that can be used to seize and hold territory.
China, a major arms producer, refused to take part in today's vote, even though it participated in talks with the other four permanent members of the Security Council in Paris last summer on curbing arms sales to the Middle East. 
China offered no explanation for its stand. 
But some diplomats said the Chinese action might reflect the importance that arms sales has acquired for China as a source of foreign currency as well as resentment at the pressure to go along with the register from the United States and other Western supporters.
In today's vote, 150 countries approved the resolution establishing the register and procedures for gradually expanding its scope to cover not only heavy arms shipments but also lighter weapons, arms production and national weapon stocks. 
While no nation voted against, Cuba and Iraq abstained.
During the debate in committee, many developing countries complained that the register would discriminate against poorer nations, which import their arms, by requiring them to disclose their purchases while protecting richer nations with indigenous arms industries against revealing their military strength.
As a result, the resolution calls on the Secretary General to set up an expert group to report next year on ways of extending the register to include lighter arms as well as production sites and national weapon stocks. 
This could transform the register from a list of arms sales into one for conventional arms that includes transfers.
Purchases by developing countries account for about 75 to 80 percent of the international arms trade, which peaked at $57 billion in 1987 before declining, according to the latest report of the United States Arms Control and Disarmament Agency.
The United States earned $14 billion from selling arms overseas in 1988, the last year for which Government figures are available, accounting for 29 percent of the world market. 
According to the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency, world arms exports fell 13 percent from $57 billion in 1987 to $49 billion in 1988, the lowest level in 10 years. 
But in average terms, the agency says, sales have been declining 3 percent a year since 1983.
"For the first time in history, perhaps, the favorable prospects for controlling the transfer of conventional weapons appear to outweigh the negative," Prof. Stephanie Neuman, an arms control expert at Columbia University, said in a paper for the American Association for the Advancement of Science. 
Professor Neuman attributes the downward trend to the increasing sophistication of weapons, deteriorating economic conditions and "the new political order."
But at a recent meeting of arms control scholars at Wisconsin University, Michael Klare of Hampshire College said Iraq's defeat in the gulf war might encourage developing countries to shift from their preference for large tank and infantry formations to a greater emphasis on aircraft, helicopters and precision-guided munitions.

file: U.S. Acts to Free 2 Chinese Dissidents.txt
text:
ï»¿
The national security adviser, Brent Scowcroft, asked the Chinese authorities last weekend to allow Fang Lizhi, China's most famous dissident, and his wife to leave the country, senior Administration officials said today. 
He came away hopeful that their fate will be resolved soon.
Mr. Fang, an astrophysicist, and his wife, Li Shuxian, who is also a leading critic of China's Communist Party, took refuge in the United States Embassy a few days after Chinese troops crushed the pro-democracy movement last June, and they remain there. 
Their plight was discussed last weekend by Mr. Scowcroft and Deputy Secretary of State Lawrence S. Eagleburger in their meetings with Chinese officials.
Under the arrangement under discussion, Mr. Fang and his wife would migrate not to the United States, where they would be quite visible, but to a more neutral country. 
The release could come within a few weeks, the officials said.
Â 
A Request Deemed Unacceptable
The Chinese authorities have insisted that the couple be prevented from continuing their political activities from abroad, but Administration officials said the United States is unable and unwilling to give such assurances.
The effort by the United States and China to reach a deal to release the dissidents from their six-month confinement was first reported in The Los Angeles Times today, but senior officials said they were still unsure of whether the Chinese would carry out a release.
Administration officials are reluctant to discuss the highly delicate matter, concerned that advance word could lead the Chinese to back out. 
But they acknowledge that the release of Mr. Fang (his name is pronounced fahng lee-jur, rhyming with burr) and his wife (her name is pronounced lee shoo-shyen) would help the Administration. 
It would do so by blunting the sharp criticism of Democratic lawmakers and some China specialists and political analysts that secretly dispatching such a high-level delegation to Beijing was unwise and sent the wrong signal to Beijing.
These critics have argued that while Mr. Bush has pressed for democratic reform in Eastern Europe, he has subjected China to far less rigorous standards.
Â 
Expectations of Reciprocity
In response to criticism that Mr. Bush received nothing in return for his bold diplomatic move, White House officials have hinted that they expect a reciprocal gesture before relations can improve. 
In conversations with Republican lawmakers after the visit, Mr. Scowcroft hinted that they should stay with the Administration because something tangible might come out of the trip.
Administration officials have raised the issue of the couple's fate a number of times since last summer, stressing that the matter must be resolved before relations between the two countries can return to normal.
The status of Mr. Fang and his wife was also broached to the Chinese both by former President Richard M. Nixon and former Secretary of State Henry A. Kissinger during their separate trips to China last month. 
In a meeting with President Bush after the trip, Mr. Kissinger said he was fairly optimistic that the issue could be negotiated, according to officials familiar with the discussion.
In an interview with the Cable News Network on Thursday, Mr. Kissinger said Mr. Fang's release to a third country so that he could pursue nonpolitical activities was desirable. 
Asked about Mr. Fang, he replied, ''If the Chinese understand American concerns, a way should be found that makes it possible for him to leave and move to a country in which he has an opportunity to pursue his scientific career.''
Â 
Sign of a Concession
In an important signal that the Chinese are changing their position on the status of Mr. Fang and his wife, China's Foreign Ministry spokesman, Jin Guihua, said at a weekly news briefing Thursday that their confinement was ''inappropriate'' and called the sheltering of him in the United States Embassy ''a sensitive question'' that involved China's sovereignty and international law. 
In an acknowledgment that China must help to resolve the matter, he added, ''Solving the problem will require effort on both sides.''
Until now, Chinese leaders have branded Mr. Fang a traitor and counterrevolutionary and demanded that the United States turn him over to the authorities.
Chase Untermeyer, an aide close to Mr. Bush who was part of the delegation in Beijing, today denied reports that he had discussed the two dissidents privately with two Chinese friends of Mr. Bush, who is a former Ambassador to China.

file: U.S. Bars Chinese Role At Talks on Air Pollution.txt
text:
ï»¿
To avoid violating sanctions imposed on China last year because of its crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators, the Administration has excluded Beijing from an international conference on air pollution and climatic change, even though the Chinese burn more industrial coal than any other country, officials said today.
The conference, to be held here on Tuesday and Wednesday, will include the rest of the world's most industrialized or populous nations, and White House officials said they normally would have considered Chinese participation an important element of such a meeting.
The White House Conference on Scientific and Economic Research Related to Global Change is part of President Bush's effort to spur research into the way pollution may be changing the global climate and to allay criticism of his environmental policies. 
Mr. Bush will address the gathering on Tuesday morning and Wednesday afternoon.
The conference is to focus on the kind of research the industrialized and developing nations should conduct on the theory of global warming, which postulates that certain kinds of pollutants are causing the Earth's temperature to rise. 
The burning of coal is the primary source of carbon dioxide, a chemical that is believed to be a major cause of this phenomenon.
Criteria Explained
In drawing up the guest list for the conference, the White House selected countries ''that have substantial populations, large land masses, industrial economies or heavy future energy needs,'' said Stephen Hart, a White House spokesman.
China, which has the world's largest population, about 1 billion people, burns more coal than any other country and is expected to increase its consumption dramatically in an industrialization drive. 
At present, it is the third largest producer of carbon dioxide in the world, after the United States and the Soviet Union, according to United Nations statistics.
''China has the potential to emit a lot of carbon dioxide as they continue to develop, as well as chlorofluorocarbons, and under different circumstances they probably would have been invited to this meeting,'' Mr. Hart said.
Scientists say chlorofluorocarbons, chemicals used for such purposes as propellants in aerosol sprays and coolants in refrigerators and air conditioners, damage the ozone layer, increasing the amount of harmful radiation reaching the earth's surface.
Â 
High-Level Exchanges Banned
But Mr. Hart said China was excluded from the list because of the sanctions Mr. Bush imposed against the Beijing Government last year after its nationwide crackdown on political dissent, which culminated in the violence in Tiananmen Square last June.
Among those measures was a ban on high-level exchanges between the two nations. 
Mr. Hart said the White House determined that the rule would apply to the conference since the invitations went out to government officials of ministerial level.
Officials said that even if China's participation might have been useful, the Administration wanted to avoid the kind of severe criticism it drew last year after it was disclosed that Brent Scowcroft, the President's national security adviser, and Lawrence S. Eagleburger, the Deputy Secretary of State, had made two trips to China after the sanctions were imposed. 
The White House took the position at the time that the Scowcroft-Eagleburger mission was not an exchange.
The United States signed the 1987 Montreal Protocol, which called for a reduction of 50 percent in the production of chlorofluorocarbons. 
The 80 nations that signed the document are now negotiating a deadline for a complete ban on the chemicals. 
China has not ratified the protocol.
Sending delegations to the conference besides the United States are Australia, Brazil, Canada, West Germany, France, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Mexico, the Netherlands, Nigeria, Norway, Poland, the Soviet Union, Britain and Zaire, as well as the European Community and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.

file: U.S. Calls North Korea Atom Plan a Global Concern.txt
text:
ï»¿
Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d told South Korea today that Washington considered North Korea's suspected development of nuclear weapons a matter of urgent global concern and that it was now actively exploring with Japan, China and the Soviet Union ways to curtail the move.
South Korea's Foreign Minister, Lee Sang Ock, endorsed the American initiative to try to further isolate North Korea economically and diplomatically until it opened its nuclear installation to international inspection and halted work on what is suspected to be a reprocessing plant capable of producing hundreds of pounds of weapons-grade plutonimum, a senior Korean official said.
In his meeting with the South Korean Foreign Minister, Mr. Baker said Washington had come to see curtailment of the North Korean nuclear development as a "matter of urgency," and something that was "not just a Korean issue but a matter of global concern," according to a Korean official who attended the talks. 
The North Korean nuclear activity is at Yongbyon, a nuclear complex 60 miles north of Pyongyang.
While Mr. Baker is in Seoul for the annual meeting of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, to discuss Asian trade issues, many of his private discussions have focused on how to generate pressures to halt the North Korean nuclear program before it sets off a nuclear arms race in Asia that could prompt South Korea and Japan to try to develop nuclear weapons.
Â 
Forcing Inspections
Having been slow to react to the Iraqi nuclear bomb program, the Bush Administration is trying to make sure that it does not repeat the mistake by underestimating North Korea's moves.
For now, American officials say they are concentrating their efforts on finding ways to squeeze the North Koreans diplomatically and economically in order to force them to open their nuclear installation to the International Atomic Energy Agency for inspection, which the North is obliged to do as a signer of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
But a senior State Department official told reporters traveling with Mr. Baker today that while it is important to compel North Korea to open itself up to international inspection, "we need to go beyond that -- there should not be a reprocessing facility there at all."
Up to now, North Korea has refused to allow any inspection of its nuclear installations and has spurned a South Korean offer on Nov. 
8 that both nations agree to forego development of any weapons of mass destruction.
Â 
Tokyo's Important Gesture
The first sign of the multilateral American approach was manifested Tuesday when Japan, at Mr. Baker's behest, pledged that it would not go ahead with plans to establish diplomatic relations with North Korea unless it scrapped its center for reprocessing nuclear fuel. 
Japan's Foreign Minister, Michio Watanabe, who met Mr. Baker in Tokyo on Monday, made the pledge during a meeting in Seoul with his Korean counterpart.
That gesture was important to the South Koreans, who were annoyed by a visit to North Korea by senior members of Japan's governing Liberal Democratic Party. 
Privately, some South Korean diplomats suspect that the Japanese would prefer that the peninsula remain divided so they would never have to compete with a unified Korea -- much the way many European countries preferred a divided Germany.
In addition, on Tuesday Korea's President, Roh Tae Woo, formally requested China's help in halting the North Korean nuclear program. 
The request was made in Seoul during the first meeting between a Chinese Foreign Minister and a south Korean President. 
The two countries still do not have diplomatic relations.
The Korean pres agency quoted President Roh as telling Foreign Minister Qian Qichen that continued North Korean nuclear development "would endanger stability, not only on the Korean Peninsula, but also in northeast Asia and the whole world."
Â 
Last Major Benefactor
American officials said that in their tentative discussions with the Chinese on the issue, Beijing had indicated some willingness to be helpful, but the extent of cooperation remained to be seen.
With the Soviet Union having already slashed its economic aid to Pyongyang, and demanding to be paid in hard currency for its oil exports to North Korea, China remains the last major benefactor to the isolated Government of Kim Il Sung.
Speaking generally of the evolving American strategy on the North Korean nuclear issue, a senior State Department official said: "What we are doing at this stage is first trying to raise the profile of the issue as a way of starting to build some multilateral diplomacy to deal with it. 
Second, we are starting to discuss specific steps people might take. 
The overall strategy is to heighten the sense of isolation of the North Koreans."
Korean officials said Foreign Minister Lee indicated to the Secretary that while his country wanted to see the North Korean nuclear program stopped immediately, it was ambivalent about involving outside powers in too formal a manner.
Â 
Role of 4 Powers
While the Koreans recognize that without outside pressure there is little hope that the North Koreans will respond, they have long maintained that the fate of the Korean Peninsuala, particularly questions involving unification and relations between north and south, should be resolved in a direct dialogue between Seoul and Pyongyang.
That is because the North insists that the South is simply a colonial creation of the United States and therefore it will only discuss security issues with Washington and not Seoul. 
The North wants to conclude a peace treaty with Washington that would ultimately lead to a withdrawal of American forces from the South.
As The Korea Times said in a lead editorial today: "The two-plus-four formula, or German unification method, is not applicable to the Korean case, as the Korean question is fundamentally in the South and North's own hands, whereas German unification required the sanction of the four allied forces -- the United States, the Soviet Union, France and Britain. 
Yet, it is the stark reality that Korean problems will be hardly unravelled without assistance and guarantees of the four neighboring powers."
Mr. Baker, Korean officials said, assured Mr. Lee that while Washington sought to enlist the help of Japan, China and the Soviet Union, it would not be in any institutionalized form -- as with the German unification process -- and that the United States still believed that the political future of Korea should be determined in direct talks between the North and the South.
Korean officials quoted Mr. Baker as saying that neverthless, "because of the urgency of the matter all interested countries should be involved."

file: U.S. Envoy to China Has Quarrel With Rights Protestors in Seattle.txt
text:

The United States Ambassador to China, James Lilley, called demonstrators against Chinese human-rights abuses "cowards" when they confronted him here Saturday night, and he suggested that one man, a Tibetan, "go back to China and serve China."
But in a speech a few minutes later, Mr. Lilley said the United States wanted to see "concrete improvement on China's human rights record," and referred to the lifting of martial law in Tibet as "window dressing."
Representative John Miller, Republican of Washington, said today that Mr. Lilley should apologize for his remarks, made to protesters outside the closing ceremony of a four-day trade exposition and symposium on relations between the United States and China.
Mr. Lilley got into the argument with a handful of demonstrators outside Union Station before going inside to make his speech.
Most of those outside the former train station did not notice the exchange, but it was taped by a Seattle television station, KIRO.
Mr. Lilley and China's Ambassador to the United States, Zhu Quizhen, arrived in cars at the side of the station. 
About 50 demonstrators were at the front of the building, waving signs andchanting slogans condemning the Chinese Government's slaying of hundreds of demonstrators in Beijing in June 1989 and its 40-year occupation of Tibet.
Jim Berman, a Seattle resident whose wife is Tibetan, said he and a half-dozen others left the main group on the chance the ambassadors might use a side entrance.
They chanted "China -- human rights!", "Tibet for Tibetans!" and "Remember Tiananmen Square!" he said.
Mr. Zhu ignored the demonstrators and went inside, Mr. Berman said.
But Mr. Berman said, and the KIROvideotape corroborated, that Mr. Lilley suddenly shouted, "Were you at Tiananmen Square?
I was there."
"So what?"
Mr. Berman said he replied. 
"I know it wasn't the greatest retort," Mr. Berman said afterward, "but I certainly didn't expect his outburst."
Mr. Lilley then shouted to a Tibetan man: "What are you doing about it?
I'm doing something about it.

file: U.S. GRANTS BOEING A WAIVER TO SELL JETLINERS TO CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
Granting a waiver of the sanctions announced by President Bush last month, State Department officials said today that the Boeing Company could sell four commercial jetliners to China.
The waiver involves only the four 757-200 aircraft. 
But State Department officials said the decision could have important long-term implications for Boeing, which hopes to remain active in China's potentially lucrative market for civilian aircraft.
The decision to grant the waiver was made by Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d and was coordinated with the White House, the officials said.
A White House spokesman said tonight that he did not know who in the White House had coordinated the decision, but said of Mr. Bush, ''I'm sure he's aware of it.''
Â 
No Softening Seen
The State Department asserted that the waiver did not represent a softening of the sanctions that President Bush had already put into place.
''I don't think the President ever intended to put a stop to this transaction,'' a State Department official said.
The decision to grant the waiver was quickly criticized by some members of Congress who have lobbied President Bush for tougher sanctions against China. 
Last month, Mr. Bush halted the sale of hardware and items of military value to increase the diplomatic pressure on Beijing after its crackdown on the pro-democracy movement.
''My concern is that there are powerful forces in this country that are ready to do business with China irrespective of what Chinese human rights are,'' said Representative Tom Lantos, a California Democrat who is a member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. 
''These people have many spokesmen within the Administration.''
Â 
Exports to Communist Nations
The State Department officials said the Boeing deal had been been held up because the plane's navigation system was on the State Department's munitions control list that applies to exports to Communist countries. 
The Bush sanctions blocked the sale of all items on that list.
But the officials said the navigation systems would be used in civilian aircraft and would have no important military value for the Chinese. 
''Our decision is in keeping with the President's intent not to disrupt nonmilitary commercial trade,'' a State Department spokesman said.
A State Department official said the McDonnell Douglas Corporation, Boeing's principal rival, has also applied for a waiver of President Bush's sanctions, so that it might ship its navigation systems to Shanghai, where it is building its MD-82 midsize aircraft in a joint venture with the Chinese.
The State Department also authorized Honeywell Inc. to maintain navigation equipment in planes sold to China, arguing that this action was needed to protect the safety of Chinese airline passengers.
The four Boeing 757's are narrow-body 200-passenger planes, with a total value of about $200 million. 
They are part of an 11-plane order, but Administration officials said the exemption applies only to the four planes, which were scheduled for delivery in June.
Delivery of the remaining planes in the order depends on developments in China, the officials said. 
Boeing has already sent five 757's to China under a previous order, a company spokesman said.
The State Department officials said Boeing, which is based in Seattle, had pressed hard for a waiver, provoking some criticism in Congress.
Â 
Action With Allies Urged
Representative Lantos said the Administration should try to work out sanctions with allies to block the sale of commercial jetliners to China.
Such a move would ''exact a price,'' he said, adding, ''The Chinese must understand that massacres will not go unpunished.''
A State Department official said it would be a mistake to block American companies from selling planes to China, allowing airplane manufacturers from other countries to make the sales.
Representative Gerald B. H. Solomon, a Republican from Glens Falls, N.Y., who had also called for sanctions tougher than the Administration's, complained about the waiver, saying it sent the wrong message to the Chinese.
''We ought to be going to our allies to get them to join us in putting our foot down with the Chinese, instead of just saying that if we do not sell airliners to the Chinese somebody else will,'' he said.
Mr. Solomon said the decision to allow the sale might be a sign that the Administration also plans to allow the export of American communications satellites to China for launching on Chinese rockets under an agreement reached last year.
Â 
Also on Control List
The sanctions prevent the export of American-manufactured satellites to China since they are also on the munitions control list although do not have military use. 
An Australian consortium and a British-Chinese consortium, both of which arranged the Chinese launchings, are asking for exceptions from the sanctions.
Mr. Solomon has sponsored an amendment that would prohibit the export licensing for the satellites because of China's crackdown on the democracy movement. 
China has drawn customers for its launching of satellites because its prices are cheaper than those of American and Western European companies.
Boeing and McDonnell Douglas, which is based in St. Louis, have been competing for China's aircraft market.
Last month, China announced that it would buy 90 planes in the next four years to add to its commercial fleet of 420.
Boeing has sold 61 planes to China since the early 1970's for about $2.35 billion.
Some experts said China is significant more as a potential market than as a immediate purchaser of American planes.
''There is no doubt China represents a potentially huge market,'' said Jack A. Modzelewski, vice president of research for Paine Webber Inc. 
''But we do not see China as a major source of buying potential for aircraft in the next three to five years.''
Â 
Constraints on Purchases
Mr. Modzelewski said aircraft purchases would be constrained over the next several years because of slow economic growth in China and China's limited supplies of hard currency.
In response to questions, Boeing said in a statement that the company did not believe that the licenses for the navigation equipment on the four 757-200 planes should have been suspended. 
It said it had ''discussed that issue at length with appropriate Government agencies.''
An Administration official provided one example of Boeing's activity on the issue. 
He said Boeing helped draft language that was included in House legislation that stated items on the control list intended for civilian use should not be blocked.
It said the four planes would be delivered to Guangzhou Airlines and Shanghai Airlines as soon as possible.

file: U.S. Lifts Its Sanctions on China Over High-Technology Transfers.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Bush Administration lifted sanctions against China's transfer of high technology today after accepting its promise to abide by restrictions on the sale of missiles and missile technology to the Middle East.
The decision was pushed by the White House and the State Department despite recent intelligence reports that China is continuing to sell missile technology to Syria, Iran and Pakistan and nuclear technology to Iran, according to some senior Administration officials and lawmakers.
Lifting the sanctions, which prevented the sale of American satellite parts and high-speed computers to China, is important because it removes the obstacle to China's signing of the Missile Technology Control Regime, a 1987 international agreement restricting the export of missiles and missile technology. 
In November, Beijing promised Secretary of State James A. Baker that it would adhere to the agreement if Washington lifted the sanctions.
The decision also reflects Mr. Bush's firm belief that the way to moderate China's behavior is through contact and trust as well as the Administration's willingness to give the country the benefit of the doubt on the missile issue.
Despite the announcement, there is division within the Administration and among lawmakers about China's intentions and the wisdom of lifting the sanctions.
In explaining the reasons, Lawrence S. Eagleburger, the Deputy Secretary of State, and other Administration officials argued that adherence to the missile control regime was an important gesture and could signify the first step toward achieving similar concessions in other contentious areas, like the transfer of nuclear technology and intellectual property rights.
But these officials stopped short of stating categorically that China had ceased the sale or delivery of missile technology that would violate the missile control regime. 
Instead, one official explained, they said only that the Administration "has thus far not determined that the Chinese have engaged in activities that would bring about sanctions."
They also argue that there is no evidence to support the claim that China shipped technology after the pledge made to Mr. Baker.
Other Government analysts cite intelligence reports indicating that Chinese exports continue, including, for example, the recent shipments of chemicals needed to make missiles to Syria and Iran. 
They also say they believe that China has accelerated the delivery of some nuclear technology to Iran in anticipation of signing the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty. 
China has said it favored signing the treaty, but has not yet done so.
Â 
A Letter From China
The Bush Administration has made the issue of nonproliferation the linchpin of its post-cold-war foreign policy, and is especially eager to halt the transfer of nuclear, chemical and biological weapons and ballistic missiles to the developing world.
Today's decision follows a letter three weeks ago from Foreign Minister Qian Qichen of China formally agreeing to abide by the guidelines of the Missile Technology Control Regime, Margaret D. Tutwiler, the State Department spokeswoman, said in a statement today.
"China's written commitment to abide by M.T.C.R. guidelines and parameters is an important step forward in securing Chinese support for ballistic missile nonproliferation," Miss Tutwiler said.
In recent days, Mr. Eagleburger has met with a number of Republican Senators, both to inform them that the Administration was lifting the sanctions as well as to urge them to renew most-favored-nation trade status for China when the current certification expires in June. 
The trade privileges allow China's goods to enter the market at the lowest tariff rates.
Â 
Closed-Door Session Urged
On Thursday, some Senators briefed by intelligence analysts came away convinced that sales were continuing and concerned about the scope of the pending Chinese contracts that are believed to involve billions of dollars and extend over several years.
The Senate vote on the trade status is set for Tuesday, but many are urging the Senate majority leader, George J. Mitchell, Democrat of Maine to hold a rare closed-door session to discuss the recent intelligence findings.
Â 
No Response
In criticizing the lifting of the sanctions, Senator Mitchell said in a statement today: "The Chinese leaders have again failed to keep their word, but President Bush has once again placated their demands without any tangible substantive evidence in their policy of repression and deceit.
"In doing so, he has continued his failed policy regarding China, and has increased the threat to peace," he said.
Early this month, a bipartisan group of 17 Senators sent a classified letter to Mr. Baker complaining about recent arms sales by China to the Middle East. 
The letter, signed by Senator Mitchell and leading members of the Senate Foreign Relations, Armed Services and Intelligence Committees, was an effort to prevent the Administration from going forward with the agreement made by Mr. Baker in November. 
No response has been received, Senate staff members said.
The Administration had delayed lifting the sanctions pending China's clarification of several issues, including its agreement not to deliver missiles and technology that were contracted for before its pledge to Mr. Baker.
The sanctions, which are unrelated to those imposed after the military crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Beijing in 1989, were imposed last June after American officials discovered that China had sent launchers for its newly developed M-11 missiles to Pakistan.
When the sanctions were announced, the Commerce Department had 20 pending license applications to allow the sale to China of about $30 million worth of high-speed computers, Administration officials said.
A number of senators are also upset that the Bush Administration has not fulfilled its obligation under last year's State Department Authorization Bill to submit a report by Jan. 
26 detailing China's arms transfer practices.
Â 
Report 'Stuck,' Some Say
Senator Joseph R. Biden, the Delaware Democrat, said in a statement today that what "angers" him is that the report has been delayed. 
"I have been told by the Administration that this report is 'stuck in the State Deparmtent,' " he said. 
"What I suspect that means is that the report contains information confirming that the Chinese have not changed their ways and are already breaking their promises to the Bush Administration, promises that led to the lifting of sanctions on Friday."
The State Department denied that the report was "stuck," but could give no explanation for the delay.
According to some Administration officials, China has complained that the Administration is demanding too many restrictions on the sale of arms-related technology. 
Although there is a detailed annex to the Missile Technology Control Regime, which lists the forbidden materials and equipment, there is some disagreement within the Administration on what constitutes a violation.

file: U.S. Lodges Protest With China_ A Taiwan Journalist Is Arrested.txt
text:
ï»¿
The American Embassy today formally protested what it called a ''premeditated'' attack on a foreigners' residential compound here a month ago. 
It said certain apartments of American diplomats and others were ''deliberately targeted'' by the Chinese Army.
American officials said the Chinese Foreign Ministry, which received the protest, had no immediate response.
The unusual American protest, which was accompanied by the release of an embassy study of the incident here on June 7, seems bound to do further damage to relations already strained by American criticism of China's crackdown on protests on June 4 and the harsh repression that has followed.
As the embassy issued the protest, a Taiwan journalist was arrested outside his hotel this morning about 24 hours after he reportedly met with Wang Dan, a student leader of the protest movement, who had eluded a national manhunt under way since the June 4 crackdown. 
It appeared that Mr. Wang may have also been arrested.
Â 
Car Was Being Followed
Colleagues of Huang Teh-pei, the arrested Taiwan reporter, said that he and Mr. Wang, who knew each other well, met in Beijing on Sunday. 
They said that Mr. Wang, a 20-year-old history student at Beijing University who is generally regarded as one of the three major student leaders of the democracy movement, had returned secretly to the Chinese capital after hiding for several weeks in the south of the country.
The colleagues of Mr. Huang, Antonio Chiang and Hsu Lu, both reporters from Taiwan, said that Mr. Huang and Mr. Wang were traveling in a car on Sunday driven by a common friend of theirs. 
When they discovered that the car was being followed, Mr. Huang jumped out. 
As the car continued on its way in the northeast part of Beijing, it was still followed by another car and a motorcycle of the type generally used by the Public Security Bureau.
Chinese news programs today announced the arrest of five more students in Beijing, accusing them of possessing weapons and ammunition taken from the army during the confrontation in and around Tiananmen Square a month ago.
There were no official reports of the arrest of Mr. Wang, one of 21 student leaders on a most-wanted list.
If he was arrested, Mr. Wang would be the seventh of the 21 leaders to be taken into police custody.
The American protest was delivered to the Foreign Ministry today by the charge d'affaires, Raymond Burghardt. 
It concerned an incident in which Chinese troops raked the facade of one of the high-rise buildings inside a guarded, walled compound where diplomats and other foreign residents of Beijing are required to live.
The official Chinese explanation for the episode, which took place three days after the suppression of the protest movement, was that a sniper was in the compound firing on troops on the broad avenue below. 
After the troops fired at the building, Chinese plainclothes police officers entered the compound and, after searching it, appeared to have apprehended a suspect.
But the American Embassy report on the incident, released to reporters here, takes sharp issue with this version of events. 
It says that the arrest of the sniper ''appeared to be staged, since the sniper did not appear to be distressed nor did the P.L.A. appear to be using expected force during the 'arrest.'
'' The P.L.A. is the People's Liberation Army.
''There is no doubt in this embassy's opinion that certain apartments were deliberately targeted by the P.L.A.,'' the report concludes. 
Some of the ''hits'' sustained by the apartments resulted from direct fire from a building across the avenue from the diplomatic compound, which had been occupied by Chinese troops the day before, the report said.
''Events on June 6 and 7 indicate that this action appears to have been premeditated and that specific apartments were targeted,'' the report says.
Many have noted here that the firing on the diplomatic compound took place the day after Fang Lizhi, China's leading dissident, was given refuge inside the American Embassy.

file: U.S. READY TO LET SATELLITES GO UP ON SOVIET ROCKETS.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Bush Administration has decided to allow American commercial satellites to be launched on Soviet rockets for the first time, Government and industry officials say.
As a result of decisions made at the White House this week, an Australian commercial venture, the Cape York Space Agency, will be permitted to hire an American company to run a base in northern Australia from which Soviet rockets will carry satellites into orbit for customers from around the world, perhaps as early as 1995, the officials said.
The project provides a major opportunity for the Soviet Union to expand its international space business and is expected to increase foreign competitive pressures on the American rocket industry.
Â 
Industry Is Divided
Domestic rocket companies had opposed letting the Soviet Union provide launching services for American customers, but the satellite makers had favored opening up the market. 
Representatives for both groups said the Administration's decision seemed evenhanded, since it includes provisions intended to insure that the Soviet Union prices its rockets fairly.
In recent years, the United States has shifted the job of launching privately owned satellites from the Government's space agency to aerospace companies. 
In August the McDonnell Douglas Corporation became the first company to conduct a commercial launching in the United States, and nearly a dozen launchings by several companies are expected this year.
Â 
Among Thorniest of Issues
But the domestic industry faces intense competition from the European consortium Arianespace, and the availability of inexpensive rockets from China and the Soviet Union is also a worry. 
The domestic industry has invested hundreds of millions of dollars in a business fraught with technical risks.
This week the National Space Council, an interagency committee headed by Vice President Dan Quayle, completed a broad set of recommendations on the international launching business. 
The decision to approve the Cape York project was among the thorniest issues in the council's policy review.
Last year China won limited approval from the United States Government to launch a few American satellites from Chinese territory. 
But despite the warming in Soviet-American relations, and considerable interest from American satellite companies in using Soviet launching services, there has never been any sign that the United States was ready to abandon its opposition to a cooperative arrangement, especially if it meant launching American satellites from Soviet soil. 
Rocket and satellite technologies are strictly controlled because of their military applications.
Â 
The Australian Arrangement
Now the State Department, with the approval of the White House, intends to grant an initial export license to the USBI division of the United Technologies Corporation to operate the Cape York station, where Soviet Zenit rockets could be launched beginning in 1995. 
The project, estimated to cost nearly $500 million, is backed by an Australian real estate development company and would not receive any Australian Government money. 
The Soviet space agency, Glavkosmos, would supply rockets and engineers, but would not own a share in the venture.
Despite strong opposition from American rocket manufacturers and some skepticism by other Federal agencies, the State Department is expected to issue the Cape York license once President Bush approves the new policy governing the international trade in rocket-launching services, several officials said.
The proposal for the Australian launchings of Soviet rockets first surfaced last year, but the Bush Administration decided not to make a decision on it without conducting a broad review of its policies for promoting the domestic commercial space industry. 
The Reagan Administration had never considered letting the Soviet Union launch American satellites, but improving relations between the two countries made the Australian proposal palatable to the Bush Administration.
Although the National Space Council's recommendations will not become final until formally approved by President Bush, the new policy has already been explained by White House officials to a few Congressional aides, and after several weeks of intense review virtually all the details have been agreed to by senior officials on the space council.
Â 
'A Middle Approach'
Dawn Gifford, a Washington lawyer who is director of the Competitive Alliance for Space Enterprise, an industry group that represents rocket makers and satellite makers, said the Administration had taken ''a reasonable approach'' in its policy review. 
''My impression is that they have taken a middle approach that will wash well with both sides,'' Ms. Gifford said of the industry's reaction.
One rocket industry official said the new policy appeared to include safeguards against unfair competition from the Soviet Union, but this executive cautioned that enforcing those provisions might be difficult.
Satellite manufacturers tend to favor letting the Soviet Union supply launching services.
Although more licenses would be needed later for American-made satellites to be launched from Cape York, the decision to allow an American company to manage the operation in effect insures the approval of subsequent licenses as long as Australia and the Soviet Union adhere to conditions laid down by the United States.
Those conditions, as outlined in the space council's recommendations, include a Soviet promise to limit its overseas launching to a single site and to abide by an international agreement controlling the export of ballistic missile technologies, which have commercial and military uses.
Domestic rocket manufacturers, supported by officials from agencies as diverse as the Defense Department and the Transportation Department, have argued that the domestic rocket industry would suffer unfairly in a head-to-head competition with Soviet suppliers.
But the State Department viewed the Soviet-Australian proposal favorably, and American satellite companies warned that if they were prevented from putting their payloads on the cheapest available rockets they would eventually lose business to emerging foreign satellite makers who faced no such restrictions.
Â 
Australians Eager for Business
The Australians had pressed the proposal vigorously because they are eager to play a bigger role in the potentially lucrative aerospace business.
The Administration's policy statement declares it is in the economic and national security interests of the United States to maintain a healthy commercial industry for launching satellites. 
But it seeks to foster that industry by promoting further research into advanced rockets that would cost less and be more reliable, rather than by using trade barriers.
An official said the policy called for negotiating new ''rules of the road'' with the European Space Agency, which controls Arianespace. 
The official said such rules might include limiting subsidies and defining fair pricing for launching satellites.
The Soviet Union and China would be expected to adhere to the same fair-trade policies in pricing their rockets on the world markets, even though it is very difficult to estimate fair prices for rockets designed and built in controlled economies. 
How to Enforce Fair Pricing?
One major point that remains to be resolved is how the United States and other Western nations would enforce the fair-pricing rules.
Some Administration officials favor using export licenses as the enforcement mechanism. 
For example, if the United States determines that the Soviet Union is pricing its rockets too low, licenses would be refused for future American launchings from Cape York, shutting the Australian base off from its biggest source of customers.
But the State Department is arguing that the export control laws, which it administers, are meant only to prevent the sale of militarily useful technologies to potential adversaries, and not to enforce fair-trade rules.
The domestic rocket manufacturers are already complaining that China has violated the agreement it signed last year, when the United States first allowed that country to launch a few American satellites on Chinese rockets. 
The American companies say China submitted an unreasonably low bid when it recently won a contract to launch a communications satellite for an Arab consortium.
The American companies, supported by their European competitors, are urging the State Department to revoke licenses for the Chinese to launch more American satellites if the United States determines that the Chinese bids have been unfairly priced.

file: U.S. Sees Months of Talks Needed for World Trade Pact.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Bush Administration said today that weeks or months of negotiations would be required before it could accept a proposed GATT agreement to pull down international trade barriers.
With the European Community already unhappy about reductions in agricultural subsidies called for by the proposal, the Administration reaction today insured that the five-year-old talks known as the Uruguay Round, for the country in which they began, will drag into the spring on a wide range of issues. 
There are 108 countries in the negotiations, which seek to reduce obstacles to trade and broaden the authority of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, the Geneva-based organization that sets rules for international trade.
Julius Katz, the deputy trade representative overseeing the United States negotiating team, told the House Agriculture Committee today that "considerable work remains to be done with respect to the negotiations on market access for goods and services and the schedules for internal support and export subsidy in agriculture, and only when these negotiations are completed can we assess the true worth of the entire package of agreements."
The United States and other countries will give their formal responses to the proposal in Geneva on Monday. 
Originally envisioned as a chance for countries to endorse or turn down the pact, the meeting now is likely to be the beginning of further talks.
One requirement of the current proposal, presented by GATT's Director General, Arthur Dunkel, in late December, is for countries to reduce their spending on agricultural export subsidies by at least 36 percent in six years and the tonnage by at least 24 percent. 
Farmers picketed President Bush during his visit to Australia last week to protest America's wheat-export subsidies, which were enacted by Congress in response to Europe's even larger farm-export subsidies.
The proposal would also reduce some Japanese trade barriers that have resisted American efforts during President Bush's current visit to Tokyo, such as Japanese limits on imported rice.
President Bush in Tokyo and several Administration officials here said today that the broad proposal put forward on Dec. 
20 was a step forward but would require changes and clarifications. 
Administration officials had hoped that they would need very few amendments to the text.
"Both the United States and Japan believe that Director General Dunkel's proposed text is an important step that helps establish momentum to bring the Uruguay Round to a successful conclusion," said a communique issued at the end of President Bush's meetings with Prime Minister Kiichi Miyazawa of Japan. 
"Of course, the Dunkel proposal is not a final text."
The United States trade representative, Carla A. Hills, said Mr. Dunkel's text "is probably where we should have been a year ago."
But the Administration believes the proposal still does not address enough subjects in adequate detail for the plan to win any immediate endorsement.

Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d said today that the summit meeting was ''not something that the United States ought to be worried about.''

Another Administration official said: ''We have not reacted negatively or nervously.

Mr. Bush's comments would have alarmed conservatives 15 years ago.

''Washington should welcome the thaw between Moscow and Beijing,'' said Roger A. Brooks, director of Asian studies at the Heritage Foundation.

file: U.S. Solar Sensor Is Launched by Chinese Rocket.txt
text:
ï»¿
A big Chinese rocket roared into orbit yesterday, carrying an advanced American-built sensor that is expected to help electric power producers around the world avert blackouts caused by storms on the Sun.
The $1.2 million instrument, built at the Applied Physics Laboratory of Johns Hopkins University, was given a free ride into space on a Swedish satellite named Freja, which also carried instruments from Sweden, Canada, France and Germany. 
Sweden offered Johns Hopkins space on its satellite in return for access to data the instrument collects. 
The satellite was launched by a Long March 2-C rocket from Jiuquan in the Gobi Desert.
Dr. Lawrence J. Zanetti, leader of the Johns Hopkins group that built the Magnetic Field Experiment, said in an earlier interview the instrument would trigger a warning the instant a major disturbance of the Earth's magnetosphere begins. 
Timely warning will permit power companies to take steps to prevent blackouts like the one that knocked out electricity throughout Quebec on March 13, 1989, an incident that also caused $8 million in damage to the Salem nuclear power plant in New Jersey and damaged other plants across North America.
Magnetic storms begin when the Sun blasts electrically charged nuclear particles into space toward the Earth. 
A few of the speediest particles reach the Earth in about eight minutes, but most of the lower-energy particles, traveling at speeds up to 590 miles per second, take 2 to 12 days. 
When they reach the Earth, they not only produce spectacular auroral displays but also deform the Earth's magnetic field.
"It's as if a huge metal mallet were striking the Earth's magnetosphere," said Dr. Thomas Potemra, a lead designer of the project.
The shifting of the magnetic field caused by this particle shower induces electrical current in the Earth's crust, and when this current interacts with electricity passing through power lines, it causes surges. 
Such disruptions can make entire power distribution grids crash if operators do not respond quickly, and this can cause widespread blackouts and damage to equipment. 
Among the many possible consequences is the disabling of control systems at nuclear power plants. 
Magnetic storms also disrupt global radio and telephone communications.
The Swedish satellite was carried into orbit along with a much larger Chinese military reconnaissance satellite. 
After both satellites reached an orbit extending to 197 miles above the Earth, Freja's rockets were fired to boost the Swedish satellite to an elliptical orbit over the Earth's poles, ranging in altitude from 375 to 970 miles. 
The satellite is being tracked by an arctic station near Kiruna, Sweden.
The Chinese satellite is designed to return to Earth in about two weeks, but Johns Hopkins scientists expect the Freja satellite to operate for about two years, during which the Magnetic Field Experiment, similar in principle to the magnetometers used at airports to detect concealed weapons, will collect information about the effects of solar storms on the Earth's magnetic field.
Although the experiment will offer only a few minutes' warning, it can help power operators make emergency decisions. 
Ordinarily, automatic safety locks close down individual power plants when they detect surges, but when whole power networks are affected by solar storms, operators must override safety devices to keep power.

The White House announced today that it was suspending high-level meetings between United States officials and the Chinese Government.

file: U.S. WEIGHS MOVES ON CHINESE TRADE.txt
text:

On the eve of a vote on the issue in the House, the Administration is still trying to decide whether to make a series of concessions to persuade a hostile Congress to extend normal trading privileges to China for another year.
The House is now expected to vote overwhelmingly to renew the so-called most-favored-nation status for China, but with conditions for future renewal, such as the improved observance of human rights, that the White House has promised to veto. 
Instead, the Administration is leaning toward making a series of promises, including a possible major shift on United States policy toward Taiwan, that would satisfy some Congressional objections without being set in legislation.
At stake is not only the level of Chinese-American relations but also President Bush's reputation for consistently being able to persuade Congress to support his foreign policy positions.
Â 
Private Sector of Economy
Many Democrats and some Republicans have contended, sometimes heatedly, that China's poor human rights record, arms exports and ballooning trade surplus with the United States justify limits on Chinese access to the American market. 
But the Administration has countered that raising tariffs would seriously hurt American-Chinese relations and would hurt the private sector of the Chinese economy, the group the United States would most like to see succeed.

file: U.S.-China Diplomat Quarrel Grows.txt
text:
ï»¿
A dispute between China and the United States about restrictions on diplomatic movements has grown into a case study in how negotiation strategies can go awry.
Chinese-American relations are generally friendly, and the United States characterizes the dispute as only an ''irritant'' in a cordial overall relationship. 
But no one knows how to remove the irritant, and instead of going away it has become worse.
The dispute originated in 1984, when the United States opened a consulate in the northeastern city of Shenyang. 
The small American diplomatic staff there was forbidden to travel by private car beyond the city limits, although they could travel to any open area by train or plane.
In fact, there are hardly any cities nearby that any diplomat could or would want to visit by car, so the restriction was not a major difficulty.
Â 
China Pressed to Relax Rule
It is not completely clear why the Chinese banned car travel in the area in the first place, except that the area may be sensitive because of its proximity to the North Korean border and because many companies in the military industry are believed to be in the northeast.
For some of the same reasons, the Americans may have wanted greater freedom to look around. 
So in negotiations beginning in 1987 the United States pressed China to relax the rule and warned that otherwise the State Department would be obliged by law to adopt reciprocal restrictions on Chinese diplomats based in the United States.
In October the United States finally adopted what officials felt was a measured response: Chinese diplomats based in Chicago were forbidden from driving by car outside Cook County, which includes Chicago. 
In fact, the Chinese were probably affected by the restriction more than the Americans in Shenyang had been, because they traveled more than their American counterparts and because when they traveled they were far more likely to drive.
In November, the Chinese responded by decreeing that American diplomats based in Shenyang and Shanghai would have to get permission 48 hours in advance before leaving those cities by any means, even public transportation.
Â 
Angry Chinese Response Feared
''We consider the Chinese restrictions unreasonable, since they go well beyond the restrictions on P.R.C. diplomats here,'' Phyllis E. Oakley, deputy to the State Department spokesman, said at a press briefing last week.
Li Zhaoxing, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman, said, ''It is entirely unreasonable for the U.S. 
State Department spokesman to say that.''
After the restrictions put in October on the Chinese Consulate in Chicago, he said, the Chinese side had no choice but to increase restrictions on the consulates in Shanghai and Shenyang.
Now the United States is in a difficult position. 
If it retaliates, as it is obliged to by law, by restricting movements of Chinese diplomats in New York or Houston or elsewhere, that might lead to an angry Chinese response and further escalation of what began as a minor frustration.
''We don't want to have a downward spiral,'' said an American diplomat in Beijing. 
The legislation requiring reciprocity includes no deadline, so the State Department can wait indefinitely before retaliating, in the hope that the threat will remove the restrictions.
Â 
Law Worked Well in Mexico
In the past, the reciprocity law has sometimes worked well. 
Mexico, for example, used to forbid diplomats stationed there from buying imported cars. 
After the United States responded by prohibiting Mexican diplomats stationed in the United States from buying imported cars, the rule was lifted.
So far in China, however, the reciprocal restrictions have increased the limits on travel instead of reducing them, and negotiators here are concerned that if the United States appears heavy-handed, that would do more harm than good.
''If you get their backs up and excite the strain in them that's upset by 100 years of Western domination, then that doesn't help,'' an American diplomat said.
Some diplomats also worry that if the Chinese are backed into a corner, they will apply reciprocity in ways that would not be welcome to American diplomats.
Â 
Frustrations With Beijing
For example, diplomats in Beijing are given badges that allow them to walk wherever they want to in airports. 
That is a useful privilege when receiving arriving dignitaries, and the United States would like to continue to enjoy it without giving Chinese diplomats license to roam at will through American airports.
On the American side, there are other frustrations with the Chinese. 
About 10 American diplomats are living in hotels in Beijing because China has not provided housing for them as promised. 
In early 1986, China pledged that it would provide 23 new apartments for the United States Embassy in Beijing by the end of 1987, but only eight were made available in that time. 
The reason was apparently construction delays.
Another problem for diplomats in China is that since April 1987, their spouses have not been able to hold jobs without giving up their diplomatic immunity. 
Since the State Department is not willing to allow spouses to give up their immunity, the spouses have usually had to give up their careers if their partner is assigned to Beijing.
An American official said there were some signs that the problem could be resolved soon with a bilateral agreement allowing spouses to retain immunity while holding jobs.
