file: UPHEAVAL IN CHINA_Yearnings of Youth_ An Old Pattern.txt
text:
ï»¿
When one of China's student hunger strikers said last week that his demand was for ''a beautiful, perfect system,'' he was not merely being naive. 
He was reflecting in somewhat naive-sounding terms the yearning for restored national greatness that has led Chinese youth several times this century to take to the streets to demand change from what they saw as incompetent or dictatorial governments.
Protests by Chinese youths, which go back at least 70 years, have always shown a combination of utopianism and practicality, self-interest and patriotism. 
They have also been among the most important elements pressing for change - and sometimes merely turmoil - in a country whose recent history has been among the world's most tumultuous.
But if the students leading an extraordinary month of protests against their country's leaders belong to a tradition well-established this century, there are important differences of style and tactics between them and their predecessors.
Despite the streak of utopianism and occasional episodes of naivete shown by many in the demonstrations, the students seem far more sophisticated, mature and knowledgeable about the world than any of their predecessors.
This has astonished many experts on China, virtually all of whom admit that they never believed it possible for hundreds of thousands of students to conduct a mass movement of civil disobedience worthy of a Gandhi or a Martin Luther King Jr. 
The explanation for the extraordinary development is that China has been changing rapidly and irreversibly; the students' dramatically increased sophistication reflects those changes.
Â 
Old Slogan Reappears
Historians cite an episode 70 years ago known as the May 4 movement as the grandfather of the student movement. 
The May 4 movement started as a march through central Beijing in 1919 to protest China's weakness in the face of Japanese aggressiveness. 
But it turned into a long and heated examination of China itself in an effort to find out why it had lost its place among the world's pre-eminent nations.
There was a striking reminder of the May 4 generation when the protesters recently held up the slogan ''Democracy and Science'' as one of their demands. 
''Democracy and Science'' is the most remembered slogan of the May 4 movement, which largely introduced the idea that tradition had to be replaced by freedom and rationality if China was to take its place among leading nations.
Sixty years later in Beijing, during a short-lived protest movement known as the Democracy Wall period, which lasted from late 1978 until early 1980, a similar slogan emerged. 
It was ''The Fifth Modernization - Democracy,'' which alluded to the so-called Four Modernizations of the economy.
The most important recent instance of student activism in China came as part of the near anarchic Cultural Revolution of 1966-76, a complex and violent episode that among other things involved the effort by Mao Zedong to exploit youthful idealism to eliminate his rivals for influence among China's senior leaders.
Mao encouraged the formation of immense bands of young Red Guards, a group remarkably different in temperament from today's youth. 
Stoked to a frenzy by Mao's demagogic appeal, the Red Guards believed they were patriots serving China's interests.
Â 
A Contrast on Violence
In this sense, they were similar both to the generation of May 4 and to the current protesters. 
But they were also different in that they were anti-democratic extremists who obeyed no laws as they persecuted those thought to be the enemies of Mao's revolution.
They broke into homes, confiscated property and beat and humiliated the perceived enemies in kangaroo courts until finally Mao, who first egged them on from the sidelines, called in the army to restore order.
The present student generation seems, in striking contrast, to be genuinely committed both to democratic methods and nonviolence. 
When the protesters confronted soldiers with handshakes, Popsicles and exhortations to disobey the Government's order to suppress the movement, the students were invoking a new and far more sophisticated tactic than anything their forebears in the Cultural Revolution ever tried.
''The Red Guards were full of faith in Mao and in the leadership,'' said Prof. Andrew J. Nathan, a specialist on contemporary China at Columbia University. 
''They really and truly believed in Maoism. 
It was only after Mao cracked down on them in 1967 that people woke up, some sooner, some later. 
Many of the Red Guards were sent to the countryside, and they discovered that life was miserable there, so they started doing some thinking about what was wrong.
''Today's students, it seems to me, don't believe in the party. 
They are still idealistic. 
But the ones I've spoken to have lost all faith in Marxism and socialism.
''Partly it is that their own professional prospects are bleak because of the extreme underfunding of education and the low pay of educated people in all walks of life. 
More fundamentally, the experience of Maoism and a national reflection on what that meant has now come to a head with virtually all the intellectuals inside the party and outside of it concluding that the Chiniese system is fundamentally a bad one.''
Â 
A Culmination of Trends
Many experts on China in the United States see the current movement as a culmination of trends that have been developing slowly since the death of Mao in 1976 and the institution of a far more moderate Government ready to tolerate a greater measure of free expression.
Several smaller student-led protests have already taken place, including the Democracy Wall movement of the late 1970's, named for a stretch of street in Beijing where free expression was briefly allowed. 
After a period of euphoric activity, that movement was suppressed by the authorities and its leaders were jailed.
In the meantime, there have been student marches in important university cities like Shanghai and Nanjing, all of them rigorously suppressed, all of them reappearing now.
But even experts who have closely watched developments in China have been surprised by the apparent skills and maturity of the current protesters, including their use of English, both in interviews with American television networks and on protest banners, signaling an ability to appeal to international public opinion.
Â 
'A New Approach'
''The parents of these kids, many of whom were intellectuals who suffered in the Cultural Revolution, have told them about it,'' said Thomas Gold, a professor of sociology at Berkeley who has spent time among Chinese students in China. 
''And maybe their parents said: 'Look, you don't get anywhere with violence. 
You have to take a new approach.'
''
The changes also include China's far greater openness to the outside world, which included the dispatch of tens of thousands of students to study abroad, and its ambitious program of economic changes.
At the same time, economic changes have unsettled Chinese society in ways that have been deeply dissatisfying to intellectuals.
''On the one hand, economic reforms haven't given students and intellectuals the economic benefits that others, especially those who have gone into private business, have gotten,'' said Prof. Susan Shirk, a political scientist at the University of California at San Diego. 
''College graduates have suffered a relative decline in their economic status compared with people who operate in the free sector.''
Â 
The Philippines Example
''On the other hand,'' Professor Shirk said, ''the students are more willing to take risks because there are other options now. 
You can go off and join a private consulting firm. 
You can become a private entrepreneur. 
So the system is less monolithic.''
Perhaps more important, the students have gotten information about the use of ''people power'' in the Philippines to overthrew the Marcos dictatorship.
''The students are very plugged in,'' Professor Gold said. 
''If you look on the magazine racks you'll see a great deal of information about what happens in the rest of the world. 
They listen to the Voice of America and the BBC. 
They have friends and siblings in the United States, and they get information about what life is like in this country. 
A lot of them are planning to go abroad, so they want to know more about what is happening.''
''And,'' he continued, ''because they are frustrated with their own leaders, they've really been casting about for ideas. 
They really keep in touch.''

President Bush said today that he had ''no second thoughts at all'' about sending envoys to China last week. 
But he added that he did not believe that it was time for the United States or other countries to remove sanctions against China, imposed after the killings of students protesting for democracy in Beijing.
''To those suggesting that I have normalized the relationship with this power because of one visit, they simply are wrong, off the reservation on this point,'' Mr. Bush said, referring to the visit to Beijing last weekend of Brent Scowcroft, the national security adviser, and Lawrence S. Eagleburger, the Deputy Secretary of State.
''I think we've made the right step,'' Mr. Bush said, ''and only time will tell how this leadership in China views the mission.''
Mr. Bush's remarks came during a news conference held this afternoon with President Francois Mitterrand of France after the two leaders met to discuss the changes transforming Europe and the Soviet Union.
Â 
'Responsive' to East Germany
President Bush, speaking in a voice hoarse from a cold, also said the United States would be ''very responsive'' if East Germany requested emergency food aid to get through the winter.
He said he had not received a request for such assistance from the East Germans. 
But when Secretary of State James A. Baker 3d met on Tuesday in Potsdam with Prime Minister Hans Modrow, the East German said his country could face food and energy shortages in the winter, a situation that could hasten the push for unity as East Germans demand what West Germans have.
Mr. Mitterrand had positive remarks for Mr. Baker's proposal this week on changing the North Atlantic Treaty Organization from a military to a more political grouping and on establishing a closer American relationship with the European Community.
''There are quite a few elements in this very important statement which obviously meet with my approval,'' Mr. Mitterrand said. 
''It is very important to become aware of the future of the community, and of the necessary acceleration strengthening its structures.''
He added that Mr. Baker had shown ''great understanding'' about Europe.
Traditionally, France has viewed NATO as America's vehicle for influencing Western policy in Europe, and the community as its own vehicle.
The fact that Mr. Mitterrand was receptive to a new vision of alliances suggests some success in President Bush's efforts to coordinate American and French policy more tightly. 
As unification of the two Germanys becomes a real prospect, it also reflects a more sympathetic attitude by France and other Western European nations toward a more prominent American role in Europe to counter the weight of Germany.
The two leaders, casually dressed, met for an hour under a striped tent on the beach at L'Habitation de Lonvilliers, a hotel on the French side of this this Dutch-French resort island in the West Indies. 
Then they continued their discussion in English without a translator as they walked on the powdery sand and as they ate a lunch of lobster, goat cheese, Chassagne Montrachet wine and chocolate tarts.
Â 
Moving at the Same Gait
At the news conference, the French President said that he and Mr. Bush agreed that they must deal with the ''German problem'' in a ''harmonious'' way.
''I made this comparison,'' Mr. Mitterrand said, speaking through a translator. 
''If the horses of the team don't move at the same speed, there'll be an accident.''
''We need to know and observe the evolution of the forthcoming months, which remains uncertain,'' Mr. Mitterrand said of the German situation.
Mr. Bush said that France and the United States had not reached any agreement on seeking to slow the West German Chancellor, Helmut Kohl, in his drive for reunification with the East. 
Mr. Mitterrand said that Mr. Kohl should proceed carefully, however. 
He said he had been assured by Mr. Kohl that he was not ''precipitating events'' even though the Chancellor hopes for reunification.
Today's meeting, which marks the sixth time the two have met in the last 10 months, was part of Mr. Bush's continuing effort to emphasize to France that the United States will continue to play a major but not domineering role in Europe.
President Bush has gone out of his way to reorient America's ties with Europe from the days of the Reagan Administration. 
While Mr. Reagan worked largely through Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher of Britain, Mr. Bush has sought to establish a close relationship with Mr. Mitterrand and with Chancellor Kohl.
Mr. Mitterrand said he and Mr. Bush got along well today, as they did when the French President visited the American President at his home in Kennebunkport, Me.
Â 
No Competition With Thatcher
Asked whether he had replaced Mrs. Thatcher somewhat in the affections of the United States Government, Mr. Mitterrand said a poet had written that ''one may have one's heart open to several friendships in life.''
This provoked laughter from the press corps.
''We're not in a sentimental competition,'' the French President said of Mrs. Thatcher.
At a meeting of NATO Foreign Ministers in Brussels this week, the French were the most outspoken in casting doubt on Mr. Baker's proposal that traditional institutions like NATO and the European Community assume new roles.
Today, Mr. Mitterrand agreed that ''we cannot stay where we were before the collapse of all the walls that existed between peoples of Europe.''

China issued a bitter protest today against a Congressional decision to impose sanctions and said lifting the curbs was a ''necessary condition'' for normalizing relations with the United States.
The protest, which was delivered to the United States Ambassador, James R. Lilley, by Vice Foreign Minister Liu Huaqiu, expressed China's ''utmost indignation'' at the legislation, adopted on Tuesday in the Senate and earlier by the House of Representatives. 
Mr. Liu said the United States had ''willfully trampled on the basic norms governing international relations.''
The criticism was surprisingly harsh, since the sanctions bill attracted little notice here or elsewhere. 
The bill is largely symbolic because it reflects measures already adopted by the Bush Administration last summer after the military crackdown in June on demonstrators seeking democracy.
The sanctions bill, which President Bush is expected to sign, asks the Export-Import Bank to continue to postpone financing for United States exports to China and suspends financial support from the Overseas Private Investment Corporation and the Trade and Development Program.
Â 
President Could Waive Sanctions
It would also suspend sales of controlled munitions or crime-control and detection equipment, exports of American satellites and the liberalization of multilateral export controls. 
Mr. Bush would be authorized to waive the sanctions if he deemed it in the national interest or if he could show Chinese improvement on human rights.
There have been repeated mixed signals from the Chinese authorities on a range of issues in recent months, and it is not clear whether the protest signaled anything more than ruffled tempers in the Chinese Government. 
In the last month, relations between China and the United States appeared to be warming after months of tension.
''The present problems in Sino-U.S. relations are entirely caused by the U.S. side,'' the official New China News Agency quoted Mr. Liu as saying. 
''The U.S. 
Government has repeatedly expressed its hope to see Sino-U.S. relations back on a positive track, to which China expresses its welcome.
''The Chinese side shares the hope that Sino-U.S. relations will soon return to normal and has made efforts this end,'' the agency's account of Mr. Liu's remarks continued. 
''To lift the sanctions by the United States against China is a necessary condition for the return to normal of the bilateral relations.''
The United States Embassy declined to comment today.

Connection With Dissidents

file: Using Yak Hair to Woo Business.txt
text:
ï»¿
Dwarfed by the bedraggled red curtain that covers the faded pink walls of the Hotel Intourist dining room here in the Soviet Far East, a Japanese businessman taps relentlessly through dinner at a shiny laptop computer. 
Continuing even after a stern, slow waitress flicks an abacus to tally his check, he is straddling two very different worlds: one breaking out of the late 19th century, another hurtling into the 21st.
The long-cloistered Soviet Far East is a huge but sparsely populated region rich in forests, fisheries, minerals and wildlife, and it is beginning - ever so slowly - to venture into the 20th century's international economy.
''We are actively seeking contact with Pacific Rim countries,'' said Pavel L. Morosov, deputy chairman of the executive committee of Khabarovsk Krai, one of seven jurisdictions that make up the Soviet Far East.
For years, Soviet Far East officials who hungered for economic development had to look west thousands of miles and seven time zones to Moscow and they received little but scraps. 
Now, as the Soviet Union reaches out to build trade with the West under Mikhail S. Gorbachev's economic restructuring program of perestroika, the Soviet Far East wants to forge its own ties with the commercially vibrant Pacific Rim nations - and particularly Japan.
But although foreign business executives are beginning to venture into this area, the bureaucratic obstacles blocking these efforts are formidable and plans are moving at a snail's pace, at least by Western standards.
The Russians say ''handsome rewards'' await foreign investors supplying the Far East with technological expertise and equipment for sawmills, pulp mills, reforestation, fisheries processing, mining, construction and a host of other projects. 
But they offer few details.
Mr. Gorbachev, a strong booster of Far East development, said the region could be a magnet for sorely needed hard currency. 
Yet no one is able to estimate what the potential sums would be.
Furthermore, the products targeted for export from the Far East are hardly forcing trading partners to scramble for orders. 
Although forest products and coal are on the 67-item list, most of the others are such things as yak hair, birch sap, horse heart, reindeer antlers, beeswax, fir pitch and moss. 
Dalintorg, a Soviet Far East international trade organization serving as a conduit to Soviet-Pacific exports, has targeted these products mainly because of their availability.
The process of trading, too, is complex. 
Dalintorg has had no authority from Moscow to deal with American companies, which means they must contact Soviet Far East enterprises on an individual basis. 
And while Japanese companies are permitted to do business with the Soviet Union, no treaties exist regarding economic cooperation or investment.
Dependability of supplies and a shortage of roads and rail lines remain a problem. 
And complicating the situation is the fact that the Soviet Union lacks convertible currency, which means trading partners must accept barter deals, work out other arrangements for payment or maneuver in other currencies.
''People must not underestimate the excruciating difficulty of trade,'' warned a senior commercial attache with a Western embassy in Moscow, who asked not to be identified. 
''That doesn't mean that there won't be some nuggets of gold in the Far East'' for companies trying to profit from the well-documented Soviet shortages of consumer goods, he said. 
But he warned that companies ''trying to sell chrome bird cages or something'' will not find a ready market.
Western diplomats in Moscow remain skeptical about the potential for increased trading with the Far East. 
They point to a lack of specifics in Soviet plans to attract foreign companies accustomed to favorable terms offered elsewhere in the highly competitive Pacific region.
They cite vagueness in a 1987 Soviet Far East economic development plan, and note that none of seven Soviet jurisdictions to be granted economic autonomy in an experiment beginning in 1990 is located in the Far East. 
Figures on existing international business volume are not readily available.
''There is a strong political desire to develop the Far East and to make the Soviet Union an economic power in Asia,'' said one Western economic attache, who asked not to be identified. 
''It's more a hope, a goal, than it is a political reality now or even in the next five or 10 years.''
A Japanese businessman interviewed during a two-and-a-half-hour flight from Niigata, Japan, to Khabarovsk cited some stumbling blocks to investment. 
The executive, who asked that his name and that of his company not be used, noted, for example, that he had to go all the way to Moscow to initiate business, despite the fact that the Soviet Far East faces Japan. 
And because the Soviet Union lacks convertible currency, the factory he is supplying with equipment could pay only by bartering its future production. 
Furthermore, he could not visit other plants because they were located in large tracts that are off-limits to foreigners.
Conditions at the Hotel Intourist are primitive, especially by Japanese standards, and a phone call to the home office can cost $10 per minute before it gets cut off in mid-sentence. 
And with the lack of legal guarantees, a chronic labor shortage, a historically transient work force and international travel restrictions on Soviet partners, the business climate seems as harsh as a Far East winter.
Despite the difficulties, Western and Asian executives are looking at the Soviet Far East with growing interest, considering whether to brave the harsh conditions to gain a foot in the door to its eventual markets. 
Westerners are betting on the long term - say 10 or 15 years in the future - hoping that they can arrange deals by then for much broader trading partnerships.
Right now, the Japanese seem most interested in getting into this market first. 
Of the seven joint ventures known by the Japanese Government to be operating between Japanese companies and the Soviet Union, four are located in the Soviet Far East and involve catching, raising or processing fish products.
Of the four, two have combined capital of $1 million and the other two have total capital of 28.6 million rubles, or $45.8 million. 
At the current exchange rate, which is set by the Soviet Government and greatly overvalues the ruble, a ruble is worth $1.60. 
No figures are available for the value of trade between Japan and the Soviet Far East.
Other arrangements are either underway or planned for the region. 
Mr. Morosov, the Khabarovsk official, outlined several:
* Barter or currency plays. 
The ruble is not convertible to American or other Western currencies and cannot be taken out of the country. 
To avoid having to accept rubles for their goods and services, a foreign company may trade products or use other currencies.
* Joint ventures. 
The Soviet-Nippon Company processes fish; Swedes and Russians work together to catch deep-sea crab; Russians team up with North Koreans and Cubans to process timber. 
In its first joint venture, Khabarovsk Krai and the Chinese recently built a stylish Chinese restaurant in Khabarovsk.
* Cooperation. 
A Soviet enterprise sends cloth to Vietnam and North Korea, where workers assemble shirts. 
Those shirts are then sold in the countries in which they are assembled. 
Profits are split between that country and the Soviet Union.
* Compensation in kind or output. 
A Japanese company supplies equipment to build a wood-chip plant, and is reimbursed in wood chips once production begins.
These arrangements are tiny compared with multinational special economic zones envisaged by Mr. Gorbachev. Those zones, he said, ''would have an easy regime of customs duties, licensing of foreign economic transactions and taxation, and where reduced payments for natural and manpower resources would exist.''
Japanese economists have advocated the concept of zones in which the Soviet Union would supply resources and development opportunities and other countries, including Japan, the United States, China, North Korea and South Korea, would supply labor, capital, consumer goods and equipment.
The zones dominated discussion in October at a Soviet-sponsored conference in Vladivostok, which drew academics, business executives and diplomats from around the Pacific region. 
The Malaysian Ambassador to Moscow, Renji Sathiah, who attended it, said he believed Japan is ''the key'' to Soviet intentions in the Far East. 
''It's really the country they're looking at,'' he said. 
''It's the one with the big bucks and with the demand for the resources they have.''
But Japanese companies' dealings with the Soviet Union are carefully limited by Tokyo, which continues to predicate normalized relations on the return of four northern islands held by the Soviet Union since the close of World War II. 
The disagreement leaves the two nations without a peace treaty; as a result, Japanese companies doing business in the Far East - or trying to - have been taking a low profile.
''They need a political breakthrough before anything will happen on the economic front,'' Mr. Sathiah said. 
The Russians, meanwhile, are seeking membership in the Pacific Economic Cooperation Council, a group of political and economic authorities.
Mr. Gorbachev's interest in opening the Far East was clear during a September speech in the Siberian city of Krasnoyarsk. 
Beyond that, Far East officials take heart from new laws. 
Enterprises may now determine product distribution, and joint ventures with foreign companies are liberated from initial import taxes, onerous customs fees and requirements that local citizens retain majority ownership and top management jobs.
For Soviet enterprises, the changes pose challenges. 
Energomash, a plant outside Khabarovsk producing turbines and compressors, has received the right to trade directly on foreign markets. 
This year, the portion of the plant's production covered by state orders will drop to 10 percent from 80 and managers must now scramble to learn such basics as world prices.
Not surprisingly, some enterprises are slow to pick up the beat. 
''There is opposition to perestroika,'' said Mikhail Postnikov, a Khabarovsk government economist. 
''You can't point to individuals. 
If you ask anyone, they will say they are for it.''
Soviet economists have criticized Dalsprom, a Far East institution handling forest products, for sitting on American and South Korean proposals for joint ventures to produce chopsticks for the Asian market.
Despite the difficulties, supporters of Mr. Gorbachev's trade initiatives say the effects of those efforts are spreading, even to long-neglected parts of the Soviet Union like the Far East.
''The soul, the feeling of perestroika has reached the outskirt regions,'' said Valentin V. Romanov, director of the Khabarovsk Pedagogical Institute, which trains teachers. 
''We can feel it here now.''

The influx of nearly 100,000 Asians over the last decade, many of them Chinese entrepreneurs from Hong Kong, has transformed the look and character of Canada's third-largest city and helped shield it from cold economic winds blowing across the rest of the country.
As a result of new Canadian immigration policies and worries in Hong Kong about absorption by China in 1997, Vancouver, which now counts 15 percent of its 1.5 million people as ethnic Chinese, has emerged as a bustling Pacific Rim finance and trading center.
It is a harbor city of gleaming towers, silvery hills and crisscrossing ferries, and already looks much like Hong Kong.
In recent years, the similarities have increased sharply. 
In some Vancouver schools, more than 90 percent of the students are ethnic Chinese; bilingual signs are now widespread; Chinese-language newspapers can be found in in hotels and shopping centers, and Hong Kong institutions like the Hong Kong Bank of Canada and Cathay Pacific Airways have established a presence in the city.
Terms like "feng shui," meaning the positioning of a house so that it brings good fortune to a family, have also emerged in everyday language.
Â 
Encouraged by Government
Fearing for the future in Hong Kong under Communism, many of the immigrants have bought their right to live here. 
They have come under new Government programs offering "landed immigrant" status, which is almost as good as citizenship, to those who commit at least $250,000 or start businesses employing at least three people.
These entrepreneurs are acquiring businesses ranging from ginseng, chopstick making, doughnuts and garments to computer software.
They are building $1 million homes and gobbling up commercial real estate. 
One official estimate says that Asian-Canadians now own 7 percent of the land in the downtown area, including Canada's biggest real estate development, the giant Pacific Place of Li Ka-shing, a billionaire and one of Hong Kong's richest men.
Mr. Li bought 204 acres on the Expo 86 site next to Chinatown for $320 million in 1987, and hopes to complete a huge waterfront commercial and residential center in the next 10 to 12 years.
Some older Canadians of European extraction talk of an ethnic Chinese takeover of the city. 
Resentment is expressed over perceived competition for jobs, real estate and services, over Chinese clannishness, and over occasional violence by Asian street gangs.
The magazine Vancouver has just published an article, titled "Look What They've Done to My Neighborhood," that laments a pattern of residential building by Hong Kong millionaires in which modest, airy old houses surrounded by gardens and trees are replaced by pretentious mansions with all sorts of extra bathrooms, hot-tub rooms, rec rooms and exercise rooms.
Â 
'Greed Now Calls the Shots'
"It's megabucks and build to the max," an author, Kerry McPhedran, wrote. 
Where modesty once dictated design in this city, he said, "greed now calls the shots.
Tung Chan, a Hong Kong-born banker who is the only ethnic Chinese member of the Vancouver city council, accuses critics of using a double standard. 
"When a European family has a large house," he said, "people call it an estate. 
When a Chinese family has a large house it's called a 'monster house.'
"
Still, he is urging the new Canadians to be more restrained in their housing tastes to avoid "racist backlash."
He quotes an old Chinese saying, "When you go into a river, you follow the flow of the stream."
In spite of friction, just about everyone agrees that the economic effect of the new immigration wave and the accompanying investment of $2 billion a year for the region have been positive.
"The heavy Chinese immigration is one reason why Vancouver outperforms the rest of the country," said Prof. Don J. DeVoretz, an immigration economist at Simon Fraser University here. 
"It has created jobs."
Â 
The Need to Hustle
The employment situation is hardly good, but not as bad as in Canada's two largest cities. 
While unemployment in Vancover rose from 7 percent to 8 percent in the last year, the rate in Toronto nearly doubled, from 5.8 percent to 10.4 percent, and Montreal's rose from 10 percent to 12 percent.
"We're in a situation where we have to get out and hustle," said Sid Fancy, manager of Vancouver's economic development office, "and our friends from Hong Kong are showing us how."
Longtime businesses are divided on how to respond. 
"Some are still resentful," said Peter Ladner, editor and publisher of the weekly Business in Vancouver. 
"Others want to accept the challenge and say, 'Let's learn something.'
"
One sign of the resentment is the absence of Chinese faces in the Vancouver Club, inner sanctum for the city's business aristocracy. 
At the nearby Terminal City Club, though, Hong Kong Chinese sit on the governing board.
Not all the immigrants are buying factories and building shopping centers. 
Many Asian newcomers arrive without jobs, hardly speak English and must adjust to a very different way of life.
To ease the fears and frustrations, the United Chinese Community Enrichment Services Society offers employment seminars, English-language training and orientation classes.
Georgina Lane, herself from Hong Kong, and a mortgage specialist at the Royal Bank, is a volunteer teacher at the agency. 
Her class on mortgage financing is one of the most popular.
"Their response is tremendous," she said of her students. 
"They want to know everything they can about mortgages."

text:

CATHAY
A Journey in Search of Old China.
By Fergus M. Bordewich.
Introduction by Jan Morris.
304 pp. 
New York:
A Destinations Book/Prentice Hall Press. 
$19.95.
The Chinese claim that theirs is the oldest culture on earth, and even now it is so deep-rooted that it has been shaken only superficially by the West. 
The homogeneity of this vast nation is always more striking than its diversities, and the waves of invasion that have swept over it have been absorbed as naturally as the periodic floods of its great rivers.
Yet the Western challenge has posed problems that no other invader has equaled. 
Other insurgents had nothing to teach the Celestial Kingdom, whereas Western ideas -- Communism and democracy among them -- have endangered its very essence. 
Above all, the Cultural Revolution, which engulfed the country for 10 years beginning in 1966, dealt out destruction to the older civilization with a terrible evangelism. 
"Build the new, destroy the old!" rang the Maoist battle cry -- and no more un-Chinese slogan could be envisaged. 
The Chinese world had been built on a Confucian concept of the past -- on the myth of a Golden Time -- and in theory the Chinese always strove to return to this era of imagined purity, as if the centuries were simply fading echoes of an ancient harmony. 
In China, age and precedent have always been revered.
Today, after decades of destruction and modernization in China, the traveler enters a country of superficial monotony, in which the greater palaces and temples (built, fatally, of wood) have mostly been burned away, and the old scholars and es thetes who were the repositories of the past are disappearing -- either killed, "reformed" or made redundant by events.
In "Cathay: A Journey in Search of Old China," Fergus M. Bordewich sets out to discover "how much of Old China had survived behind the blank mask of communism, and to ask how much of post-Communist China might be a reincarnation of the old."
He answers the first question with affectionate and vivid portraits of places and people. 
But the second, more ambitious task -- to diagnose the past in the living present -- eludes him.
This failure partly stems from his having taken the easy option of visiting familiar tourist sites. 
He entered the country from the unexpected direction of Hunza, beginning his journey in the "vast emptiness" of China's far western frontier, but then traveled the Silk Road eastward through Xinjiang Province to Xian, site of the great Tang dynasty (A.D. 618-907) capital, and on down the gorges of the Yangtze. 
After exploring the rambling complex of Confucius' home at Qufu, he visited the sacred mountain of Taishan; Jiuhuashan, the site of many venerable Buddhist temples; the garden city of Suzhou; the old Southern Sung dynasty (A.D. 1127-1279) capital of Hangzhou; the holy island of Putuoshan, and at last Beijing.
These are, on the whole, conventional destinations, and it is sad that this author's passion for his subject did not lead him to experience what remained of ancient China in country villages and lesser-known towns.
Yet he is a receptive and hardy traveler, and he writes memorably about some of the people he met: Tung, the caretaker of an art collection housed in a garden pavilion in Suzhou, who slowly comes to trust him; the art teacher Peng, who takes refuge from his own ambiguous past in a passion for scroll paintings; the absurd dilettante Chen, who dreams of becoming a monk on Putuoshan, but who discovers at the last moment that life in the monastery there is as corrupt as life outside.
"Cathay" is a frankly romantic and nostalgic search for a way of life that, the author acknowledges, coexisted in its day with bitter poverty and callousness. 
This was the culture of the private scholar and esthete, or of the monk. 
It is crystallized in the Sung dynasty paintings of idealized landscapes and contented hermits, in allusive poetry and chrysanthemum-gazing, in the subtle love of simple things.
Mr. Bordewich, who was an adviser to the Xinhua News Agency in Beijing in the early 1980's, writes of all this in a style that is sometimes evocative and often lush. 
His is a Western romantic's response to this most restrained and economical of cultures. 
Yet he recognizes the limitations of the Old China, and those of its spokesmen. 
"Nearly all served in the imperial bureaucracy," he writes, "but they were also painters, calligraphers, scholars, and connoisseurs. 
The rarefied life that they lived was difficult to imagine, or to respect entirely, in the democratic twentieth century. 
. . . Imperial service bred disdain for the less favored."
And what, in the end, does he find?
The Cultural Revolution did not, of course, extinguish the past. 
No political movement can. 
The past goes on existing in the national psyche and announces itself in new guises. 
Once the glaze of Westernism is chipped away, the old Chinese reticence and politesse, the attachment to form and precedent, the pomposity and delicacy are all in place. 
But Mr. Bordewich is less concerned with dissecting the subtleties of national character than with discovering physical evidence of the past he romanticizes. 
And he does, sometimes, find it -- in the depleted but still active Buddhist monasteries, in architectural leftovers, in the memories of old men.
That this past pervades the whole national psyche is a phenomenon that is beyond this author (or perhaps any author) adequately to compass. 
The Chinese application of Communism -- so different from its Soviet or Western counterparts -- is a fascinating story that has yet to be properly written. 
It betrays more about the Old China than any scroll painting.
But even the gentle, esthetic (and rather pedantic) past that Mr. Bordewich eulogizes proves, in the end, elusive -- like the pigeon-flutes whose music haunts him. 
These curious instruments are still occasionally whittled from bamboo or tiny gourds and then attached to the tail feathers of pigeons. 
When the birds fly, they make an eerie, whining music. 
It haunted the author like the old culture itself, coming and going in the sky, half sensed and half imagined.
The past is like that in China still. 
Mr. Bordewich has sometimes caught it in flight, sometimes not.

Responding to the unrest in China, the Voice of America has begun sending television signals to China, the first time that the agency has taken that step, the director of the agency said today.
The Voice of America signal is going directly to about 2,000 satellite dishes in China, operated mostly by the People's Liberation Army. 
The V.O.A. director, Richard W. Carlson, said there was no way to tell whether the transmission was being watched by the military or being passed along other channels.
The United States Embassy in Beijing is receiving the signal ''loud and clear'' on a satellite dish, Mr. Carlson said. 
The transmission began on Tuesday.
The broadcast of news to the military is significant because of reports that units backing the pro-democracy demonstrators may have exchanged fire with units supporting the crackdown.
Â 
Broadcasts Available to Military
''We are sending a television signal that is available to every major military installation in China,'' Mr. Carlson said. 
The signal originates in the United States and bounces off satellites over the Indian and Pacific Oceans. 
The signal can be received all over China.
''It makes available to the Chinese military information about what is going on in China,'' he said. 
''Information that may not otherwise be available to the Chinese military.''
Television and radio sets cannot receive direct satellite signals. 
The transmissions must be received by satellite dishes and rebroadcast in a signal accessible to individual receivers.
The radio service, which broadcasts radio programs in many languages around the world, including transmissions directed at Communist nations, has never used a television signal before, Mr. Carlson said.
Â 
Radio Broadcasts Increased
''It seemed like the right thing to do,'' he said. 
Mr. Carlson said he made the decision and informed a special State Department task force monitoring the events in China.
''The State Deparment is aware of it,'' he said. 
''No one has objected.''
The service usually beams 8 hours of Mandarin-language radio broadcasts to China each day, but it increased that to 11 hours in response to the student demonstrations in Beijing.
''Chinese authorities have said that we have a regular listening audience of 60 million,'' Mr. Carlson said. 
''We believe that we are over 100 million now. 
We are clearly the most pervasive non-Chinese source of news in the country.'
Â 
Jamming of Radio Broadcasts
The Voice of America's television image shows a broadcaster reading the news as a Chinese-language script scrolls across the lower part of the screen. 
The service has not tried to broadcast television pictures of the demonstrations or the aftermath.
During the unrest, Mr. Carlson said, the Chinese authorities tried to jam the service's Chinese-language radio broadcasts, but they have not tried to jam its English-language broadcasts.
The service has a bureau with two correspondents in Beijing, and it uses other Western news services, which have been reporting a different story than the official Chinese news organizations.
''The Chinese media have been very dishonest about the student demonstrations and the role of the military,'' said Mr. Carlson.
''Chinese media have said there were 300 dead, and that they were mostly soldiers, which is not true,'' he said. 
''The Red Cross says 3,000 people died.''
Some Western sources in Beijing have estimated the dead at 7,000.

text:

The real news does not travel fast in this Communist country, at least through official channels. 
So when the streets here swell with protesters, people all over China tune in the Voice of America.
During the turmoil of recent weeks, people in offices, factories and schools throughout China have clustered by the radio to listen to the latest episodes in the saga of student protest. 
At Beijing University, students huddle around posters that report the latest Voice bulletins, and the other day, hundreds of students crowded around a dormitory window listening to a dispatch.
Voice of America Has Won the Ear of China
The United States Government radio network hardly competes with China's Central People's Broadcasting station, which probably has the largest number of listeners in the world. 
But during times of unrest, China's news organizations tend to be silent about what many Chinese people are most interested in, sending waves of would-be listeners to the American competition.
''I always listen to V.O.A.,'' said Xi Rimo, a 28-year-old chemistry student at Beijing University. 
''Some news takes a long time to get to us, and some news we never hear at all. 
V.O.A. helps us understand what's going on in our own country.''
In times of turmoil, Chinese people have always scrambled for access to foreign news reports.
The Voice of America has enjoyed a much wider audience than the BBC partly because it offers nine hours of news in Chinese every day, compared with two and a half hours at the BBC. 
While more Chinese tune in these days to the English-language news programs, the great majority still listen to Chinese programs.
Because it has some 60 million listeners in China, the Voice at times seems to have a greater effect on local politics than do China's own news organizations.
Perhaps the peak of the Voice's influence here came during nationwide student demonstrations in December 1986, when many people said the Voice was partly responsible for the spread of the protests from city to city, as people learned from the broadcasts what was happening elsewhere and decided to join in.
''Our listenership goes through the roof during protests,'' said David W. Hess, chief of the China branch at the Voice of America in Washington.
Because of the station's political influence here, its broadcasts have sometimes become an irritant in Chinese-American diplomatic relations. 
China protested the broadcasts during the 1986 student demonstrations, and five months ago during racial unrest in the city of Nanjing, the official People's Daily called a Voice report ''nonsense.''
Last August the Foreign Ministry turned down a request for press accreditation from a Voice correspondent, giving no explanation.
So far the Government has not made any comment about the Voice's coverage of the protests, and last week it accredited a second journalist for the station's Beijing bureau. 
In addition, China's television and radio and newspapers now are reporting limited information about the protests, and so the Voice is not playing so pivotal a role.
Â 
Some Special Attention
Newsmakers sometimes give the Voice special attention. 
Indeed, in the middle of a demonstration, or a march on the Communist Party headquarters, when other foreign correspondents are stalking students to interview, the students are stalking the Voice reporter.
''Have you seen the V.O.A. reporter here?'' a student demonstrator asked a foreign reporter recently.
Yet some students now seem disappointed with the Voice's coverage, complaining that it has not been as aggressive as before.
''We have very little information about what goes on in Beijing,'' said Zhang Z., a 24-year-old electrical engineering student who had come here from Fudan University in Shanghai. 
''Of course we listen to V.O.A., but V.O.A. has been rather moderate in its news reports of the student protests, not like in 1986.''
The Voice of America insists that its coverage of this round of protests essentially has not changed, although it relied more heavily during the first week of unrest on news-agency reports.

text:
ï»¿
Two months ago the story would have provoked shouted inquiries to the President as he boarded his helicopter and hasty news conferences by members of Congress eager to take a stand. 
But on Aug. 
28, 1989, the report provoked only silence.
The State Department prepared special guidance for its spokesmen on the report, but when no journalists asked about it at the daily briefing, the department did not volunteer a comment.
The report was brief: The Associated Press said a student in Beijing had been sentenced to nine years in prison for allegedly spreading rumors to the Voice of America. 
Attributing the report to a Chinese newspaper, the news agency said it was the first sentencing of a student to prison for participating in the spring democracy movement.
Through television Americans survey a vast world from their living rooms. 
With every new crisis, their attention turns and last week's news begins to fade out. 
As democracy bloomed in Poland and the drug war exploded in Colombia, China seemed to fade out. 
What ever happened to American outrage over the repression of the democracy movement?
To begin with, the Chinese are learning the lesson of South Africa: what American news organizations cannot see, the average American will not feel. 
Although the arrests and repression in China today are far more sustained than the fleeting explosion of violence in Tiananmen Square, they are taking place beyond the glare of television cameras. 
It is hard for Americans to summon outrage from file footage.
''The Chinese will never make the mistake again of allowing television cameras to show their tanks running over people in Beijing,'' an Asia expert in the State Department said. 
''What is happening there today may actually be worse - the slow dribbling out of arrests and convictions -but it lacks drama. 
It's not on television. 
It's not in Beijing. 
It is people being arrested in the middle of the night.''
Indeed, television has both cultivated and reflected the very short attention span Americans have toward foreign news. 
Stories on television, unlike in real life, always contain bold dramas and quick endings. 
The viewing public has become accustomed to news packaged in this format. 
When it cannot be packaged this way, the channel gets changed.
China's democracy movement attracted Americans' attention as a rare glimmer of democratic possibilities, like Hungary in 1956. 
But such moments lack staying power. 
At best they become memories that inspire the long boring haul of reform and institution building, which make for good history and awful ratings.
There are other explanations. 
With China, Americans seem to be experiencing the humility that comes from discovering that a nation they thought they knew was actually a stranger. 
It was as though the United States awoke one morning and realized that it did not know China, that it was not, as many hoped, on a steady course toward Westernization.
Americans learned the hard way that they would have to wait for China to sort out its own path, that this regime has much more staying power than many would like to believe and that its leaders have no intention of paying for American friendship with their own power. 
As that became more apparent, the policy debate on China assumed a new modesty.
This was reinforced from above. 
No one has more power to shape a debate than the President. 
But instinctively, President Bush seemed to realize that the students were never going to capture power, so he dampened expectations about the democracy movement.
In addition, strategic interests dictated that he not abandon the implicit Chinese-American alliance against the Soviet Union simply because so many students were gunned down. 
So Mr. Bush flashed just enough anger to appease the momentary sense of outrage and to prevent Congress from legislating its own sanctions, but not so much anger as to break relations with China or to keep its drama in the headlines an extra day.

Thirty-five members of the Fezziwigs, a suburban New York-Connecticut-New Jersey branch of the International Order of Dickens Fellows, usually meet on the last Saturday of each month from September through June to indulge their passion for the works of Charles Dickens. 
Visitors will be welcome at the next session, which is scheduled from 1 to 3 P.M. Saturday in the French Parlor of Reid Hall at Manhattanville College in Purchase. 
Admission is free.
''In ordinary contact with people, you don't come across many who are avid Dickens readers,'' said Claire Davis, president of the chapter, ''and you like to talk to someone about what you read.''
Each year the three-year-old branch chooses a Dickens book to read and discuss under the leadership of Dr. Nancy Schaumburger, professor of English at Manhattanville. 
This year's project is ''Hard Times.''
Founded in London in 1902, the International Order of Dickens Fellows has a total of 80 branches worldwide - 30 in England, 20 in the United States and varying numbers in Canada, Italy, France, the Netherlands, Japan, New Zealand, Sri Lanka and Argentina. 
''Each branch chooses its own name,'' Mrs. Davis said, ''usually a character in one of the books.''
Fezziwig was the family name of the woman who jilted Scrooge in his youth.
In addition to the meetings, the chapters hold a Christmas party and a Dickens birthday party each year, raising money for charity. 
''Last year we gave to Hale House,'' Mrs. Davis said, referring to the Manhattan refuge for AIDS-infected babies.
The gift was given in compliance with one of the stated objects of the international fellowship: ''To knit together in a common bond of friendship lovers of that great master of humor and pathos, Charles Dickens. 
To spread the love of humanity, which is the keynote of all his work; to take such measures as may be expedient to remedy those existing social evils, the amelioration of which would have appealed so strongly to the heart of Charles Dickens, and to help in every possible direction in the cause of the poor and oppressed; to assist in the preservation and purchase of buildings and objects associated with his name or mentioned in his works.''
To that end the London fellowship purchased and established its headquarters in Dickens's home at 48 Doughty Street, where he wrote ''Oliver Twist,'' ''The Pickwick Papers'' and ''Nicholas Nickelby.''
Membership in the local chapter is $15 a year and includes meetings, parties and a newsletter.

text:
ï»¿
OUT of the teapot comes more than the soothing or ceremonial cup. 
Tea can add subtle flavor and rich color to a variety of foods.
While Westerners generally think of tea only as a beverage, the Chinese have used it as a seasoning for centuries. 
And now as more American and French chefs are blending Asian flavors and techniques into their cooking, they too have discovered the pleasures of flavoring with tea.
Perhaps the most traditional use of tea in Chinese cooking is for tea-leaf eggs, a specialty often served on the Chinese New Year because eggs represent rebirth and good fortune.
After hard-boiled eggs are prepared, their shells are gently cracked all over but not removed. 
The eggs are then simmered for about an hour in a mixture of water, soy sauce, star anise and tea leaves. 
The dark, flavorful broth penetrates the cracked shells so when the eggs are finally cooled and peeled they have the look of marbelized porcelain.
Today tea is most frequently used for smoking poultry. 
Nina Simonds, the author of ''Classic Chinese Cuisine'' and ''Chinese Seasons'' (Houghton Mifflin, 1982 and 1986), said the smoking technique originated as a way to preserve foods in the warmer provinces of Sichuan, Hunan and Hubei. 
''A number of flavoring and coloring agents were used,'' she said in a recent interview, ''and among them were camphor, cyprus, bamboo and tea.''
She added that the use of smoke in China has evolved strictly as a flavoring now.''
Among the Chinese restaurants in New York that serve tea-smoked duck are Chin Chin on East 49th Street and Shun Lee West on West 65th Street.
Charles Palmer, the chef and a co-owner of Aureole in Manhattan, serves tea-smoked squab. 
''I do it differently from the Chinese,'' he said. 
''I don't cook the squab first. 
I smoke raw squabs for about 40 minutes, then roast them.''
Mr. Palmer said he first tasted classic tea-smoked duck at Chin Chin. 
''I liked the flavor because it was not as pungent as the taste you get from wood smoking,'' he said. 
''I didn't know exactly how the Chinese did it so I experimented.''
He uses branches of green Greek mountain tea that he buys in Astoria, Queens.
Ken Hom, an author and cooking teacher, said he saw a lot of young American chefs experimenting with tea smoking because ''it's new for them and different from using hickory chips.''
The type of tea used is extremely important. 
''It should be fresh, not old, so it imparts the best flavor and color,'' Ms. Simonds said. 
She prefers China black tea but also said that Lapsang souchong, which has a smoky taste, was very effective.
Not only are smoked foods more popular than ever, but the ease and simplicity of the Chinese technique adds to its appeal. 
It can be done on the kitchen stove in a wok.
The wok is lined with aluminum foil and in it are placed the tea leaves and, usually, some sugar. 
Some recipes also include raw rice with the tea leaves. 
Star anise, dried tangerine peel or cinnamon sticks may also be included for flavor. 
Whole duck, chicken or squab that has been steamed or poached in an aromatic broth is set on a rack over the tea mixture. 
The wok is covered tightly. 
Within minutes after the heat is turned on the tea mixture begins to smoke, seasoning the food and deepening its color.
After 10 to 15 minutes, the heat can be turned off and the food left in the wok to cool.
Occasionally tea leaves are used for stir-frying. 
A specialty of Hangzhou in southern China is stir-fried shrimp seasoned with fresh green dragon well tea leaves. 
In her book ''Chinese Cooking for the American Kitchen'' (Atheneum, 1976), Karen Lee includes a recipe for stir-fried beef with black tea. 
She also uses steeped black tea in sesame paste when making sesame noodles as well as in marinades for barbecuing.
Regardless of the cooking technique, Mr. Hom said it was important not to overdo the tea flavor. 
''It should add subtle depths but not overwhelm,'' he said.
Delicate teas can season rice. 
Yannick Cam, the chef and owner of Le Pavillon in Washington, sometimes uses jasmine tea instead of water for cooking rice to serve with Thai curries. 
In Elizabeth Andoh's first book, ''At Home With Japanese Cooking'' (Alfred A. Knopf, 1980), a dish of rice and chicken or fish is served moistened with hot green tea.
Tea even adds exotic perfume to desserts. 
Green tea has become a standard ice-cream flavor in Chinese and Japanese restaurants. 
Using tea in dessert is also popular among French and American chefs.
Jasmine is used to season a custard at Restaurant Troisgros in Roanne, France. 
Alain Senderens, chef and co-owner of Lucas Carton in Paris, steeps prunes in brandy and black tea. 
A parfait of tea and raisins with warm praline-champagne sauce is also on the menu at Beau Geste, a new French restaurant on the Upper West Side in New York.
In ''Chez Panisse Desserts'' (Random House, 1985), Leslie Remolif Shere includes a recipe for fruit poached in sauterne and seasoned with Darjeeling tea. 
Mr. Palmer uses jasmine tea and tangerine to add subtle flavor to ice cream.
''I think tea is an interesting flavor,'' he said. 
''There's such variation in teas. 
And the funny thing is I never particularly drink tea, but now I use it for cooking.''

1 1/2 pounds fresh chicken livers
3 1/2 quarts water
1/2 cup China black tea leaves tied in a square of cheesecloth
1/4 cup rice wine
1/4 cup soy sauce
4 whole star anise
6 slices fresh ginger root, peeled.
1.Lightly rinse the chicken livers, drain thoroughly and separate the lobes.
2.Heat two quarts of water until boiling and blanch the livers for about two minutes. 
Drain.
3.In a heavy saucepan combine the remaining 1 1/2 quarts of water with the tea leaves, rice wine and soy sauce. 
Lightly smash the anise and ginger root with the side of a cleaver and add them. 
Simmer this mixture for 20 minutes.
4.Add the chicken livers and once the mixture returns to a simmer cook for 15 minutes. 
Remove from heat and allow the chicken livers to cool in the liquid.
5.Remove the cooled livers from the cooking liquid and slice them thin. 
Serve cold or at room temperature on slices of toast or in a salad.
Yield: 6 servings.
Â 
Tea-Smoked Squab
Â 
(Adapted from ''Bruce Cost's Asian Ingredients,'' William Morrow & Company, 1988)
Â 
Preparation time: 10 minutes plus marinating and cooling time
Â 
Cooking time:
One hour, 30 minutes, in stages
Â 
4 whole squabs
2 tablespoons coarse salt
2 teaspoons Sichuan peppercorns
6 star anise
2 2-inch cinnamon sticks
2 teaspoons dark soy sauce
1/2 cup uncooked rice
1/2 cup light brown sugar
1/4 cup black tea leaves
Peanut oil for deep frying.
1.Rinse and dry the squabs thoroughly.
2.Place the salt, peppercorns, star anise and cinnamon sticks in a dry skillet and toast by shaking over medium heat until the mixture begins to smoke and the salt begins to turn brown. 
Allow to cool. 
Discard the star anise and cinnamon and rub salt and peppercorns over the squabs, inside and out. 
Cover the squabs loosely and set in a cool place or in the refrigerator for eight hours or overnight.
3.Place the squabs, breast side down, on a heat-proof plate. 
Place in a steamer or a covered wok fitted with a rack and steam 30 minutes. 
Allow squabs to cool, then rub with soy sauce.
4.Cover the bottom of a wok with aluminum foil. 
Place the rice, brown sugar and tea in it. 
Place a rack in the wok and arrange the squabs breast side up on the rack. 
Line the cover of the wok with foil, cover the wok and seal the edge of the cover with dampened paper towels to keep the smoke from escaping.
5.Turn the heat to medium high and when you smell smoke leave the heat on for 15 minutes. 
Turn the heat off and keep the birds in the covered wok for 45 minutes.
6.In a large wok or deep fryer heat the oil, add the squabs one at a time and deep fry them for five minutes to crisp the skin. 
Pat dry with paper towels. 
Serve warm or at room temperature.
Yield: 8 to 10 servings.
NOTE: Instead of deep frying, the squabs can be roasted for 10 minutes at 450 degrees.
Â 
Green Tea Ice Cream
Â 
(Adapted from ''An American Taste of Japan'' by Elizabeth Andoh, Alfred A. Knopf, 1986)
Â 
Preparation time: 25 minutes plus freezing
Â 
Cooking time: 8 minutes
Â 
Y cup sugar
Y cup water
1/2 teaspoon mirin (Japanese rice wine)
2 teaspoons matcha (powdered Japanese green tea)
1/2 cup whole milk
1/2 cup half and half.
1.In a small saucepan, combine the sugar and water and stir over low heat until the sugar melts. 
Simmer 5 minutes longer, then stir in the rice wine. 
Remove from heat.
2.In a small dish, dissolve the tea in one tablespoon of the sugar syrup, then stir the tea mixture back into the rest of the syrup.
3.Stir in the milk and half and half. 
Chill.
4.When the mixture is cold, place it in an ice-cream maker and churn it until thickened and smooth. 
Transfer to a container and freeze for an hour or two to firm it.
Yield: 1 pint.

text:

President Bush can always count on hundreds of millions of fans in China this fall. 
People here regard him as an old friend and still talk about how he and his wife, Barbara, used to ride their bicycles around Beijing when they lived here in the early 1970's.
Friendship aside, the Government also has another reason to support the incumbent: President Bush will fight Congress to keep China's unconditional "most favored nation" trade status, despite human rights abuses. 
Bill Clinton probably would not. 
That makes this, from China's point of view, a one-issue race.
One indication of Mr. Clinton's thinking is that two exiled dissidents that Beijing considers "counter-revolutionary criminals," Chai Ling and Li Lu, were invited to speak at the Democratic Convention.
Beyond that, most Chinese are not familiar with the campaign issues, and newspapers have devoted little space to the race. 
For example, on the convention's third day the People's Daily published 190 words about the opening ceremony. 
For balance, it also carried a 277-word article describing a Tibetan arts troupe's visit to New York.

The President today directed that the U.S. 
Government suspend participation in all high-level exchanges of Government officials with the People's Republic of China, in addition to the suspension of military exchanges previously announced. 
This action is being taken in response to the wave of violence and reprisals by the Chinese authorities against those who have called for democracy. 
The United States has supported the legitimate democratic aspirations for freedom of peoples throughout the world. 
The United States will continue to voice its concern and its support for these aspirations.
The United States hopes that the current tragedy in China be brought to a peaceful end and that dialogue will replace the atmosphere of suspicion and reprisal.
