file: WHAT_S DOING IN_ Hong Kong.txt
text:
ï»¿
It is this time of year, as winter slips into spring and residents shed their furs and overcoats, that Hong Kong's eternal bustle accelerates a bit. 
Instead of hurtling about inside their office towers and shopping arcades, people careen along the sidewalks in their rush to get somewhere. 
The frenzy moves outdoors, to the markets, to the parks and to the harbor with its European yachts and Chinese junks.
Defining Hong Kong is a bit like defining a stew, for this is a territory with a bit of everything. 
Mirrored skyscrapers, sprawling mansions in the hills and spacious shopping malls with water-splashing fountains create a picture of modernism. 
I. M. Pei's stark, geometric monument for the mainland's Bank of China juts out in the skyline, as below, specks of white that are the yachts of the wealthy glide silently through the ''fragrant harbor,'' as Hong Kong is called in Chinese.
Just a few blocks away the image shifts to an older, poorer Hong Kong, where fish and vegetables are sold in the street, where fruit and meats are offered to the ancestral gods and where English is barely understood.
Hong Kong's 5.7 million people fit snugly onto this 413-square-mile territory off the southern coast of China, and yet while it is crowded - overwhelmingly so at times - it is a good spot for walking. 
Streets are small and the shops, which line them everywhere, make the streets more lively to walk through. 
A taxi can easily be hired, but it is more fun to walk and cars often seem to be too big for the roads one wants to go down. 
Buses are also convenient, and the subway system embarrasses the American varieties with its combination of efficiency and low cost. 
The cost of a bus or subway ride varies depending on the length of the trip, but it is generally between 20 and 85 cents.
Shopping is perhaps the prime activity in Hong Kong. 
But there are other things to do in the city, where the flavors of ancient customs still linger in the back alleys, the hidden temples and old teahouses.
Â 
Things to See
The Peak is far more than just a tall, pointy mountain. 
It is physically beautiful, even when the mist wafts in during the sunsets; on a fresh, clear day it offers one of the most expansive views of Hong Kong. 
By day, a sharp-eyed visitor may be able to see the New Territories to the north; by night the sparkling lights of the city glisten against the water in the still harbor below.
Such views have made the Peak one of the most coveted residential areas, a symbol for many of the rich local inhabitants that this is an enclave one attains through accomplishment. 
It is also a place where many foreign expatriates live and the home of elegant dinner parties, small private swimming pools and beautiful gardens.
For those who want to exercise, there are plenty of small roads that wind through small woods and grass. 
Try Mount Austin Road, where one can stroll - and perspire a little - and peer out over the mountainside at the expanse of the surrounding colony. 
The Peak Tram, more than 100 years old, will make you grab for a handle because of the sensation that the back is where the feet should be. 
The tram station is one block above the Hilton Hotel in the Central district, and the ride up, about every 15 minutes, costs around $1.70.
Hong Kong is divided into districts, among them Central, Tsim Sha Tsui and Wanchai. 
The subway, or Mass Transit Railway, stops at each of these places, but if you want to get to Tsim Sha Tsui from Central (or vice versa), take the Star Ferry. 
The stark contrast between the modern glass buildings and the strong, salty breeze during this short trip across the harbor is one of the hallmarks that keeps Hong Kong from being just another big city. 
The Star Ferry, which costs about 13 cents, leaves from the terminal by the docks in Central.
The south side of Hong Kong Island is very scenic, and its sandy beaches attract hundreds of people.
A visit to Stanley Market, Repulse Bay and Aberdeen would make a pleasant afternoon. 
Catch Bus No. 6 or 260 to Stanley at the Exchange Square Terminal in Central (a taxi would be a bit more than $6). 
Although Stanley is a residential area with long, sandy beaches, its main attraction for tourists is the sprawling street market. 
A patient shopper should enjoy walking through the narrow streets packed with stalls and stores, where famous-brand jeans (often less than $20), sweaters and all sorts of cheaper clothing are sometimes piled up on a counter. 
The clothes may be overruns, imitations or irregulars from the many factory outlets, so be careful.
One of the most interesting temples is the Wong Tai Sin temple, near the M.T.R. 
Wong Tai Sin Station on the Kowloon side. 
There on a weekend people can be seen praying to Taoist gods. 
It is a large smoke-filled complex, with several different halls, where people present all sorts of elaborately prepared meats and other offerings to the deities.
Â 
Shopping
It is often fun just to wander through the small shops or the large malls in Tsim Sha Tsui, or the Japanese department stores and clothing boutiques in Causeway Bay. 
Individual shops have their own business hours but generally close around 8 P.M. here, and after they close there is always the night street market on Temple Street, near Jordan Road.
A shopping guide is invaluable. 
There are several books on the subject, but the Hong Kong Tourist Association puts out a free publication, ''The Official Guide to Shopping and Eating Out,'' which lists shops as well as restaurants approved for membership by the association. 
Virtually anything can be found on sale, from Chinese art to Indian rugs to furs to computers to furniture to watches to jewelry.
Hong Kong is one of the world's major markets for diamonds and other gemstones, partly because there is no tax or duty on jewelry. 
In general, shoppers should be wary, especially when buying jewels or antiques, and it may be better to stick to the more reputable stores, even if their prices are a bit higher. 
The tourist association book is a good guideline, and make sure that the receipt shows a full description of the precious metal or gem. 
All the top hotels should have reliable jewelry shops. 
One good place to visit is Town and Country Jewellery (31 Queen's Road Central, in Central; 5225843).
Women's clothes are sold virtually everywhere. 
Some of the best buys can be found in the factory outlets upstairs in the Pedder Building, 12 Pedder Street, in Central. 
The shops across the street in the Landmark Building, and then farther east in the Prince's Building and Mandarin Oriental Hotel also have designer wear, at designer prices. 
For lower quality goods at rock bottom prices, try Li Yuen Street East and Li Yuen Street West, which brim with leather purses and bags, scarves, watches and blouses.
Hong Kong is full of tailors, most of whom specialize in men's suits. 
A tailored suit will cost somewhat more than a comparable suit off the rack at home, but the fit is usually much better. 
Tailors generally require a week and at least two fittings to make suits. 
Try A-Man Hing Cheong (unit M10, mezzanine floor of the Mandarin Oriental Hotel in Central; 5223336). 
Wool men's suits at A-Man start at about $450.
Â 
Eating Out
Hong Kong offers both Western and Asian food, but naturally, Chinese food is its specialty. 
It is best to make reservations at the best places, and even so, one may have to wait. 
Cantonese food, stir-fried quickly at high heat, is the most widely available, but all kinds of Chinese cuisines are represented. 
Try the roast duck at the Grand House of Yung Kee Restaurant, which is usually full, even though it has floors and floors of space (36-40 Wellington Street, in Central; 5221624). 
About $12 to $15 a person. 
The seafood at Tai Woo Restaurant, just across the street, is very tasty (15-19 Wellington Street; 5245618). 
About $15 a person.
For some of the best Shanghainese cuisine try the Wu Kong Shanghai Restaurant (27 Nathan Road, Alpha House Basement, Kowloon; 3667244). 
About $10 a person. 
Cleveland Szechuan Restaurant is good for the spicy Chinese cooking - especially the sizzling prawns - from Sichuan Province in the heartland of China (6 Cleveland Street, Flat C, Causeway Bay; 5763876). 
About $13 a person.
For Cantonese dim sum, which are dumplings served at lunchtime, try the Luk Yu Tea House and Restaurant (26 Stanley Street, in Central; 5235464). 
This is a favorite spot for old Chinese. 
There are no carts, which is what many dim sum houses use to bring around the food. 
If there isn't an English-speaking waiter available you may have to point, but the culinary experience is worth it, and costs only about $6 a person.
For a quieter atmosphere, try the Rainbow Room at the Lee Gardens Hotel (Hysan Avenue, Causeway Bay; 8953311). 
About $13 a person.
Â 
Where to Stay
Accommodations are not cheap, but they are generally excellent. 
The two most convenient districts are Tsim Sha Tsui and Central. 
Hotel rates change frequently, and visitors should ask for special winter rates, which some places offer. 
Add a 10 to 15 percent service charge and 5 percent government tax to all regular hotel rates. 
All prices quoted are for a standard double room.
The Regent, perhaps the most luxurious hotel, is a clay-red modern building with a spectacular view of the harbor. 
Rooms are $190 without a view, $256 with a view (Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon; 7211211).
Across the way is the grande dame of Hong Kong hotels, the Peninsula, oozing charm and history. 
Parts of it will be renovated this spring. 
Standard rooms are $276 (Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon; 3666251); The Mandarin Oriental (5 Connaught Road, Central; 5220111) is often ranked among the top three in the world. 
Rooms run from $192 (standard) to $308 (deluxe). 
At the well-located Hilton, rooms run $185 (2 Queen's Road, Central; 5233111). 
For those who want to stay as close to the shopping as possible, and yet save some money, try the Royal Garden, where excellent accommodations are $135 (69 Mody Road, Tsim Sha Tsui East, Kowloon; 7215215).
It may be a little out of the way, but the newly opened Grand Hyatt offers standard rooms for about $140 (1 Harbour Road, Wanchai; 8611234). 
Standard rooms at the New World, by the harbor right next to the Regent, run about $154, but there are smaller, cheaper rooms for $101 (22 Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon; 3694111). 
At the Y.M.C.A. 
(Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon; 3692211) rooms cost $62. 
Book as far in advance as possible.
Budget choice: Harbour View International House (4 Harbour Road, Wanchai; 5201111) Rooms are $64.

file: WHAT_S DOING IN_ Singapore.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a remarkable combination of will, foresight and happenstance, what began as a swampy island only 85 miles from the Equator has been transformed into the most modern, efficient and simply the cleanest city of Southeast Asia. 
The last is not a bad attribute in a part of the world where sanitation is more talked about than practiced.
Singapore, a city-state of just 2.6 million people and possessing almost no natural resources except its harbor, rides along on a swift current of capital and financial services. 
It is, with Hong Kong, the most unashamedly materialistic society in the region - status conscious, a touch insecure, eager to taste, hear, see or drink what someone, usually in the West, has decided is ''the latest.''
So everything from Indonesian batik to Italian designers, from Chinese silk to the newest Japanese electronic devices, is available here, and usually at low, open-to-bargaining prices comparable to Hong Kong's.
A multiracial society of immigrants, Singapore's mosaic of Asian cultures can be enthralling, with significant contributions from the Chinese, the Malays and the Indians, who, respectively, make up 76 percent, 15 percent and 6.5 percent of the population. 
Conveniently for the American visitor, however, this variety is in the context of a largely English-speaking society, and people live amid a low degree of racial tension.
Altogether, then, Singapore is the easiest introduction any foreigner can have to Asia, a comfortable place with fine hotels, transportation and tourist services, with lots of stuff for the kids, restaurants of nearly every recognized cuisine and yet still the living embodiment of some of exotic Asia's most important cultural and religious influences.
Slowly, even a paternalistic Government obsessed with modernity and convinced that any problem can be solved by ''twiddling the knobs'' of social control has learned to try to preserve the city's cultural and architectural heritage - and just in time, too, before the last Chinese shop-house died for the 100th skyscraper.
Singapore's paternalism also has an element of social control and collective propriety. 
For the residents, this includes restrictions on the kinds of dogs allowed in public housing and fines for littering, not flushing the toilet or urinating in elevators.
For tourists, however, these are not normally major difficulties, though there are increasingly stiff restrictions on where one can smoke. 
In addition one risks the death penalty for drug use, and long hair on men has been sometimes known to create difficulties at immigration counters.
But the pleasures of picking at Singapore's contradictions, which are, of course, as fascinating as its felicities, can wait for a second or third visit.
It's a place where you can shop till you drop, eat till you pop and then plop into the swimming pool. 
Then you can do penance by seeing a Chinese temple or a Malay cultural show, or by taking the kids to one of the best zoos (cageless, in the modern style) or bird parks in Asia. 
The Singapore Zoological Gardens is on Mandai Lake Road and is open 8:30 A.M. to 6 P.M. daily. 
Admission: $2.65, $1.30 for children under 12; telephone 269-3411. 
The Jurong Bird Park is on Jalan Ahmed Ibrahim, open 9 A.M. to 6 P.M., with shows at 10, 10:30, 3 and 4, featuring swooping eagles, hawks, owls and even a condor. 
Admission is the same as the zoo; 265-0022.
Â 
Things to See
Two popular attractions, the National Museum and the eccentric Tiger Balm Gardens, a Chinese Disneyland built by the Aw brothers with their fortune from Tiger Balm, the the liniment, are closed for renovation, at least until the middle of next year.
Empress Place, one of the most successful renovation projects in Singapore, is worth a morning. 
It was built in 1854 as a courthouse, and has been carefully transformed into a museum and exhibition center. 
Until March the museum is showing artifacts from China's Qing dynasty, its last, on loan from the Shenyang Palace Museum. 
Open 9:30 A.M. to 9:30 P.M. daily. 
Admission $3.15; children $1.60.
Singaporeans love birds, and another nice diversion are the songbird cafes, which are less hokey than they sound. 
At the corner of Tiong Bahru and Seng Poh Roads is an unassuming coffee shop, its lot surmounted by poles. 
Handcarved wooden and wicker cages hang from them, while the songbirds inside go through their paces, apparently learning from their neighbors.
Don't forget to note the grasshopper vendor near the coffee shop who provides the birds' munchies. 
The coffee isn't great, but it's a nice way to spend part of a morning. 
The times are roughly 7 A.M. to 11 A.M.; Sundays at 8 A.M. there is a sort of concert.
Â 
Neighborhoods
Given Singapore's size, a standard city tour will provide good orientation and it barely takes a morning. 
Tours cost about $11, $6 for children; most include a sort of ''instant Asia'' cultural show. 
Ask at your hotel or the Singapore Tourist Promotion Board, Raffles City Tower, 250 North Bridge Road (339-6622). 
There is also a potted ''Contrasting Culture'' tour that will take you through what's left of the ethnic neighborhoods.
You'll see Arab Street, in the southeast, a Muslim sector, Chinatown and Little India, along Serangoon Road.
But go back on your own to chat and browse, particularly in Chinatown. 
On Telok Ayer Street is a favorite temple, Thian Hock Keng, the Temple of Heavenly Happiness, where new migrants to Singapore came to pay their respects to Ma Chu Poh, the goddess of the sea.
What began as a josshouse is now a relatively stately temple, with an iron gate imported from Glasgow. 
But the grounds also served as a place of rest and refuge for weary immigrants from Hokkien, many of whom used to smoke opium to relax after a long day of aching labor. 
They would smear opium on the mouths of the goddess's guardians, two statues that flank her own, and give them more to smoke.
Opium, like all such drugs, is illegal now in Singapore. 
Yet even today, what appears to be fresh opium is found smeared on the mouths of the guardians. 
Sometimes, in the evenings, from the rear of the temple grounds, comes the sickly smell of burning opium, tolerated still, or so it seems, for a founding generation quickly passing.
Â 
Getting Around
Singapore has a new subway system, called the M.R.T., or Mass Rapid Transit, and it is clean, quiet and cheap, with fares from about a quarter to 75 cents. 
It works with a magnetic ticket, rather like the Washington, D.C., subway. 
Sometime next year all 42 stations will be in operation.
Recently more stations opened on the east-west lines, so residential areas for the Malay community are accessible. 
One such district, on the east coast, is known as Geylang Serai. 
If you get off at the Eunos Station, you can look at the local market, a lively emporium where the prices are cheap, bargaining is good-natured (and hence serious) and the tour buses don't go. 
It's a good place to meet people and talk to them about their lives, while picking up some batik.
The bus system offers Explorer tickets good for one ($2.60) or three days ($6.30), available at hotels, tour agents and the bus authority (205 Braddell Road; 287-2727).
Taxis are also reasonable, and all are metered and clean. 
And in this carefully regulated city the taxi drivers are honest, or else.
Â 
Orchard Road
One of Singapore's most genuine sights, of course, is the area around Orchard Road, which is devoted to shopping, eating and people-watching. 
The place to start bargain hunting is the Tangs store at No. 320. Swiss watches, gold jewelry, perfume, cosmetics and electrical items are especially good buys. 
Also, surprisingly, Oriental carpets. 
Stay away from the cheap tailors - go to Hong Kong or even Bangkok for that.
It is perfectly legal, by the way, to change money with the many money changers, and the rates are better than at the bank.
Â 
Where to Stay
The days of ready discounts in Singapore hotels are over, at least until a lot more rooms are added in 1991. 
It's worth getting your travel agent to ask, but don't expect miracles. 
All hotels charge a 3 percent tax, soon to be 4 percent, and a 10 percent service charge on top of rates. 
They discourage further tipping but that doesn't mean you can't.
For Orchard Road shopping trips, the Hilton is almost ideally situated at No. 581 (737-2233). 
Doubles go for about $126, and it's a decent, well-run place. 
In roughly the same area and price category, the Hyatt Regency, at 10-12 Scotts Road (733-1188), offers doubles for $131.
Also on Scotts Road, at No. 22, is the Goodwood Park Hotel, a whimsical-looking building, formerly the German Club, that has pleasant public spaces and excellent Asian food.
The Shangri-La Hotel, 22 Orange Grove Road (737-3644), offers some doubles for $121. 
It's a fine hotel, but a bit far to walk from Orchard Road.
For a slightly cheaper stay: the pagoda-like Dynasty Hotel, attached to Tang's at 320 Orchard Road (734-9900). 
Doubles start at $110.
Bargain choices: The Ladyhill Hotel, 1 Ladyhill Road (737-2111), owned by the Goodwood Group, with doubles at $63, or the Cockpit Hotel, 67 Oxley Rise Penang Road (737-9111), with doubles at $74. 
The Cockpit has the sanction of Raffles Hotel, now closed for renovations until mid-1991, to make the original Singapore Sling, which is better than the imitations.
Â 
Where to Eat
For a good Malay meal in a cozy setting: Aziza's Restaurant, 36 Emerald Hill Road; 235-1130 or 732-9491. 
A meal for two with wine or beer: $40.
For Indonesian-Malay food, try the Sanur Indonesian Restaurant, fourth level, Centrepoint Shopping Center, 176 Orchard Road; 734-2192 or 734-2249. 
Meal for two: $20.
The Hyatt Regency has a nouvelle-American restaurant, Nutmegs, that can make a nice break from a long bout of Asian cuisine. 
Good crab cakes and ice cream, especially a mango sorbet of unmatched texture and perfume. 
Dinner for two, with wine and sorbet: about $95.
At the Goodwood Park Hotel, the Min Jiang is thought by many to be the best Sichuan restaurant in Singapore (about $50 for two, with beer). 
A new and elegant Shanghainese restaurant at the same hotel, the Chang Jiang, still has some teething problems, but a compelling menu (about $65 for two, if you stay away from shark's fin and abalone).
For excellent and inexpensive North Indian food, try Moti Mahal, 18 Murray Street (Food Alley); 221-4338. 
A meal for two with wine or beer: $25.

file: Worker Departures Vex Hong Kong.txt
text:
ï»¿
It is the prospect of increasing business with China that brings more foreign companies here each year, and it is the threat of China's eventual dominance over business that drives away their potential employees.
Finding and keeping Chinese employees is developing into a major problem as companies with offices here seek to strengthen ties to China.
''We've said goodbye to a lot of people,'' said Robert J. Schmitt, regional marketing manager at the Digital Equipment Corporation in Hong Kong. 
45,000 Emigrated Last Year Some 45,000 Hong Kong Chinese emigrated last year, out of a labor force of about 2.8 million - worsening the problem of an unemployment rate that is so small it can barely be calculated. 
Many Hong Kong Chinese leave because of concern about what will happen to the territory after 1997, when Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule. 
Most people expect the numbers of emigrants to grow, particularly among white-collar professionals who are not convinced that the Chinese Communist Party will keep its promises to let Hong Kong continue its capitalist ways.
On the other hand, with economies in Asia expanding and costs rising in other financial centers like Japan, companies are moving support staff to Hong Kong, or fortifying or relocating their regional headquarters here.
Yet, as their offices here grow, banks, software companies, accounting firms and other corporations are watching the pool of skilled Chinese professionals shrink. 
They are seeing a territory once famed for its cheap, hard-working labor turn into an expensive auction house for bright Hong Kong professionals.
Â 
Measures to Combat Emigration
While some employers do not think there are any measures to combat effectively the tide of emigration, others have revised their compensation systems, enhanced company perquisites and replaced manpower with machines.
The Hong Kong offices of some American companies are advertising in newspapers in the United States and Canada, not for Americans or Canadians but for skilled Hong Kong Chinese who have already emigrated.
''If someone has another passport, that is an added positive aspect in the total evaluation of the person,'' said Eoghan M. McMillan, regional managing partner at Arthur Andersen & Company in Hong Kong.
Knowing that companies value a foreign passport highly, the Chinese who return to work in Hong Kong can command higher salaries as they shop for employers.
Â 
'Incessant Job Hopping'
''The marketplace is characterized by the most incessant job hopping I've seen here in the region,'' said Vangell Rafael, managing director of Paris-based Econocom Far East Ltd., which sells computer software and hardware.
In some cases, companies are paying as much as 50 percent more than last year in salaries for trained experts or middle-level managers.
Mr. Rafael said that a few months ago when he was at his former company, he hired a computer analyst with a United States passport at a salary of $50,000. 
A year earlier, he would have paid about $35,000.
''We bite the bullet and pay more money,'' Mr. Rafael said.
Â 
Creating a Buffer
Companies also try to hire 10 percent to 15 percent more employees than they actually need to create a buffer against people who leave on short notice.
Technology, finance and engineering companies have been experiencing turnover rates as high as 25 percent a year. 
More significantly, those who emigrate tend to be critically important employees with five to eight years' experience.
''In general, the quality of systems might have gone down,'' said Stephen Lau, a member of the Hong Kong Computer Society. 
Mr. Lau, who is director of information technology at Citicorp in Hong Kong, said that as a result, work is sometimes shifted to other offices in the Pacific Basin.
Â 
Working Through Headhunters
To lure employees, some companies are working though headhunters, while others are plucking talent directly from competitors. 
The incentives include service awards and prizes, intensive training and preferred mortgage rates.
''Some companies are using financial incentives like the 1997 handshake,'' said John C. Wilson, managing director of Russell Reynolds Associates Inc., a New York-based executive recruiting firm in Hong Kong. 
''A multinational would say to someone that if you stay with us until 1997, you will receive 'X' amount of U.S. dollars.''
Citicorp in Hong Kong said it is trying to raise morale by adding merit badges and monetary prizes pegged to performance and by improving training of junior employees.
Â 
Transfers to Other Locations
When possible, companies transfer or rehire Hong Kong Chinese in other locations. 
Digital Equipment, for instance, has 44 former employees from Hong Kong in its Toronto office.

text:
ï»¿
Not only a call for democracy, but also anger over inflation and corruption, seemed to impel the tens of thousands of workers who joined students today in demonstrating in Tiananmen Square in the center of the capital.
So far most of the workers seem bitter enough to be willing to join the students, but not so angry that they will stage demonstrations or strikes of their own.
In interviews today, many of the workers said that while they believed in the students' cause, they are reluctant to join formally in the march for fear of losing their jobs.
Many workers said their supervisors had warned them not even to watch the demonstration for risk of punishment. 
But the workers' dissatisfaction with pocketbook issues, and in some cases the lack of democracy and freedom of the press, carried them into the streets today to shout and shove alongside their junior comrades.
Â 
'The Economic Risk'
''Workers won't dare march by themselves because the economic risk is too great for the ordinary man,'' said a factory worker who was taking part in the demonstration. 
''If they fail to appear at their factory in the morning, they won't get their day's bread.''
Few seemed to care deeply that today's march also marked the 70th anniversary of the nationalist demonstrations that later influenced democratic and radical thought in China. 
Some complained that the real lesson of the demonstration was that the demands for democracy were still unrealized after seven decades of struggle.
Many called for freedom of the press, seeing news organizations as a way to supervise Government officials, whom they see as members of a new privileged class.
''It's a problem with the system, because those in power are not under any effective control,'' said Z. Z. Pi, a 34-year-old technician. 
''There is no mechanism, such as the media, to supervise them.''
''If this movement can push political reform forward, then I think it will be a success,'' Mr. Pi said. 
''Essentially, it is a matter of redistribution of the benefits of economic and political power.''
''Any reform won't be successful until the masses receive benefits,'' said Wan Zhicheng, a 25-year-old factory worker. 
''We say we oppose corruption, but ultimately, it is the entire system.''
''Before an earthquake, small animals know it and run for cover,'' he said. 
''They are the intellectuals,'' he said, referring to the thousands of Chinese who have gone abroad to study and perhaps live. 
''And a great earthquake isn't far away.''
''A corrupt country calls for help,'' Mr. Wan said. 
''Its end is near.''
Onlookers cheering from the window of a building in Beijing as demonstrators marched by yesterday (Reuters)

file: Workers_ Resistance Lags in Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
Zhang Quan slipped out of work several times earlier this month to join pro-democracy rallies, and he donated $27, two-thirds of his monthly salary, to the student demonstrators.
But like tens of thousands of other workers, he bowed out of Sunday's demonstration. 
He said he was too busy.
''The students and the citizens are tired,'' the 23-year-old cake seller said. 
''The movement has lasted for so long and we citizens have done our best to support the students. 
We have given them bread rolls, clothing and quilts. 
But as ordinary citizens, we are not rich. 
We are exhausted and we are disillusioned.''
The challenge for China's university students is to reawaken the enthusiasm of workers like Mr. Zhang. Such workers added a new dimension to the movement and vastly increased its scale, but now many seem to be settling back into silence.
Â 
Fear and Exhaustion
For a brief moment two weeks ago, workers and citizens, like Mr. Zhang, by the hundreds of thousands, seemed to come out of nowhere to support the hunger-striking students. 
But since martial law was declared nine days ago, the citizens seemed to be steadily disappearing from the streets.
The first few nights after martial law was imposed, citizens poured out in waves to block the troops from entering the city center. 
But during the week, many large work units have issued stern warnings against taking part in demonstrations, or even watching them, and some units have apparently promised bonuses for workers who stay inside and deductions for those who do not.
This seems to have frightened many workers, especially those with families to support. 
Mr. Zhang has no wife or children, but he still lives at home with his parents, who constantly urge him not to go out to the square.
Mr. Zhang says that the nature of his work often takes him out of the office, so that marching with the students was not that difficult. 
But as the papers and errands piled up he fell behind in his work.He spent Sunday settling his accounts and clearing up paper work.
Â 
'They Were Not Selfish'
Nonetheless, Mr. Zhang has not abandoned the movement. 
In fact he has been the most active of the workers in his unit.
''One reason I supported the students is that they were not selfish,'' Mr. Zhang said. 
''They don't stand to gain anything for themselves, like food, drink or jobs, from the movement. 
Why did they stage it?
For the citizens. 
And the movement has awakened our people.''
Mr. Zhang went to Tiananmen Square for several demonstrations, but after martial law was declared, he passed all his evenings except one at home.
Now, he says that the movement is at a lull, that thus far it has failed and dampened the spirit among the citizens and workers. 
But he says he expects the tide of protest to rise as June 20 approaches, the date when the standing committee of the National People's Congress, China's legislature, is scheduled to meet.
Â 
'Shall I Continue to Donate'
Still, like so many others, he is willing to take part only if the masses do, and so when a smaller crowd of students shows up for a demonstration, as happened on Sunday, he is hesitant about risking his job. 
And if there are going to be arrests, he said, the police will arrest citizens before students.
''I've already donated $27 of my April salary to the students,'' said Mr. Zhang, who says he only makes about $40 a month. 
''And now, I'm wondering, shall I continue to donate?
What's the point?''
Mr. Zhang insists that he has not switched sides, and opposes a crackdown by the Government. 
But as he listens to the rumors about the downfall of the Communist Party leader, Zhao Ziyang, and the apparent rise of Prime Minister Li Peng, he insists that the Government under Mr. Li cannot last for long since it does not have the support of the people.
Â 
Not Organized Enough
But at the same time, he acknowledges that the people are not organized enough to make a difference.
''The problem with Chinese is that we are not so united. 
About 30 percent would simply prefer to stand on the sidelines with their arms folded, and about 20 percent simply don't care. 
The remaining 50 percent want do something, but they still have a hard time uniting among each other.''
The fundamental problem, he said, is that Chinese are simply too tolerant.
''We Chinese can tolerate almost everything,' Mr. Zhang said. 
''As long as we have something to eat and to drink, we will not rebel unless there is nothing left for us to eat but leaves.''

file: World Markets_Out of China, a Boost for Hong Kong.txt
text:
ï»¿
ORDINARY Chinese must be wondering what could have happened in their country to have sent the Hong Kong stock market bouncing to new heights this week. 
For while their markets, in the cities of Shanghai and Shenzhen, were creeping downward, the Hong Kong market rose to a new record, mostly on the news from China.
The prime shaker in the Hong Kong exchange is not a central bank. 
It is a coterie of elderly men, most in their 80's, who rule China and who with a cough or a stumble can send the markets reeling. 
They essentially determine the pace of China's economic growth -- the direction is invariably up -- and therefore the action in Hong Kong.
Last week, the action was in the Hang Seng index, which surged to a peak of 6,329.12 on Thursday, dropped by 66.58 points on Friday to 6,262.54, but even so was up 277.21 points, or 4.6 percent, for the week.
Underlying the market's rise is a change in perceptions about Hong Kong's relations with China. 
For years, Hong Kong's proximity to China and its scheduled return to Chinese control in 1997 have provoked anxiety, dampening investor confidence and lowering price-earnings ratios in Hong Kong.
But these days, a growing number of investors see China as an opportunity, rather than a threat. 
They argue that Hong Kong companies are able to participate in one of the greatest economic booms anywhere, and that the boom will continue for many years.
"Hong Kong is always a proxy to China," said Wai-keung Wan, sales director at the Jardine Fleming brokerage house. 
"China is embarking on a long-term growth trend. 
In the 1990's, any country that can produce economic growth can reasonably command a premium. 
Therefore, people feel very positive about China."
Hong Kong's stock exchange, once a wayward cowboy market of which Americans were wary, has been rising on and off since the beginning of this year. 
A buying frenzy in Hong Kong seized investors last week because they thought China had cleared a number of political and economic uncertainties.
Investors were reassured by the new leadership team that the Communist Party announced a week ago, feeling that the seven members of the new Politburo Standing Committee are reform-oriented. 
In fact, the appointments were largely expected, but the market seized upon the news to leap ahead.
In the process, the market ignored some bad news: China's Communist leaders criticized and snubbed Hong Kong's new Governor, Christopher Patten, signalling that relations may become tougher between Hong Kong and China. 
Mr. Patten had come to China to discuss his proposals for broadening democracy in Hong Kong and for financing a $16 billion airport. 
"On the face of it, it was quite negative," said James K. Osborn, assistant director at Baring Securities (Hong Kong) Ltd. 
"But on sheer fact, it was not a worse surprise than what was expected."
On Friday, however, after Mr. Patten departed for Hong Kong, China said it would retaliate if Mr. Patten's proposals for democracy and the airport were implemented without Beijing's consent. 
China's comments are certain to influence the direction of the market next week. 
Disappointment with the trip -- coupled with profit-taking -- accounted for the market's fall on Friday.
The underlying reason for the Hong Kong market's euphoria recently has been the 14th Communist Party Congress, which culminated Monday with the announcement of the new leadership team. 
The congress declared that China would develop a "socialist market economy" with the emphasis on "market."
Moreover, China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, who is 88 years old and holds no posts, appeared on public television on Monday. 
Investors took that as good news -- dispelling fears that he was virtually on his death bed -- instead of focusing on the fact that his health seemed much worse than the last time he appeared on TV, in February.
Mr. Deng exerts the greatest influence in the country, and now he is determined to lock China onto a course of building a market economy. 
The congress hailed him and his commitment to economic reform.
The previous week also brought news that lifted the market. 
Chinese and American trade negotiators broke a stalemate in discussions over American exporters' access to the Chinese market. 
The result was that China agreed to import more American goods, thereby avoiding punitive duties on as much as $3.9 billion worth of Chinese exports to the United States.
Money has been pouring in these last couple of weeks from the United States, as well as from Asia, analysts said. 
Although trading is conducted in Hong Kong dollars, the currency is pegged at a rate of about 7.8 Hong Kong dollars to the United States dollar. 
"One beauty of the Hong Kong stock market is that it is really a U.S. dollar market because of the peg," said Allan Ng, a senior analyst at S. G. Warburg Securities (Far East) Ltd. 
"No matter what happens, there's not currency risk."
Many of Hong Kong's large companies have shed the undeserved fly-by-night reputation they had a decade ago. 
The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation recently acquired the British bank Midland Bank P.L.C. 
Among the major China plays in the market are Hopewell Holdings Ltd., a construction firm building a highway in China.
Not surprisingly, most of the buying focused on blue chip companies, such as the Hong Kong Bank, and on Cheung Kong, Hong Kong's largest conglomerate, run by its richest man, Li Ka-shing.

file: Writers in China Are Asked to Write, But Not Subversively.txt
text:
ï»¿
Literature is like groceries, says Ma Feng, the earthy ''old revolutionary'' who is China's new literary czar: in both cases the government should encourage what is nutritious and ban what is poisonous.
These days it is largely up to Mr. Ma, a lean man of 68 who joined the Communist rebellion in 1938 at the age of 16, to enforce that regulatory vision. 
It is a formidable task because many authors loathe the regime and develop a writer's block when they are asked to ''serve socialism.''
This leaves Mr. Ma in an awkward position as the effective head of the Chinese Writers Association. 
He comes from a different world - the countryside of north-central China - and he made his name writing short stories and film scripts about peasants who brim with decency and enthusiasm for the Communist Party. 
Nothing could be further from the urban frustration and alienation that inspire many Chinese writers today.
''I don't like Beijing - too many people,'' he chuckled the other day while puffing on his beloved Zhongnanhai cigarettes in an interview. 
Mr. Ma was living in his native Shanxi Province, 260 miles southwest of Beijing, when the crackdown on democratic impulses came last year and led to his summons to Beijing.
Early this year, Mr. Ma was formally named vice chairman and party secretary of the Chinese Writers Association, meaning that he would take charge of it. 
The nominal chairman, the writer Ba Jin, lives in Shanghai and is 86 years old and infirm. 
He had few responsibilities even before he lost his influence by supporting the student demonstrators seeking democracy.
Â 
Not Just a Club
There is no parallel to the Chinese Writers Association in the West, for it is far more than simply an authors' club. 
In China, the association is the work unit of the country's 3,500 authors: it is the employer, the source of housing and salaries, the organizer of political study sessions and the arbiter of who can travel abroad. 
Chinese publishers pay royalties, but these are less important than the association's salaries, and in any case it is difficult to be published without the association's blessing.
Mr. Ma sounds a conciliatory line, asserting that Chinese writers can write about whatever they choose, but they must not criticize their country or subvert Communism. 
His catechism is taken from the works of Mao Zedong, who argued that art is inseparable from politics and must serve the proletarian revolutionary cause.
''Writers should serve socialism and they should serve the people,'' Mr. Ma said, adding that authors should leave the ivory tower to understand the land they write about.
''If you write about society, you must study it,'' he said. 
''If you write about a factory, you should work in a factory. 
If you write about the countryside, you should spend time in a village, rather than sitting around the house writing blindly.''
Â 
Justifying Curbs
In the last few years, a group of young writers very different from the ''old revolutionaries'' has won prominence and acclaim for their attempts to probe the spirit of post-Mao China, but Mr. Ma asserts that they had only a small following. 
Asked about Bei Dao, a highly respected poet who was one of this circle of younger authors, Mr. Ma said he found such writers unimpressive.
''They had an impact on some younger arts circles, but if you go to a factory in Shanxi Province, no one will have heard of them,'' Mr. Ma said, adding that ordinary people do not want to read such books.
''They were just a small group of people,'' Mr. Ma said. 
''Many good writers are needed by the people, but in the late 1980's only their writings could be published. 
Now we want to publish books needed by ordinary people in factories and farms.''
Â 
Talk of Revenge
Many others see it differently and believe that the ''old revolutionaries'' behind the cultural purges - leaders like Vice President Wang Zhen and Acting Culture Minister He Jingzhi as well as Mr. Ma himself - now are relishing the opportunity to strike back at those who in recent years looked with contempt at their orthodox Marxist view of culture.
''It's revenge and it's petty,'' said Geremie Barme, an Australian scholar who recently visited China.
One Western diplomat said he thought the general attitude toward someone like Ma Feng was one of contempt. 
He said that Mr. Ma had stuck to his ideological line for many years and suddenly been vindicated, and that he was an opportunist turning that to his own advantage.
Some other diplomats and Chinese are not so harsh, portraying Mr. Ma as a decent man placed in an impossible position. 
They say he is among the better revolutionary writers but that he has never been an intellectual, in the sense of possessing a doubting or inquiring mind, and that he is out of touch with the main current of writers today.
Â 
A Conciliatory Sound
Mr. Ma, well aware of the antagonisms in the field, takes pains to sound a conciliatory line. 
He even explained the ousting of Liu Binyan, a dissident who was vice chairman of the association, not on the basis of Mr. Liu's heretical views but on the ground that Mr. Liu is in the United States and does not seem likely to return soon.
''In our association, some people took part in the turmoil,'' Mr. Ma said. 
''They won't be punished; they will be educated. 
I'm sure they will change their minds.''
''We've received many manuscripts for publication, criticizing various writers,'' Mr. Ma added. 
''But we don't want to publish them and crush the writers. 
We want to join forces with them and help them write more things that people want to read. 
If we criticize them, who will write for us?
What will be left of the Writers Association?''
Â 
The Purge Proceeds
Still, the authorities are going ahead with their purge in cultural circles. 
The top executives of several publishing houses and journals, including the most prominent, People's Literature, have been replaced. 
Some writers reportedly may not be published, although Mr. Ma denies the existence of any blacklist, and others have had trouble going abroad. 
And there has been a yearlong process of investigations, self-criticisms and political study sessions to return writers to the straight, narrow and sometimes winding path of Marxist orthodoxy.
So far this crackdown has had mixed results. 
In general, there is less experimentation and less writing about the problems of urban, alienated young people and about political discontent. 
But some works, like Harvest, a Shanghai literary journal, are still remarkably bold, and recent books are probably more lively and interesting than the leaders might have in mind.
''The new policies have had the effect of making people miserable and angry, and it's harder to get things done,'' said a Western diplomat. 
''But at the end of the day similar things end up being written and published.''
Â 
A Broader Effort
The selection of Mr. Ma to head the writers' association appears to be part of a broad effort to evoke the glories of the Communist Party in its heyday in China in the 1950's and early 1960's. 
To read People's Daily, watch television or listen to official speeches is to find a resurrection of the themes that emerged in Maoist days. 
Lei Feng, a model Communist and heroic soldier, is again an object of official adoration; songs like ''Good Socialism'' have been re-released, and industrial heroes like ''Iron Man Wang'' have been dusted off and hailed in the newspapers.
Mr. Ma fits neatly into this backdrop. 
After joining the Communist revolution at the age of 16, he won fame in 1944 with a novel about Communist troops, ''Heroes of Luliang Mountains.''
While his father was a scholar who won success in the old imperial examinations, Mr. Ma's characters are largely simple, decent peasants who evoke tu - the earth and an agrarian charm that goes with it. 
One of his books, a collection of short stories, has been translated into English.
These days, however, Mr. Ma says he is too busy to write any new stories.

file: Wuhan Journal_At 102, He_s Back in School, With Many Like Him.txt
text:
ï»¿
Qian Likun is a model university student, the kind of diligent scholar-athlete who joins in foot races, excels in his studies and is never distracted by a woman's short skirt.
Mr. Qian is also five times older than most university students. 
He is 102 years old, and while ordinary students study the Boxer Rebellion of 1900 and the fall of the Ching Dynasty in 1911, Mr. Qian has no such problem: he remembers them.
The University for the Aged, where Mr. Qian studies, has 8,000 students here in Wuhan, a major city on the Yangtze River of central China. 
Founded five years ago, it is part of a network of more than 800 such institutions for the elderly in China, all founded in the last eight years.
China has traditionally revered the aged, and this nation's programs for the elderly are very impressive for a developing country. 
Some Chinese villages have a special "house for the aged," where senior citizens can live if they have no children to depend on, and most cities have a range of physical fitness, entertainment and educational programs for retired citizens.
Â 
Questions for the U.S.
One question that Chinese often ask Americans is why families sometimes put their parents in institutions, why such a rich country cannot do more for its elderly. 
The questions include a hint of reproach, but mostly wonder at the breach of filial piety.
"We want to help the elderly help themselves, so that they can reduce their dependence on their families and on society," said Lu Jianye, the vice president of the Wuhan University for the Aged. 
"We also want to help them increase their contribution to society, and to develop hobbies such as art, calligraphy or even massage, so that they can enjoy their later years."
The university here, which charges tuition of less than $5 a term, offers courses in 123 subjects. 
These include painting, disco dancing, calligraphy, bridge, cooking, English, literature and health care for the elderly.
Â 
Canes Beside the Chairs
Most people in Wuhan are literate, but the university also arranges classes in some neighborhoods to teach reading and writing to the elderly, mostly women who never went to school.
China, with a population of 1.1 billion, has some 115 million people over the retirement age, which is normally 60 for men and 55 for women. 
The proportion of the aged will rise sharply in coming decades as baby boom generations grow older and family planning policies reduce the number of young people.
On a recent visit, the classrooms of the Wuhan University for the Aged were full of animated students, some with canes beside their chairs, enthusiastically commenting on each other's paintings, reciting standard phrases of English and dissecting ancient poetry.
"We don't want to get senile," said Yan Bin, a 56-year-old woman who retired recently as a professional singer. 
She was sitting around a table with three partners, working on her skills at bridge, the card game favored by Deng Xiaoping and countless other elderly Chinese.
"I never studied bridge before," said Mu Youqing, a silver-haired woman of 64 years who is a retired doctor. 
"But it's very highbrow and cultured, and it has a long history in China."
Â 
A Boost for the Brains
The baby of the foursome, 56-year-old Shao Kanfu, a lean, tall man who retired early, added, "I wanted to look after my health and give my brains a boost."
Most elderly people in China live with their children, and often they are responsible for caring for their grandchildren. 
So the University for the Aged holds classes in the midmorning and again in the early afternoon, when the students' children are at work and their grandchildren are at school.
In addition, because some of the old people cannot get around easily, the university has set up 13 branches around the city in residential areas. 
The university depends for money on tuition fees and also on generous grants from the city government. 
The faculty consists mostly of professors at nearby universities who are delighted to moonlight for a small fee.
"The teaching level isn't as high as at a regular university, and we don't go into as much depth as we would with younger students," said Zhou Wu, a junior high school instructor who teaches Chinese literature on the side at a branch campus of the University for the Aged. 
"But some of the older folks bring a good deal of enthusiasm as well as diverse experience to the classroom, so it's often more interesting to teach them than to teach my regular students."
Â 
Along for the 'Fun Run'
One of Mr. Zhou's most diligent students is Mr. Qian, the 102-year-old. 
A retired agricultural researcher, Mr. Qian diligently prepares for each class session and offers some pointed views.
"This poem isn't very good by Tang Dynasty standards," he said the other day as Mr. Zhou dissected a poem on the blackboard. 
"But it's better than anything we have today."
Mr. Qian manages to walk to the class on his own, and he hears and sees well enough to follow the teacher most of the time. 
The first class he took was on health care for the elderly, and he says he found it very useful in looking after his wife, who died a few months ago at the age of 100, and his daughter, who is 81 years old and in fading health.
When the university held a "fun run" this spring, some 300 old people ran about 2.3 miles to complete the race. 
Mr. Qian was ong them, but the university staff acknowledges that his pace was more of a hobble than a jog.
A lover of traditional poetry, Mr. Qian scarcely paused when asked for a few lines of his favorite poem. 
The room fell silent as he recited from memory this ancient Chinese poem:
The clouds are wispy this morning, the breeze is light.
As I pass the pond, I see flowers and willow trees.
The passers-by don't know the joy in my heart.
I'm like a kid at play.

file: Xiamen Journal_Chinese Isle Bewitched (and Bothered) by Taiwan.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a tiny electronics shop in this coastal Chinese town, on the poor side of the thin stretch of water called the Taiwan Strait, the proprietor is exploiting the longing to be like the Wangs and the Chens across the waterway.
His lure is a video of a young woman singing into a microphone, her gown rippling as she dances, and it seems to work. 
A crowd gathers inside the shop, eyes fixed on the singer, whose style and dress shows that she is from Taiwan.
As with many stores in this special economic zone, a Taiwan signature helps draw business, just as it has helped transform this once-backward tiny island of Amoy, as it used to be called, into a bustling metropolis.
But in a back room of the electronics shop, away from the music and the Taiwan glitter, a handful of Chinese explained their feelings about their Taiwan compatriots, revealing sentiments that were not entirely loving.
Â 
'Dregs of Society'
"They may be rich, but they aren't very polite," said a customs official who was helping the shop owner. 
"Lots of the Taiwanese who come here are the dregs of society. 
They bring over the worst of their world, and when we see them smuggling or going out with hookers, naturally we're turned off."
Xiamen is absorbed by the love-hate relationship that many Chinese feel toward their Taiwan brethren. 
Mainland Chinese and Taiwan Chinese may share the same forebears, but with more and more Taiwan residents visiting the mainland, the clash of ideologies, styles and levels of wealth has created headaches for Chinese leaders.
"It is true that the local people resent us a bit," said a Taiwan businessman who has been in Xiamen for several years. 
"The smugglers and boatmen came over here before the businessmen, and they were very crude people. 
This left a deep impression on the locals."
Tsay Mingshan of Taiwan, who is senior manager at a wholly owned Taiwan enterprise called Eupa, said: "Many Taiwanese thought that this was a 'yellow earth,' a new playground that you could dig into as you pleased. 
They didn't realize that if they came over here, people would watch their behavior and form opinions."
Trade between China and Taiwan for the first 11 months of last year reached $5.15 billion, up 41 percent over the same period in 1990, according to Taiwan statistics. 
Taiwanese investment in the mainland was $840 million for the first nine months of last year, nearly as much as for all of 1990, Chinese statistics show.
The relationship, which is much closer than it has been for most of the four decades since Chiang Kai-shek and his army fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the civil war to the Communists, seems bound to get better. 
China is thirsty for Taiwanese capital, just as Taiwan is eager to use the mainland's cheap labor and raw materials. 
China is also trying to forge closer ties as a means to bring Taiwan back under its territorial domain.
The Communist Party General Secretary, Jiang Zemin, visited Xiamen in December to commemorate the 10th anniversary of the special economic zone. 
Many businessmen say this was partly to impress the Taiwanese. 
But his visit also seems to have unleashed a spirit of expansion in Xiamen, which has lagged somewhat behind China's four other special economic zones.
"If Deng Xiaoping called for faster development, now that would be even better," said Zhang Zongxu, the Deputy Mayor of Xiamen, referring to the Chinese leader. 
Mr. Zhang, a former Chinese Consul General in Houston, said that Taiwanese investment had certainly helped Xiamen develop, but added that the audacity of some Taiwanese behavior rubbed him the wrong way.
"They play around with women, or one week they go around with one secretary and the next week it's another one," he said. 
"Or they go eating and drinking at the nightclubs. 
Afterward, they walk over to the singer and stuff a big tip into her bra."
Local residents have been overwhelmed in the last three years by the flood of rich Taiwan visitors. 
Some of the businessmen have come flashing their thick wallets and expensive tastes. 
These are the very "bourgeois" influences that China accuses Westerners of spreading and that, in fact, the Taiwan Chinese are probably even better at disseminating because of the common language.
Â 
Taiwan's Influence Is Strong
Moreover, to the Government's dismay, the island is an enclave for prostitution and smuggling. 
Scores of boats go back and forth across the strait, often carrying contraband like cigarettes, videotapes, books and other goods from Taiwan. 
Last year, security officials caught more than 200 people involved in prostitution rings, Mr. Zhang said.
Xiamen's economic development is still at least two decades behind that of Taipei. 
But Taiwanese investment is the fastest growing source of foreign capital, and when the Taiwan Government approves direct air and shipping links, perhaps in the next couple of years, Xiamen could become, in many ways, a virtual colony of Taiwan.
Meanwhile, Taiwan music, videos, books and fashions have almost become a way of life here. 
Multisystem televisions, which enable viewers to receive Taiwan stations, are among the hottest purchases.
Residents here speak the same Chinese dialect as about 80 percent of the people in Taiwan, and half a million Taiwan tourists have visited the island in the last four years. 
"Xiamen is turning into a Little Taipei," said a Chinese involved in trade with Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao.
Until the middle of last year, the Chinese military still broadcast Communist propaganda from the tip of Xiamen through a dozen huge loudspeakers aimed at nearby Taiwan-controlled islands.
Taiwan doubled the decibels, broadcasting its Nationalist propaganda from at least two dozen loudspeakers on the nearby island of Quemoy. 
Today, the Taiwanese speakers are still there, but the Taiwan Government seems to have discovered a more effective means of propaganda: they often play Taiwan pop songs.

file: Year Later, Chinese Father Grieves and Fears.txt
text:
ï»¿
A year after soldiers shot dead his only son, the father's own odyssey through faith, heartbreak, bitterness and disillusionment with the Chinese Communist Party still leaves him confused and fearful.
The atmosphere in his shabby, simply furnished three-room apartment changes from bickering and laughter, when the 14 family members and relatives gather together, to a ghostly quiet, as memories turn to the son of this house and that time during the June 4 military crackdown when his life ended at 21 years as he rode a bicycle to his part-time job in a garage.
While most of the dead were killed while protesting against the attacking troops, this young man was shot in the back while bicycling to work on a side street four miles from Tiananmen Square. 
People who saw the shooting told his family that a small group of soldiers was on the street and apparently shot him at random. 
Neither he nor his family was active in the democracy movement, and family members agreed to be interviewed on condition that they not be identified, for fear of reprisals from the authorities.
Long Silences at Dinnertime
The father, a Communist Party member, is 61 now - his newly graying hair betrays the real aging that has taken place over the last 12 months - and the immediate despair over his son has faded into long silences at dinnertime. 
He tries to fend off the memories by channeling his energies into raising the 18 pigeons he keeps in a large cage outside his living-room window.
Since the day his son was cremated and the appropriate certificates turned over to the authorities as proof of his son's innocence when he was killed, no one from the Government has sent a letter of acknowledgment or sympathy or even come to ask about him, either to brand him a counterrevolutionary rebel or a martyr.
''The Government never said we were counterrevolutionaries or not,'' one of the son's relatives said. 
''They never said we were good or bad. 
They never asked us.''
Throughout Beijing and the rest of the country, hundreds of families are remembering their loved ones who were killed on June 4 last year, when troops opened fire on crowds of demonstrators in the center of Beijing.
Last year, the Government said it would compensate the families of victims innocently killed in the crackdown. 
It also prepared a list of the victims for possible release, but then said it would not release the list because of objections from the families.
Â 
No Compensation Evident
Each time such announcements were made, the father waited for a visit, but so far, he has received neither compensation nor consultation on the release of his son's name. 
The Government did not disclose how much the compensation would be, and apparently has not paid it to any of the victims' families.
It is this silence from the authorities that stirs anger in the father, the mother and four sisters. 
Some families have received visits by the authorities, especially if the victims were students who took part in the movement. 
This family does not even know if the son has become a statistic.
''This child was too young,'' the father said. 
''He wasn't even old enough to make his contribution to the nation. 
He had just started working. 
Such a small life, terminated, just like that. 
Such a loss.''
For the father, the death of the son was especially distressful. 
The son had pleaded with the father not to venture out, but the father adamantly insisted on going to work that early morning on June 4. 
The son followed the example, setting out to work on his own.
Â 
Fury Replaced by Fear
Yet, for the father, the fury has subsided slowly, and in its place is more fear than cynicism or courage borne out of pain. 
He has not complained to his ''work unit,'' where he is partly retired, and he has not tried to contact the authorities. 
He rarely speaks against the Government, only sometimes around family members.
His distance from the party has grown considerably, since the early days when his hope for China lay in the party, and he did not take part in any political study sessions during the year. 
The party is carrying out its nationwide re-registration for its members, and those whom it deems unsuitable may be expelled. 
The father says he will not officially resign from the party, nor will he officially re-register.
Like many Chinese whose anger over the crackdown has blended into their daily lives, the family is waiting for the Government to change, but in the meantime, their disaffection is turning into indifference.
''They are too busy to come see us,'' the father said, his voice soft and calm. 
''For a common man like me there is only patience and hope.''
Later, he added, ''The time of hope has already passed.''
The mother has taken to fits of craziness, talking in a rambling manner, family members say, and they have removed all of the son's belongings from the house because of the memories they inspire. 
She retired late last year, and then sought a part-time job after two weeks at home. 
She was spending her time at home thinking about her son.
Â 
His Ashes Are Visited
In honor of the son, the family has followed a Chinese tradition of burning fake paper money many times in the last year, and it has refrained from setting off firecrackers, because they symbolize happiness. 
Now, his ashes are kept at a state funeral parlor, and the family often goes to pay its respects.
''We go there to burn paper money and to burn the things he used to like to eat, like shrimps, apples, oranges and fish,'' said the mother, a thin woman, whose coarse, wrinkled skin makes her look older than her 51 years.
When a classmate of the son stopped in to pay his respects and to ask about visiting the funeral parlor, the parents jumped up to tend to him. 
The father returned to the living room, his face showing a mixture of pain and appreciation.
''My spirit is better these days,'' he said. 
''But I dread the visits of his classmates.''

text:
ï»¿
Saying he needed to "restore order" and protect the reformist core of Russia's Government, President Boris N. Yeltsin cut short his visit to China this morning and headed back to Moscow.
His new Prime Minister, Viktor S. Chernomyrdin, whom Mr. Yeltsin chose this week after parliamentary pressure forced him to abandon acting Prime Minister Yegor T. Gaidar, was on his own visit to Kazakhstan, and Moscow itself seemed quiet early this morning.
But Mr. Yeltsin, who has a flair for the dramatic gesture, announced that he had been informed overnight of a concerted effort to replace the reformist core of Mr. Gaidar's team of young, Westernized economists, some of whom accompanied Mr. Yeltsin to China.
"They have begun too early to fight for portfolios, to pull apart the Cabinet, and so the master must return and restore order there," Mr. Yeltsin said at Beijing airport.
Â 
Core Must Remain
"Gaidar brought his own team with him, his young inner core," Mr. Yeltsin said. 
"The new prime minister wants to bring in his own team but the core of Gaidar's reformers must not under any circumstances be pulled apart."
Some Cabinet posts can be changed, he said, but most of Mr. Gaidar's team must remain.
Out of 30 people or so in the Cabinet, Mr. Yeltsin said, "three, four or five can be replaced."
But "the rest of the main figures" must remain, he said.
Earlier, China's official Xinhua News Agency mentioned Mr. Yeltsin's early departure, citing only his "busy schedule at home."
He was scheduled to leave later today in any event. 
The statement added that Yeltsin's visit to China "has been very smooth and successful."
There have been reports in Moscow that Arkady Volsky, the lobbyist leader of the main opposition grouping, Civic Union, had said on a visit to Tokyo that he was pushing Mr. Chernomyrdin to replace Mr. Gaidar's team with more conservative economists closer to industry. 
But Mr. Volsky said on Friday that he had been misquoted.
But there was a sense on Friday that Mr. Chernomyrdin was trying to make a fast start. 
He began making good on his promises to help industry in just the manner Western economists feared, proposing to a compliant Russian Pprliament an additional 200 billion rubles (about $480 million) in immediate credits to the energy sector he used to run.
Before flying to Kazakhstan for talks to promote better cooperation with Russia, especially in oil and gas, Mr. Chernomyrdin added an amendment to the 1992 budget law calling for the new credits this year. 
The Supreme Soviet, which had approved the budget law in principle earlier this week, passed it Friday with the new funding, pushing the budget deficit to 1.17 trillion rubles ($2.8 billion) for the year.
Finance Minister Vasily Barchuk had argued that the higher deficit would increase inflation and could damage Russia's ability to pay for needed imports.
Mr. Gaidar has encouraged his "team" of young, Westernized, like-minded economists to remain in the Cabinet if they could pursue and protect economic reform, and Anatoly B. Chubais, the deputy prime minister in charge of the crucial privatization policy, has already agreed to stay on. 
He extended the period in which Russians may pick up their free privatization voucher, with a face value of 10,000 rubles, another month, until the end of January.
Â 
Gaidar Team Open to Staying
In Beijing, where he was accompanying Mr. Yeltsin, another deputy prime minister, Aleksandr Shokhin, told Interfax that the Gaidar team would not "slam the door" if Mr. Chernomyrdin wanted them to stay on. 
But they wanted assurances about "the core of the Government and its policies."
Mr. Shokhin said he was encouraged that Mr. Chernomyrdin did not campaign to be Prime Minister and got the job "unexpectedly."
While Mr. Chernomyrdin "is a very experienced economist who worked in a key branch of the economy," Mr. Shokhin said "it is one thing to be a director and quite another to be a Prime Minister."
On Friday the Russian President announced that Moscow and Beijing had agreed in principle to cooperate on military and technological projects as part of an array of accords intended to deepen the relationship between the two countries.
The agreements, though overshadowed by Mr. Yeltsin's assertion that he would meet with President Bush next month to sign a new strategic arms reduction treaty, appear to broaden Russia's contacts with China, a former adversary, and sweep aside ideological differences in the relationship.
On the second day of what was to have been a three-day trip to China, Mr. Yeltsin and his entourage signed 24 agreements covering cultural, trade and scientific exchanges, food credits, the construction of a nuclear power plant and the reduction of troops along the Russian-Chinese border.
"An important step has been made in the development of bilateral relations and a new page has been opened in our friendly relations," Mr. Yeltsin told reporters tonight at a press conference. 
"Let's talk less and do more."
The two sides cemented their budding new relationship with the signing of a joint declaration of friendship, renouncing the use of a nuclear first strike against the other country and pledging not to enter into treaties "prejudicing the sovereignty and security interests of the other party."
Mr. Yeltsin said that at the last-minute insistence of the Chinese Prime Minister, Li Peng, the two sides signed a memorandum of understanding that laid down the general principles for closer cooperation on military and technological projects.
Mr. Yeltsin would not say what kinds of projects would be covered under the arrangement, but he said a "real agreement" would be worked out within a month by the two countries' defense ministers.
China would not comment on the agreement on military cooperation. 
It did, however, make public the text of the joint declaration, which says that China and Russia will set up exchange programs that will help build "cooperation in the military field."
A Russian Deputy Prime Minister, Aleksandr N. Shokhin, said that Moscow would extend a long-term $2.5 billion credit to finance the building of a nuclear power station that would conform to international standards. 
He added that restrictions on the secondary transfer of the technology would be very strict. 
The loan for the power plant, which is to be built in the northeastern province of Liaoning, would be spread over 10 to 12 years.
Mr. Yeltsin said that China had agreed to extend a credit worth about $52 million, mainly to allow Russia to buy food and feedstock. 
He added that China planned to sell 10 million tons of grain to Russia at world prices.
