In the free markets of the new China, young men are coming to realize that there is something even more precious than a new car, an electronic pager or a Swiss-made watch.
And that rare commodity -- an unmarried woman -- is becoming harder and harder to find.
There are not nearly enough of them, a situation that is creating anguish for millions of Chinese men and has at least the potential of revolutionizing the status of women in this traditionally sexist society.
"What sort of woman do I want?" said Xu Wenyuan, a lonely 30-year-old who agreed to dress up in a sky-blue satin suit and to warble a few bars of "Song for the Motherland" on a television matchmaking show in Beijing. 
"It doesn't matter."
If he had hoped to prove his desperation in the search for a wife, Mr. Xu succeeded in those two minutes in front of the cameras. 
"Women are so hard to find now," he explained. 
"And I just want one."
For Mr. Xu and other Chinese men in search of love, the offerings of the Chinese State Statistical Bureau are downright heartbreaking. 
The 1990 census showed that of a total population of 1.2 billion, about 205 million Chinese over the age of 15 are single. 
And of those, there are nearly three men for every two women.
A 3-to-2 ratio might seem bad enough to most men. 
But the numbers suggest that the situation becomes far, far bleaker for a Chinese man the longer he stays unmarried.
The Government's figures show that while the vast majority of Chinese adults marry by the time they turn 30, eight million people in their 30's were still single in 1990. 
And in that age group, the men outnumbered the women by nearly 10 to 1.
There is an ugly explanation for the relative scarcity of unmarried women: the desire among many Chinese couples for boys at almost any cost.
The preference for boys has meant that millions of Chinese girls have not survived to adulthood because of poor nutrition, inadequate medical care, desertion and even murder at the hands of their parents.
China's strict rule of one child per family, imposed in the late 1970's and meant to defuse a population time bomb, has only worsened the insistence on having male heirs. 
Ultrasound machines and ready access to abortion have made it relatively simple for parents to guarantee that their one child is a boy.
Â 
Nature's Revenge
But after generations of tampering with nature, nature has begun to exact its revenge. 
The numbers suggest that tens of millions of men alive at the turn of the century will be lifelong bachelors because there will not be enough women available as wives.
"Of the young people who come into this office, at least 70 percent are men," said Li Xiaotong, a Beijing social worker whose Government-sponsored computer dating service is swamped by eager men searching for a mate.
"The girls are very happy with this service," Ms. Li said, "because they can set their standards very high for a prospective husband -- intelligence, education, money -- and then have a good chance of finding a man who meets their standards."
Her grin suggested that there was some justice in all of this.
"The men always ask for beautiful girls," she said, "and I tell them that they must be realistic. 
The goals they set must not be too high, because there are not enough women."
Apart from having their pick of prospective husbands, Chinese women may find another silver lining in the numbers churned out by the Government's demographers.
In a China newly receptive to capitalism, people are being reminded that in the free market, scarcity equals value. 
And so it could be for Chinese women after centuries in which the supply of potential brides equaled demand, and they could be -- and were -- treated as chattel.
"I do think that to some extent this shortage of women will play a positive role in improving the status of all women," said Guo Daofu, a senior economist for the State Statistical Bureau. 
"I think this will lead to changes in society. 
Men will have to become more open-minded."
He said a new open-mindedness could be of particular benefit to older unmarried women, who have traditionally had almost no hope of finding a husband. 
Custom here holds that a man should marry a woman at least several years younger, and that the bride should have less education. 
A result is that even after the age of 30, women, especially educated ones, have few prospects.
"There is a saying in the countryside that a man who marries a woman who is three years older has found a bar of gold -- that he can benefit from her maturity," Mr. Guo said. 
"Now, I think many more men will act" on this proverb.
There are several theories about how a badly lopsided sex ratio would affect -- and probably improve -- the status of Chinese women. 
A Western diplomat who has studied the situation said the Government might be forced to offer incentives, like educational benefits and tax breaks, to encourage couples to have girls.
"If this Government made it not only acceptable but in some cases preferable to have girls, you'd see a huge change in the way women are treated throughout society," he said.
While China's leaders tend to welcome anything that will limit population growth in the world's most populous country, there is alarm about the consequences of so many single men in a society that values the family above all else.
Chinese sociologists and journalists have suggested that with men unable to find wives as sexual partners, there could be an increase in prostitution, rape and -- among men -- suicide.
"This discrepancy between the sexes is a matter of serious discussion among our Government leaders," said Wang Wei, a professor of ethics at the People's University in Beijing. 
He pointed to a series of kidnappings in which city women have been abducted by bounty hunters who deliver them to rural farmers desperate for brides. 
"You could see more of that," he said.
Although the problem is more serious here if only because of its vast population, China is not the only country facing a crush of single men.
Figures compiled by the United Nations show that the world's second most populous nation, India, with nearly 900 million people, has nearly 133 single men for every 100 single women. 
As in China, Indian custom demands that couples produce male heirs.
In the industrialized world, the ratios are much smaller, and in some countries single women outnumber single men. 
According to the 1990 census in the United States, there were more unmarried American women than unmarried men, about 54 percent of unmarried adults to 46 percent. 
A similar ratio was found in Japan in a 1985 survey.
Perhaps no one knows more about the scarcity of unmarried women than China's best-known matchmaker: Yang Guang, the host of "We Meet Tonight," the popular matchmaking television show.
Â 
Bachelors Get Bold
For 20 minutes every Friday night, Ms. Yang invites a group of single men and women to make a televised pitch for a mate in a cross between "Dating Game" and a talent show.
"We receive very few applications from young women who are willing to appear as contestants," said Ms. Yang, whose show takes credit for 274 marriages since it went on the air four years ago. 
"The men are much more bold about agreeing to appear. 
And they are bold because they have to be."
During the show, viewers are invited to write in for a date, and the plight of China's single men becomes all the clearer when the mailbags begin to arrive in the studio the next day.
"Maybe a man who appears on the show will get 30 letters," Ms. Yang said. 
"But a woman will get over 50, sometimes 60. 
Sometimes many more. 
Our record-holder is a 24-year-old woman who got more than 500 letters."
Many Chinese men are being driven to look at what are, certainly by Chinese standards, unconventional ways of finding a bride.
The first computer dating service, the Great Wall Information Company, opened in Beijing in 1989, and others have followed. 
Some provincial and city governments have stepped in with their own matchmaking services. 
But whether high-tech or traditional, the marriage brokers all suffer from the same problem: a dearth of available women.
Â 
Lonely Hearts on Street
The quandary of the lonely Chinese male is evident in the hangdog looks of the young men who gather on Saturday afternoons to watch the passing crowds along Wangfujing Street, the heart of Beijing's central shopping district.
Rows of these lonely hearts lean against the storefronts, hoping that some young woman will return their stares. 
It rarely happens, they say with a moan.
"Sometimes the girls are very stuck up, very choosy about whether they will consider a boy for a husband," said Wang Jian, an engineering student who, at 22, worries that he may never find a mate.
His friend Meng Yuchang, 23, was even more inconsolable. 
"Without enough women, maybe we will all become monks," he said, kicking the toe of his sneaker against the sidewalk. 
"This whole generation of Chinese men will become monks. 
And maybe then the women will feel sorry for us."

file: A Designer_s Careful Leap to Success.txt
text:
ï»¿
As the old fable tells us, sometimes slow and steady wins the race.
While some designers make a big splash with their first collections and then fade away when they can't follow through, others start quietly and work their way up to a breakthrough collection. 
By the time success comes, these slow starters have proved that they have more than one idea and don't have to play the same note over and over again.
It took Han Feng eight years to achieve her breakthrough. 
It happened at her fall show last month when she made the leap from being a maker of pleated scarfs and dresses to becoming a designer of coats, tailored suits, evening dresses and furs.
"I wanted to show I could do fitted clothes as well as pleats," she said last week in the showroom she maintains in her apartment on the Upper West Side.
Her business office is in the garment center, but 30-odd blocks uptown, retailers can see and touch the clothes in a round room with light streaming in from three big windows. 
It's a peaceful oasis where the designer serves freshly brewed mint tea while her birds chirp in the background.
Han Feng studied graphic design, not fashion design, in China, where she was born and lived until 10 years ago.
"I was born during the Cultural Revolution, and we had no fashion," the 32-year-old designer said. 
"But I wanted to be a designer. 
I got a T-shirt and jeans and grew my hair long so I would stand out."
To stand out in New York, she now wears her hair in a crew cut.
"I don't have formal training in designing and I don't know what traditional styles are, so I design what I like," she said. 
"I like a small silhouette, very simple, with covered-up legs and breasts and unexpected slits on the sides or in back. 
I like to play with shape. 
I don't sketch. 
I play on the mannequin, drawing on the body to show the pattern maker what I want."
All her clothes are made in New York. 
The fall collection is based on curves. 
There are curved seams that bring jackets close to the body, curved collars that frame the neck, curved backs that give a cocoonlike shape to pleated silk evening jackets and velvet coats.
She used silk duoppioni for the jackets, silk velvet for the coats, silk and wool blends for coats, silk satin for shirts and tunics, silk georgette for evening dresses and silk organza for ball-gown skirts that are poufed with little ribbon ties.
Han Feng's love of silk goes back to her hometown, Hangzhou, near Shanghai, in an area noted for silk and green tea. 
She met her husband, Stuart Schonberger, while she was a student at an art school in Hangzhou and he was teaching English there.
"He grew up in Westchester and went to China after college because his parents had traveled there and wanted him to see it," she said. 
"When we came to New York in 1985, I knew no English. 
I studied English for six months and got a job as a saleswoman at Bloomingdale's.
"My husband got his M.B.A. and worked in a bank for five years, then went back to China. 
He runs an auto repair school in China now with his partners, an Israeli and a Chinese, but he travels back and forth to New York."
Han Feng said she always knew she would come to this country. 
"A psychic in China told me that when I was born, everything was facing America," she said. 
"So I had to come here."
Han (pronounced HAHN) is her Chinese surname and Feng (pronounced FANG), which means red leaf, is her given name, but she always uses the two names together. 
"To help people remember, I tell them to think of 'have fun,' " she said, "and they remember."
Like many hopeful designers, Han Feng started by making clothes for herself. 
After leaving Bloomingdale's because her limited English kept her from a promotion to buyer, she worked for S. Shamash & Sons, a silk importer in New York. 
There she cut swatches and dealt with some of the company's small customers. 
When people admired clothes she made, she took a pleated skirt and top to a shop in SoHo, which bought them and offered to buy anything else she made.
"I quit my job and started making clothes for the shop, but it went out of business six months later and I was left with all this fabric," she said. 
"So I made scarfs and took them to Henri Bendel and Barneys, to Bergdorf Goodman and Neiman Marcus."
When she went to Chicago for Bendel's to make a store appearance, the buyer asked her to make a blouse for the holiday selling period.
"I made two," she said. 
"Dramatic blouses. 
And the buyer reordered. 
So I decided this was a quicker way to make money than scarfs. 
I made six pieces for spring and they sold out."
By 1993, she was ready for a show, albeit a small one, just 20 pieces modeled at the Alternative Museum in SoHo. 
In April of last year, she graduated to the Seventh on Sixth shows in Bryant Park, but with a collection that was still basically pleated.
The full-fledged collection she showed last month attracted many new buyers from specialty and department stores, including Dayton Hudson in this country, Brown's in London and Isetan in Malaysia and Singapore. 
Neiman Marcus has added her clothes to more of its branches, and Henri Bendel will sell the entire collection as her exclusive outlet in New York.
On May 24, Han Feng will be one of eight designers of Asian ancestry to be honored by the Asian American Federation of New York at a dinner dance at the United Nations. 
She'll be in good company. 
The other honorees include Anna Sui, Josie Natori, Yeohlee Teng and Vera Wang.

file: A DIRECTORY OF CRUISES WORLDWIDE_The Yangtze_s Gorges.txt
text:
ï»¿
IT is at dawn that the murky waters of the Yangtze River are most mysterious. 
As little cargo boats emerge from the mist like apparitions, it seems entirely possible that the Three Gorges here in central China were formed not by geological forces but by the goddess Yao Ji and the 12 dragons.
The 12 dragons, as local folk can tell you, used to bully and oppress the peasants along the Yangtze. 
Then Yao Ji showed up on the top of a nearby cloud and pointed her finger at the dragons, killing them. 
Unfortunately, the goddess hadn't thought the problem through. 
The bodies of the dragons left 12 huge mountains that blocked the river and turned the region into a huge sea.
Then the goddess figured out a way to carve a channel through the dragon-mountains. 
That channel became the Yangtze River gorges, and the goddess stayed behind in the form of a rock pinnacle.
The Three Gorges, extending 120 miles in the midreaches of the Yangtze River, remain one of the most famous tourist sites in China. 
Thousands of foreigners and even more Chinese each year take a leisurely three- to five-day cruise up or down the river through the belly of China. 
Several dozen cruise boats, some with swimming pools, discos and karaoke bars, ply the Yangtze. 
Now the trips are particularly in demand because of fears that a huge dam just beginning construction will flood the entire area and destroy the scenery.
I traveled through the Three Gorges in late May on one of the best boats, the Yangtze Paradise. 
Some 285 feet long, the Paradise has 70 cabins, an observation deck, a couple of coffee shops, a souvenir shop, a bar and a tiny swimming pool that was empty during my voyage. 
Perhaps more important, it has clean sheets, decent food and better commitment to modern hygiene.
Like most travelers, I boarded the ship in Chongqing and traveled downriver. 
For those with time on their hands, however, the journey upriver is a good alternative, because the boats have fewer passengers and the pace is somewhat slower. 
The downriver journey takes three to four days, while it takes a day longer traveling against the current.
Chongqing, which used to be known as Chungking, is a crowded, polluted rabbit warren of a city in Sichuan Province, 900 miles southwest of Beijing. 
Yet the city, divided by two rivers and built against a hillside, offers a much more authentic glimpse of China than the cities tourists normally see, Beijing and Shanghai.
The sailing was set for 8 A.M., so by 7:30 I was at the dock, a frenzied herd of would-be porters surrounding my car and pressing against the windows. 
"If you get a porter to help you with your luggage, be sure to fix the amount before he touches your suitcase," the driver warned. 
"A while ago I took some Germans here, and the porters helped them to the boat. 
But the porters refused to give them back their luggage until they paid some outrageous amount. 
The Germans almost missed their boat."
With that warning, I decided to carry my own bags and slipped through the throngs of porters down a steep set of stairs to the water's edge and across a gangplank to the Yangtze Paradise.
"Hi, my name is Ben," said a tall Chinese man in his mid-20's, in fluent English. 
"I'm the cruise director."
After picking up my key, I inspected my cabin. 
It was scarcely bigger than a king-sized bed, but contained two single beds -- I was traveling with a Canadian journalist -- a night table, a desk, a stuffed chair and a small bathroom with a shower. 
A narrow door opened onto a balcony with just enough room for the two chairs provided, and over the next few days the balcony proved a wonderful escape from the cabin.
The cabin was clean and air-conditioned, perfectly comfortable but a bit worn and dowdy. 
Facilities in Communist countries often look old and faded within a week of opening, and so it was with the cabin. 
My wallpaper, for example, was stained to a degree that in other countries it would have been replaced; in China, the staff would have regarded it as perfectly silly to discard wallpaper just because of a few character-building stains.
The Yangtze Paradise was much the same. 
From a distance, it looked sleek and graceful, a swan compared to the rusty hulks carrying freight up and down the river. 
But up close, nothing ever worked quite as well as it was supposed to. 
The coffee shops were mostly unstaffed, so that it was a major triumph to get service. 
There was a nice fitness center, but the stationary bicycle and most of the other equipment was broken. 
And the rat . . . but wait, I'm getting ahead of my story.
The Yangtze Paradise, as Ben explained to all the passengers as we gathered in the lounge shortly after departure, was launched in 1991. 
It can accommodate 130 guests; only 91 were on board. 
This perplexed me, as when I made the booking -- three months earlier -- I was told that the Paradise was booked solid, and it was only after considerable time and effort that I was able to reserve a ticket. 
One couple at my table had paid a bribe to get tickets, for they were told that everything was sold out.
The cities along the Yangtze are known as the "furnaces" of China, because of their unrelenting summers, and so I had brought several pairs of shorts and short-sleeve shirts. 
I thought about that as I huddled in a windbreaker on deck, occasional raindrops plunking down on me, watching the landscape. 
From May through September, the temperature is normally very hot, often well above 90 degrees, but my trip was a reminder that the weather is unreliable. 
I wish I could say that I stared over the deck rail at the churning waters and the river bank, overwhelmed by the beauty and mysteries of China. 
Instead, I gazed at the filth and litter in the water, contemplating how polluted the Yangtze has become. 
Beyond the opaque brown river, the river banks were ugly and industrial, with one hulking factory next to another.
The Yangtze, of course, is one of the most important rivers in Asia. 
Some 35 percent of all Chinese, accounting for 8 percent of all humanity, live in the Yangtze basin. 
It is a crucial economic highway for the development of interior provinces.
But an important river is not necessarily a beautiful river, and I decided that at least the stretch below Chongqing is not very scenic. 
Perhaps the gorges themselves would be.
That evening the boat made the first of five stops, in the grimy Sichuanese county seat of Wanxian. 
The night market in the center of town -- a mile from the dock -- is a jumble of peddlers selling everything from live chickens to wicker chairs to racy magazines. 
It's worth a walk around, not because it's charming, but because it's bleak and ugly: Wanxian is fairly typical of the county towns all over China that foreign tourists do not normally visit.
The next morning, after a pleasant sleep in my cabin, we reached the first of the Three Gorges. 
The Yangtze Paradise has a spacious observation deck that offers a full view in every direction while guests sit in comfortable chairs and sip lukewarm tar -- well, the waitress said it was coffee.
As the boat entered the gorge, with high mountains rising on each side, I didn't hear many "oohs" or "aaahs" from the other travelers. 
Instead, there were plenty of appreciative "mmmmm's," and that was how I felt. 
With steep cliffs on either side of the narrow channel, it was certainly scenic, but not so spectacular that I would advise someone to travel halfway around the world to see it. 
.
The same was also true of the second gorge, which we saw that evening, and the third, which we passed through the next morning. 
In fact, those of us on the observation deck were getting impatient for the second gorge and finally asked a waitress when we would enter it. 
"Don't you know?" she said, shocked. 
"This is the second gorge. 
We've been in it for 20 minutes now."
Most of the other people with whom I talked on the boat had a similar reaction to the Three Gorges, but we were genuinely impressed by a side trip on the second day to the Lesser Three Gorges. 
These are on the Daning River, a tributary of the Yangtze, and nearly all cruise boats make the seven-hour side trip.
Because the Daning is narrow and shallow, we transferred to a group of motorboats that could each carry about 20 people. 
With the motorboat's awning pulled back and the spray of the rapids around us, the boat ride was much more engaging than the one on the Yangtze. 
The toilets on the small boat were so dirty that we all limited our intake of beverages.
The Daning is a pretty little river, a refreshing turquoise after the brown of the Yangtze, flanked alternately by steep cliffs and gentle tree-lined slopes. 
The boatmen point to odd-shaped formations that are thought, with some stretch of the imagination, to resemble pandas, Buddhas and goddesses.
Perhaps the most interesting stop was Zigui, a county seat where we docked for the second night of the cruise. 
A famous poet and statesman, Qu Yuan, committed suicide in about 288 B.C. by leaping into the river here. 
His suicide is commemmorated each spring with dragon boat races, held especially for tourists, who can participate, whenever a cruise boat pulls up. 
It's all rather hokey, but everybody seemed to have fun. 
We also explored Zigui and visited a temple honoring Qu Yuan.
Trips to the Three Gorges have been particularly popular in the last few years because of fears that the area will be inundated by the Three Gorges Dam, but "farewell tours" seem a bit premature. 
Opposition to the dam, which would be the world's largest hydro-electric project if it is completed when scheduled, about 17 years from now, remains considerable, and there is some prospect that the scheme will be quietly dropped after the death of China's 89-year-old senior leader, Deng Xiaoping.
Although the 607-foot-high dam would not destroy the landscape, it would change it radically, raising the level of the water and making the vistas less dramatic -- something that already happened with the construction of the Gezhouba Dam in the 1970's and 1980's. 
Accounts from several decades ago describe the Three Gorges as exciting rapids with boulders and whirlpools. 
Now the gorges are placid and much deeper than they used to be.
Some American friends who have taken Three Gorges cruises complain that the other passengers were mostly Taiwanese who could not speak English and with whom they had little in common.
BUT on the Yangtze Paradise, the passengers -- primarily Americans, with smaller numbers of Europeans, Japanese and Taiwanese -- were very companionable, and we enjoyed long and friendly meals with new friends. 
The meals were large and reasonably good, all served in a modern and spacious dining room with clean tablecloths. 
The food was all Chinese, except that Western breakfasts -- toast and eggs -- were also offered. 
A typical lunch or dinner included rice, a diced chicken dish, a stir-fried vegetable or two, spicy minced pork and a fish, with fruit for dessert.
Among those assigned to my table were two young Britons who turned out to be the Earl and Countess of Dalkeith. 
They were pleasant conversationalists who enjoyed the trip, at least until the final morning.
It was about 5 A.M., in their cabin, that the Earl suddenly was awakened by a pain in his finger. 
He looked down to see a rat (or perhaps just a mouse) nibbling his hand. 
It ran away, leaving only a bit of blood, considerable commotion, and anxiety about rabies and other diseases. 
The boat had a Chinese doctor on board, but she turned out to be an ophthalmologist who spoke no English and knew nothing about animal bites. 
Perhaps the most distressing aspect of the incident was that the boat staff did not seem particularly surprised. 
In fact, I discovered rat poison beneath my bed as well, and a crew member explained that, on the Yangtze, rats come with the river.
Now that I've ruined the sleep of any reader who takes a Yangtze cruise any time soon, I should add that I have never heard of any other foreigner's seeing a rat on board a foreign cruise boat on the Yangtze. 
Still, like many visitors, I found the Yangtze Gorges fell short of my expectations. 
There are plenty of sights in China that are far more captivating: the Forbidden City in Beijing, the terra cotta warriors of Xian, the Potala palace in Lhasa, Tibet, the huge carved Buddhas of Datong, the painted caves of Dunhuang, sacred Mount Tai in Shandong Province, even the day cruises along the Li River in Guilin.
Yet, for all that, floating down the Yangtze past the Three Gorges is a pleasant break, a respite from the trains and planes that normally whisk tourists around the country. 
But temper your expectations, because some of the praise for the gorges can be attributed to poetic license -- like these lines of Guo Moruo earlier in this century:
Â 
Cliffs rise like walls on both banks,
Guarding the river's zigzag course.
Rosy cloud brightens the army hats,
And the river roars in the mist.
Â 
Â 
Â 
A VISITOR'S GUIDE TO CRUISING IN CHINA
Getting There
The shortest Three Gorges cruise is just two-and-a-half days on the water from Chongqing to the rather dull city of Yichang. 
However, Yichang does not now have a functioning airport, and so disembarking passengers must take an overnight train -- quite comfortable -- to the major industrial city of Wuhan and fly from there. 
It is also possible to continue on the boat from Yichang to Wuhan, although this adds a day to the schedule.
Many cruise guides say that the Yangtze Paradise is the best boat on the river; other relatively good ones include the Bashan, the Yangzijiang, the Yangtze Pearl and the Yangtze Princess. 
Two new boats, China Glory and China Dream, are supposed to go into service next year. 
But all 20 of the boats for foreigners are reasonably clean and comfortable.
When side trips such as the Lesser Three Gorges visit are included, a four-day Chongqing-Wuhan cruise on the Paradise costs $690 a person sharing a standard double cabin. 
The price is about $510 in July and August, when the Three Gorges are extremely hot, or in the late fall or early spring, when the area can approach freezing. 
The longer upriver journey costs $620 in the peak season and $480 in the slack season. 
(Probably the best time to go is May to June and from late August to early October.) These figures include meals, but a cabin with a balcony -- much recommended -- is $50 more a person. 
Less luxurious boats than the Paradise are a bit cheaper.
Generally, single-occupancy cabins cost 75 percent more than the price of a bed in a double. 
There are also deluxe double cabins for as much as $1,200 a person.
Travel agents sometimes tack on their own profit margins, and so visitors frequently spend much more than the sums mentioned above. 
An American biochemist at my dining table paid $1,600 each for himself and his wife for the Three Gorges trip, including air fare from Hong Kong, two nights in a hotel in Chongqing and one night in Wuhan.
Even in Beijing, I found that prices varied by 50 percent or more for identical Three Gorges packages. 
Within China, the most reasonable and efficient travel agency that I could find for booking Three Gorges tours was the Hubei China International Travel Service, 48 Jianghan Yilu, Hankou, Wuhan, Hubei Province 430021, China; phone (86-27) 221-265, fax 211-891. 
The sales director is Wu Dandan. 
While it may be more convenient to book through an American travel agent, Ms. Wu can accept overseas orders.
The trip is not physically demanding, but at several of the ports of call there are gangplanks and dozens of steps. 
This might not be the best cruise for those who have difficulty getting about.
Â 
Where to Stay
The best place to stay in Chongqing is the Holiday Inn, 15 Nan Ping Bei Lu, Chongqing 630064; (86-811) 203-380, fax 200-884; $97.75 a night for a double room including tax.
In Wuhan, the best accommodations are at the Asia Hotel, 300 Jie Fang Da Dao, Hankou, Wuhan 430030; (86-27) 568-777, fax 559-372. 
Double rooms are $69 a night including tax. 
Both the Asia Hotel and the Chongqing Holiday Inn can pick up guests at the airport for an extra charge if arranged in advance.
It is safest to plan on having an extra day in Chongqing, for otherwise a delayed flight could cause you to miss your cruise.
If you are traveling to the dock yourself to board the boat, be sure to find out from your hotel the number of the dock assigned to your cruise boat. 
Otherwise, you may find yourself frantically searching for your boat at departure time.
Â 
What to Take
The cruises are very informal, as is China generally, so there is no need to take suits or fancy dresses. 
Shorts and T-shirts are very much accepted.
A useful picture book with text, "The Three Gorges on the Yangtze River," is available in Chongqing and on some of the boats. 
Also useful is "The Three Gorges of the Yangtze River, a Guide for Tourists," but this is rather more difficult to find.
English books and magazines are generally harder to find in China.

file: A HALF-CENTURY IN CHINA_The Bright Young Stars of China_s Future.txt
text:
ï»¿
Officially, power in China is concentrated in the hands of a small number of men, all career Communist politicians who were alive when the People's Republic was declared on Oct. 
1, 1949.
But today a new class of leaders is emerging that will form China's public face in the decades to come. 
They are men and women in their 30's and 40's whose aims and experiences exemplify the growing diversity of China after two decades of market-oriented change.
While ultimate power remains tightly linked to Communist Party politics, many members of the new generation exert influence in a wide variety of other fields, like business, art and science. 
And they tend to differ from the ruling generation, more flexible and cosmopolitan in their ideas.
"They automatically accept reform; they know it must happen," said Li Qiang, a sociologist at People's University in Beijing. 
"They have often been abroad and welcome the cultures of other countries."
Born toward the end of the tumultuous Maoist era, many younger adults did not internalize the fear and caution so essential to survival then.
"Most older Chinese have the habit of listening to the radio in the morning, because they did so every day in the 1960's to learn what Mao wanted them to do," Professor Li said. 
"The younger generation is more independent; it doesn't look for instructions."
Some emerging leaders, to be sure, join the Communist Party and pursue Government careers. 
In a country where the party still has the final say in every field, most people who are out to make a mark are careful to cultivate official ties.
The individuals profiled below represent an arbitrary selection, in Beijing, from the multitudes of rising young stars. 
Together, they provide a taste of the China being born.Â

file: A LA CARTE_Chinese Cooking Without the Deep Frying.txt
text:
ï»¿
THERE is a story behind every restaurant. 
Even the tiniest takeout has a tale to tell. 
The modest Good Earth, which opened recently at 399 New York Avenue at Huntington Village (421-1414), is a case in point.
The combination of unlikely people, events and ideas that led to its establishment are straight out of an adventure story. 
They include a Mexican who was the executive chef of the Ritz Hotel in London, a kosher caterer in Hewlett, a trip to Shanghai, China, and an unusual, creative idea.
Faz Esmizadeh, the Mexican chef came to this country from London eight years ago and became the kitchen commander at Victor Mayer Kosher Catering in Hewlett, where he met Stanley Chi, a chef from Shanghai who was in charge of the caterer's Chinese station. 
Mr. Esmizadeh was impressed by the Asian chef's cooking, style and speed and learned from him.
Five years ago, Mr. Chi returned to China and although the two men stayed in contact, Mr. Esmizadeh put his catering job and new-found interest in Chinese food behind him and opened the Tortilla Grill, on Route 110 in Huntington Village. 
There he began cooking healthful Mexican food that emphasized fresh ingredients and eliminated preservatives, oils and frying.
As his nontraditional Mexican take out grew in popularity and became a modest restaurant as well, Mr. Esmizadeh once again turned his attention to Chinese cuisine. 
For two years he experimented at home, attempting to apply the same principles to Chinese cooking that he had to Mexican dishes. 
Eight months ago, he felt ready enough to visit China, seek out Mr. Chi and urge him to return to the United States and open the Good Earth.
When Mr. Esmizadeh told his friend of his plans for a different kind of Chinese takeout restaurant, one with no frozen ingredients, lard, microwave, artificial coloring or spices, monosodium glutamate or cornstarch, he was greeted with interest. 
But when he said the Good Earth would be "the only Chinese restaurant in the world without a deep fryer," Mr. Chi replied: "That's impossible. 
How are you going to make an egg roll?"
The answer was, "Bake it."
Mr. Esmizadeh perservered, peppering the Chinese chef with his ideas for fresh, light cooking. 
"With my ideas and your ability we can do this," he said. 
"We will cook sweet and sour chicken in a wok, not fried in oil. 
We will use only high quality olive oil and very little of it. 
No cornstarch, only potato starch, and let's forget that sticky white rice and use fluffy, tasty basmati instead. 
We can offer Chinese food that will not leave a knot in people's stomachs."
Mr. Chi liked what he heard and returned to Long Island, where he recruited two veteran chefs from Manhattan: Benny Wong of Hong Kong and Shao Shai of Shanghai. 
Last month the four chefs opened the bright, little Good Earth, "a Chinese spot like no other," said Mr. Esmizadeh.

text:
ï»¿
FALLING LEAVES
The True Story of an Unwanted
Chinese Daughter.
By Adeline Yen Mah.
Illustrated. 278 pp. 
New York:
John Wiley & Sons. 
$22.95.
ADELINE Yen Mah's "Falling Leaves: The True Story of an Unwanted Chinese Daughter" opens with the reading of the first page of her father's will in the opulent office of a Hong Kong attorney. 
Joseph Yen's entire estate is left to his second wife, Jeanne, who declares that since there is nothing left -- without explanation, her husband's two tons of gold bullion, stocks and shares, and worldwide real estate holdings have disappeared -- the rest of the will is meaningless. 
With that, the siblings are instructed to hand over their copies, which, because they have been bullied by this woman their entire lives long, they do.
Mah alludes to a traditional Chinese aphorism -- "falling leaves return to their roots" -- to describe her narrative journey back in time to the roots of her Shanghai family. 
Although the early stories are inspiring and even heartwarming -- Mah's great-aunt defies tradition by resolutely refusing to have her feet bound and founds the Shanghai Women's Bank; another aunt exudes unconditional love -- "Falling Leaves" is nothing if not a traditional memoir of a bad childhood.
These early memories are soon supplanted by a litany of abuses. 
The family irrationally blames Mah for the death of her mother, who died in childbirth. 
Her father, Joseph Yen, soon takes up with Jeanne Prosperi, the 17-year-old daughter of a French father and a Chinese mother. 
With her European ancestry, great beauty and convent education, she is seen as the ultimate trophy wife. 
By the age of 23, Jeanne has two children of her own in addition to her five stepchildren, whose Chinese names she immediately bans. 
Overnight they become Lydia, Gregory, Edgar, James and Adeline, and are subjected to verbal degradation. 
"I do think Adeline is getting uglier and uglier as she grows older and taller," Jeanne observes at one point. 
This Mommy Dearest beats her own baby daughter, and Adeline, a plucky first grader, is the only person to object. 
"I shall never forget or forgive your insolence," Jeanne announces. 
"Never!
Never!
Never!"
She keeps her word. 
Just as the Japanese invade, Adeline is sent away to boarding school, where she is abandoned for years. 
So beguiled is Joseph by his luscious and headstrong wife that he never intervenes on his children's behalf.
To be fair, this entire family seems almost psychotically cruel. 
Adeline's brothers urinate into her orange juice. 
When one of those brothers writes that he'd like to become a professional bridge player, his father sends a telegram: "Why don't you become a pimp instead?"
The elder Yens repeatedly pit one child against the other. 
Those who dare to protest are disowned and disinherited. 
Through it all, Adeline never stops longing for her family's love and acceptance. 
But with the exceptions of Adeline and her half sister Susan (herself married to a Hong Kong billionaire), these are people who plot and scheme to the very end for their father's long hidden and greatly depleted fortune of $30 million.
Mah's story is almost a casebook study of the effects of long-term abuse, but she doesn't seem to have the self-awareness to place it in this context. 
So when her first love affair is with someone emotionally abusive, or her first husband is a batterer, she sees these interludes, which so clearly follow the pattern of victimization, as just two more bad things that happen to her. 
Only rarely does she offer a glimpse into her sex's historical plight, even though abortion, infanticide and abandonment of female children occur routinely in Chinese culture even now. 
Still, in many ways the turbulence of Mah's family life mirrors the great conflicts of China during the last century. 
"Bear many sons. 
Sublimate your own desires. 
Become the willing . . . spittoon of the Yens and we will be proud of you," Mah's grandmother was told on the eve of her wedding. 
Even her radically independent aunts are eventually stripped of power and position, condemned and persecuted. 
Humbled, they eke out their last days without protest.
Like so many memoirists, Mah finally triumphs over adversity. 
While never winning the Yens' love, she becomes a respected physician, marries a fine man and starts her own family. 
It's hard not to admire her persistence and perseverance, or to think of those siblings scattered around the world, spending their inheritances and maybe taking a peek at their sister's scorching and vivid account.

text:
ï»¿
Not long ago, Tsingtao Brewery looked unbeatable.
With a high quality product, a well established name, a booming beer market and ambitious plans to quadruple production in five years, Tsingtao seemed perfectly positioned to ride China's locomotive-like economic growth. 
In 1993, when the Government allowed China's top companies to list shares on Hong Kong's stock exchange, Tsingtao was chosen to go first, and its stock was one of the hottest issues of the year.
Yet Tsingtao (pronounced ching-dow) is going nowhere. 
Its profits are sagging, its stock is near an all-time low, and its expansion plans have stalled. 
Tsingtao managers have been reluctant to explain why the $190 million they raised in 1993 has not been invested in expansion.
Tsingtao's story straddles a central paradox in China today. 
In this nation's wrenching shift from a planned to a market economy, explosive growth has been accompanied by bumbling financial operations mired in a hopelessly inefficient system run by the Communist Party. 
The heralded entry of Chinese stocks into securities markets in Hong Kong and Shanghai has been a dud.
"Even by the year 2000 China could become an economic giant but remain a financial pygmy," Timothy Beardson, chairman of Crosby Securities in Hong Kong, said at a recent conference in Beijing.
The contradiction is striking: China has emerged as a magnet for international investment, as manufacturers like Motorola, Coca-Cola and General Motors pour in. 
Economic growth has averaged a sparkling 12 percent annually for four years, and an awakening demand for consumer goods and services is likely to continue for decades.
Yet the financial system envisioned by China's leaders is stuck in its infancy. 
China's stock markets remain tiny and lackluster: in the past six months, as the Dow Jones industrial average kept racking up new highs, Chinese shares on the Hong Kong and Shanghai markets have drifted lower and lower.
Unforeseen difficulties are inevitable, of course, when capital markets are being built from scratch. 
In China, though, such problems are compounded by a situation that most Western investors have a hard time fathoming: companies that say they want to make money are still run by Communist Party bureaucrats who care more about meetings and Government policy than revenues or profit margins.
Many businesses survive on Government subsidies and loans that banks are ordered to give them, and those selected to issue shares are picked as much for political reasons as for financial ones.
Tsingtao's difficulties are especially striking because the opportunity is so great. 
China's beer market is now about 118 million barrels annually, roughly 15 times as big as it was in 1980 and growing so fast it has overtaken Germany to become the world's second largest, after the United States.
But Tsingtao, unused to entertaining questions from anyone but Government officials, is almost completely indifferent to investors and analysts, offering them little information.
Of the 17 China-based companies now listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, only one, Shanghai Petrochemical, trades at more than its original listing price. 
And Brilliance China Automotive Holdings, a Bermuda-registered company that promoted itself as China's first listing on the New York Stock Exchange, shot up to $30 shortly after its debut in 1992, but now trades at around $4.
American investment banks like Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs and Smith Barney, after big expansions into China in 1993, now have little business here.
Any analyst can list a number of reasons Chinese stocks are down this year: Many have suffered from Beijing's tight-credit policy, others were hit by unexpected tax increases, still others were simply priced badly. 
But the main problem is that it has gradually dawned on investors that they understand little about how Chinese companies are run. 
When they do get a peek inside, they don't like what they see.
Tsingtao is a prime example. 
It has been making beer here since the Germans opened the brewery in 1903, when they colonized a section of the Shandong peninsula in northeast China. 
As it earned a reputation for making the best beer in China, Tsingtao gained a robust 70 percent of China's beer exports.
When they announced plans to list shares as the first of many "red chip," or mainland Chinese, stocks in Hong Kong, Tsingtao executives boldly proclaimed plans to dominate China's fragmented beer market, in which more than 800 breweries compete.
Response was overwhelming, and the initial offering was so oversubscribed -- more than 100 times -- that few investors could get in.
After Tsingtao was listed at 36 cents a share, it climbed to $1.40, a towering 98 times earnings, in 1994. 
The Anheuser-Busch Companies, the American beer giant, bought a 5 percent stake.
But bad news began emerging about Tsingtao in the middle of this year.
Profit in the first half fell 49 percent, as prices of raw materials rose sharply but competition prevented Tsingtao from charging more for its beer. 
More troubling, analysts looking over the company's puzzlingly vague annual report discovered that Tsingtao's managers had taken nearly half of the $190 million from their share issue and, rather than investing it in plant expansion -- as had been promised in a prospectus -- lent it to other Chinese companies that Tsingtao will not identify.
With its new capital thus mysteriously tied up, Tsingtao had to scale back expansion plans and cut projected growth in beer production, which is now at about three million barrels a year, by half. 
Worse, it remains unclear how much of Tsingtao's loans will be repaid: China's state-owned enterprises are famous for losing money and remaining immune to demands for repayment.
"When we called with questions, they wouldn't come to the phone," said Lim Cheang Yee, an analyst for H. G. Asia in Hong Kong. 
"They screwed around with minority shareholders' money, but wouldn't explain anything."
Ms. Lim said that Tsingtao had apparently recovered much of its loan money in recent months, and had even become more responsive to questions. 
But she said that it would still take a long time to repair the damage done to its credibility.
Talks between Anheuser-Busch and Tsingtao about expanding the American company's stake to 15 percent or more went sour. 
Anheuser-Busch executives have told colleagues at other beer companies that the deeper they looked into Tsingtao, the more pessimistic they became about the company's ability to expand its share of this fragmented market.
While Tsingtao is one of China's largest breweries and clearly its best known, it has just 2.2 percent of the market. 
And though its 70 percent share of China's beer exports sounds good, that accounts for just 10 percent of Tsingtao's sales over all. 
Moreover, those sales are blurred by the complex set of distribution rights, which vary from market to market, that the company agreed to when first entering international markets several years ago.
"They're amazingly arrogant," said a distributor who works with Tsingtao managers. 
"They say, 'We're Tsingtao, we don't need to advertise.'
It's so ridiculous. 
Even Coca-Cola has to advertise."
The markets have judged Tsingtao harshly as well, with the stock now trading at less than $2 and its American depository receipts selling for pennies. 
[On Tuesday, the company's shares closed at 1.82 Hong Kong dollars, and its A.D.R.'s closed at 23 cents.]
Tsingtao executives brush away questions about their unorthodox lending.
"I don't see what the fuss is about," said Qiao Qijian, a senior executive at Tsingtao, in an interview at company headquarters here during which he downed three glasses of Tsingtao draft. 
"Many investors from Hong Kong are concerned. 
But when they come to visit, they can see that everything is going fine."
Mr. Qiao said Tsingtao had been unable to invest its newly raised capital immediately because of shifting policy in Beijing, and had to delay its planning throughout 1994 until a meeting was held in February 1995. 
At that time, Beijing officials informed company executives about the need to shift China's alcoholic consumption away from the traditional favorite, grain alcohol, because of a growing shortage of grain.
That means beer and wine production is to be encouraged, which sounds good for Tsingtao. 
Yet the fact that a leading beer company's expansion was dictated by a Government meeting, itself most concerned with the politics of grain production, was an indication of how the emphasis remains on Government planning rather than on market demand.
Moreover, Mr. Qiao conceded that the financing of increased beer production was not even discussed at the meeting.
That seems short-sighted. 
China's beer market is entering an intensely competitive stage, with foreign breweries marching into China every day. 
Asahi and Kirin of Japan and Foster's of Australia recently announced plans to expand, and Beck's of Germany and Pabst of Milwaukee are already making beer in China.
With prospects for Tsingtao bleak, Anheuser-Busch went ahead with a joint venture to produce Budweiser with a different brewery in the central Chinese city of Wuhan.
"Our greatest concern with the company has always been that competition will force Tsingtao to cap price growth," Ms. Lim of H. G. Asia wrote in an analysis of the brewery, recommending that shareholders sell. 
"Profit growth will therefore have to depend on volume growth."
On paper, Tsingtao's expansion plans call for a fourfold production increase by the year 2000, which would come to 10 percent of today's domestic market. 
But Mr. Qiao, the Tsingtao executive, conceded that with all the delays it has encountered, the company would be pleased to achieve half as much.
Even with scaled-back plans, it is unclear where additional financing will come from, since China is in the midst of a tight credit policy that shows no signs of easing.
Mr. Qiao leaned back in a puffy chair and took a deep breath when asked about this.
"We have three options: bank loans, Government subsidies or another share issue," he said.
Unfortunately, he added, none of those look feasible anytime soon.

text:

Asia's largest investment bank outside Japan, Peregrine Investments Holdings, was forced to shut down today, the first major casualty of the economic and currency crisis that has swept through the region since summer.
Moreover, Peregrine's collapse is the first major bankruptcy in Hong Kong since the territory reverted to Chinese rule last July.
News of Peregrine's failure shook Hong Kong's stock market, which was already rattled by the growing financial difficulties in Indonesia. 
Stock prices plunged today, with the Hang Seng market index falling985.51 points, or 11.1 percent, to 7,909.13, by the midday trading break.
The shutdown of Peregrine came after a weekend of frenzied negotiations with potential rescuers.
"It looks like liquidation this afternoon," said Tom Grimmer, a Peregrine spokesman. 
"Bankers didn't go for any sort of rescue operation last night. 
There are no alternatives left."
Founded a decade ago by a former British race car driver and a local investment banker with support from an array of Hong Kong's leading tycoons, Peregrine quickly emerged as the principal underwriter for Chinese companies listing in Hong Kong and the largest brokerage firm here.
Peregrine earned a reputation for daring and rapid decision-making, and for a formidable network of connections with Hong Kong and China's most powerful financial figures.
But as rapidly as the bank soared, it was pulled down as quickly by mounting economic turmoil in Asia, especially in Indonesia, where Peregrine had committed one-third of its capital as a loan to a Jakarta taxi and bus company.
Last summer, Peregrine decided to back Jopie Widjaya, the owner of Steady Safe, a taxi company listed on the Jakarta stock exchange. 
Mr. Widjaya sought financing to expand into ferries and toll roads, plans apparently supported by the daughter of President Suharto. 
Like many of Peregrine's deals, Mr. Widjaya's connections seem to have played a key role in the decision to loan Steady Safe $270 million.
Since the loan, however, the Indonesian rupiah began a swift decline from 2,400 rupiah to the dollar to nearly 10,000 rupiah to the dollar last week. 
Steady Safe found itself unable to meet its obligations and over the weekend its doors in Jakarta were shuttered and locked. 
Peregrine was left with a gaping hole in its balance sheet.
In November, Peregrine announced that it had reached a deal with the Zurich Group of Switzerland to take a 24.1 percent stake in the bank, in what would have amounted to a bailout. 
That deal fell apart as the rupiah continued its slide and the depths of Peregrine's problems became apparent.
As a last-ditch effort, Peregrine approached the Bank of China, but according to a Bank of China executive, senior officials in Beijing ruled out the possibility of taking a stake in the troubled bank.
Over the weekend, Hong Kong's senior civil servants sought to calm the waters as anxieties over the economy mounted, but Donald Tsang, Hong Kong's financial secretary, said the Government would not intervene to save Peregrine.
Zurich Group's withdrawal sent Peregrine's co-founders, Philip Tose and Francis P. T. Leung, into a frenetic search for a savior for their bank. 
Apart from the Bank of China, Deutsche Bank A.G. glanced briefly at Peregrine before shying away.
In Beijing, there was some consternation that Peregrine had even dared to approach the Bank of China, a move that some Chinese bankers saw as running counter to the deliberate policy of insuring Hong Kong's virtual autonomy from Beijing.
And none of Peregrine's original backers, some of the most high-profile tycoons in Hong Kong, appeared willing to come to the rescue of the bank.
As one banker put it this morning: "No one really knows what Peregrine's liabilities are or what it's exposure to Southeast Asia is. 
How could you step in at the last minute?"
About 700 Peregrine employees are expected to be laid off in Hong Kong, with another 1,000 losing their jobs elsewhere in Asia.
