text:
ï»¿
The architecture of Dan Hinkley's garden on the Kitsap Peninsula in Washington State is native, shaped by old Douglas firs and a seeping bog. 
But in the cultivated understory, he has convened plants from all around the globe, reuniting the tribes of the botanical diaspora. 
More than 50 kinds of arisaemas -- called jack-in-the-pulpit in North America -- rocket from the soil, and one, Arisaema nepenthoides, stands fully erect, a single cobralike spathe beside a rotting stump crowned with ferns. 
Thirty-five varieties of Solomon's seals, or polygonatums, from China, Japan, Taiwan, Nepal and Sikkim unspiral from their early growth, and dozens of types of hellebore have just passed their prime. 
Throughout the garden, hydrangeas and viburnums are beginning to dispense their leaves; Stachyurus and Edgeworthia, winter-flowering shrubs from Asia, are leafing out. 
On some loops of the garden trail, where a Cardiocrinum giganteum thrusts its antediluvian seedpod six feet into the air, you almost expect to see a dinosaur wander past. 
Bud-break has stirred among an orderly chaos of growth-forms.
The man behind this collection of plants is Daniel Hinkley, a 45-year-old native of northern Michigan who has come to be regarded as one of the pre-eminent plant explorers in the world. 
Hinkley is the co-owner and chief plantsman of Heronswood Nursery, started in 1987, which lies within the visual domain of the Olympic Mountains across Puget Sound from Seattle. 
Heronswood is Hinkley's personal garden, his trial garden and a two-and-a-half-acre commercial nursery rolled in one. 
It's also Hinkley's home, which he shares with his partner, Robert Jones, an architect who is to the mailing list, the account books and the commercial operations at Heronswood what Hinkley is to the plants.
Here are more than 9,500 plants sprung from seed gathered all over the world. 
Most are numbered and listed in a loose-leaf binder that Hinkley calls the Big Bang, a compilation of plants already for sale and those that someday will be. 
The binder listing current inventory is called the Grand Mal. 
To most gardeners, the plants on these lists would be unfamiliar. 
Instead of the classic Hosta "Frances Williams," for instance, there is Hosta kiyosumiensis, which Hinkley collected from Mount Kiyosume in Japan's Chiba Prefecture in 1995. 
Instead of hybridized Asiatic and Oriental lilies, there is Lilium nanum, collected by Hinkley during a joint expedition to the Himalayas in 1995. 
Instead of a Norway maple or a David Austin rose, there is Acer rufinerve, a striped-bark maple he gathered in central Japan in 1997, and a rose of as yet undetermined species collected from an altitude of 10,800 feet in China's Yunnan province in 1996.
From this garden each year also comes the Heronswood catalogue, a major literary artifact in the world of gardening ephemera. 
Printed solidly in small type, it begins with Hinkley's wry musings on the imperfect art of running a mail-order nursery and ends 300 pages and some 2,500 plants later. 
The catalogue is a saga of botanical excitement and a chronicle of adjectival fatigue, the fate of a man driven to travel the world searching for remarkable plants and then doomed to write a terse, descriptive paragraph about one $6 or $8 clone after another, beginning with Abies balsamea "Nana" in the "Conifers" section and ending with the New Zealand sedge Uncinia unciniata, the final plant in the section on grasses.
Though it advertises nowhere and admits visitors only by appointment, Heronswood Nursery mailed 35,000 copies of the 1999 catalogue, and subscription requests are currently arriving at the rate of 100 a week. 
At $8 for a two-year subscription, the catalogue just pays for itself, unless you count the cost of Hinkley's writing time, in which case it is grossly underpriced. 
Subscribers pleasantly lost among Hinkley's paragraphs can be forgiven for wondering whether the nursery exists to justify the catalogue, or vice versa. 
Still, appealing to a newly adventurous generation of gardeners, Heronswood was an almost instant success. 
In 1993, the year after it incorporated, it had a gross income of $220,000. 
In 1998, it was five times larger, $1,100,000. 
These days, as Robert Jones says, he and Hinkley are trying to choose their limits, trying to let Hinkley's interests, rather than mere economic growth, continue to shape their offerings.
Plant introduction has traditionally been one of the reasons public agencies, public gardens and university arboretums -- like the United States Department of Agriculture, the New York Botanical Garden and the Arnold Arboretum at Harvard University -- have mounted collecting expeditions. 
But such institutions, as even they sometimes admit, usually do a far better job of collecting and studying plants than they do releasing them to the public. 
There is a historic rivalry between the public gardens and commercial nurseries like Heronswood, which dates to well before the days when the legendary plant hunter Ernest Henry Wilson combed turn-of-the-century China first for Veitch's nursery and then for the Arnold Arboretum. 
It's a rivalry, as the academics would put it, between science and mere trade or, as the tradesmen might put it, between exclusivity and openness. 
But these days, in fact, many public gardens and arboretums buy directly from Hinkley, sometimes taking a share in his plant-collecting expeditions, which entitles them to a portion of the seeds Hinkley gathers. 
"They're some of my best customers," he says.
Mid-April is the peak of the spring plant-shipping season at Heronswood, where overworked staff members try to meet the florid expectations of gardeners by selling them plants that are not only garden-worthy but that also carry, for many customers, an echo of the exotic places where Hinkley has collected -- Nepal, Sikkim, China, Japan, Korea, Tasmania, Mexico and Chile. 
The nursery office, an attractive prairie farmhouse of sorts, is surrounded by open shade-canopies sheltering tables crowded with flats, each marked with a customer's name and shipping date.
Hinkley's Michigan drawl crackles over a walkie-talkie clipped to a plant-packer's belt. 
Concealed somewhere in the woodland garden, he is the ghost in this botanic machine, enjoying a 10-day respite from a busy spring speaking schedule and preparing for a collecting trip to Japan. 
A path leads into the benign enveloping shade characteristic of the Northwest woods. 
The light falling on the mounded garden beds seems detached from its source, and what it illuminates has a freshness that is an attribute of the early season and of the vegetation itself. 
A hundred yards down the path, Hinkley works in mottled shade helping a new crew member shovel steer manure from a garden cart onto a planting site. 
No matter how exotic his expeditions may be, this is the end point of every collecting trip -- making a hole in the ground, sprinkling a little 20-20-20 fertilizer in it and grubbing the earth back into place by hand around the stem of a newly propagated plant.
Hinkley speaks quietly, slowly, but there is a sense of haste about him, the result of living in what he calls "a perfect madness of plants," a garden that needs to be brought into peak condition within the next few weeks. 
"At this point it feels like it's moving day," he says. 
"But as long as I keep bringing new plants into trial, it's always going to be like this. 
I get tired of one plant, or it's just not doing for me, so I get rid of it and start over again. 
But every time you do that you want to rejuvenate the soil, and to do that you've got to move another plant."
Hinkley kneels on the ground, chopping at the soil with a border spade and looking up from time to time as he talks. 
He is direct and delicate at the same time, handling plants with none of the hesitation of the amateur gardener. 
He overflows with affection for the garden he has made, and yet his criticism of each individual plant-form -- a kind of veiled self-criticism in fact -- is unsparing.
Hinkley is bearded and balding, and he wears wide suspenders over a T-shirt from the J.C. 
Raulston Arboretum at North Carolina State University. 
Raulston, who died at 56 in a car accident three years ago, was one of Hinkley's mentors and a widely respected emblem of intellectual and horticultural generosity. 
Hinkley has dedicated his next book, "The Explorer's Garden," which Timber Press will publish in the fall, to Raulston and to Gerald Straley of the University of British Columbia, another gardening mentor who died in his 50's. 
"J.C.'s everywhere in this garden," Hinkley said. 
"Every day, I could take out a plant that he gave me, and I would never run out of plants. 
He knew, he sensed what a good plant was."
To sense what a good plant is -- to recognize it in the wild and then confirm it in his own garden -- is the essence of Hinkley's work. 
At Heronswood, there are really three different kinds of garden and, hence, of garden-worthiness. 
Among the greenhouses, for instance, there is the denatured, rationalized garden, which consists of plants grouped by size and species -- garden-worthy, in Hinkley's judgment, but also able to withstand shipping. 
In the woodland garden, tested and marketed varieties of plants compete with untested kin. 
The search here is for better form, greater hardiness, a distinctive virtue -- variegation or a more upright or prostrate habit -- or simply for the illumination, vital to Hinkley's task, that comes from growing many related species in proximity to each other. 
"For me," Hinkley says, "it makes a more complete, more understandable portrait of plants if I get the opportunity to grow many different relatives together."
And then there is the private garden surrounding the house, which is set at the back of the property. 
This is a place where Hinkley has tried to set aside at least some of the cultural limitations that frame our sense of what makes a garden. 
It is a subject he understands very well. 
"We have all this Lutheran guilt," he says. 
"We all moved west from the Midwest where we couldn't have winter gardens, and so our gardens in Seattle and Portland and Vancouver are amazingly timid as far as what our climate can actually do."
But there is no timidity in this garden. 
What takes it beyond timidity isn't massed plantings or vibrant color or expansive scale or even mere exoticism. 
It is Hinkley's subtle reliance on the globally diverse forms of individual plants. 
Each plant, grown well, reveals itself and reveals something, too, about its neighbor. 
What creeps grows next to what climbs. 
The fastigiate and the pendulous conspire. 
Bark peels, thorns protrude, vines finger their way across an arbor, and what unites it all, what makes these plants garden-worthy, is the interest they bestow upon each other.
There are few explicit canons for deciding what makes a plant garden-worthy, but one of them -- a base line below the realm of the esthetic -- is lack of ecological invasiveness. 
Most gardeners are familiar with species that tend to be invasive in the garden, like Ajuga reptans, sometimes called carpet bugle. 
But what haunts Hinkley is the thought of plants that can break loose from cultivation and run rampant across the landscape -- purple loosestrife, kudzu, tamarisk, honeysuckle. 
"My greatest concern," he says, "is the introduction of a bad plant."
To help prevent that, Hinkley has hired Sarah Reichard as a consultant. 
Reichard, an ecologist at the University of Washington's Center for Urban Horticulture and a founder of Washington's Native Plant Society, began to wonder while collecting seed in South America as a graduate student whether any of those plants would prove invasive in the Pacific Northwest. 
She has constructed a model -- a decision tree, based on a plant's observed characteristics, which asks questions about how quickly the species reproduces and whether it belongs to a family or genus already strongly invasive in North America -- that indicates whether a plant is likely to become invasive.
On the burn pile at Heronswood lay one of the results of Reichard's work. 
There, atop other horticultural debris, was Ligustrum delavayanum, a species of privet named after the French priest and botanist Jean Marie Delavay, who collected plants in China in the late 19th century. 
This ligustrum bore fruit in Hinkley's garden for the first time in October, and it caught the attention of Roy Lancaster, the English dean of plant explorers, who was visiting Heronswood at the time. 
"He said he'd never seen a more beautiful form of it," Hinkley told me. 
"But it's a broad-leafed evergreen, and those do really well in the Northwest. 
I looked at it all winter long and battled with it in my conscience. 
You've probably seen what Ligustrum sinense has done in the Southeast. 
It's everywhere. 
Finally we had Sarah run it through her model, and she said, Reject."
Invasiveness is a hot issue, and it inspires a botanical xenophobia, a fear that just because a plant is exotic -- i.e., non-native -- it's inevitably invasive or otherwise harmful to the suite of native plants, changing the balance of nitrogen in the soil, for instance, or causing the water table to dip below the roots of native plants. 
But in horticulture, as in agriculture, the distinction between exotic and native has been blurred by the ancient, extensive exchange of plants for their economic or ornamental value. 
Because plant material -- seeds, cuttings, fruits -- moves as readily as humans do, human plant collecting, like the invention of agriculture, predates history itself. 
Gardening may be a way of enclosing a distinctive botanical world -- separating the cultivated from the uncultivated -- but few gardeners have ever restricted themselves to growing only native plants. 
The literature of gardening is underwritten by the literature of plant trafficking -- Robert Fortune, Joseph Hooker, Joseph Banks, Armand David, Ernest Henry Wilson and a host of predecessors traversed temperate Asia searching for plants of botanical and horticultural interest. 
Their motto, and Hinkley's as well, might be the words of William Bartram, who explored America in the late 18th century, when it was still the gardening world's China. 
"Let us advance to the spot in which nature has seated them," Bartram wrote of the plants he sought.
If there's an ecological argument to be made against plant collecting, there are many to be made for it. 
The term itself is a misnomer. 
Hinkley does not collect plants. 
As he notes in the Heronswood catalogue, "Our wild collections are primarily of seed, which we collect in a very conservative manner."
This means collecting only when there is abundant seed, adhering to the terms of local permits and customs and making sure the seed is carefully prepared to meet U.S.D.A. restrictions (free of any potentially contaminating soil, insects and so on). 
The image of ship decks full of Wardian cases -- the enclosed, portable greenhouses that made the 19th-century boom in plant hunting possible -- has been replaced by the image of tired botanists cleaning seeds for U.S.D.A. inspection under less-than-ideal conditions. 
"It isn't necessarily a fun thing to do," Hinkley says, remembering a trip to Nepal, "especially when you're doing it in a tent at night and it's raining cats and dogs outside and the only light is a headlamp."
Gathering seed from wild plant populations is also a means of preserving genetic diversity in the face of widespread environmental degradation. 
In Nepal, for instance, a grazing yak-cow hybrid, the dzo, has had a grave impact on alpine plant communities. 
In China, deforestation is proceeding at a rate that far outstrips the ability of Chinese and foreign botanists to inventory and collect seeds from endangered plants. 
Even in a gardening culture as traditional as Japan's, there's a tendency to overlook native species in favor of the exotic -- which in the case of Japan means American species. 
After searching Shikoku Island in 1997 for a wild Japanese hydrangea called Hydrangea sikokiana, Hinkley began scouting Japanese nurseries, hoping to find the plant in cultivation. 
"We thought we'd see it from a distance in every single nursery, and we'd go up to it and it was our native Hydrangea quercifolia. 
No one we talked to had even heard of sikokiana. 
They had no interest in growing it because they had this very exotic, much, much more exciting hydrangea from America."
The exotic sikokiana is now growing at Heronswood, not far up the woodland path from the native quercifolia.
But the ultimate rationale for Hinkley's work is the garden itself. 
He shapes his expeditions by looking for climates similar to that of the Pacific Northwest, traveling to places where plants show similar hardiness because of elevation or latitude, and are accustomed to similar rainfall patterns. 
Sometimes a collecting trip broadens the gene pool for a plant that has already been collected, like Paris polyphylla, a Nepalese trillium relative Hinkley had grown at Heronswood for a decade but was the only clone in North America. 
Often a trip leads to a new understanding of how, as Hinkley puts it, a plant "wants" to grow. 
It can also be a means of expanding the idea of the garden philosophically and esthetically by allowing Hinkley to see cultivated species and their wild near kin in their native habitat. 
Perhaps, Hinkley says, re-collecting seed "will bring additional hardiness or additional insect or disease resistance, so I never pass up a plant if it's in seed, if indeed I think it's a plant that deserves to be in cultivation."
Hinkley's garden feels like a glimpse of another creation, a place where the monoculture of the mind is disturbed by a willingness to push beyond the familiar botanical forms into a realm of pleasing visual discomfort. 
Walking along the woodland trails at Heronswood, Hinkley points out some of the plants he admires -- like Podophyllum delavayi, a May apple from Sichuan, which, he says, "deserves to be worshiped" -- and some of the plants he thinks will become important to American gardeners in the years ahead, not only among "plant nerds," as he puts it, but also among gardeners generally. 
He points out a group called the woodland lilies -- Smilacinas, Polygonatums, Uvularias, Disporums and Disporopsis.
But above all he points out Hepatica -- Hepatica acutiloba, an American native and Hepatica maxima, which grows only on one island in the Japan Sea, Hepatica in a single clone, in many clones, in enough clones one day to sell. 
To a casual visitor, these are perplexing plants, modest, growing in low mounds with rather formal, old-fashioned leaves and small flowers, not half as striking as the arisaemas and trilliums that are rioting in the woodland. 
But besides being a "simply good" plant, Hepatica maxima, for one, is also very rare in cultivation, which makes its goodness no longer simple. 
It goes about its business in a quiet corner of the garden, reaffirming a strange premise of life itself, for being there at all is part of its beauty.

file: A Savory Guide To the Exotica Of Chinatown_s Food Vendors.txt
text:
ï»¿
A THOUSAND years ago, in the villages of China at the beginning of the Sung dynasty, before there were restaurants, and before peasants had ovens, food vendors roamed mud streets.
From morning to night, the vendors hawked fried puffy breads, sweet sticky rice and plump barbecued chickens. 
They brought the food from larger, nearby towns where the chickens were roasted in ovens, then tucked into tiered bamboo baskets that hung on poles slung across their shoulders. 
The food was humble, but tasty -- tasty enough that the tradition is alive today on the streets of Beijing, Hong Kong and Manhattan.
In Manhattan's Chinatown, there are six or seven vendors along the south side of Canal Street, starting at Centre Street and heading east five short blocks to the Bowery, and several more vendors are located on the Bowery, south one block to Bayard Street.
To operate legally, each vendor must pass an inspection to receive a license and permit from New York City's Department of Health. 
As proof, the vendor numbers are prominently displayed on the front of each cart. 
The vendors offer the foods of 1,000 years ago, and people queue up to buy fried scallion pancakes, braised honeycomb tripe, barbecued duck and the snacks of both northern and southern China.
Very little has changed.
Gone are the bamboo baskets, and in their place are stainless steel carts equipped with steam tables, griddles and plastic take-out containers. 
White plastic forks and spoons have replaced chopsticks.
An informal tasting of the foods offered by these street vendors was conducted in three visits in the last three weeks. 
The vendors stake their claim to particular spots on the sidewalk and work six days a week, usually from 9 A.M. to 6 P.M. Kee Lim, a vendor who sets up in front of 226 Canal Street, was a street vendor in Hong Kong for six years before moving to New York.
Some vendors, like Mr. Lim, were chatty in Cantonese. 
A few spoke minimal English, enough to understand that a customer wanted one pancake, or four dumplings. 
The provenance of the food was a mystery. 
A few, like Mr. Lim, bought from restaurants, but they wouldn't say which ones. 
Still others said nothing. 
They cooked, they sold, but they did not reveal sources.
To find the best food, go where the crowds are, and assume that in dishes like dumplings or braised meats, there will be a bit of monosodium glutamate.
People clustered and gawked at the Hong Kee Food Corporation's street stall -- an extension of the take-out food store -- that sells traditional Chinese snacks at 234 Canal Street (Centre Street). 
Working on a griddle, Shirley Kong took a roll of silky white rice noodle and wrapped it around crisp-on-the-outside, chewy-on-the-inside fried dough, a breakfast food that was both soothing and was filling ($1). 
To warm the roll up, she lightly sauteed it on the griddle, and to offset its bland flavor, she drizzled it with thinned-out soy sauce that had been simmered with sugar, scallions, ginger, garlic and broth.
On the other side of the griddle, rectangles of turnip pudding were sizzling. 
Made of grated white Chinese turnips seasoned with ginger and garlic, the pudding was steamed, sliced and pan-fried until crisp and golden on both sides (three slices for $1). 
It slithered down the throat, slippery and savory. 
It is best eaten with a sprinkle of oyster sauce. 
If the cook doesn't offer the oyster sauce, ask for it. 
Hong Kee's vendor number is 19863.
Where street food stands apart from homemade or high-quality restaurant food is usually in the degree of refinement or luxuriousness of ingredients. 
At a good dim sum parlor, the turnip pudding is sometimes studded with bits of dried shrimp and Chinese sausage. 
At Hong Kee, the turnip pudding lacked the shrimp and sausage. 
But who complained?
Judging from the crowds, the answer was no one.
About three steps to the east of Hong Kee, Shu Chen, No. 16592, was one of two vendors on Canal Street selling deep-fried scallion pancakes, a Shanghai specialty. 
Filled with freshly chopped scallions, the perfect pancake is crisp on the outside, greaseless, slightly salty, with the scallions adding a sweet flavor. 
Here, the pancake (50 cents) was imperfect -- somewhat tough, and scanty on the scallions. 
But the fried chicken wings, which tasted like they were marinated briefly in soy sauce and a splash of wine, were warm, crisp and greaseless (two for 50 cents).
The other purveyor of scallion pancakes was Sung M. Wong, No. 19890, who operated in front of 228 Canal Street. 
His pancakes looked like the others, were priced the same (50 cents each), but were much closer to the ideal of crisp outside and tender within.
He also sold one of the most ancient of Chinese snacks, the dumpling or jiao tze, a pleated pouch traditionally filled with minced cabbage and pork, and seasoned with ginger, soy sauce and sesame oil. 
The historical importance of the dumpling was discovered in the 1960's when the Chinese unearthed a pair of preserved dumplings that dated from the eighth or ninth century, the time of the Tang dynasty, which lasted from 618 to 907 A.D. More than 1,000 years later, the crescent shape of the jiao tze, and the number of pleats, is unchanged.
Here, the dough was thick, somewhat crude and chewy, but the filling of minced Chinese chives and pork, along with the highly familiar dash of MSG, was both pungent and tasty (four for $1).
Farther east down Canal Street is Mr. Lim, one of the friendlier vendors. 
He hovered over a stainless steel cart that is divided into compartments, each holding a different hot dish, none of which he had cooked. 
Instead, like the food vendors of the Sung dynasty, he bought the food from different restaurants or suppliers.
He offered rice gruel, also called jook; slippery rolled sheets of rice noodle; curried squid, and braised beef tripe cooked with turnip. 
The tripe, made into a honeycomb with chunks of white turnip, was cooked in a rich, aromatic broth of soy sauce, rice wine, garlic, ginger, soy sauce, water, sugar, salt and star anise. 
The tripe was tender, the turnip soft ($1.25 for a container). 
The food "is Hong Kong style," Mr. Lim said. 
To spot him, look for No. 16872.
Culinary treasures like roast ducks, soy sauce chickens, roast pork and braised barbecued pork are sold at bargain prices by Ying Chun Hui, whose cart, No. 16982, is usually in front of 208 Canal Street. 
But, surrounded by crowds, it's not hard to find.
One recent weekend, a woman waited in line to buy a duck to be presented as an offering at a temple. 
Another woman was struck by the prices, and said, "The duck is cheaper than Ollie's!"
She was referring to the popular chain of restaurants with three locations on the west side of Manhattan, where a whole roast duck sells for $17.50. 
At Kam Man, a Chinese grocery store at 200 Canal Street, the roast duck was $13. 
Mr. Hui sold ducks for $10 apiece -- and they were flawless. 
Each day, he said, he sells at least 20 ducks.
The skin was burnished and crisp, the tender meat subtly flavored by the marinade of scallions, garlic, bean sauce, soy sauce, chicken stock and sugar that filled the cavity of the duck as it roasted. 
(The same sauce is traditionally retained to be poured over the duck at serving time.)
The roast pork (not to be confused with the red-tinged strips of barbecued pork) had crisp, golden blistered skin -- like cracklings. 
When served, the pork is considered perfectly cooked when there are three distinct layers: the thick crunchy skin, a slender layer of sweet fat, and a thicker layer of lean yet moist meat ($5 a pound.) Mr. Hui's pork was perfect.
Who cooked these meats?
And where?
Mr. Hui would say only that the cook was a professional who moved from Hong Kong to New York and once worked in a local restaurant.
Scattered along Canal and the Bowery are vendors who sell egg-shaped cookies made from a batter of egg, flour, sugar and milk. 
They pour the batter into an iron griddle that has egg-shaped indentations and resembles a waffle iron. 
The cookies tasted like warm sponge cakes. 
Whenever an adult stood in line to buy the cookies (20 for $1), there was often a child hovering nearby, seeming to salivate.
At the corner of the Bowery and Bayard Street, in front of the National Westminster Bank, a husband and wife sold their specialty -- tripe and turnips -- which drew a steady line of customers, often six deep. 
The man, Chuck Au, said, "This is the best tripe."
Mr. Au was not a braggart; he spoke a humble gastronomic truth. 
The tripe almost melted in the mouth but still had a little crunch. 
The turnips were tender. 
But it was the flavor -- the classic combination of soy sauce, star anise and sugar -- that ran deep.
One customer bought four containers of tripe at $1.25 each. 
Others bought the rice gruel, which was subtly flavored with dried fish and blanched peanuts ($1). 
The cart is No. 16816.
When asked how their popular tripe was prepared, Mrs. Au, who did not want to give her first name, said, "Buy it, boil it and let it dry before you season it."
She paused, poured some water into the steam table, and said, "It's hard work."
But the results are delicious.

file: A Specialist In Esthetics Of Offbeat Violence.txt
text:
ï»¿
His films are notable for cascading glass, falling bodies and enough bullets to touch off a war. 
But John Woo, Hong Kong's most celebrated filmmaker, whose movies are almost operatic in their excess, insisted that the flamboyant violence stamping his work resembles a ballet, almost ethereal, even otherworldly.
"It's like dancing," the 51-year-old director remarked the other day as he nervously awaited the opening of "Face/Off," his most ambitious American film, starring John Travolta and Nicolas Cage, which opened No. 1 at the box office this weekend. 
"My actors are amusing and exciting. 
I grew up on films like 'Singin' in the Rain' and 'Seven Brides for Seven Brothers.'
That's what I want!
It's like a cartoon."
And the anarchic violence in his films?
The BBC once called Mr. Woo "the Mozart of mayhem."
"Violence in real life is horrid, frightening," Mr. Woo said. 
"The news on television is scary, not movies. 
Movies are fake, not real. 
People know the movies are not real."
Mr. Woo, who moved to Los Angeles five years ago to flee what he termed the creative constraints of Hong Kong, is now poised to become an American success story after a 1993 misstep with "Hard Target," starring Jean-Claude Van Damme, and the far more successful 1996 movie "Broken Arrow," with Mr. Travolta and Christian Slater.
Thus far, however, Mr. Woo's fame rests on Hong Kong movies that have been lauded by directors like Martin Scorsese and Quentin Tarantino. 
Films like "A Better Tomorrow" (1986), "The Killer" (1988) and "Hard Boiled" (1992) transformed the traditionally low-budget king-fu action genre into bizarrely over-the-top fantasies inevitably involving two men inextricably linked and hurtling toward a fatal collision.
"Face/Off," a film released by Paramount, which received the best reviews of Mr. Woo's career, is a weird saga involving a law enforcement officer, played by Mr. Travolta, who undergoes radical surgery to "borrow" the face of Mr. Cage, a psychopath bent on destroying Los Angeles. 
Mr. Travolta wants to find the site of a poison gas bomb. 
Of course, things go awry. 
Mr. Cage awakens from a coma with the face of Mr. Travolta. The film has Mr. Woo's trademarks: a dizzy plot, hypercharged editing, blunt religious symbolism, offbeat humor and unimaginably creepy villains. 
Subtlety is not Mr. Woo's strong point.
In its opening as No. 1 this weekend, the film grossed $22.7 million, said the Exhibitor Relations Company, which tracks ticket sales. 
It outflanked Disney's "Hercules" as well as "Batman and Robin," which was No. 3 at the box office and dropped off so sharply in its second week that it looms as a major disappointment.
Referring to the movie, Mr. Woo said the duality of good and evil is central to the film and to his work. 
"It's my usual theme, always good and evil mirroring each other," he said, in an office near the 20th Century Fox studios in West Los Angeles, where he is starting work on a new film. 
"I like imperfect characters. 
Perfect heroes bore me."
Mr. Woo's films, with their choreographed and often slow-motion violence, seem surprisingly funny and bloodless, as if all that killing were not horrific. 
His sources, he said, are rooted in films by directors of the 1950's and 60's: Sam Peckinpah, Stanley Kubrick, Akira Kurosawa, Alfred Hitchcock and Arthur Penn.
As Peter Rainer, chairman of the National Board of Film Critics, wrote last week in the newspaper New Times: "Woo openly courts -- and satisfies -- our primal desire to see people pulverized. 
Even five years ago his brand of mayhem might have seemed too way out for American audiences, but because of the increasingly heightened violence in our movies -- and especially because of the Hong Kong movie influence in the films of Quentin Tarantino -- Woo may soon be anointed as Hollywood's new crown prince of estheticized gore."
Mr. Woo said he moved to Los Angeles in 1992 partly because he felt stymied in Hong Kong -- "The Government in Hong Kong, the police, treat filmmakers like beggars" -- and partly to spend more time with his family. 
"I worked seven days a week in Hong Kong. 
My children hardly saw my face, they never really had a father and there were misunderstandings, difficulties," said Mr. Woo, a compact man with a wide smile and an open, engaging manner. 
"I was guilty, very guilty."
"Now I stay home after work," said Mr. Woo, who lives with his wife, 15-year-old son and two daughters, 17 and 20. 
"I try to be a good father. 
I cook for them."
Mr. Woo himself is part of a vanguard of Hong Kong filmmakers working increasingly in Los Angeles and clearly a bit uneasy about the end of colonial rule after 156 years when Britain hands the colony back to China on Tuesday. 
.
"Some people say it will be tough on the film business at first," he said. 
"There will be censorship, but perhaps this will be temporary. 
I don't see many problems."
Mike Simpson, senior vice president of the William Morris agency, which represents many of Hong Kong's top filmmakers, agreed that there was some nervousness within the movie business there -- as well as anticipation.
Among the filmmakers the agency represents are Mr. Woo; Jackie Chan, the action star of "Rumble in the Bronx" and "Supercop"; Chow Yun-Fat, a frequent star of Mr. Woo's films who is making his Hollywood debut early next year opposite Mira Sorvino in "The Replacement Killers"; Stanley Tong, director of "Rumble in the Bronx," who is now making "Mr. 
Magoo" for Disney, and Michelle Yeoh, one of Hong Kong's top female movie stars, who appears in the new James Bond film, "Tomorrow Never Dies."
"There is some feeling of apprehension or wariness, of uncertainty," Mr. Simpson said. 
"There's also a sense of excitement."
Mr. Simpson said the migration of Chinese talent to Los Angeles had little to do with the handover. 
"The level and quality of films made there just began to go down and down," he said. 
"They were remaking bad versions of good films they made earlier."
He also noted that American action films had simply usurped many Chinese-language films in the Asian marketplace in recent years, leading to a deteriorating financial base for Hong Kong films and a decline in quality.
As for Mr. Woo, he said his next movie, called "King's Ransom," which is set to start filming later in the year, is a comedy.
A John Woo comedy?
Mr. Woo smiled. 
"It's like the 1960's heist movies, like 'To Catch a Thief' or 'The Thomas Crown Affair,' " he said. 
"It will, I hope, be funny and charming and elegant. 
Only a little bit of shooting."

file: A Top Dissident Flees China And Is Admitted to the U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
A dissident who ranked third on the Chinese Government's list of "most wanted" student protesters after the 1989 Tiananmen Square demonstrations has been admitted to the United States after fleeing China, the White House confirmed today.
The dissident, Liu Gang, 35, was arrested in June 1989 and sentenced to six years in prison and two years' deprivation of political rights. 
From remote Lingyuan Labor-Reform Camp in Liaoning Province, he smuggled out a letter accusing the authorities of torturing him, and he staged several hunger strikes.
After his release in June 1995, he was kept in isolation in his remote hometown of Liaoyan, with his phone cut off. 
He said he was unable to find a job or to live with his family. 
He violated his parole last month to go to Beijing, and from there he was smuggled to the United States.
In a telephone interview from Cambridge, Mass., where he is staying, Mr. Liu said he arrived in Boston on Thursday. 
But he refused to describe his route, saying he does not want to jeopardize the safety of his relatives in China and Hong Kong.
He said he expected to stay in the United States and attend school.
"I've just applied to go to school now, to some universities in Boston and other places," said Mr. Liu, who has a master's degree in physics.
He has not applied for political asylum, officials said. 
He was allowed into the United States under a provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act allowing entry "temporarily for immediate emergency reasons or the public interest."
The United States and China are sparring over the spread of nuclear weapons, intellectual piracy, Taiwan and human rights, with the expectation that Washington will soon impose billions of dollars in sanctions on the weapons and piracy issues.
The White House spokesman, Michael D. McCurry, said the Liu case should not further damage relations with China. 
"We are confident we can maintain the broad constructive engagement with China which reflects the status of our current bilateral relations," he said.
Regarding Taiwan, the State Department spokesman, Nicholas Burns, confirmed a report in The Washington Post that senior American officials met with Taiwan's national security adviser, Ting Mou-Shih, on March 11 in New York, to urge Taiwan to avoid provocative actions during China's military exercises at that time.
The American officials were Under Secretary of State Peter Tarnoff and Samuel R. Berger, deputy national security adviser. 
The meeting was one of the highest-level contacts since 1979, when Washington broke off diplomatic relations with Taipei.
Mr. Burns said he was unaware of any formal Chinese expression of unhappiness about the meeting. 
"In light of the tensions in the Taiwan Strait," he said, "the U.S. 
Government believed it was important to communicate directly and at a high level with both the People's Republic of China and with Taiwan."

text:
ï»¿
INTERESTED in a trip around the world that will cost almost nothing?
You can visit this country without ever leaving Long Island.
Italy and China have always been easy destinations for hungry, value-conscious diners. 
Spain, Japan, Germany, Mexico, Greece, France, Ireland, India and Portugal have also become popular ports of call. 
But not until recently did Vietnam, Russia, Poland, Persia, El Salvador, the Dominican Republic, Turkey, Thailand and Afghanistan, among others, become accessible in terms of cuisine. 
Add some of the penny-wise, new American regional restaurants popping up locally and you have a diverse culinary chain on Long Island that circles the globe. 
The opportunity to eat your way around the world, without eating at all deeply into the family budget, is now a reality.
Most of the multi-national cuisine being served in Nassau and Suffolk originates in humble hang-outs brimming with authentic atmosphere that reflect each country's culture and spirit. 
In fact these ethnic spots, many of which are listed below, represent Long Island's best restaurant values.
Â 
AFGHANI
Kabul, at 1153 East Jericho Turnpike, in Huntington (549-5506), is one of the Island's most foreign restaurants, with its dissonant Middle-Eastern music, hanging leather and macrame lamps, hand-made rugs and filigreed curtains of hanging gourds. 
The most expensive entree, two lamb chops on a skewer, is also the best. 
But be sure to sample all the inexpensive appetizers, the aush soup, shish leek (a lamb and vegetable saute), sauteed pumpkin and all desserts.
Â 
CHINESE
There is no chow mein, chop suey, egg roll or egg foo young at the exceptional Fortune Wheel Seafood Restaurant in Levittown.
Asian and Western purists consider such menu mainstays gimmicky. 
Chinese food aficionados flock to the Fortune Wheel in the Nassau Mall at 3601 Hempstead Turnpike (579-4700), between Pathmark and Rickels. 
It is one of the Island's best choices for diners serious about Chinese meals. 
Although food of this sort is available in some Chinatown restaurants in Manhattan and Flushing, and many Hong Kong eating places, it is rarely found on the Island.
Â 
GERMAN
Koenig's, at 85 Tyson Avenue (354-2300), in Floral Park, has been serving mammoth portions of hefty, hearty, German food at modest prices for over a half century. 
It is especially well known for dishes like rouladen (rolled beef with onions, bacon, mustard and pickle), kassler rippchen, (smoked pork chops), a wurst platter of knackwurst, bauernwurst and bratwurst, tender beef goulash and pan-fried steak topped with crisp onions.
Â 
GREEK
The Mediterranean Snack Bar, a long-time local institution with the spirit of a neighborhood taverna, at 360 New York Avenue in Huntington (423-8982), gets my vote for the best bargain Greek restaurant on Long Island. 
This well- run, clean cafe, with its quick service, moderate prices and earthy authentic Greek dishes has, from its beginning, nearly a quarter of a century ago, had lines of diners waiting for tables. 
That is still the case, despite an expansion that doubled its capacity.
Although few of the expected Greek classics, like gyros, falafel, spanekopeta and moussaka are missing from the menu here, the Mediterranean Snack Bar excels with seafood.
The owner is a knowledgeable fisherman with a feel for the preparation of fish. 
In fact, he catches many of the blue fish, striped bass and other local varieties served at this store-front spot.
Â 
INDIAN
Soothing sitar music fills the air, tuxedoed waiters glide by, diners savor an array of dishes in an atmosphere of elegant serenity, amidst ornate Indian antiques, temple carvings and art. 
Bombay?
Calcutta?
Manhattan?
No, Jericho Turnpike in Syosset at mid-day, where an elaborate Indian buffet is served seven days a week at the Jewel of India, 347 Jericho Turnpike (677-9898).
This dinner-sized lunch costs $8.95 weekdays and $9.95 on weekends when it is even more bountiful. 
It is one of the Island's most outstanding luxury-value combinations. 
The Syosset restaurant is the Island branch of the well-regarded Jewel of India, which has been serving classic Indian cuisine in Manhattan for more than six years (a similar lunch costs $13.95 there).
The buffet, with soup, eight hot dishes, salad bar and condiments aplenty, provides an opportunity to sample from dishes that are familiar and foreign, spicy hot and mild and assertive and subtle. 
That is an especially welcome prospect for those who want to try Indian cuisine but are not secure enough to order any single dish.
Â 
IRISH
Dublin Delights Cafe, 244 Lake Avenue, St. James (862-6900), is a tiny sparkling shamrock of a place. 
Behind its multi-paned cottage windows are just six tables and a small bar. 
Inside the bright, cheery, clean cafe, diners in sweaters, plaid shirts and jeans eat Irish and English style pub food considerably superior to that usually found in Dublin or London. 
The wee Irish gem, hidden away in a shopping center, serves authentic dishes like bubble and squeak, shepherd's pie, Lancashire pot pie, Scotch eggs and, of course, corned beef and cabbage.
Â 
JAPANESE
Japanese food lovers and haters will find Restaurant Yamaguchi at 63 Main Street (883-3500) in Port Washington to their liking. 
Many familiar Japanese standbys are available as entrees or in smaller portions as appetizers. 
Tempuras, shrimp and vegetable, are lacy, crisp and delectable. 
Negima-yaki, tender beef rolled around scallions, broiled and served with teriyaki, is also done well at Yamaguchi as is sushi and sashimi. 
Conservative diners will find happiness with the tenderloin steak spiked by a tasty mustard sauce.
Restaurant Yamaguchi has wide appeal for its high quality food, inviting atmosphere, affordable prices and caring staff.
Â 
MEXICAN
Everything at Los Compadres, 243 Walt Whitman Road, Huntington Station (351-8384), is plastic, except the food. 
That means that the clean, modest Mexican luncheonette style restaurant is quite different from most of its suburban counterparts. 
The restaurant has a brisk takeout business at the same counter where sit-down diners place their orders. 
In fact, its slogan is "The Hottest Takeout in Town."
But whether eating in or taking out at this fast service spot with sombreros on the walls and a neon sign in the window, the prices are amazing, the greeting is friendly and the food says Mexico.
Â 
PORTUGUESE
The 100-seat Churrasquiera Bairrada, at 144 Jericho Turnpike in Mineola (739-3856), is a very different type Portuguese spot, with its wood-burning barbecue and herb-flavored authentic dishes like roast suckling pig and kid. 
Two people can split a whole barbecued chicken, accompanied by salad, rice, potatoes and vegetables for $14.95 or order rodizio, a dinner of unlimited quantities of five to seven meats served on skewers and presented tableside. 
It is accompanied by all the chopped cabbage or other green vegetable, black beans, rice and fried bananas anyone desires.
Â 
REGIONAL AMERICAN
The Cooke's In serves far more food than anyone has a right to expect for the prices it charges. 
Generosity, warmth and smiles are the keynotes at this modest storefront at 210 Depot Road in Huntington Station (424-2181). 
The restaurant specializes in hearty down-home Southern and American heartland dishes. 
Diners receive a complimentary fruit starter, bottomless glasses of iced tea and cups of coffee, both sweet and white potatoes, an entree, warm crusty bread, a family style bowl of salad, two vegetables and whatever else Juanita Cooke, the chef and owner, happens to have on hand.
Two entrees -- Southern fried chicken, four sizable pieces, and fried catfish with a zippy barbecue-like dipping sauce (both $8.95) -- boast light herb-infused crisp coatings that encase moist meat running with juices.
Â 
RUSSIAN
Russian restaurants have always been rare on Long Island. 
But the sparkling 40-seat storefront Cafe Samovar, opened by a warm, hospitable Russian family, at 2245 Long Beach Road in Oceanside (764-7676), has the potential to be around for quite a while.
Its hearty specialties consistently provide the earthy flavor bang of peasant food from Russia's heartland. 
Especially impressive are the pirogis ($5.25), varenikis ($4.95) and pelminis ($4.95), dumplings of various sizes and shapes.
Â 
SALVADORAN
Rincon Guanaco, a gleaming luncheonette-style storefront in Copaigue at 492 Oak Street (264-0324) is the largest and most accessible of a growing number of Central and South American restaurants to open on the Island.
Although this restaurant Salvadoreno, like the others, appeals mainly to Hispanic people who have settled in the region in recent years, an increasing number of adventurous longtime residents are visiting it as well. 
They are attracted by its tasty food, rock-bottom prices and warm atmosphere.
This bilingual restaurant knows what it is about, and that is reproducing the dishes of El Salvador. 
Included among them is the country's national dish, pupusas. 
A pupusa is made up of two corn or masa tortillas that form a pita-like pocket stuffed with the Central American version of chicharron -- pork, tomatoes and spices that are virtually cooked into a spread -- and warmed on a comal, or Mayan pottery griddle.
Â 
THAI
Siam Lotus again proves that good things come in small packages. 
The tiny Bay Shore restaurant at 1664 Union Boulevard (968-8196), jump starts bored palates with some of the best Thai food on the Island. 
The winning formula is familiar. 
The owners are ever-present. 
The husband is in the front and the wife in the kitchen. 
He is a gracious host and waiter and she is a talented chef.
Portions here are smaller than those at Chinese restaurants, but prices are rock bottom, enabling patrons to sample many dishes.
Â 
TURKISH
Although most Middle Eastern restaurants are modest storefront spots, the new Medeast Chalet at 5 Railroad Avenue in Roslyn (621-7975), has retained the enchanting Early American charm of the previous occupant, The Chalet. 
Despite its rugged stone taproom, appealing fireplaces and tree-covered deck, the prices here are modest (most entrees cost between $12 and $16) and much of the food delivers a flavor rush from the first bite. 
This is an Eastern Mediterranean restaurant specializing in tasty Turkish dishes, especially those that feature eggplant.
Â 
VIETNAMESE
Although a number of hole-in-the-wall Vietnamese spots have failed on the Island, Maxia, in Bethpage might well have staying power.
This modestly priced Southeast Asian outpost at 560 Stewart Avenue (942-0776) is an authentic place to sample Vietnamese cooking, which has its own distinctive character. 
It is a lighter, more subtle Chinese spinoff with Indonesian, French and Thai overtones that stress ingredients like fish sauce, coconuts and coconut milk, white rice, lemongrass, cilantro, cinnamon and plum sauce.
Although many of the dishes look and sound like familiar Chinese favorites, they rarely taste the same. 
The greaseless chicken spring roll ($3.95) starter, for example, a mix of mushrooms, chicken and shrimp cooked with oyster sauce, rock sugar, sesame oil and white pepper, among other ingredients, is quite different from its Chinese counterpart. 
Even fried won tons ($2.45), a Chinese standard-bearer, contain an intricate blend of honey, cilantro, dried bean curd and the ever-present fish sauce at their meaty middles.

file: A VISIT FROM CHINA_ NEW SPY CASE_Intelligence Report Points To 2d China Nuclear Leak.txt
text:
ï»¿
In early 1996, the United States received a startling report from one of its Chinese spies. 
Officials inside China's intelligence service, the spy said, were boasting that they had just stolen secrets from the United States and had used them to improve Beijing's neutron bomb, according to American officials.
The spy had provided reliable information in the past, and officials said investigators took the report seriously.
China first built and tested a neutron warhead in the 1980's, using what American officials have said publicly was secret data stolen from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California, one of America's key nuclear weapons laboratories.
But the design did not work properly. 
American officials say that China's 1988 test of the neutron bomb, which kills people with enhanced radiation while leaving buildings intact, was not successful.
Now, the spy was suggesting, Chinese agents had solved the problem by coming back to the United States in 1995 to steal more secrets. 
The spy even provided details of how the information was transferred from the United States to China, officials said.
The report prompted a Federal criminal investigation, but American officials say they have found no evidence that China has produced an improved neutron bomb.
Samuel R. Berger, who is now the National Security Adviser, was first told of a possible new theft of neutron bomb data in 1996, according to officials who took part in the meeting or read the highly classified materials used to prepare for it.
The briefing, these officials said, came weeks after the Federal Bureau of Investigation gave the Energy Department a report about the spy's information.
David C. Leavy, a spokesman for the National Security Council, said that Mr. Berger and another N.S.C. official who attended the 1996 briefing do not believe the neutron bomb issue was mentioned. 
Mr. Leavy said that Mr. Berger did not learn of the suspicions until a more detailed briefing in July 1997.
The spy's report arrived as American intelligence agencies were examining a separate suspected Chinese espionage coup: the theft of designs of America's most modern nuclear warhead, the W-88.
The disclosure of this previously unknown 1996 intelligence report about the neutron bomb is significant for several reasons.
Until now, Clinton Administration officials have portrayed reports of China's nuclear spying as an old story.
In a series of public statements, Administration officials have emphasized that the loss of the W-88 design occurred in the 1980's, which was while Republicans held the White House. 
They have suggested that there is no evidence that Chinese nuclear spying continued into the Clinton Administration.
They have also said that President Clinton acted quickly in response to concerns about security breaches at the nuclear weapons laboratories by issuing a Presidential order in February 1998.
Accounts by Government officials about the neutron bomb case call both assertions into question.
According to the officials, the April 1996 briefing of Mr. Berger included evidence of the theft of the W-88 design, the need to increase security at the weapons laboratories and the report about the loss of neutron bomb data.
The White House said Mr. Berger did not tell the President or take any further action until more than a year later, in July 1997, when he received a more detailed briefing about the W-88 theft, the neutron bomb and the ongoing Chinese espionage.
Soon after, Mr. Leavy said, Mr. Berger told the President about the security weaknesses at the laboratories and China's spying. 
Asked whether he mentioned the neutron bomb case, Mr. Leavy would reply only that he did not detail "each and every allegation."
A bipartisan Congressional report on China's acquisition of United States technology includes a detailed, but still secret, account of Beijing's efforts to obtain neutron bomb secrets, including reports of efforts during the Clinton Presidency. 
But Government officials say that the Clinton Administration is resisting requests from Congress to make the more recent material public.
Mr. Leavy said the Administration is cooperating with Congress to declassify as much material as possible consistent with law enforcement and intelligence requirements.
Several agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Central Intelligence Agency and the Energy Department are continuing to examine the case.
The F.B.I. has not identified a suspect in the case.
The April 1996 briefing came at a critical moment in U.S.-China relations.
The Clinton Administration's continuing effort to expand commercial and diplomatic ties with China had been upset by Beijing's test in March of missiles off the coast of Taiwan.
Mr. Berger has said that the April 1996 briefing was not sufficiently detailed to prompt action.
Appearing on NBC's "Meet the Press" last month, he said the information he was told three years ago was "very general and very preliminary."
In addition, he said, "we did not have a suspect" in the theft of the W-88 technology.
But other officials offered a different account of Mr. Berger's briefing. 
The White House said it believes the briefing occurred on April 13, 1996, but is not sure of the exact date and has no records of what was said that day.
The officials said the briefing was more detailed than Mr. Berger has described and was the culmination of a five-month inter-agency study of the W-88 theft and related issues. 
"It was a pretty specific briefing," one American official who was present said.
Charles Curtis, the Deputy Secretary of Energy, led the Energy Department's delegation at the White House briefing. 
The main briefer was Notra Trulock, then the Energy Department's chief of intelligence.
Mr. Trulock's briefing, officials said, specifically covered the theft of the W-88 technology and concluded that China had likely obtained data about the miniaturized warhead, officials said.
The officials said Mr. Berger was also told that investigators had identified a prime suspect in the theft and would shortly turn their information over to the F.B.I. for a formal criminal inquiry.
Mr. Berger and Mr. Curtis agreed that the Congressional intelligence committees would be briefed on the W-88 matter following the referral to the F.B.I. 
(Congress was informed that summer.)
According to the officials, the 1996 White House briefing also discussed how the stolen technology could fit into Beijing's nuclear strategy. 
Mr. Trulock suggested that China could use the W-88 technology as part of a plan to rely on the mobility of truck-launched missiles with small warheads to better survive nuclear attacks, officials said.
At the end of the April briefing, officials said, Mr. Trulock said there was new information that China may recently have stolen neutron bomb data. 
He was referring to the spy's report, which had been received by the Energy Department from the F.B.I. on March 27, 1996, the officials said.
The neutron bomb intelligence was "hot off the press," and it was included to warn the White House of the possibility of continuing Chinese espionage, one official said.
Mr. Curtis told Mr. Trulock at the meeting to follow up the neutron bomb information with a broader inquiry into Chinese espionage efforts at the weapons labs, one official said.
The Energy Department completed an analysis of the neutron bomb case in July 1996, and it unearthed some intriguing connections. 
The study, officials said, raised the possibility that the chief suspect in the W-88, a computer scientist in Los Alamos, had also been involved in the transfer to China of neutron bomb secrets.
The suspect, Wen Ho Lee, was dismissed from his job last month after the Energy Department said he violated security regulations. 
No criminal charges have been filed against him. 
Officials said the F.B.I. has investigated the Energy Department's theory but has not been able to establish that Mr. Lee has any connection to the neutron bomb case.
As they investigated further, Energy Department officials discovered that Mr. Lee had attended a classified meeting in 1992 in which solutions to the neutron bomb's design flaw were discussed, officials said.
The F.B.I., officials said, had also found that Mr. Lee had made at least one telephone call to the scientist at Lawrence Livermore who was suspected of having provided the Chinese with the original neutron bomb data in the late 1970's and early 1980's.
According to the F.B.I.'s informant, Chinese officials were boasting in 1995 about obtaining new data from the United States but did not specifically mention the Government's weapons laboratories. 
American officials say the F.B.I. has not found any evidence linking the weapons laboratories to the suspected theft of neutron bomb secrets.
Government officials said it is difficult to evaluate China's progress on developing a neutron bomb because they have not detected any testing of such a weapon since 1996, when Beijing agreed to a moratorium on tests.
The informant's report, however, was one of several pieces of intelligence pointing to the vulnerability of the laboratories to espionage.
In November 1996, shortly before he left the Government, Mr. Curtis ordered a series of measures to tighten security. 
But the White House was apparently not notified of Mr. Curtis's directives, most of which were ignored or delayed by Energy Department officials.
In July 1997 Mr. Trulock returned to the White House to present his wider findings to Mr. Berger, who had become Mr. Clinton's National Security Adviser.
Mr. Berger, in turn, now says that that briefing prompted him to tell Mr. Clinton about China's nuclear espionage and concerns about lab security. 
But late last year, in a sworn reply to the select House commitee headed by Christopher Cox, a Republican from California, Mr. Berger said the President was not told about the espionage until 1998.
Asked to explain the discrepancy, Mr. Leavy said "after the Cox Committee process we've remembered more."
Mr. Clinton has said that he was not aware of any Chinese espionage taking place during his Administration.
"To the best of my knowledge, no one has said anything to me about any espionage which occurred by the Chinese against the labs, during my Presidency," he said at a news conference last month.
Mr. Leavy declined to say whether Mr. Clinton has been briefed on the intelligence about the possible theft of neutron bomb data during his Presidency.
Two months ago, Mr. Cox and the ranking Democrat on the committee, Norm Dicks of Washington, wrote President Clinton requesting a meeting to discuss their report. 
Mr. Leavy said the White House was working on scheduling a meeting. 
The committee has completed its work but is still consulting with the Administration over how much of its final report can be made public.Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: Administration Details Defense Of Controls on Satellite Exports.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Clinton Administration mounted the most detailed defense of its satellite export control policy today. 
Three top officials said that China's military had not benefited from transfers of sensitive American technology and that safeguards were in place to prevent any such leakage.
The spirited rebuttals by senior officials from the Departments of Commerce, State and Defense marked a counteroffensive against a growing Republican-led attack on the Administration's handling of satellite exports to China, a policy that Republicans have charged threatens American national security.
"We do not believe that the commercial space launch activities that have been authorized by licenses and monitored under these procedures have benefited China's missile or military satellite companies," John D. Holum, an acting undersecretary of state, told a House hearing today.
And Jan M. Lodal, the principal deputy undersecretary of defense for policy, said, "The current system protects national security."
The Administration officials said intelligence agencies have found no proof that any sensitive technology was transferred to the Chinese military through normal licensing channels. 
They asserted that adequate safeguards were in place to protect against that. 
But they did not rule out that there might have been unauthorized transfers. 
That is a question the Justice Department is looking into in the case of two American satellite companies.
But critics say it is very hard to tell whether there was a transfer of technology because the Chinese missiles that launch American satellites are very similar to the Chinese missiles that carry nuclear warheads. 
Improving the reliability of the commercial missiles might help the Chinese military, even inadvertently, with its nuclear program.
Despite the united front at today's hearings, cracks of dissension within the Administration's ranks and among usually loyal Democrats broke through.
The Government's arms control agency warned last year that waiving a ban on satellite exports to China to entice Beijing to curb missile sales had accomplished "nothing."
The warning by the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency, contained in a memorandum apparently sent to State Department officials, was made public at the House hearing. 
The memo undercut a fundamental reason for granting waivers to allow satellite exports to China despite a ban imposed after the 1989 massacre in Tiananmen Square.
"History has proven that the only time we have gotten movement from the Chinese on missile proliferation has been in the face of a penalty being imposed," the memo said. 
"Carrots have gotten us nothing."
But the agency's advisory was not included in the State Department's official recommendation to the White House earlier this year. 
President Clinton approved the waiver last February, despite objections from the Justice Department that it would undermine an ongoing criminal inquiry into whether two satellite makers divulged sensitive information to Chinese rocket scientists.
Mr. Holum, who also heads the arms control agency, told an unusual joint hearing of two House committees, National Security and International Relations, that the warning was not adopted because "it would have been very disruptive" to broader American commercial interests.
In an afternoon Senate hearing, Senator Max W. Cleland of Georgia became one of the first Democrats to openly criticize the White House's shift of licensing authority for all commercial satellites to the Commerce Department from the State Department in 1996. 
"I've got more and more concern about Commerce becoming the lead dog here," said Senator Cleland. 
"I'd rather hedge my bets and put national security first and commerce second."
The back-to-back hearings over seven hours featuring the Administration witnesses capped a frenzied day on Capitol Hill over the wide-ranging China accusations, and came just a week before Mr. Clinton visits China.
The Director of Central Intelligence, George J. Tenet, updated the House Intelligence Committee in a closed, two-and-a-half hour briefing on a series of conflicting Government assessments. 
They involve whether two satellite makers who are the focus of the Justice inquiry -- Loral Space & Communications and Hughes Electronics -- jeopardized national security by discussing results of their independent review of a failed launch of a satellite on a Chinese Long March missile in February 1996.
With little dissension, the House approved a resolution, 409 to 10, to create a special select committee to lead its inquiry on the China accusations. 
The 10 who voted against the resolution were Democrats.
Despite bipartisan backing for the resolution, Democrats criticized Republicans during the debate for spending too much money on duplicate investigations of President Clinton and Democratic fund-raising practices. 
And they expressed concern that the work of the select committee would fall captive to what they labeled a Republican witchhunt to tarnish Mr. Clinton and curry favor with conservative voters.
At the House and Senate hearings, Administration officials said allowing American satellites to be launched on Chinese rockets was a "wise" policy inititally set by Republican Presidents Ronald Reagan and George Bush to help make up for a shortage of American launching services.
And by transferring commercial satellite licensing authority to the Commerce Department, the Clinton aides said, the Administration was completing a shift that President Bush started in 1992. 
In a nutshell, the State Department considers national security implications for sensitive exports, while the Commerce Department also weighs American commercial interests.
Or, as William A. Reinsch, undersecretary of commerce for export administration, told Senators: "Commerce is an open, transparent, time-sensitive approach. 
State's is not. 
We've developed a 'process-friendly' " approach.
The General Accounting Office said the shift in licensing authority had loosened controls of satellite exports. 
But Mr. Reinsch disagreed, saying the Administration had added safeguards, including a broader role for the Pentagon and intelligence agencies to review export applications. 
Critics say those protections still fall far short of the State Department's regime.
"The existing Commerce licensing system fully protects our national security and foreign policy concerns," Mr. Reinsch said.

file: After Four Decades of Bitterness, China and Taiwan Plan to Meet.txt
text:
ï»¿
An envoy from Taiwan today concluded five days of talks with mainland China officials, clearing the way for a historic meeting between senior representatives of each side to try to turn four decades of enmity into a cooperative future.
The meeting will mark the first time since 1949 -- when the Communists defeated the Nationalist Government and forced it to flee to Taiwan -- that top representatives of the two rival Governments get together to discuss their differences. 
Officials from both sides said they expected the meeting to be held in Singapore, and China said it would take place on April 27 and 28.
Â 
Opening a Dialogue
The meeting is not expected to deal with the weightiest questions between Taiwan and mainland China, like possible reunification. 
But it is intended to result in cooperation between the rival Governments to fight crime and smuggling and to protect the investments on the mainland by Taiwanian businesses.
Perhaps most important, the talks will begin a high-level dialogue between rivals who regularly shelled each other throughout the 1950's, 60's and 70's. 
Both sides officially regard Taiwan as part of China, and each claims to be the legitimate government of all China. 
Even now, tensions remain high, and the mainland openly reserves the right to attack Taiwan.
There has been occasional talk of possible secret meetings between the sides in the 1980's but there is no evidence that they ever took place.
Chinese television news showed a beaming Wang Daohan, who will lead the Chinese delegation to the Singapore talks, pumping the hand of Cheyne J. Y. Chiu, a former Taiwan presidential aide. 
Mr. Chiu returned tonight to Taipei to brief Taiwanian leaders including C. F. Koo, a member of the governing Nationalist Party's highest echelon, who will lead the Taiwanian delegation to the talks in Singapore.
Mr. Wang is a former Mayor of Shanghai who heads the Chinese organization that deals with practical problems relating to Taiwan, like repatriating criminals, smuggling across the Taiwan Strait and inheritance of property. 
Mr. Koo, a close associate of President Lee Teng-hui, is in charge of a similar organization in Taiwan.
President Lee has cautioned that the talks in Singapore are mainly intended to build mutual trust.
"We must be very patient in forging rapprochement with the mainland," Mr. Lee said recently. 
"Exchanges across the Taiwan Strait remain at non-official levels and the Koo-Wang meeting aims to resolve administrative and technical problems arising from such exchanges."
The meeting will come at a time when Taiwan's relationship with the mainland seems to be at a crossroads, perhaps a dangerous crossroads.
On the one hand, economic and cultural contacts across the 100-mile Taiwan Strait are growing rapidly. 
A Chinese Peking Opera troupe just left to perform in Taipei, and bilateral trade last year -- almost all via third places like Hong Kong -- rose nearly 28 percent to a record $7.4 billion.
On the other hand, many people on Taiwan say they do not want the mainland back even if it is offered to them. 
The first direct presidential election on Taiwan is to be held in 1996, and it is possible -- though unlikely -- that an opposition candidate will win and call for Taiwan to declare itself an independent nation, separate from the Chinese mainland.
China has repeatedly said that in such circumstances it will use military force to prevent Taiwan from becoming independent. 
A Hong Kong magazine, The Mirror, which has good ties to Beijing, recently published what it said was a confidential speech by Deng Xiaoping, China's senior leader, underscoring the threat of military intervention.
"The two sides must be unified," the magazine quoted Mr. Deng as saying.
"If Taiwan engages in 'one China, one Taiwan' or in Taiwan independence, if it colludes with foreign forces to interfere in China's internal affairs, we'll have no choice," Mr. Deng reportedly added. 
"We'll have to use force to solve the Taiwan question."
Â 
Trading and Visiting
Mr. Deng acknowledged that such intervention would force China to pay an enormous price, but he added, "We must pay, and we can afford the cost."
Taiwan and mainland China have no formal relations and no direct flights or other transportation links. 
But Taiwan seems to be moving toward permitting some direct links, perhaps within the next year, and there are growing calls for an informal mechanism for handling problems arising from the booming trade and tourism across the Taiwan Strait.
According to accounts in the official Chinese press of the meetings in the last few days, both sides agreed to establish "a systematic channel for exchanges."
This is likely to include an informal Taiwan office in Beijing, with Taiwan representatives.
During the discussions in Beijing, leaders of each side initialed agreements that will speed registered mail between Taiwan and China and that will make it easier for a notarized document from one place to be recognized in the other.
The opposition party in Taiwan, the Democratic Progressive Party, has warned that Taiwan Nationalists and the Chinese Communists may reach a secret agreement for eventual reunification. 
Its requests to sit in on the talks in Singapore have been rejected by both sides.

file: AIDE TO FIRST LADY WAS GIVEN CHECK AT WHITE HOUSE.txt
text:
ï»¿
The chief of staff to Hillary Rodham Clinton accepted a $50,000 donation to the Democratic Party in 1995 in the White House from a California businessman who has emerged as a central figure in the criminal and Congressional investigations into improper fund-raising by the Democrats, Administration officials said tonight.
The donation by Johnny Chung through Margaret A. Williams to the Democratic National Committee is the first known instance in which a campaign check was handed to an Administration official at the White House during the last four years. 
It is likely to fuel criticism that the Clinton Administration had inadequate safeguards for separating politics and fund-raising from the business of governing.
A Federal law makes it "unlawful for any person to solicit or receive any contribution" in "any room or building occupied in the discharge of official duties," such as the White House. 
Just this week, Vice President Al Gore found himself on the defensive as he explained his occasional practice of telephoning potential donors from his office.
White House aides defended Miss Williams today, saying that she had simply passed along a check that was given to her by a frequent White House guest and devoted fan of Mrs. Clinton.
"This was legal and proper and she was following established procedures," said Ann Lewis, deputy White House communications director.
But it was unclear why Miss Williams did not tell Mr. Chung to give the check directly to the D.N.C. 
That same week, Mr. Chung met with D.N.C. officials in Washington, according to his lawyer.
Lawyers outside the Administration criticized the acceptance of a campaign contribution in the White House, and some questioned why Mr. Chung was giving a payment to a top aide to Mrs. Clinton rather than simply giving the check to officials at the D.N.C.
"It is totally improper," said Joseph E. diGenova, a Republican and former United States Attorney in Washington. 
"It is illegal to receive Federal campaign funds on property at the White House or at the Executive Office Building."
The payment by Mr. Chung was made the same week that he escorted some officials from the Chinese Government to a taping of President Clinton's weekly radio address at the White House. 
The group included Huang Jichun, the vice president of a Chinese conglomerate that trades weapons.
After that visit, President Clinton told his aides that he "wasn't sure we'd want photos of him with these people circulating around," according to a White House document made public last month.
And Robert L. Suettinger, a China specialist on the National Security Council, warned that Mr. Chung was "a hustler" who appeared "to be involved in setting up some kind of consulting operation that will thrive by bringing Chinese entrepreneurs into town for exposure to high-level U.S. officials."
Later that summer, Mr. Chung also tried to insert himself as a negotiator between Chinese and American officials after China imprisoned a leading critic of that country's human rights policy, Harry Wu. 
Mr. Suettinger then warned the White House that Mr. Chung could "conceivably do damage" to American-Chinese relations.
Referring to Mr. Chung and Miss Williams, Brian A. Sun, Mr. Chung's lawyer, said: "I can confirm that he had discussions with her about the donation in the First Lady's office. 
But I would not go so far as to describe it that she solicited the donation."
Mr. Sun said that Mr. Chung had discussions with Miss Williams and at least one other person in Mrs. Clinton's office "talking about the fact that the party needed help."
"But I will not say who said what to whom," Mr. Sun said.

file: Aides Meet Today on Dispute Over Sales to Iran and China.txt
text:
