The Commerce Department has scheduled an interagency meeting for Tuesday in a final effort to approve the sale of crop-duster aircraft to Iran and jet engines and satellite gear to China before President Bush leaves office, Administration officials said today.
The sales are strongly opposed by the Defense Department, which is worried about increasing the military power of the two countries, and about the precedent the sale could set for the export of even more advanced commercial equipment with potential military applications.
The Administration is also considering whether to allow the sale of a petrochemical factory to Iran but will not decide this issue on Tuesday. 
The factory would produce as a byproduct large quantities of hydrogen cyanide, a primitive chemical-warfare gas that, unlike a related chemical, potassium cyanide, is not considered militarily useful, an Administration official said this afternoon.
Â 
First Sale of Planes in Decade
If approved, the delivery of 10 single-seat crop-dusters to Iran would be the first sale of American aircraft to Teheran since the bombing of the United States Marine barracks in Lebanon in October 1983, when 241 Americans were killed. 
Iran was suspected of involvement in the bombing.
The jet engines are intended for use in Chinese military training aircraft, but a Defense Department analysis found that their components could also be used to build cruise missiles that could fly farther and carry a heavier payload than anything now in the Chinese arsenal.
The satellite gear consists of a cesium-beam laser component that would be used as a clock to coordinate other satellite systems.
Â 
Commerce vs. Defense
Federal law requires Government approval for the transfer of technology with potential military applications to nations that have Communist governments or have been labeled by the State Department as supporters of terrorism, as Iran has.
The approval process has deeply divided the Administration, three officials said.
The Commerce Department has advocated the sales as necessary to insure that United States businesses do not lose foreign markets.
State Department officials have been busy with the arms control agreement with Russia signed on Sunday and have not taken an active role in the dispute, said all three officials, who insisted on anonymity.
Â 
Some Find Consensus Unlikely
The Policy Coordinating Committee on technology transfers, which has representatives from the State, Defense and Commerce Departments, will meet Tuesday at the request of the Commerce Department to try to form a consensus on the sales. 
One official predicted that the committee would be unable to reach a consensus because of the Defense Department's concerns, and would forward the issue to a top interagency committee, which is unlikely to meet before Mr. Bush leaves office on Jan. 
20.
But another official said many in the Administration felt that because the sales deals had been struck during Mr. Bush's tenure, there was an obligation to resolve them rather than leave them to President-elect Bill Clinton.
The crop-dusters represent the most difficult issue because many people associated them with gas warfare.
Â 
Use in Gas Warfare Disputed
Iraq has long been rumored to have used crop-dusters to dump lethal chemical gases on Kurdish civilians, but no evidence has ever been found to prove that crop-dusters were used, said Anthony H. Cordesman, an adjunct professor of national security studies at Georgetown University. 
A recent study by the Defense Department and the Central Intelligence Agency found that crop-dusters would be very difficult to use for chemical warfare because the pilots would be likely to be killed by the gas.
The United States has already allowed the sale of several European jetliners with American parts to Iran, but has barred any sale of completely American-made planes. 
The Boeing Company tentatively agreed last year to sell nearly $1 billion worth of jetliners to Iran Air if American policy were to change and allow such sales.
If the United States does not sell the crop-dusters, other countries will do so, said Fred P. Ayres, the chairman and owner of the Ayres Corporation. 
The company, based in Albany, Ga., is seeking permission to export 10 of its Ayres Turbo Thrush crop-dusters to Iran. 
Poland and Russia are already leasing 100 crop-dusters to Iran, he said.

file: Amendment Killed, Way Is Cleared for China Trade Bill.txt
text:
ï»¿
With surprising and decisive ease, the Senate cleared the last major hurdle today to passing a trade bill with China and handing President Clinton one of his top remaining foreign policy goals.
Senators rejected a contentious amendment to impose sanctions on Chinese companies that export sophisticated weapons to hostile nations, setting the stage to vote in a few days on legislation to give China permanent normal trading privileges.
The amendment was defeated on a bipartisan vote, 65 to 32, after a furious last-minute lobbying campaign this week by pro-trade business leaders and several of Mr. Clinton's cabinet officers, who argued that the measure was redundant and could scuttle the bill.
The vote virtually assures that the Senate will join the House in ending the annual Congressional review of China's trade status, a ritual for 20 years that Beijing considers humiliating but that opponents argue is a lever for improving human rights. 
More than 70 senators are generally expected to vote for the overall bill.
"This is the big enchilada," said Senator Max Baucus of Montana, a pro-trade Democrat who led the fight against the amendment. 
"We've got it now."
Unlike the situation in the House, where the trade bill survived intense opposition from a coalition of labor and religious groups, final passage in the Senate was never been in doubt, only the course to get there.
Supporters of the legislation have pressed for a bill free of amendments because they say there is not enough time before Election Day to reconcile an amended Senate bill with the version that the House passed in May.
One after another, amendments to improve human rights, religious freedom and labor standards in China have fallen by lopsided votes this week, not because senators opposed them on merit but because of their potential harm to the underlying bill.
But the amendment sponsored by Fred Thompson, Republican of Tennessee, and Robert G. Torricelli, Democrat of New Jersey, to penalize Chinese companies that traffic in nuclear, chemical and biological weapons, as well as long-range missiles, struck a strong chord with lawmakers who are increasingly alarmed by intelligence reports of Chinese arms exports.
Under the amendment, the president would have been required to conduct an annual review of China's proliferation activities. 
If Chinese companies trafficked in the prohibited weapons, Mr. Clinton could have cut off sensitive technology exports and United States government loans or credits. 
The president could have waived the sanctions if it was in the national security interest of the United States.
"Senator Thompson is asking us to put national security ahead of greed," said Senator Robert C. Byrd, a West Virginia Democrat who supported the amendment. 
"What's wrong with that?"
Senator Mike DeWine, Republican of Ohio, added: "This amendment is not just about holding other nations accountable as proliferators. 
It is also about holding our President accountable as the world's principle proliferation enforcer."
But other senators, including Phil Gramm, Republican of Texas, voiced support for the overall bill and its trade benefits and objected to any amendments that could imperil them.
Mr. Thompson mocked Mr. Gramm for naively believing that trade could help reverse Beijing's penchant for selling missiles and missile technology to countries like North Korea and Pakistan.
"His response is trade with them, and one day we will magically wake up and they will be dismantling their armaments," said Mr. Thompson, who has clashed with Mr. Gramm in recent months over a bill to govern export controls. 
"When that happens, I will present the tooth fairy on the floor of this body."
Even after Mr. Thompson had watered down his amendment to address administration complaints that it focused too narrowly on China and that its sanctions would hurt American farmers, the Clinton administration strongly objected.
This week, several cabinet members, including Defense Secretary William S. Cohen and the national security adviser, Samuel R. Berger, telephoned senators who were wavering on the amendment, warning that it overlapped existing law and hindered the president's ability to compel China to curb proliferation.
In the end, 35 Democrats and 30 Republicans voted against Mr. Thompson's measure, while 23 Republicans and 9 Democrats voted for it. 
Several Republicans, who favored the amendment as a separate bill, including Thad Cochran of Mississippi, Connie Mack of Florida and Don Nickles of Oklahoma, voted against it as an amendment.
"This is it, it's settled, it's all over but for the shouting," said Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan, a New York Democrat who has championed the trade bill.
After the vote, Mr. Thompson's aides said he had not ruled out bringing up the measure again before the Senate adjourns.
The United States and China reached agreement last fall on a deal to help pave China's eventual entry into the World Trade Organization, the 135-member trade group that sets the rules for global commerce. 
China will enter the W.T.O. no matter how the Senate votes. 
But without Congress's blessing, Beijing could withhold some of the trade benefits, including lower tariffs, from the American farmers and companies that it will extend to other members of the trade group.
Business leaders hailed the surprisingly wide margin of the vote and predicted speedy passage of the overall bill, perhaps as early as Thursday.

file: American Deported From China Kept Secret Diary of Life in Jail.txt
text:
ï»¿
"I lied to them," said the human rights campaigner Harry Wu, leaning forward in his study today as he recounted his two months of imprisonment in China, "and so what?"
"I said that if they released me I would stay away from politics and have a good life with my wife," he said in an interview just hours after his expulsion from China and return to his home here, 30 miles south of San Francisco.
Mr. Wu, whose arrest had become an irritant in United States-Chinese relations, declined to say whether he would continue his secret forays into China investigating forced labor camps. 
But he said would continue his human rights work.
"Why should I be honest with them?" he said. 
"I deal with men as men deal with me, and they lied to me from the very beginning."
And then he turned to politics, and the decision by Hillary Rodham Clinton to attend a women's conference in Beijing next month.
"She had to judge by herself to go or not to go," he said. 
"But if my release is part of a deal, if this is a condition for Mrs. Clinton to go to China, I will be angry about it."
He added: "The release of Harry Wu does not mean the Chinese human rights record has improved. 
The police told me, 'You are lucky you are an American citizen.'
This made me very sad."
In a detailed account of his ordeal, Mr. Wu said he was keenly aware of the special treatment he received as an American. 
He was kept in an air-conditioned room in a medical building, was fed the same food as his guards and was told to shave before the monthly visits of an American consular official.
Mr. Wu, 58, who spent 19 years in Chinese camps as a young man before coming to the United States in 1985 and becoming a citizen, has made a career of publicizing abuses in the labor camp system, returning in secret to China four times to compile his reports.
It was during his most recent visit, on June 19, that he was seized at the border. 
This week he was convicted of spying and stealing state secrets and sentenced to 15 years of imprisonment and expulsion. 
Immediately after his sentence was read, he said, the judge smiled, patted him on the arm, and told him he could go home.
Today was Mr. Wu's chance to tell the story of his most recent stint in a Chinese prison, in the first person, and his words began flowing before he had even taken his seat -- about the cell he was forced to share with three guards, the duel he played with his interrogators, and the secret diary he kept, in tiny Chinese characters, in the inner margins of a fat Chinese-English dictionary.
An expert on the tricks prisoners play, Mr. Wu made a thin glue from rice and water and sealed the inner edges of the pages together to hide his journal entries. 
As he gingerly pulled them apart today, his hidden chronicle of pressures and interrogation sprang to light.
The page numbers denoted the month and day of the entry. 
On page 704, July 4, two weeks after his arrest, the entry reads: "Got fresh air for the first time."
Page 710, July 10, reads: "They take away my ring and my watch. 
I request medicine. 
I protest that I wrote a letter to my wife and they did not send it."
July 11: "Talked to them about my back pain."
July 18: "Two doctors from the medical university examined me. 
Talked about my counter-revolutionary crimes from 10 to 12 o'clock. 
Afternoon interrogation about my activities in China in 1994."
Mr. Wu said he broke his back in a coal mine accident while serving in a labor camp 20 years ago. 
As a result, he said, without medication his left leg was in constant pain.
At the start of his two months of interrogations, Mr. Wu said, "I played it tough because I didn't know what they wanted. 
They said, 'Do you know what is your problem?
You have caused us big trouble. 
We have wanted you for a long time.'
"I said, 'Here I am, like meat on the chopping block for you. 
Whatever you want, you can chop."'
Later, he said, he asked his interrogators, "Why are you doing this?
You are making me a hero. 
Are you crazy?
Maybe my books will sell well again."
The interrogations focused on television documentaries he had made about conditions in Chinese labor camps, Mr. Wu said, and he won some points and lost some points.
"I admitted violating the law," he said. 
"It is true. 
If America has a speed limit of 55 and China has a speed limit of 40 and you go 55 in China, then you break the law. 
If a watchtower is a secret and you film the watchtower, what can I say?"
Last night, with the time change and the exhilaration of his release, Mr. Wu said, he could hardly sleep. 
Only hours before, he had expected to spend the next 15 years in prison.
"But something funny happened," Mr. Wu said today. 
"After the sentence was read, they did not put handcuffs on me. 
The police very kindly said, 'Now we can go.'
"
Within two days, Mr. Wu said, he was put on a Chinese commercial flight from Shanghai to San Francisco.
"As soon as I boarded, the door closed, and an hour later the American consul was informed of my departure," Mr. Wu said. 
"Everything was prearranged. 
A pretty good show."

file: Americans Enjoy 70 Healthy Years, Behind Europe, U.N. Says.txt
text:

The United States falls behind almost every country in Europe as well as Canada, Australia and Israel in what the World Health Organization calls "healthy life expectancy," according to a report released today.
With the report, the organization joins a trend toward measuring life expectancy in a new way, for the first time factoring in the diseases and disabilities that are likely to rob people of a lifetime of good health.
By this adjusted measure, Japan leads the world in healthy life expectancy, according to W.H.O., which is part of the United Nations system. 
A Japanese citizen can expect to lead a life of 74.5 healthy years, it said. 
At the very bottom of the scale is battered Sierra Leone, where a child born in 1999 can expect to live a healthy life of fewer than 26 years.
Almost every country with a healthy life expectancy below 40 is in Africa, where AIDS and warfare are lowering life spans significantly. 
The group estimates that H.I.V.-AIDS has cut 15 to 20 years off life expectancy in southern Africa, and 5 to 10 years in other parts of the continent.
As in other measures of well-being, the study found, the United States loses ground against other industrial nations because it has its own "third worlds" within its population. 
Not surprisingly, the health agency says, years lost to disease, injury and other disabilities are substantially higher in poorer countries, and poorer communities in richer nations.
The new study lists poor health among American minorities, the effects of AIDS, tobacco-related cancers, heart disease and violence as factors in reducing a healthy life expectancy in the United States.
At the Population Reference Bureau, a private demographic research organization in Washington, Carl Haub, who compiles annual statistics on world population, said the American ranking is not particularly surprising.
"We have a 25 percent minority population that has lower life expectancies," he said, adding that even by traditional measures of mortality, the United States does not rank among the nations with the highest levels of longevity. 
"If you look at the U.S. by ethnic group, you see a somewhat different result. 
African-Americans in the U.S. have a much lower life expectancy, particularly males."
Using traditional methods, the United States had a life expectancy of 76.7 years in 1998, Mr. Haub said, with men at 73.9 years and women at 79.4.
The World Health Organization table of healthy life expectancy lowers the level to 70 years for Americans overall, with 67.5 years for men and 72.6 years for women.
Nicholas Eberstadt, who follows demographic surveys at the American Enterprise Institute in Washington, said there has been a trend, beginning in Europe, to add new dimensions to the study of longevity. 
"There has been an enormous amount of work done on healthy life expectancy," he said. 
"Some of these efforts have been inventive, but none have been particularly compelling."
Mr. Eberstadt said that a number of surveys have factored in perceptions about health and well-being among populations, which can vary dramatically from one country or region to another despite the statistical similarities.
The World Health Organization survey does not deal with perceptions, but does include projections based on what is known about major health factors like heart disease or lung cancer related to smoking. 
In Japan, for example, the new survey says that lung cancer rates for men "are expected to jump in coming years as the long-term effects of the post-World War II smoking popularity begin to hit."
China, the world's most populous nation, with one-fifth of the world's people, was found to have a healthy life expectancy of 62.3, well ahead of the second-largest country, India, at 53.2. 
The Chinese figure is considered particularly impressive, given the country's income level, W.H.O. says. 
China outranks not only India in a healthier life but also Russia and many nations in Central Asia, the Middle East and North Africa.Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: ANNUAL U.N. RITUAL CONDEMNING CHINA LOSES U.S. SUPPORT.txt
text:

Only days after deciding to move up a Presidential trip to Beijing, the Administration has given China another important boost by dropping American sponsorship of an annual United Nations resolution condemning China's record on human rights.
The move, which effectively kills a resolution before the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva, was described by senior officials today as a response to Beijing's recent efforts to improve its rights record, including its decision this week to sign an important international human rights treaty.
"China still has an enormous way to go, and we intend to press them at every opportunity," a senior Administration official said. 
"But in light of these steps, we have decided not to sponsor the resolution. 
It's certainly not a reward. 
It is being done as a calculation. 
It is being done because we believe it is the way to make progress in the future."
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, hinted strongly that China had agreed to release a number of prominent political prisoners if the United States dropped its sponsorship of the resolution. 
"I believe there will be further releases," he said, declining further comment. 
"Lives are at stake."
The Administration's decision was denounced by human rights groups, which said the Administration was abandoning one of its best tools to press Beijing to end what the Administration agrees are widespread human rights violations.
The annual resolution, first introduced at the commission in 1990 after the massacre of unarmed civilians at Tiananmen Square the year before, has infuriated China, even though it has never been adopted by the 53-member commission. 
The commission is to open its annual meeting in Geneva next week.
"If the President visits China without clear human rights preconditions and also drops any resolution at the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva, what leverage will the United States use to press for concrete progress?" asked Mike Jendrzejczyk, Washington director of Human Rights Watch Asia. 
"They've caved."
The White House announced this week that Mr. Clinton, who would be the first President to visit China since the 1989 crackdown on the democracy advocates, had moved up his trip to June from November in order to build on progress made during the visit by President Jiang Zemin of China to the United States last fall.
Chinese officials leapt at the proposal for an earlier meeting.
The Administration's steps to improve relations with China came as President Clinton sought to play down the importance of new evidence that China had tried to sell nuclear technology and equipment to Iran.
The President told reporters at the White House that the sale, first disclosed by the State Department in testimony before Congress on Thursday, was halted in response to an American protest last month.
"The Chinese followed through on it and kept their agreement to the letter," the President said. 
"I am well pleased, actually, with the way that issue came out."
Administration officials said that soon after President Jiang agreed during last year's summit talks to halt nuclear cooperation with Iran, the United States learned about negotiations concerning the sale to Iran of tons of chemicals that could enrich uranium for nuclear weapons.
Far from seeing the incident as a violation of the American-Chinese pact, Administration officials said today that only low-level Chinese officials had negotiated with the Iranians and that senior Chinese Government leaders had blocked the sale as soon as it was brought to their attention by the United States.
"Chinese authorities investigated the matter and promptly informed us that a transaction like that had not been agreed to and that China had no intention of making such a transaction," said James P. Rubin, the State Department spokesman. 
"This is a case that demonstrates how nonproliferation works."
The Administration's critics on Capitol Hill, however, viewed the incident as fresh evidence that China's commitment to its nuclear agreement with the United States was still in question.
Senator John Ashcroft, a Missouri Republican who is a member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, described the potential deal as troubling and said President Clinton had a "policy of blind engagement" toward Beijing.
The committee chairman, Senator Jesse Helms, Republican of North Carolina, said through a spokesman, "We now have the spectacle of the Clinton Administration questioning China on whether it is continuing to provide nuclear weapons assistance to various countries even while, at the same time, a Presidential certification to the contrary is pending before the Senate."
Administration officials said -- and human rights groups agreed -- that the decision to drop sponsorship of the human rights resolution probably meant that no resolution against China would be offered this year.
Last year the resolution, sponsored by the United States and Denmark, was defeated, 27 to 17, after a vigorous lobbying campaign by the Chinese Government, which labeled the resolution "an outrageous distortion of China's reality."
A senior Administration official said Washington decided not to seek a new resolution because of recent actions taken by China at the request of the United States and other nations. 
These included the release of several prominent political prisoners and this week's announcement by China that it would sign the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.
The covenant, a United Nations treaty, is intended to provide guarantees of freedom of expression, religion, assembly and movement, and equality before the law. 
By signing the treaty, China would be required to file periodic reports on its human rights record that would be subject to review by international human rights experts.
"This is an important step that we have been seeking for several years," an Administration official said, describing the covenant as a "far better mechanism" to force changes in China than the sight of another United Nations resolution going down to defeat in Geneva.

file: ANTIQUES_Tang Horses Are Out In Full Force.txt
text:
ï»¿
According to the Chinese zodiac, this is not the Year of the Horse. 
But it should be. 
Ancient Chinese horse sculptures are showing up all over.
There are four life-size terra-cotta chariot horses from the Qin dynasty (221-207 B.C.) in "The Golden Age of Chinese Archeology," a show at the National Gallery of Art in Washington that opened on Sept. 
19 and runs through Jan. 
2. These horses, with ears forward and nostrils dilated, are part of a group of 500 horses and soldiers excavated from tombs in Shaanxi province in 1976.
Ten horses from the Tang dynasty (618-906 A.D.) are among the works in "Abstraction and Reality: Chinese Art From the Warring States to the Liao," which opened two days ago at the Chinese Porcelain Company, a gallery at Park Avenue and 58th Street. 
Some of the horses are glazed, in glorious blue, green, amber and cream, with tasseled bridles and elaborate saddle blankets. 
Others are unglazed, which makes them look modern to Western sensibilities.
One unglazed pale taupe horse has its head raised, neighing. 
Another twists its neck to catch a fly. 
Still another has its muzzle to the ground. 
They are subtly modeled to catch the light and create shadows.
"These are very rare models," said Jim Lally, who runs J. J. Lally, at 41 East 57th Street, and specializes in ancient Chinese art. 
"The Tang was a moment in Chinese art when there was a strong move toward realism and a strong decorative impulse. 
Horses imported from the Near East were precious. 
In Tang China, the horse was the emblem of wealth and power. 
They are meant to embody rank and speed."
Mr. Lally, who sells Tang horse sculptures, currently has a classic example in pale green glaze with an amber saddle cloth, for $100,000.
In addition, there is a herd of nine Tang horses for sale at E. & J. Frankel Oriental Art, 1040 Madison Avenue, at 79th Street, and there are a few more at the Alvin Lo Gallery, 5 East 57th Street.
China's love affair with the horse probably began in the Shang dynasty (circa 1600 to 1100 B.C.), when real horses and human charioteers were interred with Shang emperors. 
Initially, the Chinese had only small, sturdy horses they used as draft animals. 
After the Chinese were attacked by enemies riding larger, stronger horses, they began importing horses from the Middle East, breeding them and training them for warfare and sport.
This all came together in the Tang dynasty. 
Mario Prodan wrote in "The Art of the Tang Potter" (Viking, 1961), "This is China's moment of greatness, artistic, political, military and cultural."
He continued, "Whenever the Chinese dream of imitating nature, of achieving the unbroken line, may have begun, it is certain that it is at last fulfilled in the art of the Tang potter."
The horse was a favorite subject of these artists, but the horse has always been a source of inspiration in China. 
Chinese composers and poets wrote songs and poems about horses, and artists painted them, carved their portraits in stone and created pottery sculptures.
Today, Tang pottery pieces are the most valued of Chinese horse sculptures. 
They range in price from a few thousand dollars to millions. 
Unlike jade, a Tang horse offers a buyer a certain comfort level because thermoluminescence tests can prove its age and fakes can be detected.
The popularity of these works was proved again in Christie's New York sale of Chinese sculpture on Sept. 
16. One horse, which was estimated to sell for $60,000 to $80,000, went for $266,500.
Unglazed, it had its head lowered toward its left foreleg, which was slightly raised. 
There was a grooved channel running the length of the arched neck, where a real horsehair mane would have been inserted, and there was a hole for a horsehair tail.
An amber glazed horse with a textured fur saddle blanket glazed green went for $310,000. 
It was not unlike one that Sotheby's London sold in 1989 for the British Rail Pension Fund for $6.1 million, the world record for a Chinese work of art.
"Tang horses are the most widely popular image of Chinese art," Mr. Lally said, "because they are immediately accessible to everyone. 
You don't have to read a book on Chinese art to love a Tang horse."
Among the horses in the Chinese Porcelain Company show is a cream-colored, glazed one decorated with splashes of cobalt blue. 
Khalil Rizk, co-owner of the gallery, said: "Only 5 percent of Tang horses have blue glaze. 
Cobalt was put on during the last firing. 
Cobalt was a treasured commodity imported from the Middle East; it was more valuable than gold. 
Its use means the horse was for someone of the highest rank."
This horse is 15 inches tall and turns its head to the left. 
It has an ornamental harness and bridle. 
Originally, Mr. Rizk said, it would have had bronze decorations as well.
"Generally speaking, glazed horses used to be more sought after, especially in Japan," Mr. Rizk said. 
"But some horses were so well sculpted they may have been deliberately left unglazed."

file: AOL Merger Is Unlikely to Reshape AsianInternet Business.txt
text:
ï»¿
It was hardly Paris, but Shanghai played a part in the brief, intense courtship between America Online and Time Warner.
America Online's chairman, Stephen M. Case, attended a Fortune magazine conference there in October, during which he mingled with Time Warner's top executives, including Gerald M. Levin and Ted Turner. 
Later, the executives traveled to Beijing for the 50th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China. 
A Time Warner executive who was there recalls a teasing exchange between Mr. Case and Mr. Turner, when the two found themselves stranded in the rain outside the Great Hall of the People.
"Ted, your big, merged company isn't getting you off the steps," Mr. Case shouted to Mr. Turner.
"Steve," he replied, "your billions ain't getting you anywhere either."
It is not clear, even after America Online's extraordinary bid for Time Warner, that this huge merged company will be able to get off the steps in China -- or elsewhere in Asia. 
In contrast to Europe, where America Online has built a valuable regional franchise through its partnership with Bertelsmann A.G., the Internet in Asia remains a fractured business with few large competitors and virtually none that cross national boundaries.
"AOL and Time Warner have tremendous critical mass in the United States and, through AOL and Compuserve, in Europe as well," said Michael J. Wolf, the partner in charge of the media practice at Booz, Allen & Hamilton, the New York-based consultancy. 
"But to a large extent, Asia is up for grabs."
America Online operates an on-line service in Japan, and recently started one in Hong Kong. 
But it has yet to enter the Chinese mainland, where Yahoo, the Internet portal service, is one of the few major American Internet companies to have established a foothold. 
Time Warner distributes movies and music in China -- as well as CNN and Time magazine, when they are not being banned by the Chinese government. 
But like most other American media companies, Time Warner has not been able to make deep inroads in the country because of hazards ranging from piracy to onerous regulations and political pressure. 
The proposed merger will not eliminate those.
Some analysts said that America Online would benefit more from a deal than Time Warner because its credibility will be burnished in the eyes of the Chinese government. 
Although Beijing, after months of equivocation, recently indicated that it would allow foreign companies to invest in the Internet, officials seem likely to pick and choose among potential entrants. 
Analysts said America Online's odds of receiving favorable treatment would be higher if it tied up with a media giant like Time Warner.
"CNN and Ted Turner will open doors for this company politically, allowing it to do things that other companies may not be able to," Mr. Wolf of Booz, Allen & Hamilton said.
Brian C. Lippey, chief executive of Tokai Asia, a hedge fund based in Hong Kong, added: "The merger gives AOL international credibility. 
Time Warner is a good old-fashioned multinational."
And although a combined company's prospects in Asia are uncertain, news of the huge deal reverberated through the region, prompting talk of more mergers and strategic alliances involving Asian companies. 
Shares of local media companies and Internet access providers soared on Tuesday, though most fell back as the initial giddiness over the announcement subsided.
This may reflect some basic truths about Asia. 
Lehman Brothers noted in a report that the ownership of many Asian media companies is concentrated in the hands of one or two big investors. 
That would make huge, widely held combinations like AOL-Time Warner unlikely, at least in the short term.
Cultural, linguistic and regulatory differences among Asian countries also militate against the creation of pan-Asian companies. 
Two decades after CNN was founded in the United States, Star TV, a satellite television unit of the News Corporation, remains the only genuinely regional media service based in Asia.
"If you look at Japan, there are some wonderful media companies, but very little of their material sees the light of day outside Japan," said Alexander A. Arena, the group managing director of Pacific Century Cyberworks, a Hong Kong company that is designing a satellite-delivered Internet service.
Still, analysts and stock pickers were quick to draw up lists of Asian companies they contended would benefit from the changes suggested by a merger of America Online and Time Warner. 
Leading the list are obvious candidates like Sony, the Japanese electronics giant, and less obvious ones like TVB, a Hong Kong television broadcaster that owns the world's largest library of Chinese-language programming.
Analysts said that Pacific Century Cyberworks and other companies that aspire to deliver information and entertainment to subscribers over high-capacity wires would also benefit. 
Hong Kong's dominant local phone company, Cable and Wireless HKT, may also come into favor because of its recent alliance with Star TV, in which the two plan to offer television programming to the phone company's customers.
For all the excitement, Asian reactions to the AOL-Time Warner deal have had an unfocused quality. 
Experts said that reflects the Internet's relative lack of development here, which makes picking winners and predicting the future even chancier than in the United States.
"It's a simple question of supply and demand," Mr. Lippey said. 
"There aren't that many quality Internet companies in Asia."

text:

Reflections Abroad
Anthony Giordano Gallery, Dowling College, Idle Hour Boulevard, Oakdale. 
Through Nov. 
24. 244-3016.
For 10 years, and more intensively after the Government crushed the pro-democracy movement in his native China, Zhang Hongtu has examined the image of Chairman Mao Zedong as a symbol of pervasive power. 
His current exhibition surveys the decade, during which he turned from introspection to an overt critique of the Chinese Communism.
The earliest works in this selection, like "Portrait -- The Back," are literally inward-looking, a kind of interior dialogue between the artist and his materials. 
In the late 1980's, however, Mr. Zhang began using cultural icons as motifs. 
Unlike Andy Warhol, for whom Mao was one celebrity among the many he portrayed, Mr. Zhang focused on the political, social and moral implications of Mao's pervasive presence in the China of his youth.
Among the earliest works in this series is "Chairmen Mao," a group of laser-print manipulations that deconstruct the leader's features. 
With a Dadaist sense of disrespectful satire, Mr. Zhang exercises a freedom of expression that would be denied to him at home, while at the same time suggesting that, despite distortion and caricature, Mao survives.
Even as a silhouette or cutout shape, the Chairman's presence is strongly felt. 
In the "Material Mao" series, his unseen image is surrounded by basic raw materials, including corn, rice, wood and iron, on which society depends. 
Metaphorically Mao is in the food, the buildings, even the Ping-Pong table memorializing the sport that paved the way for diplomacy with the West.
In the silhouette drawings, soy sauce is substituted for ink, while the paper is recycled pages of Mao's "Red Book."
By alluding to traditional Chinese art, and especially by rendering the image in a staple of the Chinese diet, Mr. Zhang comments on Mao's program to remake China in his own image and nourish its people with his omnipotence.
The exhibition culminates in a non-Mao piece, "Flying Blues," Mr. Zhang's homage to the spirit that survives in spite of repression. 
Emanating from a Daoist diagram, feathers suspended by strings over a cloud pattern in sand symbolize imagined freedom restrained by ties to the past. 
Paradoxically, the sky is below and the earth above, a comment on the fact that, for the artist, the ground on which we stand represents openness, while freedom in China is still a celestial ideal.

Archeologies
Omni Gallery, 333 Earl Ovington Boulevard, Uniondale. 
Through Nov. 
25. 794-7800.
The artist and the archeologist have much in common. 
Both engage in excavation, look for evidence and contribute to cultural understanding. 
But while the archeologist searches for past meanings, the artist invents new ones.
In this group show, three artists engage in personal excavations that reveal as much about themselves as about the objects or images they uncover. 
The evidence they collect is more a means to an end than an end in itself.
Mary Leto actually begins with artifacts scavenged from building ruins and natural sites. 
Many are incorporated into her wall reliefs, but the most massive elements, pieces of broken concrete, are cast in paper made of pulverized texts. 
Thus "Sow and Reap" is not only a demonstration of how civilization's structures collapse on themselves, crushing the works of man and nature, but also a comment on how words and ideas are integral to those structures.
In Gail Cohen Edelman's mixed-media works, burial sites of several cultures serve as generic sacred spaces. 
Her two "Chapel of Bones" pieces use abstracted skeletons to link areas, like trails taking us from one site to another and emphasizing the universality of ancestor worship.
"The Opening of the Ark" and "You Can't Predict" are more specific, alluding to concentration camps and mass burials -- grisly relics of contempt for the living and the dead.
Naomi Grossman digs into human relations, using the body as her field of exploration. 
In her sculptures of wire, wax and shredded paper, figures are torn by conflict and imperfectly mended, surviving more by inertia than by volition.
"Holding Herself Together" summarizes female resignation, while "Memories of Youth" blatantly parodies lost virility. 
Although women as the victims of men's domination are Ms. Grossman's main concern, male vulnerability is also acknowledged, even if only as a stereotype.
Â 
Shades of Blue
Alfred Van Loen Gallery, South Huntington Public Library, 2 Melville Road, Huntington Station. 
Through Nov. 
30. 549-4411.
Members of the TANA artists' group are again exhibiting works in which a color is the only common factor. 
Last time it was red, and now we have blue as the harmonizing influence.
Water and sky are obvious subjects for artists who favor blue, and several works allude to those elements. 
Julienne Saslaw captures the mystery of an overcast evening in "Nuit Bleu," with its swirling clouds enveloping a lambent moon. 
A more sinister atmosphere invades Lorraine Baron's "Cloud of Annihilation," a plastic painting that seems to melt before our eyes.
The clever use of collaged holograms enlivens "Halley's Comet," Celia Kushner's evocation of a celestial phenomenon notable for its transcience. 
The comet's icy heart is suggested by the crystalline hologram fragments, while the dark void through which it hurtles is nicely imagined.
Judy Golden's all-over abstraction is titled simply "Blue," yet the composition incorporates flakes of gold leaf that offer a visual pun on the artist's name. 
Gladys Goldberg's "Blues Are Running" is also a double entendre, featuring blue fish, or is it bluefish, accompanied by ghostly afterimages that might be blueprints.
"Pompeii," by Vi Koch, imitates the surface of an ancient wall, scoured by time and the ravages of nature. 
The subtle interplay between surface and ground allows us to imagine the piece as a remnant from ages past. 
"Blue Guardian," Gloria Frey Yudkin's monoprint, also has archaic overtones, with its sentinel figure doubling as a gateway that seems to have its own internal watchman.

file: ART_Maybe Not on the High Road, but They Travel Well.txt
text:
ï»¿
JON THOMPSON, DIRECTOR OF cultural affairs for the city of Memphis, faced a challenge in Beijing a few years ago. 
He had to persuade the Chinese Government to allow more than 250 relics and fine-art objects out of the country for almost three years. 
Worse, he had to explain that its cherished national treasures were not going to some world-renowned museum.
Instead, they were to be the heart of a touring blockbuster exhibition series called "Wonders," which would open at a convention center in downtown Memphis just a few miles from Elvis Presley's Graceland. 
The show would then go on to Portland, Ore.; Provo, Utah, and Denver before ending up in Orlando, Fla., just a few miles from Disney World.
But Mr. Thompson, a genteel Southerner who also happens to be a veteran marketing man, had his sales pitch ready. 
Knowing China was eager to win American admirers, he began by describing a "cultural corridor," running from New York to Washington, through Chicago and on to Los Angeles, saying it was in these cities that most major arts events occur in the United States.
"So why don't we create our own countercultural corridor," he suggested, "going from Oregon to Florida diagonally across the U.S. in the opposite direction?"
The Chinese were sold.
As a result, "The Imperial Tombs of China" opened in Memphis in 1995. 
Last Thursday, the exhibition opened at the Orlando Museum of Art, the last leg of its planned five-city tour. 
More than 1.5 million people have seen the show so far.
Predictably, some members of America's museum establishment are not particularly receptive to Mr. Thompson's road show. 
In fact, the concept of the "Wonders" blockbuster runs so counter to their notions of high culture that they may never completely accept it.
"Wonders: The Memphis International Series," which Mr. Thompson heads, was started after the city sponsored an exhibition in 1987 called "Rameses the Great."
It drew 675,000 people and went on to be seen by almost eight million people on an eight-city North American tour. 
Then came "Wonders" exhibitions on Catherine the Great, the Ottomans, the Etruscans, Napoleon and China, all staged in the Memphis convention center. 
The city's seventh blockbuster, "Titanic: The Exhibition," opened last month in the basement of Memphis's largest indoor sports arena, where it will remain through September.
The "Wonders" shows have even inspired a few spinoffs. 
James E. Broughton, the organization's original director, left Memphis and set up a similar series of three shows on Egypt, Russia and Greece in St. Petersburg, Fla. 
In Jackson, Miss., another former "Wonders" staffer, Jack Kyle, staged "The Palaces of St. Petersburg" in cooperation with Russia's Hermitage Museum last summer. 
Attendance was more than 550,000, second last year only to the Cezanne exhibition in Philadelphia.
Unlike blockbusters that are composed strictly of fine-arts objects, "Wonders" shows combine fine art, natural history and Smithsonian-like cultural history. 
Every exhibition is designed to make a strong emotional impact through elaborate sets and a story line. 
A free audio guide is narrated by a celebrity: Leonard Nimoy for the Chinese exhibition, Lauren Bacall for Catherine the Great. 
Non-art objects are often a big draw, too: bricks from the Great Wall of China, Catherine the Great's coronation carriage and every item in the art-free Titanic show, from jewelry and money to a steward's jacket and a jar of green olives.
"There is a real hunger for this kind of thing in second- and third-tier cities that do not have a Metropolitan Museum on their doorstep," Mr. Thompson said.
MANY FROM THE MUSEUM world are reluctant to dismiss the "Wonders" concept totally, but they express concern that the shows may warp the public's perception of what museum professionals do.
" 'Wonders' is a great draw for the city," said Kate Gooch, president of the Memphis Arts Council. 
"It is kind of the Boston Pops of art. 
But it is not a substitute for a museum."
Edward H. Able, president of the American Association of Museums, an organization of 3,000 museums across the country, also has reservations about the "Wonders" concept. 
"These are one-time events that come and go," he said. 
"They seem to be mostly entrepreneurial activities to make money, unlike museums, which are committed to continuing programs, education, scholarship and a broader and more complex mission."
Some museum officials are also troubled by the fact that "Wonders" is an arm of local government, not a museum. 
John Buchanan, director of the Portland Museum of Art in Oregon, said his museum took the China exhibition last summer because of its artistic value, but he noted that the idea of city bureaucrats initiating art exchanges raises questions. 
"The opening salvo in these negotiations came from the governments," he said. 
"And that was nervous-making to my colleagues, who are used to talking curator to curator."
But to city leaders, any doubts about the shows are overshadowed by the bottom line: the tourism they attract stimulates local economies. 
Even when a "Wonders" show operated at a loss, which some have, the city of Memphis still earned $3.54 in tax revenue for every dollar invested, a city study showed.
That is a major reason Memphis keeps the nonprofit series solvent through a revolving $4.2 million loan. 
Any profit from "Wonders" ticket- and gift-shop sales is funneled back into the next exhibition. 
Organizers keep the expenses low by using more than 2,000 volunteers and sharing costs with other cities on the tours.
For this and other reasons, the people behind "Wonders" and its spinoffs do not apologize for their efforts. 
Instead, they say their work complements that of museums, and they cite a number of reasons.
Not having a permanent museum collection, they say, enables them to focus all their resources on display. 
They pay fees for the works they borrow because the "Wonders" organization, unlike big museums, cannot trade on prestige or the promise of reciprocal loans.
Education is a built-in part of the concept. 
Free study guides are sent to every teacher in the area, and thousands of children are given free tours. 
Shows are staged in uncommon venues only when local museums do not have enough space to handle the large exhibitions and huge crowds.
Their most heartfelt defense is that the "Wonders" exhibitions do not commercialize art; they popularize it. 
"I'm a populist," said Mr. Kyle, the former "Wonders" staff member. 
"I believe art is for the people."
He and his colleagues argue that there is nothing wrong with bringing the exhibitions to people who may never be able to afford a trip to New York, much less Russia or China, or to those who find museums intimidating.
Cheryl Reddick, who drove 12 hours from Georgia with a friend to see the Titanic show, is one of those people. 
"Museums are too overwhelming," she said. 
"With 'Wonders' you can see the whole exhibit in a couple of hours."
If nothing else, the "Wonders" concept democratizes art, said J. Carter Brown, director emeritus of the National Gallery of Art in Washington and the creator of a blockbuster of his own last summer at the Olympics in Atlanta. 
"I think these exhibits challenge the idea that only the priesthood can see art and the great unwashed cannot," he said.
It's a view shared by Thomas Hoving, the former director of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, who is credited with originating the blockbuster phenomenon when he brought the King Tut show to America in 1977. 
" 'Wonders' is a trailer-park blockbuster," he said. 
"But it's good. 
They reach a whole group of people who never got an art education, and it might end up drawing them into other museums. 
Half a generation from now, I bet there will be bunches of people who will remember 'Wonders' and say it is what got them interested in art as a child."
He added, "The shows are great, not second-rate at all."
For each show, organizers recruit recognized experts to be guest curators. 
The Napoleon exhibit was curated by Bernard Chevallier, director of Malmaison in France, who gathered more than 175 pieces of art from 50 museums all over the world. 
"The people they get to curate are the top people in their fields," Mr. Hoving said.
FOR ALL THE SUCCESS OF these shows, however, a "Wonders" exhibition can still be a risky proposition. 
St. Petersburg is struggling with an $11 million loss on its series, mainly because of lower-than-expected attendance and a financial arrangement in which much of the gift-shop revenue went to Mr. Broughton, the original "Wonders" director, instead of to the city.
Mr. Broughton has left to form an independent company to produce similar shows for other cities. 
His next show will be called "Nicholas and Alexandra."
Meanwhile, in Memphis, an exhibition of several hundred ancient Peruvian treasures will open next spring. 
An exhibition from Versailles is set for next summer in Jackson. 
And cities like Topeka, Kan., and Wilmington, Del., have discussed beginning their own series.
Despite challenges and naysayers, the "Wonders" concept persists. 
"The elitist crowd has some valid points of criticism," said Mr. Hoving. "But these shows are going to keep coming."

file: ART_Works From China, Many Political but Conveyed With Wit.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE Lehman College Art Gallery here has a history of mounting shows of the art of different cultures. 
The current exhibition, "Contemporary Chinese Art and the Literary Culture of China," is focused and lively. 
Little of the writing is on the usual surfaces: it is embedded in all sorts of sculpture installations, many of which use communications technology.
Four of the artists whose works are in the show now live in the United States, at least part time, and are represented by large, elaborate pieces. 
Six others have remained in China and are represented through photographs and computer-generated images of recent endeavors. 
The audience here thus has only a partial view of their endeavors. 
It was expected that art from contemporary China would be political, and much of the art made in China is. 
But it is covert politics, often conveyed with wit or paradox.
"Heaven Is on a Flying Dragon" by Wang Huaxiang, for example, is a simple juxtaposition of a European Renaissance prince, who was no doubt steeped in Machiavelli, and of the Chinese leader Hua Guofeng, a like-minded ruler, who is applauding the prince. 
Another artist, Liu Yan, has sent photographs of his "Amber Series."
Yellowing newspapers reporting extraordinary events in China's history since the establishment of the Communist Party in 1949 are cast in yellow plastic, but not before dumplings filled with Chinese soil are scattered over them, giving the newspapers a lasting dimension.
Zhang Dali has been called the Keith Haring of China for his furtive spray painting of heads in profile. 
Some of the profiles have been his own and are meant to be witnesses to the myriad abuses and crimes committed on the streets of Beijing. 
By contrast, Zhu Jingshi extols monumentality. 
He once covered every inch of a huge column with small pieces of rice paper, a tribute to the staple of Chinese life. 
Shang Yang's paintings, rooted in collage technique, are a personal diary that does not spare events, which are not usually depicted, like his recovery from heart surgery.
If his technique is somewhat old-fashioned, so is part of Huang Yan's process: he makes rubbings. 
But he has put these ghostly images into futuristic computer-generated compositions. 
He once made rubbings of a wooden chair; a new rubbing was made every time he pared down the chair with a knife, and at the end he had rubbings of wood chips.
The four artists living in America get the most out of being present. 
In two installations, Xing Fei celebrates a style of writing, dating from the eighth century, known as "grass script" because the elongated characters resemble individual stalks in a field. 
In "The Grass Script I," Ms. Xing hangs a bevy of yarn-covered characters from the ceiling, creating a forest. 
A nearby wall is plastered with computer-generated wallpaper bearing this wiggly script.
Sculptures and flat characters interact, illustrating how Chinese characters are created through intersection and overlapping. 
"The Grass Script II" has roughly the same format, but the hanging pieces are made of wire and, complementing the length of the wire elements, the writing on the wall is on scrolls.
There is hidden political content in these works, which superficially show reverence for the past. 
The writing is unintelligible, and the pieces are ultimately about a lack of faith in communication. 
Ms. Xing has remarked that the words on the wallpaper and scrolls are reminiscent of leaflets plastered on walls during the Cultural Revolution. 
Their sternness is the opposite of the playfulness of the hanging characters.
Masses of information-laden paper are Longbin Chen's primary material. 
A viewer can see the back of his large sculptured head and its shelves packed with New York City telephone books. 
To carve the features of "Big Face," Mr. Chen took a chain saw to the dense surface made by the exposed pages of the books. 
The face seems to be awakening from a long slumber and is beginning to move its lips. 
Similarly, the recumbent figures in Mr. Chen's "Endless" look asleep, but they are not cast in alabaster. 
They are cut with a chain saw from reams of computer printouts, sometimes extended and often compacted into blocks. 
A wish to put life or the human touch back into the increasingly depersonalized workplace would seem to be Mr. Chen's message. 
Meanwhile a flying figure, named "Twist Angel" and made of musty old books, is oblivious to the issues articulated beneath him.
The work of Xu Bing is the most portable. 
He can make it on the spot, as he did for the placard announcing this exhibition. 
Superficially, the logo looks like a grid of six characters or ideograms, but closer inspection will reveal to the viewer that he can decipher them. 
In each character Mr. Xu has artfully woven the letters of the Western alphabet to make each of the English words in the exhibition's title. 
Likewise the Western alphabet is the basis for "ABC," another of his works. 
Projecting from a wall are terra cotta bricks bearing the Chinese characters that most closely match the English pronunciation of each letter.
Zhao Suikang appears to be the most idealistic of the artists, in his wish to bring out the commonality of the people of the world. 
Two of his works here are attempts to unite texts from the major religions of the world: "Color Fluorescent Pamphlets" has the exotic allure that fluorescence can impart, while "Polyphonic Realities" involves computer-generated spiritual writing in several alphabets being projected and woven together before our eyes. 
Mr. Zhao loses his pious image with a "Red Fish Tank," stocked with goldfish that dart around red script in several writing systems. 
Red is the appropriate color, for these are linguistic juxtapositions of erotic prose.
The closing date is Jan. 
15, and the information number is (718) 960-8731.

file: As China Threatens Taiwan, It Makes Sure U.S. Listens.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese leadership has sent unusually explicit warnings to the Clinton Administration that China has completed plans for a limited attack on Taiwan that could be mounted in the weeks after Taiwan's President, Lee Teng-hui, wins the first democratic balloting for the presidency in March.
The purpose of this saber-rattling is apparently to prod the United States to rein in Taiwan and President Lee, whose push for greater recognition for the island of 21 million people, has been condemned here as a drive for independence.
While no one familiar with the threats thinks China is on the verge of risking a catastrophic war against Taiwan, some China experts fear that the Taiwan issue has become such a test of national pride for Chinese leaders that the danger of war should be taken seriously.
A senior American official said the Administration has "no independent confirmation or even credible evidence" that the Chinese are contemplating an attack, and spoke almost dismissively of the prospect. 
"They can fire missiles, but Taiwan has some teeth of its own," the official said. 
"And does China want to risk that and the international effects?"
The most pointed of the Chinese warnings was conveyed recently through a former Assistant Secretary of Defense, Chas. 
W. Freeman Jr., who traveled to China this winter for discussions with senior Chinese officials. 
On Jan. 
4, after returning to Washington, Mr. Freeman informed President Clinton's national security adviser, Anthony Lake, that the People's Liberation Army had prepared plans for a missile attack against Taiwan consisting of one conventional missile strike a day for 30 days.
This warning followed similar statements relayed to Administration officials by John W. Lewis, a Stanford University political scientist who meets frequently with senior Chinese military figures here.
These warnings do not mean that an attack on Taiwan is certain or imminent. 
Instead, a number of China specialists say that China, through "credible preparations" for an attack, hopes to intimidate the Taiwanese and to influence American policy toward Taiwan. 
The goal, these experts say, is to force Taiwan to abandon the campaign initiated by President Lee, including his effort to have Taiwan seated at the United Nations, and to end high-profile visits by President Lee to the United States and to other countries.
If the threats fail to rein in Mr. Lee, however, a number of experts now express the view that China could resort to force, despite the enormous consequences for its economy and for stabilityI in Asia.
Since last summer, when the White House allowed Mr. Lee to visit the United States, the Chinese leadership has escalated its attacks on the Taiwan leader, accusing him of seeking to "split the motherland" and undermine the "one China" policy that had been the bedrock of relations between Beijing and its estranged province since 1949.
A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman, asked to comment on reports that the Chinese military has prepared plans for military action against Taiwan, said he was awaiting a response from his superiors. 
Last month, a senior ministry official said privately that China's obvious preparations for military action have been intended to head off an unwanted conflict.
"We have been trying to do all we can to avoid a scenario in which we are confronted in the end with no other option but a military one," the official said. 
He said that if China does not succeed in changing Taiwan's course, "then I am afraid there is going to be a war."
Mr. Freeman described the most recent warning during a meeting Mr. Lake had called with nongovernmental China specialists.
Participants said that Mr. Freeman's presentation was arresting as he described being told by a Chinese official of the advanced state of planning. 
Preparations for a missile attack on Taiwan, he said, have been completed and await a decision by the Politburo in Beijing.
One of the most dramatic moments came when Mr. Freeman quoted a Chinese official as asserting that China could act militarily against Taiwan without fear of intervention by the United States because American leaders "care more about Los Angeles than they do about Taiwan," a statement that Mr. Freeman characterized as an indirect threat by China to use nuclear weapons against the United States.
An account of the White House meeting was provided by some of the participants. 
Mr. Freeman, reached by telephone, confirmed the gist of his remarks, reiterating that he believes that while "Beijing clearly prefers negotiation to combat," there is a new sense of urgency in Beijing to end Taiwan's quest for "independent international status."
Mr. Freeman said that President Lee's behavior "in the weeks following his re-election will determine" whether China's Communist Party leaders feel they must act militarily to change his behavior.
In recent months, Mr. Freeman said he has relayed a number of warnings to United States Government officials. 
"I have quoted senior Chinese who told me" that China "would sacrifice 'millions of men' and 'entire cities' to assure the unity of China and who opined that the United States would not make comparable sacrifices."
He also asserted that "some in Beijing may be prepared to engage in nuclear blackmail against the U.S. to insure that Americans do no obstruct" efforts by the People's Liberation Army "to defend the principles of Chinese sovereignty over Taiwan and Chinese national unity."
Some specialists at the meeting wondered if Mr. Freeman's presentation was too alarmist and suggested that parliamentary elections on Taiwan in December had resulted in losses for the ruling Nationalist Party and that President Lee appeared to be moderating his behavior to avoid a crisis.
"I am not alarmist at this point," said one specialist, who would not comment on the substance of the White House meeting. 
"I don't think the evidence is developing in that direction."
Other participants in the meeting, who said they would not violate the confidentiality pledge of the private session, separately expressed their concern that a potential military crisis is building in the Taiwan Strait.
"I think there is evidence to suggest that the Chinese are creating at least the option to apply military pressure to Taiwan if they feel that Taiwan is effectively moving out of China's orbit politically," said Kenneth Lieberthal, a China scholar at the University of Michigan.
Mr. Lieberthal, who also has traveled to China in recent months, said Beijing has redeployed forces from other parts of the country to the coastal areas facing Taiwan and set up new command structures "for various kinds of military action against Taiwan."
"They have done all this in a fashion they know Taiwan can monitor," he said, "so as to become credible on the use of force."
"I believe there has been no decision to use military force," he continued, "and they recognize that it would be a policy failure for them to have to resort to force; but they have set up the option, they have communicated that in the most credible fashion and, I believe, the danger is that they would exercise it in certain circumstances."
Several experts cited their concern that actions by Congress in the aftermath of President Lee's expected election could be a critical factor contributing to a military confrontation. 
If President Lee perceives that he has a strong base of support in the United States Congress and presses forward with his campaign to raise Taiwan's status, the risk of a military crisis is greater, they said. 
A chief concern is that Congress would seek to invite the Taiwan leader back to the United States as a gesture of American support. 
A Chinese military leader warned in November that such a step could have "explosive" results.
In recent months, American statements on whether United States forces would defend Taiwan if it came under attack have been deliberately vague so as to deter Beijing through a posture of what the Pentagon calls "strategic ambiguity."
Some members of Congress assert that the Taiwan Relations Act of 1979 includes an implicit pledge to defend Taiwan if attacked, but Administration officials say that a decision would depend on the timing, pretext and nature of Chinese aggression.
