file: China, the Oldest Culture, in Mega-Tomes.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE first book in a projected 75-volume series on Chinese culture being published by Yale University Press in New Haven is described by staffers there as an effort to pierce China's other great wall, that of Western neglect for the world's longest-lived culture.
"Three Thousand Years of Chinese Painting," which hit book stores last month, provides an overview of pictorial art ranging from cave petroglyphs of sun priests to naturalistic depictions of World War II refugees. 
More than 300 color plates supplement a 354-page text authored by six leading scholars of Chinese art.
It also comes with a $75 price tag, which the Yale University Press director, John Ryden, hopes will not stop potential buyers of the series. 
Much depends on the commercial success of the first volume, not least of which is the continuation of an unprecedented, ambitious collaboration between the nonprofit publishing arm of Yale University and China.
"We're only beginning to take on board the immensity of it," Mr. Ryden said. 
"For too long, China has been a closed book to us in the West. 
Now there is a new willingness from China to open that book."
Indeed, when Chinese President Jiang Zemin came to the United States in late October, he had with him advance copies of "Three Thousand Years of Chinese Painting" for President Clinton and Vice President Gore as well as Republican legislative leaders. 
Chinese scholars and publishers are excited as well, hoping it will break through the barrier Chinese authors come up against when shopping books to the West.
"Hopefully, this will make China more understandable," said the vice president of the Chinese International Publishing Group, Huang Youyi. 
A coalition of book and magazine publishers, the group counts among its members the Foreign Languages Press in Beijing, which is publishing the series with Yale.
Gracing a wall in Mr. Ryden's corner office is a brushwork scroll displaying a single Chinese character, that of the dragon. 
A gift during a visit to Beijing, it seems an apt symbol of the task Yale University Press has undertaken. 
No stranger either to art books or multi-volume collections, the Yale press faces what may well be an unprecedented challenge in its century-old history: 75 books in 25 years.
Can it be done?
By comparison, Yale University Press produced 48 volumes of the correspondence of Horace Walpole, starting in 1932 and finishing in 1983. 
A collection of Benjamin Franklin's papers, begun in 1959, has yet to be completed and is expected to top out at 45 books.
Many of the books in the Culture and Civilization of China series will be translations of great works of Chinese literature, some never before published in the West. 
Eight to 10 large-format original books now in the works, on subjects ranging from sculpture to Buddhism, will require the same sort of years-long scholarship and design work as did "Chinese Painting," a $500,000-plus investment for Yale.
An advisor to the series, James C.Y. 
Watt, calls the 25-year timeline unrealistic. 
In a recent interview, Mr. Ryden also called the 75-book total, a projection rather than a firm number. 
Yet he then started to talk about the possibility of producing a second series of volumes, to focus on particular types of Chinese painting and art.
For some, like its executive editor, James Peck, the series is ambitious because it must be: "We need to correct the historical imbalance. 
When you look at how little we know about a culture that goes back so long, then you view this as a modest step toward the kind of knowledge we need."
The project began life in 1985 in far different form and with a different publisher, Random House. 
Mr. Peck and Robert Bernstein, then-Random House chairman, worked out an exclusive joint publishing arrangement with China to produce various non-connected books, including a Chinese-English dictionary.
Mr. Bernstein was ousted from Random House in 1989, and Mr. Peck left shortly afterward. 
That same year, China imposed martial law as its soldiers fired on protesting students at Tiananmen Square. 
Suddenly, the future for a cooperative publishing venture seemed very dim.
Two years later, Mr. Bernstein and Mr. Peck were in Mr. Ryden's office, pitching the concept. 
"China wasn't interested in continuing at Random House," Mr. Ryden said. 
"Their allegiance was with Peck and Bernstein."
While the main idea appealed to Mr. Ryden, the books that Random House had worked on were not as interesting. 
"There were other reference books and children's books," he said. 
"That's not our kind of work."
So the project became transformed, into what will be if completed a comprehensive look at a civilization that took root more than 3,500 years ago. 
"And unlike the rise and fall of the Pharaohs, or Greece of the Golden Age, there has been a continuum," Mr. Ryden said.
Mr. Ryden initially worried that a link with the Chinese Government in the wake of Tiananmen might make Yale University Press appear an apologist in some eyes. 
But the more he thought about it, he said, the more convinced he became that the object of the series, that of explaining China and its culture to the West, was more vital.
"I think and hope that the people who encounter these books will see them as a legitimate effort to understand the people and the mind of China," he said. 
"What we are doing is saying that if you want to understand a people, you have to understand where they are coming from."
Mr. Ryden hastened to add that the Chinese Government has set no restrictions on series content. 
"It does not need or get any kind of seal of approval," he said.
What is in it for China?
For many of its people, both in and out of government, there is said to be a strong feeling that China is misunderstood by the West, which the series would help resolve. 
And then there is another potential benefit.
"An old Chinese proverb says that you can see a mountain better when you look at it from a distance than when you are standing at the top of it," Mr. Huang said. 
"China is very eager to see how Westerners interpret their culture. 
American authors pick up on things that are interesting."
As an example of this, Mr. Huang pointed to one of two introductions to "Three Thousand Years of Chinese Painting," written by James Cahill, professor emeritus of art history at the University of California, Berkeley. 
Mr. Cahill wrote that Chinese painting follows different basic rules than its Western counterpart, intended not "to be read illusionistically as windows into another space" but rather as a visual reference to common themes and touchstones of Chinese culture.
For Mr. Huang, 25 years is not an overly ambitious time frame. 
In fact, he would like it completed sooner. 
Nothing less than the posterity of Chinese culture for its own people is at stake, he said.
"With the classical translations, the fact they were written in classical Chinese means fewer people today are able to read it," he explained. 
"The people working as translators now are in their 50's, 60's and 70's. 
In 15 years' time, it will be harder to find translators."
In an interview, Mr. Cahill noted that past scholarship of Chinese painting has focused on a comparatively small art collection at the National Palace Museum in Taiwan. 
"Most of the paintings are going to be unfamiliar, except to specialists in the West," he said. 
"There is quite a lot of new material, especially in the early period. 
A lot of that has been newly discovered."
For scholars like Mr. Watt, the Brooke Russell Astor Senior Curator at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in Manhattan, the series is particularly valuable to the Western reader for the combination of Chinese and non-Chinese viewpoints. 
"This joint approach will be very helpful to the Western reader," he said. 
"There is no lack of interest in China in this country. 
The trouble has always been a lack of good books."
Much depends on the reception accorded "Three Thousand Years of Chinese Painting," which is being simultaneously published in France as well as China and the United States. 
Kirkus Reviews has called it "the Janson's of Chinese painting" and it is currently a Book-of-the-Month Club selection. 
But sales, as well as the excitement the book generates with foundations and other would-be donors, can have a tremendous influence on the speed with which the rest of the series is produced. 
That is one reason a book of painting was chosen to be first, as it would be "less exotic" and more marketable to Western tastes.
Three more large-format volumes -- on Chinese archeology, architecture and sculpture -- are scheduled to appear over the next 18 months. 
Mr. Ryden, Yale University Press's director since 1979, agreed the series, if completed, could be the crown jewel of his tenure.
"I spoke at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing on Oct. 
21 to launch the series," he said. 
"It was a big event, with many senior officials in attendance. 
I told them that our hope with this series is to create a university without walls. 
It is necessary to understand the long and complicated history of this people. 
A lack of understanding is a dangerous thing."

text:

Last November, representatives from the communications firm of Robinson Lerer Sawyer Miller were invited to the Chinese Embassy to present an ambitious three-year public-relations strategy for Beijing.
Focus on "hot-button issues" like human rights and weapons sales, the Chinese were told, according to people familiar with the day-long presentation. 
Put on a road show of Chinese athletes during the summer Olympics. 
Create a "command center" to handle crises. 
Set up a news bureau with television links and an on-line information system. 
The firm boasted that it operated "well behind the scenes" and represented corporate giants like Microsoft and Chrysler and the Governments of countries like the Philippines, Columbia, Chile and Indonesia.
The Chinese listened politely and thanked their guests. 
Officials at the firm say they have not heard back since.
Given China's historic suspicion of outside interference, the encounter was highly unusual, as were China's tentative overtures to other American lobbying firms. 
The search for a hired gun was part of an awkward effort to defeat Taiwan -- not with a missile attack across the Taiwan Strait, but with a public relations campaign in the United States.
On this battlefield, however, even a nuclear power of 1.2 billion people and the fastest-growing economy in the world is no match for a small island of 20 million inhabitants that has assiduously worked Washington for decades.
"It's hard to think of anybody who does this kind of thing worse," said Stanley Roth, director of studies at the U.S. 
Institute for Peace, who was the senior Asia specialist at the White House until last month. 
"The Chinese come in and tell you what they want to do and you're supposed to say 'good.'
They are not willing to compete in the realm of ideas nor do they recognize that the key to lobbying is education over time."
But ever since the Clinton Administration bent to Congressional pressure and allowed President Lee Teng-hui of Taiwan to visit the United States last summer, the Chinese have seemed determined to sell their message better.
President Jiang Zemin has admitted the need for China to develop its skills in dealing with other nations, telling U.S. 
News and World report last year: "We have not developed the practice of picking up the phone and saying 'hello' to President Clinton. 
I think we need to improve this. 
We certainly haven't done enough lobbying of the U.S. 
Congress."
Late last year, according to press reports, the Chinese created an entity called the "Central Leading Working Group on the U.S. 
Congress," which reports indirectly to Mr. Jiang and whose mandate is to study and understand Capitol Hill. 
But the group is either so low-profile or so new that even China specialists at the Central Intelligence Agency and James Sasser, the newly confirmed American Ambassador to China, know nothing about it.
To help burnish their image, the Chinese are pressing members of Congress to visit and treating them like heads of state when they come.
Last month, when three Democratic senators -- Diane Feinstein of California, John Glenn of Ohio and Sam Nunn of Georgia -- visited Beijing, President Jiang showed them Mao's bedroom, billard room and indoor swimming pool, telling them that they were the first foreigners to step foot in that part of the palace since the Chinese leader died.
But when it came to the tough policy issues that divide the two countries -- like Taiwan, human rights and missile sales to Pakistan -- Mr. Jiang and his subordinates turned tone deaf, Senator Glenn said.
When Deputy Foreign Minister Liu Huaqiu, China's top specialist on the United States, suggested during one meeting that Congress not bring up anything negative about the relationship between the two countries during the election year, the Senator lost his patience.
"I told him 'You just don't understand our form of government if you think anybody could tell a particular Congressmen or Senator not to bring up something about China,' " Senator Glenn said. 
"We're not that kind of country. 
China has a few top leaders who decide what the country is going to do and it happens. 
In our country, every individual is a king."
That exchange underscores why China experts, businessmen and lawmakers like Senator Feinstein, who has emerged as a chief defender of China on Capitol Hill, have begun to urge the Chinese to look to Taiwan as an example of how to mold American public opinion.
Even though the United States Government considers Taiwan part of China (its diplomats cannot even enter the State Department), its lobbying efforts have led 24 states to pass resolutions to treat Taiwan like any other country.
Taiwan has 13 regional offices to push cultural and trade ties; it buys good will with donations to universities and first-class trips to Taiwan for Congressional staff members, rotary clubs, state legislators and veterans groups. 
As Governor of Arkansas, Bill Clinton visited Taiwan four times; he has never visited the People's Republic of China.
The Chinese are well aware that Taiwan is paying $4.5 million over three years to the Washington lobbying firm of Cassidy & Associates, which helped get President Lee a visa last year.
"I say to the Chinese you have a lot to learn here," said Robert Kapp, president of the U.S.-China Business Council. 
"I say to them, 'America is not a mystery.'
I say to them, 'If you're going to talk to Congress, you have to talk the talk and walk the walk.'
"
Among his specific advice is for the Chinese to assign younger people with strong language skills to reach out to Congress, state legislatures and the American people.
Although China's Ambassador, Li Daoyu, gives an occasional speech and makes an occasional trip to Capitol Hill, his embassy keeps an exceptionally low profile. 
The only time many American journalists step foot inside the embassy is trick-or-treating with their children at Halloween.
When Lu Wenxiang, the ever-polite embassy spokesman, was asked to comment on China's efforts to reach out, he said he would call back. 
He did not.
The Chinese can expect to get some help with Congress from Ambassador Sasser, who spent 18 years in the Senate and pledged during his confirmation hearings last October to have "as many senators as possible" visit him in Beijing.
"Part of my role is going to be -- how should I say it -- to more fully inform the Chinese of the importance of good relations with the U.S. 
Congress and of the way our Government functions," said Mr. Sasser, who leaves for Beijing on Saturday.
A few months ago, China sent out tentative feelers to several leading public relations and lobbying firms, but has yet to proceed with serious negotiations, a number of China specialists said.
One of those approached was Fleischman-Hillard, Inc., whose clients include Sony and MasterCard and the governments of Angola and Turkey, and which already has a trade office in Beijing. 
The company had presented the Chinese with a plan to promote American trade and investment, and has talked to independent China experts about developing a public-relations proposal for Beijing, according to people familiar with the company's activities.
For now, the single best lobbyist on behalf of China is probably former Secretary of State Henry A. Kissinger, who is not paid by China but who advises American companies doing business there. 
Mr. Kissinger's meetings with Speaker Newt Gingrich last year led him to back off his call for Taiwan's independence.
But even Mr. Kissinger's efforts have not been enough to make Mr. Gingrich a friend of China.
Just last Saturday, in a town meeting outside of Atlanta, Mr. Gingrich warned of a future nuclear threat from "China or Iran or Korea or some place like that," adding that an angry China might some day decide to launch a missile at Los Angeles.

text:

China and the United States made new progress today in resuming a program of high-level military contacts by agreeing to an exchange of visits of their top military officers next year.
But American defense officials visiting here this week reported that during private conversations they encountered trenchant rhetoric and signs of unrelenting determination by Beijing's military and civilian leaders to undermine the rule of the President of Taiwan, Lee Teng-hui.
In recent days, China has restated its intention to use all means, including military intimidation and force if necessary, to end what Beijing considers a drive by Mr. Lee to achieve independence for Taiwan.
Mr. Lee insists he is only seeking greater international recognition for the island, which has been estranged from the mainland since the Nationalists fled there after their defeat by the Communists in 1949.
As three days of talks ended, the Pentagon was receiving reports that China had begun a new military exercise off its southeastern coast near Taiwan, military officials here said.
It followed a Taiwanese drill earlier in the week intended to demonstrate the island's ability to repulse an invasion from the mainland.
The visit of the American delegation led by Joseph S. Nye, the Assistant Secretary of Defense for International Security Affairs, was the first by American military officials since the diplomatic rift that followed a White House decision to allow Mr. Lee to make a private visit to the United States in June.
And it demonstrated that United States-China relations are recovering at a time of unremitting military tension across the Taiwan Strait that could lead to another rupture in relations and, perhaps, military conflict.
"The Chinese have a military operation starting right now," an official traveling with Mr. Nye said tonight. 
"And what is clear is that China is brushing off military plans and operational contingencies that they haven't thought about since the 1950's. 
This is an issue we are very concerned about."
Mr. Nye and officials traveling with him said that communication between China and the United States is improving in some areas, but "there was no give whatsoever" on Taiwan, one official said.
"Every single person referred to Taiwan, and their point was that every Chinese is united on this question," the official said.
"It was interesting because they made a comparison with our system. 
They said you may have differences in your Congress, but in China we are all united that there is only one China and Taiwan is part of China."
Chinese military leaders, during extensive closed door talks with the American delegation, engaged in "subtle exploration" of how the United States would respond in the event of a military crisis over Taiwan, one official said.
But the American officials refused to discuss United States contingency planning. 
"We stand for peaceful resolution of disputes across the Taiwan Strait," Mr. Nye said at a news conference today.
Any use of force by China against Taiwan "would be a serious mistake" and, he added, continued military exercises near Taiwan "are not helpful."
Mr. Nye announced that the Chinese Defense Minister, Gen. Chi Haotian, would visit Washington next year and that Gen. John Shalikashvili, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, would pay a reciprocal visit to Beijing.
Visits by American and Chinese warships to each other's ports will also resume, Mr. Nye said.

text:

Early in January a group of Hong Kong's wealthiest tycoons boarded an Air China flight to Beijing for three days of meetings to promote the territory's interests with some of China's most senior officials. 
The visit reached its climax in a meeting with Li Peng, China's Prime Minister, the man widely regarded as having ordered the 1989 massacre of protesters at Tiananmen Square.
The tycoons assembled in the Pavilion of the Purple Light, one of the ceremonial halls of the old imperial compound in the heart of Beijing. 
Bit by bit the flattery and obsequiousness seeped out.
One member of the delegation asked whether Li's feelings had been hurt by the relentless negative coverage he had received in Hong Kong's free press. 
Another suggested that China buy a television station in Hong Kong so that it could more easily propagandize the people there. 
And another raised eyebrows even among his sycophantic colleagues when he praised Li for his "extraordinary leadership" of China's Communist Party. 
Li himself was taken aback at this. 
"I'm not the leader," Li reminded him. 
"President Jiang Zemin is."
The Union Jack still has 16 or so months to fly on Hong Kong's flagpoles, but many members of the city's elite are hurrying to cozy up to their new colonial master. 
Yet Hong Kong doesn't have to travel to China for that. 
In some respects the master is already there. 
You can find him on the top three floors of the old Bank of China, where China's Communist cadres once hung streaming banners denouncing British colonialism and hailing the glories of Mao Zedong. 
David Tang remembers those days. 
"One of my early memories was how mysterious that building was," says the 41-year-old Tang. 
"And there was a distinct smell. 
There was a Communist smell about it."
Today, Tang wishes he could bottle that smell because, for him, it is the smell of China. 
Tang is selling China, or at least the romance of it, here at the China Club, where nearly 2,000 of Hong Kong's toniest have shelled out $19,500 in membership fees for the privilege of eating fairly ordinary Cantonese food in a Chinese memory palace.
Waiters pad about in black slippers on worn plank floors. 
Dark wood columns are sconced with faintly Art Deco lamps. 
Rotary telephones sit beside old stuffed-leather chairs draped with antimacassars. 
And paintings of Mao cover the walls. 
Mao orating to the masses. 
Mao cheek by jowl with Whitney Houston.
Many of those who live in Hong Kong now were once victims of Maoist persecutions, but Tang, the founding spirit and part owner of the club, doesn't worry about the paradoxes. 
"Mao is an intrinsic part of Chinese history," he says. 
"We are not condoning everything Mao has done. 
I think people ought to be a little more relaxed about these kinds of things."
The transfer of Hong Kong will soon become part of Chinese history, too, and relaxing about Mao, and about China, is the message of the day in some of its inner circles.
"The message of the China Club is to create a new Chinese superiority based on being Chinese, based on being privileged Chinese," says a prominent Hong Kong lawyer. 
"And who are the privileged Hong Kong Chinese?
Those with relations with privileged Chinese. 
This is the new comprador class. 
The China Club is the new symbol."

file: China_s Arrest of Pennsylvania Librarian Alarms Scholars.txt
text:
ï»¿
The arrest here of a Pennsylvania-based Chinese researcher as he collected documents from the Maoist era has caused an uproar among Western scholars, who say it imperils academic research and exchanges with China.
Today, 101 China scholars, including many leading experts from American, Australian and British universities who favor broader ties with China, released a letter to President Jiang Zemin calling for the immediate release of the researcher, Yongyi Song.
The letter warns that Mr. Song's arrest -- on vague charges of providing confidential information to foreigners -- could undermine support for the academic exchanges that China has fostered over the last two decades as it sought to modernize and end its former isolation. 
Each year, thousands of Chinese students and professors study abroad while smaller numbers of Western experts visit China to study its history, politics and society.
"Continued prosecution of this case will make it impossible for foreign scholars or Chinese scholars associated with foreign universities to conduct research in open sources in China with the confidence that they will be safe from criminal prosecution," says the letter, which was faxed to the Chinese Embassy in Washington today.
One of the signers, Michel Oksenberg, a political scientist at Stanford University and a former White House adviser on China policy, said in an interview that by arresting an academic researcher who was apparently seeking materials already in the public domain, China may have violated basic principles on which scholarly exchanges are based.
"As a sponsor and adviser of students who wish to do research in China," Mr. Oksenberg said, "I have some responsibility to insure that their research will not place them, or those in China who assist them, at risk."
Mr. Song, 50, is a scholar and librarian at Dickinson College in Carlisle, Pa., and an authority on the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution, when China was in turmoil and largely closed to outsiders. 
Mr. Song has written a book and numerous articles in Chinese, but is best known for his exhaustive bibliographic work on that chaotic decade.
Last summer -- as he often had before -- he visited China to collect materials from the period, such as newspapers of the radical young Red Guards, old books and mimeographed records that lurk in second-hand book stores, street markets and private collections.
Many Western and Chinese scholars, including Chinese graduate students at American universities, routinely engage in the same kind of historical treasure hunt here.
But on Aug. 
7, Mr. Song -- a Chinese who was on the verge of becoming an American citizen -- was detained by security forces in Beijing.
After months of interrogations, on Dec. 
24 he was charged with "the purchase and illegal provision of intelligence to foreigners."
The charge is less severe than that for divulging "state secrets," but depending on how the courts define the gravity of his offense, Mr. Song could receive anything from a light sentence to more than 10 years in prison. 
No trial date has been announced.
The Chinese authorities have not revealed which of his activities resulted in the arrest. 
Mr. Song's wife, Helen Yao, a jewelry designer who was detained along with her husband and held for over two months, said in a recent interview that when security officers asked him about particular government documents he had acquired, he argued that each had formerly been published.
Roderick MacFarquhar, a Harvard professor and author of a multi-volume history of the origins of the Cultural Revolution, said that the prosecution of Mr. Song would create two classes of China scholars abroad: "Westerners who can come and go with relative freedom, and current or former Chinese citizens who will have to tread very carefully for fear of being arrested or at least having their relatives harassed."
Perhaps most affected will be Chinese scholars who live and work in China, who fear that their already limited ability to pursue historical evidence may shrink even further. 
One historian in Beijing said that he and his colleagues also fear that collaborative research with foreigners may become more dangerous.
The international group of scholars, organized by David Strand, a historian of China at Dickinson, also sent a copy of today's letter to President Clinton and Secretary of State Madeleine K. Albright in the hope that the administration will step up efforts on his behalf.
A spokesman for the American Embassy in Beijing said today that senior Embassy officials have "brought up the matter of Yongyi Song several times" with the Chinese government.
A subject of endless fascination for historians, the Cultural Revolution remains among China's most politically sensitive topics, and accounts published here are carefully censored in an effort to protect the legitimacy of the Communist Party.
Under Mao's banner of continuing revolution, millions of people were persecuted, imprisoned or killed, schooling came to a halt and the economy was nearly destroyed.
After Mao's death in 1976, his successors declared the Cultural Revolution to have been a disastrous mistake and said that Mao had erred under the baleful influence of a small group of leaders, including the "Gang of Four."
But Mao's achievements greatly outweighed his missteps, the official line declared, and his memory as the heroic father of the People's Republic has been carefully nurtured ever since.
Many key documents from the Cultural Revolution remain in closed archives, including Beijing directives that might implicate Mao or other leaders such as the late, revered Prime Minister Zhou Enlai in vicious purges or other misdeeds.
But during the early years of the Cultural Revolution in particular, fanatical young Maoists often published leaders' speeches and other documents. 
Such materials have been avidly collected by scholars and libraries, largely without trouble until now.
In recent weeks, as word spread about the criminal charges against Mr. Song, members of Congress and the State Department have expressed concern and China scholars have been up in arms.
"Because of its unpredictability and the absence of clearly stated rules," said Thomas P. Bernstein, an expert on Chinese politics at Columbia University, the case "is dangerous from the point of view of anyone doing research on contemporary China."
Mr. Strand, Mr. Song's colleague at Dickinson, said today, "This case strikes at every aspect of the work we do, both practical and ethical."
"Every day I think of Song in his jail cell," he said.

file: China_s Fickle Rivers_ Dry Farms, Needy Industry Bring a Water Crisis.txt
text:
ï»¿
The one time this spring that there was actually enough water in the Yellow River to flow all the way to its mouth on the Bohai Sea, the peasants in this village of brick and mud homes were not allowed to use it.
Just a month away from the summer wheat harvest, the farmers here were forced to stand by as hundreds of millions of gallons of water flowed past their thirsty crops to a state-run oil field downstream at Dongying. 
The oil company's directors had pleaded to Communist Party officials in Beijing that without the water they would be forced to shut down crucial pumping operations.
Tempers flared and earthy epithets flew when the peasants discovered that guards had been stationed at the valves to their fields.
"All this water started flowing but we were told it was restricted for use only by the oil company and we were not allowed to use it," said Li Lixing, a 28-year-old farmer in the village, where almost everyone is named Li and whose residents have farmed the banks of the Yellow River for centuries. 
"We had to go at night and secretly take some for our crops," Mr. Li said, shaking his head and concluding, "The life of a peasant is pretty pitiful."
What happened along the lower reaches of the Yellow River this spring was another portent of China's developing water crisis. 
And the anxiety that has seized this farming village is the anxiety of 120 million Chinese whose lives, agriculture and industry depend on the Yellow River. 
They want to know: Will there be enough water?
The answer is probably no, say Chinese and Western water experts, unless China undertakes extensive conservation measures and builds some of the largest dam and aqueduct projects ever conceived, requiring the dislocation of hundreds of thousands of Chinese at tremendous cost to the economy.
Indeed, the key to the future of the Yellow River may be the Yangtze River, whose virtually inexhaustible flow has prompted Chinese leaders to consider building mammoth waterworks to divert a part of its volume to northern China. 
These waterworks would be even larger and more costly than the Three Gorges Dam, the world's largest hydroelectric project, which is now under construction on the lower Yangtze.
"These are the world's largest engineering schemes," said Pieter Bottelier, the World Bank's resident director in China. 
"Even if they build a series of dams and reservoirs on the Yellow River, they will still have to do the south-to-north water diversion scheme. 
That is the judgment of our engineers."
Until then, the Yellow River basin and the broad, northern plain of China face a growing water shortage as economic growth, a surging population and the contamination of water supplies combine to squeeze the country's available water resources.
Known as the cradle of Chinese civilization and also as "China's Sorrow" for the millions it has killed in floods, the Yellow River has gone dry in its lower reaches for an average of 70 days a year in each of the last 10 years. 
In 1995, the dry period stretched to 122 days, as water users all along its course diverted its flow for some of the most extensive irrigation networks ever built.
And so, this spring, the oil company officials at Dongying sent their urgent appeal to Beijing, warning that without a guaranteed water supply, the oil field -- critical to China's energy needs -- might have to shut down.
The Government declared a state of emergency to force farmers and factories along a 400-mile stretch of the river in Henan and Shandong provinces to close sluice gates so the water, released by the upstream dam at Sanmenxia, would reach Dongying, the last stop on the Yellow River's course to the sea.
The oil field got the water, but the crisis continues.
More than 100 large Chinese cities, but particularly those in northern China, have acute water supply problems and only 6 cities can meet safe drinking water standards due to growing pollution of water sources from untreated sewage, industrial waste and agricultural chemicals.
This year, Shanxi province, China's coal-producing center, is so parched that drinking water is being rationed and most people in Taiyuan, the capital, get nothing when they turn on the taps in their homes.
In China's arid northwest, peasants travel up to 10 miles a day under back-breaking conditions to secure their daily water supplies.
Even in Beijing, the water demands of the luxurious new hotels and office buildings have so overstressed supplies that farmers in the broad agricultural belt outside the city have been cut off from traditional water sources. 
The capital is rapidly outgrowing the two small reservoirs that serve it and the city is expected to enter a period of serious shortfall within a decade.
Chinese Government scientists now predict that demand for Yellow River water will outstrip available supplies by 250 billion cubic feet in the year 2000. 
A World Bank assessment says the shortage could reach 280 billion to 425 billion cubic feet, or about 20 percent of the river's flow.
"The current level of water supply cannot hope to meet the demands of the provinces," said Huang Ziqiang, a senior engineer at the Yellow River Conservancy Commission in Zhengzhou. 
"If the eight provinces along the river got everything they wanted, they would want a total of 92 trillion cubic feet by the year 2000, but the total water resources of the river are only 71 trillion, so that is a big difference."
Â 
Erratic Resource
Plenty of Water At Wrong Times
At first it seems counterintuitive that China could be running short of water. 
Its geography has created dozens of mighty rivers that form in the western part of the country high on the Qinghai-Tibetan plateau. 
They cascade down from two-mile heights through spectacular gorges before emerging onto alluvial plains in the east. 
Their scenes of violence and beauty have inspired Chinese poets and artists over two millennia.
China ranks sixth in the world in total water resources, but the average Chinese uses less than a quarter of the world's per capita consumption.
The core of the problem is the seasonal nature of China's rainfall and the lack of control over its rivers as they run to the sea, sometimes in devastating floods. 
Beijing gets more annual rainfall than Paris, Berlin or even London, but most of it falls during an eight-week period in summer.
"China has abundant water resources, but it is often found in the wrong place at the wrong time, so we have shortages," said Chen Chuanyou, a leading water and irrigation expert at the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
Li Zunyao, 73, one of the oldest farmers in Litingzhuang, which means "village of Li households," complained, "It seems that when you don't need the water, like in winter, there is plenty of it, and when you really need it for planting crops in the spring, there is never enough."
Â 
'China's Sorrow'
Managing Control Of the Yellow River
Because it is the dominant water system in northern China, the Yellow River is the key to the future of the region, where industrial and mining output are expected to double the demand for water over the next five years.
From its headwaters, the Yellow River travels 3,000 miles to the sea. 
In its upper reaches, its waters are crystal clear. 
It is only when it makes a long serpentine loop through Inner Mongolia and around the loess plateau that the river becomes the muddiest in the world, gathering the "yellow earth" at sediment concentrations 10 to 30 times as dense as in the Mississippi River, itself often called the Big Muddy.
"In some places, the river resembles more a flowing mudslide than a river," said Michel Oksenberg, a China specialist at Stanford University.
There is now no longer any dispute that within five years demand for Yellow River water will be well beyond its capacity to deliver it, leading to what the World Bank terms "severe crop stress" in the vast farmlands the river now supports.
In part, the problem is management.
The river is so choked with mud that roughly a third of its annual flow is used each year to "flush" the mud downstream.
The rest is parceled out by a series of dams under a water management plan that is chaotic at the best of times.
"Fundamentally, the Yellow River is out of control from an overall planning standpoint," said Arthur N. Holcombe, director of the United Nations Development Fund in Beijing.
Chinese officials in charge of the river seem to agree.
"The management of our water supply is very poor," said Wu Zhiyao, the chief engineer of the Yellow River Conservancy Commission in Zhengzhou. 
"So many cities and industries along the river are greedy for water and they take more than they need without any regard to the people downstream."
In theory, he added, the commission has the authority to manage the Yellow River's water, but in reality, provincial leaders can flout any water management plan until Beijing intervenes to sort out water priorities, as it did this spring at Dongying.
After the Three Gorges project, the second largest dam project under way in China is the Xiaolangdi Dam, which has received little notice. 
But its construction will force the relocation of 400,000 peasants by the time it is completed in 2002. 
The $3 billion dam is being built with the help of a $500 million World Bank loan and will be designed to protect the lower reaches of the Yellow River valley from the hypothetical flood that occurs every 1,000 years and could kill a million Chinese.
Indeed, China's prime concern in planning a series of new dams costing a total of $12 billion to $15 billion on the Yellow River is flood control.
"The Yellow River is very dangerous when it comes out of the mountains and onto the open plain," said Mr. Bottelier, the head of the World Bank mission in Beijing. 
"It is always a threat to break out of its levies."
Â 
Diversion Project
Enormous Plan To Tap the Yangtze
Even if the Yellow River's water were used with maximal efficiency, it could not meet the demands of expanding irrigation and industry.
This spring, Government scientists and engineers are deliberating over an enormous water diversion plan that would tap central China's Yangtze River at five points and convey the water north through huge tunnels and aqueducts that would bore through mountains and traverse plains.
The proposed diversion has prompted a major debate among China's scientists and significant opposition from those who favor conservation over massive engineering projects.
"There is lots of internal opposition, more than that against the Three Gorges Dam," said Vaclav Smil, a scientist at the University of Manitoba who studies China's environmental problems.
"But I think they will go ahead with these schemes," Mr. Smil said, "because to them it will be the simpler solution to increase the supply of water rather than manage the supply through conservation. 
That is the typical Communist Party solution."
The Yangtze, with 15 times the flow of the Yellow River, "has virtually limitless water resources," said Mr. Bottelier of the World Bank, and may be the only long-term solution to north China's water shortage.
Although the cost of these water diversion plans is still being calculated, together they far exceed the estimated $17 billion cost of the Three Gorges Dam.
"I think they will make their decision this year," said Mr. Wu, the chief engineer of the Yellow River Conservancy Commission. 
"but there is a big debate going on."
Even the peasants in Litingzhuang have heard about the water diversion plans.
"It is said that the future is bright and the Yellow River can be controlled so that when we need the water it will be released and when we don't it will be stored," said Li Zhonghua, 31.
In the meantime, said Li Chengliang, a carpenter who makes horse carts, "Life here is not so good, but it is interesting."

file: China_s Leader Flexing Muscle on Several Fronts at Once.txt
text:
ï»¿
These are politically perilous days for President Jiang Zemin. 
Yet he is deliberately fighting on several fronts at once, using an atmosphere of crisis to exert his personal authority in new ways.
Faced with an exceedingly difficult political challenge from Taiwan, where President Lee Tung-hui seems to be spoiling Beijing's dream of reunification, Mr. Jiang is not retreating, but is rather taking the offensive.
At the same time that he threatens force against Taiwan, Mr. Jiang is conducting twin political campaigns: one against Falun Gong, the spiritual movement that was outlawed last month, and the other against laxness in the Communist Party apparatus.
Today, state media reported a major policy address by Mr. Jiang, his first since the leadership emerged from an annual summer conclave at the seaside report of Beidaihe. 
Mr. Jiang spoke not about Taiwan or Falun Gong, or even about Communist Party discipline. 
Instead, he ventured into a fourth area where he would like to make a personal imprint: economic reform.
Why juggle so many balls in the air at one time?
With the Taiwan issue virtually unsolvable, political experts here say, Mr. Jiang is taking the offensive in other areas to extend and strengthen his authority in case Taiwan does not turn out well.
"October 1 is the key date," a political analyst in Beijing said, referring to the 50th anniversary of Communist Party rule, an occasion for an enormous political pageant. 
"Jiang is reacting to events, but he is also asserting himself in a way that makes him the unquestioned leader at an important time."
Each year, when China's leaders conclude their highly secretive summer conclave, experts look for clues to what was decided, and characteristically come up with little. 
While many guess at whether moderates or conservatives scored more points, all appearances this year point to a stronger hand for Mr. Jiang, who likes to portray himself as being simultaneously in the middle and above it all.
On Monday, political experts in Beijing were surprised by a headline that streamed across the top of the People's Daily, the Communist Party's mouthpiece: "Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Jiang Zemin Discuss Materialism and Atheism."
That might sound like so much Communist Party drivel to an outsider, but party historians doubtless noted the milestone. 
It was the first time that the newspaper had placed Mr. Jiang on an even stage with Mao and Deng, each considered giants of China's revolutionary struggle, and the timing of such a grand assertion can hardly be coincidental.
When Deng passed ultimate control of China's leadership to Mr. Jiang in the early 1990's, Mr. Jiang chose Taiwan as one of the main issues that would define his leadership. 
The goal of reunifying Taiwan with mainland China had been beyond the grasp of Mao and Deng, and this was clearly an issue where Mr. Jiang could distinguish himself.
Mr. Jiang chose his trusted mentor, the former Shanghai Mayor Wang Daohan, to open negotiations with Taiwan. 
Mr. Wang, a flexible and creative politician, began talks with a Taiwan counterpart in 1993.
Yet Taiwan has proved more difficult than Mr. Jiang seemed to expect. 
President Lee rebuffed repeated attempts to give the talks substance, and then shocked Beijing in July this year by asserting that Taiwan would now see China in a "special state-to-state relationship," discarding the earlier framework that saw the two as part of one conceptual nation.
Seeing Mr. Lee's move as an possibly irreparable step away from reunification, Mr. Jiang now faces an excruciating dilemma. 
Acquiescing to Mr. Lee's action opens Mr. Jiang to attack from hawkish critics that he is losing Taiwan. 
Yet taking military action risks the great humiliation that would come from an effective counterattack by Taiwan's forces, and from drawing United States forces to Taiwan's defense.
A major element of Mr. Jiang's leadership has been to bring China into closer cooperation with the United States, China's biggest trading partner. 
That stance could be ruined by a conflict with Taiwan.
Chinese officials recently warned Washington that they may be forced to "punish" Taiwan with some kind of military strike, a message that China's media have been trumpeting for weeks, apparently in the hope that Washington might force Mr. Lee to retract his stance. 
Yet Mr. Lee shows no sign of retreating.
Mr. Jiang may try to muddle through a middle ground, making a limited military move that satisfies China's hawks, without causing the disruption that would come from an all-out war. 
Yet on such a delicate issue, mixing the potentially explosive matters of sovereignty and military might, the situation is highly unpredictable.
Another plank of Mr. Jiang's leadership is economic growth, which many experts believe is crucial to maintaining the acceptance of Communist Party rule by restive workers in urban areas, where unemployment is growing fast. 
Economic growth could also be severely damaged by any military action.
In today's policy address, Mr. Jiang seemed to try to steer a middle course, stressing the need for economic growth while being vigilant on military issues.
"Competitiveness in our overall national strength is increasingly a decisive factor in shaping a country's fate," Mr. Jiang said. 
"We are on the verge of a new and rare opportunity, but at the same time we face grave new challenges.
"Only by unceasingly enhancing our economic strength, defensive strength and national cohesiveness can we establish an unbeatable position in international competition that grows more intense each day, and effectively protect our national sovereignty and national dignity."
Until recently, Prime Minister Zhu Rongji was seen to be in charge of China's economic reform program. 
Yet Mr. Zhu's position appears to have been weakened after his trip in April to the United States, where he was accused by conservative rivals of having offered too many concessions to try to win China's entry to the World Trade Organization.
On Thursday, appearing at an international horticultural exhibition in Kunming, in China's southwest, Mr. Zhu denied reports that he might resign. 
Yet while other leaders met at Beidaihe, he was pictured prominently in the media as he inspected flood waters in central China.
Mr. Zhu was also conspicuously absent from the stage in northeast China where Mr. Jiang delivered his policy address on economic reform, where several other leading officials did appear. 
Instead, Mr. Zhu was pictured in today's media at the horticultural exhibition.
Although Mr. Zhu does not appear to have been completely sidelined, his authority over economic reform seems to have been curtailed. 
That paves the way for a greater hand in economic reform for Mr. Jiang.
Some Chinese experts believe that Mr. Jiang opened the campaign against Falun Gong 10 days after the Taiwan crisis erupted in order to engage in an easily winnable political movement to draw attention away from a more difficult one.
Yet Mr. Jiang appears to have detected in Falun Gong a genuine threat to the Communist Party's role as the undisputed power in the nation, and also saw an opportunity to mobilize the Communist Party apparatus behind him as Falun Gong is stamped out.
Meantime, China's official bluster about Taiwan continues. 
One newspaper, the China Business Times, devoted its front page on Thursday to an analysis of potential military conflict, confidently predicting that Taiwan forces would not be able to withstand an onslaught from the mainland for more than four or five days.
Military experts say, however, that the Chinese Army is woefully inequipped for an amphibious assault on Taiwan. 
That may be why, during the last crisis in 1996, China lobbed a few missiles into the ocean near Taiwan, talking tough as it took essentially harmless action.
Limited military action is still possible, military experts say, like the seizing of one of the small islands that Taiwan controls, even though they hug the coast of China. 
But tough-sounding threats from Beijing have been part of official policy for 50 years, during which China has yet to actually move on Taiwan.

file: China_s Rulers on Guard as Spiritual Sect Pushes the Envelope.txt
text:
ï»¿
The police were out in force in several Chinese cities this weekend, seeking to head off rumored plans for new demonstrations by a spiritual sect that staged a giant vigil in Beijing a week ago.
No incidents have been reported, and national leaders are pondering how to deal with the group, called Buddhist Law, which has gained millions of fervent followers. 
The Government normally maintains control over mass movements and religions and does not allow social groups to be directed from abroad, as this group is.
Though it is not political and insists that it is not a religion, Buddhist Law has pushed the edge of what is allowed. 
With last week's demonstration by 10,000 members seeking legal approval, the group also showed a remarkable ability to muster its believers.
The Communist rulers have tried to avoid provoking the organization, whose members are seen as decent citizens. 
But the leadership cannot be happy to see the emergence of a social wild card.
Buddhist Law, or Falun Gong, was first preached in 1992 by Li Hongzhi, who was already a master of the ancient art of qigong (pronounced che-goong) in which breathing and meditation are used to channel vital forces. 
Mr. Li, now 48, combined concepts from qigong, Buddhism and Taoism with his own mystical theories. 
Last year, saying he was under official pressure, Mr. Li moved to New York, but he remains the sect's absolute leader.
The word Falun means "law wheel," a high-energy rotating body said to be in a practitioner's abdomen that harnesses cosmic forces and expels bad elements. 
Followers are told to harness this power, rather than using medicines, to cure disease.
Traditional martial arts like qigong were suppressed here as superstition in the 1960's and 1970's, but in the more open climate that followed they have revived. 
Leaders of traditional groups here who blatantly cross over into fraud have been imprisoned.
Although it obviously has great popular appeal, particularly among retirees and middle-aged women, Mr. Li's new sect has had critics. 
More traditional qigong sects are mainly devoted to health and fitness. 
The Government's limited oversight is wielded through the martial arts department of the Sports Commission.
Last year, that department began evaluating qigong sects for legal approval. 
But a scholar who advised the department, Luo Shao, said that the evaluation methods were ill-defined and that many officials were followers of qigong, insuring a lack of critical oversight.
So far the agency has studied only 11 sects out of hundreds, not including Buddhist Law, and approved them all, said Mr. Luo, an expert on Buddhist history at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and a strong critic of the group.
New offshoots like this one, with charismatic leaders and broad-ranging mystical beliefs, have been attacked as heretical cults by some scholars here as well as by mainstream qigong groups and Buddhist leaders. 
Members resent the characterization.
Buddhist Law was accepted into the semi-official China Qigong Science Association in 1993, but expelled in 1996 for what were considered its extreme claims. 
In a letter sent to followers in December, Mr. Li said he had withdrawn because the purpose of "so-called fitness-maintenance qigong" is to "swindle money."Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: China_s Sniping Heeded By Some Taiwan Voters.txt
text:
ï»¿
With Taiwan's presidential election only 10 days away, China has uncorked its vitriol on the Democratic Progressive Party candidate, Chen Shui-bian, calling him a separatist and a silver-tongued liar. 
To hear Mr. Chen tell it, Beijing is doing him a favor.
"We have a precedent here," he said in an interview during a campaign swing that took him from Taipei to this southern port city. 
"The person China hates, Taiwan voters love."
When Beijing fired missiles into the ocean near Taiwan before the 1996 election, hoping to scare people away from President Lee Teng-hui, they responded by re-electing him in a landslide. 
Mr. Chen, who is viewed as less acceptable to Beijing than either of his two main rivals, said China's latest barrage of threats would play to his advantage as well by raising the hackles of voters.
But Chen Shui-bian is not Lee Teng-hui, and this is not 1996.
Interviews with party officials, political analysts and voters this week suggest that Mr. Chen's identification with the cause of Taiwanese independence could hurt him, particularly among the one-quarter of the electorate that is still undecided.
Mr. Chen is running neck-and-neck with Vice President Lien Chan and James Soong, an independent. 
Mr. Chen's campaign manager figures the election will hinge on 200,000 to 300,000 voters, who may not make up their minds until they step into the polling booth.
In the meantime, these people are being subjected to a daily drumbeat from Beijing. 
On Monday, the Chinese Army accused a "prominent figure" -- read Chen Shui-bian -- of pushing for independence and said it had put its troops on alert to crush such a move.
"Under no circumstances should we be fooled by his sweet talk," said the army's newspaper, Liberation Army Daily, in a front-page editorial. 
"One minute he is brazenly howling 'Long live Taiwan independence,' while the next he is using beautiful and pleasant words to lie that he wants 'good will, reconciliation, vigorous cooperation and everlasting peace' with the mainland."
Today in Beijing, President Jiang Zemin told a group of foreign journalists, "If you seek Taiwan independence, it will be a case of brother fighting brother."
One of those who is listening is Chen Yen-yang, 22, a political science student at National Taiwan University. 
Mr. Chen, who will cast his first vote in this election, said he always assumed he would support Chen Shui-bian. 
But he starts compulsory military service next year. 
That has changed his mind, and he now plans to vote for Vice President Lien of the governing Nationalist Party.
"Everybody around me, my family and friends, is talking about the possibility of war between Taiwan and China," Mr. Chen said. 
"I can't ignore that."
His classmate, Chen Yu-wen, said, "I think Chen Shui-bian underestimates China's willingness to take military action against Taiwan."
She said she planned to vote for Mr. Lien because the Nationalist Party "understands China."
"They know how to deal with them," she said.
Mr. Chen's rivals have seized the chance to portray him as a threat to peace. 
The Nationalists are running a newspaper advertisement that shows a man in army fatigues, his face hidden by a black gas mask, staring into a wall of flames. 
The figure represents Taiwan in the aftermath of a Chen victory.
Mr. Chen counters these charges by noting he is the only candidate with a son who would be drafted into the military if Taiwan were invaded by China. 
"As a father, I understand the fear of parents who don't want to put their children into danger," he said.
In his zeal to appear moderate, Mr. Chen rivals even the hypercautious Mr. Lien. If elected, he has pledged not to declare independence, not to hold a referendum on the issue, and not to put the phrase "special state-to-state" relations into Taiwan's Constitution. 
Those words, which President Lee uttered last July, infuriated China and set off a war of words across the Strait of Taiwan.
The problem for Mr. Chen is the platform of the Democratic Progressive Party, which calls for "the establishment of a sovereign and independent Republic of Taiwan."
Mr. Chen insisted today that such a move would come only after a plebiscite, the timing of which would be up to the people.
Some political analysts dismissed Mr. Chen's more conciliatory tone as a political ploy rather than a shift in his bedrock beliefs. 
And they said the fervor of 1996 -- in which Taiwanese people rose up to defend their first native-born president -- was missing from this election.
"People in this country are no longer fanatical," said Wang Jin-pyng, a Nationalist Party stalwart who is the president of Taiwan's legislature. 
"They believe that maintenance of stabilityI is the best policy. 
If the threats from China reduce Chen's support by 3 percent, he will lose the election."
Kaohsiung is one of Mr. Chen's strongholds, and tonight thousands of his supporters turned out here for an earsplitting, and defiant, rally.
Lee Chia-shin, 27, who has a mix of mainland Chinese and native Taiwanese roots, said she did not worry about China's hostility. 
"I think Chen Shui-bian will be flexible enough to deal with it," she said.
Cheng Wen-shiung, a 47-year-old tailor, also said the threats from China would not intimidate him.
"We Taiwanese have the courage to repel any invader," he said. 
But he added, "Of course, some people won't vote for Chen because of China."

file: China_s Top Justice Official Ousted, Some Say for Corruption.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's minister of justice was removed from office this week, officials acknowledged today, and according to some accounts he is under investigation for corruption.
As of tonight, the departure of the minister, Gao Changli, 63, had not been announced. 
But during the day, as rumors swirled in legal circles, Justice Ministry employees were told that Mr. Gao had quit because of poor health, a ministry worker said.
If his departure involves financial improprieties, Mr. Gao's case would be another blow for the Communist Party, which is reeling at the scope of corruption coming to light.
Adding to the party's concern is a legal battle brewing in Vancouver, Canada, over the fate of China's most wanted suspect, Lai Changxing. 
Chinese officials say he was the mastermind of a smuggling operation in the southern city of Xiamen that drew hundreds of high party, police and customs officials into crime.
Officials said Mr. Gao had been replaced by Zhang Fusen, deputy secretary of the Beijing Communist Party and a former deputy justice minister.
Over the last two days, a few newspapers in Hong Kong and the West have reported that sources in the ministry were saying that Mr. Gao had been detained for interrogation about economic misdeeds. 
While some legal officials also said today that he was under investigation, others said that they were unaware of it, and details could not be confirmed.
Mr. Gao rose to power in Shandong Province, then in 1993 became a senior member of the national Supreme People's Court before being appointed to the top justice post in 1998.
Though traditionally weak, the ministry oversees prisons and legal education and regulates the legal profession. 
While Mr. Gao had no direct power over prosecutors and courts, which are notoriously susceptible to political control and corruption, he had taken a leading role in promoting the rule of law, a professed goal of the top leaders as China opens to the global economy.
Mr. Lai, the detained businessman, began as a barely educated farmer in Fujian Province but by the 1990's was a corporate kingpin living in Hong Kong, with his Yuanhua Group a dominant corporate presence back in Xiamen, a port in Fujian. 
The authorities say that by spreading bribes widely, Mr. Lai, 42, imported more than $5 billion worth of cars, fuel and other goods without paying duties. 
By the time the case broke earlier this year, Mr. Lai had disappeared. 
Now, with the detention of him and his wife, Tsang Mingna, by Canadian immigration authorities last week, it is known that Mr. Lai, his wife and three teenage children fled to Vancouver in August 1999, using Hong Kong passports.
The couple's detention has put Canada in a delicate spot. 
In hearings this week, officials made it clear that they hope to deport them to China, stressing that Canada does not want to be seen as a refuge for criminals. 
But Canada does not have an extradition treaty with China or a death penalty and has often declined to extradite criminals to countries where they are likely to be executed.
Eleven others in the smuggling case have been sentenced to death, and Mr. Lai would be almost certain to receive the same punishment.
In a court statement this week, Mr. Lai denied the smuggling charges and gave sensational but unverified details of past ties to senior Hong Kong and Chinese officials as well as his work as a Chinese double-agent against Taiwan.
Mr. Lai said that he met three times in 1999 with Chinese prosecutors who wanted him to help frame the vice minister for public security, Li Jizhou, who had been a longtime friend. 
It was his refusal to cooperate in a political struggle, Mr. Lai said, that led prosecutors to go after him.
In contrast, accounts leaking from government sources say Mr. Lai kept a pleasure house in Xiamen where he set up Mr. Li and other officials with mistresses, ensuring cooperation in his scheme.

file: China_s Trade Status Remains _Open Question_ as Vote Nears.txt
text:
ï»¿
With animosity toward China growing on the right and left in Congress, President Clinton's national security adviser, Samuel R. Berger, said yesterday that it remained "an open question" whether Congress would vote to revoke China's normal trading status.
Mr. Berger spoke as the Republican leadership in the House rescheduled this year's vote on the trading status for late June, a month earlier than expected, to assure a vote before the return of Hong Kong to Chinese rule on July 1.
Mr. Berger said that even a close vote that preserved China's status could prove "corrosive," undercutting the Administration's efforts to deal with China's leaders on a variety of issues, from the environment to the spread of weapons.
"It is difficult for us to move this relationship to a new level where we have a greater chance of solving problems if we don't have a national consensus behind the policy," Mr. Berger said in an interview in his office at the White House.
The trade arrangement is called "most favored nation" status, although it is the normal trading arrangement accorded most countries by the United States. 
China's status is currently subject to yearly review, and advocates of renewal this year have been concerned that any problem in the handover of Hong Kong, especially televised protests that could provoke police reaction, could jeopardize passage.
One Republican aide said yesterday that the vote was being moved up to deny opponents the opportunity to rally support. 
That suggested confidence that the House will preserve the status but concern that opposition could be stronger than it has been in recent years.
In a speech delivered in New York at the Council on Foreign Relations, Mr. Berger said that the fight to revoke China's status was the "one development" that could undercut American policy toward China and "do grievous injury to the interests of the United States."
In his speech, Mr. Berger defended the Administration's policy, which seeks to engage China through trade and economic development, while making clear American objections to violations of human rights, among other things. 
He also said the United States would monitor how China takes control of Hong Kong to insure that its traditions and freedoms thrive, but that punishing China by revoking its trading status would only isolate Hong Kong.
"The goals of the opponents to normal trading relations with China are ones we share -- advocating human rights and religious freedom, promoting fair trade, strengthening regional and global security," he said in his speech. 
"But the method they have chosen -- destroying our economic relations with China -- is profoundly misguided."
In the interview, Mr. Berger said the Administration was articulating what he called a "clear and coherent" policy toward China as Congress moves toward what is expected to be a pitched fight.
The Administration hoped this year would bring calmer relations with China, culminating in a summit meeting between President Clinton and President Jiang Zemin in the fall. 
Last year's debate ended quickly, as members in the House voted solidly -- 286 to 141 -- to renew China's status.
But this year the debate has flared, driven by a lack of improvement in China's human rights record, the impending takeover of Hong Kong and the controversy over campaign finance.
Mr. Berger argued that critics of China had chosen the wrong way to register their outrage. 
He said that the United States had "an arsenal of tools" to punish China, including more targeted sanctions, like those imposed last month on two Chinese companies for helping Iran develop chemical weapons.
As for Hong Kong, he said the United States expected China to abide by the agreement reached with Britain in 1984 to maintain Hong Kong's freedoms under autonomy. 
The United States would gauge that, he said, by seeing whether elections for a new legislature take place soon, the civil service and judiciary continue to work unmolested, the economy remains open, and freedom of religion, speech and association is maintained.
"Living up to that pledge is as much in China's interest as it is in Hong Kong or in ours," he said in the speech.
"A smooth reversion will promote China's international prestige," he said. 
"Handled badly, the transition will tarnish China."
He did not, however, specify what steps the United States would take if China at some point in the future violated those standards.

file: China_s Transport Gridlock_ Cars vs. Mass Transit.txt
text:
ï»¿
Until recently, officials of this port city famous for its Tsing Tao beer and its German architecture boasted that they were investing heavily in basic infrastructure as part of their strategy to attract more foreign industries.
Last fall, Deputy Mayor Min Xiangchao could hardly contain his enthusiasm when he told an interviewer that "the pace of growth of Qingdao is difficult to hold back now" because the city had won approval from the central Government in Beijing to build a subway system, a cross-harbor tunnel connecting the city's industrial zone with its downtown area, which are on opposite sides of Jiaozhou Bay, and a 10-mile bridge to span the bay.
"These will be the engines of growth in later years," he predicted.
Today, however, these projects have been suspended for lack of financing.
What has happened here in the last 12 months is happening all over China: basic transportation projects, especially mass transportation, are being canceled or cut back dramatically for lack of capital and as Beijing's leaders debate the best way to move 1.3 billion Chinese from one place to another in the next century.
While money is a key issue, basic issues of transportation policy also remain unsettled.
Although most Chinese still walk, bicycle or ride a farm animal to get around, the migration by millions of people to urban centers is creating a transportation crisis.
Where there is public transport, bus and train fares stay frozen for years, part of the cradle-to-grave subsidy system under socialism that has undermined new investment. 
Meanwhile, in dozens of large cities, traffic gridlock is threatening the very growth that must occur to meet the transport needs of tens of millions of new job seekers arriving in the cities over the next five years.
In large part, the policy debate centers on whether scarce money should be directed more toward better roads for the swelling number of automobiles, or toward mass transit. 
Which way China goes will have enormous environmental consequences not only for urban residents here, already choking in smoggy air, but for the whole world -- a vast new fleet of cars in China would use up so many resources and add to the problem of planetary warming.
The debate over how to manage this crisis has pitted the powerful Ministry of Machine-Building Industry and its two million workers in dozens of automobile plants against China's scientific establishment and many municipal authorities, who see their streets descending into a choking paroxysm of traffic and pollution.
The ministry is busy implementing the "pillar industry" strategy formulated in 1994 by China's State Council under Prime Minister Li Peng. 
Its aim is to create a half-dozen giant Chinese automakers in partnership with General Motors, Volkswagen and other foreign companies to feed the growing demand by newly rich Chinese for cars.
The ministry wants China's central and local governments to divert more money into highway and road construction to support an automobile-based economy.
But China's scientific community, in a major report last summer, began a campaign to challenge this policy.
"It would be inappropriate for China to encourage the use of family cars on a large scale in the next few years because of the country's serious shortage of land, oil and other resources and its huge population," the scientists' report said. 
It recommended "a public transportation network that is convenient, complete and radiating in all directions."
As it is, China's relatively small road network is already under strain. 
For every one million Chinese, there are only 541 miles of roads, most of them unpaved and rutted. 
By comparison, there are 15,195 miles of paved road per one million Americans, 5,457 miles per one million Japanese and 1,070 miles per one million Indians.
One of China's leading physicists, Prof. He Zuoxiu, who worked on the country's first atomic bomb, has thrust himself into the transportation debate by trying to persuade the Communist Party leadership to get behind mass transit.
Ticking off the problems of China's future energy supplies, worsening pollution and the shortage of land, Professor He said in a recent interview in Beijing that "China just simply cannot sustain the development of a car economy."
Professor He said that he fears that Government policy is being driven by a desire to keep two million auto workers employed. 
In addition, many top officials in Prime Minister Li's Cabinet come from the auto industry. 
Even President Jiang Zemin got his start as a Soviet-trained electrical engineer.
"Right now, the Government still has no clear policy and so this issue is still very much under debate," Professor He said, even though "almost every scientist in China favors the development of mass transit systems."
As the debate rages, many experts say other factors are influencing China's choices, notably the country's inability to attract the kind of capital needed to construct a modern transport system.
Limits set by Chinese authorities on rates of return foreigners can earn on long-term investments in power plants and toll highways in China have engendered a wariness in world capital markets about making long-term commitments here.
Still, there is a sense of urgency.
China's infrastructure bill includes the Yangtze River's Three Gorges Dam, the largest hydro-electric project in the world, and dozens of major power plants that must be completed to meet electrical demand and stop the blackouts that idle many industries.
In addition, money must be found for an aquaduct system to save northern China from perpetual drought, for new rail networks to open China's internal markets, for oil refineries, an updated telecommunications system and dozens of new airports and shipping terminals.
The central Government's budget revenues, chronically weak, cannot hope to pay for such a prodigious agenda, estimated by the World Bank to cost $300 billion or more during the 1996-2000 period.
"China's needs today are enormous and immediate," concluded a recent study by Nicholas Bradbury of The Economist Intelligence Unit in Hong Kong. 
"Without dramatic improvements to its infrastructure, and foreign expertise to implement them, China's economic progress will stall."
In December, China's State Council, or cabinet, issued orders to shut down subway and light rail projects in Qingdao and three other major cities -- Nanjing, Shenyang and Tianjin. 
The order was not made public until late March.
"Funds needed for metro construction are beyond the means of the central and local government and operating expenses are too high," the semi-official China Daily newspaper quoted a Cabinet statement as saying.
The latest estimates show that the cost of subway construction have soared in the last decade and now range from $53 million to $91.5 million per kilometer.
"These programs are extremely capital intensive," said Robert S. O'Neil, president of De Leuw, Cather & Company, a Washington, D.C., subway design and consulting company now working on Shanghai's subway system. 
"They don't pay for themselves," he added.
Wang Yuexian, a senior transportation planner at the State Planning Commission in Beijing, said that under the cabinet edict, only subways planned for Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou would go forward, and even in these cities, schedules would be stretched out and work limited to a single line.
"A total of 17 cities have applied for subway financing," said Jiao Ying, a senior engineer at the Ministry of Railways, who has stayed behind in Qingdao to complete a test tunnel section should the project ever be revived. 
"But the Government only considers three or four of them important, and the rest will have to wait," he added.
In Beijing, a new eight-mile subway line that was to open in 1997 will now be delayed another 10 years. 
Shanghai will be allowed to complete a new 16-mile line and Guangzhou will complete an 11-mile line.
The central Government edict has done little to dampen enthusiasm in Qingdao.
Xue Liai, the vice director of the city's Major Projects Office, said in an interview that "we still hope we can build the subway because every citizen here wants it."
Construction crews had nearly completed the largest station on the first 10-mile segment of the Qingdao system when the order to stop work came in December. 
City officials quickly shifted their plans and persuaded the Miramar Hotel group from Hong Kong to convert the station into an underground shopping mall.
Now, where the trains should be running, there is an endless line of boutiques, and above ground on the streets -- gridlock.

text:

China's troops streamed into this new Chinese territory today, in a joyful procession that revealed how deeply people here yearn for law and order after the gangsterism that stained the last years of Portuguese colonial rule.
At noon, 12 hours after the ceremony in which China gained sovereignty over Macao, a convoy of armored personnel carriers, buses and trucks rumbled across the border from Zhuhai, on the Chinese mainland. 
Less than an hour later, the 500 troops secured their objective: a makeshift barracks in a vacant apartment building in the center of Macao.
Tens of thousands of people lined the route, cheering and waving Chinese flags, in a largely unscripted expression of hospitality. 
It was a contrast to the handover of Hong Kong two years ago, when the arrival of the Chinese Army was met with a mixture of curiosity and dread.
"I am thrilled because the soldiers give me confidence," said Lau Kit Leng, 34, a homemaker. 
"Security has been such a big problem in Macao. 
The troops give me a reason to hope."
The Chinese Army seems destined to play a very different role in Macao than in Hong Kong. 
In well-policed Hong Kong, the troops have kept a very low profile. 
They arrived in predawn darkness on July 1, 1997, and headed to their barracks, where they have essentially remained.
In Macao, where the colonial administration could not stop a gang war for control of the territory's lucrative casinos, officials said the army would play a powerful symbolic role in restoring law and order. 
On the streets today, several people said that if the local police were not up to the job, they would be happy to see the army go after the gangsters.
Edmund Ho, the new chief executive of Macao, insisted that the troops would not be used for police work. 
But he said they would give people a sense of safety. 
And he added that having a garrison nearby would help him reform the Macao police force, which has been plagued by corruption.
The deployment of troops was a bone of contention between China and Portugal in an otherwise smooth handover. 
Portugal withdrew its soldiers shortly after its revolution in 1974, and Portuguese officials said the joint declaration governing the return of the colony did not provide for stationing troops there.
But early this year, China's deputy prime minister, Qian Qichen, said the government planned to send an advance guard to the colony even before the handover.
In March, President Jorge Sampaio of Portugal briefly threatened to boycott the handover ceremony if the Chinese did not explain why they were not abiding by the agreement.
In an interview here on Sunday, Mr. Sampaio seemed eager to wash his hands of the issue. 
"China is China," he said.
