file: Chinese Stock Markets Bounce Back, Rising 30_.txt
text:
ï»¿
Chinese stock prices surged more than 30 percent yesterday after the Government's announcement late last week that it had halted the listing of new stock issues.
On the Shanghai stock market, an index of class A shares, meant for domestic investors, rose by 36 percent. 
And on the smaller exchange in the southern city of Shenzhen, across from Hong Kong, the A share index increased by 34 percent. 
Both markets had fallen by more than 75 percent from their highs last year.
The upward momentum appeared to be continuing today. 
At mid-morning, Shanghai A shares were up 10.3 percent, while those in Shenzhen had gained 11.25 percent.
Last Friday's halt on listing new stock issues was part of a Chinese Government effort to reduce inflation, which has risen to about 25 percent a year in large cities, through restricting capital formation. 
Last year, Beijing raised interest rates and restricted credit to curb price increases. 
As a result, many state-owned enterprises turned to selling stock as a way to raise capital.
Moving to prop up stock prices should attract investors who might otherwise spend their cash, said Philip J. Suttle, head of emerging-markets research at J. P. Morgan. 
"They are trying to build up the savings side of the economy, and the last thing you need is a stock market that is declining."
The move is only the latest of several moratoriums on new share issues by the Chinese. 
The previous halt occurred in February, but was lifted several weeks later. 
Some foreign investors applauded this step, but cautioned that it was a stopgap.
"The move would be meaningless now if that's all they are going to do," said Mary Yee, an analyst with Smith Barney, adding: "The problem really stems from the lack of regulation and the poor disclosure requirements. 
Some companies have been listed for two or three years and have not issued an annual report."
The halt is not likely to last much longer than six months, predicted James Polacheck, an Asian markets analyst for Baring Securities in New York. 
There is a backlog of about 1,700 companies waiting to issue shares, he said. 
These concerns have already sold restricted stock to employees and other insiders, and those people are waiting for a public listing in order to cash out their investments at large profits.
Yet, these future issues have hung over the markets, helping to depress shares of the 200 or so companies already listed domestically. 
The Chinese markets are quite volatile because trading volume is low and because they are dominated by individual speculators often operating without access to the most basic corporate reports or financial statements.
"The volatility is a reflection of a very junior, immature market," Mr. Suttle of J. P. Morgan said.
Chinese companies can issue two types of shares that foreign investors can buy. 
Class B shares are traded on the domestic exchanges, and the other category, class H shares, are traded in Hong Kong and New York. 
Companies that issue H shares are subject to much more stringent disclosure requirements and therefore attract money from Western institutional investors. 
B shares are more popular in Hong Kong and with expatriate Chinese, and are much more volatile.
The market capitalization of the A share market is about $60 billion, compared with $5 billion for the B share market, Mr. Polacheck said.
The prices of A and B shares of the same company have often been quite different, depending on the demand for each. 
Many foreign investors have wanted the two markets to merge in order to eliminate this discrepancy and create greater liquidity. 
Chinese officials have indicated that they would like to move in that direction, but that it is difficult until the nation fully eliminates currency controls.
On Friday, however, the Government said it would create a means for foreign investors to buy class A shares through fund-management companies.
In the meantime, stocks in Hong Kong also rose yesterday, in part a reaction to the China markets. 
The benchmark Hang Seng index of 33 stocks increased by 2.6 percent. 
This morning, though, it gave up part of yesterday's gains.
China's budget deficit has sharply increased recently. 
More problematic, Beijing has been running a trade deficit as it has imported equipment, raw material and, increasingly, luxury goods. 
This deficit, however, has been reduced this year. 
And foreign currency reserves have increased by 50 percent as the deficit has been more than offset by an increase in foreign investment, Mr. Suttle said.
"It looks as though the Chinese are going to have the soft landing they are aiming for," he added. 
As a result international investors are becoming a little less negative on China.

file: Chinese Stocks Surge 9_ On the Hong Kong Market.txt
text:
ï»¿
Shares of Chinese and China-related companies surged here today as investors concluded that a landmark trade agreement between the United States and China -- and the competition it promises -- would help Chinese companies more than it would hurt them.
The Hong Kong Stock Exchange's "red chip" index, which tracks the performance of Hong Kong-based, Chinese-controlled companies, soared 9.8 percent after the news broke that American and Chinese negotiators had achieved a deal in Beijing after six days of talks. 
The H share index, which tracks companies based in mainland China, jumped 9.69 percent.
Hong Kong's broader Hang Seng index rose 2.64 percent, to close at 14,564.79 -- its highest close in more than two years. 
Shares also rose strongly on the stock exchanges in Shanghai and Shenzhen, though not as spectacularly as China-related stocks in the Hong Kong market.
The Hong Kong market was stronger in morning trading on Tuesday, with the Hang Seng up seven-tenths of a percent at noon.
Analysts said that the trade agreement, which removes a major barrier to China's entry into the World Trade Organization, would strengthen Chinese companies, simply by exposing them to competition. 
Although few details of the agreement have been disclosed, officials said it would open China's telecommunications, banking and insurance industries to American companies.
"If China joins the trading world, its companies are going to be forced to change," said Andy Xie, an economist at Morgan Stanley, Dean Witter here.
Such optimism is far from conventional wisdom in mainland China. 
Indeed, a main reason this trade agreement took so long to reach was that some Chinese government officials feared that the country's state-owned corporations -- many of them bloated relics of a command economy -- would be thrashed by more nimble rivals from the United States or Europe.
Those fears have not gone away. 
But Mr. Xie said they were outweighed by the prospect that foreign companies could help Chinese companies as partners or investors. 
One of the oft-mentioned candidates for such a partnership, China Telecom (Hong Kong) Ltd., recorded an 8.5 percent increase in its shares.
China Telecom is a prime example of a company that could be transformed by China's entry into the World Trade Organization. 
As the dominant player in China's burgeoning mobile phone business, it would be an instant candidate for an alliance with a European or American cellular carrier, when outsiders are allowed to own stakes in Chinese telecommunications providers.
As if to dramatize that point, one of Hong Kong's leading telecommunications providers, Hutchinson Whampoa Ltd., announced a $1.2 billion joint venture today with Global Crossing Ltd., the operator of a worldwide fiber optic network. 
The new venture, to be called China Crossing, will build a high-speed fiber optic voice and data network, initially in Hong Kong but later aiming at the mainland China market.
Some analysts contend that Chinese fears of foreign competition are overblown. 
American companies have stumbled in China in businesses as diverse as insurance and beer, and not always because of trade barriers.
"The obstacles to making money in China are not just those that have to be removed as part of W.T.O. accession," said Richard Margolis, a regional strategist at Merrill Lynch here. 
He cited issues like pricing and marketing.
Not all the Chinese companies that benefited from today's announcement are on the frontier of technology or communications. 
Two old-style shipping companies, Cosco Pacific and China Shipping Development, recorded 12 percent and 13.69 percent increases in their shares, respectively, because of hopes that the trade pact would expand the amount of cargo flowing between the United States and China.
Mr. Xie said the agreement also raised the odds that several big Chinese state-owned companies would be able to issue shares in the Hong Kong market the next year. 
Beijing hopes to raise more than $20 million by offering shares in companies like China National Petroleum and the Bank of China.

file: Chinese Take-Away.txt
text:
ï»¿
KOWLOON TONG
By Paul Theroux.
243 pp. 
Boston:
Houghton Mifflin Company. 
$23.
Like Graham Greene, Paul Theroux generates forward momentum in his novels by displacing people: the not-quite-public-school fix-it Englishman on the fringes of both white and Chinese society in the Singapore of "Saint Jack," the Massachusetts handyman in the Central American jungle of "The Mosquito Coast," the academically endowed prostitute in the London of "Half Moon Street."
But no one has been more displaced than the Mullards, mother and son, of Hong Kong in "Kowloon Tong."
Aging Betty Mullard, who likes to take "just a flutter" on the races at Happy Valley and Sha Tin, is an old Hong Kong hand, assiduously British in an early post-World-War-II manner. 
No shift of history has ever caused her to refer to the local people as anything but "Chinky-Chonks," and she takes it as a given that apart from Mr. Chuck, her late husband's partner, they are perverse in tastes and politics and simply crazy in motivation. 
Though a Hong Kong resident for 45 years, she has never since the opening of China in the early 1970's had enough curiosity to take the one-hour train ride from Kowloon into Shenzhen on the mainland. 
Nor has she ever tasted Chinese food. 
"Not a chance," she announces. 
"I don't eat that muck."
But now she is facing "the Chinese take-away," as she and her son call it -- the return of Hong Kong to the Chinese Government. 
"They could make us take Chinky-Chonk nationality," she realizes, the scales falling from her eyes.
Neville (Bunt) Mullard, her son, is even more on the margins of time and place. 
At 43, not only has he never been to China but, except for one vaguely remembered childhood visit, he hasn't been to England either. 
But China is now coming to him, and Bunt Mullard is bright enough to know that it might wash him away from neat Albion Cottage on the Peak back to a Thatcherite England better imagined than lived in. 
Mr. Theroux defines the Mullards' impasse with his typical piquancy: "They had been liberated by Hong Kong, they had money and a sense of the exotic, they were superior here. 
Going home meant defeat -- snubs and meagerness and middle-class making do. 
The trouble was that the idea of England was easier to sustain the farther they were from the place."
In the last year of British rule in Hong Kong, Bunt and Betty do their best to ignore these realities. 
They do not listen to the "take-away" news on their British-made bakelite radio and gratefully eat the bacon and eggs and roast beef that Betty has taught their Chinese servant, Wang, to cook. 
Bunt drives off in his father's 1958 Rover to Imperial Stitching, the family factory in Kowloon Tong, which the Mullards own with a Chinese-hating Chinese entrepreneur named Mr. Chuck. Typically, it will take a Chinese mainlander to let Bunt know that "Kowloon Tong" is Cantonese for "Nine Dragons' Pond."
"Everything means something," Bunt sniffs, with the dragon's breath already on him.
Before the late George Mullard and Mr. Chuck chose the site for Imperial Stitching, they had a geomancer check the feng shui, the balance of elements, of the place, and proclaim it propitiously located. 
But in this last British year, the feng shui is driven crazily out of balance. 
As the novel opens, Mr. Chuck has perished in uncertain circumstances, leaving his share of the business to Bunt. 
What at first seems to enlarge Bunt's prospects now enlarges him as a target. 
A man named Mr. Hung, with "a soldier's way of walking and an officer's arrogance," turns up in that supremely British institution, the Hong Kong Cricket Club, and makes Bunt an offer on Imperial Stitching -- that is, on Bunt's very identity. 
Mr. Hung admits that his job is "the acquisition of strategic sites for the People's Liberation Army," and Bunt is appalled to find that Betty has already given her assent to the sale.
Until now, Bunt has noticed with some contempt that all around him the apparently British residents of Hong Kong are seeking alternative identities. 
The British-born family lawyer, his very name Brittain and his background Jewish, has become an Austrian citizen. 
"Monty, you're a Kraut?" asks Bunt bemusedly. 
Others talk about Canadian, Tongan, Cayman Island, Belizean and Panamanian citizenship. 
"I've got a Guinea-Bissau passport," boasts an American, who may work for the C.I.A. or merely want to stay, but for whom an American passport might not be convenient after the takeover.
On the floor of Imperial Stitching, as in the Cricket Club, people have a sense of time running out. 
Thus a charming seamstress, Mei-ping, an illegal immigrant from China, shyly accedes to Bunt's sexual overtures. 
Bunt, like his father before him, is a habitue of the "blue hotels" around his factory in Kowloon Tong. 
"A big, needy gweilo," he drinks beer and eats the sandwiches his mother has packed for him, then goes off to one of the rooms with a girl. 
Sex is what has most powerfully assimilated Bunt into Hong Kong. 
He knows the four characters that proclaim sun-dou-bak-mui ("new girl from north"), and he is well aware that yet lau, yet feng means "one room, one phoenix" -- that is, one working girl without a pimp. 
He has had sex only once with a European, a Portuguese prostitute in Macao.
Sniffing out Bunt's every weakness, Mr. Hung becomes a relentless pursuer of Imperial Stitching. 
"If you do not sell," he warns, "you will not be happy next year."
He forces Bunt to go out with him for a meal, where Bunt watches him devour chicken feet and paw two girls from the factory. 
When Bunt agrees to sell and then equivocates, his employees begin to vanish.
Hong Kong on the eve of the take-over is itself a major character in this book, possessing both a Chinese and a British substance, and Mr. Theroux brings to it his gift for aphorism: "Whoever said the Chinese were enigmatic might have met one Chinese person but had not met two. 
. . . They carried on their lives in whispers and their business in shouts."
Mr. Theroux's considerable charm as a narrator will keep his readers engaged to the end. 
But this is one of those books about which people say of the central character, "I would like to give him a good shake."
The threat of Mr. Hung might have the whole weight of China behind it, and Bunt seems to give way to that threat at every turn. 
He walks out of confrontations at the stage where the next question begs to be asked. 
"He was glad to go," Mr. Theroux writes of Bunt at the end of a particularly challenging scene, yet Bunt's habitual tactic is flight.
Betty is a wonderful character, vulgar-genteel, and in her way as toughly determined to survive as Bunt's Chinese adversary. 
Mr. Hung, with impeccable English and the uncompromising manners of a talented but brutal peasant, is a credibly menacing figure. 
But Bunt is the passive center of all the plot's movement. 
We are given occasional glimpses of why Bunt -- who detests Mr. Hung and has half a mind to stay in Hong Kong, who believes in British institutions -- does not report Mr. Hung to the police. 
But they do not add up to a full motivation for Bunt's aimlessness. 
To give one example that may help make the point without betraying the novel's denouement: when Bunt takes a terrified Mei-ping to Macao, books a room and then accidentally encounters his mother at a gaming table, it takes just one command from Betty -- "Stop faffing around and come along. 
You too, duckie" -- to bring the lovers meekly back to Hong Kong. 
The tension inherent in weak men in novels derives from our sense that they will ultimately be tempted to defiance. 
In Bunt's case, that tension is never exploited. 
If the point is that he is so displaced that he has no core, then one wonders why the author gives him so many highly dramatic chances to transcend himself.
Whatever the problems with Bunt, Mr. Theroux's astringent misanthropy and narrative momentum are powerful propellants. 
And since the tale is told from within the consciousness of the Mullards, China in the person of Mr. Hung possesses an ominousness that fills the horizon. 
The takeover is so close, and yet no one can predict with any certainty what it will mean for the Bettys, Bunts and Mei-pings of the city.
As one character says, "Hong Kong is an accident of history that is about to be rectified."
Hong Kong was first taken by gunboat diplomacy. 
Its present boundaries were finally established by Britain's strong-arming of a weak Manchu dynasty. 
If Paul Theroux's novel can be believed, the mainland Chinese are retrieving it in the same spirit in which it was taken.

China continued its testing of a new generation of ballistic missile warheads by exploding a nuclear device beneath its far western desert at Lop Nor today.
In Washington, the White House said it "deeply regrets" the Chinese test, and the State Department called on China to abide by a moratorium on nuclear testing, which has been honored by the other nuclear powers since 1992. 
"We continue to urge China to consider the changed circumstances of global security affecting the role of nuclear weapons," the department spokesman, Michael McCurry, said.
Today's test, like an earlier one in June and another one a year ago, is part of a series that China has undertaken to verify the reliability of warheads designed during the 1980's, experts said.
One Chinese scientist who worked inside China's ballistic missile program said the new warheads were intended to be smaller than China's older ones, yet more powerful in their explosive yield.
"Right now, China is testing its miniaturization program," the scientist said in a recent interview. 
"If China obeys the international request to stop testing nuclear weapons, then it means China would have to cancel its ballistic missile program without developing its second-generation ballistic missiles."
China's nuclear strategy is based on assuring it the ability to retaliate after any nuclear first strike against it by another country.
The detonation was detected by the Australian Seismological Center in Canberra at 11:25 A.M. today Chinese time (11:25 P.M. Thursday E.D.T.). 
Center officials estimated its explosive strength at 40 to 150 kilotons, the equivalent of 40,000 to 150,000 tons of TNT.
The Chinese Foreign Ministry later confirmed the test, saying Beijing would put an end to its nuclear tests as soon as negotiations on a comprehensive nuclear test ban treaty were completed in 1996.
"Among all the nuclear states, China has conducted the least nuclear tests," the ministry's statement said. 
"It has always exercised great restraint on the question of nuclear tests and will continue to do so in the future."
It was China's 41st nuclear test since 1964, compared with 44 tests by Britain, 210 by France and more than 1,000 by the United States.
In 1993 the Clinton Administration invested a substantial amount of energy trying to persuade the Chinese leadership to abandon its testing program. 
After China's test last October, President Clinton instructed Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary to begin reviewing options to resume American testing at the Nevada test range.
When this threat drew no response from the Chinese, the White House conceded that nothing it could do in the form of pressure could dissuade Beijing, and the effort was abandoned.
But Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, during a visit to Washington this week, agreed to work with the United States to ban the production of weapons-grade uranium and plutonium to prevent proliferation and, eventually, to halt the production of nuclear material for use in new weapons by the countries that have nuclear weapons.

file: CHOICE TABLES_Exotic Blends From Miami Chefs.txt
text:
ï»¿
AMERICA'S gastronomic weather vane is increasingly twisting southward, toward the homey regional fare of the coastal Carolinas and extending all the way to Louisiana and Texas. 
And some of the most vibrant restaurant scenes are found in South Florida, specifically Miami and Miami Beach.
Trying to keep up with restaurant comings and goings, particularly in Miami Beach, sometimes seems like counting ocean waves. 
A mighty Darwinian struggle is raging among restaurateurs to capture the renascent tourist business and the growing year-round trade of Miamians. 
Many are doing so by offering a unique and diverting cuisine that melds traditional American fare with products and techniques from the Caribbean.
Some chefs have rather grandiosely begun calling it New World Cuisine. 
No matter. 
When this fusion cooking succeeds, it can be exhilarating; when it flops, however, it goes down like a screen-bottomed sailboat.
Following are four greater Miami restaurants that are not only afloat but making waves.
Â 
Nemo
At the south end of Miami Beach is a winsome cafe called Nemo that looks like too much fun to serve good food -- but it does. 
Under Michael Schwartz, a self-taught chef, the small open kitchen turns out an impressive array of stagey creations that are as delectable as they are architectural. 
Mr. Schwartz reaches into the Caribbean pantry to invigorate his cooking but also borrows liberally from Japan and Southeast Asia.
Nemo's main dining room is as multihued and radiant as the islands themselves, with a bleached blue ceiling, terra cotta walls, color-splashed banquettes, high-tech copper lanterns dangling overhead and a spacious outdoor terrace framed by palm trees. 
The small open kitchen is so close to diners that from certain tables you might be privy to the romantic woes of the fellow who debones chicken breasts. 
Two other sizable rooms bring seating capacity to about 200.
A good way to start is with thick cubes of polenta fries that are crisp and greaseless outside and almost creamy at the center, served with spicy ketchup -- close to a meal in themselves. 
As a counterpoint, two friends and I sampled dainty garlic-cured salmon rolls cushioned with filaments of alfalfa sprouts and served with a mild wasabi mayonnaise. 
Big meaty prawns gift-wrapped in shredded filo were nicely cooked but sorely needed a dipping sauce.
This chef loves to stoke the jalapeno fires, so ask the waiter about B.T.U. levels in dishes described as spicy. 
A Vietnamese beef salad -- strips of skirt steak layered over a mound of sliced sweet peppers, onions, mung bean sprouts, and peanuts -- made my point. 
Within this innocent looking dish, on the beef itself, was an incendiary salsa that had nearly everyone at my table gulping water -- not really the Vietnamese style of seasoning. 
A safer bet is the mixed green salad with shaved Parmesan and crispy rings of cleanly fried calamari in a Caesar-style dressing.
Typical of Mr. Schwartz at his best is an entree of wok-charred salmon, rosy in the center, flecked with toasted pumpkin seeds -- a wonderful marriage of texture and flavor. 
It was sitting atop a salad composed of four kinds of sprouts (you see a lot of these here) and sweet peppers tossed in a cleansing soy-lime vinaigrette. 
At lunch one day we tried a hefty sandwich of roasted duck, aromatic with tamarind, on a roll along with melted fontina cheese -- the duck was actually good enough to have carried the show without the cheesy understudy. 
It came with fragile, crisp homemade potato chips.
The desserts by Hedy Goldsmith, the pastry chef, were a highlight of the tour of Miami restaurants. 
Strikingly beautiful but not contrived, they are marvels of texture and balance. 
Among her many memorable creations are malted milk flan ringed with tangerine caramel and orange, served with a chocolate-almond biscotti, Key lime napoleon with a Caribbean fruit salsa, and Jamaican ginger cake with tamarind-pineapple chutney and macadamia brittle ice cream.
Nemo's offers a wide and eclectic range of wines, including a number of relative unknowns. 
Prices start in the $20 range but escalate fast.
Â 
Norman's
About half an hour's drive down the coast in Coral Gables is one of the hottest new dining spots in Greater Miami, called Norman's. 
The owner and chef, Norman Van Aken, has been on the scene for more than a decade with several restaurants, most recently a Mano. 
His exuberant approach to Caribbean-American cooking, which includes hints of Asian and Mexican flavors, is carried out with intelligence and visual flair.
Just reading the exacting menu at Norman's is an event. 
Here's an example from the dinner menu: "Pork Tenderloin with Haitian Grits, 21st Century Mole, Smoky Plantain Crema and a Red Onion, Black Bean and Sweet Corn Salsa."
We couldn't ascertain what made grits from Haiti superior to others, nor could our server enlighten us about the chronological reference to mole -- but it was fun trying. 
All this scholarship was in vain anyway, for the wood-fired pork was dry and tough -- the only disappointment in an otherwise exciting and illuminating meal.
Norman's is a big, airy place done in terra cotta and stucco, with Moorish arches, two capacious wood-burning ovens, and flattering lighting.
Because we had made an accidental detour into what seemed like part of the Everglades and arrived 45 minutes late, we had to wait at the bar until a table opened upstairs. 
While the balcony tables are pleasant, you would be better off asking for a table in the festive main dining room (and read your map carefully).
As for the food, several appetizers alone are worth hitchhiking down to Coral Gables. 
Conch chowder is a brilliant combination of long, exceptionally tender strips of conch in a saffron-tinged cream with hints of fresh orange, star anise and coconut. 
The season's first soft shell crabs were terrific when dusted with cornmeal, perfectly cooked, and set over citric lime butter along with purple potatoes and red onions. 
Bacalao (cod) fritters were cleanly fried and meaty, not as peppery as they might have been, but satisfying with a dipping sauce of aioli enlivened with ancho peppers.
The array of main courses is daunting. 
Seafood is certainly a high point as judged by the beautifully sauteed yellowtail snapper in citrus butter with asparagus spears and wonderfully chunky mashed potatoes. 
Also excellent are the grilled "diver-harvested' scallops perched on fluffy mashed sweet potatoes, fresh corn and a lemon-vinaigrette holding chunks of salty pancetta -- quite a mouthful, but it works.
One creation that sank under its own weight was a ravioli filled with a mass of tiny shrimp and blue crab along with portobellos, leeks, tomatoes, mustard cream and balsamic vinegar.
Among many delectable dishes was the unremittingly rich loin lamb chops in a lustrous reduction of lamb shank ragout, wild mushrooms and red wine.
Servers at Norman's have a challenge keeping up with the chef's fancy footwork, but they try hard. 
On Saturday night service was slow and scattered.
And a restaurant of this caliber should know better than to print its wine list in eye-straining small agate type. 
The international selections are mostly big-name standards with prices starting in the mid-$20 range and going up.
Desserts are as polymorphic as the rest of the menu. 
Try the vertical strudel filled with dates paired with ginger ice cream and a thyme-honey sauce; the banana-rum flan with caramelized bananas and a crunchy spiced cookie; and the sharp-sweet cinnamon poached Granny Smith apple with gianduja (a chocolate hazelnut flavoring) ice cream.
Â 
Chef Allen's
That a kid from Brooklyn, trained at a local technical college and apprenticed at the classically oriented Le Cirque in Manhattan would find his way to Florida and become a pioneer of Caribbean-American cuisine might seem peculiar -- but Allen Susser believes that his unconventional road has been an asset.
"If you know the basics of French cuisine then you can build on it or modify it," said the genial, soft-spoken chef while making the rounds recently in his innovative restaurant, Chef Allen's, in Aventura (formerly North Miami Beach).
Mr. Susser, who succeeds as much as or more than most, infuses his food with the sunny flavors of mango, papaya, starfruit, mamey (a sweet, football-shaped fruit with a granular texture), coconut, and tangerines. 
Other products that are common on his menu include wahoo and cobia (two local fish), mussels and shrimp, pompano, and conch. 
While the notion of combining fruit with seafood might seem about as appealing as mixing gin with milk, Susser has built his ever-changing menu around such unlikely juxtapositions.
"A lot of the fruits have high acid levels, and that balances the sweetness," said the soft-spoken Mr. Susser while making the rounds of his Art Deco dining room. 
"It's all a question of balance."
Chef Allen's 120-seat, pink-toned, neon-accented dining room with well spaced tables facing a glass-enclosed working kitchen seems an appropriate place for this kind of fare. 
Our menu got off the mark nicely with a mound of rich tuna belly tartare crowned with beluga caviar and set over shaved fresh coconut and a puddle of semisweet coconut cream -- surprisingly, the coconut did not bully the tuna and caviar, but rather provided a sprightly, sweetish foundation. 
Less successful, however, was seared foie gras paired with boniato (a root vegetable) and a sweetish mango ketchup -- flavors were scattered in every direction.
Charred red snapper, an especially delicate fish, was wonderful over a sweet-tart fresh corn vinaigrette and black bean salsa. 
A surprising side dish was refreshing slaw of calabaza (a winter squash), which has a crunchy texture and semisweet flavor. 
If soft shell crabs are in season try the version coated with pine nuts in an Indian River orange sauce.
Another palate-popping creation is called "spicy citrus-blasted local calamari with baby fennel, blood orange and Bermuda onions."
This is a salad, and the combination of hot spice and sweet orange, followed by cooling fennel, is memorable. 
So is the tangerine-barbecued duck with cranberry-orange preserve, a deft balance of sweet and tart.
Mr. Susser has assembled an earnest and unpretentious service staff who understand the boss's food and convey it with authority. 
The international wine selection is broad and well chosen, but expensive.
Â 
China Grill
About a year and a half ago one of Manhattan's more popular cross-cultural restaurants, China Grill, a Cal-Asian hybrid, transported its dramatic, family style dining to South Beach -- and judging from the crowds you would think they were giving away Broadway theater tickets with each order of dumplings. 
Actually, the reason China Grill is so mobbed is because the food is light, inventive and invigorating.
The cavernous, theatrical dining room has the nightclub look with a black ceiling, artsy, saucer-shaped lanterns hanging from above, black tiled walls, penitential pop music, a giant circular bar, and an immense kitchen populated by enough cooks to operate a moderately sized Carnival Cruise liner. 
But the strategy works, for food emerges from the kitchen quickly and absolutely fresh and hot.
Our server informed us that the food at China Grill was served "as soon as it is ready," not necessarily when the customer is ready. 
"O.K.," we shrugged. 
"We're good sports."
The food here could not be defined as New World or New Floridian (I would call it Gulf Stream Cuisine), but its Asian approach incorporates many tropical products. 
The first dish to arrive was stir-fried sesame-citrus noodles, as good as they sounded -- citric, with a touch of soy, and faintly crunchy. 
Lobster pancakes were a delight, too, thin, scallion-flavored crepes holding sweet chunks of lobster cooked in coconut milk with shiitake mushrooms, scallions and enough red chilies to give a kick. 
One of the best dishes overall, and a copious one, is the Peking duck salad -- a mountain of mixed greens tossed in a lovely citric dressing supporting crispy strips of duck meat and skin as well as meaty, succulent duck legs.
Some of the main courses are equally intriguing. 
A dish of charred Szechuan beef -- marinated in sake, soy and cilantro -- was cooked perfectly, medium rare with a slightly salty, barbecue flavor. 
We ordered mashed potatoes, which were fluffy and moist and had a lingering bite of wasabi mustard.
Another dish to try is rosy barbecued salmon swabbed with a Chinese mustard sauce and accompanied by stir-fried greens. 
The only low point of the meal was the listless grilled shrimp over bland black fettuccine.
The expensive, mostly California wine list focuses appropriately on sharp, high-acid wines that can stand up to these flavors.
For dessert, the pleasant apple cake was paired with harsh, bitter cinnamon ice cream. 
Go instead with the crazy-sounding wasabi tiramisu with chocolate espresso sauce -- unauthentic, but who cares when it's this good?
Â 
Diner's guide
Â 
All four restaurants accept major credit cards. 
Unless otherwise noted, the prices below are for a three-course dinner for two, including a glass of wine each, and tax.
Â 
Nemo, 100 Collins Avenue (at First Street), Miami Beach; (305) 532-4550. 
Open daily for lunch (they call it brunch on Sunday) and dinner. 
Smoking is allowed in the open-air sections of the dining rooms. 
$100.
Â 
Norman's, 21 Almeria Avenue, Coral Gables; (305) 446-6767. 
Open Monday to Friday for lunch, Monday to Saturday for dinner, closed Sunday. 
Smoking allowed in the bar. 
$100.
Â 
Chef Allen's, 19088 Northeast 29th Avenue, Aventura (formerly North Miami Beach); (305) 935-2900. 
Open for dinner daily. 
The dining room has a smoking section. 
$95 to $105.
Â 
China Grill, 404 Washington Street, at Fifth Street; (305) 534-2211. 
Open for lunch and dinner Monday to Friday, dinner only Saturday and Sunday. 
Smoking allowed in most of the restaurant. 
$90 to $110.Â Â Â B.M.

file: CHOICE TABLES_For Eclectic, Ethnic Asian Cuisine_ A World of Flavors in Singapore.txt
text:
ï»¿
I USED to avoid Singapore, dismissing it as a somewhat sterile, westernized city that had little to offer in the way of authentic Asian cooking. 
Instead, I traveled to Hong Kong, for years Asia's leading culinary mecca.
But times have changed: Move over Hong Kong and make room for Singapore. 
About 10 years ago, I spent four days in Singapore, and was stunned by the eclectic selection of dishes. 
That was the beginning of a love affair, and I now return each year.
In Singapore, as in much of Malaysia, there is an overwhelming supply of delicious food that reflects the cooking of its residents who are Malaysian, Chinese, Indian, European, Thai and Vietnamese. 
Some years back, once the government realized that tourists were interested in ethnic delicacies, the restaurant scene began to thrive -- with refined places to eat as well as the countless hawker stalls.
And since the city government rules over sanitary codes with an iron fist, tourists can safely eat off the street.
Â 
Au Jardin Les Amis
On a trip last December, the city was abuzz over a new, small restaurant. 
I resisted going, since the idea of a fancy European restaurant in the heart of Asia really put me off. 
But Au Jardin Les Amis, in a charming, colonial-style bungalow smack in the middle of the lush Botanic Gardens, is positively enchanting.
Justin Quek, the shy but charming native Singaporean chef, first started cooking in 1982, but his formal training began three years later, in Singapore, Bangkok, then Europe. 
There he worked in such notable restaurants as the Hotel de Crillon in Paris and L'Oasis on the Cote d'Azur. 
While Mr. Quek has been inspired and influenced by his mentors, he uses local Asian ingredients to create his own innovative, distinctive style of cooking.
A superb, three-course tasting lunch (which cost about $35 a person, not including wine, at 1.6 Singapore dollars to the U.S. dollar) began with a carpaccio of tuna served with a smoked eel parfait. 
The clean, fresh flavor of the paper-thin fish slices contrasted beautifully with the satiny texture of the savory mousse. 
My companion's appetizer was equally delicious: circles of watermelon flesh topped with a tomato "jelly" and drizzled with aged balsamic vinegar and olive oil. 
We ravaged a plate of tender ravioli stuffed with celery root, sprinkled with truffle shavings served on top of a perfectly poached egg yolk, mopping up with freshly baked French bread. 
Meltingly tender smoked salmon slices were dotted with roe and drizzled with a touch of mirin (sweetened rice wine). 
My lunch entree of braised veal cheeks with a black truffle sauce was slightly heavy, but memorable.
The meal ended on a high note of refreshingly cold ice, flavored with vodka and fresh lime, served with a soursop (a tangy local fruit) mousse. 
The menu changes each week. 
The wine list is extensive with 900 offerings.
Â 
The Imperial Hot Wok
I have long been singing praises of the Imperial Herbal restaurant, one of my favorite Singapore haunts, where Chinese master chefs collaborate with a traditional herbalist to create superb food. 
Now the Imperial Herbal has spawned a cousin, the Imperial Hot Wok, a casual Chinese bistro in the heart of the newly restored financial district known as Far East Square. 
The decor may remind you of Soho, but the menu offers unfailingly authentic Hakka, Beijing, Sichuan and Cantonese specialties.
The favorite dish of our group of four (and the house special), which I had never tasted outside of a Hakka home, is the Hakka village rice special set. 
We were first given a large bowl of fragrant jasmine rice, lightly seasoned with chopped shallots and dried shrimp. 
It was accompanied by stir-fried vegetable side dishes including tofu seasoned with leeks, chopped, cooked long beans, and minced pickled radish. 
Each customer then helps himself, starting with a bowl of rice and adding spoonfuls of the cooked vegetables with chopped peanuts. 
The end result is a bowl of delicious-tasting custom-made fried rice, but the flavor is much better.
We also tried the succulently tender steamed herbal chicken, which was stuffed with red dates, wolf berries, other (unidentifiable) Chinese herbs and lightly seasoned with a rich oyster sauce. 
Steamed sea bass was unusual -- but delicious -- with its Thai-influenced tangy lime dressing, and the boiled garlic chive and shrimp dumplings were satisfyingly homespun. 
For dessert, we shared spoonfuls of freshly made coconut ice cream with a sumptuous, sweetened red bean topping and calamasi sherbet made from a pungent local lime.
Prices are extremely reasonable. 
There is a decent selection of moderately priced wines, mainly from Australia. 
My drink of choice is the Hawthorn Spritzer, a tart fruit and soda water drink.
Â 
Blue Ginger
To taste the true food of Singapore, you must sample home cooking, but the next best thing is to eat is at Blue Ginger, a bit of a local institution, with two locations. 
Some Singaporean friends claim that the food can be inconsistent, but on a good evening the kitchen (especially at the older restaurant on Tanjong Road) can turn out very good nonya specialties.
Nonya is the the local, high-bred cuisine, which originated when Chinese traders settling in Singapore, Penang and Malacca took Malay wives; it reflects a melting pot of many different cultures. 
The Chinese, who were from southern China, were accustomed to robust foods cooked with dark soy sauce, leeks, garlic and onions. 
The Malaysian influence is apparent in the use of ingredients like coconut milk, tamarind, screw pine and fresh lime leaves. 
Indian seasonings such as cumin, cardamom and curry mixtures are as prevalent as Thai flavorings like lemongrass and shrimp paste. 
The abundant use of chili peppers, both fresh and dried, impart a fiery brilliance.
Traditionally, the food is cooked by women, and this custom is preserved at Blue Ginger where Vivien Lian, who is the niece of a famous nonya cook, Leong Yee Soo, has developed a menu that reflects the best aspects of the nonya style.
The Tanjong Pagar Road restaurant, which I visited recently, is like stepping back in time to colonial Singapore. 
Antique wooden door panels, vibrant folk-art paintings and gilt mirrors give Blue Ginger an elegant but cozy atmosphere.
We started with a simple, traditional soup, bakwan kepeting, garnished with plump chopped pork and crabmeat balls and thin bamboo slices. 
The broth was light and flavorful and the pork balls were tender. 
Another unusual and delightful appetizer is kuah pie tee, small homemade pastry cups filled with a mixture of shredded bamboo shoot and turnips seasoned with garlic and bean paste and topped with a slice of shrimp and a sprinkling of chilies.
Stewed pork shoulder (babi pong tay) was succulently tender and redolent of star anise. 
My Singaporean friend insisted that we try another beef dish, beef randang, made of braised cubes of meat rich with the flavors of lemongrass, ginger, curry and coconut milk. 
Another classic, ayam buah keluak, a stew made with chicken and stuffed keluak nuts, which are seasoned with lemongrass, galangal and turmeric, was slightly heavy, but de rigueur for a nonya meal. 
The fish cakes, steamed in banana leaves (otak otak), were nicely flavored with turmeric and lime. 
We also tried ikan goreng chili garam, a gorgeous, crispy-fried sea bass topped with a fiery chili paste and then squeezed with fresh calamasi lime juice.
For dessert, I cast caution to the wind and ordered durian chendol, sweetened red beans and jelly surrounded by coconut milk, topped with a durian puree. 
Durian is infamous for its odor, and the flavor is definitely an acquired taste. 
But the puree is made with palm sugar so the taste was similar to caramel. 
When paired with the coconut milk and red beans, it was sublime. 
Another winning dessert was longan pulot itam, a traditional recipe made with black rice cooked with dried longans, then topped with coconut milk. 
There is a decent wine selection, but we opted for beer and glasses of freshly squeezed calamasi juice.
Â 
The Seafood International Market Restaurant
Have you ever dreamed of a restaurant where you walk in, grab a grocery cart and fill it with all the ingredients of your dinner, fresh from a produce bin and row on row of fish tanks?
You then hand the fresh food over to a chef, tell him whether you want it cooked a la Thai, Vietnamese, Chinese or Malaysian and, shortly, the dishes are delivered to your table.
Well, this is no fantasy; it's the way it's done at the Seafood International Market Restaurant near the airport. 
No matter how many times I visit, I still feel a child's delight at the process of selecting the food and watching the chefs cook it.
The decor is definitely no frills bordering on funky. 
Diners are given the choice of eating in air-conditioned comfort inside or outside on a huge veranda-type room. 
(Since Singaporean nights can be pleasantly balmy, I generally opt for the fresh air.)
Forget the decor; the attraction is fresh seafood.
My Singaporean friends and I have our favorite dishes: usually we start with tom yam kung, a Thai hot and sour seafood soup garnished with plump shrimp and generously seasoned with lemongrass, kaffir lime leaves, hot chilies, fish sauce and cilantro. 
The Seafood International version is heavy on the chilies, leaving your taste buds slightly numb.
If I'm being treated, or feeling expansive, I order the lobster sashimi -- so fresh and simple that it's quite amazing -- especially with the presentation: The head is placed at the front of the platter and usually the antennae are still twitching (not for the fainthearted). 
Drunken prawns are another winner. 
The shrimp or prawns are brought out to the table in a plastic bag, freshly plucked from the tank, and cooked tableside with some Shaoxing rice wine, similar in flavor to a very dry sherry. 
The shrimp steam in their own juices. 
You eat them with your fingers.
Other special dishes are the Singapore chili crab served with a spicy tomato-based sweet and sour sauce that is generously seasoned with garlic and ginger. 
I love to mop up the sauce with an order of garlic toast, a custom I learned from one of my native buddies. 
The crab or lobster is stir-fried simply in the Cantonese manner with scallions and ginger.
For the end of the meal, there is a table of wonderful Thai desserts. 
Most are sumptuous and slightly heavy, but the sweet rice pudding flavored with coconut milk, the coconut tapioca pudding served with cooked yam or taro, and the mango pudding are delicious.
Beer, wine and soft drinks are offered.
Â 
The Banana Leaf Apollo Restaurant
In the heart of Little India on Racecourse Road, the Banana Leaf Apollo Restaurant can be combined with a visit to this part of the city with its spice shops, clothing bazaar and stalls where cooks make wonderful Indian breads and snacks.
After a recent renovation, the Banana Leaf is now rather stylish with gleaming granite floors and air-conditioning. 
The restaurant is only a step up from cafeteria style, but the food is quite delicious, inexpensive and well worth a trip.
Once seated, customers are given large banana leaves instead of plates. 
Steaming-hot white rice or fragrant biryani rice flavored with saffron and turmeric is spooned into the center. 
You then choose a type of main entree, which includes a number of curries as well as fried chicken and mutton. 
The most famous dish is the fish head curry, the head and meat served in a fiery red curry sauce redolent of turmeric, ginger, cumin, chili powder, coconut milk and tamarind.
My companion, who has a rather unadventurous palate, ordered the tender tikka chicken, a classic Indian dish marinated in salt, pepper, chili peppers and fresh lime juice, then baked in a tandoor oven. 
I preferred the chicken masala with its sumptuous sauce flavored with an abundance of spices and thickened with cashews and almonds.
Other enticing entrees are spicy fish sambal and mutton curry. 
The meal also comes with assorted side vegetables -- cabbage, long beans and "lady fingers" (an Asian vegetable with a texture similar to okra).
A delicious, filling meal is easily under $10 a person.
Â 
Bill of fare
Au Jardin Les Amis is at the EJH Corner House in the Singapore Botanic Gardens, Cluny Road; (65) 466-8812, fax (65) 466-8227. 
Open for lunch and dinner. 
An eight-course degustation dinner is $65 a person, not including wine. 
Reservations are not easily come by since the restaurant has only 12 tables, but they can be made up to a month in advance (for Saturday night the restaurant suggests calling three weeks ahead).
The Imperial Hot Wok Restaurant is at 01-01 Far East Square, 72 Telok Ayer Street in the financial district; (65) 438-8918, fax (65) 438-8919. 
Lunch costs about $12 a person; dinner, $20 to $25 a person, not including wine or beer.

text:

Secretary of State Warren Christopher came under fire today both by lawmakers who oppose sanctions against China over its human rights record and those who favor tough measures to pressure Beijing.
In a visit to Capitol Hill, Mr. Christopher indicated that President Clinton would adopt a middle-of-the-road approach, signaling that the Administration would renew China's favorable trade status, while at the same time pinning some lesser sanctions on China.
At a meeting with Senator Max Baucus of Montana and other opponents of trade sanctions, Mr. Christopher was urged not even to impose partial trade sanctions, such as denying favorable tariffs to products made by state-owned companies.
After the meeting, Mr. Baucus and several other legislators sent a letter to Mr. Clinton asserting that partial sanctions were "likely to prove unworkable."
Last June Mr. Clinton issued an executive order saying that China's most favored nation trading status would be renewed only if Beijing made substantial overall progress on human rights.
In his letter, Mr. Baucus said that revoking the special trade benefits "for goods produced by 'state enterprises' does not seem even theoretically possible," adding: "China has no sharp distinction between 'public' and 'private' sectors.
"We hope you will avoid a political compromise that is very likely to prove unworkable."
The letter was also signed by Senator John Danforth, a Missouri Republican, Representative Robert Matsui, a California Democrat, and Representative Jim Kolbe, an Arizona Republican.
Mr. Christopher also met with Representative Nancy Pelosi, a California Democrat, and others who support strong measures to pressure China to improve its human rights performance.
In an interview, Ms. Pelosi said she told Mr. Christopher, "China has not made overall significant progress and therefore hasn't complied with the President's executive order."
She said it would be wholly inadequate for Mr. Clinton to punish China, as some lawmakers have suggested, by only banning sales of Chinese handguns or semiautomatic weapons.
"That wouldn't be sufficient, not even close," she said. 
"Let's get real about this. 
It is important for us to have sanctions that are real and that pressure the Chinese."
She said she supported partial sanctions that would end favorable tariffs for China's state-owned industries or those run by the Chinese military.
Late this afternoon Mr. Clinton's top foreign policy and economic advisers met to discuss what decison to make on China. 
Some Administration officials say he will announce his decision in the next few days.

file: CLASSICAL VIEW_Freshly Minted, an Orchestral _Tradition_.txt
text:
ï»¿
LAST MONTH, ON THE VERY DAY Deng Xiaoping's death was announced, some of us were at Carnegie Hall learning that "xiao" can also be the name for a kind of flute, and that a number of xiaos, together with erhus, pipas, shengs and other instruments, can make a kind of orchestra. 
We were learning, because here was something new to us: this concert by the National Traditional Orchestra of China, based in Beijing, was the first given by such a group on the Carnegie stage, though a similar ensemble from Hong Kong played at Alice Tully Hall last season.
Orchestras of this sort are also pretty new to the world. 
In this respect, the "traditional" in the Beijing outfit's title should be understood as advertising rather than fact. 
The Carnegie program book, a masterpiece of prevarication, deftly eluded the question of how deep into the past the group can trace its history, but the answer seems to be "not far."
The 1949 revolution precipitated an energetic effort to adapt Chinese traditional melodies and instruments to Western norms, as understood by Soviet advisers. 
Before that period, Chinese culture was blissfully ignorant of the notion of orchestral performance, and though the idea rapidly took off in Taiwan and Hong Kong, one must regard the National Traditional Orchestra as an expression of that strange hybrid of patriotic and international cultural strategy typical of Communist states. 
It has about as much authenticity as the Red Army Choir.
Indeed, one doesn't have to delve into origins to sniff an esthetic problem here: it is enough to listen, and to look. 
The National Traditional Orchestra of China is, on the face of it, so preposterous a parody of the Western orchestra as to be a little sad, a little charming. 
The musicians adopt every ritual of the philharmonic but two: they wear long silk robes, and they don't tune up, for the elementary reason that they don't intend to play in tune.
Their instruments, though based on Chinese prototypes, shamelessly take over functions from the West. 
As in Vienna or Cleveland, the orchestra's foundation is a large complement of strings, but with erhus in different sizes instead of violins, violas, cellos and basses. 
Similarly, xiaos replace flutes and suonas stand in for oboes. 
Lacking an indigenous alternative, the orchestra finds its timpani in timpani. 
Shengs -- portable organs played by means of a mouthpiece, including one instrument the size of a small tree -- are among the few instruments without a clear Western counterpart.
Then there's the music. 
Perhaps the only evidence still surviving of the Sino-Soviet friendship of the early 1950's is in the Russian flavor of the Chinese "traditional" repertory, which seems to consist entirely of folk tunes harmonized and colored with all the skills Rimsky-Korsakov knew, of picture postcards in the manner of Glinka and Borodin, and of symphonic poems as graphic as those of Tchaikovsky. 
But where those 19th-century Russian composers were concerned with the exotic, here are people who really are Chinese making a musical portrait of themselves as outlandish. 
Weird.
What listeners heard was Chinese chinoiserie. 
The pentatonic tunes, lively or soulful, were no doubt home-grown, as were the nasal sonorities and the sudden changes of rhythm. 
But the arrangements estranged all these things, and in that sense the National Traditional Orchestra is as far from any notion of tradition as it is possible to be. 
Within a tradition, people speak of what is theirs, which they can then communicate to others, whereas here an alien medium, the orchestra, was dividing people from their own. 
Listeners were asked to gaze but not touch, or be touched. 
That is the way of movie music.
But hold on a moment. 
Before we write off the National Traditional Orchestra of China as a wholly synthetic institution, we should take a closer look at Western musical culture. 
An Arab or Persian visitor to a concert in Europe around 1700 might have felt much as a Western listener does today when confronted with this newly traditional Chinese music, though for opposite reasons. 
That visitor would have found familiar instruments (string instruments and oboes came out of the Islamic world) used to unfamiliar purposes, whereas the Chinese ensemble shows us unfamiliar instruments in an entirely familiar context. 
That visitor might also have felt as shocked, amused, despairing and curious as we do at the spectacle of cultural miscegenation.
THOUGHTS OF THE EARLY days of the Western orchestra were aroused specifically by the rowdiness of the Chinese group. 
Its instruments may be adapted to the same scale, and to that degree homogenized, but they fight against concord. 
They sound much the way period-instrument orchestras did in the 1970's, before experience began to tell, and no doubt the way period-instrument orchestras did in the 1770's, when no music stayed around long enough for anyone to gain experience in playing it.
The National Traditional Orchestra of China may, therefore, be traditional after all, but situated at the start of a new tradition, as the Western orchestra was two or three centuries ago. 
Everything of human devising must start out as a ramshackle experiment: in the case of the Western orchestra, an assembly of instruments from different sources, meant for different uses, including strings from Islamic courts, horns from the hunting field and, lest we forget, gongs from China.
Time has given this miscellany the patina of reputability, but it has not given us the right to be sniffy about parallel developments that we catch in an earlier phase. 
The distinction is not between the fake and the genuine but rather between new fakes and old ones.

file: Clinton Administration Tightens Rules on Supercomputer Sales to 13 Foreign Groups.txt
text:
ï»¿
Addressing concerns over the sale of American supercomputers to Russia and China, the Clinton Administration added 13 foreign organizations today to its list of groups that are involved in secretly producing nuclear weapons and will now require special Federal approval to buy American technology.
Six organizations in Russia and China will now be on "an alert to exporters" and additional names will be added soon, said William A. Reinsch, Under Secretary of Commerce for Export Administration.
Critics said, however, that today's publication is too little and too late after recent disclosures that dozens of American supercomputers, many with possible military applications, have been sold to Russia and China since 1996 without Federal licenses.
These sales did not require Government approval because they were made under greatly relaxed export controls for supercomputers issued by President Clinton in 1995. 
Under those rules, the Government transferred to companies the responsibility for screening buyers to insure they were not diverting sensitive technology to military uses.
"This is a good first step, but it's a baby step, and in the case of the Russian nuclear weapons lab, it comes too late," said Gary Milhollin, the director of the Wisconsin Project on Nuclear Arms Control.
Mr. Milhollin was referring to the All-Russian Scientific Research Institute of Technical Physics, which was added to the list today. 
Last year Silicon Graphics Inc. in Mountain View, Calif., sold supercomputers to the institute, saying it did not seek Government approval because it was unaware that the institute was also a weapons lab.
But the Russian institute's nuclear weapons role has long been widely known, so much so that the Commerce Department felt no urgency, until recently, to include it on the list, according to Commerce Department officials. 
Had the institute been put on the blacklist earlier, the sale would have been subject to Federal review and probably would not have happened, the officials also said.
The Department of Justice has opened a criminal investigation into Russia's purchase of supercomputers.
When announcing the 1995 deregulation, the White House promised to keep exporters informed of "potential proliferation and other security risks."
But in early 1996 the Clinton Administration turned down a request by Federal nuclear experts to fulfill that obligation, out of fear of offending some countries or compromising intelligence-gathering methods, officials said.
The Administration only published the first name on the list this year after Russia stunned proliferation experts by announcing that its nuclear weapons laboratories had acquired American supercomputers. 
Today's list, published in the Federal Register, includes organizations in India, Israel and Pakistan as well as three Chinese scientific organizations and two research institutes and a ministry in Russia.
Congress raised concerns after the disclosure of the sales to Russia and the discovery that China had obtained 47 supercomputers. 
American intelligence officials said the Chinese could use the computers to design more efficient or lighter nuclear warheads that could be put on missiles able to reach the United States.
Two weeks ago the House of Representatives passed an amendment to the defense authorization bill to reinstitute tighter controls over supercomputer exports. 
One sponsor, Floyd D. Spence, Republican of South Carolina, said it "would put Government officials back to where they belong, protecting our security interests instead of remaining on the sidelines while Russia, China and other nations of proliferation concern go on a shopping spree."
Senators Thad Cochran, Republican of Mississippi, and Richard J. Durbin, Democrat of Illinois, have offered a similar amendment in the Senate.
The Clinton Administration strongly opposes both amendments, arguing that export controls should he handled by the executive branch.Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: CLINTON AIDE SAYS CHINA TRIP DELAY WOULD BE MISTAKE.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Clinton's national security adviser said today that "it would be an enormous mistake" to postpone Mr. Clinton's trip to China next month simply because of the current political storm over the export of satellite technology.
Nonetheless, White House officials are already scrambling to find diplomatic offerings they can bring to Beijing without worsening the controversy, since many of the initiatives Mr. Clinton is considering would use access to American satellites and joint space research as a lure for China to take further steps in limiting weapons proliferation.
Appearing on the CBS News program "Face the Nation," Samuel R. Berger, the national security adviser, dismissed calls by virtually all the Republican leaders in Congress for Mr. Clinton to cancel his trip. 
Among those leaders was Speaker Newt Gingrich, who said on the CNN program "Late Edition," "Until we know the truth about what was going on, it is very inappropriate for the President to go to China."
Mr. Gingrich added that "it would be an embarrassment to both countries to have the meeting."
White House officials say there is virtually no chance Mr. Clinton will cancel plans for his meeting with Chinese leaders in late June, which Mr. Berger said comes at a critical moment in relations with Beijing. 
Noting India's recent tests of nuclear weapons and the turmoil caused by the Asian financial crisis, Mr. Berger said, "China is key to all of those."
At the same time, a continuing criminal investigation and the opening of several Congressional inquiries into the actions of two satellite makers are bound to affect the agenda of the trip, according to several officials and informal advisers to the Administration on China.
"It's obvious that a lot of what we had hoped to offer in return for Chinese commitments on proliferation -- especially in the space and technology area -- are going to have to be reviewed," one senior adviser to Mr. Clinton said. 
"That's just the political reality."
For example, a month ago Administration officials were discussing with the Chinese the possibility of a blanket waiver of sanctions imposed after the killing of demonstrators in Tiananmen Square in 1989. 
The waiver would allow China to launch American-made satellites without case-by-case Presidential review. 
In return, the White House was looking for a commitment from China to join the Missile Technology Control Regime, the main international group that limits exports of missile technologies.
But in the current political climate, that proposal appears all but dead. 
Not only would it cause an uproar in Congress, according to Administration and other officials, but China has so far not indicated a willingness to join the missile regime, though it already adheres to some of its principles.
There are also questions about another major proposal: an agreement between the National Aeronautics and Space Administration and its Chinese counterpart to conduct scientific observations from space.
Before the current controversy, Administration officials say, the Pentagon and the nation's intelligence agencies had insisted on restrictions to make sure that the space accord did not enable China to improve its spy satellite capability, or its ability to use global positioning satellites to allow more precise targeting of ballistic missiles. 
The cooperation agreement was focused mostly on observing agricultural changes and pollution.
"Even with that," one Administration official said this weekend, "people are going to look at this carefully because it has the words 'space' and 'satellite' in it."
It is unclear how, or even if, the satellite controversy will affect other offerings to the Chinese. 
Some are not technology-related: for example, the Administration has considered lifting an eight-year-old ban that has prevented two Government agencies, the Overseas Private Investment Corporation and the Trade and Development Agency, from promoting deals between American companies and the Chinese Government.
The Overseas Private Investment Corporation provides political risk insurance to American companies for a fee. 
The Trade and Development Agency finances feasibility studies of overseas projects that could create jobs for American workers.
Last week, the House of Representatives overwhelmingly passed amendments to a military spending bill that would prohibit virtually all satellite exports to China. 
Among the House members who voted for the bill were a number who had urged Mr. Clinton to allow such exports in the past, rather than let the business go to rival European companies.
Mr. Berger suggested today that Congress had acted prematurely and emotionally. 
"I always thought we went from accusation to fact to conclusion to remedy," he said.
On the talk shows today and on Capitol Hill last week, participants in the debate often conflated three separate issues into a broad argument over whether the Clinton Administration has taken actions that could compromise national security.
The first of those issues concerns a waiver President Clinton signed earlier this year allowing Loral Space and Communications, a major military contractor, to export a satellite that is scheduled to be launched by the Chinese in November. 
The President's decision was complicated by the fact that Federal prosecutors have been investigating a 1996 incident in which Loral's engineers are accused of having breached security by advising the Chinese on how to build more reliable rockets.
That advice followed an investigation into the causes of the explosion of a Long March rocket, the mainstay of China's commercial rocket fleet and its nuclear arsenal. 
Classified memorandums, made public by the White House on Friday, show that there was intense debate within the Clinton Administration over whether to approve this year's launching.
The question is whether the White House was influenced by appeals from Loral to sign the waiver quickly, before contractual penalties of more than $4 million were imposed by the Chinese for a delay in delivering the satellite. 
Mr. Berger defended the decision to allow the export, saying that "no technology was being transferred by the license."
He noted that the license could still be revoked if the investigation led to an indictment of the company or any of its employees.
The second issue concerns Mr. Clinton's pattern of issuing waivers that allow such launchings. 
The White House has noted that President George Bush did the same, signing nine waivers between December 1989 -- only six months after the Tiananmen Square killings -- and 1992. 
Mr. Clinton has signed 11 waivers since July 1993.
Documents shown to reporters on Friday made it clear that the waivers are given to the Chinese as a reward for an action that pleases Washington, or used as an incentive for future action. 
For example, the State Department recommended that Mr. Clinton approve the February waiver because it would "provide an incentive for China to observe M.T.C.R. missile proliferation guidelines."
But the waivers are also motivated by a desire to assure that American companies remain ahead of their European competitors in the race to get satellites aloft, serving telephone users and television viewers around the world.
Thus the Administration is open to charges that it has twisted its security judgments for the benefit of American companies, including those whose officers are known to have made large campaign contributions. 
The issue is complicated by the fact that some of the waivers clearly aided the China Aerospace Group, a conglomerate owned by the Chinese Government. 
An executive of China Aerospace, Liu Chaoying, is believed to have been the conduit for surreptitious donations to the Democratic Party in 1996. 
Ms. Liu has denied the accusation.
And almost lost in the Washington debate is what may be the most critical question: why President Clinton, in March 1996, overrode his Secretary of State, Warren M. Christopher, by ruling that satellites would no longer be classified as munitions. 
That eased the process of getting export waivers approved.
"I am convinced the national security was not compromised by any decision that we made," Mr. Berger said today.
