file: Clinton Defends Engagement With China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Declaring the isolation of China to be "unworkable, counterproductive and potentially dangerous," President Clinton today defended his policy of engagement with China as fundamental to America's economic and security interests.
The President's 25-minute address to a small group of Asia experts at Voice of America headquarters here was broadcast to a global radio audience estimated at 100 million, and was meant to lay a foundation for next week's summit meeting with President Jiang Zemin of China. 
It was the first time in his Presidency that Mr. Clinton has devoted an entire speech to a broad treatment of the relationship between America and China.
He said that even though he is having a high-profile meeting with Mr. Jiang -- the first Chinese state visit in a dozen years -- significant problems remained between Washington and Beijing. 
China stifles dissent, supplies weapons components to rogue states and does not adhere to international trading regimes, the President said. 
But the relationship with China is too important to base solely on points of friction, he asserted.
"As always, America must be prepared to live and flourish in a world in which we are at odds with China," he said. 
"But that is not the world we want. 
Our objective is not containment and conflict; it is cooperation. 
We will far better serve our interests, and our principles, if we work with a China that shares that objective with us."
The President touched all the bases of China policy without lingering very long on any one -- human rights, trade, environmental protection, Chinese political liberalization and American security interests in Asia.
The audience of diplomats, China scholars and Government officials interrupted the President with polite applause only twice, when he made his most forceful statements on American determination to call attention to continuing human rights abuses in China.
Mr. Clinton sought to inoculate himself against critics who claim that the United States should not act so cooperatively toward a repeat violator of press and religious freedoms, but should rather use its political and economic muscle to press Beijing toward more openness.
The President spoke of the profound economic changes under way in China and predicted that the growth of a market economy would bring with it greater political freedom.
"In the process, however, they have stifled political dissent to a degree and in ways that we believe are fundamentally wrong," he said.
"This approach has caused problems within China and in its relationship to the United States," he continued. 
"Chinese leaders believe it is necessary to hold the nation together to keep it growing, to keep moving toward its destiny. 
But it will become increasingly difficult to maintain the closed political system in an ever more open economy and society."
Despite these differences, the President insisted, the United States could not afford to contain or isolate Beijing, nor could it succeed in doing so because such an approach would embolden the enemies of freedom in China and give European and Asian business competitors a jump on the world's largest emerging market.
"A pragmatic policy of engagement is the best way to advance our fundamental interests and values," the President said.
Representative Nancy Pelosi, a California Democrat, criticized the President's speech as having glossed over Chinese human rights violations, however.
"President Clinton's China speech was masterful in its craftiness in whitewashing China's record," Ms. Pelosi said. 
"With this speech, President Clinton has tried to justify the failure of his trade policy and the failure of his human rights policy with a fiction of China's cooperation on proliferation of weapons of mass destruction."
Although the President's Washington audience consisted chiefly of professional China experts, he aimed his message at listeners in China and across the United States.
Evelyn Lieberman, director of Voice of America, said the speech was being broadcast into China in Mandarin and would be rebroadcast over the next several days. 
Foreign radio broadcasts into China are sometimes jammed.
The President spelled out six reasons it is in American interests to work with China on a range of issues, and said they would figure in next week's summit agenda. 
He maintained that policing the unpredictable post-cold-war world would be much simpler with China as a partner, that the security of American allies and trading partners in Asia depended on China's peaceful role in resolving disputes there, and that global efforts to curb the spread of weapons of mass destruction would fail unless China agreed to stop selling dangerous technology to unreliable nations.
In addition, he said China could be a crucial partner in stemming the regional and global flow of drugs, arms and aliens; that China represented the richest potential market for American goods at a time when American economic growth depends on the growth of exports, and that China had a large role to play in efforts to reduce energy consumption and protect the environment.
He closed by approvingly quoting Richard M. Nixon, who as President brought about the historic modern opening of China to the West. 
Even in 1967, before winning the Presidency, he said, Mr. Nixon recognized the futility of trying to isolate the world's most populous nation, warning that "there is no place on this small planet for a billion of its potentially most able people to live in angry isolation."

file: Clinton Defends His Policies In Kosovo, China and Mexico.txt
text:
ï»¿
With surprises abroad and critics at home bedeviling his foreign policy, President Clinton today defended his efforts to cooperate with Mexico in fighting drugs, to engage with China to promote political freedom, and to threaten force to bring peace to Kosovo.
Mr. Clinton tried to step back on a jumbled day of scattershot developments and locate coherent themes in a foreign policy that his critics have long complained reacts to world events more than it anticipates them, and abides the abuses of nations more than it prevents or punishes them.
Twice in his broad-gauged, 50-minute speech here, he spoke of the "inexorable logic of globalization."
He warned that while increased trade and economic growth might knit nations closer together, without active American leadership they would not guarantee peace, wealth or environmental protection.
"The promise of our future lies in the world," Mr. Clinton said. 
"Therefore we must work hard with the world -- to defeat the dangers we face together and to build this hopeful moment together, in a generation of peace, prosperity, and freedom."
He went on to list regions and issues where he planned to use the country's troops, trade, aid and cooperation -- rather than its broad, cold shoulder -- to advance his goals.
On Kosovo, the Clinton Administration has faced criticism for setting a deadline for peace talks between Serbs and ethnic Albanian rebels, and then letting it slip.
In his speech, the President declared his intent to certify to Congress that Mexico is cooperating in the fight on drugs, despite the widely held view in his Administration that corruption in the Mexican Government has resulted in less cooperation in the last year. 
A6.
Mr. Clinton warned Slobodan Milosevic, Yugoslavia's President, to exert "restraint, not repression" during the pause in the troubled peace negotiations with the Albanian rebels in the once-autonomous region of Kosovo. 
"If he does not, NATO is prepared to act," he said. 
But he did not specify what actions might prompt the long-threatened bombing raids.
And on the day that his State Department issued a scathing summary of China's rights abuses in the annual Human Rights Report, Mr. Clinton called for "principled and purposeful engagement with China, its Government and its people."
Without referring specifically to the State Department's findings, he suggested that China was "moving away from the rule of fear" but was "not yet rooted in the rule of law."
"I do not believe we can hope to bring change to China if we isolate China from the forces of change," he said. 
Secretary of State Madeleine K. Albright, who is preparing to leave for China this weekend, sat to Mr. Clinton's left as he delivered his speech, in a hotel's basement ballroom here. 
He spoke to the Pacific Council for Globalization, the Commonwealth Club and the World Affairs Council.
With Israelis and Palestinians at an impasse over the President's latest intervention for peace, the Wye River Agreement, Mr. Clinton declared today, "I intend to use the time I have remaining in this office to push for a comprehensive peace in the Middle East," adding, "The people of the Middle East can do it, but time is precious, and they can't afford to waste any more of it."
He began his survey of the world -- which his national security adviser, Samuel R. Berger, called a "State of the Union for foreign policy" -- with an upbeat appraisal of the times. 
"For the first time since before the rise of Fascism early in this century, there is no overriding threat to our survival or our freedom," he said. 
He then described a fifteenfold jump in world trade since the end of World War II that has raised "living standards on every continent."
But, calling for "a little humility," he read a long quotation declaring that an extraordinary increase in trade, travel and information flow had insured that "isolation is no longer possible."
The words were said 100 years ago by President William McKinley, Mr. Clinton said, noting that McKinley's optimism was followed by two world wars, the Holocaust, the Great Depression and Communism.
"Had leading nations acted decisively then, perhaps these disasters might have been prevented," he said.
As a result of that experience, he warned: "We cannot assume today that globalization alone will wash away the forces of destruction at the dawn of the 21st century, any more than it did at the dawn of the 20th century. 
We cannot assume it will bring freedom and prosperity to ordinary citizens around the world who long for them. 
We cannot assume it will avoid environmental and public health disasters."
Cautioning against what he called an American tendency to withdraw from the world during good times, the President went on to slot his top foreign policy concerns into overlapping categories, listing five "challenges" to the United States in the coming century: building a "more peaceful 21st century world;" bringing Russia and China "into the international system as open, prosperous, stable nations;" protecting against dangers of weapons proliferation, terrorism, drugs and climate change; creating a world trading and financial system that benefits ordinary people, and maintaining freedom as "a top goal."
His aides say that after regarding foreign policy as a regrettable but necessary distraction at the beginning of his first term, Mr. Clinton came to relish the world stage, particularly after 1994, when a Republican Congress stymied much of his domestic agenda. 
He also became increasingly convinced of the benefits of global trade to American business and of the potential of commercial ties and international organizations to enmesh potentially rogue nations and enforce peace, foster democracy and protect human rights.
Taking more control over his policy, he replaced the mentors of his first term -- notably Secretary of State Warren M. Christopher -- with advisers like Mr. Berger and Ms. Albright whom he regards as peers.
But while he has been credited in his two terms with advances in the Middle East, Haiti and Northern Ireland, Mr. Clinton has been repeatedly criticized for ignoring festering problems, like those in Bosnia and Rwanda. 
He has been unable to build enough support in his own party to win the special negotiating authority from Congress necessary to strike the free-trade deals that he regards as central to his policy. 
And critics have accused him of naive optimism that the flow of products and information will ultimately force China and other repressive governments to open their political systems.
Further, Mr. Clinton's go-go optimism for free markets, both of goods and of capital -- encouraged by his Treasury Secretary, Robert E. Rubin -- may have blinded him, critics charge, to the risks posed by furious currency trading to the fragile economies of South East Asia, Latin America and Russia.
Today, he appealed to his audience for help in figuring out what to do about such sloshing of capital in and out of developing countries. 
"We have got to find a way to facilitate the movement of money -- without which trade and investment cannot occur -- in a way that avoids these dramatic cycles of boom and then bust, which have led to the collapse of economic activity in so many countries around the world," he said.
On a six-day trip through the west, Mr. Clinton flew this afternoon to Los Angeles to attend a fund-raiser this evening. 
On Saturday, he planned to fly to Utah for a three-day vacation with his family, to celebrate the 19th birthday of his daughter, Chelsea.
At a fund-raiser here Thursday night, he said he had made "no progress" in resolving tensions between Turkey and Greece, or between India and Pakistan. 
He did not speak so starkly today, but he observed that the standoff in South Asia was a reminder that "the next big war could still be nuclear."

"But if we don't stop the conflict now, it clearly will spread. 
And then we will not be able to stop it, except at far greater cost and risk."

A former senior Chinese official who was jailed for opposing the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown has been warned a third time by the Chinese authorities to stop talking to foreign journalists.
The latest warning came on Sunday, only a day after President Clinton's news conference with the Chinese President, Jiang Zemin. 
But the former official, Bao Tong, has continued to speak out, giving an interview on Tuesday to the Voice of America.
Senior American officials said today that Mr. Bao's fate is "a topic of significant interest" to the Clinton Administration. 
But they added that they could not say whether Mr. Clinton had raised Mr. Bao's case with Mr. Jiang.
Mr. Bao, 66, is no dissident. 
He served as chief of staff to the former Communist Party Secretary, Zhao Ziyang, who was ousted days before the June 1989 crackdown and who remains under house arrest.
Mr. Bao, who was jailed then for seven years followed by two years on probation that ended in late May, has used Mr. Clinton's visit to speak out about the Government's failings. 
Mr. Zhao himself circulated a letter to the party's Central Committee just before Mr. Clinton arrived, calling on it to reverse its condemnation of the demonstrations in the square, which are officially considered a "counterrevolutionary rebellion."
In the episode leading to the latest warning, Mr. Bao gave an interview to CBS News, which was televised on Monday. 
Mr. Bao's son, Bao Pu, said in an interview that the security police came to his father's Beijing apartment after the taping on Sunday, and spent two hours there.
Reached by telephone on Thursday in Beijing, Mr. Bao confirmed that he had been visited by public security agents three times in June, most recently on Sunday when three agents came to his house. 
"They were polite and not threatening," Mr. Bao said. 
He said they confirmed that he does enjoy freedom of speech. 
However, he said, they again warned him that he should not give interviews to overseas journalists without the approval of the Government. 
Such interviews are illegal, they told him. 
"I hope this is just a misunderstanding and does not reflect the guiding principles of the government," Mr. Bao said, speaking over a telephone line that was probably tapped by security agents.
Under Chinese regulations that are often ignored, foreign journalists are supposed to get official permission before conducting interviews.
Mr. Bao's son said that Mr. Bao told the agents that President Jiang himself had said the day before that "every Chinese citizen is given freedom of speech by the Constitution."
Also on Sunday, Mr. Bao gave an interview to The Los Angeles Times, which printed an article the next day.

file: CLINTON IN CHINA_ FANFARE_Chinese Agog at Clinton, a Hero (Like Nixon).txt
text:
ï»¿
In his global vision, it seems, Bill Clinton ranks right up there with Richard M. Nixon.
Nixon will forever be revered here for reviving ties between the United States and the once isolated China.
Now, in the days before Mr. Clinton arrives for his first state visit to China, he is being lionized in the official press and among elements of the intelligentsia as a far-sighted statesman who had the wisdom to change course with China, by shifting from his initial attacks to his current policy of close engagement.
It's a politician's dream: newspapers, magazines and television shows are showing a deep fascination with Mr. Clinton the political leader, dissecting his recent speeches on China policy and extolling his courage in the face of the China-haters who are trying to derail the emerging "strategic partnership."
One newspaper ran a large picture of the President in a suit of armor, while Chinese journalists who visited Arkansas reveled in Mr. Clinton's record as Governor in promoting education, not Whitewater. 
(So far, oddly, there has been relatively little attention to Hillary Rodham Clinton, who will accompany him on the visit, which begins on Thursday.)
The adulation was evident this afternoon at the monthly salon of the XSH Book Club, in its headquarters in the middle of a park in northwest Beijing. 
The directors of the club -- which markets books at a discount to its thousands of members through catalogues and seminars -- assembled foreign policy experts and a few dozen Chinese journalists and book lovers to discuss three American titles recently published in Chinese.
The first was Mr. Clinton's "Between Hope and History: Meeting America's Challenges for the 21st Century" (Random House, 1996), the manifesto of his second Administration, written with William Nothdurft. 
This month, the book went into its second printing in China. 
("Not quite a 'Titanic,' " said the book club editor, Xi Hong, "but a consistent top-seller over the last year.")
The second featured title, just published here after a rush translation job, was Monica Crowley's new memoir, "Nixon in Winter" (Random House, 1998). 
The third was Henry Kissinger's 1994 tome "Diplomacy" (Simon & Schuster), which appeared in Chinese last year.
Whatever American critics may have made of the Clinton book and Ms. Crowley's deferential memoir of the former President who took her under his wing in his final years, the assembled professors here treated these works seriously, as offering insightinto the men who made today's emerging Chinese-American partnership possible.
Qian Wenrong, deputy director of the Xinhua World Issues Research Institute, noted that by the time Mr. Clinton published his book, he had already made his momentous shift in China policy, and recognized the leading role China will play in world affairs. 
Back in the 1970's, Mr. Qian said, Nixon too had presciently seen China's inevitable rise.
Wang Yizhou of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences called the Nixon book "excellent, a reminder of how far-sighted the man was."
He declared Mr. Kissinger's book a classic. 
"The Kissinger book is very deep," he said, "but I like the Clinton book better."
Jia Qingguo, a political scientist at Beijing University who spent several years in the United States, was less taken, but noted that through Mr. Clinton's book, and his rags-to-riches story, Chinese could better understand the American Dream.
A fourth scholar, Huang Annian, a historian at Beijing Normal University, listed the three most important American Presidents from China's perspective. 
The first was Franklin D. Roosevelt, leader during World War II, "the most glorious period in Chinese-U.S. relations" as the countries fought together against Japan.
The second was Nixon, who set the process in motion that led to normalized relations. 
And third was Mr. Clinton, who despite concerns over human rights and other issues has realized that the isolation of China does not serve America's interest.
"These three men -- they all have strategic vision," Mr. Huang said.
Even greater praise has appeared in the official media.
After Mr. Clinton gave an interview to visiting Chinese journalists in Washington last week, an article in The Economic Daily here said, "The 40-minute interview was unforgettable."
Mr. Clinton's "foresight, courage and insight deeply impressed the Chinese correspondents," the article said.

file: CLINTON IN CHINA_ HONG KONG_Hong Kong Surprise_ Politics Steady but Economy Falters.txt
text:
ï»¿
His hometown is marking the first anniversary of its return to China on July 1, but Loon Wai-ting is in no mood to celebrate. 
Mr. Loon has spent the year without a job. 
On a recent sauna-like afternoon, in the teeming neighborhood of Mong Kok, he stood before a government labor office, fruitlessly searching a bulletin board for job listings.
"When the British were here, there was a lot of business in Hong Kong," said Mr. Loon, a 51-year-old merchant seaman, whose deeply lined face bespeaks both a lifetime at sea and a worrisome year as the unemployed father of four. 
"When the British left, the business left with them."
Of course, Britain's exit from Hong Kong has had little to do with the economic downturn of its former colony, which sits at the crossroads of a becalmed Asia and has suffered along with its neighbors. 
But Mr. Loon speaks for many Hong Kong people, who are being ravaged by rising unemployment, a 20 percent drop in the stock market and a 40 percent decline in the property market in the last six months.
For this embattled outpost of commerce, celebrating the passage of a year under Chinese rule seems almost beside the point.
Hong Kong is staging a flurry of events on Wednesday, including a flag-raising, a cultural pageant and back-to-back visits on Wednesday and Thursday from the Chinese President, Jiang Zemin, and President Clinton. 
But the government has scrapped gaudier elements of last year's celebration, like the laser and fireworks shows, because they seem ill-suited to these hard times.
The subdued tone of Hong Kong's anniversary is all the more notable because until six months ago, the government here would have had much to crow about. 
Politically, Hong Kong has scarcely changed in the year since this capitalist bastion became part of a Communist empire. 
Defying predictions by experts here and in the West, Beijing has left Hong Kong largely untouched.
Since last July 1, Hong Kong voters have turned out in record numbers to elect a new legislature, enjoyed a lively news media and marked the ninth anniversary of the Tiananmen Square massacre with a huge, candlelight vigil -- one of more than 1,400 protests against everything from human rights abuses in China to the plummeting value of apartments in Hong Kong.
But there are rumors that Chinese officials are seeking to influence Hong Kong's leaders through hints delivered in back-channel conversations. 
And the government recently raised fears about the integrity of Hong Kong's legal system by amending laws in ways that seem to favor Beijing. 
But fears about wholesale meddling or the muzzling of the media have so far proved unwarranted.
"Hong Kong is a graveyard for political prognosticators," said Daniel R. Fung, the Solicitor General of Hong Kong and a defender of the government. 
"Everybody predicted we'd have a bumpy ride politically but the economy would take care of itself. 
Exactly the opposite has happened."
Mr. Fung said Beijing delivered on its promise of "one country, two systems," a political arrangement that guarantees Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy as a special administrative region of China. 
That agreement was secured in years of often-rancorous negotiations between Britain and China.
But while the British colonial government was laying the groundwork for Hong Kong's political future, it was also presiding over a spectacular inflation of the colony's property market -- creating an Asian Xanadu with more billionaires and Rolls-Royces per square mile than any other city in the world.
When the financial crisis tore through Asia last fall, it devastated Hong Kong's exports and humbled its stock market. 
While Hong Kong fought off the symptoms of the Asian flu longer than its neighbors, it finally succumbed -- slipping into a recession for the first time in 13 years.
If economic collapse was not enough, Hong Kong has also been hit by several calamities: a deadly outbreak of bird flu in December, a string of cholera cases and a creeping red algae tide in Hong Kong's coastal waters.
The flood of bad news has left people traumatized. 
And it has prompted them to question Hong Kong's government and its chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, the conservative shipping magnate who was chosen by Beijing to lead the territory. 
Such dissent is uncharacteristic for Hong Kong, where the British colonial governor ruled in close cooperation with the business elite.
"Economic prosperity was the major connecting thread between the old Hong Kong and new Hong Kong," said Michael DeGolyer, a professor of government at Baptist University here who studied public attitudes toward the handover. 
"Now Hong Kong people are getting very irritated."
Anger may have been one reason people voted in record numbers in Hong Kong's legislative elections last month. 
In a gesture of defiance to the local government and Beijing, the voters elected pro-democracy candidates to a majority of the popularly elected seats. 
Many of those politicians had been sent into political exile when Beijing dissolved Hong Kong's last democratically elected legislature before the handover and replaced it with a hand-picked body.
Pro-democracy politicians say Hong Kong's people are even more committed to a pluralistic system than they were before the handover, when the city's political independence under China seemed at risk. 
Being a part of China, they say, has made democracy seem more precious.
"Of the 1.2 billion people in China, we -- the 6.6 million people of Hong Kong -- are the only people who have the vote," said Martin Lee, the head of the Democratic Party, who regained his legislative seat.
Still, Mr. Lee admitted that concerns about civil rights and individual freedoms are being overshadowed by economic issues. 
Indeed, the Democratic Party teamed up with pro-business and pro-Beijing parties to mount a coordinated assault on the policies of Mr. Tung. The group is calling on the government to use its vast financial reserves to lessen the burden on people by cutting taxes.
Bowing to pressure, the government recently announced a package of measures, including a one-time tax rebate, to stimulate the economy.
For all the noise generated by the newly elected legislators, Hong Kong is still firmly controlled by Mr. Tung. Though Mr. Lee and his colleagues won more than half of the popular vote, they will hold fewer than one-third of the seats in the legislature. 
And the legislature does not have the power to introduce bills on major issues without the acquiescence of the chief executive.
Mr. Lee is demanding that the government accelerate the timetable for full democracy here. 
Under the current timetable, voters here will not be able to elect all legislators directly until 2007. 
But given that the chief executive and the National People's Congress in China would have to approve such an amendment to Hong Kong's constitution, Mr. Lee's crusade seems quixotic.
A more pressing concern for some pro-democracy politicians is the rule of law in Hong Kong. 
Although the territory has retained British common law as the foundation of its legal code, some critics say the government is making subtle changes that may whittle away citizen's rights.
Most notably, the government in April granted the Chinese Government the same immunity from local laws that the British Crown had. 
The trouble is, the Hong Kong authorities defined the Chinese Government broadly enough to include the New China News Agency, which has historically functioned as Beijing's eyes and ears in the territory.
The agency still inspires fear among pro-democracy leaders here, and the prospect that it will hold immunity from local laws is doubly frightening to them. 
"The last year has been little short of hair-raising," said Margaret Ng, a lawyer and pro-democracy politician who was also recently elected to the legislature.
Despite their qualms, even pro-democracy politicians credit Beijing with masterly public relations. 
After marching into Hong Kong at midnight on June 30, the Chinese Army troops retreated into their barracks and have been kept there since. 
A single soldier stands guard outside the garrison in central Hong Kong.
China's conduct has given Hong Kong's pro-Beijing politicians a keen sense of vindication. 
Tsang Yok-sing, an avowed Marxist who heads the main pro-Beijing party, said President Jiang had been scrupulous in maintaining the principle of "one country, two systems" -- even discouraging pro-Beijing people in Hong Kong from airing criticisms of the territory while on the mainland.
For people here who are intent on reaffirming their Chinese identity, however, China's low profile poses some ticklish problems. 
Hong Kong's top civil servant, Anson Chan, said in a recent speech in Washington that she had felt an "emotional and spiritual connection" in seeing the Chinese flag hoisted over Hong Kong to celebrate the national day of the People's Republic on Oct. 
1.
But Ms. Chan's speech was greeted with ambivalence at home. 
Mr. Lee, whose family fled to Hong Kong from neighboring Guangdong Province, said, "How can I feel warm when I see the flag go up when so many of my people are deprived of basic human rights?"
Even staunchly pro-Beijing people are not ready to predict that Hong Kong will never again clash with China. 
Though few believe that the Chinese Government will clamp down on Hong Kong over political issues, a growing number of politicians and business executives worry that Hong Kong's languishing economy might provoke China to take a more intrusive approach.
Beijing's financial stake in Hong Kong is vast and growing.The stock exchange here is the primary means for Chinese companies to raise capital. 
With Prime Minister Zhu Ronji pushing to privatize state-owned enterprises, Hong Kong will become an even more vital window between China and the global market.
The social contract between Beijing and Hong Kong is predicated on a simple idea: As long as Hong Kong makes money, Beijing will leave it alone. 
If Hong Kong stops making money, people here say, all bets are off.
Or as the Hong Kong author and publisher Louis Cha, put it: "Suppose Hong Kong Bank lends me $1 million and I run my business well. 
They will leave me alone. 
But if I run my business poorly and can't repay my loans, it's very possible they will send somebody to look at my books."

file: CLINTON IN CHINA_ IN HONG KONG_Manhattan Of Asia_ Indifferent To Clinton.txt
text:
ï»¿
They call this city the Manhattan of Asia. 
And today, as President Clinton wound up his visit to China by motoring around town to give a speech, attend some meetings and do a bit of shopping, Hong Kong treated the leader of the free world with New York-style indifference.
"I'm not paying any attention to him," Chu Shu-san, a 48-year-old newsstand vendor, said with a shrug as he sold copies of papers with Mr. Clinton's picture on the front page. 
"He's just in transit anyway."
To be fair, Mr. Clinton attracted a good crowd for a speech this morning about the relationship between the United States and Asia. 
But the audience of local and foreign business leaders responded tepidly to his call for a speedier introduction of democracy to this former British colony, which reverted to Chinese rule a year ago.
"We debated this issue for five years in the 1980's," said Vincent Lo, a leading property developer, in a somewhat grumpy tone, as he rose to leave after Mr. Clinton's half-hour speech. 
"We know the good points and the bad points of democracy, and we know we musn't rush into it."
Mr. Clinton, the first President to visit Hong Kong while in office, came here three times before entering the White House, and he clearly likes the place. 
"I think it's quite appropriate for our trip to end in Hong Kong, because, for us Americans, Hong Kong is China's window on the world," he said.
Still, the 24-hour stop lacked the high drama of his televised debate with President Jiang Zemin, his freewheeling give-and-take with students at Beijing University or even the solemn welcoming ceremony at Tiananmen Square.
On a rainy day here, few people lined the streets to see Mr. Clinton's motorcade. 
When Hillary Rodham Clinton and her daughter, Chelsea, slipped away to do some shopping at Shanghai Tang, a boutique that specializes in updated Mao-style clothing, they barely drew a crowd.
Even "Primary Colors," the film adaptation of the thinly disguised satire on the Clinton Presidency, has flopped here. 
The movie, which opened in Hong Kong the day after Mr. Clinton arrived in China, has earned just a fraction of the box-office of the most popular current film, "True Mob Story."
One reason for the lack of drama is that Hong Kong's troubles are more economic than political. 
People here are worried about the swooning stock market, the plummeting value of real estate and the stabilityII of the Hong Kong dollar -- topics that do not lend themselves to soaring rhetoric or street theater.
Mr. Clinton praised Hong Kong and China for not devaluing their currencies and he endorsed a $200 billion plan announced on Thursday by the Japanese Government to take over failing banks and protect depositors.
Of course the President did not ignore political issues. 
He applauded the record voter turnout in Hong Kong's legislative elections of two months ago, saying, "The results were a mandate for more democracy, not less, and faster, not slower, strides toward political freedom."
After his speech, Mr. Clinton met privately for 20 minutes with Martin Lee, Hong Kong's most prominent democratic politician. 
Mr. Lee, who lost his seat in the legislature when Beijing dissolved the body before the handover and regained it in the recent elections, told the President he hoped that half of the council's 60 seats would be directly elected in 2000 -- compared with 20 seats today.
Samuel R. Berger, the national security adviser, said Mr. Clinton listened attentively to Mr. Lee but did not express an opinion on any specific proposals for speeding up democracy in Hong Kong. 
"I don't think it's for us to get into the specifics of what the timetable of that might be," Mr. Berger said.
Despite Mr. Clinton's reluctance to talk numbers, Mr. Lee said the meeting was "terrific."
He said the President responded positively to his argument that the "Hong Kong Government should be encouraged to develop democracy, so they can see that it works well under Chinese rule."
Later Mr. Clinton met several other democratically elected legislators. 
One participant, Tsang Yok-sing, the head of Hong Kong's largest pro-Beijing party, said the President "showed that he has a positive attitude toward developing a constructive relationship with the Chinese leadership."
After his news conference, Mr. Clinton and his family stopped off for some last-minute shopping on their way to Hong Kong's new $20 billion airport. 
The President's use of the airport is about the only part of his visit that has generated local interest. 
Air Force One landed six hours after the departure of President Jiang, who had been in Hong Kong to mark the first anniversary of the handover.
The Hong Kong Standard devoted much of its article on Mr. Clinton today to a discussion of the dual presidential flights.

file: CLINTON IN CHINA_ TAIWAN_As the Chinese See It, Taiwan Remains Most Important Issue.txt
text:
ï»¿
From China's point of view the most explosive issue in its relationship with the United States is Taiwan. 
Chinese officials consistently argue that the level of American arms sales to the island violates Washington's pledge to reduce and, ultimately, phase out such sales.
To press its point, Beijing contends that its help to Pakistan and Iran's military and missile programs, which Washington is trying to limit, is comparable to Washington's military assistance to Taiwan. 
In negotiations, Beijing has suggested trading off its missile cooperation in the Middle East for American commitments to cut arms sales sharply to Taiwan, a possibility criticized by American Republicans like the former American Ambassador to China and representative to Taiwan, James R. Lilley.
The United States has argued that Chinese missile assistance to countries like Iran, which may use the weapons offensively, is quite different from its select supplies of defensive weaponry to Taiwan.
Since 1979, when Washington recognized Beijing as the sole legal Government of China and acknowledged that Taiwan is part of China, Washington has been committed to sell Taiwan whatever it needs to defend itself, language in the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act and passed by Congress.
But in August 1982, in what became known as the third communique, President Ronald Reagan agreed that the United States would gradually reduce arms sales to Taipei from the levels of that era, $830 million a year. 
For a time the Administration cut spending $20 million a year.
Although Administration officials, then and now, argue that nothing in the 1982 communique contradicts the 1979 law, "the problem is that the two are not consistent, and it's not hard to find ways in which they are in conflict," said Prof. Kenneth Lieberthal of the University of Michigan.
The 1979 act, which Congress regards as pre-eminently the law of the land, speaks of no reductions. 
The communique, which China regards as superseding the law, promises reductions of sales to Taiwan, "leading over a period of time to a final resolution."
The issue was not prominent, however, until 1992. 
Then, in the midst of his campaign for re-election, President George Bush agreed to sell Taiwan 150 advanced F-16 fighters, worth more than $5 billion and produced in the pivotal state of Texas. 
That one sale drove the fiscal 1992 arms sales to Taiwan of $478 million, to $6.275 billion for fiscal year 1993, before falling back to figures below $500 million each year since then, according to unclassified Congressional notifications under the Export Control Act and assembled by the Congressional Research Service.
In the last few years the Clinton Administration has also notified Congress of some major sales, including, in January, three Knox-class frigates and anti-submarine missiles and launchers worth $300 million; last year 21 AH-1W Super Cobra attack helicopters worth $479 million, and, in 1996, two sales of Stinger ground-to-air missiles and launchers that totaled 1,764 missiles for $885 million.
China has been particularly concerned about past sales of Patriot-equivalent air-defense systems and wants to forestall future American sales of a "theater missile defense system" to Taiwan, a system that has not been developed yet.
In the 1982 communique Beijing promised a peaceful resolution of the question of Taiwan, which Washington interprets as directly linked to its promise to reduce arms sales, an assumption that Beijing rejects. 
Some officials here have argued that China's severe reaction to pressure by President Lee Teng-hui of Taiwan for independence, including Chinese missile launchings that bracketed Taiwan before its elections in March 1996, was also a violation by Beijing of the communique.
"We have a legal and moral obligation to provide for Taiwan's security, and if Taiwan feels secure there's more likelihood for a real cross-straits dialogue between Beijing and Taipei about the future," said Winston Lord, former Assistant Secretary of State for East Asia and a former Ambassador to China.
Even the sales of F-16's, Mr. Lord argued, "though a stretch," were nonetheless legitimate, given China's growing military capacity.

United States officials expressed concern to the Government today over reports that several dissidents had been detained and others harassed in connection with President Clinton's visit.
"We're very concerned that some dissidents may have been detained or otherwise disrupted," the White House spokesman, Michael D. McCurry, told reporters soon after Mr. Clinton's arrival in Xian this evening. 
He said the United States Ambassador, James R. Sasser, had conveyed this to Chinese officials.

He added, "If true, this represents not China at its best, not China looking forward, but looking backward."
Among those detained, Yang Hai of Xian, one of about 70 people who had called on Mr. Clinton to meet with dissidents during his visit, was taken away by the police today, according to the Information Center of Human Rights and Democratic Movement in China, a Hong Kong-based monitoring group.

Still, in the months since the Chinese Government released the prominent dissident Wei Jingsheng into exile in the United States last November, scores of people around the country have signed petitions and written open letters calling for democracy and a reappraisal of the military crackdown in Tiananmen Square in 1989, in which hundreds of civilians were killed.

file: CLINTON IN CHINA_ THE DRAMA_Lincoln Center_s Unhappy Prospect_ The Opera With the Empty Costumes.txt
text:
ï»¿
At precisely the same time that President Clinton arrived to a colorfully choreographed welcoming ceremony in Xian this evening, a remarkable drama about a different strand of China-United States relations was wrapping up at Shanghai International Airport.
In a seedy-looking departure lounge, Nigel Redden, director of the Lincoln Center Festival, sat down for what he took to be a final talk with Ma Bomin, the director of Shanghai's Bureau of Culture, who has been blocking the classic Chinese opera "The Peony Pavilion" from making it to New York in time for its scheduled opening on July 7.
Mr. Redden's flight was scheduled for 7:40 P.M., and he was informed in the late afternoon that Ms. Ma would go to the airport to see him off, because she had something to say.
At 7 P.M. in the bar, Ms. Ma informed Mr. Redden that her bureau was now willing to compromise on the matter that kicked off this whole drama a week ago: blocking the shipment of elaborate sets, costumes and props. 
The shipment, Ms. Ma said, could now proceed.
Mr. Redden, suspicious after days of fruitless negotiations, quickly asked a pertinent question: What about the actors?
Would they be allowed to go too ?
No, Ms. Ma said with a grimace, the actors of the Kunqu Opera Company would not yet be allowed to perform, as she had said over and over, unless the opera was fully restaged to fit Government guidelines.
Costumes, but no actors. 
So a high-profile example of cultural exchange between the United States and China lay in ruins, on the day President Clinton arrived for a state visit, precisely the time when Chinese and United States officials are most eager to clear away unnecessary public conflict.
To an arts executive like Mr. Redden, it is stunning that Chinese authorities would want to prevent any ancient Chinese opera from being performed in New York (especially since Lincoln Center is paying). 
But it became clear in recent days that Chinese officialdom was not against "The Peony Pavilion," so much as one particular official was, and her name is Ma.
Ms. Ma's comments suggest that some petty political motives -- power over artistic troupes, professional jealousy, the right to censor -- may play as big a role as the artistic objections she cited, in her complaints that the work was a national treasure that needed to be protected from unorthodox interpretations.
And the reluctance of any higher Chinese authority to rein her in suggests that she wields considerable political clout.
Negotiating in China, it often seems, is never over. 
Mr. Redden knew that if he left, he might be called back to Shanghai the next day for a new round of talks.
"We keep asking about it, and the reaction is always 'It's extremely complicated,' " said Raymond Burghardt, United States Consul General in Shanghai. 
"Well, why is it so complicated?"
Mr. Burghardt was asking the question rhetorically, since as a diplomat with long experience in China he knows that calling a matter "extremely complicated" is a polite way of saying that there are a lot of politics involved.
Yet Mr. Burghardt fudged when asked whether President Clinton would inquire about the opera, even though one polite question from Mr. Clinton, voiced to a Chinese leader, could conceivably solve the issue in an instant.
At the airport this evening, Mr. Redden began to let his frustration show after making such little headway, particularly when Ms. Ma, a former opera singer, tried to tell reporters who had been hastily assembled that her compromise showed how her bureau had been flexible in these talks.
"There has been no flexibility at all," Mr. Redden protested. 
"I've been here since Monday, and have been met with no cooperation whatsoever."
As her aides started insisting that Mr. Redden leave because his flight was boarding, Ms. Ma turned to the reporters again to say, in Chinese, that perhaps both sides should continue to keep talking, since there were more avenues to be pursued.
When the comment was translated to Mr. Redden, he apparently thought Ms. Ma had actually meant what she said. 
He immediately ripped up his boarding pass and said, "So let's talk."
Looking shocked, as though a major headache on the verge of flying away had decided to stick around, Ms. Ma again described her concern about the opera's script, and how it would be necessary to unpack the costumes to rehearse. 
So maybe, she said, that shipment should not actually be allowed to go to New York. 
And before long, Mr. Redden was presented with a new boarding pass.
After Mr. Redden left, Ms. Ma turned to the reporters again and made another pitch: maybe Lincoln Center would accept a safer version of "The Peony Pavilion," one that was simpler to stage, that used none of the innovative techniques of Chen Shi-Zheng, the director hired by Lincoln Center, whom Ms. Ma, to put it mildly, does not like.
"We have already started rehearsing," Ms. Ma said, brightening. 
"We could certainly take it to Lincoln Center in time for their festival."
Mr. Chen, dejected by the opera's demise, lamented that bureaucrats like Ms. Ma seemed to have no sense that a serious arts festival like Lincoln Center's valued artistic integrity and vision, and would not simply slap in a replacement performance by another troupe if the original was blocked.
"You know, 'The Peony Pavilion' itself is about pursuing a dream, and how you need it to survive," said Mr. Chen, now an American citizen. 
Musing about his own dream of staging the opera in its original 55-act form, he said, "In China today, it is so clear, that kind of spirit is not allowed to live."

file: CLINTON IN CHINA_ THE MEDIA_Live Debate On Television Is a Rarity For Chinese.txt
text:
ï»¿
What is perhaps most remarkable about today's exchange between President Clinton and President Jiang Zemin is that the debate, covering sensitive topics from human rights to Tibet, was broadcast live all over China, via China Central Television-1, the Government's main television station.
"I think this is a first," said a senior editor from the station, who spoke on condition of anonymity. 
"We've never done live coverage of a press conference between Chinese leaders and leaders from another country before."
In fact, live television coverage of important political events is a relatively new development here. 
Last fall, when President Jiang visited the United States, all events were taped, edited and shown later. 
Difficult discussions, like portions of the joint news conference between the Chinese and American Presidents in Washington, or possibly embarrassing scenes, like Mr. Jiang swimming in Hawaii, were edited out.
But today, any Chinese citizen could have watched the two Presidents debate the merits of arresting dissidents and the 1989 crackdown on student-led demonstrators in Tiananmen Square. 
Any citizen, that is, who happened to be tuned to CCTV-1 at midday on a blisteringly hot summer Saturday.
For although the news conference was broadcast live in its entirety, it was never listed on television schedules or otherwise advertised. 
And, hours after a lively debate in which both Presidents performed admirably, the conference effectively disappeared -- replaced by an edited version for the evening news.
Chinese television has just recently moved toward live coverage of important political events -- although clearly with great ambivalence. 
Aside from a brief period in the spring of 1989, when press controls were eased and some episodes in the democracy movement were broadcast live, only highly ceremonial events, like treaty signings, or scripted speeches by Chinese leaders were shown as they happened.
State television produced 10 live broadcasts from the National People's Congress session in March, including a somewhat controversial news conference in which a Western reporter asked the newly elected Prime Minister, Zhu Rongi, to comment on the Tiananmen crackdown.
But Mr. Zhu, after all, is a reliable party man. 
This time, who knew what President Clinton might say?
Nonetheless, said the CCTV editor, the station's leaders decided to go ahead with a broadcast. 
He said the decision was partly a reflection of the Government-controlled media's greater openness, and partly an acknowledgment that it has become harder to conceal news from Chinese citizens these days.
"We didn't hesitate to show it live even though we knew that lots of sensitive topics could come up," the editor said. 
"But if we didn't do it there are other ways for people to get news, from other stations or from the Internet."
So it was there for an hour. 
And then it was gone -- to the disappointment of the many Chinese excited about the Clinton visit who said they would have tuned in if only they had known.
The handling of the news conference followed what is becoming a familiar pattern: sensitive moments from live broadcasts of the National People's Congress, including some of Prime Minister Zhu's remarks and the retirement of the popular Foreign Minister, Qian Qichen, were also later relegated to the cutting-room floor.
Today, hours after the news conference, extensive reports by the official New China News Agency omitted President Clinton's statement that the "tragic loss of life" in Tiananmen Square was "wrong."
Nor did they include an American reporter's question about the detention of four dissidents in Xian and 2,000 other dissidents reported to be in jail. 
They did, however, obliquely acknowledge that President Clinton has raised the issues of Tiananmen, Tibet and human rights and gave President Jiang's responses.
The 7 P.M. news showed brief, bland segments of each President's opening remarks, and a picture of the American reporter asking the question on dissidents -- with the sound deleted. 
A 9 P.M. "special report" carried a five-minute account of the state banquet this evening, followed by a segment on trains.
In the process, some interesting television was lost. 
At the end of the live midday broadcast, the CCTV anchor for what had been scheduled as a 15-minute news conference but turned into a major impromptu political debate, came up with a most fitting epilogue:
"It seems that to communicate with each other takes time," he said, adding, "Anyhow, face to face is better than back to back."

file: CLINTON IN CHINA_ THE OVERVIEW_Clinton Sends Dual Message To China in Interview on TV.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Clinton, in his last opportunity to address a mass audience in China, said Wednesday that he would continue to speak out on behalf of democracy and individual liberty, but that the United States did not seek to dictate the path of China's development.
In an interview with China's main Government-run television network to be broadcast today, Mr. Clinton said that China's current course of economic liberalization and greater personal freedom was "morally right," and that the status of the United States as the world's lone superpower did not give it the right to use economic and military might to impose its values on China or any other nation.
In the course of the interview, Mr. Clinton sent subtle and somewhat contradictory messages to different audiences in China. 
His words offered reassurance to President Jiang Zemin and other leaders in Beijing that the United States would not and could not impose its will on China. 
But he also signaled to ordinary Chinese -- and to domestic critics of his policy of engagement with China -- that he would continue to press Beijing to allow greater personal freedom and take steps toward a more open political system.
"I think there's a genuine movement toward openness and freedom in China, which obviously as an American, and as an American President, I hope will continue and increase and which I believe is right -- morally right -- but I also think it's good for China," Mr. Clinton said.
Mr. Clinton was asked whether the world needed a single leader to mediate disputes within and among nations. 
"The short answer to your question is yes, the world needs a leader, but not in the sense of one country telling everyone else what to do," Mr. Clinton said. 
"So it's a different sort of world leadership than in the past where it's just a question of who has the biggest army gets to send a list of instructions to another country and you think it will be done. 
That's not the way the world works now."
He gave as examples the United States' intervention in Bosnia and Haiti and its efforts to mobilize other nations to combat drug trafficking, weapons proliferation and ethnic conflict. 
He said the way to get results in the post-cold-war world was to forge alliances to exert influence, rather than trying to act unilaterally. 
"And so the United States' role I think is to try to create a structure where more likely than not the right things will be done when problems arise -- not to just do it all ourselves or tell other people what to do," Mr. Clinton said.
The White House sought this interview because an earlier one with CCTV, held before Mr. Clinton left Washington, was heavily edited by the Chinese authorities and received little notice in China. 
United States officials said they had received assurances that Wednesday's interview would be broadcast in its entirety. 
It was conducted by Shui Junyi, anchor of CCTV-1's public affairs program "Focus" and Chen Xiaowei, an anchor on CCTV-4, thenetwork's international channel and host of a Sunday news program.
The questioning was gentle compared to the grilling Mr. Clinton got Monday from students at Beijing University who challenged him on United States policy toward Taiwan and human rights in America. 
Asked when he became interested in China, he gave a vintage Clintonian response. 
He said he was 8 or 9 years old and reading an encyclopedia when he came across the entry about China.
"And I was fascinated by what I read," Mr. Clinton said. 
"I always wanted to come here from that time on."
He said the most gratifying thing about his trip was the decision by Mr. Jiang to allow their Saturday press conference and his speech at Beijing University to be carried live on Chinese television. 
He said he was surprised and pleased by the decision to allow the "open, sweeping communication" with the Chinese people that those two events afforded.
"That I think was very good," Mr. Clinton said. 
"I think it was also good for the Chinese leaders."
Mr. Clinton sat for the 20-minute interview at the modern Shanghai Stock Exchange, where he received a rousing welcome from traders on the floor. 
Mr. Clinton conducted a round-table discussion with young entrepreneurs, who told him of the difficulties in starting a new business, securing venture capital and dealing with the bureaucracy. 
Mr. Clinton told the business people they were an important force for change in China, and a source of the new jobs that will be needed as state-owned enterprises close.
In the afternoon, Mr. Clinton visited a housing development to witness a relatively new phenomenon in China -- private ownership of homes. 
The Jin Hui Gardens complex opened five years ago, offering Chinese families the opportunity to buy their own apartments for $42,200 to $96,500, according to figures provided by the developers.
Mr. Clinton told families assembled at the development that home ownership represents an investment in society and the bedrock of middle-class life.
"All China benefits from more home owners because that means more jobs, a stronger economy, stronger families," Mr. Clinton said as low clouds threatened rain. 
"And, of course, when people own their own homes, they are free to take new jobs without worrying about losing housing benefits. 
We also see around the world that home owners take more responsibility for the communities in which they live."
The President announced a new joint United States-China program to promote the construction of affordable, energy-efficient housing. 
He also said that American officials would work with Beijing to create a middle-income mortgage-lending market and to strengthen legal rights for property owners.
Today, the President flew to Guilin, a picturesque city on the Li River, where he delivered an address on the environment. 
He continues on to Hong Kong, where on Friday he will give a speech on the turmoil in the Asian economy to business leaders and conduct a news conference before returning to Washington on Friday night.

file: CLINTON IN CHINA_ THE REPUBLICANS_G.O.P. Delivers Unusual Praise On Clinton Trip.txt
text:
ï»¿
Even before President Clinton's return from China, many prominent Republicans concede that the trip has been a political success that could deprive their party of a potent election-year issue.
In a series of interviews Republicans said they still had serious questions about the wisdom of Mr. Clinton's policy approaches toward Beijing.
But as a political matter, there seems to be a consensus among Republicans that, at least for now, Mr. Clinton has overcome fears among Democrats that the trip would expose the President to damaging attacks on issues like human rights, the exporting of satellite technology to China and campaign finance irregularities.
"I think it was a huge success," said Jack F. Kemp, the Republican Vice Presidential nominee in 1996, who faults the President for seeming to side with China against Japan. 
"That presents a problem to those Republicans or conservatives who want to make it an issue. 
I can't imagine that there's any great political benefit to be derived, because the President handled himself very well."
James R. Lilley, the Ambassador to China in the Bush Administration, put it this way: "Clinton got control of the agenda. 
He ran it like a campaign. 
And he made it into a political success story."
Republicans say the President gave a polished performance throughout the trip and avoided gaffes. 
His defense of human rights, and criticism of the 1989 crackdown at Tiananmen Square, at a news conference with President Jiang Zemin, struck the right note, the Republicans said. 
Mr. Clinton also defended religious freedom in China and Tibet, as well as economic liberalization.
Mr. Lilley said he had advised Republican Congressional leaders to hold their fire and rethink how to handle China as a political issue. 
"I've counseled them to pull back on this one. 
Don't hit Clinton at his high point -- or it's going to sound like sour grapes."
But Mr. Lilley did say he thought that the President had "swept under the rug" the issue of Chinese military modernization."
Weeks ago, House Speaker Newt Gingrich called on Mr. Clinton to postpone the trip until the Justice Department had determined whether two American companies gave sensitive missile information to Beijing in 1996.
But speaking to reporters on Wednesday in San Antonio, where he was attending a Republican fund-raising event, he praised Mr. Clinton. "I think the President did a pretty good job talking on Chinese radio and TV," Mr. Gingrich said. 
"It's less expensive to be friends than to be enemies."
Rich Galen, a phrase maker to the Speaker, said: "They set the bar so low for success that the arrival ceremony looked like a limbo dance, and he did better than expectations. 
You have to say this has been a successful trip for the President."
One explanation for Mr. Gingrich's praise is that he has been trying to repair relations with corporate executives who have soured on giving money to Republicans, and who have championed intensified trade with China.
The positive notices from Mr. Clinton's trip have already affected Republican legislative strategy. 
The Senate had been expected to vote next week on a package of amendments sponsored by Senator Tim Hutchinson, Republican of Arkansas, that among other features would deny visas to Chinese officials involved in forced-abortion policies and prohibit new American-backed international loans to China.
But today Senate officials said that the vote had been put off by at least a week, partly out of concern that the amendments might not win a positive reception in the afterglow of the summit.
The upbeat reaction even led White House officials to take the unusual step of pointing out an editorial on Tuesday in The Wall Street Journal, whose editorial page is better known for harsh rebukes of the President. 
The White House communications director, Ann F. Lewis, said she was so stunned by the unexpected praise that "I looked again -- it did not say April 1."
The editorial said, "So we may break convention among the President's critics by saying we think Mr. Clinton has been doing well in China."
The Journal backed off today in an editorial, accusing Mr. Clinton of "kowtowing" to China over Taiwan.
Many Republicans, and Democrats, say they do not expect the relative silence on Mr. Clinton and China to last. 
Several Republicans said that would depend in part on what polls show about the public reaction to the trip.
And some Republicans may be more willing to speak out against Mr. Clinton after his arrival in Washington -- he is due back early Saturday morning -- out of a tradition that it is inappropriate to denounce a President while he is overseas.
Although most polling organizations are waiting until the end of the trip to question Americans about whether it was a success, surveys beforehand showed wide public support for the trip. 
A New York Times/ CBS News Poll early last month found that about half of Republicans and two-thirds of Democrats said that Mr. Clinton should go to China.
Representative Benjamin A. Gilman, the Republican of Middletown, N.Y., who heads the International Relations Committee, said it was too early to know how the trip would play politically.
"The opportunity to talk to the Chinese people without any restrictions and focusing on the rights of individuals was a plus," Mr. Gilman said. 
"The key question is how much else was accomplished?
The Chinese achieved a number of important goals at our expense."
The chairman of the Republican National Committee, Jim Nicholson, said he believed that Republicans could eventually score political points over China.
"It will take time for the splash of the trip and the media coverage to wear off and for the real substance of what went on to surface," Mr. Nicholson said. 
"As that happens and people begin to see the way he gave away the store, they're not going to like it."
Mr. Nicholson said he was deeply concerned by the President's comments about Taiwanese reunification with China, the fund-raising scandals, Mr. Clinton's failure to meet dissidents and the laxity of China's agreement not to point nuclear missiles at the United States. 
"It was all carrot and no stick," he said.
Still, as with many other Republicans, Mr. Nicholson's language was tamer than before the trip, when he said the President would "walk on the blood of those brave pro-democracy protesters."
Gov. Roy Romer of Colorado, general chairman of the Democratic National Committee, countered that Mr. Clinton's performance had exceeded his expectations. 
Mr. Romer had been particularly concerned, he said, about how the President would be perceived at the arrival ceremonies at Tiananmen Square, site of the Government's bloody crackdown in 1989.
"I didn't know how he would perform personally," Mr. Romer said. 
"There was tension with the Tiananmen Square thing. 
I was apprehensive."
But he said of Republicans: "I think they've lost it as an issue. 
People understand that one-quarter of the world's population is sitting in the middle of that Asian economy. 
We've got to know them better, and they've got to be partners of ours."
A Republican media consultant, Michael Murphy, predicted that the trip would provide nothing more than a short-term boost for Mr. Clinton, saying: "It's not unlike the proverbial Chinese dinner -- short-term in its splendor. 
It was a successful photo op, which is what they wanted."

Just because you're President of the United States doesn't mean you can't get stuck in an elevator. 
It happened to Bill Clinton today -- for 10 long minutes.
Finally the doors were pried open and Mr. Clinton was freed, along with his wife, Hillary Rodham Clinton; his chief of staff, Erskine Bowles, and Secret Service agents.
Apparently a lightning bolt during a thunderstorm triggered a power surge that knocked out a computer at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Center, which stopped Mr. Clinton's elevator as he was leaving after speaking to business leaders.
A reserve power supply allowed the elevator to move to a floor but the doors would not open, a White House spokesman, Barry Toiv, said.

They were cracking jokes about it, the President and everybody."

file: CLINTON LAUNCHES EFFORT TO RENEW CHINA TRADE TIES.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Clinton began a campaign today to win Congressional renewal of normal trading status for China, in an annual exercise that threatens to be more contentious than ever this year.
In an announcement before a group of business executives, Mr. Clinton said that trade ties are "the best way to bring China into the family of nations and to secure our interests and our ideals."
Mr. Clinton is facing growing anti-China sentiment on both the right and the left in Congress, with an unlikely combination of opponents lining up against renewing China's trade privileges. 
The coalition ranges from labor, which is concerned about economics and human rights issues, to the Christian right, which is opposing China on human rights grounds as well.
Once Mr. Clinton formally sends his decision to grant China what is known as "most-favored-nation status," the House and Senate have 90 days in which they can try to overturn his recommendation.
Originally the White House had hoped that this year relations with China could be put on a firmer footing. 
Mr. Clinton is expected to hold a summit meeting with President Jiang Zemin of China later this year, and the Administration is negotiating with China over entry into the World Trade Organization.
Admitting that it would not have the votes, the White House quietly shelved any hope that it might be able to win permanent, instead of annual, approval of normal trade ties for China this year.
The only debate inside the Administration, officials said, was over how much the President should personally put himself on the line to support China in the face of the campaign finance controversy.
The President won an important ally of sorts today in Representative Newt Gingrich, the Speaker of the House. 
Although Mr. Gingrich assailed Mr. Clinton as being "virtually absent without leadership on issues of religious tolerance, human rights, and democratic freedoms," he said he would support normal trade relations with China.
Other irritants in this year's debate are China's transfer of missiles to Iran and its huge trade surplus with the United States. 
Congress is also swayed this year by increasing concerns over Hong Kong. 
The assumption in Washington is that the handover of the British colony to China will go smoothly. 
If it doesn't, as one senior Administration official conceded this afternoon, "this whole effort sinks in the Pacific."
The White House today sought to address concerns about Hong Kong's transition by noting that Hong Kong's governor, Chris Patton, and Hong Kong's most prominent advocates of democracy , like Martin Lee, the leader of Hong Kong's Democratic Party, support extension of China's trade status.
"Even those people in Hong Kong that have been most passionately identified with the cause of freedom and human rights and have been most in conflict with the Chinese have argued that we have to maintain an open trading relationship with them so we can continue to work with them," Mr. Clinton said.
Other Administration officials argued that Hong Kong is the gateway of trade between the United States and China and that to cut off China's trade status at this moment would deal a blow to Hong Kong precisely at this crucial moment of transition.
While last year's announcement about China's trade status was made in a major speech on Asia policy, this year the President made the announcement at the business leaders' event, which was held in the Old Executive Office Building.
Mr. Clinton said that stopping normal trade relations would "cut off our contact with the Chinese people and undermine our influence with the Chinese Government."
Mr. Clinton originally came into office accusing President Bush of "coddling dictators," but in the spring of 1994, under pressure from American business groups, Mr. Clinton backed down from his early attempt to link China's most-favored-nation status to significant progress in human rights. 
Since then Mr. Clinton has called for renewal of China's trade status annually.
Mr. Clinton has argued that economic engagement is the best way to get China to improve its treatment of dissidents. 
But his national security adviser, Samuel R. Berger, had to concede at a White House briefing today that "we cannot say that human rights conditions in China are better today than they were a year ago."
But Mr. Berger argued that commercial cooperation and openness to the world would eventually change the Beijing Government's behavior.
Yet the Administration's admissions that little has changed in human rights encouraged those who argue that Mr. Clinton's attempt to use commerce in the service of human rights has failed.
"They have to change the subject from human rights because they have nothing to point to," said Gary L. Bauer, the president of the Family Research Council, which is pressing its traditional Republican allies to abandon the party's longstanding support for renewing China's ordinary trading rights.
"It's a corrosive debate," Mr. Berger said in an interview in his office this afternoon. 
"Everyone in Congress knows that cutting off trade relations is far too blunt an instrument. 
Instead of debating how to influence China, how to shape the direction, we wind up debating a piece of the relationship. 
It doesn't work."
Mr. Clinton said today that "the United States has a huge stake in the continued emergence of China in a way that is open economically and stable politically. 
Of course we hope that it will come to respect human rights more and the rule of law more."
But Human Rights Watch/Asia immediately issued a statement asking how the Administration planned to exert influence on China on human rights, noting that the Administration's efforts to condemn China's human-rights practices in Geneva last month had failed. 
"What other measures is the Administration willing to use?" asked Mike Jendrzejcyk, the group's Washington director. 
"Or has it abandoned human rights altogether?"
Despite the growing anti-China sentiment in Congress, Administration officials and opponents of most-favored-nation trade status say that Mr. Clinton would ultimately have the votes to prevail on the issue.
The United States has economic incentives to continue the trade relationship. 
United States officials say that 170,000 American jobs are dependent on exports to China and that ending normal trade status would cost consumers $600 million annually in higher prices on certain consumer goods.
In fact, at this point the United States and China are so economically intertwined that even many members of the growing anti-China lobby in Congress concede that denying trade privileges to China would be tantamount to breaking off political relations with the world's most populous nation.
As the debate plays out over the next months, the only question, officials say, is whether the President will be forced into a bruising veto fight to preserve most-favored-nation status. 
That would occur if the House and Senate pass a joint resolution turning down normal trade status. 
Both chambers would then have to muster two-thirds votes to override the President's veto.
The last time there was such a confrontation over China was in 1992, a Presidential camapign year, when Congress tried to stop most-favored nation status but failed to override Mr. Bush's veto.
