file: CORRESPONDENT_S REPORT_Something New in China_ Environmental Cleanup.txt
text:
ï»¿
SUZHOU CREEK is where the bodies are buried.
In Shanghai's glory days of the 1920's and 30's, when British bankers strolled along the waterfront and French chefs concocted culinary delights for the city's elite restaurants, Chinese gangsters ruled the night. 
When someone got in their way, and a corpse had to be disposed of, Suzhou Creek was often the preferred dumping location.
Since the Communist takeover in 1949, the principal dumping into the Suzhou Creek has been industrial, and it became one of China's most polluted waterways, black as tar and home to a colorful collection of floating refuse.
A rescue, of sorts, has now come. 
Efforts to clean up Suzhou Creek, whose industrial smell became so intense that many residents along its banks had to close their windows in the heat of a summer afternoon, are finally starting to pay off.
"A year ago, it was black," said Yao Jianguo, who supervision of river boat deliveries brings him to Suzhou Creek each day. 
"Now it's gray. 
Maybe in a few years it will actually be clear."
For the first-time visitor to Shanghai, a trip to the city's waterfront is essential, either for a view of the European buildings that look out over bustling river traffic, or for a trip up the modernistic Oriental Television Tower across the way in East Shanghai.
For those who like to walk, turning the corner off the waterfront onto Suzhou Creek and following it into the gritty innards of Shanghai is an option that requires little map-toting navigation, and that now offers a cleaner river. 
Just stick by the creek, as it winds its way past rows of ramshackle houses with red tile roofs and dilapidated warehouses, where the daily commerce of squalid city life is on view at close range.
Dozens of low-lying canal boats that transport goods to Shanghai from inland areas are moored against the river bank on any given day, and the families who live aboard let their children play on the flat decks while parents hang laundry to dry on "People who live on these boats wash their hands in it now," said Mr. Yao of the river. 
"A year ago, they wouldn't even do that."
If the water looks better than it used to, it isn't exactly what anyone would call clean. 
One recent morning, watermelon rind, plastic sandals, and discarded white Kentucky Fried Chicken cups could be seen drifting downstream on the gray water.
"Suzhou Creek is still our worst waterway," said Gu Youzhi, an engineer who works on the cleanup project. 
"It's a lot better, but there is still a long way to go."
The cleanup effort actually began in 1988, with the construction of a series of pipelines to discharge human and industrial waste into the city's huge sewage treatment system. 
It was done with the aid of a $145 million loan from the World Bank and completed just over a year ago.
In their eagerness to hail the success of the cleanup, city officials proclaimed their ambition to make the Suzhou Creek as lovely an attraction as the Seine in Paris.
Mr. Gu is a little more realistic, saying the river's cleanup is less than half complete and will require more infrastructure. 
Sixty percent of the waste is industrial, he said, while the rest comes from spill that feeds into the river from city streets each time a hard rain falls, and from the refuse chucked over the side of boats.
"You see these boats packed against the river bank?" asked Xu Yongcai, who operates one of the garbage collection boats that lift floating refuse into a small boat. 
"They'll stay for a few days, and when they pull out, all this garbage will be left behind."
Protecting the environment is still a new idea in China, Mr. Yao pointed out, and teaching ordinary people something as simple as throwing garbage into a refuse bin rather than directly into the river will doubtless take time.
"People are only starting to have this idea of cleaning up the environment around them," he said. 
"At least the government is doing something about it."

file: Crayons Produced in China Are Recalled as Lead Risk.txt
text:
ï»¿
Hundreds of thousands of boxes of crayons imported from China were recalled today after the Government said they contained traces of lead that could poison children who ate the crayons.
The recalled crayons, most of which were manufactured a few years ago, amount to only a small fraction of the millions of boxes sold each year.
Although very few tainted crayons are thought to be on store shelves, many may be in use and should be discarded or returned to stores for refunds, the Consumer Products Safety Commission said.
The agency said parents and schools should buy crayons and other art materials only if they carry the label "Conforms to ASTM D-4236," or a similar phrase, indicating that a toxicologist has determined that the product poses no chronic hazard.
Â 
Main Brand Is Found Safe
The recall highlights a continuing, broad effort to eliminate sources of possible lead exposure, a danger to children that is well established by toxicologists but not fully appreciated by many parents and health professionals.
Agency tests of Crayola crayons, the dominant brand with about half the United States market, found them safe.
Among the brands recalled was one sold by the nationwide chain Toys "R" Us, and labeled as Safe 48 Nontoxic I'm A Toys "R" Us Kid!
Crayons. The chain sold 100,000 boxes of the crayons in 1990 and 1991, and more than 2,000 boxes since then.
The recall order to importers and distributors came after a nationwide survey of crayons from China. 
The survey, undertaken after a Phoenix infant suffered lead poisoning from eating a crayon, found three brands that investigators determined to have had enough lead to pose a definite hazard to children and eight brands with smaller amounts.
Although many recalled crayons probably do not have enough lead to raise a child's level to what is defined as poisonous, a child who is also exposed to small amounts of lead from other sources could be harmed by the additional exposure from the crayons, the agency warned.
Lead poisoning in children is officially defined as 10 micrograms of lead per deciliter of blood.
Exposure to lead is considered the most serious pollution problem facing children. 
It can come from many sources, including paint dust or chips, and solder in cans and plumbing, and cumulative exposure can cause permanent brain damage or even death. 
Surveys indicate that millions of children have unsafe levels of lead.
Mental health specialists now recognize that even low levels of lead exposure can cause developmental delays and intellectual impairment, and recent research has found no safe level of lead exposure for children.
"While there are other causes of lead poisoning, such as lead paint, no children's product, especially crayons, should contain lead," said Ann Brown, the consumer agency's chairwoman.
Â 
Most Imported Before 1990
Most crayons recalled today were imported before a new law took effect in 1990. 
It requires children's art supplies to be free of toxic materials including lead, and all art supplies must indicate on the label whether they contain toxins.
Toys "R" Us removed all the remaining crayons from its stores last week, after it and other suppliers were notified of the problem so they could prepare for the recall. 
Toy "R" Us no longer buys these or any other crayons from China, a company spokeswoman said.
Toys "R" Us said an independent toxicologist sampled the crayons and found them to be safe after the consumer agency notified the company of the potential hazard. 
But the agency said the Toys "R" Us crayons it tested had enough lead to present a poisoning hazard.
Another brand, marked 64 Crayons CR 64-64 CT, was widely distributed in the New York City area by Baum Imports, the agency said. 
The company sold 80,400 boxes of 64 crayons.
In one case, the agency found that a brand carrying the proper label still had toxic levels of lead. 
That brand, marked 12 Crayons, Glory, was imported by the Glory Stationery Manufacturing Company in Los Angeles. 
The company told the agency that none of the crayons were in retail stores and that all would be retrieved from distributors and destroyed.

file: CRISIS IN THE BALKANS_ APOLOGY_Beijing Calls U.S. Explanation of Embassy Bombing _Unconvincing_.txt
text:
ï»¿
One day after Under Secretary of State Thomas R. Pickering presented Chinese officials with a detailed explanation of how NATO warplanes could have accidentally bombed the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade last month, the Chinese Government rejected it today as "unconvincing."
Mr. Pickering spent hours on Wednesday briefing Foreign Minister Tang Jiaxuan and other officials about the conclusions of an investigation into the bombing, which killed three Chinese and set off angry anti-American protests here.
Tonight, the report's findings were featured on state-run television and carried by the official New China News Agency -- along with a detailed Chinese Government analysis concluding that the American explanations were inadequate.
"This irrelevant explanation only shows that the United States lacks any sincerity," said People's Daily, the Communist Party newspaper.
Beijing's rejection of the American version of events marked another setback for Chinese-American relations, which were at a low point at the time of the bombing, but recently had seemed to be mending somewhat.
"There was an opportunity here to move forward on W.T.O. and other big issues, but instead something in the Chinese foreign-policy-making process made them want to rachet this up again," said David Zweig, a China expert at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.
But some Chinese were more optimistic, seeing the exchanges on this issue as a first step in a healing process. 
"From the Chinese perspective the explanation is not convincing," said Jia Qingguo, a professor of international politics at Beijing University. 
"But I think China wants further clarification so it can get over its doubts, so that it can move on in the relationship."
Most Chinese have been convinced from the start that the United States intentionally bombed the embassy, though few can say why the United States would want to do that. 
Many believe it was intended to test China's resolve or to punish China for its vocal opposition to the NATO air campaign in Yugoslavia.
The Clinton Administration has promised to provide a fuller briefing to Congress and news organizations when Mr. Pickering returns to Washington next week, James B. Foley, the deputy State Department spokesman, said today.
"I think you've seen Chinese spokesmen on television this morning indicating that they were not fully satisfied with the report."
Mr. Foley said. 
"I would like to point out, though, that from our perspective, we believe that the information Ambassador Pickering provided is sufficient to demonstrate that the bombing was a terrible mistake."
An Administration official, who spoke only on condition that he not be identified, suggested that the hostile Chinese response to the explanation may be partly for internal consumption. 
State media spent the last month decrying the bombing as an act of imperialist aggression, a position that may be politically difficult to reverse overnight.
The New China News Agency said that Mr. Pickering told the Chinese that the intended target was the Yugoslav Federal Directorate for Supply and Procurement, but that these errors resulted in striking the embassy instead:
*American intelligence used three maps, two produced in Yugoslavia and one by a United States Government agency in 1997, none of which specifically identified the Directorate or the correct location of the Chinese Embassy.
*An American intelligence officer -- "in breach of operational rules" -- preliminarily located the target by extrapolating from "the pattern and numbering system" of parallel streets. 
He mistakenly picked out the Chinese Embassy.
*Military and targeting databases had not been updated and contained an old address for the Chinese Embassy, so the error was not detected.
*Targeting reviews also failed to pick up the mistake, and the air crew, flying high and at night, could not see identifying markers.
Government commentaries rejected this explanation today. 
An analysis released by the New China News Agency pointed out that many current maps have the correct location of the Chinese Embassy, and that the Chinese Embassy is distant from and looks nothing like the Yugoslav Government building.
It treated with disbelief the notion that American databases were so out of date or that NATO would allow an intelligence officer to pick a bombing target using imprecise techniques.
Still, Government statements made clear that China's goal is renewed engagement, and urged Washington to "take practical action and handle this incident properly so as to create necessary conditions and an atmosphere for bilateral relations to return to a normal track."
But it was unclear what action would satisfy the Chinese -- or what further information Washington might provide.

file: CRISIS IN THE BALKANS_ BEIJING_China Students Are Caught Up By Nationalism.txt
text:
ï»¿
Exactly 10 years ago, with protesters in Tiananmen Square, a small grassy triangle in the center of Beijing University became a shrine to democracy, plastered with tracts about liberty and freedom. 
In recent years it had become a temple for the professions, filled with notices about computers and law examinations.
But in the last four days, the plaza has been transformed anew, into a museum of frenzied nationalism and anti-American sentiment. 
Hundreds of handwritten letters and posters decorate the fence, the trees and nearby billboards in a vitriolic reaction to the bombing of the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade, the Yugoslav capital.
"Support Yugoslavia and Resist America," one poster read. 
"Adolph Clinton," another read. 
A letter suggested that students should cover the American Embassy with garbage.
A poem read, in part: "Resist America Beginning with Cola, Attack McDonald's, Storm K.F.C."
University students here led the angry and sometimes violent protests at the American Embassy over the bombing. 
With the authorities' permission, the students have vented and displayed for the world the fury that many Chinese say they feel.
But even after four days of nearly continuous demonstrations, it is clear that there remains an extremely deep wellspring of angry emotion on college campuses that students say could percolate for months or years.
For many people, Chinese friendship toward the United States has always been tinged with a drop of suspicion, and the bombings have allowed dormant nationalism and anti-Western sentiments to surge to the surface.
The demonstrations have quickly become a formative experience for college students, who are in some cases making dramatic life decisions like forgoing overseas study based on their new views.
A generation raised on rock music and Coca-Cola is experiencing a complicated shift. 
"Many of my classmates have been going through their things and planning to burn all American products, at least those they can do without," said a 22-year-old marketing major at Beijing University, whose surname is Zhao.
Many students who cheered Michael Jordan last year and welcomed President Clinton on his recent visit are turning their backs or even lashing out at all things American.
At People's University on Sunday, several American students were surrounded by a group of Chinese students who were screaming, "Blood must be repaid with blood!"
Such incidents are rare, but Westerners who were walking on the Beijing University campus were subject to hard stares, as well as the occasional impromptu lecture on imperialism and anti-American taunts tossed out of dormitory windows.
The scene is a jarring about-face at universities where two months ago the highest achievement was to obtain a place at an American graduate school. 
In some departments at Beijing University, more than half the students have gone to the United States after graduation in the last few years.
Some students said they worried that rash actions now could haunt China for years. 
"There is a tone of irrational extremism, and people aren't thinking clearly about what they think and write," said Yu Jie, a popular liberal essayist who is a graduate student at the university. 
"I think this will have a very bad effect on the economic, social and cultural development of China."
Since Saturday, the universitieshere have sent busloads of students to the American Embassy area. 
On campuses, students talk of little else, and they have organized accompanying on-campus study sessions and protest rallies.
"I protested because I'm extremely outraged at this trampling on the dignity of the Chinese people," said Chen Wanyi, 20, who marched last weekend.
Although many students opposed the rock throwing that has battered the embassy, they said they understood why it had occurred.
"I know the protest looked extreme," said Lin Yijin, a trendily dressed 28-year-old journalism student at People's University, who protested on Saturday and Sunday. 
"But I think compared to what we were responding to, it was pretty restrained, just bottles and rocks and things like that."
Students said they believed that the United States had intentionally bombed the embassy in Belgrade, although few explained why Washington might have wanted to do that.
Unlike average Chinese, who can see only state-controlled media, the elite university students generally have Internet access. 
They read Mr. Clinton's expressions of regret and the NATO explanation, both of which the students dismissed as unbelievable or inadequate.
At the Beijing University triangle, students have posted a full English transcript of the NATO news conference in which officials first explained the bombing. 
It is covered with comments like "pure lies."
"Chinese are furious, and although we've now heard the apologies, we still feel that the response from NATO and the United States has been superficial," a 22-year-old international business major from northeastern China with the surname Wei. 
"If you'd seen the pictures of the three corpses, you'd understand why."
Although a number of students said they continued to feel friendly toward the American people, they were keeping their distance for now. 
Students said they were boycotting American products. 
Near the university, the usually bustling McDonald's and Pizza Hut restaurants stood mostly empty today.
"Give up the poison of American-style fast food and cultural opium -- Coca-Cola, Pepsi, McDonald's, K.F.C.," read a poster on the triangle.
A Dairy Queen store near the protests was closed this evening, and a Baskin-Robbins store was also closed, hiding its sign under red cloth and placing banners that said, "Down With Imperialism," on its doors.
The anti-American atmosphere is so intense that some students said they were contemplating whether to continue English classes, take jobs with American companies or pursue hard-won acceptances to Harvard University.
Many are clearly torn between the moment's anger and pragmatism. 
Some said the protest groups were probably smaller than usual today because students were busily cramming for a national English test tomorrow and standardized tests this weekend that are required for American graduate schools.
A group of students at the National Minorities University in Beijing said it wanted to go to Yugoslavia to join the army, and it has posted fliers on other campuses urging others to join.
But a number of students who strongly support the protests said the excesses frightened them. 
"Are we still in the revolutionary era?" an essay posted on a wall at People's University asked. 
"Must we answer barbarity with barbarity?"
Jiao Li, 20, a student at the Beijing Transport Technology College, said: "I think this is a passing thing when students are inflamed with patriotism and very emotional. 
So it's natural for now to respond by not drinking Coke, for example. 
But I don't think that refusing to work for an American firm will solve any problems."
Students said the anger would fade slowly and only if NATO and the United States offered acceptable apologies.
"What the Chinese want is an explanation and an apology that will restore our dignity," Lin Yijin said. 
"I wouldn't take the stuff about 'Blood for blood' and 'Attack NATO' too seriously. 
For us this is about saving face."

file: CRISIS IN THE BALKANS_ BELGRADE_Embassy Attack Followed By Defiance Toward NATO.txt
text:
ï»¿
Chinese demonstrators protesting the bombing of their embassy here on Friday night held up a banner in the main square of the capital today, where a crowd was gathered for the daily rock concert: "America the loser, Yugoslavia the winner," it read.
That summed up the defiant mood here in Belgrade. 
Although the bombing of the embassy has shocked Serbs and Chinese alike, dashed burgeoning hopes of peace, and fed the fear of living under the threat of air strikes, it has also convinced many residents that they are being deliberately targeted by NATO, and hardened their determination to resist.
In a series of conversations this weekend, virtually every Belgrader interviewed seemed convinced that the United States had intended to hit the Chinese Embassy. 
They gave various reasons: NATO's alleged intention to spark a greater crisis by dragging in China, an attempt by the United States to show its superiority as the world's only superpower, or as part of a cynical campaign to hit more and more civilian targets.
"Would you believe that with all their sophisticated weapons, they can miss?" said a pensioner, Vlade Smiljanic, who was examining bomb damage to Government buildings on a main Belgrade street across the Sava River from the New Belgrade district where the Chinese Embassy is located.
"Why did they not bomb the American, German, French and Canadian embassies along here?" shouted his companion, Djordje. 
"Just you see, they will hit the Russian Embassy next and spark a third world war."
Downtown, in a bookshop cafe where intellectuals gather, the views were the same. 
"It was a provocation by the United States," said Zoran Arsic, a computer systems manager who was drinking a morning coffee with a friend. 
"They did it on purpose to show the whole world that they are the only remaining superpower. 
To say to us: 'How can such a small power do anything, when the U.S. can do this to China,' "
Mr. Arsic said he was sure that the latest bombing, the heaviest Belgrade has experienced, signaled NATO's new determination to hit at the civilian population. 
"Now they are going to bomb by day to scare the people," he said.
The embassy bombing has rattled many people, who are showing the stress of nearly six weeks of on-off bombing. 
They say it was a sign that anything is a target. 
Saturday night was quiet in the capital, but NATO planes continued their bombing around the country. 
People in the city are bracing for more.
"This has completely changed our views," said Mr. Smiljanic. "Things are worse now. 
I am more calm but my wife has psychological problems with all the sirens going off again and again. 
I never go to the bunker, because I am so old it does not matter, but these young girls should go," he said gesturing to a 9-year-old girl on the street.
"They have water in their ears," he said of NATO. 
"They are disoriented. 
They don't know what to hit next."
Some Serbian reasoning defies logic. 
The people can be simultaneously nervous and supremely indifferent, even fatalistic. 
They are often scared, but few bother to go down to the bunkers at night and almost no one reacts when air raid sirens sound during the day.
Vladan Markovic, a 24-year-old mechanical engineering student, was in his apartment just behind the Chinese Embassy compound when the missiles hit on Friday. 
"I never felt it that way before," he said. 
"My knees began to shake. 
I went to the cellar first, but what should I do there?
It is only the old people there."
Many Serbian interpretations of NATO's aims and intentions in this war are wayward, or warped by propaganda and old Communist suspicions.
Bombing people into submission is always senseless, they say, but particularly senseless when it comes to Serbs because they will resist even harder. 
"It is the wrong politics of the West," Mr. Arsic said. 
"They do not know our thinking."
But his friend, Misa Popovic, who was drinking coffee with him, countered: "They are very clever. 
They know how Serbs will resist, because they know we will not be conquered."
His reasoning was that the Serbs would fight to the end, and so be destroyed by the West or reduced to slaves, which, he argued, is what the West has wanted all along.
"Now they have shown what their real goal is," Mr. Arsic added. 
"They do not want to allow Yugoslavia to live under its own authority, and they do not want to see Yugoslavia as a partner in business or politics."

file: CRISIS IN THE BALKANS_ CHINA_CHINA PROTESTERS RAGE AT AMERICA.txt
text:
ï»¿
Large, angry protests erupted around American Government offices in several cities after Chinese learned that NATO bombs had hit their embassy in Belgrade, killing at least three people sleeping inside. 
By this morning, the demonstration had left a consulate in flames and the embassy here in a state of siege with most of its windows broken by rocks.
In Chengdu, in western China, several thousand protesters threw rocks and bottle-rockets, setting a consulate building on fire. 
The police used tear gas to disperse the crowd, said an embassy spokesman here.
At dawn today in Beijing, the streets were briefly quiet. 
But by 9 A.M. tens of thousands of students were streaming toward the American Embassy where, despite a heavy police presence, they barraged embassy buildings with a continuous stream of rocks and firecrackers.
In Beijing on Saturday, thousands of well-organized university students cheered on by other Beijing residents held noisy protests on the streets surrounding the American Embassy as the police looked on. 
Small groups of students and residents threw rocks through embassy windows, pummeled cars belonging to embassy employees and burned American flags.
It was by far the largest anti-American demonstration in China since well before President Nixon's historic visit to China in 1972 and the largest political protest since the student rallies in Tiananmen Square 10 years ago.
"Now we hate America," said Ma Zhanglu, 20, a student with shoulder-length dyed hair, who had just hurled a rock at the embassy. 
"China has been especially friendly to the American people," he said. 
"But we have been rebuffed and now the Americans have broken international law."
The protests marked an extraordinary moment in a controlled country where such outbursts are normally forbidden and almost never occur, though Saturday's demonstrations clearly had some measure of Government approval. 
The protests also come just two weeks after Buddhist Law, a spiritual group seeking official recognition, held another huge rally in the city center.
In Shanghai, a large chanting crowd threw rocks and bottles at the American Consulate. 
Similar demonstrations were reported in Guangzhou.
In Beijing after nightfall on Saturday, large unruly throngs roamed the embassy district, defying police requests to go home. 
Several times crowds pushed against lines of police officers, who held them away from the American and British Embassies, shouting "Don't you protect Americans?"
At one point, a group of 50 demonstrators burst through police lines, only to be stopped by a row of police five deep about 50 yards from the American Embassy compound. 
The police, who did not carry weapons, made no arrests.
An embassy spokesman said the embassy had "strongly protested" inadequate police protection, after students were allowed to press up against the embassy's street-side gates and throw rocks through windows of an office building still holding 15 to 20 embassy staff members, including James Sasser, the American Ambassador.
Virtually all protesters said they thought the bombing was intentional.
The protests began early Saturday afternoon when angry people started gathering on the tree-lined streets in front of the embassy in Beijing. 
Around 4 P.M., they were joined by thousands of angry, chanting students, not die-hard Communist Party cadres but thoroughly Westernized youths, wearing baseball caps and Nike sweat pants.
The Beijing students marched in groups of several hundred behind their university banners carrying hand-painted signs, some in English, like "U.S.A. 
Nazi Killers" and chanting slogans like "The blood of Chinese must be repaid."
Each group paused in front of the iron gate at the embassy, just 15 feet from its front door, to chant, sing patriotic songs and deliver a variety of petitions. 
At first, an officer from the embassy's political section came out solemnly to accept the papers. 
But the protests quickly turned violent, as students from several universities pelted the embassy with rocks and water bottles. 
Each broken light and window was greeted with thunderous cheers.
Although most students returned to their campuses around nightfall, many remained in the embassy district, and by 9 P.M. raucous students and other demonstrators had regrouped near the embassy, jostling with unarmed police officers and smashing cars with American Embassy plates, identifiable by the red character for embassy, followed by the number 224.
Although the police presence was heavy, the officers, generally equipped at most with cell phones, at first did little to stop the rock throwing. 
The embassy warned Americans living in Beijing to increase personal security and to avoid any protests.
As the fever pitch increased, reinforcements were brought in and made some serious efforts, though often with little effect. 
Police officers stood by as hundreds of protesters burned an American flag.
The well-planned afternoon march was clearly condoned by the Government. 
Official student organizations arranged for buses, and students said that the Beijing Municipal government had approved the protest.
Foreign reporters, who are generally shooed away by public security officers from even minor car accidents, were given freedom to interview and photograph protesters on Saturday.
But the anger was deep and genuine both from the students and the thousands of Beijing residents who apparently gathered spontaneously, many with children, after they had found out about the protest from friends or on the Internet.
"As a young Chinese I've always felt a very friendly attitude toward the U.S. and its people," said Wang Bin, an interpreter, who decided early Saturday afternoon to stand peacefully outside the embassy in protest. 
"But now I feel a deep internal disgust and anger."
Chinese public opinion has been violently opposed to the NATO war over Kosovo, in part because the Government-controlled press did not report on the Serbian purge of Kosovo Albanians. 
But most also agree with their Government that Kovoso's internal ethnic conflicts should not be solved by "a foreign bully" wielding bombs. 
They now regard President Slobodan Milosevic of Yugoslavia as a hero for standing up to NATO and the Serbs as an oppressed people.
"I'd always thought that Kosovo should be considered an internal affair and that NATO shouldn't be there," said Guo Qionghu, a student at the National Minorities University. 
"But today this issue has fallen directly on the heads of the Chinese people, and that's why our emotions are so aroused."
The evening television news carried China's furious official condemnations of the attack as "barbarian" and a "gross violation of China's sovereignty" and featured the students' demonstrations.
The three Chinese known to have died in the Belgrade attack were identified as Shao Yunhuan, a 40-year-old woman who was a reporter for the New China News Agency; Xu Xinghu, the resident correspondent in Belgrade for the newspaper Guangming Daily, and Mr. Xu's wife, Zhu Yin, an employee in the advertising section of the newspaper. 
The couple had only been married for a year.
Before being trapped in the embassy compound, Ambassador Sasser had been called in to the Chinese Foreign Ministry to receive its strong protest.
In a country where there is often a huge divide between official pronouncements and public opinion, China now appeared to react as one.
"They did it on purpose," said Yu He, a bank employee in Shanghai, adding. 
"Of course I'm angry now they're attacking us too."
Even before the protests, a Chinese Internet chat room about Kosovo that has been popular in recent weeks was deluged with vituperative messages, including "Tonight, let's lay siege to the U.S. 
Embassy."
Liberal Chinese who have supported engagement with the United States called reporters with a deep sense of disbelief and betrayal, looking for explanations. 
Students at the Beijing demonstration, some of whom had welcomed President Clinton to China a year ago, said they also felt betrayed.
Kicking off the protest, student delegations from China's most prominent universities -- Beijing University, Qinghua University and People's University -- marched in lines, waving red flags and banners, chanting slogans like "Down with Imperialism" and singing patriotic songs.
Some students carried hand-painted signs condemning NATO or the United States and wore targets like those worn in protest by civilians in Serbia.
The crowd turned violent when the group of 200 students from Beijing Polytechnic turned onto the road that bisects the two grassy office compounds of the American Embassy. 
Piles of rocks and cement squares lined the sidewalks, which are being re-laid as part of the campaign to dress up Beijing for the nation's 50th anniversary this fall.
The building material along the narrow street provided ample weaponry for the students in the dense crowd, who hurled the rocks through the windows of the embassy's visa office and an administrative building just behind the fence.
The embassy is a hodgepodge of older buildings in three different sites, all within 15 to 20 feet of the road. 
The street that divides the two main office sites, home to the day's protests, has been closed to nonembassy automotive traffic since the bombings in Africa last summer.
Police had clearly been girding since early in the day, when they closed a nearby popular outdoor market, Silk Alley, where tourists flock to buy Beanie Babies, Chinese qipao dresses and fake Prada bags.
But they were certainly unprepared for the outpouring of anger that gathered throughout the day and into the late evening, when thousands of angry protesters moved from the American Embassy to the nearby British Embassy and on to the American Ambassador's house.

file: CRISIS IN THE BALKANS_ DIPLOMACY_China Suspends Some Ties as Bombing Adds Strains to Already Tense R.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Chinese Government tonight suspended high-level military ties and a new human rights dialogue with the United States in response to the mistaken NATO bombing of its embassy in Belgrade last week.
Talks on arms control, international security and preventing arms proliferation were also being postponed, the official New China News Agency said.
The announcement by Beijing seemed intended to signal China's displeasure without disrupting the main elements of its battered relationship with Washington. 
But the bomb attack has already proven its potential to do far greater harm to ties with Beijing than to frustrate any peace settlement for Kosovo, Administration officials said today.
The accidental bombing by NATO, portrayed in China as deliberate, played to one of China's historical sensitivities: humiliation at the hands of foreigners.
With no letup today in street protests in Beijing against the United States, the Administration scrambled to try and persuade the Chinese that it regretted the loss of lives.
Worried that the embassy bombing may strengthen the hands of conservatives in Beijing's secretive leadership, Administration officials also emphasized the continuing desire for a "strategic partnership" with China, a relationship already badly frayed over allegations of espionage, and issues of human rights and trade.
President Clinton today sent a letter to China's President, Jiang Zemin, that expressed condolences and set out NATO's cause against Yugoslavia, a White House spokesman said. 
The letter concluded by saying the President would continue to work on improving relations, the spokesman said. 
To date, however, China has resolutely opposed NATO's bombing, and its controlled media have not reported on the plight of Kosovo's Albanians, but rather on the suffering of Serbs.
Around midnight on Saturday, Secretary of State, Madeleine K. Albright, accompanied by Undersecretary of State, Thomas Pickering, went to the Chinese Embassy to speak with Ambassador Li Zhaoxing to express sorrow at the accident, a State Department spokesman said. 
The Secretary, he said, explained to the Ambassador that the accident was an "intelligence failure."
How much effect the late-night visit had was not clear.
Appearing on the ABC television program "This Week" today, Ambassador Li declared that the bombing was a "horrifying atrocity, something rarely seen in the entire history of the worst diplomacy."
Mr. Li said his Government was demanding an investigation of the bombing by NATO and after the results of the inquiry would determine what "further actions" to take.
Speaking from the American Embassy in Beijing on the CBS News program "Face the Nation," America's Ambassador to China, James Sasser, said the Chinese Government was tolerating or even encouraging the street demonstrations in Beijing, which he called a risky policy.
"You get a sense of widespread indignation within officialdom itself here about this tragic bombing of the Chinese Embassy," he said, even as the demonstrations continued outside his compound. 
"This is, I think, really a national thought to some extent, and one of our more perceptive foreign service officers here today said, perhaps the Chinese want us to feel their pain."
It was probably inevitable, a senior Administration official said, that the bombing would be exploited by the conservative elements in the Beijing Government who have been against the more modernizing trends led by President Zemin and Prime Minister Zhu Rongji. 
"This is a major complicating factor in the United States-China relationship," the official said.
On the other hand, the official said, the Administration's policy of working toward a "strategic partnership" with China may have shown some dividends in the current crisis.
With personal contacts established between Mr. Clinton and Mr. Jiang during their visits to each other's countries in the last two years, it was slightly harder for the Chinese to return immediately to the mentality of the cold war.
But the pressures on the more Western-leaning officials, particularly as China faces the 10th anniversary next month of the killing of hundreds of civilians by the military at the Tiananmen demonstrations, would only mount in the wake of the Belgrade bombing.
"There has been a debate in China mirroring that in the United States in which the military and the hard-liners have accused Prime Minister Zhu of being too soft," said Winston Lord, a former American Ambassador to China. 
"There is the danger that in the coming weeks that those who want to be constructive will be on the defensive. 
This is going to give ammunition to the hard-liners."
While China, as a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, is needed for any United Nations-brokered resolution of the Kosovo war, the most immediate long-term issue at stake for Washington is China's entry into the World Trade Organization, the Geneva-based body that governs world commerce. 
China's admission has been going through a rocky phase after the visit of Prime Minister Zhu to Washington last month.
Mr. Zhu, who came to the United States with far more concessions on market openings than the Administration expected, was aggrieved when President Clinton failed to sign an agreement that would have paved the way for China's entry.
But just before Mr. Zhu left the United States, Mr. Clinton backtracked somewhat, telephoning the Prime Minister with a pledge that the United States would back China's membership in the trade organization as long China stood by the major concessions on foreign investment in telecommunications, banking and insurance.
By last week, however, those concessions had been withdrawn, apparently the victim of Chinese Government officials who believed that Mr. Zhu had given away too much to the West. 
With anti-Americanism now raging in the media and on the streets of Beijing, these conservative officials could well prevail, a Clinton Administration official said.
Even without the bombing of the embassy, the next three weeks are critical in the World Trade Organization process. 
President Clinton faces a June 3 deadline for telling Congress whether he intends to renew China's trading status. 
If China becomes a member of the trade body, Congress would have to normalize China's trading status, a move likely to set off a major political brawl for the White House.
On the question of human rights, the Administration infuriated Beijing by filing a resolution condemning China's practices at the annual meeting of the United Nations this spring in Geneva. 
The recent State Department annual report on human rights around the world was particularly critical of China.
The relationship has also soured over allegations from United States intelligence agencies that China posed an "acute intelligence threat" to nuclear weapons laboratories.Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: CRISIS IN THE BALKANS_ DIPLOMACY_U.S. Struggles to Contain Damage To Diplomacy and Air Campaign.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Clinton Administration struggled today to prevent the accidental bombing of the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade from either hobbling NATO's air campaign or stifling the nascent diplomatic search for a way to end the war over Kosovo.
The White House said the American Ambassador in Beijing, James Sasser, had apologized to the Chinese Government and would continue to provide Chinese officials with information on how the accident happened.
In an attempt to show sympathy with China, Administration officials said NATO would guarantee safe passage for a Chinese plane being sent to Belgrade to evacuate embassy staff members who survived the bombing. 
But there was no suggestion of any letup in the air strikes, a step urged by both China and Russia.
The attack against the Chinese Embassy came just as the diplomatic process to end the Kosovo war had begun to gather steam, raising concerns that the efforts could stall, particularly at the United Nations Security Council, where China and Russia are both permanent members and denounced the attack overnight as a flagrant affront to international order.
President Clinton, speaking to reporters in Del City, Okla., where he inspected tornado damage, described the embassy bombing as a "tragic mistake."
But he insisted that the alliance's air strikes would continue until President Slobodan Milosevic of Yugoslavia accepted NATO's terms, including a NATO military presence to enforce a peace in Kosovo.
Asked about Russian denunciations of the bombing as barbaric, Mr. Clinton replied: "Well, it isn't barbaric. 
What is barbaric is what Mr. Milosevic has done. 
What is barbaric is the intentional ethnic cleansing that he has provoked for a decade now."
"I believe that Russia recognizes that, which is why they have shown so much leadership on the diplomatic front," he said. 
"And I would encourage them to stay on that course."
The Russian envoy, Viktor S. Chernomyrdin, was in Germany today for talks with Chancellor Gerhard Schroder and was expected to move on to Belgrade on Sunday.
The Western allies are banking on Russia's and China's support for a Security Council resolution to authorize an international security force in Kosovo.
Administration and NATO officials expressed confidence that the emotional outpourings in Beijing, in Moscow and at the United Nations would be short-lived. 
They even suggested that the accident might actually add urgency to the diplomatic efforts.
"We will just have to ride it out," a senior Administration official said. 
"Everyone recognizes this is an unfortunate development."
The official said the Administration had prepared itself for more civilian casualties and mistaken hits as the price of a more expanded air campaign, but had not counted on hitting the embassy of a key Security Council member. 
There was little doubt that the NATO military planners would take extreme caution in the coming days about their targeting, the official said.
Officials from the United States and other NATO countries argued that since a United Nations resolution on the security force was at least some weeks away, the accident need not affect the final vote. 
It was unlikely, they said, that if Russia backed a resolution, China would stand alone and veto it.
"We believe there is broad agreement to the contours of a settlement and that the Chinese would not block it," a spokesman for the National security Council, David Leavy, said.
The national security adviser, Samuel R. Berger, met with the United Nations Secretary General, Kofi Annan, at the White House today. 
Mr. Leavy said Mr. Berger had expressed regret but had vowed that the air campaign would go on. 
Before the meeting, Mr. Annan, speaking to reporters briefly in Washington, said he was "rather shocked" about the damage to the embassy.
"This is a reason for continuing peace talks," he said. 
"I hope it will not unduly complicate our search for peace."
But he added, "Obviously it is not going to make matters easy."
The Pentagon said today that the accidental bombing of the embassy would not affect the basic direction of its air campaign. 
There will be no pauses in the bombing, said the Pentagon spokesman, Kenneth H. Bacon, nor will NATO give advance warning of its targets to neutral parties.
"NATO is determined to continue this campaign and to intensify the campaign," Mr. Bacon said. 
"I don't anticipate there will be a pause. 
In fact, I see that there will be broadening attacks as NATO continues to work toward its goals."
The round-the-clock air campaign has grown to include around 600 missions daily.
In a step toward a diplomatic solution, the Russians agreed with the Western allies on Thursday that a security force was necessary in Kosovo to guarantee the return of the ethnic Albanian refugees.
There are still considerable gaps between Russia and the allies on the composition of the force.
It was possible, a NATO official said, that the attack on the embassy could weaken the hand of the allies a little as they bargain with the Russians on who should take part in the peacekeeping operation.
But overall, this official said, the attack should "encourage the Russians to be more forthright in sorting out the problems and encourage the Russians to lean on Milosevic."
The NATO Secretary General, Javier Solana, called the bombing of the embassy "a tragic mistake."
Apparently determined to show that it would not deflect attention from the military campaign, NATO and Administration officials stressed today the successful hits in Belgrade on Friday night, including a bunker complex they said was used by Mr. Milosevic.
Mr. Solana said in a statement in Brussels that NATO would continue its military campaign and at the same time back the diplomatic track.
While publicly confident that the attack on the embassy would not have a lasting impact on their diplomatic efforts, the Administration appeared to be doing what it could to mollify the Chinese.
Secretary of State Madeleine K. Albright was trying to call the Chinese Foreign Minister, Tang Jiaxuan, to express her sympathy, a State Department spokesman said.
In a statement, the State Department said it deeply regretted the loss of life in the bombing, in which at least three people were killed. 
The United States still looks forward to working with China on matters of mutual concern, including the Kosovo crisis, the statement added.
Despite the outward confidence, the embassy attack comes as relations between Washington and Beijing have soured over a number of issues. 
The Chinese have been very critical of the NATO assaults against Yugoslavia, largely because they fear that a precedent is being set that could allow interference in Tibet. 
Trade disputes and allegations of Chinese espionage have complicated relations further.
The Chinese showed earlier this year how they can wield their diplomatic weight when they vetoed a Security Council resolution to extend the mandate for a United Nations peacekeeping operation in Macedonia. 
The veto was an expression of China's anger at Macedonia's diplomatic recognition of Taiwan.
Emotions ran high at a Security Council session called by China on Friday night. 
China called the strike a "war crime."
The Russian delegate to the United Nations, Sergey V. Lavrov, accused NATO of trying to "destroy world order."

file: CRISIS IN THE BALKANS_ EMBASSY BOMBING_Two Victims In U.S. Raid Reportedly Were Spies.txt
text:
ï»¿
The American bombs that struck the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade on May 7 destroyed the compound's intelligence-gathering nerve center, and two of the three Chinese killed were not journalists but intelligence officers, American officials and a Western diplomat said today.
The highly sensitive nature of the parts of the embassy that were bombed suggests why the Chinese, despite assurances from President Clinton and other senior United States officials that the complex was erroneously targeted, insist the bombing was no accident.
"That's exactly why they don't buy our explanation," said one exasperated Pentagon official familiar with the incident that also wounded about 20 people.
The officials interviewed said they learned of the location of the intelligence operation only after the bombing. 
American officials traveled to Beijing last week to explain that an outdated map and a bureaucratic chain of errors failed to catch the misidentification of the building.
The bombing, which came at a critical time in the 11-week air war, deeply embarrassed United States officials and dealt a serious setback to relations with Beijing.
Indeed, China and the United States were close to hammering out a deal on China's entry to the World Trade Organization, but China suspended negotiations after the bombing.
In the assessment immediately after three satellite-guided 2,000-pound bombs from an American B-2 ripped into the embassy, military officials said the intended target had been the headquarters of a Yugoslav arms agency that is actually about 200 yards south of the embassy.
At the Pentagon today, spokesman Kenneth H. Bacon sought to clarify reports that a midlevel analyst at the Central Intelligence Agency questioned whether military planners had picked the right building shortly before the embassy was struck, but that his concerns went unheeded.
The analyst, who was not identified, was not involved in selecting the target but knew about the arms agency headquarters. 
When he examined C.I.A. maps and spy satellite photographs of the proposed target, he sensed something was wrong.
"He did not say, 'You're about to hit an embassy,' " Mr. Bacon told reporters. 
"He said, 'I believe you're going after an appropriate target but maybe not the best target.'
"
On May 4, three days before the bombing, the analyst called a midlevel officer at a NATO command in Naples to express his doubts. 
At the same time, the analyst tried to arrange a meeting within the C.I.A. to clarify his concerns. 
But he was unable to schedule the meeting before he left on two days of training.
"He didn't have a great sense of urgency about this because he had no idea of when the building was to be targeted," Mr. Bacon told reporters.
When the analyst returned on May 7, he again called Naples but spoke to a different officer. 
The analyst learned that the B-2 was already en route to Belgrade from Whiteman Air Force Base in Missouri on one of 50 missions that these warplanes flew during the war.
"The military officer recalls asking the C.I.A. analyst if there was any reason to cancel the strike and being told there was no reason to call off the attack," Mr. Bacon said in a statement put out tonight, clarifying remarks he made earlier in the day.
The slightly conflicting accounts of the timing and specificity of the warning and Mr. Bacon's clarification underscore the murky nature of the whole incident.
The Central Intelligence Agency's Inspector General conducted its own review, and found that the analyst's concerns went unheeded. 
Now the Pentagon plans a review headed by a deputy Defense secretary, John Hamre, and by Gen. Joseph W. Ralston, the vice chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. 
The two officials are to present their findings in closed session before the House Intelligence Committee on July 1.
"There's some fog here, and I expect to be fully informed by next Thursday," said Representative Porter J. Goss, a Florida Republican who heads the intelligence panel.
Mr. Goss, whose committee received a classified briefing on June 10 from George J. Tenet, the Director of Central Intelligence, on the embassy bombing, said he would hold a public hearing in mid-July.
Today's explanation from the Pentagon did little to assuage Chinese officials, many of whom suspect that NATO deliberately bombed their embassy because of Beijing's sympathies toward Yugoslavia. 
China's Deputy Ambassador to the United Nations, Shen Guofang, commented, "So far the explanation from the U.S. side is not convincing."

file: CRISIS IN THE BALKANS_ UNITED NATIONS_Security Council Backs Peace Plan and a NATO-Led Force.txt
text:
ï»¿
After more than a day of frantic diplomatic maneuvering, the United Nations Security Council approved a resolution today sending a large NATO-led force into Kosovo to keep the peace and placing the United Nations in administrative charge of the province.
Fourteen of the Council's 15 members voted in favor of the resolution. 
China, which had pressed for changes in the text, only two of which were adopted, abstained.
Approval of the resolution bestows United Nations legitimacy on the peace plan and the NATO-led military operations in Kosovo. 
NATO's bombing campaign, by contrast, never secured the world body's explicit blessing, since resolutions authorizing it would have been blocked by Russia and China.
The vote also gave a vast, challenging role to the United Nations, which had been politically sidelined until now by American insistence that NATO and Russia take the lead in efforts to end the conflict.
"Today we are seeing at least the beginning of the end of a dark and desolate chapter in the history of the Balkans," said Secretary General Kofi Annan, who nevertheless warned against being "triumphalist," and spoke of "difficulties and dangers ahead."
United Nations officials, struggling with budget cutbacks and demands that they do more with fewer resources, said they were pleased but daunted by the task ahead. 
For the resolution approved today turns Kosovo at least temporarily into a virtual United Nations protectorate.
Shashi Tharoor, the director of communication, said the war "was a NATO war; the peace will be a United Nations peace."
NATO members of the Council, bowing to China's sensibilities, adopted a nonsubstantive change in the wording of the resolution's preamble. 
But the Chinese representative, Shen Guofang, regretted that the Council did not accept other changes, adding that the resolution "makes no mention of the disaster caused by NATO bombing."
China tried to fix a firm 12-month limit on the life of the force, to soften criticism of Yugoslavia, and to limit the circumstances under which the NATO-led troops could use military force in carrying out the resolution. 
It succeeded in none of these.
Most of the 20 representatives who gave often impassioned speeches in the Council today defended NATO's campaign and endorsed the peace plan. 
Peter Van Walsum, the representative of the Netherlands, said the vote reflected a profound shift in the balance between respect for human rights and for national sovereignty. 
"Today," he said, "no sovereign state has the right to terrorize its own citizens."
Sir Jeremy Greenstock, the British representative, asserted that President Slobodan Milosevic of Yugoslavia had been "defeated" in his attempt to destroy the Kosovar people.
Russia's representative, Sergei V. Lavrov, one of the resolution's 13 co-sponsors, said, nevertheless, that his country "sternly condemned the NATO aggression" against Yugoslavia. 
The bombing, he said, had transformed a humanitarian crisis into a "humanitarian catastrophe."
A far harsher note was sounded by Cuba, whose representative heatedly attacked the United States and its NATO allies for the bombing, accusing the allies of conducting a "genocide" in Serbia. 
This, in turn, elicited equally sharp critiques of Cuba's human rights record from the United States, the Netherlands and Croatia, among others.
Yugoslavia's representative, Vladislav Jovanovic, also expressed disappointment that the resolution had authorized participation in the United Nations mission by "countries which have taken an active part in the aggression."
The NATO-led force, which is to be number about 50,000 troops, will include civilian experts as well as soldiers. 
It will supervise the refugees' return and the withdrawal of Serbian forces and paramilitary policemen. 
It will consult with the Secretary General, but will not be directed by him.
Another unusual feature of the resolution, a senior United Nations official said, is its unlimited authorization of the NATO-led force. 
While the resolution authorizes the force for an "initial period of 12 months," it can continue to operate there "unless the Security Council decides otherwise."
The Council gave sweeping powers to both the NATO-forces and the United Nations. 
Specifically, it charges NATO with "deterring renewed hostilities," "demilitarizing the Kosovo Liberation Army," and establishing "a secure environment" for refugees to return home. 
Placing these powers under Chapter 7 of the United Nations Charter, means that the NATO-led soldiers can use force to insure that the Yugoslavs fulfill their commitments to the Council.
The resolution authorizes the Secretary General to establish an "interim administration" for Kosovo, guaranteeing "substantial autonomy" and providing for free elections.

This weekend is the last chance to see "Splendors of Imperial China: Treasures From the National Palace Museum, Taipei" at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, before it moves on to Chicago, San Francisco and Washington.
First-time visitors will find work so reticent that it may come as a shock to the city-jangled nervous system. 
Those returning for a second look are in for surprises of a different kind: since mid-April more than 50 light-sensitive paintings in the original installation have been replaced by comparably astonishing works.
