file: Critic_s Choice_Film_Mixing Humanity and History to Illustrate the Flux of Family Life in China.txt
text:
ï»¿
With exquisite simplicity, the astonishing Chinese film maker Zhang Yimou tells stories that pierce the heart. 
"To Live," his latest (after "Raise the Red Lantern," "Ju Dou" and "The Story of Qiu Ju"), is one more stirring example of this director's ability to mix humanity with history, letting a politically charged drama unfold on the most intimate, affecting scale. 
Mr. Zhang's daringly iconoclastic work remains banned in China, but it deserves to be admired in every corner of the globe.
"To Live," an eloquent and devastating chronicle of family life in modern China, spans three decades in the marriage of a couple (played wonderfully by Ge You and Gong Li) buffeted by political upheaval. 
Those changes manifest themselves in indirect ways, but family tragedies and reversals of fortune are inextricably linked to larger changes in Chinese life. 
That theme is familiar among today's Chinese film makers, but Mr. Zhang makes it particularly personal and moving. 
He also sets forth this sad story with a superb eye for revealing detail.
"To Live," one of this year's very best foreign films, will also be notable as a no-show in the Oscar race, giving one more black mark to the arcane nominating procedures of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. 
China, which now bans some of its most distinguished film makers from traveling abroad and even working, required Mr. Zhang to produce a written apology for "To Live" and isn't likely to submit his scathing film as a possible nominee.
The academy still relies on nominations made by a film's country of origin. 
Aside from allowing politics to influence the process, this system works against international co-productions, which are more and more present. 
So Krzysztof Kieslowski's haunting "Red," a nominally Swiss film with a Polish director and French producer, is considered unacceptable as a candidate from any of those countries.
"To Live" and "Red" will not be the only impressive films unreasonably overlooked by the Oscars. 
There's a casualty of the academy's television rule, which disqualifies films if they were seen on television before their American theatrical release. 
Best-actress nominees will be elusive this year, and Linda Fiorentino's scarifying performance as a ruthless con woman looks like a real contender. 
But "The Last Seduction" was first shown on HBO, so it hasn't got a chance.Â Â Â JANET MASLIN

file: Critic_s Notebook_The Vanishing Haute Cuisine.txt
text:
ï»¿
"IN my opinion, Chinese chefs are much more skilled than French chefs," Ching Yun Pu said. 
And then he added, "Although we do not brag the way French chefs do."
It was 1981, and Mr. Pu, a master chef trained in pre-revolutionary China, was working in a restaurant in San Francisco's Chinatown. 
I was working at a magazine there, trying to find the best Chinese restaurants in the state. 
I couldn't do it on my own, so I enlisted the help of Chinese friends (among them, Wayne Wang, then an unknown filmmaker). 
They read the ads in Chinese-language newspapers, talked to their parents and consulted employment agencies that placed cooks. 
And then we started eating; before we were done we had found 50 astonishingly good restaurants cooking regional Chinese food and catering almost exclusively to a Chinese clientele.
I had been to China the year before, but I gained a new respect for Chinese food in America. 
As I ate Sichuan minced squab soup, Chiu Chow crab roll and Hakka stuffed bean curd, I learned about the enormous impact politics and immigration laws have had on the Chinese restaurants of America. 
It was not an accident that regional Chinese cooking became a craze during the late 1960's; the Hart-Celler Act of 1965 allowed many more Chinese people into the country and brought new chefs to our shores.
America got Chiu Chow food as a result of turmoil in Southeast Asia. 
The first wave of Hong Kong cooking was due to the Cultural Revolution, which drove many people out of South China to Hong Kong and from there to the United States. 
The second wave came courtesy of the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986, which increased the Hong Kong immigration quota. 
Tasting the flavors these new immigrants brought with them was exciting, and I became convinced that America was about to experience an explosion of Chinese cooking. 
I was positive that before long the country would have as many notable Chinese restaurants as French ones.
Almost 20 years later, I have to admit that I was wrong. 
It is still possible to find a good Chinese meal in the United States. 
As more Chinese people have come into the country, the number and quality of small, regional restaurants have certainly increased. 
If you want the Chinese equivalent of French bistro cooking, you can easily find it.
But China, like France, also has a venerable tradition of haute cuisine. 
While expensive French restaurants in New York can hold their own against many places in Paris, if you want to move beyond steamed dumplings and stir-fries to experience the complexity of Chinese banquet cuisine, the possibilities grow dimmer each year. 
Why?
Chinese food experts in this country contemplate this culinary disappointment with deep sadness. 
The reasons, they say, range from the apathy and lack of sophistication of American diners to a shortage of great Chinese chefs.
Twenty years ago, San Francisco had the benefit of master chefs like Mr. Pu. New York's Chinese restaurants of that period also showed the influence of T. T. Wang, who opened the original Shun Lee restaurants; Uncle Lou, a renowned banquet chef, and the chefs from mainland China who opened Sichuan Pavilion. 
They had all been classically trained, a process that can take years.
"Our training was very hard," said Mr. Pu, who served a formal apprenticeship in Beijing in the 1940's with one of China's most powerful families. 
"We were sometimes beaten when we made mistakes. 
And we had to prepare each dish according to the classic method, no matter what the conditions. 
In the winter we had to peel shrimps, washing them with cold water because warm would have changed their taste. 
No matter that our hands were burning from cuts and stinging from the cold."
The revolution, of course, put an end to all that. 
"Who wanted to be a chef in China from 1949 to 1985?" said Michael Tong, the owner of Shun Lee Palace and Shun Lee West, both in Manhattan.
But today's China is a different place. 
Tourism is booming, along with national wealth. 
Hotels are being built. 
Restaurants are opening. 
The market, Mr. Tong says, is getting bigger, and there are not enough chefs. 
"Over the years we must have had 500 chefs coming and going at Shun Lee Palace," he said, "and only 5 percent were trained in China."
Mr. Tong also talks of the old system of apprenticeship, in which young people who worked for famous chefs lived behind the kitchen and did everything from making their beds to heating their wine. 
But prosperity has changed that, as well. 
"China has never thought of being a chef as a high profession, and there is no tradition of celebrity chefs," Mr. Tong said. 
"Young people aren't being trained as they used to."
The result is intense global competition for top Chinese chefs. 
And rising salaries.
A good chef in Hong Kong, says Philip Chiang, the owner of the Mandarin Restaurant in Beverly Hills, Calif., can make more than $100,000 a year. 
After taxes. 
If a restaurant in the United States wants a chef of that caliber, it has to match those dollars. 
Few chefs in the United States, no matter what their style of cuisine, are paid that much money. 
"Chinese chefs are better paid than French ones," Mr. Chiang said.
The Chinese, though, with their growing tourist economy and new freedom to enjoy luxuries in public, are increasingly willing to pay whatever it takes to hire great chefs.
MOST Chinese experts are too tactful to say so, but money is only one part of the equation.
"Why should Chinese cooks come here?" asked Bruce Cost, the restaurateur and author of several Chinese cookbooks. 
Mr. Cost, who is not Chinese, was the chef and an owner of Monsoon in San Francisco. 
He is now an owner of Big Bowl in Chicago. 
"Anybody who can cook can make a good living in Asia," he said. 
"And if you're a Chinese chef, you want to feed Chinese people."
Nina Simonds, a cookbook author and another non-Chinese expert in Asian cooking, agrees. 
"The best Chinese chefs," she said, "don't cater to Westerners."
It is true that many Chinese are convinced that Americans do not value Chinese food. 
Mr. Tong is among them. 
"Americans appreciate French culture more than Chinese culture," he said. 
"And Americans have much more knowledge of French food."
He noted, rather heatedly, that he sometimes goes to Restaurant Daniel in Manhattan and watches incredulously as people devour squabs. 
"They even eat them rare!" he added. 
"I used to put squab on the menu; maybe I would sell two or three. 
And if I put eel, duck webs or sliced kidneys on the menu, nobody orders that."
Mr. Cost said: "There is a difference in what people like to eat. 
The Chinese eat bones and innards. 
Americans don't."
Or as Ms. Simonds said, "In this country the audience is not there to appreciate really great Chinese food."
Mr. Tong blames himself. 
"In the 70's we invented all these dishes: orange beef and crispy sea bass. 
There's no such thing in classic Chinese cooking. 
When Americans eat Chinese food now, they want crispness. 
They want sweetness. 
They want spicy. 
If I try to give them red-cooked dishes, they don't understand or want it."
Which is a shame. 
Red-cooking is a classic Chinese technique that involves searing meat or fish in oil and then slowly stewing it in a mixture of soy, sherry, rock sugar and spices like star anise. 
The result is a glistening sauce with a complex flavor that is simultaneously salty, sweet and rich.
Not long ago, I was invited to an elaborate banquet at Shun Lee West, given by a friend eager to prove that Chinese food can be as impressive as anything produced by the French. 
It was testimony to the fact that when Shun Lee wants to pull out all the stops, the kitchen is equal to the task.
The meal began with cold hors d'oeuvres surrounding an edible landscape, in which pandas carved out of vegetables cavorted around a gelatin lake. 
Eight cold plates were set around it: crisp slices of pig's ear in hot oil crunched pleasantly when you ate them. 
Dried bean curd was cut into noodles and tossed with fava beans. 
Pork kidneys had been soaked in many changes of water until they were pure texture, little clouds under a hailstorm of Sichuan peppercorns. 
Fish was richly smoked. 
Jellied pate rivaled anything on the Champs-Elysees. 
"They just don't sell," Mr. Tong said. 
"We sell one cold hors d'oeuvre for every 30 hot ones like egg rolls, dumplings or spare ribs."
Twenty years ago, Mr. Pu was already lamenting what had become of his native food in American hands. 
Speaking of the Hunan food that was then the rage in San Francisco, he said: "What is often called Hunanese food is something made up to please the American palate. 
Once the pattern of spiciness and the overuse of garlic was established, nothing could change it."
THERE is another attitude that nothing seems to be able to change, either. 
Drew Nieporent, the restaurateur and an owner of Nobu, TriBeCa Grill and Montrachet in Manhattan, has been considering opening a Chinese restaurant. 
But he said: "One thing worries me -- price. 
There's a certain conditioning about Chinese restaurants that they shouldn't be expensive."
Mr. Tong said flatly, "American people won't come if you charge more than $75" per person.
Mr. Cost said: "Think about Hong Kong, where a single abalone dish can cost $1,100. 
And then ask why the restaurants here aren't as good."
It is true: the most expensive meal I have ever had was in a Hong Kong restaurant where dinner for two, without alcohol, was almost $1,000, in American dollars. 
The crabs alone, with delicious fat down to the end of their claws, cost $400. 
Would Americans be willing to pay those prices?
"No, they would not," said Mr. Cost, who still becomes angry when he thinks about the reviews of his now-defunct San Francisco restaurant, Monsoon. 
"One review called it Asian food at European prices. 
I was buying the same raw ingredients as Chez Panisse, but there was an attitude that Chinese food had to be cheap."
It is a prejudice that extends even to cookbooks, Ms. Simonds maintains. 
"Publishers tell me that people will pay more for an Italian or French cookbook than a Chinese one," she said.
Prejudice, however, goes both ways, and even if you were willing to spend a fortune on a Chinese meal, you might not succeed. 
There are many small restaurants serving good regional Chinese food, and they will feed you well. 
But when you get to the next level, eating well becomes more difficult. 
Consider the Chinese food palaces that opened when Hong Kong money was flooding into the United States in the early 90's.
"Hong Kong money is only invested in Chinatown and Flushing," Mr. Tong said. 
"They only want to cater to Chinese people. 
They have no interest in taking care of Caucasians."
The reasons are mainly pragmatic. 
"The Chinese spend more money," he said. 
"They eat more quickly. 
Caucasians come in, just a few of them, and they want to have a drink first. 
Then, when you want them to order, they say, 'Don't rush me.'
"
The Chinese also arrive in bigger numbers, he said. 
"Look around," he said. 
"The Chinese go in groups. 
It's a cuisine of sharing. 
In a Chinese restaurant there are no tables for two or four; there are only big tables and private rooms."
Chinese people, Mr. Tong said, even order differently when they go out to eat. 
"They always," he said, "order ahead."
Scott Haas, a Boston food writer, recently had a meal at one of that city's best Chinese restaurants, New Shanghai. 
Julia Child and Ms. Simonds were seated nearby, and he noted that their food looked much more appealing than what was on his own table. 
When he asked C. K. Sau, the chef and an owner of the restaurant, the reason for it, Mr. Sau replied: "When Julia and Nina come in, they don't order. 
They call me the day before and say 'C. 
K., go to the market, get something fresh, get something that's in season.'
They never order from the menu."
But is the culture gap unbridgeable?
Probably not. 
Americans could certainly become more knowledgeable consumers of Chinese cuisine. 
Chinese restaurateurs could learn to trust American customers.
But it may be too late. 
Ed Schoenfeld, one of the first non-Chinese to take Chinese food seriously, recalls that when he was a manager at Uncle Tai's Hunan Yuan in Manhattan in 1973, the chefs were extraordinary. 
"The three top chefs each had 25 years' experience," he said. 
"The No. 10 chef had 10 years' experience. 
The rest had learned in Hong Kong and Taiwan. 
The food was wonderful. 
There aren't so many Chinese chefs of that caliber in New York anymore."
There may not, in fact, be many chefs of that caliber anyplace anymore. 
Ms. Simonds has just returned from Asia. 
She said that although she ate spendidly in Taiwan and Hong Kong, it was getting harder to find good food there, as well.
"My mentor, T. C. Lai, becomes very upset when he starts talking about the general level of cooking there," she said. 
"He is one of the most knowledgeable people about Chinese food, and he thinks the standard has gone down."

file: Dam_s Inexorable Future Spells Doom for Yangtze Valley_s Rich Past.txt
text:
ï»¿
Two years after the start of construction on the world's largest dam in the scenic Three Gorges area of central China, the extensive rescue effort envisioned to save some of the country's best-known cultural antiquities has yet to begin. 
It has become mired in a rancorous dispute pitting hundreds of historians, archeologists and other scholars against Government engineers who are racing against time and a shortage of financing to complete the mammoth project.
In an unusual public challenge to Communist Party authorities, 56 leading cultural figures have petitioned President Jiang Zemin to intervene in the dispute, to insure that the cultural treasures of the Yangtze River region are preserved. 
If he fails to do so, Yu Weichao, director of the National Museum of Chinese History and an archeology professor at Beijing University, has threatened to dramatize the Government's lack of interest by making public an inventory of archeological and cultural sites and the plans for how they can be saved.
What is needed, Mr. Yu and other scholars say, is a rescue operation many times larger than the one conducted in Egypt to save the temples of Ramses II and Queen Nefertari behind the Aswan Dam three decades ago.
The scholars' appeal has drawn an angry response from the chief engineer of the Three Gorges project, Wei Tingcheng. 
In a interview, he accused the cultural preservationists of exceeding their mandate by devising "grandiose" schemes for museums and "palaces" to house the treasures of the Yangtze valley. 
More to the point, he asserted, the Chinese people are not that interested in cultural preservation.
"To tell you the truth," he said, "the common people of China have such a low education level that they will not be able to enjoy these cultural relics, and only some of these experts will go to these museums."
The sudden collision on the Three Gorges preservation issue reflects the deep divisions caused by the project, which will cost $17 billion to $30 billion. 
By the time it is completed in 2009, it is expected to boost China's electrical generating output by 10 percent and to provide critical flood protection for millions of people downstream. 
But it has also raised serious concerns about its environmental impact and the planned resettlement of at least 1.13 million people before the dam can make its serpentine lake, stretching 400 miles from Yichang to Chongqing.
The senior engineer's belittling of the preservation issue reflects not only the financial jitters of the construction organization but also the priorities of the engineering culture, which dominates the Communist Party leadership today.
"Li Peng is making this dam impossible to stop, though it could have many problems in the future," said Sun Changjiang, a leading party intellectual of the 1980's; he was referring to China's Prime Minister, a Soviet-trained engineer and the dam's chief proponent in the Government. 
"The scholars will be told to 'look at the larger picture' of China's energy and flood control needs," he said, adding that when it came to preservation, they would have to settle for less.
Towering Fortress The Gods Can't Save
Among the national treasures that may be lost beneath the waters of the man-made lake that will form behind the dam is the one here at Shibaozhai, which means "stone rock fortress."
Generations of Chinese have built their temples on the towering rock formation that rises from the mists here to stand watch over a sweeping turn of the Yangtze River on its way to the sea.
One legend holds that an ancient goddess was trying to plug a hole in the heavens ripped open by a shower of comets when this 100-foot-high shard of limestone slipped from her grasp and thundered to earth. 
In the 18th century, a magnificent 12-story pagoda was added to the rock face to ease the ascent of those who come to pray on the summit.
"Without Shibaozhai, there are only mountains and poverty here," said Zhou Kangwu, who lives in the village below the rock.
Not far downstream from Shibaozhai, a Chinese Hercules named Zhang Fei was killed by rivals. 
The residents of nearby Yunyang have spent 1,700 years crafting and adding to the memorial temple that honors him. 
Now they wonder whether it will be saved.
And up a winding tributary called the Daning River, the residents of the ancient village of Dachang still live in houses that are the best examples of Ming Dynasty (1368-1644) structural art remaining in rural China. 
These living museums are also in danger, the scholars say.
In their challenge to Communist Party leaders, 56 Chinese scholars wrote: "At the moment when the Three Gorges cultural relics are about to be destroyed on a large scale, we respectfully present to you this letter in the hope that the Three Gorges project departments realize the importance of the cultural relics in the area and carry out rescue work."
The letter, dated Aug. 
8, was also sent to Prime Minister Li and the other six members of the Politburo's Standing Committee.
Among its signers were Chai Zemin, former Ambassador to the United States; Wang Meng, former Minister of Culture; Jia Lanpo, a discoverer of Peking man, and professors from Beijing University and other leading academic institutions. 
Professor Yu, the director of the national history museum, helped organize the petition. 
For seven months he supervised the work of 300 scholars and technical experts who drafted the 30-volume rescue plan presented to the Three Gorges construction office in May. 
It calls for spending $230 million over 10 years.
Opportunities Lost As Pressure Mounts
The plan has remained in limbo; no money has been allocated for rescue operations that were to have started this year, even though the dam project itself races forward. 
Mr. Wei, the chief engineer, would not comment except to say there were "different ideas about the protection of cultural relics."
Professor Yu disagrees, asserting that there is broad consensus among archeologists and historians about how to preserve the region's cultural heritage.
"Now we have missed a year and a lot of things can't be done," Professor Yu said, adding, "unless we have the cooperation of all of our colleagues in the world."
But so far, Prime Minister Li has rejected any option calling for international assistance.
Of particular concern to archeologists are excavations that are not yet complete near the dam site at Sandouping.
"This area was the site of some of the earliest civilized developments in Chinese history," the petition letter reads. 
One of them, an early civilization known as the Ba people, is at risk. 
Skilled as warriors and artisans, the Ba helped topple the Shang Dynasty about 1100 B.C. and established their own kingdom. 
"Archeological excavation will allow us to reconstruct the Ba culture," the scholars wrote. 
"But if not rescued in a timely fashion, the Ba will disappear with the construction of the reservoir -- an irreversible error."
"Some ancient graves and cultural relics have already been destroyed by giant earth-moving equipment," the scholars continued in the letter, saying that in recent weeks, a stone carving known as "Conversing About Beautiful Mountains and Rivers" had been dynamited by project engineers.
Mr. Wei, the engineer, who is 70 and has been preparing to build the Three Gorges Dam since he was 25, said he did not see the need to build new museums and "palaces" for rescued artifacts.
"Right now," he said, "to spend so much money to build museums does not conform to the interests of the state."
He added that China's top leaders were aware of the issues raised by the scholars' letter but declined to say how they would respond.
There are credible reports that the Three Gorges engineers are feeling intense pressure from the office of Prime Minister Li, who is said to fear any obstacle to progress on the dam. 
Mr. Li's second and final term as Prime Minister ends in March 1998, and it is widely understood that he would like to oversee two milestones that would push the dam project past the point of no return.
One comes late next year when the Yangtze River will be blocked with a huge rock berm to allow construction on the main span of the dam and its powerhouse. 
The contract for building the berm was awarded last month. 
The second milestone will be the awarding of multibillion-dollar contracts, also in 1997, for the dam's giant turbines and generators. 
Four international consortia, one of which includes General Electric Co., are in competition.
Some scholars have long suspected that cultural sites would be sacrificed by engineers more interested in meeting their construction deadlines than in protecting the national heritage.
"Time is very precious, "Professor Yu said. 
"Even if we get a lot of money in the final stage, it will be of no use."
Preservation Plans Awaiting Support
Here at Shibaozhai recently, Zhou Kangwu, an attendant at the site, hiked up and down the monolithic rock formation to show a visitor its intricate temples and the commanding view from its promontory.
The preservationists' plan, developed at the Beijing Construction Engineering College, is to surround the rock fortress with an oval-shaped wall that would make it an island in the new lake, 1,200 feet around and accessible by a bridge. 
The wall would rise 80 feet above the surface of the lake. 
The bright red pagoda would thus be protected and would cut a striking new profile on the lake.
Downstream at Yunyang, Zhang Fei's temple is inextricably tied to the identity of the town, which will also be inundated.
"Many people have built their family tombs near the temple," said Tan Zhong, 34, who runs a restaurant at the busy port across from the temple.
A preservation plan developed at Qinghua University in Beijing calls for dismantling the oldest part of the temple by 2003 and moving it 15 miles upstream opposite the relocated town of Yunyang on the new lake.
In the Ming Dynasty village of Dachang, the houses in the old quarter are bunched together along narrow lanes. 
Delicate stone carvings adorn roof lines, and hand-carved lattices can still be found in some rooms. 
A plan to relocate a dozen Ming Dynasty houses is estimated to cost about $4.5 million.
But planning for preservation has been hampered by secrecy and mistrust. 
Professor Yu complains that the Three Gorges engineers will not disclose exactly when they will begin raising the level of the lake, which is to begin forming as early as late 1997.
Engineers like Mr. Wei insist that the water level will not rise in 1997 because a diversion channel will remain open. 
But municipal officials along the river say they have been told to expect higher water.
"We have had to find out through our own informal sources what the water level will be after they close the river," Professor Yu said, "and we believe that after the river is closed in 1997, more than 100 cultural sites will be flooded."

file: DANCE_When Battle and Ballet Become Synonymous.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE director Ang Lee's shimmering new film, "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon," which opens in New York on Friday, flows with the rhythms of dance. 
Although indebted to fantasy-filled Cantonese wuxia pian films popular in Hong Kong in the 1950's and early 60's, in which chivalrous warriors sailed through the air with swords and daggers flashing, Mr. Lee's movie takes that martial-arts genre to a whole new level. 
By informing the film's thrilling displays of physical prowess with psychological insight and choreographic sophistication, Mr. Lee touches the heart.
Although known for his versatility, Mr. Lee, who was born in Taiwan, had given no hint in his previous work of his lifelong interest in martial-arts novels and films. 
It seemed unlikely that the director of "The Wedding Banquet" (1993), "Eat Drink Man Woman" (1994), "Sense and Sensibility" (1995) and "The Ice Storm" (1997), or even "Ride With the Devil" (1999) -- all centered on human relationships -- would also like what is often considered B-movie material.
"I grew up with the genre," Mr. Lee, 46, said on a visit in September to the mid-Manhattan offices of Sony Pictures Classics, the film's distributor. 
"I felt I wouldn't be a real filmmaker until I made this type of film, although mine deals with real feelings, which is unusual."
Following a story line common to the wuxia pian genre, the film takes as its hero an honorable martial-arts warrior who sets out to reclaim his stolen weapon, a beautiful jade sword, and to disclose his lifelong love for a female warrior who matches him in skill and courage. 
His course is irrevocably interrupted when a young aristocratic woman tries to throw off her family's constraints by entering into an affair with a dashing bandit.
The Asian film idol Chow Yun Fat and the martial-arts film star Michelle Yeoh play the warriors, with Zhang Ziyi and Chang Chen taking the roles of the rebellious lovers. 
Against panoramic backgrounds of desert wilds, cloud-shrouded mountain ranges, silvery bamboo forests and a re-creation of early 19th-century Beijing, they contend for the sword, twisting, leaping, spinning and flying in encounters as meticulously choreographed as Balanchine ballets. 
As in many martial-arts films, the women fight as fiercely as the men.
There are good reasons for the film's choreographic magic. 
Working with the master action-choreographer Yuen Wo-Ping, whose techniques propelled Jackie Chan to fame as a comic stuntman in "Drunken Master" (1978) and who provided "The Matrix" (1999) with its free-wheeling battles, Mr. Lee created 30 minutes of fight sequences for his 119-minute spectacle, each sequence with its own rhythms, colors and tone -- and only one that turns bloody. 
Eighty of the 100 shooting days were devoted to these scenes. 
"We sometimes took a month on one battle," Mr. Lee said.
In this kind of film, the director and the martial-arts choreographer often work independently. 
But for the making of "Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon," Mr. Lee held all the reins. 
"It's not that Wo-Ping isn't brilliant," he said, "but too often in this genre, a film comes across as if it were two films in one -- one by the action choreographer, and the other by the director. 
I didn't want that to happen."
The idea was to maintain the plot's coherence without interrupting the flow with incongruous, if rousing, fights. 
Consequently, the movie maintains an unbroken, underlying rhythm -- a breakthrough for the genre. 
Just as a good choreographer uses movement and gesture to indicate developments to come, so Mr. Lee sets the stage for combat and just as consciously brings it to its natural conclusion. 
None of the fighting is mindless, for the combatants' beliefs, emotions and personalities are illuminated by their physicality. 
The more they fight, the better we know them.
The only cast members accomplished in the martial arts, besides Ms. Yeoh, were Cheng Pei-Pei, a famed martial-arts actress in the 1960's, and Gao Xian, a martial-arts instructor in New York as well as an actor and director. 
Everyone else had to take crash courses to learn the requisite skills. 
But even the professionals needed intensive coaching to be brought up to snuff. 
A good deal of the teaching fell to Mr. Gao. "Ang wanted them to look like totally professional martial artists," he said in an interview at a Manhattan restaurant last month. 
He appeared fit enough to take on the whole room if required.
"That meant not only learning the basic fighting stances, but how to wield a sword at the same time," he said. 
"Coordination and flexibility are key. 
Nothing should look abrupt. 
It might sound strange, but martial-arts encounters should be spare and beautiful. 
They take an enormous amount of control. 
Ang also wanted their body language to express their personalities -- not usually a consideration in this type of film. 
Playing an older woman, Michelle fights closer to the ground than the youthful Ziyi. 
She wants to bring her down to earth. 
Ziyi's character wants to fly."
Both Ms. Yeoh and Ms. Zhang studied ballet, which Mr. Gao says gives them a good foundation for martial arts, particularly balance, posture and timing. 
For his own understanding, Mr. Lee also took lessons. 
"He became very good," Mr. Gao said.
The first combat scene, as much a chase as a fight, occurs only a few minutes into the film and begins with a masked figure skimming over moonlit temple rooftops and silkily flying up walls. 
Like all the airborne scenes, this one was accomplished by suspending actors in harnesses from wires, a technique, borrowed from the circus, called wirework or wire fu. 
Until computers, directors would try to disguise the wires; now they can be removed digitally.
But the actors are still stuck with the discomfort of wearing harnesses, which greatly inhibit movement of the torso. 
In scenes where this could be a problem, the choreography emphasizes the fluidity of the arms and legs. 
For one stunning sequence, an aerial pas de deux, Mr. Lee took the technique to the extreme, hoisting Mr. Chow and Ms. Zhang by crane and suspending them 80 feet above the ground, at the top of a bamboo forest, with nothing below them but a shallow creek. 
"It was kind of dangerous," Mr. Lee admitted. 
"I won't do it again."
Stuntmen filled in for only the most perilous feats.
Mr. Lee sees Chinese martial arts as more about choreography than about battle, and martial-arts films as closer to musical theater than to shoot-'em-up Westerns. 
The roots of the genre bear him out. 
Although violent, these works often have a strikingly dancelike quality, even when Bruce Lee, the first international martial-arts superstar, forces his opponents to their knees in "Enter the Dragon" (1973) or when Mr. Chan leaps from buildings in "Police Story III: Supercop" (1992). 
To achieve this quality, directors draw on the traditions of Chinese opera, which combines song, dance, acrobatics, mime and swordplay. 
They also use concepts from ancient Chinese medicine that underlie the martial arts, chiefly a belief in the unity of opposites. 
Among other things, this means a martial artist should be mobile and stationary, defensive and offensive, all at the same time. 
That's why in battle scenes it is common to see swift kicks followed by abrupt rests or poses, and why as much emphasis is placed on blocking a blow as on delivering one.
In the decades since the 1920's, when Shanghai filmmakers first developed the genre, Chinese directors have mined the vast trove of popular stories -- similar to Arthurian legends and tales of the American West -- that exist in the annals of martial arts.
While Mr. Lee's film will open a new world to many Americans, other Chinese directors have used similar themes and choreographic methods. 
In 1983, the producer and director Tsui Hark, now a major figure in Hong Kong cinema, introduced groundbreaking, wire-enhanced fight choreography in his film "Zu, Warriors From the Magic Mountain."
He took it even further in "Swordsman II" (1991), in which the action-choreographer Ching Siu-Tung staged fights on top of stalks of grass and combatants swirled in the sky.
One of several Chinese action directors imported by Hollywood for their choreographic talents, the lean, cigar-smoking Mr. Tsui has made three films in the United States: "The Master" (1991), "Double Team" (1997) and "Knock Off" (1998). 
In a conversation in July, he played down the importance of his various cinematic breakthroughs. 
"It's our job to invent new elements that will generate new energy," he said, talking above the ringing phones at his production company, Film Workshop, in Kowloon, across Victoria Harbor from Hong Kong.
"Our choreography always depends on how we shoot," he said. 
"To create flow in a fistfight or during swordplay, we use long takes and a panning camera. 
The point is to be very clear and precise in order to capture the movements and gestures that best tell the story. 
The pauses between bursts of action are as important as the action. 
They increase the intensity -- just like a dancer pausing before a leap or fast turn. 
A good fight should be like a good dance work."

text:
ï»¿
Since 1987, the beige row house at 1249 41st Street in Borough Park, Brooklyn, has been home to four generations of the Zhao family, from the great-grandmother who grew up in the tiny village of Taishan in southern China, now 97, to Yan Zhen Zhao, 16, the studious aspiring doctor who was the family's youngest, brightest light.
Like countless other immigrant families, each generation of the Zhaos had struggled and saved, investing its meager funds and rich hopes in the next generation. 
All four of Yan Zhen's grandparents came to the United States in the 1960's, toiling in Chinese garment factories until they were allowed to bring their children and grandchildren to the United States after China's Cultural Revolution.
The girl's father, Xian Ming, worked as a cook in a Chinese restaurant near City Hall, and her mother, Mila, as a seamstress in a Chinatown garment factory. 
But their children, they believed, would reach higher. 
Miss Zhao's older brothers and cousins include a biochemist, a computer programmer and a college sophomore.
But the Zhao family's faith in the future fell apart on Friday, when bricks tumbling from a school construction project struck Miss Zhao, fracturing her skull and leaving her comatose and tethered to life support.
"You work all your life and give your children the best," Mr. Zhao said. 
"But suddenly, something like this happens. 
What can you think?"
Although officials at Kings County Hospital Center refused to comment in detail on her condition yesterday, family members said that they were told on Monday that there was little chance for her recovery. 
They said they had been asked to consider the option of taking Miss Zhao off life support.
But the Zhaos were not ready to lose her. 
Family members gathered at her bedside in shifts yesterday and took turns praying for a miracle. 
"We know the chances are slim," Mr. Zhao said, weeping uncontrollably. 
"But we can't give up hope."
The accident occurred as Miss Zhao, an 11th grader at John Dewey High School in Coney Island, was walking with a friend to Public School 131, at 4305 Fort Hamilton Parkway in Borough Park, to pick up the friend's younger sister. 
School officials said a contractor doing work at the school, Espo Construction of the Bronx, was apparently using bricks to hold down tarpaulins on the edge of the school's roof, despite earlier warnings to stop the practice. 
City officials suspended the company the night the accident happened and have since inspected other schools that are undergoing construction to look for possible safety hazards.
But those steps did not lessen the anger of Miss Zhao's family. 
"How could the city allow something like this to happen?"
Mr. Zhao asked yesterday in the living room of his home. 
"This is so irresponsible."
Of his three children, Miss Zhao, who everyone calls Zhen and who is his only daughter, has always been his favorite, the pearl in his palm, Mr. Zhao said. 
She studied hard, he said, but also kept her four grandparents and her great-grandmother company and helped them prepare meals.
A cousin who emigrated from China last year said Miss Zhao helped her learn English and offered words of encouragement. 
The cousin, who did not want her name to be used, also said Miss Zhao ironed her brothers' shirts before she went to school each morning.
"She loved everybody," the cousin said.
Despite their meager earnings, Mr. and Mrs. Zhao were determined to help their children succeed. 
Two years ago, they spent $2,000 of their savings on a computer. 
Mr. Zhao said his daughter spent much of her time studying in the local branch of the New York Public Library or on the computer, mostly seeking out information on the field of medicine -- she wanted to become a nurse or a heart surgeon, he said.
And she had plenty of encouragement from her extended family in the row house on 41st Street. 
Miss Zhao's two cousins, the son and daughter of an aunt who lives on the third floor, work as a biochemist and a computer programmer. 
An uncle, Thomas Zhao, who lives on the second floor, works in a bank. 
Her eldest brother, Fong, 22, is a sophomore at Borough of Manhattan Community College, while Ken, 20, is a senior in high school.
Mr. and Mrs. Zhao became citizens some years ago; Miss Zhao, who has lived here since she was 2 years old, had recently applied for citizenship herself, Mr. Zhao said.
David Sobiloff, a lawyer representing the Zhao family, said last night that he would file notice this morning that the family intended to sue the city, the Board of Education and the School Construction Authority. 
He said he also expected to seek damages from Espo Construction.
Last evening, friends gathered at a flower-laden makeshift memorial at P.S. 
131. "She was fun and outgoing and had a lot of friends," said Angelo Soto, a classmate. 
"Everybody's just been down. 
Everybody is angry at the construction people that are working here. 
It's too late to do anything for Zhen."
Miss Zhao's family members kept up their vigil at the hospital, at a time when most Chinese families are preparing to celebrate the Chinese New Year, which begins on Jan. 
28. Relatives said Miss Zhao was especially looking forward to this year's family feast because she planned to introduce her boyfriend, Danny Lee, 16, whom she had been seeing for the last year.
Before he left the hospital yesterday, Mr. Zhao repeated his prayer over and over again: "Zhen, come home, come home."

file: DECISION IN TAIWAN_ MAN IN THE NEWS_A Determined Fighter Who Paid a Price.txt
text:
ï»¿
People here who know Taiwan's president-elect, Chen Shui-bian, often describe him as remote and impersonal. 
In interviews, the 49-year-old politician comes across as almost robotic, reciting policy positions with a blank gaze and a frozen smile.
Yet for many Taiwanese, not least those who swept him to victory today and ended more than 50 years of rule by the Nationalist Party, Mr. Chen's public image was fixed by a supremely personal tragedy.
When Mr. Chen was greeting supporters at a rally in 1985 after losing a county election, his wife, Wu Shu-jen, was hit by a truck. 
His supporters say the accident, which left Ms. Wu paralyzed from the chest down, was politically motivated. 
Evidence for that is sketchy, but it cemented Mr. Chen's reputation as a man who paid a high price for his beliefs.
"There are two sides to the Taiwanese spirit: the fighter, and those who want to maintain the good life," said Paul S. P. Hsu, a lawyer here. 
"Chen Shui-bian is a fighter."
Mr. Chen's grim determination has fueled a political career of vertiginous highs and pitiful lows. 
And it has now made him Taiwan's first leader from outside the long-ruling Nationalist Party.
Mr. Chen's Democratic Progressive Party formally favors an independent Taiwan -- a position dangerously at odds with that of China. 
Mr. Chen has said he will not declare independence, though it is far from certain that this will mollify the leaders in Beijing, who view Taiwan as a renegade province.
Born on Feb. 
18, 1951, in a farming village in southwestern Taiwan, Mr. Chen is the son of illiterate parents who worked as day laborers. 
Life for the Chen family was bleak. 
They lived in a mud house with little furniture and the constant fear of destitution. 
At school, the young Mr. Chen often went without lunch.
But he was an extraordinarily diligent student, and education became his ticket out of deprivation. 
He graduated from primary school first in the country. 
In 1969, he enrolled in National Taiwan University, where he studied law and graduated with yet more accolades in 1975.
In those days, Taiwan was still firmly under the grip of the Nationalists -- followers of Chiang Kai-shek who fled China after the Communist takeover in 1949 and established a government in exile on the island. 
Chiang dreamed that Taiwan would reunify with the mainland, and he brooked no dissent. 
Yet there were already stirrings of an opposition movement, which advocated independence for Taiwan. 
That movement would later became the Democratic Progressive Party.
As an ambitious young lawyer in the 1970's, Mr. Chen initially had scant interest in politics. 
He joined a prestigious maritime law firm and married Ms. Wu, the daughter of a wealthy doctor, in 1976.
Mr. Chen entered politics by accident in 1980. 
He was asked to defend two pro-independence leaders who had been charged with sedition, after a protest in the port city of Kaohsiung. 
Among the other defendants was Annette Lu, a lawyer trained in the United States, who was Mr. Chen's running mate in this campaign and will become Taiwan's first female vice president.
To nobody's surprise, in an island firmly controlled by the ruling Nationalists, Mr. Chen lost the case. 
But his political senses were piqued.
"I realized this experience was not just a legal issue," he said in an official biography published in 1998. 
"I came to accept the defendants' political arguments and ideals. 
I became a believer. 
We should have two separate countries across the Taiwan -- one country on each side of the straits."
That belief was to become both the root of Mr. Chen's appeal and a cudgel in the hands of his political enemies. 
Supporters, particularly native Taiwanese, flocked to Mr. Chen. But the Nationalists, and more recently the Chinese government, portrayed the studious lawyer as a wild-eyed zealot who was intent on dragging Taiwan into a dangerous and futile split from its Chinese motherland.
Mr. Chen began his political career with a successful bid for the Taipei City Council, where he acquired a reputation as a crusader. 
But his fortunes soon reversed. 
He lost the race in his native Tainan County, and his wife was injured. 
Worse, in 1986, he was jailed for eight months after losing a libel case filed by a Nationalist official, whom he had accused of plagiarizing a doctoral thesis.
Mr. Chen's release from prison in 1987 coincided with the Nationalist government's decision to suspend martial law and legalize political parties. 
Mr. Chen joined the Democratic Progressive Party, where his keen intellect and indefatigable work habits made him a star.
In 1994, he was elected mayor of Taipei, and swept into the city like an avenging angel, shutting down its sex trade and evicting apartment dwellers to build public parks. 
After a stormy term, during which he managed to make enemies and alienate friends, he was turned out of office.
Political analysts said the defeat matured Mr. Chen, forcing him to shed his dogmatism. 
Never the zealot that his opponents claimed, he has now become a master of political nuance. 
He recognizes that very few Taiwanese are willing to risk their material well-being on a lunge for independence. 
"You can see that he has basically abandoned the idea of a Republic of Taiwan," Mr. Hsu said.
Indeed, the verbal traps that Mr. Chen must avoid in discussing Taiwan and China may be one reason he is so programmed. 
In an interview last week, he noted that he was the only candidate with a son who would be drafted if Taiwan were invaded by China, he said, "As a father, I understand the fear of parents who don't want to put their children into danger."

file: DECISION IN TAIWAN_ THE NATIONALISTS_Party Undone by Liberty It Nurtured.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Taiwanese election marks a huge defeat for the Nationalist Party, which in the 20th century controlled first China and then Taiwan, and which presided over the emergence of the very democratic forces that ultimately upended it.
Dr. Sun Yat-sen, the great Chinese nationalist and revolutionary, formed a predecessor organization of the Nationalist Party in 1894 while he was living in exile in Hawaii. 
The party's initial aim was to overthrow the corrupt Qing Dynasty, which was already disintegrating and finally collapsed in 1911-12.
The party dominated China for the next few tumultuous decades, although power was also divided among warlords and for a time the Japanese invaders. 
Party leaders, such as Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, were initially impressed by the organization of the Soviet Communist Party and modeled the Nationalist Party along Leninist principles, even calling each other "comrade."
While they had a good deal of support from Americans, the Nationalists became detested in China because of their corruption, brutality and failure to fight the Japanese invaders. 
In 1949, the Communists under Mao Zedong defeated the Nationalists and forced them to flee and move their seat of government to the offshore island of Taiwan, which had just been recovered from Japan in 1945.
Some two million Nationalist soldiers and officials settled on Taiwan, where they were bitterly resented by many local people. 
In particular, the Nationalists were hated for massacring local people during upheavals that began on Feb. 
28, 1947, and ever since then the phrase "2-28" has been a sensitive code word in Taiwan that conjures those antagonisms between local people and the mainlanders.
The Communists might well have seized Taiwan in the early 1950's, because Generalissimo Chiang's army was in chaos and America was unwilling to help it. 
But then fate intervened: In 1950, North Korea invaded South Korea, and Americans became increasingly fearful of Communism around the world. 
The upshot was that President Truman sent the Seventh Fleet to protect Taiwan. 
Ever since, the United States has either promised or hinted that it would protect Taiwan from a mainland Chinese attack.
In ruling Taiwan, the Nationalist Party had little ideology other than self-aggrandizement and self-enrichment. 
Particularly in the 1950's and 1960's, the security forces under Chiang and his son and successor, Chiang Ching-kuo, often dragged away critics of the regime. 
Initially, they were often killed immediately; later they tended to face torture and sham trials.
The Nationalists imposed their ideas and language on Taiwan, and children were forced to speak Mandarin Chinese and punished if they spoke the Taiwanese or Hakka dialects that they spoke at home. 
There was almost no teaching of local history, and instead children learned about distant mainland Chinese provinces that they could never visit.
Yet the Nationalist Party redistributed land, promoted education and encouraged the Taiwanese people to form businesses and get rich. 
The result was an economic and educational revolution in Taiwan that laid the seeds for a political one as well.
In the 1980's, the Nationalists responded to popular aspirations and began to permit opposition party activities -- although even then critics of the Nationalists were tortured and occasionally killed. 
The playing field was never level, for the Nationalists manipulated the news media and owned companies that gave them huge economic resources, but they gradually allowed opposition figures to win local elections and form local power bases.
The greatest changes came after the death of Chiang Ching-kuo in 1988. 
Control of the Nationalist Party passed uneasily to Lee Teng-hui, a Taiwanese who as vice president was Taiwan's new president. 
Mr. Lee transformed the Nationalist Party by democratizing it, distancing it from its mainland Chinese roots, and ultimately by creating a more pluralistic Taiwan in which an opposition victory became possible.

file: DECISION IN TAIWAN_ THE OVERVIEW_Taiwan Nationalists Ousted After Half-Century Reign.txt
text:
ï»¿
Chen Shui-bian, an opposition politician who long advocated Taiwan's independence, was elected its new president today, ending more than half a century of Nationalist rule and risking dangerous new tensions with mainland China.
Mr. Chen, a 49-year-old lawyer who served as mayor of Taipei and struggled against martial law in the 1980's, won with 39 percent of the vote in a bitter three-way race. 
The Nationalist candidate slumped to third place.
The opposition's victory, the first transition of power in Taiwan's young democracy, was made possible by a schism in the Nationalist Party that led one of its stars, James Soong, to mount an independent candidacy. 
Mr. Soong, a populist former governor of Taipei province, came in second with a strong 37 percent showing; Lien Chan, the Nationalist, got just 23 percent.
For years, Mr. Chen and his Democratic Progressive Party called for independence from the mainland, which considers Taiwan a wayward region that must return to the motherland. 
The president-elect, who will take office on May 20, succeeding Taiwan's first elected president, Lee Teng-hui, has recently moderated that position, saying no declaration of independence is needed because Taiwan is already sovereign.
But Beijing has called Mr. Chen deceitful and issued dire warnings against his election, with Prime Minister Zhu Rongji all but saying last week that it could provoke a war.
To reassure nervous citizens and governments abroad -- including Washington, which has pledged to help Taiwan defend itself if attacked -- Mr. Chen tried to reach out to the Chinese in his victory speech tonight.
He avoided inflammatory references to Taiwanese "statehood," and said he would seek deeper economic ties and "a permanent peace."
He has promised that he will not declare independence or hold a referendum on the issue unless Taiwan comes under attack.
However, in a statement certain to anger Beijing, he also pledged, "We won't let Taiwan become another Hong Kong or Macao."
Those former colonies have been handed back to China, which has granted them broad autonomy.
The initial reaction from Beijing tonight was terse and noncommittal. 
Page 18.
In Washington, President Clintonsaid he saw the election as a demonstration of the vitality of democracy and an opportunity for Taiwan and China to open a new dialogue. 
"The United States strongly supports such dialogue," he said.
Some 83 percent of Taiwan's voters turned out after a campaign dominated by worries over relations with China and public impatience with the corrupt political practices of the Nationalists.
Mr. Chen faces a legislature still dominated by the Nationalists, who have ruled firmly since Chiang Kai-shek retreated here from the Communist-dominated mainland in 1949. 
The country is in for a period of unprecedented political reshuffling and uncertainty, even as it faces a possible confrontation with China.
Speaking to thousands of cheering supporters, Mr. Chen declared that his success "is not a victory for the Democratic Progressive Party -- it is a victory for democracy."
In a subtle friendly gesture to China and to some of his fiercest enemies at home -- those who fled the mainland after the Communist victory in 1949 -- Mr. Chen gave his acceptance speech in Mandarin Chinese rather than in the Taiwanese dialect he often used in campaign rallies.
But Mr. Chen refuses to accept China's hallowed notion of "One China," and in answer to a question tonight he said China's "one country, two systems" formula for enlisting Taiwan as an autonomous region "would never be accepted by the Taiwanese people."
"We are determined to defend this island but we are also determined to seek peace and stabilityI," he said.
In an effort to reassure foreign governments that he will not take reckless actions, Mr. Chen has promised to retain the current defense minister, top national security officials and the military chief of staff.
Mr. Chen, like 85 percent of the island's population and many supporters of his political party, is considered an ethnic Taiwanese, descended from people who immigrated from the mainland centuries ago.
Mr. Chen became involved in opposition as a defense lawyer for dissidents who favored democracy and independence. 
After martial law was lifted in 1987, he entered politics, he joined the Democratic Progressives who became the main opposition party. 
For many of the party's supporters, the victory tonight is an emotional culmination of decades of struggle.
The Nationalists, for their part, have been thrown into turmoil and their powerful chairman, President Lee, is now on the spot. 
Mr. Lee's feud with Mr. Soong helped cause the devastating defeat and the party could suffer a permanent split if the popular Mr. Soong tries to form his own party now, as he signaled tonight he would.
Already tonight, Huang Quen-huei, the secretary general of the Nationalists, offered his resignation.
Late tonight, a large crowd of Mr. Soong's supporters, most of then longtime Nationalists who felt Mr. Lee had betrayed the party by snubbing Mr. Soong, marched to Mr. Lee's official residence and his party's headquarters in central Taipei to shout for Mr. Lee to step down as party boss. 
Both buildings were surrounded by riot policemen and there were some scuffles.
Mr. Chen has called for disclosure of the Nationalists' multibillion-dollar investments and confiscation of any properties that should belong to the state rather than the party.
But Mr. Chen also said tonight that he bore no animosity toward his campaign opponents and that he hoped to work with the Nationalists to build a "cross-party alliance," though he did not offer specifics.
His ability to forge a coalition will be crucial to his success.
"Chen Shui-bian's immediate challenge is that he has to act as a president, not just a leader of an opposition movement," said Chu Yun-han, a political scientist at National Taiwan University. 
"Nearly two-thirds of the electorate didn't vote for him, and many are deeply suspicious of his approach to the mainland."
The defeated Nationalist candidate, Mr. Lien, had used scare tactics in the final weeks of the campaign, suggesting that Mr. Chen could bring disaster to the island.
Tonight he was more gracious in conceding, calling the transition a milestone for Taiwan's democracy. 
"I hope the new president will handle state matters properly, leading our country into a new era," he said before a crestfallen line of party leaders. 
"We can still regroup. 
From today we need to engage in self-examination and reform."
Mr. Lee remained silent and secluded in his residence, where he summoned the military chief of staff and the defense minister. 
There have been reports here of Chinese troop movements on the mainland, although no one expects imminent military action.
Mr. Chen's victory reflected, in part, a demographic trend that bodes ill for the Nationalists and also for China's hope of peaceful reunification: many younger people have no allegiance to the Nationalist Party their parents long served, and think of China as a distant concept.
Since the first presidential election in 1996, more than one million young people became eligible to vote, Mr. Chu noted. 
And fully half of them said in recent surveys that they were voting for Mr. Chen, who is seen as representing youthful energy and cleaned-up politics.
China's military threats do not intimidate such people. 
A typical example is Yang Jie-lung, a 27-year-old graphic designer. 
Approached this morning as he left the polling booth, he would not discuss his preferences until his mother, a lifelong Nationalist, was out of earshot.
"I hope Chen Shui-bian can win," he said. 
"He's the best one to clean up the problems left by the Nationalists, and as mayor he did a pretty good job."
As for the mainland's dark warnings, he said: "We are not obliged to take any advice from China. 
We are electing our own president."
Even in Mr. Lee's hometown of Sanchi, northwest of Taipei, voters rebuffed the president's plea to keep the Nationalists in power.
"Why should I listen to Lee Teng-hui?" asked Pan Yue-ching, 38, a homemaker. 
"I have my own opinions."
The voters also appeared mainly unimpressed with the threats from China. 
"It's always the same between these two countries," said Lee Fung-lin, also 38 and an unemployed restaurant worker. 
"They just shout at each other."

file: DEMOCRATS HOPED TO RAISE $7 MILLION FROM ASIANS IN U.S.txt
text:
ï»¿
A White House official and a leading fund-raiser for the Democratic National Committee helped devise a strategy to raise an unprecedented $7 million from Asian-Americans partly by offering rewards to the largest donors, including special access to the White House, the committee's records show.
The strategy is laid out in a "National Asian Pacific American Campaign Plan," which was among 3,000 pages of the committee's records made public over the last week. 
Those records, drawn largely from the files of John Huang, the committee's chief fund-raiser in Asian-American communities, suggest that the party's goal of raising the $7 million helped create a high-pressure atmosphere that led to at least $1.2 million in improper donations.
The records, and interviews with donors, show that Mr. Huang told potential contributors that the time was ripe for them to win the political clout that had eluded Asian-Americans for a century. 
Political contributions were the path to power, he told them. 
Writing big checks would open doors for this generation and the next.
In many instances, Mr. Huang meant that quite literally. 
His files -- including business cards, campaign memorandums and canceled checks from contributors -- leave little doubt that the quid pro quo for large donations was in many cases a face-to-face meeting with the President.
Mr. Huang and Doris Matsui, a deputy assistant to President Clinton and the wife of Representative Robert T. Matsui, a California Democrat, helped create the fund-raising strategy, the records show. 
As part of that strategy, members of the Asian Pacific American Leadership Council -- a title conferred on people who gave at least $10,000 and companies that gave at least $15,000 to the Democratic committee -- were to receive an invitation to the White House.
The plan was to "reward Apalc members by inviting them to special White House or other events" with Mr. Clinton and to "solicit input" from them, the records show. 
Responsibility for orchestrating that reward fell to the White House, the Clinton-Gore campaign and the Democratic committee.
Those meetings often featured discussions of Mr. Clinton's policies toward Asian nations, especially China, though no evidence has surfaced suggesting that the donors won changes in policy. 
Instead, the Democratic Party capitalized on decisions the President had already made -- to extend China's preferential trading rights, to come to Taiwan's defense, to seek changes to the immigration and naturalization laws -- to lure Asian-American donors.
The Justice Department is examining the legality of the donations solicited by Mr. Huang. They are also being scrutinized by a Congressional panel that asked the Democratic National Committee to make the documents available last week. 
Although Amy Weiss Tobe, a committee spokeswoman, declined to comment on the strategy plan, Lanny J. Davis, the White House special counsel, said, "We will review this document and have a reaction to it, if appropriate, in the next several days."
As the pressure to raise money intensified this spring to pay for television commercials and other campaign expenses, Mr. Huang, who joined the Democratic committee in December 1995 after a stint as a mid-level Commerce Department official, veered into forbidden territory.
He took donations improperly from foreign corporations and from people who were neither American citizens nor foreign citizens living legally in the United States. 
And when Mr. Huang's fund-raising efforts went wrong, they usually went wrong with very large checks.
In some cases, those checks were drafted on the same day that a meeting was set up with Mr. Clinton. In one case, $250,000 bought a brief meeting at the Sheraton Carlton Hotel here between Mr. Clinton and a South Korean entrepreneur who had vague plans to build an electronics plant in Carson, Calif.
The entrepreneur spoke no English. 
Rather than labor through an uncomfortable conversation, he had his picture taken with the President and then left the dinner, eating instead with his entourage at a nearby Chinese restaurant.
In another case, Mr. Clinton's meeting with three business executives from the C.P. 
Group, a huge Thai conglomerate with interests in China and elsewhere in Asia, came within days of $185,000 in contributions from a Thai-American businesswoman, Pauline Kanchanalak. 
The Democratic committee later returned those donations, saying the money might not have come directly from Ms. Kanchanalak, as required by campaign law. 
The committee has offered a vague explanation, saying the money may have been given by a relative of hers.
And there are hundreds of thousands of dollars in checks from Arief and Soraya Wiriadinata, an Indonesian couple who appear on seating charts at a private dinner with Vice President Al Gore along with Mr. Huang and Charlie Yah Lin Trie, an Arkansas restaurateur and self-styled Asian trade adviser who delivered $639,000 in improper contributions to the President's legal defense fund this year. 
Those contributions have also been returned.
In March, Mr. Trie arranged for one of China's top weapons dealers to attend a private briefing with Mr. Clinton. Mr. Clinton now says he did not know who the Chinese official was, and says his attendance at the small briefing was "inappropriate."
In total, at least $1.2 million of the $3.4 million Mr. Huang raised came from questionable sources and has been returned. 
That money has become the greatest sum of campaign cash to come under Federal investigation since President Richard M. Nixon's 1972 re-election drive.
The Asian-American fund-raising effort was conceived by the Democratic committee and coordinated with the White House and the Clinton-Gore campaign, the records show. 
It was driven by a single stark statistic: Mr. Clinton received only 31 percent of the Asian-American vote in 1992 while President George Bush won 55 percent. 
Campaign money had flowed accordingly.
To reverse that situation, Mr. Huang joined the Democratic committee in December 1995 and served on the committee's Asian Pacific American Working Group.
The group, formed in February, included Ms. Matsui, the highest-ranking Asian-American in the White House; Maria Haley, director of the Export-Import Bank of the United States, who played a role in helping Mr. Huang obtain his job as a Commerce Department official in 1994; Ginger Lew, general counsel to the Commerce Department, and several staff members of the Democratic National Committee.
Its goal was to "coordinate all White House, Democratic National Committee and Clinton/Gore 1996 activities for the Asian Pacific American community," with an emphasis on fund raising, a strategy paper in the committee's records show. 
"Legal constraints" required the committee to raise the money, but the White House would help with the politics, said the paper, drafted in March and completed in April.
Mr. Huang had already organized "the largest Asian Pacific American fund-raising event in D.N.C. history," garnering more than $1 million at a Feb. 
19 dinner with Mr. Clinton and a Feb. 
20 breakfast with Mr. Gore, the paper said. 
But the goal, it said, was $7 million. 
And the pressure to reach that goal led to the string of questionable donations.
In March, Mr. Huang was approached by the Mayor of Carson, Calif., who also was a consultant for Japanese, Korean and Chinese enterprises. 
The Mayor, Michael I. Mitoma, had a client who wanted to meet the President. 
Mr. Huang solicited a $250,000 donation -- since returned -- from the client, called Cheong Am America, Inc., the Los Angeles subsidiary of a little-known South Korean company.
The donation was illegal. 
Cheong Am had no revenues in the United States, meaning that the funds in the April 8 check, a copy of which was in Mr. Huang's files, were funneled to the Democratic National Committee from abroad.
Handwritten notes in Mr. Huang's files strongly suggest that the Democrats could have known Cheong Am had no business activities in the United States. 
A flow chart of the Cheong Am Business Group, also in the files, shows no American subsidiary.
The company's chairman, a South Korean known as John Lee, had convinced Mr. Mitoma that his company might spend $150 million to build a giant outdoor television-screen factory in the city. 
But he wanted to talk to the President about it.
"Is it possible to have Lee meet Clinton privately for 30 minutes in Korea when he visits instead of the private meeting in Washington?"
Mayor Mitoma asked in a fax to Mr. Huang a week before the dinner. 
"If possible let me know how what kind of fund raising would be appropriate. 
How should the donation check be made payable?"
In a telephone conversation, Mr. Mitoma said Mr. Lee had wanted to buy every seat at the dinner, at a cost of $500,000. 
But the Democratic committee would not let him.
So, he said, Mr. Clinton "just smiled, stood for a picture and said 'adios' " to Mr. Lee. "I would have been livid, if it had been my money," Mr. Mitoma said. 
But Mr. Lee, he said, "went away happy."
After Mr. Clinton's brief meeting with Mr. Lee at the Sheraton Carlton Hotel in Washington, Mayor Mitoma wrote the President suggesting more meetings when he visited South Korea later that month. 
He asked to introduce the President to "Chairman Chong who heads the largest industrial group in Korea," misspelling the group's name as Hundai.
He appeared to be referring to the honorary chairman of the Hyundai Group, Chung Ju Yung, who unsuccessfully ran for President of South Korea in 1992 and was subsequently convicted of diverting $62 million of the company's funds to his campaign. 
His company was convicted earlier this year of bribing former South Korean leaders.
The meeting never took place. 
A handwritten notation to Mr. Huang from another Democratic committee official, who signed the note only as "D," says: "President Clinton cannot see these folks in Korea. 
This is important."
There is no question that Mr. Huang's legal fund raising struck a chord with many Asian-Americans who felt that they had long been excluded by the political and policy-making process. 
Chi Wang, a Library of Congress employee, said he had been persuaded by Mr. Huang to buy $25,000 worth of tickets to a Clinton fund-raising party.
"I've lived in Washington a long time, 40 years," Mr. Wang said in an interview. 
"Nobody had ever asked me for a large contribution. 
Huang said Asian-Americans don't get involved in American policy. 
And he tried to tell me that I should participate."
In any case, the Asian-American vote, which was 1 percent of the total Presidential balloting, gave Mr. Clinton 43 percent, Bob Dole 48 percent and Ross Perot 8 percent. 
Yet the controversy has also angered some of the Asian-Americans whom Mr. Huang said he wanted to escort to political power.
"Now everybody asks us questions," said Richard Yeh, an executive of Kang Long Agriculture in South El Monte, Calif., whose company gave a legal donation of $12,500 at Mr. Huang's behest. 
"I think that no one now will want to donate when they are asked next time."
Correction
An article on Dec. 
28 and an editorial on Dec. 
31 about questions raised by contributions to the Democratic National Committee and President Clinton's legal defense fund misstated the citizenship of Pauline Kanchanalak, a businesswoman and political contributor. 
She is a citizen of Thailand and a legal resident of the United States; she is not a Thai-American.
An article on Dec. 
28, 1996, described a Democratic National Committee report about that year's election campaign financing. 
The report, written in April 1996 and later turned over to a Congressional committee investigating campaign finance, referred to the role of Doris Matsui, then a White House aide. 
Ms. Matsui served as chairwoman of a private group that drafted a plan to enlist Asian-Americans in supporting President Clinton's re-election.
The Democratic National Committee document asserted that Ms. Matsui's group set a fund-raising goal for Asian-Americans. 
But later investigations by Congress and the Justice Department into White House and committee fund-raising unearthed no evidence that her group played any role in fund-raising or that she ever engaged in improper conduct. 
Ms. Matsui, who left the White House in December 1998 and is now working for a private law firm in Washington, asked The Times to bring its account up to date in fairness to her.
