file: Despite Tensions, Clinton Urges Renewal of China_s Trade Status.txt
text:
ï»¿
Despite a conflict with China over pirated American computer software, movies and music, President Clinton called today for unconditional renewal of preferential trade status for China, saying the step would be "a vote for America's interests" and "not a referendum on all China's policies."
Mr. Clinton's speech began a full-scale Administration lobbying effort to win Congressional approval for the extension of most-favored-nation trade status for China, even though tensions linger over major issues like nuclear proliferation and human rights abuses as well as trade.
The President's address to the Pacific Basin Economic Council also came close to being a point-by-point response to a withering election-year attack by Bob Dole, the presumptive Republican presidential nominee, on Mr. Clinton earlier this month for "weakness, indecision, double talk and incoherence" in foreign policy, especially toward the Pacific Basin.
Reviewing his Asia policy, Mr. Clinton emphasized the "firmness and steadiness" with which his Administration secured the shutdown of reactors producing weapons-grade plutonium in North Korea. 
He said the United States must also be "steady and firm" in pushing for a stable, open and prosperous China.
And while Mr. Dole had cited a merchandise trade deficit with Japan last year of $60 billion, higher than when Mr. Clinton took office, the President today countered with his own trade statistics. 
He said that the trade deficit with Japan was down 25 percent from last year.
Four years ago as a candidate, Mr. Clinton denounced President George Bush for his position that engaging China rather than threatening it with trade sanctions was the best way to promote human rights and protect America's interest in Asia. 
But once in office, Mr. Clinton came around to a similar policy of engagement.
Last week, after months of warnings regarding the violations of an agreement protecting intellectual property rights -- which include pirating of software, videotapes and music -- the Administration published a list of $3 billion of goods exported from China to the United States annually that could be subject to the largest trade sanctions ever imposed by Washington.
But Mr. Clinton has long made clear his intentions to push to continue the trade benefits, and his action today was expected. 
His speech displayed the kinds of arguments he will be making during the next few months as Congress weighs whether to vote to revoke China's trade benefits and force Mr. Clinton to exercise a veto. 
Although the President almost certainly would defeat an override attempt, the battle would make him look weaker on the world stage.
[On Tuesday, a Vice Premier of China, Li Lanqing, welcomed Mr. Clinton's effort to renew the trade status but warned Washington not to impose sanctions over trade disputes, Reuters reported.
["This, of course, is good news," Mr. Li told a seminar in Beijing. 
"I feel that it is harmful to long-term Chinese-U.S. economic and trade cooperation for China and the United States to argue about this problem each year. 
It will create psychological instability on both sides and will have no good results."
[Referring to looming tit-for-tat sanctions announced by Beijing and Washington in the dispute over copyright piracy, Mr. Li said: "I don't know who will be imposing sanctions on whom or who will be containing whom. 
I feel that this is inappropriate. 
We are not willing to see a trade war."]
Mr. Clinton noted today that China is Asia's only "declared nuclear weapons state" and has the world's largest standing army. 
In less than two decades, he said, it could be the world's largest economy.
Faced with such an economic and military behemoth, he argued, it would not be in America's interest to drive China toward isolation by denying the "most favored" trade status that is given routinely to most trading partners in the world and allows China to export its products to the United States at the lowest possible tariffs. 
The sanctions for violating the piracy agreement amount to only a small fraction of China's total imports to the United States.
Revoking the status, Mr. Clinton said, "would drive us back into a period of mutual isolation and recrimination that would harm America's interests, not advance them."
"Rather than strengthening China's respect for human rights," Mr. Clinton said, "it would lessen our contact with the Chinese people. 
Rather than limiting the spread of weapons of mass destruction, it would limit the prospect for future cooperation in this area. 
Rather than bringing stabilityI to the region, it would increase instability as the leaders of Hong Kong, Taiwan and all of the nations of the region have stated repeatedly."
Mr. Dole earlier this month spurned the conservative wing of his own party and said he too backed the current status for China, though he sharply criticized Mr. Clinton's overall policy toward Asia.
"President Clinton's long silence and his history of zigzags on China has put extension of M.F.N. in serious doubt this year," Mr. Dole said today in a statement. 
"The President still needs to articulate a coherent policy toward China and how M.F.N. extension fits into that policy."
Patrick J. Buchanan, Mr. Dole's erstwhile competitor for the Republican nomination, called Mr. Clinton's move to renew China's trading privileges "an act of economic, moral and military appeasement."
He added: "For the Republican Party this will be a defining moment: Do we stand with Bill Clinton or do we stand by the values that made us a Congressional majority. 
Do we love trade more than we loathe tyranny?"
Administration officials said Mr. Clinton would formally notify Congress of his decision to extend the trade preferences on June 3, starting the time-clock for action. 
Beginning a month later, on July 3, the House and Senate have 60 days in which they could vote to revoke China's benefits.
Republicans say that there has been rising frustration on Capitol Hill with what is seen as Administration leniency toward China as well as with Beijing's conduct on several issues ranging across the areas of trade, human rights, diplomacy and arms control. 
The White House press secretary, Michael D. McCurry, today also acknowledged a tough fight ahead and said that is why Mr. Clinton announced his decision early.
"We are worried enough that we are not taking anything for granted," Mr. McCurry said. 
A variety of Administration officials were to be deployed to begin making the Administration's case, with Defense Secretary William J. Perry, for example, scheduled to make an address concerning China on Wednesday.
Officials predict that the House will vote against trade preferences or make the benefits conditional because of liberal and conservative concerns alike about China's human rights record and failure to live up to international accords.
Mr. Clinton has stronger support in the more moderate Senate. 
But even there, Republicans say, the balance could tilt depending on whether the size of the House vote puts pressure on Democrats to split with the President and stand up for human rights or if the United States and China are in the midst of a trade war over intellectual property.

file: Detained Editor_s Brother Is Arrested in Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
The police have detained the younger brother of a Boston-based poet arrested in Beijing last week, apparently for his involvement in a literary journal that has sometimes published work by Chinese dissidents.
The poet, Bei Ling, a Chinese citizen with an American green card, was taken into custody on Aug. 
12 during a visit to Beijing. 
His younger brother, Huang Feng, 32, a writer who lives in Beijing, was detained Thursday night.
It is unclear exactly what charges are being brought against the two, although Mr. Bei, 40, is being held in criminal detention, which suggests that they could be serious.
It is at least the second time in about a year that a Chinese intellectual with permanent resident status in the United States has been arrested in Beijing. 
Last summer, Song Yongyi of Dickinson College in Carlisle, Pa., was arrested in connection with studies of the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution, a period embarrassing to China's leaders.
An aggressive campaign by American politicians and scholars helped secure Mr. Song's release after six months. 
Similar forces seem to be gathering in Mr. Bei's defense.
At a news conference on Thursday to promote a major cultural exchange, the American envoy, Joseph Prueher, said of Mr. Bei: "We have officially expressed our concern to the Chinese government about him. 
Obviously the issue of freedom of expression is a core point."
Others noted that the Bei case could prove a public relations nightmare for China. 
Within the next three weeks both President Jiang Zemin and Li Peng, the head of Parliament, will be at the United Nations. 
Also, as part of the announced cultural exchange, a Chinese exhibit will tour American cities.
"It will cause a great deal of embarrassment to a useful cultural effort if they continue to hold him this way," said Jerome Cohen, a New York lawyer who helped secure Mr. Song's release. 
"They will not want to have demonstrators protesting outside the Javits Center."
At the time of Mr. Bei's arrest, the police confiscated hundreds of copies of Tendency, the quarterly journal he edits. 
Published in the United States, Tendency is not legally available in China.
All magazines there must have a government sponsor that formally takes responsibility for their content. 
Foreign magazines like Mr. Bei's, which combines work by Western and Chinese authors, must have permits for import, although many circulate in intellectual circles and essays published overseas are often available on the Chinese Internet.
It was unclear what level of the bureaucracy initiated the brothers' arrests and whether they were meant as a larger signal.
"Sometimes when we look into cases it's not a government plan, but the action of a small entity," Mr. Prueher said at the news conference.

file: Dingjiaergou Journal_Remains of a Day, Unearthed, Enrich Another.txt
text:
ï»¿
In Ding Yaohong's tiny sitting room, mud walls are etched with deep cracks and two tattered chairs vie for space with roosting chickens, signs of this remote region's desperate poverty. 
But the new centerpiece of the room, displacing a small, rotting table, is the valuable fossilized spine of an ancient spade-toothed elephant that Mr. Ding recently unearthed -- portending a more prosperous future.
For years, the farmers here struggled to coax wheat and corn to grow on these arid, rocky hills, but the land gave little in return. 
"Plant a handful of seed and you get a handful of crops," a local saying goes.
But recently this barren, brown wasteland has yielded a lucrative new crop that stands to repay the village for its generations of suffering: a cache of nearly intact 15 million-year-old fossils, which the villagers plan to sell.
"We've been digging for fossils for more than 10 years, but this is the first time we've hit upon anything like this," Mr. Ding said.
His home is now littered with valuable specimens excavated in the last two months, including ancient crocodiles, rhinos and pigs. 
"When the experts come to buy, I hope it will be a very good harvest," he said.
As China has moved toward a market economy, peasants all over rural China have had to devise ways to buy goods and services that were once provided for free by the state, like education and medicine. 
Where land is good they farm. 
Near cities, they turn to migrant labor.
But Dingjiaergou, whose residents belong to China's Hui Muslim minority (and are mostly surnamed Ding), is 15 miles from the nearest paved road. 
The village is in a county with a per capita income of less than $100 a year, in one of China's poorest areas, the Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. 
Villagers got electricity several years ago, but houses still lack running water, phones and heat, even though winter temperatures drop well below zero.
So peasants here have turned to large-scale fossil excavation to make ends meet -- a unique if dangerous (and probably illegal) sideline.
When not tending their crops, the men of Dingjiaergou can often be found tunneling like groundhogs 10 feet under the region's hills, in the hopes of finding ancient bones.
Two months ago Mr. Ding and 17 other villagers hit gold burrowing their way into the underground cache. 
Now, the three-room mud-brick house he shares with his wife and three children resembles a museum storeroom, with the spine in the sitting room, piles of skulls in the bedroom, and the huge-tusked skull of a spade-toothed elephant blocking access to the family kang, a traditional brick bed built over an oven to provide winter warmth.
Scientists have long known that this arid land in Tongxin County was once a richly forested terrain, filled with lakes and rivers, said Ye Jie, deputy director of the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing.
In the 1960's and 70's some farmers picked up spare cash by digging up and selling "dragon bones" -- fossil shards used to make traditional medicines for treating stomach troubles and scars. 
In the next two decades, Chinese scientists occasionally made research expeditions to this remote region, cataloguing its past.
But farmers here say they only recently realized that there was big money in excavations, and began carving out their peculiar niche in China's emerging market economy.
"In the beginning we didn't know how valuable this stuff was," said Ding Yuzhu, a grizzled 50-year-old in a Mao jacket and white skullcap who is the younger Mr. Ding's nephew.
He said that in the last few years, Chinese scientists as well as foreign experts had come to view -- and buy -- their wares. 
"Now we have discovered we could do this to make a living," he said.
Ding Yaohong, a burly man of 38, said that even before the major discovery this spring, most of his income in recent years had come from fossils. 
He makes about $35 a year from growing wheat and corn -- and $125 a month selling the smaller fossils and bone shards he unearthed in the past.
With this year's jackpot, his second income stands to increase many times. 
He and his partners say they will price the elephant skull alone at $4,000 to $6,000. 
Mr. Ding says they plan to sell the fossils to the Natural History Museum in Beijing, but experts predict that many will end up on a lucrative black market.
Neither farmers nor local officials seem terribly perturbed that their digging might be illegal. 
"In fact we don't have much choice," the older Mr. Ding said, "since our land is so poor we would starve otherwise."
The officials have done little to intervene, noting that the region's government does not have the money for proper excavation anyhow.
Still, many scientists are concerned that these amateur fossil hunters may be destroying valuable scientific evidence with their rudimentary picks and shovels.
"Most scientists are opposed to this unscientific digging, even though it has been a convenient way to get specimens," said Mr. Ye of the Academy of Sciences. 
"The peasants' goal is to sell fossils -- not to gather related scientific information -- so things are lost. 
And because of their limited knowledge they often damage valuable things which they think of as unimportant."
To get to the fossils, groups of villagers first dig a hole down several yards into the earth, and then often tunnel laterally hundreds of yards.
This spring, the 18-man team from Dingjiaergou tunneled 500 yards before they found fossils, which Mr. Ding said could be distinguished from the surrounding rocks by their color and also their unique taste.
"We found so many things there," he said, "but it was hard since the tunnel was only 1.5 yards high -- you couldn't stand up and only one person could go in at a time."
Each fossil had to be dragged out of the narrow tunnel using ropes. 
And scientists complain that the villagers inevitably chop up large specimens to get them up through their maze, destroying evidence in the process.
It is a dangerous after-hours job that has killed two men from Dingjiaergou in the last 10 years. 
Since there are no trees in this desertlike region to provide beams to reinforce the tunnels, they are prone to collapse.
"This is our first big find after years of looking," the elder Mr. Ding said, "and two people have died doing it. 
That's why the bones are so expensive."
The villagers say that over the last few years, visiting experts have taught them how to handle the fossils more carefully and brought scientific charts that help them identify bones from ancient mammals.
But some of the fossils remain inscrutable to the peasants.
"What's that?" a visitor asked, pointing to a pear-shaped 15-inch skull on the dirt floor, with dull yellow teeth protruding at odd angles.
"Oh that, that's some kind of monster," the elder Mr. Ding said with assurance.

text:
ï»¿
The eminent industrialist made his prediction with confidence: If the opposition party's candidate wins the presidency next month, the Taiwan stock market will crash, no question about it, because investors fearing hostilities with China will yank out their money.
The speaker, in an interview today, was C. Y. Kao -- chairman of the National Federation of Industries, chief executive of the giant Uni-President Group conglomerate and, not coincidentally, a leader of the Nationalist Party, which has governed Taiwan for half a century and now faces possible defeat.
Mr. Kao's warning of economic catastrophe, if extreme, was one of many dire predictions by political opponents who say the election of Chen Shui-bian on March 18 would cause dangerous tensions, and perhaps war, with China.
Speculation about China's view of Mr. Chen intensified after China warned in a report this week that any step toward formal independence, or even an indefinite delay in negotiations toward reunification, could lead to a military attack.
The report did not directly discuss Mr. Chen or the Democratic Progressive Party. 
But from its founding in the 1980's, the party has called for Taiwan's formal independence -- which China calls a cause for war. 
Recently the party has moderated that stance.
The warnings about China's possible reaction and the questions about the sincerity of his pullback from outright independence are a source of endless exasperation for Mr. Chen. In truth, he argued in an interview today, perhaps only his party can -- in the manner of President Richard M. Nixon, a fervent anti-Communist who achieved a historic opening to China -- reach a lasting accord with the mainland.
"I'm a peacemaker, not a troublemaker," he insisted, his voice croaking from incessant campaigning.
His basic position, and his rationale for backing away from his original, harder line, is that since Taiwan is already an independent state in practice, there is no need to codify it.
In practice, that leaves his policy little different from that of the governing party of President Lee Teng-hui, although the Nationalists still pay lip service to a distant goal of unifying in some way with the mainland they fled after their defeat to the Communists in 1949.
Though dogged by charges that he would provoke a crisis, Mr. Chen has a good chance of winning in the race against Lien Chan of the Nationalist Party and James Soong, a longtime Nationalist who is running independently and hence dividing the party's traditionally large vote.
In his doomsday prediction today, Mr. Kao, the Nationalist and industry chief, was remarkably specific: Right after Mr. Chen's election, he said, the stock market would plummet to one-third of its current level.
"Many people will wire part of their money out of Taiwan just to play it safe," Mr. Kao said, charging that Mr. Chen, 49, and his colleagues are too young and inexperienced to guide Taiwan safely. 
And who can be sure, he and other critics ask, that once in office they will not let their true pro-independence colors show?
Told of the dire prediction, Mr. Chen smiled and recalled that his opponents made similar efforts to "terrorize people" in 1994 when he was elected mayor of Taipei.
"The day after I won, the stock market actually rose by hundreds of points," he said. 
Mr. Chen then listed, as he often has done in speeches and interviews and meetings with foreign diplomats, the new policies he and his party have adopted to avoid trouble with China.
If elected, he said, he would not try to write Taiwan's sovereign status as a "state" into the Constitution. 
He would not, as his party once promised, call a referendum on Taiwan's future or to change its official name from Republic of China to Republic of Taiwan. 
Only if Taiwan is attacked, he said, would he ask the public to consider such changes.
And as a first step toward smoother relations with the mainland, Mr. Chen said, he will -- subject to national security concerns -- ease the current government's restrictions on direct shipping, transportation and communications across the straits, and on large-scale investment projects in the mainland.
Mr. Kao made it clear today that he has never been happy about his own Nationalist Party's restrictive policy. 
"We just want to pursue trade and investment," he said of Taiwan's businessmen. 
"We hope politics won't have any impact."
This evening, the powerful industry association he heads announced that Mr. Kao will travel to Beijing soon after the March elections to discuss improving economic ties. 
He is certain to be feted by senior Chinese leaders.
As for Mr. Chen, even with his economic olive branch, he and his party may be a hard sell in Beijing. 
China may prefer almost anyone to President Lee, who has riled them by bluntly asserting that Taiwan is sovereign and equal and that the two sides should talk on a "state to state" basis.
Some finessing of concepts may be needed for China to agree to talk on those terms. 
But, realistically or not, Mr. Chen says he sees a chance to overcome deeply rooted enmities.
"The recent cross-straits tensions originate in the historical hatred between the Nationalist Party and the Chinese Communist Party," he said. 
"They can only be ended by a party without that burden."

The Walt Disney Company is seeking $77,000 in damages from three Chinese publishing houses accused of pirating Mickey Mouse, Peter Pan, Cinderella and Snow White, an official report said on Friday.
The copyright infringement case is the largest brought by a United States company in China this year, the English-language newspaper China Daily reported. 
Chinese businesses are widely accused of pirating copyrighted and patented material, and United States companies say such infringements cost them $800 million last year.
Disney is suing the publishing companies and accusing them of violating its copyrights in nine picture-story books that feature the four Disney characters, the newspaper reported. 
The publishers reportedly produced and marketed 300,000 copies of the books in 1991, 1993 and 1994.
Hearings began on Wednesday and more are scheduled before a verdict will be announced, the newspaper said. 
Disney is also seeking to stop the printing.
At the hearing, the lower court determined that there was evidence of copyright violation and agreed to hear a case.
According to the newspaper, the publishers say the books were published under an agreement with the Grand World Publishing Corporation, which is said to have signed a publishing contract with an unidentified British corporation based in Hong Kong. 
The newspaper did not say where Grand World Publishing was based.

file: Dispatches From a Culinary Frontier.txt
text:
ï»¿
BETWEEN carrying on about Ian Thorpe, the young swimmer with feet almost as big as a kangaroo's, and marveling at Sydney's magnificent harbor and opera house, the writers and broadcasters covering the Olympic Games have somehow found time to rave about the food and wine they have discovered in Australia.
About that, at least, they do not exaggerate. 
Only a generation or two ago, a can of Foster's and a few shrimp on the barbie defined the epicurean horizons of most people down under, but no more. 
Sydney has become one of the world's great restaurant towns, Australian cuisine is a topic of global interest instead of an oxymoron and Australian wine has long since outgrown the Monty Python troupe's taunts about Perth pink and Nuits-St.-Wagga-Wagga.
But to most Americans, it's all hearsay, as remote as dinner on Mars. 
Even in the jet age, Australia is many hours and thousands of dollars away, which makes a clutch of new and nearly new Australian cookbooks all the more welcome as guidebooks for the armchair gastronomic traveler. 
Their publication reflects the world's growing fascination with the culinary scene on the smallest continent, and a couple of them, one in particular, are just as useful at a stove as in an armchair.
What, you may well ask, is Australian cuisine?
Tough question. 
Some cuisines can be defined by the starches on which they rely -- rice in China, for example, pasta in southern Italy and potatoes in northern Europe. 
Or the cooking fat they use -- olive oil in the Mediterranean, lard in central Europe and butter in northern France. 
But Australians, like Americans, use a little of this and a little of that.
The reason, of course, is that modern Australian cooking, like modern American cooking, is New World cooking, evolved not from generations of peasant tradition but from the application of Old World techniques to local ingredients by gifted chefs. 
It reflects "cosmopolitan influences from everywhere," in the words of Australia's leading purveyor of fancy groceries, Simon Johnson.
Until the relatively recent (and by no means universally successful) vogue for fusion cooking in the United States, French and Italian and Chinese and Japanese and Lebanese and Afghan foods have kept mostly to themselves in this country, often modified to meet local tastes but seldom mixed. 
In Australia, synthesis is the norm. 
Chefs shamelessly plunder ideas and ingredients from the whole wide world.
As Alan Saunders writes in "Australian Food" (Ten Speed Press, 1999), the taste of Australia is "the flavor of change, adaptation and -- in the very best sense of the word -- compromise."
Take Janni Kyritsis, the chef at MG Garage in Sydney, who is one of the luminaries featured in Mr. Saunders's book. 
Greek-born, he cooks red mullet coated with gremolata bread crumbs. 
Greek enough. 
But he adds a Sicilian dimension by stuffing the fish with a mixture including currants and pine nuts. 
Or Stefano Manfredi, who runs Bel Mondo, in my view Australia's best Italian restaurant. 
He serves pasta, to be sure, but he is as likely to serve it with un-Italian things like abalone and shiitakes as with tomatoes.
The unsung hero of the Australian gastronomic explosion is Gough Whitlam, the former prime minister, who in the 1970's began encouraging immigration by Asians. 
Today, if Australia is not quite an Asian country, Asia influences what Australia eats to a degree unknown elsewhere in the Western world -- in superb Asian establishments like Gilbert Lau's Flower Drum in Melbourne, possibly the best Cantonese restaurant anywhere, but in Western restaurants, too.
Cheong Liew, who cooks at the Grange, the dining room of the Adelaide Hilton, was born of a Chinese family in Malaysia, which perhaps gave him a head start in melding different culinary traditions. 
So did his apprenticeship. 
He worked in Greek, Indian, Southeast Asian, French and Chinese kitchens, and his own restaurant was the first one anywhere, to the best of my knowledge, to perfect a fusion style.
"I can cook a dish the traditional way," Mr. Liew said last year, "but I like to put in an element from somewhere else in the globe to remind people of their own culture. 
There is a cultural freedom in Australia that accepts this."
Multicultural cooking works only if it tastes good, and it tastes good only if a discriminating sensibility is at work. 
Believe me, Mr. Liew's dishes -- like his red snapper, red-roasted in Chinese fashion, with a green Southeast Asian jus of coriander, spring onions and chilies, served with a French-inspired leek fondue -- never cross the very narrow line that divides fusion from confusion.
Tetsuya Wakuda, the Japanese-born chef whom many have tried to lure to the United States, produces food Faberge -- fillets of a perchlike fish known as barramundi, for example, served with peaches, endive, truffle oil and wakame seaweed. 
(Think Charlie Trotter crossed with Nobu Matsuhisa.) You will find the recipe in Mr. Saunders's book, lacking, alas, any suggestions as to what North American fish might work in case your neighborhood supermarket has run out of barramundi. 
Mr. Wakuda's forthcoming book, I am told, will be available here soon.
Not that all the chefs who have shaped modern Australian cooking are immigrants. 
Christine Manfield ranges the world for inspiration for her book, "Spice" (Viking, 1999), and for her restaurant, Paramount, in the prosperous Sydney suburb of Potts Point. 
But she is Australian born and bred, and she proves it with a vertical fantasy consisting (reading from south to north) of a disk of nori omelet, a potato pancake sparked with wasabi, strips of quick-seared kangaroo, horseradish cream and a liberal dusting of chives. 
(Yes, they sometimes eat kangaroo; no, it's not a staple. 
Rather more like buffalo here -- lean, healthy, tasty, favored by the cognoscenti rather than rank-and-file.)
Like California, Australia benefits from its climate. 
It is blessed with tropical and temperate fruits in profusion. 
It grows vegetables of all kinds, Asian as well as European in origin. 
Its relatively unpolluted seas, with a wide range of temperatures, are equally bountiful; more than 200 kinds of fish and 90 kinds of mollusks and crustaceans are commercially available.
Some of them are exotic looking, like Coffin Bay scallops, with purple shells and magenta roe. 
Some sound more exotic than they are. 
When an Australian recipe calls for "bugs," don't reach for the ants; what's wanted instead are flattish crustaceans, found only off Australia, called either Balmain bugs (Ibacus peronii) or Moreton Bay bugs (Thenus orientalis). 
Both resemble the European squat lobster.
The abundance of prime ingredients encourages many cooks to opt for simplicity. 
One of the best at this game is a young New Zealander, Philip Johnson, who for the last five years has run a bistro called Ecco in Brisbane, in subtropical Queensland. 
His cookbook, also "Ecco" (Random House Australia, 1999), is filled with straightforward but tempting dishes like slow-cooked duck with red cabbage, bacon and hazelnuts, and fillet of beef with parsnips, baby leeks and tapenade.
Wouldn't you like to try grilled quail with wet polenta and asparagus sometime soon?
Dishes like that -- "lovingly crafted, basic but perfectly cooked food," in the magazine's words -- won Mr. Johnson the 1997 Restaurant of the Year award given by The Australian Gourmet Traveller, one of the country's top food magazines.
But you needn't be a celebrated chef to play in this league. 
The other night, when I had only a scant hour and a half to make dinner for myself; my wife, Betsey; and four guests, my eye fell upon "New Food Fast" (Whitecap Books, 1999) by Donna Hay, an overachieving 30-year-old food writer with two best-sellers already to her credit. 
It offers sections headed "10 Minutes (or So)," "20 Minutes" and "30 Minutes" -- and I found the timings accurate.
Something light, Betsey said. 
Mussels poached in a quick broth flavored with ginger and lemon grass, to which I added a chopped hot pepper and a bit of garlic, got us under way. 
Then came scallops of swordfish sauteed with sage leaves and a shower of grated lemon rind, with a side of very slowly roasted tomatoes with basil, served lukewarm, and kadota figs in vanilla and white port sauce.
My jury approved, and it gave the blue ribbon to the swordfish. 
Cutting the fish steaks in half horizontally and cooking them in olive oil for a minute on each side produced something much moister and subtler in flavor than grilling the slabs whole over coals.
Had I been feeling more ambitious, I admit, I would have tried something dreamed up by Neil Perry, my favorite Australian chef -- maybe his passion-fruit custard tart or, if I had been feeling truly foolhardy, his king prawn cake and scallops with spicy prawn sauce, a little number with a mere 48 ingredients, many of them Asian (galangal, turmeric, kaffir lime, palm sugar, coconut cream, coriander roots, lemon grass). 
A slight, ebullient, ponytailed man, he is every bit as fastidious about his raw materials as he is about technique.
Or maybe I would have jumped on a plane for Sydney and headed for one of Mr. Perry's restaurants, either Rockpool, which is formal, or Wockpool, which is more casual and more overtly Asian. 
Maybe I'd have ordered his aged rump steak, cut two inches thick, rare inside, a crisp smoky crust on the outside, a chunk of anchovy butter on top, plus a bottle or two of Penfolds Grange shiraz to wash it all down. 
With food and drink like that, who needs a ticket for the Olympics?

Scouting Out the Books
Â 
NEW FOOD FAST" by Donna Hay and "Australian Food" by Alan Saunders are available in major bookstores. 
"Spice" by Christine Manfield and "Ecco" by Philip Johnson are available at specialty booksellers like Kitchen Arts & Letters, 1435 Lexington Avenue (93rd Street), or online through amazon.co.uk and dymocks.com.au, among others.

SWORDFISH FRIED IN SAGE OLIVE OIL
Adapted from "New Food Fast" by Donna Hay
Time: 10 minutes
Â 
3 tablespoons fruity extra virgin olive oil
8 large fresh sage leaves
2 teaspoons grated lemon zest
1/2 teaspoon cracked black pepper
4 thin ( 3/4-inch) swordfish steaks.
1. Heat olive oil in a large saute pan over medium-high heat. 
Add the sage leaves, lemon zest and cracked black pepper. 
Saute until sage is crisp, about 2 minutes.
2. Add swordfish, and saute about 1 minute on each side, or until just cooked through; be careful not to overcook. 
Quickly transfer to serving plates, and drizzle with the oil and sage from the pan. 
Serve immediately.
Yield: 4 servings.
Â 
ORANGE, DATE AND CARDAMOM TART
Adapted from "Spice" by Christine Manfield
Time: 2 hours, plus overnight refrigeration and 3 hours' cooling
Â 
1/2 cup confectioners' sugar
3/4 cup flour
5 1/2 tablespoons chilled unsalted butter, cut into cubes
2 large egg yolks
1/2 vanilla bean, split
4 large eggs
3/4 cup plus 2 tablespoons extra-fine
granulated sugar
Zest of two oranges
1/4 cup fresh orange juice
Seeds from 4 green cardamom pods, ground
1/3 cup heavy cream
18 fresh dates, halved lengthwise.
1. Sift together powdered sugar and flour, and place in food processor. 
Add butter, and pulse until mixture resembles fine bread crumbs. 
Add egg yolks, and scrape in pulp from vanilla bean. 
Blend until dough just comes together in a soft ball. 
Wrap in plastic film, and refrigerate overnight.
2. In a medium bowl combine eggs and sugar, and whisk until pale and creamy. 
Add orange zest, juice, cardamom and cream. 
Mix well, and refrigerate overnight.
3. Lightly dust a work surface with flour, and roll dough into 10-inch circle. 
Fold into quarters to transfer to a 9 1/2-inch nonstick tart pan. 
Unfold and fit snugly into pan, trimming and patching as necessary. 
Refrigerate 30 minutes.
4. Preheat oven to 325 degrees. 
Prick tart shell all over with a fork, and bake just until dry and golden, about 15 minutes.
5. Strain egg mixture through a fine sieve. 
Place tart shell on baking sheet, and arrange dates inside. 
Gently pour in egg mixture.
6. If edges of the tart shell are already browned, cover with strips of foil to prevent burning. 
Bake until custard is lightly browned and set, about 30 minutes. 
Allow to cool at least 3 hours before removing from pan.
Yield: One 9 1/2-inch tart (8 servings).
Â 
WARM SALAD OF BARBECUED LAMB
Adapted from "Australian Food"
Time: 1 hour and 15 minutes
Â 
2 tablespoons Asian plum sauce
2 tablespoons light soy sauce
1 tablespoon mirin (sweetened rice wine) or sherry
3 tablespoons light vegetable oil
1 teaspoon sesame oil
1 tablespoon rice vinegar
Chili oil, optional
4 cups mixed baby spinach, arugula and tatsoi
18 green beans, trimmed
4 lamb loin chops, boned and trimmed of fat
1/4 cup char sui sauce or Asian plum sauce
1/4 cup Sichuan peppercorns, finely crushed with a rolling pin
3 tablespoons vegetable oil
12 oyster mushrooms
15 snow peas, ends trimmed, each cut diagonally into two
3 tablespoons bean sprouts
6 fresh water chestnuts, peeled and sliced, or 1/3 cup canned whole water chestnuts, thinly sliced.
1. In a small bowl, combine 2 tablespoons plum sauce, soy sauce, mirin, light vegetable oil, sesame oil and vinegar. 
Mix well, and add chili oil to taste. 
Set aside.
2. Prepare a grill, or lightly oil a heavy ridged or flat skillet. 
Place spinach mixture in a bowl, and set aside. 
Bring a pot of lightly salted water to a boil, and blanch green beans until just tender. 
Rinse under cold water, drain and set aside.
3. Coat lamb chops with char sui sauce, and roll very lightly in peppercorns. 
Allow meat to rest 30 minutes. 
Grill or sear over high heat until charred but pink in the center, about 2 1/2 minutes on the first side, and 1 1/2 minutes on the second. 
Transfer to a plate, cover with a bowl and let rest for 2 to 3 minutes.
4. Heat vegetable oil in a separate skillet, and fry mushrooms until crisp. 
Add to spinach mixture. 
Add snow peas and green beans to skillet, and saute for 30 seconds. 
Add bean sprouts and water chestnuts, and toss just until heated. 
Add to spinach mixture.
5. To serve, whisk dressing until blended, and add to spinach mixture. 
Toss gently, and place an equal portion in the center of each of four serving plates. 
Slice the lamb thinly on the diagonal, and arrange over greens. 
Serve immediately.
Yield: 4 servings.

Less than a month ago, Wei Jingsheng was in a Chinese prison, jailed for advocating democracy.
Today Mr. Wei, China's most prominent dissident, had a private meeting with President Clinton in the White House and urged him to continue pressing Beijing to improve its record on human rights and democracy.
"I told him about some of my experiences in dealing with the Chinese Communists," Mr. Wei told reporters at a briefing later, "and I expressed the hope that in dealing with the Chinese Communists, the United States would not be deceived. 
My personal feeling is that President Clinton is not someone who is easily deceived."
Mr. Wei's release on Nov. 
16 came two weeks after President Jiang Zemin of China made a state visit to the United States, and the release was widely interpreted as a conciliatory gesture in response to criticism of China's human rights record.
Mr. Clinton had requested the meeting with Mr. Wei. But the White House, sensitive to Beijing's concerns and not wanting to jeopardize future releases of political prisoners, declined to comment on the 35-minute session, held in Mr. Clinton's private West Wing office.
The Chinese were annoyed nonetheless. 
In a statement on Tuesday carried by the official New China News Agency and reported by Reuters, the Government said, "This act of the U.S. side is totally wrong, and the Chinese side expresses its strong resentment against and firm opposition to the meeting."
When dealing with the Beijing Government, Mr. Wei said he warned Mr. Clinton, "do not pay before the goods are delivered."
"In the West, you go by credibility, by the rule of law, by rules and regulation," Mr. Wei said, speaking through an interpreter. 
"That is never the case with the Chinese Communists. 
They can make any promises, and they can go back on any promises. 
It is like a sports match, where one side must obey all the rules and the other side doesn't have to."
In today's meeting, Mr. Wei said Mr. Clinton seemed sincere about his commitment to human rights. 
Mr. Wei said he had "differing views" from Mr. Clinton on certain issues, but declined to say what they were. 
He also sidestepped a question about whether he endorsed Mr. Clinton's plans to visit China next year.
Mr. Wei, 47, a former electrician at the Beijing Zoo, won fame for an essay in December 1978 suggesting that Deng Xiaopeng should expand his campaign to achieve the "Four Modernizations" -- of industry, agriculture, science and technology, and national defense -- to include a "fifth modernization," democracy. 
He was arrested, and since 1979 he spent all but six months in prison.
Ostensibly released for poor health, Mr. Wei appeared fit today, although he said he had "a number" of problems that were not life-threatening. 
He has suffered from heart disease, high blood pressure and an irregular heartbeat.
Mr. Clinton has retreated from the campaign of trade pressure on China that he advocated at the beginning of his Administration, arguing that "engagement," not confrontation, was more likely to yield improved human rights conditions in China.
Asked today if he believed that the strategy had made China a freer society, Mr. Wei said, "In my own personal view, no such thing has happened."

text:

A Chinese dissident on a weeklong hunger strike to protest China's crackdown on a fledgling democratic party was released from Bellevue Hospital Center yesterday after being taken there Saturday, a hospital spokesman said.
The dissident, Wang Xizhe, one of China's first pro-democracy activists, began his hunger strike during a protest on Dec. 
27 in front of the United Nations headquarters, said Wang Bingzhang, an organizer. 
Wang Xizhe returned to his home yesterday, but hopes to continue his hunger strike for at least two more days, Wang Bingzhang said.
Last month, the Chinese Government sentenced three men in China to prison terms of more than a decade each after they tried to organize the Chinese Democracy Party as a formal opposition to the Chinese Communist Party. 
Wang Xizhe, the secretary of the overseas committee of the Democracy Party, was joined by about 15 others who staged shorter hunger strikes last week, said Wang Bingzhang, no relation, who is an adviser to the Democracy Party.
"We organized this hunger strike to protest the arrests by the Chinese Government and to urge the United Nations and international society to do something to stop these persecutions," he said.
Pro-democracy activists had hoped that the Chinese Government would relax political controls after President Clinton's trip to China in June, and leaders began applying to register their party with the Government. 
But those expectations were quickly abandoned after the first arrests and a speech last month by President Jiang Zemin, who said that challenges to one-party rule in China would be "annihilated."
Wang Bingzhang said he and Wang Xizhe were to testify about the arrests later this week before the House of Representatives.
"We advised him to eat," Wang Bingzhang said. 
"He has to recover his health to go to Washington."

Wei Jingsheng, China's most prominent democracy advocate, said in an interview in New York yesterday that he would tell President Clinton that only continued pressure from the West could help free more Chinese political prisoners.

"This will be the very first issue that we discuss," said Mr. Wei, who is expected to meet Mr. Clinton later this month or early in December.

Excerpts, page A5.

Mr. Wei's assertions that he intends to become a strong public advocate for improvements in China's human rights situation could complicate relations between Washington and Beijing.
Mr. Wei's message may prove controversial to the Clinton Administration, which won praise yesterday from rights organizations for pressing Mr. Wei's case in private meetings with Chinese leaders in the last three years. 
Mr. Clinton has stepped back from the campaign of trade pressure on China that he advocated at the outset of his Administration, arguing that "engagement," not confrontation, was more likely to produce improved rights conditions in China.
Speaking at a news conference in New York and in an interview afterward, Mr. Wei said he saw himself becoming an evangelist for greater freedom and democratic reform in China using the Voice of America, Radio Free Asia and other news media that would enable him to build an audience among the Chinese.
Many people in China do not recognize his name because it is banned from being mentioned by state-run news outlets and because he has been imprisoned almost continuously since March 1979.
"Most of the Chinese people would very much like to hear other voices," he said. 
"Otherwise they would not know that they have choices. 
That is why this is very important."
He quarreled good-naturedly in the interview at being labeled a dissident. 
"Most of the Chinese people all want democracy," he asserted. 
"And the people who are different are just this little group of ruling elites of the Chinese Communist Party, so they are really the dissidents."
In the news conference, he exhorted China's democracy forces, saying, "You should not pay attention to the immediate low tide, because after a low tide there is always a high tide that follows."
The State Department earlier this year reported that political dissent in China had effectively been completely stifled through a campaign of repressive measures including jailings and forced exiles.
Mr. Wei's entrance this morning into a large hall at the New York Public Library packed by waiting reporters and well-wishers was greeted by applause and cheers. 
The 47-year-old activist wore a brown corduroy jacket and a red plaid shirt, his uneven prison crew cut looking in need of a trim.
In an opening statement, Mr. Wei thanked the "people and governments around the world that have made enormous efforts to press the Chinese Government for the release of political prisoners" and admonished those who already live in freedom in the world not to become complacent about those who do not.
"Democracy and freedom are among the loftiest ideals of humanity, and they are the most sacred rights of mankind," he said. 
"Those who already enjoy democracy, liberty and human rights, in particular, should not allow their own personal happiness to numb them into forgetting the many others who are still struggling against tyranny, slavery and poverty, and all of those who are suffering from unimaginable forms of oppression, exploitation and massacres."
Though he evaded questions during the news conference about what message he would deliver to Mr. Clinton, during the interview afterward, Mr. Wei was emphatic that he would seek continued pressure from Washington and other Western capitals for improvement of rights conditions in China and the release of prisoners.
The only reason Chinese leaders have ever engaged in dialogue over the country's internal human rights conditions has been pressure from the United States and other countries whose markets have become important export destinations for Chinese goods and a source of technology for China's modernization.
Mr. Wei said he would like to visit all parts of the United States in the coming months. 
While in New York, he has been assigned a New York police detective as a bodyguard. 
Columbia University and the University of California at Berkeley have offered him office space and living quarters to pursue academic studies and pro-democracy work.
His immediate plans are to write a book about the beatings, abuse and psychological pressure that the Chinese prison authorities used to try to break him and, ultimately, to force him into exile by refusing him further medical treatment in prison.
Among the techniques were shutting off heat in his cell, using other inmates to torment or beat him and housing him in a cell where lights were left on 24 hours a day as a way of denying him sleep.
Mr. Wei was released from Jidong Prison, about 150 miles southeast of Beijing. 
"When I was a prisoner there in 1989, they used to brag that they were the largest salt factory in Asia, exporting to Japan and many other countries. 
But when I returned in 1993, I asked them if they were still exporting salt to other countries, and they denied it."
Mr. Wei indicated that international criticism of China's use of prison labor for exported products had caused the prison authorities to change their story.
He said that if he becomes active as an opposition figure in the United States, he is concerned that the Communist authorities might retaliate against members of his family left behind in China.
"I am concerned about their security," he said at the news conference. 
"They have suffered a lot. 
But there are hundreds of millions of Chinese who have been oppressed, and I am concerned about them equally."
Beijing's leaders are apparently calculating that with Mr. Wei out of the country, his threat to rekindle a democracy movement has been neutralized and his effectiveness as a political troublemaker will be minimized by his distance from China.
But rights groups based in the United States, with Mr. Wei's cooperation, already appear to be developing a strategy to give him a new voice in China, something he has scarcely had since 1978-79, when he pasted his pro-democracy essays on a stretch of wall in central Beijing that became known as the Democracy Wall.
Among Mr. Wei's first interviews yesterday were with correspondents for the Chinese-language service of the Voice of America, Radio Free Asia and a major Chinese daily newspaper in Hong Kong. 
He was also interviewed by The New York Times.
For a man who has spent long years in solitary confinement and watched as more than a dozen teeth dropped out from years of malnutrition because of a poor prison diet, Mr. Wei seemed to enjoy parrying the questions of a New York news conference.
Asked about his views on Taiwan and Tibet, where there are strong independence movements with support in the United States, Mr. Wei was careful not to challenge China's claims of sovereignty over both territories.
"On Tibet," he said, "this is a rather complex question. 
I don't agree with the Government's policy of oppressing and killing Tibetans and carrying out the destruction of Tibetan culture, but as to how to resolve this issue, I think that calm Chinese and Tibetans should sit down and figure out a good solution."
Asked to tell the greatest lesson he learned from his 16 years of imprisonment for the views he expressed during the Democracy Wall period, Mr. Wei said: "I have learned many things in prison, but the most important thing is that for a human being, there is no difficulty that cannot be overcome. 
You just have to rely on yourself and you can get through anything."
The man most responsible for Mr. Wei's jailing was Deng Xiaoping, the Chinese leader who emerged in the years after the death of Mao in 1976 and opened an era of economic reform that is turning the nation of 1.2 billion into an Asian powerhouse.
Mr. Wei's trenchant essays on Democracy Wall pointedly criticized Deng for failing to carry through with his promises of democracy as part of the program for China's modernization. 
When Mr. Wei called Deng a dictator in early 1979, he was arrested and Democracy Wall was torn down.
Mr. Wei said he sent a letter of condolence to Deng's family when the 92-year-old leader died in February.
"If he could have expanded reform to the political arena," Mr. Wei said, "then -- even if he had abused me even worse than he has -- I still would not hate him."
Mr. Wei took questions for a little more than 40 minutes at the library hall and then asked politely that he be excused because he was feeling tired and dizzy.

file: Ecologists Improve Production in Chinese Farming Village.txt
text:
ï»¿
BY examining the flow of nutrients and energy in a typical Chinese farming village, scientists have found ways to increase production while reducing dependence on synthetic fertilizers.
In a paper published recently in The Journal of Applied Ecology, the scientists described an experiment conducted by Dr. James Y. Guo, now at the University of Singapore, that treated Zhang Zhuang, a small farming village in Jiangsu Province, as an ecological system that could be enhanced through proper management.
The village grew rice in the summer and wheat in the winter. 
The more than 2,300 residents also raised more than 1,500 pigs a year for their own consumption and for sale. 
The village, typical of many in China, had been a self-sustaining farming system for more than 2,000 years.
But a population growth of one-quarter of 1 percent a year for 40 years put a strain on the farming system. 
Even small crop fluctuations caused tremendous problems for the people. 
They turned to synthetic fertilizer rich in nitrogen, the use of which doubled over a 10-year period. 
And fertilizer leaching and soil erosion damaged the environment, particularly the fish ponds and water channels running through the village.
Dr. Guo's team grew grasses in the land around the fish ponds and planted water vegetation in the irrigation canals. 
The team also dug out the fish ponds to bring in more light so more algae would grow. 
The new vegetation was fed to the fish and the pigs.
The researchers also made an effort to recycle the wastes from the crops, pigs and fish to fertilize the fields. 
And they dug wastes from the bottom of the ponds to add to this manure mixture.
There was no substantial difference in the amount of crops produced or the number or size of the pigs raised. 
But the yield of fish increased 370 percent in the deepened ponds. 
And the village cut back on its use of synthetic fertilizer by 46 percent, and was able to eat better and sell more produce as a result of the new system.
"It is an analysis of traditional efforts that reminds us that it is possible to have intensive agriculture which is totally balanced and which can, if properly managed, go on for 5,000 years," said Dr. Anthony D. Bradshaw, a retired professor from the University of Liverpool in England who published the study with Dr. Guo. "I believe that if we're really going to understand our environment, we've got to do much more of it."
Less detailed but larger-scale studies have been made recently in various regions of China. 
One team of researchers from the Institute of Applied Ecology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences looked at the plains of northeastern China, where soil erosion and water shortages have become severe problems since the 1950's.
The group, led by Dr. Dazhong Wen, studied the possibilities of rehabilitating the region in order to continue farming for its fast-growing population, which is expected to equal that of the United States within 20 years. 
The study outlines several areas where government regulations could help stem practices that are devastating the land.
The study calls for more crop rotation and more planting of different crops in alternate rows to counter insects and diseases. 
The researchers also recommend using minimum tillage techniques instead of deep plowing to ease soil erosion, and shallow irrigation for rice to conserve water. 
They also stress the need for using more organic fertilizer and combining farming with animal husbandry to make better use of the crop wastes, as in the Zhang Zhuang study.

file: Economic Scene_Players in the Asian crisis_ Are they up to the solution_.txt
text:
ï»¿
WHILE the pronouncements from the Pacific summit meeting in Vancouver were short on substance, the subtext was clear enough: If the ailing Asian tigers are prepared to let free markets work their healing wonders, the industrial powers will do what is necessary to prevent collateral damage.
That message is certainly reassuring, and seemingly credible: By the benchmark of say, Latin America in 1982 or Eastern Europe in 1991, Asia is in decent shape. 
But it is far from clear that the folks who make the rules will do their part in smoothing the road back to rapid growth. 
Indeed, there are reasons to doubt they have the policy sense and political fortitude to prevent the crisis from deepening.
Consider the major players:
CHINA Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia and South Korea are all counting on currency depreciation to invigorate their exports and service foreign debts. 
But increased foreign sales are likely to come at the expense of Chinese exports because China's currency, the yuan, has appreciated 25 percent against the dollar since 1994. 
If China responds by devaluing the yuan, it could set off another wave of currency instability.
China still has some leeway. 
With $130 billion in reserves, little short-term debt to foreigners and currency-conversion limits that inhibit capital flight, speculators cannot force Beijing to devalue.
But sooner or later Chinese leaders will have to let the yuan fall. 
"China's underlying problems -- an overvalued currency and an insolvent banking system -- are exactly the same as Korea's and Thailand's," says Nick Lardy, an economist at the Brookings Institution.
JAPAN Unlike the rest of Asia, Japan is a net creditor to the world with big trade and current account surpluses -- and thus needs no external help to solve its financial crisis. 
But thus far, Japan has shown little will to dig its way out by paying off depositors in insolvent banks or by forcing hundreds of moribund companies into bankruptcy. 
Nor does the Government seem inclined to try a dose of Keynesian fiscal stimulus, for fear of running a bigger budget deficit. 
As a result there is little prospect that Japan will escape another recession.
Would a chronically ailing Japan lend tens of billions of dollars to financial institutions elsewhere in Asia when the Government cannot manage a domestic financial fix?
Would a deeply depressed Japanese economy be in any position to absorb more exports from South Korea, China and Southeast Asia?
Who's kidding whom?
UNITED STATES The International Monetary Fund will have to come up with $20 billion -- and, most likely, two or three times that amount -- to allow South Korea to convert its short-term foreign currency debts into manageable long-term debt. 
But after financial rescues in Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines, the cupboard is no longer well stocked and Washington is showing no signs of renewed generosity. 
"Congress refused to bail out the 'crooks' in Indonesia," noted John Makin, a senior fellow in the American Enterprise Institute's Asian Studies Program. 
"Why would they bail out the 'crooks' in Korea?"
Unlike Japan, the United States is in a position to buy the surplus consumer goods spewing out of Asia. 
Indeed, cheap imports are just what the doctor ordered to prevent the American economy from overheating. 
But what's good for America is not necessarily good for General Motors -- or 100 other industries that must compete with imports. 
And after the failure to pass legislation that would give the President enhanced authority to negotiate trade agreements, it is a safe bet that Congress will counter a ballooning trade deficit with protectionism.
I.M.F. On paper the International Monetary Fund is a creature of the major economic powers; in practice, its bureaucracy runs the show. 
And in the case of Asia, that authority could prove counterproductive.
Long used to dealing with the problems of basket-case economies with low savings rates and little fiscal or monetary discipline, the fund is demanding a balanced budget and high interest rates as the price of assistance in refinancing Asia's external debts. 
But Steve Radelet, an economist at the Institute for International Development at Harvard, argues that in Korea as well as Indonesia, the problems are institutional, not fiscal. 
"It makes no sense to ask for austerity from countries that have excess production capacity and are still saving 30 percent of their income," he added.
The global economy is surely less vulnerable to a deflationary panic than it was in 1930. 
But the sequence of events in Asia -- stock and property market crashes, followed by bank failures and competitive currency devaluations -- is eerily similar. 
And while economists have a better understanding of how to contain such a crisis, policy makers have yet to prove they have mastered the situation. 
"They're whistling in the dark, hoping it will all go away," Mr. Lardy concludes.

file: Economic Scene_Should Clinton embrace the China trade deal_ Some say yes.txt
text:
ï»¿
GRAB it. 
So say many economists, referring to the bold trade deal that China offered the United States in April and President Clinton rejected in what many deem a serious foreign policy blunder. 
Mr. Clinton can reverse course when he meets President Jiang Zemin on Sunday in Australia.
China wants to enter the World Trade Organization in time for the group's next meeting in Seattle in November, when the member nations are expected to embark on a new round of world trade talks. 
But before China can join, it needs the approval of Mr. Clinton and Congress. 
So it offered huge "concessions" on nearly every front.
Concessions is the lingo of tradespeak. 
But the term is wholly misleading. 
China's promise to open its economy to foreign goods and investment would serve its own self-interest yet would be largely irrelevant to the economic fortunes of the United States. 
Some concession.
Critics make three arguments for rejecting the offer. 
Delay could achieve better terms in the future. 
The deal's nice-sounding terms are unenforceable. 
And China's entry into the trade group would flood American markets with cheap textiles and apparel.
But judging from an analysis of Daniel H. Rosen and his colleagues at the Institute for International Economics, the first criticism appears weak, the second misleading and the third misguided.
The precise terms of China's offer remain unpublished, though the Administration published a summary. 
The breadth of the offer is stunning. 
China would drastically cut tariffs to levels less than those of most United States trade partners. 
It would eliminate export subsidies, phase out quotas on industrial products and comply immediately with World Trade Organization rules for protecting foreign investors and intellectual property.
China also agreed to phase out regulations that restrict foreign companies from importing, exporting, wholesaling and retailing. 
The offer would permit foreign companies to buy substantial stakes in insurance and telecommunications companies. 
China also agreed to have its state-owned enterprises make purchases on nondiscriminatory terms, based solely on price, quality and other commercial considerations.
Jeffrey Schott of the institute said that these terms were "substantially more liberal than those the United States had hoped to get out of negotiations and substantially more liberal than those which a number of existing W.T.O. members, like India, currently adhere to. 
You can't say that the terms of the agreement don't measure up."
Greg Mastel of the New American Foundation, a prominent critic, says that the deal is deficient on telecommunications and financial services. 
He has a point. 
There is, for example, no firm provision to eliminate nonperforming loans from banks, which serve as disguised subsidies to state-owned enterprises. 
This omission raises questions about China's commitment to run its state-owned enterprises on a commercial basis.
Mr. Mastel also criticizes the deal because, he says, it cannot be enforced. 
China is not, he warned, "a rule-based society" that makes decisions in ways that can be monitored and challenged. 
He points to China's repeated violations of patent and copyright protections.
But here the Administration must ask, what is the alternative?
In the absence of membership, China could continue many of its protectionist ways with impunity. 
But as a member, China is subject to the trade group's disciplinary process that has proven to be impartial and unflinching.
The United States would lose the right to impose unilateral trade sanctions against China once it joins the group. 
But the United States would gain international backing for sanctions so that every dispute does not turn into a bilateral foreign policy spat. 
Also, China would be responsible for meeting market-opening commitments that go well beyond anything the United States can now demand.
Critics point to the fact that as a member of the World Trade Organization, China would escape restrictions now in place on its exports of textiles and apparel to the United States. 
But Marcus Noland of the institute estimates that most Chinese sales here come at the expense of imports from other countries, not American manufacturers. 
Indeed, the institute estimates that American exports to China under the trade deal would rise by about $3 billion. 
Imports from China would rise by slightly more, so the overall effect on the $8 trillion American economy would be minute.
For the most part, the United States already provides China nondiscriminatory access. 
So why does China fight for admission to a club whose benefits it largely enjoys already?
Prime Minister Zhu Rongji apparently needs the weight of international commitments to help overcome domestic opposition to his ambitious plan to drive his economy away from state controls and toward markets. 
That would seem to be an ambition that Mr. Clinton would want to propel rather than sabotage.

file: Economic Scene_The Chinese way_ spend out of trouble like Keynesians.txt
text:
ï»¿
JOHN MAYNARD KEYNES may be out of fashion in the West. 
But in one of the odder twists to the unfolding Asian crisis, his prophets have resurfaced in Beijing.
To keep the Chinese economy out of recession -- and to prevent the urban proletariat from taking to the barricades -- China's pragmatic Communist leadership is calling for a heady dose of fiscal stimulus that would have made Keynes proud.
Acknowledging that fiscal intervention is needed to sustain annual growth of more than 8 percent is one thing; delivering on that promise is quite another for the Chinese Government. 
For even if the early reports have exaggerated the amount that China will spend on roads, housing and other public works, any significant increase in outlays is bound to complicate its plans to modernize the half-socialist, half-capitalist economy.
"There's just no easy way out of their predicament," said Nicholas Lardy, a specialist in the Chinese economy at the Brookings Institution.
At first glance, the case for spending is strong. 
China's ability to modernize has been constrained in recent years by electricity and transportation bottlenecks. 
And the timing is propitious, since spending could offset economic pain. 
The combination of currency depreciation and falling output in the rest of Asia is widely expected to reduce the demand for Chinese exports by about $20 billion this year. 
Meanwhile, the continuing effort to trim China's bloated state enterprises is expected to push several million people out of jobs.
Rather than accept a sharp drop in employment and growth, Chinese leaders have said they will increase spending, with $750 billion to $1 trillion devoted to new construction over three years. 
Even by the widest definition of infrastructure spending, the Government would have to increase outlays by 60 percent to hit the $750 billion mark -- virtually impossible short of a total mobilization of the economy in the manner of Chairman Mao's Great Leap Forward.
But even a 10 to 20 percent increase, as is deemed plausible by Wing Thye Woo, an economist at the University of California at Davis, would conflict with China's other policy goals. 
The only practical way to increase spending rapidly is to funnel the cash to state enterprises -- many of which are industrial dinosaurs with a long history of wasting resources. 
"All the politics says the Government will give the money to China's equivalent of the Korean chaebols," Mr. Woo said.
Moreover, new public spending is likely to displace money that would have been used to recapitalize China's insolvent state banks. 
Bank reform can wait. 
The banks can easily meet their current obligations to foreigners, and domestic depositors have no place else to go with their money. 
But the longer the delay, the longer it will take to create the disciplined, efficient market for capital that the economy desperately needs to sustain growth.
China could try to both recapitalize the banks and prime the fiscal pump by opting to run a big deficit. 
On paper, the risks would be modest: With the cost of living actually falling in recent months, inflation is not a major worry. 
And with a very small Government debt, China would have little difficulty selling bonds to finance spending. 
But Jeffrey Sachs, the director of Harvard's Institute for International Development, warns that China's finances are more precarious than the official numbers suggest.
The state banks' bad debts, which may be the equivalent of several hundred billion dollars, are effectively part of the national debt. 
Worse, what appears to be a nearly balanced budget is actually deeply in the red because the official expenditures do not include subsidies to state enterprises disguised as bank loans. 
"China is sitting on a mountain of fiscal problems already," Mr. Sachs concluded.
All this points toward a strategy of big talk and modest action. 
China's leaders, whose political legitimacy is tightly linked to their competence as economic managers, cannot afford to look as if they are ignoring rising unemployment and insolvent banks. 
By the same token, they cannot afford to risk China's hard-won reputation as fiscally conservative -- a reputation that has prevented capital flight from Hong Kong and allowed the newly installed Government to hold the line on exchange rates.
Beijing appears to have undertaken the delicate task of having it both ways. 
"These guys know what they're doing," argued Lawrence Kreicher, chief economist for Alliance Capital.

file: ECONOMIC VIEW_Lighting Up A Lesson In China Trade.txt
text:
ï»¿
WANDERING through a flea market in Shanghai earlier this year with Craig Smith, The Times's new correspondent there, I stopped at a stall that was selling cheap cigarette lighters with pictures of Mao Zedong pasted on them. 
Flick one open, and it plays the tune of "The East Is Red."
I don't smoke, but I couldn't resist buying a handful.
Not far away, another merchant offered hundreds of hand-painted posters from the days of the Cultural Revolution. 
I bought one dated 1976, showing a smiling Mao leading a parade of workers and students into the promised land. 
We bargained a bit before settling on a price of about $5.
Say what you will about capitalism, but you must admit it has a marvelous way of turning even the most violent and earthshaking upheavals into safe, salable kitsch.
And that, above all, is why it is worth continuing to encourage Beijing to move along the path toward freer markets, private investment and open trade. 
Karl Marx (remember him?) said it as well as anybody in, of all places, the Communist Manifesto:
"The bourgeoisie, by the rapid improvement of all instruments of production, by the immensely facilitated means of communication, draws all nations, even the most barbarian, into civilization. 
The cheap prices of its commodities are the heavy artillery with which it batters down all Chinese walls, with which it forces the barbarians' intensely obstinate hatred of foreigners to capitulate."
What does this have to do with today's debate over China?
Plenty.
The choice facing Congress this week over granting China what is called "permanent normal trade relations" -- part of a deal to admit China to the World Trade Organization -- turns on conflicting views of how to best induce change in China's authoritarian regime.
On one side -- opposed to normalizing trade -- are those who argue that Congress should vote every year on China's trade status, thus maintaining outside pressure on Beijing to respond to complaints of human rights abuses. 
The annual vote should not be given up, they say, because it is Washington's only stick for persuading China to ease repression and to free dissidents. 
Treating China as a normal trading partner, they say, will just entrench the current regime and encourage its belligerence.
Opposing that view are those who believe that change inside China can exert greater leverage for reform than any diplomatic pressure. 
Through broader trade and contact with the outside world, the Chinese people will be exposed to the full range of Western life, from the sublime to the ridiculous. 
In the end, the temptation will prove irresistible. 
Treat China as a normal country, this side argues, and it will eventually turn into one.
"Openness is a two-way street," Nicholas Lardy, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, said last week in a telephone interview from Beijing. 
"Already there are thousands of foreigners living in China and interacting on a daily basis across a very broad spectrum. 
That will only grow as China joins the W.T.O. 
At the same time, tens of thousands of the most promising Chinese have gone to the West as students. 
They've come back -- often to very high positions in government, banking and business -- changed for good."
I VISITED China for the first time this year. 
But even without an earlier point of reference, it was clear that though the economy remains very basic, the country has changed immensely in the last two decades.
As recently as the early 1980's, nearly everybody in Shanghai, the most Westernized city in China, still wore the famous blue Mao suits. 
Only top officials had cars; everyone else pedaled bicycles or rode buses. 
Lights were dim. 
Public restaurants and private enterprises barely existed. 
Architecture seemed frozen in a pre-World War II time warp. 
Today, everything is different: jeans and khakis are ubiquitous; cars and taxis compete with bikes on crowded streets; glass-sheathed skyscrapers abound; Shanghai throbs with activity day and night.
"We tend to forget," Mr. Lardy said, "how much change has already occurred."
As private enterprise spreads and markets open to real competition from domestic and foreign companies alike, tens of millions of Chinese are shedding their dependence on the state. 
They are richer and freer. 
It's not democracy, but it is the first step toward a genuinely pluralistic society.
And that is just the beginning.
"China now feels competitive heat across continents and oceans," Robert Wright wrote in a recent issue of The New Republic. 
"It must face the same logic the rest of the world faces. 
In the age of the Internet, even more than in the age of industry and print, granting enough liberty for cutting-edge prosperity while denying political liberty is a tall order."
