A majority of Senate Republicans today urged their leader, Trent Lott, to delay until September a vote on a major bill establishing permanent normal trade relations with China, an approach that Democrats and business leaders said could imperil the measure.
Mr. Lott said he had made no decision, and renewed his promise to try to cut through several procedural and political hurdles and bring up the measure by the end of this month, before Congress adjourns for its five-week summer recess.
But in his strongest signal yet that imminent passage of the China trade bill was in jeopardy, Mr. Lott told reporters that waiting until September "is not as big a problem as some people fear."
Business leaders and President Clinton have pressed the Senate to follow the House's lead, and quickly pass a bill that would end Congress's annual review of China's trade status, before it gets caught up in election-year politics. 
In a telephone conversation today, Mr. Clinton again asked Mr. Lott to schedule a vote by month's end.
Supporters of the bill have at least 70 votes, more than enough to defeat a filibuster. 
Even so, the final vote has been delayed since the House passed the measure in May because Mr. Lott has given a higher priorty to passing several spending bills. 
Also complicating speedy passage is the prospect of several amendments that could force the measure back to the House for a second vote.
But Democrats accused Republicans of postponing action on the trade bill to extract concessions onspending bills and to allow an issue that divides Democrats to fester on through the party's nominating convention in August.
"Delay is danger," said Senator Max S. Baucus, a Montana Democrat. 
"This is putting politics above policy."
But at their private weekly luncheon today, several Senate Republicans recommended that Mr. Lott use the remaining two and a half weeks before the recess to focus on top-priority tax and spending bills, and set a date in September for the China trade bill vote.
"I don't think it makes a difference if we wait until September," said Senator Rod Grams, a Minnesota Republican who three weeks ago had urged Mr. Lott to hold a vote by July 4. 
"We need to vote on it, but I know we have other priorities."
Unlike supporters in the House, who fought for votes until the final minutes, backers of the bill in the Senate have always had the votes to lock up a large victory. 
But supporters want to approve a clean version of the House bill, free from amendments that would force the measure back to the House for a potentially volatile second vote.
Several senators, including Jesse Helms of North Carolina and Phil Gramm of Texas, both Republicans, as well as Paul Wellstone, a Minnesota Democrat, have signaled their intention to offer amendments on China's record on human rights, religious liberties and labor conditions.
But the biggest hurdle has been a measure sponsored by Senators Fred Thompson, a Tennessee Republican, and Robert G. Torricelli, a New Jersey Democrat.
Their measure would require the administration to monitor China's record on the spread of nuclear weapons. 
It would impose automatic sanctions on China if there is "credible evidence" of exports of certain types of prohibited weaponry.
Mr. Clinton would have discretion to waive some penalties, but others would be automatic. 
Nonetheless, the administration and business leaders have opposed the measure as unnecessary, and harmful to United States diplomacy and American companies that trade with China.
"If the Senate is on record with this harsh rhetoric and these extraordinarily harmful sanctions, I think it could seriously poison the well" with China, said Senator Tom Daschle of South Dakota, the Democratic leader.
Mr. Daschle said he might be able to support the antiproliferation measure if significant changes were made, including removing the bill's focus on China.
In response, Mr. Thompson said today he has dropped sanctions affecting food and medicine. 
Republican aides said they were also modifying other provisions, including the steps that triggered sanctions, to appease critics.
Mr. Thompson has insisted that the Senate vote on his measure before taking up the China trade bill. 
He has threatened to offer it as an amendment if that does not happen.
In the Senate, process is important, and Mr. Lott said he was trying to work out all the competing parties and proposals. 
"The Senate is going to pass China P.N.T.R.," Mr. Lott said. 
"It's not a question of 'if.'
It's a question of when and in what condition."

file: GARDEN NOTEBOOK_The Global Backyard_ Weird Is In.txt
text:
ï»¿
JOHN TREXLER, a plant connoisseur in Boylston, Mass., is obsessed with Gunnera tinctoria, a Chilean plant with enormous crinkled leaves and large furry buds that looks like something H. G. Wells could have dreamed up for "The War of the Worlds."
So what if it has to spend the rugged New England winter under pine needles and a whisky barrel to survive?
Tony Avent, a nurseryman from Raleigh, N.C., had his heart snatched by a foreigner at the bottom of a cliff in China. 
"It was a six-foot-tall clumping perennial loaded with snapdragonlike flowers," Mr. Avent marveled. 
"Each flower had a wine-purple upper lip and a pure white lower lip."
The call of the wild hellebore, a perverse little plant that blooms in the winter, has lured an English mathematician named Will McLewin to risk his life collecting plants in war-torn Bosnia and Croatia. 
"People tell us we're mad, but it's no more dangerous, I suppose, than the Bronx," said Mr. McLewin, who now grows 5,000 hellebores (both species and hybrids) in his experimental nursery near Manchester, England.
Weird and wonderful plants are tumbling into gardens at a velocity not seen since the Victorian era, when intrepid explorers roamed the mountains of China in search of the elusive dove tree.
Explorers from North Carolina are going to southern China for exotic ferns and salvias that can stand up to the Deep South's heat and humidity. 
Chicago horticulturalists are heading for Siberia for oaks hardy enough to survive a Midwestern winter. 
A Denver plantsman climbed the Drakensberg Mountains in South Africa and returned with brilliantly colored ice plants and fuchsias perfectly suited to the dry, temperate climate of Colorado.
The spring crop of cutting-edge catalogues has it all -- from natives, like a five-foot, hot-pink Mississippi phlox that doesn't mildew, to erotic-looking gingers from Japan and six-foot striped cannas from South Africa.
"Weird is in," said Ken Druse, the garden writer and photographer, who gardens rather fanatically in both Brooklyn and New Jersey. 
He has liked weird plants since childhood, when his nature-loving mother used to show him jack-in-the-pulpits in the wilds of New Jersey and tell him, "Never pick one."
But now he can order its far more exotic cousins -- like Japanese cobra lilies, with strange whips extending from their colorful mouths -- from creme de la creme catalogues showcasing these "it" plants of the year.
Variegation -- white or yellow or even pink infiltrating green leaves -- is hot, hot, hot. 
"I'm desperate for a variegated horseradish," said Mr. Druse, referring to Armoracia rusticana Variegata, a mutation of an Asian native. 
Its scrambled genes produce three-foot crinkly white leaves with green blotches. 
This from the man who fanned the native plant movement three years ago, urging gardeners to cordon off all exotics (in botanical lingo, foreign plants), as if in quarantine on Ellis Island.
Mr. Druse's latest book, "The Collector's Garden" (Clarkson Potter, 1996), leaps his own fence and declares: "If it's rare, we want it. 
If it's tiny and impossible to grow, we've got to have it. 
If it's brown, looks dead and has black flowers, we'll kill for it."
While only a few catalogues offer these rarities at the moment, the ones that are easily propagated through cuttings and tissue culture will probably show up in good local nurseries in the next few years. 
Meanwhile, orders are soaring.
"Sales have gone up 700 percent over the past five years," said Mr. Avent, who sells thousands of native and exotic plants through his mail-order company, Plant Delights Nursery, in Raleigh. 
The odd ducks -- you can tell them by their names -- call to their own soulmates.
Five years ago, Mr. Avent sold two voodoo lilies. 
"Now they're selling in the hundreds," he said. 
"Even the $200 one sold out last year."
The $200 voodoo lily, Amorphophallus titanum, from Indonesia, sports a lone red 15-foot flower that smells like rotting meat (it's pollinated by flies).
What's going on?
Maybe it's the confidence of maturity, like having a martini and not apologizing (and offering one to your voodoo lily).
Ten years ago, American gardeners were suffering through adolescence, throwing out all those fluffy delphiniums from Mother England while discovering the sturdy natives growing in oblivion in their own ditches and bogs. 
They declared a holy war against invaders like bamboo and ornamental grasses.
But then even the die-hards began to feel a little silly. 
They missed their Chinese witch hazels and Japanese maples. 
Then they saw their first wild Japanese ginger and lost their hearts, all over again, to foreigners.
And there's always some Marco Polo out there willing to risk life and limb to collect one.
"We were in a small wooden boat in the Yellow Sea heading toward an island off the coast of Korea when a typhoon blew up," said Barry Yinger, a plant hunter with a research nursery in southern Pennsylvania, who has made at least 40 collecting trips to Japan. 
"The motor conked out, and the wind and waves were taking us toward the rocks. 
We were being blown toward a rocky cliff. 
There were six people in the boat, and only about three could swim, so I was trying to decide which one I liked well enough to try to save, when we got the motor started."
Mr. Yinger has brought about 75 species of asarums, or gingers, back from Japan, and they are slowly entering the catalogues. 
These plants, with their mottled green leaves and strange flowers, make beautiful ground covers. 
But they cannot be grown without knowledge and care.
The explosion of interest in exotic plants reminds Mr. Yinger of his grandmother's day. 
"My grandmother grew up in a time when people were more involved with plants -- the ferns and grasses, the old-fashioned perennials, the butterfly bushes, the trumpet flowers and brugmansias -- that are popular again today," he said.
It was also an era of great plant explorations, with lilacs, kiwis, flowering cherries, lilies, mimosas and all kinds of other ornamentals flooding in from Asia. 
All that was interrupted by World War I, the Depression and World War II.
Mr. Yinger made his first trip to Japan as a student from the University of Maryland more than 20 years ago. 
He checked into a rooming house, and on his second day he went to the neighborhood bathhouse.
"I went into the dressing room, and there, on a big table, was a display of bonsai trees of Prunus mume in bloom," he said, referring to tiny apricot trees. 
"And there was a man who looked like a garbage-truck driver, very dirty from his day's work, with his boy, and they were walking around the table while he explained what was going on. 
This was an epiphany for me, how different Japanese society was for men who loved plants. 
Because I grew up at a time when most people thought it was not quite normal for boys to be interested in plants."
This increased worldliness has not slowed interest in native plants; it has just broadened gardeners' ideas of what is possible.
When Mr. Avent, the Raleigh nurseryman, and his wife, Michelle, started their first garden there almost 20 years ago, they didn't have much to choose from. 
"In North Carolina, there were about 20 basic plants," Mr. Avent said. 
Now, Plant Delights carries 5,500 plants, from 200 hostas and 18 lobelias (make-overs of the American red cardinal flower) to a six-foot green-and-white striped leaf called Canna Stuttgart. 
That beauty made its way from South Africa to Germany to the Brooklyn Botanic Garden and on down to Raleigh.
"I still love natives," said Kim Hawks, who started Niche Gardens in Chapel Hill, N.C., 11 years ago to encourage the use of forgotten American plants. 
"It goes hand in hand with ecology issues. 
If you're doing a wetlands planting, you're going to use natives of that region."
But, she added, "bringing other plants from other parts of the world gives us a bigger gene pool to draw from."
Last fall she fell in love with the wild landscape of southern China. 
"The mountains were just awesome, very jagged and ancient and snow-capped," she said. 
"We saw peonies and buddleia, ligularia, rodgersia."
Ms. Hawks returned home with 500 seeds and 100 plants and is testing them out in her garden.
As for that brave bloomer, the hellebore, Mr. McLewin, the Englishman, continues to collect seeds in Bosnia and Croatia, and his plants are showing up in the Heronswood Nursery in Kingston, Wash.
He lost his mathematician's heart to the species about 11 years ago, driven to understand its complexity before the rarest ones disappear. 
"I can look at a thousand hellebores in one wild colony," he said, "and every one is different."
Four years ago, he came upon a red hellebore in Eastern Slavonia, which he says is not available anywhere. 
There were only three red ones, so he didn't dig up even one. 
"The next year, we went back and a new road had been built," he said. 
"The whole colony was gone."
In Colorado, Panayoti Kelaidis, the rock-alpine garden curator and plants-evaluation coordinator at the Denver Botanic Garden, made a beeline for South Africa as soon as apartheid laws were abolished.
About 12,000 feet up, he found a little succulent ice plant with shimmering yellow, daisylike flowers called Delosperma nubigenum, which means "where the clouds are born" in Latin. 
The drought-tolerant wildling not only survives frost, but also turns an attractive red in the cold and back to green again come spring, So, back home in Denver, it's all the rage as a ground cover.
South Africa "has one-tenth of all the plants in the world," Mr. Kelaidis said, adding, "It's Mecca for temperate botanists."
In Massachusetts, Mr. Trexler, the executive director of the Worcester County Horticultural Society, has spent 11 years building the Tower Hill Botanic Garden in Boylston out of a 132-acre farm, which has hundreds of specimens rugged enough for a New England winter.
But this man of the world wants dessert. 
"You want all those wonderful sweet pastries," Mr. Trexler said, "like the epimediums and the hellebores."
(And that Gunnera tinctoria, which he coddles at the first sign of frost like a baby in a blanket.)
It's that growing-up thing again. 
"As you get more mature, you get more uninhibited," he said, "more baroque, whether it's art or music, or gardening, and it's due to being an older society and an older individual."
Is that how you explain the return of the dreaded coleus?
That red leaf from Grandmother's garden and, before that, from Java. 
It has returned to haunt us in ruffles and hot colors: chartreuse, screaming yellow, hot pink, variegated, even black!
"It's like these retro clothing fashions coming back from 1975," said Ken Selody, who grows 100 different kinds of coleuses at his nursery, Atlock Farm, in Somerset, N.J. 
"I guarantee some fashion designer who sees a newly planted park -- where everything's replaced with coleus -- is going to put those colors on people's backs, and you'll see them all seated around a dinner table."
Give them all martinis and pass around the Rolaids.
Â 
Relax, You Don't Have to Travel
Catalogues from these nurseries have become bibles for those in search of good native and exotic plants.
Â 
FORESTFARM -- 990 Tetherow Road, Williams, Ore. 
97544; (541)846-7269; $4. 
It has 7,000 trees and shrubs, like clethra, fothergilla, ceanothus and, from China, the fragrant seven-sons plant (Heptacodium miconioides).
Â 
HERONSWOOD NURSERY -- 7530 Northeast 288th Street, Kingston, Wash. 
98346; (360) 297-4172; $4. 
This nursery has 2,400 plants, like chamaecyparis trees, hydrangeas, hellebores, gunneras, coleuses and cobra lilies.
Â 
NICHE GARDENS -- 1111 Dawson Road, Chapel Hill, N.C. 
27516; (919) 967-0078; $3. 
There are about 450 unusual native plants, like Baptisia Purple Smoke and Phlox paniculata Robert Poore, a mildew-resistant phlox.
Â 
PLANT DELIGHTS NURSERY -- 9241 Sauls Road, Raleigh, N.C. 
27603; (919) 772-4794; price printed on catalogue: "10 stamps or a box of chocolates."
There are 5,500 different plants, from cobra lilies to lobelias.
Â 
SISKIYOU RARE PLANT NURSERY -- 2825 Cummings Road, Medford, Ore. 
97501; (541) 772-6846; $3. 
It has 1,650 dwarf conifers, hardy perennials and alpine plants. 
Its cover girl is Zaluzianskya ovata (above), from South Africa.

file: GARDENING_Admiring Beauty That_s Only Skin Deep.txt
text:
ï»¿
FEBRUARY is the month when nearly everyone catches cabin fever. 
The cure?
A long walk on a fine day. 
During one of these walks, the birch trees were discovered. 
Oh, they had been growing in the park for many years. 
But they were never really seen until just a few days ago. 
They had no leaves to block the view; they just stood there with their long, high trunks glistening white in the sunshine.
This group of white, or paper, birch trees was mature enough so that their trunks had that clean chalky quality. 
The trees had several stems, which is a birch trait. 
The view was dramatic. 
And the tree count?
Maybe seven or more.
Displays such as this set the mood for the day. 
Surely there must be others to see. 
Not far from the birches was another handsome specimen with rather unusual bark. 
This one was a maple, the paperbark maple (Acer griseum). 
The park planter must have been intrigued with tree bark that suggested paper and so a small collection was started.
The paperbark maple was not the giant that most maples are. 
Later it was learned that this maple can be 20 to 25 feet tall, but most garden specimens are only about half that. 
The cinnamon-colored bark of this tree is its most spectacular asset. 
When the sun shines, it glistens. 
The bark peels off, too, in paper-thin sheets.
The plant explorer Ernest Wilson found this splendid tree growing in central China, and thanks to his efforts, the tree was introduced to this country. 
But until recently, it has almost been a horticultural secret. 
Paperbark maple is not the easiest specimen for nurseries to propagate. 
But more knowledgeable propagators are learning how and the tree is beginning to be found at nurseries.
Another relatively unknown shrub, stewartia, is planted more for its showy bark. 
It can be particularly spectacular now when there are no leaves in competition. 
Stewartia bark resembles that of the sycamore tree, but because the shrub is smaller in stature, the mottling is easier to see. 
The stewartia can be planted for its camellia-like flowers that appear in late summer.
Although several stewartia species are available, most of them are from Asia. 
But the mountain stewartia is a stalwart. 
This one is a native American species and is probably well known to those who may have hiked throughout the Carolina woods.
Although the stewartia is relatively disease-free, it has a bad reputation as being difficult to transplant. 
In these days of container-grown plants, home gardeners will have a better chance of success. 
When the plants are purchased in spring, select carefully. 
Have the nurseryman knock the plant out of the container to be sure that it does not have a serpentine collar of roots inside the pot. 
This would mean that the shrub has been in the container too long. 
A younger, actively growing specimen will be much easier to transfer to the home ground.
Just as showy on the landscape is the lacebark pine (Pinus bungeana). 
This one also resembles the sycamore, but in a more stately fashion. 
This pine needs a place of its own, preferably in an open sunny location where the soil drains well. 
The exfoliation does not occur in the very youngest trees although the bark will be interesting. 
When mature, the lacebark pine assumes the mottled effect of green-white-yellow-brown patches that are ever so handsome.
The lacebark pine was introduced from China, too, where it was first seen growing in a temple garden near Beijing. 
Although the tree was introduced in the 1840's, it has not gained the use it should have.
In the same category, a little-known elm tree deserves much more attention than it has been receiving. 
This one is the lacebark elm (Ulmus parvifolia). 
The first time I saw it, it boggled my mind. 
I never knew that such a handsome elm existed.
The United States Arboretum in Washington is introducing a fine selection of this elm, which it has named Ohio. 
The arboretum can supply a limited supply of budwood or rooted cuttings to qualified nurseries. 
More stock will be made available in the future as more nurseries tackle this one. 
At present only a limited number of cultivated varieties are on the market.
One cautionary note: Though this lacebark elm species is native to China, and sometimes called Chinese elm, it is not to be confused with a somewhat inferior elm species, Ulmus pumila, which is sold as the Chinese elm. 
(The need to know Latin binomials can be critical).
The lacebark elm is a big shade tree, as are all elms. 
But the distinctive character, its handsome bark, makes it particularly appealing. 
Thus far the tree has excellent resistance to the elm-leaf beetle and Dutch elm disease. 
And its future may be forthcoming because this elm also has the desirable vase-shaped crown.

text:
ï»¿
In a setback for the Clinton administration, the House Democratic leader, Richard A. Gephardt, intends to oppose granting China permanent normal trading privileges, several people familiar with his decision said today.
For months, Mr. Gephardt refused to say how he would vote, hesitating to worsen divisions among Democrats on the issue and jeopardize his greater goal of reclaiming the House this fall and becoming speaker.
He is expected to announce on Wednesday in St. Louis, his hometown, that alternatives to Congress's annual review of China's trading status fall short of giving lawmakers enough leverage over Beijing's behavior on human rights, religious tolerance and the environment.
The timing of the expected announcement is important, since the House began a two-week recess today, and during their time at home, undecided lawmakers will be the target of intense lobbying and advertising campaigns from both sides.
The Democratic leader is also expected to tell his rank-and-file to vote their consciences and the best interests of their districts. 
That would free some of them to vote for the pact, strengthening them in campaigns against pro-trade Republicans this fall.
Both sides say the House vote, scheduled for the week of May 22, is too close to call. 
The Senate is considered certain to back the change.
The vote on China's trade status will determine to what degree America benefits from China's expected entry into the World Trade Organization.
Mr. Gephardt's decision is a victory for the coalition of labor, environmental and human rights groups, and their allies on Capitol Hill, who oppose the measure as an undeserved reward to a repressive regime.
"I never had any doubt that Dick would come down on the right side of the issue, where his heart is," said Representative Peter A. DeFazio, an Oregon Democrat who opposes permanent normal trade status for China.
It also complicates President Clinton's efforts to rally dozens of uncommitted Democrats to support one of his most important remaining foreign policy goals. 
Given Mr. Gephardt's stature, his position could give wavering Democrats political cover to vote no on the agreement, which is an important step in China's entry into the World Trade Organization.
"Obviously, we're disappointed and wished he were able to be for this," Commerce Secretary William Daley, Mr. Clinton's point man on the vote, said in a telephone interview. 
"But we'll continue to make the case with Democrats and Republicans that this is good for national security and our overall world leadership position."
On Friday, Mr. Daley suffered an embarrassment when he was forced to cancel a trip with both Democratic and Republican lawmakers to China when most of the dozen invited legislators opted for various reasons to pull out.
Mr. Gephardt's decision is not surprising. 
On virtually every nettlesome trade issue of the Clinton administration, Mr. Gephardt has joined the opposing charge, calling for tougher labor, environmental and human rights standards. 
He opposed the 1993 North American Free Trade Agreement, which Mr. Clinton won, and the bill to give the President special authority to negotiate trade accords, which Mr. Clinton lost.
Over the years, Mr. Gephardt has voted against granting China normal trading status in the annual review. 
He is a staunch ally of organized labor, which is aggressively fighting the measure to give China the same permanent lower tariffs the United States gives most every other country.
Republicans never took Mr. Gephardt's silence seriously. 
The No. 2 House Democrat, David E. Bonior of Michigan, is leading the attack against the measure, but top House Republicans, especially Dick Armey of Texas, the majority leader, have always lumped Mr. Gephardt in with its foes.
Trade policy has long played in important role in defining Mr. Gephardt's political agenda. 
The centerpiece of his failed 1988 presidential campaign was a measure that would have forced retaliation against nations that gained large trade surpluses with the United States through unfair means.
Mr. Gephardt has recently intensified his courtship of corporate America, especially high-tech companies, to dispel his label as a traditional, old-style Democrat. 
But many trade advocates said it would have been unfathomable for Mr. Gephardt to switch his trade stripes so quickly.
"We anticipated this, and the fact Dick is not making this a litmus test is very important to all of us," said Representative Robert T. Matsui of California, the top Democratic vote-counter in favor of the measure.
Clearly, the significance of the China vote has weighed on Mr. Gephardt. Last month, he said he was trying to broker a compromise with the administration, labor unions, business groups and House Democrats.
Such an alternative, he said, would include "a methodical way" to ensure that China abides by its treaties, a mechanism to evaluate its human rights record and a code of conduct for American companies doing business in China.
It would also permit the United States to impose sanctions against China if it violated the agreement, as long as the penalties were consistent with the World Trade Organization rules.
But some critics questioned Mr. Gephardt's commitment to finding a third way. 
He has been dismissive of a popular effort along those lines by Representative Sander M. Levin of Michigan, one of the uncommitted Democrats.Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: Gore_s Staff Did Not Object To Temple Event, Aide Says.txt
text:
ï»¿
Despite a warning from the National Security Council that a fund-raising luncheon at a Buddhist temple should be approached with "great, great caution," Vice President Al Gore made the appearance anyway after his own national security adviser raised no objections to the trip, Mr. Gore's spokeswoman said today.
The issue arose today after documents released by the White House showed that in an E-mail exchange of messages between John J. Norris, a member of Mr. Gore's national security staff, and Robert L. Suettinger, one of the National Security Council's Asia affairs specialists, Mr. Suettinger raised concerns about how the 1996 event would be perceived by China. 
He also suggested that the donors might have a "hidden agenda."
The computer messages are also the latest document to make clear that members of the Vice President's staff were aware beforehand that the luncheon at the temple was intended to raise campaign money, despite Mr. Gore's initial assertion in the face of news reports last fall that he had thought it a "community event" and not a fund-raiser.
"Hsing Yun would host a fund-raising lunch for about 150 people in the V.P.'s honor," Mr. Norris said in a message to Mr. Suettinger on April 15, referring to Venerable Master Hsing Yun, a Taiwanese Buddhist leader. 
"Any problems with the V.P. participating in this event from the perspective of U.S.-China relations?"
On April 19, Mr. Suettinger replied: "This is terra incognita to me. 
Certainly from the perspective of Taiwan/China balancing, this would be clearly a Taiwan event, and would be seen as such. 
I guess my reaction would be one of great, great caution. 
They may have a hidden agenda."
Mr. Norris's E-mail message said the fund-raising event would be held at the end of June. 
In fact, it was held 10 days after Mr. Suettinger issued his words of caution. 
Mr. Gore appeared on April 29, as the main speaker at the Hsi Lai Temple, which is in the Los Angeles suburb of Hacienda Heights and is described by its founders as the Western Hemisphere's largest Buddhist monastery.
Lorraine Voles, the Vice President's spokeswoman, said today thathis office had taken the words of caution from the National Security Council "very seriously."
But, she said, Mr. Gore nonetheless went ahead with the event because his own national security adviser, Leon S. Fuerth, after consultation with the council and a separate inquiry to the State Department, "posed no objection to the event from a foreign policy standpoint."
Mr. Gore's appearance came at a tense time between the United States and China, just a month after the Administration had sent United States warships near Taiwan in response to Chinese military exercises that were timed to Taiwan's first direct presidential election.
Mr. Gore's stop at the temple has been a continuing source of controversy, because $140,000 in campaign money was raised in a religious institution and also because of questions about the true source of some of the money.
In addition, Mr. Gore has amended his account of what he knew about the event.
The Democratic National Committee has said that in hindsight, it considers the raising of donations in a religious institution, which has tax-exempt status, to have been a mistake. 
The Democrats reimbursed the temple for the $15,000 it spent on food and other expenses for the event, and later returned some of the campaign money.
The documents released today show that Mr. Gore's foreign policy staff was concerned enough about his appearance to inquire about its propriety. 
Ms. Voles said that on the advice of the State Department, Mr. Gore's staff had worked with the organizers of the event "to minimize any risk of negative reaction from the Chinese Government" by making sure that the luncheon was not identified as a Taiwan event, that there was no display of Taiwanese flags or political symbols and that no politicians from Taiwan "were allowed to exploit the event."
Ms. Voles also said Mr. Norris's description of the luncheon as a fund-raising event was not inconsistent with Mr. Gore's own remarks. 
"Some members of our staff may have known the event was a fund raiser, but he did not," she said. 
"The briefing paper provided for him did not say it was a fund raiser."
She added: "I'm not saying there wasn't a disconnect here. 
The senior political staff traveling with the Vice President also did not know it was a fund raiser."
Last autumn Mr. Gore initially said he had believed that he was attending a "community event" for Asian supporters of the Democrats. 
Then, in December, the White House released thousands of pages of documents that included one on the luncheon that had been sent to the Vice President's office by the Democratic National Committee's fund-raising division. 
Mr. Gore then acknowledged that he had known that the Asian Pacific Leadership Council, which he addressed, required membership payments to the Democratic Party. 
But he said he had not known that the luncheon itself was intended to raise money.

file: GRADING THE SECRETARY_ A special report._Albright, a Bold Voice Abroad, Finds Her Role Limited at Ho.txt
text:
ï»¿
With her bold public stands undermined by irresolution in the White House and her experience rendered less relevant by new economic crises, Madeleine K. Albright has had a tough 20 months as Secretary of State.
Ms. Albright remains the Clinton Administration's principal foreign-policy voice and the liaison with a recalcitrant Republican Congress, and is greeted like a celebrity very popular in the country beyond Washington. 
But a President averse to military risk, preoccupied by the fallout from his relationship with an intern and unwilling to offend core Democratic constituencies has not supported her on key issues like the Middle East and Kosovo.
Her assiduous courtship of Congress was instrumental in winning Senate ratification of NATO expansion and the Chemical Weapons Convention from a Congress verging on isolationism. 
But Ms. Albright has had little to do with the few other Clinton successes of the second term: a settlement in Northern Ireland and a reinvigoration of relations with China.
And now, as Russia melts, tainting one of the relationships of which Mr. Clinton has been proudest, this is a particularly vulnerable period for the Administration's foreign policy. 
Russia was part of widening international crisis that has now hit Wall Street, threatening the booming economy that has kept his popularity afloat.
But Ms. Albright and the State Department have not been crucial players, White House officials say. 
With Mr. Clinton so distracted, it is not immediately clear who is in charge.
The evidence appears to favor the national security adviser, Samuel R. Berger, and the Treasury Secretary, Robert E. Rubin, though, instead of Ms. Albright.
In a recent interview, Ms. Albright bristled at specific criticism, but says it is only natural that the economic experts take the lead on their issues.
"For me, what's important is what people think in years hence," Ms. Albright said. 
"Whether I used this four-year period in a way that ultimately accomplished what I want: to create the underpinnings for the American role in the next century, while taking care of what needs to be done to problem-solve."
Ms. Albright attended only one recent meeting of the National Economic Council, the functional equivalent of the National Security Council, and that was on Japan.
She and her officials did regularly urge a broader view of American interests in Asia than simply the financial, including security and the stabilization of democratizing Asian allies, and coordinated interagency aid packages for Thailand and Indonesia.
But her call for President Suharto of Indonesia to step down occurred only hours before he did so anyway, and in general, Ms. Albright and her department have let Treasury run the show.
Was this an opportunity missed, or simply, as Ms. Albright and her aides contend, the most efficient and collegial way to coordinate a post-Soviet world with new, nontraditional challenges?
In the Middle East, on the other hand, Ms. Albright has been central, trying to coax and cajole Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel into a compromise that would refresh a deterioriating peace and help restore American credibility in the Arab world. 
But her intensive efforts have not yet produced the clear personal triumph that zero-sum Washington seems to require.
In May, she gambled that public pressure and an ultimatum would move Mr. Netanyahu, but the White House failed to support her in the face of a lobbying firestorm stoked by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.
She kept the Administration engaged in Bosnia, where it could not reasonably retreat.
Here in Sarajevo on Sunday and again today, Ms. Albright spoke passionately and effectively about the effort required to make a multinational, democratic Bosnia come to pass, and she was eager to make it vividly clear that American aid would only come to those who worked to carry out the Dayton accords.
But her advocacy of an aggressive approach -- including a credible threat of air strikes -- toward the Serbian leader Slobodan Milosevic, over his crackdown on ethnic Albanian separatists in Kosovo Province did not find wide support within NATO and was rejected by Mr. Clinton in the spring.
Her vow in March that "we are not going to stand by and watch the Serbian authorities do in Kosovo what they can no longer get away with doing in Bosnia" has proven hollow.
Other American threats have seemed equally empty -- against Iraq to defend United Nations weapons inspections, for example.
That has called into question the American commitment to a sustained war on terrorism, a commitment Ms. Albright and others pledged would begin with the missile strikes against Afghanistan and Sudan.
Â 
Some Early Victories For a New Secretary
Ms. Albright's accession as Secretary of State, becoming the highest-ranking woman in American history, prompted enormous popular and media interest. 
She attracted attention for her newly discovered Jewish background as well as for successful efforts to expand NATO and to her push to articulate a more forceful American position than her dry, quiet predecessor, Warren M. Christopher.
She quickly earned respect from her French, Russian, Chinese and Arab colleagues. 
Early victories in Congress were hailed, and she has won important policy shifts on Iran and Cuba, while helping to prevent a trade war with Europe over sanctions.
But with domestic problems undercutting Mr. Clinton's international credibility, the Administration foreign policy seems ever more reactive. 
And with the bombing of American Embassies in Kenya and Tanzania, followed by missile strikes in Afghanistan and the Sudan, with civil war in Kosovo, nuclear tests by India and Pakistan, the Russian economic and political problems and the unresolved crisis in Iraq flaring again, the world seems a more dangerous and unstable place than when Ms. Albright came to office.
Ms. Albright's greatest virtues -- clarity and an intelligent, forceful voice connecting with the public and Congress -- have not diminished, said a senior White House official who admires her. 
But as the Administration faces diverse and less manageable problems, many due to the economic problems that began in Asia, "her virtues seem less impressive or timely," the official said, "because neither economics nor strategy are her strengths, and her depth lies in European issues, not Asian ones."
Even Ms. Albright's hard work with Congress -- in particular with Senator Jesse Helms, Republican of North Carolina -- has not yet produced a deal to repay Washington's debt to the United Nations or funds to replenish the International Monetary Fund reserves, both described as high priorities by her aides. 
Compromises have been stymied by a fight with House Republicans over abortion policy.
"My predecessors had a different world to deal with in which the parameters were fairly set," Ms. Albright said. 
"They had the possibility of focusing all their attention on one or two issues."
By contrast, she said, she is trying to "put into play a lot of issues that I see as challenges we're facing," like nuclear nonproliferation, economics and the effective use of sanctions, issues that were at the center of a January review of priorities.
Â 
The Land Mines And the War Crimes
Ms. Albright has failed to achieve some of the human-rights goals she described as among the most important to her. 
She was an early champion of a ban on land mines. 
Last year, however, in Ottawa, the United States was nearly alone in opposing a treaty.
As a Central European whose family fled first the Nazis and then the Communists, she has been especially concerned about crimes against humanity. 
She created an Ambassador for War Crimes and lobbied for a permanent international tribunal to prosecute them.
But at a Rome conference to accomplish that goal, the United States was part of a small minority refusing to sign a treaty to create a permanent tribunal. 
In both cases, the Pentagon and Congress successfully argued that the only superpower required special exceptions.
Ms. Albright said she continues to champion her principles, but she cannot forget America's responsibilities. 
"I have to balance enunciating the principles and leading the way with the pragmatism of getting things done and the power of the United States," she said.
But there is now a new expression in diplomatic circles -- "to pull an Ottawa" -- which means to promote a new initiative and then abandon it at the end.
Ms. Albright's fierce rhetorical battles with the Iraqis at the United Nations helped catapult her into the Secretary's elegant office on the seventh floor. 
And in a corridor leading off from it, she keeps a comic shrine, a collection of cartoons, newspaper cuttings and other mementos of her tussles with Iraq.
But the Iraq problem persists. 
The latest crisis is an outgrowth of the inconclusive standoff last March, which did little for the reputation of Mr. Clinton's foreign-policy team.
Iraq continues to serve as a reminder of the limits of American power, of the post-Soviet difficulties in orchestrating allies and of the continuing reluctance of Mr. Clinton to use force in risky circumstances.
Â 
The Big Fiasco In Columbus
But the televised town hall meeting in Columbus, Ohio, in February, was the most visible fiasco. 
Ms. Albright and Mr. Berger, the security adviser, and Defense Secretary William S. Cohen were unable to silence hecklers or to sound convincing about why a nearly isolated United States might need to bomb Iraq.
The Ohio meeting -- organized by the White House to use Ms. Albright's skills and popularity -- began the erosion of her reputation among the foreign-policy elite of which she has been a member for so long.
"If you look around the world for the big challenges now, where's the Secretary of State?" asked Robert B. Zoellick, former Under Secretary of State for James A. Baker 3d, who enjoyed a level of access to his President, George Bush, and influence over him that seems denied to Ms. Albright. "To an outsider, she's M.I.A. 
People run issues case by case, but there's a sense the show is being managed by Berger."
The Administration manages crises but has no clear strategic framework, Mr. Zoellick said. 
"How do different problems relate to one another?
It starts with the President, but it's not her forte or Berger's. 
If you don't have a sense of where you want to take the country, you won't get there."
Michael Mandelbaum, of Johns Hopkins University, who criticized first-term foreign policy as "social work," thinks the current team is doing decently at managing the smaller crises of the post-cold-war era, which have less to do with national security and diplomacy.
"Certainly in this second presidential term, by far the most important figures in foreign policy" are Treasury Secretary Rubin and his deputy, Lawrence H. Summers, Mr. Mandelbaum said. 
"For that we should be grateful. 
A world with a financial crisis is far safer than a world with a military crisis, and they've been doing pretty well. 
But Albright doesn't seem to be a player in all this."
Â 
Success With China: Who Gets Credit?
Richard N. Haass of the Brookings Institution, who was on the National Security Council staff under President Bush, said "the one significant accomplishment in the second term" has been to renew relations with China. 
"There you can see a policy initiative and presidential investment," he said. 
"One senses that the engine for that has been the President and the National Security Council."
In the interview, Ms. Albright defended her involvement and that of her strong team in the full range of foreign policy, from Asia and China to Iran and Cuba. 
On financial matters, she said, she has been working to insure that the diplomatic, human and security aspects are fully grasped.
As a former academic, she has been happy to reach down to the regional assistant secretaries and to urge them "to think outside the box," wanting career officers to compete for ideas with outsiders. 
She has encouraged Under Secretaries Thomas R. Pickering and Stuart E. Eizenstat, and Deputy Secretary Strobe Talbott, "to drive policy and make things happen," an official said.
"Economic issues we have brought right into the department," Ms. Albright said, "and we have an Under Secretary who's strong -- Stu Eizenstat -- really working on sanctions issues and on trying to meld the financial with the assistance part of the Asian financial crisis."
She has pushed hard, as she promised him she would, Mr. Eizenstat said, to make State a serious player again on economic issues. 
Treasury gets the headlines over Asia, he said, "but we and she have been intimately involved with the humanitarian and political dimensions."
She is confident about her managing role as Secretary of State, as the prime foreign-policy spokesman for the Administration and as a formulator of key policy. 
And she rejects the notion that Mr. Clinton's choice of Richard C. Holbrooke to be chief American delegate to the United Nations -- someone who was said to have been a candidate for Secretary of State before Ms. Albright was chosen -- is a sign that her own star is waning or wanting.
"Washington is what it is," she said, shrugging. 
"People think you're terrific, and then they think you're too terrific, so then they let you know that you're not. 
You can't be in a position of being the visible voice for the United States and not be out there to be praised and criticized."
Ms. Albright and Mr. Berger have a friendship dating back to the presidential campaign of Michael S. Dukakis of Massachusetts, when Ms. Albright was the chief foreign-policy adviser to a candidate who took almost unremitting heat for not having a strong foreign-policy view. 
Despite moments of annoyance -- usually over personnel -- presidential briefings or second-guessing about the results of specific diplomatic missions, Ms. Albright and Mr. Berger are each other's closest advisers. 
They hash out policy in advance and speak many times a day -- a sharp contrast to the tension between Mr. Christopher and Anthony Lake, or the raging warfare under Jimmy Carter -- the last Democratic President -- between Cyrus R. Vance and Zbigniew Brzezinski.
Â 
Albright and Berger Are Both Pragmatists
"This is not the foreign-policy President who wakes up thinking what notes he can pen to his foreign colleagues," a senior Administration official said, a reference, apparently, to Mr. Bush, who was famous for his hand-written correspondence to world leaders. 
"So Berger becomes the guy who doesn't make foreign policy so much as broker it."
In meetings, another senior White House official said, "she is pragmatic and a consensus builder, like Berger, despite her reputation outside as an uncompromising, six-gun shooting moralist."
She arrives well-briefed and armed with a collective department view, in contrast to Mr. Cohen, whose well-armed Pentagon often gets its way regardless. 
She is "articulate on issues she knows well, and tends to put aside the talking points and draw from her own experience, and she's best when she does that."
Ms. Albright dealt movingly with the emotional and security crisis surrounding the bombing of the American Embassies in Kenya and Tanzania and the deaths of many of her employees, and she has handled Mr. Clinton's personal troubles with dignity.
But her finest policy moment lately has been a shift in the treatment of Iran after the election of the moderate Mohammad Khatami as President. 
While maintaining demands for a halt to terrorism and Iran's nuclear, chemical and missile programs, she pushed Mr. Clinton to a more receptive Iran policy.
"It was hard and had internal criticism, but she got it done with Sandy and the President," avoiding an interagency battle, an official said.
After her recent speech laying out the new policy -- to which Iran has not yet responded -- the President took her aside to congratulate her, she said, "for threading the needle."
Similarly, she used contacts with Pope John Paul II, the Congress and Cuban exiles in Miami to allow direct relief flights from the United States to Cuba to resume and to let relatives send money.
Ms. Albright is also praised for her work with the Russian Foreign Minister, Yevgeny M. Primakov, which helped forge a new relationship between NATO and Russia.
At one point, aides remember, as Mr. Primakov argued for secondary military status for new NATO members, Ms. Albright said: "Neither the President nor I will negotiate over the heads of the peoples of Central Europe. 
That happened once before and it's not going to happen again."
Mr. Primakov was silent, then diverted the conversation, and never pressed the issue so hard again, the aides say.
But Russian policy is generally run by Mr. Talbott and is dominated by the economic and political crisis, making Mr. Primakov -- and Ms. Albright -- less important.
Ms. Albright also pushed the Pentagon to act more decisively in support of political goals in Bosnia and to keep troops there without a deadline.
Her conversations with the Bosnian Serb President, Biljana Plavsic, were crucial in encouraging her to challenge Radovan Karadzic.
On Kosovo, she argues that -- unlike in Bosnia -- Washington and NATO were involved early and got Europe to act. 
A resolution is not yet clear, she says, but the ground is prepared.
Ms. Albright is also proud of using her unprecedented telephone relationship with the Chinese Foreign Minister to organize the Security Council's five permanent members -- the United States, Russia, China, France and Britain -- to condemn nuclear tests by India and Pakistan.
At their June meeting in Geneva, she told the others that they are "always talking about a multipolar and not a unipolar world."
This was their chance to prove it, she said, "so one country doesn't take a principled stand and the others sign up the contracts."
Â 
She Will Await History's Judgment
With all the "profound ideological confusion" facing a post-cold-war Secretary of State, said Moises Naim, editor of Foreign Policy, this is not a period for "grand strategy."
Ms. Albright's role, he said, is inevitably one of a goalkeeper.
But Secretaries of State are often defined by challenges. 
Mr. Baker, for instance, had a great crisis thrust upon him, the Persian Gulf war, and a great opportunity, the collapse of Communism.
So far, Ms. Albright has not had such a test or made such an opportunity of the growing world economic problems.
"I can't operate on the basis of instant gratification on any part of my daily work," she said.
"The policies that are being put into place are longer term. 
It may be the next Secretary of State will reap the rewards of what I've done. 
Sitting in this chair you get the sense that you are a part of history."
She noted her recent induction into the national Women's Hall of Fame. 
"When they say I'm the highest-ranking woman in the history of the United States, that's pretty amazing. 
I don't mind occasionally having someone criticize me."
Judith Kipper of the Council on Foreign Relations, while a fierce critic of United States Middle East policy, praises Ms. Albright for showing the way.
"She can be soft with her children, motherly and nice, and go shopping and be all the things a decent person can be," Ms. Kipper said.
"But when it comes to the work, she's tough and serious. 
There's no gender in the work."

file: Hard Choice for White House On Hillary Clinton and China.txt
text:
ï»¿
Of all the powerful people in the White House, there is probably no one -- not even the President -- to whom aides less like to say no. 
So Hillary Rodham Clinton's strong wish to lead the American delegation to the United Nations Conference on Women in Beijing next month has prompted much hand-wringing among senior diplomatic officials who are not sure she should go.
The geopolitics are plain enough: should the most prominent woman in the United States lend her presence to a conference on women's rights that happens to be held in a country with an abysmal record on human rights -- especially when China is holding the American human rights advocate Harry Wu on espionage charges and Chinese-American relations are rubbed raw.
The domestic politics are clear, too: Congressional Republicans are chomping to seize the issue as an example of the mishandling of foreign policy by Mr. Clinton, and to accuse him of coddling dictators as he once accused George Bush of being too soft on China. 
House and Senate leaders have called for an American boycott of the conference.
The office politics are murkier: knowing Mrs. Clinton's desire to lead the charge on an issue that has long concerned her, Administration officials, including the President in his news conference last week, have studiously avoided saying no, and some are ambivalent about the risks and benefits involved.
For her part, Mrs. Clinton argues -- as she did in a speech to a women's group in Denver last month that her aides took pains to fax to a reporter today -- that the conference is "an important opportunity to focus attention on women."
She said that the American delegation should "play a very big leadership role in shaping the agenda" and that "the United States should do all that it can to make sure that barriers to women's participation are broken down, and that training and credit and political involvement and health care and education are available to all women."
As the Clintons began the first full day of a 17-day vacation in the Grand Tetons this morning, the official word from the White House was that there was no official word. 
Unofficially, senior Administration aides in Washington gave slightly conflicting status reports.
Some in the West Wing and the State Department said the current plan was to wait a few more days to see if Mr. Wu might be released, before making a decision by next Monday, which they described as the last realistic point at which the logistical arrangements for such a trip could be made.
Aides to the First Lady insisted there was no "drop dead date," but they acknowledged pressure to make a decision soon, since Mrs. Clinton would leave for Beijing from V-J Day commemorations in Hawaii over the Labor Day weekend, and perhaps visit Mongolia, Cambodia and Thailand as well.
On Monday, Secretary of State Warren M. Christopher and the deputy national security adviser, Samuel R. Berger, met separately with Mrs. Clinton to go over the pros and cons. 
Aides to both the First Lady and the President said today that Mrs. Clinton would rely on their judgment in making her decision.
Moreover, at least some officials outside the First Lady's staff have argued that Mrs. Clinton's visit could be good for Chinese-American relations in the long run. 
Winston Lord, the Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific Affairs and former Ambassador to Beijing, switched his vacation plans to be available to escort her.
The matter remains complicated, balancing the enormous attention Mrs. Clinton would win among the 50,000 delegates and reporters at the conference with practicalities as particular as the fate of one man.
Over the weekend, Mr. Wu's wife, Ching Lee, wrote to the First Lady, imploring her not to go. 
Mrs. Clinton has not yet replied, but officials said there was general agreement that it would be extremely problematic for Mrs. Clinton to attend if Mr. Wu remained in custody.
At the same time, these aides said the Administration was determined not to link Mrs. Clinton's decision too closely to Mr. Wu's fate, or to the status of Chinese-American relations in general, but to the mission of the conference.
Washington will be well represented at the once-a-decade conference in any event. 
The chief United States delegate to the United Nations, Madeleine K. Albright, is the official head of the American delegation, which includes the Secretary of Health and Human Services, Donna E. Shalala, and former Gov. Thomas Kean of New Jersey. 
Mrs. Clinton would be the honorary chairwoman.
Officials said today that if she went, Mrs. Clinton would most likely stay in Beijing one day, address the conference, spend the night and then move on, holding no meetings with Chinese Government officials or dissidents to emphasize that she was attending an international conference, not honoring the Chinese.
But among the Administration's concerns is that however brief her stay, Mrs. Clinton could easily become embroiled in disputes or demonstrations by the various delegations at the conference, and that her visit would almost certainly be interpreted by the Chinese as a sign of American nonchalance about its human rights record.Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: Hong Kong Asks Its High Court to Clarify Ruling Beijing Dislikes.txt
text:
ï»¿
Seeking to quell a bitter dispute with mainland China, Hong Kong's government asked its high court today to clarify a landmark ruling that provoked objections from Beijing.
"We have looked at the concerns expressed by a lot of parties," said a government spokesman, Stephen Lam. 
"Because there has been such great concern in the community, we have decided to seek clarification."
Late last month, the Hong Kong Court of Final Appeal ruled that children born on the mainland who have at least one parent living in Hong Kong have the right to residency here. 
Officials in Beijing criticized the decision as a violation of the Chinese Constitution and warned that they wanted it "rectified."
Far from calming the waters, today's move rattled legal experts, who said the Hong Kong government appeared to be pressing the court to retreat from the ruling before the Chinese Government forced its hand.
"This is close to a government subversion of the court," said Yash Ghai, an expert on constitutional law at Hong Kong University. 
"I would almost prefer if China took the action itself and bore the responsibility."
Lawyers here have said that if China overturned the decision, it would ignite a constitutional crisis. 
Under the agreement between Britain and China -- known as "one country, two systems" -- Hong Kong is supposed to be a semi-autonomous region within China, with its own legal system.
China has not formally demanded that Hong Kong overturn the ruling. 
But many people here believe that if the local government does not mollify Beijing, the Chinese Government will probably repudiate parts of the decision during the annual meeting of the Chinese National People's Congress next month.
Such a move could stain Hong Kong's reputation as an international financial center, which depends in part on having courts that operate without meddling from Beijing. 
The dispute has already set off a crisis of confidence among Western diplomats and business executives, some of whom fear that the rule of law could become a relic of Hong Kong's colonial past.
"This ruling is central to Hong Kong's autonomy," Professor Ghai said.

file: Hong Kong Court Upholds China_s Rule.txt
text:
ï»¿
A constitutional challenge to China's rule in Hong Kong was rebuffed today when a three-judge panel ruled unanimously that the territory was powerless to question Beijing's decisions, particularly the scuttling of Hong Kong's elected legislature and its replacement by a handpicked assembly.
The challenge, which grew out of a criminal case involving the theft of a Rolex watch at a ferry terminal, claimed that the existence of Beijing's legislature violated the Basic Law, the mini-constitution that Beijing drafted for Hong Kong before China took over here from Britain. 
The Basic Law provides for a legislature that is in part elected, but it does not provide for an appointed assembly.
In the narrow sense, the case revolved merely around the survival of a criminal indictment through the transition from British to Chinese sovereignty, but more broadly, the ruling by the Court of Appeal, the second-highest court in Hong Kong, found that China has the power to impose its will on Hong Kong.
The case itself marked a significant moment in the era of Communist rule in China. 
For the first time in the history of the People's Republic of China, judges deliberated on constitutional matters affecting Beijing's governance.
Indeed, remarkably, only one of the three judges was Chinese, making this the first time that judges of foreign nationality have deliberated on Chinese laws; all Hong Kong's judges retained their appointments after China resumed sovereignty over Hong Kong on July 1.
It was not immediately clear what the complete implications of today's decisions are for Hong Kong's autonomy, or whether the jurisdiction of Hong Kong's courts has been circumscribed. 
The Government insisted afterward that the rule of law and the integrity of the courts had been maintained. 
But lawyers who brought the case, and other critics, warned of the consequences of the ruling and hinted at an appeal.
At stake was the fate not only of Beijing's appointed legislature, known as the Provisional Legislative Council, but also of the laws it has passed, including an omnibus law to insure the continuation of common law in Hong Kong as well as the appointment of the appeals court judges themselves.
In reading his opinion today, Chief Justice Patrick Chan said, "I am inclined to hold that the Provisional Legislative Council has been validly established under Chinese law and was ratified by the National People's Congress," China's rubber-stamp Parliament.
Addressing a courtroom packed with observers lining the walls and spilling out the double wooden doors, Mr. Chan said of the appointed legislature: "Its formation is an interim measure out of necessity."
He said, "It was not done as an intentional breach of the Basic Law. 
It is, strictly speaking, not a Legislative Council under Article 60 of the Basic Law," the provision that requires a partially elected legislature.
In a precisely reasoned ruling, Justice Chan took pains to support his ruling on principles of common law and under Chinese laws passed by China's parliament, as well as the decisions of various Chinese-appointed bodies and the text of the Basic Law itself. 
At no point did anyone, including harsh critics of the decision, suggest that Mr. Chan and his colleagues were pressured by Beijing to rule a certain way.
Ever since China declared it would abolish Hong Kong's elected legislature, because the elections in 1995 were held without its approval, there has been a debate here, especially among legal experts, over whether an appointed assembly would satisfy the constitution.
Both the Bar Council, which represents barristers, the lawyers who appear in court, and the Law Society, representing solicitors, lawyers who deal with clients, have maintained that the Provisional Legislature is not in accord with the Basic Law.
That argument was powerfully presented in this case last week by Gladys Li, a former chairman of the Bar Council and one of the most respected barristers in Hong Kong.
Opposite her was the Government's chief legal officer, the Solicitor General, Daniel Fung, who insisted that China had the authority to erect the governmental structure it deemed appropriate for Hong Kong and that in any event, the courts had no power to rule on those decisions.
Clearly relieved at the court's posture, Mr. Fung said afterward, "We welcome the Court of Appeal's decision, which was unanimous that the Provisional Legislative Council is a valid, competent body established by the National People's Congress."
"This has settled a constitutional controversy and we welcome the clearing of the air," said Mr. Fung, who, like the other barristers and judges, appeared in court in elaborate regalia of robes, starched collars and horsehair wigs.
Tung Chee-hwa, the shipping magnate appointed by Beijing to administer Hong Kong, also praised the ruling. 
"The rule of law is one of the important factors contributing to Hong Kong's success," said a statement issued by Mr. Tung's office. 
"The litigation demonstrates the respect the society have towards the rule of law."
Across Hong Kong, however, many pro-democracy activists, including lawmakers who had been dismissed from the legislature by China, were critical of the court's ruling and suggested that the issue would be raised again in Hong Kong's highest court, the Court of Final Appeal.
Martin Lee, the leader of Hong Kong's largest political party, the Democratic Party, which lost all 19 of its legislative seats, was equally critical. 
"This case raises very serious implications for the future of Hong Kong's rule of law and autonomy," said Mr. Lee.
"There must be something seriously wrong if the Chinese central Government can introduce an appointed body, ignore the Basic Law at will, and Hong Kong courts cannot do anything about it," he said.
Nihal Jayawickrama, a professor of law at Hong Kong University, called the implications of the ruling "quite serious."
He explained, "What they are saying is that the National People's Congress is supreme and whatever it does, the court will apply. 
That's not what the Basic Law says. 
The National People's Congress has no relevance in Hong Kong. 
If they can do this, where does the Basic Law stand?"
While it was unclear tonight whether there would be an appeal to the territory's highest court, Mr. Fung expressed confidence that today's ruling would be upheld. 
"There is no question the common law is part of the law of Hong Kong," said an ebullient Mr. Fung after the ruling. 
"We all accept the difference in nature and development between the Hong Kong system and the Chinese system. 
But we have to respect the basic law and the structure under which we were created."

file: Hong Kong Faces Loss Of Luster to Mainland.txt
text:
ï»¿
For a city that has prospered as an intermediary between the Chinese economy and the outside world, Hong Kong has lobbied hard to help China win full membership in the world's club of trading nations.
Now that the United States House of Representatives has voted to give China permanent normal trade status -- bringing normalized trade relations closer and easing China's accession to the World Trade Organization -- Hong Kong has to begin facing the consequences of its successful campaign.
A China more open to commerce with the outside world, many experts say, will jeopardize Hong Kong's historic role as a trading post.
"There's no question that companies are going to do business directly with China," said Robert C. Broadfoot, the managing director of the Political and Economic Risk Consultancy here. 
"It's not a question of if, but when, you're going to have shocks to Hong Kong's role."
Mr. Broadfoot contends that in the long run Hong Kong will benefit from China's integration into the global economy as the overall volume of China-related trade grows.
But in the short term, China's march into the World Trade Organization will pose a thorny challenge. 
As a former British colony and now a semiautonomous region of China, Hong Kong is a separate trading entity that already has its own membership in the W.T.O.
Hong Kong's stock market reflected this ambivalence, falling slightly today while shares in the mainland Chinese cities of Shanghai and Shenzhen roared ahead.
In 1998, more than $52 billion worth of goods passed through Hong Kong's port bound for mainland destinations. 
Mr. Broadfoot estimates that a third of that traffic will disappear after the United States and other countries start shipping directly to mainland ports.
Likewise in air travel, Hong Kong could lose its role as a gateway to China. 
As part of the W.T.O. negotiations last year between the United States and China, Beijing agreed to increase the frequency of commercial flights, which would enable more American cities to have more direct flights to mainland Chinese cities.
That could hurt Dragonair, a Hong Kong carrier that serves many mainland cities. 
It stands to lose Western passengers who fly to Hong Kong and transfer to planes to popular Chinese destinations like Xian or Guilin.
Hong Kong's position is further threatened by Taiwan, whose new President, Chen Shui-bian, has signaled that he is open to negotiating direct trade links with China. 
In 1998, Hong Kong's container port handled nearly $10 billion worth of Taiwanese exports bound for China. 
If Taiwan and China were to break down these barriers, some of that trade would also bypass Hong Kong.
"Once China gets into the W.T.O., Taiwan would presumably get into the W.T.O. soon as well," said Eden Woon, director of the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce. 
"That means that Taiwan would have to deal more directly with China."
With all the troubling implications, why did Mr. Woon and other Hong Kong officials push so energetically for the House to pass the bill?
Part of the reason is political. 
Beijing has made entry into the trade organization the centerpiece of its economic agenda. 
In Hong Kong, where politicians and business leaders try to outdo each other to be seen as loyal to the motherland, supporting the trade campaign was a natural.
Even Martin Lee, Hong Kong's most prominent pro-democracy leader, traveled to Washington to lobby for the bill. 
Mr. Lee, a longtime critic of Beijing, said his motives were political rather than economic.
"I went to support the 1.2 billion people of China, not the Chinese government," Mr. Lee said. 
"I see in this bill a reasonable possibility that China will change its culture toward observing the rule of law."
Other supporters argue that Hong Kong can retain its middleman role -- with a few tweaks -- as a provider of services to the next generation of foreign companies that try to get into China. 
Hong Kong, with its legions of lawyers, accountants and consultants, is quite likely to remain a valuable guide for those companies.
"In order to handle all this trade, China will have to have a very well-developed service sector," said Victor K. Fung, the chairman of the Hong Kong Trade Development Council and the owner of a trading firm. 
"In the short run, it will be very difficult for China to ramp up those services."
But some more old-line Hong Kong industries will have to redefine themselves. 
With the United States set to lift import quotas on Chinese textiles and textile products by 2005, Mr. Woon predicted that many Hong Kong clothing makers would move their factories to the mainland to take advantage of lower production costs. 
Hong Kong, he suggested, could recast itself as a center for Asian fashion design, rather than a manufacturing center.
China's entry into the trade organization is also quite likely to deprive Hong Kong of its thriving gray market in goods like oil, cigarettes and agricultural products. 
Those are smuggled from mainland China by the truckload and exported from Hong Kong so that they will be subject to lower tariffs.
Despite its expected negative effects on some Hong Kong industries, China's trade campaign has made people here recognize that their economic fortunes are inextricably tied to the mainland. 
It seemed no coincidence that last week Hong Kong announced a $12 billion expansion of its rail system, including a direct link between central Hong Kong and Shenzhen.
Hong Kong's government estimates that China's joining the W.T.O. would add more than 5 percent to the territory's gross domestic product over the next decade. 
It also predicts that investment by Hong Kong companies in China will explode. 
Local companies have already poured in a cumulative $156 billion.
Because Hong Kong and China would retain separate memberships in the World Trade Organization, officials said Hong Kong would not necessarily gain access to Chinese markets earlier than other countries. 
But business people here are lobbying for special treatment. 
Even without it, officials say, Hong Kong will flourish.
"We do not mind if multinational companies go directly to China," the government's chief spokesman, Stephen Lam, said. 
"As long as the pie gets bigger, even if we get a smaller piece, it will still be more than enough for us."

text:

Long accustomed to their boisterous, muckraking press, Hong Kong's journalists and news organizations are reeling from a series of body punches delivered by a senior Beijing official over the future of press freedom here.
Lu Ping, the Chinese official charged with setting up Hong Kong's new government after China retakes the territory from Britain on July 1, 1997, has issued a procession of comments starkly warning the crown colony's press that there will be limits on what can be published here under Chinese rule.
"It's all right if reporters objectively report," said Mr. Lu, while on a visit to Japan this month in his role as director of China's Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office. 
"But if they advocate, it is an act. 
It has nothing to do with freedom of the press."
Mr. Lu's reference to "an act" appeared to invoke Article 23 of the Basic Law, which China has pledged to respect and is often described as Hong Kong's future constitution. 
Article 23 allows the banning of any "act" deemed treasonous, subversive or secessionist. 
Mr. Lu went on to specify that advocacy of Taiwan's independence could be prosecuted under Article 23.
Hong Kong's 59 newspapers and 675 periodicals are filled with columns of advocacy, blistering articles of opinion and untempered appeals for community and political activism. 
With China's reassertion of suzerainty now in sight, anxieties among Hong Kong's journalists are mounting.
"The message is pretty clear," said Ivan Tong, president of the Hong Kong Journalists Association. 
"On the one hand he is talking about Hong Kong people retaining the same degree of press freedom after 1997. 
On the other hand he's talking about a bottom line, a limit on press freedom. 
It's not press freedom at all."
In addition to Hong Kong's huge Chinese-language press, there are many international news magazines published in Hong Kong, including The Asian Wall Street Journal, Time and Newsweek's Asian editions, the Far Eastern Economic Review and Asia Week. 
And while all insist publicly that they intend to remain here under Chinese sovereignty, many publications are quietly looking at alternatives to Hong Kong.
"Our plan is to remain in Hong Kong," Donald M. Morrison, the editor of Time's Asian edition, said. 
"Not only are we staying in Hong Kong, we are expanding."
But he also cautioned, "As for 1997, obviously we will wait and see what the climate is in terms of freedom of information."
Now in its 50th year, the Far Eastern Economic Review, widely regarded as the region's preeminent weekly and now owned by Dow Jones, also insists that it intends to remain in Hong Kong after 1997, and seems more optimistic about the future climate for journalism here.
"We have every intention of remaining in Hong Kong," said L. Gordon Crovitz, the magazine's editor and publisher. 
"It's important to us that we always be able to report fairly and accurately and we have every expectation that we will be able to do that from our base in Hong Kong."
Urban C. Lehner, the editor of another Dow Jones publication, The Asian Wall Street Journal, said that the paper would also continue to be based in Hong Kong after 1997.

"We're committed to being in Hong Kong. 
We think Hong Kong is the place to be. 
It's the central spot in Asia. 
It's the heart of covering the best story in Asia, which is China."

"Losing Hong Kong is one fifth of our readers," he said. 
"Advertisers want those readers. 
Not delivering a morning paper to those readers would be the biggest loss. 
But basically, we could move in a minute."
For most of Hong Kong's printed press, however, the option of moving after 1997 does not exist, and editors here are taking a grim view of Mr. Lu's recent statements.
"His comments brought out the anxieties journalists have had for a long time," said Daisy Yet Wah Li, a senior editor at Ming Pao, one of the territory's most serious newspapers. 
"Is merely reporting on Tibetan independence or Taiwan independence advocacy?

What about a survey that Hong Kong people want independence and we put it on the front page?

John Schidlovsky, director of the Freedom Forum Asian Center, an independent research center on press issues and a training center for journalists here, said Mr. Lu's comments reflected an unfamiliarity with the role a free press plays in a free society.

text:
