In the shadow of an old Buddhist temple, a curving alleyway known as Soothsayer's Arcade is full of tiny stalls where fortunetellers routinely predict the future and, for a few dollars extra, unlock some of life's deepest mysteries.
Yet even here, in icon-laden booths that reek of incense and the mystical power of Chinese fortunetelling, no one seems willing to venture a prediction about what will happen in Hong Kong after July 1, when China takes over from Britain.
"How can you know?" asked Leung Tin-che, a 50-year-old fortune-teller whose inviting smile turned to a puzzled frown when he was asked about Hong Kong's future. 
"None of my customers ask about that anyway. 
They want to know about their career, or love."
As Hong Kong nears its fateful date, people all over the world are wondering what will happen in a political situation that history has no script for. 
In Hong Kong itself, however, many people seem to accept that their future remains firmly in the realm of the unknowable.
But in a telling indication of the way things are going, in Soothsayer's Arcade and in so much of Hong Kong, new customers now come mostly from mainland China.
Fortunetellers say that many of the mainland visitors are actually mid-level Communist Party officials, who ignore the Party's rejection of superstitious practices when they come for a session.
"It makes sense if you think about it," said Chung Tak-ching, another fortuneteller. 
"If you're from the Communist Party, and no one believes in Communism anymore, wouldn't you have questions about your future?"
Probably no place is as obsessed with lucky numbers and talismans and fortunetelling as Hong Kong, perhaps because its very existence -- as a precarious dot on the long coast of China -- seems to have tempted fate over the years. 
Bankers and lawyers regularly consult fortunetellers, as do housewives and delivery boys, and the 200 fortunetellers in Soothsayer's Arcade may be the largest such grouping in the world.
A decade ago, despite China's promises to leave Hong Kong untouched, many people here feared that 1997 would mean the closing of places like fortunetelling stalls and nightclubs and race tracks, long banned in China as remnants of a misguided, and capitalist, past.
But few fear such a crackdown now, since change in recent years has brought capitalist pastimes like stock markets and nightlife to the mainland. 
Even if Chinese control does mean a loss of civil liberties, several fortunetellers said they found it hard to imagine their trade being affected.
"They come here as customers themselves, so why would they want to shut us down?" asked Priscilla Lam, a matronly fortuneteller who has brushed up on her Mandarin to accommodate mainland clients. 
"Maybe they'll figure out a way to make money off us."
In a simple example, Ms. Lam seemed to put her finger on some critical forces verging on Hong Kong's future: China's enthusiasm for capitalism, the eagerness of Chinese officials to enjoy the forbidden fruit within, as well as these officials' tendency to try to make money off anyone who is making money.
Yet all the reasons why China should leave Hong Kong alone may have to be balanced against Beijing's deepest concern: to control anything it perceives as a threat.
"We are not a danger to anyone," Ms. Lam said firmly. 
"No one here would ever make a prediction that is politically sensitive."
Described on her business card as a "physignomist," Ms. Lam prefers to divine an individual's future by examining palms and nose and eye shape, and by crossing her findings against one of many ancient charts listing personality characteristics based on year, date and hour of birth.
One customer, Evelyn Lau, a 24-year-old bank clerk wearing purple lipstick, came to ask about her prospects with a man she recently met. 
She demurred when asked what her palm-reading disclosed.
"I want to know about big issues that will affect me for my whole life," she said, trying to surpress a nervous giggle. 
Egged on by a friend, she admitted, "I really like this guy."
Mr. Leung said that, although most of his prognostications also deal with romantic concerns, there was a surge in the fortunetelling business about five years ago when many Hong Kong people were trying to decide whether to emigrate and to where.
"Everyone was afraid of the future back then," he said. 
"But everything depends on what happens in China, and China is changing fast."
Despite his own reluctance to predict Hong Kong's future, Mr. Leung said he had noticed a few things about people who do make predictions.
Hong Kong's most vocally optimistic people, he observed, are wealthy businessmen and women who, although they have the most to lose, also have the easiest ways out. 
Most of them arranged foreign passports or other escape routes years ago.
In contrast, he said, many working-class people are pessimistic about the future, though they have little to lose but their freedom.
"They're the ones with nowhere to go," he said. 
"Like me."
Ms. Lam has also advised many customers on choices about emigration, but she said it was always a question about where, not if.
"Everyone with enough money emigrates," she said simply.
With the fortunetelling business slow, Mr. Leung allowed that he makes his real money as a master of feng shui, the ancient art of geomancy, advising a tenant or home-owner on the proper placement and design of an office or dwelling. 
Even though the practice was banned in the mainland long ago, Mr. Leung thinks it inconceivable that Chinese officials would try to restrict it here.
Ms. Lam also complained that since much of her business now comes from mainland visitors, business has been slow this month, because Chinese authorities feared an onslaught of mainland visitors in the weeks just before and after the handover and put restrictions on how many could come.
"We'll have to wait until late July 1 before things pick up again," she said.

On clear days at this time of the year, Barrie Cook used to take out-of-town visitors to the top of Victoria Peak, where they could see the gleaming skyscrapers of Macao, a Portuguese colony 38 miles away. 
Now, he said, "you can barely see to the bottom of the hill."
For much of this winter, Hong Kong has been shrouded in a yellowish haze that has blotted out its legendary vistas. 
This is not brooding, rainy mist of the sort that supplies atmosphere in James Clavell novels. 
It is a dry, gritty smog that catches in the throat and gives the city an odd sepia-tinted glow.
As the haze has become an every-other-day phenomenon in this city of 6.7 million, it is setting off alarm bells in some unlikely quarters.
"If this is allowed to deteriorate further, it's going to be a major problem for the economy," said Mr. Cook, who runs a cement and concrete company for Hong Kong's most famous tycoon, Li Ka-shing. 
"Companies are very concerned about employees working in a deteriorating environment. 
They won't want to invest here. 
They won't want to put people or facilities here."
In Hong Kong, tackling pollution raises ticklish political issues. 
Much of the smog is generated across the border in mainland China, where a forest of smoke-belching factories has risen in Guangdong Province over the last two decades. 
In the winter, northerly winds blow the fumes into Hong Kong, where they mix with exhaust from buses and taxis to create what Kim Salkeld, the government's spokesman on the environment, calls a "horrendous cocktail."
Mr. Salkeld said the percentage of days when pollution reduced visibility to less than five miles doubled from 1991 to 1997, to more than 8 percent. 
Hong Kong hit a new low on Jan. 
19, when a particularly murky brew cut visibility to less than 3,000 feet, despite sunny skies. 
Ships in the harbor were forced to sound their foghorns as they crept forward in the midday gloom.
Hong Kong is still less polluted than Beijing or Shanghai -- not to mention famously blighted Asian cities like Bangkok and Manila. 
But experts here worry that Hong Kong could soon slip into their ranks.
With China's economy still humming, more factories are likely to spring up in Guangdong.
And Hong Kong, which is clawing its way out of an economic quagmire, may be reluctant to turn away industrial development, even if it degrades the environment and alienates foreign businesses.
"It really depends on what we're willing to put up with," said William Barron, a professor at the Center for Urban Planning and Environmental Management at the University of Hong Kong. 
"What we see in a place like Bangkok is how bad things can get, but the government still doesn't address the problem."
Mr. Barron said that while the Hong Kong government regards pollution as a major threat, it has been loath to confront China about its role in fouling its newest possession. 
"They don't even want to talk about the pollution coming across the border," he said. 
"It is way too sensitive."
Partly this is because of Hong Kong's general reluctance to ruffle the feathers of its new sovereign, whether it be over issues of judicial independence or environmental policy. 
But partly it is because the government knows that many of the factories in Guangdong are owned by Hong Kong companies.
Hong Kong also has no shortage of home-grown pollution. 
The number of cars, taxis and buses has soared in recent years as more people have moved into the New Territories, a once-bucolic hinterland that separates Kowloon from the mainland.
In Hong Kong's popular shopping district, Causeway Bay, the pollution readings are often so high that the government urges people with respiratory conditions to stay indoors. 
On a recent afternoon there, the fumes from taxis and double-decker buses all but choked two women who were standing on the sidewalk, handing out invitations to join a health club.
"In 15 years, Hong Kong will not be livable," Cindy Ho said as she packed her things and headed for a restaurant. 
"Everybody will be dead."
Mr. Salkeld said the government was determined to clear the air by banning leaded gasoline, converting taxis from diesel to liquefied petroleum gas, and expanding the rail system by 40 percent. 
But Hong Kong's close ties to southern China are not helping. 
Many trucks burn low-grade diesel fuel that is smuggled into Hong Kong from the mainland. 
The police recently uncovered an illegal pipeline that carried the cheap and far more polluting fuel across the border.
Politicians here said the government could no longer afford to tiptoe around China. 
Hong Kong's chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, declared in a speech last month that the environment would be "at the forefront of our agenda next year, year after next, and every year thereafter."
But Mr. Tung, a shipping magnate appointed by Beijing, has said little about cross-border pollution.
"What I don't want to see is the government saying, 'Just because the problem is from over there, we can't do anything about it,' " said Christine Loh, a pro-democracy leader who is active in environmental issues.
As a practical matter, it is not clear that Hong Kong can do much to influence Beijing's environmental policies. 
Mr. Salkeld said the two governments were cooperating to harmonize fuel standards. 
And they pledged $3 million each to install a pollution-monitoring system in Guangdong. 
But Mr. Salkeld noted that China's population and economic demands were so vast that they could make any environmental initiative seem hopelessly inadequate.
And anyway, he added, the seasonal wind currents work against China, too. 
"During the summer," he said, "when Hong Kong's air quality is pretty good, the wind is blowing our pollution into the mainland."

text:

Tendrils of steam plumed from the teapot's spout as Yip Wai-man splashed the parchment-thin ceramic thimbles with boiling water. 
Then, in a liquid ballet, he filled a tiny red clay pot with water, spilled tea into a blue and white china jug and carefully poured a mouthful of pale amber liquid into each thimble.
"This is Iron Buddha tea," Mr. Yip said, balancing the translucent china thimble in his fingertips. 
"Smell the bouquet and then sip it carefully."
In the frenzy of Hong Kong's day, executives in crisp suits scurrying into glass towers, the 24-hour roar of construction equipment, the buzz of business over hurried lunches, Mr. Yip preaches the need for tranquillity and harmony -- elements of the traditional Chinese tea ceremony. 
It is a ritual, he insists, that has been all but lost here.
"Basically everything of tradition in China was destroyed with the fall of the Qing dynasty," Mr. Yip said, referring to the collapse of China's last dynasty in 1911. 
"When I went to China, I was devastated to find there was no one to teach me about tea.
"Frankly speaking, China is not so useful; they've lost everything related to the tea culture. 
Nobody talks about the Chinese tea ceremony, only the Japanese ceremony. 
Of course, its origin was in China."
With nervousness growing as Hong Kong braces for the takeover by mainland China on July 1, 1997, Mr. Yip, cherubic in a Beatle-ish mop and white cotton Chinese jacket, extols the virtues of "cha dao," or "the way of tea," as a political healer and social pacifier.
In a city with some of the busiest McDonald's anywhere, where Coke and cognac consumption spirals upward and where tea is more an afterthought than passion, Mr. Yip's obsession nears the quixotic. 
But he is undeterred.
"I used to drink Coke," said Mr. Yip, 37, a former social worker. 
"I was like the Hong Kong masses. 
I was totally not into tea. 
I didn't even think it tasted good. 
Then I became interested in China's history and culture. 
It arose from my concerns about 1997, to dig into my past, my thoughts about being Chinese."
Being Chinese is apparently not at the forefront of many Hong Kongers' sensibility. 
A recent poll by the Chinese University of Hong Kong found that only 36 percent of Hong Kong's people see themselves as Chinese, while 49 percent identify themselves as "Hongkongese."
Mr. Yip said that escaping history was not so easy. 
"I realized that because of jitters over '97 and my sense of the growing distance between people here in Hong Kong, I want to use tea to spread harmony," he said. 
"What I want is a new Hong Kong tea culture, a product of the combination of the old and new China, of north and south and the ingestion of Western influences."
Already he has staked out land in the New Territories, Hong Kong's bit of the mainland, for a tea farm and the site of his members-only International China Tea Club.
Intended as a refuge from the frazzled existence of urban Hong Kong, the Tea Club, to open in September, will be a traditional two-story Chinese teahouse where the elaborate ritual of tea drinking can take place in leisure and relative solitude, a privilege that will cost the equivalent of about $6,500 a year.
"The idea is to relax, drink tea and make teapots if you wish," he said.
To be sure, Hong Kong is not lacking in tea. 
There is not a restaurant here where tea is not a staple. 
But hunched behind his desk in his tea shop on Argyle Street in Kowloon, Mr. Yip disdains the plebeian practice of sloshing plain green tea into mug-like teacups.
In his Jabbok Tea Shop, the paraphernalia of the tea ritual -- what he insisted are the essentials of the tea experience -- sit carefully on well-lighted shelves and in glass cases. 
On three glass shelves, 15 palm-sized red clay teapots are arrayed under spotlights.
"These are very special," Mr. Yip said, adding that they cost about $8,800 each.
Along the wall, fat canisters of tea displayed the profusion of regional vintages, from Pu-er to Long-jing, from Mu-dan to Iron Buddha, teas in a rainbow of colors, smells and tastes, with prices from $5 to well over $1,000 for a bit more than a pound of tea leaves.
"Tea," Mr. Yip declared, "is like French wine. 
It matters where the leaves are grown, on a hill or a valley, and when they are harvested, in the spring or autumn."
Mr. Yip spreads his devotion to tea, to the esoterica of ritual and his faith in the tea ceremony's palliative properties, in courses he teaches -- more than 8,000 students over the last decade, he said. 
But a few other tea masters in Hong Kong, less fervent perhaps, have brought the ferocity of competition to the genteel world of tea sipping.
Vesper Cha, the proprietor of the Best Tea House, a small chain of tea shops in Hong Kong, sells a wide range of ordinary and rare teas, teapots and the assorted utensils used in a traditional ceremony. 
But Mr. Cha, a former dealer in industrial lubricants, saw the lack of high-quality teas in Hong Kong as a marketing challenge.
"All over Hong Kong, I could not find one high-quality tea," he said. 
"So this was a big chance for me to open a shop with high-quality tea. 
My first shop was only 400 square feet."
Today, he has shops in Hong Kong and Canada.
Still, the infatuation of Hong Kong's young people for Coca-Cola and beer remains a hurdle.
"If your only customers are old people, you're doomed," he said with a laugh. 
"When people are too young, they don't know how to appreciate a cup of good tea. 
They have too much energy. 
But hopefully when they get to be 30, they learn to enjoy real tea."
Mr. Yip, who admitted that he is not immune to market pressures, insisted that his more refined approach to the tea business, and to tea culture, would endure.
"Tea has always been closely related to Chinese life for the last 3,000 years," he said. 
"It brings out the concept of harmony, which is a central theme of Chinese civilization. 
Tea is a real instrument of furthering harmony. 
It is a real linkage in relationships."

After a year of economic despair, relentless criticism and growing doubts about his leadership, Hong Kong's chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, finally got a break last week.
Prime Minister Tony Blair of Britain, making his first visit here since this former British colony reverted to China, praised Mr. Tung for how steadily he was leading Hong Kong through the Asian financial crisis.
That the chief executive's most prominent defender these days is the former colonial ruler of this territory must be cold comfort to Mr. Tung, 61, a former shipping tycoon who took over Hong Kong when it was the pulsing heart of the Asian economy and has watched as it has gone into cardiac arrest.
"Am I frustrated?" asked Mr. Tung in a rare interview on Friday. 
"At times, I would say. 
But the important thing is to zero in on the things you can do and also zero in on the long-term perspective, because the turmoil will be over."
As if to underscore his point, Mr. Tung showed off a scroll that China's President, Jiang Zemin, painted and gave to Hong Kong as a gift during the handover. 
"Hong Kong will be better tomorrow," it says in Chinese calligraphy.
But to many people here, the economic crisis has settled into a debilitating illness, with little hope of a cure. 
Hong Kong's stock market has fallen by roughly half since its peak in August 1997, property prices have plummeted by as much as 60 percent and unemployment is soaring.
"People respect Tung as a sincere, elderly person," said Joseph Cheng, a professor of political science at the City University of Hong Kong. 
"His heart is in the right place, but people are looking for results."
As the man China chose to run Hong Kong, Mr. Tung faces a quandary unique among Asian leaders. 
He does not have a popular mandate, yet he must serve two very different constituencies: the 6.6 million people of Hong Kong and the Communist bosses in Beijing. 
Unless he comes to grips with the economic crisis, his critics say, Mr. Tung risks losing the faith of both groups.
With its economy in a free fall, some observers said they also feared that Hong Kong was turning away from the global market. 
In August the government intervened in the stock market to foil overseas hedge funds, which it accused of manipulating Hong Kong's markets.
In defending the intervention, senior officials played heavily on fears of unnamed "foreign traders," while a prominent member of the legislature referred to foreigners by a derogatory Cantonese word.
Mr. Tung said such remarks reflected public frustration with the hedge funds, which he said had destabilized Hong Kong's economy. 
But as someone who lived in Boston and New York for nine years and watches the football games of his favorite team, the San Francisco 49ers, on videocassette, Mr. Tung seemed disturbed by suggestions that Hong Kong had become xenophobic.
"The whole of Hong Kong overwhelmingly understands that Hong Kong is an international city, and the future of Hong Kong, the success of Hong Kong, is closely tied to being an international city," he said.
When it comes to domestic issues, critics said Mr. Tung seemed to miss the forest for the trees. 
In his annual policy address last week, he proposed to turn Hong Kong into a center for Chinese medicine, but he offered no major remedies for restoring the property market. 
During a radio call-in show with Mr. Tung after the 135-minute speech, one caller bluntly told him to resign.
"Obviously, you can understand it when the public is unhappy," Mr. Tung said. 
But he added, "Hong Kong is a very free-market economy, and what the government can do is really not a lot."
Some politicians here say Mr. Tung may be miscast in his role. 
Before the transfer to China, when Hong Kong was booming, a conservative businessman might have seemed an obvious choice to keep the cash registers ringing. 
Now, with the economy in a shambles and Hong Kong's confidence shaken, people here are yearning for more than Mr. Tung's gray-flannel style.
"He would make an excellent chief executive in Singapore, where the people are Chinese but are more old-fashioned," said Martin Lee, Hong Kong's most prominent pro-democracy politician.
Unlike his British predecessor, Christopher Patten, who was a Tory party leader before coming to Hong Kong, Mr. Tung does not relish kissing babies, glad-handing on the street or racing to accident scenes.
"This is one area in which I really have to learn a whole lot more -- transforming myself from a businessman," Mr. Tung said. 
"Could I communicate better?
Yes, I can and I will communicate better."
But while Mr. Tung wants to hone his political skills, he is not about to embrace the rough-and-tumble of democracy. 
Hong Kong held direct elections for one-third of the seats in its legislature in May, and pro-democracy candidates, who did well, are pressing for a speedier transition to full democracy.
Mr. Tung said the economic crisis made him more determined to stick to the timetable, which would not put his job or the full legislature up for election until after 2007.
"Right now we just have too many things going on," he said. 
"If you look at the changes that are around us, we need a stable environment."
In the final analysis, Mr. Tung's future depends on his relationship with the leaders in Beijing. 
And despite Hong Kong's travails, there is no evidence that he has lost their faith. 
Likewise, Mr. Tung's support among Hong Kong's powerful property tycoons remains generally solid.
Mr. Tung has worked hard to establish his credentials as the leader of a Chinese city. 
In his speech last week, he said Hong Kong people should be inspired by their brethren in China, who built earthen walls to hold back the waters during the recent floods on the Yangtze River.
But critics say the flood would not have been so calamitous if China had protected its environment. 
Hong Kong, they say, needs policies that avoid disaster, rather than appeals to heroism after disaster has struck.

A Window on Prosperity
"They hope by rhetoric and bullying and shouting at the present time to bring about a result more acceptable to China," said James D. McGregor, a Hong Kong legislator and chairman of Asia Securities International Ltd. 
"At the same time, I don't think they have any intention of seriously damaging the great capability of this place to deliver the golden eggs for China."
The current dispute intensified on Friday, when Chris Patten, the British governor of Hong Kong, formally introduced legislation to broaden democracy in the crown colony. 
China has reacted with outrage.
And today, Lu Ping, a senior Chinese official with responsibility for Hong Kong affairs, denounced Mr. Patten as it has denounced no other major foreign official in several years.

"Stock market volatility doesn't mean that the real economy is being affected accordingly," said K. K. Chan, senior economist at the Hong Kong Bank.

file: Hong Kong Still Carries Britannia_s Indelible Mark.txt
text:
ï»¿
Over the last two centuries or so, Britain has ruled great chunks of the globe -- an empire, it was said, on which the sun never set.
Now, in a matter of hours, this easternmost shard of that empire will be relinquished, returned to China after 156 years of colonial suzerainty, leaving Britain with little more than a handful of islands, mostly in the Caribbean. 
Yet, the Hong Kong that returns to China is in many ways recognizable less as a place Chinese than a place indelibly touched by the ways of the West.
There are, to be sure, the obvious remainders of colonial rule -- coins with Queen Elizabeth's portrait still jingling in pockets, motorists hewing to the left side of the road, the local yacht club clinging stubbornly to its appellation "Royal," the tea and scones served on fine china at the Mandarin Hotel, and above all the use of English.
Yet, Britain has bequeathed Hong Kong more than visible trinkets of its reign.
Derek Davies, for decades the helmsman of Asia's pre-eminent news magazine, the Far Eastern Economic Review, assayed colonialism's central accomplishment in a speech he delivered not long ago titled, "Two Cheers for Colonialism."
"The British," he asserted, "were the Romans, the builders and administrators, no intellectual nonsense, although certainly they thought they were bringing civilization -- industry, modernity, the Christian religion."
"Harbors, roads, railways and imperial cities," were built, he continued, "in addition to less palpable but more important benefits such as the rule of law, the legal system, parliamentary democracy and a free press."
There are some here who are unimpressed by this heritage, preferring instead to see Hong Kong's entire colonial experience as an affront to Chinese history and civilization. 
Propounding this view most forcefully in the last year has been Zhou Nan, the senior Chinese official here, who invariably describes the return to Chinese sovereignty as the moment "when the yoke of colonialism" is shrugged off.
Indeed, Britain's resort to war from 1839 to 1842 to force the Chinese to buy opium from the firm of Jardine, Matheson and its wresting of the island of Hong Kong as booty from Beijing hardly presaged much in the way of morality or benevolence.
Official Chinese lamentations over British perfidy neatly overlook the venality and collaboration of a huge measure of Qing dynasty officialdom with the opium trade. 
Yet the fact remains that force of arms won Hong Kong for the British empire and cemented it, in 1898, with a 99-year lease on adjoining mainland territory.
In many ways, however, Hong Kong was different from other British colonial possessions, whether in the New World, Africa or the Indian subcontinent, virtually all of which are now long independent.
"I think Hong Kong is not a typical colonial situation," said Charles Aylmer, head of the University Library's Chinese Department at Pembroke College, Cambridge. 
"Rather paradoxically, I think the reason Hong Kong outlasted all the other colonies is because of the really strange situation with the lease."
"It is because everyone knew it was coming to an end that it lasted as long as it has," he said. 
"If it had been a simple occupied territory, there is no reason it would not have ended in 1949," the year Mao Zedong established the People's Republic of China.
The crude barbarity with which Hong Kong passed into British control was quickly supplanted by the rudiments of an administrative and legal system modeled on Britain's own. 
Democracy was not in the cards, though, for more than a century.
Still, Britain's last Governor, Christopher Patten, has been buoyantly defending the record of British stewardship. 
In his final appearance before Hong Kong's legislature, a fully elected body that China will dismiss on Tuesday, Mr. Patten summarized what he believes to be British colonialism's bequest to its last Asian territory.
"I think that Hong Kong is an astonishing Chinese success story," he told the 60-member legislature. 
"But I think it's a success story with British characteristics. 
I think that what Britain has helped provide as a result of the accidents of history is a framework within which people, particularly in the last 50 difficult years in this region, a framework within which Chinese men and women -- ordinary Chinese men and women -- have been able to do extraordinary things. 
I don't think any fair-minded observer would deny any role for British administrators or the rule of law in what has happened. 
But equally, any British observer, any of my predecessors as Governor, like this Governor, would stand back in awe at what Chinese men and women have managed to do here in Hong Kong given the chance, given the chance to be free in an economic and political sense."
More than any of his 27 predecessors, Mr. Patten in his five-year tenure moved Hong Kong toward a genuine measure of democratic governance and accountability. 
In 1995, for the first time, Hong Kong's Legislative Council was fully elected, directly and indirectly. 
Other local councils are all filled by elected members. 
It is one British legacy that will be nullified.
China will dismantle those institutions of governance on Tuesday. 
Indeed, the senior member of the new government's incoming Cabinet, Sir Sze-Yuen Chung, said this week that assemblies with appointed members marked "a step forward for democracy."
When the royal yacht Britannia, bearing Prince Charles and Mr. Patten, slips its mooring here on Tuesday, the Chinese flag will already be flying above them. 
But not all those who came here in the service of colonialism will follow.
Among those bits of empire that will remain are the likes of the stout and ruddy-faded Police Superintendent, Stephen Grinley Evans, who oversees a police team that watches the border for illegal immigrants passing into Hong Kong from China.
"I'm not ashamed to say I'm a bloody dinosaur," he said, laughing. 
"I came here from Scotland and I've been here since 1977. 
As long as they'll pay me, I'll stay."
And there is David T. Browning, a senior civil servant in the Customs and Excise Department who has seen the Union Jack lowered twice before on bits of empire.
"I joined the colonial service, partly for adventure and partly because I didn't really fancy staying in England," he said, hoisting a silver tankard of ale to his lips.
"I stayed on in Zambia after independence," he continued. 
"But I left the New Hebrides after it went independent."
The New Hebrides are now Vanuatu. 
"A friend in London said 'Why don't you go to Hong Kong?'
" he said. 
"Of course, I had in the back of my mind the impermanence of colonial regimes."
Now the last remaining British civil servant of 5,000 in his department, Mr. Browning said that Chinese rule would mean a rapid winnowing of the slightly more than 1,000 British citizens working in the Hong Kong Government.
"There are enough well-qualified, diligent, intelligent people here," Mr. Browning said. 
"The main thing is they have to maintain stabilityI under the S.A.R."
-- the Special Administrative Region, as Hong Kong will be known under Chinese rule. 
"I don't think it will be very many years before the expats leave," he continued. 
"Nobody's indispensable."
But for Governor Patten, his major regret, he insists, is not the disappearance of British civil servants -- for the civil service remains -- but the scuttling of democratic governance.
"I think there is a sadness," Mr. Patten said, "that this is the first time in recorded history that decolonization is followed by less democratization, not more."

Instead, several Hong Kong officials will join the talks as consultants.
Mr. Patten's proposals essentially try to increase the number of Hong Kong residents who can directly or indirectly elect the territory's legislators. 
While the proposals fall far short of democracy as it is practiced in the West, they have outraged China, which at one point threatened to unravel the political structure if Hong Kong's legislature approved and enacted them.
The announcement today is likely to arouse concern among democracy campaigners in Hong Kong that the British Government, having raised their hopes, is now caving in to Beijing. 
Pro-democracy organizations have warned that British officials are under strong pressure to reach some pact with China, even it it means agreeing to Chinese proposals that would narrowly constrict the role of elections in the territory.
Last month China said it would "set up a new kitchen," a vague Chinese idiom that was interpreted by many as meaning China would set up a shadow government or at least a second power structure to rival the British.
But Lu Ping, the Chinese official responsible for Hong Kong affairs, has recently tried to construe the term more narrowly, so that it refers merely to Chinese preparations for the takeover of the territory. 
Mr. Lu went out of his way to criticize Mr. Patten last month -- calling him a "man to be condemned by history" -- but he also appeared to try to reassure investors, saying China wants to insure stabilityI and prosperity in Hong Kong.
Mr. Lu also made a gesture of peace by reiterating China's support for a new $16 billion airport project, which has been delayed ever since it was announced more than three years ago.

file: Hong Kong, Takeover Near, In Wary Dance With Destiny.txt
text:
ï»¿
Tucked among the coffin makers just off Wing Lok Street, on the edge of a hankie-sized park where old men play Chinese chess, a fading photograph shows a waterfront site, Possession Point -- the spot where the British flag was first planted, by Capt. Edward Belcher at 8:15 A.M. on Jan. 
26, 1841.
Today Possession Point -- now Hollywood Road Park -- is well inland from Hong Kong's shrinking harbor. 
The coffin makers lounge on low stools, smoke from their loosely fingered cigarettes drifting in the pudding-thick humidity, as they wait for their next customers and watch the last faint moments of British rule unwind.
One year from today, at midnight's stroke on June 30, 1997, the territory's last colonial governor will sail from Hong Kong, relinquishing Britain's final Asian outpost and its 6.2 million people to one of the world's last remaining Communist governments. 
It is a moment that is riveted in people's minds and emotions, a date with a destiny many fear and others exult in.
In Beijing, where an immense digital clock flicks glowing red seconds inexorably toward zero hour, Hong Kong's return to China will be a decisive righting of historical wrongs -- the return of a piece of the motherland sundered after Britain forced China to buy its opium. 
The "yoke of colonialism," as Zhou Nan, China's senior official here, repeatedly puts it, is being shucked off.
Under that yoke, however, Hong Kong has become Asia's pre-eminent financial center, a city feverishly at work on the globe's largest civil engineering project -- involving a new airport, town, railroads, two immense bridges and two tunnels under Hong Kong's harbor. 
Hong Kong is the place where money is made with relish and spent with abandon, where a two-bedroom apartment can run $10,000 a month and tycoons tool around in limousines originally designed for the Japanese emperor.
Yet even in this city of soaring financial prowess -- a place of robust debate and newly spread political wings -- pride at the ending of colonialism is stirred by a widening sense of apprehension about the future under a Communist sovereign.
"I'm very pessimistic about the near future," said Martin C. M. Lee, the leader of Hong Kong's Democratic Party, which won the largest number of seats in last year's legislative elections. 
"They don't trust us, so they want to control us from Beijing."
Indeed, after 14 years of preparing for China to retake Hong Kong, virtually none of the major issues confronting the territory have been resolved, including most prominently who will lead the territory. 
A committee chosen by Beijing is nominally charged with settling these issues, but it meets only in secret, consults with carefully selected segments of Hong Kong's people behind closed doors and has banished dissenting voices from its proceedings.
China has promised that it will leave Hong Kong unchanged and "with a high degree of autonomy" for 50 years. 
Yet in the past year, China has proceeded clumsily and mostly in secret as it lays its plans to resume sovereignty.
What is clear is that Beijing has said it will abolish Hong Kong's elected legislature and replace it with handpicked lawmakers, scuttle its Bill of Rights ordinance and revive a slew of repressive laws. 
What is also clear is that the transition is well under way; China is already the largest investor here, with more than 1,100 mainland companies, from banks to trading houses, garment manufacturers to tour operators, doing business here.
Â 
The Growing Signs Of China's Presence
Already the pace of Hong Kong's absorption into China is quickening. 
At the Department of Government Supplies, Nigel Shipmen has taken surveys of Government buildings to determine how many of China's five-starred red flags will be needed on July 1, 1997, and how many of Hong Kong's new flag, featuring a five-petaled bauhinia flower.
Insignias for the police, fire department, immigration and prison officers are all being redesigned.
Beyond the external flourishes however, China's presence and influence are already considerable here. 
Swire Pacific, one of the great British hongs, or trading houses, has been pressed to reduce its holdings in the airline run by Hong Kong to a minority share. 
The British telecommunications giant Cable and Wireless is expected to cave in to Chinese pressure and become a minority shareholder in the territory's local phone company.
"It is natural for China to want some control of the commanding heights of the economy -- aviation, electronics, telecommunications and maybe banking -- but I am not comfortable," said Miron Mushkat, the managing director of Lehman Brothers here, at an American Chamber of Commerce conference. 
"It is not the Hong Kong way, and it is a form of nationalization."
For years, companies that traditionally have done most of their business with the London-based Hongkong & Shanghai Bank have been shifting business to the Bank of China. 
"It just makes sense," said the director of one company. 
"These are the guys we have to deal with."
But Hong Kongers themselves are not easily abandoning their sense of themselves as distinct from China's people, not merely because of social and political differences, but culturally and linguistically.
Â 
A Sense of Identity Apart From China
Last spring Eric K. W. Ma, a journalism professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, sent his students to an exhibit on Hong Kong's history, telling them to return and write about who they felt they were.
"My purpose was to trigger them to see whether they are local Hong Kong people or are they Chinese," he said. 
"Most of them were born in Hong Kong and most have very remote ideas about the Chinese."
More often than not, Hong Kong's people see themselves not as Chinese, but as Hong Kongers -- with a way of life far removed from China's mix of avariciousness born of rapid economic growth and insularity born of political repression, and with an ease with the world around them that China's people do not share.
In an effort to lend some statistical shape to Hong Kong's amorphous sense of identity, Timothy K. Y. Wong, of the Hong Kong Institute of Asia-Pacific Studies, conducted a poll. 
"We found that Hong Kong people still maintain a strong indigenous identity, although this identity is declining somewhat over the years," he said. 
Indeed, 49 percent of those surveyed regard themselves as Hong Kongers, with only 36 percent seeing themselves as Chinese.
One answer to the search for identity, among many, springs from the pages of the essays Mr. Ma collected. 
A student who left China in 1981 described her transformation after the Tiananmen massacre of June 4, 1989, from a "Hong Kong Chinese" to a "Chinese Hong Konger."
"The more I was influenced by Hong Kong's culture and ideas, the more I became a Hong Konger through and through," she wrote.
Â 
Confidence, Yes, But Keep Passports
One of the starker signs of the chasm between Beijing and Hong Kong is the refusal of Chinese officials here to speak Cantonese in public. 
Instead they insist on speaking Beijing-accented Mandarin, a language scarcely understood here. 
Yet there remains a vast range of intentions toward China's looming sovereignty.
Six years ago, Chui Kei Kong returned to Hong Kong from Vancouver, British Columbia. 
"You can't earn as much in Canada as here," said Mr. Chui, an electrical engineer. 
He had moved to Canada 10 years ago, but the allure of business opportunity pulled him back. 
His wife and daughter remain in Canada.
"I don't worry too much about 1997 because I'm a Canadian citizen," said Mr. Chui, who now owns a factory over the border in Shenzhen. 
"If the situation is very bad next year, I'll go back to Canada. 
Even though I can earn more in Hong Kong, I'd rather stay in a peaceful and civilized place."
Invariably, conversations these days swing toward contingency plans, and above all that means possession of a foreign passport. 
There are no precise data, but the Government estimates that 600,000 Hong Kongers hold such passports. 
In fact, more than half the members of Beijing's hand-picked Preparatory Committee, the body that China created to chart the transition from British to Chinese rule, carry foreign passports.
Yet many Hong Kongers are eager to live in a Hong Kong that is a rightful part of China. 
Chung Lee Wai, a 22-year-old university student who said he plans to work in community development, is harshly critical of China's political system yet equally fierce in his patriotism.
"The first step is for China to control Hong Kong," he said. 
"We need to go back to China. 
Hong Kong went to Britain because of the Opium War. 
I don't believe in independence for Hong Kong. 
I'm staying."
Chan Siu Hong is equally adamant. 
"Of course things may become very harsh in 1997, but I would like to stay here to try my best to take advantage of the opportunities here," said the 26-year-old owner of a video production company. 
"Why should I go abroad where I'll be looked down on by foreigners?"
Yet even some of the most ardent boosters for Chinese rule have hedged their bets. 
Henry Cheng, one of the world's richest men and the managing director of the New World property conglomerate, is chairman of the Better Hong Kong Foundation, a pro-China business group that actively promotes the territory's prospects and regularly meets with China's senior leaders.
Still, when asked recently what passport he held, he replied, "a French passport as a matter of confidence."
Quickly, though, he corrected himself. 
"I mean as a matter of convenience."
Â 
Little Understanding Of a Free Society
Much of Hong Kong's anxiety stems not only from the opacity of the process leading to Chinese rule, but from the stream of comments from Chinese officials that appear to threaten elements of Hong Kong's way of life, and the silence emanating from the territory's own leading citizens. 
Beijing's insistence on secrecy and conformity among the Hong Kongers it chooses to steer the territory toward Chinese rule is regarded as particularly ominous.
When Frederick Kin Kee Fung, a member of the Preparatory Committee, announced that he intended to vote against plans to abolish Hong Kong's legislature, he was aggressively lobbied by senior Chinese officials. 
On the day the committee voted to install a legislature picked by China, Mr. Fung cast the solitary negative vote.
"I wanted to let them understand, through words and actions, what is Hong Kong political culture," Mr. Fung said. 
"At the Preparatory Committee they just read out documents and said whoever supports it raise their hands. 
It's the Chinese way. 
I was told that if I voted no, I would be off the provisional legislature" -- the council that China will impose on July 1, 1997.
Mr. Fung did vote no, and he has been barred from participating in any discussions over the new legislature or the chief executive.
Many Hong Kongers, including Mr. Fung, believe that Chinese officials fundamentally do not comprehend Hong Kong.
Hong Kong's Governor, Christopher Patten, argues that much of the blame for Beijing's ignorance of and insensitivity toward Hong Kong is a consequence of the type of advice it has sought. 
"I think that one of the tragedies of the last few years is this," Mr. Patten said in an interview. 
"It's understandable that senior Chinese officials, given their backgrounds, find it difficult understanding the nature of a free society, what makes Hong Kong tick.
"They require a bit of assistance in learning about Hong Kong.
"They haven't always gotten the assistance they deserve from their appointed advisers in Hong Kong, who have believed that they should go and tell Chinese officials what they think Chinese officials want to hear. 
Senior Chinese officials deserve honesty, and too often they've gotten shoe shining."
In the meantime, Hong Kong waits and watches.

file: Hong Kong_s Business Elite Tells Americans_ Don_t Panic.txt
text:
ï»¿
On a warm spring night last month, the entrepreneurs and billionaires who built modern-day Hong Kong held an opulent dinner here at the Four Seasons Hotel to send the Washington establishment an urgent message: Calm down.
Don't overreact to every Chinese pronouncement about the future of Hong Kong, they warned members of Congress and Administration officials. 
Don't assume the worst about restrictions on civil liberties. 
And most important, let us handle Beijing.
"We are not in trouble," Victor Fung, a prominent property owner, insisted that night to members of Congress and Administration officials who deal daily with Asia. 
"We are not panicked."
In truth, the Hong Kong business elite is panicked -- but about how to manage Washington, not Beijing. 
The executives' fear is that Congress, with no other tools than economic sanctions at hand, might lash out in response to a minor roundup of protesters or a modest political crackdown, and send an already rocky relationship between the United States and China into a costly and bitter deterioration.
Formally, the United States will simply be an observer on July 1 when Prince Charles ends Britain's 155-year-long control over Hong Kong, the booming financial capital of Southeast Asia, and the Chinese reclaim a territory whose success has profoundly changed China's direction. 
But as a matter of economic Realpolitik, Washington is the central player.
All sides in the arguments and political maneuvering leading up to the turnover agree that America is the key to Hong Kong's future, both as a huge investor and trading partner, and as the single loudest international power calling for Beijing to respect Hong Kong's autonomy.
And in recent months everyone from the departing British to the bullish-sounding billionaires of the Better Hong Kong Foundation, and from labor unionists to Martin Lee, the chief democracy advocate, have come here in hopes of manipulating the political and economic levers in Washington's hands, to their own ends.
The executives are calling for Washington to do nothing, arguing that strong reactions can only anger Beijing. 
The unions and democracy advocates see the United States as their only brake on Beijing but decline to specify how Washington should use its leverage.
Meanwhile, the Clinton Administration has begun a lobbying campaign of its own in Hong Kong. 
In a series of strong but precisely worded warnings, it has argued that the markets rather than the White House or Congress will ultimately punish the Chinese if Hong Kong's autonomy and civil liberties are trampled.
"My message is simple," Lawrence H. Summers, the Deputy Treasury Secretary, said in Hong Kong recently. 
"There is no firewall between economic freedom and freedom in its many other dimensions.
"The free flow of information, the ability of people to remain free, to enter into transactions, to speak out: these are all the essential elements of free markets and a strong financial system," he said.
The Administration is betting that Mr. Summers' economic credentials make it easier to deflect Chinese criticism that Washington is interfering in its economic affairs.
To Americans doing business in Hong Kong, Mr. Summers is even more direct, cautioning executives about the risks of becoming apologists for the Chinese or the new Beijing-appointed Hong Kong Government. 
"If the two systems are going to merge," he said, "it is in everyone's interest that China become more like Hong Kong than the other way around."
But it is far from clear that the message is winning converts in Hong Kong. 
And in Washington, what was once a clear policy to treat Hong Kong as a completely autonomous entity, even after Beijing takes control, has been muddied by the debate about relations with China.
In a nonbinding resolution passed overwhelmingly this spring, Congress threatened to place huge sanctions against Hong Kong exports if China were to crack down on civil rights. 
Within days, that strategy was bitterly criticized by all sides in Hong Kong, from pro-Beijing executives to democracy advocates and Governor Chris Patten, who said it would "deprive Hong Kong of its livelihood at the moment it most needs support."
Since then, Congressional leaders have backed away from that strategy. 
But on Tuesday, Senator Jesse Helms, the chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee, opened a new front: He introduced a resolution to deny China "most favored nation" trading status, an annual exercise that this year could turn into a tough fight. 
He linked the matter to China's handling of the succession.
Mr. Helms declared that it was foolish to treat Hong Kong as a separate entity if the Chinese will not, and argued that China has already reneged on many promises to keep Hong Kong's political freedoms. 
"Yet the United States has failed to prevent or reverse a single violation" of the 1984 accords on the handover, he said.
On Thursday, Treasury Secretary Robert E. Rubin is expected to respond, telling American executives who have pressed for permanent trade status for China that revoking the trade status would "harm Hong Kong in the name of helping it."
Â 
Primary Investor
Roads Lead to U.S., Not Britain or Japan
Hong Kong is known around the world as a Chinese city with a distinctly British flavor, down to the daily high tea at the Peninsula Hotel. 
But amid the giant towers of Exchange Square, home of the booming Hong Kong stock exchange, it is taken for granted that the territory's economic interests are far more enmeshed with the United States, whose consulate sits just below the Governor's Mansion.
"There is a reason that everyone with an interest in Hong Kong's future is running to Washington these days, not to London or even Tokyo," said Robert Broadfoot who runs a political-risk consulting firm in the city.
The linkage has been tightened by the long recession and stock-market fall in Japan. 
Despite China's looming control, many American companies have cut back their Tokyo offices and moved their Asian headquarters to Hong Kong in the last five years, hoping to use Hong Kong as a beachhead into both China and the booming nations of Southeast Asia.
Today there are more than 1,100 American companies with regional bases in Hong Kong, led by investment houses like Morgan Stanley and banks like Citicorp. 
The American Chamber of Commerce estimates, perhaps stretching the numbers a bit, that American-based companies employ 10 percent of Hong Kong's work force of 2.5 million.
During the cold war, the American Consulate in Hong Kong was a major outpost for the Central Intelligence Agency. 
Today it is a base for issues at the forefront of American relations with Asia: the crackdown on drug trafficking, organized crime and counterfeiting of American currency and American-made products. 
"For a long time the U.S. policy in Hong Kong was that the handover is a British problem, and we're sure they'll work it out," said Jeffrey S. Muir, a senior executive for Seagram Asia Pacific who has lived in Hong Kong for more than two decades. 
"People don't think that way any more."
As a matter of both law and official policy, Washington's stance toward Hong Kong after the transition is to treat it as a completely separate entity from China, building on China's commitment to treat Hong Kong under the doctrine of "one country, two systems."
"We can't insist that China respect Hong Kong's autonomy unless we do as well," Jeffrey Bader, the deputy assistant secretary of state for East Asia, said to Congress earlier this year.
But carrying out that policy creates difficult anomalies. 
Hong Kong will continue to have a separate textile quota from China's, even though Chinese manufacturers have cheated on those quotas for years by placing Hong Kong labels in Chinese-made goods. 
The Commerce Department will continue to keep separate trade statistics for the territory, rather than lump Hong Kong trade with China's.
Hong Kong will continue to have its own vote at the World Trade Organization in Geneva, infuriating Chinese officials, who say it is an outrage that the territory belongs to the organization while China is in a tense negotiation to enter. 
Nonetheless, Hong Kong officials insist that they, not Beijing, will decide how to vote within the organization.
There will even be separate export controls. 
Electronics makers, for example, will be able to ship sensitive technologies to Hong Kong that could not be sent without licenses to Beijing.
"The whole system presumes that the Chinese will truly respect their border with Hong Kong," a senior Western official said in Hong Kong recently. 
"The first time some supercomputer whisks through Hong Kong and shows up in a nuclear weapons lab in Shanghai, the assumptions begin to crack apart."
An American official here with a more jaundiced view of the policy -- and of its assumption that Hong Kong courts, customs service and financial regulators will remain completely independent -- put it another way.
"Here's the deal," he said. 
"After July 1 we pretend that Hong Kong isn't part of China, even though it is. 
And we still insist that Taiwan is still part of China, even though it isn't."
Â 
Civics Lesson
Market Strength Is Tied to Freedom
The Clinton Administration's political strategy before the transition is to constantly repeat Mr. Summers's argument that China cannot reap the financial benefits of a booming Hong Kong unless the city remains a place of open dissent, corruption-free courts and markets that are less rigged than in most of Asia.
"This was the best way we could think of to convey our message to the Chinese," a senior Western diplomat in Hong Kong argued recently.
"Lecturing them about human rights is a proven failure," he said. 
"So we are simply trying to make the point that if you want to have a solid stock market that people trust, you have to have newspapers that are free to write about the Dalai Lama, or the state of the independence movement in Taiwan. 
These are all subjects that deeply affect the atmosphere for investors."
So far, there are reasons to question whether the message has got through. 
In interviews in Hong Kong, many of the city's tycoons and market players dismissed that argument as overblown, saying that only Americans believe that free markets require American-style liberties.
Several Hong Kong leaders say that C. H. Tung, Hong Kong's chief executive-designate, has asked many of them, "If it works in Singapore, why not the new Hong Kong?"
The Japanese send a similar signal, telling Hong Kong's Government that Japanese investors want stabilityI above all else.
Perhaps the biggest test of Hong Kong's ability to separate the economic from the political lies in how it handles the "red chips," huge state-owned Chinese companies that have become the hottest properties on the Hong Kong exchange.
The companies come from a tradition of enormous secrecy, and they bridle at Hong Kong's requirement that companies publish extensive financial data, including subsidies they received from Beijing. 
In fact, their chief asset, the one propelling their share prices into the stratosphere, is their "guanxi," or connections to the Chinese leadership.
That means their future is completely bound up in the most delicate political decisions facing China's leadership -- for example, whether the leaders are willing to risk millions of jobs because the world demands that China open its domestic market and strip away the protections that have allowed some state-owned companies to operate as monopolies for decades.
Already some analysts for Western brokerage houses say they feel subtle pressure from their employers not to write anything too critical about the "red chips," for fear that Beijing will take lucrative business elsewhere. 
They would be hesitant, several said, to declare that a state-run company was cooking its books or bloated with far too many workers.
And Western investors wonder whether, after the transition, Hong Kong regulatory authorities will remain independent and uncowed by their new masters in Beijing, who many expect will press for less strict standards for companies with friends in high places.
"Watch what happens the first time the Hong Kong authorities delist some stock that has plenty of connections," the head of an American brokerage in Hong Kong said recently.
"The risk in Hong Kong," said a British official who is pessimistic about its future, "is that a stifling political correctness sets in."
If that happens, he adds, Beijing will discover that the markets are "self-sanctioning."
Â 
Anxieties at Home
Executives Object To Democracy Card
Hong Kong boosters say that Beijing understands that the markets must be free to exert such discipline on political meddling. 
The vast lobbying campaign that the city's rich and powerful have waged in Washington was prompted by the fear that Congress will feel compelled to do something anyway, egged on by prominent leaders of the Hong Kong opposition like Martin Lee, who reminded Congress during a visit here in April that the 1992 Hong Kong Relations Act "commits your Government to support a free, elected legislature in Hong Kong."
Mr. Lee's sympathetic reception on Capitol Hill infuriated many of Hong Kong's rich and powerful. 
"You want to know what would be a good American policy toward Hong Kong?"
Ronnie C. Chan, one of the most outspoken of the American-educated members of the Hong Kong elite leading the lobbying campaign in America, asked over dinner recently at Hong Kong's glistening cultural center. 
"This may sound simplistic, but try it: Leave us alone."
Mr. Chan is hardly alone in that view. 
So when major American magazines began predicting Hong Kong's demise under Chinese rule, he and other members of the city's wealthy elite began inviting journalists from around the world to visit Hong Kong, at the expense of the Better Hong Kong Foundation, to persuade them to paint a more flattering picture. 
Other executives have begun denouncing the American media, arguing that it is exaggerating the threat to make a better story when China takes the reins.
"The American view of what will happen is wildly out of whack," said Mr. Fung, who heads the Hong Kong Trade and Development Council. 
"Look, we have a barometer of Hong Kong's future -- the stock market. 
And investor confidence is very, very high. 
Who would have guessed that just a few years ago?"
In fact, polling data suggest a huge perception gap between Americans and Hong Kong residents.
A study just released by Wirthlin Worldwide, a political polling group, found that 60 percent of Americans polled believe that the people of Hong Kong would choose to become independent, but only 14 percent of the Hong Kong respondents agreed. 
A scant 4 percent of Americans thought Hong Kong would choose to become part of China, while 62 percent of Hong Kong residents thought their fellow citizens would elect Chinese rule. 
The margin of sampling error in the poll was 4.9 percent.
The poll numbers understate the concerns in places like the soda-can-strewn offices of the Hong Kong Federation of Trade Unions, on the third floor of a neighborhood of bars and brothels where tourists rarely tread.
There, elderly men who mix cement on the edge of Hong Kong harbor and drivers who deliver Coca-Cola say their links to the United States are their best protection after July 1. 
In April, just a day after Hong Kong's government-in-waiting announced new restrictions on political demonstrations to go into effect within hours of the turnover, a dozen or so of these workers met with John Sweeney, the president of the A.F.L.-C.I.O.
"Political activity is how we fight for workers' rights," Lee Cheuk Yan, the general secretary of the federation told the visiting American labor chief. 
"Is a strike over wages a 'political activity?'
"
When the American union leader conveyed those concerns the next day to Mr. Tung, Hong Kong's future leader offered assurances that unions would not be affected by bans on political actions. 
But after Mr. Sweeney launched into a brief monologue on why Hong Kong must observe basic rights, Mr. Tung paused for a moment, then remarked, "You're too caring."

file: Hong Kong_s Leader Heads for U.S. to Correct _Misconceptions_.txt
text:
ï»¿
Tung Chee-hwa, the man chosen by Beijing to run Hong Kong, left today for his first visit to the United States since Britain returned this territory to Chinese control on July 1. 
He said the visit was intended to correct American "misconceptions" about Hong Kong.
The Hong Kong that Mr. Tung will discuss with President Clinton, members of Congress and interested Americans is flourishing economically. 
But it has no democratic institutions, has undergone a sharp contraction of civil liberties and apparently has three times the number of people it did 25 years ago who are living in poverty, in part because of an aging population and the large number of immigrants from China who do not have the skills that enable them to work in an increasingly non-manufacturing ecnonomy.
"I'm looking forward to going to the U.S.," said Mr. Tung, a shipping tycoon. 
"Really to tell my friends in America what is happening in Hong Kong, not only about the transition, but what is going on."
Mr. Tung was dissuaded from visiting the United States in the months leading up to Chinese rule, in part because of criticism over his decision to roll back certain rights.
Now, however, with two months of calm behind him, Mr. Tung said he is ready to spread news of Hong Kong's success under Chinese rule to skeptics in the United States, particularly to members of Congress who have been critical of Beijing.
Mr. Tung said he expected to meet with President Clinton, who met last spring with Martin Lee of Hong Kong's Democratic Party, which opposed Beijing's move to disband the elected legislature. 
He also hopes to meet with other Administration officials and key members of Congress.
"The Government is functioning as normal," said Mr. Tung. "The financial market is moving. 
Demonstrations are continuing, arguments everywhere. 
The legislative body is just as assertive as before, challenging everything we want to do."
Still, many people here, including Mr. Tung himself, believe he will face a hostile audience in explaining why Hong Kong is considered not ready for democracy.
Mr. Tung has proposed an electoral system that would give Hong Kong's leading companies and banks a major say in the legislature's composition.
Under his proposal, seats would be distributed to parties according to their proportion of total votes. 
A third of the seats would be chosen by companies, banks and professional associations. 
This arrangement is likely to prevent the Democratic Party, which won the largest share of seats in the fully elected legislature of 1995, from winning a large number of seats in elections next May. 
Because even losers in the elections will gain legislative seats, as permitted under a proportional voting system, and because companies are dominated by conservative business people, the Democratic Party's share of seats is almost certain to fall sharply.
Mr. Tung's view of how things are going is not shared by legislators who were removed from office by China on July 1 and replaced with a body of lawmakers of its choosing.
"It is a step backward -- it's highly undemocratic," said Mr. Lee, describing Mr. Tung's proposal.
The rosy picture painted by Mr. Tung was clouded somewhat today by a report by a group of university academics, the Hong Kong Social Security Society, which found that 856,000 people, 14 percent of the territory's population, are living beneath the poverty line of $358 a month.

file: HOUSE APPROVES EXPANSION OF TIES TO TAIWAN_S ARMY.txt
text:
ï»¿
The House voted overwhelmingly today to expand military ties between Taiwan and the United States, a move that China and the Clinton administration warned could aggravate regional tensions and jeopardize a landmark trade agreement.
The bill, approved by a bipartisan vote of 341 to 70, calls for the United States to establish direct military communications between Washington and Taipei, expand American training of Taiwan military officers and conduct an annual review on threats to Taiwan's security.
While the provisions of the Taiwan Security Enhancement Act are more symbolic than substantive -- American administrations have been empowered to give Taiwan military aid for more than two decades -- moving toward more formal military relations could have damaging diplomatic consequences with China.
If enacted, critics said, the bill would upset Washington's deliberately ambiguous "one China" policy, which treats Taiwan as a part of China and recognizes Beijing as China's capital, but also allows the United States to provide Taiwan with defensive weaponry.
"It would bring about very serious damage to China-U.S. relations," Yu Shuning, a spokesman for the Chinese Embassy here, said in a telephone interview. 
Beijing, which has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since the defeated Chinese Nationalists fled there in 1949, has not renounced the use of force to achieve eventual reunification.
But senior Republicans, led by Representative Tom DeLay of Texas, the powerful majority whip, chose the security measure as the first major bill for floor consideration this year precisely because it would challenge China.
The measure marked the opening salvo in what is likely to be a contentious series of votes involving China in this campaign-compressed year. 
It was a popular bill with Mr. DeLay's conservative base as well as with many Democrats. 
And it sought to paint Republicans as champions of democratic Taiwan, while leaving the administration to appear more interested in trade benefits with rival China.
Opposition from Democrats and some Republicans last fall had forced the bill's sponsors to strip out its most contentious language, including authorization to sell Taiwan specific weapons like missile defenses, air-to-air missiles and diesel-powered submarines. 
With those changes in mind, 140 Democrats felt free today to join 200 Republicans and 1 independent in saluting Taiwan's democratic government and its formidable lobby here.
"This is far less confrontational than the original legislation," said Representative Sam Gejdenson of Connecticut, the senior Democrat on the House International Relations Committee. 
Administration officials said they were saving their lobbying fire for the Senate, where the watered-down version still faces stiff opposition and possible defeat.
Senator Trent Lott of Mississippi, the majority leader, who is a strong supporter of Taiwan, urged caution against complicating United States-China relations. 
"We should proceed with due diligence," he said.
President Clinton's national security aides have advised him to veto the measure if Congress approves it, arguing that it goes well beyond the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act. 
That measure allows the United States to arm Taiwan with defensive weapons and implicitly commits Washington to defend Taiwan against attack.
The administration had backed up its commitment to Taiwan in recent years. 
The Pentagon dispatched two aircraft carrier battle groups toward the region in 1996 after China fired missiles near Taiwan. 
Between 1994 and 1998 alone, Mr. Gejdenson said, the United States approved $2 billion in arms to Taipei.
But the timing of the bill is a major headache for the administration, especially as American officials have tried to mend relations with China since the bombing of the Chinese Embassy in Yugoslavia last May.
"This bill would mandate a number of new security and military arrangements with Taiwan that could create dangerous, false and inaccurate expectations on both sides of the Taiwan Straits," said an administration policy statement.
But an influential Taiwanese lobbyist said the vote would play well among the candidates in the presidential elections in Taiwan next month, although security as taken a back seat in the campaign to other issues like coruption.
"Symbolically, Congress has sent a very strong signal to the people of Taiwan that the U.S. is committed to their security," said Wenyen Chen, president of the Formosan Association for Public Affairs, a lobbying group for Taiwan.

Supporters, led by Mr. DeLay, said the measure clarified and reaffirmed Washington's commitment to Taiwan's security in the face of a Chinese military buildup.
"Given the volatility of the situation in the Taiwan Straits, any mixed signals by our government can easily be read by the Communist Chinese as complacency," Mr. DeLay said.
But critics said the bill was unnecessary and counterproductive, and could create a new barrier to a vote later this year on granting China permanent trade benefits.
