file: Lawyers, Split Along Party Lines, Tangle Over Immunity for Huang.txt
text:
ï»¿
A sometimes testy three-hour meeting between lawyers for John Huang, the central figure in the Democratic fund-raising controversy, and lawyers for the Senate committee investigating campaign finance abuses ended today with Republican and Democratic lawyers clashing over whether Mr. Huang should be given a grant of immunity to testify.
The Republicans are reluctant to let Mr. Huang testify for fear that his testimony may jeopardize possible prosecutions. 
The Democrats say they want him to appear as a witness to rebut Republican allegations of a Chinese Government plot to influence last year's elections.
This behind-the-scenes debate continues even though some who have seen Mr. Huang's videotaped deposition in a related case said he might make for a surprisingly undramatic witness, one who often obfuscates.
After three days of hearings this week before the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, the debate over Mr. Huang's possible testimony has taken on enormous political and legal implications. 
Many had hoped that he would be the star witness, one who even the Democrats say was involved in questionable fund-raising. 
Without such a breakthrough witness, even Republican staff members acknowledge that the hearings have produced few fireworks and few revelations.
Ultimately, the decision on immunity will require the approval of two-thirds of the committee, with the Republican majority expected to take its cue from the committee's chairman, Senator Fred Thompson, Republican of Tennessee.
Democrats, who first raised the issue of immunity, have said all week that they are confident that Mr. Huang's testimony will vindicate their position that his fund-raising efforts, however questionable, will not support the Republican allegations against China.
"There's no evidence John Huang is anything but what he appears to be -- a politically active and ambitious fund-raiser who cut corners," said James Jordan, a spokesman for the Democratic minority on the committee. 
"Anything more than that is just flimsy inferences."
In the opening week of the hearings, the Republicans were often upstaged by an aggressive Democratic public relations campaign and by the surprise offer by Democrats for Mr. Huang to testify. 
And, with public interest in the hearings flagging, the Republicans may need to produce a high-profile witness, like Mr. Huang, as a star attraction to keep attention focused on their allegations.
So far, the Republicans have failed to generate the kind of excitement with these hearings that has surrounded past Congressional investigations, like Watergate and the Iran-contra hearings.
The Republican's lead witness, Richard Sullivan, a former finance director of the Democratic National Committee, not only failed to support Senator Thompson's charges regarding China but also tried to affirm the basic Democratic position that Mr. Huang was an exception to Democratic fund-raising practices.
Still, both sides continue to negotiate over whether Mr. Huang will testify. 
After the meeting today, Mr. Huang's lawyer, Ty Cobb, said he remained "cautiously optimistic" that his client would testify before the committee, although perhaps not until the fall.
In a surprise move on Tuesday, the opening day of hearings, Senator John Glenn of Ohio, the committee's ranking Democrat, announced that Mr. Huang would testify if given a grant of immunity on several lesser legal issues. 
But Mr. Huang agreed to testify without the protection of immunity on some of the major allegations against him.
"The discussions today were very constructive and professional," Mr. Cobb said. 
"There were some occasional rough spots. 
But from my perspective, we are hopeful it will move forward to the end that we had hoped for. 
We remain cautiously optimistic. 
But it may take more time to resolve this than the public may expect."
Mr. Jordan, the spokesman for the committee's Democrats, said: "Mr. 
Cobb is interested in a way to make it happen. 
And Senator Glenn is hopeful the attorneys can find a way to satisfy the concerns of all and make it possible for Mr. Huang to appear before the committee to answer some of the serious charges against him."
Paul Clark, a spokesman for the committee's Republican majority, had no comment, saying that the Republican members "haven't had time to digest" the results of today's meeting.
Committee Republicans have been concerned that granting any form of immunity to Mr. Huang will prevent him from facing prosecution. 
The precedent for this was set after the Iran-Contra hearings when a three-judge panel overturned the convictions of Oliver L. North and John M. Poindexter on the ground that testimony taken under a Congressional grant of immunity had tainted evidence in their criminal trials.
In addition, Attorney General Janet Reno has objected to any grant of immunity. 
Ms. Reno has not stated specifically the reasons for her objection, but the Justice Department has serious concerns over any arrangement that would impede its investigation into Mr. Huang's fund-raising actions and could undermine possible prosecutions.
"It's a mess in some ways," said Alan Strasser, a former United States Attorney and a lawyer in the Washington office of Kutak, Rock. 
"To some extent, the Democrats have Ollie North in mind. 
If Huang talks, he won't be prosecuted and they would just as soon see that. 
Each party has an expectation of what Mr. Huang's testimony will be: the Republicans don't think it will be helpful to them, and the Democrats think they can benefit from it."
But Joseph E. diGenova, also a former United States Attorney and now in private practice said giving immunity "is a serious matter" and added: "This is just not the kind of thing that you do lightly. 
You run the possibility of ruining a serious criminal investigation. 
Attorney General Reno has made herself very clear on that and someone has got to pay homage to that."
Mr. diGenova added that was possible for the lawyers to agree to withhold the granting of immunity immediately and wait to see whether the Justice Department indicates whether there is a serious case against Mr. Huang. If it appears that the case is not strong, Mr. diGenova said, then allowing Mr. Huang to testify would be less of a risk.

The Government of China today put Wang Dan, its most noted dissident, on an airplane bound for the United States after releasing him for medical reasons, according to the official Chinese news agency, Xinhua, in Beijing.

16. Mr. Wei was also released on medical grounds on condition that he, too, leave China and go into exile.

file: Legislator Urges Diplomacy to Improve Rights in China.txt
text:

The chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee said today that he expects China to meet President Clinton's human rights demands as a condition to renewing Beijing's trade status. 
If it does, he said, the Administration should stop threatening China with sanctions and use other means to promote human rights.
The chairman, Representative Lee Hamilton, an influential foreign-policy voice, also urged President Clinton to lay the groundwork for a policy that will take account of United States trade, security and political interests.
"I believe the President has not always provided the personal articulation and justification that his policies need," Mr. Hamilton said in a speech at the American Enterprise Institute.
"On China, we need a broader understanding of our national interest. 
We need a skillful balancing of economic, security and human rights interests, rather than a single-minded emphasis on one objective."
Mr. Hamilton thus highlighted an intensifying debate, just three weeks before President Clinton must decide whether to renew China's trade benefits as a "most favored nation."
Senior Administration officials said they are involved in an intense dialogue with China to try to get Beijing to demonstrate as much progress on human rights as possible in the next few weeks.
While no one at the White House will say so out loud, it is now widely assumed within the Administration and on Capitol Hill that Mr. Clinton will find a way to renew all or most of China's trade benefits, which allow it to export products to the United States at the lowest tariff rates.
The only real question is what political steps the President will take to get down from the tall tree he climbed a year ago, when he declared that he would not renew trade benefits without "overall significant progress" on human rights. 
While China has made some progress, and Administration officials hope for more, how "significant" it will be remains to be seen.
One option was endorsed by Mr. Hamilton today, when he said "I hope and I expect" that China will do enough by June 3 -- like accounting for political prisoners -- that the President will be able to declare that Beijing has met his conditions.
Mr. Hamilton said President Clinton should then renew China's trade status, and retire permanantly the threat of a revocation. 
Instead, he said, Mr. Clinton should try to influence China by fostering "change through personal diplomacy and our economic ties."
Under another option, some lawmakers and human rights organizations argue that, barring some dramatic move, China at best will only fulfill some of the President's human rights demands before the deadline.
They contend that the President, for his own political credibility, cannot renew China's trade benefits across the board, given the spotty progress Beijing has made on human rights. 
Instead, they advocate renewing the most-favored-nation status for China's private exports, but withholding it for selected exports from Government-owned or army-owned factories.
Like the White House, this school understands that the economic stakes are too great -- more than $40 billion a year in trade -- for Washington to totally revoke the trade benefits. 
But they want to keep up the pressure.
Â 
Describing the Targets
"I honestly believe that if the Chinese do not make overall significant progress, the President will honor his executive order and have some revocation" of the trade benefits, Representative Nancy Pelosi, a California Democrat who has been a leader of the get-tough policy.
She said one possible target is China's state-owned military industries, which export everything from clothing to AK-47 assault weapons to the United States.
Senior officials say the final decision will come down to a political judgment for the President. 
If he gets just enough progress from Beijing, he could swallow hard, renew China's trade status and take the criticism from editorial writers and some members of Congress, who will inevitably point up the differences between his oratory and his actions.
Or he could choose the politically more attractive route of renewing trade benefits selectively, thus remaining true to his campaign promises while not aborting the trading relationship.
Not only the President has a political interest in such a compromise; so do many of the most outspoken Democratic lawmakers who have advocated a tough line on China since the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre. 
Although many Administration officials believe a selective approach is unworkable, given the difficulty of sorting out whether a company is privately owned or state-owned, it may turn out for political reasons to be the policy.

file: Likely to Be a Best Seller in China_ It_s No Mystery.txt
text:
ï»¿
Officials have been streaming into government bookstores in recent days and hauling away stacks of a hot new product: a 74-page, 50-cent booklet called "A Great Program for Comprehensively Strengthening Party-Building."
This must-read item consists of two recent speeches by the man who is the Communist Party chief and president of China, Jiang Zemin, and a collection of editorials describing the "brilliant thesis" and "essential compass" that Mr. Jiang has laid out -- a purported breakthrough in Communist doctrine labeled the "Three Represents."
To prosper in a new century, Mr. Jiang says in these speeches, the Communist Party "must always represent the development needs of China's advanced productive forces, must always represent the forward direction of China's advanced culture and must always represent the fundamental interests of China's broadest number of people."
In a classic propaganda campaign that has gathered full force this month, Mr. Jiang's supposed breakthrough has been pounded home almost daily in laudatory editorials and televised testimonials by leaders from every province and officially recognized social group.
If this sounds anachronistic for a leader who is promoting a wider opening to the West, it reflects enduring rituals of power within the Chinese Communist Party. 
The booklet's contents may be vague and tedious, insiders say, but that is beside the point: Mr. Jiang is making officials go through the panegyrics as a show of his leadership, as a public blow in his maneuvering to retain supreme power in the decade ahead.
Mr. Jiang is expected to resign as the party's general secretary at the 16th Communist Party Congress in 2002, when he will be 76. 
He is expected to give up the presidency the year after. 
But with no strong successors in sight, Mr. Jiang, who has led the party since 1989 and served as president since 1993, is widely believed to want to continue pulling strings from behind the scenes, as Deng Xiaoping did in the 1980's and 1990's.
And so while Mr. Jiang cultivates the stature he hopes will transcend formal retirement, officials anxious to hold on to their own jobs loudly sing his praises.
"It's like in ancient times, when the emperor would test his ministers by bringing out a donkey and calling it a horse," said an editor at a major party-affiliated newspaper. 
"If you maintained that it was a donkey you lost your head. 
If you called it a horse, then you got a promotion."
Closely related to Mr. Jiang's effort to fortify his image, insiders say, is his effort to secure himself a place in the Chinese Communist pantheon, after Mao and Deng, as an important theorist. 
Not surprisingly, considering Mr. Jiang's current unrivaled position, his "breakthrough" statement on the "Three Represents" is garnering rave reviews and has become a staple of high-level study sessions in provincial capitals.
"A brilliant thesis drawn from insight into the future," said the party's official paper, People's Daily, on May 22 in a typical description. 
"A concentrated embodiment of the fundamental nature of the party and the essence of socialism."
In other newspapers, officials have called Mr. Jiang's prosaic statement "pregnant with connotations and meanings," "a scientific summation of our party's nearly 80 years of historical importance" and "a great program for party-building in the new century."
The Liberation Army Daily hailed it as "an essential compass for military, ideological and political construction in the new era," while the Federation of Trade Unions, not to be outdone, said Mr. Jiang "answers the question of why and how the working class is relied on the during the process of building socialism with Chinese characteristics."
The China Women's News proclaimed, "The 'Three Represents' are the criteria for women's work."
The campaign is, of course, low-key compared with the vicious political winds of the Mao era, and much of the population today can simply tune it out. 
At the popular Xinhua Bookstore in central Beijing today, most customers walked right past the rack up front that featured the booklet on Mr. Jiang's speeches.
But the booklet is a best seller at the Party Documents Bookstore, where officials are buying it in bulk for their colleagues, and ambitious party and government leaders can hardly afford to ignore the new catch phrases.
"Quite apart from substance, the campaign is a test of whether subordinates and local leaders in the provinces are staying in step," the editor said. 
"That's why in recent days we've seen one local leader after another coming forward -- it's a way to affirm their allegiance and keep their jobs."
This new campaign went into overdrive even before last year's "Three Stresses" campaign (theoretical study, political awareness and good conduct) had fully run its course, causing complaints about the sheer waste of time and energy.
In that campaign, still continuing in far-flung local branches, party and government officials have been required to spend weeks at a time studying Deng and Jiang speeches and engaging in self-criticism. 
The process was intended to spot new talent and bring discipline to an organization seen as increasingly lax and corrupt.
"Nobody really cares about this stuff, and people feel disgusted when they have to study it," a former party propaganda department official said of Mr. Jiang's latest ideological offerings. 
"What about Taiwan or the World Trade Organization?
People have even started making off-color jokes about Jiang Zemin's love of 'threesomes.'
"
The current campaign, many believe, is just a prelude to the probable publication this year of Mr. Jiang's collected speeches and writings, providing a showcase for his works.
"It has always been the case here that the party leader is expected to put forth his own thinking," the newspaper editor said. 
"Otherwise he has no prestige."
Party experts have noted that Mr. Jiang opened the new campaign with speeches in the south, beginning in Guangdong Province, in a parallel with Deng's last great act, when he kicked off a new wave of market reforms and economic growth with a celebrated southern tour in 1992.
Whatever his strengths as a power broker, Mr. Jiang is not regarded as a bold theorist, and some officials are quietly grumbling about self-aggrandizement.
But in Mr. Jiang's defense, insiders note, he has not yet tried to elevate himself into a Mao or Deng. 
Up to now, at least, he has not granted his own ideas the official status of a body of thought, as in Mao Zedong Thought, or theory, as in Deng Xiaoping Theory.

file: Lonely Song of a Chinese Minstrel Bares a Migrant_s Lament.txt
text:
ï»¿
Over the clatter of Chinese meal-making in the outdoor food stalls that overflow with diners on a hot summer evening, Shen Ping sings with a lonely voice.
A long-faced young woman with wide eyes, Ms. Shen wanders with a friend from one stall to the next through a back alley in this southern city, offering to strum her guitar for any customer willing to throw a dollar her way.
Stopping beside a low-lying table piled high with dishes and surrounded by six men on small wooden stools, Ms. Shen and her partner sing a duet earnestly, if a little off-key. 
It is a sentimental love song, something about being far from home, which is apt enough for the two young women, since they are migrants.
Hundreds of thousands of outsiders looking for easy money have flocked to this part of Hainan Island, touted as China's Hawaii by development-hungry local officials. 
Most of them, like Ms. Shen and her friend, Lan Feng, have to settle for something less.
A leader in free-wheeling economic reforms, Hainan, off China's southern coast, rode a real-estate boom in 1990-1992, only to suffer badly from a crash in 1993. 
Thousands of half-built hotels lie vacant, like ghosts of another era.
But young people like Ms. Shen still pour into Hainan because, even with a downturn, China's coastal areas offer more opportunity than most of the slower-growing interior.
"Mainlanders do the kind of jobs that locals would never want," said Hong Yansheng, a food stall manager, referring to the migrants. 
"A local resident would never sing for money. 
You lose too much face."
In many nations, immigrants often do the kind of work that native-born residents look down on. 
In China, migrants from other parts of the country play that role, on an enormous scale.
More than 100 million of China's 1.2 billion people are estimated to be on the move, leaving their homes to look for work elsewhere. 
This floating population is causing an enormous but largely unmeasured social upheaval across the country.
When Ms. Shen, 23, left her village in Anhui province four months ago, she came to Hainan because a friend told her she could easily find a job in a hotel. 
But Ms. Shen found that one hotel after another would only offer work in a massage parlor, which she declined to do.
Instead, she bought a guitar and teamed up with Ms. Lan.
"I get tired of the men who pinch my rear end, but I can always walk away," said Ms. Shen.
Ms. Shen said she made about $25 to $35 a night, more than 10 times what she made working as a store clerk in her hometown. 
She sends $50 home to her parents each month, but will not tell them the truth about how she earns her living.
"They think it's bad for a girl to work on the street," she said. 
"I tell them I am an attendant in a hotel."
At another food stall, a diner who was red-faced from beer-drinking called Ms. Shen and her partner over to play.
"Where are you from, little sister?" he asked.
Ms. Shen eyed him warily, and did not answer. 
Instead she asked if he had any requests.
"As you like," said the man. 
"Sing a beautiful one."
Ms. Shen had hardly begun her song when the man waved her off.
"That's terrible!" he said loudly. 
"Sing another!"
Letting her finish this time, the man reluctantly gave Ms. Shen the equivalent of $1.25. 
She and Ms. Lan headed for the next stall.

file: Macao Journal_If Life_s a Crap Game, the Isle of Casinos Is Smiling.txt
text:
ï»¿
Polished to a spit shine, Macao welcomed its leader, President Jiang Zemin of China, as he landed here today to mark the former Portuguese colony's first year under Chinese sovereignty.
Such scrubbings are customary for visits by China's top brass. 
But this may be a rare case where the cleansing is more than skin deep.
A year after Portugal decamped from its last colonial possession -- leaving behind a territory riven by gang violence, drained by recession, and demoralized by decades of neglect -- Macao is cleaner, inside and out.
Thanks to a crackdown by the Chinese government, the so-called triad gangs that used to terrorize Macao are in retreat. 
The most notorious triad boss, Wan Kuok-koi, was convicted by the Portuguese just before they left. 
He is now in a heavily fortified jail and nobody is laying claim to his mantle. 
"It would be foolhardy to say that triads don't exist in Macao; they do," said Eric T. M. Yeung, a leading local businessman. 
"But there are clear boundaries. 
The sheer presence of a crack force from the Chinese military is a deterrent."
By putting the triads on a tight leash, China has all but ended the drive-by shootings, car bombings, and mafia-like mayhem that gave Macao an unwanted reputation as the Wild West city of the east.
Every now and again, flames erupt on sleepy side-streets as vandals set ablaze a car or motorcycle belonging to a triad member. 
But with most other violent crime down sharply this year -- particularly around the casinos that are Macao's economic lifeblood -- people are breathing easier.
"Incarcerating Broken Tooth made a big difference," said Ricardo Pinto, a Portuguese journalist, using Wan Kuok-koi's nickname. 
"There is a sense among the triads that they now have a rival to be respected."
The downside of law and order in Macao is a growing intolerance of dissent, not least on politically sensitive occasions like this anniversary. 
The police detained several members of the Falun Gong sect today, after they threatened to protest during Mr. Jiang's visit. 
About 20 members of the sect who came from nearby Hong Kong this morning were turned back at the ferry terminal.
Falun Gong, a spiritual movement with traces of Buddhism, is outlawed in China. 
But it remains legal in Macao and Hong Kong, which have their own legal systems.
Political protesters also come under pressure here. 
Lei Kin Yung, 21, a democracy advocate, said he was detained three times in the last six days for handing out leaflets.
"The authorities don't want Jiang to hear any voices from the other side," Mr. Lei said. 
"It has become worse under the Chinese."
The trouble for Mr. Lei is that he and others in the democracy camp elicit little sympathy from Macao's 430,000 residents. 
Unlike their Hong Kong neighbors, who are covetous of the rights they inherited from Britain, people here had little exposure to democratic political institutions under the Portuguese.
"They have a stronger interest in public affairs than they did a year ago, but not yet in political affairs," said Ng Kuok Cheong, the lone advocate of democracy in Macao's legislative assembly.
Still, Mr. Ng said he was cheered that people were now more engaged in solving the problems of Macao. 
Among the most pressing is the economy, which was mired in recession for four years because the crime wave scared off visiting gamblers. 
With safer streets, Macao's economy bounced back a bit in 2000.
Edmund Ho, the banker chosen by Beijing to run Macao, hopes to give legs to this recovery by opening the gambling industry to competition next year for the first time in decades. 
That decision is bad news for Stanley Ho, the Hong Kong tycoon who has held the sole license to operate casinos since 1962. 
But it cemented Edmund Ho's authority (Edmund and Stanley Ho are not related).
"We have a very smart politician as our leader," Mr. Yeung said. 
"He is also backed to the hilt by the Chinese leadership."
Critics worry that inviting other companies to build casinos here could rekindle the triad wars. 
A few note that while Wan Kuok-koi's gang, 14K, has been defanged, its archrival, known as Water Room, has kept its grip on the private rooms in the casinos where the high-rollers make their bets.
Aware of these risks, Macao is moving slowly. 
It hired the consulting firm Arthur Andersen to study the industry, and it seems likely to push for a small number of competitors, including Stanley Ho's company, rather than unbridled competition.
Mr. Ho has little choice but to acquiesce. 
He thrived on his close ties to the Portuguese colonial administrators. 
And despite having been here for 442 years, Portugual's legacy is waning like an autumnal sun.
Fueling the sense of good riddance was the disclosure that a few days before the handover last Dec. 
19, the departing governor, Gen. Vasco Rocha Vieira, transferred almost $20 million from a foundation he controlled in Macao to another in Portugal. 
An independent panel in Macao said his action had taken place in a "gray area of the law," but he refused to return the money.
"For the Portuguese community here, it was an awful way to start a new era," said Mr. Pinto, one of 1,000 Portuguese still left in Macao.

file: Macao Journal_Packing Up, Portugal Polishes Image.txt
text:
ï»¿
In less than two months, Portugal will give up this vest-pocket colony to China. 
Like well-mannered guests in a summer rental, the Portuguese are spending their last days tidying up after themselves.
Sidewalks are being repaved, lush gardens planted and a boxy glass pavilion is rising on the waterfront. 
Designed to resemble a giant Chinese lantern, the building is to be the site of the handover ceremony. 
There, at midnight on Dec. 
19, China will claim sovereignty over Macao, ending 442 years of colonial rule.
Over at the courthouse, the Portuguese authorities are busy with another kind of house-cleaning. 
They are prosecuting a 45-year-old Chinese man suspected of being the most powerful organized crime leader in Macao.
The man, Wan Kuok-koi, is accused of masterminding a string of shootings and bombings that have frustrated the police, scared off tourists, and turned this normally drowsy enclave into an Asian replica of the Wild West.
Mr. Wan, who goes by the nickname Broken Tooth Koi, has become the colony's most celebrated resident -- and Exhibit A for those who say Portugal has allowed Macao to decay from merely seedy to scary. 
Fears of violence during the trial have prompted the government to import security troops from Portugal, who patrol the courthouse with submachine guns.
To say that Portugal would like to resolve Mr. Wan's case before the handover understates its sense of urgency. 
The presiding judge, Fernando Estrela, holds hearings every day from 9:30 A.M. to 7:30 P.M. When Mr. Wan's lawyers ask windy questions, the judge cuts them off in an impatient tone.
"They are rushing because hundreds of foreign journalists are coming to Macao for the handover," said Ricardo Pinto, the editor of Ponto Final, a Portuguese-language newspaper here. 
"From an image point of view, it would be terrible for Portugal to have this business unfinished."
Government officials say that Mr. Wan's trial is not being rushed to avoid bad publicity. 
But they acknowledge that the Portuguese administration would prefer not to punt the case to Macao's new rulers.
"People said we were just going to wait for the handover, but we have confronted our problem," said Lieut. 
Col. Manuel A. Geraldes, a Portuguese Army officer who is a spokesman for Macao's Security Department. 
"One of the legacies we will leave Macao is respect for the law."
Resolving Mr. Wan's case is a top priority because last week, Portugal and China removed one of the few other remaining hurdles to a smooth transition. 
Earlier this year, Portugal protested China's decision to send troops to Macao before the handover. 
Portugal's President, Jorge Sampaio, even threatened to boycott the ceremony unless Beijing reversed itself.
During a visit to Lisbon on Tuesday by China's President, Jiang Zemin, the two sides agreed on a compromise: China will dispatch "technical delegation" to Macao before the handover to prepare for a military garrison. 
But it will delay sending troops until after Dec. 
19.
For Joao Manuel Costa Antunes, the Portuguese official coordinating the handover, it was welcome news. 
Mr. Antunes has designed Macao's handover events to emphasize the continuity between Portuguese and Chinese rule. 
He noted that, unlike Hong Kong, which was ceded to the British in 1842 at the end of the Opium War, Macao was settled by Portuguese seafarers in 1557 with the consent of China. 
"We never had a war with China, so for Macao, the handover should be a very smooth process," Mr. Antunes said.
Hong Kong's handover was a brittle affair. 
After the transfer of power, the head of the British delegation, Prince Charles, left abruptly on the royal yacht, Britannia. 
In Macao, by contrast, the Portuguese delegation -- including Mr. Sampaio -- will stay on to watch Mr. Jiang swear in the new government.
"We don't feel like we're losing something and China is gaining something," Mr. Antunes said. 
"We're coming to the end of a long period of historical involvement, and we want to go out with dignity."
With China and Portugal no longer squabbling over troops, the only hurdle to a dignified handover is the man known as Broken Tooth. 
Normally under Portuguese law, criminal trials last about a month -- meaning that Mr. Wan's trial could be wrapped up by mid-November.
But his lawyers are hoping to delay the trial until after the handover, when it would be heard by a Chinese court.
Such a strategy carries high risks. 
China's legal system can be brutal to gangsters. 
Cheung Tze-keung, a Hong Kong crime boss known as Big Spender, was executed last December after being convicted of kidnapping and arms trafficking. 
The crimes Mr. Wan is accused of carry a penalty of 5 to 15 years.
But Mr. Wan's lawyers said they had no reason to believe that he would fare worse in a Chinese court.
One noted that Portugal, as one of its last contributions to Macao, was building a maximum-security prison with only 12 cells. 
He believes the jail is being built with only one occupant in mind: his client.

file: Major Shift for Communist China_ Big State Industries Will Be Sold.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's leaders have agreed to sell off most of the nation's big state-owned industries, and outlined plans today at the opening of a Communist Party congress that is setting the nation's political and economic agenda for the post-Deng era.
A central theme of the congress, the party's 15th, will be endorsing a ground-breaking shift from socialist-style state ownership to a system of share-holding. 
More than 10,000 of China's 13,000 large and medium-sized state enterprises are likely to be sold, though many issues -- like who the buyers will be -- remain unclear.
Elder party members have objected that China may be dissolving the last solid pillar of its socialist system, but President Jiang Zemin has apparently persuaded decision-makers that they can no longer afford the burden of inefficient and money-losing industries, no matter the risks.
Still ruled by a party that calls itself Communist, however, Mr. Jiang and his allies are relying on semantical gymnastics to justify the move. 
Avoiding the word "privatization," they instead insists that when ordinary people buy shares of stock it is a form of "public ownership."
"Even if the state-owned sector accounts for a smaller proportion of the economy, this will not affect the socialist nature of our country," Mr. Jiang said today in a speech at the opening of the congress.
By whatever name, Chinese leaders are essentially abandoning what has been a central principle of Communist rule since the revolution here nearly 50 years ago: that the state would retain its position as the dominant owner of industry.
"What is socialism?" said Dong Fureng, a senior economist advising government leaders on how to make the shift to share-holding. 
"It means seeking social equality, not that the state has to keep a majority stake in every industry."
The long-term effect of changing such a critical system of ownership, perhaps lying beyond the political calculus of leaders now consumed by short-term crises, seems destined to move China's economy toward an even more capitalist and free market system, one where the Communist Party may have difficulty preserving the role it has today.
For now, however, the party dominates politics in this country, and the congress, with more than 2,000 delegates, is the most important political gathering here since the last party congress five years ago. 
With the main policy issue already decided, the principal drama at the weeklong congress is expected to lie in changes in the top leadership.
Since China's leaders still select themselves and make important decisions in secret, with little accountability to public opinion, high-level politics resemble a continuous campaign of infighting and ever-shifting alliances among the 19 members of the Politburo, particularly among the top three: President Jiang, Prime Minister Li Peng and the legislative chief, Qiao Shi.
A party congress is generally stage-managed to display an aura of unity to the public, while the senior leaders are actually involved in intense power struggles backstage, sometimes yielding important decisions only at the last minute.
One of the most-watched issues at this year's congress is what jobs await Mr. Jiang's top colleagues and rivals, Mr. Li and Mr. Qiao, both of whom are expected to relinquish their current positions. 
Though the congress has begun, the answers remain uncertain.
Like all capital cities, Beijing thrives on rumors and intrigue. 
But the center of power here is so well concealed by secretive tradition, and insulated by loyal aides, that outsiders rarely learn much about inside politics until well after the fact, if then.
It is clear, however, that the 15th party congress -- coming six months after the death of Deng Xiaoping -- is well timed to showcase Mr. Jiang as the leader likely to dominate the near future. 
A move to enshrine "Deng Xiaoping theory" in China's Constitution alongside "Mao Zedong Thought" appears to be an effort to line Mr. Jiang up as a leader on a par with Mao and Deng.
Although economic reality is helping force Mr. Jiang's hand on state enterprises, the political timetable of the party congress may have spurred him to act sooner than he would otherwise. 
Mr. Jiang needs to show he can be bold and is not just a follower of Deng, and reforming state ownership is the issue he has grasped.
Shifting ownership is a tremendously complex legal and organizational challenge, several economists said, with a serious danger that state assets will disappear into the pockets of factory managers during the transition. 
Industrial managers, traditionally an important constituency in China, are likely either to become corporate executives, or to get left out of the new system altogether if they cannot adjust.
Many officials argue that despite the planned changes, the state may remain the main owner in China for some time, since in many cases the shift to a share-holding system will transfer ownership to shares controlled by a specific government-run organization or company.
Since the plans have not yet been announced in detail, it is unclear exactly what role the state will play. 
Yet a vast sale of state assets will sharply reduce central control over large enterprises.
At greatest risk may be tens of millions of urban workers whose jobs are at stake. 
Yet leaders seem to think their best hope is to brave layoffs, which are inevitable, at a time when the overall economy is growing fast and some labor can be absorbed by non-state companies that are expanding.
After all, China's recent economic history has confounded most experts, domestic and foreign.
Not long ago, it was inconceivable that ordinary people in China would be able to buy and sell shares of stock freely, or have access to almost any consumer goods on the world market. 
Or that such choice would be accompanied by a significant loosening of government control over daily life, like choosing a job or where to live.
Perhaps the greatest paradox in China today is the way its enormous economic and social change over the last decade has seen virtually no corresponding alteration of the political structure, which is still dominated by Communist Party officials.
"There is no real point in talking about political reform at this point," said a Chinese political scientist in Beijing. 
"Leaders will not change the system themselves, they will only respond to demands from society. 
So ownership reform is very meaningful in that it gives ordinary people a voice."
In recent years, though the private sector of China's economy has grown fast while the state sector atrophied, leaders seemed stymied about what to do with state industries, which have always been described as the unshakable core of China's economic system. 
Before starting any bold initiatives, it seemed, leaders were waiting for Mr. Deng's death, which finally came this year on Feb. 
19.
Mr. Jiang broached the topic of ownership reform in May in a speech at the Central Committee's Party School, winning consensus from other leaders over the summer.
On Sept. 
2, the New China News Agency carried an authoritative report specifying that more than 10,000 of the nation's 13,000 large and medium-sized enterprises would be "encouraged to switch to various forms of public ownership."
"The financial dilemma of the state sector continues to be the outstanding problem of the Chinese economy," the agency said. 
"But hope returned when Chinese President Jiang Zemin called for a powerful change in economic reform."
The same dispatch was accompanied by a spirited rejection of any suggestion that Mr. Jiang might be endorsing privatization, which has always been a bad word in Communist China's political lexicon.
"The share-holding system has nothing to do with privatization," said Wang Jiaqiu, vice president of the Party School, the news agency reported. 
"The system only provides a method to achieve public ownership and will bring no change to the present economic structure where public ownership is in the leading position."
Stressing "public ownership," while selling state industry, recalls Chinese slogans like "a socialist market economy" or "socialism with Chinese characteristics," that justify a capitalist economic necessity by invoking socialist ideology.
A key role in Mr. Jiang's efforts to push through approval of a share-holding system will be played by the man most likely to carry it out: Deputy Prime Minister Zhu Rongji, who is widely expected to become Prime Minister next year. 
Sometimes called "China's Gorbachev" by Westerners who see him as a strict manager and visionary, Mr. Zhu is said to hate the name, worrying that it exposes him to accusations that his leadership might lead to the undermining of the party.
A former Mayor and party chief of Shanghai, where he battled an entrenched bureaucracy and began a stunning economic transformation, Mr. Zhu moved to Beijing in 1993 to take the seemingly impossible task of bringing order to China's economy. 
Inflation had surged to 24 percent and raised fears that it would provoke unrest among China's low-paid factory workers.
Mr. Zhu dismissed the head of China's central bank, assuming the job himself and instituting a strict credit policy that was deeply unpopular with factory heads, who were used to getting whatever subsidies and loans they needed. 
To virtually everyone's surprise, Mr. Zhu stuck to his position, and inflation fell to 2 percent in this year's second quarter, without hampering China's overall economic growth rate.
Now Mr. Zhu has pledged that he will attack state-owned enterprises with the same vigor to achieve their reform within three years.
"The key problem in China's industry is that ownership is unclear," said He Yang, a former official who now runs his own investment company. 
"People say 'the state,' but who is that?
The central government?
A certain ministry?
A local government?
Everyone wants to exert authority, and take profit, but no one wants to take responsibility when there are losses."
Mr. He cited a typical predicament for a large electronics company: the State Planning Commission supervises its investment plans, the Ministry of Electronics Industry appoints its leaders and the Ministry of Internal Trade looks after its sales.
"They all want power, none want responsibility," Mr. He said. 
"No one, and I mean no one, takes responsibility when a company fails. 
It's always someone else's fault."

text:
ï»¿
CHINA'S stock markets have been showing signs of irrational exuberance again.
With so much excess cash swirling around, and an anything-goes mentality at work, China's markets have become prone to wild swings of buying and selling. 
Stock prices surged more than 60 percent in this year's first four months, one of the sharpest rises in the world.
Yet China's central authorities were so alarmed by the buying frenzy they took several steps to cool it last week, sending the market down nearly 10 percent in a single day.
Now, it is anyone's guess whether the buyers -- the retailers of securities and individual investors -- will spring back into action, and if they do, how regulators will respond.
"What's going on is a battle between the regulatory authorities and the retailers," said Peter Alexander, director of Direct Pacific Financial Services in Shanghai. 
"Lately, the retailers have been winning."
Buyers had been betting that Beijing's efforts to calm the market would be mild, Mr. Alexander explained, because of a belief that the Government does not want to take drastic action before July, when Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule.
So, as if on a dare, regulatory authorities in Beijing decided last week that their past methods -- an editorial in The People's Daily cooled a similar buying craze last December -- would not be enough this time.
To try to absorb the free-flowing cash that has been flooding the market this year -- driven in part by falling interest rates -- the authorities announced plans Thursday to raise their quota for new share offerings this year to $3.6 billion, or double the 1996 figure. 
They also increased the transaction fee charged on each trade to five-tenths of 1 percent from three-tenths of 1 percent.
The following day, the authorities suspended trading in four listed companies that had shown abnormal price movements. 
Because market manipulation is believed to be rampant, the prospect of a crackdown hit home, and the market plunged.
It can hardly be coincidence that word also began circulating in the markets last week that Zhou Daojiong, who heads the Securities Regulatory Commission -- China's version of the Securities and Exchange Commission -- would soon be replaced by an official who better understands markets and the benefits of aggressive regulation. 
No announcement has yet been made.
The market was lackluster yesterday, though trading in the suspended shares was resumed. 
The Shanghai market's index for dollar-denominated shares -- those available to outside investors -- edged up just 0.52 point, to 84.96, though the index that tracks shares available to domestic investors posted a larger gain.
With interest rates falling, said John Pinkel, head of China research for Merrill Lynch in Hong Kong, investors have been less willing to put their savings in the bank. 
When the market began to surge this spring, many new investors stepped forward. 
"The fundamental problem is a lack of investment opportunities," he said.
In April, the Shanghai Securities Exchange processed 1.3 million new accounts, nearly 10 percent of its total.
"The really staggering thing is that the volume is even larger than Hong Kong's," Mr. Pinkel said.
The value of shares changing hands in Shanghai and at China's other market, in Shenzhen, reached a combined $4 billion a day at its peak last week, more than twice the volume in Hong Kong, where the overall market is significantly larger.
The exuberance among China's investors, irrational or not, may look similar to the enthusiasm that has pushed the New York Stock Exchange to levels that made United States regulators, including Alan Greenspan, the chairman of the Federal Reserve, express concern.
But with their wild swings, their reliance on rumor and their uneven regulation, China's markets look like those in the United States early this century. 
Or, perhaps, like a less exalted venue for placing financial bets.
"Compare it to an OTB parlor at 42d Street and Sixth Avenue," said Mr. Alexander, referring to the off-track betting centers in New York. 
"There are people staring at a huge screen; there's some guy crying in the corner that he just blew his daughter's college tuition, and the boss is in the back counting all the money. 
Exactly the same."
Many investors in China, he added, are still uncomfortable with the idea of leaving their money overnight in something as abstract as a stock. 
"They all want out by the end of the day," Mr. Alexander said. 
"And then they'll go back in the next morning."Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: Market Place_Communists Are Coming, And Stocks Are Soaring.txt
text:
ï»¿
Just like its older cousin in New York, the Hong Kong stock market is benefiting from a robust economy and stable interest rates, and last week it hit highs and saw record volume.
The difference is that Hong Kong is about to be absorbed by Communist China.
With just days to go before Hong Kong is handed from Britain to China on July 1, the market here is confounding even optimistic forecasters, virtually none of whom foresaw this bullish sentiment on the eve of such a precarious historical moment.
Not long ago, Hong Kong's stock market and property markets were expected to be suffering badly in 1997, on the assumption that mainland Chinese rule would devastate economic and political life here. 
Instead, both markets are near their highs.
Optimism about China's surging economy and growing openness have been the moving force. 
In the last 12 months, while Asia as a whole has been a tepid region for investors, Hong Kong's benchmark Hang Seng index has climbed more than 30 percent, bursting through the previously unreached barrier of 15,000 last Friday. 
It has not been an uninterrupted ascent, of course, with gains punctuated by periods of volatility and price weakness.
"The Hong Kong market in recent years has been trading at a discount because of the coming change," said Christopher Wood, Asian and Emerging Markets strategist at Peregrine, a Hong Kong-based investment bank. 
"What's been happening this year is that the discount has narrowed as people become more confident that the hand-over will go smoothly."
One factor, other analysts said, is a widespread expectation that Chinese authorities will take steps to insure that Hong Kong's market remains buoyant during and after the hand-over, part of an effort to show the world how confident Hong Kong is about its future.
"Everyone figures, 'China will make sure the market stays high, so I may as well get in beforehand,' " said a senior executive at Merrill Lynch in Hong Kong. 
"But no one expected it to get this high."
In fact, the market got even hotter than Beijing wanted, partly because of a rush to sell new offerings of shares by companies with mainland interests, locally known as red chips, which have climbed even faster than the rest of the market this year.
Last Friday, partly to cool the feverish interest in these mainland companies, Beijing announced new measures that make it harder for red chips to win approval to raise money in Hong Kong. 
Until now, red chip companies have enjoyed significantly less regulation than Chinese companies listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges.
The new measures came as a surprise -- no one expected Beijing to introduce new market-cooling regulations so close to the hand-over. 
Yet China's regulators seemed concerned by the near-frenzy of buying in Hong Kong stocks and apparently calculated that their new rules would rein in some exuberance without causing too sharp a drop.
As it turned out, the market indeed fell somewhat in Monday's and today's sessions. 
The Hang Seng index closed today at 14,890.96, down 130.27.
Even as it cools slightly, the general exuberance in Hong Kong's market still seems dangerously high, some economists say, if not quite irrational.
"Overexcitement can lead to underexcitement," said Miron Mushkat, chief economist at Lehman Brothers in Hong Kong. 
"If everything collapses six months later, these gains will be viewed as having been an artificial bubble. 
That will be very disappointing."
Even so, Mr. Mushkat said he saw positive signs that the market would remain strong for the rest of the year, a sentiment that is widely echoed by other economists and analysts and brokers.
Hong Kong's long-term future seems harder to predict. 
Envisioning possible outcomes has almost become a parlor game in the city's financial community, and everyone seems to have an opinion.
Gary Coull, chief executive of Credit Lyonnais Securities Asia, predicted that Hong Kong would grow steadily as a financial center in the coming decades, even if it tended to act more as a place for Chinese companies to raise capital than as an international center.
"The Hong Kong financial community will easily grow to supplant other centers in Asia," Mr. Coull said. 
"The idea of Hong Kong as an international financial center might suffer, but its role for China will more than compensate."
With 350,000 enterprises in China that need money, Mr. Coull predicted, 300 or so will probably attempt public offerings each year for the next 20 years, and many of those will undoubtedly be in Hong Kong.
In contrast, an economist, Marc Faber, foresees the demise of Hong Kong's singular position over the next decade, primarily because with high real estate and other prices, it could lose its competitive edge.
"It was the only bridge to China for a long time," Mr. Faber said. 
"But you can have lots of bridges to China now, so you can't keep charging a high toll."
Known in Hong Kong for his contrarian gloominess, which has earned him the name "Dr. 
Doom," Mr. Faber predicted that within 10 years, Hong Kong would simply be one of 20 large cities in southern China, with few of its privileges left.
Then again, a decade ago, when the transition to Chinese rule was only in the distant future, that is what many people expected Hong Kong to be by now. 
Since then, moves like the appointment of a shipping magnate, Tung Chee-hwa, as the future leader of Hong Kong, have reassured some investors.
"If you'd said 10 years ago that the stock and property markets would be at an all-time high," Mr. Wood of Peregrine said, "that senior members of the civil service would all be staying on, that a businessman like C. H. Tung would be chief executive, well, no one would have believed you."

file: Maverick Chinese Province Fears Opening of Trade.txt
text:
ï»¿
Every Monday for seven years, Wang Tai-ching has boarded a ferry in Hong Kong and chugged up the muddy waters of the Pearl River delta. 
His destination is a factory in Zhongshan, one of the slapdash cities that have sprouted in Guangdong Province over the last decade, crowding out rice paddies and duck ponds with smokestacks and elevated highways.
Mr. Wang, and thousands of Hong Kong entrepreneurs like him, have helped transform Guangdong into the fastest-growing region in China -- a capitalist hothouse on the South China Sea. 
As China moves closer to its dream of entering the World Trade Organization, however, people here are nervous.
Far from relishing the prospect of free trade and wide-open markets, they worry that the new competition could threaten their livelihood. 
To enter the W.T.O., China will have to throw open its doors to foreign companies. 
And by reducing tariffs on imports, it will level its commercial playing field -- depriving the frontier capitalists in Guangdong of many of their advantages.
"The beauty of W.T.O. is that it is a signal to foreigners to come in," said Mr. Wang, 55, who bunks in a spartan dormitory with his workers during the week. 
"But it's different for the people who are already here. 
I don't know how many will survive and how many will fail."
Mr. Wang's factory makes disposable diapers. 
His company, Disposable Soft Goods, is one of 15 such manufacturers in China -- a remarkable statistic for a country that regarded throw-away diapers as an unattainable luxury a few years ago. 
Procter & Gamble began selling Pampers throughout China last October, setting off a ferocious price war.
For Mr. Wang, that is just the beginning of his headaches. 
As part of its agreement to join the W.T.O., China is committed to reducing duties on imported raw materials like plastic and fabric by 40 percent, and to open up its tightly controlled distribution system. 
This will greatly benefit global manufacturers like Procter & Gamble, enabling them to cut their prices even further.
"It's going to be very tough for the local companies to survive," said Andy Xie, an economist who specializes in China at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter in Hong Kong. 
"The W.T.O. deal means that in industries with large economies of scale, the American companies will dominate."
As one bounces along the pothole-pocked roads here, Zhongshan seems the very picture of a swaggering gold-rush town. 
Tacky hotels and karaoke bars line the streets, while prostitutes troll for visiting businessmen. 
But there is something new in the air these days: fear.
"The local people are scared," said Mr. Wang, who employs 130 workers, most of them women. 
"They're worried about losing their jobs. 
They're worried about their factories being closed. 
To them, this is a revolution."
Of course, the threat to Chinese-owned companies is not confined to Guangdong Province. 
But it resonates powerfully here because of Guangdong's hard-won prosperity. 
An economic backwater as recently as 1984, this province of 60 million people capitalized on its proximity to Hong Kong and its distance from Beijing to transform itself into a free-market powerhouse.
Initially, companies moved their factories across the border to escape rising labor costs in Hong Kong, a former British colony. 
The increasingly blurry line between Guangdong and Hong Kong enabled the garment industry to evade strict quotas placed on clothing exported from China.
Later, business people from Taiwan came, attracted by Guangdong's anything-goes atmosphere and the access to Hong Kong's duty-free port. 
More than 4,000 Taiwanese companies set up footwear, electronics and other factories.
By the early 1990's, Guangdong was producing two-thirds of China's exports. 
When Deng Xiaoping made a famous visit here in 1992, he held up the province as a model for China. 
Guangdong, he declared, would become the "fifth tiger of Asia," alongside Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan and South Korea.
But the political winds have shifted, and the country's leaders are now promoting development around Shanghai and in the northern provinces. 
Guangdong's economic growth slowed to 9.4 percent last year from 10.2 percent in 1998. 
Although it still grows faster than China as a whole, its share of the country's exports dropped to 41 percent in 1999 and 38 percent in the first quarter of this year.
"The focus of China's economic development is moving north," Mr. Xie said. 
"Guangdong will remain successful, but it will no longer be central to China's growth."
In some industries, the Chinese government is trying to accelerate this process. 
Earlier this year, Beijing began requiring garment manufacturers here to pay a deposit equal to 30 percent of the value of their exports. 
Factory owners complained.
"We think the Chinese government is trying to drive us out of business to move the industry up north," said Laurie Jim, whose Hong Kong garment-trading company works with dozens of factories in Guangdong. 
"Eventually in southern China, there won't be any garment factories at all."
The outcry from the apparel makers was so loud that the government shelved its policy. 
But Ms. Jim believes it is only a temporary reprieve. 
As China seeks to establish normal trading relations with the United States to and enter the World Trade Organization, she contends, China will intensify its efforts to move labor-intensive production from Guangdong to the less-developed northern regions.
Even without state intervention, Guangdong's advantages are slipping away. 
Today, many apparel companies here make a portion of each piece -- a sleeve or collar -- in Hong Kong, so they can claim it is "Made in Hong Kong," and ship it out under the territory's less-restrictive trade quotas.
By 2005, however, the United States is scheduled to lift quotas on textiles from China. 
That would erase the advantage of splitting production between Guangdong and Hong Kong. 
And with labor costs significantly lower in northern China -- not to mention countries like Mauritius and Bangladesh -- it would rob the apparel companies of one of the main reasons to build factories here.
"Guangdong has been very good in taking advantage of loopholes," Mr. Xie said. 
"But when the rule of law is strengthened, it will be tougher to do that."
Like other coastal provinces, Guangdong has a thriving underground economy in smuggled oil, cigarettes and food products. 
China's prime minister, Zhu Rongji, has made cracking down on smuggling the centerpiece of his anticorruption campaign.
Guangdong also led the way in the creation -- and subsequent downfall -- of investment trusts. 
These state-run companies borrowed heavily to invest in often-dubious real estate ventures. 
When Beijing decided to make an example of one of them by throwing it into bankruptcy, it chose Guangdong International Trust and Investment, the flagship venture of the provincial government.
In some ways, Guangdong is suffering the same growing pains as any region that struggles up the economic ladder. 
With its labor costs the highest in China outside of Shanghai, it is trying to attract more capital-intensive industries, like telecommunications, computers and software. 
It is also trying to hold on to the higher-end segments of its traditional manufacturing industries.
"What Guangdong needs to do is move up the value chain," said Vincent Chen, the founder of Texwatch.com, a Web site that tracks the garment industry. 
"They will be known for making high-quality products, like polo shirts."
As China seeks to catch the technology wave, however, Guangdong may find itself handicapped by its dearth of good universities and its less-educated work force. 
China's Internet industry is centered in Beijing -- home to the top-notch Beijing and Qinghua universities.
For all its weaknesses, experts say that Guangdong is still far more competitive and resilient than other parts of China. 
They note that the Pearl River delta is dominated by private entrepreneurs -- a stark contrast to the sclerotic state-owned enterprises of northern China.
"None of those grievous problems that you see up north blight the Pearl River delta," said David Dodwell, who has written extensively about the region. 
"Most of the companies here are leaner, meaner, and better equipped to confront international competition."
Indeed, Wang Tai-ching is not about to wave a white flag. 
He notes that he, too, will benefit from lower duties on imported raw materials. 
Lower duties on machinery will allow him to install another assembly line in his factory.
To counter the threat from Procter & Gamble, he wants to build warehouses in the north to deliver diapers in Shanghai and Beijing. 
Eventually, Mr. Wang predicts, his factory will produce 300 million diapers a year. 
With 19 million babies born in China every year, he says there are more than enough bottoms to go around.
"I'm very optimistic about W.T.O.," Mr. Wang said gamely. 
"But the changes haven't happened yet."

text:

There was a certain tautness to Mayor Rudolph W. Giuliani's face yesterday, a vague twitch of impatience, as he stood next to the recently released Chinese dissident, Wei Jingsheng, in the Blue Room of City Hall. 
The Chinese reporters in the room were asking endless questions about China, everyone was looking at Mr. Wei and no one was asking the question the Mayor wanted asked.
So finally he just had to ask it himself.
"Can you tell us," the Mayor inquired, "your first impressions of New York City?"
He smiled a feline smile, as if he knew what the answer would be, which it turned out he did. 
Sure enough, Mr. Wei, who was released from 18 years in a Chinese prison last week and flown to the United States, could not have answered more congenially if he had spent as much time on the Mayor's staff.
"There are not as many violent crimes and criminals as the Chinese Communist propaganda media said," Mr. Wei said, through a translator, to raucous laughter all around.
Other mayors, particularly Edward I. Koch and Fiorello La Guardia, Mr. Giuliani's favorites, loved to dispense foreign policy advice to governments around the world, instructing Russians, South Africans and Nazis to behave themselves. 
Mr. Giuliani has demonized his share of unpopular world figures -- Yasir Arafat, Fidel Castro, double-parking diplomats -- but for the most part has stayed out of international disputes. 
He may love to stand next to a hero of democracy, but his real interests are strictly local.
He criticized the Chinese government only indirectly yesterday in lamenting the lack of human dignity in China. 
Instead, he made it clear that China and similar countries could learn a lesson in tolerance from the city over which he presides.
"This is a city that's built on an understanding of human freedom, founded very largely because people wanted to practice their religion the way they would like, not the way the government would tell them to do it," he explained to Mr. Wei, who has spent the last several days in New York. 
"It's a city that has accepted people from all over the world and grown as a result of that. 
And it's a place that is unafraid of new people, because we understand that new people allow us to grow even more."
Nothing in the room was too small to be turned into a object lesson in local virtues. 
When television camera operators got into their usual shouting match with still photographers, Mr. Giuliani described it as the price of free expression in a free country. 
When he held up a copy of Mr. Wei's book of prison writings, "The Courage to Stand Alone," he explained to Mr. Wei that it might help sell the book, "which is one of the things a capitalist country has to offer."
In an hourlong private meeting with the Mayor that preceded the news conference, Mr. Wei signed a copy of his book and discussed human rights, trade policy and his life in prison. 
That was also where he revealed that Mr. Giuliani's achievement of lowering crime in New York City had not reached the ears of the Chinese Communist leadership.
Aides to the Mayor agreed later that even if Mr. Wei hadn't made the remark about reduced crime, he still would have received the key to the city, putting him in the company of the 1996 New York Yankees, former Police Commissioner William J. Bratton and Pope John Paul II.
At the news conference, Mr. Wei dismissed criticism made by some of his fellow dissidents in China on Monday that he had become arrogant and was too soft on Deng Xiaoping, China's former leader.

And he had nothing but praise for Mr. Giuliani's support of his human-rights crusade.

"Because Mr. Mayor knows that what happens on another side of the planet is not irrelevant to what happens on this side.

When Thomas F. McLarty 3d was President Clinton's chief of staff, he approved a 1994 meeting that brought inside the White House several Chinese businessmen working on a project with the controversial Lippo Group, documents show.

Mark Middleton, a White House aide at the time, greeted the Chinese businessmen and a Lippo executive on the afternoon on April 22, 1994. 
Mr. Huang, then a Lippo employee, and his wife met with Mr. Middleton earlier in the day at the White House, Mr. Middleton's calendars show.
The Huangs made $20,000 in donations to the Democratic Party the month before the meeting and a $5,000 contribution a week after it, Federal election records show. 
Mr. Huang later joined the Commerce Department and, at Mr. Giroir's urging, became a Democratic fund-raiser.

The disclosure marks the first time a meeting is known to have taken place inside the White House related to a proposed $1 billion project to build a power plant in China.

Mr. Middleton set up the meeting after being directed to do so by Mr. McLarty, said Bob Luskin, Mr. Middleton's lawyer.

Mr. Middleton has left the White House since then and has a consulting arrangement with Mr. Giroir.

In a statement on Friday, a White House spokesman, Lanny J. Davis, said, "Mr.

file: MEXICO, IN SWITCH, DECIDES TO RETURN STRANDED CHINESE.txt
text:
ï»¿
In a sudden reversal, the Mexican Government apparently bowed to American pressure today and agreed to take responsibility for 659 Chinese refugees aboard three ships about 60 miles off the Mexican coast that were intercepted by the Coast Guard while headed for the United States.
Only hours after officials here had reiterated their stance that the smuggled Chinese were an American problem, a senior official announced that Mexico would allow the ships into port and then immediately return the immigrants to China.
The official, Andres Rozental, Under Secretary of Foreign Relations in Charge of North America, said in an interview tonight that Mexico was taking charge of the Chinese "purely on humanitarian grounds," because of the deteriorating shipboard conditions.
Â 
Pressure From Washington
But privately, Mexican and American officials confirmed that the United States had pressed Mexico hard to help resolve the problem, which embarrassed the Clinton Administration only weeks after it announced a new policy to discourage illegal immigration.
Some American officials had voiced concern that Mexico's tough rejection of the United States request came at a particularly inopportune time.
Only four months from now, the United States Congress is to cast the decisive vote on the North American Free Trade Agreement that is intended to eventually unite the United States, Mexico and Canada in a single, tariff-free zone. 
Mexico's demonstrated willingness to cooperate with the United States on non-trade issues is certain to weigh heavily in the vote.
Mr. Rozental said that Alexander Watson, the United States Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American affairs, raised the issue of the immigrants in talks with senior Mexican diplomats in Mexico City on Monday. 
But Mr. Rozental said, "I don't think there was any major pressure or anything."
Still, the episode was the latest in a series that have seemed to define the relationship between the two countries on the basis of Mexico's overwhelming desire to see the trade agreement passed. 
The accord is expected to increase jobs and wages in Mexico only slowly, but it is expected to quicken the flow of much-needed foreign investment in Mexico right away.
Over the last year, Mexico has prominently reversed itself several times in disputes with the United States, and almost every time Mexican officials have acknowledged their fears for the trade agreement as a leading factor.
A United States official said that tonight, even while senior officials in the Mexican Foreign Secretariat were publicly insisting that Mexico was not negotiating over the fate of the Chinese, and would not, other officials under President Carlos Salinas de Gortari were continuing to hold out the possibility of Mexican help.
Â 
Decision Is Welcomed
"Throughout this thing, there were some Mexican officials who were irritated and were unwilling to cooperate on this, and others who were willing to cooperate to work this situation out," the American official said.
In a public statement in Washington, Martin Judge, a State Department spokesman, said: "We welcome Mexico's humanitarian decision. 
Our discussions with Mexico continue, and we are willing to cooperate with the Mexican Government in this matter."
Mr. Judge said "consultations" on the immigation issue would continue Thursday in Mexico City.
Tonight in Washington, National Security Council and State Department officials were so sensitive about the appearance of having pressured Mexico that they would not discuss the nature of the talks that took place with Mexico this week.
On Monday, Mr. Watson met in Mexico City with Foreign Minister Fernando Solana Morales to discuss the request that Mexico accept the Chinese refugees, Mexican officials said. 
But the Foreign Minister expressed his displeasure at the request and its timing, four days after the request was first reported in American newspapers, and the talks faltered, Mexican officials said.
Â 
Treatment of Mexicans
Mexican diplomats had shown their ire at the American request for help with the Chinese openly. 
They suggested it was almost hypocritical to seek Mexico's aid with the problem when, Mexico maintains, the United States habitually mistreats some of the estimated two million Mexican citizens who cross illegally into the United States each year.
For more than a year now, Mexico also has been pushing the United States to change its immigration policies to guarantee undocumented Mexican immigrants better treatment and to allow more Mexicans living on the Mexican side of the border and working in the United States to be allowed to cross legally. 
Mexican officials said they feared that the Clinton Administration's new harder-line policy on keeping illegal immigrants out could have negative consequences for those goals.
But Mr. Rozental insisted that Mexico did not change its position. 
In its written appeal to Mexico for help last Friday, Mr. Rozental said, the United States had asked that Mexico bring the three Chinese boats into Mexican ports, then process the smuggled aliens jointly with the United States and the United Nations High Commission on Refugees to determine the validity of any claims of political persecution. 
The United States said it would then assume the cost of sending the rest of the Chinese, most of whom are believed to have paid thousands of dollars to be passed like chattel across the Pacific.
Â 
Mexico's Own Plan
Rather than accept those conditions, Mexico came up with its own plan, Mr. Rozental said.
He said the Mexican authorities would only tow the Chinese ships into port once they had made their way from their current position, about 70miles out to sea, to the 12-mile limit of Mexican territorial waters. 
Since one of the three ships is disabled and another is believed to be in precarious mechanical shape, Mexican officials said they expected the United States to take charge of assisting the boats to the 12-mile limit.
Mexican officials added that, as is their policy, they would not hear any claims of asylum from the immigrants. 
And though they have consistently accepted American compensation for processing third-country immigrants in the past, they said they would reject an offer of United States financing this time.
"These people were in really bad shape and in order not to prolong their suffering, we felt that we should get them back to China as soon as possible," Mr. Rozental said.
Â 
Persecuted or Not?
A Mexican official added: "We know very well that none of these people who are coming here are being persecuted. 
The U.S. knows that, too. 
The only difference is that in the United States, the only thing you have to do is to step on American soil and cry asylum, and you get a hearing."
Mr. Rozental said Mexican diplomats had ascertained that more than 100 Chinese repatriated by Mexico in May had not been punished by the Communist Government. 
But American immigration officials said an additional 112 Chinese whom the United States repatriated around the same time were subsequently jailed and fined.
Mexico has long prided itself on a generous policy of providing asylum to peoples fleeing politically motivated repression.
But last year, as Mexico struggled to begin the repatriation of more than 40,000 Guatemalan refugees who have been camped on its southern border for a decade, it expelled 123,050 illegal immigrants, many of whom it said were trying to cross into the United States for economic reasons. 
They included people from India, Latin Americans and Asians, 427 of them Chinese.
Mexico was especially angered in May, when about 200 Chinese from a group seized in Baja California escaped from the Mexicali airport and fled toward the United States. 
Most were caught, but Mexico was livid when the American authorities refused to allow the Mexican plane deporting them to even refuel on Alaskan soil.

file: Mindful of China, U.S. Agrees To Weapons Deal for Taiwan.txt
text:
