A group of 13 Nobel Prize-winning economists signed a letter today that backs China's bid to join the World Trade Organization. 
But the letter, released in a ceremony with top Clinton administration officials, was at least as notable for what it left out.
The four-paragraph letter, endorsed by 149 economists including the Nobel laureates, makes no mention of what the White House has called its top remaining legislative and foreign policy priority: persuading Congress to grant China permanent normal trade relations. 
The omission was conspicuous. 
As the administration has stressed many times, Congress has no say in whether China joins the trade body. 
Congress votes only on whether to elevate the trade ties, a step that is necessary if American companies are to benefit fully from China's membership in the W.T.O.
Clinton administration officials said the letter did not mention the vote because the administration sought to attract support from a broad array of economists. 
Some economists might not have agreed to sign the letter if it explicitly mentioned a political issue before Congress, the officials acknowledged. 
The officials said that they thought most of the economists who signed the letter personally support permanent normal trade relations, but that some do not and that others felt uncomfortable taking a political stand.
Qualms about delving into politics did not stop 200 corporate chief executives from endorsing permanent normal trade relations in a letter released earlier this month. 
And a group of former Treasury and State Department secretaries spanning five administrations explicitly backed the Clinton administration's position on the vote this month. 
So did 47 governors in a letter released in late March.
The White House released the economists' letter in high-profile fashion, kicking off the final month of an intense effort to persuade wavering lawmakers in the House to back permanent trade ties. 
The vote is expected in late May and the tally in the House is considered too close to call.
Treasury Secretary Lawrence H. Summers; Gene Sperling, the director of the National Economic Council; and Martin N. Baily, chairman of the council of economic advisers, were on hand to present the letter to reporters. 
Robert M. Solow, a Nobel laureate from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, also came to Washington to speak in support.
"It's a once-in-a-generation event that Bob Solow and Milton Friedman, Paul Samuelson and Merton Miller are signing a letter on the same side of a major public policy issue," Mr. Summers said. 
He was referring to four of the Nobel-winning economists who signed the letter but have often taken opposing positions on other economic issues.
The lack of a clear stand on the issue before Congress also comes at a time when the administration is under scrutiny for its lobbying efforts on behalf of increased trade with China. 
A complaint from Representative Frank R. Wolf, a Virginia Republican who opposes making China's trade status permanent, prompted the General Accounting Office to open an investigation this month into whether the administration violated legal restrictions on lobbying Congress when it set up a White House "war room" to coordinate the campaign. 
That investigation is continuing.
When first asked why the economists' letter made no mention of permanent normal trade relations, Mr. Sperling said the administration had to abide by legal restrictions on what it could urge outsiders to say on a matter before Congress. 
But Mr. Sperling and other officials later said that explanation was incorrect.
They said that there were no legal restrictions at issue in choosing whether to mention the Congressional vote in the letter, and that it was drafted well before the G.A.O. began its investigation. 
The letter did not mention permanent normal trade relations because the administration was seeking support from a wide spectrum of economists on the left and right, some of whom might not want to weigh in publicly on a Clinton administration legislative priority, they said.
"The economists all believe that it's important to have open trade," said Commerce Secretary William M. Daley, who is leading the administration's lobbying campaign on the China vote. 
"But they want to stay out of the political fight."

file: North Korea Agrees to Join 4-Party Talks.txt
text:
ï»¿
Forty-four years after the Korean War ended with a bitter, tenuous cease-fire, North Korea agreed yesterday to hold talks with South Korea, the United States and China in an effort to negotiate a lasting peace.
The two Koreas remain profoundly divided, and intractable issues must still be resolved, but the agreement represents a breakthrough in efforts to forge peace on the Korean Peninsula, which remains one of the world's most troublesome, potentially explosive regions.
North Korea's agreement cleared the way for "preparatory talks" to begin in New York on Aug. 
5 between delegations from the two Koreas and their principal allies during the war, China and the United States.
The agreement was announced yesterday after a final day of wrangling over details between senior delegations from North Korea, South Korea and the United States at the New York Palace Hotel in midtown Manhattan. 
Yesterday's meeting was the third in four months. 
The previous meetings ended in frustration.
In impromptu remarks to reporters on East 51st Street, the head of North Korea's delegation, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Kim Gye Gwan, said his country would enter the "four-party" talks, calling them "very conducive to the peace and security on the Korean Peninsula."
While senior officials of the two Koreas have met before, the talks would be the first between the North and South to address directly some framework for peace, including mutual recognition, improvement of relations and, many officials believe, an eventual reunification.
President Clinton and President Kim Young Sam of South Korea proposed the "four-party" talks last April as a way of overcoming North Korea's unwillingness to negotiate directly with its enemy. 
The North had long sought talks only with the United States, hoping to isolate the South.
Secretary of State Madeleine K. Albright welcomed North Korea's decision to take part in what she called "this historic process."
In a statement from Hong Kong, where she attended ceremonies marking the return of the British colony to Chinese rule, Ms. Albright said the talks were meant "to reduce tensions and build confidence on the Korean Peninsula with the aim of putting a formal end to the hostilities of the Korean War."
While an armistice ended the fighting in July 1953, the two countries technically remain in a state of war, with the border between them the most heavily armed in the world.
In the previous meetings in New York, Mr. Kim, of North Korea, had signaled a willingness to hold peace talks, but continued to raise objections, insisting that any agreement had to include substantial donations of food aid to cope with growing shortages in the North. 
The United States and South Korea, while responding to international appeals for emergency aid with donations, refused to link the aid to North Korea's participation in talks.
By yesterday, North Korea had dropped its insistence on food aid, though American and South Korea officials said that Mr. Kim's delegation raised the issue again. 
"They again repeated that they have an urgent and substantial need for additional food aid," a senior Administration official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
A senior South Korean official said the shortages in the North, which have become dire according to many reports, were "something structural and elemental" and would be part of future peace talks.
The progress toward the negotiating table follows a year of tumultuous relations between the North and South, which included the incursion of a North Korean submarine into South Korea's coastal waters last fall, and the defection of a senior North Korean minister. 
It also comes at a time when North Korea's ruler, Kim Jong Il, prepares to assume in July the official mantle of his father, Kim Il Sung, on the third anniversary of his death.
In a joint statement, the three delegations said the preparatory talks in August would resolve "procedural matters" for the future talks, including "the earliest agreeable date, venue and agenda."
The United States and South Korea had apprised China and received its commitment to take part, the officials said.
Despite North Korea's agreement to attend talks, the officials cautioned that much remained to be resolved before a peace treaty could be reached. 
After all, it took more than a year and a host of high- and low-level meetings to persuade the North simply to agree to attend talks.
"While this is a very important step," the Administration official said, "it doesn't bring us 100 percent of the way."Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: Not (Yet) Gone the Way of All Asia.txt
text:
ï»¿
First Thailand, then Malaysia, Indonesia and South Korea collapsed. 
Then Hong Kong and Singapore fell ill. 
Japan, the onetime powerhouse, sank back into recession. 
Not to mention neighbor Russia's fall into the gutter.
Through it all China has continued to slog along, its economy bowed but not entirely broken.
If its growth so far this year, officially said to be something more than 7 percent, is sluggish by recent Chinese standards, it looks spectacular compared to the rest of Asia's economies. 
And despite months of intense global speculation, China's currency has not been devalued.
On Monday, President Jiang Zemin will go with some pride to Malaysia for a summit meeting of Asian and Pacific leaders.
Yet China has definitely entered a politically dangerous era of slower growth and rising unemployment. 
The signs of trouble are everywhere: it is hard to find a family in which at least someone has not been laid off in the last year or two, and in cities like Shanghai and Beijing, new commercial buildings stand half-empty. 
Around the country, protests by laid-off workers or retirees demanding overdue welfare or pension payments are almost routine.
Still, there is no sense of panic, and for every empty building, another restaurant or shopping center seems to open.
China's leaders, anxious to head off a severe slump and social unrest, are using every Keynesian tool at their disposal to stimulate domestic investment and demand. 
At the same time, they have delayed the badly needed overhaul of bloated state industries and overstretched banks. 
Critics say China is creating even bigger, more costly problems later on for its banks and industries. 
But officials say they had no choice.
"Maintaining growth and fighting unemployment had to get the top priority," said Li Shantong, a senior economist at the Development Research Center of the State Council, or Cabinet. 
"Unless these two goals are met, you can't address the other problems like banking and state enterprise reform."
The program of monetary and fiscal stimulus measures has already pushed tens of billions of extra dollars into state enterprises, and data from the first nine months of this year show that investments in capital projects, technology and real estate have jumped 20 percent over last year and are accelerating.
A central question is just how soundly the extra funds are being spent. 
How much is going to build needed roads and irrigation canals and innovative factories, as the Government says it intends?
How much to build unnecessary office space and to help doomed companies produce unsalable stockpiles, as critics charge?
Because of some deft policy moves, longstanding controls on currency trading and the sheer size of its economy, China does not appear to face an immediate risk of repeating its neighbors' debacles. 
Rather, the main concern involves the longer-term costs of its all-out program to wrench up the 1998 growth rate to an arbitrarily set target of 8 percent.
"The danger is not a short-term economic collapse," said Barry Naughton, an economist at the University of California at San Diego, "but excess slackening of pressure on state-owned firms, leading to serious problems a few years down the road."
Still, Mr. Naughton praises the stimulus program as sensible.
When Zhu Rongji became Prime Minister early this year, he boldly vowed to speed reforms that are essential to future prosperity. 
Outmoded, money-draining state enterprises would be drastically pruned and the survivors made to stand on their own. 
The giant state banks, courting insolvency because they had long funneled money to dubious state industries, would only lend on sound commercial terms.
These changes, and the inevitable layoffs of tens of millions of long-loyal and cosseted workers, would be difficult under the best of conditions. 
Now they have been put on ice as the Government pumps a new flood of money through the banks into public companies and projects.
"Political pressures have forced the Chinese leaders to make some decisions that will come back to haunt them," said Nicholas Lardy, an economist at the Brookings Institution in Washington, one of China's sharpest critics on this subject.
Mr. Lardy credits the Chinese with some skillful moves of late, like curbing foreign debt by imposing new limits on foreign borrowing by companies and banks. 
But he warned, "The dangers of a banking system failure are going up."
Other experts say the banking problem should be manageable. 
But at best, after the current frenzy of Government-induced spending, shaking out the state-owned companies and ridding banks of their albatross of bad loans will be all the harder, the ultimate price all the higher.
The Asian crisis hit at a time when China was already facing an economic slowdown. 
Earlier in the decade the country had spectacular double-digit growth, but also spectacular inflation.
Tight monetary and fiscal policies tamed the inflation dragon without a recession -- China's renowned "soft landing" -- but by 1997, with an 8.8 percent economic growth rate, the country entered a time of deflation and excess production capacity. 
Some said the tight policies had overshot the mark.
On top of this, global economic strains and the collapse of regional trading partners took their toll. 
This year the growth in exports has slowed sharply, and the inflow of foreign investment has fallen.
These twin reversals alone would cut two to three percentage points from economic growth, said Yukon Huang, Beijing representative of the World Bank. 
The Government's stimulus package is intended to recapture as much of that potential growth as possible, Mr. Huang said.
"The Chinese are walking a fine line," he added. 
"They need to keep the economy growing so they can pursue the reforms.
"One lesson of the Asian crisis is that in a seriously contracting economy it's difficult for basically sound enterprises, as well as bad ones, to repay their loans."
But the stimulus measures have definitely come at a cost. 
In a series of changes this year and last, China's banks were told they would be held responsible for bad loans, and would no longer be forced to dole out funds uncritically to state enterprises and local governments with pet projects.
But over the summer, as part of the emergency program to bolster economic activity, banks were directed to expand lending to state companies, again exposing the financial system to trouble as it propped up moribund industries.
This fall the Government has used more direct fiscal methods, issuing $12 billion worth of bonds to support infrastructure projects and requiring the banks to lend an equivalent amount for the same purpose.
Ms. Li, the State Council economist, acknowledged that the lending standards of banks had been relaxed, but again said that without economic growth, all else would be lost.
Official statistics show that both lending and investment have jumped, but there is no way to sort out how that money is being spent, and how soundly. 
Much of the extra punch may be seen next year, experts say.
Critics like Mr. Lardy ask why more of the new lending was not directed to the emerging private sector -- virtually ignored by Chinese banks for years -- which might spend it more productively. 
Government officials say that is impractical on such short notice.
In that, the officials are supported by Ma Guonan, co-director of Asia-Pacific research at Salomon Smith Barney in Hong Kong, who notes that a transition to a sound system of private commercial lending will take time.
"Most state banks only know how to lend to state enterprises," Mr. Ma said. 
"They just don't have the training to know how to evaluate risk in lending to private companies."
This year's growth rate has become a matter of some contention. 
Seeking to exude confidence, Mr. Zhu, in the best old style of the planned economy, has firmly declared and repeated that growth this year would reach 8 percent. 
Some critics say that even the 7 percent-plus figures registered in the first nine months do not seem credible, compared with other indicators like falling imports and slower growth in power use and freight transportation, as well as declining prices.
This week even a senior Government economist, Lu Benqiang, also of the State Council's Development Research Center, told Chinese journalists that local governments might be fabricating numbers or investing in useless projects simply to increase the growth rate.
If output in the final quarter of this year truly rose enough to pull the annual average up to 8 percent, that would actually be "terrible news," said Mr. Naughton, because it would imply such a high level of wasteful investment.
China's neighbors, and the United States, are closely watching for signs that the Government might relent in its political determination not to devalue its currency, the yuan. 
Over the last year, China was said to be suffering a competitive disadvantage as other Asian countries devalued, making their exports relatively cheaper.
In fact, there has been lengthy debate among economists as to whether China, with its particular mix of imports and exports, would benefit from a weaker yuan.
Many experts feel that the case for a devaluation will strengthen next year if countries like Thailand and Indonesia, still reeling from the current crisis, begin to recover. 
So far, stricken countries in the region have been in such turmoil that few companies have been tempted to move in to take advantage of the low exchange rates, investing in export industries.
But if those countries stabilize, with exchange rates still lower than in the past, they may begin to reap some of the competitive advantages -- at the expense of China's foreign investment and exports.
With sluggish growth, declining prices and large unused productive capacity, China's economy would benefit more generally from a devaluation and the modest inflation it would promote, said Andy Xie, chief China economist at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter in Hong Kong.
Expert opinion is divided as to whether there will be growth next year at close to this year's level, whatever it really is, or somewhat lower -- a dismal prospect for a country that is trying to refashion its economy and that has so many underemployed people. 
Much will depend on trends in the region and world, affecting China's trade and foreign investment prospects. 
A prolonged global slump could be China's undoing, since this year's stimulus measures cannot continue indefinitely.
Since his audacious announcement of reform measures last March, Prime Minister Zhu has kept a low profile on that topic, saying little in public as many of his hard-won goals have been set aside.
Still, there is no indication that China's leaders have dropped the goals in principle, and no indication that his power as economic czar in this perplexing time has diminished.
"There's no alternative to Zhu Rongji," Mr. Xie said, "and Jiang Zemin knows that."

file: Notoriety Now for Movement_s Leader.txt
text:
ï»¿
On Sunday, followers of Buddhist Law staged the largest protest in Beijing since the Tiananmen Square movement 10 years ago, but the New York-based spiritual leader who developed the doctrine rarely shows his face.
The leader, Li Hongzhi, a 47-year-old native of Changchun in northeastern China who now calls New York home, keeps a low public profile even as his books, audio and video tapes and Web sites spread his message to tens of millions of people around the world.
Close associates say they do not know where he is now. 
They assert that he has no formal organization. 
Like a rebel leader on the run, he sometimes appears at conferences his followers sponsor in Asia, North America or Europe, but with little advance notice.
"We have no organization," said Yi Rong, an assocaite of Mr. Li based in New York. 
"No one talks to him regularly except maybe his family. 
We had a research society in China once but this has been abolished."
Despite that elusiveness, or maybe because of it, Mr. Li has become a guru of a movement that even by Chinese Government estimates has more members than the Communist Party. 
Beijing puts the tally of his followers at 70 million. 
Practitioners say they do not dispute those numbers, but they say they have no way of knowing for sure, in part because they have no central membership lists.
Amorphousness makes practical sense. 
The Communist Party suppresses unauthorized organizations of any kind, whether they explicitly oppose Communist rule or not.
The demonstration on Sunday in Beijing involved more than 10,000 followers. 
But Ms. Yi insisted that Mr. Li had no advance notice of the demonstration. 
"I'm quite sure that not only did he not organize this, but he did not even know about it. 
We all learned about it just yesterday," she said, but she acknowledged that her certainty was tempered by her inability to contact Mr. Li or to pinpoint his whereabouts.
Mr. Li has fashioned a mind and body spiritual exercise program intended to allow adherents to live a moral life, remain free of disease and achieve enlightenment. 
He is a master of what the Chinese call qigong, an ancient practice than spans a spectrum from martial arts to soothsaying.
In the early 1990's, people who follow Mr. Li said, he build up a network of students around China, lecturing thousands at a time. 
Last year, under pressure from the Government, he left China for the United States.
Exile appeared to do nothing to limit his popularity in China, even as he spread his gospel to Americans and Europeans. 
Mr. Li, who followers say is always on the road, was the guest of honor at a recent qigong conference in Sweden, where most of the practitioners were locals.
"He is like qigong masters everywhere but claims to be one level above them," said Chen Maiping, a Chinese who attended a seminar with Mr. Li in Sweden but does not follow Mr. Li's teaching. 
"He treats it like religion. 
He has a complete philosophy of life and death."
In some ways the movement resembles a religion. 
It has a central treatise, called the Zhuan Falun. 
Like some ancient Chinese philosophy, the text is a little obtuse.
"The reason why cultivation can be called cultivation is that there is a way for cultivation, a road for you to walk on," begins a chapter entitled "Not Cultivating the Dao" (which means the way and is sometimes spelled Tao). 
"There was such a saying in the past: The man does not cultivate the Dao, yet he is already in the Dao. 
Such a man abides by the small way and pays attention to Nothingness or Emptiness."
Despite these quasireligious overtones, followers of Mr. Li insist that his movement is not religious. 
It has no churches, no ordained priests, no hierarchy of any kind, says Ms. Yi.
"There are no conditions for membership, and people can come or go at any time," she said. 
"We have no structure or hierarchy. 
That's why we strongly state that we are not a religion."

file: OFFICIAL ASSERTS SPY CASE SUSPECT WAS A BIAS VICTIM.txt
text:
ï»¿
The former head of counterintelligence at the Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico said yesterday that Wen Ho Lee, the American scientist who is the top suspect in the Chinese atomic spy case, was unfairly singled out for Federal investigation because of his ethnicity.
"It was a key factor," the former counterintelligence leader, Robert S. Vrooman, who himself is to be disciplined for his handling of the case, said in an interview. 
"There were 83 people who went to China" from the New Mexico weapons laboratory in the 1980's, he said, any one of whom might have leaked secrets.
"A lot of Caucasians" were not investigated, Mr. Vrooman said, even though they had access to weapons secrets. 
"And they made contact with the same people that Lee was in contact with," added Mr. Vrooman, who investigated the case for nearly three years and is still a consultant to the laboratory.
Though intelligence experts eventually discovered that Dr. Lee had downloaded secret weapons-related computer codes onto an unsecure computer, Mr. Vrooman said yesterday that Dr. Lee's ethnic background "was a major factor" in initially making him the top suspect. 
He has not been charged with any crime.
Dr. Lee, who says he is innocent of spy accusations, is a Taiwan-born scientist who worked at Los Alamos for more than two decades before being fired in March for violations of security rules. 
After he was fired, investigators discovered he had transferred vast amounts of secret nuclear data from Los Alamos's classified computer system to an open network. 
The data included the legacy codes, mathematical approximations of nuclear weapons designs.
Counterintelligence experts say racial focusing is not uncommon in spy investigations because foreign intelligence services often target people who may have sympathies with foreign states.
Mr. Vrooman is apparently the first investigator in the case to raise the issue of racial bias publicly, though some Chinese-American rights groups had previously done so. 
His remarks were first reported yesterday in The Washington Post.
Energy Secretary Bill Richardson and other managers at Los Alamos have denied that Dr. Lee's Asian ancestry sparked suspicions that he was involved in possible espionage.
Mr. Vrooman's comments come as Secretary Richardson last Thursday called for Mr. Vrooman and two other Los Alamos officials to be disciplined for failing to handle the laboratory's investigation properly. 
Mr. Vrooman was not named in the department's news release, but officials disclosed his name to reporters. 
Mr. Vrooman was criticized specifically for allowing Dr. Lee continued access to nuclear secrets.
Los Alamos officials said yesterday that a decision on any disciplinary action would probably not be made for weeks. 
Mr. Richardson has recommended terminating Mr. Vrooman's contract as a consultant.
In the interviews yesterday, Mr. Vrooman strongly defended his actions, accused the department of playing politics and said the nation's nuclear weapons laboratories had been unfairly made targets. 
Though China has obtained secret weapons information, he said, it is more likely that information came from the military or defense contractors than from weapons laboratories.
"It was not design information," he said of the lost secrets. 
"It was engineering data. 
If you were a Las Vegas odds maker, you'd put your money on D.O.D.," or the Department of Defense.
Mr. Vrooman said Federal investigators had found that secret data on the warhead at the center of the investigation, the W-88, the most modern in the American arsenal, had been made available throughout the Federal bureaucracy to hundreds of people.
"A rather detailed description of the W-88 had a distribution of 548 copies," he said, most to the Defense Department, the military services, the National Guard, Federal agencies and contractors like the Lockheed Missile and Space Corporation. 
"Please note that I am referring to 548 mailing addresses, not people."
Mr. Vrooman's criticisms that the investigation prematurely focused on Dr. Lee echo the more general findings of the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, which earlier this month made public a report on the China espionage investigation. 
It said Federal investigators erred early on when they focused on Dr. Lee without having adequately reviewed other possible suspects.
The spy scandal erupted in March when the House select committee on Chinese espionage, led by Representative Christopher Cox, neared completion of a report saying China stole secrets about seven of America's most advanced warheads. 
Dr. Lee was not mentioned by name when the report was publicly released in May, but his identity had emerged months before then. 
All along, he has maintained his innocence.
In a televised interview on the CBS News program "60 Minutes" several weeks ago, Dr. Lee said that he was a victim of ethnic bias and that he had downloaded secret files to protect them. 
He denied giving the material to anyone.
In interviews last week, the Los Alamos director, John Browne, and other laboratory managers strongly disagreed with Dr. Lee's explanations about why he violated security rules by transferring millions of lines of classified computer code.
"We have no evidence that anyone has ever done anything like this before at Los Alamos," Mr. Browne said.
Mr. Vrooman, a former case officer at the Central Intelligence Agency, said yesterday in interviews and in a two-page statement that Federal investigators had "not one shred of evidence" that linked Dr. Lee to Chinese espionage. 
He said he scrutinized the case for nearly three years, from June 1995 until he retired from Los Alamos in March 1998.
Mr. Vrooman said the Energy Department's Office of Counterintelligence had identified Dr. Lee as "the prime suspect based on, at best, cursory investigation at only two facilities."
They were Los Alamos, the birthplace of the bomb, and the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California, the nation's other main center for the design of nuclear arms. 
"The investigation lacked intellectual rigor," he said. 
"They missed a lot of people. 
It was a mess."
Last week, in recommending the disciplinary action against Mr. Vrooman, the Energy Department pointed to Dr. Lee's continued access to classified information.
The department's inspector general reported to Secretary Richardson last week that in 1997 the Albuquerque field office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation told Mr. Vrooman that there was no longer any investigative reason to keep Dr. Lee in his position with access to classified information. 
Mr. Vrooman did not take any action to move Dr. Lee and did not tell the managers at Los Alamos about the bureau's finding, the department said.
But yesterday, Mr. Vrooman said his decision to continue Dr. Lee's access had been made in concert with officials of the F.B.I. and the Energy Department's chief intelligence officer, Notra Trulock. 
Mr. Trulock, who first raised the alarm about China's theft of American nuclear secrets, did not return calls yesterday seeking comment.
"It is important to note that executive order 12333 specifies that the F.B.I. has responsibility for counterintelligence investigations within the United States," Mr. Vrooman said in his statement. 
The internal security office at Los Alamos, he added, "can only provide support to the F.B.I."
Mr. Vrooman added that he had been made the target for disciplinary action because he opposed the Energy's Department's view that the Chinese espionage had occurred in its warrens rather than elsewhere.
Energy officials have "put constraints on us that are going to destroy" the Los Alamos laboratory, Mr. Vrooman said. 
"This is a national treasure. 
I don't want to see it destroyed based on false allegations."

file: On Eve of Geneva Rights Talks, China Agrees to Sign U.N. Pact.txt
text:
ï»¿
China said today that it was ready to sign a United Nations covenant protecting political and civil liberties, in a move to head off criticism of its human-rights record.
"The Chinese Government is preparing to sign the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights," Foreign Minister Qian Qichen said at a news conference. 
"The Chinese Government has always attached great importance to international covenants on human rights."
China is anxious to avoid censure at a meeting of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights that is to open in Geneva on Monday.
The European Union, citing progress on human rights in China, agreed not to sponsor a resolution this year critical of Beijing's record. 
But the United States has said it could throw its weight behind a critical resolution.
Last month, a European Union delegation visited China for discussions and workshops that focused on legal changes China would need to make to subscribe to the United Nations political covenant. 
Topics covered police torture and detention without trial.
Pressing China to sign the pact has become one of the chief targets of European Union diplomacy.
The European Union has been criticized by human-rights groups and politicians for its decision to let China off the hook in Geneva. 
Member nations are now anxious for concessions from Beijing.
The political covenant covers freedom of expression and religion, assembly, participation in public affairs and elections, freedom of movement and equality before the law.
In its annual human-rights report, the American State Department said there was progress in Beijing's protection of fundamental freedoms but that serious abuses remained.
Amnesty International said in a report this month that despite human rights concessions, little had changed in practice in China. 
The report said thousands of Chinese had been detained without trial, and that trials were "grossly unfair."
It said torture was widespread.
Mr. Qian's pledge during the National People's Congress was the latest in a series of high-profile gestures by Beijing to polish its human rights image, still tarnished by the 1989 army crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in Beijing.
Beijing late last year released a jailed dissident, Wei Jingsheng, on medical parole and has invited the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Mary Robinson, to visit.
In February, three clerics from the United States arrived in China at the invitation of President Jiang Zemin to investigate religious worship.
Washington has backed resolutions criticizing China in Geneva each year since the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre.
But Beijing has always mustered enough support to quash the moves, and critics say the resolution has become an empty exercise that only fuels China's anger.
Â 
--------------------
U.S. Praises Beijing Move
WASHINGTON, March 12 (Reuters) -- The United States today hailed China's decision to sign the rights covenant, and hinted that Beijing might escape American censure at Geneva next week.
The State Department spokesman, James P. Rubin, said the Chinese announcement would have a "significant impact" on whether Washington would sponsor a resolution critical of China, but that no decision had been made.
"Clearly, this is a step forward." he said. 
"It's the kind of step on human rights that the world has long called for."
"By announcing its intention to sign the covenant, China has indicated in more concrete terms than ever before that it accepts the universality of human rights," Mr. Rubin said.
