file: TAIWAN_S LEADER WINS ITS ELECTION AND A MANDATE.txt
text:
ï»¿
President Lee Teng-hui swept to an election victory today that exceeded all expectations and served as a forceful rebuke to mainland China. 
This island's voters gave Mr. Lee a strong mandate in their first democratic balloting for President.
Final results showed that 54 percent of the nearly 11 million Taiwanese who cast ballots voted for Mr. Lee. His tally was more than double that of his closest challenger in a field of four candidates.
A strong sense of crisis over mainland China's threatening series of military exercises apparently caused significant numbers of voters to defect from Taiwan's largest opposition group, the pro-independence Democratic Progressive Party, to Mr. Lee's camp.
In Beijing, the official New China News Agency interpreted the election results as a sign that the voters of Taiwan opposed the idea of separation from the mainland. 
[Page 16.]
Mr. Lee's efforts to create a more independent international image for Taiwan have given him a broad appeal among voters of conflicting ideologies, including those who would like Mr. Lee to dump the island's longstanding commitment to a "one China" policy in favor of independence.
"This was a plebiscite without the label of plebiscite, and I hope that China got the message," said Parris H. Chang, a pro-independence member of Taiwan's legislature. 
"And the message is that Taiwan does not want to reunify with the mainland."
But other people watching the election closely said Mr. Lee would take the mandate and seek a new dialogue with Beijing in the hope of reducing military tensions.
Those tensions caused the Clinton Administration to send two aircraft carrier battle groups to waters near Taiwan to signal China that it should not interfere in Taiwan's democratic process.
[In Washington, a White House spokeswoman, Mary Ellen Glyn, said, "We congratulate the people of Taiwan on their first election."
She added: "We hope to see tensions in the Taiwan Straits greatly reduced in the days to come."
[But American officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said that no formal congratulations would be offered, because the United States does not have diplomatic relations with Taiwan.]
Mr. Lee had said before the vote that the next president's main job would be to work on cross-strait relations, and many took that to mean that Mr. Lee was preparing a post-election effort to cool tensions.
But the 73-year-old leader has given no clue as to whether he is willing to make substantive concessions to Beijing, like moderating Taiwan's drive for a seat at the United Nations. 
Beijing considers that effort to be part of an unacceptable "two China" strategy.
The pro-independence candidate, Peng Ming-min, 72, a longtime dissident who was only allowed to return to Taiwan from exile in 1992, turned out the poorest showing the opposition has made in the last three islandwide elections. 
The Democratic Progressive Party chairman, Shih Min-teh, announced his resignation at a news conference tonight, saying, "Someone has to take the responsibility" for the loss.
Two other tickets, headed by Lin Yang-kang and Chen Li-an, both breakaway members of Mr. Lee's governing Nationalist Party, polled 15 percent and 10 percent, respectively.
In a victory appearance at his campaign headquarters in downtown Taipei, Mr. Lee greeted a cheering and flag-waving crowd and said: "This is a historic moment. 
The door of democracy is now completely open."
Speaking in turn in Mandarin Chinese, English and his native Taiwanese dialect, Mr. Lee made only one reference to the campaign of military pressure mounted by mainland China during the last 10 months to weaken his hold on power.
"In this very difficult and dangerous moment with threats coming from the outside, we have completed our mission," he said.
The election was cheered in other parts of the region.
"This is a proud day for all Chinese people around the world," said Martin Lee, head of Hong Kong's Democratic Party. 
"It is the first time in China's history that a leader is elected on a one-person, one-vote basis on Chinese soil."
During the day, a crush of voters streamed to polling places registering a turnout that surpassed 76 percent, election officials said.
The results reflected a remarkable response to Mr. Lee's plea for a mandate to open a new round of negotiations with Beijing over Taiwan's future.
"From now on we should focus on economic development and strengthen the cross-strait economic and trade ties and cooperation," said Taiwan's Economics Minister, Chiang Pin-kung. 
Taiwan's central bank governor, Sheu Yuan-dong, also sought to reassure the island's investors and business community that pressure on the value of the Taiwan dollar caused by the flight of capital in recent weeks would return to normal.
Some analysts said that the true measure of Taiwan's rebuke to Beijing's Communist Party leadership could be seen in adding Mr. Lee's and Mr. Peng's tallies together, which represented 75 percent of the votes cast.
"The message from 75 percent of the voters is that what the mainland tried to accomplish by coercion and the threat of force, failed badly," said Mr. Chang, the legislator.
While Mr. Lee's vote tallies were strong throughout Taiwan, his total in this capital city was among the weakest, at 39 percent. 
Mr. Lin and his running mate, former Prime Minister Hau Pei-tsun, registered their strongest showing in Taipei, with nearly 25 percent of the vote.
By contrast, in the southern port city of Kaohsiung, a hotbed of independence sentiment, Mr. Lee took nearly 51 percent of the ballots and Mr. Lin took only 13 percent.
Appearing on Taiwan television tonight from a studio in Washington, the former American Ambassador to China, James R. Lilley, said that the election would serve to make China recognize "that power does not grow out of the barrel of a gun," as Mao Zedong once said, "it grows out of the ballot box."
But Mr. Lilley added that he believed that Mr. Lee is now well-equipped with a mandate to "start talking to China again and get the relationship going again" in order to reduce military tensions in the area.
In conceding defeat, all of the other candidates congratulated Mr. Lee and his running mate, Lien Chan. 
Though deep personal animosities were visible during the campaign, each sought to take the high road, although Hsieh Chang-ting, the Democratic Progressives' vice presidential candidate, seemed to be reminding the winning ticket of its obligation to pro-independence voters who crossed over.
"We hope the people who got elected will not betray the people who voted for them," he said. 
Less than a week ago, Mr. Hsieh reminded voters that President Lee had referred to himself as Moses last year and had promised to lead the people of Taiwan out of the "red" sea, meaning a sea dominated by China.
Mr. Hsieh had warned voters in the pro-independence party not to cross over to support Mr. Lee because the defections might go to Mr. Lee's head.
"Lee Teng-hui thinks he's Moses right now, but if he gets a mandate, he will think he is God," Mr. Hsieh said.
But it seems that many voters did not take this advice.
"Of course I voted for Lee Teng-hui," said Chen Bo-jui, a 42-year-old businessman, after he cast his ballot in midmorning. 
"He is a strong leader, and we have to be strong in order to talk to mainland China. 
Otherwise, they will just tell us what to do."

file: Taiwan_s New Leader and Beijing Testing Each Other.txt
text:
ï»¿
A day after Beijing hinted at new flexibility in dealing with Taiwan and its new president, it hastened to restate that its "one China" principle was an absolute precondition of strengthening ties.
"Acceptance or rejection of the one-China principle is the touchstone to test whether one sincerely wants to improve cross-straits relations," said a commentary by the official New China News Agency, issued in response to the inaugural speech on Saturday by President Chen Shui-bian of Taiwan.
"Anybody who dares insist on splitting Taiwan from China," the press agency said, "must bear responsibility for all the serious consequences."
In his speech on Saturday, Mr. Chen tried to reassure Beijing that he wanted reconciliation, but he did not satisfy the Chinese leaders' demand that he unequivocally call Taiwan a part of China.
In an official response on Saturday that was largely repeated in today's article, Beijing accused Mr. Chen of insincerity and evasiveness. 
But the statement also emphasized China's desire to seek closer economic ties across the Taiwan Strait.
And, for the first time since Mr. Chen's election in March, Beijing said negotiations could start under two conditions: if both sides "express in their own way orally" that they adhere to the one-China principle, as China says both did in 1992, and if Taiwan does not call itself an equal state.
Today, in his second day as president, Mr. Chen offered a potential plum if the two sides can start talking. 
He said he hoped to negotiate an end to what he called Taiwan's outdated ban on direct trade, shipping and postal links.
Beijing has long sought such direct ties, known as the "three links," not just to save the cost of sending goods and flights via Hong Kong but as a way to draw Taiwan to the mainland.
Taiwan, professing security concerns, has kept the ban as a bargaining chip, but its own business leaders, who have invested billions in China and send it a huge amount of exports, are increasingly chafing at the costs.
Political experts in China and Taiwan said the varying statements during the last two days were predictable as the sides continued to test each other as Mr. Chen assumed power. 
In particular, Beijing is probing to see how far Mr. Chen has moved from his longtime advocacy of formal independence for Taiwan.
"I think Chen Shui-bian's speech offered something positive, and we should catch the opportunity," said a Chinese specialist in foreign policy, Shen Dingli of Fudan University in Shanghai. 
"But Beijing will continue to put pressure on him over 'one China' to keep him moving in the right direction."
When he was preparing to run for president, Mr. Chen stopped calling for formal independence, though he emphasized that Taiwan was already sovereign in practice and intended to stay that way.
China's statement today, compared with Saturday's, included more emphatic reminders that the one-China principle was a non-negotiable precondition for talks.
Mr. Chen described his goal of relaxing commercial restrictions today as he visited the outlying Taiwan-controlled island of Jinmen, or Quemoy, which is near the mainland and would greatly benefit from direct commerce.
"Under the precondition that national security can be assured," Mr. Chen said, "we are willing to review the outdated, rigid and inflexible three-links policy."
He said the admission of China and Taiwan to the World Trade Organization, which could happen as early as September, would provide a natural forum for discussing such impediments to direct trade.
Julian Kuo, a political scientist at Soochow University in Taipei and an adviser to Taiwan's Foreign Ministry, said it was "a good sign" that Beijing had mentioned reviving the 1992 political formula and its desire to strengthen economic ties.
Mr. Kuo warned that rapid progress was unlikely, especially before China's leaders make crucial decisions about Taiwan at their annual seaside retreat in August.
But he also said that membership of China and Taiwan in the trade organization could provide an opportunity to "sort out economic issues" and end the ban on direct commerce. 
China and other countries have agreed in principle that Taiwan can join the trade group on a special, non-state basis.

file: Taiwan_s Overtures to U.S. Backfire.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Taiwan ruling party's efforts to influence American policy by hiring a high-priced Washington lobbying firm and fostering donations to the Democratic Party seems to have backfired, and critics here fear they have done serious harm to Taiwan's image.
Taiwan, once widely seen abroad as a right-wing holdover from a past era, has proudly promoted a new image as a booming Asian democracy, under threat from the military might of China.
But officials and lawmakers here fear that this positive image has been tarred by several recent developments.
Best known in the United States is the controversy involving a senior fund-raiser for the Democratic National Committee, John Huang.
Mr. Huang, who was educated in Taiwan, took the unusual step of traveling here to solicit funds from Taiwanese corporations that operate in the United States. 
The donations were apparently legal, but have been criticized by some as inappropriate.
Another, murkier incident involved a fund-raising event on April 29 at a Buddhist temple in California that is an offshoot of a temple in Taiwan. 
At the event, attended by Vice President Al Gore, hundreds of thousands of dollars were raised, but the Democrats have returned some of the money because of questions about the source and legality of the donations.
In Taiwan itself, a furor was stirred up by allegations that the ruling Nationalist Party offered to donate $15 million to President Clinton's re-election campaign, after being solicited by a former White House staff member, Mark Middleton. 
The Nationalist Party has denied making the offer.
"Image-wise of course it has an effect," Shen Lu-hsun, the senior Foreign Ministry official in charge of north American affairs, said in an interview.
Some legislators are concerned that the problem is deeper than that.
"It has been rather unfortunate that the impression has been given that U.S. support for Taiwan by sending aircraft carriers to protect us, or granting a visa for President Lee Teng-hui, is due to money," said Parris H. Chang, an opposition party lawmaker.
Last spring, after China conducted a series of missile tests near Taiwan, the Clinton Administration sent two aircraft carrier battle groups to patrol the waters near the islands. 
The missile tests themselves occurred 10 months after a "private" visit by Mr. Lee to the United States, a visit that China denounced.
Taiwan, which has had no diplomatic relations with the United States since relations were severed when Washington recognized Beijing in 1979, treads a delicate path between the Administration and Congress.
But President Lee Teng-hui, who became the first popularly elected leader of Taiwan earlier this year, has reportedly been dismayed by what he believed was the timidity of his Foreign Ministry in presenting Taiwan's case to the American Congress and the Clinton Administration, according to people familiar with Nationalist Party affairs.
As a result, he ordered his ruling party to hire a high-profile, aggressive lobbying firm in Washington, Cassidy & Associates.
Close advisers to Mr. Lee said he believes that the lobbying efforts were ultimately successful in winning him a visa to visit Cornell University, his alma mater, in June 1995, the visit that enraged Beijing and catapulted United States-China relations into disarray. 
Mr. Lee's visa was issued by President Clinton only after an overwhelming vote by Congress, which also was an object of lobbying by Cassidy & Associates.
For its part, the State Department vigorously opposed Mr. Lee's visit, arguing that it would damage relations with China. 
But evidently the problems caused by Mr. Lee's trip to Cornell stirred disquiet at the White House as well.
In at least one meeting here in Taipei during the last year, Mr. Middleton, the former White House aide accused of soliciting donations, urged a senior Nationalist Party official, Liu Tai-ying, to dump Cassidy as the party's lobbying arm in Washington, according to those present at the meeting.
The Arkansas friend of Mr. Clinton's who was appointed chairman of the semiofficial American Institute in Taiwan, James C. Wood, told Taiwanese officials that Cassidy was a liability for them, according to people familiar with these discussions.
As far as Taiwan's Foreign Ministry was concerned, the sooner Cassidy was dismissed the better. 
In the Chinese-language Chinese Times last week, former Foreign Minister Fred Chien assailed Cassidy's hiring as causing "disastrous" problems for the Government.
Mr. Shen, the Foreign Ministry official, said that there was nothing the Taiwan Government could do to impede the Nationalist Party and Cassidy.
Yet even as the Foreign Ministry continued to fight a guerrilla war with the Nationalist Party over the conduct of foreign policy, Taiwanese business was insuring that it retained solid links with the Democratic Party, the party that throughout the last year seemed destined to retain control of the White House.
At a celebratory dinner after the Democratic convention, selected Taiwanese politicians and business executives were scattered at tables in $1,000 seats. 
Among them was Annette Hsiu-lian Lu, a member of the political opposition, but a rising political force here.
"I was at one of the head tables," said Ms. Lu, a former legislator who was a founder of Taiwan's women's movement and who spent years in Kuomintang prisons. 
"I was supposed to sit next to Mr. Clinton, but somebody decided that was not a good idea."
The political symbiosis was cemented by the frequent trips of Mr. Middleton to Taipei, where, according to people here, he approached many of the country's wealthiest business executives for donations.
The exposure of divisions within the Government and ruling party over approaches to American foreign policy as well as the criticisms of Taiwanese political contributions to the Democratic Party have, in the view of some lawmakers here, jeopardized the strength of Taiwan's links to Washington.
"My worry," said Mr. Chang, the opposition lawmaker, "is that in the future, any Senator or Congressman inclined to speak out for Taiwan may not because of the suspicion that they are on the take."

file: Taking In the Sites_Factions Weigh In on Hong Kong Under Chinese Rule.txt
text:
ï»¿
There must be a reason so many of the World Wide Web sites about Hong Kong open with a scene of that city's skyline.
Not that there is anything tedious about the view south from Kowloon toward downtown Hong Kong. 
Despite the prohibition on big blinking lights (to avoid distracting airline pilots), Hong Kong's panorama of steel and glass has long been one of the more beautifully crowded urban vistas.
But as the jewel of the British Empire prepares to be remounted in a Chinese setting, Hong Kong's skyline may be one of the few aspects of the place that is certain not to be changed after sovereignty shifts to Beijing on June 30.
And the fact that perhaps not everything is up for grabs may be a comforting thought to Web designers of all political flavors.
As put in a candid and readable essay on the American Chamber of Commerce's Hong Kong site: "In Hong Kong, there is widespread cynicism about the real intentions and agenda of the British colonial rulers in the final days of the transition. 
Paradoxically, there is also concern that Hong Kong will become a de facto colonial outpost of P.R.C. interests, with less autonomy than hoped and agreed."
P.R.C. stands for People's Republic of China, and China's official Hong Kong Web site, when it can be reached, makes quite clear the view that the territory should have been part of the P.R.C. a long time ago.
But beyond the flattering portraits of China's hand-picked leaders for the new Special Administrative Region, the press releases showing popular support for cutbacks in civil liberties and the clock counting down to the hand-over, the most interesting thing about the official China site is its roster of advertisers.
One day last week Intel, I.B.M., Eastman Kodak, Microsoft and U.S. 
Robotics all offered "warmest wishes for the prosperity of Hong Kong."
Bay Networks and Oracle went further, "commemorating the return of Hong Kong to the motherland."
The ad for Mitsubishi Motors, a Japanese company, was pointedly different, "commemorating the return of Hong Kong to China."
Whether or not China is the motherland appears to be of little concern to the British Government's Foreign and Commonwealth Office, which runs a Web site that is almost wry in its resigned but dubious attitude about the hand-over.
Hong Kong's civil authorities are much more enthusiastic. 
The Hong Kong Government and Trade Office's in San Francisco has a Web site that offers a wealth of business information and gives the impression that the hand-over will be little more than an administrative detail. 
Likewise, the Hong Kong Tourist Association assures visitors that English will remain on street signs and that visa requirements will not change.
The Hong Kong Government's information site offers next to nothing of the territory's history, but includes a long section dedicated to explaining "myths and facts" about the change-over.
For example, fact 16 says (in part) that "public demand for the democratic process to stay on course and develop after 1997 will be irresistible."
That is not much comfort to those who fear Chinese rule.
Emily Lau, a pro-democracy Hong Kong legislator who is almost certain to lose her job after the change-over, runs a site that is half personal campaign literature and half general human rights advocacy. 
The Hong Kong Democratic Foundation, which appears to be more libertarian think tank than political action group, also has a site.
The Hong Kong Democratic Party and pro-democracy groups called Frontier and the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of the Patriotic and Democratic Movement in China, among others, run extensive Chinese-language sites.

file: Tension in Asia Over Wealth Under the Sea.txt
text:
ï»¿
In the seas between Japan and China are potential oil reserves, fishing grounds, mineral deposits and a few specks of rock that together amount to prime international real estate.
The disputes about who owns the resources are becoming more serious, for Japan, China and South Korea will soon be tussling over competing claims under the Law of the Sea Treaty. 
No one expects war any time soon, but some diplomats and government officials warn that in the long term, the disagreements could become a source of major conflict.
"I think there's a potential here for more than just diplomatic wrangling," said Kent E. Calder, a Princeton University scholar who has just published a book, "Pacific Defense," (William Morrow & Company), about security risks in the region. 
"Beyond that, the disputed areas are part of a larger danger of tensions between China and Japan.
"This will be a central issue in Sino-Japanese security for the next 5 to 10 years and perhaps beyond."
The backdrop is the growing unease in Japan about the military implications of the rise of China. 
Japanese Government officials often say that in the long run, the most important external issue facing their country is China.
Just this month five Chinese research ships conducted sonar exploration of what Japan regards as its seabed. 
Last fall a Chinese ship searched for oil on what Japan considers its side of the dividing line in the seas between them.
Japan occasionally scrambles its fighter aircraft when Chinese warplanes approach the Senkaku Islands, a few uninhabited islets that both countries claim. 
But some Japanese officials acknowledge that their warplanes and warships are a bit like dogs chasing cars, and that if the Chinese ever fired a missile, the Japanese forces would beat a hasty retreat.
One complication is oil, for the East China Sea bears promising geological formations that some experts say resemble those of the North Sea, with its huge oil reserves. 
Japan is acutely aware of its vulnerability on imported oil, and China has been a net oil importer since 1993. 
So both sides are dazzled by estimates that the East China Sea may contain 10 billion to 100 billion barrels of oil.
China's oil exploration in the disputed area last fall may be a sign that it will try to exploit reserves in the sea. 
So far Japan's Foreign Ministry has discouraged Japanese oil companies from drilling in the area, but if China goes ahead there would be strong political pressure for Japan to do so as well.
Sadayuki Hayashi, Deputy Foreign Minister of Japan, said in an interview that it was important to work toward finding common boundaries under the Law of the Sea Treaty. 
But he added that Japan would draw its exclusive economic zone on the basis that the Senkakus are a part of Japan.
"It is very clear that this is part of Japan," Mr. Hayashi said. 
He noted that China had not much contested Japan's sovereignty until reports surfaced that the area includes a lot of oil.
The issue has arisen because Asia, like most of the world, is moving to the Law of the Sea Treaty as the new framework for determining who controls the ocean's resources. 
South Korea ratified the treaty late last year, China did so on Wednesday, and Japan is expected to do so in the coming month.
The treaty allows nations to establish 200-mile "exclusive economic zones" in adjacent waters -- but the problem is that China and Japan and South Korea are less than 400 miles apart. 
This means that they have to figure out how to draw the line dividing their zones.
China's claims are raising anxieties to its south as well as its east. 
On Friday the Philippines and Vietnam reportedly denounced Beijing's claims under the Law of the Sea Treaty to a vast stretch of water in the South China Sea.
Japan proposes drawing the line at the halfway mark, although for this purpose it conveniently ignores a sometimes-submerged island off the Chinese coast. 
China, on the other hand, makes a sweeping claim to "inviolable sovereignty" over its continental shelf, which it argues juts into the ocean most of the way to Japan.
China also has disputes about maritime boundaries with South and North Korea. 
Although North Korea and China often hail their friendship, North Korean gunboats are said to have fired on Chinese fishing boats that stray into what North Korea regards as its waters.
Ji Guoxing, a Chinese scholar in Shanghai who has written extensively about maritime disputes in the seas around China, said it would take China some time after it ratifies the Law of the Sea Treaty to fix its exclusive economic zones. 
Mr. Ji added that while disagreements may be difficult to resolve, a war is unlikely.
"This may be an area of potential conflict, but I don't see a real battle there," he said. 
"Both Japan and China will exercise restraint while sticking to their own claims."
To solve the disputes, the parties could refer the matter to the International Court of Justice or seek mediation or arbitration.
For now, though, the countries have been taking the alternative approach of bolstering their navies. 
China and South Korea have been pouring money into their navies in recent years, and Japan, which already has a very credible navy, is considering whether to upgrade it further.

file: TENSION IN TAIWAN_ THE POLITICS_War Games Play Well for Taiwan_s Leader.txt
text:
ï»¿
"We hate China and we will fight to the death for Taiwan!"
Chang Ting-sen, an otherwise temperate-mannered professor of Chinese literature, shouted those words into the din of a packed stadium rally in Chiayi, a southern stronghold of Taiwan's pro-independence forces, and then smiled with satisfaction and yelled it again.
As the night sky crackled with fireworks and loudspeakers warmed up the crowd with a torrent of political bombast, he and 20,000 banner-waving Taiwanese packed the sports arena on Tuesday to cheer their candidate, Peng Ming-min, of the pro-independence Democratic Progressive Party.
Like many in Taiwan, the crowd had been roused to indignation by the missile tests and war games China has carried out in an attempt to intimidate the 12 million voters of Taiwan, who on Saturday will hold their first direct presidential election.
But even many independence advocates conceded that they are not the real beneficiaries of the confrontation with China. 
No one has profited more than Lee Teng-hui, the incumbent and native-born Taiwanese leader, whose own vision of Taiwan's future with the mainland is ambiguous.
Fundamentally, this is President Lee's confrontation with Beijing, brought on by his pursuit of a distinct and independent image for the island of 21 million people. 
It has transformed the election into a referendum on who should lead Taiwan in its time of crisis. 
By all accounts, Mr. Lee will win the contest handily.
His critics say this is exactly what the 73-year-old President wanted, an international emergency that would insure his victory and mobilize the United States to strengthen its guarantee of Taiwan's security with a show of naval force and the sale of new weapons.
In whistle-stop appearances through the island and in rousing speeches with nationalistic themes, Mr. Lee, a prodigious campaigner, is siphoning off voters from the pro-independence camp, while holding on to an opposing constituency that simply craves stabilityII, the status quo and a strong leader to face China.
He does so without ever betraying whether he favors reunification or some form of independence.
With the balloting about to begin, the pollsters here say that only his margin of victory is in doubt.
Just a year ago, Mr. Lee's political fortunes were in decline. 
The legislative majority of his governing Nationalist Party, which has been in power here since 1949, when Chiang Kai-shek appropriated the island as his exile home, was splintering under an assault of anti-corruption sentiment and reformist zeal.
But Mr. Lee's trip to the United States in June, a first for any Taiwan leader and made possible by a well-financed lobbying campaign in Congress, touched off a bellicose response from Beijing that still may not have reached its militaristic peak.
The Communist leaders in Beijing assume that Mr. Lee's image-building campaign is just another way to declare Taiwan's independence and undermine the "one China" principle by which China and Taiwan have lived since 1949.
Â 
Vagueness on Goals Is a Lee Strategy
But Mr. Lee is deliberately vague about his true colors, so much so that even close associates who have known him for many years are unwilling to venture a guess as to his overall objective.
Chang Tso-chang, president of the island's most influential newspaper, described Mr. Lee this way: "In his heart, he wants independence, but he has never been able to say it. 
And he is not willing to reunify with the mainland, but he also has never been able to say that."
Added the chairman of a major Taiwan corporation who has known Mr. Lee for many years: "I think Lee Teng-hui shows many different faces to many different people. 
That's why people are confused by his statements."
Still others see an innate pragmatism in Mr. Lee and a wily political instinct to keep the Communist mainland guessing and at arm's length, while searching for more "living space" for Taiwan in regional and international affairs.
Most Taiwanese today are willing to support such a strategy until some form of greater Chinese democracy emerges in which Taiwan could be confederated. 
Until then, few people in Taiwan are willing to put themselves in Beijing's hands, as Hong Kong's residents must do in 1997 when the British colony reverts to Chinese rule.
Mr. Peng, the candidate of the pro-independence Democratic Progressive Party, put it more bluntly at this week's rally in Chaiyi. 
"Lots of people in China are trying to escape their own country," he said. 
"Why would we want to be a part of China?
If you choose reunification, you are out of your mind."
This campaign is taking place in the midst of the worst political and military crisis here since 1958, when Mao Zedong's threat to send troops across the Taiwan Strait to reclaim China's long-separated province was blocked by the United States Seventh Fleet.
Â 
China and U.S. 
Exchange Demands
Now, with two American carrier battle groups steaming protectively in the western Pacific, one near Taiwan and the other expected to arrive this weekend, the crisis has led to harsh exchanges between Washington and Beijing.
Chinese Government spokesmen accuse the United States almost daily of "gross interference" in China's internal affairs, first for sending warships to the region and second for selling, most recently, Stinger missiles and other advanced, defensive weapons to Mr. Lee's 400,000-member armed forces.
In the final days of the campaign, the polemics have only increased with Chinese admonitions that American warships stay out of the Taiwan Strait and Washington's assertion of right of passage through the international waterway.
The Communist leadership in Beijing appears to expect that its display of military fireworks this month will reduce Mr. Lee's margin of victory or sober him to the threat China could mount against the island's economy. 
That, Beijing may believe, would render Mr. Lee more pliant in negotiations to open direct trade and transportation links across the strait, which China sees as the first step toward reunification.
But experience has shown that Mr. Lee, as a tactician, is not to be underestimated.
"Taiwan has created an economic miracle, and we have built a democracy without bloodshed," Mr. Lee told more than 600 foreign journalists who have arrived to cover what he characterized as democracy in the "shadow of war."
Mr. Lee has shrewdly said his victory would represent a mandate from voters to deal with Beijing from a position of strength. 
It appears he will get it.
"He has asked the Taiwanese to give him a mandate, to support him in this crisis," said Tim Ting, chief consultant to the polling company, Gallup Taiwan. 
"I believe he wanted a confrontation with the mainland because it has internationalized the problem of Taiwan. 
He is getting CNN live coverage, and he is drawing world attention to the threat of Chinese nationalism, while also building up Taiwanese nationalism."
In the field of four candidates, Mr. Ting added, it has been clear for some months that Mr. Lee has a lock on 40 to 50 percent of the vote, well ahead of any challenger.
But Mr. Lee's strategy is not without risks, and there are signs of stress fractures everywhere.
First, there was the sudden deployment this week of a phalanx of security men armed with M-16 rifles to protect all four presidential candidates after reports of an assassination plot detected by the National Security Bureau.
The details were sketchy, but Mr. Peng, the Democratic Progressive candidate, said he had been told that the plot involved a team of mainland Chinese infiltrators who were paid $5 million to kill one or more of the candidates. 
Government officials confirmed that a plot had been detected, but there was no allegation that Beijing was behind it.
Then, there was the Government intervention in Taiwan's stock market, where central bankers thus far have pumped more than $3 billion to give the appearance of stabilityII in this crucial week before the voting.
Mr. Lee has also sought to calm financial markets with hints that he will seek a new accommodation with the mainland to insure that the $25 billion to $30 billion in Taiwan investment on the mainland is protected.
Still, most of the island's business leaders are panicky over a drop in orders for Taiwan's exports and the flight of capital out of the country.
As a native-born Taiwanese, educated in Japan and the United States, Mr. Lee shows little affinity for the mainland or the mainlanders in his party. 
The mainlanders are often disparaged here as "wai sheng," or foreign-born, intruders who took over the island when Chiang Kai-shek fled the Communist victory and who, for many years, used martial law rule to suppress indigenous democratic stirrings and to build a corrupt party machine, which today is still accused of vote buying and "money politics."
Â 
Unpredictability Confounds Critics
With his 6-foot-plus frame, striking silver hair and a disarming, Cheshire cat smile, Mr. Lee continues to confound his critics with unpredictable political tactics. 
He has promised that he could make another landmark trip after the election to a capital that "no one could imagine."
"The people like Lee Teng-hui because he is a strong leader and he stands up for them in the face of China's dictators," said Chen Shui-bian, the popular mayor of Taipei who is a rising star in the pro-independence camp, but who concedes a grudging admiration for Mr. Lee's political style.
Aside from the fact that Mr. Lee sits atop a party machinery that controls the island's television networks and billions of dollars in assets, his greatest advantage is his own formidable campaigning skills arrayed against an opposition that is seriously diluted.
His appeal straddles the colliding politics of reunification versus independence, infuriating some in both groups.
"Mr. Lee Teng-hui directs and acts the play himself and leads the two sides to the edge of war," said one critic, Lin Yang-kang, the candidate of the New Party. 
Mr. Lin, 69, is among several stalwarts of the governing Nationalist Party who have given up party posts and privileges to work for Mr. Lee's defeat.
Mr. Lin and his running-mate, Hau Pei-tsun, 77, who were both deputy chairmen of the governing Nationalist Party and once close advisers to Mr. Lee, opened their presidential campaign this winter, accusing Mr. Lee of betraying the Nationalist cause, which is to work for the reunification with the mainland.
The Lin campaign now calls for "peace" with the mainland, but ever since the missiles were launched at target sites near Taiwan's ports this month, their approach has been portrayed by Mr. Lee as surrender to "terror."
In the south, where the independence movement was born, Mr. Lee has never uttered a commitment to declaring independence from the mainland. 
He does not have to. 
Taiwan's independence forces believe that he is with them.
He speaks the slang of the southern ports and factory towns, riding bull-horn trucks with local candidates and setting off firecrackers to please the deities of local temples.
"There is no question that he is a native of Taiwan and he thinks like us," says Parris H. Chang, a pro-independence legislator, "and there is nothing in his blood or his system that makes him want reunification."

file: THE 2000 CAMPAIGN_ WORLD VIEWS_A special report._Rivals Differ On U.S. Role In the World.txt
text:
ï»¿
If elected president, Al Gore says he will use America's military power to halt Bosnia-style massacres, its economic influence to press failing states to adopt democracy, and the carrot of trade accords to encourage adoption of Western-style labor and environmental standards.
Yet when asked in a recent interview how he would deal with all the festering resentments that American power engenders around the world, he paused for a moment and uttered two words: "Strategic humility."
He smiled at the phrase as he coined it, but never elaborated on how it would mesh with his interventionist inclinations.
George W. Bush, in contrast, argues that an overextended American military should gradually pull out of the Balkans -- a step that the Europeans view as abandonment. 
He insists on charging ahead with a national missile defense system -- which Russia and China have vowed to defeat by building up new nuclear forces to overwhelm defensive interceptors.
Yet Mr. Bush, asked in the second presidential debate to describe his philosophy for projecting American power, sounded startlingly like Mr. Gore. "If we are an arrogant nation, they will resent us," he said. 
"If we're a humble nation, but strong, they'll welcome us."
At a moment of unchallenged American primacy, it is understandable that both candidates want to convince the rest of the world that they would step lightly. 
Beneath their words, however, lie very different priorities, and probably very different styles, in managing America's relations with both allies and enemies.
In his debate performances, interviews and speeches on foreign and economic policy, the vice president has repeatedly portrayed himself as a man who has come to believe in vigorous American intervention abroad, a reversal of Democratic philosophy for most of the time since the end of the war in Vietnam.
He describes how the experience of seeing the Clinton administration move too slowly to end the killing in Bosnia drove him to conclude that America must be prepared to prevent disaster, and how two successive global financial crises reshaped his understanding of the central role economic stability must play in the foreign policy agenda.
Mr. Bush has woven a middle ground between two battling factions of his party -- internationalists who support engagement with great powers like China and isolationists who are deeply suspicious of the United Nations, the International Monetary Fund and the World Trade Organization.
Drawing on the advice of Gen. Colin L. Powell, widely viewed as a potential secretary of state in a Bush administration, Mr. Bush is far more tentative about committing American troops and rules out their use for what he dismisses as nation building. 
"There may be some moments when we use our troops as peacekeepers, but not often," he said in the final presidential debate. 
In the second debate he suggested a broader philosophical disagreement with Mr. Gore: "I'm not so sure the role of the United States is to go around the world and say, 'This is the way it's got to be.'
"
Any comparison of foreign policy between the two candidates is inherently unbalanced: Mr. Gore has a long record, in the Senate and as vice president, while during Mr. Bush's time as governor, his only real foreign focus has been Mexico, whose long border with Texas is a major matter of state and local politics.
Mr. Gore is always eager to mention his extensive dealings with foreign leaders and to analyze international events; he granted an hour-long interview for this article.
Mr. Bush took four weeks to consider repeated invitations to be interviewed on his foreign policy views. 
In the end he declined.
Â 
Seeing the World From Texas
The Texas governor has traveled frequently to Mexico, and says that as president he would focus on Latin America far more intensively than the Clinton Administration. 
But beyond those trips Mr. Bush, now 54, has left America's shores only three times in his adult life. 
He spent five or six weeks in China in 1975, on a break from graduate school when his father was American envoy to Beijing. 
When his father was president, he led an American delegation to the Gambia for a celebration of the country's independence.
In 1998, when he was considering a run for the presidency, he visited his daughter in Italy and then joined other governors on a tour of the Middle East. 
He stopped in Egypt and met President Hosni Mubarak, then went on to Israel, where he met the current prime minister, Ehud Barak and toured the West Bank with Ariel Sharon, a hard-liner now in negotiations about creating an emergency government with Mr. Barak.
The Bush campaign also provided a list of 150 foreign officials Mr. Bush has met with in Texas and elsewhere, mostly diplomats and trade officials, but also representatives of Russian energy firms. 
He saw the foreign minister of Russia, Igor Ivanov, this year.
Mr. Bush's aides say these meetings have left him at least as well prepared for the presidency as three past governors: Bill Clinton, Ronald Reagan and Jimmy Carter. 
Nonetheless, Mr. Bush makes foreign policy by committee, and prefers to have his coterie of advisers answer all the questions.
Mr. Gore's eagerness to place America's imprint on the world has clearly grown in his seven years in the vice presidency, which have featured dozens of trips abroad and many meetings with world leaders. 
White House advisers recall him making an impassioned plea to President Clinton in the summer of 1995 to threaten bombing Serbian forces after they overran a United Nations safe area in Bosnia, a moment that one aide said was now "seared on the front of Al Gore's brain."
The former United States trade representative, Mickey Kantor, recalls bringing Mr. Gore to meetings about how to confront Japan on opening its economy "so that I would sound like only the second-most vociferous guy in the room."
What Mr. Bush derides as nation building, Mr. Gore calls a natural evolution, decades later, of the Marshall Plan -- when American willpower and capital, and some American troops, helped rebuild Europe.
That difference was accentuated this month when Mr. Bush's chief foreign policy adviser, Condoleezza Rice, said the Republican contender would, if elected, gradually pull the remaining American troops out of the Balkans, after consulting with NATO allies. 
That prompted Mr. Gore and Secretary of State Madeleine K. Albright to shoot back that Mr. Bush would squander a nascent American victory in rebuilding the former Yugoslavia, where there are now some 11,400 troops, less than 20 percent of the total peacekeeping presence in Bosnia and Kosovo.
Lurking just beneath the surface of that dispute are questions that both candidates have left unanswered. 
Mr. Bush has never defined what kind of mission is in the "vital national interest."
Mr. Gore has never said how long he would keep troops in place to build a democratic state. 
Mr. Bush, in short, won't say when he'll wade into a crisis, and Mr. Gore won't say when he'll get out.
These positions reflect, in many ways, the advisers who surround the two men. 
Mr. Gore depends heavily on Leon Fuerth, his national security aide for two decades, who urged him to break with the Democrats and vote for going to war with Iraq in 1991. 
Richard Holbrooke, the United Nations ambassador, supported Mr. Gore's ill-fated run for the presidency in 1988, a political risk one aide says "the vice president has not forgotten."
He is often mentioned as candidate for secretary of state. 
And Mr. Gore has grown closer to Treasury Secretary Lawrence H. Summers, the architect of the Clinton administration's biggest financial interventions, from the Mexican bailout to the Asian crisis.
Mr. Bush relies heavily on Ms. Rice and a large cast of other graduates of his father's administration. 
Their influence is evident: Long before Mr. Bush ever criticized the International Monetary Fund, another close adviser, former Secretary of State George P. Shultz, said it should be shut down.
Both candidates insist that they would never seek to throw America's weight around. 
When it serves their purposes, though, each is quick to jettison his commitment to American humility.
Mr. Bush has made it clear that he will go ahead with a missile defense shield no matter what America's allies think -- and despite the harm it might inflict on America's fundamental relationships with Russia and China. 
Mr. Gore has repeatedly expressed a desire to incorporate environmental and labor rules in every future trade accord -- even though poorer nations view that as an unvarnished effort to assure that developing nations remain less competitive with American manufacturers.
Â 
Gore and Globalization
Not surprisingly, Mr. Gore tries to portray himself as the candidate best prepared to delve into the newest and most complex territory of foreign affairs, the challenges of economic globalization. 
The vice president's aides whisper that Mr. Bush's advisers are lost in the thicket of 1980's era problems, and are unprepared for a world in which global capital flows can cause as much havoc as global arms sales.
In a speech last spring in Boston, Mr. Gore charged that his rival was "stuck in a cold war mindset," that "continues to view Russia and China primarily as present or future enemies."
At one point he said that "Governor Bush's foreign policy is noticeably blank."
Mr. Gore has never repeated that charge, but his aides do what they can to sow doubts about Mr. Bush's competence as a potential world leader and a recent New York Times poll indicated that roughly half of American voters have their doubts on that score.
Mr. Bush's campaign officials say that in the second presidential debate their candidate established himself as respectably conversant in the major international issues of the day. 
Mr. Bush himself was comfortable enough to joke shortly afterward about his trouble wrapping his tongue around the names of world leaders. 
"I was especially pleased that Mr. Milosevic has stepped down," he said after the Yugoslav leader bowed to a street revolt. 
"It's one less polysyllabic name for me to remember."
Mr. Gore, in his interview, showed that he indeed has absorbed seven years of daily intelligence briefings -- and that he can name names with ease. 
He spoke with authority about the differences between the separatist movements in two parts of Indonesia, and discussed what kind of opposition movements in Iraq the United States could exploit to help unseat Saddam Hussein.
But Mr. Gore frequently passes up opportunities to describe a sweeping vision of how he would position the United States in the world. 
Mr. Clinton, by contrast, has mastered that patter, rarely missing a chance to draw the link between economic integration and the spread of capitalism and democracy.
Â 
Managing the Nuclear Rivals
China and Russia are huge powers in the midst of huge transitions, whose weaknesses and strengths pose some of Washington's biggest challenges. 
In either nation, an economic collapse or a military buildup could cause tremendous instability, not only in Asia and Europe, but around the world.
Yet those challenges have hardly been discussed in the final months of the campaign, for different reasons on each side.
Mr. Gore knows Asia well. 
He talks about his priorities there more crisply than many of his foreign policy advisers do. 
(Sometimes, in fact, he is too crisp: When he backed anti-government protesters in Malaysia two years ago, using their rallying cry of "reformasi," in a speech, Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad deftly used the moment to whip up a nationalist backlash against America that squashed the reform movement.)
But as one of his informal advisers says, "all the imagery is bad for him" in Asia. 
Raising broad visions of how to deal with China, for example, invites the Bush campaign to play up the photos of Mr. Gore bowing at the Buddhist temple in California that became the subject of lengthy campaign finance investigation. 
(The temple was linked to Taiwan, not China, but such subtleties are lost in campaigns.)
So Mr. Gore's campaign has indicated that he would continue in the Clinton mode of using economic ties to encourage China to greater openness, democracy and capitalism. 
But as China's leaders have stepped up the arrest of political and religious dissidents in the last year, Mr. Bush has homed in on the Clinton administration's oratory about a "strategic relationship" with Beijing. 
(Mr. Gore does not use that term.)
"China is a competitor, not a strategic partner," Mr. Bush often says. 
And he has indicated that he would sharply depart from the Clinton script in two ways: by pursuing the national missile defense, which China vigorously opposes and would counter with more and better intercontinental missiles, and perhaps by announcing a break with longstanding policy and pledging that the United States would come to Taiwan's aid if it was attacked by China.
Previous presidents have left that commitment vague, and critics warn that an explicit security guarantee would antagonize China while increasing the risk that Taiwan would take steps toward independence. 
Such moves, in turn, could increase chances of a conflict with the mainland.
There has been more talk about Russia, where Mr. Gore played a leading role, though a commission he co-chaired with former Prime Minister Viktor S. Chernomyrdin. Mr. Gore knew from the outset that an active role in guiding Russia toward a new role in the world would distinguish him from any potential rival for the presidency. 
And the effort had some early successes, including an agreement to return to Russia the nuclear weapons that had been stationed in Ukraine, Belarus and Kazakhstan. 
But American hopes of guiding economic reforms went off-track, and recent disclosures indicate that Mr. Gore failed to get Russia to halt arms sales to Iran by this year.
Mr. Bush argues that the administration was naive, "focusing our aid and attention on a corrupt and favored elite" that sometimes failed to fulfill promises made to Mr. Gore. "When Bill Clinton compared Boris Yeltsin in Chechnya to Abraham Lincoln, what signal did that send to states around Russia's periphery?" asks Ms. Rice, a Russia expert. 
"When the Russians didn't follow the favorable and attractive script we wrote for them, we continued to pretend they were carrying out their part of the bargain. 
They lost respect for us as a result."
(While Mr. Clinton in 1996 did make a glancing comparison of the Chechnya rebellion to the Civil War, he also said then that "a free country has to have a free association" and Russia would have to find "a diplomatic solution.")
Mr. Bush has offered only generalities about how he would handle Russia differently, and has never said how he would persuade Moscow to accept the missile defense system that could require quitting the Antiballistic Missile Treaty. 
(Ms. Rice says that Mr. Bush would review "the size of the American arsenal," and perhaps reduce it).
On the Middle East, Mr. Bush has gone to some lengths not to criticize Mr. Clinton's handling of a volatile and deteriorating situation -- at least not directly. 
And Mr. Gore has been almost completely uninvolved in managing the failed Camp David talks and diplomacy that followed -- until he flew back to Washington 10 days ago to sit in on the meetings planning Mr. Clinton's summit meeting with Yasir Arafat, the Palestinian leader, and Mr. Barak.
Indirectly, though, Mr. Bush has thrown a few jabs. 
"You can't put the Middle East peace process on our timetable," he said in a not-so-subtle suggestion that Mr. Clinton rushed into Camp David in hopes of a comprehensive agreement before he left office.
Both candidates are quick to tick off their criteria for sending America's troops to intervene. 
But ask them for their criteria for using taxpayer dollars to choke off a market crash or a global financial crisis -- the kind that struck Mexico in 1995, and Asia two years later, then spread around the world -- and specificity vanishes.
Mr. Bush stumbled when asked in the first debate how he would handle a stock market crisis -- and then announced that he would summon his top advisers.
Mr. Gore pointed to Robert E. Rubin, the former treasury secretary, in the audience, a man regarded in Washington and on Wall Street as a cool manager of such crises. 
He seemed to suggest that he would call his old friend -- now a top executive at Citigroup -- and then he changed the subject. 
"He clearly wasn't prepared for that one," one of his close economic advisers said.
In his interview, Mr. Gore was similarly vague about his standards for economic intervention. 
"I'm not sure there is a handy cookie cutter on that one," he said. 
"I think there are so many variables that you have to know it when you see it."
He referred an interviewer to Mr. Summers, who said that he would recommend using America's financial might to right another country if "there was a material impact on the U.S. economy or the global economy," provided the loans came with conditions to assure reform in the country getting assistance, "a credible assurance we will be repaid" and a "prospect of success in restoring market confidence."
Ms. Rice said in an interview that Mr. Bush's first criteria for bailing out a foreign nation would be "whether the countries we are helping have the political will to make economic reforms."
Clearly Russia in 1998 -- a bailout Mr. Gore helped coordinate -- did not fit her test. 
Other Bush aides tick off economic criteria closely parallel to that of Mr. Summers.
Â 
Bush and the I.M.F.
Mr. Bush is more leery of the role of the International Monetary Fund. 
"I think a lot of times we just spend aid and say we feel better about it and it ends up being spent the wrong way," he said in the second presidential debate. 
He charged that the fund -- which the United States effectively controls as its largest shareholder -- often sends the message to international bankers that "if you make a bad loan, we'll bail you out."
He also charged that much of the $4.8 billion lent to Russia in 1998 ended up "in the pockets" of Mr. Chernomyrdin. Mr. Chernomyrdin denied it, threatening to sue Mr. Bush for defamation. 
The I.M.F. says independent auditors have found no evidence that the money was diverted, and the Bush campaign has cited no evidence to back up the charge.
Ms. Rice insisted that Mr. Bush's broader point was correct. 
"Once the Russians were flaunting it, cooking the books, and once their privatization effort went awry, we kept pumping I.M.F. money in," she said. 
"That weakened the I.M.F., and it allowed the Russians to have a kind of drug on which they became dependent. 
It was a mistake. 
A big one."
Economic sanctions create a sticky problem for both candidates. 
Mr. Gore defends the slow lifting of sanctions against North Korea, saying, "Incredibly enough, we have seen a positive response to initiatives there," but refuses to consider trying the same approach on Cuba. 
"I'm a hard-liner on Castro," he said, ticking off the Cuban leader's list of offenses, and ignoring a similarly long list for North Korea.
Cuba, of course, is a highly emotional issue in Florida, whose 25 electoral votes are hotly contested. 
So Mr. Bush has taken a similarly tough line. 
But he has also distanced himself from the views of his running mate, Dick Cheney. 
In 1998, while running Halliburton, the oil services company, Mr. Cheney said unilateral sanctions almost always fail and hurt the competitiveness of American businesses. 
He called for lifting sanctions on Iran, saying the United States could no longer rely on them "as a club that we can use to punish those who disagree with policies or goals or objectives of the United States."
Mr. Bush has said pointedly that he is not ready to lift sanctions on Iran.
Â 
Free Traders, but Not Always
Everyone in this race is a free trader. 
Except, of course, when campaigning in Michigan or West Virginia, or anywhere else where overseas competition seems a mixed blessing, threatening old jobs even as it creates new markets for American goods.
Mr. Gore is accustomed to weaving between his free-trading boss and the labor unions that make up his core support. 
Those unions have opposed every major free trade initiative by the administration, from the North American Free Trade Agreement in 1993 to the China trade bill that passed last month, and some threatened to bolt from Mr. Gore. In the end, they backed down.
This year, Mr. Gore backed the China trade legislation, just as he backed the North American trade pact in 1993. 
It did not include standards for protecting workers or preserving the environment that he said in his interview he would, if elected, try to get included in all trade negotiations. 
A free trade agreement with Jordan, signed by Mr. Clinton last week, is the first to include all of those standards in the core of the accord.
Mr. Bush insists that he would aggressively press new accords -- without labor and environmental provisions -- and expand the North American pact to include much of the rest of Latin America.
In short, he sounds like a true free-trader. 
Yet in coal country, Mr. Bush has also bent over backward to draw in union workers who have become disaffected with Mr. Gore. Earlier this month he visited a coal-rich area of West Virginia, and was introduced by a laid-off miner who is president of a United Mine Workers local. 
"This is an administration that fears coal," he said. 
"They see it as a threat. 
I see it as an opportunity to make us less dependent on big, foreign oil."

file: THE ASIAN CRISIS_ BEIJING_China Vows Not to Overrule Hong Kong Officials.txt
text:
ï»¿
Faced with their first major crisis since resuming sovereignty over Hong Kong, where the stock market went into free fall and lost 10.4 percent of its value today, Chinese officials responded calmly with promises not to intervene or overrule Hong Kong authorities.
Displaying a sophisticated understanding of market pressure, and pointing to the "one-country, two-systems" formula that Beijing has pledged to keep in Hong Kong, China's top banker employed caution and expressed confidence that Hong Kong's financial authorities would handle the situation.
"The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has the competence and capability to maintain the stabilityI of the Hong Kong dollar," Dai Xianglong, governor of the People's Bank of China, told a Hong Kong newspaper in an interview to be printed Friday.
At the same time, Mr. Dai sent a signal to speculators by declaring that China was prepared to support the Hong Kong currency, if asked.
One of the main concerns in Hong Kong about Beijing's new rule has been that Chinese officials unfamiliar with modern financial markets might panic or interfere in a crisis.
Technically, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has sole say in the territory's fiscal matters. 
But if a serious disagreement arose between Hong Kong and Beijing during a financial crisis, it is anyone's guess who would prevail.
In a sense, today was the first test.
Acting calmly, Mr. Dai and other bank officials indicated that even before they took control of Hong Kong on July 1, they had anticipated just such a market meltdown. 
"We are fully prepared for this kind of situation," Mr. Dai said. 
"I have full confidence in the Hong Kong dollar."
Economists have been watching with growing bemusement over the last year as China's foreign exchange reserves grew ever higher, reaching $134 billion by the end of September. 
Mr. Dai acknowledged today that one of the reasons was to protect the Hong Kong and Chinese currencies in a crisis.
In view of the market turbulence spreading across the globe, Mr. Dai said, "The reserves are currently sufficient, not excessive."
Hong Kong's own reserves total $80 billion, and officials at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority have pledged to use what is necessary to defend the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the United States dollar of 7.75 to 1.
Just prior to the handover of power to Beijing, there was wide speculation in Hong Kong about whether Chinese authorities would try to support the Hong Kong stock market if it came under heavy pressure. 
Now that that has happened, however, a senior economist at the Bank of China insisted that it was inconceivable Beijing would authorize such a defensive operation.
"A lot of analysts thought the market became overvalued in the last few months, especially red chips," the economist said, referring to China-based companies listed in Hong Kong. 
"It makes no sense to support the stock market. 
It will rise and fall. 
The currency is what needs to remain stable."
Shen Guofang, a Foreign Ministry spokesman, echoed that sentiment. 
"No administrative agencies will interfere or intervene in the operations of the stock market," Mr. Shen told reporters. 
"We believe the 'one country, two systems' is being applied well in Hong Kong."
Eden Woon, director of Hong Kong's General Chamber of Commerce, said most business leaders supported the Government's policy. 
"This is a very political issue," Mr. Woon said. 
"Everyone sees it as an extremely important sign of stabilityI and confidence in the territory. 
People know that a loosening of the peg would cost a great deal."

file: The Bamboo Chair Sings a Sweet Song.txt
text:
ï»¿
WHEN William Lipton talks about Chinese bamboo furniture, he sounds more like a philosopher than a merchant. 
"They say without meat, a man grows thin; without bamboo, he can't build a house," he said this week. 
"And when you sit in a bamboo chair, it should sing. 
You know bamboo chairs were built to make that creaking sound."
Mr. Lipton, 44, a New York dealer, has been thinking a lot about bamboo furniture since he came upon a few rare pieces in two warehouses in Beijing in 1993 and realized there might be more. 
Over the next two years, and several trips back to China, he amassed enough to put together the first exhibition of such furniture in this country.
"Honorable Gentlemen: Bamboo Furniture and Objects from China," a show in Mr. Lipton's shop at 27 East 61st Street, offers some 50 chairs, tables and cabinets that were produced for use in Imperial palaces and homes of wealthy merchants, mostly in the 18th and 19th centuries. 
These pieces have the dignity and proportions of formal hardwood Chinese furniture. 
They imitate its lacy look in the use of latticelike panels to fill the backs of chairs, form the bases of tables and embellish the fronts of chests.
Mr. Lipton said this style of bamboo furniture flourished only in Shanxi province in northern China and largely remained there until recently because of the difficulty and expense of shipping goods in China.
His below-street-level shop in a converted town house is chockablock with furniture. 
Round tables, octagonal chairs, squarish footstools and rectangular cabinets are grouped together or stacked, covering every inch of the tiny shop.
"The layering and density achieve a certain effect," he said. 
"It's calculated to produce a sense of mystery."
Always the merchant, he added, "I also want people to see how things are different, how things are not alike."
The shop is supposed to look like an old Chinese tea house with a garden out back planted with bamboos and Chinese plants. 
Mr. Lipton said that in China many people lived in heavily furnished rooms, combining very simple pieces with ornate ones "as we have in this shop."
The earliest piece on display is a lacquered Ming cabinet of woven split bamboo embellished with a dragon on top from the 17th century. 
"We know the bamboo tradition goes back further than that," Mr. Lipton said, noting that there are tables and chairs depicted in Song paintings from the 13th century. 
Most of the early bamboo furniture has not survived. 
"Bamboo is so vulnerable, and because it was so common throughout China, people didn't treasure it as they did rarer pieces," he said.
Even so, Mr. Lipton's shop offers an amazing selection, in both the types of furniture and the detailing of the bamboo patterns. 
There are chairs with horseshoe-shaped or square backs, others with hexagonal seats. 
Tables come in all sizes and shapes. 
Some were used for serving tea, others in scholars' studies.
Each piece of latticework on the bamboo furniture is carved with little pins and slots that function like mortise and tenon joinery. 
The legs are made of bamboo, and the stretchers are also single pieces of bamboo that are wrapped around them. 
"I think the way bamboo furniture is lovingly embellished with this wrapping technique shows how the makers in Shanxi prized this material," he said.
Everything in Mr. Lipton's show is for sale. 
The prices range from $2,000 for a tea stand to $12,000 for a side table. 
The exhibition runs through October. 
(A catalogue will be available on Nov. 
1 for $50.)
Coincidentally, the Lipton show comes at a time when there is growing international interest in Chinese furniture. 
A major exhibition is currently on display at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, and when the Shanghai Museum reopens in its new building next week, it will feature a gallery devoted to Chinese furniture. 
Last month, the first comprehensive collection of such furniture brought record prices at Christie's.
Mr. Lipton traces his interest in Chinese furniture to his childhood, when he tagged along with his parents on their weekly visit to an antiques shop in San Francisco's Chinatown. 
He says the tiny lacquer boxes, the porcelain cups and carved jade buckles he saw in the glass cases "looked so mysterious."
He studied textile design at the School of Art in Basel, Switzerland, and then went to Bangkok, Thailand, where he was the design director at the Jim Thompson Thai Silk Company in the 1970's. 
Later, he designed textiles for General Motors in Southfield, Mich. 
He came to the antiques trade after honing his eye for 20 years as a collector of Asian decorative arts and opened his shop in 1990.
When Mr. Lipton began buying bamboo furniture in Beijing he was reminded of an encounter he had had with an old Chinese furniture maker in Thailand. 
"He had a chair that had belonged to his father, and I wanted to buy it," Mr. Lipton said. 
"But he couldn't sell it because he liked the noise it made."
Mr. Lipton also likes the noise. 
"The creaking happens as the bamboo stretches and the joints squeak, the way crickets sound rubbing their legs together," he said. 
"Crickets are prized in China for their song."
Now, with Mr. Lipton's help, the gentle squeaking of bamboo furniture may be valued, too.

file: THE CHINA TRADE VOTE_ BEIJING_Chinese Express Joy and Relief at Passage of Trade Bill.txt
text:
ï»¿
News that the House voted to grant China permanent normal trade status with the United States was generally greeted with joy here today, tempered by worries about the wrenching economic changes that are expected as China frees up its markets to outsiders.
"That's fantastic," said Zhang Linan, 24, an accountant, as he heard the news on the way to work. 
"I think it will be a boost for our economic development and personally it means more choices for us."
But the government, in its first official reaction, expressed "severe concern and dissatisfaction" about conditions that the House attached to the bill, including a new annual review of human rights, calling it an unacceptable effort to "interfere in China's internal affairs and damage China's interests."
Many Chinese have placed enormous hopes on membership in the World Trade Organization, with its rules for market opening, as a force for dismantling inefficient state industries and modernizing the country. 
The trade bill's passage was expected to help China's entry to the WTO.
And since most people yearn especially for cooperation with the United States, which they see as the world's economic and cultural leader, defeat of the trade bill would have been seen as a stinging betrayal.
"It's so good that it passed," said Luo Hui, 36, a computer programmer. 
"If Congress hadn't passed this law, it would have been a shock, a setback, a big international incident. 
Now we can get on with business."
While the government felt obliged to object to intrusive conditions the House attached to the trade bill, the top leaders were undoubtedly pleased with its passage. 
President Jiang Zemin and Prime Minister Zhu Rongji have staked their prestige on China's entry into the global trading regime and on closer economic ties with the United States.
The official statement, issued by the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation, said "it was wise of the House of Representatives to pass" the bill to normalize trade relations. 
"The resolution of this issue will benefit the healthy and stable development of Sino-American bilateral trade on a basis of equality and reciprocity."
At the same time, the government put a strong protest on the record. 
The conditions included in the bill, the official statement said, are "unacceptable to the Chinese government."
The news from Washington should speed along what is already a remarkable revival in Chinese-American relations since the bombing of China's embassy in Belgrade last year, during the NATO campaign against Yugoslavia. 
Still, foreign policy experts warn of pitfalls ahead.
"Before the trade vote in Congress, two big problems threatened Chinese-American relations, trade relations and Taiwan," said Xiong Zhiyong, dean of the Foreign Affairs College here. 
"Now there's only one."

text:

Chinese Pavilion Featured
Workers from Westchester's sister city Jingzhou in China completed construction of a traditional pavilion and garden in May at Lasdon Park and Arboretum in Somers, a property of the county's Department of Parks, Recreation and Conservation.
Called the Chinese Friendship Pavilion, it was built by Chinese artisans sent to Westchester along with all the construction and finishing materials they would need. 
The building, dedicated on June 2, will be featured on a free tour of the park today at 2 P.M. Typically Chinese in its architectural style, it is the sort of structure one would have seen in the gardens of royalty. 
Painted orange, turquoise and red, it has a tile roof and is open on all sides, the better to contemplate the surrounding landscape and a pond. 
The interior ceiling and overhang are painted with 108 dragons flying among clouds.
Also on the tour are the arboretum's many species of trees, shrubs and perennials and a native American chestnut tree grove where the American Chestnut Foundation does research.
In 1991 the 180-acre preserve established a continuing project called the Famous and Historic Tree Grove, where seeds taken from trees at significant locations or dating from centuries ago are planted.
Some of them are from the homes of American Presidents. 
Among them are an Overcup Oak from Abraham Lincoln's home and seeds from trees at the homes of George Washington and Franklin D. Roosevelt. A yellowwood seedling was obtained from John F. Kennedy's grave site at Arlington Cemetery, and a water oak seed was taken from the grounds of the Brown African Methodist Episcopal Chapel in Alabama, where the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. spoke at the start of the march to Montgomery.
Battles also figure in the collection of seeds. 
A Saratoga red oak represents a 1777 victory for the American Revolutionary forces at that site, and a northern white cedar seed was taken from Fort Ticonderoga, commemorating a 1759 battle in which the British took the fort from the French. 
A seed from the rare Franklinia Tree, prized for its fragrant white flowers, which bloom in July and August, is a descendant of the original, planted in the 1600's by John Bartram, an American botanist.
Admission to the tour is $3. 
Call 232-9147 for more information.

Teun Hocks's painted photograph "Untitled," exemplifies the theme of an exhibition opening Tuesday and remaining through Oct. 
25 at the Castle Gallery of the College of New Rochelle. 
"The Waking Dream: Psychological Realism in Contemporary Art" tries to explore the lighter and darker sides of life as expressed enigmatically by 21 artists. 
Viewers will read whatever they wish into the results.
D. Dominick Lombardi and Steven Lowey were the guest curators, and they will give free gallery talks at a reception on Sept. 
20 from 1:30 to 4 P.M. The artists' names would not be familiar to most people, but they are all professionals. 
They include Mike Cockrill, Julie Harvey, Antonio Petracca, Steven Skollar and Lisa Zwerling.

Candid Shots in China
Forty-four color photographs of people in some of China's major cities will be on display in the Somers Public Library from Tuesday through Sept. 
29. They were taken by C. Richard Donahue, a clinical social worker who recently traveled through Hong Kong, Beijing, Xian, Guilin and Guangzhou with a group of colleagues.
"I'm a people person, and most of the pictures are of people I would see from the time they went to work at 6 in the morning through the rest of the day," he said.He photographed many fathers tending their children, which surprised him. 
"They are very family oriented," he said. 
"And they are doing simple, unusual entrepreneurial things that they would have been arrested for 20 years ago."
He recalled a man who had set up a little business by the side of a road well traveled by people on bicycles -- the most prevalent mode of transportation. 
"He had a canvas spread on the ground, with a complete set of bike repair tools."
Struck by the unexpected freedom that the Chinese have to travel, he said, "They were streaming into Hong Kong and experiencing unprecedented growth and expansion."
Unframed prints of the photographs may be bought for $25 each. 
An indication of their content is in the titles: "Haircut on the Street in Beijing," "Mother and Child at the Market in Guangzhou," "Life on the Li River in Guilin," "Young Girl in a Newsstand in Beijing," "Art Student at the Children's Palace in Xian," "Women Waiting for a Bus in Guilin" and shots of families in the temple, an old woman begging, a woman hanging wash and a customer in a butcher shop.

The Flag as Chronicle
An unusual exhibition of antique American flags can be seen at the Darien Library through Sept. 
14. Ken Reiss, curator of the show, is co-owner with his wife, Catherine, of many of the flags on view. 
"It has often been said," he said, "that the American flag is unique in providing an ongoing chronicle of the growth of the nation it represents."
Upholding that premise are flags tracking 10 changes in design from 1861 to 1912. 
Different patterns of stars in rows or circles reflected individuals and manufacturers' concepts, sometimes to the point of adding new stars in anticipation of new states. 
The flags and related materials, some from the Darien Historical Society collection, mostly date from the half century after the start of the Civil War.

text:
