file: THE MARKETS_ Market Place_U.S. Investors Salivate Over Chinese Stocks In Pact_s Wake.txt
text:
ï»¿
MAYBE it depends which side of the Pacific you're on.
In the days since China and the United States signed a deal that may lead to Chinese admission into the World Trade Organization, the Chinese stock market has made small gains, with indexes of mainland stocks up about 1 percent. 
Hong Kong stocks did better, with the leading index of such shares up 3.6 percent since Friday.
But most of the relatively small number of Chinese stocks traded on major American stock markets have risen sharply. 
In some cases they have gone absolutely berserk. 
Suddenly, any stock with China in its name seems to have willing buyers.
The biggest gains have gone to stocks that previously had been of little interest to American investors. 
By contrast, China Telecom (Hong Kong), which provides cellular telephone services in China and has been an institutional favorite in America, rose on Monday and Tuesday but fell $5.9375, to $86.5625, yesterday, and is up just 2 percent for the week.
But such languid performance is more than offset by other stocks that have skyrocketed. 
A list of nine stocks -- all traded on the New York Stock Exchange or Nasdaq and all with the word "China" in their names -- shows increases of at least 60 percent for six of the nine since Friday. 
Investors who put an equal amount of money into each of the stocks on Friday -- the last trading day before the W.T.O. agreement was announced -- would have more than quadrupled their money by yesterday's close.
The most amazing move came in the shares of China Prosperity International Holdings, a company that does property renovations in China -- but that has also been talking about doing something related to the Internet.
China Prosperity was once something of a hot stock, moving as high as $37 a share in Nasdaq trading in 1996 -- adjusted for a later reverse split. 
But it had fallen out of investors favor, and by Monday was trading at $1 a share.
Then on Tuesday, the stock leaped to $11.06, trading as high as $14, and volume rose to 521,100 shares, or more than had traded in the previous year. 
That however, was just the prelude. 
Yesterday, volume totaled 4.4 million shares, or more than the total volume in this country since the company went public in 1995. 
The price leaped as high as $80, then began to slide before ending at $32.0625.
There was no announcement from the company, but the same could not be said for another suddenly highflier. 
China Resources Development, a distributor of natural rubber, reported that its losses were growing. 
It added that it had no explanation for the stock's movement in Nasdaq small-cap trading.
That stock jumped $19, to $25 a share, in trading yesterday, on volume of 906,800 shares. 
That volume is nearly twice the total number of shares outstanding.
Another amazing performance was turned in by the Dransfield China Paper Corporation, which rarely trades on Nasdaq. 
During October, there were only two days when shares in the company, which distributes paper products and is building pulp mills in China, were traded. 
The price then was $1 a share. 
It fell to 43.75 cents on Monday, and then did not trade Tuesday.
But yesterday, with anything named China looking hot, 1.3 million shares were traded -- more than triple the total volume traded since the company was listed on Nasdaq in 1997 -- and the price rose as high as $29 before closing at $12.
China.com, a company based in Hong Kong that provides a portal for Chinese users of the Internet, leaped from $58 on Friday to a close of $105 yesterday, trading as high as $137. 
It had gone public, at $20 a share, in July.
Even China Tire, a company that makes car and truck tires, got in on the action. 
Since Friday, it is up 77 percent, to $10.625.
It is not easy to explain such moves based on expectations of what will happen if China is successful in entering the World Trade Organization, something that could yet be derailed by Congressional opposition. 
Changes in the Chinese economy will arrive over a period of years, and the opening of the economy to competition from foreign companies may damage some Chinese businesses even as others are helped.
But there seems to have been little in the way of such analysis regarding many of the stocks that were moving yesterday. 
Instead, Internet chat rooms were full of comments about how certain stocks were sure to keep moving because there were relatively few shares available for trading. 
Traders were chasing performance, and in the process they were creating it.

file: The Nation_Searching Only in Profiles Can Hide a Spy_s Face.txt
text:
ï»¿
WHEN investigators were trying to find out who might have given sensitive weapons secrets to China, they paid special attention to Wen Ho Lee in part because of his Chinese ancestry. 
But last week, when the Taiwanese-born American scientist pleaded guilty only to downloading sensitive information onto an insecure computer and prosecutors conceded they had no further case to make against him in open court, the quick association of Mr. Lee's ethnic origins with suspicions about his loyalty seemed mostly an embarrassment for the government.
Accusations of "racial profiling" in Mr. Lee's case didn't just offer a new example of the historic tension in America between concerns about national security and civil liberties principles. 
There were also practical arguments, offered by experts on counterintelligence, against zeroing in early on an espionage suspect primarily on the basis of ethnicity.
To be sure, some Justice Department investigators felt last week that they were the ones who had been treated unfairly. 
To them, it was thoroughly legitimate to consider Mr. Lee's ethnic background, among several other factors, in forming suspicions that he might have helped Beijing. 
It was especially logical, they said, because the Chinese government has a well-documented history of using ethnic Chinese in other countries to help gather intelligence.
Those investigators said they are obliged to make their best effort to narrow the list of suspects when trying to determine the source of a leak of information and should not be hampered by notions that to do so might offend some group.
But many experts are now saying that such an approach is not only inherently offensive but also potentially counterproductive.
Experts on espionage have long accepted that using factors like ethnicity carries a risk of reprising historically corrosive assertions that some Americans have a dual loyalty based on their heritage.
For many years, it was fear of that very accusation that lay behind an Israeli government policy of not using American Jews to gather intelligence in the United States. 
When Jonathan Pollard, an American Jew and civilian analyst for the Navy, was arrested in 1987 on charges of spying for Israel, the shock was all the greater for that reason, and the Israeli government made a point of insisting that the intelligence unit that recruited Mr. Pollard had been a renegade outfit.
Phillip B. Heymann, a Harvard law professor who served as the deputy attorney general in the early Clinton years, said that using a suspect's heritage is not only offensive to concepts of civil rights but is also often a lazy form of stereotyping that can do more to hamper a counterintelligence investigation than help it. 
"At the early stage of an investigation, you have to identify a relatively limited number of suspects and do so in a relatively inexpensive way," he said in an interview. 
"And then you can work harder on that smaller group."
Mr. Heymann, who oversaw the Justice Department's counterintelligence operations, said that the most important factor in narrowing a list of suspects is determining who had access to the information and motive to provide it to a foreign power.
"Motivation and opportunity are the two things you look for," he said. 
"You might look at who had unusual debts, who is bitter and angry, who has the opportunity to make contact with the country that received the material."
Ethnicity, he said, can serve as a misleading surrogate for those factors. 
"What you're getting out of knowing that Wen Ho Lee is Chinese is an extremely crude estimate of the larger list of factors about motive and opportunity. 
It comes very cheap but it isn't nearly as probative as the others.
"Ethnicity turns out to be a very difficult factor to use properly," he said. 
"There are so many steps between the initial observation of someone's ethnicity and making an intelligent use of it that it's really not worth using. 
And if you use it to focus too quickly on a narrow category of people, you're giving a pass to other people in other categories."
John L. Martin, who supervised the Justice Department's investigation and prosecution of espionage cases for 26 years until 1997, said in an interview that "what should lead a good investigator are the facts and not necessarily the ethnicity of anybody in the pool of suspects."
Mr. Martin now heads the Washington office of the OSO Group Ltd., an international investigative company. 
He said that most spies of recent vintage were mercenaries, people who chose to help foreign governments for money. 
"You would be wasting your resources if you pursued a potential suspect largely on the basis of ethnicity and not all the underlying facts," he said.
In the case of Mr. Lee, he said, it seemed that his Chinese heritage had increased suspicion of him because he had traveled to China and had met with Chinese government scientists in the United States. 
"But it appears a flaw in the Wen Ho Lee case was that there were non-Chinese scientists who made some of the same trips and had some of the same contacts" but were not investigated as closely, he said.
Another feature of the Lee case that strongly suggests that investigators were too quick to rely on Mr. Lee's ethnic heritage was that in the end they weren't sure which foreign country he might have been motivated to help. 
Some investigators suspected China, but because Mr. Lee had been born in Taiwan, others thought it might have been that country, which is the People's Republic of China's most resolute foe.
It may never be fully clear to the public just how much Mr. Lee's ethnicity was a factor in singling him out because the plea agreement that ended the case also halted an inquiry on that matter by the federal judge hearing the case. 
But the issue has already had other consequences. 
Last week, lawyers for several Muslims charged in connection with the plot to bomb two United States embassies in Africa in 1998 said they would use the Lee case to argue that the prosecutors had unfairly singled out their clients on the basis of their religion.
And just as the "racial profiling" of minorities for special suspicion of involvement in crime can backfire on law enforcement by arousing a whole community's resentment, there was evidence that the Wen Ho Lee case may have actually cost American security research some valuable talent. 
Chinese-American civil rights groups said that Chinese-Americans are now greatly reluctant to take government positions at the national laboratories.

file: The Nonproliferation Treaty Bares Its Toothlessness.txt
text:
ï»¿
ONLY a few months ago North Korea seemed like a pathbreaking example of how the world's great powers can set aside other differences to make sure that fanatical leaders and nuclear bombs are kept apart. 
Faced with overwhelming evidence that the hard-line Communist regime of Kim Il Sung was building a bomb, the United States harnessed the West, and then Russia and China, to stop the project from turning into a nightmare. 
For most of last year, it looked like the strategy was working.
Beneath his usual cloud of defiant oratory, the 80-year old Mr. Kim finally agreed to live up to his obligations under the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty. 
He allowed international inspectors to visit the mysterious nuclear site called Yongbyon. 
His motives seemed clear. 
He sought the trade and investment he desperately needs, especially now that there are reports of food riots and troops stand on rail-side coal piles to keep the residents from stealing enough to heat their homes.
On Friday, though, it was Washington's seeming success that turned to coal -- and along with it, much of the world's confidence in the workability of the treaty that 153 nations have signed. 
In an unnerving and perhaps self-destructive act of defiance, North Korea became the first nation ever to renounce the treaty, barring the door completely to international inspectors who were on the scent of a secret cache of plutonium. 
Vice Foreign Minister Kang Sok Ju declared that the North had signed the accord in 1985 to reduce what he termed a nuclear threat from South Korea and the United States, and said "We are now withdrawing from it because it is being abused to destroy our republic."
Surprised and more than a little scared, Japan and South Korea denounced the action as destabilizing and dangerous. 
At the same time, though, there were second thoughts about whether the safeguards designed 25 years ago, in an age of superpower patrons for countries like North Korea, still have any teeth.
Â 
Something Fishy
What use is a treaty that allowed a country to develop nuclear weapons for seven years while it barred inspectors -- and that is renounced as soon as the first inspectors in the door smell something fishy?
Is the International Atomic Energy Agency, a United Nations affiliate with no enforcement powers, the right institution to keep countries like North Korea in line?
And even if the issue goes to the Security Council, what can you take away from a country that has nothing?
"The treaty is no longer quite so sacrosanct today," said Leonard Spector, head of a project on nuclear proliferation on the Korean Peninsula at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. 
"Now that one country has pulled out, others obviously can begin to think about it."
In many ways the North Korean experience is significantly different from the challenges the West has faced in dealing with nonsignatories -- including India, Pakistan, Israel and Algeria -- and even with countries that have signed and dodged, like Iraq. 
First, by all accounts, Saddam Hussein seems much farther from realizing his dreams than Kim Il Sung is. 
Estimates vary widely, but more and more analysts in the United States Government seem to agree that North Korea already has the raw material for at least one bomb, and a few think some crude, still-untested devices may have already been built. 
Second, North Korea has turned weaponry into its only successful export business; it ships home-grown missiles to the Middle East, and presumably would have few qualms about shipping nuclear weapons.
But perhaps most important, rather than play an Iraq-style game of hide-and-seek with the inspectors, the North has used the access to its nuclear facilities guaranteed by the treaty itself as a bargaining chip. 
In its statement Friday it said it would only return to the regime if "the United States stops its nuclear threats against the North" -- which was interpreted as a reference to the annual "Team Spirit" military exercises now under way between South Korea and the United States -- and if the atomic energy agency "returns to its principle of independence and impartiality."
In short, Mr. Kim turned a situation in which it held no cards -- he was trying to hold off a "special inspection" of two sites that American spy satellites have identified as waste dumps that would probably show how much plutonium he has produced -- into a situation in which he now holds at least one: re-entry into the treaty. 
In fact, once a three-month waiting period to exit the treaty expires, his bomb-development work will become legal.
"From the start it was always assumed that if a country did withdraw from the treaty, it would be a signal that they had decided to make a bomb," Gary Milhollin, the head of the Wisconsin Project on Nuclear Arms Control, said recently. 
"If not, why take the political heat?"
What got everyone to this point is a 25-year-old system that acknowledges the right of every nation to use nuclear materials for peaceful purposes, even if those same materials, especially plutonium, are relatively simple to rework into weapons. 
It is the "safeguards" system of inspection that is supposed to assure that materials intended for civilian plants stay in civilian use.
The biggest advocates of that system are countries like Japan, which is already extracting plutonium from nuclear waste, much as North Korea is trying to do, as part of its aggressive civilian nuclear power program. 
These days the Japanese find themselves in the diplomatically embarrassing position of arguing that they have every right to do so because the world recognizes them as a solid international citizen, while at the same time arguing that their North Korean neighbors must be denied the right because they have an attitude problem.
Â 
Plutonium Politics
The North Koreans, naturally, say that their intentions are benign and that the I.A.E.A. is "tacitly approving" moves by Japan and South Korea to secretly arm themselves.
"We are seeing the breakdown of a regime that believed that plutonium and bomb-grade material are O.K. as long as they are under safeguard," said Paul L. Leventhal, president of the Nuclear Control Institute and a harsh critic of the precedent set by Japan's plutonium effort.
Officials in Japan and South Korea, naturally, say they have no interest in nuclear arms. 
The Japanese have long renounced them, and South Korea stopped developing them after the United States got wind of its project in the late 1970's. 
But preventing such an arms race has always depended on Seoul and Tokyo remaining unshakably confident that the United States' support, and its nuclear umbrella, extends over them.
Though few will say it publicly, that is what the Team Spirit exercise, which was suspended last year when the North looked like it was beginning to cooperate, is all about. 
This year the United States brought the B-1B bomber and other nuclear-capable equipment to South Korea for the exercises, presumably to make a point. 
And it was exactly that which sent the North into a frenzy, declaring early last week that they were going on a "semi-war footing" because invasion was imminent.
Now Washington is in the position of having few attractive options. 
Some officials, including many in Japan and a few members of the two-week old South Korean Government, argue that going ahead with the 125,000-troop Team Spirit exercise this year is an unnecessary provocation. 
But it is too late to back down. 
Though the American military has endless scenarios for eradicating Yongbyon, everyone acknowledges they are of little use: If the North retaliated on Seoul, only 35 miles from the border, or on South Korean civilian nuclear plants, it would be disastrous.
Economic sanctions are likely to have little effect on a country that is already isolated from virtually all of its neighbors except China. 
Getting the Chinese to seal off that border, and with it food and fuel, is unlikely.
"It may not be over yet," said Mr. Spector. "We are about to see an intense diplomatic effort to get this turned around."
But it may be, he said, that the world has little cause to be optimistic: Perhaps the North Koreans knew that they were about to get caught, he said, and the only solution was to jettison the one treaty that could betray them.

file: THE TRADE DEAL_ THE CHINESE_Joy, Worry and Indifference in Streets of Beijing.txt
text:
ï»¿
Many Chinese were pinching themselves this afternoon, filled with disbelief that after more than a decade of false starts, China had actually taken the plunge into the international economy, signing a landmark trade agreement with the United States.
On a chilly gray afternoon in Beijing, many people were ebullient when they first heard the news. 
For most people, it raised the prospect of new opportunities to make money as well as new chances to consume. 
The agreement drops many current restrictions on trade and investment and reduces import taxes.
"It's signed?" said Li Dayong, 29, who works for an American pharmaceutical firm. 
"That's great!
I'm thrilled!
We've been wanting this for so many years."
Some took a macro view, welcoming the treaty as a sign of bigger things: China's new economic muscle, an immutable commitment to further economic reform and a renewal of relations with the United States that had been ravaged by the bombing of the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade in May.
But Beijingers also seemed keenly aware that there will be individual winners and losers along China's new path. 
Most are paying careful attention to the micro view, calculating what the trade agreement -- which is widely expected to lead to World Trade Organization membership -- means for them.
"This is great news: I had planned to change my Daewoo for a better car soon and now I'll buy an imported American one," said Xu Yiang, a stock investor, referring to the car he now owns.
Mr. Xu said he also plans to change his investment strategy, buying telecommunications stocks that he deems likely to attract foreign investment.
But Luan Wenqiang, a worker at the Beijing Light Truck Company, predicted that the agreement would drive him out of his already tenuous job. 
"Our factory is already in bad shape," he said. 
"Most workers are on leave and are called back only when there is work to do. 
This will open China to better and cheaper U.S. trucks. 
I don't believe we will survive."
Under the agreement, duties on imported vehicles will drop dramatically, from the current rate of 80 to 100 percent.
For the hundreds of millions of Chinese who farm the land or work as low-wage laborers in small cities and towns, today's triumphant treaty was a big bang in another universe -- although many will probably feel its effects.
Half a dozen migrant workers interviewed in Beijing said they had never heard of the trade organization, which has had only fleeting recent mention in the press despite the frantic negotiations here.
"It has nothing to do with my life," said a middle-aged man, a worker in a small machine factory, strapping a huge box of cabbage to the back of an ancient bicycle.
The new treaty will certainly bring both new investment and intense competition to China and the outcome will vary from industry to industry. 
But many corporate leaders seemed to relish the challenge of being able to compete in the world arena.
"I'm extremely happy to hear about this," said Duan Yongji, the Chairman of China's giant Stone Group, a technology company. 
"Everyone knows that entry will make the country more open and that will bring more competitive pressure.
"But we shouldn't need a greenhouse to protect us. 
And we also hope that entry will open more opportunities for collaboration and cooperation between Chinese and foreign companies."
Mr. Duan added that, at a personal level, he was relieved to hear the government renew its vows, so to speak, to principles like economic overhaul and engagement with the West. 
The Chinese government has often appeared lukewarm on such concepts.
In Beijing's business districts, many owners of small businesses likewise focused more on the opportunities of today's deal than its risks.
Many foreign companies have opened offices here in the last five years -- though their activities were extremely circumscribed by Chinese law -- gambling that this huge economy would one day open. 
Today people dared to imagine the payoff.
Li Dayong, an American drug company employee, said that until today his company has not been able to import many of its medicines to China. 
"Now I think it should become easier to bring foreign medical products in," he said.
Dai Liming, 35, well dressed in a sweater vest and suit, saw only possibilities when he heard the news. 
Mr. Dai, who works as a representative for a domestic trading company, predicted that "the deal will bring my company new opportunities for foreign trade."
But others offered more sober assessments, noting that many of China's service industries -- from insurance to the Internet to personal banking -- are young and ill prepared to compete on the world stage.
"We are already facing fierce competition from foreign companies in some areas and if further concessions are made in the insurance sector we'll be facing a grimmer future," said Lu Youquan, manager of Antai Life Insurance Company in Shanghai.

file: THE TRADE DEAL_ THE OVERVIEW_U.S. REACHES AN ACCORD TO OPEN CHINA ECONOMY AS WORLDWIDE MARKET.txt
text:
ï»¿
American and Chinese negotiators reached a landmark agreement today that would open the economy of China, the world's most populous nation, to foreign competitors and would also make it a full partner in the world's trading system.
After six days of arduous negotiations, the United States trade representative, Charlene Barshefsky, and China's trade minister, Shi Guangsheng, signed the papers at 3:50 p.m., shook hands and raised a Champagne toast to an agreement that capped 13 years of on-and-off negotiations on China's entry into the World Trade Organization.
Under the deal, Beijing would reduce tariffs on various industrial and agricultural products. 
It would also lift many of the barriers that have hamstrung American banks and insurance and telephone companies that want to expand their operations and investments in China.
In exchange, the United States agreed to support China's bid for membership in the global trade group, the 135-member organization that sets the rules for international commerce.
China still must complete agreements with the European Union, Canada and some developing countries, including Brazil, before its application can be taken up by the group's member states.
"Let me just say that this is a profound and historic moment in U.S.-China relations," said a clearly exultant Ms. Barshefsky, adding that the agreement would not only aid the economies of both countries, but also serve as an anchor in their tumultuous political relationship.
The last six days of day-and-night negotiations were conducted in a "win-win spirit," Mr. Shi said, "and finally we reached an agreement that serves the interests of both China and the United States."
For all the rejoicing, the agreement faces tough resistance in the United States, where it is opposed by labor unions and some critics of China. 
Congress will not vote on the deal itself, but must vote to put an end to its annual review of Chinese trade and to establish normal -- and permanent -- trade relations with Beijing.
For China, membership in the trade group would mean a long-sought acceptance into the "club" of world powers. 
The W.T.O.'s elaborate rules would help protect China from unfair trade policies abroad, but would also impose a body of international rules on China's own fitful progress toward a market economy.
The accord goes to the heart of China's transition to an open, market economy. 
It would put Beijing, for the first time, under the jurisdiction of the rules set by the World Trade Organization, which are enforced by a trade court.
Full membership would be a victory for President Jiang Zemin, who sees achieving economic modernization as his legacy even as he tries to ensure continuation of Communist rule. 
At the same time, membership would cheer the more liberal, reform-oriented factions led by Prime Minister Zhu Rongji, since it locks China onto a path that could force China's state-owned industries to become efficient.
The step is a politically risky one for China, coming at a time when those state-run companies are already shedding millions of workers.
For President Clinton, today's agreement provides a badly needed centerpiece to his fraying policy of engagement with China, offering the prospect of tangible gains to many companies and to consumers. 
It is also a stunning recovery from what his own top aides describe as a huge mistake: his decision to walk away from the surprisingly sweeping deal, largely identical to today's, offered in April by Mr. Zhu.
After the signing today, Ms. Barshefsky and Gene Sperling, the White House chief of economic policy -- who opposed the April deal and attended the talks as a symbol of Mr. Clinton's renewed commitment -- were driven to the secluded leadership compound for a brief meeting with Mr. Jiang, who twice in the past month conducted telephone talks with Mr. Clinton.
Speaking in Turkey today, Mr. Clinton said: "I think this is a good agreement for China, for America and for the world."
But Mr. Clinton's struggle to make this accord a central foreign policy achievement is far from over.
Congress will essentially review the accord when it prepares to vote on the biggest single American concession: granting permanent trading rights to China rather than reviewing those rights annually, a Capitol Hill ritual that has turned into an annual debate about human rights and arms proliferation.
Mr. Clinton has spoken often of "integrating China into the world economy" and gradually getting the country to embrace "the rule of law," starting with commercial law. 
But without closing a World Trade Organization agreement, his aides said, he would have little progress to point to.
The agreement may also help to repair the damage done to Chinese-American relations by charges of Chinese spying in the United States, the American bombing of the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade in May and China's continuing suspicion that the United States is attempting to "contain" Chinese military and economic power.
"Successful completion of W.T.O. will go a long way to smooth out some of the extreme oscillation that we have seen in Sino-American relations in recent years," said Joseph Fewsmith, a China expert at Boston University. 
"I think it gives us a chance to build some substance into a relationship that has been badly damaged."
Today's agreement is a huge step toward membership for China, but it very likely comes too late, experts said, for China to be admitted before Nov. 
30, when a new round of global trade talks begins in Seattle.
But today's accord means that China can take a larger role in setting the agenda there. 
And past trade rounds have lasted for years.
From the beginning, the American goal was not just to press China for large reductions in tariffs on imported farm products and industrial goods like automobiles. 
In measures that may ultimately have a far more profound impact, China had to commit itself to allowing foreign companies to take majority investments in many industrial and service sectors.
The final six days, and usually nights, of negotiations went through several rough spots. 
Several times Ms. Barshefsky and Mr. Sperling suggested they were packing up to leave, threats Ms. Barshefsky said in an interview today were "largely tactical, to force the Chinese to make some progress."
"Clearly," she said, "they were not going to let us leave."
In an interview from Hong Kong today, Ms. Barshefsky said that the key Chinese player in the talks appeared to be Prime Minister Zhu, who twice stepped in to break an impasse and ultimately directed his negotiators to make several key concessions -- allowing American companies to take a 50 percent stake in China's booming telecommunications companies, for example. 
But all his decisions, analysts here said, were almost certainly cleared by the top party leadership.
The outlines of an agreement had been worked out last April, when Mr. Zhu visited Washington. 
But President Clinton backed away from any agreement at the time, fearing Congressional opposition. 
Most of today's pact follows the April understandings, and in resolving areas of continued dispute, Ms. Barshefsky asserted -- in a statement sure to be scrutinized by skeptics in Congress -- "I think we achieved an overall strengthening of this agreement."
The agreement involves a general reduction in China's import tariffs from the current average of 22.1 percent down to 17 percent, with tariffs on major American farm products cut sharply to 15 percent or less.
Tariffs on automobile imports, which now range up to 100 percent to protect China's inefficient producers, would be reduced over a six-year period to 25 percent, with the quickest reduction in the initial years. 
That is one year longer than China offered in April.
But equally important, American officials said, foreign auto companies and banks would for the first time be able to offer consumer loans for cars, a critical concession in a country where few can lay out the money for such a large purchase.
Thus, Chinese consumers may soon be buying General Motors cars, for example, with the "G.M.A.C." loans so familiar to Americans.
Two of the most contentious issues in recent days, Ms. Barshefsky said, involved the American demands for ways to respond to surges of imports into the United States and for use of a method to identify when the Chinese might be illegally selling products below cost, or "dumping."
China wanted such measures to phase out quickly, but in the end agreed to surge protections for a 12-year period, and the anti-dumping regime for 15 years. 
Without those concessions, Ms. Barshefsky told her Chinese counterparts, Congress could easily balk at the accord.
For the first time, China also agreed to allow foreign companies to distribute their own goods, rather than forcing them to distribute food or industrial components through Chinese companies. 
They would also be able to repair and support their products directly.
In terms of textiles, one of the most politically sensitive topics in the United States, it was the Americans calling for restrictions on free trade. 
The Chinese wanted to scale back the American demand to continue existing textile import quotas for another 10 years. 
In the end, the United States agreed to end quotas after five years, but with special anti-surge safeguards for another four years after that.
The anti-dumping and textile provisions are charged issues for Vice President Al Gore. 
He hopes to keep the support of organized labor in his presidential bid, but such groups oppose the trade accord.
Foreign investment in China's telecommunications sector had become a sore point inside China, where some saw it as an issue of national security. 
The Americans fought for 51 percent ownership rights -- which Mr. Zhu had offered in April -- but finally agreed that foreign firms could take up to 50 percent ownership of companies in this booming sector, beginning two years after China enters the trade organization.
"It became clear that this was an incredibly emotional issue for the Chinese," Mr. Sperling said in an interview.
Important provisions would open Chinese retail banking to foreign firms over several years, and also improve market access for insurance companies, and legal and accounting firms. 
But the American negotiators got far less in China's infant and high-risk financial securities market, where they would be limited to minority stakes in activities like underwriting stock issues.
For China -- which is still unraveling the legacy of Mao Zedong's cloistered, command economy -- entry into the World Trade Organization will carry profound implications.
Many economists here compare entry to Deng Xiaoping's landmark opening of the economy to market forces and foreign influence in the late 1970's.
"The opening of China to the outside world began with Mao Zedong's meeting with Richard Nixon in 1972," said Hu Angang, a leading economist here at the Chinese Academy of Sciences. 
"The second major stage was marked by Deng Xiaoping's visit to the United States in 1979."
"Joining W.T.O. will represent a whole new stage in China's opening to the world," he said. 
"It will signify a shift from partial to comprehensive opening and reform," he said, "and a shift from an opening based on domestic rules to an opening based on internationally defined rules."
China's embrace of more open markets reflects the desire of President Jiang and other top leaders to push ahead with a radical overhaul of the domestic economy, opening it to global competition and bringing in more foreign capital and technology.
President Jiang and his fellow Communist Party leaders see economic transformation as vital if China is to become a great power in the century ahead. 
They also know that if they do not provide steadily rising incomes to their people, the party's rule is in trouble.
So the renewed opening is perhaps unavoidable, but it is a risky step for the leaders, who can expect to see some cherished state enterprises crushed even as others are energized. 
In the short run, at least, already impoverished farmers may be harmed by cheap imports and more urban workers might lose their jobs.
The impact of today's agreement on the power of Mr. Zhu, who is nominally number three in the party hierarchy, is unclear. 
Over the last six months or so, his influence appeared to slip, as the country took a more conservative and nationalistic turn, and Mr. Jiang took a stronger role in economic matters. 
By many accounts, Mr. Zhu lost his former control over policy on the World Trade Organization and the reform of state enterprises.
But Ms. Barshefsky said today that in a phone call between Mr. Clinton and Mr. Jiang last month, "Jiang said that Zhu Rongji is in charge of these negotiations."
"And," she said, "it looked very much as if he had taken ownership of it."
Today's agreement put Mr. Zhu and his ideas back in the limelight, but Chinese television reports this evening featured President Jiang, and both Chinese and foreign analysts continue to speculate about power shifts in the secretive Communist hierarchy.
On paper, the changes China has promised are breathtaking in scope. 
But even the most optimistic American officials concede that threatened ministries and provinces are likely to find ways to delay implementation of many provisions. 
This suspicion is likely to feed controversy in the United States about the pact.
Still, both Democrats and Republicans say the agreement will almost certainly be approved in Congress sometime early next year, after a spirited debate.

file: THE TRADE DEAL_ THE PARADOXES_Riding Winds of Reform, Yet Mired in Orthodoxy.txt
text:
ï»¿
On Monday, President Jiang Zemin warmly played host to American officials at the Chinese leadership compound to celebrate the major trade agreement committing China to far-reaching economic reforms and broad international ties.
Today, on the other side of Chang An Avenue, Mr. Jiang's security police forcibly detained more than a dozen members of the banned Falun Gong spiritual movement who had dared to unfurl a yellow banner and meditate in Tiananmen Square.
The two events, only 24 hours apart, illustrated the contradictory impulses driving China, a country that one moment seems to be hurtling toward a more open future and the next seems mired in Communist orthodoxy and intolerance.
Today, one day after the announcement of a trade deal that is likely to lead to membership in the World Trade Organization soon, China's state-controlled news media uniformly gushed over the deal's benefits for business as well as for foreign relations. 
The pact will "improve relations with other major powers, particularly the U.S.," said the Beijing Youth Daily, a newspaper that just four months ago was castigating the United States as an imperialist invader for the bombing in Kosovo.
"There are a lot of paradoxes in China now that are difficult to resolve," said Minxin Pei, a senior associate at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington.
Many experts in and outside China, as well as President Clinton, have predicted that the opening of the economy required for entry into the World Trade Organization would ultimately push China to liberalize in noneconomic spheres as well -- promoting, for example, more freedom of the press and a more even-handed legal system.
But for now, the contradictory facets of China remain mostly uncoupled, creating the odd juxtapositions.
"The economic dimension of China has been transformed to allow for market forces and private property," said He Qinglian, a Shenzhen author and economist. 
"But the other dimensions -- politics and ideology -- have changed very little. 
The political system has changed only as much as demanded by economic change. 
And in ideology, there's been very little change at all."
This is partly because China's leaders are much more unified on the need for economic reform than for political reform, said Mr. Pei. And Chinese citizens are, for the moment, far more concerned with improving living standards than with voting, he added.
But other experts point out that there is a unifying impulse behind the leaders' seemingly contradictory actions: to maintain the power of the Communist Party.
"The furthering of reform and opening characterized by the W.T.O. deal and the intensified crackdown on the sect and dissidents are both fully in line with Deng Xiaoping theory, which calls for 'both hands being aggressive,' " said a researcher at the Institute of Marxism, Leninism and Mao Zedong Theory of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences in Beijing.
He said the leaders hoped that the trade deal would bring foreign investment to maintain high economic growth, which would in turn promote stabilityI. 
"If they can achieve these goals, it can help consolidate the rule of the Communist Party, which -- remember -- is the most important of Deng's Four Cardinal Principles."
In the past year, the Chinese government has grown increasingly at home living in this divided world, making little effort to link liberalizing economic and social policies with politics at home.
In 1997 and 98, in the months preceding the exchange of state visits by Mr. Jiang and Mr. Clinton, the Chinese routinely released dissidents as a good-will gesture, held only a few political trials and even tolerated the development of an embryonic democratic party.
But this fall, even as Mr. Jiang toured Europe and chatted on the phone with Mr. Clinton in pursuit of a trade agreement, Chinese courts were sentencing pro-democracy activists to long prison terms after brief trials without lawyers. 
And the Chinese police were detaining thousands of Falun Gong members for practicing a banned form of exercise and meditation.
Falun Gong is an idiosyncratic blend of traditional Chinese exercises and Buddhist and Taoist religious beliefs that was widely popular -- before it was banned in July -- among middle-aged Chinese for its supposed health benefits.
Ever since, the government has been conducting an old-style Maoist propaganda campaign to wipe out what it has labeled an "evil sect," complete with re-education for members, and detention or labor camps for those who have publicly continued its practices.
But in a China now filled with Internet cafes and Hong Kong cable television, campaigns do not work as they used to, and this one has fallen flat both among more devoted practitioners and among the many Chinese who see the group as mostly harmless.
Today, on a crisp fall morning, in Tiananmen Square, a dozen or so practitioners unfurled a banner reading "The Great Law of Falun" and held out their hands to begin their exercises, a small protest to attract the attention of the United Nations Secretary General, Kofi Annan, who is visiting Beijing.
Police in uniforms and plainclothes -- on bicycles, in vans and on foot -- were out in large numbers. 
The protesters, some of whom were kicked, were then shoved into vans, which sped out of the square, witnesses said.
There was another small demonstration Wednesday morning by four women, a man and a young child who performed slow meditation exercises, The Associated Press reported. 
The police bundled the group into a van and drove them away.
Experts say it is unclear how long China's leaders can aggressively open their economy to the outside world while pursuing a totally closed political system at home.
"I think the whole process of economic pluralism inevitably leads to pluralism in ideology and other spheres, because it leads to diversity of economic interests which in turn produces distinctive needs and values," said Ms. He, the economist.
She said that at a time when China is changing so rapidly, the country's sustaining value systems, Confucianism and Communism, are both collapsing -- leading to the rise of groups like Falun Gong.
"China still adheres to a monolithic ideology," she said. 
"But a specialized professional society like China is becoming requires a more innovative, pluralistic ideology."
Also, after an initial surge in response to the trade agreement, China's stock prices tapered off today, and investors and economists in China seemed uncertain that opening the economy would, by itself, lead to the economic growth that the Communist Party wants and needs.
"The kind of paradoxes we see today can last for some time," said Mr. Pei of the Carnegie Endowment. 
"But no society can tolerate that kind of dissonance forever."

file: THE TRADE DEAL_ THE POLITICS_Agreement Presents a Split for Republicans in Presidential Race.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Clinton administration's agreement to support China's membership in the World Trade Organization today laid bare the deep divisions among Republican candidates for president on the nature of relations between the United States and China.
Gov. George W. Bush of Texas and Senator John McCain of Arizona gave qualified endorsements of the trade deal, saying that bringing China into the global trading scheme would help moderate its economic and political behavior.
But the more conservative candidates for the Republican presidential nomination condemned it, accusing the administration of ignoring gross human rights violations in its eagerness to expand commerce with China.
The two Democratic candidates, Vice President Al Gore and former Senator Bill Bradley, applauded the trade agreement, although aides said that Mr. Bradley would reserve final judgment until he had a chance to study its terms. 
Both candidates are seeking a way to embrace free trade with China while not alienating important Democratic constituencies -- including organized labor and some human rights advocates -- who oppose it.
The initial reaction signals that the coming political battles on China and trade will take place largely within the major political parties, rather than between them.
"The more heated debate will be within the Republican Party," said Gary Bauer, a Republican presidential candidate and vehement opponent of the trade deal. 
"There will be a Reagan wing making my argument, and the trade wing -- the Bush wing -- unfortunately siding with Clinton and Gore on this."
Mr. Bush said in a statement that he has consistently supported membership of China in the World Trading Organization, a position also advocated by his father, former President Bush.
"I welcome news of an agreement that will open China's markets to American products and help introduce American values into China," Governor Bush said. 
"The agreement should give American farmers, ranchers and businesses access to China's growing market, and help introduce American values along with American products. 
An agreement with China should also open the door for Taiwan's admission to the W.T.O., which is long overdue."
Mr. Bauer's view, which is largely shared by his fellow conservative candidates, Steve Forbes and Alan Keyes, is that China's record on trade, human rights, weapons proliferation and threats to Taiwan has worsened in recent years. 
He said the administration should have sought significant changes in the way Beijing does business before agreeing to sponsor its membership in the trade organization.
Mr. Forbes, a millionaire magazine publisher who is largely financing his own campaign, said last week in a speech on China policy that he strongly opposes allowing China to join the global trade group.
"Let me be clear," Mr. Forbes said in an address at the Nixon Library in Yorba Linda, Calif.: "Yes to Taiwan in the W.T.O. 
No to China. 
Beijing hasn't earned it, and we shouldn't give it. 
Period. It is time for our government to reward freedom and democracy -- not force and demagoguery -- and let us never forget it."
Mr. Bradley did not directly address the China trade agreement today. 
But an aide said that Mr. Bradley supports China's membership in the trade group as long as it has to meet the same legal and economic requirements as any other nation.
"Senator Bradley believes it is better to have China inside W.T.O. subject to universal rules rather than outside cutting unilateral deals," said Kristin Ludecke, a spokeswoman for him.
Mr. Gore supports the administration's position on trade with China, but he is also trying to finesse the issue because of the fervent opposition of the A.F.L.-C.I.O., which has endorsed his presidential bid.
John Sweeney, the A.F.L.-C.I.O. president, criticized the agreement as a "grave mistake" and accused the administration of being "disgustingly hypocritical" in claiming that trade deals help to moderate Chinese behavior.
A spokesman for Mr. Gore, Christopher Lehane, said in response to Mr. Sweeney's criticism, "Al Gore has made absolutely clear -- as he did at the A.F.L.-C.I.O. convention last month -- that all future trade agreements he would negotiate as president would include labor, environmental and human rights agreements as part, and they would be enforceable."
Patrick J. Buchanan, who is seeking the Reform Party's presidential nomination, has long opposed what he considers one-sided trade deals that hurt American workers.
"This is the latest administration capitulation to Beijing at the expense of working American families and for the benefit of transnational corporations," Mr. Buchanan said in a statement. 
"It is a cave-in, pure and simple, to a regime that even today persecutes religious minorities and aims nuclear rockets at the United States of America.

file: THE TRADE DEAL_ THE PROSPECTS_White House and Business Groups To Push Congress on China Pact.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Clinton administration and business groups prepared an intense campaign today to win approval in Congress for China's entry into the World Trade Organization, facing opposition from conservatives who object to almost any dealings with China and liberals who say the trade pact would be bad for workers.
Members of both parties said the deal would most likely be approved in the House, the more difficult of the two Congressional battlegrounds, based on the solid bipartisan majority that granted China a one-year extension of favorable trading terms earlier this year. 
The Senate tends to be more supportive of free trade measures than the House.
But neither the supporters nor the opponents were taking the outcome for granted, given the volatility of the relationship between the United States and China and the political sensitivity of trade issues heading into an election year.
"It's going to take an awful lot of work," said Representative David Dreier, a California Republican who is chairman of the House Rules Committee and a leading advocate of bringing China into the trade group.
Congress would not vote on the agreement itself, but on whether the United States should permanently grant China normal trading privileges, which is in effect a condition of the deal. 
Since 1974, Congress has had to vote annually on whether to retain a normal trading relationship with China, a process that critics of China have used to express their displeasure with Beijing.
Eager to win greater access to the huge market in China -- and stung by criticism that they had been ineffectual in rallying support for past trade votes -- business groups promised an all-out campaign to get the deal enacted.
"We were asked by the administration if we could deliver the votes," said L. Craig Johnstone, senior vice president for international economic and national security affairs at the United States Chamber of Commerce. 
"We said we could and we will."
Many industries -- commercial banking, auto and aircraft manufacturing, farming and food processing, investment banking, electronics, money management, filmmaking -- hailed the agreement today as an opportunity to expand rapidly into the giant Chinese market. 
Business groups had complained to the administration last spring when the president rejected an earlier deal with the Chinese. 
Mr. Clinton had walked away from the proposal fearing that he would have been unable to secure sufficient support in Congress.
Republican Congressional leaders have been generally supportive of a deal with China, but were cautious in their reaction today. 
Senator Trent Lott of Mississippi, the majority leader, said that there were still "significant questions" about the deal's effects on human rights, religious freedom and the economic relationship between the two countries, and that he was reserving judgment until he could study the agreement.
Even if, as expected, the Republican leadership ultimately joins the White House in pushing for the agreement, the proposal is still sure to set off a bitter debate uniting some of the most conservative Republicans and the most liberal Democrats against centrists in both parties.
Citing what they said were human rights abuses, the spread of nuclear and conventional arms, a lack of concern for environmental issues and the prospect that increased trade would result in some American workers' losing their jobs, a spectrum of groups said they would try to block or modify the agreement.
John Sweeney, the president of the A.F.L.-C.I.O., called the deal "a grave mistake," and said it was "disgustingly hypocritical" of the administration to claim to be keeping the interests of working people in mind even as it negotiated with a regime that routinely violates human rights.
Opposition to the deal by human rights advocates could also give an opportunity to conservative Republican candidates like Steve Forbes and Gary Bauer to win support from the right wing of their party, whose leading candidate, Gov. George W. Bush of Texas, supports the deal.
Representative Dana Rohrabacher, a Republican from California, said the agreement was a "raw deal" for workers and consumers because it would institutionalize tariff advantages held by China.
"On top of that, we'd be putting our stamp of approval on having a gangster regime coming into yet another international body and thinking that in some way that body is going to civilize the regime," he said, "when in fact it's more likely that the organization itself will be corrupted by having the world's worst human rights violator in its midst."
Administration officials said they would press hard to get the deal approved, probably in the first few months of next year.
Samuel R. Berger, the national security adviser, told reporters in Turkey, where President Clinton was traveling today: "I believe that when Congress has an opportunity to study the terms of this, recognize the tremendous benefits to American industry and American workers around the country, and the protections that we obtain for import-sensitive industries in this agreement, that there will be broad support for it."
The administration won support today from Human Rights Watch, an advocacy group that said China's entry into the trade organization "could increase pressure for greater openness, more press freedom, enhanced rights for workers and an independent judiciary."
But the White House is primarily counting on business groups. 
Administration officials have consulted with business lobbyists to gauge support for a deal in Congress and to plan strategy for winning approval.
The Business Roundtable, which represents the country's largest corporations, has readied a plan to tout the benefits of the deal in 71 key Congressional districts. 
In Iowa, for instance, the group has hired a political organizer, Bill Menner, to get businesses and interest groups working on behalf of the agreement.
Mr. Menner said he planned to turn to groups like the Iowa Farm Bureau Federation and other employers in the state, like Diamond V Mills, a soybean processor in Cedar Rapids, and the headquarters of Roto-Rooter in West Des Moines, to make a public case for the deal and call their members of Congress.
The Business Roundtable also plans to run newspaper advertising in Iowa emphasizing the economic benefits the deal would bring to farmers and other groups.
"We hope that when push comes to shove," Mr. Menner said, "the case we can make about the benefits of trade with China will carry the day."Â Â Â Â Â Â

file: THE U.N. AT 50_ CLINTON AND JIANG_CHINA_S PRESIDENT AND CLINTON MEET TO REPAIR FENCES.txt
text:
ï»¿
Meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations anniversary celebration, President Clinton and President Jiang Zemin of China made their best effort yesterday to repair a relationship that has been seriously strained by disagreements over Taiwan and human rights.
No concrete agreements emerged from the two-hour session at Lincoln Center, and there was no public display of unity comparable to Mr. Clinton's joint appearance on Monday with President Boris N. Yeltsin of Russia at Franklin D. Roosevelt's Hudson Valley estate.
But White House officials expressed confidence that the momentum developed at the intense session yesterday would allow the two nations to move forward with further discussions in a range of areas of concern, from arms control to trade relations.
Michael D. McCurry, the White House Press Secretary, said Mr. Clinton described his encounter with Mr. Jiang as a "very good, very positive meeting and the best of three meetings he has held to date" with the Chinese leader.
"He's confident that we have begun a process that will lead to a series of dialogues that will help improve the opportunity for comprehensive engagement with China," Mr. McCurry said.
Chen Jian, the spokesman for President Jiang's delegation, told reporters at a separate briefing that the meeting had been "candid, friendly, positive and useful."
"It will be useful for the improvement and growth of the bilateral relationship," Mr. Chen said.
Clinton Administration officials said the two leaders covered a range of issues including Taiwan, human rights, China's desire to join the World Trade Organization and nonproliferation of nuclear weapons. 
The officials said Mr. Clinton emphasized that while the two major powers were bound to have their differences, they can manage them better through honest dialogue.
"Neither side would claim that there aren't serious differences remaining," Assistant Secretary of State Winston Lord said after the meeting. 
"There are serious differences."
But he said the relationship had "resumed momentum."
The Administration had hoped to capitalize on Russia's agreement on Monday to halt all nuclear testing in 1996 as a way to persuade China to do the same. 
But the Administration received only a promise to pursue the issue further. 
Though China has agreed to pursue a comprehensive test ban in 1996, it is the last of the five major nuclear powers not to sign on to the idea of zero testing.
Mr. Clinton raised the issue of human rights with China, bringing up specific cases as well as the issue of Tibet, which has been under Chinese control since 1950. 
But at a briefing after the meeting, Mr. Lord refused to identify the specific human rights victims discussed. 
That was in marked contrast to Mr. Clinton's meeting with Mr. Jiang in Seattle in 1993 where the public announcement of names helped get dissidents freed.
Mr. Clinton deflected questions about human rights issues and Taiwan from reporters who quizzed him and Mr. Jiang at a picture-taking session before their meeting.
"The important thing is that we're going to have this meeting," he said. 
"These are two great countries that have a real interest in maintaining a constructive dialogue with each other and wherever possible a partnership, and we need to go to work on it.'
Mr. Chen sidestepped a question about whether President Clinton had raised individual human rights cases with President Jiang.
"It is true that both countries have different views" on human rights, Mr. Chen said. 
"We can have dialogue on it instead of confrontation."
As expected, the Chinese brought up the issue of Taiwan, and Mr. Chen described it as "the most major and sensitive issue affecting the relationship."
But American officials said they were gratified that it did not dominate the agenda as it did in the aftermath of the United States' decision to allow the Taiwanese President, Lee Teng-hui, to make a private visit to the United States this spring.
Despite the Administration's insistence that the visit did not constitute a break with Washington's longstanding "one China" policy, Beijing recalled its Ambassador in protest.
Mr. Clinton's aides said that at the meeting today the President reaffirmed that the United States recognized only one China, but that the United States would not promise to ban any visits by Taiwan officials. 
He said such visits would remain "unofficial, private and rare."
Ever since Mr. Clinton took office the relationship with Beijing has been one of the most difficult to keep on track. 
With the end of the cold war and the breakup of the Soviet Union, China and the United States no longer have the same pragmatic need to use each other as counterweights against the former adversary. 
China's leaders have been unsettled by a struggle over who will be the successor to the 91-year-old Deng Xiaoping. 
And the personal relationship between Mr. Clinton and Mr. Jiang has been cool, Administration officials acknowledge.
The United States has also been concerned about China's arrest and trial of Harry Wu, an American human rights advocate who was jailed in China and convicted of stealing state secrets.
Since then both countries have moved back from the brink. 
Beijing released Mr. Wu; Hillary Rodham Clinton visited Beijing for a United Nations women's conference, and China announced in late September that it would suspend a contract to sell two nuclear power reactors to Iran.
Still, a successful meeting between Mr. Clinton and Mr. Jiang yesterday was not assured.
At the last moment, the Chinese demanded that the meeting site be changed because the planned venue, the New York Public Library, was featuring an exhibit that included a handbill from the 1989 student democracy movement, which was crushed in Beijing's Tiananmen Square. 
The exhibit also contains footage of the Chinese military suppression of the demonstrations, in which hundreds were killed.
And just hours before the two world leaders sat down together, Mr. Jiang used his speech at the United Nations celebrations to charge that "certain big powers, often under the cover of freedom, democracy and human rights, set out to encroach upon the sovereignty of other countries, interfere in their internal affairs and undermine their national unity and ethnic harmony."
Mr. Jiang also repeated Beijing's longstanding position that Taiwan remains an "inalienable part of China's territory."
Nonetheless, both the American and Chinese officials were eager yesterday to bring relations back to the point where the two nations could have normal diplomatic exchanges.
Other issues that came up yesterday included joint law enforcement efforts, narcotics enforcement and trade relations. 
China's admission to the World Trade Organization is one of Beijing's major diplomatic objectives. 
And Mr. Lord said the President stressed that China needed to make more progress in the area of intellectual rights protection as a step toward its goal.
Mr. Chen said that the two leaders would meet again at the summit conference of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation Group in Osaka, Japan, next month. 
"The Osaka meeting will build on this meeting and move the process forward," he said.

file: The Usual Spats Over Nominees For Foreign Films.txt
text:
ï»¿
THIS YEAR SEEMS typical when it comes to the Oscar race for best foreign-language film. 
That is to say, complaints and conspiracy theories are rampant. 
And, as usual, they center on why certain films were not nominated by their respective counpries and how difficult it is to change the eligibility rules. 
The five selected films will be announced on Tuesday, along with other Oscar nominations.
Some of the most talked-about foreign-language films released here last year will not be among the nominees because they were not offered up by their home countries. 
These include several that were critically praised: "Shanghai Triad," from China; "The Postman" ("Il Postino") and "Lamerica," from Italy, and "Wild Reeds" and "Les Miserables," from France. 
"Les Miserables" won the Golden Globe award three weeks ago.
Even eligible films have encountered significant problems. 
The Iranian film "The White Balloon," the story of a young girl's quest to buy a goldfish, narrowly escaped being withdrawn. 
Teheran tried to pull it back, saying Washington planned a covert operation against the Iranian Government. 
The Academy of Motion Pictures Arts and Sciences refused on the grounds that the foreign-language film committee members had already begun screening "The White Balloon."
Another political squabble has swirled around "Underground," a film from Yugoslavia about two small-time gangsters who join the Communist Party at the beginning of World War II. 
Since "Underground" won the prize for best film at the Cannes International Film Festival last year, it has been the subject of a heated debate in France centering on the politics and loyalties of its director, Emir Kusturica.
"Underground" has also become the subject of a legal debate. 
Days before it was scheduled to be shown to the Academy's committee, the film's distributor, Ciby 2000, asked that the screening be postponed on the grounds that the film contained potentially libelous material about an individual who believed he was being parodied. 
The problem was resolved when a shorter, 25-minute version of the film, also released in Yugoslavia, was submitted.
Despite its problems, "The White Balloon" is still considered a contender for a nomination, according to some members of the Academy's committee. 
Other films that have been mentioned are "Antonia's Line," from the Netherlands; Bo Widerberg's "All Things Fair," from Sweden; Pedro Almodovar's "Flower of My Secret," from Spain; Giuseppe Tornatore's "Star Maker," from Italy, and two dark-horse candidates, an Algerian film called "Dust of Life" and "Wild Horses" from Argentina.
This year, only about 400 of the Academy's more than 5,000 voting members volunteered to judge the 41 eligible foreign-language films. 
(Only countries belonging to the United Nations may submit a film, and only one film per country may be entered.) The films were divided into two groups, which were each shown to half of the members. 
To vote, members must see roughly 16 of the films in their assigned group. 
According to Bruce Davis, executive director of the Academy, about 325 members were qualified to vote this year.
Because of the investment of time required to see 16 films, the committee is composed mostly of retired Academy members. 
The director Paul Bartel, the producer Mark Johnson and the cinematographer John Bailey are among the few working film makers who participate.
As in past years, there has been considerable carping about the films being offered by selection committees in foreign countries. 
Chinese politics may have played a role in the exclusion of "Shanghai Triad," Zhang Yimou's drama set in the 1930's. 
It was passed over by the Chinese selection committee in favor of "Red Cherry," directed by Ye Ying.
"Red Cherry" is about two children who are sent to the Soviet Union to be educated. 
Though "Red Cherry" was the most popular film last year in China, many observers believe that politics was involved in the Chinese Government's nomination of Mr. Ye's film instead of Mr. Zhang's.
Mr. Ye's father was sent to the Soviet Union to be educated; there, he was a classmate of Li Peng, the Chinese Prime Minister. 
Mr. Ye's grandfather was General Ye Ting, a member of Mao's army; the general is regarded as a Communist martyr.
It should also be remembered that last year the Chinese Government forbade Mr. Zhang to attend the New York Film Festival for the opening night of "Shanghai Triad."
In 1994, he was not allowed to go to the Cannes film festival when his film "To Live" was shown there. 
And in 1990, the Chinese Government tried but failed to withdraw his film "Ju Dou" from being considered for an Oscar nomination.
"It's really obvious that the Chinese Government wants to keep Zhang Yimou down," said Michael Barker, co-president of Sony Pictures Classics, the company that is distributing "Shanghai Triad."
Critics of the current system have suggested that all foreign films released theatrically in the United States during the past year be eligible for a nomination. 
If this were the case, "Shanghai Triad" and "The Postman" would have been eligible this year. 
The films "Wild Reeds" and "Les Miserables," which were passed over by France in favor of "French Twist," also would have qualified.
But the current rule of one film per country is apparently not going to change. 
"We would rather keep the category eccentric and manageable," said Mr. Davis. "We can make this category go away if it becomes too difficult to administer or if we are making more people angry than happy."
Bruce Feldman, a committee member who used to be a marketing executive at Universal, adds, "If any Academy members have a problem with the selection committee, they should serve on it."
As an added inducement, this year's screenings, which ended last Sunday, were accompanied by fudge, crudites and the occasional steamed dumpling instead of the packaged cookies of years past.

file: The View From_White Plains_Recalling Yangtze River In Song for the New Year.txt
text:
ï»¿
THERE was a moment that was so moving it actually sent shivers into the scalp at the Chinese New Year celebration last weekend at the County Center here. 
Ke-Zaheng Wen, a 70-year-old internationally known bass-baritone originally from China, was singing "Ol' Man River."
The power of his voice was wonderful, but most stunning were his inflections and phrasing, the way he sang the words, in Chinese-accented English, as if they had been written for him:
"I get weary and sick of trying, I'm tired of living and scared of dying, but Ol' Man River, he just keeps rolling along."
This quintessentially American song, he said after the performance, moves him from the heart. 
Although in Jerome Kern's "Show Boat," it is sung by a poor 19th-century black man, Mr. Wen said he found in it something pertinent to his life. 
"In China, when the Cultural Revolution came, it was not the workers who were oppressed and persecuted, it was the artists and intellectuals," he said through an interpreter. 
"For many of us, it was a nightmare."
The river, he added, could have been the Yangtze as well as the Mississippi; the fatalistic sorrow, his own at the time of China's upheaval. 
In English, he said, "This song, I have very much deep feeling for."
In similar but less dramatic ways, the blend of Chinese and American and Eastern and Western cultures was evident throughout the evening. 
Sponsored by the local branch of the National Organization of Chinese Americans, which focuses on immigration and other legal issues, and the Westchester Chinese Association, a nonprofit cultural group, it was a festivity heralding the arrival of the Year of the Rabbit. 
Virtually everyone there had been born either in China or Taiwan or had parents who had been. 
There were plenty of traditional Chinese dances and songs; almost all of the 600 people attending wore at least some red, the traditional color of good luck.
But there were many American influences as well. 
Teen-agers who on stage wore silk robes and pajamas of fuchsia and lime appeared afterward in blue jeans and leather jackets. 
Not everyone munched red bean cakes or dumplings, the traditional New Year's foods, but pizza and fries from the concession stand. 
And the night ended with adults and children doing the macarena to music played by a disk jockey.
"It's really good to feel both Chinese and American," said Petula Shyu, a 16-year-old student at Scarsdale High School and, on Saturdays, at the Chinese School of Southern Westchester in Edgemont, where she learns Mandarin Chinese. 
"I was born here. 
I am an American, but I'm also Chinese. 
With my family, a big part of that is respecting your ancestors. 
On the actual New Year -- this year, it was Tuesday, Feb. 
16 -- we go to see my maternal grandmother in Brooklyn. 
She is 88. 
Then we go visit other relatives and friends, in the traditional way."
Smiling and nodding approval were Betty Hsieh, who works at International Business Machines, and her husband, Wen Hsieh, who owns a consulting company. 
The Hsiehs, who live in Scarsdale, have children in college and high school. 
"I grew up in Taiwan," Mr. Hsieh said. 
"Chinese culture stresses family values, a lot of respect for the family. 
This is good. 
In America, everything is so individualistic. 
But that too is good. 
Nowhere else is society so open, so full of opportunity. 
The best thing is to combine the best of both worlds."
Petula was among the teen-agers who performed on the stage of the little theater. 
She and Vivian Yee, also a 16-year-old from Scarsdale, were part of a folk dance called "Embroidered Purse."
As the girls executed graceful movements, Rose Kaung, a mathematics professor at Westchester Community College, whispered to an audience member, "This is the story of a young woman whose love is far away, who embroiders a silk purse for him."
Suddenly a tiny brocade pouch struck someone lightly on the shoulder. 
"Oh! that is good luck," Mrs. Kaung said. 
"The dancers throw those into the audience and whoever gets one is supposed to prosper in the new year."
Folk music is also performed by Hsing Lih Chou. 
Mr. Chou, an entertainer clad in black slacks and a collarless jacket -- "the students' 'uniform' in China," he said -- played guitar and sang Taiwanese songs. 
Born 48 years ago in Taiwan and now living in Manhattan, he teaches Asian-American studies in Manhattan and is principal of the Chinese School of Southern Westchester. 
Like its counterparts, the Chinese School of Northern Westchester in Somers and the Huaxia Chinese School in Hartsdale, it holds classes on weekends for elementary, middle and high school-age youngsters in Chinese language and culture.
"I like to put emotion into what I do," Mr. Chou said, after his spirited performance. 
"One of these folk songs sounds like something by American Indians, don't you think?
The same kind of sad, wailing, chanting sound. 
In school when I teach, I try to make the students feel things. 
You cannot just tell them things, you need to relate them to what they know. 
I don't focus on, say, the word for lo mein; instead, I will teach them how to say spaghetti in Chinese.
"When I first came to America, Oct. 
29. 1976, I experienced culture shock. 
I flew into J.F.K. 
A friend picks me up and we go through Queens and across the Queensboro Bridge. 
I see a subway car. 
I see all this ugly, dirty graffiti. 
I said to my friend, what is this, the train that goes to the garbage dump?
He said, get used to it. 
That's the train you'll be traveling on every day. 
Not only did I get used to it, now I love it."
For some, the transition was not so easy. 
Generally, people of Chinese descent living in Taiwan who came to America did so completely voluntarily, for a chance at a better career or education. 
For some from the mainland, however, the situation was more complicated. 
Mingjian Gao, a 40-year-old United Nations translator now living in Scarsdale, left Beijing when he was 28. 
His mother, who was visiting Scarsdale for the New Year, still lives there.
"She likes to stay among her friends and what is familiar," he said. 
No permission was needed for Mr. Gao to leave -- "By then everything was reformed," he said -- but he does have memories of the Red Guard ransacking his house when he was a child. 
"My father was a math teacher," he said simply as an explanation. 
"It only happened once."
Like so many others, his life is now a mix of Chinese and American customs. 
For the New Year, he ate dumplings, considered in northern China to be a lucky New Year food. 
He did not, however, get to see the glowing displays of fireworks as he once did in China. 
"That we could not provide," Brenda Sun, a real estate broker from Scarsdale who is one of the festival's organizers, said with a laugh. 
Mr. Gao added: "Even in New York City, this year, they could not have fireworks in Chinatown. 
People missed them. 
I understand they used fake ones, little paper explosions, which was all the Mayor would allow. 
That's too bad. 
It was part of a Happy New Year celebration."
