Q: Do you think of yourself as a political dissident?
I don't want to get involved in politics. 
I don't care for it. 
Governments focus only on the problem at hand, instead of looking at what has caused this problem in the first place. 
If ordinary people's society does not become more virtuous, any number of problems may occur, and I cannot concern myself with this prospect. 
I am only responsible to the practitioners of Falun Gong.
But you've recently been described as one of the most influential people in Asia. 
Does this new high profile help you?
I think it has done quite a bit of damage to me, personally. 
Were cultivators of Falun Gong to know that I was ranked among the influential people of the world, they would most likely laugh at me. 
As cultivators, we do not seek fame and profit. 
My masters are all practicing in the mountains. 
If they don't want to be seen, even I couldn't find them. 
I "came out" only because they said that I should. 
Otherwise I would not.
For the past three years you've been in America. 
During that time, what differences did you find between Chinese and American culture?
The difference is quite enormous. 
Chinese people's mentality is deeply influenced by their ancient cultural heritage. 
But Americans are unfettered by ancient culture. 
In terms of human characteristics, because Chinese people are so rational, they will consider the substance of what they do. 
A Westerner will make sure that it is done well on the surface. 
For instance, everyone knows Chinese food is quite delicious. 
But when it comes to surface qualities, it is not very particular. 
Chinese restaurants are often very casual, and all you really need is a pair of chopsticks. 
But Western cuisine, while it doesn't necessarily taste any better, pays much closer attention to exactly which fork is to be used when eating a certain food. 
Chinese people are concerned with the inner quality of culture, whereas Westerners are concerned with the surface qualities of culture.
Those can be loaded terms. 
Do you disapprove of American culture?
Personally, I have no opposition to it. 
I need to have a quiet and calm place to concentrate on the practice. 
So I don't watch TV and movies often. 
But I know they have created irreversible pollution to the world. 
And human beings can never reverse the pollution and get back to its purest state, no matter how hard we try.
You were supposedly living underground until very recently. 
With all the Chinese immigrants in your neighborhood, didn't anyone recognize you?
If they do not look carefully they will not recognize me. 
I seldom communicate with others because of the language barrier, and because of my personal practice, I seldom walk down the street. 
Sometimes on weekends, we go to the mall. 
You know, sometimes I help my wife do the grocery shopping. 
I love that I can get Chinese sauces in New York.
Are you settling into life in New York?
Or will you return to China?
My wife and I have registered our own small company. 
We are preparing to publish my books. 
But I've been thinking, if the Chinese Government would not treat their people as they do now, and if they were willing to solve the issues through dialogue, I think that would be good for the Chinese Government and people as well. 
If they want me back, I would go back. 
But the Government is nervous and they don't want me back. 
I don't want to be any trouble to them. 
I can live wherever I am.
Unlike in China, however -- where you are said to have millions of followers -- here in America very few people understand your movement.
Is Falun Gong a religion?
Does it require faith?
It is a practice that can remove illnesses, keep people fit and make one live longer. 
Like tai chi, it's a morning exercise. 
People practicing Falun Gong are expected to follow the principles of truthfulness, compassion and forbearance. 
And they must speak truthfully, have compassion, be benevolent, be tolerant. 
But whether people have other faiths or not, they can all practice Falun Gong. 
We do not get involved in faiths. 
We respect all of them.
Falun Gong has been described as a cult. 
Is that description fair?
A cult advocates end-of-the-world theories and leads people to do many bad things. 
I am only teaching people the practice for healing and fitness. 
Not only that, I am teaching people to have good moral characters. 
I think this is good and meaningful to society. 
The Chinese Government accused me of advocating a doomsday and of saying I can delay the end of the world by 30 years. 
That's really ridiculous. 
And very often people assume that in order to study the Great Way of Falun they would have to live like a monk and give up everything. 
Actually, all practitioners are members of society; they do ordinary things just like anyone else.
Perhaps more specifically, cults don't tolerate dissent. 
Do practitioners of Falun Gong have differing opinions?
Or do they tend to be of one mind on most things?
Normally people who do not like the principles of truthfulness, compassion and tolerance would not be very likely to study Falun Gong. 
Only the people who like these principles would come to learn. 
But people come and go as they please, you know; it's voluntary.Â Â Â Jonathan S. Landreth and J. S. Greenberg - Translated from the Chinese.

text:

He sniffs the cigarettes first, draws them lengthwise under his nose and then lights them one after the other, the smoke curling in the soft bronze light that flows through his west window. 
"River light," the novelist John Cheever called that luminescence peculiar to New York City mornings. 
It does seem to rise off the Hudson before it enters the room where Wei Jingsheng sits and talks about the regime that imprisoned him for all but a few months of the last 18 years, before releasing him into exile in November.
"The Chinese Communist Party is indeed the evil empire," he says, echoing President Reagan. 
"If the Soviet Union was the evil empire, then the Chinese Communist regime is an even greater one -- or at least a slyer one."
That's a reference to the recent scandals involving the satellite industry and campaign contributions by Chinese nationals to the Democratic Party. 
"The Chinese Government is continuously trying to spread its influence and build its strength," he says. 
"The Chinese Communists have always used these methods. 
Perhaps only now with this evidence will more Americans pay more attention to it, and to their schemes. 
It should serve as a very clear warning."
Under the circumstances, Wei says, President Clinton clearly should have canceled the trip he is scheduled to embark on this week. 
"I believe Clinton, under these conditions, should not go. 
Clinton has not said what he plans to say or do, so I feel that he won't stray from the path of the wishes of the Chinese Communists. 
If he doesn't say clearly what he will do, then I believe it is a mistake to go under these conditions.
"If he does finally appear at Tiananmen Square -- although I think that would be a major political mistake -- then he should state clearly his support for the struggle, his sympathy for those who were killed and injured and his commitment to pressing for the release of the democracy activists still in prison. 
If he doesn't do these things, then his appearance may damage his standing in the eyes of every single Chinese. 
He should not adhere to the conditions attached by the Communists."
The President's trip is a kind of benchmark for Wei, who, with Wang Dan, a leading figure in the 1989 Tiananmen Square uprising, shares billing as China's most famous dissident. 
Clinton's presence in China, surrounded by his beaming hosts, provides a platform that has been largely missing in Wei's seven months of exile. 
The attention could help him press his campaign against Clinton's policy of "engagement" and cement his position as the primary spokesman for the dissidents. 
But it could just as easily backfire, if his ideas are brushed aside or, as Beijing so fervently hopes, dismissed as irrelevant.
Certainly, Wei is not silent; his recorded message to a crowd of thousands in Hong Kong in early June -- commemorating the ninth anniversary of the Tiananmen Square massacre -- made headlines around the world. 
But the questions linger: How many are listening?
Whom does he speak for?
And not just in the West, but in China as well. 
More immediately, did Wei make the right decision when he relented and accepted Beijing's offer of exile?
To most people, there would have been no choice whatsoever: whether to remain in prison or to accept an offer of medical parole and exile. 
But Wei is not like most people.
If he were, he never would have been imprisoned in the first place, for the crime of speaking his mind. 
He never would have endured, merely for refusing to recant his belief in democracy, solitary confinement in a cell where a bright light burned 24 hours a day, frequent beatings from other inmates and conditions so abysmal that he lost a dozen teeth and contracted high blood pressure, heart disease, arthritis and hepatitis during his two separate incarcerations.
In 1995, at the beginning of his second prison term, he was made an offer that few thought he could refuse: he would be freed if he accepted exile in the United States. 
He had become an international cause celebre, and the regime of President Jiang Zemin wanted to be rid of him. 
He had written, besides his incendiary public essays, impertinent (and often humorous) letters to Deng Xiaoping, China's late paramount leader, and was now making Jiang his new pen pal.
Execution was one option, but Wei was too famous to be dealt with so crudely. 
China wanted trade with the West, and international respectability. 
Clearly, the only thing to do with Wei was to export him. 
But he declined the offer, not once but twice.
"Wei didn't want to leave China because by being there, he would be a player," explains Philip Cunningham, a journalist and China scholar who edited a collection of Wei's prison letters to Deng and Jiang. 
"He wanted to be there even in jail rather than free in exile because the danger of exile is that you become irrelevant."
But last fall, Wei finally accepted banishment. 
On Nov. 
16, 1997, he was released from prison, taken to a Northwest Airlines plane in Beijing and flown to the United States.
What made him change his stand?
We are in the small but comfortable apartment he occupies at Columbia University, where he is a visiting scholar. 
He is a stocky man of about 5 feet 8 or 9 inches, 48 years old, with a full head of black hair. 
There is no hint of gray. 
His youthful, robust appearance is miraculous, considering what he has been through.
"Two reasons," he answers through an interpreter. 
"My health was quickly deteriorating. 
So I had two choices. 
One was to leave the country, the other to die in prison. 
I felt there was no reason for me to die in prison for no worthy cause."
Wei slips another Marlboro out of the pack and lights up. 
"The second, which is more important, is that in recent years, the position of the Western countries toward the Chinese Communist Party has been softening, which has dealt a blow to the confidence of the Chinese people. 
It is important for me to come out and tell Western Governments the real situation, the realities in China and what effective roles they can play, and also to convey what the Chinese people would really like to say to the people of the Western countries."
That ought to be enough to keep 10 men busy. 
But after some thought, Wei gives me a third reason: he hopes to coordinate the activities of pro-democracy dissidents abroad. 
In effect, he would become the leader of the dissident movement, which could be far more difficult than persuading Western Governments to amend their China policies. 
The 500 or so active dissidents in this country are hopelessly fragmented by petty squabbles, jealousies and differences in opinion about how best to deal with Beijing.
It's a difficult agenda for a man who has little support other than his name and the enormous respect and good will it commands. 
Columbia provides Wei with an office and clerical assistance, but he does not teach or lecture on a regular basis. 
Rising at 9 A.M., he usually works late into the night, conferring with other dissidents.
Wei is determined not to retire to the scholar's cloister, as many other exiled dissidents have done. 
And yet, looking at him, dressed in slippers, a beige cotton shirt and gray trousers held up by black suspenders, his legs folded on a threadbare couch as he sips tea and smokes and smokes, it is hard to picture him maneuvering in the corridors of power.
He has tried, but to little effect. 
This winter, he traveled to London, Paris and Brussels, where he lobbied the European Union to ratify a United Nations resolution condemning China's human rights record. 
In the spring, after the 15-nation European Union voted not even to introduce the resolution, much less to pass it, Wei embarked on a 12-nation, seven-week tour of European capitals, calling on foreign secretaries and members of parliament to explain their decision.
He fared no better with the Clinton Administration, which in a reversal of longstanding policy, also withdrew support for the resolution this year. 
And now, in a further disappointment, President Clinton is off to China.
To Wei, there is no compromise with Beijing, no engagement and no partnership. 
"Clinton has an opportunity. 
I want him to make his support for human rights and democracy clear. 
If he does not do this, then he will not help the movement and he will not help the standing of himself and the United States in the eyes of the Chinese people. 
I think that Clinton's use of the word 'partnership' is completely wrong, since the Chinese Communists use the word 'enemy' in describing the United States. 
I don't think the American people want a partner like the Chinese Communists."
When Wei speaks, his baritone barely changes inflection and, whatever may be going on inside him, he gives an outward impression of serenity. 
Yet the position he has staked out for himself is nearly impossible. 
Here is a man without a political party or power of any kind beyond the moral authority vouchsafed by his sufferings, appointing himself roving ambassador for one-fifth of the world's population, trying to shape American foreign policy. 
I wonder if I'm in the presence of a Chinese Don Quixote, or a man who could become to China what Vaclav Havel is to the Czech Republic or Nelson Mandela is to South Africa.
There is a certain purity about Wei, but it's hard to tell sometimes if it is the purity of an egomaniac or a saint. 
Others have commented on Wei's saintly qualities: his lack of bitterness, his heroic readiness to sacrifice himself on the altar of principle, his unflagging composure. 
But in time, I realize that Wei is neither saint nor egomaniac. 
He is a man of integrity -- integrity in its fundamental meaning: he is united within himself. 
God knows, he had plenty of time, in the isolation of his cell, to think things through. 
He has emerged as a man with a seamless confidence in himself and in the truth of his ideas.
Wei has hundreds, if not thousands, of admirers and supporters in the West. 
Among many Chinese dissidents, he is an icon. 
Even those who disagree with his views on China are in awe of his courage and his ability to write and argue in clear, direct, forceful language.
But will that be enough?
Now that Wei is out of prison and no longer a myth, there are dissidents as well as Western diplomats and scholars who think that his ideas are outdated and that Wei himself, though unquestionably a hero, is a hero from a bygone era. 
They question whether he is the right candidate to lead the dissident movement and to convey realities in China to Western leaders. 
They say that Wei, having been isolated for so long, clings to views and rhetoric frozen in the amber of the cold war.
"The more Wei speaks out, the more he reveals that he doesn't know the current situation," says Merle Goldman, a professor of Chinese history at Boston University and an expert on the dissident movement. 
"Through no fault of his own -- he was in prison for all but a few months of the last 18 years -- he has no clear idea what is going on in China or abroad."
The China of the 1990's is not the China of the 1970's under Mao, she notes. 
A rudimentary democracy has taken hold at the village level, where elections have been held this year. 
Although open dissent is still prohibited, citizens privately criticize the Government in ways that would have been unthinkable 25 years ago. 
It is a much more prosperous and at least somewhat freer country. 
When I mention to her that Wei has said that "millions of workers and peasants in China are truly starving," she exclaims, "That's not true!" and adds that Wei's penchant for injudicious comments like that could undermine his credibility.
Wei's defenders say it's too early to judge him, after only a little more than seven months in exile. 
"We're honoring him for his courage, not necessarily because he's an astute politician," says Robert Bernstein, the founding chairman of Human Rights Watch. 
"We don't know about that yet. 
Wei has sacrificed for his ideas and deserves a chance. 
Besides, it never hurts to put pressure on the regime."
Chen Xiaoping, a 36-year-old former journalist and law professor now studying at Harvard, was forced to leave China because of his pro-democracy activities. 
He says the youngest dissidents -- of whom Wang Dan is the most prominent -- almost literally don't understand the language that Wei speaks. 
When Wei gave a talk at Harvard, Chen says, "Some students asked him: 'Where are you coming from?
This is traditional, not modern discourse.'
He was talking like somebody from the Cultural Revolution.
"Wei is too old," Chen adds flatly. 
"In jail for 18 years, and because he was in prison for such a long time, he cannot understand the modern China."
The obvious implication is that the 29-year-old Wang, who was serving an 11-year sentence when released to American doctors this spring, understands China better -- the China, that is, of young entrepreneurs bearing cell phones instead of Mao's little red book. 
Wang's opinion on Clinton's visit does seem to be more nuanced than Wei's. 
"I feel extremely uncomfortable when I think about President Clinton walking on Tiananmen Square," Wang says. 
"But I understand that United States policy toward China should represent the interests of the American people. 
I just hope it also represents the moral standards of the American people."
Aware of the force his words carry in the dissident community, Wang, who is spending the summer at Harvard, adds diplomatically: "Both Mr. Wei Jingsheng and I believe that to promote a peaceful transformation toward democracy in China, international influence is crucial."
Almost no one disagrees with Wei's objectives: building a China where people aren't arrested without charges and tortured in prison, where workers trying to organize independent labor unions aren't crushed and freedom of speech and expression are not repressed.
Besides, as Bernstein points out, it's not as though the younger dissidents are accomplishing any more than Wei. 
"They aren't getting results, either," he says. 
"Of course there's more economic freedom. 
Of course the party is giving ground politically -- it has no choice."
The difference between Wei and his loyal critics is in figuring out how to get there from here. 
For Wei, the correct approach -- the only approach -- is to get tough. 
But this does not mean the complete suspension of relations, says Xiao Qiang of the organization Human Rights in China. 
"We don't want to fall into the trap of isolation versus engagement," he says. 
"We want a strong and effective human rights policy, on an equal footing with trade and security policy."
Wei puts it more succinctly. 
Dealing with China, he says, is like dealing with a "scoundrel on the street": the nicer you are, the more likely you are to get mugged.
Wei's history is a history of fighting dragons. 
He was born in 1950 in Beijing, where his father was a high-level official in the foreign ministry while his mother was a party cadre in a shoe-and-hat factory. 
A self-described "fanatical Maoist" as a teen-ager, he graduated in 1966 from a top high school reserved for party higher-ups and went into the countryside as a Red Guard during the tumultuous Cultural Revolution. 
But the stunning poverty he saw, and the unspeakable horrors wrought by Mao's policies -- like a village so ravaged by starvation that people sold their dying infants as food -- led him to condemn the Great Helmsman.
Wei gained international fame with the publication of his classic essay, "The Fifth Modernization: Democracy."
Posted on the Democracy Wall in Beijing on Dec. 
5, 1978, the essay exploded the myth that Deng Xiaoping's "four modernizations" -- radical economic reforms that excluded any political change -- would improve the lot of the masses. 
Wei argued that without true democracy all promises of a better life for China would remain just that.
Later, in another essay, "Do We Want Democracy or New Autocracy," he dared to attack Deng by name. 
Within a week, he was arrested, and then was sentenced to the first of his prison terms. 
Though he'd been held incommunicado, he remained defiant at his trial. 
Refusing to repudiate his criticisms, he proved himself to be not the passive victim of an authoritarian state but an agent of history, the author of his own tragic destiny.
Orville Schell, a China scholar at Berkeley and a strong Wei supporter, portrays him as both militant and ascetic, a kind of warrior monk who "stripped himself bare" of material possessions and emotional attachments so he could wage his lonely battle with despots unencumbered.
My own impression is of a solitary existential rebel straight out of the pages of Camus. 
Martyr, warrior-monk, existential rebel, I can hear all three incarnations speaking to me in the Manhattan apartment as he tells me that Clinton should demand greater democratization from Jiang's Government as a quid pro quo for a greater share of the American market.
So far, he says, the only beneficiaries of United States-China trade have been a few large corporations -- and Jiang's regime. 
The profits reaped by companies like Boeing and Motorola, as well as from European enterprises in China, have strengthened Beijing's hand and emboldened it to stifle all political opposition. 
"It's these corporations coming to China and cooperating closely with the Chinese Communist Party that has created a very bad image among the Chinese people of the U.S., of the American people, who they think care only about money and don't care about democracy and human rights."
Proponents of engagement contend that modernization is creating a middle and professional class that could eventually form the nucleus of a political opposition, and that a take-no-prisoners policy would isolate China and prove counterproductive. 
The examples of North Korea, Iraq, Libya and Cuba suggest that isolation, embargo, military action and other hardball tactics tend to perpetuate dictatorships rather than eliminate them.
But Wei finds his critics' arguments lacking in substance. 
Rather than re-examine his thinking, they should "re-examine their thinking," he says. 
"I don't believe my thinking at any point over the past 20 years has once been outdated. 
But I ask, What evidence is there to support their new thinking?
Is the new thinking to cozy up to the Chinese Communist Government and turn away from their behavior?
Where has that gotten us?"
Each year, gathering around a polished oval table in the Art Nouveau meeting room of the Norwegian Nobel Institute in Oslo, five members of the Nobel committee decide who will be the recipient of its Peace Prize. 
The award is given to pioneers of organized peace work, politicians and, in recent times, to human rights advocates. 
Wei has been nominated for the prize four years in a row, the last two years in concert with Wang Dan.
"Wei has stood up in the finest traditions of an Andrei Sakharov," Schell says. 
"All alone, he has stood against the gale force of a very powerful and intimidating state with dignity and intellectual clarity."
Former laureates like Oscar Arias Sanchez, Elie Wiesel and the Dalai Lama, American legislators like Jesse Helms and Nancy Pelosi, a Democratic representative from California, and several hundred professors from around the world have signed on to Wei's nomination.
In its glossy official booklet, the Nobel Institute makes it clear that well-organized campaigns have little influence on the committee's decisions and "may in fact be counterproductive."
Thus, the effort to promote Wei's candidacy is almost by design low key and ad hoc.
The Chinese Government, meanwhile, has been doing what it can to undermine the nomination. 
Its campaign is also low key, for if the committee frowns at stumping for a particular candidate, attempts to knock a candidate out of the running really make it bristle.
But it is no secret that one of the last things President Jiang wants to see on CNN this December is Wei Jingsheng marching side by side with Wang Dan into the Oslo Town Hall to make a laureate's speech. 
Such a scene would represent several dangers for the Chinese Communist Party. 
For one, the prize could enhance Wei's already considerable stature, turning him into a giant around whom the fragmented dissident movement abroad might finally rally and unite. 
Pelosi notes that the prize would also encourage dissidents inside China.
Finally, there is the danger to China's pride.
The Nobel Prize sounds prestigious to people in China," says Xiao Qiang, of Human Rights in China. 
The 36-year-old former astrophysicist, who turned dissident after the Tiananmen Square crackdown, notes that no citizen of the People's Republic of China has ever won a Nobel in any category. 
It would be a symbolic blow to Jiang and his Government if the first were to be shared by two dissidents who had spent years in jail.
This perception has led to speculation that the regime has taken advantage of the fissures and jealousies within the democracy movement and recruited dissidents to discredit Wei and derail his nomination. 
Last year, a prominent dissident in China, Ren Wanding, sent an open letter to the Nobel committee, pleading with its members not to give the prize to Wei. 
The 52-year-old Wanding, who himself spent 11 years in prison, then called a news conference in Beijing and told foreign reporters that Wei was "not a symbol of Chinese democracy," and that his Western supporters were making a god of him. 
In November, a week after Wei's release, another veteran dissident, Xu Wenli, publicly rapped Wei for being conceited, for failing to recognize other dissidents' achievements and for being too soft on Deng Xiaoping.
Were Ren's and Xu's comments another example of disarray in the movement, or was something more sinister going on?
Xiao leans toward the darker view.
"For the last two years, no dissident in China can call a press conference to say anything," he tells me amid the boxes and file folders of his cramped office. 
"They're not even allowed to have a birthday party.. 
. .Wanding, Xu, all dissidents are under 24-hour surveillance. 
The Government knows where they're at, what they're doing. 
Ren Wanding then calls a press conference for foreign reporters in Bejing to speak against Wei?
It never would have happened without Government sanction or tolerance. 
Draw your own conclusions."
Wei has already drawn his. 
After telling me that he initially did not take the attacks too seriously, regarding Ren and Xu as "old friends," he says in a tone of regret that the two men have gone over to the other side. 
"We have no direct evidence or proofs of any sort," he quickly adds. 
"However, this is definitely not coincidental that after many years of silence, they should voice these criticisms. 
They are coordinating with the Chinese Communists to sabotage the work of the democracy movement."
There are nevertheless China scholars -- as well as Chinese dissidents definitely not in collusion with Beijing -- who also question Wei's nomination. 
They say he doesn't deserve it any more than several others who have suffered for their commitment to democracy.
Zhang Weiguo, a 42-year-old exile who posts a dissident Website, "New Century Net," out of his office in Berkeley, Calif., explains that some of these critics are merely envious, while others have legitimate concerns. 
"Why are there different opinions about Wei?"
Zhang asks. 
"If Wei becomes the authority for democracy, then some fear their voices will be overwhelmed. 
If Wei is conferred with the mantle of democracy, then, these people fear, he will become a kind of cult figure, defeating the whole purpose of pluralism."
Those who view Wei in this light say he is wasting his energies and valuable moral capital, charging off in different directions, criticizing Western policies before he's had time to study the issues thoroughly. 
What he should do now, they advise, is learn English, work on his autobiography, establish his credentials as a political thinker and build support in the dissident community.
In the end, it is impossible to form a single opinion or impression of so complex a man. 
The skepticism voiced about his ideas and approach to the West's China policies appeals to the mind; but Wei's unflagging spirit, commitment and courage appeal to the heart. 
A lot of his critics are intellectuals, and intellectuals tend to distrust clarity, simplicity and directness even when what's clear and simple is the truth. 
And I think that Wei does speak the truth when he says that the interests of the Chinese Communist Party will never be the same as, but ever in opposition to, the real interests of the Chinese people.
As for Wei's spirit, those scholars and friends advising him to retire to the study and write and develop his intellectual resources may not be misleading him, but they are probably misreading him. 
Besides, there is something tepid about such counsel. 
To borrow an old, old phrase, it does not have the power to stir men's souls. 
Many other dissidents have followed that route, and it doesn't appear to have helped the cause of democracy in China or to have unified Chinese political exiles.
That said, Wei does need to brief himself on current conditions, in this country and his own. 
In the words of Cunningham, Wei's editor, Wei may not be a "first-class intellectual, but of all the prominent dissidents, he has "the appeal and spirit, the personality and the charisma, all the credentials to unify that fractious movement."
But he will lose credibility if he doesn't catch up on all that happened in the world while he was in prison. 
It does neither himself nor his cause any good to paint Jiang's China in the chiaroscuro pigments of Mao's China, where people, literally, were forced to devour their children.

The Chinese invented silk, gunpowder -- and the pet rock. 
Actually, they are scholar's rocks and they have been objects of connoisseurship since at least the Sung Dynasty (960-1279). 
They are still collected today.
Seventy of these rocks are on exhibit through Aug. 
18 in a show called "Worlds Within Worlds: The Richard Rosenblum Collection of Chinese Scholars' Rocks" at the Asia Society, 725 Park Avenue (70th Street).
In China, they sat on a scholar's table for contemplation. 
"Like landscape paintings, the rocks represented a microcosm of the universe on which the scholar could meditate within the confines of the studio," said Robert D. Mowry, the curator of Chinese art at the Arthur M. Sackler Museum at Harvard University and curator of the show.
Vishakha N. Desai, the director of the galleries at the Asia Society, said: "The more you look, the more you find in it -- worlds within worlds, animal creatures, miniature abysses."
The rocks are from ancient caves, where they have been eroded by underground streams into highly textured shapes with glossy surfaces.

text:
ï»¿
LAST week, while governments and the press abroad dwelled on the harsh sentences meted out to Chinese dissidents, exuberant middle-class couples crowded into the newly opened Ikea warehouse store here, snapping up stylish, modestly priced furniture and housewares.
As the Chinese and American Governments sparred over human rights, moviegoers rushed to see the season's hit, "Be There or Be Square," a romantic comedy filmed in Los Angeles that affectionately caricatures the United States and the Chinese who go there to seek their fortunes.
Among ordinary Chinese people, it would seem, the current crackdown on democracy activists has registered only faintly, if at all. 
Ask even well-educated professionals what they think about people like Xu Wenli or Wang Youcai, two of the four democracy advocates who received prison terms of a decade or more, and they are apt to call them brave but stupid men who sacrificed themselves with no chance of success. 
Many Chinese are bewildered by all the attention outsiders give these cases, asserting, as one lawyer did, that "these things just have no affect on our daily lives now."
It's not that people are entirely unaware of the virtues of free speech and politics. 
But they know that while there is little room for dissent these days, they can pursue exciting new options in their own lives. 
Many of them just assume that the society will eventually have to liberalize. 
The biggest threat to their personal freedoms, many say, would be a souring of Chinese-American relations that might strengthen conservative forces here.
Though audiences are streaming to see "Be There or Be Square" for a good laugh rather than for a sociology lesson, the movie's popularity and themes are revealing. 
The film, which is directed by Feng Xiaogang, deftly plays on Chinese stereotypes about America and about themselves, and viewers are sophisticated enough to see past the caricatures.
The image of Los Angeles is horrid: Robbers lurk around every corner and wide-eyed immigrants at first seem destined for drudgery or jail. 
But as the two main characters zoom about in their cars, have amusing encounters with the police and create their own niches, the essential, refreshing freedom of California shines through.
The male lead, played by the comic actor Ge You, is an appealing but shiftless man who has spent a decade living in a trailer, selling other Chinese immigrants everything from dubious insurance policies to graveyard plots. 
When the female lead, played by Xu Fan, arrives in town, pretty but penniless, he warns her that there is good news and bad news about America.
"Go back to China," he says. 
"This is a terrible place."
"O.K., so what is the good news?" she asks.
"That was the good news," he replies. 
Then: "Do you want to work as a stripper?"
She declines the offer and after years of perseverance she achieves a decent living in the promised land and, of course, the two fall in love. 
America is a land of opportunity after all.
Americans here sometimes have a hard time understanding how many Chinese can simultaneously appreciate the freedom of the West -- a growing number of professionals have studied in the United States -- and readily dismiss the dissidents as foolish idealists. 
The vast majority feel they are finally getting a chance to savor freedom in their personal lives and work, and they want to enjoy the fruits of modern society. 
The last thing most of them want is upheaval.
Unlike most Chinese, dissidents like Xu Wenli are devoting their lives to an abstract cause. 
The late philosopher Isaiah Berlin famously said there are two types of intellectuals, the foxes who know many things and the hedgehogs who know one big thing. 
Mr. Xu and many of his colleagues in the democracy movement are hedgehogs, with their minds focused laserlike on their quest and a determination that transcends bravery.
Mr. Xu has already spent 12 years in prison and he assumed, when he started speaking out again this year, that he would probably be imprisoned again. 
In the face of repeated warnings and detentions, he stepped up the organization of a new political party and other activities to promote freedom.
And what did he talk about after his sham trial on Dec. 
22, when he was granted a final half-hour with his wife before starting a 13-year prison sentence?
"He said that the charge of subverting state power made no sense," his wife later said in an interview.
"He said it was legally irrational because state power comes from the citizens," she said as she recounted, proudly, the detailed legal and political analysis her husband gave her in their final minutes together. 
He told her his prison term would give him time to "think things over very calmly and reflect on what has happened and what should be done."
He did, before he was finished, express concern about their daughter and tell his wife -- a remarkably dedicated person in her own right -- to look after her health.
IN interviews, some of the veteran dissidents sound almost robotic ticking off their latest analysis of the global forces and domestic politics that affect the democracy movement. 
But the analysis is often brilliant, and the monotone reflects minds that are wholly concentrated.
What sustains these dissidents is an article of faith: that freedom of speech and association is central to the good of a modern society. 
If a single idea drives them, it is a big idea, however pushed aside it is in today's China.
As many citizens and even Government officials will tell you, Chinese today can think what they want and say what they want so long as they do not organize against the Communist Party. 
First-time visitors, having read about repression here, are often surprised at how ordinary things appear: lively newspapers and magazines, fast-paced television news programs and endless commercials for cosmetics and electronic gear. 
Severe repression singles out a small number of people, and most of the rest accept the Party's limits, with little apparent pain.
Harder to gauge is the cost to people in terms of cynicism and even moral corrosion of blanking out certain kinds of thoughts; of mouthing hackneyed party phrases in some settings while speaking one's true mind in others, and of taking it for granted that all news is subtly crafted to serve the interests of the Communists.
It may be true that social evolution, propelled by economic and technical change, will eventually bring a free and democratic China, though there is no sign this will happen any time soon. 
In the meantime people like Xu Wenli and Wei Jingsheng, who is now in exile in the United States after spending much of his adult life in prison, will keep pushing as they can. 
Only time will tell whether their countrymen will some day honor them for their persistence, and their suffering.

text:
ï»¿
There does not appear the slightest probability that, under any circumstances, Hong Kong will ever become a place of trade. 
It is worse than folly to persist in a course begun in error, and which, if continued, must eventually end in disappointment and in national loss and degradation.
-- Robert Montgomery Martin, the British colonial treasurer, reporting home during a visit to Hong Kong in 1844.
SO perhaps not every Brit who sailed into the glorious cavern of Victoria Harbor after the Opium War immediately grasped the magnificence of what his country had just stolen. 
Eventually, though, the defenders of the 19th century's biggest drug cartel figured the place out. 
And even today, at a time when business lives by modem, Hong Kong serves as living proof that in politics, trade and the creation of great cities, geography still matters.
Â 
Magic
Though many have tried -- from Singapore to Vancouver to Taipei -- no one has ever managed to replicate the formula that transformed Hong Kong from a steep, humid, scarcely populated island into one of the world's capitals of commerce.
But what exactly is the magic of Hong Kong?
Its success, of course, is all about proximity -- to the most complex, the most infuriating and now the fastest-growing emerging market on earth. 
The source of its dynamism, though, is far more complex. 
Hong Kong thrived precisely because it was on the edge of, but never mired in, the politics and turmoil of China. 
That separateness allowed it to create one of the world's most wired, global cities -- a narrow, ridiculously crowded place where Western law, Asian culture, Japanese design, American financing and greed from seven continents all mixed together to make money.
So China celebrates Hong Kong's return not only because it ends a century and a half of humiliation, but because the barren island it lost to gunship diplomacy returns to Chinese control tomorrow as the city of the future. 
The question is whether the magic can survive the transition.
When Britain's sovereignty ends amid fireworks and network-TV special reports at midnight on June 30 -- noon on the East Coast of the United States -- so does the detachment that long insulated Hong Kong from the political control, rampant corruption and endemic cronyism of modern-day China. 
But it may take decades to answer the question looming over the ceremonies -- whether as Hong Kong and China converge, the country will come to look more like the island or the island more like the country.
In the sunny study of his official mansion recently, Christopher Patten, the 28th and last Governor of Hong Kong, who will sail into the sunset tomorrow as President Jiang Zemin and his army take control, framed the issue this way: "In 10 years' time, will Hong Kong be more than just the richest city in China?"
"The way China treats Hong Kong," he added, "goes to the heart of what China will be like -- whether it can move from boomtown capitalism to a well-regulated, sophisticated economy that is able to accommodate political change."
Both China and the Hong Kong tycoons who have spent millions preparing the ground for its assumption of control say such comments are arrogant. 
It is Chinese energy more than British foresight that made Hong Kong, they argue, and that explains why Hong Kong's per capita income, an astounding $27,500 last year, long ago outstripped Britain's. 
Having battled Mr. Patten's five-year campaign to create democratic institutions, one of the city's pro-Beijing millionaires suggested recently that Mr. Patten's departure tomorrow night will be his greatest contribution to Hong Kong's future.
The markets don't exactly disagree: they hit heights last week so dizzying that the head of the colony's central bank, in his last act as a servant of the Crown, offered a warning to investors against "undue exuberance."
Â 
An Elusive Formula
The truth, though, is that no one is quite sure what will happen to Hong Kong because no one is quite sure which ingredients made it both Asia's greatest trading center and one of the world's most captivating cities. 
Maybe it's the majesty of the setting -- the glass set against rock, the winding streets, the cacophonous markets improbably etched into a mountain rising from the South China Sea. 
Or perhaps the style of the place -- the chic restaurants, the escalators that run at double speed so that no one is late to a deal, the Mao watches (his mechanical hand waves once a second), the impish spirit that gives rise to fast-food restaurants named the Deli Lama.
Or maybe it is the sight of starched investment bankers and dock workers simultaneously yammering into cell phones in English and Cantonese on the lumbering Star Ferry, where a commute across the worlds most fascinating harbor still costs only 13 cents.
Those are all images television viewers can expect to see today and tomorrow. 
But the formula that has made Hong Kong work -- first as a British outpost in Asia and then as a Chinese city with American and Japanese capital and British eccentricities -- is far more opaque.
The obvious factor is location: Hong Kong is a quick boat and train ride from the biggest labor force and the biggest market on earth, yet it has not had to pay the social costs of sustaining either. 
But there is more.
British rule of law created an advanced framework for capitalism in Hong Kong before anyone thought that capitalism comes in different flavors -- Asian, Western, global. 
British law meant the markets were regulated well enough so that investors were willing to take the risk of putting their money into companies. 
It meant companies were willing to sign contracts, knowing that they could seek enforcement through an independent judiciary where precedent mattered more than who your friends were.
Â 
Low Taxes, Iron Hand
Those were only the start. 
Hong Kong's taxes are among the lowest in the developed world. 
Until Mr. Patten introduced his democratic reforms, which China now threatens to undo, the territory was ruled with an iron hand that limited domestic politics, eliminating a distraction from making money. 
(This is an inconvenient fact for those in Washington who argue that democracy is integral to Hong Kong's economic success.)
None of the country's productive resources went toward national defense -- that was Britain's problem. 
Nor was it spent on a burdensome social security system. 
That's why Hong Kong's phenomenal wealth -- count the Daimlers parked outside the bars of Wanchai -- is mixed with considerable urban squalor, a jarring contrast that the territory's new, Beijing-appointed leader, Tung Chee-hwa, says is no longer acceptable.
It's no wonder that Milton Friedman, the famed economist, once said that "If you want to see capitalism at work, go to Hong Kong."
There are many imitators, but none has quite pulled off another Hong Kong. 
A few years ago, Vancouver, another spectacular city on the sea, was a favorite site for jet-setting "astronauts" who insured themselves against China's takeover of Hong Kong by establishing residencies in that safe corner of the British Commonwealth.
The sleepy Canadian outpost benefited from an injection of capital, entrepreneurial spirit and great Cantonese restaurants. 
But Canada and Confucianism were a marriage of convenience. 
Astronauts earned their title by parking their families and their brokerage accounts on Vancouver's quiet streets and rocketing back to the fray.
Taiwan, where the British briefly considered building a Hong Kong when the island was still known as Formosa, also aspired to be a great financial center. 
It succeeded at creating tremendous wealth. 
But until recently it had no direct trade links to China. 
That limitation, combined with tremendous trade barriers, deep corruption, huge defense costs and deeply divisive politics, meant Taiwan never made the leap.
Â 
Singapore: Tough Option
Hong Kong closest real rival is Singapore, another glittering, onetime British colony, which impresses first-time visitors with its cleanliness, efficiency, spectacular airport and corruption-free traditions. 
Its location, between Indonesia and Malaysia, takes second place to Hong Kong's.
But while Hong Kong is about risk, Singapore is about order. 
It is run by control freaks who believe prosperity can proceed quite nicely, thank you, without political freedom -- which is exactly why the Chinese so admire the "Singapore model."
In response, American and British officials are telling the Chinese that politics and economics cannot be separated if the aim is a truly vibrant market that investors around the world will trust; they have to know they can wake up in Hong Kong and read about a financial scandal in Jiang Zemin's family, then flip on CNN and see uncensored footage of an uprising in Tibet.
China clearly has its own ideas about Hong Kong's future, and most involve Shanghai. 
For years now, China has been importing what it likes from Hong Kong -- the stock market, the glitz, the entrepreneurial spirit -- but it has left behind the political freedom, strict regulations and clean courts that Western investors demand. 
It is unclear whether the ultimate plan is to supplant Hong Kong as the international financial center or simply use Shanghai as a faucet to tap the savings of Chinese in a market that requires less disclosure and runs by Chinese rules.
And what of Hong Kong?
Perhaps its tycoons are right: all this handwringing is the preoccupation of a Western press fixated on individual liberties instead of common prosperity. 
Or perhaps Hong Kong's first newspaper, Friend of China, was closer to the truth in 1842 when it said Hong Kong was destined to "revolutionize, or subvert, the existing state of things in China."

file: The World_ Protecting Xanadu_Hong Kong Seeks Its Own Chinese Wall.txt
text:
ï»¿
CHINA'S newest city is crowded, expensive, polluted and mired in its worst recession since World War II. 
And yet to listen to Hong Kong's leaders, every person in mainland China with the slightest claim to live here would scramble across the border if the gates were opened.
Since January, Hong Kong has been in a lather over the prospect that it is about to be inundated by Chinese immigrants. 
The fears, which began after a court here granted residency to mainland Chinese who have at least one parent in Hong Kong, escalated into near-hysteria when the Government estimated that more than 1.6 million people would be eligible for residency.
"It is clear that Hong Kong cannot bear the burden of these 1.67 million people," said Tung Chee-hwa, the territory's chief executive, in a typically charged response. 
"The consequences are unimaginable."
Last week Mr. Tung asked Beijing, in effect, to overrule the court by reinterpreting a part of Hong Kong's constitution that deals with residency rights. 
Pro-democracy leaders accuse Mr. Tung of flouting the rule of law, which has been the cornerstone of Hong Kong's economic success and was supposed to survive the transition from British to Chinese rule.
That Hong Kong would put its legal system at risk to keep out an influx from the mainland shows how vulnerable this enclave still feels. 
Nearly two years after Hong Kong reverted to Chinese sovereignty -- in a grand experiment known as "one country, two systems" -- people here regard Hong Kong as a Xanadu that could be spoiled by the masses from the vast Chinese hinterland.
"It's a typical immigrant mentality that says 'I got in, now close the door behind me,' " said Martin Lee, the leader of Hong Kong's Democratic Party. 
"This whole debate has brought out the worst in people."
Despite Hong Kong's woes, there is no disputing its allure. 
It generates a gross domestic product of $25,200 per person, 33 times that of the rest of China. 
It has more Rolls-Royces per square mile than any city in the world. 
In a country of 1.2 billion people, half of whom have not made their first phone call, Hong Kong has so many cellular phones that movie theaters ask patrons not to talk on them during love scenes.
It may be one country, but measured by almost any economic yardstick, it remains resolutely two systems.
David Tang, founder of the Shanghai Tang boutiques in Hong Kong and New York, speaks for many here when he asks: "Do we want millions of immigrants coming into a stable and bourgeois society?
Our starting point is different than 150 years ago, when this place was a barren rock."
The debate has put Hong Kong's residents in an awkward spot. 
Most are the children or grandchildren of Chinese refugees who came in waves after the Communist takeover in 1949 or during the Cultural Revolution. 
While many still distrust the regime, the motherland evokes genuine patriotism. 
Protesters mobbed the United States Consulate here to denounce the errant bombing of the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade, pelting it with tomatoes rather than rocks, as protesters did in Beijing.
But when it comes to sharing their schools or neighborhoods with mainland Chinese, Hong Kong's citizens wrinkle their noses. 
In a survey of residents conducted shortly after the handover in July 1997, the words they most frequently used to describe mainlanders were ignorant, impolite, dirty and greedy.
PART of this has to do with changing demographics. 
Many of the mainland Chinese who poured into Hong Kong after 1949 were members of the commercial elite. 
Those who came during the Cultural Revolution tended to be scholars and intellectuals. 
The latest batch, from neighboring Guangdong Province, are mostly young, male and uneducated.
"It's a form of class discrimination," said a 40-year-old woman from Guangdong Province whose husband lives in Hong Kong. 
"Many people in China have not had the chance to receive an education."
The woman, who identified herself as Mrs. Siu, is trying to gain residency for her 16-year-old daughter. 
Mrs. Siu's husband migrated to Hong Kong in the 1970's, returning to China in 1981 to find a wife. 
After the couple had their daughter, they discovered that Hong Kong's immigration laws barred her from moving here. 
So Mrs. Siu stayed with the daughter in China, while her husband moved back.
Attitudes toward mainland Chinese have also hardened in the wake of the Asian economic crisis. 
With Hong Kong limping through its second year of recession, blue-collar workers here worry that more newcomers could crowd them out of the job market. 
Policy makers fear that an influx of unskilled people would make Hong Kong less competitive than Taiwan and Singapore, both of which have immigration policies that favor highly skilled applicants.
Critics say Hong Kong has exaggerated the projected number of immigrants to scare the public and win support for reversing the court ruling. 
"It's probably the grossest misuse of numbers I've ever seen by a government," said Michael DeGolyer, the director of an academic project that conducts surveys on public attitudes about Hong Kong's return to China.
Mr. DeGolyer said some realities of Hong Kong life -- like its stratospheric real estate prices -- would keep mainlanders away. 
In fact, he said, some locals stay only because of its hospitals and schools. 
"If Hong Kong opened its border 24 hours a day," he said, "and if it built schools and medical facilities near the border, at least 200,000 people would move out immediately."

text:
ï»¿
A NEW way of measuring the world's economies has vaulted China from the ranks of third-world nations to those of the economic powerhouses. 
Under calculations being introduced by the International Monetary Fund this week, relying on the buying power of each nation's currency rather than its dollar value, China's economy comes out four times bigger than most previous estimates. 
That makes it the world's third-largest, after the United States and Japan.
But the confirmation of China's enormous economic power helps to obscure the unevenness of the nation's economic development. 
China may be the world's fastest-growing economy on its way to becoming the world's largest market, but that represents primarily the activity along the country's coastal rim, from the northeastern tip of Manchuria all the way down past Hong Kong.
In fact, what has emerged in the past few years is a two-tier economy that is broadening the gap between rich and poor. 
This is worrisome to China's leaders because the same sort of gap prompted Communist guerrillas like Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping to fight to overthrow the old order in the 1930's and '40's.
In its more Communist days, China was relatively egalitarian as countries go, for no one had much of anything. 
Indeed, the economic restructuring begun in 1978 by Mr. Deng, the nation's senior leader, initially created a more equal society. 
By stimulating growth in the countryside, it raised living standards closer to those of the cities.
But last week, Deputy Prime Minister Zhu Rongji warned that over the past six months disparities between China's different regions had "widened to some extent."
That seems an understatement. 
All indications are that income disparities have been growing since the mid-1980's, and that the pace is now accelerating.
"That could provoke a great deal of disenchantment and impatience among those whose lives are lacking," said Carl A. Riskin, a specialist on the Chinese economy at Queens College in New York.
In Guizhou, a landlocked southern province, the poverty is striking. 
In the mountainous countryside surrounding the city, a handful of children, their small bellies slightly distended, run around half-naked because their parents can't afford to buy them clothes. 
Huts are made of tree trunks, branches and straw. 
The typical resident's income was $123 last year, about one-sixth the average income in Shanghai.
China's 30 provinces were never all that much alike in the first place, but in their earlier years the Communists diligently played Robin Hood. 
They milked rich places like Shanghai to give to poorer regions. 
But the policy has shifted dramatically over the years, and now the contrast is sharp. 
The coast is vibrant, with executives striking thousands of deals every day with the outside world. 
The interior is crawling -- admittedly, faster than before -- yet even Chinese refer to this four-fifths of the nation as "China's third world."
Â 
Rich Get Richer
Guizhou belongs to this other world. 
For the past dozen years, while provinces like Guangdong and Jiangsu were given economic privileges to develop, Guizhou was asked to supply its coal, timber and other raw materials at fixed state prices. 
The logic was that economic activity would "trickle in" to remote areas, as land, labor and transport costs rose in more developed regions.
The problem is that such a process is likely to take decades. 
Meanwhile, poorer areas are still subsidizing richer coastal areas with cheap raw materials. 
Officials tacitly acknowledge this phenomenon, but they defend it as imperative for progress.
"Development must be stable and orderly," said Zhao Jiaxing, vice director of Guizhou Economic Commission. 
"Actually, China can't develop evenly. 
But after the coastal areas get rich, their people will come here."
By some accounts, the nation has four or five million millionaires as calculated in local currency. 
(A million yuan is equivalent to about $175,000 at the official rate of exchange.) Some Chinese believe that such estimates, reported in the Chinese press, are exaggerations, but they have aroused some resentment.
"A certain level of gap encourages people to work," said Zhu Qingfang, who researches income differences at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. 
"But if the gap is too big, it makes people feel uneasy."
In any case, the disparities are creating strains. 
Conspicuous consumption is growing in the cities, leading official newspapers to denounce "money worship."
Huge migrations are creating headaches, as millions of peasants flock to cities in search of work. 
In the past, China restricted labor movements, but it has relaxed those rules, partly to allow urban economies along the coast to soak up surplus labor in the countryside.
One result is a talent drain from the poorer inland regions in China's northwest. 
The "floating population" has also made it tricky for the Government to control the birth rate. 
The Government's overriding fear is that the new inequities will provoke unrest. 
But some Chinese argue that even the poor are better off and therefore will not challenge the system.
"We know from TV that life in Guangdong may be better than here, but Guiyang is better than before," said Zhang Jinghui, a peasant who recently got a job as a vendor in this city in Guizhou. 
"And anyway, you can't believe everything you see on television."

file: THE WORLD_China Chooses Not to Prod North Korea.txt
text:
ï»¿
AS brothers in arms, China and North Korea have a long history of standing shoulder to shoulder against Western "hegemony" in Asia. 
Perhaps half a million Chinese soldiers died defending the right of Kim Il Sung, North Korea's longtime dictator, to commit one of the century's great military blunders in attacking South Korea on June 25, 1950.
Today, the world is anxiously waiting to see how a much different China, one desperately seeking an era of stabilityII in which to lift its 1.2 billion citizens to prosperity, is going to help North Korea escape its most serious confrontation with the West since Harry Truman was forced to send a general named MacArthur onto the beach at Inchon.
There are many signs that China's leaders are torn over which course to take, whether to back the doddering, 81-year-old general in Pyongyang, thereby supporting his quest to become Asia's second nuclear power, or join a United Nations pressure campaign to stop him.
Either way, China could lose, and that is why few analysts here expect China's untested new President and Communist Party boss, Jiang Zemin, a fence-sitter all his career, to take a leading role in Korean diplomacy.
This month in Seattle, Mr. Jiang, in his first performance on the world stage as China's leader, clearly demurred when Pacific leaders looked to him to exert some influence on his North Korean comrades.
Instead, Mr. Jiang told Prime Minister Mirohiro Hosokawa of Japan in private that China has little influence these days over Kim Il Sung and, therefore, could not be counted on to change North Korea's ways.
This must have added to the disappointment of President Clinton, who has little to show for upgrading relations with China at some political risk this fall -- including meeting with Mr. Jiang in Seattle. 
Afterward, he returned to Washington to strike a shoulder-to-shoulder stand last week with South Korea's President, Kim Young Sam, but avoided the more bellicose vocabulary that his Administration has recently directed at North Korea. 
And Mr. Clinton held out an unexpected carrot.
If North Korea allows inspections of its nuclear installations and resumes its dialogue with the South, the United States would consider standing down from the annual "Team Spirit" war maneuvers it conducts with South Korea -- war maneuvers that North Korea, through its paranoic lens, views as a prelude to invasion.
Asian diplomats say Mr. Clinton's offer, including other incentives like aid and the possibility of normal relations, was not self-inspired. 
Japan, South Korea and China have all warned that painting the prickly North Korean dictator into a corner is counterproductive. 
Mr. Clinton last week said he got the message.
Asian leaders also felt that the American oratory was too far out in front of the politics. 
They say no Asian power, especially those most threatened by the prospect of a nuclear North Korea, is now ready to support United Nations sanctions for the simple reason that they won't yield any result except perhaps a war devastating to the region's vibrant economies.
Japan and South Korea have made it clear they eventually may go along with a United Nations campaign of pressure and sanctions, but neither feels the threat has "ripened," as one Japanese diplomat said. 
After a briefing from Defense Secretary Les Aspin in Tokyo last month, a Japanese official said, "We still are not persuaded that North Korea has a full nuclear capability or an effective means to carry a nuclear weapon."
Such statements raise the question of whether the Administration and its Asian allies agree on what constitutes a North Korean nuclear capability. 
If North Korea has extracted enough plutonium from its five-megawatt research reactor to assemble one or several crude, untested nuclear bombs -- but is still far from actually assembling a device -- is this a threat so severe as to warrant an immediate United States-led military assault aimed at leveling North Korea's well-dispersed nuclear complex?
Presented with such a scenario, an Asian diplomat will warn of the enormous flow of Korean refugees to the Chinese border in a military conflict, or about how the peninsula's economy could be set back decades, or of heavy casualties.
Now, as diplomacy approaches the brink over North Korea, the key players seem focused on different schedules.
The United States remains riveted on the International Atomic Energy Agency's inability to inspect North Korea's nuclear labs or assure the Security Council that North Korean scientists have not yet tightened the last screw on their first nuclear bomb.
Â 
The Long View
At a meeting next month, the atomic-energy agency may well conclude that, having been thwarted since the spring, it can no longer guarantee North Korea is in compliance as a signer of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. 
That could trigger an unwelcome escalation of the crisis.
China's leaders seem to take greater comfort in focusing on the long term in North Korea -- the prospect that the death of Kim Il Sung will bring an era of change for a country caught in what Secretary of State Warren Christopher calls a "time warp."
Implicit in China's strategy is that it might tolerate the development of a nuclear bomb until it could persuade a successor regime to return to non-nuclear status, as South Africa did under President F. W. de Klerk. 
A Western diplomat here said that beneath China's noncommital statements on the need to avoid pressure is the hope "that they can somehow manage the collapse of the Kim dynasty and bring about a transition to a Communist regime that is more like China or Vietnam, one that is open and interested in economic development, but which is still Communist and retains stabilityI."
If Mr. Clinton succeeds in his new policy of broader diplomatic engagement with what seems a hopelessly isolated regime, he will have scored a major Asian policy success, as well as a blow for nuclear non-proliferation. 
But the North Korean problem may also demonstrate a new imperative about the new world order -- that commercial interests and stability outweigh all but the most advanced, the most "ripened," of security risks.

file: THE WORLD_China, the Conglomerate, Seeks a New Unifying Principle.txt
text:
ï»¿
AFTER holding China together for four decades, Communism is like a yellowing, cracking layer of glue, slowly losing its grip. 
The ideology and -- when that wasn't enough -- the fear that Mao used to keep distant provinces in the orbit of Beijing are no longer sufficient, and Chinese leaders are searching for a new unifying force, a new adhesive, to keep the empire together.
"In Russia, there's no state, but there is a society," said a prominent Chinese journalist. 
"Here it's more like the reverse. 
In Russia, people still line up even if there's no bread on the shelves, while here it'd be chaos in that kind of situation. 
There's nothing to hold us together. 
It's only a question of time before everything falls apart."
Not everyone is that pessimistic, but even the authorities are aware of the risks. 
They have in mind two possible replacements for ideology as a national glue. 
One is a sustained economic boom to raise living standards and thus give the Government a new legitimacy and the people a sense of common purpose. 
The second is nationalism.
There are problems with both. 
China's economic boom has tended to worsen regional disparities and tensions rather than alleviate them. 
Tibetans feel left out, while prosperous Guangdong Province is growing so fast it feels dragged down by the rest of the country.
And Chinese nationalism could threaten Asian stabilityII. 
China has boundary disputes with at least seven of its neighbors, including Japan, Vietnam, Russia and India. 
The neighbors are naturally anxious that rising nationalism could encourage China to become more aggressive, particularly as it is engaged in a far-reaching military buildup. 
China insists that its intentions are wholly friendly, but it seems to be doing what it can to encourage more nationalism.
"The new unifying force in China is patriotism," said He Xin, a social commentator with close ties to the hard-liners, using a more benign term for nationalism. 
"It's already emerged."
Empires have had a way of falling apart in this century, as the British, the French and lately the Russians have discovered. 
Today the Chinese empire -- stretching from Buddhist Tibet to Korean enclaves in Manchuria, from Muslim Xinjiang near Pakistan to Cantonese-speaking Guangdong next to Hong Kong -- is arguably the last great multi-ethnic trans-continental empire left in the world. 
And while its grasp is enormous, its reach is even greater: Chinese claims stretch across seas to encompass Taiwan and the Spratly Islands near the Philippines and Malaysia.
For decades and sometimes centuries at a time, China has been more like Europe -- sometimes Europe at war -- than like a country. 
As recently as the first half of this century, China was a hodgepodge of fiefs run by competing warlords. 
As Lucian W. Pye, an American specialist on Asia, writes in the most recent issue of the Australian Journal of Chinese Affairs: "Put bluntly, the fundamental problem in China's modernization is that China is really a civilization pretending to be a nation-state."
Today many Chinese are particularly fearful about what will happen after the death of Deng Xiaoping, the country's 88-year-old senior leader. 
Few questions may be so important to Asia in coming decades as whether China develops some new cohesive force to keep it together.
Â 
At the Edges
Already, decentralization is gaining momentum, and local leaders are increasingly bold about defying national policies. 
Separatist movements appear to be gaining in Tibet, Xinjiang and Inner Mongolia; Taiwan, as well, is debating whether to declare its formal independence from Chinese sovereignty.
It seems less likely that China's other provinces would want to leave, but in places like Guangdong the possibility of eventual secession cannot be ruled out. 
Indeed, in China, almost nothing should be ruled out.
Leaders from Mr. Deng on down have warned that the West should not look forward with glee to the prospect of Communism collapsing in China. 
Given past experience, including the flight of millions of Chinese abroad when past dynasties crumbled, the authorities may have a point.
"Should there be a disintegration of China or a continued chaos with the 1.16 billion people divided and fighting and starving, the disastrous consequences would spill over the border and endanger the stabilityI of our neighbors, and Hong Kong may witness a flow of millions of people across the border," Ma Yuzhen, the Chinese Ambassador to Britain, warned in a recent speech.
While China's neighbors are worried not just about the possibility of China collapsing but also about the emergence of nationalism as a new unifier, there is little sign now that militant nationalism could be a threat. 
Nationalism is clearly on the rise only among ethnic minorities, and in their case is directed against China.
The only nationalist issue that seems to fire up the general public is the conduct of Japan. 
Many Chinese blame Japan for failing to provide more compensation for wartime injuries, for laying claim to islands that China regards as its own, and for supposedly waging economic imperialism by flooding China with Japanese products.
Paradoxically, this manifestation of nationalism seems to do more harm than good to the central Government's legitimacy.
Many ordinary Chinese protest that the Communist authorities are being too friendly to Japan, and are trying to prevent anti-Japan organizations in China from speaking out. 
The party rose to power partly because it gained nationalistic credentials by fighting Japan; today it is losing some of its dwindling legitimacy because it is widely seen as too chummy with those still known in Chinese as the wokou, the "Japanese bandits" -- a term often pronounced with a real hatred.
While wary of the way nationalism could turn against them, the authorities seem to believe that they have little alternative but to press ahead and cultivate national pride.
"The amount of patriotism will depend in part on how we play our propaganda," said a mid-level Government official. 
"So we're trying to step up our propaganda now in schools and in the news media to encourage more patriotism."

text:
