file: Under Scrutiny_ Citibank_s Handling Of High-Profile Foreigners_ Accounts.txt
text:
ï»¿
Two Congressional investigations, set off from different starting points, are examining Citibank and the confidential world of private banking, a growing and highly lucrative service.
The investigations, led by lawmakers who rarely find common cause, are examining how Citibank -- and a handful of other institutions -- handle the private accounts of foreign officials and their relatives. 
The investigations are likely to result in the closest scrutiny yet by Congress of private banking.
The investigations are led by Representative Dan Burton, a conservative Indiana Republican, and Senator Carl Levin, a Michigan Democrat.
Mr. Burton is looking at allegations of Chinese involvement in the financing of the 1996 American election campaign, including $300,000 in Chinese Government money for the Democratic Party that was wired from Citibank's Hong Kong branch.
Senator Levin, aides say, wants to know how half a dozen American banks managed sensitive foreign accounts, including Citibank's work for powerful families in Asia, Africa and Central America.
Citibank, a unit of Citigroup Inc., entered the private-banking business in the 1970's, taking some business away from the highly secretive Swiss banks. 
Citibank is a leader in global finance, and while its private bank is relatively small, it has attracted elite clients.
But some customers have come under intense law enforcement scrutiny, and so too has the private bank.
First came Raul Salinas de Gortari, who is the brother of Mexico's former President and who is currently in jail in Mexico. 
Raul Salinas secreted millions in a Citibank account, money that investigators suspect came from illicit activities.
Then came the husband of Pakistan's former Prime Minister, who is also in jail for corruption.
More recently there was Liu Chaoying, the daughter of China's former top military official and the reported paymaster for $300,000 in Chinese military money intended for the Democratic Party in 1996, according to testimony from a participant in the payment.
The Salinas investigation has caused Citibank to tighten its policies.
"Since the Salinas episode, the bank's policy on accepting public figures as customers has toughened," said Tom Lahiff, a vice president and lawyer for Citibank. 
"Public figures are not a target market," he said, adding that public figures who do become clients are reviewed annually by top executives.
In 1992 Citibank Private Bank accepted Mr. Salinas as a client and then helped him move tens of millions of dollars out of Mexico. 
Other banks refused to do business with the Salinas family but Citibank, then the only American bank licensed in Mexico, opened the account with what investigators later found was scant review.
That case prompted a Federal criminal investigation of Citibank. 
No charges have been brought against Citibank and the bank denies any wrongdoing.
Congressional investigators and Federal bank regulators, however, are continuing to investigate Citibank's handling of other politically prominent foreign clients, examining whether Citibank has been more concerned with protecting the clients than cooperating with inquiries.
Last week Mr. Burton, chairman of the House Committee on Government Reform, complained in a letter to Citibank about "undue delays" and a "seeming lack of compliance" with a committee subpoena for records on the $300,000 wired to a Democratic fund raiser. 
Bank records list the sender as Ms. Liu, a Chinese military officer and aerospace executive whose father was then China's senior military official.
"We've been quite responsive to the committee in a short time frame," Mr. Lahiff said. 
"We sent an additional document today and by the end of the week we will have given them everything we can."
Ms. Liu transferred the money a few days after the head of Chinese military intelligence told her and the fund raiser, Johnny Chung, that he would soon have Ms. Liu forward $300,000 to Mr. Chung to support President Clinton and the Democratic Party, according to Mr. Chung's testimony last May before Mr. Burton's committee. 
Mr. Chung pleaded guilty to campaign-related charges, and was sentenced to probation after cooperating with investigators.
In his letter last week, Mr. Burton also questioned the lack of authorized signatures for Citibank accounts held by the People's Bank of China, the country's central bank. 
Last year Federal bank regulators had similar questions about these accounts as they tried to trace tens of millions of dollars from the central bank to an account at Citibank Private Bank that was controlled by the daughter of one of the Communist Party's old guard, Government documents show. 
The woman is the sister-in-law of Ms. Liu and a former official at a small California bank that served the Chinese business community.
Mr. Lahiff said the incomplete documentation stemmed from banking laws, common in some countries, including China, that "prohibit our production of certain information."
The Democrats on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, where Mr. Levin is the ranking Democrat, are looking at Citibank from a different angle, asking whether offshore private banks, in their desire to offer clients extra confidentiality, may leave themselves vulnerable to money laundering.
A primary focus of the Senate panel is how Citibank Private Bank handled accounts for top foreign officials and their relatives, and whether advising foreign leaders about their investments affects Citibank's business dealings with those foreign countries, committee aides said.
Mr. Lahiff said Citibank had turned over "a lot of documents" to the Senate committee.
The Senate inquiry intensified after a General Accounting Office report last December found that executives at Citibank Private Bank ignored one of the bank's own safeguards in helping to move up to $100 million for Raul Salinas while his brother, Carlos Salinas de Gortari, was President of Mexico.
Mr. Lahiff said the G.A.O. report contained "a lot of errors," but he declined to specify them.
Another case under review by the Senate committee, aides said, involves Pakistan's corruption investigation of Benazir Bhutto, the former Prime Minister of Pakistan, and her husband, Asif Ali Zadari. 
The two were convicted of corruption earlier this year in Islamabad. 
Documents show that Citibank Private Bank in Geneva handled tens of millions of dollars for Mr. Zadari.
Citibank was not cited for any wrongdoing and the corrupt proceeds at issue in the trial did not involve Citibank, one lawyer familiar with the case said.
Private banking, a Citibank official testified in 1994, is a "white-gloved kind of environment" for wealthy clients who "usually come from countries that are in turmoil of some sort" and seek to shelter their money.
At the heart of all these investigations lies a banking practice termed "know your customer."
According to a G.A.O. report last year on money laundering and offshore private banking, Federal banking regulators "consider 'know your customer' policies one of the most important components of an institution's measures for understanding whom it is doing business with, recognizing unusual transactions and detecting illegal or suspicious activities."
When American bank regulators investigated possible money laundering involving the People's Bank of China and Ms. Liu's sister-in-law at the California bank, they raised questions about whether some American banks knew enough about their customers, according to a lengthy report last year by the Comptroller of the Currency.
Money from the People's Bank of China flowed through a number of American financial institutions, but the Comptroller pushed for more information about the Citibank accounts because that bank handled a significant part of the total. 
But Citibank gave the same explanation offered by Mr. Lahiff: Chinese law prohibited disclosure of much information.
Unlike the laws in Switzerland and other r countries, American regulations do not require banks to "know their customer," but most banks do. 
Still, there remains the question of whether pushing too hard for more disclosure will scare customers away.
"The dilemma becomes: how far down the line do you push the customer," said Peter Sperling, a former Citibank executive who helped set up Citibank's private international bank in the early 1970's.
According to one G.A.O. report, "Citibank made no attempt to investigate Mr. Salinas's background before accepting him" as a customer in 1992. 
Mr. Salinas, who was referred to the bank by a prominent Mexican businessman, was arrested in 1995, and his Citibank accounts were later closed.
For prosecutors to show that a bank violated money-laundering statutes, they have to prove that the money was derived from an unlawful source and that the bank knew or should have known this.
But the Federal inquiry into the tens of millions of dollars in transfers by China's central bank in the mid-1990's -- like the inquiry into Citibank's handling of Mr. Salinas's wealth -- has produced no charges.
By now, the China trail is cold or incomplete. 
But Representative Burton continues to press the matter beyond where Federal investigators have gone.
He is trying to trace the $300,000 that Ms. Liu wired to Mr. Chung, a small fraction of which wound up with the Democratic National Committee. 
A select House committee concluded that the payment was an attempt by Ms. Liu to "better her position in the United States to acquire computer, missile and satellite technologies."
Mr. Burton's next stop will be Ms. Liu's account at Citibank Private Bank in Hong Kong.

AMERICAN foreign policy is going through a noble phase just at the moment.

In the Middle East, it is rededicating itself to the peace process, a task so thankless that a saintly glow illuminates anyone fool enough to undertake it.

America's dealings with Japan have seldom been about human rights or justice or peace mediation. 
They have been about profits and guns. 
In 1851 Japan was minding its own business when President Millard Fillmore wrote the Emperor a letter demanding that the two countries commence trade; since then, the American clamor for access to Japan's markets has continued unabated. 
In the early 1940's, after commercial rivalry in continental Asia got out of hand, the two nations fought a horrendous war; at other times, their armies have lined up on the same side.

Principle was just about irrelevant.
This is how the Japanese wanted it. 
When Japan was forced out of isolation by Fillmore's letter, Asia was being carved up by colonists spouting fine principles from the decks of their gunboats. 
Japan resolved to escape principled subjugation by amassing commercial and military power, and by shutting its ears to foreigners' beguiling rhetoric. 
As a result, Japan has traded with America only when it stood to gain; it has never believed (until recently, at least) that a consistent commitment to free trade is good on principle. 
Equally, Japan has entered security alliances with America only on terms that suited its narrow interests. 
It has been indifferent (again, until recently) to abstractions like human rights and international justice.
Japan's determined Realpolitik, and America's response, lie at the heart of two scholarly new books on the bilateral relationship. 
In "The Clash," Walter LaFeber, a diplomatic historian at Cornell University, takes the story back to the 1850's. 
Michael Schaller, a professor of history at the University of Arizona, deals with the period after 1945 in "Altered States."
Both offer dense chronological accounts that are not for the fainthearted. 
Both draw few general lessons from their research, which may disappoint nonspecialist readers. 
Nevertheless, both books suggest that today's noble phase in foreign policy may soon bump up against its limits.
The noble foreign policy is based on two ideas: that America has the power to force other countries to behave in a principled way, and that its power allows it to take its core security for granted. 
The history of Japan policy shows that both assumptions are dangerous. 
Even at times when America boasted overwhelming power vis-a-vis Japan, it has not been able to make its principles stick. 
And, despite American power, Japan has often behaved in ways that threatened American security.
Consider first America's failure to make Japan accept its principles. 
For 150 years, as LaFeber shows, America has preached the value of free trade; for 150 years Japan has listened only when convenient. 
In the late 19th century, Japan was weak, so it backed America's "open door" policy on Chinese trade and grabbed the commercial opportunities that this policy created. 
In the early 20th century, Japan was strong, so it reversed its attitude to the open door and seized a chunk of China for its own companies. 
After 1945, America continued to explain that free trade yields benefits for everyone. 
Japan pretended to listen.
Japan, LaFeber tells us, has defied the United States on more than just trade. 
In 1904 Japan took advantage of American diplomatic support to go to war against Russia. 
This did not prevent Japan from entering into an alliance with Russia in 1910 to thwart American policy in China. 
After World War I, the United States emerged as the most powerful nation on earth: its industry had escaped destruction, its Navy was building formidable new ships, foreigners (including the Japanese) depended on New York for capital. 
But at the Versailles conference Japan steadfastly refused to bend to Woodrow Wilson's request that it should give up some territorial gains. 
"Wilson found himself now controlling the world's greatest economic and military power," LaFeber writes, "but it was not enough to have his way with Japan."
After World War II, this pattern continued. 
America's relative power increased; its military bases in Japan protected the Japanese from Communism. 
But this did not stop the Japanese from defying America repeatedly, refusing to rearm as rapidly as Washington wanted, demanding that the southern island of Okinawa be returned, undermining the American boycott of China after the Tiananmen massacre. 
Japanese leftists wanted the alliance revoked; when, in 1960, America's Ambassador in Tokyo met Japan's Foreign Minister to exchange signed copies of the security pact, arrangements had to be made for the two to escape over a back wall if rioting mobs caught up with them. 
Even the pro-American right wing has doubted the security alliance. 
In 1972, according to a poll cited by Schaller, only 44 percent of Liberal Democrat candidates for the Diet supported it strongly.
The high point of American power over Japan came right after 1945, when America's occupation force thought it could remake Japan in its own image. 
As a biographer of Douglas MacArthur, the general who reigned over occupied Japan, Schaller is especially expert on this folly. 
The United States started out by purging militarists from public life, hoping that new leaders would sprout up who shared American principles. 
When the vacuum seemed likelier to be filled by a pro-Communist left wing, Washington changed course. 
Nearly 200,000 Japanese had their purge orders revoked; these ex-militarists accounted for 42 percent of the new members of the Diet's lower house after the 1952 election. 
In 1957, Nobusuke Kishi, who had cosigned the declaration of war against the United States in 1941 and been imprisoned for war crimes, visited America as Japan's Prime Minister and Eisenhower's guest. 
Schaller mentions that he was invited to throw out the first ball at a game between the New York Yankees and the Chicago White Sox.
This visit was humiliating; but it teaches a useful lesson about the limits to American power, and so the limits to its ability to pursue principled foreign policy. 
On principle, America should have punished war criminals. 
But it simply could not afford the risk that Japan might acquire weak or Communist leadership. 
On principle, today, America is right to push Japan to open its markets and shoulder more of the defense burden in Asia. 
But perhaps it cannot afford to risk a Japanese backlash -- just as it must beware of provoking Southeast Asians when it speaks up for human rights and Russians when it enlarges NATO. 
It is not a pleasant thing to say, but noble ideals can sometimes be a poor guide to foreign policy.

The Government indicated today that it was essentially pleased with remarks over the weekend by Newt Gingrich, who said last week during a visit to China that he accepted a one-China policy but asserted that the United States would defend Taiwan militarily if it was attacked.
The one-China policy has been at the heart of relations between the United States and China since President Nixon established ties with Beijing in 1972. 
In signing the Shanghai Communique then, the United States and China effectively deferred the issue of a resolution to the simmering civil war that has kept Taiwan and the mainland divided since 1949. 
In the meantime, a robust economic boom in the region has drawn the two enemies close together.
At a news briefing today, Shen Guofang, China's Foreign Ministry spokesman, said of the House Speaker's visit: "Mr. 
Gingrich mentioned several times in Beijing that he opposed Taiwan independence and approved the principle of one China. 
He also expressed that the American Government and the American Congress will stick to the principle of one China."
With little rancor, Mr. Shen highlighted the positive points in Mr. Gingrich's remarks, which were made to reporters in Shanghai on Sunday, before the Speaker and his party of 12 members of Congress left for Tokyo and a final stop in Taiwan before returning to the United States.
Mr. Shen did not take issue with Mr. Gingrich's pointed warning that if the mainland should use military force against Taiwan, "we will defend Taiwan. 
Period."
The Chinese spokesman said: "Referring to what he said in Shanghai, China has always stood for the position of peaceful unification" with Taiwan.
"However," Mr. Shen said, "the Chinese side will take necessary measures if Taiwan declares independence or if foreign powers interfere in the Taiwan issue."
What those measures might turn out to be, he said, "is the internal affair of China."
Mr. Gingrich's remarks on defending Taiwan seemed to undermine the "strategic ambiguity" by which the United States has avoided issuing a direct warning to China over the use of force, in part because such a warning might incite the pro-independence forces on Taiwan.
The White House issued a statement on Sunday that while it did not rebuke Mr. Gingrich, said that he "was speaking for himself."
The statement reiterated that the United States was committed by the Taiwan Relations Act to provide an "adequate self-defense" for Taiwan, while also insisting that both parties "peacefully address the Taiwan issue."
But some China specialists argued today that Mr. Gingrich's formulation, balanced between his public commitment to "one China" and a determination that no party can solve the Taiwan issue by force, amounted to a clear statement of American political sentiment in the wake of the 1996 Taiwan crisis.

file: Vancouver_ Where the Far East Now Begins.txt
text:
ï»¿
THE waiter leaned down, presenting a basket in which several wiggling spotted prawns, just fetched from the fish tank, were awaiting our pleasure. 
Did we want them cooked quickly in wine and oil?
In a good Chinese restaurant, it is always best to take the waiter's hints.
The preparation was tableside, and the prawns continued to flip around until they were added to the pot. 
The air was perfumed with the aroma of rosewater, the prawns unbelievably tender and sweet.
The best Chinese restaurants in Vancouver, like Sun Sui Wah in the up-and-coming Mount Pleasant neighborhood, know what their patrons -- mostly wealthy Chinese emigres from Hong Kong -- expect.
An enormous immigration from Hong Kong over the past decade has made Vancouver one of the most Asian cities in North America -- and, many would say, the best city in the world, outside of Hong Kong, to eat Chinese food. 
An estimated 110,000 Hong Kong Chinese have flowed into this city of 525,000 since the early 1980's in anticipation of the Chinese takeover.
And many arrived with the wherewithal to indulge their connoisseurship of the fine points of Chinese cuisine: the Canadian Government made citizenship easy to obtain for those who could show several hundred thousand dollars in assets. 
Not for nothing has the city earned the nickname Hongcouver.
Chefs from Hong Kong's best restaurants soon followed these emigres, bringing with them a level of sophistication that is seldom seen outside that city. 
So, for example, when Marco Wong, who heads a shipping company in Manhattan, wants the very best Chinese food in North America, he knows to look for it in Vancouver, where his brother, Stephen Wong, is a food consultant and cookbook author.
"It's like the difference between going to a very good bistro and going to Alain Ducasse," said Marco Wong, referring to France's only six-star chef. 
"Nowhere else comes close."
If some of the Chinese food I ate during my five-day stay were French, it would be called haute cuisine.
The Hong Kong connection is evident to the visitor the moment Vancouver comes into view: a city on the water with new, tall, slim towers sprouting like mushrooms, many of them built with Hong Kong money. 
One hears grumbling from old-timers about the new "monster houses" built by wealthy newcomers where modest bungalows once stood. 
And about the new need for classes in English as a second language in the schools. 
But there is no grumbling about the new culinary influences on the Vancouver scene. 
Here is where I discovered that contrary to popular belief, the Chinese can make pastries as fine and flaky as the most expert French baker, that soy sauce comes in at least 60 varieties and that the latest fad among young Chinese, bubble pearl tea, is one that ought to sweep America.
The chefs' demand for the ingredients so readily available to them in Hong Kong has brought those ingredients not just to Vancouver, but also to places like Richmond, a city south of Vancouver whose population is now 40 percent Chinese.
It was at the modern sprawling T & T Supermarket in Richmond that I found those 60 kinds of soy sauce on the shelves, as well as bean curd in at least two dozen different forms, ranging from one labeled "smelly" to one shaped like a chicken and made for vegetarians. 
There are black chickens, duck tongue, geese intestines and taro root ice cream, too. 
Looking almost exotic in this setting were North American staples like Sara Lee strawberry cheesecake, maple syrup and Ritz crackers.
In Richmond you find fish tanks in the supermarkets. 
One tank after another is filled with live sea creatures that are the foundation of much Hong Kong cooking. 
T & T has a sign in English above the crabs:
Â 
WARNING LIVE CRABS DO BITE
Live is the operative word. 
The freshness of seafood is crucial for Cantonese food because the recipes are quite simple, to show off the quality of the ingredients.
Even the fast food in the food courts of the Richmond shopping malls (where it is possible to go an entire day without hearing a word of English spoken) is intriguing. 
The stalls are similar to those in Asian cities, and they offer an amazing display of quick, cheap, mouthwatering dishes. 
In the Yaohan Center, Pak Tak Chiu Chow serves dishes like savory duck cooked with five-spice powder and soy accompanied by a dip of garlic and rice vinegar. 
The Curry House has a subtly hot lamb curry served with a delicious rice cooked in chicken broth with chicken fat, garlic and ginger.
But one of the most intriguing concoctions is the bubble pearl tea, imported from Taiwan, that is the latest fad among young Chinese. 
It is a fad I would happily embrace: sweetened iced tea frothed with milk, sometimes idiosyncratically flavored with anything from litchi nuts to Ovaltine. 
What makes it so appealing are the gelatinous pearls made of potato flour placed in the bottom of the glass that are sipped through an extra-wide straw. 
The pearls sort of rumble as you slurp them up. 
(Sadly, these giant Taiwanese pearls do not seem to have reached the East Coast yet.) Vancouver has no less than 30 establishments that specialize in these drinks.
Given the inventiveness of Chinese chefs, it's not surprising to find refreshing fusion dishes here as well. 
Chinese restaurant menus turn up such surprises as pan-fried ostrich dumplings and Japanese udon noodles and teriyaki sauce; such oddities as lobster with cream and butter sauce, an import from Hong Kong via France; pomfret with Miracle Whip and a favorite dim sum dessert, a crisp spring roll filled with canned fruit salad and mayonnaise.
Only in a place sure of its Chinese roots would a chef dare to create these fusion dishes, even if they don't all work. 
The fusion goes both ways. 
"We use a lot of Chinese ingredients," said Adrienne O'Callaghan, the chef at a downtown restaurant with the resoundingly un-Chinese name of Irish Heather. 
"We don't think of them as Chinese. 
We think of them as mainstream: Chinese vegetables, rice vinegar, sesame oil, all kinds of noodles, shrimp paste. 
You don't bat an eyelash anymore."
Vancouver has had a Chinese presence since the 1850's, decades before the city's incorporation. 
It's just that the Chinese profile has risen so sharply, so fast.
"Chinese food and Chinese people were always around," said Murray McMillen, the food editor of The Vancouver Sun, "but I didn't feel the culinary influence when I was growing up."
The culinary impact of the large Chinese population in the city has become so pervasive that people here treat Chinese ingredients the way people in Houston treat salsa.
Raazhan Rae, a schoolteacher, used to shop in Chinatown, but now she can find what she needs in her own neighborhood, where most of the residents are westerners. 
"The vegetable department where I shop probably has one-third Oriental vegetables," she said, "and it has fish tanks."
Kasey Wilson, the author of several guidebooks and the co-host of a radio food show, has noticed the difference among her circle of friends. 
"Westerners buy a lot of prepared dim sum, steam them in little Chinese steamer baskets they have at home and serve them as appetizers. 
The fact that you can just pick up a Peking duck and serve it with lingonberry sauce, that barbecued duck is used to top pizzas, that chefs are buying them for their restaurants and cutting them in strips for appetizers . . . "
Those in the know, Chinese or not, who are looking for the best and cheapest fish, shop in Chinatown. 
Sylvia Molnar, a cooking teacher, goes there at least once a week to buy live fish, especially sturgeon and carp.
Visitors to Vancouver are most likely to encounter its Chinese specialties in the restaurants. 
Sun Sui Wah is renowned for its squab and its live fish. 
The restaurant's weekend dim sum are just as sophisticated as its dinner fare. 
For Westerners who want to dip no more than a toe into shark's fin dishes, shark's fin dumplings are the route. 
The glutinous shark's fin makes a pleasing contrast to the shrimp and ham in the filling, all encased in a very tender dough. 
The savvy diner saves room for fresh-from-the-oven egg tarts and the best sponge cake on the planet.
The Shanghai Bistro in downtown Vancouver also puts on an impressive dim sum banquet at lunch every day, and a standout is the silky handmade noodles with spicy eggplant, all cooked to sweet perfection. 
This is also the place for steamed buns filled with pork and cilantro, perfectly cooked so that the buns do not taste, as they often do, like uncooked dough. 
Shanghai scallion pancakes are toasty brown on the outside and soft inside.
The best winter melon soup I had in Vancouver was at the Grand King Seafood Restaurant, improbably in a Holiday Inn. 
(Don't let the locations of Chinese restaurants put you off.)
In Richmond, the President Chinese Seafood Restaurant, in the Radisson Hotel (which also houses a Buddhist temple), does a superb suckling pig and a refined shark's fin soup with a rich, clear broth. 
The deep-fried Alaskan king crab announced its arrival by sending waves of fragrant garlic to the table, and what the Chinese call hollow vegetable but others call water spinach, is superb with ginger, garlic, hot pepper and preserved bean curd.
If you want to try the ovaries of the snow frog, guaranteed to make you beautiful, improve your complexion and clean your system, says Melina Hung, communications director of the Radisson, have them in the pudding. 
You'll never know they are there.
Alas, some of the very best of these restaurants see few westerners. 
"I've had a hard time convincing Caucasians to come to these restaurants," said Stephen Wong, the cookbook author. 
"They won't spend money on pea shoots," a reference to one of the most popular vegetables.
On the other hand, these top restaurateurs have not gone out of their way to welcome westerners. 
But now that some of those wealthy Hong Kong Chinese are returning home, the restaurants may find they have to step up their outreach programs.
Â 
FIVE-SPICE MAPLE-CURED SALMON
Â 
Adapted from "New World Noodles" (Firefly Books, 1997) by Bill Jones and Stephen Wong
Time: 15 minutes plus marinating
Â 
1 side of salmon, about 2 pounds
1/2 cup salt, preferably sea salt
1/2 cup maple syrup
2 tablespoons soy sauce
1 tablespoon grated ginger
1 teaspoon five-spice powder.
Â 
1. Prepare the salmon by removing all bones and trimming the fat. 
Place the salmon in a long stainless-steel, glass or plastic container.
Â 
2. In a small bowl combine the salt, maple syrup, soy sauce, ginger and five-spice powder. 
Pour the mixture over the fish, turning to coat it evenly. 
Leave the salmon skin side down, cover with plastic wrap and place a roasting pan on top weighted down with a couple of bricks or cans. 
Refrigerate for at least 12 hours and up to 3 or 4 days.
Â 
3. Remove the salmon from the curing mixture, and rinse off any excess spices. 
Lay the salmon skin side down on a cutting board, and slice on a diagonal into thin slices, as you would smoked salmon, without cutting down to the skin, which should be discarded.
Â 
Yield: 12 servings.
Â 
CLASSIC BUBBLE TEA
Â 
Adapted from Stephen Wong
Time: 3 minutes
Â 
1/2 cup chilled, cooked large Chinese tapioca pearls (if substituting regular small tapioca, use 1/3 cup)
1 cup crushed ice
1 cup very strong chilled black tea (or substitute orange pekoe tea or Chinese litchi tea)
1 cup milk, or to taste
Honey or sugar to taste.
Â 
1. Place the pearls in a large parfait glass.
Â 
2. Combine all remaining ingredients in a cocktail shaker, and shake vigorously until the mixture is frothy. 
Pour into the glass, and serve with extra-thick straws.
Â 
Yield: One 16-ounce drink.

file: VERDICT IN BEIJING_ THE OVERVIEW_Beijing Sends a Strong Warning With Long Sentence for Dissenter.txt
text:
ï»¿
By convicting Wei Jingsheng in a closed trial today of "conspiring to subvert the Government" and sentencing him to 14 years in prison, China again silenced the most powerful pro-democracy voice in the country and sent a strong warning about the limits of dissent.
Mr. Wei, 45, a onetime electrician at the Beijing Zoo who helped father China's democracy movement in 1978, was also denied his political rights for three years beyond the prison term. 
The harsh sentence drew expressions of anger and indignation from members of Mr. Wei's family, human rights organizations and governments around the world.
[The Clinton Administration criticized China but stopped short of threatening specific retaliatory action. 
But some members of Congress warned that Mr. Wei's imprisonment could lead to renewal of the linkage that Washington once made between trade privileges for Beijing and its rights record. 
Page A20.]
The verdict comes at a time when China's Communist Party leadership has reached a peak of sensitivity and defensiveness in foreign and domestic affairs, in part related to a struggle for pre-eminence among potential successors to Deng Xiaoping, China's 91-year-old paramount leader, who is in extremely frail health.
Over the last 12 months, Beijing has taken increasingly belligerent or intransigent positions on a range of issues from human rights and trade negotiations, to religious freedom in Tibet and political developments in Hong Kong and Taiwan. 
In the case of Taiwan, China has threatened more explicitly to go to war to recover its estranged province than at any time in decades.
The judgment against Mr. Wei sends a powerful signal to a nation in the midst of an economic revolution that any public talk of political revolution, democratic reforms and democracy can be considered seditious.
To many in China, these constraints are not as burdensome as they seem to many foreigners. 
Free speech, even criticism to senior leaders, is tolerated as long as it is private. 
Millions of Chinese crave stabilityII and are not interested in the politics of confrontation that marked the democracy movements of the 1980's.
Outside of intellectual circles, Mr. Wei may be less a symbol and more a curiosity, but the Communist leadership fears that his attack on Communist rule and passion for democracy could take hold among the millions of disaffected Chinese who are not taking part equally in the fruits of China's economic boom.
Thus, Mr. Wei is the largest and most obvious target for this new Government crackdown.
His mordant style first drew public attention and outraged some party leaders when he scrawled it on a poster and hung it on a stretch of wall in Western Beijing that came to be known as Democracy Wall. 
Mr. Deng was among the first to feel his barb in 1979, and Mr. Deng is believed to have ordered Mr. Wei jailed and Democracy Wall torn down.
After serving 14 1/2 years of an initial 15-year sentence, Mr. Wei emerged in September 1993 with the same fearlessness to take on Mr. Deng again, as well as his potential successors.
"The present leaders were the most outspoken group of men, shouting their support of human rights and democracy before they ascended to power," he wrote in an essay on the Op-Ed page of The New York Times in November 1993. 
"But their subsequent dictatorship made clear that they have no intention of making good on the promises they once made to the masses."
In April 1994, after a number of run-ins with the authorities, Mr. Wei was rearrested.
With the dispatch of Mr. Wei back to a prison cell, where he has spent all but six months of the last 16 years, China's security services have now jailed or placed under close control all of the prominent pro-democracy leaders who remain from the Democracy Wall or Tiananmen periods.
Wang Dan, a student leader of the pro-democracy demonstrations at Tiananmen Square in Beijing in 1989, whom the Bush Administration invested great effort to free, has been held without charge since May. 
So has the writer Liu Xiaobo.
Chen Zeming, one of the so-called "black hands" behind the Tiananmen uprising, was released in May 1994 as a special concession to President Clinton, but Mr. Chen, who is suffering from cancer, was abruptly jailed again last June. 
Another student leader who was released last summer, Liu Gang, lives as a virtual prisoner in his home in Liaoning Province.
In Beijing today, many democracy campaigners awoke on the day of Mr. Wei's trial to find themselves under house arrest.
At a courthouse swept by the first snow of winter here, Mr. Wei made an appearance at the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court and spoke on his own behalf during the six-hour trial. 
Although Mr. Wei was represented by a respected private attorney, Zhang Sizhi, and was allowed to present his defense, the verdict was preordained by the Communist Party leadership, Chinese and Western experts say.
"Wei was defended by a lawyer hired by Wei's relatives, and was allowed to represent himself fully," a Government statement said tonight. 
"After debate between the opposing lawyers, Wei made his closing statement."
Under today's ruling, Mr. Wei would not be able to publish another essay about democracy in China, criticize the Communist Party regime or speak to a foreign reporter until the year 2012, assuming that he survives another long prison term.
No record of today's proceedings at the No. 1 Intermediate People's Court was made public, but tonight, China's Government-run central television and press agency issued a statement that was extraordinary in its acknowledgment that Mr. Wei was engaged in nothing more sinister than publishing and fund-raising activities in support of China's democracy movement.
"The court's investigation showed that Wei, in attempting to overthrow the Government, developed a plan of action," the Government statement said, "which included establishing an organization to raise funds to support democratic movement activities, purchasing newspapers, setting up a company in charge of organizing cultural activities, and organizing non-governmental painting exhibitions, performances and publications with the aim of setting up a propaganda and liaison base, attempting to raise a storm powerful enough to shake up the present Government."
The Government statement made no assertion that Mr. Wei had formed a group, or written a charter or manifesto with the stated aim of toppling the Communist Party or overthrowing the Chinese Government. 
Moreover, there was no assertion that Mr. Wei advocated violence or any activity beyond publishing and cultural performances in support of democratic reforms in China.
"The trial and sentence are an outrage, and a clear effort by Beijing to subvert the rule of law," Human Rights Watch said in a statement.
Outside the courthouse, several dozen foreign reporters and photographers gathered in hopes of witnessing the proceedings, or at least recording the coming and going of the unidentified few Chinese who were allowed to witness it. 
But Public Security officers kept foreign journalists more than 100 feet away from the gate of the courthouse.
Some members of Mr. Wei's family were allowed to attend the trial, but their telephones were not working afterward.
Two of Mr. Wei's personal friends who came to the courthouse despite earlier warnings by the police to stay away were arrested after they mingled with journalists and expressed their concern for Mr. Wei's fate.
"As Wei's friends, we are concerned about him," Jin Cheng said. 
"I think all dissidents are deeply concerned about the trial. 
If Wei is convicted, we don't know what's going to happen to us."
Mr. Jin chatted as plainclothes policemen, who later arrested him, stood close by seeking to overhear or record his comments to reporters.
"What is more important," he continued, "is that Wei is the symbol of China's democracy movement and we are concerned about the fate of the movement."
Reached in Washington, one of Mr. Wei's sisters also expressed her alarm over the verdict.
"This verdict shows how shameful the Chinese Government is," said Wei Shanshan, who is lobbying for White House and Congressional support on her brother's behalf.
"The only thing he did was speak out his thoughts, and this is not a violation of the Chinese Constitution," she said, adding, "he hasn't formed any anti-Government organizations or engaged in any anti-Government activities."

file: Vladivostok Journal_A New Capitalist Goes Foreign Shopping for Profit.txt
text:
ï»¿
With their easy banter, upscale clothes and shared bottles of imported vodka, the large group of young Russians on the eight-hour Moscow-to-Vladivostok flight were obviously people who did this often.
Halfway through the overnight flight, when most of his group had dozed off, Roman, the leader, agreed to explain who they were and what they did. 
It was a variation on a story often heard among Russian entrepreneurs trying to break out of the encrusted mold of socialism.
They were on a "shopping tour" to China, he said -- not of the tourist sort, but to pick up goods to resell in Moscow. 
Most in the group planned to bring back inexpensive track suits and running shoes, but there were also buyers of electronics and household appliances.
The 23 members of the group were independent buyers who had banded together to form a company that organized the visas, travel and hotels. 
The trip cost each of them $500, and each carried anywhere from $3,000 to $5,000 in cash in American dollars in their money belts to spend in China.
Â 
Other Destinations
There were thousands like them, Roman said, from all over Russia and other former Soviet republics. 
China was the current draw, because visas were easy and the prices were right, but there were also "shopping tours" to Turkey, Poland and elsewhere. 
Some went from Vladivostok to the Polish border and sold their goods to Poles who moved it westward.
The group banded together partly for protection, Roman said. 
They were obvious targets, since bandits knew full well what they were up to. 
It was no coincidence that most of the group were men of an athletic build in their late 20's or early 30's, but in the end there was no guarantee against robbery, he said. 
They had all been hit, most more than once.
On arrival in Vladivostok, they would spend a night in some hotel and then take a train to Harbin in China. 
There they would spend a few days haggling and buying. 
Then, toting their bales of products, they would return to Vladivostok and arrange to ship their wares on the Trans-Siberian Railway back to Moscow. 
In seven days the goods would be in Moscow.
Roman's business was "rags," mostly track suits. 
Back in Moscow, he had six people working with him. 
Most of them would fan out to various flea markets and peddle the clothes.
Â 
Profits and Risks Both High
The profits were good: Roman said he could sell a track suit for seven times the purchase price. 
But risks and costs were high. 
There were the arduous trips, roughly one per month, the risk of robbery, the long hours, several people to pay and constantly changing costs. 
There was the inherent insecurity of the operation, which could be cut off at any moment by the Russians, the Chinese, Aeroflot or a dozen other unexpected problems.
A current problem is with passports. 
Russia had decreed that new passports are needed for travel abroad. 
But the Chinese were never advised, and Russians with new passports were turned away at the border.
"These people come up to me at the tolkuchki," Roman said, referring to the new outdoor markets that have sprung up in every Russian neighborhood and village, named from the word to "push."
"And they scream at me, 'How dare you sell for these prices!'
'We know what you're buying this for!'
'You have no shame!'
"
"That hurts a lot." he said. 
"I want to tell them, 'Do you think I enjoy doing this?
Do you think I like sitting in these long overnight Aeroflot flights, haggling with Chinese, staying in God-awful hotels?
Do you think this is the life I want to live?'
I'd much prefer to spend the time with my wife and daughter."
Â 
A Welder by Trade
Handsome and well-spoken, Roman had completed his studies in welding at a technical school and gone on to an institute to do research in welding exotic metals. 
He liked the work, but the institute could not pay a living wage.
So he dipped into the new free market. 
On a trip to Czechoslovakia, he saw that the Russian matryoshka dolls -- the brightly colored wooden figures in diminishing sizes that fit into one large doll -- were selling briskly.
He negotiated to supply them at a lower price. 
He then contracted to buy them directly from artists in Russia. 
The shipments soon started moving to Prague, to everyone's satisfaction: Several artists were making money, he was making money, and the Czechs were making money.
One day the customs agent stopped him. 
"Are these wood?"
"Of course they're wooden."
"Then you need a special permit," the agent said. 
"The Government has decreed wood a strategic export. 
Sorry."
The decree was intended to control exports of raw lumber. 
But a permit would have required extreme effort. 
Roman's business was dead.
Next, when the first cheap Chinese track suits began to filter into Moscow, he thought they could be made even cheaper in Russia. 
He contracted with a textile factory in Ivanovo for the cloth, got a dozen seamstresses together and started putting out Russian track suits.
Â 
Done In by Taxes
Then the taxes and the payoffs began. 
A 28 percent value-added tax, a 32 percent tax on profits -- in the end, Roman said, he was giving away 90 percent of his profits. 
The business folded.
So he began taking "shopping tours" to China. 
There were no customs on imported goods valued under $5,000. 
Taxes could be evaded in the tolkuchki, and if you kept mobile, you could elude the protection rackets.
Why does he use dollars?
Because there is no other way to carry cash, he said. 
Russia has no travelers' checks or money orders, and $5,000 at the current exchange rate was 5 million rubles -- a bag full of bills.
Roman said he still dreamed of a small business. 
He had some capital saved up. 
All he needed was a dollop of stability.

text:
ï»¿
VICTORIA ENG and Timothy Chin both grew up in New York and have fast-paced, high-tech jobs: Mr. Chin is an assistant futures trader for Citibank and Ms. Eng is an actuary systems specialist at the Teachers Insurance Annuity Association. 
But their wedding was full of echoes from ancient China.
Like many Chinese-American couples, they chose the year of their wedding according to the Chinese lunar calendar. 
It showed that 1993 would be a year filled with light to guide people in new ventures.
"Nineteen ninety-four is the blind year," the bride said. 
"That means there's no spring. 
It's the year of darkness. 
Nineteen ninety-three is the year of two springs, and that occurs very rarely, once every blue moon. 
The year of the two springs is a very happy year."
Ms. Eng and Mr. Chin, both 30, carefully chose the day for the wedding, Dec. 
18, as well. 
Many Chinese believe the number 8 symbolizes prosperity and wealth and that 18 means definite prosperity and wealth.
"The Chinese pick days for everything," said Dawn Chin, the bridegroom's sister. 
"You don't say, 'Oh, I'll be free that day.'
There are good days and bad days."
But there were a few rituals the couple skipped. 
For instance, it is a Chinese custom to hand-deliver wedding invitations. 
Weeks before the wedding, Ms. Eng said, "If I can get away with mailing them, I'm going to."
(She did.)
On the morning of the wedding, as the Chinese have done for centuries, Ms. Eng and Mr. Chin formally poured tea for the bride's parents. 
"It's a farewell tea ceremony," the bride said. 
"My parents are saying goodbye to me because after I get married, I'm no longer part of the family. 
I'm gone. 
I'm history. 
In the old days in China, when women got married, it was like they were going to another world."
The actual wedding ceremony was nothing like one in ancient China. 
The couple -- she in a white lacy dress, and he in a dinner jacket -- were married at the Marriott Financial Center Hotel. 
As 200 guests watched, they exchanged vows before the Rev. Jim Covington, a Unitarian-Universalist minister. 
Afterward, 450 guests attended a traditional 12-course wedding banquet at the Silver Palace restaurant in Chinatown.
As is the Chinese custom, the bride changed clothes throughout the night. 
She arrived at the banquet in a red (for good luck) Chinese wedding outfit, a long skirt and a cropped jacket with dragon and phoenix designs. 
Later, she changed into a cherry-red velvet dress with multicolored beading on the front, so that she sparkled like fireworks on the dance floor.
As dish after dish was served (beginning with long jellyfish noodles, which symbolize longevity), the couple and many younger guests congregated on the dance floor to play Chinese wedding games that involved raw eggs, ice cubes and blindfolds, all aimed at pestering the newlyweds.
William Lin, a guest, noted that the games would probably go on very late into the night. 
"Traditionally, friends crash the bridal suite and steal all of their clothes," he said.
In their new apartment, the couple will also follow old traditions. 
"The first night together, we have to sleep in a new bed with red sheets," the bride said. 
"The bed has to be new, and it has to be a gift. 
The groom's mother buys it because the groom's mother wants heirs."

file: WAITING FOR CHINA_ Anxious Artists_Flowering In the Face Of a Giant Unknown.txt
text:
ï»¿
HONG KONG'S 6.3 MILLION PEOPLE produce more wealth in a year per capita than their British counterparts, yet there is no Globe Theater here. 
Hong Kong's streets are clogged with more Rolls-Royces than London's, yet there is nothing akin to the British Museum. 
Hong Kong, it is said, and it is widely believed, is a single-minded place, and its mind is on money. 
Hong Kong, it is widely believed, and it is routinely said, is a cultural wasteland.
But tucked away in tiny studios or down red-brick arcades or in small mirrored halls, canvases are being daubed with oils, actors struggle with new scripts, and dancers pirouette over worn boards. 
Indeed, art is being born here, in solitude and collaboratively, in defiance, almost, of a social esthetic that prizes money above all else. 
And it is art, often, that is rooted not in any grand Chinese tradition but in Hong Kong's peculiar circumstances and culture. 
It is art, as well, that at times shudders at the prospect of impending unity with the giant totalitarian neighbor to the north.
"For the true Hong Kong artists," explains Johnson Chang, the owner of Hanart, a gallery that displays both prominent mainland painters and Hong Kong artists, "it's always in the back of their mind: the awareness of this historical era, of this unknown, is very unsettling. 
But it is what makes Hong Kong Hong Kong. 
The one thing that has changed quite a bit in the last few years is that people are looking at specifically what makes Hong Kong Hong Kong."
Over the last 150 years, Hong Kong has been ruled mostly by plumed, beribboned and brocaded emissaries from London who, over the decades, were buttressed by legions of mostly second-rate British bureaucrats (Filth, as they've been known: Failed in London, Try Hong Kong), all in the service of the great British trading houses. 
Nowhere in their thinking was there much room for Hong Kong's local population, whom until recent memory were barred from the clubs, management suites and halls of government. 
British colonial culture here consisted largely of Chinese seascapes by British artists, and portraits, traveling string quartets and the Christmas pantomime, which more often than not poked fun at local ways.
To the colonialists, and the foreign traders and bankers who followed them, this was Hong Kong's culture. 
But here, as Hong Kong grew from a cluster of villages to one of the world's foremost economies, the territory's culture evolved in ways neither completely Chinese nor mimetically British -- in ways that were distinctly Hong Kong, suffused by the transient nature of life here and by the influx of millions of refugees fleeing Communism, and epitomized by a language that emerged at some distance from that spoken just over the fence in China.
Now, with China resuming sovereignty of Hong Kong in less than five months, many of Hong Kong's leading artists are contemplating a future littered with more unknowns than certainties. 
Questions of artistic freedom, sources of financing, the looming shadow of mainland artistry, whether state-sponsored or not, all linger on a horizon that has grown startlingly close. 
And while some artists continue to work unruffled by the thought of impending Chinese suzerainty, others find the prospect threatening, not only because of the censorship and pressures so prevalent on the mainland but especially because the nurturing of an indigenous culture and art scene is so very recent and, in the eyes of some, so very fragile.
"Part of the colonial strategy," argues Oscar Ho Hing-kay, an artist who has moved gracefully from sculpture to drawing in charcoal, "has been to get people to make money. 
This has been the whole model of educational philosophy here. 
Look at how insignificant art courses are here."
(Hong Kong does not possess a full-time academy.) "And the nice thing about this for colonial rule is that you don't ask ideological questions. 
You just make money. 
Art is about asking questions, being rebellious."
Leafing through heavy ivory-colored sheets dark with charcoal images of Hong Kong, cornered with colophons in a dense tumble of Chinese -- not the Chinese of China, but the Chinese of Hong Kong -- Mr. Ho fingers a recent work. 
Under a heavy sky with a hint of central Hong Kong in the distance, two flattened figures peer from beneath large boulders, a work he titles "Strange Rock Disease."
In a choppy, vernacular Cantonese that falls on local ears the way Brooklynese may sound in Los Angeles, a colophon explains: "A bizarre epidemic has broken out in a place near Tuen Mun. 
Those struck down by it have a rock that grows out of their back. 
The rock gets bigger and bigger until it crushes the patient to death. 
It seems like this disease is spreading. 
The medical authorities are so worried that they've classified this disease as highly confidential."
This drawing, part of Mr. Ho's series "Tales Around Town," is drawn from the cornucopia of local myths and folk tales that he has gathered in his explorations of Hong Kong, or simply in his daily encounters. 
"The 'Tales Around Town' are almost like a diary," he explains. 
"You hear them, and you come home and do them."
Mr. Chang of Hanart Gallery, who has displayed Mr. Ho's work, sees in it disturbing images of life and imagination. 
"They're more like paranoia and nightmares about Hong Kong," he suggests. 
"They are like folk ghost stories; he actually didn't make them up. 
There is one in particular that is very dark, this one of the rumor about the stone lion in front of the old Bank of China that devours people."
"Stone Lion Turns Into Demon" is the fifth in the "Tales" series, a blackened, representation of a stone-hewn lion stretching suddenly from its pedestal to snare a passer-by. 
"One of the pair of stone lions outside the old Bank of China building in Central has turned into a demon and has been attacking people around midnight. 
Those in the know say that if you pour red paint on the lion's head it can stop the lion demon."
Despite the apparent blatancy of the symbolism at work in this piece (since 1949, the Bank of China has been Beijing's most prominent granite presence in this British colony), Mr. Ho emphasizes the oral taletelling of the work that is imbedded in Hong Kong life. 
"This is Hong Kong mythology," he says, "twisted around."
Visions of Meaning From a Windowless Room
Gaylord Chan, a snowdrift of white hair pushed back from his face, squeezed past a table of earnest children raptly brushing ideographs onto large sheets of paper and padded into a windowless room bathed by fluorescent tubes. 
Easels with unfinished canvases crowded together, stacks of stretched canvases tipped against walls hung with framed and frameless paintings.
"This is where I work," he said, his hand flitting over the jumble before him. 
From this brightly lighted cave, Hong Kong's eldest, and perhaps its most important, artist has produced a formidable oeuvre. 
But it is not his paintings that have paid the bills; it is the gaggle of children in the front rooms who come to his school for art and calligraphy, as well as older students.
His paintings now are large, boldly defined acrylics on canvas, abstract shapes that suggest urban life and passions. 
The local critic Tsong-zung Chang wrote that Mr. Chan's canvases "are inspired by the mundane signs and symbols of the city: neon lights, billboards, traffic signs."
"These images speak to him," the review continued. 
"They are suggestive of special meanings and hidden messages, secrets unbeknown to the graphic artists who created them."
They show a world that Mr. Chan and many of his colleagues see as destined to be transformed. 
Mr. Chan contends that artists, and the art scene in Hong Kong, will inevitably change under Chinese rule. 
"The audience will change to some extent," he says. 
"Some artists will respond to that. 
But those artists who do art for the sake of art, they wouldn't care less. 
Some will be influenced by what comes from the north, of course. 
If Hong Kong were suddenly taken by Italians, you would see change in that direction."
A Return to Roots To Get Ready for Change
Yet other artists, like Lucia Cheung, stress the Chinese roots of their work, roots inherent in the wash of Chinese cultural and social forces. 
Although she trained in Italy, Ms. Cheung gradually moved in the last decade or so from a distinctly Western style in her paintings to more discernibly Chinese overtones. 
"I found more and more I cling to Chinese work," she explains, showing a visitor through a range of her work hung in her vast apartment. 
"I found something that is so intimate, something more satisfying. 
There's a lot to say through a flower, a petal. 
You can also write down a poem. 
In Chinese painting it is not the process, but afterward. 
Maybe because I am Chinese."
From a long series of somber ink-wash paintings of austere, virtually lifeless landscapes huddled under scowling skies -- paintings reflecting deep angst over the death of her only son -- Ms. Cheung has in the last year or so produced a series of witty paintings of Hong Kong on gold-flecked handmade paper, pondering in many cases the territory's return to Chinese sovereignty. 
One, titled "Meeting as Usual," depicts Hong Kong's skyline and race track, with stylized Tang horses on the track, all suggesting normal life. 
Yet the sky in the scene is the red-starred ceiling of Beijing's Great Hall of the People, the vast hall where the Chinese Communist Party meets every five years.
The advent of Chinese rule is but one constraint facing artists in Hong Kong, according to Ms. Cheung. More troubling in some ways, she feels, is an esthetic indifference to Hong Kong's own artists, a feeling that the only thing of value in Hong Kong is money and how it is made.
"Before, nobody cared about art in Hong Kong," she explains. 
"Now it's changing a bit. 
But people pay much more attention to imported art. 
Local art is not good enough."
"Certainly artists in China face more difficulties than we do," she says. 
"In Hong Kong we are so free. 
There's no lack of materials. 
But you don't have the space, the atmosphere that gives you encouragement. 
Hong Kong is a British colony. 
We are so free to receive everything. 
But you must be wise enough to chose what is good for you. 
To find the balance is difficult. 
You need to look for your identity."
Â 
On an Open Stage, a Wealth of Styles
At a gallery and theater space called the Fringe, its director, Benny Chia, insisted that the diversity of artistic impulse and creativity, whether on stage or in galleries, were both important expressions of Hong Kong's identity and a vibrant sign of a blossoming, independent culture.
Indeed, the Fringe, a tiny gallery and a somewhat battered stage in one of the few surviving colonial buildings in the high-rent Central district, is the one place in Hong Kong where artists, whether widely known or not, or playwrights, whether working on first plays or on a string of stage successes, can display their work.
But with Chinese rule looming, Mr. Chia wonders what the landscape for artists will look like in six months. 
"It must occur to every artist whether there will be the same degree of freedom after 1997," he says. 
"We know you can create impressive works of art in the most repressive environment. 
But as far as I can tell, the Government has no wish to close its doors on the rest of the world."
On the other hand, Mr. Chia argues, "There are a number of things Hong Kong will benefit from after 1997. 
Psychologically, you will feel like you belong to a larger space. 
In vision, Hong Kong is a very small place. 
People will start to look at what you can do with China."
Mr. Chang, of Hanart, contends that Hong Kong artists will continue to face obstacles simply because of the kind of society Hong Kong is. 
"In Hong Kong, artists are really an underground," he says. 
"Nobody buys their work. 
Nobody is interested in their work. 
Nobody takes them seriously. 
There is no art scene in Hong Kong, like you have in New York. 
The real reason is, Hong Kong is an emigre society. 
Most people consider the real native culture China, not here. 
'True' Chinese art must be from the mainland."
Â 
A Focus on Home While Looking Ahead
Nonetheless, the growth of Hong Kong's indigenous cultural expression does seem to be well rooted. 
Although a product of British theatrical efforts, the Chung Ying Theater Company under its new artistic director and its first Chinese director, Ko Tin-lung, has dumped Shakespeare in favor of the works of local playwrights like Emily Cheng, Cheung Tat-ming and, most often, Mr. Ko's own prodigious output.
A former actor who worked for a time in the United States, Mr. Ko returned to Hong Kong in 1989 and was named Chung Ying's artistic director in 1993. 
In an early-20th-century red-brick colonial building rimmed with graceful arcades, Mr. Ko puts his 17 professional actors through their paces for his newest production, "A Chronicle of Lights and Shadows," a play exploring the frenzied history of Hong Kong's film industry.
Written in the Cantonese dialect of Hong Kong, the play follows the career of a sometimes working, sometimes out-of-work assistant director, and her loves and betrayals as the film industry alternately soars and swoons.
Despite his central focus on Hong Kong themes, Mr. Ko admits that Hong Kong's internationalism demands some foreign threads. 
"I think we do focus very much on developing new playwrights and new plays," he offers. 
"However I think we have to keep in contact with the world. 
I do think theater is a global village."
A global village perhaps, but one that reaches the stage of Chung Ying very deliberately in Cantonese.
"There's a controversy about whether we should perform in Mandarin after 1997," says Mr. Ko, referring to the official dialect of China. 
"This is an issue. 
Of course you could have two versions of a play. 
But some people say that if you want to retain your identity, you must perform in Cantonese. 
I don't think Chung Ying will have Mandarin versions of its plays."
He laughs and then adds, "Very practically, my actors don't speak Mandarin."
Â 
Looking at China With Hope and Dread
Although his plays and those he commissions are hardly political, Mr. Ko feels that Chinese rule does pose risks for Hong Kong artists. 
"I think whether we have problems in '97 or not, we will still do what we are doing. 
I think it is an artistic choice. 
If I chose a certain playwright and the play had a sensitive political issue in it, I would support it. 
I do think we in Hong Kong are quite concerned about freedom of expression."
Even closer to the bone, though, is the potential to undermine artistic freedom by withholding government financing. 
Corporate support of the arts is almost unheard-of in Hong Kong. 
Rather, the arts are heavily subsidized by the Government; the Chung Ying company in particular receives about $1 million a year. 
Mr. Ko worries that this financing could be vulnerable to political pressure. 
"In Hong Kong, about 95 percent of local arts activities are either directly or indirectly supported by the Government," he said.
As the cadence of China's march toward Hong Kong grows louder, this territory's almost newborn, and admittedly fragile, art world wonders about the future, as does the rest of the territory. 
And while there seems little that any individual artist is doing to prepare for the raising of China's red flag, there is a general certainty that Hong Kong is different from China, and different from everywhere else.
"We really don't have any contact, emotional or otherwise, with China, with communist China," explains Oscar Ho, the artist who draws local myths. 
"Now, this baby-boom generation here is at its prime just as Hong Kong goes to China."
"We love to see the end of colonialism," exudes Mr. Ho, his boyish, somewhat lopsided grin cleaving his face. 
"We rejoice. 
But at the same time, we dread the return to China. 
So, you see, with this complexity, things are not black-and-white."

text:

Further stepping up its military pressure on Taiwan, China said tonight that it would close a huge swath of the Taiwan Strait on Tuesday to conduct "live fire" exercises with naval ships and warplanes as a series of missile tests neared completion.
It will be the first time that China has tried to close such a large portion of the international waterway between Taiwan and the mainland.
The announcement raised immediate questions of whether Beijing was challenging the right of passage by United States naval vessels through the sensitive area.
A United States Navy battle group led by the aircraft carrier Nimitz traversed the Taiwan Strait on Dec. 
19, and Clinton Administration officials have hinted in recent days that they may be considering additional transits by American warships through the strait.
[The White House and Pentagon, which have repeatedly condemned Chinese missile tests close to Taiwan, had no immediate comment. 
A Clinton Administration official said the new exercises had been expected and would probably not hinder shipping. 
"According to the shipping companies, it's only a minor inconvenience," the official said.]
On Friday, China began ballistic missile tests within a few dozen miles of two of Taiwan's major ports, Keelung and Kaohsiung. 
Three Chinese M-9 missiles have been fired into the zones so far without incident.
The announcement of new maneuvers was issued by the official New China News Agency. 
"From March 12 to 20, 1996, the Chinese People's Liberation Army will conduct naval and air force exercises," it said. 
"For the sake of safety, the Chinese Government requests the governments of relevant countries" to notify "ships and aircraft of their countries not to enter the said sea area and airspace during this period."
In Taiwan today, President Lee Teng-hui said the expanding war games would not interfere with Taiwan's first direct presidential election, on March 23.
"The aim of Communist China's exercises is to interfere with the elections and to reduce the votes of the President," he said in a televised address. 
Mr. Lee is expected to win easily but has said he would like at least 50 percent of the vote.
China has been seeking to weaken Mr. Lee's hold on power because it suspects that his drive for greater international recognition for Taiwan, which Beijing views as a renegade province, is a strategy to undermine the official "one China" policy of his Nationalist Party.
"In my recollection, China has never gone this far toward closing the strait," said James R. Lilley, a former Ambassador to China and now a fellow at the American Enterprise Insitute in Washington. 
"It is a challenge, because they are beginning to take us on in international waters, and that is pretty dangerous."
Kenneth G. Lieberthal, a China scholar at the University of Michigan, said the new set of exercises represented an "upping of the ante" against Taiwan.
"If you look at what China has done to date," he said, "it seems to have been very well thought through."
He said the Chinese military had "created the maximum sense of pressure and alarm on Taiwan without exceeding the boundaries of what a sovereign state is allowed to do."
"So without a blockade," he continued, "without attacking any shipping, China has raised the temperature without violating international law. 
And these actions suggest it is playing a very tough game."
The Chinese security authorities today expelled two Taiwanese journalists who had been detained on Thursday on China's southern coast. 
They were accused of "illegally" videotaping "military targets."
China identified the journalists as Sui An-teh and Chuang Chi-wei, a cameraman, both of Taiwan Television, and said they had been admitted to China to cover the annual session of the National People's Congress in Beijing.

A senior Republican Senator said today that the White House knew as early as 1995 that China might try to influence American elections, a year earlier than White House aides say they were warned.
The lawmaker, Senator Orrin G. Hatch of Utah, said that despite those warnings, the White House continued to rely on fund-raisers who had close ties to Beijing.
Senator Hatch said that beginning in 1995, the Federal Bureau of Investigation had told the State Department, the Central Intelligence Agency, the Justice Department, the House and Senate Intelligence Committees and at least seven lawmakers that China would try to funnel illegal contributions to Congressional races in 1996.
"They knew about it," Mr. Hatch, the chairman of the Judiciary Committee and a member of the Intelligence Committee, said on the CBS News program "Face the Nation."
The White House immediately denied Mr. Hatch's accusations, in unusually sharp language.
"His information is contrary to what is being communicated to me and contrary to what I've briefed you," Michael D. McCurry, the White House spokesman, told reporters today. 
"I suspect that this is another case of a Senator hyperventilating on a Sunday talk show. 
But if he has information or knowledge, factual knowledge of that, he should come forth and produce it."
The F.B.I. warned two officials of the White House National Security Council in June 1996 that China might be trying to influence Congressional races, but President Clinton has said that he and his senior staff were not told. 
The White House and the F.B.I. blamed each other last week for the embarrassing lapse.
The F.B.I.'s top spokesman, John Collingwood, said today that the bureau would not comment on Mr. Hatch's accusations. 
But Mr. Hatch has received sensitive briefings from the F.B.I. on China's connection to the 1996 elections.

It was unclear from Mr. Hatch's remarks which agencies and lawmakers the F.B.I. warned in 1995 and which it warned in 1996, and if any of them ever told Mr. Clinton. One lawmaker who was warned in 1996, Representative Nancy Pelosi, Democrat of California, has also said that F.B.I. agents first approached her in 1991 or 1992 to caution her that China might try to funnel money into her campaign.
Senator Arlen Specter, a Pennsylvania Republican who headed the Intelligence Committee in 1995 and 1996, said today on the ABC News program "This Week" that he was told by the F.B.I. in 1996 that "the Chinese were looking to co-opt the Congress and state legislatures."
Mr. Hatch declined to say exactly what he thought the Administration knew in 1995. 
"I can't tell you the exact findings, because that would disclose too much here," Mr. Hatch said.

Mr. Hatch also criticized Democrats for relying on questionable fund-raisers with Asian connections, notably John Huang, a former Commerce Department and Democratic National Committee official, when there were clear warnings from the F.B.I. that the Chinese were trying to buy influence.
