file: Sites for the Socially Conscious.txt
text:
ï»¿
THERE are many Web sites devoted to criticizing industries and companies. 
Many are of the ''Wal-Mart Watch'' variety (walmartwatch.com) and are decidedly one-sided.
There are also services like the Dow Jones sustainability indexes (www.sustainability-indexes.com), and the many sites for ''socially conscious'' investors. 
These, according to a recent article in The Harvard Business Review, amount to a ''cacophony of self-appointed scorekeepers'' that make up a ''jumble of largely meaningless rankings, allowing almost any company to boast that it meets some measure of social responsibility.''
Now comes Do The Right Thing (dotherightthing.com), a site introduced this month. 
It works like Digg.com in having users make submissions, which are then voted on by readers. 
''All are welcome,'' the site announces, including ''people who buy the stuff, who make the stuff, who live in communities where the stuff is made, and who have transcendent abilities to speak on behalf of that which cannot speak (like wildlife and the environment).''
Once companies are submitted, they are evaluated for 60 days. 
Users submit evidence for or against the company, votes are tallied, and a ''social performance'' score is given. 
After the initial evaluation, the score can still change with further submissions and voting.
''Its important to create a system that has a balance of accountability and free form,'' Ryan Mickle, the site's founder, told David Cohn of newassignment.net. 
It is based on Digg, he said, because ''it's a balance between a wiki and a forum, and neither [alone] would have worked for Do The Right Thing.''
This may not yield a fully balanced assessment of every company, but only time will tell that. 
While it seems at least possible that most users will be predisposed to take a negative view of a given company, the site is open to people with all points of view.
''Google does EVIL by allowing censorship in China,'' is the headline on one recent submission, which referred to an article on TechCrunch.com. 
But the article was about a Google founder, Sergey Brin, recently expressing regret over Google's earlier decision to allow China to censor its search results. 
When several other users pointed this out to the submitter, he referred to a different article about Chinese censorship that referred to Google only peripherally. 
Most users gave the post a thumbs-down, and it ended up with a below-zero score. 
Still, as of Thursday, 67 users had voted positively on the submission, essentially agreeing that it should count against Google.
One user questions the very nature of the site, asserting that it is based on false premises. 
Many things companies do, this user noted, have both good and bad consequences. 
Should complicated matters really be measured with a simple thumbs-up or down?
''Is outsourcing really not the right thing?'' he asked. 
''Are you sure?''
The user concluded, ''I recommend using and posting to this site with trepidation.''
That, and perhaps not writing off those ''self-appointed scorekeepers'' so quickly.CREDIT SCORE MISTAKES -- People trying to repair their credit often operate from ignorance of how credit scores are determined. 
For them, the Simple Dollar (thesimpledollar.com) offers the ''10 Common Tactical Mistakes When Dealing With The Credit Score Blues.''
For instance, canceling old credit cards is not always a good idea, because the length of a person's credit history is a big factor on a credit score. 
Also, the site advises, ''if you have balances on other cards, canceling an old credit card can also worsen your debt ratio, which makes up 30 percent of your score.''DEDUCTIVE REASONING -- Bankrate.com offers the wild and the wacky from the world of tax deductions. 
More than one person has tried to write off the cost of day care for a dog. 
One Amish man wanted to write off his buggy, on which he had spent about $1,000 to install dashboard lights, kickplates, a tinted windshield and a velvet interior. 
Not all offbeat deductions are illegal, though. 
One man successfully wrote off his comic-book collection because he wrote his doctoral thesis on the societal impact of comics. 
DAN MITCHELLComplete links are at nytimes.com/business.

file: Skype Text Is Monitored In China.txt
text:
ï»¿
SAN FRANCISCO -- A group of Canadian human-rights activists and computer security researchers has discovered a huge surveillance system in China that monitors and archives certain Internet text conversations that include politically charged words.
The system tracks text messages sent by customers of Tom-Skype, a joint venture between a Chinese wireless operator and eBay, the Web auctioneer that owns Skype, an online phone and text messaging service.
The discovery draws more attention to the Chinese government's Internet monitoring and filtering efforts, which created controversy this summer during the Beijing Olympics. 
Researchers in China have estimated that 30,000 or more ''Internet police'' monitor online traffic, Web sites and blogs for political and other offending content in what is called the Golden Shield Project or the Great Firewall of China.
The activists, who are based at Citizen Lab, a research group that focuses on politics and the Internet at the University of Toronto, discovered the surveillance operation last month. 
They said a cluster of eight message-logging computers in China contained more than a million censored messages. 
They examined the text messages and reconstructed a list of restricted words.
The list includes words related to the religious group Falun Gong, Taiwan independence and the Chinese Communist Party, according to the researchers. 
It includes not only words like democracy, but also earthquake and milk powder. 
(Chinese officials are facing criticism over the handling of earthquake relief and chemicals tainting milk powder.)
The list also serves as a filter to restrict text conversations. 
The encrypted list of words inside the Tom-Skype software blocks the transmission of those words and a copy of the message is sent to a server. 
The Chinese servers retained personal information about the customers who sent the messages. 
They also recorded chat conversations between Tom-Skype users and Skype users outside China. 
The system recorded text messages and Skype caller identification, but did not record the content of Skype voice calls.
In just two months, the servers archived more than 166,000 censored messages from 44,000 users, according to a report that was published on the Information Warfare Monitor Web site at the university.
The researchers were able to download and analyze copies of the surveillance data because the Chinese computers were improperly configured, leaving them accessible. 
The researchers said they did not know who was operating the surveillance system, but they said they suspected that it was the Chinese wireless firm, possibly with cooperation from Chinese police.
Independent executives from the instant message industry say the discovery is an indication of a spiraling computer war that is tracking the introduction of new communications technologies.
''I can see an arms race going on,'' said Pat Peterson, vice president for technology at Cisco's Ironport group, which provides messaging security systems. 
''China is one of the more wired places of the world and they are fighting a war with their populace.''
The Chinese government is not alone in its Internet surveillance efforts. 
In 2005, The New York Times reported that the National Security Agency was monitoring large volumes of telephone and Internet communications flowing into and out of the United States as part of the eavesdropping program, intended to hunt for evidence of terrorist activity, that President Bush approved after the Sept. 
11 attacks.
The researchers said their discovery contradicted a public statement made by Skype executives in 2006 after the content filtering of the Skype conversations was reported. 
At the time the company said that the conversations were protected and private.
The Citizen Lab researchers issued a report on Wednesday, which details an analysis of data on the servers. 
''We were able to download millions of messages that identify users,'' said Ronald J. Deibert, an associate professor of political science at the University of Toronto. 
''This is the worst nightmares of the conspiracy theorists around surveillance coming true. 
It's 'X-Files' without the aliens.''
Jennifer Caukin, an eBay spokeswoman, said, ''The security and privacy of our users is very important to Skype.''
But the company spoke to the accessibility of the messages, not their monitoring. 
''The security breach does not affect Skype's core technology or functionality,'' she said. 
''It exists within an administrative layer on Tom Online servers. 
We have expressed our concern to Tom Online about the security issue and they have informed us that a fix to the problem will be completed within 24 hours.''
EBay had no comment on the monitoring.
Other American companies have been caught in controversy after cooperating with Chinese officials. 
In 2005, Yahoo supplied information to the Chinese authorities, who then sentenced a reporter, Shi Tao, to 10 years in prison for leaking what the government considered state secrets. 
The company said it was following Chinese law.
EBay created the joint venture with the Tom Group, which holds the majority stake, in September 2005. 
The Tom Group itself was founded in October 1999 as a joint venture among Hutchison Whampoa, Cheung Kong Holdings and other investors. 
In its annual report this year, the Tom Group, based in Hong Kong, said that the number of Tom-Skype registered users had reached 69 million in the first half of 2008 and revenue had increased tenfold in the last year.
The researchers stumbled upon the surveillance system when Nart Villeneuve, a senior research fellow at Citizen Lab, began using an analysis tool to monitor data that was generated by the Tom-Skype software, which is meant to permit voice and text conversations from a personal computer. 
By observing the data generated by the program, he determined that each time he typed a particular swear word into the text messaging program an encrypted message was sent to an unidentified Internet address.
To his surprise, the coded messages were being stored on Tom Online computers. 
When he examined the machines over the Internet, he discovered that they had been misconfigured and that the computer directories were readable with a simple Web browser.
One directory on each machine contained a series of files in which the messages, in encrypted form, were being deposited. 
Hunting further, Mr. Villeneuve soon found a file that contained the numerical key that permitted him to decode the encrypted log files.
What he uncovered were hundreds of files, each containing thousands of records of messages that had been captured and then stored by the filtering software. 
The records revealed Internet addresses and user names as well as message content. 
Also stored on the computers were calling records for Skype voice conversations containing names and in some cases phone numbers of the calling parties.
Mr. Villeneuve downloaded the messages, decrypted them and used machine translation software to convert the Chinese messages to English. 
He then used word frequency counts to identify the key words that were flagging the messages. 
The exact criteria used by the filtering software is still unclear, he said, because some messages on the servers contained no known key word. 
He said that in addition to capturing the Skype messages sent between Tom-Skype users, international conversations were recorded as well, meaning that users of standard Skype software outside China were also vulnerable to the surveillance system when they had text conversations with Chinese users.

file: So Many Stores, So Little Time and Money.txt
text:
ï»¿
BORSCHT. It's not a dish many people associate with Hong Kong, and probably not what most would order for dinner their first night in this former British colony. 
Roast pork, sure. 
A whole fish steamed with ginger, absolutely. 
But beet soup?
It hardly seems Chinese.
Yet borscht is certainly Hong Kongese, a not uncommon sight on dinner menus and an essential component of a meal at Queen's Cafe, the dim, cozy, wood-paneled restaurant where I spent one Friday evening earlier this year. 
Opened in 1952 by White Russian emigres and immortalized in the 1991 Wong Kar-wai movie ''Days of Being Wild,'' the cafe was filled with a cross-section of Hong Kong: hip kids in black glasses and cowboy boots, office workers embarking on the weekend, and first-daters, all tucking into roast chicken, rib-eye steaks, shrimp cocktail and bowls of that tangy borscht.
I was there alone, and so I brooded over my prix fixe meal of borscht and ''sharshlik'' fillet -- garlicky and a little overcooked, just the way I like it -- which cost 128 Hong Kong dollars, or $16.45 at 7.77 Hong Kong dollars to the U.S. dollar, plus a pair of Carlsberg beers for 35 Hong Kong dollars each. 
Dining with oneself for company can be difficult in any city, more so in one as jam-packed with human beings as Hong Kong: seven million inhabit the 425 square miles of this special administrative region of China, more than two-thirds of which is rural land or protected greenspace. 
Don't think sardines; think transistors on the latest Intel chip.
Adding to the challenge was my two-day budget of $500, including lodging, which in Hong Kong can go a long way -- or nowhere at all. 
Fleabags abound, noodle soups cost next to nothing, and trendy, disposable clothes are worn by everyone under the age of 40. 
At the other end of the spectrum is the Hong Kong of the bankers, the developers, the movie stars: InterContinentals and Mandarin Orientals, glittering Louis Vuitton boutiques, and private clubs whose ''Members Only'' plaques glare at you from semisecret entrances to Art Deco skyscrapers.
I wanted to live that life, but on a rickshaw-puller's salary, and so far, I'd succeeded. 
I had checked into the Cosmopolitan, a new hotel whose clean, modern rooms occupy the former premises of the Xinhua News Agency, China's official news outlet. 
The Cosmopolitan and its infinitesimally cheaper sibling, the Cosmo, lay across the street from the Happy Valley racetrack, about 10 minutes from the Causeway Bay subway station.
Reserving two nights through hotels.com set me back $176.12, and the remainder I'd calculated at approximately 2,600 Hong Kong dollars, about $334, of which I'd spent almost nothing. 
Lunch had been a noodle soup with roast pork and wontons (23 Hong Kong dollars), and the subway trip to Central, Hong Kong's downtown (5 Hong Kong dollars), put me within walking distance of the Peak Tram, the funicular (30 Hong Kong dollars round trip) that for 118 years has heaved sightseers up steep slopes to Victoria Peak. 
Or, rather, to the Peak Galeria, where I bought bags of dried mangoes and spicy dried cuttlefish (10 Hong Kong dollars each; the latter was buy-one-get-one-free!) before marching to the real peak.
The 20-minute hike along winding Mount Austin Road took me past ritzy apartment complexes and the peaceful, deep-green Victoria Peak Garden before topping out in a plaza 1,818 feet above sea level. 
Up there, families strolled paths lined with mountain laurels and azaleas, while I looked down on the city: the 50-story apartment buildings arising from the hills; the misty harbor, stocked with ferries and container ships; the black kites wheeling lazily in the sky, sighting a rodent dinner far below.
Later that day, I received a call from Tim, a childhood friend who had been living in Hong Kong for several years. 
We met for a drink at Opia, a dark bar-restaurant that would not be out of place in New York. 
Its prices, too, struck me as familiar: 132 Hong Kong dollars for my South gin martini meant, alas, that one would be my limit. 
Still, there was always Saturday.
SHOPPING in Hong Kong is more than a pastime; it's an undertaking, a scholarly pursuit. 
There was no way I could hit every shopping district in a mere 24 hours, but I was determined to do my best. 
I began with Hollywood Road, stopping first for an airy scrambled-egg-and-corned-beef sandwich (33 Hong Kong dollars with a cup of coffee) at Tsui Wah, a hectic plastic-boothed diner that serves fish-ball noodle soup alongside baked pork chops with tomato sauce.
One of the oldest streets in Hong Kong, Hollywood Road is famous for its antiques shops, art galleries and the boutique zones of Soho and Noho. 
But the very first store I walked into was of more recent vintage: G.O.D., or Goods of Desire, a minichain that applies Hong Kong street style to Ikea-like home decor, clothing and stationery. 
Here were pajamas printed with classified ads from Chinese newspapers, Lucite frames bearing stock shots of people from the 1960's, and rather comfy-looking sofas that might have been a tad difficult to ship back home. 
(Dear G.O.D., please open a New York branch.)
On I soldiered, glancing at the contemporary Vietnamese paintings at Arch Angel Gallery (53-55 Hollywood Road) and sampling the premium men's denim at Jeanious before happening upon Wattis Fine Art, which was the host of a show of Arthur Hacker's pen-and-ink drawings of 1970's Hong Kong.
Mr. Hacker, a British writer and artist who has lived in the city since 1967, renders street life with a strong, funny, simple line, carefully tracing the flower print on a hippie's shirt or the precarious-looking bamboo scaffolding still used on construction sites today. 
No catalog was available, and the drawings cost 8,500 Hong Kong dollars and up, but a lithograph of his ''Evolution of the Hong Kong Bar Girl'' was a relative bargain at 500 Hong Kong dollars; I snapped one up.
Lunchtime!
I met my friend Fed at Isola, a trendy Italian restaurant with a magnificent harbor view and an equally magnificent set menu (218 Hong Kong dollars): an antipasto buffet (from olives to octopus salad and beyond), a main course (gnochetti al ragu, red mullet) and a dessert bar (panna cotta, fruit salad, creme brulee, chocolate mousse, apple tart ).
Over the gut-busting meal, Fed, a consummate shopper, gave me advice: Skip the glossy shops of Central, and make for Tsim Sha Tsui in Kowloon, Paterson Street in Causeway Bay, and the area around 3 Pacific Place in Wan Chai.
I splurged on a scenic cruise across the harbor on the Star Ferry, dropping 2.20 Hong Kong dollars for an upper-deck seat (the lower deck is 1.70). 
The ferry, in operation since 1888, has the advantage of being fast as well as atmospheric, and landed me in Tsim Sha Tsui in under 10 minutes.
For Tsim Sha Tsui bargains, there is one destination: the third floor of the Silvercord Center, where the I.T. 
Sale Shop has off-season fashions from brands like Paul Smith and Cacharel at up to 90 percent off. 
I found an A.P.C. suit down from 6,199 Hong Kong dollars to 3,100 -- cheap, but not quite frugal.
A few flights down, however, was a warren of stores operated by I.T., a fashion conglomerate with 230 shops across Greater China. 
Some sell international brands; others offer I.T.'s own labels, of which Izzue has become my favorite, seeming to take my best memories of the Gap and Urban Outfitters and give them an amusing Hong Kong twist. 
I walked out with lightweight olive-green pants and a rumpled blue-striped button-down (698 Hong Kong dollars).
After a restorative nap at the Cosmopolitan, I went in search of 3 Pacific Place and Flea n Cents, (34-38 Queen's Road East, Wan Chai) whose world-spanning collection of vintagetoys, furniture and tchotchkes Fed was certain I'd love. 
It was closed. 
A nearby Illy Cafe, however, was open, and sold a wide array of CD's -- classic reggae and soul, the new Neko Case and ''Xiang Gang Electric,'' a compilation of local D.J.'s, which I bought for 128 Hong Kong dollars.
Time for dinner. 
Again, I was alone. 
(My friend Tim works for a large newsweekly based in Hong Kong, and a breaking story kept him in the office.) But Xi Yan Sweets, a Chinese restaurant whose up-and-coming chef, Jacky Yu, takes cues from Southeast Asia, knows how to treat the solo diner. 
My waitress endorsed my selections -- a smoked-duck noodle soup and fried radish cakes with XO sauce -- with a welcome enthusiasm. 
The room was stark red and white, with high ceilings, marble-topped tables and exposed ductwork, and I slurped my noodles (smoked duck tastes surprisingly like really good ham) undisturbed.
After dinner (154 Hong Kong dollars), I heard from Fed. 
He and some friends were meeting in Lan Kwai Fong, Central's hopping night-life district; would I like to join?
Yes, I said, then changed my mind. 
There is something quite wonderful about walking the streets of a megalopolis at night, with lamps glowing in the apartments above and a million dramas taking place as people close up shop, get drunk, argue on cellphones, and neck quietly in the dark corners of empty office plazas.
Sunday morning brought a hunger that reminded me of when, at the age of 18 months (so my parents recount), I stood up in my chair at a slow-to-serve restaurant and cried out, ''I want Chinese food!
Give me Chinese food!''
No more fusion -- I wanted the classics. 
I wanted dim sum. 
Make that Dim Sum, a retro-traditional dumpling parlor 15 minutes' walk from the Cosmopolitan, past a series of cemeteries -- Muslim, Roman Catholic, Protestant, Parsee and Hindu -- whose multilingual tombstones reminded me of Hong Kong's tourism slogan: ''Asia's World City.''
Dim Sum was also directly across the street from Tim's apartment; he woke up just as I arrived and joined me for two kinds of shrimp dumplings, fried pork dumplings, roast pork buns, chive boxes and -- because I'd heard Calvin Trillin loves it -- sweet fried milk. 
The little plates fulfilled that 30-year-old hunger, but, since the bill was just 91 Hong Kong dollars each, left me with one last dilemma: How to spend the last 400 or so in my pocket before my flight?
Dim Sum's neighborhood, Tim informed me, happens to be known for its foot-massage parlors. 
The name Foot Joy intrigued me, and for the next 50 minutes (and for 198 Hong Kong dollars), my feet underwent a process that left them soft, limp and close to joyful.
In fact, they felt so good that before I knew it, I had walked back to Happy Valley, where a series of horse races from Macao were being projected on a video screen. 
(Live races run Wednesdays.) I paid my entry fee of 5 Hong Kong dollars, and split my last 200 between two horses: Sea Treasure, a sure thing at 3.4-1, and Oh Great, the 99-1 long shot. 
One minute 50.3 seconds later, it was time to go home.

file: South Korea Cuts Interest Rate to 3_, a Record.txt
text:
ï»¿
South Korea's central bank on Thursday announced the deepest cut in interest in its history in an attempt to cushion its economy from the global downturn.
The announcement followed China's disclosure that its economic indicators for November showed the country's economy slowing much more rapidly than expected, increasing expectations that Beijing will accelerate efforts to bolster growth.
The Bank of Korea's cut on Thursday was its fourth in two months, and took its key interest rate down a full percentage point to 3 percent, a much bigger cut than economists had predicted. 
The bank's governor, Lee Seong-tae, said South Korea was ''on the verge of an emergency situation that may need more drastic policy,'' Reuters reported.
Central banks around the world have delivered a cascade of cuts as the speed of the economic slowdown -- and outright recession in the United States, Canada, Japan and much of Europe -- becomes apparent.
In Taiwan, the central bank cut its main rate by 0.75 points, to 2 percent, on Thursday, the fifth such move in two months. 
The rate cut, which was announced after the close of the market, was the biggest in 26 years.
In China, data for November showed a sharp fall in consumer price inflation -- to 2.4 percent, from 4 percent the previous month -- as demand fell in line with slowing growth. 
On Wednesday, trade data showed import growth dropping sharply and exports shrinking for the first time in years as domestic and overseas demand shrank.
The Chinese data added to the sense of worry about the extent to which Asia's economies are being affected by the economic downturn that was set off last year by the subprime mortgage crisis in the United States. 
It also dashed hopes that China's economy could act as a buffer by taking up the slack from the slumping United States, Europe and Japan.
China's double-digit growth is expected to slow to around 8 percent next year, and growth across the region is also forecast to decline as demand in Europe and the United States and within the region shrinks.
The Asian Development Bank on Thursday said it expected growth in Asia's developing nations to slow to 5.8 percent next year, from 9 percent in 2007 and a projected 6.9 percent this year. 
The estimates echoed those issued by the World Bank earlier this week.
Jong-Wha Lee, head of the Asian Development Bank's s office of regional economic integration, said that ''2009 is likely to be a very difficult year for developing Asia.''
The bank called on governments to step up efforts to bolster their economies. 
''While the region's economies and financial systems are fundamentally sound and appear better cushioned to withstand the immediate effects of the crisis than in other parts of the world,'' the bank said it was concerned ''that the global credit crunch is now spilling over into domestic banking systems, squeezing funding resources for corporate investment.''

file: Spaghetti Stir-Fry and Hambagoo_ Japan Looks West.txt
text:
ï»¿
IN New York or Los Angeles, fans of Japanese cuisine can rattle off orders for uni and o-toro, or urbanely express a preference for soba over udon. 
But what about ''Napolitan,'' cooked spaghetti that is rinsed in cold water, then stir-fried with vegetables in ketchup?
Or ''menchi katsu,'' hamburger covered in bread crumbs and deep-fried?
Or ''omu rice,'' an omelet lying over a mound of ketchup-flavored rice?
At once familiar and alien, these dishes may make Americans feel, with some justification, that they have wandered into a parallel culinary universe. 
All are standards of a style of Japanese cuisine known as yoshoku, or ''Western food,'' in which European or American dishes were imported and, in true Japanese fashion, shaped and reshaped to fit local tastes.
Today yoshoku is thoroughly Japanese. 
It is a staple of television cooking shows and mainstream magazines. 
The lines outside venerable upscale yoshoku restaurants here in Tokyo are as long as ever, mostly with older Japanese for whom yoshoku provided a first taste of a Western world they had not seen. 
Yoshoku restaurants are also a requisite of the trendiest new shopping districts, like Midtown and Roppongi Hills, where they cater to younger Japanese whose mothers made the food at home.
And yet it is virtually unknown to foreigners. 
The first Michelin guide to Tokyo, published in the fall of 2007, listed 150 restaurants; not one was a yoshoku establishment. 
Indeed, visitors to Japan seldom enter the places where yoshoku is served: homes, chain diners, family-owned neighborhood restaurants or upscale yoshoku establishments of long standing. 
Outside Japan, yoshoku is rarely seen except in former Japanese colonies like South Korea and Taiwan, which were introduced to Western cuisine through Japan.
Shiseido Parlor is a storied yoshoku establishment in the heart of Tokyo's Ginza district, a restaurant to which many Japanese make a pilgrimage at least once. 
But the restaurant, the flagship of what is now a chain, is rarely mentioned in Western travel guides, and few Westerners ever wander in.
''Probably this thing called 'yoshoku' is difficult to grasp from a foreigner's perspective,'' said Tatsuya Yokokawa, an executive at Shiseido Parlor. 
''If it's not traditional Japanese cuisine, and it's neither French nor Italian, they're thinking, What is it?
And so they're unlikely to give it a try.''
But the story of yoshoku goes beyond the familiar one of fusion cuisine. 
It sheds light on Japan's tumultuous modern history, from its traumatic early encounters with the West to its often uneasy embrace of Western values.
Yoshoku was born during Japan's Meiji Restoration, the period that followed this isolationist country's forced opening by America's so-called Black Ships in 1854. 
Japanese were dispatched to Europe and America to learn about Western laws, weapons and industry. 
They also brought back the cuisine. 
Shocked to discover how much shorter they were than Westerners, Japanese determined that they would catch up not only economically and militarily but also physically, by eating their food.
That desire survived at least until the 1970's, when a businessman named Den Fujita established McDonald's in Japan and claimed that its menu would make Japanese as tall and attractive as Americans.
''Japanese are poorly built because they eat rice,'' he said at the time. 
''We'll change that with hamburgers. 
After eating hamburgers for a thousand years, Japanese will even have blond hair.''
The yoshoku category is broad, and includes dishes that have become so integral to the diet that many Japanese wouldn't consider them Japanized Western food at all, but simply Japanese food.
Still, all yoshoku dishes have their roots in Western counterparts. 
A key ingredient or a step in the cooking has been altered, or violated outright, with surprisingly delicious results. 
Instead of being served as soon as it is cooked, Napolitan spaghetti is allowed to sit, then reheated and stir-fried with vegetables; it was the only pasta known to most Japanese until a couple of decades ago, when ketchup was still widely considered an Italian sauce. 
Done well, menchi katsu, bread crumb-covered ground beef, or tonkatsu, a thicker version of pork cutlet, are deep-fried but manage to remain juicy inside.
A demiglace sauce with tomato juice served over hashed beef was named hayashi sauce -- because the words sounded similar, by one theory, though a rival one suggests that it was the invention of a Mr. Hayashi. A stewlike curry with onions, potatoes and carrots, served over rice, became ''kare rice.''
Hamburgers were considered American food and called ''hambagah,'' but the yoshoku version was called ''hambagoo.''
(The burger was served without the bun and often covered with demiglace -- the real thing at expensive restaurants, but mostly out of a bottle elsewhere.) Au gratin dishes, breaded oysters and various croquettes -- cream of crab croquettes with white sauce is considered a classic -- rounded out the yoshoku menu.
Most yoshoku dishes can be accompanied by rice and eaten with chopsticks, although better yoshoku restaurants have silverware and an option offered only in this style of Japanese cuisine: ''rice or bread.''
The dishes come with traditional Western sauces, or their Japanized versions, like demiglace, white sauce, Worcestershire or ketchup.
The yoshoku menu has changed little over the decades, said Hiroshi Modegi, 40, whose grandfather founded Taimeiken, a famous yoshoku restaurant in Tokyo's Nihonbashi district, in 1931.
''Our customers want the old favorites,'' said Mr. Modegi, now the restaurant's head chef, explaining that nostalgia was a big part of yoshoku's appeal. 
''It's O.K. to change the menu once in a while, but not too much, because they're basically coming here to eat things like your standard omu rice.''
The standard fare, though, is fairly new, considering the stretch of Japan's history. 
For 1,200 years, an imperial edict banned the eating of meat because of a Japanese Buddhist belief that it was unclean. 
Fish was central to the Japanese diet, and meat was consumed furtively, only for medicinal purposes.
Then in 1872, the emperor lifted the ban.
''To catch up with and overtake the superior culture of the West, Emperor Meiji believed that eating habits had to be changed first,'' said Tetsu Okada, an expert on Japan's culinary culture and an author of a history on tonkatsu. 
''He told everyone to eat meat, and to get the ball rolling, ate it himself.''
The first Japanese to go overseas brought back dishes -- filled with meat, butter, unfamiliar spices and other ingredients utterly foreign to the Japanese diet -- that eventually became the basis of yoshoku. 
In contrast, Japan's neighbors, China and Korea, dealt with the threat from the West by first rejecting it. 
To this day, neither Chinese nor Korean cuisine has much Western influence.
Japan borrowed from Germany to modernize its legal system and from Britain to reform its military and industry. 
For the food that would eventually become yoshoku, it looked mostly to France. 
But the cuisine had other, unexpected sources. 
The Japanese Imperial Navy, which modeled itself after Britain's, is said to have introduced to Japanese of the late 19th century a dish popular among British naval officers: Indian curry, which eventually became the kare rice eaten in homes, school cafeterias and restaurants today.
''It wasn't curry from India, but curry from Europe, that we now find everywhere in this country,'' said Takeshi Ninomiya, the executive chef at Nakamuraya, a famous Indian curry restaurant in Tokyo. 
''This dish that came from Britain, and was considered Western food, was then assimilated here.''
Yoshoku's popularity reached its peak in the decades following World War II. 
For mothers, it was easier to prepare than traditional Japanese food. 
For children, a big treat was an ''okosama lunch,'' or ''kid's lunch,'' at a department store restaurant, consisting of small portions on a single plate of Napolitan spaghetti, hambagoo and ketchup-flavored rice with a little flag of a country like Switzerland or New Zealand on top.
Meanwhile, in the decades before most Japanese could afford to fly overseas, upscale yoshoku restaurants grew into symbols of the longed-for, glamorous Western world. 
The most famous, Shiseido Parlor, became a gathering place for artists, intellectuals and writers, and appeared in the work of many novelists, including Yasunari Kawabata and Yukio Mishima. 
Ordinary Japanese dined there, blowing a week's salary on a meal.
''Japanese who had never set their eyes on this thing called the Western world probably used their imagination and were able to see it in yoshoku,'' Mr. Yokokawa of Shiseido Parlor said.
Until the economic boom of the 1970's and 1980's, yoshoku was the only version of Western food known to many Japanese. 
Ingredients to make authentic French or Italian dishes were simply unavailable. 
Before expressions like ''pasta'' and ''al dente'' became known in Japan, there was only Napolitan spaghetti or ''spaghetti with meat sauce.''
That changed in the 1980's, when the yen grew so strong that Japan could import anything from anywhere. 
Restaurateurs from all over the world began gravitating here. 
Nowadays, in a neighborhood like Roppongi, you can find just about anything: French and Italian, American steaks, even Nigerian pounded yam and egusi soup.
But this does not mean yoshoku is in danger of disappearing. 
In fact, yoshoku dishes make up the bulk of the menus at Japan's biggest chain diners, or family restaurants, like Jonathan's, Royal Host and Denny's.
That's right: Denny's. 
Several years after arriving in Japan in the 1970's, Denny's gave up its American fare for a menu heavy on yoshoku. 
So, as some homesick Americans seeking comfort food have found out, a Denny's in Japan has no Grand Slam breakfasts or hamburgers.
But it's just the place to go when you want omu rice, Napolitan spaghetti and a hambagoo.

text:
ï»¿
Anne-Marie Slaughter, an international lawyer and the dean of the Woodrow Wilson School at Princeton University. 
She is the author âThe Idea that is America,â and she is spending this academic year in Shanghai.
There is a poster all over Shangai of a Downs Syndrome kid with a medal hanging around his neck covered in lipstick kisses â an ad for the Special Olympics that were held in Shanghai last month. 
Professor William Alford, my friend and former colleague from the Harvard Law School, was deeply involved in making the Special Olympics happen. 
I asked him to write up a post about it. 
He describes a sea-change in Chinaâs attitude toward disabled kids â kids who have long been hidden away were in the spotlight, applauded by a proud nation.
When I first began to study China almost 45 years ago, Chairman Mao had yet to launch the Cultural Revolution. 
There was no United States foreign investment in the Peopleâs Republic of China nor any PRC students in the United States. 
China was so inwardly focused that few, if any, in or outside the country could have imagined it becoming a global economic and military powerhouse.
Over these decades, Iâve had a front-row seat to epic changes, both hopeful and tragic. 
But nothing compares with the extraordinary events I witnessed this autumn through my pro bono work with the Special Olympics, an NGO headquartered in the United States that provides free sports, health, educational and family support services worldwide to persons with intellectual disabilities.
Special Olympics held its Summer World Games in Shanghai during the first half of October. 
It was the largest sporting event of any type held in the world this year, with some 7,500 athletes with intellectual disabilities from 165 nations having taken part. 
But far more noteworthy is the change it expresses and what that tells us about China.
The disabled have never been treated especially well in China, but that hardly distinguishes it from the history, at least until fairly recently, of every other nation. 
In the United States, for instance, it was Oliver Wendell Holmes, among the most revered of Supreme Court justices, who in upholding involuntary sterilization wrote that âthree generations of idiots is enough.â
The change that Iâm referring to was most dramatically manifest at the moment on October 2 when the Chinese team, composed of hundreds of
persons with intellectual disabilities, entered Shanghai Stadium. 
The crowd of more than 90,000 â including Chinaâs President and many of the Chinese worldâs most prominent public figures including the actor Jackie Chan, the cellist Yo-Yo Ma and the hoopster Yao Ming â exploded in prolonged exuberant standing applause. 
A population that had long been shunted aside or worse, now stood center stage, celebrated as the countryâs representatives before a national television audience running into the hundreds of millions. 
At least for that evening, they were the focal point of the intense pride that Chinese feel in their nationâs domestic resurgence and ascendance on the world stage. 
Having devoted a lifetime to scrutinizing the Middle Kingdom, I found it a profoundly moving experience.
Skepticism comes naturally among professional observers of China and one may be tempted to wonder whether there is anything more to the magic of the opening ceremony than a good show for officials intent on creating an image of humanitarian concern, or doing a dry run for the 2008 Beijing Olympics. 
Clearly, only time will tell whether the authorities are willing to do what it takes to ensure full inclusion for their tens of millions of disabled citizens and, as importantly, whether age-old attitudes among the populace have changed throughout this continent-sized land of 1.32 billion people. 
That said, there are reasons for optimism.
At the official level, busy as they were with final preparations for the 17th Party Congress, President Hu Jintao and other senior leaders, including Shanghai Party Secretary Xi Jinping, who was designated at that conclave as Huâs likely successor, devoted considerable time, personal prestige and resources to the World Games. 
The example of the usually earnest president happily embracing individuals with intellectual disabilities has more force in China than would its counterpart here, whatever the motivation.
But however one reads official actions, there was far more at play during the Games. 
Qin Yi, the Katharine Hepburn of China, and other eminent Chinese actors appeared on national television talk shows to discuss the challenges they faced in raising children with serious intellectual disabilities. 
Leaders from academe, business, sports and other sectors of Chinese life joined foreign counterparts in a day-long symposium designed to share best practices in their respective fields. 
Representatives of families of the intellectually disabled from across the nation convened to express powerfully their desire for better treatment. 
And, most importantly, individuals with intellectual disabilities spoke for themselves â on national television, at the aforementioned symposium and, it seemed, everywhere.
The circle of people touched was not limited to those directly affected by or professionally concerned with intellectual disability. 
More than 40,000 individuals â most, but not all, from China â served as volunteers, including thousands who housed total strangers from abroad and a valiant team from Shanghaiâs Fudan University and the University of North Carolina who pulled numerous all-nighters to ensure that every athleteâs accomplishments was available online for family and friends unable to attend. 
And hundreds of thousands of other Chinese took in the competitions, cheering on the athletes, whether they were from China or playing against the home team.
China, I dare say from the perspective of 40 yearsâ viewing, will never be the same.
William Alford is the Henry L. Stimson Professor, Vice Dean, and Director of East Asian Legal Studies, Harvard Law School and a member of the board of directors of Special Olympics.

file: Standoff Brings Calls to Boycott Chinese Goods.txt
text:
ï»¿
Kmart has received thousands of calls and e-mail messages from customers urging the discount retailer to stop buying so many of its shoes, fishing rods, T-shirts and stereos from China, prompting the company to warn Chinese diplomats that it will seek new suppliers unless the crew of an American surveillance aircraft is released promptly, company executives said today.
The complaints that have streamed into Kmart's customer service line in Troy, Mich., in recent days were an unprecedented and apparently spontaneous response to the overseas crisis, the executives said. 
Store managers have also telephoned headquarters to relay concerns that customers were annoyed that the stores stocked so many "made in China" goods when American military personnel were being held in that country against their will, they said.
"Our customers are telling us to quit doing business in China -- that they're not going to buy things made there anymore," said Dale Apley, vice president for public policy. 
"These are just the people taking time out of their schedule to contact us. 
How many other people out there are thinking the same thing?"
The outpouring of anger may indicate that the continuing standoff may have started to shake one of the foundations of the United States-China relationship: the partnership of trade and investment that has grown rapidly despite regular disruptions in bilateral ties during the last decade and a half.
Unlike China's bloody crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Beijing in 1989 or its efforts to intimidate Taiwan by lobbing missiles off that island's coast five years ago, the current impasse directly affects United States military personnel. 
Business leaders said that made this crisis uniquely sensitive because the public put the safety of the crew above abstract notions of geopolitical stability or human rights for Chinese citizens.
Like Wal-Mart, Target and other discount leaders, Kmart sells billions of dollars of Chinese-manufactured consumer goods each year. 
Total trade volumes have soared, and often, from month to month, the United States trade deficit with China tops the one with Japan. 
The most recent Commerce Department statistics showed that the United States trade deficit with China increased 19.3 percent in January, rising to $7.2 billion, while the deficit with Japan narrowed slightly, to $5.9 billion, the lowest in 13 months.
Mr. Apley said Kmart had no plans to pull Chinese goods off its shelves and would like to continue to do business with factories there. 
But he said the customer response had prompted executives to put Chinese business contacts on notice that Kmart would have no choice but to "diversify its suppliers" unless the matter was resolved quickly.
At Target Stores, based in Minneapolis, Patty Morris, a spokeswoman, said the company had decided not to answer media questions about customer complaints or product sourcing policies. 
She said that the company might have received a few calls related to the China standoff, but that the volume "was not alarming to us and does not warrant getting involved in the dialogue."
Most corporate executives who have worked for years to cultivate cordial ties with Chinese officials are reluctant to say anything about the crisis in public, hoping that a low-key approach will encourage a speedy resolution that leaves few scars. 
United States companies accounted for almost half of the $40 billion in foreign investment in China last year, and many of the largest -- Boeing, Motorola and General Motors -- have declined comment or said talks should be left to diplomats.
But some business leaders in Washington share Kmart's alarm. 
Lobbyists here say they worry that the detention of the crew will make it hard to hold back a tide of anti-China sentiment. 
"We have been the most vocal advocates of open and expanded trade with China," said Thomas Donohue, president of the United States Chamber of Commerce. 
"But we are going to support these young men and women being held over there. 
If this goes on much longer, the economic advances are going to be hard to sustain."
The crisis is so sensitive that some Chinese-American business leaders have expressed rare public opposition to China's diplomatic behavior.
Susan Au Allen, head of the United States Pan-Asian Chamber of Commerce, a group of Asian-American business executives, said she wrote a letter to the Chinese Embassy today saying her group had decided to cancel a May meeting on investment opportunities with Chinese trade officials in Washington.
"There is a glaring difference between this crisis and all the other issues with China because they are holding Americans against their will," said Ms. Allen, who was born in Guangzhou. 
"China does not need any more excuses. 
They have to grow up and act like big boys."
Unlike the fight in Congress last year over whether to grant China permanent normal trade relations, when the battle resonated only lightly outside the capital, the current standoff appears to have set off a grass-roots response that could affect the way Washington reacts.
Recent polls have found that a majority of people consider the military detainees to be hostages, though the Bush administration has not used that term. 
The polls also show that a majority do not want the administration to apologize for the incident.
Mr. Apley of Kmart said the company at first suspected that the volume of complaints indicated that an anti-China group had begun an organized campaign, but company officials found no evidence of that.
Still, some unions that have opposed expanding trade ties with China are using this as an opportunity to drive home their message.
The United Association of Union Plumbers, Pipefitters and Sprinkler Fitters has devoted $500,000 to buy radio advertisements during baseball games around the country urging a boycott. 
"The crew of an American plane, forced to make an emergency landing in China, is held hostage by the Chinese government," the commercial says. 
"Think about that. 
And vow to buy no Chinese products until the servicemen and women are released."

file: Start a New Career at 50_ In Syracuse, Life After Layoffs.txt
text:
ï»¿
When factories close, the workers who are laid off often feel like dinosaurs in a fast-disappearing industrial age. 
But when the Carrier Corporation shut down its huge air-conditioning factory here last year, Joseph Huppman saw it as a golden opportunity.
Mr. Huppman, who worked at Carrier for five years after spending 17 years in the Air Force, took advantage of his layoff to pursue a career that had long beckoned to him.
''I always wanted to be a nurse, and the opportunity never came up before,'' he said. 
''Carrier, by sending my job to China, made the opportunity come up.''
Now, after nearly a year back at school, Mr. Huppman, 50, is a licensed practical nurse, working at the local veterans hospital.
After Carrier, long this city's largest employer, moved the last of its Syracuse manufacturing operations to China and Singapore, many of the 1,200 laid-off workers felt as if they had been plunged into a real-life version of ''Survivor,'' although not on a Pacific Island. 
But now hundreds of these workers are pursuing a survival strategy that seems to be working: concluding that they had to reinvent themselves for post-industrial America, they are training for new careers.
Helped by federal and state aid and generous tuition assistance from Carrier, nearly 500 laid-off workers have enrolled in a variety of college or vocational courses: respiratory therapy, education, trucking, human resources, hotel management, even geographic informational systems.
''We were pleased to see that a lot more of these workers went back to school than we usually see after layoffs,'' said Kelli Owens, the central New York regional administrator for the state's employment services office. 
''Our goal has been to train these workers for a job they can move into.''
With manufacturing withering in Syracuse and many other cities that were once blue-collar meccas, state, city and union officials urged the Carrier workers to train for new fields, and a large number heeded that advice.
Two programs eased the way. 
First, Carrier promised to pay tuition for workers for up to four years, sweetening the pot by offering a $10,000 bonus to those who received bachelor's degrees and $5,000 to those who received community college degrees. 
Second, federal retraining money for factory workers who lose their jobs when their companies move operations overseas provided many Carrier workers unemployment benefits for as long as they remained in school, for a maximum of two years. 
Usually workers receive only six months of such benefits.
But education has not been a cure-all. 
It does not ensure that the workers will find jobs or, if they do, that the jobs will pay as well as Carrier did. 
Happy as he is to be a nurse, Mr. Huppman is earning $30,000 a year, half what he earned at Carrier, where he earned $17 an hour and worked hundreds of hours of overtime.
''They all got to accept they're not going to earn the same money they earned while at Carrier, even if they go back to school,'' said Rick Simone, business manager for the Sheet Metal Workers local at Carrier. 
He estimated that those who found new jobs took pay cuts of 30 to 40 percent, on average.
Betty Haley, a career adviser with CNY Works, a government-financed training and employment agency in Syracuse, said the workers did not have it easy.
''Looking for a job is very overwhelming when you haven't done that for 25, 35 years,'' she said. 
''We've helped them with interviewing skills, resumes and networking, all these skills they haven't used in forever.''
Stephanie Liddle, another Carrier castoff, took a six-month course to become a medical assistant in a doctor's office, but her job search has come up dry.
Now 59 and having problems paying her rent, she is at a point that she thought she would never reach: She has decided to move in with her 85-year-old mother.
''I've sent out resumes to at least five places a week, but without any luck,'' she said, having just hauled two dressers out of her apartment to the curb for anyone to take.
Still, Irwin Davis, the president of the Metropolitan Development Association of Syracuse, said that as a whole, the former Carrier workers were doing better than expected.
''If this were 10-plus years ago, a majority of these people would have simply hit the interstate and headed south and gotten a job there,'' Mr. Davis said. 
''The interesting thing is some 500 of these workers have returned to school, and that shows they think there is opportunity here.''
Roger A. Evans, an economist with the state Labor Department, was bearish about this city's prospects. 
''This area is doing very well outside the manufacturing sector,'' he said, noting that the number of nonmanufacturing jobs in the area had risen by 8,700 to 287,400 in the last three years, while factory jobs fell by 5,200 to 33,000.
Some workers have scoured the Internet to find industries that are hiring. 
A Web search convinced Chris Fiacchi, 34, that he should study respiratory therapy.
''A lot of us chose medical fields,'' he said. 
''With all the aging baby boomers, there's going to be a large increase in medical staffing. 
You don't have to worry about layoffs there.''
Thirty years ago, Barbara Ann Goss left Syracuse University after her freshman year and went to work at Carrier. 
Now she has returned to college to study health information technology.
''Manufacturing, which I love, hardly exists any more in Upstate New York, and I'm not about to move to China,'' said Ms. Goss, who worked at Carrier for 26 years. 
''I'm not about to leave the region, and about the only field I see growing here is health care. 
But I'm not cut out to be a nurse. 
I can't do blood and guts.''
There are indisputable success stories. 
After studying to become a surgical technologist, Dale Carpenter, 37, landed a job in an operating room at St. Joseph's Hospital Health Center here.
''The layoff was the best thing that ever happened to me,'' he said. 
''Now I don't have to worry week to week about being laid off. 
Now I won't ever have to worry about looking for work again.''
Patrick Sullivan, 52, sounds as if he has discovered the fountain of youth, so enthusiastic is he about studying for a degree in geographic informational systems, which involves interpreting satellite photos.
''Like most other parents, I told my kids, 'If you get a chance to go to college, you should,''' said Mr. Sullivan, who worked at Carrier for 27 years. 
''Well, I finally had the chance to go to college, and I took it.''
Even with their new skills, some former Carrier workers have been frustrated by the job hunt. 
Gary Galipeau, 57, who is married to Ms. Goss, will soon have a bachelor's degree in human resources from Empire State College. 
But he has repeatedly been rejected for jobs in the field, despite his expertise from having been the top employee benefits official for the union at Carrier.
''I feel a need to continue working, financially and emotionally,'' said Mr. Galipeau, who worked at Carrier for 37 years. 
''I was interviewed by a headhunter, but the subtle feedback was, I'm too old for what they're looking for.
''A lot of Carrier people worked 50, 60 hours a week for many, many years, and now, suddenly, they're considered too old to work.''
Mr. Galipeau contrasted today's job market with the one in 1967, when General Electric laid him off from its now-closed television factory here.
''At that point in time, you could roll out of bed into a manufacturing job,'' he said, voicing concern that the region's high-paying factory jobs were giving way to lower-paying service jobs.
''I'm scared about the future for central New York,'' he said. 
''You can't base an economy on selling hamburgers and insurance policies to each other.''

file: Still Wary, Taiwan Split Over Change On Mainland.txt
text:
ï»¿
Government and business leaders here welcomed today the orderly transfer of power in Beijing and a series of Chinese overtures to Taiwan, but a deep split is evident on how to respond.
Tsai Ing-wen, Taiwan's minister for relations with China, said conciliatory statements by President Jiang Zemin and Deputy Prime Minister Qian Qichen during and just before the Communist Party Congress in Beijing showed a new willingness on the mainland to negotiate closer links with Taiwan. 
At the congress, Hu Jintao replaced Mr. Jiang as head of the party.
"The position of both sides, after consideration of what has been said by both sides, is closer than before," Ms. Tsai said in an interview today.
But Ms. Tsai was wary about moving quickly to conclude any new deals with Beijing, even after recent comments by Mr. Qian, who has called for closer transportation links across the Taiwan Strait and has softened some of China's demands before that can happen.
"We still have reservations in the sense that we have to wait for some time to see if what he said is going to be a stable and consistent policy of China," she said.
Taiwan business leaders were much less cautious today, calling for a quick opening of direct flights and shipping routes to the mainland.
"I just hope they can negotiate a deal as quickly as possible," said Y. C. Wang, chairman of the Formosa Plastics Group and Taiwan's richest and best-known industrialist.
Focused on Iraq and the campaign against terrorism, the United States has urged China and Taiwan to avoid confrontations in the coming months like the dispute that erupted in August when President Chen Shui-bian of Taiwan briefly hinted at a more pro-independence stance. 
Beijing regards Taiwan as rightfully a province of China.
Some warming of relations is already apparent. 
Taipei announced on Tuesday that it would allow chartered flights between Taiwan and Shanghai for Chinese New Year early next year. 
That would address the annual problem of tens of thousands of Taiwan business executives trying to return home for the holidays on a limited number of flights.
But Taipei said the chartered planes would have to fly via Hong Kong or Macao, taking six or seven hours instead of the 80 minutes a nonstop flight would require, because the Taiwan Strait is less than 100 miles wide. 
If direct flights were allowed they would approach Taipei so quickly that air defense systems might have trouble distinguishing them from a military attack.
Taiwan businesses have been the biggest "foreign" investors in China in the last decade, and they contend that the lack of direct transportation links and closer governmental relations have hurt their competitiveness. 
Beijing has welcomed the investment and has increasingly tried to draw Taiwan into a close economic embrace, a policy especially apparent in speeches at the Communist Party Congress.
Taiwan's government has been more wary, especially since the election two years ago of Mr. Chen, of the Democratic Progressive Party, which leans toward greater independence. 
The party tends to represent less-affluent voters who are wary of competition from low-wage businesses in China.
The opposition Nationalist Party, which ran Taiwan from 1949 to 2000, is closer to the island's business community and favors eventual reunification with the mainland.
In an interview on Thursday, Lien Chan, the party's chairman, said the Democratic Progressive Party was trying to placate those voters who strongly favor independence from the mainland. 
"If you do something to please them, you are sure to have 30 percent of them packed up for you," he said. 
"This is Chen Shui-bian's grand strategy."
Ms. Tsai declined to respond publicly to the criticism.

The United States markets, though still distressed, are increasingly finding buyers in governments overseas. 
Recently, Citigroup sold $7.5 billion worth of shares to the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority.
Central banks have also been working to help bring demand back to the tight credit markets, which froze up over the summer as mortgage defaults spiked.
